'If we burn, you burn with us!': Why a Gen Z youth wave of protest is sweeping Europe - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:04:38 UTC
19:04:38 KST

Maya Gourdel, a 19-year-old student in Brussels, sits at a desk writing slogans against those running her country: “If we burn, you burn with us!” The slogan, taken from the 2012 film "The Hunger Games" that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth movements globally, reflects the anger, frustration and desire for change driving Gen Z-led protests around Europe.
From the suburbs of Paris to the squares of Belgrade, thousands have taken to the streets.
The demands are various but often overlapping – frustrations with shabby schooling facilities, perceived lack of economic opportunity, cost of living, corruption, housing and a sense of not being listened to. At times those protests triggered violence – with thousands of shops in France alone being damaged or looted in recent weeks – and police firing stun grenades and water cannons.
This weekend they also brought real change – student-led protests culminated in the toppling of an election of Serbia’s long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism.
“Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom," said student protester Stasa Piletic. "Personally, I feel a sense of victory. I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility."
'An explosion of rage'
Chiara, a 21-year-old student in protest-hit Milan, believes “it's vital to take part in people's spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible.”
"I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream," she said.
She said Italian students were confronting a reality of schools without enough teachers and crumbling buildings.
“And all of this with the prospect of an underpaid job which we didn't qualify for and the prospect of living in a tiny, overpriced house, probably away from our city, which we didn't want to live in."
Protests led by Gen Z have caused a global ruckus as the generation born roughly between 1997 and 2012 found its voice, from Bangladesh in 2024 and Nepal in 2025, to India this year. Now Europe has become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living are a concern for 40% of 16-30-year-olds, according to a European Union survey published in 2025.
Among the 92.7 million people in the EU who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, the highest risk was recorded for young adults aged 18-24 years, at 26.3%, while the lowest was recorded for adults aged 65 years or over, at 18.8%.
Younger people are also wary of shouldering the financial burden of an older generation that tends to vote in greater numbers. People over 60 in France make up a quarter of the population but own 60% of France's wealth, according to the OFCE think tank.
French pensions are by far the biggest public expense, on track to reach 14% of economic output, as the population ages and voters resist raising the retirement age or reducing benefits. That is still less than Greece or Italy, which spend the largest proportion of national income on public pensions among OECD countries, at around 16% of GDP, according to OECD figures in 2025. But it is much more than Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland or South Korea, which spent less than 4% of GDP on public pensions, according to the OECD.
'Young people in Europe are united'
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris, has been protesting against “deplorable” conditions and staff shortages at his school. “There used to be rats,” he said. Students were evacuated last year when a roof collapsed on the courtyard; though no one was hurt, he said.
Protests showed “that young people in Europe are united”, he said, adding, "we all agree on one point: that young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren't listened to enough.”
A French government report in October said pension spending had risen by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023 while that for education had declined by 0.5 percentage points. It also showed 32% of the education ministry’s budget went towards pensions, crowding out money for other areas.
Gourdel, too, has been protesting for better conditions in schools in Belgium.
“We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It's only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us,” she said.
The protests are still spreading, with a demonstration planned in Germany this weekend over the cost of living, inequality, war and the state of schools.
Unrest has also hit Albania, where student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government, fueled by anger over perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, engulfed Tirana and spread to other cities.
“Our Prime Minister spent 130 days not listening to us,” said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.
“If you ask a student in Albania, 'where do you see your future?' Everyone says 'outside this country'," she said, arguing that at home, even if you have talent, someone with "connections is always going to beat you."
Serbia’s student movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of.
Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing – something neither the students nor their candidates have any experience of. Luka Stojakovic, another protester, brushes that aside. "We have seen where people with political experience have brought us."

The latest controversy centers on the OCAC’s celebration of Hsu’s departure during Thursday’s farewell banquet for council members, per UDN. Attendees said that approximately 30 minutes of the two-hour event were dedicated specifically to Hsu, who reportedly spent more time onstage than Acting OCAC Minister Lee Yen-hui (李姸慧).
When asked about the banquet, Cho said the event was intended to express gratitude to OCAC members who return annually for important meetings, per ETtoday. He said no public funds were used for personal purposes but acknowledged that the council needed to communicate such arrangements more clearly in the future.
Cho added that an investigation into allegations of Hsu’s misuse of public resources would be completed within three months, per Rti.
Banquet attendees alleged that Hsu received treatment comparable to that afforded to the premier or the legislative speaker. When Lee took the stage, she reportedly said that controversies surrounding the OCAC were campaign tactics and slander.
The council also reportedly produced a video highlighting Hsu’s achievements during her six-year tenure as minister.
In response to the reports, the OCAC said council members had petitioned for Hsu’s participation the night before the banquet, emphasizing that the celebrations honoring her did not involve public expenditures, per CNA. France-based council member Sandy Hsueh (薛雅俶) said the nation is facing cognitive warfare, adding that attacks against the council could undermine public trust and societal resilience, per China Times.

Former envoy to New Zealand Jieh Wen-chieh (介文汲) said that because Hsu resigned amid allegations of public resource misuse, allowing her to receive well-wishes and flowers at an official OCAC event was unacceptable, per China Times. He stressed that civil servants should not repurpose public events for personal use.
Jieh called on the Control Yuan to intervene and investigate the event.
In related news, KMT Legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) urged DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) to comment on the allegations surrounding the former minister, per Tai Sounds. TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China’s political interference is stalling Taiwan’s bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said Wednesday.
Speaking at a Legislative Yuan Foreign and National Defense Committee meeting, Lin said China opposes Taiwan’s accession despite failing to meet the CPTPP’s membership criteria itself, per CNA. Some member countries have privately acknowledged that China’s political interference remains the main obstacle, he added.
Taiwan submitted its membership application in September 2021.
The country continues to lobby CPTPP member economies through visits and other channels to get its application on the agenda, Lin said, CNA reported. Although the rotating chair’s final decision remains difficult to predict, Taiwan has garnered support from friendly countries, some of which are also privately advocating on its behalf, he said.
Lin said the CPTPP is reviewing its accession process to address the current backlog, according to CNA. One proposal under consideration is to establish multiple working groups simultaneously, with different member economies serving as conveners and reviewing applications in parallel rather than sequentially.
If the bloc adopts parallel reviews, Taiwan could be assessed alongside other applicants, an approach the foreign ministry is working to promote, he said.
The foreign minister added that the ministry hopes to establish a mechanism requiring any member opposing an applicant to provide specific reasons, CNA reported. Without such a mechanism, some members may be reluctant to support Taiwan publicly because of political pressure, he said.

The Amarna letters

First discovered in Egypt in the late 19th century, the collection of clay tablets known as the Amarna letters is one of our richest windows into the ancient world. The letters are extraordinary not only for their contents – diplomatic communications exchanged between Egyptian pharaohs and other nearby rulers in the 14th century BCE – but also for their script: they were written not in Egyptian hieroglyphs but largely in cuneiform, a writing system most often associated with ancient Mesopotamia. In this video from the British Museum, the always entertaining Assyriologist Irving Finkel details how the letters came to be and how they were discovered, and delves into the fascinating correspondence itself, which includes petty disputes over perceived slights, leaders lobbying for military support and more than a few requests for gold.

Horror isn’t just intense fear, new psychology study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

Reading a news headline about a violent tragedy can provoke an unsettled, sickening jolt that feels very different from the anxiety of facing a personal threat. A new study published in Cognition and Emotion suggests that when descriptions of harm involve extreme outcomes or vivid, gory details, they tend to heighten horror much more than fear, in part because they make the event seem more abnormal. The findings provide evidence that horror is not merely an intense version of fear, but a distinct emotional reaction to events that violate our basic expectations of how the world works.
In everyday conversation and dictionary definitions, horror is often treated as a synonym for extreme fear. In psychology, however, the two terms can represent different ways of interpreting and categorizing a harmful event. Fear functions as a threat-detection system that alerts a person to potential danger and motivates self-defense or escape. Some emotion researchers define real-world horror, by contrast, as an emotional and mental shock experienced when witnessing or learning about actual harm that contradicts a person’s fundamental assumptions about human safety and how the world operates.
“‘Horror’ is one of dozens of English words we have to label our emotional responses to harm, but it remains largely unstudied,” study author Pamela Marie Taylor, an assistant professor in the Faculty of Global Connectivity at Akita International University, told PsyPost. “This neglect might be because research in the 1980s categorized horror as a subtype of fear, or because it has become closely associated with the fictional genre of horror films. However, people use the word ‘horror’ to describe their responses to real events, and do so in a way that is meaningfully different from how they use the word ‘fear’.”
“For example, ‘horrified’ is often paired with verbs like ‘learn’, ‘realize’ and ‘discover’ that indicate a response to extreme novelty or abnormality (e.g., ‘I was horrified to learn’),” Taylor explained. “In contrast, people typically use the word ‘fear’ to describe the anticipation of some possible harm (e.g., ‘fear the worst’, ‘fear of snakes’). This study was done to test if horror can be differentiated from fear based on how abnormal a harmful event is seen to be.”
How people evaluate unusual events plays a central role in shaping their emotional reactions. In a 1986 theoretical paper, psychologists proposed that people judge how unusual an event is by comparing it against their mental norms, and that bad outcomes preceded by abnormal circumstances provoke amplified emotional responses. Building on this idea, a 2022 experimental study by Taylor and a colleague found that people reported greater fear when facing common, mild, or personally relevant threats, whereas they reported greater horror when learning about extreme or abnormal harm that had already happened, even when the victims were strangers.
Encountering accounts of bizarre or extreme harm often leaves people struggling to reconcile the event with their worldview. Some research suggests this tension can shape how people seek explanations. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that individuals with higher morbid curiosity about unsettling events and dangerous people are more likely to seek out and believe conspiracy theories as explanations for threatening occurrences.
Although the 2022 research linked horror to abnormal harm, its experimental scenarios blended together the severity of the injury and the graphicness of the wording, leaving it uncertain which feature actually made the harm feel abnormal. To isolate these factors, Taylor designed two experiments examining how harm severity and graphic language independently shape perceptions of abnormality. She defined graphicness through the distinction between abstract and concrete language.
Taylor reasoned that abstract descriptions use broad, familiar categories, such as stating that “a person was murdered,” which allows the mind to file the event into existing mental frameworks, whereas concrete descriptions include specific sensory details, such as “a camper was slaughtered by his friend who sliced into his chest with a rusty axe,” which are harder to fit into normal expectations.
Taylor also wanted to test whether perceived abnormality is what truly separates horror from fear, or if the difference comes down to physical arousal. In psychology, arousal refers to the level of physical activation or agitation in the body’s nervous system. If horror is simply an intense form of fear, then heightened physical arousal alone should explain why people label their reaction to gruesome news as horror rather than fear.
In the first study, Taylor recruited 60 adult native English speakers in the United States through the online platform Prolific. The participants had an average age of 35.5 years, ranging from 21 to 69, and the sample was 70 percent female and 71.1 percent White. Each participant read four text stimuli presented as real news headlines adapted from The Daily Mail tabloid describing a person being harmed, with each headline remaining on the screen for seven seconds before rating questions appeared. Taylor preregistered the main prediction that severe harm and graphic descriptions would increase horror more than fear.
The headlines were systematically varied across two dimensions: the severity of the harm (moderate injuries that heal versus extreme, permanent harm such as death) and the graphicness of the description (abstract, general wording versus concrete, tangible details). After reading each headline, participants rated the perceived abnormality of the harm on a 5-point scale from 1 (“not at all”) to 5 (“extremely”) using four items assessing how unusual, abnormal, or unheard-of the event seemed.
They also rated their emotional reactions on the same 5-point scale, where scores for “horrified” and “shocked” were combined to measure horror, and scores for “scared” and “afraid” were combined to measure fear. To measure physical arousal, participants selected one of five illustrated figures ranging from a calm, closed-eyed figure to a wide-eyed figure with jagged lines depicting intense bodily activation.
To account for individual tendencies to score higher or lower on rating scales, Taylor analyzed the repeated measurements while statistically controlling for baseline differences between participants. Across the 5-point scale, where the overall average abnormality rating was 3.40, shifting from moderate to extreme harm increased perceived abnormality by 0.89 points, and shifting from abstract to concrete language increased it by 0.88 points.
Both factors also elevated horror much more strongly than fear. Across all conditions, the overall average emotion rating was 2.69, with horror averaging 0.98 points higher than fear; describing extreme rather than moderate harm boosted horror by 1.09 points compared to a 0.45-point increase in fear, while concrete rather than abstract descriptions raised horror by 0.70 points compared to a 0.22-point increase in fear.
Participants also rated the general harmfulness of each event based on whether someone suffered bodily pain or injury, and in the first study, these general harmfulness ratings predicted horror and fear equally, as the difference between the two emotions was not statistically significant. Taylor then used mediation analysis, a statistical technique that estimates how much of a relationship between an experimental condition and an outcome passes through an intermediate step, to test whether perceived abnormality explained the rise in horror.
Perceived abnormality accounted for 39 percent of the total effect of harm severity on horror and 76 percent of the effect of graphic language on horror, while explaining 63 percent and 83 percent of why severity and graphicness increased horror more than fear. In one Study 1 model, the effect of graphic language on horror over fear was no longer statistically significant once physical arousal was taken into account, and when physical arousal and perceived abnormality were tested side by side as parallel pathways, both independently explained a portion of the shift toward horror.
To verify whether these patterns would hold up in an independent sample, Taylor conducted a second study with another 60 adult native English speakers in the United States recruited via Prolific. Participants in the second group had an average age of 42.57 years, ranging from 21 to 75, and the sample was 70 percent female, 30 percent male, and 75 percent White. The procedure and rating scales were identical to the first experiment, except that one headline from Study 1 involving an animal attack was replaced with an interpersonal attack so that all four headlines depicted one human harming another.
The second study closely replicated the core findings regarding abnormality and horror. Around an average abnormality rating of 3.42 on the 5-point scale, extreme harm raised perceived abnormality by 0.85 points and concrete graphic descriptions raised it by 0.89 points. Extreme harm increased horror ratings by 1.01 points compared to 0.39 points for fear, making the effect on horror more than 2.5 times larger, while concrete descriptions increased horror by 0.62 points compared to 0.14 points for fear, an effect more than four times larger.
Unlike the first study, general ratings of bodily harmfulness in Study 2 showed a stronger association with horror than fear, though the author noted that because every headline involved harm, 12 percent of participants in Study 1 and 22 percent in Study 2 gave identical harmfulness ratings across all four headlines, limiting the precision of that specific measure.
Where the second study diverged most notably from the first was in the role of physical arousal. When arousal was tested on its own in Study 2, it again helped explain the shift toward horror, but once abnormality was added to the model, the arousal pathway was no longer statistically significant, with indirect effects of 0.11 for harm severity and 0.06 for graphicness. Perceived abnormality, by contrast, remained a strong, consistent pathway in both studies even after controlling for self-reported bodily activation. Taylor argues that whereas fear tends to arise from uncertainty about potential danger, horror arises from an excess of concrete information about severe harm that is hard to square with a person’s understanding of a safe world.
For everyday news consumers, the findings highlight how subtle shifts in phrasing can alter how a story lands emotionally. “When the same harmful event in a news headline was described using concrete language, it was rated as more abnormal than when it was described using abstract language, and caused an increase in horror that was three-to-four times greater than the increase in fear,” Taylor noted. “In other words, a person’s emotional reaction to a news event is influenced by the language with which it is told.”
“In terms of practical significance, it seems that a lot of online and political rhetoric uses abnormality to capture attention, shape discourse and influence interpretations,” Taylor said. “Therefore, people should be aware of how their emotional responses to events can be shaped by how events are described. We are increasingly aware of the dangers of online misinformation, but that focuses on the factuality of what is described. These results indicate that even in factually accurate descriptions, the language with which the event is described can influence our perception of how normal or abnormal it is, and consequently our emotional response to it.”
“We would not argue that using concrete language is bad or that headlines that use it are necessarily manipulative,” Taylor added. “The current findings examined how concrete and abstract language elicit different emotional responses without investigating the appropriateness of the language. Another way to read this study’s findings is that describing harm with abstract language can normalize it, which also has consequences when reporting on harmful events.”
There are a few additional caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because adding vivid sensory details requires extra words, the concrete headlines were naturally longer than the abstract ones, meaning word count could have contributed to the impact of the graphic descriptions. In addition, the experiments only examined short tabloid headlines about harm happening to strangers in ordinary, everyday settings, without a non-harmful baseline condition. It remains an open question whether severe harm in settings where danger is already expected, such as a combat zone, would feel less abnormal and elicit less horror.
Perceived abnormality was measured rather than manipulated, and the analyses testing it as a pathway were exploratory, added after the main results were known. The horror measure also combined “horrified” with “shocked,” a feeling that may overlap with judging an event as unusual. Both studies used nearly the same set of headlines and newly created two-item emotion scales, so it remains to be seen whether the results hold with other materials and measures.
Methodologically, participants rated perceived abnormality, physical arousal, and their emotions at the exact same time after each headline, so the statistical models cannot establish a strict chronological sequence of events. Physical arousal was also assessed through a single visual self-report scale rather than biological measures like heart rate or skin conductance.
Additionally, both study samples were 70 percent female and restricted to native English speakers in the United States. Because not all languages separate horror and fear into distinct everyday words, such as Japanese, which uses the term osore for both, future research could explore whether horror functions as a culturally specific emotion concept.
“Because many conspiracy theories seem to involve attempts to make sense of a horrifying event, I am interested in investigating if feelings of horror play a role in conspiratorial thinking,” Taylor said. “For example, can conspiracy theories act as a form of emotion regulation that people use to turn the helplessness of horror into anger, with the latter associated with a greater sense of control?”
The study, “Gruesome Details: Graphic Descriptions and Extreme Harm Differentially Elicit Horror (vs Fear) via Increased Perceptions of Abnormality,” was authored by Pamela Marie Taylor.

Cross-border network helps EU workers abroad claim wages and benefits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:39 UTC
19:00:39 KST

A cross-border network of counsellors, funded by the EU, is helping Europeans who work in other member states to claim the wages and social rights they are entitled to.
“They desperately need information, correct information, because, to a certain extent, they’re left to fend for themselves,” says Marko Tanasić, Fair Labour Mobility EU Counsellor, ZSSS Union. He is one of the counsellors from eight countries handing out leaflets at a motorway rest stop near Ljubljana, talking to drivers about their working conditions, rest time and pay.
Millions of Europeans work abroad, and some are not given the salary and benefits they are entitled to. Slovenian trucker Goran Jovanovic, Long-Distance Truck Driver, says many drivers “aren’t paid according to a collective bargaining agreement, as they should be”, and are instead paid by fixed days and per kilometre driven.
The Fair Labour Mobility EU project has a budget of 1.2 million euros this year, 90% of it from the EU, and helped nearly 3,000 workers claim their labour and social rights between 2024 and 2025. The cases range from unpaid social security contributions and work accidents to unacceptable accommodation and underpayment, often across several countries.
The European Commission has just launched its Fair Labour Mobility Package, a proposal with three key goals: faster recognition of qualifications across borders, a digital wallet to store and share social security documents, and a larger role for the European Labour Authority to beat fraud.

Ricardo Mendes, chief executive of Tekever, said: “This procurement represents an important milestone in a relationship that has been built over time through rigorous testing, open dialogue and a clear focus on delivering effective capability. We greatly value the professionalism and engagement of the USSOCOM personnel with whom we have worked, and look forward to continuing to support their evolving requirements.”
The number, model and configuration of the aircraft are not being disclosed. Tekever described the system as highly deployable and designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance in demanding environments, with a modular architecture bringing together the air platform, mission payloads, communications and mission software.
Tekever has an established presence in Fayetteville, North Carolina, where the announcement was made and which sits next to Fort Bragg, the home of United States Army special operations. The company said the purchase is a further step in its commitment to the United States and its special operations community.
The Portuguese company is familiar to British readers through its AR5 maritime surveillance aircraft, which has flown over the English Channel under Home Office contracts since 2020. It has also supplied uncrewed aircraft to Ukraine and employs more than fifteen hundred people across Portugal, the United States, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Estonia and Ukraine.

I Thought Running Would Make Me Worthy of Love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

Endurance sports are having a moment. Run clubs, marathons, and ultramarathons have never been more popular. In North America, ultramarathon finishes have roughly tripled since 2010, exceeding 150,000 runners last year, according to UltraRunning magazine.
I understand the appeal. I spent years competing in some of the world’s most difficult endurance races, finding satisfaction and eventually a professional career in seeing how far I could push myself. But as more runners test their limits, I hope they’ll also ask themselves what they need those achievements to prove. For me, winning became a way to feel worthy of love. Every finish line offered reassurance that lasted only until I started worrying about the next race.
It took losing my professional running career to understand why I needed that reassurance so badly. The story began long before I laced up a pair of shoes and entered a race.
Divorce and my parents’ own troubled upbringings made my childhood difficult. As an adult, I can now see that my parents were unable to provide the safe, nurturing, and stable environment a kid deserves.
My young mind came to a conclusion that many children do: I must not be good enough the way that I am. Love, attention, and care, I believed, were all things that you had to earn.
As a teenager, I was desperate for the attention I rarely received at home. My grades were good, but not scholarship level; I was on the cross-country team and acted in school plays, but was never the standout star in either.
Despite my best efforts, nothing worked. That is, until I found success in ultrarunning.
At 15 years old, I watched my mother train and complete her first marathon. I was mesmerized. Maybe I could win her affection by doing what I’d seen her do.
Later that year, I crossed the finish line of the San Diego Rock n’ Roll Marathon. I loved the challenge, but I wanted more. Within a few years, I was running my first 50-mile ultramarathon. As part of my senior project, I pledged to run 100 miles around my high school track while fundraising money for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society in honor of a friend who was battling cancer.
The ensuing media coverage was much more than I expected. To be honest, I loved the attention. Suddenly I felt seen by my mom. Again, I wanted more.
At 19, I finished Badwater, a 135-mile race across Death Valley in July. A year later, I flew out to Minnesota and completed the Arrowhead 135, in which I pulled a sled across the frozen landscape for nearly 54 hours. By age 20, I had attempted the Barkley Marathons for the first time, a race so difficult that in its 40-year history, only 20 people had ever officially finished. It would take me two more attempts navigating heinous trails through the hillsides of Tennessee to ultimately finish the race in 2013, becoming finisher 13.
Soon I was flying across the world, competing in 200-mile races, and living the life of a professional trail runner. It was everything I could have hoped for: the attention, the praise, the pre-race interviews, and the post-race adulation. And yet a part of me knew that if I didn’t win every race I entered, the worthlessness that I’d kept at bay for so long would drown me.
In 2018, that tidal wave finally came crashing over me. I had been diagnosed with a congenital bicuspid valve in my heart, and the resulting aortic aneurysm meant open-heart surgery.
Just like that, my professional running career was over, and with it went my path to validation. I had lived my whole life up to that point working for my worth; it was never inherent. If I couldn’t achieve results, who was I? Did I even exist? How could I be loved without having earned anything?
I spent the next five years dismantling my own self-worth from sport through therapy. The first and most pressing thing I had to face was the threat of suicide and self-harm. Running, it turns out, was protective of the deep-seated worthlessness I had developed from childhood.
Through intensive dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), medication, and an inpatient program, I curbed the more life-threatening aspects. DBT taught me awareness and the skills of emotional regulation. Later, lifespan integration and internal family systems therapy helped bring the roots of my childhood trauma to light and ultimately helped me place the hurt and shame back to their origin with my parents.
Slowly, I began to develop the understanding that I could be enough without having to achieve.
This lesson was never screamed at me. I was never explicitly told that I wasn’t enough. Instead, this anxiety whispered, quietly and convincingly, within me. It was the shaking hands of my 15-year-old self racing his heart out for the love of an absent parent. It was my 19-year-old self, slapping himself to keep going and push harder up the climb because some nebulous time or position would merit the love I never felt.
Through therapy, I came to realize I’d been fighting the wrong fight all along, and my relationship with running changed. After a full recovery from my heart surgery, I was able to begin running again, though not at the same level as I’d done before. In spite of the slower times, I was still able to get out into nature and, more importantly, spend time with my wife, whose running career was taking off.
I could hear my internal voices more clearly than ever and separate myself from it all a bit more. Eventually, I hired a running coach who, in addition to my wife, helped support me entering into shorter distance events that I’d eschewed early in my career. Not being a short-distance specialist, I’d been afraid to enter races I probably couldn’t win. Now I tried them anyway, and I had fun.
I realized I didn’t have to win a race to enjoy it or find value in it. I was finally enjoying running without needing it to be directly tied to my success.
Looking back on my career and with the perspective of both age and a tremendous amount of work, I’ve asked myself if I could have reached the same heights without that feeling that I need to win to be worthy of love.
Perhaps, and perhaps not; I’m less interested in that answer.
What I’d like to do is go back to my younger self and be there for every track meet, every race, no matter how well I performed. I’d tell myself, “I love you no matter what happens here today. There is nothing to prove. This is just a race.”
If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental-health crisis or contemplating suicide, call or text 988.

Press review: Europe seeks restoration of Russia ties as aid operation starts in Alyoshki
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Europe seeks to restore channels of communication with Russia; a humanitarian operation begins in Alyoshki; and Russia highlights the need to safeguard the global gas market. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia
Media: Europe seeks to restore channels of communication with Russia
The leaders of Russia, Norway and Finland agreed to maintain direct contact during a telephone conversation on October 27. However, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who initiated the call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, denied they were speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole, Izvestia reports.
The joint call by Finland’s president and Norway’s premier signals that Europe is getting ready for the next round of peace negotiations, Tigran Meloyan, an analyst at the Higher School of Economics’ Institute for Global Military Economics and Strategy, said. Such steps by leaders of NATO and European Union countries are always preceded by diplomatic consultations with allies, so it is safe to assume that the idea had been coordinated with Kiev and Brussels, the expert added.
Western media reports say the European Union is discussing the appointment of a special envoy for talks with Russia. Ultimately, the bloc could select several representatives, European Parliament member Fernand Kartheiser of Luxembourg said. EU member states hold widely differing positions, as some remain skeptical about the very principle of talks, while others, such as Slovakia, seek to normalize bilateral relations with Russia as much as possible. That said, appointing multiple negotiators could better represent the range of opinions within the EU, Kartheiser added.
Yegor Sergeyev, senior researcher with the Institute for International Studies at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, pointed out that it was still too early to speak of European countries becoming fully involved in the negotiation process. The analyst pointed to the lack of constructive proposals as one of the reasons.
The initiative by Stubb and Store is not part of EU diplomacy but reflects the national interests of Russia’s European neighbors, Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at the Russian State University for the Humanities, told Vedomosti. According to him, the Norwegian premier and the Finnish president did not call Putin as European envoys but as national leaders. "This does not indicate a change in attitude toward Russia or a decline in support for Kiev. This can also be viewed as an effort to avoid being left out of discussions of future European security," the expert noted.
Izvestia: Humanitarian operation begins in Alyoshki
The humanitarian operation in Alyoshki will continue until 10:59 p.m. on November 1, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said. Its main goals are to provide civilians with medicine, food and essential supplies and evacuate those wishing to leave the town. A successful outcome could pave the way for the resumption of trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev and Washington, Izvestia notes.
The Russian army suspended fire in the Alyoshki area at 4:00 a.m. on October 27 to prepare for the humanitarian mission, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Meanwhile, provocations by the Ukrainian armed forces during the ceasefire in Alyoshki cannot be ruled out, military expert Alexey Leonkov told the newspaper. In this regard, he cited 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone attacks carried out by Kiev’s forces against Alyoshki and the main roads leading to the town during the week of October 19.
"Numerous ceasefires have been announced since the start of the special military operation. Humanitarian ceasefires were also declared before that, particularly during the period when the Minsk Accords were in effect. Still, Ukraine failed to honor these agreements each time," Leonkov noted. According to him, Kiev could use the pause in fighting to deploy additional troops to this part of the front and replenish its ammunition stocks.
"Ukrainian forces are not currently staging provocations as they have to honor a promise presumably made to Melania Trump. But once the humanitarian ceasefire ends, they could resume attacks on Alyoshki and once again lay mines along roads leading to the town," military expert Viktor Litovkin pointed out. Nevertheless, the ceasefire should be used to the fullest to address humanitarian needs.
However, although humanitarian and political efforts continue in parallel, with the two processes not directly connected, a successful operation in Alyoshki could create favorable conditions for the resumption of trilateral negotiations between Moscow, Kiev and Washington. A new round of negotiations could take place after November 4.
Media: Russia highlights need to safeguard global gas market
Discussions at the Eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit in Moscow on October 27 focused on volatility in energy markets, driven by tensions in the Middle East, and sanctions on Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin and speakers from other GECF member states discussed these issues in their remarks, Vedomosti reports.
The main issue today is disruptions to gas supplies, which highlight the need to develop ways to optimize transportation routes, taking into account the geographic locations of GECF member states, the Russian leader said. Most GECF members and observer nations called for peace and security to be maintained to ensure stable gas supplies. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has demonstrated how geopolitical changes could affect the energy sector, GECF Secretary General Philip Mshelbila pointed out.
Moscow has never refused to engage in dialogue with European countries, but the European Union has made a series of short-sighted political decisions, digging a hole for itself rather than for Russia, Izvestia notes, citing Putin.
The 2026 Middle East crisis has worsened the fragmentation of gas markets, Kept expert Nikita Illeritsky said. In his opinion, US liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports are now seeking to strengthen their positions in Europe and Northeast Asia to recoup billions of dollars invested in their facilities.
Still, many European countries continue to prioritize political decisions over their economic interests. In a bid to cut Moscow’s revenues, the European Union has undermined its own economy. Abandoning stable pipeline gas supplies from Russia and shifting to the spot market, where prices are much higher, has dealt a direct blow to European industry. Nevertheless, neither restrictions nor market disruptions can halt the global trend toward a growing role for natural gas as a pillar of the global energy sector, industry and international trade.
Vedomosti: BRICS boosts its economic influence in Africa as Western presence wanes
The shares of Europe and the United States in financial and economic influence across African countries have fallen to 29% and 10%, respectively. Meanwhile, BRICS countries have broadened their presence, raising their share to 16%, according to Vedomosti estimates.
When it comes to Africa, it’s more accurate to speak of "a fragmented international security market" rather than "zones of influence," as African governments decide which external actors to work with, while global powers compete for access, influence, mineral resources and trade routes.
"This is not a division but ‘a competitive coexistence’ of numerous external forces in one space," said Mikhail Margelov, acting head of the UNESCO Department at Moscow State University’s Institute of Asian and African Studies and vice president of the Russian International Affairs Council. Formal zones of influence no longer exist in Africa, as the colonial-era division of the continent has been replaced by competition among external powers. These changes are especially evident in the Sahel region, where Russia has consolidated its position following the withdrawal of French and US troops.
African nations are increasingly seeking to balance their ties with foreign partners while reinforcing their sovereignty. The West describes this approach as multi-alignment, with countries maintaining relations with several centers of power at once, Denis Degterev, senior researcher with the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for African Studies, and professor with the Moscow State Institute of International Relations and the Higher School of Economics, explained.
Economic influence in Africa depends not only on trade and investment but also on defense and political cooperation, as well as debt burdens, Degterev noted. Creditors such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have particularly strong leverage. Even Sahel countries, which have rejected military cooperation with the West, remain reliant on these institutions. As for the European Union, it should not be viewed as a single player, because France, Germany and Italy often vie for influence.
Deeper African integration has become a crucial trend, including efforts to develop a continental free trade area, a regional payment system and financial institutions. "The only way for African nations to implement major industrial and infrastructure projects and reduce their reliance on foreign countries is to pool resources. Africa needs industrialization," Andrey Fyodorov, leading researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for African Studies, emphasized.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Resumed diesel exports could help increase Russian oil production
Russian oil refineries are ramping up diesel production after the government partially lifted its export ban. The resumption of diesel exports and higher output could help sustain domestic oil production, Rossiyskaya Gazeta notes.
Valery Andrianov, associate professor at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation, pointed out that the return to operation of refineries following scheduled maintenance was supporting Russian oil production. However, growth remains limited by Russia’s quota under the OPEC+ agreement. Earlier, domestic output fell short of the quota because demand from processing facilities had declined and logistics issues had hampered efforts to increase crude oil exports.
According to energy expert Kirill Rodionov, the current level of oil production in Russia is shaped by three factors: oil exports, domestic refining and various fuel export bans. Crude exports are currently hindered by shipping difficulties in the Black Sea. Meanwhile, domestic oil processing depends on the completion of maintenance work at Russian refineries and the regulator’s export restrictions, which are now being partially lifted.
The expert stressed that the Russia-US diesel deal would have little impact on the oil production situation because the export volumes agreed by the two countries were too small. However, a full lifting of the diesel export ban, at least for oil refineries, could pave the way to higher petroleum product exports and oil production.
In Andrianov’s view, Russia could raise oil output by 1.3 mln barrels per day. However, achieving this target will depend on the pace of refinery maintenance and the intensity of attacks on the facilities.
Rodionov identified shipping issues in the Black Sea as another risk. He does not expect Russia to achieve sustained oil production growth before 2027.

Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.
Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.
“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.
Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.
But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.
In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.
The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.
“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”
Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.
A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.
While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.
If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.
The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

Please Let the Internet Die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The internet must be put out of its misery.
Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web—and the social fabric woven there—is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself.
Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements.
Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation.
In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.
It’s not necessarily that people have gotten worse. “Dead Internet Theory”—the proposition that a vast majority of the interactions on the web are fake, bots talking to other bots—has accrued more supporting evidence recently. One cybersecurity firm concluded this spring that agents already outnumber human users, their traffic surging by 8,000 percent through 2025. No wonder seemingly everyone has at some point caught themselves scrolling through a wasteland of brainrot and asked, “What the hell am I even looking at?” Underlying that question is another: “Is it always going to be like this?”
With this anxiety hammering at my prefrontal cortex day in and out, I was more than intrigued by the absolutist title of technologist and Pulitzer-winning journalist John West’s new book, The Internet Will Die, and So Will You: On Learning to Live in Our Digital Age. In his discerning treatise, West confirms what many have suspected for a good while now: The platforms once seen as enduring archives of knowledge and communication are being cannibalized by ideological warfare and basic greed.
But that’s not the whole story. For one, West argues, people misperceive the “vastness” of the internet, which really amounts to “a vanishing fraction, a rounding error, of the human experience.” Moreover, it is remarkably fragile—West opens with the story of how a 2001 train derailment in a Baltimore tunnel took out a major bundle of fiber-optic cables, leading to internet slowdowns nationwide—and continually undergoes cycles of death and rebirth as a result of this natural instability.
If the internet is much smaller and less solid than imagined, West’s book suggests, then it’s crucial to recognize the forces that determine how those deaths unfold, or which pieces are preserved while others crumble. Because the market has falsely sold us the web as a comprehensive library of accumulated wisdom, each transient phase of this global network comes to define the present, for better and worse. Today we witness a dismal paralysis brought on by algorithmic incentives to churn out inflammatory garbage: Full-time influencers are in a losing arms race for attention with low-effort, high-volume channels that streamline production by delegating the creative process to bleeding-edge software.
West draws a sharp contrast between this holographic environment of monetization and a passionate, personalized internet that spanned from the primordial GeoCities to Tumblr, describing how these innovative communities have been gradually erased. While some endure in half-dead and highly corrupted form, others are lost. In middle school, West maintained a web page devoted to his love of anime; later, he kept a blog documenting his college years. Looking back as an adult, he’s vexed by the fates that have befallen each.
“I really wanted to delete my anime site,” West tells WIRED. “I don't have access to the AOL account anymore, and I couldn't do it.” Instead, it lives on as a zombie page, cluttered with spam ads and dead-end links. As for the college blog, he had neglected to pay domain fees toward the end of his time writing it, and so the final year of posts disappeared. “I kind of got obsessed with this idea that the things we want to last really don't, and then oftentimes the things that we kind of wish would go away hang on for way too long,” West says.
These shifting sands are a far cry from the flawless, collective, permanent memory that internet users originally believed they were building. “‘Forever’ is such a strong word, and it's the wrong word,” West says. Online spaces are memento mori, the same as individuals who self-promote across them (and that includes certain longevity-obsessed biohackers). Sure, there was a time when a celebrity could be “canceled” for tasteless posts unearthed years later, but in 2026, it’s not so easy to surface specific messages when you go hunting for them in your AI-powered Gmail account. Zeitgeist-defining platforms like Vine can be vaporized in an instant, a fact reinforced in January 2025, when Americans posted farewell TikTok videos ahead of an expected US ban on the app.
This random ephemerality, West points out, has eroded any confidence in claims previously backed up by hypertext cross-references, and thus any kind of consensus truth. An analysis of hyperlinks in articles on The New York Times website between 1996 and mid-2019 found that 25 percent of all links were inaccessible. According to a 2016 study, “three out of four citations in scholarly articles have drifted—the websites they purport to cite no longer say what they once did,” he writes. “Over half of Wikipedia’s entries contain at least one link in its references section that goes nowhere, a Pew report found.”
The impulse to drive engagement spreads to users themselves: West noticed, for instance, that when he recently reread a favorite book, Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead, he had the nagging thought that while he loved returning to the novel for the fourth or fifth time, he wouldn’t be able to count it toward his annual Goodreads stats. West says this fixation on the internet’s hollow validations creates “the exact conditions for a space to be filled by something that isn't human.”
Wouldn’t it be liberating, then, to actually deny our attention to astroturfed outrage, engineered virality, and influencer sponcon? To let the mainstream digital economies propped up by AI-enabled surveillance finally fall to ruin? If what the titans of the industry have to offer us these days are “pervert glasses” and the suppression of ads for a probably unflattering documentary, why are we helping them stay in business? Leaving their platforms for dead might be the last lever of power available to the masses.
Doing so could free people to explore dormant corners. West notes that some of the most interesting parts of the internet are the ones that nobody sees, like web portals to streams of YouTube videos that have almost no views. “Some of it’s fucking weird and creepy, but a lot of it’s just people singing a song and having a blast,” he says. West also cites the bustling, zero-revenue, circulation of poetry in web journals as proof that “you can find meaning and make meaning online all the time,” provided there is no financial motivation.
When you eliminate what the platforms want you to fixate on, it’s clear what you’ve been missing, and how you were steered away from it. Your opinions are shaped in a bubble by avatars you’ve never met, weaponized against equally hermetic rival camps. The internet doesn’t really have winners, unless you count the few without the sense to stop chasing relevance at any cost. That’s why the main characters are so malleable in their beliefs; never afraid to pivot, betray, and discard what they once held to be the core of their identity. And that’s when they stood for anything to begin with.
Absent a sudden, lasting outage due to a fresh and severe catastrophe, the internet as it exists won’t perish anytime soon. There are, however, splintering cracks in its facade, which may create room for emergent and strangely evolved life-forms. There’s no reason to assume that the present tech empire will rule the century to come; the organic and anarchic web stands to mount a triumphant renaissance if (or when) it falls.
“Look, the internet is rotting,” West says. “The question is, where are we going to put our energy?” A metaphor he often turns to in his book is compost. “Compost is just rot harnessed for a purpose,” he says. Can a decaying internet be fertilizer for something better? It’s a rosy notion, but speaking as a perennially failed composter—it’s just too gross, and I’m too lazy—I have my doubts about whether enough hardy, patient gardeners can be mobilized to make our digital landscape bloom once more.
Then again, as West’s book sought to remind me, I am destined to die as well. Maybe I’ll be mixed in with the soil.

Media groups urge EU Commission transparency as Gaza documents probe unfolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:54:15 UTC
18:54:15 KST

A group of 15 media outlets, journalist associations and press freedom organizations urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday to improve journalists’ access to public documents, as an inquiry by the EU Ombudswoman into the commission’s refusal to release documents concerning Gaza unfolds, Anadolu reports.
In an open letter to von der Leyen, the organizations called on the EU executive to address what they described as a “silent crisis” that has hampered journalists’ efforts to obtain information needed to scrutinize matters of public importance.
The appeal comes after European Ombudswoman Teresa Anjinho last week opened an inquiry into a news outlet’s complaint over the commission’s refusal to release 17 documents concerning EU-funded infrastructure projects in the Gaza Strip.
EUobserver first requested the documents in February as part of an investigation examining the extent to which Israeli attacks had destroyed infrastructure financed by the EU in the Palestinian territory.
The commission refused to release the material, arguing that there was no overriding public interest justifying disclosure. EUobserver’s subsequent appeal went unanswered.
As a first step in her inquiry, Anjinho has asked the commission to respond to the appeal by Nov. 4 at the latest. If the EU executive fails to provide a satisfactory response, she will examine the documents herself.
Against this backdrop, the 15 organizations urged the commission to commit to greater transparency, saying journalists routinely face severe delays in obtaining documents, questionable refusals and extensive redactions that render released material largely meaningless.
In some cases, they said, the commission also fails to retain and properly archive crucial documents.
The restrictions have hindered reporting on issues of major public interest, including how EU member states spent billions of euros in post-COVID recovery funds and cooperation with Israel on arms research, the letter said.
“Around Europe, public debate is being harmed. Stories which should emerge do not. Citizens cannot make important political judgements at critical moments,” it said.
The signatories called on the commission to revoke its December 2024 internal rules of procedure, which they said had made access to documents more difficult, and ensure strict implementation of the regulation on public access to EU documents.
The groups also called for a renewed action plan to improve journalists’ access to information, including implementing recommendations from the European Ombudsman, fully complying with European Court of Justice rulings and strengthening internal procedures for filing and archiving documents.
“The European Commission’s reputation for safeguarding EU democratic values is in peril. At a time when democratic norms are under attack around the world, now is the time to uphold these values,” the letter warned.
The signatories included the Committee to Protect Journalists, EUobserver, the European Federation of Journalists, Follow the Money, Forbidden Stories, the International Federation of Journalists, the International Press Institute, Investigate Europe and PEN International.

Harassed by Russian drones, Ukraine’s trains keep on rolling
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:54:06 CET
18:54:06 KST

By Yurii Kovalenko
ON A TRAIN BETWEEN DNIPRO AND ODESA, Ukraine, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Ukrainian beauty salon owner Antonina Viter is getting used to having her travel plans disrupted by the threat of Russian drone attacks, as she criss-crosses the country by rail to keep her business going.
“Every third trip, we end up evacuating once, twice or even three times,” she explained on board a train from the southeastern city of Dnipro to Odesa on the Black Sea.
“What can you do? How else do you get to your client?”
Kyiv has set new rules for rail passengers during air-raid alerts and, sure enough, soon after she spoke, the 36-year-old was standing outside under a pitch-black October sky, wrapped in a blanket, waiting for the “all-clear”.
In a country long reliant on its vast rail network, hours-long delays and repeat evacuations when air-raid sirens sound are another way in which Russia’s escalating missile and drone attacks are wrecking everyday life for civilians.
New Russian jet-powered drones that are hard to shoot down have attacked everything from shopping centres and filling stations to power plants and other critical infrastructure. And the railways are no exception.
UKRAINIAN RAILWAYS ATTACKED 1,700 TIMES THIS YEAR
The state operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, says Russia has attacked more than 1,700 rail facilities this year, including stations, locomotives and passenger wagons. Russia says its targets are objects used by Kyiv’s military.
A trip on the line from Dnipro to Odesa, some 400 km (250 miles) to the southwest, showed how Ukrainians are coping with those disruptions.
The outward journey featured eight evacuations of roughly 30 minutes each, the return journey - one more.
Direct attacks, like the drone strike that killed two train drivers on the Dnipro-Odesa line on August 13, are an ever-present threat.
But air-raid alerts can unexpectedly double the travel time on any route, and some stations in the east and south have been shut indefinitely as fighting creeps closer.
The prospect of being hit is one that 41-year-old IT worker Larysa Konstantynova - who was travelling from Dnipro to Odesa with her teenage son at the start of a holiday trip to Europe - prefers not to think about.
Like Viter, who travels at least six times a month to manage two salons in Kyiv and Dnipro, she says she is adapting.
“It’s how your mind works: you just try to be positive and survive with the way things are.”
Other attacks have included a strike on a Warsaw-bound train near the Polish border in September.
For some, overnight rail journeys - once opportunities to unwind with few distractions - are now spent in anxious anticipation.
During air raid alerts, passengers can be jolted awake and forced to scramble into fields or up and down embankments, sometimes with children or pets in tow. In the winter, temperatures are often below freezing.
RAILWAY JOURNEYS HAUNTED BY RISK OF RANDOM DEATH
Huddled outside her train with a colleague, Viter tracked a nearby drone on a cell-phone app after hearing its distinctive ‘whoosh’ overhead.
It was the third evacuation in two hours.
“Better to stand in a field for an hour than to risk never getting to see the next hour,” she said, knowing she had to teach a beauty workshop in Odesa the next day.
In fact, although delays of 5 to 12 hours are not unusual on the Dnipro-Odesa route, this train arrived just an hour and 20 minutes late.
Nevertheless, the risk of random death has soared as Russia has broadened its drone and ballistic-missile campaign, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of air defence missiles.
More than 50 railway workers have died on duty this year alone, according to Ukraine’s infrastructure minister, and dedicated staff have had to adapt their routines to maintain a network that appears to be close to their hearts.
At the beginning of each journey, conductors sweep through the carriages closing curtains to block out light that might alert a Russian drone.
“They can see us, so we have to hide a bit,” said train attendant Olha Boniuk, 49, with the air of a mother soothing her child.
After each evacuation, chief conductor Mykola Zakharchenko, 47, sits in his cramped booth diligently recording the interruption.
All the same, he smiles recalling conversations with passengers, and still enjoys watching dawn break through the carriage window: “Train work, as they say, is romance.”
Locomotive driver Mykola Kovalenko put it another way.
“If I quit,” he said, “who will drive the trains?”
(Additional reporting by Thomas Peter; Writing by Dan Peleschuk; Editing by Mike Collett-White and Kevin Liffey)

Isamaa lawyer: No ruling in criminal case to come before Riigikogu election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:54:00 UTC
18:54:00 KST

Isamaa lawyer: No ruling in criminal case to come before Riigikogu election
A criminal case against opposition party Isamaa will not reach a court ruling before the March 2027 Riigikogu elections, the party's lawyer has said.
Jaanus Tehver, Isamaa's lawyer, said prosecutors are yet to decide whether to bring charges, but will do so soon.
The suspicions date to last November, when prosecutors notified Isamaa of a prohibited donation totaling €110,234 allegedly accepted between November 2020 and April 2024.
Tehver said he will file no further requests with the Prosecutor's Office and is waiting for the formal charges, which he expects given the prosecution's stated position since spring.
The Prosecutor's Office for its part said the defense has been given until next Monday to examine the evidence materials, after which prosecutors will decide how to proceed.
According to the suspicions, prohibited donations — mainly advertising services — totaling approximately €330,000 were made to Isamaa, of which the party allegedly accepted €110,234. Isamaa and all other suspects deny the allegations.
Tehver said that, purely in terms of timing, no ruling can now be issued ahead of the elections — at best, a preliminary hearing could be held, he added.
"This means that, until the Riigikogu elections, the best that can be said is that charges have been brought before the court and that the Isamaa party is accused of this or that crime," he said. "Unfortunately, we will not know the court's position on what it thinks of these charges before the elections. Regrettable, but what can you do."
"For me, the Prosecutor's Office's position is clear, and in a situation where they have made the decision that I believe they have made, there is no point in my submitting any further requests," Tehver added.
Isamaa's hairman Urmas Reinsalu said it was in the party's interest for clarity to come quickly, but said that the proceedings had not been an issue when recruiting candidates or preparing the election campaign. "Perhaps Isamaa's opponents are more interested in that. But in my opinion, this stirring up of dust already received a public verdict at the end of last year, when we presented our expert analyses and assessments," Reinsalu said.
Reinsalu added cases like this can work the other way too and exert a sort of rallying-round-the-flag effect, as supporters come to see the charges as unfounded – while charges would attract attention, this would not be enough to distract from offering a political alternative to the Reform Party-led government, he said.
Prosecutor's Office spokesperson Kauri Sinkevicius said that if charges are brought and the case goes to court, the court will take over responsibility for the proceedings, and can take circumstances such as the upcoming elections into account when scheduling hearings.
Background:
Last November the Prosecutor's Office notified Isamaa that it was suspected of accepting a large-scale prohibited donation totaling €110,234 between November 2020 and April 2024. Tehver has previously stated the party is suspected of having benefited from coordinated activity by major donor Parvel Pruunsild, Tõnis Palts and the nonprofit MTÜ Isamaalised, who provided advertising and analysis services, with the costs covered by MTÜ Isamaalised. Under the Political Parties Act, companies and nonprofits are prohibited from financing party activities or providing free benefits with monetary value.

At least 39 killed as two high-speed trains collide in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:53:07 UTC
18:53:07 KST

At least 39 people were killed Wednesday morning when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, according to Castilla-La Mancha emergency services cited by Spanish broadcaster Antena 3. The collision, involving trains operated by Renfe and Iryo, left numerous passengers injured, with emergency crews searching damaged carriages and authorities warning that the casualty figures remained preliminary.
The crash occurred at approximately 8:54 a.m. near Urda, in Toledo province, between the towns of Mora, Orgaz and Los Yébenes. Preliminary findings indicate that a Renfe AVE train traveling from Madrid toward Seville struck the rear of an Iryo train that had stopped on the same track. Several carriages derailed, including two that plunged down an embankment.
Spain's Civil Guard reported that at least four carriages had overturned, while emergency personnel worked to rescue passengers trapped inside the wreckage. According to La Vanguardia, 397 passengers were aboard the Renfe train and another 146 were traveling on the Iryo service. The full number of injured passengers had not yet been established.
Investigators examine possible signaling failure
Spanish radio network Cadena SER, citing government sources, reported that the Iryo train had been stationary on the track when the Renfe train was allowed to continue despite a red signal. The circumstances surrounding that authorization remain unclear, and investigators have not determined the cause of the collision.
The accident triggered a major emergency response, with firefighters from Alcázar de San Juan and Orgaz, Civil Protection teams, three medical helicopters and mobile intensive care units deployed to the scene. The regional government activated its territorial emergency plan, while Renfe launched its assistance program for victims of railway accidents and their families.
One passenger described the impact as extraordinarily violent, telling Spanish media that people were thrown through the carriages. Another witness reported seeing injured passengers and emergency workers attempting to recover people trapped beneath the wreckage.
Following the collision, rail infrastructure operator Adif suspended high-speed services between Madrid and Andalusia in both directions, including connections through Ciudad Real. Renfe announced that passengers affected by the disruption would be offered free ticket changes and cancellations.
Sánchez suspends agenda as Spain faces another railway tragedy
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed shock over the disaster and said he was in constant contact with Transport Minister Óscar Puente and Castilla-La Mancha regional President Emiliano García-Page. Sánchez said emergency services were working to assist the victims and their families.
García-Page headed toward the accident site and suspended his official schedule, while Puente traveled to the rail control center at Madrid's Atocha station. Major political parties also canceled campaign activities ahead of Spain's November general election. Emergency services in Madrid established a psychological assistance point at Atocha for relatives of passengers involved in the crash.
The disaster comes nine months after a January 18 collision near Adamuz, in southern Spain's Córdoba province, which ultimately killed 46 people. That accident occurred when an Iryo train derailed and struck another train traveling in the opposite direction, becoming Spain's deadliest railway disaster since 2013, when 80 people died near Santiago de Compostela.
The January tragedy raised serious questions about railway infrastructure and safety in Spain, which operates Europe's largest high-speed rail network and the world's second-largest after China. The network extends more than 1,900 miles (3,100 kilometers), with trains capable of exceeding 155 mph (250 kph).
Wednesday's collision has renewed scrutiny of the system, particularly the signaling and safety procedures designed to prevent trains from occupying the same section of track. With rescue operations continuing, investigators will now seek to determine why the Iryo train was stopped and how the approaching Renfe service was permitted to continue.

“Disasters are growing more severe, striking communications, medical care, and transport at once. Conflicts worldwide are reaching our supply chains and energy supplies, and the military balance is shifting fast, raising the risk of collision against a vulnerable and of dangerous miscalculations,” Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, told a joint meeting of ASEAN defense chiefs in Cebu City, the Philippines, current chair of the Southeast Asian bloc.

Koizumi said the ASEAN members “are strengthening their own ability to respond and deter.”
“ASEAN as a whole is tackling shared challenges from disaster response to maritime security. These efforts complement each other, and Japan … will support both,” he said.
“Our aim is simple: to widen the options for ASEAN and for each member to understand, decide, and act on its own,” said the Japanese defense chief, urging ASEAN and Japan to “update our areas of cooperation.”
He pledged that Japan “will do everything it can” to turn ASEAN “choices into real strength.”
The meetings in Cebu City mark the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting and 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus, which also brings together the defense chiefs of US, China, South Korea, Japan, Australia, and India, although China this year did not send its defense minister.

Russia in Africa: What is Putin hoping to achieve?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
