Russia in Africa: What does the Kremlin hope to achieve?
October 28, 2026
The conflict with the West sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine prompted Russian President Vladimir Putin to seek support from other parts of the world. Africa has become a focus, with foreign minister Sergei Lavrov visiting the continent increasingly often.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova has described it as a "historic return," and declared no one and nothing could be compared to what Russia did for Africa in the 20th century.
Russia's most important African partner: Egypt
A Russia-Africa summit has been held in Russia at roughly three-year intervals since 2019. The third takes place in Moscow on October 28 and 29. The program focusses on economic cooperation. Other topics range from politics and security to science and culture. But Russia is actively working with only a few African countries, mainly in the north of the continent, and this is reflected in the trade figures.
"South Africa is still Africa's largest national economy, but its volume of trade with Russia is small, far less than with Egypt and Algeria," says Ivan Klyszcz from the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn, Estonia.
"Egypt and Algeria in particular are key partners for Russia. Egypt plays an important role in this regard. Russian diplomats and business representatives are trying to extend relationships with other countries, especially Tanzania and Ethiopia, but with no appreciable success so far."
Egypt is the second-largest economy in Africa, and the bilateral volume of trade with Russia has more than doubled since 2021; in 2025, according to Russia's Federal Customs Service, it was $10.5 billion (€9.4 billion). Consignments of Russian grain are the main drivers, followed by products of the metal industry. Egypt's exports to Russia are primarily fruit and vegetables.
There are investment projects, too. Russia is building a big nuclear power plant in the Egyptian region of El-Dabaa on the Mediterranean coast. Construction is being financed by a Russian loan of 25 billion US dollars, which covers around 85% of the costs.
Egypt is one of the few African countries with which Russia enjoys stable business relationships, as well as having extensive experience of cooperation, says Nikita Smagin, an expert on Russian policy in the Middle East. "In the long term, Egypt could become Moscow's gateway to Africa and to other markets," he says. "But Cairo is pursuing its own interests. It would be too optimistic to hope that Egypt is lending its support purely out of political solidarity."
Russia's economic role in Africa
According to the Russian customs service, around 39% of Russian–African trade in 2025 was with Egypt, and total sales between Russia and all 54 countries of the African continent came to around 27 billion US dollars. Africa's share of Russia's foreign trade is therefore very small (3.9% in 2025), and not at all commensurate with the attention Moscow is devoting to its relations with African countries.
Russia is not a significant trading partner for Africa, either. The most important partner for African countries is the European Union. In 2025, the volume of trade with the EU came to around 385 billion US dollars. African countries' statistics also show that other partners were well ahead of Russia. The volume of trade with China was in excess of 348 billion US dollars in 2025; with the United States it was almost 105 billion, and 103 billion with India.
Fidel Owusu, a Ghanaian expert with Geopolitical Intelligence Services (GIS) in Liechtenstein, comments that Russia's economic presence in Africa has not been as significant as that of China, the United States, India, or other traditional powers like France and Britain. "If you look at the volume of trade and the kind of investment," he says, "in recent times, some middle powers such as Turkey and the UAW are doing far better than Russia."
Beverly Ochieng, a senior analyst with Control Risks, a global risk and strategic intelligence consultancy in Senegal, observes: "Western countries continue to dominate in strategically important areas such as raw material extraction, finance, and the energy sector, even if their political presence in the region is declining." According to her, "Russia will compete more intensively for access to critical mineral resources and energy projects. We see this with lithium projects in Mali as well as with nuclear power initiatives across the continent."
Russian mercenaries in Africa
Russia's presence in Africa is more obvious in the military sector than in the fields of trade and investment. Starting with the arrival of the Wagner Group, Russian mercenaries have been supporting African regimes, particularly those of the unstable countries in the Sahel region. In exchange, their associated subsidiaries are granted access to raw materials. Following the death of the Wagner Group leader, Yevgeny Prigozhin, most of these operations were taken over by the Africa Corps, a paramilitary group set up and controlled by Russia's defense ministry.
According to the Congressional Research Service, the think tank of the US Congress, the largest Russian military contingents, each comprising several thousand men, are in the Central African Republic, Mali, and Libya. The Africa Corps is also keen to extend its presence in Burkina Faso and Niger. Russian mercenaries have also been spotted in Equatorial Guinea.
Irina Filatova from the University of Cape Town stresses that there are several reasons why it's important for Russia to maintain a military presence in Africa. "The countries have sizeable deposits of minerals such as gold and uranium. Through them, it's possible to exert influence over Europe's southern borders, including in matters of migration and regional security. With regard to Libya, the country is an important logistical hub for connections with the Sahel and central Africa. Goods can easily be supplied via Libya to countries without access to the sea," Filatova says.
Ultimately, Russia is still one of the biggest suppliers of arms to African countries, even though Russian exports have fallen over the course of the war in Ukraine. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates Moscow's share of the African market for the years 2021–2025 at 15%, which puts it in third place behind the United States (19%) and China (17%). Between 2020 and 2024, its share was even higher: It was in first place with 21%, followed by China with 18%, and the US with 16%.
What are Russia's diplomatic aims in Africa?
Ivan Klyszcz from the ICDS says that while Russia is not a significant economic partner for Africa, the fact that it supplies food and fertilizer and has a military presence in some countries means that Moscow's influence in Africa is far greater than is suggested by the volume of trade and investment alone.
"I believe Russia sees the diplomatic weight of Africa," says Fidel Owusu. "When I talk of diplomatic weight, I mean numbers – the continent has the largest number of countries. Russia wants that kind of support in the UN General Assembly whenever votes are cast. In recent times it has done better than in earlier votes."
The perception of Russia in Africa
In recent years, Russia has been positioning itself on the international stage as representing the interests of the Global South.
"We want to work with Africa, we are working with Africa and we will continue to do so. But our aim is not, as it was for the colonial powers, to make money or steal something from Africa, but to develop together," Russian president Vladimir Putin said recently at a conference of the Moscow-based Valdai Discussion Club.
References to the colonial past appeal to some countries but not others, says Irina Filatova. "Africa is not a country, it's a continent. There are differences in the perception of Russia, as well as in the way Russia positions itself. Also, the views of the political elites are often substantially different from those of ordinary citizens. In South Africa, for instance, the Russian narrative is received very positively. An anti-colonial agenda is also popular in other countries, but it isn't necessarily associated with Russia."
Antonio Cascais contributed to this report. It was originally written in Russian.

Iran hasn't tried to repair damaged nuclear facilities: IAEA

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

Breadcrumb
Iran hasn't tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes: IAEA chief
The head of the UN nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli military strikes this year or last year.
President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the US went to war with Iran on 28 February was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the US carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 "obliterated" the country’s atomic program.
During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the US bombed its sites last year.
Grossi said that "since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026."
Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week’s midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn’t immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi's remarks.
Iran insists its nuclear program is peaceful. Meanwhile, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity—a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
The UN meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting.
Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
Iran's UN deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the US-Israeli attacks, denouncing their "wars of aggression against Iran" and noted the US is committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
He added that "Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran."
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz called Iran a "brutal dictatorship" and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologise to Bahrain's envoy, a council member, for attacking his country.
"We've heard tireless allegations against the United States," he said. "What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran's continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations."
The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.
"Your lies are no good here," he said.

Animal rights party renews bill to ban cruel slaughter methods

Animal rights party renews bill to ban cruel slaughter methods
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The animals rights party PvdD is making a renewed effort to pass a bill that would ban a number of common and cruel livestock slaughter methods, such as electric waterbath stunning, gassing via CO2, and all non-stun methods.
The bill, sent to MPs today, was first submitted in 2025, and would also ban selling cows, pigs and horses for slaughter while they’re in the last third of a pregnancy. Tipping poultry out of crates while they’re still conscious (a common practice) would also be outlawed.
According to agriculture ministry figures for 2024, 25,895 animals – cattle, calves, sheep and goats – were slaughtered without stunning under religious rites.
In the same figures, some 10.5 million pigs were slaughtered at abattoirs that use CO2 gassing, while more than 62.7 million broiler chickens, 4.6 million ducks and nearly 4,000 turkeys were killed at slaughterhouses that use electric waterbaths.
PvdD MP Esther Ouwehand, who drafted the bill, told broadcaster NOS: “the aim of the law is to limit the suffering of animals during slaughter as much as possible.”
The party first began trying to outlaw non-stun slaughter in 2008 but was voted down in the Senate over freedom of religion concerns. But the Council of State said last year a ban would not necessarily breach freedom religion following European court rulings on bans in Belgium.

The Men Spending $50,000 Just to Reserve a Tesla Roadster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

In mid-October, CEO Elon Musk sort of made good on a long-standing promise: Tesla’s new second-gen Roadster flew through the air. Technically, the vehicle used compressed air to “thrust” itself—the “flying” lasted mere seconds, and the system takes six to seven hours to refill.
Never mind, though—some buyers were eager to unsheath their credit cards to reserve one of the cars. “I was freaking out,” says Alex Lawrence, the owner of used-electric-vehicle dealership EVAuto, who already had one reservation for a second-gen Roadster and watched the demonstration live online. “I placed another one.”
It’s not a decision most would make lightly. Tesla took years to get the sports car even close to production. The automaker first introduced the vehicle, a successor to its first car ever, as a surprise at a 2017 event, and immediately began taking $50,000 reservations. At the time, the plan was to deliver the cars in 2020; Musk and company now say the vehicle will enter production in 2028, with delivery dates unclear. (If reservation holders had put that money into Tesla stock, they would be up nearly $1 million today.)
The Roadster is also expensive to reserve—and will likely get pricier to buy. The vehicle’s base model, which doesn’t include acceleration thrusters or the flight system, still costs $50,000 to reserve. The second-tier Thrust variant, which comes with the thrusters, requires a $250,000 deposit. The actual flying car, called Rocket, is listed as “invite-only,” and even Musk has acknowledged the vehicle won’t be street legal. Meanwhile, the automaker’s reservation terms note that purchase prices are “only an estimate”—and those estimates don’t even exist yet.
Whatever! “I’m going to do everything in my power to get the flying one,” Lawrence says. When he sees the Roadster, after all, he sees money signs. His EV dealership has a large and growing social media following, and the business, not the man, technically put down the money for the Roadster reservations. “We’re going to put it on the track and use it for marketing content,” he says.
Utah-based tech founder Travis Cook upped his nearly 10-year-old reservation for the base Roadster variant to the Thrust because he actually wants to live with the thing. He calls himself a “car aficionado” and has a dealer’s license so he can buy and sell fun cars. He loves little more than driving an unusual vehicle, he told WIRED from behind the wheel of a Cybertruck as he used the company’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) feature.
“When I roll up somewhere, all the other car aficionados come out, and they're so excited,” he says. “I just get a buzz from that.”
Cook says he has no regrets about his years-old reservation, though he may get frustrated if the price shoots up closer to half a million. “I’m not sure I’m willing to drop too much money on the car—but I probably would,” he says. Close family tolerates his obsession, though his wife doesn’t enjoy going 0 to 60 in his other cars and probably won’t in the Roadster, either. “She’s not going to want to go in it,” he says.
The tech founder has faith in Musk and Tesla. The October demonstration was even crazier than he had expected. “When it launched off the top of the ramp and went and landed, my jaw was on the floor,” Cook says.
Despite the Roadster’s memeable debut, the vehicle doesn’t seem to be a top priority for Tesla. Musk has said for years now that the automaker isn’t really in the business of making cars anymore and instead is focused on robotics, artificial intelligence, and autonomy. He has touted the new Roadster as the company’s last human-driven car ever. The supercar garnered just two mentions in Tesla’s hourlong earnings call with investors this month, with Musk calling it “arguably the coolest demo of any product ever.” Musk, meanwhile, has other preoccupations—he has donated at least $445 million to Republican candidates ahead of the US midterms.
But Lawrence believes Musk will pull off what he says he will and that his own business’s investment in the Roadster will be worth it in the end. The looping, wedge-shaped car demo left him a little nostalgic, a little existential.
“We don’t do crazy stuff like this anymore, like going to the moon. There’s not a lot today that will stop you in your tracks,” he says. “I felt like I was 15, watching that.”

Russia Tracks 12.5 Million Social Media Accounts Daily, Nearly Half Over War Criticism

Russia Tracks 12.5 Million Social Media Accounts Daily, Nearly Half Over War Criticism
The Russian federal youth agency Rosmolodezh tracks 12.5 million social media accounts every day, with 6 million of those profiles linked to criticism of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the Russian military.
Denis Ashirov, deputy head of the agency, shared these details during a meeting of the Russian State Duma expert council for family protection, according to The Insider on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Data analysis indicates that these profiles account for 48% of all monitored accounts. The agency classifies such criticism as destructive and illegal information.
The agency also tracks 1.1 million profiles connected to political violence and criticism of the government, 1.5 million linked to drugs, and 906,000 associated with the promotion and rehabilitation of Nazism.
Additional categories under state monitoring include attacks on educational institutions, suicidal behavior, and criminal subcultures. Social media monitoring for Rosmolodezh is carried out by the Center for Research and Network Monitoring of the Youth Environment, an organization established by order of Vladimir Putin, according to The Insider.
The center helps identify individuals in schools and universities who are considered socially dangerous by the state. Grigory Gurov, head of Rosmolodezh, stated that work done by the center in 2024 led to about 500 criminal cases and several hundred administrative cases.
Thousands of other individuals faced preventive measures for spreading prohibited information. Court records from 2025 and the first half of 2026 show at least 48 judicial decisions where information from the center was used to prosecute citizens.
In the Novosibirsk region, criticism of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine became the most frequent category of destructive content identified by the center in 2025, followed by anarchism ideas and drug promotion.
In May 2026, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin approved a youth social prevention plan created by Rosmolodezh. The document details online tracking of teenagers to identify individuals suspected of planning illegal acts. The plan also includes setting up student cyber units to search for destructive content across social networks, messaging platforms, and online forums.
Russian authorities have increasingly focused on identifying so-called “destructive content,” monitoring political sentiment among young people, and embedding patriotic education into classrooms and extracurricular activities.
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has rolled out patriotic education programs, mandatory ideological lessons, and reporting mechanisms encouraging students and teachers to flag criticism of the war or government policies.
Officials have framed the push as a preventive measure against extremism and foreign influence, while rights advocates warn it deepens surveillance and pressure against dissent.

Mapping the siege of Yemen’s Taiz, and the price families are paying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:43:09 UTC
18:43:09 KST

Mapping the siege of Yemen’s Taiz, and the price families are paying
Three weeks into the siege of Yemen’s third-largest city, prices have doubled, and families are down to the basics.
Taiz, Yemen – In the besieged city of Taiz, Yousef Farhan’s family has run out of choices at mealtime.
“The whole day, we either eat rice or beans, whether in the morning or in the evening,” the 39-year-old father of four told Al Jazeera.
Shelling forced the family from their home years ago, and they have lived in a school in Taiz’s Wadi al-Qadi zone ever since.
Farhan used to sell cucumbers from a small cart in front of the school, earning between 4,000 and 5,000 Yemeni riyals (roughly $2.50 to $3.20) a day. The money was never steady, but it bought a gas cylinder each month and, now and then, a meal with some variety.
Then the siege closed the school, and his trade went with it. The family now cooks over firewood.
“With the suspension of the school due to the shelling and the siege, my source of income stopped, and I was unable to find alternative work since the siege caused many people’s jobs to come to a halt,” he said.
His children, aged five months to five years, depend on whatever he can find. So do his sister and her child, who joined him after their neighbourhood came under fire.
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, is home to about 1 million of the country’s roughly 43 million people.
The city has been cut off since early October, when it lost both of its land routes. The Houthis took the town of al-Turbah by October 4, severing the Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road, the main artery for goods.
A day earlier, forces loyal to the internationally recognised government closed the eastern al-Houban crossing into Houthi-held territory, citing attempted Houthi incursions.
On October 20, the United Nations warned that road closures and lack of security were blocking vital supplies.
Prices of the food and fuel still available had more than doubled, and Taiz’s water production had dropped by half.
Across Taiz, families like Farhan’s are working out what to eat and whether they can afford to cook it.
The map below shows the main Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road and three other routes out of the city, all now closed.
One day at a time
For weeks, 40-year-old Sayyun Burhan has looked no further ahead than tomorrow.
“We barely live day-to-day, waiting to see how the next day will pass,” she said.
Work is no longer available at the local store where Sayyun’s husband was employed, and his failing health makes it harder for him to find anything else. Meanwhile, the family still needs money for rent, food, water and cooking gas.
Across the city, the cost of water delivered by tankers has roughly tripled since the fighting escalated, according to UN officials.
The strain reaches beyond the kitchen. For Burhan’s children, the siege means missed lessons and long days inside, as she is afraid to let them out.
“They have been deprived of schooling and play,” she said.
Keeping both children safe and fed is becoming harder.
A city running on fumes
Fuel is behind many of Taiz’s civilian emergencies. Diesel keeps water pumps working, hospital generators running and ambulances moving. Petrol enables people can get to work, and patients to treatment. Cooking gas lets families and restaurants prepare food.
But the city’s fuel stations have been closed since October 5.
Prices gathered by Al Jazeera in Taiz show how sharply fuel costs have risen. A 20-litre (5.3-gallon) container of petrol now costs 120,000 riyals ($77), four times last year’s price of 30,000 riyals ($19).
The price of 20 litres of diesel has nearly doubled, from 46,000 riyals ($29) to 90,000 riyals ($58). A cooking gas cylinder has risen from 11,400 riyals ($7) to 40,000 riyals ($26).
Bus fares have risen from 200 riyals (13 cents) to 500 riyals (32 cents), an increase of 150 percent. Every ride now takes a bigger share of household budgets already stretched by rising food prices.
For Farhan, the move to firewood shows how far his family’s spending power has fallen. He once managed with a gas cylinder each month. Now, even a pot of rice or beans depends on what he can burn.
Water shortages are not new in Taiz, but the siege has made them worse. Diesel shortages have disrupted the pumps.
Local authorities say access restrictions are also stopping tankers from the Al-Dhabab basin, an important source of drinking water, from entering the city.
A hospital hall for a home
Fatima Khaled, 55, has kidney failure. She cannot afford repeated trips from her village west of the city to the hospital for treatment, or a room closer to the hospital. She sleeps on the floor of the dialysis hall at Al-Jumhuri General Hospital.
Closed roads and long mountain detours have made every journey for treatment exhausting and expensive.
The hospital itself is under strain. On October 22, the World Health Organization warned that 42 health facilities in Taiz were reporting severe shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and medical supplies.
“I feel like I am imprisoned here. We have no housing or shelter here. This hall is our shelter,” Fatima says.

Flávio Bolsonaro's escape: crossed into Argentina, flew overnight to Ecuador, reportedly US-bound
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:39:54 UTC
18:39:54 KST

New details emerged Wednesday about the escape of Brazilian right-wing leader Flávio Bolsonaro, who fled the country following his surprise defeat to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's presidential election, despite a court order requiring him to surrender his passports. 
Argentina confirmed Wednesday morning that Bolsonaro, his wife and their two daughters had crossed the border late Tuesday before boarding a private flight bound for Guayaquil, Ecuador. Reports suggested the family intended to continue to the United States, although their ultimate destination remained unclear.
The confirmation offered the clearest account yet of Bolsonaro's movements after he disappeared from public view Tuesday. Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win Sunday's presidential runoff, with final opinion polls showing him ahead by one or two percentage points. Instead, Lula won 51.79% of valid votes against Bolsonaro's 48.21%. The vote count began later than expected after authorities extended voting by two hours, prompting Bolsonaro to allege irregularities and refuse to recognize his defeat, echoing his father Jair Bolsonaro's response after losing to Lula in 2022.
A court order, a broken promise and a disappearance
Less than 24 hours after the election, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports within 24 hours as part of ongoing criminal investigations. The cases include suspected corruption, money laundering and tax evasion, including an investigation into efforts to secure financing for a biographical film about his father from former banker Daniel Vorcaro. Bolsonaro has denied committing any crime.
The order came amid fears that Bolsonaro might follow his father's example. After refusing to concede defeat in the 2022 election, Jair Bolsonaro traveled to the United States and remained there for several months. He eventually returned to Brazil and was later sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in a plot to overturn the election result.
Those concerns were reinforced by comments from Flávio's younger brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in the United States. Speaking to American podcaster Steven Crowder on October 23, Eduardo said he supported his brother leaving Brazil if he lost the election. "If my brother doesn't win, I'm in favor of him leaving the country," he said.
On Monday, however, Flávio Bolsonaro insisted he had no intention of fleeing. "I never thought about leaving the country," he said in an Instagram video. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this aberration, which is clearly an attempt to intimidate me. But nobody will silence me."
By Tuesday, Bolsonaro had disappeared from public view. His associates said they did not know where he was, while Brazilian media reported that he might have crossed into Argentina. When the deadline for surrendering his passports expired without his compliance, Brazilian authorities canceled the documents.
Authorities in Buenos Aires initially denied having any record of Bolsonaro entering Argentina or requesting political asylum from President Javier Milei, a political ally of the Bolsonaro family. Brazilian officials also said they had no record of his departure through an official border checkpoint. However, Brazilian citizens can enter Argentina using national identity documents rather than passports, and Bolsonaro also holds Italian citizenship.
From the Iguazú border crossing to a private flight
The breakthrough came Wednesday morning when Argentina's immigration authority confirmed that Bolsonaro and his family had entered through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, connecting Foz do Iguaçu in Brazil with Puerto Iguazú in Argentina's Misiones province. According to Argentine authorities, the family presented valid travel documents and encountered no legal obstacles to entering the country.
At approximately 11:30 p.m. Tuesday, Bolsonaro, his wife and their two daughters boarded a private aircraft operated by charter company Baires Fly at Puerto Iguazú airport. The flight plan listed Guayaquil, Ecuador, as its destination, and flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 indicated that the aircraft departed during the night.
The account raised questions about how Bolsonaro had managed to leave Brazil despite the judicial order requiring him to surrender his passports. It also contradicted earlier reports suggesting he had traveled directly to the United States. Although American and Brazilian sources indicated Tuesday that Bolsonaro was heading to the U.S., there was no confirmation Wednesday morning of his arrival or precise location. American sources said the U.S. State Department was expected to grant Bolsonaro and his family visas, but it remained unclear whether they had continued their journey.
Trump offers support, questions Brazil's election
U.S. President Donald Trump, a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, said overnight that he would support Flávio Bolsonaro's arrival in the United States. "I would support that," Trump told reporters. "I think they're good people." He also criticized the Brazilian election, describing the circumstances surrounding the vote as highly unusual. "The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible," he said. "Look at what happened to their markets."
Earlier in the week, Trump questioned the legitimacy of Lula's victory, alleging without evidence that the election appeared to have been manipulated. "I didn't interfere on behalf of either side, but it looked to me like another rigged election," he said Monday. "Elections should be beyond dispute, and this looked very bad to me."
The comments reflected Trump's longstanding political relationship with the Bolsonaro family, established during Jair Bolsonaro's presidency and maintained through his subsequent legal battles. Flávio Bolsonaro had promised during his campaign to strengthen relations with Washington if elected. His defeat represented a setback for Trump's ambitions to expand American influence across Latin America, following a series of victories by right-wing politicians in countries including Chile, Peru and Colombia.
Lula condemns escape: ‘The United States is their first homeland’
Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, sharply criticized his defeated opponent during birthday celebrations in Brasília. The Brazilian president described Bolsonaro's departure as "shameful" and argued that he should have remained in the country to answer the allegations against him and prove his innocence rather than leave after promising to cooperate with authorities.
Turning to the Bolsonaro family's close relationship with Washington, Lula added: "That's the Bolsonaro family. Brazil is their second homeland. The United States is their first homeland." He also accused Bolsonaro of subservience to Washington, saying he was "licking the boots of the United States."
Lula and Trump have repeatedly clashed over trade, regional influence and Brazil's political future. The Brazilian president accused Washington of attempting to influence the election in favor of his opponent and used his victory speech Sunday to insist that Brazil would remain independent. "Brazil is nobody's backyard," he declared.
If the United States becomes Bolsonaro's final destination, his arrival could deepen tensions between Washington and Brasília, particularly given the outstanding Brazilian court order and ongoing investigations. For now, Argentine authorities have confirmed how Bolsonaro and his family crossed the border and boarded a flight to Ecuador, but their ultimate destination remains uncertain, leaving both his legal future and the diplomatic consequences of his departure unresolved.

Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:37:49 UTC
18:37:49 KST

The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.
As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.
“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.
Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”
This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.
On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.
The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.
Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.
The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.
Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.
“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.
At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”
Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.
“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

Heat and hunger take toll on Swiss hedgehogs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:35:56 UTC
18:35:56 KST

Heat and hunger take toll on Swiss hedgehogs
Swiss hedgehogs, named Animal of the Year 2026, struggled through the scorching summer as severe food shortages left many mothers weakened and an unusually high number of cubs orphaned.
At the start of summer, hedgehog rescue centres in various regions, including cantons Bern, Basel City and Country, Aargau, Zurich and Lucerne, reported an unusual surge in the number of orphaned young hedgehogs and severely emaciated mothers, the pro Igel association said on Tuesday. Experienced foster carers had never experienced such a situation on this scale.
More
The hedgehog is named Swiss animal of the year 2026
A vet from Dätwil, canton Zurich, reported 226 hedgehogs and 336 consultations between January and the end of July. During the same period last year, the figures were 183 hedgehogs and 208 consultations. Treatment costs this year were 33% higher.
Food shortages due to drought
Hedgehogs feed mainly on small invertebrates such as beetles and insects. Prolonged heat and drought have adversely affected their living conditions and reduced their availability. The food shortage hit mother hedgehogs particularly hard during the energy-sapping period of rearing their young.
“Mothers abandoned their young because they themselves could not find enough food to survive,” explained Anja Straumann of Igelhilfe Baselbiet in the bulletin.
Long-term consequences
The consequences of the dry summer extend into autumn. Hedgehogs now need to build up sufficient energy reserves for hibernation. For late-born or already weakened young hedgehogs, the lack of reserves is life-threatening.
More
One third of Switzerland’s animal and plant species under threat
The national drought bulletin of October 22, 2026 continued to show significant to extreme soil moisture deficits in various regions.
The pro Igel association stresses that hedgehogs are already under pressure from man-made threats such as sealed surfaces, well-kept gardens and the fragmentation of their habitats. Extreme weather events have further exacerbated these difficult conditions.
+ Switzerland names 2,999 species as conservation priorities
Pro Igel recommends creating natural, interconnected habitats, as well as providing targeted supplementary feeding with high-quality, grain-free cat food and setting up water points.

ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.
The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.
Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.
Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7.
Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration's policies and espouse "anti-Christian" ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown.
Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s.
Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025.
Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area.
More than 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order.
The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them.
Their defense attorneys say the heavy charges filed against the Minnesota 15 don’t align with their alleged conduct. “This is the first time I’ve had a client who’s accused of a conspiracy and went on a speaking tour,” says Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant.
Peeking Through the Keyhole
An internal ICE document laying out the scope of Operation Puppet Master—which led to the indictment of the Minneapolis 15—ends by noting, “This case has also been accepted under CUC Op Keyhole.” According to prosecutors, Operation Keyhole is a long-standing program created by HSI’s Saint Paul office to fund “undercover activity”—primarily equipment purchases and personnel costs—in a region covering Minnesota, North and South Dakota, Iowa, and Nebraska. The program has funded at least 77 investigations into “narcotics trafficking, child sexual abuse, financial investigations, and counter-proliferation” since it started in December 2008.
The CUC prefix, per an internal 2008 DHS handbook unearthed by the independent media outlet Unicorn Riot, refers to Certified Undercover Operations, a formal designation with clearly defined oversight mechanisms, procedures, and reporting requirements. Operation Keyhole’s parameters are reviewed every six months by a committee comprising senior DOJ and DHS officials. As of June 2026, when it was last renewed, Keyhole funded six active investigations, including Project Whipple Shield, which was initiated in February to probe claims of assault, stalking, and doxing of DHS agents and other federal employees, and underpins the Minnesota 15 indictment.
At least 11 undercover agents working under Operation Keyhole infiltrated Twin Cities anti-ICE activists, participating in martial arts and know-your-rights trainings, marches, general strikes, and community meetings. They also infiltrated activists’ communications network for identifying possible undercover ICE vehicles and dispatching activists to tail them through the Twin Cities, and penetrated several activist group chats on Signal, transmitting their contents back to other HSI colleagues for analysis and eventual inclusion in the indictment.
Activist conferences as far away as Seattle, Michigan, and New York City were placed under surveillance as part of the investigation, and HSI teams photographed and ran the license plates of every car parked in the lot of a meeting location or seen transporting activists. There is also drone footage from unarmed Customs and Border Protection Reaper drones of the activists moving around the Twin Cities area.
The undercovers were part of a much broader group of more than 50 HSI agents, including at least two dozen from HSI’s little-known Special Operations Group, that took part in the investigation and surveillance of the defendants, both digital and in-person. Feds with decades of experience on complex financial crimes, drug cartel investigations, human trafficking, and organized crime were pulled into the Minnesota 15 investigation.
Several of the Minnesota 15 case agents are from out of state and appear in court records for the prosecutions of anti-ICE activists in other cities. This includes Los Angeles–based HSI agents Robert Kurtz III, who specializes in financial fraud, and Ryan Ribner, who allegedly assaulted SEIU California president David Huerta at a June 2025 protest of an ICE enforcement operation, arrested him, and then claimed the then 58-year-old Huerta attacked federal law enforcement. (Huerta’s charges were dropped in July after videos contradicting Ribner’s account surfaced.) HSI records show Ribner was also involved in at least two prosecutions of Southern California residents who physically confronted ICE and Border Patrol agents last year.
Other agents from the conspiracy investigation have also been involved in recent high-profile incidents. Tim Gerber, the “team leader” of an HSI Special Operations Group squad, led the investigation of former CNN host Don Lemon for reporting on a protest at a Minneapolis Church where an ICE agent was a pastor. Fellow SOG agent Yue Her was present at the scene of a 2025 incident when Renee Good’s killer, ICE Special Response Team agent Johnathan Ross, was dragged by the car of a man he tried to apprehend.
“This operation does not seem in any way limited to Minnesota,” says Spencer Reynolds, a former DHS attorney and counterterrorism lawyer who now works at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. “As we saw with the boots on the ground in the streets, with Greg Bovino leading CBP and Border Patrol special forces units on sweeping raids across the country, this is the intelligence and undercover investigative apparatus that is running in parallel to the door-kicking.”
Follow the Money
Mike German, a retired FBI agent who worked undercover domestic terrorism cases for years before becoming a sharp critic of post-9/11 federal law enforcement, likens the Minnesota 15 case to federal law enforcement’s long history of suppressing left-wing social movements, including the CIA’s Operation MH/Chaos, which surveilled the anti-war movement during the Vietnam War for evidence of foreign influence. One difference is the sheer scale—this time, it’s bigger.
According to a 2011 book by former CIA officer Frank Rafalko, the CIA secret investigation into suspected foreign influence on the New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement had 42 officers working the case at its peak. Court records show 62 HSI agents worked on the Minnesota 15 case alone.
“Broad monitoring of social media, communications, and financial transactions are used to link an ever increasing number of people as potential subjects of investigation and prosecution,” German says. “These are exactly the kind of intelligence activities J. Edgar Hoover adopted to suppress the Civil Rights and anti-war movements in the 1960s.”
The key difference today, German says, is the vast pool of data available to the feds.
HIS used highly invasive measures—including scrutiny of wire transfers, PayPal reimbursements, and other financial transactions; forensic digital analysis of website traffic; 15 terabytes worth of infiltrated Signal chats; and information from a commercial data broker—to identify individuals under investigation.
After a local activist uploaded a license-plate search tool on Fly.io, a developer-focused public cloud platform, to an infiltrated Signal chat, HSI agents reviewed website DNS queries and Stripe data along with data purchased from a commercial broker. This gave HSI access to SSH session logs, outbound connection records, the Fly.io account’s signup IP, and a Stripe card fingerprint on an account that had never completed a payment. Agents fused that with Minnesota DVS records and commercial data from the Thomson-Reuters CLEAR platform to produce a driver's license number, Social Security number summary, years of address history, phone numbers, property records, and jointly registered vehicles.
Documents concerning financial records requested through the Treasury Department’s 314(a) suspicious activity reporting program—created by the Patriot Act to enable speedy tracking of finances for terrorism and money-laundering investigations—show that the feds targeted records of 29 “subjects” during queries conducted on March 31, 2026. Emails viewed by WIRED between several HSI agents based in Los Angeles and Arizona show that batches of records were turned over pursuant to those inquiries, including some dealing with SEIU that a senior Minnesota HSI agent sent to a LA-based colleague to be filed “wherever these records are stored.”
HSI investigators used similar workarounds to warrants and grand jury subpoenas to obtain phone records for several journalists who covered Operation Metro Surge, as first reported by The Guardian. Court records show the feds used an administrative summons request reserved for violations of customs and taxation requirements, which does not fit the activity that made up the criminal charges filed by the Minnesota US attorney against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others.
The Minnesota 15 case is the clearest example yet of DHS pursuing the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on what have long been upheld as First Amendment–protected activities. But it’s unlikely alone.
Riach, the defense attorney, says the HSI reports show the agency is complicit in what he called “the new COINTELPRO.”
“What we saw during the immigration surges last year was that ICE is the administration’s paramilitary force, the projector of strength,” Riach says. “Here, we see that HSI are taking the FBI’s place as the investigative secret police—it’s the classic one-two punch of authoritarian regimes around the world.”

====================================================================================================

Bushfire smoke can cut solar farm output by 70 pct: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:27:21 CST
18:27:21 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Smoke from major bushfires can reduce solar electricity generation by up to 70 percent within about 50 km of fire hotspots and by up to 30 percent more than 150 km away, an Australian study finds.
Researchers used historical weather and satellite data to model how smoke and airborne particles affected solar electricity generation and panel temperatures during two major Australian bushfires, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of New South Wales (UNSW).
"Extreme bushfires are becoming more frequent and intense in several regions, including Australia, California and southern Europe. Their impacts are not confined to the areas where fires burn," said Shukla Poddar, a UNSW postdoctoral researcher and corresponding author of the study published in the journal Solar Energy.
The researchers said smoke and airborne particles reduce the sunlight reaching solar panels, lowering electricity generation. During Australia's 2019-2020 Black Summer bushfires, electricity generation fell by as much as 70 percent at locations within about 50 km of fire hotspots over several consecutive days. In regions more than 150 km away, electricity generation fell by up to 30 percent as winds carried smoke inland, the study found.
The estimated reductions in generated power during the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires in Victoria were smaller, at around 18 percent near hotspots and up to 10 percent in more distant regions, it said.
The research recommended combining bushfire information, wind patterns and smoke-trajectory modelling to help predict which solar farms could be affected. That warning could allow operators to plan inspections, schedule cleaning or adjust the position of panels before smoke arrives. ■

Economic Watch: Clean energy brings electricity, jobs to African communities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:27:15 CST
18:27:15 KST

CHANGSHA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- For 26-year-old Green, an orphan born unable to speak in remote northwestern Zambia, a new solar project job has put steady food on the table and left him a little extra cash.
Green lives in Jifumpa Village, beside the Ruida Mine. Formal work is scarce there. He once scraped by helping neighbors harvest corn and taking casual odd jobs, with no reliable income.
That changed in October 2024, when Chinese firm SANY Microgrid began building a solar-plus-storage facility nearby. Green was hired to clear land, haul materials and carry out other basic tasks. He often signals his thanks to his Chinese co-workers with smiles and hand gestures.
The site combines solar panels, battery storage and diesel generators. It delivers consistent power to the mine while trimming fossil fuel reliance.
"Beyond building power facilities, energy projects in many remote parts of Africa can also create opportunities for local disadvantaged groups to improve their lives through work," said Guo Ruiguang, chairman of SANY Microgrid.
The company now runs microgrid work across Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and other African nations. It has developed more than 60 installations for industrial parks, ports and other sites.
A June 2026 report from U.N. agencies estimates roughly 655 million people worldwide still lack access to electricity, including more than 560 million in sub-Saharan Africa.
For communities receiving their first dependable electricity supply, this green energy partnership carries wide-ranging impact.
Chen Jiequn, chairman of Chinese company Leiming Technology, still recalls one family's reaction when workers fitted a solar system to their home in rural West Africa: five children stared wide-eyed at bulbs hanging from the rafters, as light flooded their thatched hut for the first time.
Since 2016, backed by the World Bank and the United Nations Development Programme, the firm has rolled out off-grid solar schemes across Africa, bringing power to about 13 million people.
"Seeing lights dispel the darkness gives us a strong sense of fulfillment, when our products are used in local homes, schools, and hospitals," Chen said.
China-Africa green energy ties have moved beyond simple equipment sales into workforce training.
In Nigeria's Bayelsa State, Hunan Red Solar New Energy Science and Technology Co., Ltd. reworked corrosion-resistant solar hardware and materials to withstand the region's hot, humid, rainy conditions. It trains local staff to run and maintain solar and battery systems and has built up a domestic team for warehousing, technical support and after-sales care.
The effort aligns with the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation Beijing Action Plan (2025-2027). The document urges broader renewable energy cooperation covering solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal and green hydrogen, plus more skills exchanges and training for African professionals, entrepreneurs and community members.
China-backed schemes are turning the plan into realities. In Mali, China Geo-Engineering Corporation's solar demonstration village project has installed more than 1,000 solar power facilities, reaching more than 10,000 residents. At Kenya's Kakuma refugee camp, solar power enables a small cinema that broadcasts football matches.
According to figures released during the China-Africa Economic and Trade Expo in 2025, since the start of China's 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), Chinese power companies had invested a cumulative 272 million U.S. dollars in Africa's power sector. Over the same period, China had carried out about 80 solar, wind and hydropower projects in 28 African countries, including Nigeria, Zambia, Egypt and Ethiopia.
"China-Africa green energy cooperation has not only supported Africa's industrialization but also addressed the everyday needs of ordinary people," said Xiao Hao, executive dean of the Institute of African Studies at Hunan University. ■

Feature: Yasuo Fukuda, a statesman who championed China-Japan friendship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:27:01 CST
18:27:01 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who had long been committed to the China-Japan friendship, died of heart failure at a hospital in Tokyo on Oct. 22. He was 90.
Fukuda came from a prominent political family. He and his father, Takeo Fukuda, remain the only father and son to have both served as prime minister of Japan since 1885.
A longtime friend of the Chinese people, Fukuda made positive contributions to improving and developing China-Japan relations.
FROM OIL COMPANY EMPLOYEE TO PRIME MINISTER
Born in 1936, Fukuda graduated from Japan's Waseda University in 1959 and went on to work for an oil company for 17 years, an experience that gradually shaped his steady, cautious, and even-tempered character.
Fukuda originally had no plans to enter politics. But when his younger brother, seen as the family's political heir, fell ill, Fukuda, as the eldest son, took on the role.
In November 1976, shortly before his father became prime minister that December, Fukuda left the oil company to work as his father's secretary, a job he held for 13 years.
Fukuda was first elected to the House of Representatives in 1990 at the age of 53, taking over his father's former seat. Between 2000 and 2004, he served as chief cabinet secretary for three and a half years under then Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori and his successor Junichiro Koizumi.
Fukuda became prime minister in September 2007. He was 71, the same age at which his father had taken the post.
A year later, in September 2008, Fukuda abruptly announced his resignation at a time when his government was struggling to function in a divided parliament, with the opposition in control of the upper house. In 2012, he retired from politics.
COMMITTED TO CHINA-JAPAN FRIENDSHIP
Fukuda championed sound, long-term ties between China and Japan.
Of the four political documents China and Japan have signed since normalizing diplomatic relations in 1972, two are closely related to Fukuda and his father.
On Oct. 23, 1978, Takeo Fukuda, then prime minister of Japan, and Deng Xiaoping, then Chinese leader, attended the ceremony for the exchange of instruments of ratification of the 1978 Treaty of Peace and Friendship between China and Japan, bringing the treaty into force. Yasuo Fukuda, serving as his father's secretary at the time, was also present and witnessed the ceremony.
During Yasuo Fukuda's tenure as prime minister, the two countries issued the China-Japan Joint Statement on All-round Promotion of Strategic Relationship of Mutual Benefit in 2008.
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular press briefing on Monday that China expresses deep condolences over the passing of Fukuda, and offers sincere sympathies to his family.
Noting that Fukuda was an old friend of China who had made positive contributions to improving and developing China-Japan relations, Guo recalled that Fukuda once said the four political documents between China and Japan set out the principles governing bilateral relations, which must always be borne in mind, with no backtracking on these principles.
Those firm and important remarks reflected the honor and responsibility of Japan's statesmen of the older generation and should evoke self-reflection and soul-searching among those currently running the Japanese government, the spokesperson said.
In an interview with Xinhua in 2023, Fukuda said: "Geographically, Japan and China are neighbors and have very close cultural ties. Both sides must abide by the spirit of the political documents and avoid conflict in the future. This is the mission of both Japan and China."
On historical issues, Fukuda believed that visits to the Yasukuni Shrine by Japanese prime ministers did Japan itself no good, saying there was "no need to do things that offend the other side," referring to China and South Korea. Because he did not visit the shrine while in office, Fukuda was labeled "pro-China" by Japan's right-wing conservatives.
In his later years, Fukuda remained committed to China-Japan friendship. As chairman of the Boao Forum for Asia from 2010 to 2018, he witnessed China's continued opening up and rapid economic growth. He supported the China-proposed vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, and led the founding of the Japan Asian Community Culture Cooperation Organization.
In June 2018, Fukuda paid a visit to the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders in Nanjing, capital of east China's Jiangsu Province. There, he laid a wreath for the victims and wrote in calligraphy the Chinese characters "he ping dong ya," meaning "peace in East Asia." ■

Injuries reported after two trains collide in Spain

At least 10 killed after two trains collide in Spain, authorities say
High-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars, authorities said.
Two trains have crashed in central Spain, derailing two cars and killing at least 10 people, authorities said.
The crash occurred early on Wednesday near Urda, in Toledo province, south of Madrid, on a railway line connecting the capital with the southern city of Seville.
Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told Spanish public broadcaster TVE that at least 10 people died and said the death toll would “surely rise”.
Padilla said the trains had been travelling in the same direction when one struck the rear of the other, which was stationary, causing two carriages to derail.
The collision involved an AVE high-speed train operated by Spain’s state railway company Renfe, travelling from Madrid to Seville, and another operated by private rail company Iryo.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the Renfe train and 147 passengers in the Iryo train.
Two carriages of the Iryo train fell down an embankment, according to emergency service sources cited by Spanish newspaper El Pais.
The mayor of nearby Urda, Manuel Galan, told TVE that civil protection authorities had asked the town to prepare a sports pavilion to accommodate those affected.
Firefighters from surrounding towns were deployed alongside three medical helicopters and two mobile intensive care units, according to Spanish newspaper El Mundo.
Madrid’s mayor, Jose Luis Martínez-Almeida, said on X that the capital was also sending emergency medical teams and firefighters to assist with rescue efforts.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on X on Wednesday that he was shocked by the incident and remained in contact with Transport Minister Oscar Puente and Castilla-La Mancha’s regional president, Emiliano Garcia-Page, as emergency crews worked at the scene.
Spain’s railway infrastructure operator, ADIF, suspended high-speed rail services between Madrid and the southern region of Andalusia, while the Civil Guard sent a specialist disaster investigation team to the site, El Pais reported.
The cause of the collision remained unclear.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on X on Wednesday that Italy’s consulate in Madrid was checking whether any Italian nationals were among those affected by the collision and was ready to provide assistance.
The disaster comes nine months after a train derailed and struck an oncoming service in southern Spain, killing 45 people.
That crash, near the town of Adamuz, was Spain’s deadliest railway accident since 2013, when 80 people were killed.

Russia showcases submarine-launched ballistic missile (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:26:42 UTC
18:26:42 KST

Russia showcases submarine-launched ballistic missile (VIDEO)
A Russian nuclear-powered submarine has successfully test-fired an intercontinental ballistic missile, hitting a target around 6,000 km away on the other side of the country, the Defense Ministry announced on Wednesday.
The Bulava missile was launched from a submerged position by the Generalissimus Suvorov strategic missile submarine in the Far Eastern Sea of Okhotsk, near the Kamchatka Peninsula, as part of a scheduled combat training exercise.
The missile’s warheads reached the designated Chizha test range on the Kanin Peninsula in Russia’s Arkhangelsk Region, 5,500-6,000 km from the launch area. The ministry said monitoring data confirmed that the warheads arrived at their target area on schedule, declaring the exercise a success.
The ministry also released dramatic footage of the launch. The video shows the submarine cruising at sea before cutting to crew members operating control systems inside the vessel. A close-up captures the press of a launch button, followed by a nighttime shot of a blazing missile erupting from the water and streaking skyward.
The R-30 Bulava (NATO designation SS-N-32) is a submarine-launched ballistic missile designed to serve as one of the mainstays of Russia’s sea-based nuclear deterrent. Developed by the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology and officially adopted into service in May 2024, the solid-fuel missile has a reported maximum range of around 9,300 km.
Weighing approximately 37 tons, the Bulava is designed to carry multiple independently targetable nuclear warheads. It also incorporates measures intended to help it penetrate missile defenses, including a relatively short boost phase and maneuverable reentry vehicles.
The Generalissimus Suvorov is a fourth-generation Project 955A Borei-A nuclear-powered submarine assigned to Russia’s Pacific Fleet and based in Kamchatka. Built at the Sevmash shipyard, the vessel can carry up to 16 Bulava ballistic missiles, alongside torpedo armaments.
The Borei and upgraded Borei-A submarines form a key component of Russia’s strategic nuclear modernization program, replacing aging Soviet-era missile carriers. Russia currently operates eight submarines of the two classes, with additional vessels under construction.
Wednesday’s launch was intended to test the crew’s combat readiness and the submarine’s missile systems, according to the Defense Ministry.

"Dead Poets Society" sells out eight consecutive months at Teatro da Trindade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:26:10 UTC
18:26:10 KST

The stage version of the film that captivated generations is sold out at Teatro da Trindade until the end of the year, before touring nationwide.
Everyone who has seen Dead Poets Society has carried a little of it away with them. Released in 1989, it is one of those rare films capable of spanning generations like few others, and certainly one of the most beloved of all time.
The character of teacher John Keating, immortalised on the big screen by Robin Williams, has now moved to the stage in a performance by Diogo Infante that is drawing thousands of fans to Teatro da Trindade in Lisbon, where one sold-out show follows another.
Premiered in April, the production was initially meant to close in August, but its success has already forced two extensions. It is now scheduled to run until the end of the year, yet getting a ticket is impossible: every performance is already sold out.
At the start of 2027, the play will go on tour around the country and may later return to Lisbon.
What explains this success? The film left many viewers with a nostalgic feeling: "We see grandparents bringing grandchildren who have never seen the film, parents who saw the film with their children, now bringing them to show them this," says director Hélder Gamboa, of Tenda Produções, who is staging the play in partnership with Teatro da Trindade.
Gamboa adds that the script and the cast, headed by veterans Diogo Infante and Virgílio Castelo, are also key to attracting audiences: "This is a text we were needing at this moment. It is a text that gives us hope, that makes us want to be more than someone who simply belongs to a flock, that makes us want to have wings, to want to fly and to want to be ourselves," he says.
The play is a stage adaptation of the film's screenplay, written for the theatre by the screenwriter himself, Tom Schulman, who at the time was honoured for it.
Diogo Infante and the "legacy" of Robin Williams
Diogo Infante is one of Portugal's most highly regarded actors and also the artistic director of Teatro da Trindade, and he was instrumental in bringing the play to this stage.
As for the task of playing Keating, he knows it means taking on the responsibility of dealing with the memory of Robin Williams, one of the American actors most admired by audiences, who took his own life in 2014 at the age of 63.
"It is a challenge, on the one hand, because I have to, in some way, deal with the memory of Robin Williams's unforgettable performance, but on the other hand it is a profound pleasure, because it is an exceptionally well-written text, of great relevance today, which allows me, five nights a week, to speak words that are inspiring and motivating. Working with this young cast is truly refreshing, so it has been a pleasure," Infante tells Euronews.
After a full eight months of performances in Lisbon, five days a week, the play will go on tour around the country from January 2027 (source in Portuguese) (including 16 performances at Teatro Sá da Bandeira in Porto, already completely sold out) and may later return to Lisbon.
So many performances of the same text - does that become tiring for an actor? Infante is adamant: "Working in a tax office for 25 years, from nine to five, that is what is tiring. I have the privilege of working in the arts, I work in theatre, I work with emotions and passion, with full houses. That is a privilege I embrace every day. If there are days when I am more tired or less inspired, I take a deep breath and go on, because it is my duty," he says.
Diogo Infante as John Keating and Virgílio Castelo as the school's headmaster, the stern and feared Gale Nolan, lead a cast that also includes Diogo Mesquita as Mr Perry and a group of eight young actors recruited from various drama schools.
The film launched the careers of actors such as Ethan Hawke and Robert Sean Leonard, who played Professor Keating's students. This Portuguese stage version also promises to launch these young talents.
At 23, Rui Pedro Silva plays Neil Perry, the student passionate about theatre whose fate, in the story, changes the lives of his teacher and classmates forever.
Rui Pedro already knew the film, but chose not to watch it again so as not to constrain his interpretation of the character: "I wanted to distance myself from the way the story was told at the time, but it is a film that has remained very vivid in my mind and that was very important for my development as an actor, as a person and as a teenager," he tells Euronews.
The young actor sees himself in the character and says he is not the only one in the cast to feel that way: "Each of us was also chosen because of the characteristics we share with our characters. I am very much a dreamer, very sensitive; I think I am a little like Neil," he admits.
Dead Poets Society is on at Teatro da Trindade until 20 December.

Zagreb is celebrating the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:25:50 CET

To commemorate the eighth centenary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi, the Italian Embassy in Croatia organized the conference “The Relevance of St. Francis: From Coexistence to Communion and Fraternity” in Zagreb, in collaboration with the Croatian Catholic University, which hosted the event, and the Apostolic Nunciature. The conference was followed by a concert by the Ensemble Micrologus—Giullari di Dio, organized by the Italian Cultural Institute, which offered a musical journey dedicated to the Canticle of the Creatures and the ancient melodies of the Italian lauda tradition. The conference proceedings were opened by the Italian Ambassador to Croatia, Paolo Trichilo; by Monsignor Marco Malizia, ecclesiastical advisor to the Vice President of the Council of Ministers and Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Antonio Tajani; by the Apostolic Nuncio, Monsignor Leopoldo Girelli; and by the rector of the Catholic University of Croatia, Željko Tanjić. Fra Lorenzo Turchi of the Pontifical Antonianum University in Rome served as a speaker, engaging in a discussion with two Croatian professors from the universities of Split and Zagreb—both members of the Franciscan Order— on the Christian experience of St. Francis and how it can offer criteria for discernment in understanding certain dynamics of the present. The event drew a large audience and was attended by several civil and religious authorities, including Cardinal Emeritus of Zagreb Josip Bozanić, Ivan Mašina, advisor to the Croatian Minister of Foreign Affairs; and, representing the Ministry of Culture, Šime Jerčić, Director General of the Office of the Commission for Relations with Religious Communities. In his opening remarks, Ambassador Trichilo highlighted the attention given to St. Francis by Italian institutions and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as evidenced by the establishment of the national holiday on October 4 and the organization of dedicated events by the diplomatic corps. St. Francis, the ambassador emphasized, is a pivotal historical figure for Italian, European, and universal spirituality and culture. His message continues to be a source of inspiration that challenges us to reflect on the future and offers spiritual and ethical guidance for navigating the modern world. He then highlighted how the initiative takes on particular significance in Croatia, given the country’s Catholic tradition. Bishop Malizia conveyed greetings from Minister Tajani, expressing the minister’s satisfaction that the diplomatic network had accepted the invitation to promote initiatives on St. Francis and to focus on a spiritual and human witness capable of speaking to peoples, cultures, and traditions, and to contribute to the promotion of dialogue, peace, and fraternity. He also noted that Italy considers intercultural and interreligious dialogue an essential component of its international vision, emphasizing the important role played by cultural institutions, religious communities, and diplomacy—all united by the responsibility to safeguard peace through mutual understanding, respect, and cooperation. Bishop Malizia then expressed his appreciation for the conference, which represents not only a tribute to St. Francis but also a concrete opportunity to rediscover what unites us and to promote a culture of listening, solidarity, and peace.
