Russia test-fires Bulava from one of its newest missile submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:10:19 UTC
18:10:19 KST

- Russia’s Generalissimo Suvorov submarine fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- The missile was launched from underwater toward the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, and the Pacific Fleet said its warheads arrived on schedule.
The Russian Pacific Fleet’s ballistic missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from beneath the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, sending it across the country to the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The ministry said the launch was carried out from a submerged position as part of the crew’s planned combat training, and the Pacific Fleet said that, according to tracking data, the missile’s warheads arrived in the designated area at the planned time. The flight path took the missile from Russia’s Far East to the far north of its European territory, a route the Pacific Fleet uses to test the readiness of its strategic submarines.
“The crew of the Project 955A Borei-A class strategic nuclear-powered missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov of the Pacific Fleet, in accordance with the combat training plan, test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile aimed at the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region,” the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The K-553 Generalissimo Suvorov is one of Russia’s newest strategic submarines and the third of the upgraded Borei-A class, a fourth-generation design from the Rubin Central Design Bureau in St. Petersburg. The Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk laid it down on Dec. 26, 2014, and the Russian Navy commissioned it on Dec. 29, 2022. Before entering service, the submarine fired a Bulava from the White Sea on Nov. 3, 2022, with the warheads striking the Kura test range on the Kamchatka Peninsula, the opposite direction to this week’s flight.
In 2023, the submarine sailed from the Northern Fleet to the Pacific along the Northern Sea Route and arrived at its permanent base in Vilyuchinsk on Kamchatka on Oct. 16, 2023, where it joined the 25th submarine division. TASS reported that the boat’s imported components have been replaced with Russian-made equipment.
Each Borei-class submarine carries 16 Bulava missiles. The Bulava is a solid-fuel missile developed by the Moscow Institute of Thermal Engineering, the design bureau behind the Topol-M and Yars land-based missiles, and it is launched from underwater so the submarine does not have to surface and reveal its position. Each missile can carry multiple nuclear warheads that separate and fly to individual targets, and the Barents Observer has reported that each Bulava carries six. Russia formally accepted the missile into service in May 2024 after years of testing that began with a first launch in 2005.
The Sea of Okhotsk-to-Chizha route has been used before by Pacific Fleet submarines. In December 2020, the Borei-class Vladimir Monomakh fired a salvo of four Bulava missiles from the same sea toward the same range in the Arkhangelsk region, the first time a Borei had launched four missiles in a single salvo.
Russia’s Borei and Borei-A submarines are replacing the Soviet-era Delta-class boats that carried the naval leg of Russia’s nuclear deterrent for decades, with the Generalissimo Suvorov and its sister ships forming the core of the Pacific Fleet’s strategic submarine force at Kamchatka.

Another cargo ship involved in transporting military equipment has been spotted at the Russian naval base in Baltiysk, Kaliningrad region.
OSINT analysts GeoInsider and SONARROW reported this after examining satellite imagery of the Russian port.
In the image dated October 23, researchers identified the vessel LADY R (IMO 9161003) moored at the pier. A concentration of armored and logistics vehicles prepared for loading was spotted nearby.
This is the fourth vessel analysts have linked to a large-scale military equipment transport operation through Baltiysk. Earlier, on October 15–16, three other Russian dry cargo ships were observed loading equipment at the base.
These vessels are ASCALON (IMO 9198226), LADY D (IMO 9349289) and ANASTASIIA (IMO 9349291). They likely carried infantry fighting vehicles, armored personnel carriers, MRAP armored vehicles, etc.
At the time, analysts suspected additional vessels were in the port, but dense cloud cover prevented them from confirming it through satellite imagery.
Russia may be preparing one of its largest military cargo convoys. However, it remains unclear whether all four vessels will depart together and where they will deliver the equipment.
As Militarnyi previously reported, ASCALON, LADY D and ANASTASIIA have already transported Russian military cargo abroad. The latter vessel was spotted in Libya in September.
At the time, a Russian convoy comprising the cargo ships ANASTASIIA and YURIY ARSHENEVSKIY arrived at the Libyan port of Tobruk. The Project 775 landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin escorted them.
An August 11, 2026, Africa Defense Forum report said Moscow was developing infrastructure at six Libyan airbases: Al-Jufra, Al-Khadim, Al-Qardabiyah, Brak al-Shati, Maaten al-Sarra, and Tamanhint.
Russia is funding construction work at these sites and providing personnel to develop the facilities. The bases host Russian military personnel and mercenaries, air defense systems, MiG-29 fighter jets, and drones.
Russia uses infrastructure in Libya to support its presence in Africa. In particular, the port of Tobruk and local airbases serve as logistical hubs for transporting weapons and personnel. However, there is currently no confirmation that the current cargo from Baltiysk is destined for Libya.

Chinese expert points to Japan’s ability to produce thousands of nuclear warheads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:07:12 UTC
18:07:12 KST

BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan possesses more than 40 metric tons of plutonium, theoretically enough to produce several thousand nuclear warheads, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He pointed out that according to the Japanese authorities, the country possessed 44.4 tons of separated plutonium at the end of 2024, including 8.6 tons stored domestically and 35.8 tons held overseas. In addition, Japan’s stocks of spent nuclear fuel contain about 191 tons of unseparated plutonium.
"The latest report from the Japan Atomic Energy Commission, published in August 2026, says that the total amount of separated plutonium remained at about 44.4 tons at the end of 2025, with 9.9 tons stored in the country and about 34.5 tons held abroad, as the size of the stocks remained vast," Dai said.
"What does this mean? Making a simple nuclear warhead typically requires only a few kilograms of weapons-grade plutonium. According to open sources, Japan’s 44.4 tons of separated plutonium would be enough to manufacture several thousand nuclear warheads," the expert pointed out.
Dai also said that the Japanese authorities justified the country’s substantial plutonium stockpiles by citing plans to use the material as fuel for nuclear power plants. However, this remains a cause for concern amid statements by some Japanese politicians advocating the acquisition of nuclear weapons, the expert added.
"Although most of Japan’s plutonium is reactor-grade, it’s not entirely impossible to use it in nuclear devices. Notably, Japan has the technology and processing facilities needed to separate weapons-grade plutonium, making the distinction between civilian and military use extremely blurred," the expert concluded.

Chinese expert says it would take Japan only a few dozen days to develop nuclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:07:04 UTC
18:07:04 KST

BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan could develop a nuclear explosive device in a matter of weeks if its government decided to pursue nuclear weapons, according to Dai Huaicheng, Secretary-General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA). Speaking to TASS, Dai said Japan’s advanced industrial base and existing plutonium stockpiles could allow it to achieve this far more quickly than other countries. "From a technical and material standpoint, Japan is already on the ‘nuclear threshold’ when it comes to overcoming the hurdles involved in producing even a single nuclear explosive device. As one American expert aptly put it, Japan ‘only needs to turn a screwdriver’ to acquire nuclear weapons," Dai said.
"Based on statements by various Japanese officials and analyses by both domestic and foreign experts, Japan could theoretically produce a nuclear explosive device in a very short time if it chose to take that risk. Some estimates suggest the process could take just over 100 days - or perhaps even as little as a few dozen days," he added.
"On the other hand, from a technical standpoint, creating a full-scale nuclear arsenal requires completing stages such as weaponization, testing, and systems integration. However, the international community must remain on guard: Japan possesses long-standing stockpiles of nuclear materials, technologies, and delivery systems, meaning the time it would take for the country to complete this process would be significantly shorter than for other nations," the expert noted.
"This is precisely why the misguided statements and actions of the Japanese authorities in the nuclear realm pose a particular danger: they are attempting to remove the final political and legal barrier preventing Japan from crossing the 'nuclear threshold’," Dai concluded.

Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 28 that the first 30 hours of the ceasefire in the town of Oleshky had passed "without a single incident," while Russian attacks killed two people and injured 17 others in other regions of Ukraine over the past day, according to local authorities.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
The ceasefire, which took effect in the early hours of Oct. 27 and is set to last until Nov. 1, initially covered Oleshky and surrounding areas in Kherson Oblast. It is intended to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of humanitarian aid over the coming days.
At the same time, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump announced on Oct. 27 that the ceasefire had taken effect across the entire region.
Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said no strikes against critical or civilian infrastructure were reported in the region over the past day. The governor added that four people who had suffered injuries in "previous days" had sought medical care.
Pavlo Drohal, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Navy's Marine Corps, also confirmed that Ukrainian and Russian forces were observing the ceasefire as of 8 a.m. local time.
Meanwhile, Russia continued to attack other regions of Ukraine. Russian forces launched an Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missile and 88 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine, including 38 jet-powered drones, overnight on Oct. 28. Russia also used a low-cost S8000 Banderol/Dan-T cruise missile and decoy drones in the attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 71 drones, 31 of which were jet-powered.
Russian weapons struck targets at eight locations, while falling debris was reported at two others. The Air Force did not specify whether the strikes were caused by drones or the ballistic missile.
In southeastern Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, a Russian strike on the Synelnykove district killed one person and injured another, while three people were injured in the city of Dnipro on Oct. 27, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured three others over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks injured two men and two women in the regional capital of Kharkiv. Two more people were injured in other settlements across the region over the past day, the local military administration said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were injured in Russian attacks on the Zaporizhzhia District, according to the local military administration.
In northern Sumy Oblast, drone strikes injured a 51-year-old man in the Sumy community and a 43-year-old man in the Bilopillia community, the local military administration said.

Cultural Endowment chief: Casino tax break hopes based on a 'fiction'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:03:00 UTC
18:03:00 KST

Cultural Endowment chief: Casino tax break hopes based on a 'fiction'
Hopes behind Estonia's online casino tax cut were based on fiction, Cultural Endowment (Kultuurikapital) head Margus Allikmaa said.
Allikmaa told "Esimene stuudio" that information from casino operators was taken on trust more than the Finance Ministry's was, while every day at the lower rate costs culture and the Estonian state as a whole. He has called for the rate to return to its original 7 percent.
The cut, passed last December, is reducing the rate from 6 percent to 4 percent in increments by 2029. However, a hoped-for surge in casino license applications in Estonia which would have offset the tax break has not materialized.
Receipts fell 9.7 percent in the first seven months of 2026, and the Cultural Endowment expects a €6–7 million shortfall next year.
"If we now try to analyze this situation with hindsight, the intention was certainly very good. Estonia needed a large arena, and money was needed to build it. Most likely, in some way, information reached the casino operators that if the tax rate were significantly reduced, a lot of money would come in. And apparently this was seen as one possible solution, one possible way to finance this large arena. And on the strength of that belief, all these decisions were pushed through, even though, when the issue first came up, there were already quite a lot of warning signs that things might not turn out that way," Allikmaa said.
According to Allikmaa, it is very difficult to comment on why information from overseas casino operators came to be trusted more than information from Estonia's own Ministry of Finance.
Allikmaa expressed hope that the legislation will be reversed. "Every day that we continue with this low tax rate, we are losing money, and both the state budget and, in fact, the Cultural Endowment are losing out, because the Cultural Endowment receives 47.8 percent of this revenue. And for every cent less that comes in, half a cent less also goes to the Cultural Endowment. So it would be sensible to first halt the tax reduction now, so that next year there would not be another 0.5 percentage point reduction, but we would initially remain at the current 5.5 percent."
He added the rate could be kept unchanged without applying the six-month notice period, because the tax environment would not change. "And perhaps after that, either in six-month or annual steps, we should still return to the tax rate that was envisaged in the 2023 state budget strategy for the years 2024 to 2027," Allimaa said.
"In 2025, taxable turnover, according to gambling operators' data, or more precisely, according to the Estonian Gaming Association, was €450 million. This is, so to speak, the money wagered by players minus winnings, and what remains is then taxed. And if that was €450 million, then one percentage point is €4.5 million. And from here, everyone can calculate for themselves whether we give up this additional percentage point, or €4.5 million. And if it eventually reaches four percent, then we will have simply taken €10 million or more out of the state budget. Or we raise it back to seven percent and bring that money into the state budget and to culture and sports," he continued.
Regarding Eesti 200 and its MP Tanel Tein, who championed the cut, Allikmaa said they could concede their mistake.
"That's how life is sometimes: things occasionally go wrong, and sometimes you do something and it just doesn't work out. Generally speaking, I respect all these people, and they are intelligent people. An intelligent person admits their mistakes and rectifies them. I think by now everyone has realized that this did not turn out particularly well and that those expectations and hopes were based on some sort of fiction. And I very much hope that this mistake will be corrected," Allikmaa, who was ERR board chair 2007-2017, concluded.
Despite the cut, only two new license applications followed, one of them refused. The tax break applies to online casino operators whose customers are in other countries, rather than those aiming to enter the Estonian market. Such operators usually obtain gaming licenses from various jurisdictions which issue them including Malta and the Isle of Man.
The Cultural Endowment funds major culture related projects which in recent years have included the National Library renovations and the new ERR TV house. Gambling tax revenues including on operators serving customers in Estonia are a major source for cultural funding. Sport also falls under culture's remit, and a new national sports arena is planned for either Tallinn, Tartu or Pärnu.

Six out of 10 companies operating in Belgium’s nuclear sector are postponing investments due to uncertainty over the country’s energy policy, according to a survey by technology federation Agoria cited by broadcaster VRT on Wednesday.
The companies are calling on the government to provide a clear and predictable energy strategy, including concrete decisions and timelines for future nuclear projects.
Belgium has been moving toward a nuclear phase-out over the past two decades.
However, the nuclear sector continues to account for more than 8,000 full-time jobs and generate over €9 billion ($9.9 billion) in annual turnover.
Agoria said the sector has significant growth potential but needs clarity from the government on its nuclear ambitions.
“We need clear decisions and a concrete schedule for nuclear projects so that companies can prepare for the future,” Agoria CEO Bart Steukers said.
He stressed that businesses remain uncertain about which types of nuclear facilities the government intends to develop, where they would be built and when construction could begin.
“It is currently completely unclear what is going to happen and when,” he said.
Steukers said the government should clarify whether it plans to build large-scale nuclear power plants or small modular reactors (SMRs), as well as specify locations, timelines and regulatory conditions.
Agoria estimates that a clear and predictable policy could generate an additional €3 billion ($3.3 billion) in turnover and create 500 new jobs in the sector within two years.

Atlas drops seven hundred paratroopers into Germany
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:25 GMT
18:00:25 KST

Around seven hundred paratroopers have been dropped onto a German drop zone from four Atlas C1 transports across multiple waves, bringing back battlegroup-level airborne insertion using the aircraft for the first time, according to the Royal Air Force.
Exercise Rhino Titan brought together the RAF Air Mobility Force and 16 Air Assault Brigade Combat Team as a Joint Airborne Task Force, with British, French and German troops taking part. Airborne operations have long been part of British military capability, and the difference here lies in the scale and in soldiers travelling with their stores in the same aircraft.
Squadron Leader Luke, a flight commander on 30 Squadron and the airborne mission commander, said: “Rhino Titan demonstrates the return of large-scale airborne insertion as a capability. The Atlas allows us to deploy combat forces further, faster and more efficiently than previous generations of aircraft, giving Defence the ability to project force rapidly wherever it is required.”
Stores previously needed aircraft of their own, so carrying personnel and equipment together generates more combat power from the same number of airframes, and lets troops become operational almost immediately on landing. Paratroopers board carrying parachute equipment, weapons, communications systems and bergen loads of up to fifty kilograms, with air loadmasters and parachute jump instructors supervising the process before departure.
Squadron Leader Nick, officer commanding the Parachute Training Squadron at RAF Brize Norton, said: “By the time soldiers board the aircraft, a significant amount of planning and preparation has already taken place. Parachute Jump Instructors will have delivered specialist ground training, while detailed planning between aircrew, dispatchers and ground forces coordinates every aspect of the mission.”
He added: “It takes RAF aircrew, engineers, Air Loadmasters, Parachute Jump Instructors and support personnel working alongside the Army to deliver that capability safely and effectively.”
Getting to this point took eighteen months of increased activity between Brize Norton, Weston-on-the-Green and Salisbury Plain, progressing from basic parachuting serials through formation flying and simulated mass drops to integrated delivery of personnel and stores. Aircraft, crews and instructors had to be dedicated to that training while global operational commitments continued.
Squadron Leader Luke said: “The harder we train in exercises, the easier it is to deliver the capability when it’s needed.”
Pathfinders went in ahead of the main force to validate the drop zone and provide reconnaissance and surveillance before the larger force arrived. The RAF said the exercise builds on work done with NATO allies through activities such as Exercise Falcon Leap, where Atlas operators and other tactical airlift nations develop common tactics and procedures, and that dropping troops by parachute lets forces deploy beyond established infrastructure.
The A400M Atlas entered RAF service in 2014 and operates from Brize Norton with 24, 30, 70 and 206 Squadrons. The type will also be fitted for firefighting under the package the government announced last week, which is to give Britain an aerial firefighting capability permanently based in the United Kingdom for the first time.

Yvette Cooper drops plans to abolish NHS patient champion after outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:02 UTC
18:00:02 KST

Yvette Cooper has abandoned plans to abolish the NHS’s independent patient champion after an outcry from MPs across the political spectrum.
The health secretary has decided to keep and extend the role of Healthwatch England, which was due to be axed as part of the government’s reorganisation of the health service in England.
The move is the latest in a series of U-turns by ministers on core elements of the health bill since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.
Sources at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) said her decision to retain and strengthen Healthwatch and its network of branches illustrated her strong belief – which Burnham shares – in public and local accountability.
The rethink means Healthwatch England and its 150 branches will continue to collect and analyse feedback from patients about their experiences of the NHS and where its services need to improve. Its many supporters in parliament say the statutory body helps to identify areas where NHS care is lagging behind patient needs and hold the service to account.
Cooper told the Guardian: “Patients need a voice in our NHS. I’ve always been clear on the importance of people and communities having a say in local services and that’s why I said I would review all reforms in this area.
“We will retain Healthwatch England and Local Healthwatch, while strengthening them to ensure patient voices are heard and can influence real change across health and care services.”
Gillian Merron, the health minister in the Lords, will confirm the change of plan when peers debate the health bill . Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parliamentarians had criticised the planned abolition.
Healthwatch has gained respect for publishing reports highlighting issues such as declining patient access to NHS-funded dental treatment and years-long waiting times for ADHD assessments. It has also exposed flaws in the way the service communicates with patients, for example telling some of them about appointments after the date has already passed.
Cooper reprieved Healthwatch after MPs and peers from all sides in parliament raised serious concern that scrapping it would mean the loss of important oversight of the NHS.
Thea Stein, the chief executive of the Nuffield Trust thinktank and a former head of an NHS trust in Leeds, said: “Abolishing Healthwatch would have thrown away the independence that gave it credibility, without doing anything to address the reasons the NHS often don’t listen.
“It was the wrong solution to a real problem. Healthwatch has played a valuable role in making it more difficult for the NHS to ignore patients’ often frustrating experience of using it.”
Until now, the government had planned to transfer Healthwatch’s functions into NHS regional integrated care boards (ICBs) and local councils. But Healthwatch will now play a greater role in identifying recurring concerns and highlighting where action is needed to improve quality, safety and patient experience.
The Local Government Association had warned that abolishing Healthwatch “risks [NHS] organisations being seen to mark their own homework” and could create “confusion” for patients.
Other recent government climbdowns on the health bill include ministers dropping plans to:
- axe the Health Services Safety Investigations Body.
- end councils’ automatic representation on the boards of ICBs.
- remove the requirement for a nurse on every NHS foundation trust board.
The U-turns show Cooper is closely examining the legacy bequeathed to her by her predecessor, Wes Streeting, and tearing up elements of the bill she thinks are misguided.
Stein said: “This retreat needs to be followed by a cultural shift away from a health service where patients’ voices are all too often at the bottom of a long and impossible list.”

US and China share a love of "new things and innovation" says Ma Yansong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

US and China share a love of “new things and innovation” says Ma Yansong
Chinese architect Ma Yansong has completed one of the highest-profile US buildings of 2026 – the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, in California. In this interview, he explains his architecture’s international appeal as a “bridge between imagination and reality”.
Speaking over video call on the occasion of the Lucas Museum’s opening, Ma told Dezeen that the building has acted as a stable point in a rapidly changing world, with trade wars, AI races and a US federal government that has enshrined classical architecture as a national norm.
“This project took 12 years, across two countries, and the world changed around it. The building didn’t,” he said.
The long-anticipated project, funded by Star Wars creator George Lucas, was first planned for San Francisco, then Chicago, before landing in Los Angeles.
“What made it possible is that George and I come from different roots, but both love the same kind of thing – stories that belong to ordinary people, not to high culture,” said Ma.
Ma believes this shared tendency toward exploration between himself and the American filmmaker applies more widely, and the 51-year-old architect spoke positively about the potential for architecture to illuminate the similarities between China and the United States.
“I see a lot in common between the two countries,” he said. “They both like innovation and new things, and they focus on young people, on education.”
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality”
His own life mirrors this outlook. Attracted by innovation as a youth in Beijing, he travelled to Yale, where he graduated with a master’s degree in 2002.
At Yale, Ma became interested in Zaha Hadid’s parametric architecture and eventually worked at her firm in London.
Despite teaching and working mostly in the United States and Europe, Hadid cultivated her signature parametric style working in China’s early 2000s building boom.
The completion of the Lucas Museum represents a Chinese architect taking these principles abroad, a full-circle moment as Ma moved from the US to the UK, back to China, where he has completed dozens of projects, bringing his honed sensibility to California.
Buildings created in the parametric style, or design based on the specific geometries allowed by computer calculations, have been criticised for their lack of relation to sites, and for being self-referential.
The museum’s curved exterior is covered in thousands of white polymer panels, giving it a futuristic look.
Nevertheless, Ma pushes back on Dezeen’s description of the building as “spaceship-like”. Instead, he compares it to a cloud, as an enduring symbol for the imagination – an aspect of consciousness that the architect hopes is provoked by his buildings.
He worked with landscape studio SLA to design an expansive park to serve as an extension of the museum, and the building itself, according to him, features organic curves. He called the effect of these combined elements “surreal nature” and said he aims to bring the natural into the urban environment.
The suggestion of the surreal also points to his aim of provoking the imagination in his design – something the architect said he shares with Lucas and science fiction storytelling.
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality,” he said, adding that he hopes the Lucas Museum functions like the narrative art that it holds.
“You create a dream. That’s important.”
The relationship between Ma and Lucas developed around the question of narrative art since the filmmaker first tapped the architect for the project in 2014.
Ma had actually referenced a scene from Star Wars in his bulbous 2005 museum for Ordos, though he didn’t advertise the influence in his early meetings with Lucas.
“On the personal level, me and George have very easy communication,” said Ma, who famously wanted to become a science fiction director before his career in architecture.
“[George and I] are always talking about ideas, and he’s always supportive. We were constantly discussing what is narrative art,” he continued, adding that the question has led Ma to ask a question that has helped clarify his own practice – “what is narrative architecture?”
Ma said that the project has allowed him to “kind of achieve my goal as a movie maker”.
“You create a dream,” said Ma. “That’s important.”
“It’s why I like science fiction movies – because you put your imagination on the screen, and when people watch it, they believe in something.”
For Ma, this narrative approach to architecture is about opening up to different perspectives, and like science fiction and fantasy, this bridge to the imagination requires a certain suspension of disbelief.
“I’m not interested in everyone receiving the same message,” he said. “I think good public space lets everyone reflect their own experience or knowledge or thinking and share with other people.”
“So I’ve had to find a balance between abstraction and emotion.”
At the Lucas Museum, this intersection of abstraction and emotion is most evident in the massive open-air dome, where visitors can stand on the ground and look up through the panelled apex at the sky.
The space has almost a cathedral-like quality in its grandeur, but it is without ornament and other traditional figurative elements of storytelling in architecture, such as statues or text.
“The architectural space is a trigger for different people to have their own stories. I think that’s a little different from the classic buildings.”
“When you frame it and bring the light into the space, people start to look up, and they will see this connection between individuals and the universe beyond the building, so I think that’s something narrative to me.”
“I like the future, but not the cold future”
The building was also designed to evoke well-proportioned natural elements and bring nature into the city, literally in the case of the green roofs and surrounding park.
Other projects by Ma’s studio have had similar ambitions, such as the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square and One River North in Denver.
And if his architecture is futuristic, Ma hopes that a greener version of the city is the future it evokes, he said.
“I like the future, but not the cold future,” said Ma. “It’s more important that the building is warm and welcoming.”
Ma hopes that Lucas Museum will be inspiring to people, just as his younger self was inspired by the innovative architecture coming out of Yale when he was starting.
“When people see a building that’s so idealistic, that is pushing the boundary, everyone will be encouraged,” he said.
Dezeen In Depth

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry considers limiting foreign internet traffic for Russian users

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry considers limiting foreign internet traffic for Russian users
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry is discussing a plan to route all traffic from foreign domains through the country’s internet traffic filtering system (TSPU) and limit its volume, Forbes Russia reported. Several sources — including officials at the ministry and people in the IT industry — told the outlet that the measures could be included in a bill overhauling the telecommunications sector.
The ministry is expected to gain the authority to restrict foreign traffic for Russian users once it exceeds a limit that has yet to be set. From an operator’s standpoint, VPN use looks like foreign traffic.
Industry representatives polled by Forbes Russia said determining which traffic is foreign will be difficult. “A Russian website hosted abroad would be classified as foreign, while a server rented in Russia would be classified as domestic,” said a technical expert at RKS Global.
The Digital Development Ministry announced that “these issues are currently being worked out, but it would be premature to say which of them, and in what form, will be included in the final version of the amendments.”
There have been repeated reports that the Digital Development Ministry wants to charge higher fees for foreign traffic.
Demand for VPNs in Russia has surged as authorities block popular social networks, services, and messaging apps. In response, Russian authorities have intensified their fight against means of circumventing the blocks. The budget for the next three years allocates a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering.

Two high-speed trains collide in Spain, at least 10 dead
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:58:10 CET
17:58:10 KST

MADRID, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Two high-speed trains have collided in Spain on the line connecting Madrid to Spain’s southern Andalusia region, rail operator Adif said on Wednesday, killing at least 10 people.
The collision comes nine months after an accident between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators on the same line that killed 46 people.
That crash in January, which occurred after a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz, in Cordoba province, triggered a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
“Traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed rail line has been suspended following a rear-end collision between two trains,” Adif said in a message posted on X on Wednesday.
A Renfe and an Iryo train crashed just after 9 a.m. (0800 GMT), causing two Iryo wagons to derail, a government spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region said, adding that the cause and number of injuries were still being determined.
At least 10 people died in the collision, a regional government source said.
Footage by regional Castilla La Mancha Television showed a derailed train with at least one carriage remaining on an elevated section of track while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.
Rail operator Adif said the incident occurred on the line from Madrid to Seville.
Manuel Galan, mayor of nearby town of Urda, told Cadena SER that emergency services had asked the town council to prepare emergency facilities, including a sports hall, to accommodate passengers and the injured.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s agenda, published on the Spanish government’s website, had been cleared for the day. The opposition People’s Party also cancelled all campaign events, a spokesperson said.
(Reporting by David Latona, Emma Pinedo and Mireia Merino; Editing by Charlie Devereux, Toby Chopra and Alison Williams)

The banker, the basketball star, the cardiologist and the chemist: meet Serbia’s potential new leaders
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:57:40 CET
17:57:40 KST

By Aleksandar Vasovic
BELGRADE, Oct 28 (Reuters) - After a leaderless student-led protest movement swept Serbia’s former President Aleksandar Vucic from power in a historic snap election on Sunday, the country is waiting to hear who it will appoint as prime minister and to other key ministerial positions as it forms a government.
Here are some of the prominent candidates on the students’ list.
FORMER CENTRAL BANK GOVERNOR DEJAN SOSKIC, 59
Dejan Soskic, an economist and professor at the University of Belgrade’s Faculty of Economics, served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012, before resigning in protest at legislative amendments that he argued compromised the institution’s independence. He has for years been a vocal opponent of Vucic’s government.
Soskic, who was an avid biker in his youth but has mellowed into a softly spoken reformer, has frequently criticised the country’s institutional weaknesses under Vucic. In 2021, he said, without offering evidence, that systemic corruption in the Balkan state was more widespread than in neighbouring countries and that it was deterring domestic and foreign direct investment. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party have repeatedly denied accusations of corruption.
Soskic says that prudent public finances will create a stable foundation for a permanent increase in wages and pensions.
Pro-government media have criticised Soskic’s central bank record, accusing him of triggering the depreciation of the dinar during his tenure. Soskic has defended the depreciation as a reflection of the mandatory monetary policies of the time rather than a personal failure.
Nonetheless, during the election campaign, in order to increase export competitiveness, Soskic proposed correcting, or weakening, the exchange rate of the dinar - which is in a managed float against the euro - to make domestic goods cheaper in foreign currencies. An alternative, he suggested, would be to maintain a fixed, stronger exchange rate but lower costs by cutting wages.
CARDIOLOGIST AND PROFESSOR ILIJA SRDANOVIC, 55
Ilija Srdanovic, a practising cardiologist, professor at the University of Novi Sad Faculty of Medicine and a keen cyclist, became the student movement’s lead candidate when the ballot list was finalised in September.
Srdanovic’s transition to frontline politics began during the student-led anti-corruption demonstrations, where he frequently appeared as a public speaker. The physician participated in the movement’s “Guardians of the Constitution” bicycle tour across the northern Vojvodina province.
Srdanovic campaigned with the promise of a decentralised health system “at the service of citizens and based on equality for all patients”. In an interview with the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency, Srdanovic said his political objective was building “a better Serbia, nothing else is important”.
He declined an invitation from Vucic to participate in a televised debate during the campaign.
However, some of his policies do not represent a sharp departure from some of Vucic’s. He stressed the Student List position that Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008, remains an integral part of the country. He also said that European Union integration is not a current priority and that the immediate focus for the incoming administration must remain on domestic anti-corruption reforms and national “existential survival”.
FORMER BASKETBALL STAR DEJAN BODIROGA, 53
Dejan Bodiroga, the former captain of the Yugoslav national basketball team and current EuroLeague president, is one of the student movement’s most prominent public speakers.
He described Sunday’s election as a fight “for the return of a country that has been hijacked”.
The step into politics is the latest chapter in a life that has gripped the basketball-mad nation - from capturing back-to-back FIBA World Championship gold medals in 1998 and 2002 and leading the then Yugoslav team to an Olympic silver medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games to entering senior sports administration upon his retirement as a player in 2007 and being appointed as EuroLeague president in 2022.
During the election campaign, Bodiroga appeared at student rallies and took part in open-air folk dancing in rural municipalities. His fans frequently cheered him with a 1990s slogan “We have our God, his name is Bodiroga.”
CHEMISTRY PROFESSOR RADOMIR SAICIC, 64
Radomir Saicic, an organic chemistry professor and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), was the face of the students’ election win on Sunday, taking the podium at their headquarters after Vucic conceded defeat to hail the outcome as a “citizens’ victory”.
He is a specialist in medicinal chemistry whose research focuses on the synthesis of chemotherapy treatments and antiviral therapies, including a special COVID-19 project in collaboration with the Pasteur Institute.
Saicic joined the student-led anti-corruption protests that followed the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad. He became a target for pro-government tabloids after signing a petition with 24 other academics demanding Vucic’s resignation, and in May 2026 he walked out of a SANU gallery exhibition to protest an appearance by Nikola Selakovic, the minister of culture.
During the campaign, he told crowds that Serbia was “occupied from within” and said he was ready to put “even his life” at the disposal of the student movement.
Saicic says Kosovo is a “temporarily occupied territory” and backs energy ties with Russia.
Political analysts and local media have tipped him as a contender in the presidential election which will also be triggered by Vucic’s recent resignation from the post.
(Writing by Aleksandar Vasovic, editing by Kirsten Donovan and Edward McAllister)

Turkish defense giant ASELSAN adds $7.5 billion in orders in one quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:56:16 UTC
17:56:16 KST

- ASELSAN’s order backlog reached a record $30.7 billion after the third quarter of 2026, rising $7.5 billion from the previous quarter.
- Nine-month revenue rose 28% in real terms to 151.5 billion lira, while new export contracts grew 34% to $1.9 billion.
ASELSAN, Türkiye’s largest defense electronics company, ended the third quarter of 2026 with a record order backlog of $30.7 billion, after adding $7.5 billion in a single quarter and passing the $30 billion mark for the first time in its history.
The Ankara-based company reported its results for the first nine months of the year on Oct. 27 in a disclosure to Türkiye’s Public Disclosure Platform. Revenue reached 151.5 billion Turkish lira, up 28% in real terms from the same period of 2025, and new export contracts rose 34% to $1.9 billion. ASELSAN reports in inflation-adjusted lira, a requirement for Turkish listed companies, so the growth figures are measured after accounting for the country’s high inflation.
The backlog figure is the headline number because it shows how much work the company already has under contract and has yet to deliver. ASELSAN said its book-to-bill ratio, which compares the value of new orders signed to the revenue recorded in the same period, rose to 4.4, meaning it booked more than four times as much new business as it billed. The company reached the $30 billion level ahead of its own forecast: in August, when it reported a first-half backlog of $23.2 billion, chief executive Ahmet Akyol said ASELSAN expected to see levels of $30 billion from next year onward. At the end of the first quarter, the backlog stood at $20.7 billion, when the company also posted its strongest quarterly export performance in years.
“2026 is not just a year in which ASELSAN has grown, it is the year we redefined the very scale of our growth,” said ASELSAN CEO Ahmet Akyol.
Air defense, radar and electronic warfare systems led revenue in the period, alongside underwater systems, AI-powered urban security systems, guided munitions, electro-optics and communications equipment. ASELSAN’s recent product launches span much of that portfolio, from a trailer-mounted version of its 35 mm counter-drone turret to the KILIÇ underwater strike system and TUFAN unmanned surface vessel unveiled at SAHA 2026 in Istanbul in May.
Profitability rose with sales. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a common measure of operating profit, climbed 38% to 40.6 billion lira, and the margin improved by 1.9 percentage points to 26.8%. Akyol attributed the gain to the use of artificial intelligence in company processes, digital transformation and a growing share of higher-value products, and said revenue per employee rose 4% in dollar terms.
ASELSAN is spending heavily to turn that backlog into deliveries. Capital investment at its new Oğulbey Technology Base and existing campuses rose 228% to $684 million in nine months, which Akyol said is nearly twice the company’s total capital spending for all of 2025. The first phase of Oğulbey, whose foundation was laid in 2025 and which the company describes as the largest single defense industry investment in the history of the Turkish Republic, came into operation during the period, along with a new Guided Ammunition Systems Production Center and expanded robotics and automation for air, naval and land systems production.
Research and development spending increased 36% to $1.3 billion. ASELSAN said it is directing that money toward low Earth orbit satellites, quantum computing, underwater technologies, high-power microwave systems, microelectronics, and smart munitions and propulsion. The satellite effort, called ASTRALINK, was presented for the first time at the International Space Congress in Antalya.
“ASELSAN which has provided Turkish Armed Forces’ communications on land, at sea and in the air since its founding, will now also provide satellite communication services,” said Akyol.
Operating cash flow reached 23 billion lira, financial liabilities stood at 14% of total assets, and financing expenses fell 10.3% from a year earlier. ASELSAN’s equity ratio was 55%, its return on equity rose 4 percentage points to 16.6%, and its return on assets reached 9%.
ASELSAN has also climbed in international rankings this year. In August it rose three places to 40th in Defense News’ Top 100 list of defense companies and became the first Turkish defense firm included in the Forbes Global 2000.
“Our primary responsibility moving forward is to convert this portfolio into timely deliveries, expanded production capacity, and sustained technological superiority,” said Akyol.

Trump wants Ben-Gvir out of Netanyahu's next government, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:55:33 UTC
17:55:33 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump is closely monitoring Israel's evolving election results and their implications through his aides, as neither of the country's two political blocs appears to have a clear majority to form a government.
Sources close to Trump said the president wants to "make sure" that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu does not include Otzma Yehudit leader Itamar Ben-Gvir in a future government, and likely Religious Zionism leader Bezalel Smotrich as well.
Sources close to Trump say that, as far as the president is concerned, forming a government with Ben-Gvir is not an option. That is also why Trump took credit Wednesday morning for Netanyahu's electoral gains after official results began coming in as votes were counted. In doing so, Trump effectively reminded Netanyahu of the price of their deal, making clear that he has no intention of backing down on his demands.
Why Trump may push for a national unity government
With the election results continuing to come in and neither political bloc appearing to have a clear majority to form a government, the question now is whether Trump will step up his involvement in Israeli politics, after endorsing Netanyahu ahead of the election, and seek to bring about a national unity government that brings together rival political parties.
Under the agreement between Trump and Netanyahu, the two leaders would focus on Iran during the first of Trump's two remaining years in office, seeking to bring a definitive and decisive end to the war that began on February 28 of this year. During Trump's second and final year, Netanyahu may have to step down, perhaps as part of a plea bargain or another arrangement, while efforts to advance the Abraham Accords — which Trump regards as a central part of his legacy — move forward.
But there is a gap between the understandings reached by Netanyahu and Trump and the realities on the ground. Several Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia, have already made clear to the U.S. president that they will not pursue normalization of relations with Israel as long as Netanyahu remains prime minister. Trump may therefore push for a unity government with a rotating premiership to pave the way for expanding the Abraham Accords.
Ahead of Election Day, Trump intervened twice in the Israeli election, endorsing Netanyahu and urging Israelis to vote for him.
The first intervention came Sunday, October 18, when Trump posted on his Truth Social platform, describing Netanyahu as "a great warrior prime minister and an even greater partner for peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
In the same post, Trump addressed the possibility of another military campaign against Iran, saying, "We will soon finish the job." He added: "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so."
Trump's second intervention came Monday, October 26, following pressure from Netanyahu's associates. The president again urged Israelis to vote for Likud and reposted his endorsement of Netanyahu.
Addressing the Israeli public on his social media platform, Trump wrote: "To the people of Israel, to those who haven’t seen it, I am attaching the endorsement I gave one week ago to your prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu."
Trump noted that "as everyone is aware, including the enemy, Bibi and I have had a great relationship in winning together."
He also disparaged Iran, as he frequently does, describing what he claimed was its military and economic collapse, before adding: "When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister! Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!"

French Senate backs bill making protesters pay up to €10,000 for unrest damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:54:16 UTC
17:54:16 KST

Under the proposed law, which would also have to pass in the National Assembly, protesters could be required to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused during demonstrations.
France's Senate approved a bill on Wednesday that would make protesters financially responsible for damage caused during demonstrations.
The Senate passed an expanded version of the bill by 229 votes to 105, backed by a right-wing and centrist alliance which holds a majority.
The legislation now heads to the politically divided National Assembly for debate and a vote.
The bill was introduced following riots that broke out after Paris Saint-Germain defeated Arsenal in the UEFA Champions League final in May.
It has since gained new significance after protests over inequality and rising prices turned violent on 17 October, leaving thousands of businesses damaged or looted.
Speaking in parliament, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez stressed the "urgency" of responding to the damage and scenes of chaos seen on 17 October.
"We can no longer allow the vast majority of our fellow citizens to pay for a minority of vandals," he said.
Critics warn of financial impact on vulnerable families
Critics warn that people who did not personally cause damage could still be held financially responsible if they were found to have knowingly participated in a group formed to commit vandalism.
The bill would also allow welfare benefits and housing assistance to be seized to cover damages, drawing criticism from left-wing lawmakers and human rights groups.
Amnesty International warned that the measures could push "already marginalised families further into poverty".
This is not the first time a European government has implemented tougher security measures in response to violent protests.
In Italy a new security decree introduces tougher penalties for violent protests, including prison sentences of four to 12 years for organising groups involved in violent demonstrations.

"I would like to thank US First Lady Melania Trump once again for supporting the humanitarian mission and helping the residents of Alyoshki. Her personal involvement is crucial to the entire process. A huge thank-you also goes to Melania Trump’s team for their significant efforts in coordinating," the ombudswoman wrote.
Lantratova emphasized that the goal of the humanitarian mission is to assist the residents of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, and to ensure that anyone who wishes to leave the town can do so safely.
On October 23, the White House announced that Russia and Ukraine, with the assistance of Melania Trump, had reached an agreement on a ceasefire in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region starting October 29. The two countries agreed to halt all hostilities in Alyoshki to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of civilians through a designated safe corridor.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported earlier that Russian forces had ceased combat operations in the Kherson area at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27 and declared a ceasefire to prepare a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki. On October 23, Russian Armed Forces’ General Staff Chief and First Deputy Defense Minister Army General Valery Gerasimov that, to ensure the safety of civilians and the delivery of essential supplies, engineering reconnaissance would be conducted and measures would be taken to ensure the safe passage of the humanitarian convoy in Alyoshki.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the Kiev regime has been shelling roads leading to Alyoshki and extensively using drones to destroy vehicles for over two years. Ukrainian forces have also used unmanned aerial vehicles to lay mines along roads, preventing civilian evacuations and impeding the delivery of food, medicine, and other essential supplies to Alyoshki.

Switzerland seeks direct defence contracts with US manufacturers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:53:17 UTC
17:53:17 KST

Switzerland seeks direct defence contracts with US manufacturers
The Federal Office for Defence Procurement (Armasuisse) plans to purchase defence equipment directly from American manufacturers in future, rather than through the US government.
“That is one of the key lessons learnt from the F-35 purchase,” said Armasuisse chief Urs Loher in an interview on Wednesday.
But it remains to be seen whether such direct purchases are possible. This would require the go-ahead from the US authorities, Loher told the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).
More
Swiss government accepts it could have handled F-35 procurement better
He believes this might be possible for the Patriot air defence system.
“As this is a system that has been tried and tested for years, selected components are certainly available directly from the manufacturer,” said Loher. A direct purchase of state-of-the-art fighter aircraft such as the F-35 is, however, out of the question, he said.
‘Significant pitfalls’ of US scheme
Armasuisse typically handles procurements from the US via the US government’s “Foreign Military Sales” (FMS) programme. This allows the US government to retain control over which countries gain access to cutting-edge military technology, said Loher. The government also benefits from economies of scale, enabling it to purchase at lower costs itself.
More
Renewed controversy in Switzerland over US fighter jets – explained
At first glance, the government programme appears to be an “all-inclusive, worry-free package”. It spares one “lengthy negotiations with defence giants”, said Loher.
But he says Switzerland’s procurement of the F-35 fighter jets from the US has revealed “significant pitfalls”. For instance, there is no jurisdiction in the event of disputes, such as over a supposed fixed price. Also, buyers are dependent on US priorities, and in the event of delayed deliveries, contractual penalties are generally not possible.
Partial refund of Patriot advance payments
Armasuisse has experienced delivery delays and revised priorities in the delivery of the US-made Patriot system. Delivery is currently delayed by five to seven years. The federal office has therefore evaluated a second system, and a final decision is with the Federal Council, said Loher.
More
Swiss procurement of second missile defence system faces delays
Switzerland has also slipped down Washington’s list of priorities. The US intends to supply Germany with Patriot systems that were originally planned for Switzerland.
“We’ll come away empty-handed for the time being, but at least we’ll get some – if not all – of the advance payments back,” said Loher. To date, these have amounted to just over CHF1 billion. However, it is also unclear when this partial repayment will take place.

Syria reopens Jordan border crossing after mending ties

Syria reopens Jordan border crossing after mending ties
- Syria reopened the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Oct 28 after both sides tried to calm tensions caused by a deadly Jordanian strike.
- Jordan said its raid targeted “Daesh sites” after a church attack killed nine people in Karak, while Syria called the strike an “unacceptable violation” of sovereignty.
- Civilian deaths in southern Syria deepened anger, and a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet soon to discuss action against IS.
AI generated
Damascus – Syria reopened its main border crossing with Jordan on Oct 28 as the two countries reaffirmed ties that were strained by a deadly retaliatory strike by Jordanian forces.
Jordan’s strike – a reprisal against a gun attack on a church – sparked the worst crisis between the two countries since the ousting of long-time Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Syria condemned the strikes on the country’s south as an “unacceptable violation”, while Jordan said it killed more than 20 jihadist fighters in its raid.
Jordan sought to ease tensions on Oct 27, saying it had “great respect” for its neighbour and expressed regret for civilian casualties.
The main Nassib border crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, was closed following the strikes, but passenger and commercial movement will return to normal as of the morning of Oct 28, senior Syrian customs official Mazen Alloush told state news agency SANA.
Last week, gunmen opened fire during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan’s Karak governorate, killing nine people and wounding 25 – prompting a military response from Amman.
While Jordan insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus denied the claim, and Syria’s civil defence agency said the raids killed seven people, including three children.
On Oct 27, Jordan’s Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi spoke to his Syrian counterpart and emphasised Jordan’s “full respect for Syria’s sovereignty... and security”, while also expressing “sorrow and grief over the death of innocent civilian victims”, according to a joint statement.
The two officials also discussed the raids against what the statement branded as “Daesh sites”, using an acronym to refer to the Islamic State (IS) group.
Earlier, Jordan’s government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani had said that “the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh’s ranks – estimated at more than 20 fighters”.
He also said “a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation” had been destroyed.
‘Blatant violation’
Earlier, Syria’s foreign ministry issued a “condemnation and rejection” of the strikes, calling them “an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination”.
It also said the raid was “a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty”.
In the coming days, a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet to discuss the operations against IS, a government source told Syrian state news agency SANA.
Syria said five people, including a woman and three children, were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south.
“We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children – two boys and a girl – were killed,” said Nassouh al-Salim in Al-Taf, staring at a grey body bag.
An AFP reporter saw a huge crater in the family’s destroyed home, with school books, clothes and the remains of furniture strewn among the rubble.
Syrian Emergencies and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Oct 27 that both sides were handling the dispute through “diplomatic and legal channels” with the aim of securing justice for the victims.
‘Dark ideologies’
On Oct 26, Amman said the authorities had arrested three Jordanians accused of the church killings, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage.
The authorities said the suspects were hospitalised after being wounded in a shootout with security forces.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population.
“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” King Abdullah II said.
IS was territorially defeated in Syria in 2019, after it seized swathes of territory during the country’s more than 13-year civil war.
But remnants are still present, and the group occasionally claims attacks, mainly targeting Syrian security forces.
The group has previously been present in parts of Daraa province. AFP

Canada signs trade deal with UAE in push for non-US markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:50:55 UTC
17:50:55 KST

Canada signs trade deal with UAE in push for non-US markets
The agreement aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Canada and the United Arab Emirates have signed a comprehensive trade deal to lower barriers between the economies and boost investment, the governments have said.
The deal comes as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to expand trade and investment ties amid tension with the United States.
Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) on Tuesday, which aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Carney has pledged to double Ottawa’s non-US trade over the next decade as US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have rippled through Canada’s economy.
Subsequent attempts to reach a deal with Washington have broken down, which has pushed Carney to aggressively pursue trade pacts with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and the Middle East.
“Once fully implemented, the CEPA will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99 percent of current Canadian exports to the UAE,” the Prime Minister’s Office said in a statement.
“That means new markets for Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola, for manufacturers of industrial machinery and power generation equipment, for our world-class aerospace sector, and other Canadian innovators.”
“The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental, and engineering sectors,” it said, adding that CEPA is expected to enter into force in 2027.
Multiple deals
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defence cooperation.
“We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing – all of which will support our pursuit of a resilient, diversified and globally connected economy,” the UAE’s Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi said in a statement.
He signed the CEPA deal with his Canadian counterpart, Maninder Sidhu.
The UAE is the largest Middle East market for Canadian exports and a major buyer of Canadian motor vehicles and parts, and machinery.
Two-way trade between the countries was worth 3.5 billion Canadian dollars ($2.48bn) last year. It has been growing at 10 percent annually for the last few years, according to government data.
The UAE also committed up to $50bn in investment in Canada last year.

Rada reviews rejected 2027 budget amendments until 0300, to vote on 2 Wednesday

The Verkhovna Rada considered rejected amendments by MPs to the draft state budget for 2027 until 3:00 AM on Wednesday, and during the session on Wednesday, October 28, will vote separately on two of them, reported MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak (Holos faction) on his Telegram channel.
According to him, the first of these (No. 611) concerns the allocation of funds from plea bargain agreements: they must be credited exclusively to the state budget or for compensation under a civil lawsuit, and funds exceeding the damage caused—to a special fund for the monetary allowance of Ukrainian Armed Forces servicemen. The amendment also instructs the government to verify the legality of agreements for 2022–2026 and submit a report to parliament by September 1, 2027.
The second amendment (No. 1003) provides for a restriction in 2027 on the maximum monthly salary of 80,000 UAH for employees of government authorities, local self-government, budgetary institutions, as well as MPs, judges, members of the High Council of Justice, the High Qualification Commission of Judges of Ukraine, prosecutors, and NBU employees (excluding positions involved in defense).
In addition, during Wednesday's session in the assembly hall, all amendments incorporated by the Budget Committee will be put to a confirmation vote, in particular proposal No. 1279 regarding an increase in servicemen's monetary allowances.
According to information on the Rada's Telegram channel, the document will be considered in the first reading as a basis. As Zheleznyak specified, the Rada will consider it in the second reading in November.
As reported, on October 27, the Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee approved Budget Conclusions for the draft state budget for 2027, which contain 90 summary proposals formed from 5,236 deputy amendments, and recommended that parliament adopt them as a basis and send the budget draft to the government for preparation for the second reading.
The government's draft state budget for 2027 provides for general fund revenues at the level of 5.65 trillion UAH (8.7% more compared to 2026) and expenditures amounting to 7.27 trillion UAH (an increase of 13.5%).

Budget 2026 live: chancellor says scrapping gas standing charges will save 60% of homes £45 a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:50:14 UTC
17:50:14 KST

Healey also looking at removing standing charges from electricity bill, Martin Lewis says
Martin Lewissaid that, when he met John Healey this morning, the chancellor said that, having removed standing charges from gas bills, he would also like to get rid of them from electricity bills. Lewis said:
The chancellor said he will be talking to Ofgem about how they get rid of the charge on electricity as well, but that is ‘trickier’ apparently and will take longer.
Investment firms welcome reports that cut to cash Isa allowance to be reversed
The Financial Times is reporting this morning that John Healey will “use his budget to scrap controversial plans to slash the annual cash Isa allowance from £20,000 to £12,000, after concluding it was the wrong way to persuade people to invest more in stocks and shares”.
Most people in the City work on the basis that, if the FT is reporting a budget story on the day it is being delivered, it is safe to believe it is true. Investment companies have welcomed the news.
Simon Harrington, head of public affairs at PIMFA, a financial management company, said:
We welcome John Healey’s decision to reverse his predecessor’s controversial plans to slash the annual cash ISA allowance from £20,000 to £12,000. We have consistently argued that cutting the allowance was unlikely to achieve the government’s ambition of encouraging more people to invest, and risked making the stocks and shares ISA – the very wrapper it wants people to use – less attractive.
And Will Stevens, a partner at Killik & Co, a wealth management company, said:
The decision to retain the full Cash ISA allowance is a sensible one. Whilst there is a legitimate policy objective in encouraging more people to invest for long-term growth, reducing the allowance risked being perceived as penalising sensible saving behaviour rather than promoting investing.
The gas standing charges decision has also been welcomed by Nesta, a thinktank that recently published a paper arguing for exactly this policy. Andrew Sissons, director in sustainable future at Nesta, said:
Ditching the gas standing charge rightly takes a big chunk off millions of people’s energy bills, sharing costs more fairly and giving cash-strapped households a much-needed boost. This measure will provide relief to the poorest households who ration their gas use but it will also mean that switching to electric heating such as heat pumps is a better deal for some households that use more gas.
The report includes this chart showing how many households are likely to lose and gain from the measure.
Nesta estimates that, based on current TDCV (typical domestic consumption values), a typical dual-use household will save £27 a year.
But there has been a more positive response from Simon Francis, coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition. He said:
Removing the gas standing charge will bring real relief to many low-income households who use very little energy and for prepayment customers it could stop debt building up in the summer months.
It’s also welcome that the chancellor acknowledges that wider measures are needed to bring down bills and we will wait to see if he matches these words with more action in the budget later. Moving levies off electricity bills and into general taxation, as reported, would also be a positive step.
Getting rid of standing charges on gas bills really 'sleight of hand', Tories claim
The Conservatives have dismissed the chancellor’s decision to get rid of standing charges from energy bills just “sleight of hand”. In an interview on GB News, Richard Fuller, the shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, said:
We know there’s a problem with energy prices coming down the track. That’s why the Conservatives last year actually announced that cheap energy plan to get rid of VAT on people’s energy bills and roll back some of the net zero taxes that burden people’s bills.
But what Labour is doing is really sleight of hand. They’re moving it from one aspect of your energy bill or your taxes, and putting it somewhere else. Under the Conservatives, of course, we would make the tougher decisions on public spending, so the actual energy bills and people’s taxes would be coming down.
Money saving expert Martin Lewis welcomes gas standing charge abolition, and says further energy bills support likely in budget
John Healey found time to hold a meeting with Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, in Downing Street this morning. Lewis is one of the most trusted voices on personal finance in Britain, and he has been campaigning for standing charges to be removed from gas bills for some time.
Speaking to the media afterwards, Lewis said Healey was in a good mood. He said he asked the chancellor if there would be a support scheme to help people with energy bills from January, when costs are set to rise sharply. Lewis said Healey would not confirm anything, but he said that “reading between the lines” he gathered that there will be an announcement on this. Lewis speculated that this could be an increase in the warm homes discount, or it could be help for people in lower council tax bands.
The biggest issue in energy right now is that we’re expecting a 27% rise in the price cap in January. I asked the Chancellor whether he will be intervening on that. He told me I’d have to wait for the budget, but reading between the lines, yes, there will be an announcement today.
Whether it’s an increase in the Warm Home Discount, or whether it’s council tax band, or whether it’s done via a payout for people in say council tax bands A-D as a proxy for household income as Rishi Sunak did who knows.
John Healey says chancellor scrapping gas standing charges will save 60% of homes £45 a year
Good morning. When Andy Burnham became PM, he signalled that he wanted to end 40 years of neoliberalism. Judging by all the briefing about what will be in the budget today, neoliberalism is probably safe for another year or so because Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have decided not to use this as a moment for big, transformative change, but to instead opt for a more low-risk, every-little-bit-helps fiscal statement. There are radical elements in the Burnham agenda, but mostly they will have to wait for another day. In a video setting the scene for the budget, Healey sums it up with the slogan: “Breathing space today, and fresh hope for the future.”
Here is Pippa Crerar and Heather Stewart’s overnight splash story previewing the budget.
And here is an analysis by Phillip Inman setting out the main items we are expecting.
Every chancellor, though, likes to have at least one big surprise for the speech. This is the headline they want for tomorrow’s papers. We don’t know yet what Healey has chosen, but there is a lot of speculation that it will involve energy bills.
We have already had an announcement from the Treasury at 7am this morning about standing charges being removed from gas bills. Julia Kollewe has the story here.
According to the Treasury, this could save around 60% of families around £45 a year. It says:
The chancellor will announce today an end to this unfair and outdated practice. He will ask Ofgem to deliver removal of these charges – which are £108 a year for the typical household on average – in 2027 or as soon as possible after.
Instead, these fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate, which could save 60% of account-holding households around an average of £45 off their annual bill.
While this might sound like a modest cost of living measure – almost an “everyday fix” – Burnham and Healey – perhaps sensitive to the charge that there is not much radicalism in the budget – are presenting this as the start of something more ambitious. In a statement this morning, Burnham said this shows he’s “determined to reform our broken energy market” and Healey says:
My budget will draw a line in the sand on an energy policy that has failed British billpayers for years, letting extra costs on bills pile high and leaving households even more exposed to global shocks.
Healey is speaking at 12.30pm. We have also got PMQs today, but I will mostly be focusing on the budget, with reaction and analysis, and Graeme Wearden, who writes the Guardian’s business live blog, will be joining too to provide added firepower.
And we will also have comments open below the line (BTL).
Here is the agenda for the day.
8.45am:Andy Burnham chairs cabinet, where John Healey, the chancellor, will brief ministers on what’s in the budget.
Around 1.30pm: After Healey finishes, Kemi Badenoch gives a speech responding to the budget. Other MPs respond as the budget debate continues through the afternoon.
2.30pm: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, holds a press conference.
3.30pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Robert Jenrick, his Treasury spokesperson, hold a press conference to give their reaction to the budget.

Dadgar elected president of Iran’s Shooting Federation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:49:46 UTC
17:49:46 KST

Dadgar elected president of Iran’s Shooting Federation
TEHRAN – Ali Dadgar has been elected president of Iran’s Shooting Federation after securing a majority of votes in the federation’s electoral assembly.
The election was held under the chairmanship of Mohammadshervin Asbaghian, Deputy Minister of Sports and Youth for Championship and Professional Sports Development.
Dadgar was elected as the federation’s new president after receiving 26 votes from the 51 members of the assembly.
Six candidates had initially been approved to contest the election: Ebrahim Barkhordari, Ali Dadgar, Hossein Zakizadeh, Salar Mohammadnia, Abbas Mohammadipour, and Masoud Nosrati Qazvininejad.
However, Barkhordari, Mohammadnia, and Nosrati Qazvininejad withdrew their candidacies before the voting began, leaving Dadgar, Zakizadeh, and Mohammadipour to compete for the presidency.
In the first round of voting, Dadgar received 25 votes, followed by Zakizadeh with 19 and Mohammadipour with five. One ballot was declared invalid.
As no candidate secured an absolute majority in the first round, the election proceeded to a runoff between Dadgar and Zakizadeh.
In the second round, Dadgar narrowly defeated Zakizadeh by 26 votes to 25, securing the presidency of Iran’s Shooting Federation for the next four years.
Dadgar has previously served as president of the federation.

"The board, together with the executive team, acknowledges that we haven't got it right — we take responsibility for that and are committed to getting better, both on and off the field.

He added the expert would work with their AFLW sub-committee to ensure the women are set up for long-term success.
"We have a responsibility to our players, coaches, staff, members, supporters and the wider game to listen to feedback and be prepared to make meaningful, considered changes across the club to build a stronger AFLW program for everyone at Collingwood," Carp said.
Wright will coach Collingwood for the last time on Sunday against Essendon at Windy Hill. It will also be Bombers coach Natalie Wood's last game.

Despite the fallout from the 7 October attacks, three years of war and widespread public dissatisfaction, Benjamin Netanyahu emerged from Israel's election with his political position strengthened, even as neither political bloc is assured of a parliamentary majority.
