The political deadlock comes as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stages what Levy described to Euronews as an "extraordinary comeback".
"All of those are going to require someone to surrender on some very serious coalition promises," Levy said.
Netanyahu's political survival
For Netanyahu the election represents a remarkable political recovery after years of mounting pressure over the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, the subsequent war and domestic divisions.
"This is an extraordinary comeback for Netanyahu, despite the October 7th massacre that happened on his watch, despite three years of war since then, despite huge public unrest and dissatisfaction over his alliance with the ultra-orthodox parties and their demand for an exemption from military service," Levy told Euronews.
Yet his electoral gains do not necessarily translate into a governing majority.
"Netanyahu has lost his majority. It seems it's unlikely that he will hold on to a majority. But unless someone else manages to form a government, he remains the caretaker prime minister," Levy said.

Could Arab parties decide who governs Israel?

Russia conducts tests of SOVA autonomous navigation system for UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:47:50 UTC
17:47:50 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia’s SOVA (Comparative Optical Visual Authentication) autonomous navigation system, designed to ensure precise positioning of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) when GPS/GNSS signals and external communications are unavailable or jammed, has been successfully tested in the field, the Center for Unmanned Systems and Technologies (CUST) told TASS.
"The developer of the solution, VA Technologies, is a finalist in the third cohort of the CUST Special-and Dual-Use Projects Accelerator. The SOVA system is based on computer vision technology. During flight, the system compares images from an onboard camera with a satellite map of the terrain and determines the UAV’s location in real time. During testing, a drone equipped with the SOVA system completed a route that had no clear landmarks and included substantial differences between the satellite map and the actual terrain," the company said.
The CUST specified that the flight path was star-shaped. "The UAV, equipped with the autonomous navigation system, sequentially visited four waypoints and returned to its launch site. To make the task more challenging, satellite images from the spring of 2025 were used instead of an up-to-date map. Thus, the tests were conducted with a known discrepancy between the actual terrain and the map data used by the drone," the center noted.
According to the CUST, the most challenging section for the system was the stretch between the second and third waypoints. "The second waypoint on the satellite map was located over dark plowed land, while the actual terrain featured a light-colored field covered with stubble. With no landmarks to guide it, the UAV deviated from its course. However, upon reaching a tree line, the SOVA system promptly corrected its course and successfully reached the third waypoint," the company said.
VA Technologies, commenting on the situation, emphasized that such a scenario is not a failure but a standard operating condition for which the system was designed. "According to the developer, in the absence of GPS, SOVA is capable of increasing the UAV mission reliability rate to 99%," the CUST noted.

Israeli AI start-up NanoCo brings governance and security to enterprise AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:47:12 UTC
17:47:12 KST

As companies rush to adopt artificial intelligence tools across their organizations, Israeli start-up NanoCo bets the next phase of enterprise AI will require more than powerful models. Founded by brothers Lazer Cohen and Gavriel Cohen, the company focuses on building security, governance, and control layers around AI agents that can carry out tasks on employees' behalf.
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post, Lazar Cohen said that NanoCo emerged from the founders' earlier work in AI-driven communications technology.
About a year and a half ago, as interest in agentic AI and AI-powered software development accelerated, the two brothers began building what he described as a native AI public relations agency. The venture attracted clients and helped the team raise a pre-seed round for an earlier company called Quibit. During that period, the developers increasingly relied on AI agent platforms to automate recurring work.
Their experience with one of those platforms, OpenClaw, ultimately led to NanoCo's creation.
"We started using it and realized that the question was whether it could really be trusted with company data," Cohen told The Post.
Cohen leads commercial operations, while Gavriel serves as CEO and oversees product R&D.
The two viewed the challenge as both technical and operational. “We saw value in AI agents capable of completing tasks independently, but we were concerned that existing systems lacked sufficient controls for enterprise deployment,” Lazar said.
30,000+ stars on GitHub
NanoCo's answer was NanoClaw, an open-source AI agent platform designed around a simplified architecture and security-focused deployment model. Cohen explained that the platform uses a much smaller codebase than some alternatives and runs agents in isolated sandboxes designed to prevent them from accessing unauthorized data or systems.
“OpenClaw had half a million lines of code, which is impossible to audit compared to NanoCo’s 4000 lines of code,” Cohen explained.
In addition to the sandboxing technology, NanoCo developed a gateway that sits outside the AI agent environment. Requests such as accessing information or sending communications are evaluated through that gateway, where a human operator either approves or denies the request.
Cohen said the company's open-source release gained traction quickly, was adopted by hundreds of thousands of users, and accumulated more than 30,000 stars on GitHub. He added that the adoption helped attract investor attention and supported the company's growth strategy.
In 2026, NanoCo announced a $12 million seed funding round led by Valley Capital Partners, with participation from investors including Docker, Vercel, and monday.com.
In addition to NanoClaw, its open-source platform, the company’s commercial enterprise offering, NanoCo, has also been gaining traction worldwide.
Cohen told the Post that NanoCo was endorsed by Andrej Karpathy (who co-founded OpenAI) and by Singapore's Foreign Minister, Vivian Balakrishnan. Venture capitalists from leading funds have also been using the platform.
Daniel Ziv, an investor and principal at Glilot Capital Partners, explained that “a VC’s scarcest resource is attention, and a lot of our time goes to meta-work rather than judgment: scheduling, writing notes, updating the CRM, chasing diligence items, remembering what a founder said three months ago. Agents absorb that work, and because they’re always on, nothing falls through the cracks between meetings.”
Glilot is an AI-first firm instituted in Israel in 2011 as the world's first venture capital company dedicated to cybersecurity. According to Ziv, the security and privacy provided by NanoClaw have been paramount.
“We were Israel’s first cybersecurity fund, so we couldn’t compromise here. A VC handles extremely sensitive information, and NanoClaw is a security-first, privacy-aware agent infrastructure, which made it something I could actually trust with my data.”
And, with the agents doing the footwork, “that leaves me free for what stays human: creativity, like finding a smart way through a deal conflict or helping a portfolio company out of a tough spot, and relationships with founders, advisers and customers. My back-office job has shifted from doing the tasks to writing the workflows,” Ziv added.
For enterprise organizations
While NanoClaw is designed primarily for individual users and developers, NanoCo packages the technology with additional governance, management, and security controls intended for organizations.
According to Cohen, many companies do not want to manage complex AI infrastructure internally. Instead, they are seeking turnkey solutions that can be deployed and governed within existing corporate environments.
NanoCo's enterprise platform, he explained, is deployed directly into a customer's cloud environment, allowing organizations to maintain ownership and control over their data. The company does not have access to a customer's source code or internal information beyond permissions explicitly granted by the customer. NanoCo can manage enterprise deployments, including software updates and operational support. Customers can also move their agents, stored knowledge, and workflows between providers if they choose to switch AI models or infrastructure platforms.
"Companies sometimes feel like they're being left behind," Cohen said. "But it is still very early."
Tiang Lim Foo, a founding partner at Analog Ventures, said that the company built its internal agent platform, Amplify, on NanoClaw.
"Our AI analysts work in Slack alongside the team, covering investment triage, portfolio management, and investor relations. It lets a lean seed fund move like a much larger firm,” he said, adding that their agents “handle confidential founder and investor data, and NanoClaw is small enough to audit end to end, with each agent sandboxed in its own container."
NanoCo employs approximately 20 people across three countries. Most of the workforce is based in Israel, where it conducts all research and development. Team members in Spain maintain the open-source NanoClaw project, while personnel in the United States focus on marketing and growth initiatives.
The start-up is entering a crowded AI market that includes consumer-facing assistants and enterprise productivity platforms. However, Cohen said many organizations remain in the early stages of adoption.
For NanoCo, the estimation is that demand for AI agents will keep rising as businesses move from experimentation to deploying systems that can complete work autonomously under defined governance and security frameworks.
"The use of AI will only increase," Cohen said. "We are only at the beginning."

Israel's election reveals a democracy of contradictions - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

17:46:58 KST

And the people have spoken - out of both sides of their mouths. Bibi lovers can rejoice! Despite most polls predicting his loss, his Likud emerged as the largest party in the exit polls. Bibi haters can rejoice! The opposition parties together may have earned as many as 70 seats, to the coalition’s 50.
Once again, yet another Israeli election pivoted around Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s indefatigable political sorcerer. It’s remarkable. After his October 7th failures, most people expected him to resign or be hounded out of office.
Netanyahu and Israel's political tribalism
Yet three years later, Israelis voted in “droves,” and he survived. “Droves” is the trigger word Netanyahu used in 2015 to warn of mass Arab voting, before apologizing a week later. Now, having mainstreamed thugs and descended himself into divisive demagoguery, especially as he panicked, he’s not likely to backpedal this outburst of bigotry.
Netanyahu’s endurance, even without a coalition victory, reflects Israel’s political tribalism. Party membership is often a social, ethnic, and political statement, from right to left, which Netanyahu exploits with virtuosity.
But to be fair, his resurgence is not just irrational. Many of the post-October 7 moves that made Netanyahu’s brand toxic worldwide, even in America, are what resurrected his domestic political career. Even many Israelis who detest him understand that the grueling fight in Gaza against Hamas was a just war.
They acknowledge that he ultimately brought home 168 live hostages and accounted for every murdered hostage, while presiding over a war that crushed Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The fact that, as the Iranians and Americans keep skirmishing, neither side wants the Israelis fighting shows that the precious asset lost on October 7, Israeli deterrence, has been restored.
Anyone who predicts what governmental constellation will result has a better crystal ball than I have. But, once again, I am struck by three clashing perceptions: the buoyant democracy so many Israelis experienced on Tuesday; the racist oppressor Israel’s obsessive critics in the West decided they saw; and the infuriatingly successful society Israel’s enemies watched, yet again.
Israel remains one part kaleidoscope, genuinely projecting different, ever-changing, and sometimes contradictory images. It’s also one part Rorschach test, as people praise or curse the oversimplified, black-and-white Israel they imagine because the real Israel is so multi-dimensional and elusive.
This Election Day was particularly magical, given all that we have endured since October 7. So many observers noted how special it was that we have a Jewish democracy where we can vote freely, after thousands of years of being oppressed by authoritarian regimes.
Families picnicked and shopped, kids enjoyed the day off from school, and most voters, despite their constitutional Israeli excitability, waited patiently, appreciatively, in the impressively long voting lines, as 77.7 of eligible voters cast those old-fashioned paper ballots.
The joy, the calm, even the anxiety building toward the 10 p.m. exit poll announcement, illustrated Israeli democracy’s strength and sacredness. We awaited the people’s verdict.
Calm contrasted with chaos of Israeli politics
Such restraint also contrasted with the chaos and belligerence of Israeli politics. It’s the kind of contradiction every soldier, every reservist, experiences. With lots of time on their hands, they all know where everyone stands politically, religiously, ideologically. And with stakes so high, they aren’t afraid to shout about their differences, occasionally.
But when it’s time to spring into action, these distinct, often-dissimilar, hotheads become a high-functioning unit. And when reservist kids are bar mitzvahed, or fellow soldiers get married, you can always recognize the army friends’ table; while broadening the events’ demographics, they outdance everyone on the dance floor.
Obsessively anti-Semitic anti-Zionists cannot compute Israel’s many warm, human, intimate, and wonderfully democratic moments. Instead, burying the lede, they will emphasize the bigoted rants of Bibi and Itamar Ben-Gvir, rather than the remarkable results of this election wherein Ben-Gvir’s bigotry motivated many Arabs to vote.
Arabs not only have the right to vote, but their incredibly high turnout in this fair, peaceful election means they might be the next kingmakers. Exit polls estimate that Arab MKs may constitute 14 percent of oppressive, apartheid Israel’s next Knesset.
Israel emerges stronger, more united despite Oct. 7
Finally, one can only imagine what Iran’s Ayatollahs and Revolutionary Guards, what Palestinian terrorists from Gaza to Judea and Samaria, and what the dwindling ranks of Hezbollah are thinking. They, and their bots, will tweet all kinds of anti-Zionist trash talk, which their Western dupes, and too many Jews worldwide, will echo or at least buy into a bit. But our enemies know better. “Darn,” they must be thinking, “foiled again.”
Three years after the worst day in Israeli history, Israel has emerged stronger, more united despite all the noise, and even happier despite the trauma, still scoring high in all happiness indices. I kind of understand their blind hatred of us; nothing's more annoying than watching people you despise, and keep trying to destroy, bounce back from tragedy, live life to the fullest, and show the world what a successful society looks like, even with all its challenges.
Now that the votes have been cast, we Israelis need a quality that’s often in short supply these days: patience. The votes must be counted, and the counting should be finished by Friday. The inevitably excruciating negotiations have to begin. Then, if and when a new government emerges, and we escape electoral deadlock, every citizen should remember to be patriotic. Give the new government a chance to succeed, or fail, while respecting the democratic process on display so impressively this Tuesday, once again.

How the new Knesset can begin changing Israel before a coalition forms - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:46:32 UTC
17:46:32 KST

The election exit polls indicate that a decisive majority of Israeli voters have rejected the continuation of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government. Between 70 and 73 seats appear to have gone to parties outside Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc.
But that majority includes 17–18 seats won by the two Arab parties, which most of the Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu have refused to recognize as potential political partners.
That refusal could become Netanyahu's political lifeline. It does not have to be.
There is an important constitutional fact that should now become central to Israel's political debate: A new government does not have to be formed before the newly elected Knesset can begin changing the direction of the country.
The legal sequence is straightforward.
A step-by-step sequence
First, the new Knesset convenes. Its 120 members declare their allegiance to the State of Israel and its laws. The outgoing Netanyahu government continues to serve as a caretaker government until a new government is sworn in. But the new Knesset immediately possesses its constitutional authority as Israel's legislature.
Second, the new Knesset can elect a new speaker. This does not require the formation of a government or a coalition agreement. It requires a parliamentary majority in the relevant vote. If the parties opposing Netanyahu agree on a candidate, they can elect a new speaker with the support of the Arab parties. There is no legal prohibition against such cooperation.
This is not merely a theoretical possibility. In March 2020, the Supreme Court intervened when then-Knesset speaker Yuli Edelstein attempted to prevent a vote on replacing him. The Court affirmed that the parliamentary majority must be allowed to exercise its authority to elect a speaker.
Third, the Knesset establishes its parliamentary machinery. An Arrangements Committee is formed to organize parliamentary work. Temporary committees can be established, and the Knesset can create the committee framework necessary to advance legislation. This process can take place before a new government is formed.
Fourth, the new parliamentary majority can begin legislating. Members of Knesset can introduce private members' bills, and the parliamentary majority can advance them through the required legislative stages. Private members' bills ordinarily require a preliminary reading, followed by three readings and committee deliberations. Procedural waiting periods may apply, although the Knesset's rules provide mechanisms for accelerating legislation in certain circumstances.
The first priority should be legislation ensuring the establishment of an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures that led to October 7. The Knesset should also begin the process of reversing legislation that weakened Israel's judiciary and undermined democratic checks and balances.
Each legislative proposal would require the applicable majority, and some changes to Basic Laws may require an absolute majority of 61 or other special procedures. But none of these legislative processes is constitutionally dependent on the formation of a new government.
Fifth, negotiations over forming the next government continue in parallel. The president consults the parliamentary factions and assigns a member of Knesset the task of forming a government. That process can take weeks or longer. Throughout that period, Netanyahu remains prime minister of the outgoing government, but he does not automatically control the newly elected Knesset.
This distinction is crucial.
Gadi Eisenkot does not need to persuade Avigdor Liberman, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Yair Golan, Mansour Abbas and the other Arab representatives to agree on a governing coalition before they can cooperate in parliament.
They do not need to agree on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the future of the settlements, security policy or the composition of the next government. They need only agree that the voters have given them an opportunity to begin repairing Israel's democratic institutions.
Nor would parliamentary cooperation with the Arab parties require their participation in a future government. Their votes in the Knesset are as legitimate as those of every other elected representative.
The immediate challenge is therefore political, not constitutional. Can the parties opposing Netanyahu agree to exercise the parliamentary majority that the voters have apparently given them?
Liberman and Bennett may oppose forming a government dependent on Arab parliamentary support. But that is a political position, not a legal barrier to electing a new speaker or passing legislation together.
The new Knesset could begin its work while negotiations over the next government continue. A new speaker could be elected. Committees could be established. Legislation could be introduced and advanced. The process of restoring democratic accountability could begin.
None of this would automatically remove Netanyahu from the prime minister's office. That requires the formation of a new government or another constitutionally prescribed process. But it would mean that Netanyahu could no longer assume that his caretaker government also commands the legislature.
The central question is whether the leaders of the anti-Netanyahu parties will allow their disagreements over the next government to prevent them from using their majority in the new Knesset.
Israel cannot afford another prolonged period of political paralysis while its democratic institutions remain damaged and the failures of October 7 remain without a full, independent state investigation.
The voters have apparently created the possibility of change. The law provides the means to begin.
There is no reason to wait for a new government before taking the first steps.
The Knesset can begin changing Israel before Israel has a new prime minister.
The voters have spoken. Now their elected representatives must decide whether they are prepared to act.

Ukrainians back retaliatory strikes on Russian refineries even if US halts aid, 80% say – KMIS
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:46:30 EET
17:46:30 KST

More than three-quarters of Ukrainians support continuing the armed resistance against the Russian Federation despite Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the winter, and an even larger majority favors retaliatory strikes on Russian oil refineries even if the U.S cuts off military aid to Ukraine as a result, according to a survey conducted between October 16 and 25 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KMIS).
Specifically, 76% of Ukrainians maintain that even if Russia attempts to target the energy sector in winter to leave people without electricity, heat, or sewage, Ukraine must still continue its armed resistance. Meanwhile, 15% believe that under such conditions, Ukraine should agree to any Russian demands, even if they look like capitulation. Another 9% were undecided.
KMIS notes that macroeconomic breakdowns show no significant regional differences, and figures remain virtually unchanged from August-September within the margin of error.
An even greater share of respondents—80%—expressed the view that strikes on Russian oil refineries should still be carried out even if the U.S stops or limits its assistance to Ukraine. Only 11% answered that such strikes should be halted, while 8% were undecided.
During the poll, 63% of Ukrainians stated they are ready to endure the war for as long as necessary, while 5% mentioned a timeframe of 1 year. Shorter periods (several months to half a year) were cited by 21%, with the remaining 11% undecided. KMIS noted no significant changes compared to results obtained on October 8–16.
Additionally, 62% of respondents expressed trust in current Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, while 35% do not trust him (a balance of +27%). The institute noted that trust in the president stood at 43% (with 52% distrust) on October 8–9, but rose to 57% trust (and 39% distrust) by October 10–16.
"Following October 9—that is, after the 'diesel deal'—Ukraine and Ukrainians found themselves under triple pressure: from the Russian enemy and its terror campaign of jet drones and ballistic missiles (accompanied by information warfare), from certain domestic actors (some of whom insist on de facto peace at any price, while others prioritize an uncompromising struggle against the government), and from our strategic partner, the U.S... Despite these pressures, Ukrainians maintain resilience in repelling the enemy: the majority are ready to endure the war as long as needed, insist that despite a potentially difficult winter Ukraine must not yield to Russian peace terms, and believe that even with the risk of losing US support, strikes on Russian oil refineries must continue," commented KMIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetskyi on the survey results.
He also noted that despite calls from certain public figures for Zelenskyy to step down, trust in him continues to grow.
"Ukrainian society has wisely mobilized for unity during this difficult period, but the Ukrainian authorities must also learn the right lessons and avoid euphoria from success, otherwise we will quickly return to a downward trend in trust... In any case, our data demonstrate that Ukrainians, despite everything, have the will to continue resistance until an acceptable outcome in the war is achieved," Hrushetskyi concluded.
The survey was conducted via telephone interviews (CATI) based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers in all government-controlled regions of Ukraine among 828 adult respondents. Under normal conditions, the formal statistical margin of error for such a sample (with a 0.95 probability and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) does not exceed 4.4% for indicators close to 50% and 1.9% for indicators close to 5%. Under wartime conditions, certain systematic deviations are added alongside the formal margin of error, but the results retain high representativeness.

WAYFINDING system FOR Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
Located in Medora, North Dakota, the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library is embedded directly within the terrain of the Badlands. Designed by Snøhetta with architect of record JLG Architects, the library campus connects three institutions across expansive indoor and outdoor environments. Studio Loutsis was commissioned to develop the comprehensive signage, wayfinding, and donor recognition system spanning the site, treating graphic wayfinding as an architectural and landscape-driven extension of the campus.
graphic maps, architecture, and landscape into a unified system
To unify varied scales, from monumental exterior markers to pedestrian trail placards, Studio Loutsis collaborated with Commercial Type to engineer a bespoke typeface, paired with a custom iconography system. Exterior wayfinding incorporates heavy timber pylons, directional panels, campus maps, and dark metal dimensional lettering engineered to withstand North Dakota’s extreme climate while weathering alongside the building envelope.
Fabricated under stringent Living Building Challenge sustainability parameters, all materials, non-toxic coatings, and mechanical assemblies adhere to strict ecological standards. Indoors, signage mounts directly to vertically articulated timber partitions using custom-milled infill blocks, while the central lobby’s ‘Wall of Gratitude’ integrates flush donor wood panels into the primary architectural cladding.

India has invited all 10 member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), including Pakistan, to participate in its inaugural Civilisational Dialogue Forum, scheduled to be held in New Delhi from November 20 to 22, Indian media reported on Wednesday.
The invitation marks the first time since the four-day war between India and Pakistan last year that India has invited a senior Pakistani minister to the country.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh announced the initiative at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on October 20, confirming that all member states had been invited to participate.
“At the end of this year, India will host the first SCO Civilisation Dialogue Forum. We invite all SCO countries to participate in it,” Singh had said.
Pakistan Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar was present at the meeting.
Pakistan’s Minister for National Heritage and Culture Aurangzeb Khan Khichi has been invited to the forum, according to diplomatic sources cited by India Today. The forum aims to strengthen cultural ties and foster mutual understanding among SCO member states.
The invitation comes against the backdrop of strained relations between India and Pakistan following their four-day war, launched by India in May 2025 in what it described as a response to an attack in India-administered Kashmir’s Pahalgam, for which India blamed Pakistan. Pakistan firmly denied the accusations, for which India has provided no evidence.
If Khichi attends the event, it would mark the first visit by a senior Pakistani minister to India since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari participated in the SCO Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Goa in May 2023.
The proposed forum is aimed at deepening cultural engagement and promoting greater mutual understanding among the countries in the grouping.
Pakistan has yet to issue any official statement regarding its possible attendance.
Pakistan assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026-27 term on September 1. It took over the position from Kyrgyzstan following the SCO summit held in Bishkek.
The SCO has 10 member states: Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India became a full member of the organisation in 2017.

Zelensky pushes back against Musk, says Ukraine uses Starshield to defend itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

Zelensky pushes back against Musk, says Ukraine uses Starshield to defend itself
Ukraine has used SpaceX's Starshield satellite systems only to defend itself against Russian forces on its own territory, not for attacks on Russian soil, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 27.
The comments come as a rebuff of SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who claimed Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service" by using the systems for offensive drone attacks.
Ukraine widely uses both commercial Starlink terminals and their militarized version, Starshield.
Starshield was temporarily speed-restricted to 160 kilometers per hour in Ukraine earlier this month, hampering Ukrainian drone interceptors' ability to down Russian jet-powered drones and disrupting other military operations.
"When Elon Musk said that we use Starshield against the Russians — yes, against the Russians, but on our own territory. This is not offensive; it's defensive," Zelensky told journalists at a press briefing.
"But the point is that we use it against Russian troops on our territory, not on Russian territory. They came here to kill," he said.
Musk alleged that Kyiv used commercial Starlink terminals for "offensive drone strikes to kill people," adding that the "loophole" has now been closed. However, he rejected responsibility for Starshield restrictions, saying the militarized terminals are controlled by the U.S. government.
Ukrainian officials have previously rejected Musk's claims about Kyiv violating Starlink's service terms. Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that the commercial Starlink has a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers per hour and does not work on Russian territory.
Zelensky confirmed on Oct. 24 that both Starlink and Starshield are again working at full speed. Nobody has publicly claimed responsibility for the throttling of Starshield, though Trump administration officials have pointed fingers at Musk.
"Of course, civilians died while Starlink/Starshield were switched off," Zelensky said. "We're now shooting down about 90% of (Shahed-type drones). When the (latest wave of) attacks began, we were shooting down between 50% and 75–78%. Then that rate dropped back again."
The president revealed that Ukraine was just successfully testing its jet-powered Bars drone interceptors — 2,000 units of which were paid for by a European country — when the restrictions hit.
"So I really don't know who told SpaceX to do that," Zelensky said, suggesting it could either be Musk's personal decision or an instruction by a U.S. official. "I only know that, technically, SpaceX turns these systems on and off."
The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered the SpaceX CEO to lift the restrictions, while the U.S. president publicly claimed he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
The restrictions came amid deteriorating ties between the U.S. and Ukraine, with Trump easing sanctions pressure on Moscow while accusing Zelensky of not being interested in peace — despite Kyiv repeatedly backing various U.S.-backed ceasefire proposals, which were turned down by Russia.

According to Guryev, Russian products are currently available in 25 African countries. "We are ready to discuss terms for mutually beneficial cooperation with companies from the remaining 30 nations," he stated at the Russia-Africa Forum.
"The second area of cooperation is the creation of fertilizer bagging and packaging enterprises. Currently, most of our products are shipped in bulk. Packaging them into consumer containers will enable retail distribution," Guryev added. The third avenue of cooperation is scientific and technical. "We are ready to share our experience in the extraction and processing of mineral raw materials with African producers," the RAPU head said.
He added that Russia also aims to help train qualified personnel for Africa’s agricultural sector.

Elron plans to modernize trains and rent them to Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

Elron plans to modernize trains and rent them to Latvia
Estonia's state-owned passenger rail operator Elron wants to modernize the trains running between Tartu and Riga to attract more passengers to the route. It would also like to rent the trains to Latvians for use on local routes.
Elron wants to make the trains operating between Tartu and Riga more comfortable and use funds allocated for operating the route to do so, according to a letter the company sent to the Ministry of Climate.
The funds are available because the initially planned second daily departure has not yet been launched due to a shortage of trains.
The state allocates Elron €2 million annually to operate the route with two departures per day in both directions, with an additional €300,000 allocated this year for preparatory costs.
According to Elron's calculations, this year's funding would cover the operation of the route with one daily departure as well as the modernization of three trains.
Citing passenger feedback, Elron said more comfortable trains would help increase passenger numbers on the Tartu-Riga route and provide an opportunity to generate revenue by renting out the trains while they are in Latvia.
All this should help better cover the costs of the Tartu-Riga route, Elron CEO Lauri Betlem noted.
The plan to rent out trains in Latvia is linked to a procurement by Latvian passenger rail operator Vivi, which wants to rent diesel trains for three routes: Lithuanian border–Daugavpils–Riga–Daugavpils–Lithuanian border; Riga–Valga–Riga; and Riga–Daugavpils–Riga. The procurement procedure is still ongoing.
"We submitted a bid for the last route because the current direct Tallinn-Riga service arrives in Riga at around 9 p.m. and begins its return journey at 7.30 a.m. The time in between is free, during which it would make sense to put the train to work. This would also expand connections for Estonian passengers to central and southeastern Latvia," Elron's head of customer experience Kristi Unt told ERR.
New seats, carpets, footrests
Elron plans to modernize the seats in three trains, equip every seat with a power socket, replace the tables with longer ones, add footrests to standard-class seats, replace the carpet in first class and redecorate one train. There are also discussions about adding luggage areas and vending machines.
Unt said that there are no plans to completely rebuild the trains. "We are primarily talking about limited interior work," she explained.
In total, the modernization of the three trains would cost €756,000, including a small reserve, or €252,000 per train. Together with the costs of operating the route, this would amount to slightly less than €2.2 million, which is less than the state allocated to Elron this year.
Betlem said Elron can start modernizing the trains in early November when a four-car diesel train that was sent for repairs following a traffic accident in 2025 returns to service.
The ministry has given Elron preliminary approval, but final confirmation is now needed from the Ministry of Climate.
Elron currently has three two-car trains and one three-car train authorized to operate on Latvia's railway network. The European Union Agency for Railways is expected to authorize another three three-car trains soon.

TEL AVIV, October 28. /TASS/. Israel’s Likud party, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is holding on to its lead in the October 27 parliamentary elections, with 57.3% of the vote counted, according to data released by the Central Elections Committee.
The Yashar party of Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is in second place.
The Central Elections Committee is expected to announce preliminary results on October 29, with the final election outcome to be officially published no later than November 4.
TASS has compiled key details available so far.
Exit polls and seat distribution
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is holding on to its lead in the elections, with 57.3% of the vote counted, according to data released by the Central Elections Committee.
- According to this data, Netanyahu’s party is projected to win 28 seats in the 120-seat parliament.
- His main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar opposition party, is in second place with 21 seats.
- Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s bloc of parties is currently projected to win a total of 55 seats, while the opposition is expected to secure 49.
- Arab parties are projected to win 16 seats, although neither Likud nor the opposition is prepared to form a coalition with them.
- According to exit polls, the Beyachad (Together) bloc, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, ranks third with 14 seats.
- The center-left Democrats, led by Yair Golan, and the Arab Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, are expected to win ten seats each.
- Avigdor Lieberman’s party, Our Home Israel, which focuses on the interests of Israel's Russian-speaking community, is projected to win eight seats.
- The United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas, and the far-right party Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, are projected to receive seven seats each.
- The ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism, along with the far-right bloc comprising the Religious Zionist Party and Zehut, are each expected to win six seats.
- Other political forces are not expected to surpass the 3.25% electoral threshold.
- A total of 36 parties and alliances participated in the elections.
- A governing majority requires 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but, according to exit polls, no political force is expected to reach that number.
Voter turnout
- Parliamentary elections in Israel are held under a party-list system.
- A total of 7.3 mln Israeli citizens are eligible to vote.
- Voter turnout in the elections to the 26th Knesset was 77.7%, the highest level since 1999, Israel’s Channel 12 reported.
- United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas said that turnout in Arab-populated areas had reached 80%.
- He stressed that Arab voters had been more active than other voters.
Election results
- The Central Elections Committee is expected to announce preliminary results on October 29, with the final election outcome to be officially published no later than November 4.
- Once the final results are announced, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with representatives of the parties that have won seats in the Knesset before asking one of them to form a new government coalition.
Prime minister’s post
- According to Amjad Shbeita, coordinator of the Joint List coalition of Arab parties, left-wing and democratic forces have a strong chance of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
- Netanyahu previously claimed that opposition parties were trying "to steal the elections" from his bloc.
- Posts urging supporters to turn out in greater numbers appeared on Netanyahu’s X account approximately three times an hour, along with allegations that Arab parties were transporting thousands of their supporters to polling stations to secure more votes.
- As a rule, the leader of the party that wins the most seats in parliament becomes a candidate for the post of prime minister.
- However, the president may also task a politician whose party did not win the most seats with forming a cabinet, provided the party has a chance of forming a coalition.
- The first candidate for prime minister will have 28 days to form a government, with the possibility of a two-week extension.
- If the candidate fails, the president will assign the task to another lawmaker, who will have two weeks to form a cabinet, with no option for an extension.
- If no government can be formed with the support of at least 61 members of parliament, a new election will be called within 90 days.

Netanyahu likely to win most seats in Israeli polls: What happens next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:39:00 UTC
17:39:00 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies appear on track to win the most seats in Israel's parliament after an election this week, though neither he nor his main competitor, Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a majority.
Votes are now being tallied, followed by potentially long negotiations as parties try to assemble a governing coalition. If those talks fail, Israel could head to another round of elections.
Israel's Central Election Committee was tallying votes on Wednesday, and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election are known.
The committee will also tally hundreds of thousands of ballots by Israeli soldiers, as well as diplomats, who voted from outside the country.
The committee's tallying followed exit polls from major Israeli TV channels. Those polls can help give a general sense of each party’s relative strength but are not considered a reliable barometer of precise results, particularly in Israel’s fragmented political system.
The final vote tally is expected by Oct. 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on Nov. 4.
Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present Cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.

Flavio Bolsonaro on way to Ecuador from Argentina after fleeing Brazil
Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro was on his way to Ecuador after fleeing Brazil, Argentina's government said on Wednesday.
Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's runoff election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, entered Argentina on Tuesday night before boarding a flight to Ecuador, the country's National Directorate of Migration said on X.
The 45-year-old entered Argentina "with valid travel documents and no legal impediment," it added, despite a court order banning his exit.
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters boarded "a private flight operated by the company Baires Fly S.A. bound for the city of Guayaquil, Ecuador," the government agency said.
According to data from the Flightradar24 website, the flight took off just after midnight (0300 GMT) on Wednesday from the Argentine town of Puerto Iguazu in the country's northeast.
Baires Fly did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.
US media citing anonymous sources had earlier reported that Bolsonaro had arrived in the United States on Tuesday.
The US State Department said it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family but did not confirm their travel plans.
Brazil's Supreme Court banned Bolsonaro from leaving the country and ordered him to hand over his passports.
He is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity.
A police source told AFP that Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP.
'Shameful'
Reports of Bolsonaro's exit from Brazil came as a shock to his political camp.
"We still don't have any news about his whereabouts," Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho told reporters in Brasilia on Tuesday.
"I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it," he said. "That was the only communication we had."
Bolsonaro said in a video posted on Instagram a day earlier that he "never had any intention of leaving the country" and the ban on his exit was a scare tactic.
Lula, who won the election with 51.8 percent of the vote, called fleeing the country a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration.
Following his loss, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting.
Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country.
US President Donald Trump, a close ally of Flavio's father and Brazil's former leader Jair Bolsonaro, said that the elections were "rigged."
All bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month.
He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later.

Ukraine wants to meet with US and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi before any proposed talks between Washington, Moscow and Beijing, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, warning that Russia could use renewed peace negotiations to seek concessions on NATO’s military presence in Europe.

“I really don’t want this to be ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4,’ when influence is being redistributed,” Zelensky said, referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, United States and United Kingdom discussed the postwar order in Europe.
He argued that today’s fragmented, technologically advanced world was fundamentally different from the one that emerged after World War II, making a similar redistribution of power impossible.
“After Alaska, this would be Russia’s second major diplomatic advantage if things unfold as the Russians are currently suggesting, with their talk of a new ‘Yalta.’ I think Russia wants it more than anyone else,” Zelensky said.

Russia may seek NATO concessions in peace talks
Zelensky also warned NATO against accepting Russian demands to roll back the alliance’s military presence to its 1997 configuration while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.
His remarks follow an Oct. 25 report by The Telegraph, which cited diplomatic sources as saying Moscow could use renewed peace talks to secure concessions on NATO enlargement and military deployments near Russia’s borders.
According to the report, a potential Russian demand could involve withdrawing NATO forces from Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Finland, all of which border Russia.
The reported demand has not been confirmed as an official Russian negotiating position, and there is no indication that a NATO rollback has formally been added to the talks’ agenda.
The Kremlin has nevertheless signaled that it wants a broader discussion of European security. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 22 that future negotiations should address security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, as well as the “architecture of European security as a whole.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov has also argued that European countries should be involved in negotiations to end the war.
Zelensky said on Monday, Oct. 27, that Moscow’s security demands went beyond preventing Ukrainian attacks and amounted to an attempt to secure a separate agreement with NATO or the United States.
“They say: ‘If you want security guarantees for Ukraine, then we want them for Russia.’ We need to understand what Russia means by this. It is not simply about Ukraine refraining from striking Russia. For them, this is a much broader and more specific issue,” he said.
The president said discussions about broad security guarantees for Russia should wait until the terms for ending the war and Ukraine’s own security arrangements were clear.
“First, we need to resolve the issues related to this war, and only then seek answers to the questions Russia raises based on its own perceptions and expectations of security,” Zelensky said.
Moscow’s 1997 demands date back to before the invasion
Russia’s push to change NATO’s military posture in Europe predates its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In December 2021, Moscow presented the United States and NATO with draft security agreements that sought to halt further alliance enlargement, including Ukraine’s potential accession, and restrict military deployments in countries that joined NATO after May 1997.
NATO rejected Russia’s attempt to restrict its open-door policy, while saying it remained willing to discuss arms control and other security issues.
A return to NATO’s 1997 military configuration could have significant implications for the alliance’s eastern flank. Poland joined NATO in 1999, the Baltic states joined in 2004, and Finland became a member in 2023 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky said Russia’s renewed demands could reshape the wider European security architecture. He suggested Moscow had raised similar issues in talks with then-US President Joe Biden before launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
He argued that NATO members should determine the alliance’s military posture themselves, without negotiating those arrangements with Russia, which is not a member.
“Any retreat, any rollback of security, is a weakness for the alliance,” he said.
Trilateral talks could resume in November
The diplomatic maneuvering comes as Ukraine, Russia and the United States prepare to resume technical-level negotiations after a lengthy pause.
On Oct. 23, Zelensky said the next round of talks was expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi among the possible venues.
On Oct. 25, Ushakov said Moscow was ready to resume negotiations after Russia’s Nov. 4 National Unity Day holiday, describing the next meeting as preliminary and exploratory.
The format and participants remain unsettled, including whether European representatives will take part in a broader discussion of continental security.
Kyiv has insisted that any settlement must include credible security guarantees for Ukraine and prevent Russia from using a pause in hostilities to prepare for another attack.

Most of Britan’s nuclear missile submarine fleet now at sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:37:38 GMT
17:37:38 KST

Three of the Royal Navy’s four Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines are at sea at the same time, an arrangement naval sources described as unusual, according to reporting in The Times.
One of the boats is understood to be conducting the deterrent patrol, carrying Trident II D5 missiles, which is the task the Royal Navy has maintained without a break since 1969. The other two are believed to have been on sea trials and preparing to take over the patrol. HMS Victorious, the fourth boat, is at Devonport undergoing maintenance and was not among those at sea.
The Ministry of Defence declined to comment.
Having three boats out at once is not a sign of extra capacity, though, as the Vanguard class was designed around a four boat cycle in which one submarine is on patrol, one is working up or recovering, one is in training or trials, and one is in deep maintenance, and the fourth hull is what keeps continuous at sea deterrence going as the submarines age. Running three at sea at the same time means the cycle has been compressed, and it is as consistent with pressure on availability as it is with a deliberate signal.
The Times was told by a former senior naval source that the service had been operating in what submariners call 2BA, or two boat availability, for a prolonged period. In that condition only two of the four boats are available for operational tasking at any time, which leaves no margin, because a defect on the boat at sea has to be covered by a single relief.
The strain is visible in how long the boats are staying out, Navy Lookout reported in March 2025 that a Vanguard class submarine had returned to the Clyde after 204 days, breaking a record set in 2023, and patrols of more than two hundred days have since been reported again. Deterrent patrols were historically planned around three months. Crews now routinely spend five months or more submerged with no contact with their families.
Forces News reported last week, in an account of life aboard the boats, that Commander Roger Ireland, a retired submariner who served on the earlier Resolution class, described the length of modern Vanguard patrols as horrendous. Resolution boats carrying Polaris went out for around eight weeks at a time.
Maintenance has been the other great difficulty, and HMS Vanguard emerged from a refit at Devonport in 2023 that took around seven and a half years against a planned three and a half, after an unscheduled nuclear refuelling pushed the cost from roughly £200 million towards £500 million, as this publication reported when she sailed.
The four Vanguards entered service between 1993 and 1999 and were designed for around twenty five years each. All four are now beyond that, and they must hold the deterrent until the Dreadnought class arrives from the early 2030s. The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, covering Dreadnought, SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the infrastructure behind them.

Japan seeks to develop nuclear capability — China Arms Control and Disarmament Association
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:36:44 UTC
17:36:44 KST

BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan is seeking to develop a nuclear capability, according to Dai Huaicheng, Secretary-General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA).
"Since the current Japanese government took office, the country's right-wing forces have clearly demonstrated their ambitions to revive militarism, violate the 'three non-nuclear principles,' and pursue the creation of an indigenous nuclear arsenal - rapidly accelerating their progress along this misguided path. These statements are by no means isolated incidents; rather, they represent long-conceived, dangerous 'probing' steps that are part of a pre-planned strategy to 'gradually loosen restrictions in the nuclear sphere'," he stated.
Dai also noted that Japan’s current cabinet denies the country’s history of aggression during World War II, seeks to "whitewash the war crimes that were committed," and is actively pursuing remilitarization - all of which, he warned, "poses a serious threat to peace and stability in the region."
"As a non-nuclear-weapon state party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, Japan is bound under international law not to acquire, develop, possess, or proliferate nuclear weapons. There is no room for negotiation on this matter," Dai concluded.
Japan adheres to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles: not to possess, produce, or permit the introduction of nuclear weapons into its territory. Although these principles are not legally binding, successive Japanese prime ministers have reaffirmed their commitment to them. For decades, even discussing a possible revision was considered taboo. Some politicians have referred to an unwritten "fourth principle" - the prohibition on discussing the issue - and called for at least this constraint to be lifted.
Following Sanae Takaichi’s appointment as prime minister, media reports indicated that a review of Japan’s national security strategy would include discussions of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles. In particular, Takaichi was reported to be prepared to advocate lifting the ban on the introduction of US nuclear weapons into Japan.
Amid the reports, however, Takaichi stated that she had not instructed officials to revise the Three Non-Nuclear Principles as part of the deliberations on the updated national security strategy.

Villa Ginori, Versilia home of marquis Puccini dedicated La Bohème to, goes on market
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:34:42 CET
17:34:42 KST

Villa Ginori, a historic residence in the coastal Versilia area of Tuscany, in the province of Lucca, has gone onto the market with Lionard Luxury Real Estate (https://www.lionard.com/exclusive-historic-villa-on-lake-versil ia-hinterland.html). 
The home once belonged to Marquis Carlo Ginori Lisci, heir to the celebrated Ginori porcelain factory at Doccia and a close friend of Giacomo Puccini, who dedicated La Bohème to him. 
Overlooking Lake Massaciuccoli in Massarosa, the villa remains in the hands of descendants of the Ginori Lisci family. 
It preserves rooms once frequented by the composer, who lived across the lake in Torre del Lago, as well as Liberty-style decorations by Francesco Fanelli, a painter who studied under Giovanni Fattori. 
The estate owes its present appearance to Carlo Ginori Lisci. In 1887, the marquis acquired Lake Massaciuccoli and the surrounding land from the Minutoli family, transforming an existing building into a residence in the Tuscan neo-Gothic style. 
The villa's architectural character is defined by its direct relationship with the water. The lake extends beneath the building's great arches to a private covered boathouse, making it possible to reach the residence directly by boat. 
The same relationship continues inside, where the large windows of the loggia and winter garden open onto the lake. Irises, botanical motifs and Oriental-inspired lines by Fanelli, who was asked in 1900 by the marquis to decorate several rooms, echo the surrounding landscape across the walls. 
The estate comprises approximately 4,000 square metres of built space across eight buildings and 10 hectares of private land. 
Alongside the main villa, which measures about 1,200 square metres, stand an 800-square-metre 19th-century residence and a clubhouse created from a former boat shelter, as well as a chapel, a limonaia and other service buildings. 
The park, dotted with historic palm trees and exotic botanical species, is crossed by navigable canals. 
"The most authentic expression of Made in Italy is not only what we produce, but also what we have been able to build, preserve and pass on," said Dimitri Corti, Founder and CEO of Lionard Luxury Real Estate. 
"Villa Ginori represents a dimension of luxury that goes beyond the material value of a property. A building can be restored, transformed and adapted to new needs. What cannot be recreated is its history, its relationship with the people who lived there, and with the land to which it belongs. That is what makes certain places truly irreplaceable."

Chinese team reveals how brain neurons support flexible decision-making
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:56 CST
17:33:56 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese research team has revealed how brain neurons support flexible decision-making. According to a study recently published in Science, rule-related information and sensory information are compared within the same neuron, which itself takes part in cognitive computation.
Traditional theory holds that neurons are the basic structural and functional units of the nervous system. For a long time, most studies treated each neuron as a simple point-like unit that performs summation.
However, researches in brain science and artificial neural networks have found that higher cognitive functions such as flexible decision-making require the integration of massive contextual information and abstract rules, as well as dynamic adjustment of output. Such complexity is difficult to explain with the simple structure of point-like neurons.
Xu Ninglong, a researcher at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and his team designed a series of experiments in which mice heard different sounds and had to infer hidden rules. Once the mice had learned the current rules, the team changed the rules to see how quickly the mice adapted to the new logic. The team used two-photon microscopy to observe neurons in the mice's auditory cortex.
A neuron is like a tree with many branches. The cell body is the main part of the neuron, while dendrites are branch-like extensions. The distant branches are called apical dendrites.
The experiments found a clear division of labor within the same neuron. Apical dendrites mainly encode the abstract rule inferred by the mouse, while the cell body more strongly represents external auditory sensory input. The two types of signals undergo nonlinear integration within the neuron, producing a decision output that drives behavioral choice.
The experiments demonstrated that a single neuron is itself a microcomputer and that the interactions between a neuron's dendrites and cell body can perform decision-related cognitive computation. Only after a hypothesis has been verified multiple times and confirmed to be reliable does the brain slowly strengthen neuronal synapses and store the rule permanently.
The team found that although AI can also use context and existing information to adjust its answers, its mechanisms differ greatly from those of the brain. Large models mainly develop capabilities through training on data, whereas the brain combines experiential learning, internal states, and real-time information processing. Even a single neuron has a rich internal computational structure.
The team also found that the brain can support flexible behavior while using limited energy. Its biological mechanisms are worth studying for insights that could help make AI systems more flexible and more efficient. ■

Swiss village remains on alert over unstable Weisshorn Glacier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:33:45 UTC
17:33:45 KST

Swiss village remains on alert over unstable Weisshorn Glacier
The hanging glacier on the eastern side of the Weisshorn mountain above Randa, in southern Switzerland, will continue to be closely monitored and safety measures will remain in place due to the potential dangers, the authorities said on Tuesday.
Access to a local danger zone is still forbidden and access points for pedestrians and cyclists remain closed. The residential area is not affected by the current situation. Local authorities and experts are in close contact and are monitoring developments.
In mid-August, several rockfalls were recorded on the Weisshorn East hanging glacier. Due to a significant increase in movement, the authorities raised the monitoring to level 3 (on a scale of 1-5). Additional rockfalls have not been ruled out.
More
Swiss municipality raises alert level following glacier break-offs
Due to increased activity, movements on the glacier have been monitored since the end of June. A danger zone has been defined and marked out.
The first heavy snowfalls could significantly increase the risk of a glacier collapse, the Walliser Bote newspaper reported in mid-October. A block of ice measuring around 300,000 cubic metres remains suspended on the hanging glacier, moving downhill at a rate of up to 20 centimetres per day.
If a large amount of fresh snow were to fall on the Bis Glacier plateau below, a calving event could trigger a dangerous ice-and-snow avalanche. This would have a significantly greater reach than a pure ice calving event in summer.
More
Why do Swiss mountains collapse? It’s complicated
Repeated glacier break-offs on the Weisshorn
In the past, there have been repeated glacier break-offs on the Weisshorn. The largest historically documented event dates back to 1819. The avalanche triggered at that time is said to have caused extensive damage in the village of Randa. Further events in 1972 and 1973 were less severe and came to a halt on a glacier field.
The municipality of Randa has also historically been affected by other natural hazards. In 1991, a triple rockslide occurred on the Längenfluhberg. Within a few weeks, almost 50 million cubic metres of rock tumbled into the valley.
The rock masses buried the railway line and the main road. They also dammed up the River Vispa. No one was injured in the rockfalls, but livestock were killed and 33 buildings were destroyed.

Seven Chinese golfers set for Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:42 CST
17:33:42 KST

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Seven Chinese golfers, including four debutants, will compete at the 2026 Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship (AAC), which begins Thursday at Te Arai Links in New Zealand.
The 17th edition of the championship runs from October 29 to November 1 on Te Arai Links' South Course, with 120 players from 39 countries and regions competing in the 72-hole stroke-play event.
The winner will earn invitations to the 2027 Masters Tournament, the 155th Open Championship and the 131st Amateur Championship.
China's seven-player contingent comprises Zhou Ziqin, Wu Qiyou, Li Zhi, Hou Zenghao, Wang Yixiang, Liu Yiming and Cui Jingguo. Li, Wang, Liu and Cui will make their tournament debuts, while Zhou will be competing for the fifth time.
Zhou, 20, is ranked No. 55 in the World Amateur Golf Ranking and finished runner-up in 2024, one stroke behind compatriot Ding Wenyi.
"That was really close, just one shot back. But honestly, that was two years ago, and I believe my game has improved this season," Zhou said Wednesday.
"I wasn't playing my best for a period, but I played really well last season, and my game is starting to come back now."
Zhou said he was confident in his preparations but expected putting to play a decisive role on the links-style course.
"I think I did a good job preparing for this week, and I'm really ready. We have beautiful courses, and I feel like it's going to be a putting contest this week," he said.
Li, making his championship debut, said he was eager to test himself against the region's leading amateur golfers.
"I'm very happy to have the opportunity to play in the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship. Receiving the invitation is a recognition of my ability at this stage," Li said. "I believe I'll learn a lot and benefit from the experience."
Li added that the fairways, undulating greens and coastal winds would present a stern challenge.
"The fairways and greens are very firm, and the greens have considerable slopes. Combined with the wind, these factors will make the course challenging," he said.
Thailand's Fifa Laopakdee returns to defend his title in a tournament that has helped launch the careers of several leading golfers from the region.
Chinese players have won the championship five times, with Guan Tianlang claiming the title in 2012, Jin Cheng in 2015, Lin Yuxin in 2017 and 2019, and Ding Wenyi in 2024.
The championship was established by the Asia-Pacific Golf Confederation, The R&A and the Masters Tournament. ■

California governor signs orders to prepare for El Nino storms
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:31 CST
17:33:31 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom on Tuesday signed two executive orders, easing environmental requirements for flood-prevention work and requiring a risk review of Highway 1 ahead of potential El Nino storms.
The orders were signed at Crystal Cove State Park in Newport Beach, Southern California, following a statewide emergency declaration issued on Sept. 21, according to the governor's office.
One order allows the suspension of state requirements for eligible public-agency work to limit flooding, landslides, debris flows and erosion, while requiring advance eligibility approval and safeguards for fish, protected species and waterways.
The second order establishes a Highway 1 Task Force, convened by state transportation and natural resources agencies, to prepare the corridor for El Nino storms and address longer-term climate threats.
Highway 1 runs about 1,056 km along California's Pacific coast and has suffered repeated landslides and closures in the Big Sur area in recent years.
On Tuesday, the U.S. National Weather Service warned of significant coastal flooding in Orange and San Diego counties in Southern California until Thursday.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center said on Oct. 8 that there was a more than 83-percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Nino through January to March 2027. ■

Most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:27 CST
17:33:27 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families and before children turn 10, according to an Australian study.
The study analyzed Australian Child Maltreatment Study data from 8,503 Australians aged 16 and older, focusing on 2,623 individuals who reported experiencing physical abuse during childhood, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Curtin University.
One in four Australians aged 16 to 24 reported experiencing physical abuse by a family member. Family members were responsible for 85 percent of reported perpetration, while 4 percent occurred in institutional settings and 5 percent involved both family and institutional settings, the study found.
Among children abused before age 10, both parents were identified as perpetrators in one in three cases. Abuse involving both parents was also associated with the earliest onset and longest duration, according to the findings published in the journal Child Maltreatment.
Childhood physical abuse remains a major public health concern globally and is associated with substantial adverse mental, physical and social outcomes across the lifespan, said the researchers, noting that prevention efforts must extend beyond institutions and place greater emphasis on the home. ■

Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, called on Wednesday for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as partial election results showed their support would be crucial to reaching a governing coalition.
"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens (Palestinian Israelis)."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 54 seats in the 120-member Knesset, seven short of a governing majority, after 72.4 percent of votes were counted in Israel’s parliamentary elections, according to Israeli media.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 48 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were projected to win 18 seats, according to the daily Times of Israel, citing the Central Elections Committee.
Neither major bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. However, the combined projected tally for Eisenkot’s bloc and the Arab parties could exceed that threshold.
The predominantly Arab Joint List was projected to win 12 seats, while the United Arab List (Ra’am) was expected to secure four.
Among individual parties, Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to lead with 28 seats, followed by Eisenkot’s Yashar with 21.
The Together alliance was expected to secure 11.
The Democrats, United Torah Judaism and Yisrael Beiteinu were each projected to win eight seats, while Shas and Otzma Yehudit were expected to secure seven each.
Religious Zionism was projected to win six seats.
The results remain provisional and may change as vote counting continues.

‘Getting fully ready for war’: North Korea’s Kim calls for combat readiness by army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:30:39 UTC
17:30:39 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has said “primary” task of the country’s military commanders was to “getting fully ready” their units “for fighting a war,” stressing combat readiness, state media reported Wednesday.
Kim made the remarks during a photo session with participants in the third meeting of Company Leaders of the Korean People’s Army a day earlier, KCNA reported.
“The primary revolutionary task of the company leaders is to round off the combat preparations of their units for getting fully ready for fighting a war and the way for its implementation is to bring about a radical improvement in the strenuous and intensive training,” Kim said.
He called on the military commanders to “prove” their loyalty to the ruling Workers’ Party and the “revolution” through “proud successes in turning their companies into a-match-for-a-hundred ranks with firm revolutionary faith, patriotic spirit and matchless heroic mettle and fighting efficiency.”
Kim’s remarks come amid heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula following an explosion last month inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which separates North and South Korea, that wounded three South Korean soldiers.
Seoul blamed Pyongyang for the incident but said the two sides should resume military communication to ease tensions.
Pyongyang rejected the accusations and has yet to respond to the offer of talks. Both sides have written to the UN Security Council presenting their accounts of the Sept. 21 DMZ incident.

Brazil: Lula celebrates 81st birthday after re-election victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:30:31 UTC
17:30:31 KST

Standing behind a birthday cake, Lula blew out the candles, embraced supporters and addressed the gathering from a sound truck. Red Workers' Party flags waved alongside Brazilian flags as the crowd sang and cheered.
Still recovering from an exhausting election campaign, the president told supporters he needed to rest his voice. But he also took aim at his defeated rival Flávio Bolsonaro, questioning why he had reportedly left Brazil so soon after losing Sunday's presidential runoff.
Lula said he did not know Bolsonaro's exact whereabouts but wondered what guilt might drive someone to leave their country immediately after an electoral defeat. He also accused the Bolsonaro family of being excessively loyal to the United States. A senior US State Department official said Washington would grant visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family, although it remained unclear whether they had already left Brazil.
Bolsonaro, who has rejected the election result and made unsubstantiated fraud allegations, is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. A Supreme Court order required him to surrender his passports by midday Tuesday, but whether he had complied was unknown. His father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 defeat.

US Warns Gulf Countries of Possible New Military Operation Against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:30:29 UTC
17:30:29 KST

The United States has warned several Gulf Arab countries that it could resume military action against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Washington has reportedly urged regional countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign against Iran, using diplomatic and military channels to deliver the warning.
According to sources cited by the publication, the United States and Israel are considering a new wave of large-scale strikes against Iran.
The military is already taking preparatory steps. For example, flight-tracking data and information from two officials indicate that an additional Patriot air defense system is being transferred from Texas to Israel to strengthen its defenses against missile attacks.
US forces in the Middle East are replenishing ammunition stocks, while bomber and fighter aircraft prepare for possible strike operations.
In November, another carrier strike group and a Marine Corps unit could join the US force in the region, which currently consists of around 20 warships.
According to the WSJ, the US president has not yet made a final decision on a new military operation but is leaning toward large-scale strikes after the elections. Potential targets include Iran’s infrastructure and nuclear program facilities.
Tehran, in turn, has warned that it could retaliate by striking economic and civilian facilities in countries across the region. Despite previous hostilities, Iran retains a substantial stockpile of missiles and is rebuilding its ballistic weapons production capacity.
Amid the threat of renewed escalation, Iran has begun reinforcing its nuclear infrastructure and preparing its population for possible hostilities.
Militarnyi previously reported that Iran had developed a plan to attack undersea telecommunications cables in the Persian Gulf in the event of a resumption of war with the United States and Israel.
Tehran also plans to obstruct repairs to damaged cables to prolong communications disruptions across countries in the region.
