Deliver accountability for Tai Po fire tragedy or admit system is broken
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Deliver accountability for Tai Po fire tragedy or admit system is broken
Findings that result in blame for the private sector and low-level civil servants while leaving ministers untouched will not cut the ice with the public
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Mike Rowse is an independent commentator. 
One word will hang over the Hong Kong community in the run-up to next month’s anniversary of the dreadful Tai Po fire that took 168 of our fellow citizens’ lives: accountability. By the time we mark the occasion, we will know if we still have a system based on ministers taking political responsibility for failures in their policy areas or whether we must revise our constitutional arrangements.
The fire at Wang Fuk Court, which broke out on November 26 last year, traumatised the whole population of our city as well as devastating the lives of those directly involved, first responders, survivors and victims’ families alike. There was an outpouring of sympathy and support as people everywhere rallied to do what they could to help.
The government established a committee of inquiry, led by Justice David Lok Kai-hong, to ascertain what went wrong. The public hearings revealed a harrowing tale of poor professionalism, shoddy work and missed opportunities. The committee’s full report was handed over last week. Four government bodies – the Fire Services Department, Buildings Department, Labour Department and Independent Checking Unit of the Housing Bureau – were identified as being to some degree blameworthy.

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead with more than half of votes counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- As of 11:00 a.m. local time, just over 76% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."
Netanyahu's bloc trails in Israel election, exit polls say
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest single group in the Knesset, with 25 projected seats.
Challenger Gadi Eisenkot's bloc has emerged as the largest group with a projected 53, just ahead of the ruling coalition on 50, but well short of the 61 needed for a majority.
Neither bloc has a clear majority without the support of Arab parties.
These projected numbers are from public broadcaster Kan 11; other numbers vary by channel, but only slightly.
Polls closing around the country
It's now 10 p.m. across Israel, which means that polling stations around the country either should have closed or should be making preparations to do so as the last people in line cast their ballots.
Exit polls should follow shortly on Israeli television. These have a fairly good reputation overall but of course are only projections.
Results will start to trickle in through the night and are unlikely to be finalized until Wednesday.
And of course, there's every chance that even once the dust has settled and the final results are in, we will have a longer wait until there's clarity about who might be able to form a coalition government.
In any case, stick with us and we'll keep you posted.
Election commission sees 'no need to extend voting hours' after Netanyahu request
The Central Elections Committee has rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and some other groups to extend voting beyond 10 p.m. (2000 UTC/GMT).
"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.
The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.
For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.
The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.
IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign
Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.
DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.
High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc
The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.
According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.
Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.
Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.
Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.
Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.
This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.
The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.
And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.

The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.
For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.
The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.
IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign
Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.
DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.
High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc
The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.
According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.
Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.
Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.
Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.
Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.
This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.
The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.
And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.

EU: Frontex reform compounds risk of EU complicity in rights violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:28:27 UTC
17:28:27 KST

Responding to the European Commission’s proposed reform of the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation (the Frontex Regulation) that vastly expands the agency’s budget, powers, staff and mandate, without commensurately expanding its human rights safeguards and transparency obligations, Eve Geddie the Director of Amnesty International’s European Institutions Office said:
“The European Commission’s proposed changes to the Frontex mandate once again prioritize expanding the agency’s powers to deport, enforce border control, and operate beyond the EU without expanding the agency’s human rights obligations in turn.
“This includes giving Frontex new powers to carry out forced returns between non-EU countries, paving the way for a broader role in ‘return hubs’ in third countries. This reform compounds the risk of EU complicity in human rights violations and raises further hurdles to transparency and accountability. It should be rejected outright.
“Time and again we see the European Commission doubling down on Fortress Europe – increasing border security, surveillance and deportations without ever questioning the growing powers of an agency that has facilitated the trapping of people in human rights abuses.
“Frontex’s mandate explicitly requires respect, protection and promotion of human rights. Yet instead of addressing structural deficiencies and flawed approaches that fuel violations and abuses against people at Europe’s borders, today’s decision will turbocharge this flawed approach in countries outside the EU.
“As people across Europe protest over access to housing, and underfunding of education and public services, the European Commission continues to present migration control as the continent’s existential challenge, and to disproportionately pour resources into deportations and border enforcement. A fundamental reassessment of its priorities is long overdue.”
Background
On 27 October, the European Commission presented two proposals: an amendment to the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation increasing the number of Frontex officers to 30,000, giving the agency a greater role in returns and ‘crisis response’, as well as a regulation to digitalize return, readmission and reintegration procedures.
Amnesty International has long followed the work of Frontex, acting as a member of its Consultative Forum on Fundamental Rights from its inception in 2012 until the end of 2022. A series of reforms of Frontex have rapidly expanded its powers, budget, and operational capacity since its creation in 2004, with its budget ballooning to over €1 billion annually for 2026.
Amnesty International has raised concerns over the role of Frontex’s maritime aerial surveillance activities in the Mediterranean in illegal interceptions of refugees and migrants by the Libyan Coast Guard.
Amnesty International has also consistently questioned Frontex’s continuation of operations in EU countries adopting practices that are incompatible with EU law on asylum and migration, urging it to take swift action in cases of reported or alleged fundamental rights violations, and to initiate proceedings in line with the requirements in Article 46 of the existing Frontex Regulation to suspend or terminate its operations in such cases.

German drone maker unveils armed version of its Reliant spy drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:28:02 UTC
17:28:02 KST

- Quantum-Systems showed its Reliant long-range drone carrying a mixed load of 82 mm mortar rounds and 40 mm grenades.
- U.S. chief executive Dave Sharpin shared images of the armed configuration on social media and thanked partners from Orbital.
Quantum-Systems has unveiled an armed version of its Reliant long-range drone, showing the aircraft fitted with a mixed load of 82 mm mortar rounds and 40 mm grenades.
Dave Sharpin, chief executive of Quantum-Systems Inc., the U.S. arm of the German drone maker, shared images of the configuration on social media on Oct. 28, thanking partners from Orbital for their work on the project. The photos show the munitions carried on the drone’s wing hardpoints, combining two calibers on a single aircraft.
Each caliber gives the drone a different kind of strike: the 82 mm round, the standard size for medium mortars in many armies, carries a heavier explosive charge suited to larger targets, while the 40 mm grenade, the size fired by infantry grenade launchers, is smaller and lighter, so several can be carried and released one at a time against individual targets. Mixing the two lets an operator choose the right weapon for each target found during the same flight.
Reliant is a fixed-wing drone that takes off and lands vertically, so it can launch from a small clearing or a ship deck and then cruise like an airplane without a runway. Quantum-Systems introduced it at SOF Week in Tampa in May 2024 as a Group 2 aircraft with a 3.9 m (12.8-foot) wingspan and more than 10 hours of endurance from a hybrid-electric power system, and in July 2026 it announced an upgraded version with greater payload capacity, a maximum takeoff weight of 45 kg (99 pounds) and integration into the company’s MOSAIC UXS software, which lets operators control several types of unmanned systems together.
The armed configuration grows out of a version Quantum-Systems developed for U.S. customers, with hardpoints on each wing that can carry additional modules and release munitions or smaller drones. The company has also presented Reliant as a carrier for the Archer first-person-view attack drone built by U.S. manufacturer Neros, whose Archer the Pentagon has ordered in large numbers and which the U.S. Marine Corps recently flew with live warheads in Japan.
Reliant sits at the top of Quantum-Systems’ family of aircraft, above the short-range Twister and the mid-range Vector, the reconnaissance drone that made the company’s name in Ukraine. Sharpin has said Vector has flown more than 20,000 combat hours in Ukraine, and the company has fed that experience back into its designs, including after a Vector returned from a mission despite being hit 11 times by small arms fire. Quantum-Systems has also expanded production inside Ukraine, where it now builds Vector fuselages locally.
Quantum-Systems has offered Reliant to the German military as well as to U.S. buyers, and the armed version adds a strike option to an aircraft the company has so far marketed for long-range reconnaissance, surveillance and target acquisition.

Ukrainian mobile operator Kyivstar acquires cloud provider GigaCloud for nearly $50 mln

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:27:22 EET
17:27:22 KST

Kyivstar Group Ltd. (Nasdaq: KYIV), the parent company of Ukraine's largest telecommunications operator, Kyivstar, has announced the acquisition of GigaCloud, one of Ukraine's leading cloud infrastructure providers, for nearly UAH 2.28 billion (almost $50 million) to expand its cloud solutions capabilities for businesses.
"By combining these strengths with our telecommunications infrastructure, customer reach and investment capabilities, we will be able to help even more companies modernize their operations and develop a stronger technology business for the enterprise segment," Kyivstar Group Ltd. President Oleksandr Komarov was quoted as saying in a press release.
He added that the acquisition would help develop infrastructure that Ukraine will need over the long term.
The transaction is expected to close after the standard closing conditions for deals of this kind have been met. GigaCloud will continue operating as a separate business unit within Kyivstar Group Ltd., retaining its own brand and management team.
In particular, the company's founders are expected to continue running the business.
The agreement also provides for no changes to existing customer contracts, service levels or commercial terms.
"Together with Kyivstar Group Ltd., we will be able to accelerate infrastructure investment, expand our market presence and continue providing services at the level of quality our customers expect," GigaCloud CEO and co-founder Nazarii Kurochko said in the press release.
GigaCloud co-founder Anton Khvastunov, in turn, emphasized that the partnership would strengthen the company's ability to scale secure cloud services and enable it to continue contributing to Ukraine's digital development.
Kyivstar added that the investment would expand the operator's technological capabilities for the corporate sector, further strengthen its capabilities in sovereign cloud infrastructure and enable the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-based services tailored to the needs of Ukrainian businesses and government institutions.
Founded in 2016, GigaCloud currently serves more than 1,800 corporate customers. The company specializes in providing relevant services to businesses. Its clients include agricultural holding company Kernel, Naftogaz and others.
The mobile operator's press release specifies that, according to unaudited management accounts, GigaCloud generated approximately $14 million in revenue and $4.7 million in EBITDA in 2025, corresponding to an EBITDA margin of approximately 34%.
"The agreement is expected to have a positive impact on the development of Kyivstar Group Ltd. The transaction valuation takes into account GigaCloud's growth rate, expertise in cloud technologies, leading market position and the expected benefits of combining the businesses," Kyivstar said.
The transaction structure includes $41 million in acquisition consideration, up to $4 million in deferred debt obligations, approximately $3 million in payments tied to the achievement of agreed performance targets, and up to $2 million in compensation for capital expenditures (CAPEX), in accordance with the terms of the deal.
As reported in the summer of this year, the Antimonopoly Committee of Ukraine authorized Kyivstar Private Joint Stock Company to acquire control of GigaCloud LLC, the cloud provider operating under the GigaCloud brand.
In June 2025, the mobile operator launched its own cloud service for Ukrainian users, Kyivstar Cloud, which is available to small, medium-sized and large businesses, as well as public-sector organizations.
Kyivstar increased its revenue by 29.1% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, reaching UAH 28.9 billion, while revenue in U.S. dollar terms rose by 22.8% to $662 million. Kyivstar's net profit for the period increased by 36.1% compared with the first half of 2025, reaching UAH 7.1 billion, while net profit in U.S. dollar terms rose by 28.8% to $162 million.

US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion: Pentagon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:25:48 UTC
17:25:48 KST

Breadcrumb
US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion, according to Pentagon estimate
The US military has spent over $47 billion so far for the war on Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department's estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.
The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the 3 November midterm election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
The war's impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon's latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called "platform losses," which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.
Trump's initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran's defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.
Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.
While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military's Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.

Lawyers frame India's Kashmir rule as 'settler-colonial', like Israeli occupation of Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:25:28 UTC
17:25:28 KST

The Worldwide Lawyers Association (WOLAS) has accused India of implementing a dangerous plan of "assimilation, dispossession, and settler colonialism" in India-administered Kashmir, likening it to Israeli occupation practices in Palestine and announcing the initiation of legal proceedings under universal jurisdiction in foreign courts against Indian officials linked to rights abuses in the region.
Members of WOLAS, who released their damning report titled "Longest Siege: Settler Colonialism and Structural Violence in Indian Occupied Jammu Kashmir" to mark the 79th anniversary of landing of Indian troops in Jammu and Kashmir following 73 days of Kashmir's independence — an occasion commemorated by many Kashmiris and Pakistan as "Black Day" — said they aim to bring human rights violations in Kashmir before courts worldwide under universal jurisdiction.
During a press conference in Istanbul on Monday, WOLAS Chairman Enes Kafadar stressed that although Kashmir is geographically distant from Türkiye, it is "historically, culturally, and strategically close."
Kashmir was introduced to Islam in the 14th century by Turkic Sufi Bulbul Shah, Kafadar noted, recalling support of subcontinent Muslims to Türkiye during the War of Independence.
He highlighted parallels between Kashmir and Palestine, arguing, "The drones in the skies of Kashmir are Israeli-made Herons. The weapons pointed at the people in the streets are Israeli-made Tavor rifles. Lawyers, human rights defenders, and journalists are being wiretapped with Israeli-made Pegasus spyware."
"The suffering experienced by the Palestinian people and the Kashmiri people is very interconnected," the WOLAS chairman added.
Kafadar stated that WOLAS aims to activate international legal mechanisms through the reports it prepares, adding, "This report is not actually an end result, but the beginning of a legal operation."
"It is precisely at this point that we, as the Lawyers of the World Association, aim with this report to bring the human rights violations in Kashmir to many courts around the world under universal jurisdiction and to ensure that those responsible are held accountable."
'Israeli officials were present in torture centres in Kashmir'
Kafadar stated the report shows events in India-administered Kashmir are "planned assimilation and settler colonialism" by New Delhi breaching international law, not a mere security or border dispute.
He stated that several UNSC resolutions mandate Kashmir's status be decided via plebiscite, adding India's 2019 revocation of Article 370 and annexation of the region breached UN resolutions and the right to self-determination.
He said the new residency laws imposed by India in the disputed region breach the Fourth Geneva Convention, "granting outsiders rights to reduce Kashmiris to a minority in their own homeland."
"The colonial methods of repression in the occupied West Bank and Gaza are being transferred to [India-administered] Kashmir," Kafadar added.
He said that an information blackout persists in Kashmir, with journalists detained, their passports revoked, civil society organisations shut down, and books seized.
"While the Indian administration uses Bollywood productions and media manipulation to present the occupation to the world public as an 'internal security' issue, it is simultaneously implementing the colonial repression methods that Israel uses in the West Bank and Gaza in Kashmir," he added.
Kafadar said while Indian diplomats openly declare that they are basing their operations in the region on Israel's illegal settlement model, "witness statements in files submitted to the UK Metropolitan Police War Crimes Unit indicate that Israeli officials were present in interrogation and torture centres in Kashmir."
During the Israeli genocide in Gaza, the WOLAS chairman said they identified Israeli soldiers guilty of war crimes and sought Interpol Red Notices against them under universal jurisdiction, vowing to pursue Indian officials next.
"Today, we publicly announce that we are also pursuing the same legal mechanism against Indian military and civilian officials who committed crimes of torture, demolition with explosives, arbitrary executions, and demographic displacement in Kashmir," he promised.
Seven concrete steps
Hasan Basri Bulbul, a member of the WOLAS Board of Directors who presented the key issues highlighted in the 95-page report, said New Delhi has been rapidly changing the demographic structure in India-administered Kashmir since 2019.
Bulbul revealed that India had imposed 890 federal laws on the region, repealed 205 local laws, and amended 130 others, calling for the establishment of a UN Commission of Inquiry to investigate human rights violations and for those responsible to be prosecuted under universal jurisdiction.
In August 2022, he said, approximately 2.5 million new voters (a 30 percent increase) were added to the electoral rolls by granting voting rights to Indian citizens temporarily residing in the disputed region. 
Bulbul said that India-administered Kashmir has the highest military-to-civilian ratio in the world "with over 900,000-armed Indian personnel", adding "not a single military officer has been allowed to be prosecuted in civilian courts for 36 years under the Special Powers of the Armed Forces Act (AFSPA)."
Between 2019 and 2026, he said, 26,129 arbitrary detentions were recorded under draconian laws such as Public Safety Act (PSA) and the Prevention of Unlawful Activities Act (UAPA). With convictions below 1 percent, he said, massive indictments and prolonged detention serve as punishment before any verdict. 
The WOLAS official accused India of violating privacy of Kashmiris through household-level biometric registration and digital identity applications, "while the archives of local newspapers and human rights monitoring organisations are seized."
"As of September 2026, 4,249 books have been removed from circulation from universities and libraries; journalists, lawyers, and academics have had their passports revoked, systematically restricting their freedom of travel. Eid prayers at the central Friday Mosque and Eid Prayer Ground (Eidgah) in Srinagar have been blocked for eight consecutive years, including May 2026," he added.
Bulbul said the international community and legal institutions could implement seven concrete steps without requiring India’s consent or approval — implementation of UN Special Procedures and the establishment of an independent commission of inquiry, making legal applications in third states under universal jurisdiction based on documented concrete facts, implementing targeted sanctions against officials responsible for violations committed under AFSPA protection, and observance of human rights conditionality in international trade relations and defence transfers.
The steps he suggested also include continuous independent field and evidence documentation activities in accordance with international verification standards, requesting an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice via the UN General Assembly on the repeal of Article 370 and the conformity of the settlement regime with Article 49(6) of the Fourth Geneva Convention, and establishing a permanent Peoples' Tribunal that will convene at regular intervals to challenge the policy of invisibility. 
New Delhi has not responded to the report yet.
India and Pakistan each administer a part of Kashmir, but both claim the territory in its entirety. The neighbouring rivals have fought two of their three wars over the territory since they gained independence in 1947. China also administers a portion of Kashmir, known as Aksai Chin, following the defeat of India in the 1962 Sino-Indian War — making the Himalayan region the world's only nuclear tri-junction.
Rebel Kashmiris in the New Delhi-administered portion of Kashmir have been fighting Indian rule since 1989. The majority of Muslim Kashmiris support deciding the future of the region through a UN-mandated plebiscite.
India claims the Kashmir revolt is funded by Pakistan. Islamabad denies the charge and insists it only lends Kashmiris moral, political and diplomatic support. Many Kashmiris consider it a legitimate freedom struggle. Tens of thousands of civilians, rebels and Indian troops have been killed in the conflict.
India has deployed more than 500,000 troops to the region, making it one of the planet's most militarised zones.

The first snow in Kyiv - forecasters have issued a forecast
Kyiv • UNN
Precipitation is possible in Kyiv on November 6, with a probability of up to 90%. Due to temperatures around zero, it may fall as snow.
Kyiv may see its first snow as early as next week — on November 6. The probability of snowfall will reach 85%. This was reported by UNN, citing the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center.
Details
According to the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center, nighttime temperatures in Kyiv will be around +1°C. This figure is forecast at midnight, 3:00 a.m., and 6:00 a.m. In the morning, however, the temperature will rise to +2°C.
When precipitation is possible
The highest probability of precipitation is forecast at midnight — 90%. At 3:00 a.m. it will be 83%, at 6:00 a.m. — 76%, and at 9:00 a.m. it will fall to 70%. By noon, the probability of precipitation will be 63%. Due to temperatures close to zero, the precipitation may fall as snow. At the same time, the forecast does not specify the type of precipitation separately.
The Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center notes, however, that the forecast for days 6–9 is advisory in nature.

Dutch population density keeps rising, highest in mainland EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:23:53 UTC
17:23:53 KST

Dutch population density keeps rising, highest in mainland EU
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands had 539 people per square metre of land at the start of this year, up 15% since 2000, according to new figures by national statistics bureau CBS.
The population grew from 15.9 million to 18.1 million over the same period, and the country is now the most densely populated in the EU after Malta.
Single-person households are most common in university towns. In Wageningen they make up 63% of all households and in Groningen 61%. Delft, Maastricht and Leiden are all above 55%. In Amsterdam the figure is 55%, and in Utrecht and Eindhoven 51%.
Zuid Holland is the most crowded province, with more than 1,400 people per square kilometre, seven times as many as Drenthe at 193. Flevoland grew fastest, with density up 47% since 2000. In Limburg the figure has barely changed.
The Hague is the most densely populated city, with 6,900 people per square kilometre, ahead of Leiden (5,900) and Haarlem (5,800). Amsterdam has just under 5,000. Rotterdam ranks lower because its municipality includes the port, which covers 12.5 hectares of land and water and is over 40 kilometres long.
The government’s latest forecast puts the national housing shortage at 4.6%, or 384,000 homes. It expects the number of households to rise to 9.3 million by 2041. Successive cabinets have set plans to build 100,000 new homes per year, but the targets have never been met.

Two weeks before Starlink’s speed cap hit Ukraine’s drones, a Ukrainian test satellite went up on a SpaceX rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:21:56 UTC
17:21:56 KST

A test satellite for a future communications network under Ukrainian control is working in orbit, Ukraine’s Himera and Denmark’s GomSpace said on 27 October. The companies say it will work for Ukraine’s strategic security, and that the long-term aim is to rely less on foreign communications providers. Public launch records for the mission do not list a satellite by that name, though some of its objects are still unidentified.
Ukraine fights Russia on satellite links it doesn’t control, and the announcement comes two weeks after it saw what depending on an outside provider can cost. The satellite, the companies say, went up on 1 October, before that trouble began. Overnight on 14 October, Starlink and its military version, Starshield, began dropping links on fast-moving terminals, and Ukrainian officials said the cap disrupted drone missions. On 24 October, 10 days after the cap began, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported speeds restored. Who ordered the cap remains contested. That same day, Elon Musk wrote that Ukraine’s military had violated Starlink’s terms of service and that “that loophole was closed last week,” a claim a Ukrainian presidential adviser disputed.
What the companies say, and what launch records show
Obria Nano flew on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission, the release said. Aalborg-based GomSpace built it on Himera’s order, Himera co-founder and CEO Misha Rudominski wrote on Facebook. He added that the team received the first signals the next day and that the satellite is now working. Its tests are meant to inform the design of the full Obria system, the release said.
The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays
No satellite called Obria Nano appears on SpaceX’s published list for the mission, The Insider found. Public tracking catalogs show one Ukrainian satellite from that launch, named UASAT-Nano. Another 26 objects from the mission are still listed with placeholder names and no confirmed owner. The outlet said it is unclear whether the two names refer to one satellite.
UASAT-Nano is the satellite network Stetman, another Ukrainian company, is building, and its founder said the network’s first test satellite would launch in October. In April, Stetman and GomSpace agreed to set up a joint venture called UASAT and planned a first launch for fall 2026. The Obria release does not mention Stetman or UASAT.
Production in Ukraine is the stated next step
Rudominski wrote that Himera’s next stage is to produce satellites and ground terminals in Ukraine. He called it important not only to use the technology but also to gradually build domestic expertise and manufacturing.
“For us, this project is about more than launching a satellite. It is an opportunity to lay the foundation for an independent communications network for Ukraine,” Rudominski said in the release.
In the long run, the network would cover all of Ukraine and complement European satellite networks, the release said. The network does not exist yet, and Himera has given no timeline.
“Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
Replacing Starlink will not be quick. Lance Hunter, a political scientist at Augusta University, told Time that Ukraine cannot quickly swap out such technology, since diversifying it “takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of resources.” Meanwhile, one Ukrainian interceptor-drone maker has begun rethinking its air-launched designs after the slowdown.

Burials in nature are growing in popularity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:15:34 UTC
17:15:34 KST

In the Vinderhoutse Bossen in Ghent, a new site is being created to allow people to have their ashes buried in a natural way, without an urn. Funeral directors are also receiving more enquiries about this kind of option, notes funeral director Gerrit Cispa from Drongen: “The demand for new forms of burial in Ghent, closer to nature, is gradually increasing.”
Burials in nature are growing in popularity
The new natural burial site forms part of the Vinderhoutse Bossen woodland area. Unlike in a traditional cemetery, no urns are buried here. The ashes are buried in the natural environment, without an urn or any other container.
“It is not actually a cemetery, but a nature site that forms part of a nature reserve,” says Gerrit Cispa of the Cispa funeral home. “That is why no urns are buried here. In Drongen, however, an urn is required at the burial site. We are seeing an increase in the number of enquiries we receive for that location, but the whole thing is still in its infancy.”
Drongen is Ghent’s first natural burial ground and opened in 2021. Over the first four years, ashes were scattered on 46 occasions, and 67 biodegradable urns were buried. No memorials are permitted, and a plot is granted for 25 years.
Growing interest in natural burials
According to Gerrit Cispa, interest in natural burials has grown in recent years. “People are increasingly opting for a farewell ceremony in which nature plays a central role. This can be achieved by burying an urn, but also by having the ashes buried directly in nature or by choosing to scatter them.”
“There is an increasing demand for urns to be buried in a natural way, returning them to nature. It is a trend that is gradually gaining ground,” says Gerrit Cispa. “Ash scattering is also more frequently taking place at natural burial grounds.”
According to the funeral director, the traditional burial in a coffin at a conventional cemetery has been losing popularity for some time. “Those figures have been falling for quite a while. There are more new forms that are also in greater demand. People want to say their goodbyes in a more environmentally friendly way.”
Information session on Vinderhoutse Bossen
During an information session organised by the City of Ghent, Gerrit Cispa was briefed on the new site. The city has laid out new paths to guide visitors to the nature reserve. The funeral director has already visited the site himself and describes it as a beautiful, newly developed area.
However, the space available for natural burials is limited. “For the time being, part of the nature reserve has been set aside for this purpose. I believe there is currently a limit of 1,250 plots. But further expansion may be possible in the future, although that depends on the city’s future plans.”

U.S. Army pilots test MV-75 tiltrotor in simulators before its first flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:15:07 UTC
17:15:07 KST

- U.S. Army aviators and National Guard officers took part in the sixth MV-75 Cheyenne II Special User Evaluation at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, Aug. 24–28, 2026.
- Participants flew a virtual prototype, compared Chinook and Black Hawk cockpits, and practiced maintenance in virtual reality to inform the tiltrotor’s design.
U.S. Army aviators and National Guard aviation officers spent a week this summer flying a virtual MV-75 Cheyenne II, critiquing cockpits and rehearsing maintenance in virtual reality, as the service brings soldiers into the tiltrotor’s design before the first test aircraft has flown.
The sixth MV-75 Special User Evaluation ran Aug. 24 to 28 at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, according to an Army statement published Oct. 27 by the program’s acquisition office. Participants came from the MV-75 Operational Development Team, a group of aviators, crew chiefs and maintainers based at Fort Rucker, Alabama, and from a National Guard advisory working group with representatives from Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, New York and Pennsylvania. The Army has not released findings from the evaluation, and the account describes what participants did and how the program will use their feedback without saying whether any design changes resulted.
Special User Evaluations put the people who will fly and fix an aircraft into its development cycle early, so that problems with workload, human-systems integration and maintenance surface while they are still cheap to correct. For this session, crews worked through the MV-75 virtual prototype to learn the crew station and flew simulated missions over terrain to assess tiltrotor flight dynamics, vertical-lift controls and conversion from helicopter mode to high-speed airplane mode. At the Army’s Advanced Prototyping Engineering and Experimentation Laboratory, aviators compared the cockpit layouts of the CH-47 Chinook and UH-60 Black Hawk to identify features worth keeping and usability problems worth avoiding, and they flew familiarization sorties in an MD 530 helicopter with the Army Flight Test Directorate to assess its cockpit. The program office said it will consolidate that comparative feedback and use it in technical discussions with Bell, the aircraft’s builder.
Maintainers used virtual-reality interfaces to practice removing and replacing major components, and participants also reviewed cybersecurity, infrastructure and acquisition lifecycle requirements. Staff Sgt. Eric Lopez of the Operational Development Team said the aircraft’s upgraded electronics, maintenance packages and technical manuals would simplify sustainment for soldiers, an assessment that cannot yet be tested on real hardware.
The National Guard participants focused on how the aircraft would be used at home. CW4 Darren Frey of the Colorado National Guard and the High Altitude Army National Guard Aviation Training Site said the MV-75’s longer range and faster transit could let states centralize fleet maintenance at a single hub while still covering the whole state for rapid-response missions, potentially reducing infrastructure and maintenance requirements. Col. Jim Mandel of the Idaho National Guard said the officers in the working group advise their states’ adjutants general on positioning aviation assets for state and federal missions.
Maj. J.T. Hingey, deputy team chief of the Operational Development Team, said the evaluation was the team’s first in-person engagement with the project manager and the flight test directorate. He said flying the virtual prototype under the guidance of experimental test pilots with V-22 Osprey experience gave the Fort Rucker team insight it will use to improve its own simulator, refine tactics, techniques and procedures, and brief senior Army leaders. He also stressed the need for a shared understanding of the program baseline and the outside factors that affect it, so the aviation enterprise can stay aligned when funding, schedules or other variables change.
The MV-75 is the production version of Bell’s V-280 Valor demonstrator, which first flew on Dec. 18, 2017, and won the Future Long Range Assault Aircraft competition in December 2022. The program reached Milestone B, the formal start of engineering and manufacturing development, in August 2024, and in April 2026 the Army officially named the aircraft the Cheyenne II, the first all-new platform to enter its inventory since the 1980s. The 101st Airborne Division’s combat aviation brigade has been selected as the first unit to receive it.
The company completed the first MV-75 wing in February and said it took 90% fewer labor hours than the first V-22 wing, an efficiency it attributes to the aircraft’s digital design. By midsummer the first six test aircraft were in various stages of assembly, with final assembly at Amarillo, Texas, and fuselages built at a new center in Wichita, Kansas. The first gearbox has been completed, and testing on the first flight control computers has started in Bell’s weapon systems integration lab.
The schedule is less settled. The Army sharply accelerated the program in early 2026, pulling initial fielding forward to 2027 from a previous target of around 2031, but at the April naming ceremony officials declined to commit to first flight or production dates. Funding then interrupted the work: after fiscal 2026 money for the program ran out in July, the Army and Bell went through a three-month communications blackout under federal funding rules and only resumed program discussions in October. The Army’s fiscal 2027 request includes $2.1 billion in research and development funding for the MV-75, up from $350 million in fiscal 2026, and Bell said meetings with the government are planned to agree on a feasible baseline schedule.
The Operational Development Team’s work at Fort Rucker draws heavily on the V-22, the only tiltrotor in U.S. military service, which the U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Air Force have operated since 2007. The MV-75 differs from the Osprey in a key respect: its engines stay fixed in the nacelles while only the rotors and driveshafts tilt, and a driveshaft through the wing lets one engine power both rotors. The Army has never flown a tiltrotor, so the team is using virtual prototypes and joint-service V-22 lessons to build tiltrotor expertise, streamline pilot training and prepare units before the first aircraft arrive.
The aircraft’s speed will also force changes around it. The Army has said the MV-75 is designed to fly roughly twice as far and twice as fast as its current helicopters, and Army officials have noted that the AH-64 Apache, which normally escorts assault helicopters, tops out at about 300 km/h (185 mph), well below the tiltrotor’s planned cruise of more than 480 km/h (300 mph). The Black Hawk, which the MV-75 is meant to partly replace, is expected to remain in service into the 2050s.

U.S. Intelligence Reveals Images of Chinese Spaceplane for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:14:03 UTC
17:14:03 KST

China has developed a reusable spaceplane that combines aircraft and spacecraft features and resembles the American X-37B spaceplane.
The U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency released a photograph of the vehicle in its report on space threats.
The Chinese spaceplane was captured in satellite imagery taken by Maxar in 2024.
Spaceplanes can operate at the boundary between the atmosphere and space, enter orbit, and return to Earth.
For the military, these vehicles primarily provide access to space, test new technologies, and potentially support military operations.
The vehicle is believed to be called Shenlong. It is launched aboard a Long March 2F rocket.
At least four missions involving vehicles of this type are known. The first launched on September 4, 2020, the second on August 4, 2022, the third on December 14, 2023, and the fourth on February 7 of this year.
The spacecraft spent 276 days in orbit during its second mission and 266 days during its third.
Reliance on expendable spacecraft makes access to space expensive and limited.
Although reusable technologies require more complex and costly development, they can significantly reduce spaceflight costs by allowing spacecraft to be recovered, repaired, and reused.
“At present, the United States is the only country with an operational reusable launch vehicle program, while Beijing hopes to become the second,” the U.S. intelligence report states.
Chinese space companies are developing reusable launch vehicles to help Beijing achieve broader military, civilian, and commercial objectives in space.
In the United States, Boeing developed the X-37B, an unmanned spacecraft designed to carry out similar missions. NASA initiated the project but later transferred it to the military. The X-37B made its first spaceflight in 2010.
The X-37B has an 8.28-meter fuselage and a 4.6-meter wingspan. According to publicly available sources, the vehicle has a maximum takeoff weight of 4,990 kg.
The X-37B can carry a payload of up to 900 kg into space. Its stated maximum speed is approximately 28,200 km/h.

Swiss cantons give green light for modernisation of EuroAirport
The cantonal governments of Basel City and Basel Country have approved the extension of EuroAirport's terminal.
The project involves the investment of €157 million (CHF145 million) and is aimed at modernising the infrastructure and improving passenger handling.
The airport authorities will finance the project, the two Basel cantons said on Tuesday. However, the investment decision by the airport’s board of directors requires approval from the relevant authorities in Switzerland and France. On the Swiss side, this is granted by the federal government in agreement with the two cantons.
More
Euroairport Basel-Mulhouse announces eight new destinations for summer
According to an earlier statement by the airport, the plans include a 14,000-square-metre extension on the east façade of the existing terminal, as well as a comprehensive refurbishment of a 15,000-square-metre area in the old part of the airport building. Construction is set to begin in 2027, with completion planned for 2030/2031.
The government says the project will improve operational efficiency as well as the quality of service and the passenger experience. No additional capacity for aircraft handling will be created. The modernisation meets high standards of environmental sustainability both during the construction phase and in subsequent operation.

Kyiv's housing market feels the chill as residents escape ahead of winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:11:43 UTC
17:11:43 KST

As temperatures are falling in Kyiv, so are rent prices, with residents leaving the capital to escape Russian bombardment and the prospect of a winter without heating and electricity.
Over the last two months, the number of long-term rentals listed on Kyiv's market shot up by 66%, Alona Babko, head of public relations at LUN, a leading real estate portal in Ukraine, told the Kyiv Independent.
The sharp rise in vacancies started in August, as Russia stepped up attacks on Kyiv, causing civilian casualties to increase. The trend has deepened with renewed strikes on energy facilities and fears that the capital will endure another winter without heating and electricity, prompting residents to pack their bags and look elsewhere.
With more housing options on the market, and the competition it brings, rental prices have been declining since July, falling by 6% in the last month to an average of 17,000 hryvnias ($377) per month for a one-bedroom apartment — the lowest in a year — Babko said.
"We’re now seeing a trend of more and more people vacating their apartments. A lot of people are moving to safer places. Some are going abroad, while others are choosing Ukraine’s western regions," Oleksandra, a realtor in Kyiv, told the Kyiv Independent.
"It’s not just individuals, either. Companies that had branches here are relocating them to places such as Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk. Naturally, the people who work for those companies are moving there, too."
Oleksandra, as well as a landlord the Kyiv Independent spoke to for the story, declined to give their last names, citing security concerns that are not evident given the nature of the story. The request to remain anonymous may say more about the informal nature of Ukraine’s real estate sector.
Anna, a landlord who declined to provide her full name, hasn’t been able to rent out her empty apartment in central Kyiv for around a month. It used to only take her a week to find a new tenant, she told the Kyiv Independent.
Now, she is considering shaving $100 off her rent to attract renters, although she still hopes to find someone to pay the full price — $800.
read also
Unsurprisingly, rents are cheapest in parts of the city that frequently suffer attacks — usually the industrial neighborhoods on the eastern side of the Dnipro River. With Russia continuously targeting warehouses, factories, and power plants in these districts, demand is dropping as some residents relocate to the western side of the city.
The recent Russian strikes on Kyiv’s bridges connecting the western and eastern banks have also alarmed residents, Olena Haydamakha, president of Ukraine’s Association of Realtors, told the Kyiv Independent. After the first wave of strikes in early October, her colleagues in western Ukraine were flooded with calls from anxious Kyivans.
"Most people said they wanted to secure an apartment in advance. If the situation deteriorated, they would then move to that apartment," she said.
While Kyiv’s rents fall, prices in cities in western Ukraine are soaring, Babko said. Currently, rents in Lviv, Uzhhorod, and Ivano-Frankivsk have surpassed those in Kyiv — historically the country’s most expensive city — even rivaling prices in EU capitals, drawing criticism on social media.
"I read the news about the hard winter, the problems with power and heating, and decided to see how much it costs to rent housing in other Ukrainian cities. I found a one-room apartment in Uzhhorod for $1,500 a month. So if you decide to leave the capital, you’ll have to pay three to five times more for housing?" one Facebook user from Vyshhorod, Kyiv Oblast, wrote on Oct. 11.
But many Kyivans can’t afford to move away because rents are so high in other regions or because they cannot leave their jobs and families.
With no choice but to remain in the city, or because they are reluctant to leave, many are relocating to apartments on lower floors that are safer from drone attacks and easier to access when elevators don’t work during power outages.
Some apartment owners are also installing equipment like gas stoves and battery storage systems to make life more comfortable for renters during blackouts. Anna said she wants to install a $3,000 backup power unit in her apartment to help attract renters.
In online groups for renters, many landlords advertise power units in their properties as part of the deal.
LUN even launched an online map of Kyiv to show which housing units are best prepared for an energy crisis, covering information such as insulation work carried out and which services, if any, operate during power outages, including heating and water.
For now, most relocations from Kyiv are a temporary reaction to the coming winter, Babko said. When it comes to the property sales market, little has changed, indicating that residents aren’t yet willing to permanently give up their homes in the capital, she added.
Anna is optimistic that many people will continue to remain in Kyiv, even over the winter, where there are more job opportunities than in western Ukraine, and rents are cheaper.
"The city will continue to live, work, and function," she said.

Cyclone Arnab makes landfall in India’s Andhra Pradesh
Authorities evacuate 180,000 people as severe storm causes flooding, disrupting flights and train schedules.
Cyclone Arnab has made landfall on India’s east coast, causing widespread damage and bringing heavy rainfall and wind speeds of up to 135kph (84mph).
Trees fell onto highways and power supplies were disrupted after Arnab crossed into Andhra Pradesh early on Wednesday morning.
At least 180,000 people were evacuated from Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states a day earlier. Flights and train services were cancelled, and some schools were forced to close.
Authorities say more than 12 million people live in the cyclone’s expected path.
No casualties have been reported so far.
One resident of Kakinada district in Andhra Pradesh, which lies in the storm’s path, said: “No one knew whose house the water would rush into next or whose home would be submerged.”
India’s Meteorological Department forecast a storm surge of up to 1.5m above the tide level, warning that it was likely to submerge low-lying areas in Andhra Pradesh.
‘Very severe cyclonic storm’
Arnab made landfall as a “very severe cyclonic storm” – the third-highest category on its scale, before being downgraded to “severe” after moving further inland.
In neighbouring Nepal, authorities warned tourists on Tuesday not to enter high-altitude areas over fears Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches from Thursday through to Saturday.
Reuters news agency reported that authorities suspended issuing trekking permits for three days.
This is peak hiking season in Nepal, with about 750 hikers receiving permits daily.
Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic glacial mountain collapse in August, which killed more than 1,400 people and left at least 5,000 missing.
Sri Lanka has also closed schools, with its Department of Meteorology warning the storm could trigger flash floods and landslides.

Top U.S. general says AI will change how America fights its wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:07:10 UTC
17:07:10 KST

- Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called artificial intelligence one of his three strategic priorities, after the budget and ahead of operations.
- Caine used the term super intelligence, which a Sept. 29 executive order directs the executive branch to use in place of artificial intelligence.
Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has named artificial intelligence as one of his three strategic priorities, ranking it behind only securing a budget and ahead of ongoing military operations.
Caine made the remarks on Oct. 26 during a fireside chat at the National Defense Transportation Association and U.S. Transportation Command fall meeting in Grapevine, Texas, moderated by Transcom commander Gen. Randall Reed of the U.S. Air Force, according to a Pentagon News account of the session. Throughout the discussion, Caine referred to the technology as “super intelligence,” or SI, the term President Donald Trump is trying to substitute for “artificial intelligence” across the federal government.
“I have sort of three strategic priorities right now, separate from [others]. No. 1 is making sure that we have a budget. … No. 2 is [super intelligence], and No. 3 is ongoing operations,” said Caine.
The wording follows a Sept. 29 executive order that directs the executive branch, to the extent the law allows, to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI.” The order does not create a new category of technology. It defines super intelligence as the same systems already covered by the statutory definition of artificial intelligence in federal law, so when Caine says SI, he is describing the AI tools the military uses and develops today.
Trump first announced the change in his Sept. 22 speech to the United Nations General Assembly, saying all U.S. government documents would switch to the “much more accurate term.” The State Department has since ordered its staff to rename AI-related programs and systems, and military offices have started adopting the language as well; the U.S. Marine Corps aviation acquisition office this month described new maintenance tools it is pursuing as predictive super intelligence technologies.
The term already carries a different meaning in the technology field. Researchers and AI companies have long used superintelligence to describe a hypothetical future system that surpasses human intelligence, and the industry more often uses “artificial general intelligence” for AI that would match or exceed people across tasks. Critics have argued that the government’s branding blurs that distinction, and Trump has responded by calling anyone who uses the term “Artificial Intelligence” an enemy of the White House.
Caine told the Transcom audience that the technology will be essential for the joint force to win tactical engagements, run logistics and sustainment, and carry out command and control, the functions that let commanders direct forces in combat. He described a future conflict in which the number of kinetic and non-kinetic actions moving between the United States and an adversary, from missiles, rockets and bombs to cyberattacks, would be significant enough to require machine help.
“When I think of SI, …it’s going to be a game changer as we move forward,” said Caine.
The chairman stressed that the work involves training leaders as well as systems and models, so that future commanders get decision support while humans stay appropriately involved and the military balances the opportunities against the risks. He said the Joint Staff is already working on that effort.
“It’s going to be an important part of our future, [and] we need to lean in,” said Caine.
The Pentagon’s use of the technology has grown quickly over the past year. In May, Under Secretary of War Emil Michael said the number of department personnel using AI tools rose from about 80,000 to 1.5 million in a single year, spanning enterprise productivity software through classified intelligence analysis. The department is also applying AI to missile defense data fusion and has launched a pilot program that uses AI-assisted tools to manage security classification.
Transcom offers an obvious test case for the logistics side of Caine’s argument. The command moves troops, equipment and supplies worldwide by air, sea and land, and the forecasting, routing and maintenance planning behind that work are the kind of data-heavy tasks where the Pentagon has been most willing to put AI tools into daily use. Caine did not describe specific Transcom programs during the session, according to the Pentagon account.
He closed the point by saying the commercial sector is likely to set the pace if past experience holds, and that the military needs to keep up.
“And we need to match them at the same speed and tempo,” Caine said.

The banker, the basketball star, the cardiologist and the chemist: meet Serbia's potential new leaders

Here are some of the prominent candidates on the students' list.
FORMER CENTRAL BANK GOVERNOR DEJAN SOSKIC, 59
Dejan Soskic, an economist and professor at the University of Belgrade's Faculty of Economics, served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012, before resigning in protest at legislative amendments that he argued compromised the institution's independence. He has for years been a vocal opponent of Vucic's government.
Soskic, who was an avid biker in his youth but has mellowed into a softly spoken reformer, has frequently criticised the country’s institutional weaknesses under Vucic. In 2021, he said, without offering evidence, that systemic corruption in the Balkan state was more widespread than in neighbouring countries and that it was deterring domestic and foreign direct investment. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party have repeatedly denied accusations of corruption.
Soskic says that prudent public finances will create a stable foundation for a permanent increase in wages and pensions.
Pro-government media have criticised Soskic’s central bank record, accusing him of triggering the depreciation of the dinar during his tenure. Soskic has defended the depreciation as a reflection of the mandatory monetary policies of the time rather than a personal failure.
Nonetheless, during the election campaign, in order to increase export competitiveness, Soskic proposed correcting, or weakening, the exchange rate of the dinar - which is in a managed float against the euro - to make domestic goods cheaper in foreign currencies. An alternative, he suggested, would be to maintain a fixed, stronger exchange rate but lower costs by cutting wages.
CARDIOLOGIST AND PROFESSOR ILIJA SRDANOVIC, 55
Ilija Srdanovic, a practising cardiologist, professor at the University of Novi Sad Faculty of Medicine and a keen cyclist, became the student movement's lead candidate when the ballot list was finalised in September.
Srdanovic’s transition to frontline politics began during the student-led anti-corruption demonstrations, where he frequently appeared as a public speaker. The physician participated in the movement's "Guardians of the Constitution" bicycle tour across the northern Vojvodina province.
Srdanovic campaigned with the promise of a decentralised health system "at the service of citizens and based on equality for all patients". In an interview with the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency, Srdanovic said his political objective was building "a better Serbia, nothing else is important".
He declined an invitation from Vucic to participate in a televised debate during the campaign.
However, some of his policies do not represent a sharp departure from some of Vucic's. He stressed the Student List position that Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008, remains an integral part of the country. He also said that European Union integration is not a current priority and that the immediate focus for the incoming administration must remain on domestic anti-corruption reforms and national "existential survival".
FORMER BASKETBALL STAR DEJAN BODIROGA, 53
Dejan Bodiroga, the former captain of the Yugoslav national basketball team and current EuroLeague president, is one of the student movement's most prominent public speakers.
He described Sunday's election as a fight "for the return of a country that has been hijacked".
The step into politics is the latest chapter in a life that has gripped the basketball-mad nation - from capturing back-to-back FIBA World Championship gold medals in 1998 and 2002 and leading the then Yugoslav team to an Olympic silver medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games to entering senior sports administration upon his retirement as a player in 2007 and being appointed as EuroLeague president in 2022.
During the election campaign, Bodiroga appeared at student rallies and took part in open-air folk dancing in rural municipalities. His fans frequently cheered him with a 1990s slogan "We have our God, his name is Bodiroga."
CHEMISTRY PROFESSOR RADOMIR SAICIC, 64
Radomir Saicic, an organic chemistry professor and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), was the face of the students' election win on Sunday, taking the podium at their headquarters after Vucic conceded defeat to hail the outcome as a "citizens' victory".
He is a specialist in medicinal chemistry whose research focuses on the synthesis of chemotherapy treatments and antiviral therapies, including a special COVID-19 project in collaboration with the Pasteur Institute.
Saicic joined the student-led anti-corruption protests that followed the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad. He became a target for pro-government tabloids after signing a petition with 24 other academics demanding Vucic's resignation, and in May 2026 he walked out of a SANU gallery exhibition to protest an appearance by Nikola Selakovic, the minister of culture.
During the campaign, he told crowds that Serbia was "occupied from within" and said he was ready to put "even his life" at the disposal of the student movement.
Saicic says Kosovo is a "temporarily occupied territory" and backs energy ties with Russia.
Political analysts and local media have tipped him as a contender in the presidential election which will also be triggered by Vucic's recent resignation from the post. REUTERS
