Boeing gets nearly $500 million more for Apache support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:01:44 UTC
17:01:44 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Boeing a $499.8 million modification for AH-64 Apache engineering services and technical support, extending the contract to February 2031.
- The Army received one bid, and work locations and funding will be set with each order under the contract first awarded in 2021.
The U.S. Army has added nearly $500 million to a Boeing contract for engineering services and technical support on the AH-64 Apache attack helicopter, extending the work through February 2031.
Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, awarded the $499.8 million modification to Boeing’s Mesa, Arizona, operation on Feb. 21, 2026, according to the Department of War announcement. The Army solicited bids online and received one, and because work locations and funding will be set with each individual order, the announcement does not say how much money has been obligated so far or where the engineering will be done.
The modification extends a contract the Army first awarded in August 2021, when it gave Boeing a $487 million cost-plus-fixed-fee deal for the same Apache engineering and technical support, originally due to run until Feb. 6, 2026. The new action came about two weeks after that end date, adding a sum roughly equal to the original ceiling along with five more years of performance. Engineering support of this kind pays for the work that keeps an aircraft type flying and evolving after it leaves the factory, from investigating fleet problems and updating technical documentation to integrating new equipment, though the announcement does not list the specific tasks planned for the next five years.
The money arrives as the Army shrinks and reorganizes its Apache force. Under the Army Transformation Initiative announced in 2025, the service is retiring every remaining AH-64D, the older Longbow variant whose last new airframe was built in 2013, and deactivating 11 air cavalry squadrons, most of which flew the D model. The Army has been planning that drawdown for years, and as early as 2020 it sought contractors to dismantle hundreds of AH-64Ds. In April 2026, the Army’s director of aviation said the service had divested nearly 60% of its D models within a year, while procurement funding for Apaches in the fiscal 2027 budget request fell from $361.7 million to $1.5 million.
The newer AH-64E Guardian remains the Army’s only attack helicopter, but its numbers are also coming down. A Pentagon budget document reviewed by Aviation Week showed the service plans to retire some AH-64Es as well, culling the E-model fleet in greater numbers next year even as it completes the move to an all-E force.
Much of the remaining engineering effort is tied to upgrading the aircraft the Army keeps. The service’s priority is Version 6.5, an AH-64E software and hardware update that adds an open-systems interface for faster technology insertion, enhanced Link 16 data sharing for manned-unmanned teaming, and the groundwork for launched effects, the small drones an Apache can release to scout or strike ahead of it. Version 6.5 first flew in October 2023 and is meant to bring every E-model onto a single software baseline, and Boeing said in April that the Army was testing the configuration and that adding it to production would require only a modification to the existing contract.
In May 2026, the Army was investigating a newly discovered transmission problem affecting the AH-64E, at a time when funding shortfalls had forced some units to cut flight hours and speed up the retirement of their D models. The Army has not said whether any part of the new engineering modification is linked to that investigation.

‘Nobody heard us’ – why Gen Z are leading protests across Europe
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:21 CET
17:00:21 KST

By Fedja Grulovic , Alex Fraser , Bart Biesemans and Fatos Bytyci
BELGRADE/MILAN/BRUSSELS/TIRANA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Maya Gourdel, a 19-year-old student in Brussels, sits at a desk writing slogans against those running her country: “If we burn, you burn with us!” The slogan, taken from the 2012 film “The Hunger Games” that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth movements globally, reflects the anger, frustration and desire for change driving Gen Z-led protests around Europe.
From the suburbs of Paris to the squares of Belgrade, thousands have taken to the streets.
The demands are various but often overlapping – frustrations with shabby schooling facilities, perceived lack of economic opportunity, cost of living, corruption, housing and a sense of not being listened to. At times those protests triggered violence – with thousands of shops in France alone being damaged or looted in recent weeks – and police firing stun grenades and water cannons.
This weekend they also brought real change – student-led protests culminated in the toppling in an election of Serbia’s long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism.
“Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom,” said student protester Stasa Piletic. “Personally, I feel a sense of victory. I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility.”
‘AN EXPLOSION OF RAGE’
Chiara, a 21-year-old student in protest-hit Milan, believes “it’s vital to take part in people’s spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible.”
“I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream,” she said.
She said Italian students were confronting a reality of schools without enough teachers and crumbling buildings.
“And all of this with the prospect of an underpaid job which we didn’t qualify for and the prospect of living in a tiny, overpriced house, probably away from our city, which we didn’t want to live in.”
Protests led by Gen Z have caused ructions globally as the generation born roughly between 1997 and 2012 found its voice, from Bangladesh in 2024 and Nepal in 2025, to India this year. Now Europe has become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living are a concern for 40% of 16-30-year-olds, according to a European Union survey published in 2025.
Among the 92.7 million people in the EU who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, the highest risk was recorded for young adults aged 18-24 years, at 26.3%, while the lowest was recorded for adults aged 65 years or over, at 18.8%.
Younger people are also wary of shouldering the financial burden of an older generation that tends to vote in greater numbers. People over 60 in France make up a quarter of the population but own 60% of France’s wealth, according to the OFCE think tank.
French pensions are by far the biggest public expense, on track to reach 14% of economic output, as the population ages and voters resist raising the retirement age or reducing benefits. That is still less than Greece or Italy, which spend the largest proportion of national income on public pensions among OECD countries, at around 16% of GDP, according to OECD figures in 2025. But it is much more than Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland or South Korea, which spent less than 4% of GDP on public pensions, according to the OECD.
‘YOUNG PEOPLE IN EUROPE ARE UNITED’
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris, has been protesting against “deplorable” conditions and staff shortages at his school. “There used to be rats,” he said. Students were evacuated last year when a roof collapsed on the courtyard, though no one was hurt, he said.
Protests showed “that young people in Europe are united”, he said, adding, “we all agree on one point: that young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”
A French government report in October said pension spending had risen by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023 while that for education had declined 0.5. It also showed 32% of the education ministry’s budget went towards pensions, crowding out money for other areas.
Gourdel, too, has been protesting for better conditions in schools in Belgium.
“We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It’s only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us,” she said.
The protests are still spreading, with a demonstration planned in Germany this weekend over cost of living, inequality, war and the state of schools.
Unrest has also hit Albania, where student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government, fuelled by anger over perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, engulfed Tirana and spread to other cities.
“Our Prime Minister spent 130 days not listening to us,” said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.
“If you ask a student in Albania, ‘where do you see your future?’ Everyone says ‘outside this country’,” she said, arguing that at home, even if you have talent, someone with “connections is always going to beat you”.
Serbia’s student movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of.
Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing – something neither the students nor their candidates have any experience of. Luka Stojakovic, another protester, brushes that aside. “We have seen where people with political experience have brought us.”
(Reporting by Fedja Grulovic, Dragan Kastratovic, Kuba Stezycki, Anna Lubowicka, Alex Fraser, Bart Biesemans, Noemie Olive, Fatos Bytyci, Lafken Zepeda, Francesco Canepa,; Writing by Matthias Williams; Editing by Alex Richardson)

‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:00:01 UTC
17:00:01 KST

‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?
Experts say symptoms such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss can be a warning sign – but there are other factors too
TikTok is rife with influencers warning of “ferritin face”, a term they use to describe the pallor, dark circles, dry skin, and hair loss claimed to indicate low iron stores. But is this based on fact or fiction, and when is it time to head to the GP?
What is ferritin?
Iron is not made in the body, so typically we consume it in our diet. Ferritin is the protein responsible for storing iron in the body, particularly in the liver, and releasing it in a controlled manner.
By measuring ferritin levels, which can be checked via blood tests, it is possible to get an snapshot of the body’s iron reserves, although experts warn such levels are not always a reliable guide.
However “a level below 50 might be a pointer of iron deficiency,” said Sue Pavord, professor of practice in medical haematology at Oxford University hospitals.
The symptoms influencers describe include dark circles under the eyes. Photograph: Alamy/PA
The symptoms influencers describe, such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss, can be caused by a variety of factors, including genetics, stress and dehydration. But experts say low iron stores can have an effect.
“Iron is needed for every single cell of the body. So if you are iron deficient, you will be very fatigued, have brain fog, your skin will look dull and saggy, you’ll look pale and tired,” said Pavord. “While we can’t diagnose iron deficiency from the face, it might be a suggestion that there is iron deficiency.”
Prof Toby Richards of the University of East London and the Iron Clinic added such changes were particularly pronounced in people with very low iron stores. “They tend to be the really sick patients,” he said.
Why might people have low ferritin?
“Periods and pregnancies are the most common [causes],” said Pavord, but others include not getting enough iron – either from dietary choices or because of poor absorption, as can occur with coeliac disease.
Low ferritin levels can also arise as a result of blood loss linked to gastrointestinal problems, such as gastritis or polyps.
“We also sometimes see it in athletes because of the high demand for iron on their bodies,” she added.
What should people who are worried they might have low ferritin do ?
Richards said those who are at high risk of low ferritin – such as people who have heavy periods, are pregnant or have had children, or are vegetarian or vegan – should ask for a blood test, adding that should include a full blood count, ferritin level check, and test for levels of B12 and folate.
“This is a proper disease, and to put it into perspective, it’s the leading cause of disability in women of reproductive ability,” he said.
Pavord also said those who are concerned about their ferritin levels should ask for a blood test, adding it was important to understand the cause of iron deficiency.
“Older people suspecting iron deficiency would need a proper clinical assessment and investigations to look for a source of bleeding from the bowel,” she said.
Pavord said it is possible to buy iron tablets over the counter at a pharmacy.
“Taking iron tablets without confirming iron deficiency is not really going to do you any harm, particularly if you’re a young woman, because you’re losing a lot of iron with periods,” she said.
But Richards noted many products do not necessarily contain the appropriate dose. “If you are iron deficient, you need to be on a full treatment dose … and then repeat your blood results in three months’ time,” he said. “What’s marketed is normally the lower dose supplements
Is the social media focus helpful, or problematic?
Pavord was positive about the increase in awareness.
“We need to stop normalising iron deficiency,” she said. “Many women are just exhausted trying to cope with their periods, cope with their pregnancies, cope with their young children and their busy jobs, and we need to stop normalising fatigue.”
Richards agreed. “ Anything that raises the plight of women in this area is a good thing,” he said.
However Dr Asiya Maula, a GP from the private firm The Health Suite, was cautious. “The risk with social media trends is that people may see themselves in a list of symptoms and assume they have a deficiency without checking whether that is actually the cause,” she said.

A Fiat that converts from a family car into a pickup and a Peugeot with a glass-bubble roof were among six concept cars unveiled by Stellantis at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, as captured in this video carousel by Dezeen.
Automotive corporation Stellantis unveiled the six concepts at a preview event in Meudon, outside Paris, on the eve of the motor show, offering an early look at the designs before the exhibition opened to the public.
The concepts explored different approaches to future car design – from reworking historic models to experimenting with colour-changing paint and illuminated bodywork.
Among the cars presented was Fiat’s Multiplay, which combines the proportions of a family vehicle with the functionality of a pickup.
Measuring 4.45 metres long, the concept has a sliding rear section that converts its six-seat-plus-one configuration into a four-seat vehicle with an open cargo bed.
Inside, a front passenger seat called the Sunseat folds into a lounge-style position beneath the panoramic roof, while a modular Petsenger seat can accommodate a pet, a child seat or storage.
The concept was finished in bright green, with a pink floor and red and pink upholstery inspired by the colours of a watermelon.
Citroën revisited its 1948 2CV with a compact electric concept featuring an orange-red body, grey steel wheels and yellow accents.
Inside, yellow tartan upholstery echoes details of the original model, while a fabric sunroof and removable storage basket replaced some of the conventional fittings found in modern cars.
The concept also features a detachable radio called Radioën, which doubles as a portable speaker, as well as door compartments designed to hold eggs, echoing the practical requirements of the original car.
Peugeot presented its RCZ Vision concept, a low-slung coupe with a sculpted body and a glass roof with a distinctive double-bubble profile that extends from the bonnet towards the rear.
Slim horizontal headlights reinterpret the brand’s three-claw motif, while a rear spoiler deploys only when the car is moving, keeping the bodywork smooth when parked.
Inside, a square steering control called Hypersquare replaces a conventional steering wheel and transparent micro-LED displays provide driving information while reducing the visual prominence of screens.
DS Automobiles’ F3VER concept features a compact body finished in Cosmic Blue paint that changes from vivid blue to violet depending on the light.
Its two-tone finish wraps around the rear of the car, while vertical Y-shaped headlights frame the front emblem.
At the rear, 16 LED panels sit within a sculptural light assembly informed by the vaulted roof of Paris’s Grand Palais.
Opel’s STX Concept is an electric estate car with a low roofline, sharply creased bonnet and sloping rear. Its front grille, known as the Vizor, incorporates vertical animated lights around an illuminated Opel emblem.
The rear bumper features extendable aerodynamic elements, while glass light strips run from the rear side windows into the roof.
Cameras replace conventional wing mirrors and three-section alloy wheels are designed to improve aerodynamic efficiency.
Alfa Romeo’s Cuorerosso concept car explores the brand’s future sports-car design through a streamlined body, active air intakes and slim aerodynamic mirrors.
Its rear window echoes the shape of the brand’s triangular front grille, while the interior is organised around the driver, with controls concealed in the central console until needed.
Stellantis was formed in 2021 through the merger of Fiat Chrysler Automobiles and France’s PSA Group.
Its portfolio includes Alfa Romeo, Citroën, DS Automobiles, Fiat, Opel and Peugeot, among other automotive brands.

40 years on, Switzerland still sits on Haiti’s Duvalier millions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

40 years on, Switzerland still sits on Haiti’s Duvalier millions
Switzerland prides itself on returning assets belonging to former dictators. Yet, after 40 years, Bern has still not found a use for $16 million (CHF13.2 million) linked to the late Haitian dictator Jean-Claude Duvalier. This is despite Swiss aid organisations having offered their support as early as 2019.
Within 18 days in February 1986, the dictatorships in Haiti and the Philippines came to an end. Jean-Claude Duvalier, known as “Baby Doc”, fled from Port-au-Prince to France on February 7. Ferdinand Marcos fled from Manila to the US on February 25. A month later, the Federal Council, Switzerland’s executive body, froze Marcos’s assets held in Switzerland under emergency legislation, marking a turning point in Switzerland’s handling of funds illicitly held by despots.
The Duvalier case was less spectacular in that the asset freeze in mid-April was imposed following the announcement of a Haitian request for mutual legal assistance. What initially appeared to be a routine procedure, however, was to develop into the longest and most complicated case to date of so-called “asset recovery” – the restitution of illegally acquired funds.
In Haiti, criminal proceedings against Duvalier never materialised. The Caribbean state was weakened following the end of the dictatorship and experienced several attempted coups. When, in 2002, it became apparent that mutual legal assistance would fail – and that the Duvalier funds would consequently be released – the Federal Council resorted to emergency legislation after all and ordered a three-year freeze on the funds, which were then estimated at around CHF7.5 million ($4.83 million). The government explained at the time that the aim was to prevent the Swiss financial centre from being misused as a haven for assets derived from dishonest activities.
After the freeze had been extended twice, and with the help of a lawyer funded by Switzerland, Haiti resumed the mutual legal assistance proceedings in May 2008. As the Duvalier family’s account holders were unable to prove the lawful origin of the frozen funds, the Swiss authorities decided in February 2009 to return the funds to Haiti to support development projects.
More
With US in retreat, can Switzerland maintain fight against kleptocracy?
But that was not the end of the matter either. Following two unsuccessful appeals by the Duvalier clan, the Federal Court, on January 12, 2010, overturned the order for the funds to be handed over on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired and ordered the funds to be releasedExternal link. The judges appeared to have reservations about the ruling. This was indicated by their remark that the strict conditions governing mutual legal assistance needed reform.
Law aims to keep funds from Duvalier clan
On the very day that the Federal Court handed down its judgement, Haiti was struck by a devastating earthquake that claimed over 300,000 lives. “In light of the recent disaster, can we allow the Duvalier clan to keep the proceeds of its exploitation?” asks Swiss Foreign Minister Micheline Calmy-Rey in a newspaper articleExternal link. Her answer: “I don’t think so. For Switzerland, the Duvalier case is a legacy from a time when our financial centre’s defences against assets belonging to despots were still inadequate.”
On February 3, 2010, the day on which the Federal Court published its written judgement, the Federal Council once again pulled the emergency brake and froze the Duvalier funds. Parliament then responded: in October 2010, it passed a lawExternal link on the freezing, confiscation and restitution of dictators’ assets in cases where mutual legal assistance fails due to a lack of state structures in the requesting country.
This “Lex Duvalier” proved successful in that the Federal Council’s order to confiscate the former dictator’s assets became legally binding following a ruling by the Federal Administrative Court in September 2013 – 27 years after the funds were first frozen. The same law later enabled the confiscation of a further €4.2 million (CHF3.9 million), which had been deposited in a Geneva bank by the former Haitian finance minister, Frantz MerceronExternal link, and had remained undetected for a long time.
More
Explainer: Are Swiss banks still home to dirty money, or have they cleaned house?
This cleared the way for the final step in asset recovery: the restitution of the funds to Haiti. According to the law, this was to be achieved through the funding of programmes in the public interest. This was to be done either through an agreement between Switzerland and Haiti, which would regulate the nature of the programmes, the partners involved, and the control and monitoring arrangements; or by the Federal Council itself, should no agreement be reached with Haiti. Cooperation with international or national institutions is also possible in this context.
Foreign ministry cites Haiti’s precarious situation for delay
In the case of the Duvalier funds, no agreement has yet been reached with Haiti, nor has the Federal Council determined how the funds are to be used in Haiti. The sum now stands at around $16 million, as the foreign ministry announced in response to an enquiry from SWI swissinfo.ch. The funds are held in federal accounts with the Swiss National Bank and earn interest at market rates.
Explaining the further 13-year delay in the restitution, the foreign ministry stated that it had been examining projects in collaboration with various partners. Natural disasters had further weakened the country’s already fragile institutions. The situation, which remains very precarious, currently makes it impossible to resume negotiations on a restitution agreement. The search continues for programmes that can be implemented in a transparent and efficient manner.
What has not been previously reported is that, in September 2019, three Swiss non-governmental organisations (NGOs) with many years’ experience in Haiti offered Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis their support in repatriating the Duvalier funds. This was in response to a newspaper report stating that Switzerland was on the verge of reaching an agreement with UNICEF on this matter.
The aid organisations in question are Suisse-Santé-Haiti (SSH)External link, the Swiss Partnership HAS HaitiExternal link (Schweizer Partnerschaft HAS Haiti, SPHASH) and the Swiss Aid Organisation for the Work and Legacy of Albert SchweitzerExternal link (Schweizer Hilfswerk für das Werk und Gedankengut von Albert Schweitzer, SHV). “We are convinced that, thanks to our many years of practical work in Haiti in the field of healthcare – particularly in maternal and child health – we are well placed to provide competent and effective support to the Swiss authorities in achieving their objectives,” states the 2019 letter to the Swiss foreign minister.
Foreign ministry rebuffs aid groups backed by ex-minister
The NGOs requested to be involved in the evaluation of projects and gave assurances that their commitment and field experience would ensure that the funds would benefit the people of Haiti in full. At a meeting with the foreign ministry in Bern in September 2019, the NGOs were accompanied by the former justice and finance minister, Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf. She had previously campaigned against the release of the Duvalier funds.
“I am a lawyer through and through, but I do not simply follow the letter of the law. The law must also be morally justifiable,” Widmer-Schlumpf said in an interview in 2010External link. She added: “Returning the unlawfully acquired funds to the Duvalier clan would not have been justifiable, either morally or in terms of foreign policy.” However, the foreign ministry did not take up the NGOs’ offer. It said it had taken note of their explanations, but that at the time of the meeting it was already pursuing a “concrete programme approach”. But this evidently came to nothing.
More
As aid stalls in Haiti, can attack drones and soldiers end gang violence?
The fact that Switzerland is still holding on to the funds more than four decades after the fall of the Duvalier regime and 12 years after the death of the former dictator shows that the conditions for restitution are among the most difficult aspects of asset recovery. The list of returned dictatorial assetsExternal link – totalling over CHF2 billion ($2.42 billion) – which appears impressive at first glance, masks the fact that the objectives of restitution have not always been achieved. Namely, to improve the living conditions of the population in the country of origin or to strengthen the rule of law there, thereby helping to prevent impunity.
Thus, the successor legislation to the “Lex Duvalier”External link, which came into force in 2016, proved ineffective in the very cases for which it was explicitly designed. This concerned the funds of Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali (Tunisia), Hosni Mubarak (Egypt) and Muammar al-Gaddafi (Libya) – totalling over CHF1 billion ($1.2 billion) – which were frozen in Switzerland during the Arab Spring. An attempt is currently pending before the Federal Administrative Court to return the funds of the ousted Viktor Yanukovych – which have been frozen since 2014 – to the Ukrainian state.
Plans for more efficient asset recovery procedures are in place: in its response to a parliamentary motionExternal link, the Federal Council recently referred to an ongoing revision of the law.

BAE to build thirty five thousand guidance kits a year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:57:49 GMT
16:57:49 KST

BAE Systems has signed a framework agreement running up to seven years with the United States Department of War to lift production of APKWS laser guidance kits to as many as thirty five thousand a year, according to the company.
The kits turn unguided two point seven five inch rockets into precision guided munitions, and are in service with the United States Air Force, Army, Marine Corps and Navy. They are available to American allies and work in air-to-surface, surface-to-surface, surface-to-air and air-to-air engagements, including against drones.
Tom Arseneault, president and chief executive of BAE Systems, Inc., said: “APKWS delivers proven, reliable and affordable precision at scale to counter evolving threats and ensure our warfighters maintain a decisive advantage. This agreement highlights the importance of sustained investment in critical munitions to strengthen readiness and equip forces for evolving operational needs.”
Under the framework the company will increase production while negotiating a multi-year contract within it, which the company described as surge-ready support for evolving operational demands. BAE Systems said it has invested in manufacturing capacity, materials and expertise in line with the department’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy, and continues to develop upgrades, mission specific variants and new technologies.
The kits are built at BAE Systems facilities in Hudson, New Hampshire and Austin, Texas. The company delivered its hundred thousandth APKWS kit earlier, and the system is the United States government’s only programme of record for guided seventy millimetre rockets.
APKWS came to wider attention when American aircraft used the rockets against Houthi drones over the Red Sea, where a guidance kit costing a fraction of an air-to-air missile proved able to bring down one-way attack aircraft. The cost exchange problem that drove that use is the same one pushing European manufacturers towards cheaper interceptors.

Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone fleet gets radar warning software fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:55:22 UTC
16:55:22 KST

- Lockheed Martin received a $9.8 million contract to update AN/ALQ-230 radar warning software and a mission data tool for Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone helicopters.
- Canada is funding the work through Foreign Military Sales, with Naval Air Systems Command contracting and completion expected in October 2030.
Lockheed Martin will update the radar warning and electronic support software on Canada’s CH-148 Cyclone maritime helicopters under a $9.8 million contract awarded through the U.S. Navy, with work running until October 2030.
Naval Air Systems Command placed the contract with Lockheed’s Owego, New York, operation on behalf of the Canadian government, which is paying the full amount through Foreign Military Sales. It covers a new version of the operational flight program software for the helicopter’s AN/ALQ-230 electronic support measures and radar warning receiver, along with new Canadian Mission Data Load Tool software, and includes development, documentation, testing, installation and training aimed at fixing software and system trouble reports already logged against the equipment. Owego accounts for 97% of the work, with the remaining share split evenly between Ottawa, Halifax and Patuxent River, Maryland, and the contract was not competed.
The AN/ALQ-230 is the Cyclone’s passive electronic warfare sensor, a Lockheed system developed for Canada’s Maritime Helicopter Program that listens for radar emissions from ships, aircraft and air defense sites, identifies them and warns the crew when the helicopter is being tracked. The operational flight program is the software that runs the receiver itself, while the mission data load is the library of emitter signatures the system uses to recognize what it detects. A Canadian tool for building those mission data files lets the Royal Canadian Air Force prepare and update its own threat libraries, which have to change as new radars appear and as crews deploy to different regions.
The contract announcement does not describe the trouble reports or say how many have been recorded, and neither Lockheed nor the Canadian Department of National Defence has said whether the work will add capability or only correct existing faults.
The Cyclone is a militarized, fly-by-wire version of the Sikorsky S-92 built by Sikorsky, which Lockheed Martin owns, and it shares its basic airframe with the U.S. Marine Corps’ VH-92A presidential helicopter, which is also built on the S-92. Canada ordered 28 Cyclones in 2004 to replace the CH-124 Sea King, but development problems delayed deliveries until June 2015, and the helicopter did not reach initial operational capability until June 2018, the same year the last Sea Kings retired. The aircraft flies from Royal Canadian Navy Halifax-class frigates for anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare, search and rescue and utility missions, carrying a multi-mode radar, a HELRAS dipping sonar, two torpedoes and a mission system developed by General Dynamics Mission Systems-Canada in addition to the ESM suite.
National Defence puts the cost of acquiring the Cyclone, including project management, infrastructure and contingency, at C$3.75 billion, and the cost of major in-service support at C$11.17 billion. Its 2025 briefing notes set full operational capability for the fleet in September 2026 and the aircraft’s estimated life expectancy at 2043. One Cyclone was lost on April 29, 2020, while operating from HMCS Fredericton in the Ionian Sea, killing six Canadian Armed Forces members, which leaves 27 airframes from the original order.
The electronic support suite has been linked to an earlier fleet problem. Cracks found on almost all Cyclones in 2021 were caused by structural loads from the ESM and satellite communications antenna mounts in flight, according to National Defence, and Sikorsky repaired the aircraft. In April 2025, the fleet was briefly paused again after questions arose over whether some spare parts were in use beyond their service life.
Keeping the Cyclone’s mission systems current has been a recurring concern in Ottawa. Internal documents reported by CBC News in January 2024 showed the air force was worried about sustaining the helicopter’s weapon system over the medium and long term, partly because Canada is the only country flying the CH-148 and therefore bears the full cost of software and hardware updates unique to the type.
Lockheed’s Owego site also builds the AN/ALQ-210 electronic support system for the U.S. Navy’s MH-60R, and NAVAIR, which manages that work, is buying the Canadian update on Ottawa’s behalf, with part of the testing planned at Patuxent River.

Norway Allocates $45.5 Million to Strengthen Ukraine’s Energy Grid Before Winter
Norway announced the allocation of 500 million kroner ($45.5 million) to bolster Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of the upcoming winter season.
The funding will arrive through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund in November and December to enable quick repair work, equipment purchasing, and investments in critical infrastructure damaged during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian officials highlighted a specific need for new power cables to maintain stable electricity distribution across the country.
“Ukraine will soon enter another winter under war conditions. To ensure the most stable energy supply possible and avoid severe humanitarian consequences, it is crucial that Ukraine receives funds to purchase equipment for strengthening and restoring critical infrastructure damaged by Russian bombings,” stated Energy Minister Terje Aasland.
The minister noted that companies such as Nexans, based in Halden, could manufacture and supply the required subsea cables.
“Ukrainian authorities indicated that the supply of subsea cables is one of Ukraine’s top priorities. Such cables, for example, can be manufactured and delivered by Nexans from Halden,” Aasland added.
The funds form part of the 85 billion kroner ($7.73 billion) Nansen Support Programme for 2026, which designates 70 billion kroner ($6.37 billion) for military needs and 15 billion kroner ($1.36 billion) for civilian and humanitarian support.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Norway has directed over 16 billion kroner ($1.45 billion) toward gas purchases, energy infrastructure restoration, and new technological solutions.
As a harsh winter looms, Ukraine's air defenses are dangerously depleted as the country prepares for an expected surge in Russian energy strikes.
International supplies of Patriot interceptors are severely constrained, leaving Kyiv scrambling alongside European allies to secure hundreds of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles before the cold sets in.
With Ukrainian air defense intercepting only a fraction of incoming ballistic missiles, experts and officials warn that the upcoming winter threatens to bring severe energy disruptions and critical infrastructure challenges across the country.

German chemicals giant BASF raises profit guidance after Iran war price hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:54:31 UTC
16:54:31 KST

German chemicals giant BASF raised its 2026 outlook for the second time this year on Wednesday after raising prices for some products following the outbreak of the Iran war.
The maker of products ranging from automotive paints to sunscreen ingredients now expects a core profit of €7.4billion to €7.8bn ($8.2bn to $8.7bn) this year, up from a previous forecast of €6.9bn to €7.7bn.
BASF's earnings have been boosted after it hiked prices for some goods in March by up to 30% in response to surging costs for energy and other raw materials because of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
The company said Wednesday that its core profit in the third quarter rose 15% from the same period last year to €1.6bn.
Overall sales were up 14% over the period at €16.4bn.
"The increase was mainly driven by considerably higher prices (plus 12%) and slightly higher volumes (plus 2%)," the company said in a statement.
The results come as the European chemicals industry is under major pressure from high energy prices and increasingly intense competition from Asian rivals.
BASF is undertaking a major restructuring, cutting thousands of jobs at its historic German headquarters in Ludwigshafen, after opening a major chemical complex in China earlier this year to serve Asian markets.
The company is also exploring the multibillion-euro acquisition of its German rival Evonik, saying the combination could let it obtain feedstocks and precursor chemicals at lower cost.

Moscow wants a separate agreement with NATO or the U.S. that would effectively mean changing the security infrastructure of Europe and the world, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 27.

The Trump administration has been pushing Europe to take greater responsibility for its security and has publicly discussed a "review" of its military presence on the continent.

Zelensky hinted that it was Washington's diesel deal with Russia that opened the door for further demands from Moscow, though "it's hard to predict what they might be."

Media groups urge EU Commission transparency as Gaza documents probe unfolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:53:28 UTC
16:53:28 KST

Melike Pala
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
A group of 15 media outlets, journalist associations and press freedom organizations urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday to improve journalists’ access to public documents, as an inquiry by the EU Ombudswoman into the commission’s refusal to release documents concerning Gaza unfolds.
In an open letter to von der Leyen, the organizations called on the EU executive to address what they described as a “silent crisis” that has hampered journalists’ efforts to obtain information needed to scrutinize matters of public importance.
The appeal comes after European Ombudswoman Teresa Anjinho last week opened an inquiry into a news outlet’s complaint over the commission’s refusal to release 17 documents concerning EU-funded infrastructure projects in the Gaza Strip.
EUobserver first requested the documents in February as part of an investigation examining the extent to which Israeli attacks had destroyed infrastructure financed by the EU in the Palestinian territory.
The commission refused to release the material, arguing that there was no overriding public interest justifying disclosure. EUobserver’s subsequent appeal went unanswered.
As a first step in her inquiry, Anjinho has asked the commission to respond to the appeal by Nov. 4 at the latest. If the EU executive fails to provide a satisfactory response, she will examine the documents herself.
Against this backdrop, the 15 organizations urged the commission to commit to greater transparency, saying journalists routinely face severe delays in obtaining documents, questionable refusals and extensive redactions that render released material largely meaningless.
In some cases, they said, the commission also fails to retain and properly archive crucial documents.
The restrictions have hindered reporting on issues of major public interest, including how EU member states spent billions of euros in post-COVID recovery funds and cooperation with Israel on arms research, the letter said.
“Around Europe, public debate is being harmed. Stories which should emerge do not. Citizens cannot make important political judgements at critical moments,” it said.
The signatories called on the commission to revoke its December 2024 internal rules of procedure, which they said had made access to documents more difficult, and ensure strict implementation of the regulation on public access to EU documents.
The groups also called for a renewed action plan to improve journalists’ access to information, including implementing recommendations from the European Ombudsman, fully complying with European Court of Justice rulings and strengthening internal procedures for filing and archiving documents.
“The European Commission’s reputation for safeguarding EU democratic values is in peril. At a time when democratic norms are under attack around the world, now is the time to uphold these values,” the letter warned.
The signatories included the Committee to Protect Journalists, EUobserver, the European Federation of Journalists, Follow the Money, Forbidden Stories, the International Federation of Journalists, the International Press Institute, Investigate Europe and PEN International.

Hemus Magazine will continue to build bridges between Bulgarians and Hungarians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:52:59 UTC
16:52:59 KST

Author
Joan Kolev
Interview
Hemus editor-in-chief Svetla Kyoseva for Radio Bulgaria:
Hemus Magazine will continue to build bridges between Bulgarians and Hungarians
Interview with Svetla Kyoseva
Wednesday 28 October 2026 09:02
Wednesday, 28 October 2026, 09:02
PHOTO Facebook /Bolgár Országos Önkormányzat
Font size
Hemus, a bilingual Bulgarian-Hungarian magazine covering culture and public life, is celebrating the 35th anniversary of its first issue, published in 1991.
Its editor-in-chief is Svetla Kyoseva, whose life has been closely connected with Hungary since 1984. That year, she arrived in Budapest and began working at the Hristo Botev Bulgarian School, where she spent 13 years. In 2004, former pupils invited her to head the Bulgarian School for the Mother Tongue, where she remained director for 15 years. Alongside her educational work, she has pursued an active career as a translator, with more than 200 published contributions and 40 books to her name.
In recognition of her contribution to presenting and promoting Hungarian literature in Bulgaria, Svetla Kyoseva has been awarded the prestigious Baumgarten Honorary Prize for 2026. In a special interview with Radio Bulgaria, she discusses the significance of the distinction, as well as the history and future of Hemus, a magazine popular with both Bulgarian and Hungarian readers.
Svetla Kyoseva
PHOTO BTA
“This is a very interesting award that enjoyed considerable prestige between the two world wars, after which it was discontinued. It has now been revived at the initiative of citizens, with funds raised through donations. A special jury made up of writers and translators decides who should receive it. The recipients are mainly Hungarian writers, but the work of translators of Hungarian literature is also recognised,” Ms Kyoseva explained, referring to the award named after the Hungarian patron of the arts Ferenc Baumgarten.
As in previous years, Hemus publishes two issues annually, each devoted to a particular theme. This approach also defines the magazine’s character in 2026.
First issue of Hemus Magazine for 2026
PHOTO bolgarok.hu
“We call the first issue the Danube issue because we have brought together works by Bulgarian authors devoted to the River Danube. The idea was prompted by an invitation to contribute Bulgarian works to an anthology entitled The River: A Different Anthology of the Danube. It was first published in German and Hungarian, followed by translations into Romanian, Slovak and Serbian. We now feel that the time has come for a Bulgarian edition, with each country able to add works on the subject that it considers important. For this issue, we selected a range of texts, including works by the writer Yordan Yovkov and contemporary pieces, some written especially for the magazine. I hope we will soon find a suitable publisher willing to take on this exceptionally interesting anthology.”
Speaking about the second Hemus issue of the year, the editor-in-chief of the bilingual magazine says:
Second issue of Hemus Magazine for 2026
PHOTO bolgarok.hu
“It brings together Bulgarian communities in the countries neighbouring Hungary, as their histories, origins and present-day circumstances are quite similar. One common thread is Bulgarian gardening, which began spreading across Europe in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, giving rise to communities that have survived to varying degrees to this day. The issue includes an excerpt from Georgi Gospodinov’s book The Gardener and Death, as well as a text explaining to children what market gardening is.”
This issue of the magazine was officially presented during the World Meeting of Bulgarian Media in Budapest. Svetla Kyoseva chaired one of the discussion panels, entitled “Media and Enlighteners”:
Svetla Kyoseva at the World Meeting of Bulgarian Media in Budapest (20 October 2026)
PHOTO BTA
“The discussion brought together representatives of Bulgarian communities in neighbouring countries, including Diana Glasnova from Zagreb, Desislav Payakov from Vienna, and the media outlet Bulgarski Vesti, represented by its editor-in-chief, Gabriela Hadjikostova. She received an award from the 13 Centuries of Bulgaria National Endowment Fund in recognition of the contribution made by a Bulgarian-language media outlet abroad to the promotion of Bulgarian culture.”
Gabriela Hadjikostova
PHOTO BTA
As a magazine that continues to maintain a print edition, Hemus inevitably faces challenges. Unlike most Bulgarian media outlets abroad, however, which rely on targeted funding from Bulgaria to continue their work, the publication serving the Bulgarian community in Hungary does not depend on such support.
“We do not need this kind of assistance because the Bulgarian community in Hungary receives funding from the Hungarian state,” Svetla Kyoseva said. At the same time, she acknowledged that “funding is a serious problem for many Bulgarian publications abroad. Those that do not receive support from the countries where they are based face considerable difficulties in producing their publications.”
The future plans for Hemus reflect its ambition to remain a bridge between the Bulgarian community and Hungarian society by covering subjects of interest to both readerships. The magazine also aims to reach out to other communities and countries.
PHOTO Facebook /Bolgár Országos Önkormányzat
“Some colleagues and I were invited to contribute to Slovak publications on the subject of Bulgarian gardening being recognised as part of Hungary’s cultural heritage. Bulgarians in Slovakia are currently taking similar steps, which is why they showed great interest in our experience. I have also invited authors from other countries to write for the magazine.”
In 2027, one of the magazine’s issues will mark the centenary of Miklós Mázárov, a Hungarian artist of Bulgarian descent, Svetla Kyoseva announced. She added that, from this year, the gallery at the Bulgarian Cultural and Educational Centre in the Hungarian capital has also borne his name.
“After his death, his widow established an award in his name, presented to Hungarian artists. Receiving this award is a great honour. Every year, it provides an opportunity to talk not only about the artist himself, but also about Bulgaria and Bulgarian artists in Hungary, who form a very close-knit and strong community.”

Tokayev proposes three-year moratorium on small business inspections from 2027
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed introducing a new three-year moratorium on inspections of micro- and small businesses from January 1, 2027. He announced it while delivering his annual State-of-the-Nation Address in еру Qurultay today, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The Head of State called on Qurultay deputies and the Government to discuss the expediency of the measure, taking into account both the positive and negative outcomes of the previous moratorium, which was in effect from 2020 to 2023.
“In this regard, the experience of the 2020-2023 moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses will be valuable. It proved to be effective. I propose that Qurultay deputies and the Government discuss the expediency of introducing another three-year moratorium from January 1, 2027, taking into account all the positive and negative aspects of the previous one,” Tokayev said.
The President also highlighted changes in business inspection figures. According to him, the number of violations by individual entrepreneurs fell by 34% in the first half of the year, while the total amount of fines increased by nearly 11% and the number of unscheduled inspections rose tenfold.
Tokayev also called for improving the conditions for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to participate in procurement by government agencies and quasi-public sector companies. In particular, he proposed reserving a share of procurements for SMEs and easing requirements for suppliers.
The President said the proposed moratorium should serve as a strategic pause to overhaul the inspection and supervision system and transition to a digital regulatory model.
Earlier, the President ordered a new large-scale system of long-term financing for farmers.

Tokayev outlines historic mission to build a new Kazakhstan for future generations

According to the President, the National Fund’s main goal and mission is to preserve the country’s wealth, increase it, and use it for the benefit of current and future generations.
“For many years, the National Fund has fulfilled this core task, making a significant contribution to financial stability. To ensure the well-being of younger generations, we must take concrete and bold steps now. We cannot postpone addressing pressing problems. Every issue must be resolved. This is the main requirement. We must pass on to future generations a civilized, advanced and renewed state. This is our duty and responsibility to future generations,” Tokayev said.
The Head of State noted that the country’s historic responsibility to future generations involves more than leaving them financial savings in bank accounts. It also means building and passing on a fundamentally new country, one that is technologically advanced, has a strong and competitive economy, modern infrastructure and high living standards, and offers every citizen opportunities for self-realization.
“This is our main task, a mission of historic significance. It means long-term investment in human capital, improving citizens’ quality of life and, therefore, investing in the country’s future,” the President stressed.
At the same time, he said Kazakhstan must maintain a balance between accumulating funds in the National Fund and spending them.
“Funds should be directed only toward projects that bring the greatest benefit to society. Most importantly, the money spent must deliver economic and social returns. The main purpose of allocating public funds is to improve people’s well-being,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev says Kazakhstan must become leading logistics hub in Eurasia

This was stated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in his annual state-of-the-nation address, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Tokayev emphasized that logistics infrastructure is one of the key drivers of national development and called for greater attention to the sector amid the transformation of global supply chains.
Today, all countries are addressing logistics issues. Without developed transport logistics, even a country that is strong today may find itself in decline tomorrow, said the President.
President Tokayev announced that the Bakhty-Ayagoz railway line is scheduled to become operational next year. The new route is expected to increase freight capacity between Kazakhstan and China by 20 million tons.
Construction of the Aral-Caspian highway began in August. According to the President, the project will shorten the Trans-Caspian Corridor by approximately 1,000 kilometers and reduce cargo delivery times by up to three days.
The Government will ensure strict oversight of the quality and timely completion of all projects being implemented in the sector, Tokayev added.
Global logistics has entered a period of large-scale transformation and accelerated development. Vulnerabilities in maritime routes have increased the strategic importance of land transport corridors. Kazakhstan must seize this historic opportunity to become, in practice, a leading logistics hub in Eurasia, the Head of State stressed.
According to Tokayev, nearly 85% of freight transported from China to Europe already passes through Kazakhstan.
However, he warned that the country should not become complacent about its current position and must take a more active role in organizing international freight flows.
Being satisfied with the current favorable situation would condemn us to playing catch-up in the future. We must already begin positioning ourselves as a full-fledged organizer of international freight flows, Tokayev said.
He stressed the importance of developing domestic logistics operators and establishing cargo consolidation and distribution centers. The President also called for the creation of new manufacturing facilities and trading platforms around major transport hubs.
Earlier, the Kazakh President urged high-quality standards in national and local road construction.

Ukraine's intelligence names nearly 50 companies involved in developing Russia's Starlink rival
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine's intelligence names nearly 50 companies involved in developing Russia's Starlink rival
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released information on 49 Russian and Belarusian companies involved in developing Rassvet, a satellite communications system that Russia is developing as an alternative to Starlink.
Source: War&Sanctions
Quote: "The system comprises a constellation of low-Earth orbit satellites, ground-based control infrastructure, gateway stations and user terminals for fixed and mobile facilities."
Details: DIU said the project involves IT companies, microelectronics manufacturers, research centres, and entities affiliated with Russia's state space corporation Roscosmos and the Russian Defence Ministry.
According to DIU, the project's main contractor is Russia's Bureau 1440, a limited liability company that is part of the ICS Holding IT group. Other companies within the group supply components and manufacture solar panels, user terminals, printed circuit boards, electronic modules and other system components.
"Roscosmos and other companies in Russia's aerospace industry are responsible for developing and manufacturing launch vehicles and upper stages, electric propulsion engines and other satellite components, as well as adapting the satellites, preparing them for launch and placing them into orbit," DIU said.
DIU said Roscosmos head Dmitry Bakanov directly oversees the Rassvet project. He previously headed the Gonets Satellite System, which partnered with the UK's OneWeb and established a joint venture to develop low-Earth-orbit satellite communications services for the Russian market.
Entities affiliated with the Russian Defence Ministry are responsible for operating the spaceport, coordinating project participants, and eventually integrating the system into the military communications infrastructure. Russian bank VTB is among the investors in Rassvet.
According to DIU, 23 of the 49 companies and institutions involved in the project have not been sanctioned by any country in the sanctions coalition. These include Roscosmos.
The intelligence agency notes that Rassvet is primarily intended for military communications.
"Russia plans to make extensive use of the system to support its armed forces, including for strategic communications and command and control, controlling strike platforms, equipping command posts and military equipment with user terminals, supporting the combat use of unmanned systems and ensuring the operation of Russian Defence Ministry facilities," DIU said.
According to DIU, Russia plans to integrate Rassvet satellites into a space-based system that provides targeting data for missile systems and equip the command vehicles of the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system with user terminals.
"The planned coverage is primarily intended to include the territory of Ukraine and the EU. Once sufficient coverage has been achieved, Russia could use the system in hybrid acts of aggression against other countries," it warned.
The intelligence agency has called for sanctions to be imposed on companies involved in the project and for restrictions on the supply of components, equipment and software to them.
Background: According to DIU, Russia is deploying the Rassvet satellite system ahead of schedule. In March 2026, 16 satellites were placed into orbit. Russia plans to expand the constellation to 292 satellites by 2027 and 924 by 2035.

Russia has lost 1,583,350 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 28.
The number includes 1,510 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to thereport, Russia has also lost 12,448 tanks, 25,609 armored combat vehicles, 167,738 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,674 artillery systems, 2,241 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,727 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,032 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."

While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky toldFrance TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

U.S. Navy finalizes Lockheed order for F-35 power and cooling upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:47:21 UTC
16:47:21 KST

- The U.S. Navy added $13.3 million and 50,000 labor hours to a Lockheed Martin order for F135 Engine Core Upgrade integration and power and cooling work.
- The modification definitizes an earlier undefinitized order, moves the F-35’s power and thermal management upgrade into preliminary design, and runs through April 2027.
The U.S. Navy has added $13.3 million and 50,000 labor hours to a Lockheed Martin order covering integration of the F-35’s upgraded F135 engine core and the move of a new power and cooling system for the fighter into preliminary design.
Naval Air Systems Command announced the cost-plus-fixed-fee, level-of-effort modification on Oct. 27, definitizing an undefinitized contract action, which means the government and Lockheed have now agreed on final terms for work that began before the price was settled, and extending the effort to April 2027. No money was obligated at award, and the work, which supports the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps and the F-35 cooperative program partners, was not competed.
The modification sits on a delivery order NAVAIR first issued in fiscal 2025 as a not-to-exceed $107 million undefinitized order, which paid Lockheed to run trade studies and an alternatives assessment of every potential power and thermal management solution for the F-35, along with the integration work needed to fit Pratt & Whitney’s Engine Core Upgrade into Block 4 aircraft. That order was due to finish in December 2026, so the new action pushes completion back four months while shifting part of the effort from study to design as the power and thermal management upgrade enters its preliminary design phase.
Fort Worth, Texas, where Lockheed builds the F-35, accounts for 47% of the work, while Torrance and El Segundo, California, take 19% between them and two sites in Britain, Blackburn and Cheltenham, take 6% each, with the remainder spread across Haltom City, Texas; South Bend, Indiana; Windsor Locks and West Hartford, Connecticut; Rockford, Illinois; and Orlando, Florida.
The engine and cooling work both stem from the amount of heat the F-35’s electronics generate. The F-35 Joint Program Office has said Block 3 jets produce about 30 kilowatts of waste heat, a figure expected to reach 47 kilowatts in Block 4, while the current engine is optimized to absorb about 14 kilowatts. That heat is removed by the Power and Thermal Management System, or PTMS, a Honeywell unit that draws bleed air from the engine and also provides auxiliary and emergency power, engine starting and cabin environmental control, and because the PTMS takes more air from the F135 than its designers planned, the engine runs hotter and wears out faster, raising sustainment costs across the fleet.
Pratt & Whitney’s Engine Core Upgrade, or ECU, redesigns the F135’s core to produce more thrust, supply more bleed air and electrical power, and restore the engine life lost to heat, while the separate Power Thermal Management Upgrade, or PTMU, will replace or enlarge the cooling system that uses that air. In October 2024, the Joint Program Office named Lockheed the lead systems integrator for the PTMU after concluding that no other company could manage the integration, and the order modified this week is the contract vehicle for that role.
Honeywell, which builds the current PTMS, unveiled a near-term cooling option called P40 in September that would raise capacity from about 32 kilowatts to 40 kilowatts through software changes and liquid-cooling modifications, with no airframe changes and fielding planned for 2029 or 2030, and the company says the architecture could later grow to 62 kilowatts or more. Collins Aerospace, a sister company of Pratt & Whitney within RTX, is competing with a new design called the Enhanced Power and Cooling System, and the two companies have said that pairing it with the ECU would yield about a 7% gain in range and thrust along with double the cooling capacity, figures that come from the manufacturers. The modification does not say which approach Lockheed’s trade studies favored or whether preliminary design will cover one solution or several, and the government has not announced a PTMU selection.
The Pentagon chose in March 2023 to upgrade the F135 instead of re-engining the F-35 with an adaptive-cycle design from the Adaptive Engine Transition Program, citing cost and the difficulty of integrating a new engine into the short-takeoff F-35B and carrier-based F-35C. Pratt & Whitney then completed the ECU’s preliminary design review in July 2024 and later that year received a contract worth up to $1.3 billion for design maturation, rig testing and aircraft integration through March 2028.
In late August, the Navy added a modification worth up to $240.8 million to move the ECU into engineering and manufacturing development and buy long-lead hardware for a spare test engine, and Pratt & Whitney completed the upgrade’s risk reduction design review on Sept. 15. The company describes the ECU as a drop-in replacement core that can be installed on new engines or retrofitted at F135 depots, and John Sneden, the U.S. Air Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for propulsion, said in July that ground testing is planned for late 2027 and flight testing for around 2030, later than the 2029 fielding date Pratt had cited in 2024.
Lockheed’s share of the integration covers the aircraft side of the engine change, since a new core alters bleed-air flow, electrical power extraction, engine controls and heat loads, each of which affects the airframe’s fuel, cooling and mission systems. The engine and cooling upgrades also have to be timed together, because the extra cooling capacity Block 4 needs depends on both programs delivering.
The Government Accountability Office has warned of integration risks to the ECU timeline, and the Block 4 upgrade, which carries the new sensors and weapons responsible for much of the added heat, has slipped repeatedly. The fiscal 2027 budget request seeks $317.5 million for F-35 propulsion work, up from about $121 million in 2026, with much of the increase meant to accelerate the ECU and PTMU.

- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:

Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."
Netanyahu's bloc trails in Israel election, exit polls say
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest single group in the Knesset, with 25 projected seats.
Challenger Gadi Eisenkot's bloc has emerged as the largest group with a projected 53, just ahead of the ruling coalition on 50, but well short of the 61 needed for a majority.
Neither bloc has a clear majority without the support of Arab parties.
These projected numbers are from public broadcaster Kan 11; other numbers vary by channel, but only slightly.
Polls closing around the country
It's now 10 p.m. across Israel, which means that polling stations around the country either should have closed or should be making preparations to do so as the last people in line cast their ballots.
Exit polls should follow shortly on Israeli television. These have a fairly good reputation overall but of course are only projections.
Results will start to trickle in through the night and are unlikely to be finalized until Wednesday.
And of course, there's every chance that even once the dust has settled and the final results are in, we will have a longer wait until there's clarity about who might be able to form a coalition government.
In any case, stick with us and we'll keep you posted.
Election commission sees 'no need to extend voting hours' after Netanyahu request
The Central Elections Committee has rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and some other groups to extend voting beyond 10 p.m. (2000 UTC/GMT).
"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.
The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.
For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.
The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.
IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign
Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.
DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.
High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc
The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.
According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.
Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.
Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.
Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.
Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.
This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.
The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.
And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.

Minister: Economic recovery does not happen overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
