16:45:00 KST

Minister: Economic recovery does not happen overnight
Economic recovery will take a little longer for people to feel its effects, Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Liina Vahtras (Reform) said on Tuesday, commenting on the latest consumer confidence survey.
Businesses believe the economy has improved this month, but consumers were more pessimistic, data from Statistics Estonia published on Tuesday shows.
Companies have held this view for some time, so the survey results were no surprise to the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications. The industrial sector is in its strongest position in four years.
"Of course, major negative events also took place four years ago, and confidence then plummeted. By now, we have climbed out of that hole. However, according to surveys, consumer economic confidence has fallen to its lowest level in six months," said Mario Lambing, chief analyst at the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
Since May, Statistics Estonia has conducted economic confidence surveys instead of the Estonian Institute of Economic Research, and the ministry comments on the results once a quarter.
Vahtras also commented on the results.
"Economic recovery and improvement simply take a little more time; they do not happen overnight. People will feel that things have actually improved for them. And the effects of the income tax reform implemented at the beginning of the year will simply be felt a little later," she said.
High motor fuel prices and the winter heating season have made people more cautious about the future. "If this winter is colder and heating bills rise, the government will discuss how to compensate both private consumers and businesses," the minister added.
Lambing said the change in survey provider has made consumers' opinions more pessimistic.
"One factor is indeed the change in survey provider, but a bigger change may have come from the fact that consumers were now surveyed online instead of by telephone, and these methods can produce different results, even if you ask exactly the same person exactly the same question," he said.

Russia has fired more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast since 14 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his evening address on 27 October. He said partners’ air defense packages are being delayed.
Ukraine’s front-line positions are stronger than they have been in a long time, Zelenskyy said. If partners’ support for Patriots and other air defense remained just as strong, he argued, Ukraine would be in a much better position diplomatically as well. He expects trilateral talks with US and Russian representatives in November. The US, on which, he said, “almost everything concerning Patriots depends,” will be one of the three sides.
Delays and the war on logistics
Overnight on 27 October, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 280 drones, in what Zelenskyy called a serious escalation of Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s logistics. The strikes hit the State University of Trade and Economics campus and the Southern Bridge in Kyiv.
Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus, then return before dawn for the Southern Bridge again
A 46-year-old woman was killed and 15 people were injured, among them dormitory residents and two medics, the Kyiv prosecutor’s office said on the morning of 27 October.
Zelenskyy wrote that artificial and lengthy delays in interceptor packages for Patriots and NASAMS directly help Russia achieve the goals of its terror campaign. In his evening address, he added:
“And everyone hears, everyone sees that right now, it is difficult for us to defend against Russian ballistic missiles. And above all, we do not have enough missiles for Patriots.”
A month waiting on Hegseth
Earlier, on 26 October, Zelenskyy wrote that Ukraine had waited almost a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s signature on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. Kyiv is also working with Europe and other partners, he added.
Ukraine raises its stalled Patriot request with Washington again after almost a month without Hegseth’s signature
Separately, The Washington Post reported on 19 October that some transfers come from allies and need Hegseth’s approval, because the US must sign off on re-transfers. Zelenskyy’s post does not say whether his wait concerns those transfers.
Before Zelenskyy’s latest statements, US officials rejected claims of a deliberate hold. A US government official called Ukraine’s claims “not true,” the Kyiv Independent reported. On 20 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was “nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine.” Hegseth said the US had not changed its posture toward Ukraine but wants “our guys” to have as many interceptors as possible.

Q3: UBS posts $2.7 billion profit
UBS recorded a net profit of $2.7 billion (CHF2.2 billion) between July and September. The bank is on track to meet its annual targets and complete the integration of Credit Suisse this year, it said on Wednesday.
Profit before tax reached $3.6 billion in the third quarter, and $4.1 billion on a like-for-like basis, representing year-on-year increases of 27% and 14%, respectively.
The bank benefited from strong client momentum across its various market segments. Operating income rose by 5% to $13.35 billion. On a like-for-like basis, the increase was 10% to $13.39 billion, UBS said.
More
‘Switzerland has spoken’. Will UBS leave?
In wealth management, new money inflows reached $55.1 billion in the third quarter. Growth was driven by the Asia-Pacific region and the Americas.
Shareholders already have reason to be pleased, as the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio and the CET1 leverage ratio stand at 14.7% and 4.6%, respectively, paving the way for a dividend increase of around 15% and the implementation of the $3 billion share buyback programme by the time the results for the final interim period of 2026 are published.
The annual targets are within reach. Following a return on Common Equity Tier 1 (RoCET1) of 16.7% on an underlying nine-month basis (or 14.8% unadjusted), UBS believes it is on track to exceed its 2026 target, which stood at around 15% . Meanwhile, the cost-to-income ratio, which stood at 69.6% between January and September, is expected to be in line with expectations (below 70 per cent) for the full year.
More
What the too-big-to-fail Swiss parliament vote means for UBS
The results are in line with expectations, with both adjusted and unadjusted operating income, as well as adjusted pre-tax profit, even exceeding the AWP consensus estimates.
Furthermore, UBS is on track to finalise the integration of its former rival Credit Suisse by the end of the year. Additional cost savings of $0.6 billion were realised in the third-quarter results, bringing total gross savings to $13.2 billion. By the end of 2026, UBS expects to have achieved savings of $13.7 billion, compared with the $13.5 billion previously forecast.
A number of macroeconomic, political and geopolitical factors will weigh on investor confidence in the final quarterly results.

Zelenskyy: temporary Starshield restriction stops operation of 2,000 'Bars' drone interceptors
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:43:23 EET
16:43:23 KST

Ukraine received 2,000 Bars drone interceptors funded by a European country, and during testing, one of them destroyed a Russian Shahed, but Starshield restrictions halted the operation of these interceptors, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
"We found a European country. They paid for 2,000 units. I knew we had 2,000. I said: 'Let's test it. Maybe it can destroy targets.' They tested it, and it destroyed a Shahed. We were very happy. And then Starshield stopped working," Zelenskyy said at a meeting with journalists on Tuesday, an Interfax-Ukraine agency correspondent reports.
He noted that he does not know who exactly made the decision to turn off the system, which is technically turned on and off by SpaceX. Zelenskyy also explained that Ukraine uses Starshield against the Russian military on its own territory, rather than on the territory of the Russian Federation. In addition, the system is used primarily for logistics, in particular providing the military with food and water, as well as to counter "Shaheds" and jet-powered drones.
According to the President, Ukraine currently destroys about 90% of Russian Shaheds, whereas at the beginning of the attacks this figure was 50–75%, sometimes reaching 78%. Zelenskyy also stated that during the Starlink/Starshield disconnection, civilians died, although he emphasized that this happened for various reasons.
As reported, on the night of October 14, the Ukrainian military recorded restrictions on the operation of Starshield terminals – the military version of Starlink satellite communications. According to Interfax-Ukraine sources in the Ministry of Defense, terminals lost connection while moving at speeds exceeding a set threshold, which on various equipment was approximately 72–161 km/h. This complicated the tasks performed by drone interceptors and strike UAVs, as well as logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relay. The Ministry of Defense held consultations with the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners and checked backup communication channels.
On October 24, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported that Ministry of Defense monitoring systems were recording the restoration of Starlink/Starshield speed capabilities.
"We are recording speeds of more than 400 km/h, the connection is stable. This is another example of how direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yield results. And this result is primarily important for our front, for the military, drone operations, logistics, and communications," Khmara commented in response to journalists' questions on Saturday.

Fourth-tier Fleetwood stun Premier League champions Arsenal in League Cup shootout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:41:52 UTC
16:41:52 KST

Dilara Hamit
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Fourth-tier Fleetwood Town produced one of the biggest upsets in English League Cup history by eliminating Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties Tuesday.
Fleetwood won the shootout 5-3 at Highbury Stadium after the fourth-round tie ended 1-1 in normal time, reaching the competition’s quarterfinals for the first time.
The English Football League said the hosts entered the match 84 places below Arsenal in the English football pyramid.
Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave Fleetwood a surprise lead in the 21st minute, overpowering Arsenal teenager Marli Salmon before finishing past debutant goalkeeper Illan Meslier.
Arsenal controlled possession after falling behind but struggled to convert their chances against Fleetwood’s disciplined defense.
Mikel Arteta introduced captain Martin Odegaard at halftime, and Viktor Gyokeres equalized five minutes after the restart. The Swedish striker converted from close range following an attack involving 18-year-old Ceadach O’Neill, who was making his first senior start for Arsenal.
The visitors increased the pressure as the second half progressed, but goalkeeper Jay Lynch repeatedly denied them. He made important late saves against Ben White and Odegaard to send the match to penalties.
Arsenal finished the game with 10 players after 16-year-old Max Dowman was shown a red card for kicking out following a challenge by Fleetwood midfielder Harrison Neal in the 85th minute.
Fleetwood converted all five of their penalties through Ronan Coughlan, Neal, Will Davies, Andy Cannon and Conor Haughey.
Odegaard, Kai Havertz and Gyokeres scored Arsenal’s first three attempts, but Lynch saved substitute Bruno Guimaraes’ fourth penalty. Haughey then converted the decisive kick, sparking a pitch invasion and celebrations among the home supporters.
The match had also been interrupted shortly after kickoff when an unauthorized drone flew above the stadium, causing play to be suspended for several minutes.
Arteta fielded a much-changed side ahead of Arsenal’s Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday, although the starting lineup still included Gyokeres, Havertz, Martin Zubimendi, Jurrien Timber and Piero Hincapie.
Fleetwood had never previously reached the League Cup’s fourth round. Before Tuesday, they were also winless in five matches against top-flight opposition.
Arsenal’s elimination echoed their 2012 League Cup defeat to fourth-tier Bradford City, who also knocked the London club out on penalties following a 1-1 draw.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine wants Abu Dhabi trilateral meeting before potential U.S-China-Russia summit
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:41:30 EET
16:41:30 KST

Ukraine would like the tripartite meeting of the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the U.S, and Russia in Abu Dhabi to take place prior to a potential meeting between the US, China, and Russia, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
"We will see what kind of meeting this will be. We would very much like our meeting in Abu Dhabi to happen before that," Zelenskyy said at a meeting with journalists on Tuesday, an Interfax-Ukraine agency correspondent reports.
Commenting on the possible meeting of the leaders of the U.S, China, and Russia, the President noted that it will likely discuss the situation in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine.
At the same time, Zelenskyy expressed concern over the possibility of a redistribution of spheres of influence by analogy with the Yalta Conference.
"I really don't want this to be a 'Yalta – 2, 3, 4,' when there is a redistribution of influence. I would even say not influence, but opinions – that things can be redistributed this way. Today we have a different world, a fragmented world that is very different from the world of World War II, both before and after. A completely different technological world. Therefore, I think it is impossible to simply make such a redistribution between the three. Although Russia really wants to," the President emphasized.
In his opinion, such a meeting would be more beneficial to Russia than to China.
"I believe that after Alaska, this will be the second such diplomatic, serious advantage for Russia, if everything happens exactly as the Russians are now 'leaking' regarding their desires for a new 'Yalta,'" he said.
The President added that currently, holding the tripartite meeting in Abu Dhabi depends on the American side.
"The Russians have confirmed, we have confirmed. In my opinion, today this no longer depends on the Russians and not on us. Today Abu Dhabi depends on the American side," he noted.
According to him, all parties view the possibility of holding such a meeting positively, but the development of the situation in the Middle East is affecting U.S plans.
"There may be escalation there, and many are talking about it. I think there will be," the President believes.

Brussels cyclist loses sight in his left eye following serious road rage incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:40:32 UTC
16:40:32 KST

Cyclist Laurent Nyssen was the victim of a serious road rage incident in the Brussels borough of Schaarbeek. As a result of which he has probably lost sight in one eye. It all began with an argument over a blocked cycle path. “The guy got out of his car at the traffic lights; after that, I don’t remember what happened” Laurent told Brussels media outlet Bruzz.
Brussels cyclist loses sight in his left eye following serious road rage incident
On Wednesday 14 October, Laurent Nyssen was out on his bike to collect a parcel in Schaarbeek. At around 6.45 pm, he got into an altercation with a motorist on Koninklijke Sinte-Mariastraat.
“There was a traffic jam. I rang my bell at the many cars blocking the cycle path – something that happens every day in Brussels.” The street has wide cycle paths, but they are not separated from the road and the cars.
A van driver travelling behind him must have been annoyed by the ringing. “He was really worked up and gave me a proper telling-off at the traffic lights. I gave him a piece of my mind, as I often do, but at the second set of traffic lights he got out of his van. I have no memory of what happened next.”
Two witnesses did see what happened, and a CCTV camera also recorded everything. “He completely lost it,” Laurent recounts. “I was hit on the head about ten times. He hit me so hard that I fell to the ground.”
Eye surgery
Laurent was taken to hospital, but he cannot remember anything about that either. The blows left him with a broken jaw and damaged his left eye.
“I’ve had two operations on my eye, but the doctors fear I’ll never be able to see out of it again. There’s still a very small chance that some of my sight might recover over time, but it won’t ever be the same as it was before.”
At home with an ankle monitor
The man, aged around 30, who had carried out the attack was arrested that very evening. “The police came to my hospital bed in the middle of the night to tell me he’d been arrested. He spent six days in a cell and is now at home with an ankle monitor. Other than that, I know nothing about him,” says the cyclist. According to Laurent, his story is not an isolated incident. “There’s a culture of hatred towards cyclists in Brussels. It’s the law of the jungle on the streets. And the aggression towards cyclists is getting worse every year. Motorists feel like they own the roads in Brussels; they pay absolutely no attention to cyclists. And if you say anything about it, you get a proper telling-off.”
“Virtually all my friends who cycle have experienced aggression. One of them even ended up in hospital after a ‘discussion’ with a driver. Fortunately, his injuries weren’t too serious at the time.”
Food delivery riders
Laurent feels that cyclists are viewed with suspicion, particularly in the boroughs of Schaarbeek and Anderlecht. “I’m well aware that there are cyclists who don’t follow the rules. A lot of food delivery riders race through the city to get through as many orders as possible. But that’s completely out of proportion to the danger cyclists face.”
The attacker will have to answer in court in November; Laurent will be bringing a civil claim. “The police told me I was lucky to have survived. I think he should be tried for attempted manslaughter.”
Living with one eye
Laurent is recovering and trying to get his life back on track. He is at home on sick leave, preparing for a life with vision in only one eye. “The doctors have told me that the brain adapts quickly to seeing with just one eye. At first, I was worried about my job; I work as a graphic designer. I’ve realised I can manage. It’ll take a bit of getting used to it. Especially when I’m walking down the street, I find I can’t judge distances very well.”
“I’m getting a lot of support from my girlfriend and daughter, from my family and friends,” he says gratefully. “And I’m determined to start cycling again. Not straight away, but as soon as winter’s over. I won’t let anything keep me off the streets.”

Egypt, Saudi Arabia, UAE discuss regional de-escalation, with Türkiye-led mediation mechanism in focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:39:36 UTC
16:39:36 KST

Amer Solyman and Ikram Kouachi
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Egypt discussed regional de-escalation efforts with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, emphasizing coordination through a four-way ministerial mechanism involving Türkiye and Pakistan, according to the Egyptian Foreign Ministry.
Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held separate phone calls Tuesday with his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, and UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed, the ministry said in two separate statements Wednesday.
During his call with bin Farhan, Abdelatty discussed regional developments and “efforts to contain the current crisis amid growing risks of escalation,” stressing the need to “advance political and peaceful solutions through dialogue.”
The two foreign ministers agreed to “continue close consultations and coordination bilaterally and through a four-way ministerial mechanism that also includes Türkiye and Pakistan.”
The mechanism brings together Egypt, Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia to strengthen consultation and coordination on de-escalation and support political solutions to regional crises.
The call came a day after Egypt’s parliament approved, by a two-thirds majority, a mandate for President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take necessary measures to support Saudi Arabia and defend its territory, sovereignty and holy sites, in coordination with the kingdom.
It also comes amid ongoing military escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group since July, including Houthi attacks on civil aviation facilities and energy infrastructure in the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition since March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.
In a separate statement, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Abdelatty and his Emirati counterpart discussed the latest regional developments, particularly growing indications of possible escalation in the coming period.
Abdelatty stressed the need for regional countries to “unite their efforts to reach peaceful solutions and return all parties to a peaceful political track to prevent the region from sliding into a more dangerous phase of the current crisis.”
The call came as mediation efforts continue to contain tensions between Washington and Tehran amid ongoing disagreements over the conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
On Feb. 28, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US military facilities in Arab countries.
On June 18, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding and began negotiations that later collapsed over disagreements, including maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for global energy and goods supplies.

The war with Iran has already cost the United States $47.1 billion — NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:38:10 EET
16:38:10 KST

War with Iran has already cost the United States $47.1 billion - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. spending on the war with Iran has reached $47.1 billion, with more than 60% going toward munitions. The Pentagon is requesting up to another $70 billion.
For the United States, the cost of the war with Iran had risen to $47.1 billion as of October 16, with bombs, missiles and other munitions accounting for more than 60 percent of the expenditures. The Pentagon reported this to Congress last week, UNN writes, citing The New York Times.
Details
Even though U.S. President Donald Trump has so far refrained from resuming major hostilities, the Pentagon still incurred additional costs of about $3.5 billion over roughly six weeks since the estimates were presented to lawmakers last month.
These figures were the latest look at the unclassified breakdown of costs incurred by each branch of the armed forces, as well as by specific categories, such as damaged or destroyed weapons.
In the latest cost estimates, for example, the U.S. Air Force spent $7.6 billion to cover the operation of dozens of fighter and bomber squadrons. The U.S. Navy spent $1.5 billion deploying more than two dozen warships, including several aircraft carriers. And maintaining troops in the region cost the Army $2.1 billion. Overall, according to U.S. Central Command, more than 50,000 service members are involved in this military mission.
Members of Congress shared these cost estimates with The New York Times after they were provided to national security committees on Capitol Hill.
Since the war began on February 28, the U.S. military has spent $29 billion on munitions, depleting global stocks of certain critical weapons, such as Patriot interceptors, and redirecting supplies from U.S. military commands in Asia and Europe.
The Pentagon spent $6.1 billion replacing dozens of damaged or destroyed combat aircraft and other weapons and equipment. It spent $645 million deploying and supporting several thousand special forces personnel in the region.
The information also revealed spending on other important items. According to one member of Congress, the military spent $24.5 million on "internal medical support" for U.S. service members. The Pentagon reports that 18 service members have been killed in the war and more than 860 have been wounded.
According to an official, U.S. Transportation Command spent $92.2 million moving cargo and equipment, while U.S. Cyber Command spent $14 million on "cyber support operations."
According to members of Congress on Tuesday, the department's figures are almost certainly understated, as the Pentagon acknowledged that its estimate does not include $1.5 billion for fuel and other expenses that the Trump administration requested in a supplemental request to fund the war.
The information provided to Congress also did not include the costs of repairing or replacing U.S. military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks, such as the U.S. Navy base in Manama, Bahrain. The Pentagon indicated that it may close them or not rebuild them. If the military or host countries restore the facilities, the costs could amount to tens of billions of dollars, according to members of Congress.
Meanwhile, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and the Trump administration are seeking up to $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the war with Iran, as well as to purchase new weapons and personnel.

Australia moves to tighten sunscreen rules amid concerns over SPF claims
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:37:20 CST
16:37:20 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) is developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen regulation and improve consumer confidence and the reliability of sun protection factor (SPF) claims.
The proposed reforms include strengthening sunscreen testing requirements, setting quality requirements for specific ingredients and limiting the SPF claims that cosmetic sunscreens can make, according to a TGA statement released Tuesday.
The agency said it will also review good manufacturing practice guidance to clarify expectations and responsibilities and support continued confidence in the quality and performance of sunscreen products in Australia.
The reforms follow a public consultation held from March to May that received almost 120 responses from industry, testing laboratories, health professionals, consumer groups, academia and other stakeholders.
Australia has the highest incidence of skin cancer in the world, the TGA said, adding that the primary objective of sunscreen regulation was to ensure product quality, safety and efficacy in protecting consumers from harmful ultraviolet radiation, and to reduce the incidence and impact of skin cancer.
David Whiteman, a distinguished scientist at Australia's QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, backed reforms to improve the rigor and transparency of sunscreen testing and review manufacturing practices, following reports that some sunscreens failed to meet their labelled SPF in independent tests, shaking public confidence.
The TGA said further consultation on SPF labeling would take place before progressing with any proposed changes. ■

China confirms identities of 8 more volunteer soldiers killed in Korean War
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:37:08 CST
16:37:08 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- China has confirmed the identities of eight more Chinese People's Volunteers (CPV) martyrs who lost their lives during the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea (1950-1953), the Ministry of Veterans Affairs said on Wednesday.
This marks further progress in efforts to identify the remains of CPV martyrs repatriated from the Republic of Korea (ROK), the ministry said.
More than 70 years ago, the CPV crossed the Yalu River and fought alongside the army and civilians of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) against the ROK army and U.S.-led UN forces. China sent 2.9 million CPV soldiers to assist the DPRK during the war, of whom more than 360,000 were killed or injured. Most of the fallen CPV soldiers were buried on the Korean Peninsula.
According to an agreement between China and the ROK signed in late 2013, the two sides consult every year on the handover of remains of Chinese soldiers found in the ROK.
Since 2014, China and the ROK have completed 13 consecutive handovers involving the remains of 1,023 CPV martyrs.
In recent years, China has intensified efforts to identify the remains of CPV martyrs, including the creation of a DNA database for martyrs and their relatives, offering solid technical and data support to help more families find their missing loved ones.
To date, the identities of 44 of the martyrs have been confirmed and their relatives have been located. ■

Feature: Xiamen University Malaysia marks a decade of growth, cross-cultural education

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- For biotechnology graduate Ng Boon Ful, choosing the right educational institution can lay the foundation for high-quality learning and a successful career, especially amid rapid technological development.
With a thirst for multidisciplinary knowledge combining biology, chemistry, physics and even oceanography, Ng chose Xiamen University Malaysia, a renowned and highly regarded name in the sciences. He shared these thoughts with Xinhua on the sidelines of his recent graduation ceremony.
"Marine biotechnology is different and unique compared with programs related to marine science at other universities," he said, explaining that the field usually focuses on marine science in general or marine agriculture.
"This marine biotechnology course also allowed me to learn a greater variety of knowledge... This is quite a unique program that is very hard to find at other universities in Malaysia," he said, adding that he would recommend it to others interested in the field.
Ng noted that the university also gave him access to a valuable exchange program with China, providing him with access to a variety of specialized equipment and broadening the scope of his education to include marine chemistry, environmental science and other aspects of the field. "When I participated in the study exchange programs at Xiamen University and in China, I was very impressed," he said.
The university held the first ceremony of its eighth convocation on Oct. 10, with a total of 1,677 students from 23 undergraduate and seven postgraduate programs graduating at this convocation, including 978 local Malaysian students and 699 international students.
Among those in attendance were the Chief Executive Officer of the Malaysian Qualifications Agency, Mohammad Shatar Sabran, and Xiamen University President Prof. Hu Wenping.
In his remarks to the graduates, Hu reminded them of the importance not only of academic qualifications but also of growing as human beings with a broad global outlook to better prepare them for the rapidly changing world they will be entering as employees.
"What Xiamen provides is precisely a multicultural environment, where students from more than 50 countries and regions learn and interact... Years of multicultural immersion have taught you to understand differences, respect diversity, and collaborate responsibly across cultures. What this experience has given you is not just a broad perspective, but also the ability to live, work, and create with people from different cultural backgrounds," he said.
For his part, Mohammad Shatar urged the graduates to adopt a view that will help them build bridges as they continue their careers, whether locally or abroad, and to use what they have learned to build lasting bonds: "You are graduating from a university that represents something bigger: a bridge. A bridge between Malaysia and China. A bridge between East and West. A bridge between cultures. A bridge between knowledge and opportunity. And increasingly, a bridge between education and the future," he said.
The university welcomed its first batch of students in 2016, and over the past decade it has made remarkable progress, with the campus hosting more than 10,800 students from 53 countries and regions. The strength of the university has made its graduates favored not only by Chinese companies and their overseas branches but also by international companies seeking to expand into the Asian market. ■

Israel votes in a pivotal election but no clear winner emerges

16:36:28 KST

Good morning. It’s Wednesday and my name is Angela Skujins. In today’s newsletter: A new yet unclear era of Israeli politics, saying “do widzenia” to a Polish ambassador, and why energy is the chink in Europe’s defence armour. Let’s go.
Elections in Israel: Key legislative elections in Israel show incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu standing ahead of the opposition Wednesday morning after 50% of votes have been counted. This is according to figures from the Central Elections Committee. Netanyahu's bloc is projected to win 56 of the 120 seats in the parliament, compared with 49 for the opposition bloc and 15 for the Arab parties.
Eylon Levy, former Israeli government spokesperson, just said on Europe Today that there are three options facing the political elite: form a unity government, form a minority government, or fresh elections. “All of those are going to require someone to surrender on some very serious coalition promises.” Watch.
What is likely to come next is weeks of wrangling among parties to form a governing coalition and declare a new prime minister. In the meantime, Netanyahu remains as interim caretaker head of the government.
What is clear is that the country remains deeply divided over Netanyahu's leadership and remains damaged by the Hamas-led 7 October attacks and the wars that have since shaken the Middle East.
Phone a friend: The leaders of Finland and Norway spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the phone for 90-minutes on Tuesday to restart the peace process. According to statements, the two leaders urged Putin to end the full-scale invasion and engage in meaningful negotiations to reach a stable, peaceful settlement.
As my colleague Jorge Liboreiro reports, that chat was followed by a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who thanked the duo for their “active” support and called for de-escalatory steps. (More analysis of the play-by-play below).
What is important to highlight now is that the Stubb-Støre move comes as the European Commission and the European Council prepare a joint team of senior officials to be sent to the next round of talks.
As Sasha Vakulina writes, Russia, Ukraine and the US could meet in Abu Dhabi on 4 November for talks. That’s according to an announcement by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Tuesday.
According to Tusk, the provisional date emerged as European leaders coordinated diplomatic efforts with Kyiv and Washington ahead of possible negotiations. What’s interesting is that this is occurring one day after the US midterm elections scheduled for Tuesday 3 November.
The timing raises questions about what comes next for Washington's efforts to end Moscow’s war.
For those uninitiated: The midterms matter because they occur in the middle of a president’s four-year term and determine the composition of the two chambers of Congress: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
The vote not only offers an opportunity for citizens to elect lawmakers — Republican or Democrat, for example — but also serves as a temperature check on a president’s term in office. For US President Donald Trump, this is a mandate pockmarked by trade wars, hostility towards Ukraine, and a retreat from the transatlantic security architecture. Can the damage from the last 24-months be undone at the ballot box?
Keith Brannum, Truman National Security Project fellow and strategist, just told Europe Today that this Congress has been “subservient” to Trump. Democrats, however, have been “very vocal” about holding the president to account. “We are in uncertain times,” he said, with no clear projection of the future. Watch.
Brussels news: Polish ambassador Agnieszka Bartol will depart Brussels to take a cabinet position at Tusk’s government in Warsaw. She will remain his sherpa, having built on years of experience where she cut a reputation of smooth operator and became a fan-favourite of journalists in the Belgian capital. Polish Andrzej Domański is poised to become the country’s next deputy prime minister.
More Brussels news: EU energy and defence commissioners Dan Jørgensen and Andrius Kubilius will today hold talks on energy security at the Berlaymont, bringing together stakeholders including NATO officials and industry heavyweights.
According to a leaked agenda obtained by my colleague Marta Pacheco, discussions will focus on EU fuel production for defence, particularly jet fuel output and logistics to meet a “potential demand surge”.
Caspar Hobhouse, a research analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies, said Europe’s militaries primarily rely on two fuel sources: jet fuel for aviation and diesel to serve as backup power for military bases. “In the case of a military conflict, the demand is enormous,” he told me.
‘Very, very short business’: Securing these fuel supplies is becoming more difficult due to the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Without major replenishments, Europe’s current fuel reserves would leave it “very, very short business” in the event of armed aggression, Caspar said.
MEP Riho Terras, and former commander of the Estonian Defence Forces, welcomed the talks, warning that aggression is imminent and stressing the need for proper planning. “We have to be prepared,” he said, including for plan Bs. “In 2007 I served in Iraq, then the whole country experienced a very big shortage of energy, and we dealt a lot with diesel generators there. In times of war, you need to have backups,” Riho enthused.
Cash investment: A NATO spokesperson said it is “vital” that Europe’s fuel production capacity can support both civil and military demands, particularly during crises and conflicts. In July, allies approved a €27 billion NATO Fuel Supply Chain Capability Programme Plan, which includes pipelines along the alliance’s eastern and south-eastern corridors to ensure supplies for “warfighting readiness”.
So what will come out of the talks? Monitor Euronews for updates.
Life after Vučić: After 14-years of Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) rule, the status quo was shattered on Monday when election results rolled in and foretold a new era for the Western Balkan country. This is one predominantly without former president Aleksandar Vučić, a free press and a reset of EU relations.
In the days since the seismic election, onlookers have witnessed scenes unfold on social media, of the lead anchor from national broadcaster Radio Television of Vojvodina (RTV) apologising to viewers for the last decade of alleged one-sided reporting.
On Tuesday, European Council President António Costa even called Ilija Srdanović, the leader of the Student List political movement, to say that parliament and government is expected to be formed swiftly. On top of this, most importantly, he communicated that “Serbia’s place is in the European Union.”
Marko Prelec, Balkans expert at the International Crisis Group, just told Europe Today that the new political elite “clearly seek” better relations with Europe and the EU itself. But how this will actually materialise is yet to be seen. Watch.
As the EU attempts to find the right tenor when speaking with China to eradicate an eye-watering trade deficit, it seems that a French football star has irritated officials in Beijing.
Mao migraine: Top French footballer Kylian Mbappé has lost several of his biggest sponsorship deals in China after a video circulated online in which he appears to joke about Mao Zedong, the founder of the People’s Republic of China, that led to a backlash that he has now apologised for.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement he published in French, Chinese and English on Tuesday. "I apologise to everyone that my words have upset."
Ken Early, Irish football commentator, just told Europe Today that this is not the first time a political controversy has disrupted the activities on the pitch. “The German player Mesut Özil who played for Arsenal at the time, in 2019, posted on social media about the plight of the Uyghur people in China,” he said.
“In that instance, they said, ‘Okay, Arsenal won't be on Chinese television anymore.” Watch.
After months dithering, Europe shows it's ready for talks with Russia
After months of bickering, Europe is sending its strongest signals yet that it is ready to speak directly with Russia to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and decide the future of the continent's security architecture.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre marched ahead and held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the imminent restart of the peace process.
Though Stubb and Støre lacked a mandate to speak on behalf of Europe — they did so as “leaders of their respective countries” — their overture on Tuesday immediately positioned the Nordic duo as preeminent interlocutors. In its read-out, the Kremlin said that the three had "agreed to maintain direct telephone contact in the future".
The Stubb-Støre surprise move comes as the European Commission and the European Council prepare a joint team of senior officials to be sent to the next round of talks, scheduled to be held in Abu Dhabi in early November.
Is it notable that Brussels is openly stating its intention to hold the negotiations in a multilateral format, which would mean having Europeans, Ukrainians, Americans and Russians at the same table and at the same time. It is even more notable that Russia, rather than rejecting European presence, is now actively seeking it.
In his latest analysis, Jorge explains why Europe is more ready than ever to expand its diplomatic role and make its voice heard vis-a-vis Russia.

Divers explore oldest medieval warship found off Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:35:45 UTC
16:35:45 KST

Divers are exploring a remarkably well-preserved 15th-century shipwreck off Häringe, in Sweden's Stockholm archipelago. The vessel is believed to be the oldest medieval warship found in Swedish waters and could offer new insights into Scandinavian shipbuilding.
The ship was built using the carvel technique, in which planks are laid edge to edge to create a smooth hull. Researchers say it is the first known example of a ship built this way in Sweden or Denmark.
The wreck may also be connected to historical conflicts between Sweden and Denmark around 1500.
Archaeologists are documenting the buried sections of the vessel and searching for its galley, hoping to learn more about food and daily life on board.
The ongoing investigation could help researchers better understand how medieval warships were built, how they were used in regional conflicts and what life was like for the people who sailed them.

According to an analysis of publicly released footage conducted by Militarnyi, the ammonia production unit AM-70 may have been hit.
According to OSINT Varta, Novomoskovsk Azot is one of Russia’s largest chemical enterprises and is part of the EuroChem Group. The plant specializes in producing ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, methanol, and other chemical products.
The facility also produces nitric acid and ammonium nitrate, which are used not only in civilian industry but also to manufacture explosives and ammunition.
Between February 2022 and September 2024, Novomoskovsk Azot supplied nearly 5,000 tonnes of nitric acid to the Sverdlov Plant in Dzerzhinsk, Nizhny Novgorod region.
The facility produces RDX and HMX, explosives used in military munitions.
Drone attacks have repeatedly targeted Novomoskovsk Azot. In particular, on June 14, 2026, a strike destroyed one of its production workshops and damaged ammonia production units. A second attack took place on June 26.

The IDF announced that it had eliminated three members of Hamas' elite Nukhba force in separate airstrikes across the Gaza Strip last week, including an operative accused of participating in the October 7, 2023, abductions of Israeli civilians.
Ahmed Muhammad Ahmed Baraka was eliminated Thursday in an airstrike in southern Gaza, according to the IDF. The military identified Baraka as a member of Hamas' Nukhba force, the elite unit that played a central role in the October 7 attacks on southern Israel.
According to the IDF, Baraka was among the Hamas terrorists who infiltrated Kibbutz Nir Oz, one of the communities hardest hit in the attack, and participated in the kidnapping of several Israeli civilians, including Alexander Dancyg, a Holocaust educator who was abducted from his home and later died in Hamas captivity.
The IDF said Baraka also helped hold several Israeli hostages in southern Gaza during the war, including Nimrod Cohen, an Israeli soldier abducted on October 7.
In a separate airstrike Friday in northern Gaza, Israeli forces eliminated two other Hamas operatives: Omar Awadallah, identified as a Nukhba platoon commander, and Moataz Mahmoud Mohammed Al-Nimr, also a member of the elite force.
The IDF said all three men had been involved in planning attacks against Israeli troops and civilians, particularly in recent days, while working to rebuild Hamas' military capabilities.
The army described their activities as violations of the ceasefire agreement and said the strikes were intended to eliminate threats posed by the operatives.
Before carrying out the strikes, the IDF took measures to minimize harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.
Israeli forces remain deployed in parts of Gaza under the terms of the ceasefire agreement. The IDF said its troops would continue operations against what it considers security threats.

Safeguards introduced to rein in member states that do not adhere to the EU’s rules and values will “bite hard” to curb “Trojan horses” inside the bloc, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos has told TVP World.
Kos said the EU had introduced the safeguards in light of its experience with Hungary’s former pro-Moscow leadership.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If the new member states follow our rules, they will not even feel them,” she said. “But if they will go against them, then those safeguards will bite hard. So this is the main philosophy of these new safeguards.”
Kos was speaking after Sunday’s parliamentary election in Serbia—which has a history of balancing between Brussels and Moscow—was won by a political movement that grew out of widespread student-led protests against public-sector corruption.
In addition to problems with democratic fundamentals such as an independent judiciary, Serbia has been held back in its bid to join the EU by shortcomings in its “strategic alignment in the field of foreign and security policy,” Kos said.
She said if a candidate country is not strategically aligned with the European Union, “meaning being together in fighting Russia, especially in Russia’s war in Ukraine,” then it will be “very, very difficult for the country to advance,” in the accession process.
Vučić’s Defeat Is Not Yet a Victory for Serbia’s European Future
But Kos added that these issues can be addressed only when the new government has been formed in Belgrade.
Aligned with EU
The student movement that triumphed in Serbia’s parliamentary election has demands that tally with those of the EU, Kos said.
Describing the Serbian election result as “excellent,” Kos said the students’ demands—rule of law, democracy and free media, as well as fighting corruption—tally with “what we are demanding from Serbia in the accession process.”
“Serbia has been a candidate [for EU membership] for more than ten years, but... instead of advancing in the process, they were backsliding,” Kos said. “So this winning of the student list could be a new start for Serbia on the European path.”

EU Inc: Is the EU’s flagship start-up plan really dying over workers’ rights?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:32:08 UTC
16:32:08 KST

The EU’s 28th regime, the plan to help start-ups grow, has stalled in the European Parliament as political parties and trade unions warn it will deregulate workers’ rights. Watch the video!
Proposed by the Commission on 18 March, EU Inc. would be an optional company form alongside the 27 national systems, with digital registration within 48 hours, a cost of up to €100, and no minimum share capital.
Two Legal Affairs Committee votes were cancelled in October because political groups could not agree on workers’ rights. Companies would follow the employee-participation rules of their chosen country of registration. Unions and centre-left MEPs fear firms could choose weaker board-level protections. Business-friendly lawmakers say applying multiple national systems would complicate the plan.
The EU-INC campaign, backed by more than 26,000 supporters and figures linked to Stripe, Mistral AI, Klarna and Wise, says the opposite problem is real. It points to the deletion of the central EU register from the Council text and limits on harmonised stock options. Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné has said the regime cannot work without stock-option harmonisation.
A new committee vote is pencilled in for 5 November, and a first plenary vote for 12 November. Both dates are provisional. The project is not dead, but the fight is now over how much of it survives.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to his supporters at Likud party headquarters in Jerusalem after the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo)
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc led the partial election count on Oct. 28 but remained short of a majority, as opposition figures urged cooperation with Arab parties to form a government.
With 76.8 percent of ballot boxes counted, projections put Netanyahu’s bloc at 54 seats, the opposition led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot at 47 and the Joint List and Ra’am at 19, The Times of Israel reported, citing Central Elections Committee figures.
A majority requires 61 seats in the 120-member Knesset. The figures remained provisional.
Democrats leader Yair Golan urged Eisenkot’s bloc to work with the Arab parties, arguing that together they could secure a parliamentary majority.
“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he wrote on X.
Eisenkot ruled out governing with Arab parties during the campaign.
Joint List lawmaker Ofer Cassif also urged the opposition to act, telling Army Radio that responsibility now lay with Eisenkot’s bloc.
“More elections would be a gift to Netanyahu,” he said.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman called on members of Netanyahu’s Likud party to challenge his leadership. He said he had received dozens of calls from Likud members and urged them to voice their criticism publicly.
Counting continued after the Oct. 27 vote, with final results due to be published by Nov. 4.

Swedbank to cut 500 jobs, including 100 in Baltic states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:31:00 UTC
16:31:00 KST

The Swedish banking group Swedbank plans to cut about 500 jobs across its operations, including around 100 in the Baltic states, as part of a broader restructuring that could lead to further layoffs as artificial intelligence advances, the bank’s Estonian chief executive said.
Olavi Lepp, chairman of the management board and CEO of Swedbank Estonia, told Estonian public broadcaster ERR that the group was reducing its workforce while reorganising operations and investing in business development.
Swedbank employs more than 6,000 people across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, and the planned cuts will affect about 100 of them, Lepp said. Nearly 500 positions will be eliminated across the group as a whole.
The bank said it was offering existing employees opportunities to move into different roles during the restructuring, although not everyone would be able to make the transition.
“Naturally, in the process, we are also offering existing employees the opportunity to retrain for other roles, but this does not suit everyone and, unfortunately, layoffs are also needed,” Lepp said.
He explained that the restructuring followed a period of exceptionally high profitability several years ago, when the bank decided to increase investment in information technology development and projects involving data modelling.
With profitability now back at more normal levels, the bank no longer needs as many employees, he said.
“Today, when profitability is at normal levels, we do not need as many people,” Lepp said, adding that maintaining the same workforce made little sense when the bank was no longer carrying out large-scale development projects.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine receives an average of 12 Patriot missiles a month from US this year

Zelenskyy: Ukraine receives an average of 12 Patriot missiles a month from US this year
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine receives an average of 12 missiles a month for its Patriot air defence systems in 2026.
Source: Zelenskyy in a comment to the press, as reported by Ukrinform
Quote: "We buy a lot [of weapons] from the US. Europe paid for them, everything arrived, and everything was fine. But some things are a real challenge, especially Patriot missiles. In 2026, we're receiving an average of 12 missiles a month."
Details: Zelenskyy said he works every day to secure interceptor missiles and has to seek new aid packages every week to protect Ukraine from Russian ballistic missile attacks.
The president said US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has signed off on a package of 12 missiles, but approval is still needed for a further 23 missiles that Ukraine has sourced from other countries.
Quote: "The US has a package of 12 missiles, and he's signed off on it. That's great. But we've used 35 just this month. The issue now is getting approval for another 23 that I've secured from other sources."
Details: Zelenskyy also said he had asked Donald Trump during a meeting in New York to approve a "winter package" of missiles. He said he had specified how many missiles Ukraine needed and told Trump that, if the request were approved, Ukraine would not strike oil refineries.
When Trump asked where the missiles could be obtained, Zelenskyy named the countries that had them. According to the Ukrainian president, Trump replied that the US would do everything it could to help, but also needed the missiles itself and had limited supplies.
Background: On 26 October, Zelenskyy announced that Kyiv has been waiting for nearly a month for Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defence systems. He said he has instructed his team to discuss the matter with the US side again.

Malaysia foils $12M AI chip smuggling attempt at Kuala Lumpur airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:28:14 UTC
16:28:14 KST

Malaysia has foiled an attempt to smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips through Kuala Lumpur airport in a case worth more than $12 million, customs officials said on Wednesday.
The bust was the fifth case this year involving a syndicate smuggling advanced AI chips, with the total estimated value exceeding $24 million, officials said.
The Southeast Asian nation, an emerging data-centre hub, is seeking to prevent itself from being used as a transit point for restricted chips destined for other countries.
A team inspecting Kuala Lumpur airport’s free trade zone this month seized 30 server units containing advanced AI chips worth 49.5 million ringgit ($12.1 million), airport customs director Aspalila Ag Tuah said.
Malaysia tightened export and transshipment controls on US chips last year, requiring strategic trade permits and advance notification when there is suspicion of misuse or diversion.
“The servers were declared as ‘electronic components’ to avoid detection by the authorities,” Aspalila told a news conference.
“Initial investigations found that the servers were to be re-exported to another country in Asia,” she added.
The syndicate used Malaysia as a transit point to avoid restrictions during the export of the servers to their next destination, she said.
Aspalila said the servers came from “an Asian country”, declining to specify their exact origin, where the chips were manufactured or where they were headed.
“The case is still under further investigation and the company that facilitated the shipment has been called in to assist investigations,” she said.
The United States has tightened restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports through Malaysia and Thailand in an effort to curb their diversion to China.
Malaysia has also launched several investigations, including one into how servers containing US-made Nvidia chips destined for Singapore ended up in Malaysia.
Authorities said at the time they had found no evidence of illicit trade in advanced semiconductors.

‘The Story of the Panda Bears’ to be staged in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:26:56 UTC
16:26:56 KST

‘The Story of the Panda Bears’ to be staged in Tehran
TEHRAN- Iranian director Maryam Amini is set to stage “The Story of the Panda Bears Told by a Saxophonist Who Has a Girlfriend in Frankfurt,” a play by Romanian-French playwright Matei Vișniec, at the Medea Hall of Tehran Theater.
The production, translated into Persian by Hanieh Rajabi and produced by Vahid Salekfard, will begin performances on Thursday.
Iranian actors Khayyam Vaqar Kashani and Ghazaleh Akrami will perform in the two-character play, which explores an unusual encounter between a man and a woman, unfolding over nine nights and blurring the boundaries between reality, memory and imagination.
The story begins when a man wakes up to find a woman beside him whom he does not recognize. Despite the uncertainty surrounding their encounter, he asks her to stay with him for nine nights. The woman eventually agrees, and the two embark on a strange and intimate journey that gradually raises questions about their identities, their relationship and the nature of their shared experience.
Rather than following a conventional dramatic structure, the play develops through a series of encounters between its two central characters. Their conversations and interactions gradually reveal fragments of their inner worlds, leaving audiences to interpret the events and the meaning of their connection.
The play’s surreal atmosphere and poetic dialogue are characteristic of Vișniec’s theatrical writing, which frequently combines elements of the absurd with reflections on human relationships, loneliness and the instability of reality. In “The Story of the Panda Bears,” the seemingly simple premise of a man asking a stranger to remain with him becomes a framework for exploring the need for companionship and the uncertainties that shape human encounters.
The nine-night structure also provides the drama with a sense of anticipation, as each meeting adds another layer to the relationship between the man and the woman. The audience is invited to piece together the significance of their exchanges while confronting the ambiguity at the heart of the narrative.
Born in Romania in 1956, Vișniec is a playwright, poet and journalist who has established an international reputation for his works exploring the absurdities of modern life, political realities and the human condition. He moved to France in 1987 and has since written extensively for the stage, with his plays translated and performed in numerous countries.
His dramatic works often employ fragmented narratives, symbolic imagery and unconventional situations to examine questions of identity, communication and existence. His writing combines philosophical concerns with theatrical experimentation, allowing directors to approach his texts through a range of interpretations.
“The Story of the Panda Bears Told by a Saxophonist Who Has a Girlfriend in Frankfurt” will remain on stage at the Medea Hall of Tehran Theater for a month.

Japan to impose 5-year anti-dumping duties on Taiwan steel products
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:26:46 UTC
16:26:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Japan will impose definitive anti-dumping duties on nickel-added cold-rolled stainless steel products from Taiwan and China for five years starting Oct. 31, the Japanese government said Tuesday.
The relevant ordinance is set to be published Friday, with the duties taking effect the following day and remaining in force through Oct. 30, 2031, per CNA.
According to the Japan Iron and Steel Federation, duties on Taiwanese products range from 3.6% to 20.1%, while those on Chinese products range from 27.7% to 42.1%. The rates are unchanged from the provisional duties imposed in July.
The products, which contain nickel and are cold-rolled, are valued for their corrosion resistance and durability, per CNA. They are used in automotive exterior components and exhaust systems, railway carriages, and household items such as cutlery.
Japan’s Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry launched the anti-dumping investigation on July 22, 2025, following an application from Japanese steelmakers. Provisional duties took effect on July 9, 2026, after the investigation found evidence of dumped imports and material injury to Japan’s domestic industry.
After reviewing the investigation’s findings, the Council on Customs, Tariff, Foreign Exchange, and Other Transactions recommended definitive duties on Oct. 19. The government approved the five-year measure to protect Japan’s domestic steel industry.

Tehran exhibition explores Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra’s legacy through art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:26:35 UTC
16:26:35 KST

Tehran exhibition explores Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra’s legacy through art
TEHRAN – An exhibition bringing together calligraphy, traditional crafts, visual arts and religious performances to celebrate the legacy of Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA), the daughter of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), opened at Tehran’s Azadi Cultural and Artistic Complex on Monday.
Titled “The Wisdom of Zahra Was Imprinted on the World,” the event showcases works inspired by the spiritual teachings and cultural heritage associated with Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA), a revered figure in Islam whose life is widely associated with piety, compassion, modesty and devotion to her family.
The opening ceremony was attended by the CEO of the Rudaki Foundation Mohammad Allahyari Foumani, Director General of the Visual Arts Office Aydin Mahdizadeh, Rudaki Foundation Deputy for Artistic Creation Amirabbas Setayeshgar, Deputy for Coordination of Halls and Centers Reza Mardani, and Azadi Cultural and Artistic Complex Director Seyyed Mohsen Hosseini, along with artists and cultural figures.
Organized by the Azadi Cultural and Artistic Complex, the program brought together 110 artists from different disciplines. Visitors have the opportunity to view exhibitions, attend artistic workshops and speak with participating artists about their creative approaches and the religious concepts behind their works, the Rudaki Foundation reported.
One of the main sections is an exhibition dedicated to Hadith al-Kisa, a narration describing an occasion when Prophet Muhammad gathered his close family members under a cloak. In Islamic tradition, the narration is associated with the special status of the Prophet’s household, known as the Ahl al-Bayt. Seventy calligraphers participated in the exhibition by writing the Arabic text of the narration and its Persian translation.
Another 20 calligraphers contributed works featuring Ziyarat Ashura, a devotional text associated with Imam Hussein (AS), the third Shia Imam and the grandson of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
The opening ceremony also included the unveiling of a book of Ziyarat Ashura featuring the contributions of the participating calligraphers.
A separate workshop, held under the event’s title, brought together 15 artists working in engraving, qalamkari (traditional Persian textile printing), painting, miniature painting and calligraphy. The artists created works drawing on Fatemi teachings and the artistic traditions through which religious ideas have been expressed and preserved across generations.
The exhibition also features a section on modesty and hijab, supervised by artist Zohreh Abdollahi, exploring women’s identity and dress through an artistic lens. A performance by the Daughters of the Revolution choir added a ceremonial element to the program.
Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA) holds a central place in Islamic history and devotion. As the daughter of Prophet Muhammad and Khadija, she is revered by Muslims, particularly in the Shia tradition, as a model of faith, dignity and moral integrity. She was the wife of Imam Ali (AS) and the mother of Imam Hassan (AS) and Imam Hussein (AS). Her life and legacy have inspired centuries of religious literature, poetry, calligraphy and other art forms.
Events celebrating Hazrat Fatemeh Zahra (SA) are often held in connection with Fatemiyeh, a period of mourning and commemoration observed by many Shia Muslims in remembrance of her death. The occasion provides an opportunity to reflect on her place in Islamic tradition and the values associated with her life.
The exhibition’s combination of sacred texts, traditional crafts and contemporary artistic expression offers a setting for exploring these themes through Iran’s cultural heritage.
The exhibition will remain open to visitors for four days, through Friday, October 30.

73.5% of Taiwanese view CCP unfavorably
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:26:30 UTC
16:26:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Nearly three-quarters of Taiwanese view the Chinese Communist Party unfavorably, including more than half of KMT supporters, according to a survey released Tuesday by pollster Tai Li-an (戴立安).
The Taiwan Public Sentiment Survey found that 73.5% of respondents held an unfavorable view of the CCP, while 8.9% expressed a favorable opinion and 17.5% gave no clear answer, per Liberty Times. The unfavorable rating was unchanged from September, while the favorable rating rose 1.4 percentage points.
Among respondents who leaned toward the opposition pan-blue camp, 53.7% viewed the CCP unfavorably and 30.2% favorably. KMT supporters were similarly negative, with 50.3% viewing the CCP unfavorably and 34% favorably.
Among respondents who viewed the KMT favorably but the ruling DPP unfavorably, 46.8% viewed the CCP unfavorably, while 40.9% viewed it favorably, Liberty Times reported. Politically neutral respondents were more negative, with 62.5% expressing an unfavorable view and just 3.1% a favorable one.
Unfavorable ratings exceeded 75% among women, respondents aged 20 to 49, people with university-level education or higher, residents of Taichung, Changhua, Nantou, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung, and pan-green supporters.
The survey also found that 66.1% of respondents who considered Taiwan's economic situation poor viewed the CCP unfavorably, according to Liberty Times. Among those dissatisfied with President Lai Ching-te's (賴清德) performance, 60.4% viewed the CCP unfavorably, while 19.4% viewed it favorably.
Tai designed and analyzed the survey, which Beacon Market Research conducted from Oct. 20 to 22, interviewing 1,075 adults aged 20 and older across Taiwan's 22 cities and counties. The poll included 696 landline and 379 mobile telephone interviews, with a maximum sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet on Tuesday reportedly approved the immediate reassignment of Greg Lee (李冠德), Taiwan’s former envoy to Geneva, to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ Department of Treaty and Legal Affairs.
The ministry launched an investigation into Lee in August after receiving complaints from his coworkers, per TVBS. The complaints, spanning 134 pages and listing more than 200 allegations, accused Lee of reckless driving, embezzlement, waste of public funds, bullying, and other misconduct.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) later confirmed that the ministry had recalled Lee for an investigation, per UP Media. On Oct. 9, the ministry announced its findings, concluding that Lee had bullied his coworkers, per Tai Sounds.
Investigators found that Lee created an unpleasant workplace environment by loudly scolding colleagues during conferences or preventing participants from speaking. They also found that when Lee’s superiors visited Geneva to inspect certain initiatives, he used his authority to exclude some coworkers from participating in related activities.
Commenting on the reassignment, insiders said reassignment orders typically do not specify an effective date, per UDN. They explained that including the date meant Lee would immediately lose his title, as well as the associated bonuses and housing benefits.
The insiders added that the severity of the punishment was also reflected in the lack of subsidies for Lee’s accommodation and transportation expenses during his transition to the new position.
Earlier this month, TPP Legislative Caucus Director Vicky Chen (陳智菡) noted that former Overseas Community Affairs Council Minister Hsu Chia-ching (徐佳青) was mentioned several times in the complaints against Lee, per NOWNews.
Citing complaints related to Taiwan’s participation in the 2025 World Health Assembly, Chen said nearly every meeting revolved around dining arrangements for high-ranking officials. Quoting one complaint, Chen said civil servants had asked, “How much time did we spend discussing which specific meal was intended for Minister Hsu?”

Taiwan health minister warns free insurance plan could hurt poorest seniors

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) warned Wednesday that legislation covering health insurance premiums for many seniors could leave some of the poorest elderly people worse off.
Speaking before a legislative hearing, Shih raised two concerns about the changes, CNA reported. He said they could deprive vulnerable seniors of medical subsidies and undermine the National Health Insurance, per Knews.
The legislature passed amendments to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act on Oct. 16, backed by the opposition KMT and TPP. The changes would require the central government to cover health insurance premiums for people aged 65 and older whose income falls below the tax filing threshold or whose income tax rate is below 20%, subject to an income cap, per Rti.
Shih's first concern was that the amendments remove provisions requiring local governments to help seniors who cannot afford medical expenses. These include patient copayments and treatments not covered by health insurance, per Knews.
Under the previous rules, assistance could also reach seniors whose average household income was between 1.5 and 2.5 times the government's minimum living standard. Shih said these people could lose financial support even if the government pays their insurance premiums, per TVBS News.
The health ministry warned that the changes could affect subsidies for dentures, artificial lenses used in cataract surgery, and heart stents.
Shih's second concern was that the amendments conflict with the principle that people should contribute to health insurance according to their ability to pay. He said the government should focus assistance on those in financial need rather than exempt people based largely on age, per CNA.
The ministry estimates that about 83% of seniors aged 65 and older would qualify for the premium subsidy. Shih has warned that such broad coverage could place additional pressure on government finances and threaten the insurance system's long-term sustainability, per ETtoday.

====================================================================================================

Antalya agenda: COP31 can turn zero waste from a theme into a delivery discipline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:25:47 UTC
16:25:47 KST

Every climate summit is measured by what it leaves behind.
When governments gather in Antalya from November 9 to 20 for COP31, the annual UN climate conference, the real measure of success will be whether commitments begin to show up in cities, markets, landfills and household bins.
Waste is one of the places where that test is most visible, and where Türkiye has something concrete to offer.
Alongside COP31, governments will meet as the governing body of the Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol, while the climate process’s two subsidiary bodies, which provide scientific advice and oversee implementation, hold their 65th sessions during the first week.
Türkiye will host the conference and lead its Action Agenda, the track that brings governments together with cities, businesses and civil society.
Under a Türkiye-Australia partnership model, Australia’s Chris Bowen has been appointed President of Negotiations, leading the talks in consultation with Türkiye.
The negotiating agenda is long.
Under the Paris Agreement, governments are due to address several programmes, including the Global Stocktake, the United Arab Emirates Just Transition Work Programme, the Sharm el-Sheikh mitigation work programme and further guidance on countries’ national climate plans, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
The list also includes support for transparency reporting under Article 13, the Global Goal on Adaptation, loss and damage, climate finance, and international cooperation under Article 6.
Several of these issues arrive in Antalya unresolved.
Work on making the Just Transition Work Programme operational was carried over from the previous technical session, the mitigation work programme faces a decision on whether it continues, and guidance on NDCs is back on the table.
The success of COP31 will therefore depend less on the breadth of its agenda than on whether it links negotiation to implementation.
Waste to action
The Presidency has framed the conference around dialogue, consensus and action, and has said it wants COP31 to turn commitments into measurable results. That is the right yardstick.
Zero waste belongs at the heart of that implementation effort, though precision matters.
Waste, circular economy and methane reduction are not standalone items on the formal negotiating agendas.
They are, however, explicitly part of the official COP31 Presidency Action Agenda, where zero waste is described as unlocking the climate potential of waste management through scalable circular-economy solutions.
The Presidency’s thematic calendar also designates November 11 as Zero Waste Day, coinciding with the first day of the Leaders Summit.
This is more than a technicality. Negotiations produce collective decisions, rules and guidance.
The Action Agenda is where governments, cities, businesses and civil society turn those frameworks into projects and partnerships on the ground.
Rather than competing with mitigation, adaptation or finance for attention, zero waste can help make all three tangible.
The numbers support this. According to the Global Methane Assessment of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), landfills and wastewater account for about 20 per cent of human-caused methane emissions.
In 2026, UNEP also reported that food loss and waste generate 8-10 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, and that food waste alone accounts for up to 14 per cent of global methane emissions.
Preventing waste, separating it at source, managing organic waste properly and keeping resources in use are near-term climate measures, not only matters of cleanliness or recycling.
Waste also offers a bridge to national climate plans. The UN climate secretariat's NDC synthesis report, published in October 2025, covered 64 new plans, representing about 30 per cent of global emissions in 2019.
The UNFCCC itself cautioned that such a limited sample could not support wide-ranging global conclusions.
That caution is worth heeding: implementation claims at COP31 will need to hold up to scrutiny, with figures that are clear about their coverage and method.
The same rigour should apply to transparency.
Waste and methane initiatives presented at COP31 should be designed so that their emissions impact can be measured, reported and connected to national implementation systems, so that they add up to more than a series of isolated showcases.
This is where the Zero Waste Foundation has a clear and meaningful role.
Its president, Samed Agirbas, has been appointed COP31 Climate High-Level Champion, with a mandate to work with business, financial institutions, cities and regions, and civil society.
The role sits outside the formal negotiations, in which the Foundation itself holds no mandate, but it links the Foundation’s experience directly to the actors who must deliver COP31’s commitments.
UNEP has acknowledged the foundation’s role in global climate action.
At home, the foundation follows a local-to-national model. Its Istanbul Zero Waste Week programme drew participation from all 39 districts of the city and more than 1,500 project applications from public institutions, local administrations, universities, NGOs, and the private sector.
In Antalya, a foundation workshop brought together roughly 400 participants from public institutions, local governments, universities, civil society, professional chambers and business.
They worked across 16 thematic tables on issues such as food waste, plastics, circular industry, finance and data. These figures come from the foundation’s own reporting, and they show the kind of stakeholder network that turns a summit theme into local action.
Antalya agenda
The opportunity for COP31 is practical.
Governments can connect waste and methane measures to their national climate plans. Cities can build credible project pipelines to prevent food waste, separate organic waste, and cut methane from landfills.
Businesses can redesign material flows, financiers can ask for measurable climate outcomes, and civil society can help programmes earn local legitimacy.
None of this replaces progress in the negotiations on finance, adaptation, loss and damage, a just transition or mitigation. It makes those goals easier to achieve.
Delegations should leave Antalya with a simple standard for zero waste climate action: measure what is avoided, finance what can scale, disclose what is delivered and link local projects to national commitments.
The Zero Waste Foundation and other non-state actors can contribute most by convening the institutions that run waste systems, direct investment, hold data and shape public participation, and by turning visibility into verifiable results.
The official Action Agenda provides a platform to build projects that cut methane, prevent waste, and strengthen circularity, and to hold each one to that standard.
COP31 can make zero waste a delivery discipline, not just a theme.
