Russia is selling Africa dependence disguised as partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:25:41 UTC
16:25:41 KST

Russia is selling Africa dependence disguised as partnership
As African leaders gather in Moscow, the Kremlin is securing resources and protecting allied rulers while failing their people.
This week, Moscow will host the third Russia-Africa summit, bringing together African leaders as President Vladimir Putin seeks to expand Russia’s economic, military and political reach across the continent. Yet Russia’s growing influence has done far more to advance Moscow’s interests and protect allied rulers than to deliver the prosperity and security promised to ordinary Africans.
Putin is scheduled to cochair Thursday’s plenary session with Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, current chair of the African Union. Alongside the summit, a two-day economic and humanitarian forum will discuss investment, industrial production, food security, energy, technology and payment systems. Organisers have placed trade and investment at the centre of the programme with a new plan for 2027-2029 expected to advance what they call “mutually beneficial cooperation”.
On August 20, Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova outlined plans for another substantial round of intergovernmental agreements and commercial contracts at the Moscow summit. The Sochi gathering in October 2019 produced 92 agreements, and Putin pledged to double annual trade to $40bn. Four years later, the July 2023 summit in St Petersburg yielded 161 more accords and a 2023-2026 action plan.
The economic results have not matched Moscow’s promises. As the 2023-2026 plan nears its conclusion, Russia’s own trade statistics expose the shortfall: Merchandise trade with Africa reached just $27.1bn in 2025 against Putin’s $40bn target.
The trade imbalance persisted into 2026 with Russia exporting $14bn in goods to Africa during the first eight months of the year while importing just $3.2bn.
Agricultural exports help explain Africa’s significant trade deficit with Russia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Russia shipped 10.2 million tonnes of wheat to Africa, with Egypt its largest agricultural customer. These supplies meet genuine food security needs, but exports of wheat and fertiliser benefit Russian producers more than they contribute to African industrial development.
Russia’s investment record exposes a substantial gap between agreements signed and projects completed. At the 2019 summit, fertiliser producer Uralchem and Angola’s Grupo Opaia agreed to build a $1.2bn ammonia and urea complex, scheduled to begin production in 2023, but Uralchem abandoned the venture that year.
Egypt offers clearer evidence of progress: Rosatom is building four nuclear reactors at El Dabaa, where more than 18,000 Egyptians are employed in their construction. But the project is being financed largely through a $25bn Russian loan that Egypt must repay with interest.
Even when Russian-backed projects advance, the contract terms determine who stands to benefit, who bears the financial risks and how public revenues will ultimately be shared. In the Republic of Congo, a proposed petroleum-products pipeline between Pointe-Noire and Brazzaville would give Russian interests 90 percent of the joint venture and Congo’s state oil company 10 percent with a 25-year concession and guaranteed transport tariffs.
In April, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said design work would begin this year with operations planned for 2029. Russian officials have also described the pipeline as a means of protecting petroleum exports from Western sanctions imposed following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s commercial ambitions are matched by a widening military footprint. On October 8, Sweden’s Defence Research Agency identified at least 57 Russian military and security agreements involving 39 African countries, although many remain limited in practice. Others facilitate training and access to military infrastructure.
Russia initially relied on the Wagner Group, a Kremlin-linked mercenary network, before transferring many operations to the Ministry of Defence-controlled Africa Corps with Wagner remaining active in the Central African Republic. Russian personnel provide direct combat assistance, training and protection to allied governments, particularly in Mali and the Central African Republic.
Nonetheless, Mali exposes the limits of Russia’s military assistance. Wagner fighters and Malian troops captured Kidal, a strategic northern city, in November 2023, only to lose it to separatist rebels in April 2026. On October 6, Russian-backed forces regained the city after an air campaign prompted the rebels to withdraw. Moscow has helped Mali win territory, but it has failed to deliver lasting security for Malians.
According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, Malian forces and Russia’s Africa Corps carried out 49 air strikes from April to August, killing 89 civilians. Human Rights Watch reported that on July 10, Africa Corps fighters killed nine people, including four children, and burned homes in Bombori, a village in central Mali’s Mopti region.
Other abuses include beatings, electric shocks and waterboarding of noncombatants detained by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps personnel at a military base in Sevare from May to August.
For civilians caught between insurgents and forces sent to defeat them, Moscow’s military assistance has brought more violence and no dependable protection.
At the same time, Russia has proved its value to allied rulers in the region.
On August 29, Russia’s Africa Corps helped General Abdourahamane Tiani crush a mutiny in Niger. Russian troops provided ground and aerial support, and Moscow’s ambassador confirmed their role. While Tiani’s government survived, Nigeriens remain without political parties or an election timetable, and civil liberties are severely restricted. The junta also stripped five more exiled critics of their nationality on September 17.
In the Central African Republic, Moscow has helped President Faustin-Archange Touadera, in power for 10 years, tighten his grip on the country. On March 5, Touadera personally thanked Putin, acknowledging that Russian security forces had made possible December’s presidential election, which secured his third term despite an opposition boycott.
Wagner mercenaries continue to protect Touadera’s government while political opponents face repression and journalists risk arrest. Russian fighters have carried out killings, torture and attacks against civilians.
For continued protection of Touadera’s government, Moscow reportedly demanded close to 14 million euros ($15.7m) a month to deploy Africa Corps in place of Wagner while Russian-linked companies continued profiting from the Central African Republic’s gold resources.
Moscow is also helping friendly rulers shape the information their citizens receive. In July, Russia’s state broadcaster RT signed a content-sharing agreement with Tafouk TV, the new channel run by the military governments of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso.
Broadcasting from Bamako since September, the station promotes official military successes, often overlooking insurgent attacks, while local journalists face arrests, disappearances and censorship. Moscow’s campaign to shape African public opinion extends beyond state broadcasters. An April 3 investigation by France 24 uncovered nearly 650 pro-Russian articles placed in 35 West African media outlets from June to October 2024. Leaked documents listed payments of $250 to $700 per article with some outlets unaware that Russian operatives had arranged the placements.
Russian-linked efforts to shape African politics are not confined to news media. In July, an Angolan court convicted two Russians associated with Africa Politology, a political influence network with ties to the Kremlin, of terrorism and espionage. Prosecutors accused them of exploiting protests over fuel prices to incite antigovernment unrest and attempting to sway Angola’s 2027 election. Igor Ratchin received an 11-year prison sentence and Lev Lakshtanov eight years, but both denied the charges and appealed.
Russia’s expanding presence is entrenching a deeply unequal and destabilising relationship in which Moscow gains preferential access to African mineral resources, strengthens its military foothold and protects illiberal rulers.
Meanwhile, ordinary Africans are forced to endure insecurity, political repression and unfulfilled development commitments. Far from delivering shared prosperity, the Kremlin is exploiting Africa’s wealth and political vulnerabilities to advance its own economic and geopolitical interests.
No power, regardless of history, deserves exemptions.
In Moscow, Africa must demand of Russia the same standards it expects of the United States, Europe and China: fair trade, productive investment, respect for sovereignty and accountability for civilian abuses.
African lives matter, too.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Europe struggles to top up gas storage at four-year high prices ahead of winter

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. In late October, European countries continue to inject small volumes of gas into underground storage facilities (UGS) ahead of the cold season, despite prices hitting a four-year high, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Meanwhile, several countries have been net-withdrawing gas from European UGS facilities for the second consecutive week - with withdrawal volumes outstripping injections--signaling the gradual start of the heating season in the region.
To date, Europe has managed to inject only 75.5% of the gas volumes required for the upcoming winter, which amounts to 51 billion cubic meters.
As of October 26, European UGS facilities were 74.93% full, down from 82.9% a year earlier and 14.65 percentage points below the five-year average for this date. This remains the lowest level recorded for this date since monitoring began in 2011. EU storage facilities currently hold approximately 82.1 billion cubic meters of gas, which is 9.4 billion cubic meters less than last year and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that European gas inventories might fail to reach even the 75% mark, warning of a challenging autumn-winter season for the region.
Earlier TASS reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas reserves. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU nations may only manage to fill their storage capacities to 70-75%, an all-time low for the start of a heating season.
Under European Commission regulations, EU member states must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is permitted under difficult filling conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage facilities must reach at least 68 billion cubic meters to meet the requirement for the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season. However, hoping for a very mild winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower this threshold to 80% this year.

A guard at Israel's embassy in Belgrade, Serbia, was attacked by a knife-wielding assailant early on Wednesday morning, according to Serbian police.
The attacker was killed at the site shortly after midnight.
Serbia's Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said that police had increased the terror threat level to "Red," the highest possible grade, and increased their presence at vulnerable locations, according to the Associated Press.
"A minor, so far unidentified... rushed at an officer of the Gendarmerie shouting 'Allahu Akbar' and attacked him with two knives," said Dacic.
The guard was lightly wounded.
Belgrade prosecutors describe the attack
In a statement, the Belgrade-based Higher Public Prosecution Office said that an investigation showed that a black-clad unidentified individual opened the door of a guard house in front of the embassy and, armed with two knives, rushed at the policeman, identified only by the initials D.S.
"The unidentified person threw one knife in the direction of D.S., hitting him in the left cheek. After that, D.S. took out his service weapon and fired several shots at the attacker, killing him on the spot," it said, adding that the policeman's action was qualified as justified and in self-defense.
The investigation was continuing, it said.
Suspect on security services' radar prior to attack, ISIS links suspected
Dacic noted that security services had been monitoring the suspect prior to the attack.
"Based on the information available to us so far, he was known as a supporter of the Islamic State. His Instagram profile featured a black flag and symbols associated with the organization," he said, according to the Associated Press.
Dacic added that he visited the injured officer in the hospital alongside Police Director Gen. Dragan Vasiljevic, noting that the officer is in good condition and expected to be discharged for home care later today.
This was the second attack at the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in two years. In June 2024, an assailant shot a Serbian police officer in the neck with a crossbow.
Israel's Foreign Ministry noted that "there were no casualties among embassy staff, as the diplomatic mission was closed at that hour of the night."

Goodbye to the everyman who gatecrashed the greats
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:14:18 GMT
16:14:18 KST

Goodbye to the everyman who gatecrashed the greats
- Published
Whether through technique or toil, Stan Wawrinka has always been able to whip fans into a frenzy.
The ability to stir the emotions of a crowd never left him - even in what proved to be the final tour-level match of the 41-year-old Swiss star's glorious career.
Former world number three Wawrinka might have lost to Czech opponent Jiri Lehecka in front of passionate home support in Basel on Tuesday, but he did not wave farewell without showing the hallmarks of a stunning career that exceeded expectations.
The stylish one-handed backhand down the line. The finger pointing to the temple. The demand for more noise from the stands.
The roar of "Allez!" after winning a point he probably should not have won.
The temptation to snap his racquet over his knee after missing a shot he felt he should have made.
There were tears, too, of course.
Wawrinka, his family, and his team were dabbing their eyes once the reality of an honourable 7-5 7-6 (7-2) defeat dawned.
It meant a professional career spanning 23 years, 985 matches and three Grand Slam titles was over.
"All I wanted in my career was to give everything, have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100% in every match - out of respect for myself, the opponent, the tournament, the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP website., external
"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and the only way you can leave the sport - without any regrets."
Wawrinka is loved by millions of fans because he is relatable - an everyman personality who reached the pinnacle of his sport by pushing himself to the limit.
So many talented players of his generation lamented the presence of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, believing the 'Big Three' to be a blockade preventing them from becoming a Grand Slam champion.
It did not stop Wawrinka. With explosive shot-making, relentless endurance and indomitable spirit, he barrelled past the trio of superstars on his way to winning his trio of majors.
Wawrinka had been a player whose career was ticking along steadily, rather than spectacularly, until he lifted one of the sport's biggest prizes at the age of 28.
Seeded eighth at the 2014 Australian Open, he saw off Djokovic in the quarter-finals before completing an unforeseen triumph against top seed Nadal.
"I never expected to win a Grand Slam because, for me, I was not good enough to beat those guys," Wawrinka admitted as he clutched the trophy in Melbourne.
In fact, he was more than good enough - proving it again and again.
At the 2015 French Open, Wawrinka brushed past Swiss compatriot Federer in the quarter-finals, then demolished Djokovic in the final with a display of unrelenting power - a performance which must be ranked among the greatest of his era.
His last major title arrived at the 2016 US Open, when he escaped from match point down against Britain's Dan Evans in the third round and went on to beat Djokovic for the title.
It is little wonder that 24-time major champion Djokovic - considered by many the greatest player of all-time - described Wawrinka as a "legend".
"Stan's had an incredible career. The competitor he is on court, talent, strength, power, precision - he had it all," said the 39-year-old Serb, who practised with Wawrinka in Basel.
Wawrinka was good enough to win majors, but he wasn't as consistently good as his illustrious rivals.
The 'Big Three' is often expanded to a 'Big Four' featuring Britain's three-time major champion Andy Murray, who soared to world number one, won two Olympic singles gold medals and lifted the ATP Finals trophy.
Wawrinka recognises he was "really far" from creating a 'Big Five' - and the evidence underlines that.
Spending 267 weeks in the top 10, winning one Masters 1,000 tournament and claiming 15 other tour-level titles is well below Federer, Nadal, Djokovic and Murray, but it is also more than most players can dream of achieving.
The Grand Slam triumphs are what really set Wawrinka apart from most peers - and, coupled with his commendable attitude, is why 'Stan the Man' will be remembered for emerging as a great himself in a golden generation where others came up short.

Travellers are making more sustainable choices to ‘enhance’ journeys, new study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:10:50 UTC
16:10:50 KST

Sustainability is playing a larger role in how and where we travel, with a new study revealing that exploring the outdoors, scenic rail journeys and visiting lesser-known destinations can enhance experiences abroad.
Amid the rising impact of climate change, more holidaymakers are considering sustainable options for deciding when, where and how to travel, according to findings from Trip.com’s Sustainable Travel Consumer Report.
The survey of 8,777 respondents, from 29 countries across four global regions, found that 37.2% of travellers would consider destinations with a lower risk of weather disruptions. This comes after Europe experienced a summer that was the “worst on record”, according to a separate report.
Trip.com also found that 75.4% of respondents highlighted sustainability as “important when making travel decisions”, while 56.8% intentionally choose more sustainable travel options.
“Every journey depends on the world around it: the places we discover, the nature we enjoy and the communities that make each destination unique,” said Jane Sun, CEO of Trip.com Group. “For travel to thrive for generations to come, that world must thrive too.
“Sustainability is becoming an important part of what travellers value. It is not just a responsibility, but a way to experience more – from exploring nature and taking scenic rail journeys to discovering less-visited destinations.”
Among younger travellers, there is a particular interest in experience-led options, like rail journeys, outdoor activities and hotels with strong sustainability practices. Their older counterparts, however, are more interested in travelling to places with less crowds and going outside of peak seasons.
According to the report, younger travellers show “stronger engagement with more sustainable travel across intention, action and platform choice”. For Gen Z respondents, 44.3% agreed sustainability is "very important" when making travel decisions, compared to just 23% among Boomers.
Sustainable travel choices
Price remains a large consideration and perceived barrier, with 32.9% of travellers willing to pay just an additional 1%-5% for sustainable travel. However, nearly six in 10 Gen Z and Millennials are willing to pay a premium for a more sustainable travel experience.
“This suggests that price sensitivity does not necessarily translate into an unwillingness to spend more on more sustainable travel experience,” the report said.
The survey also found that exploring nature and outdoor destinations was the top sustainable travel choice thought to enhance experiences, cited by 41.6% of respondents.
This was followed by scenic rail journeys (34.1%), visiting lesser-known destinations with fewer crowds (32.7%), staying in hotels with strong sustainability practices (31.9%), and travelling during off-season (29.6%).
Extreme weather and destination appeal
Extreme weather has prompted changes to travel plans, as 29.9% of respondents have delayed or rescheduled a trip, while 23.6% changed the season or timing of travel. Further, 21.9% felt the need to change the destination.
When it comes to a destination’s appeal, 56% are attracted to good public transport or lower-carbon mobility options and 50.6% are attracted to destinations that protect natural and cultural heritage. In contrast, 37.2% of travellers would opt to travel to a place with a lower risk of weather disruptions.

In his meeting with Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, Hegseth “reaffirmed the indispensable role of the U.S.-Japan Alliance in preserving peace and stability in the Pacific,” the Pentagon said.

“America stands with allies that are serious about their own defense,” he said.

Zimbabwe’s platinum boom: Where is the wealth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:08:00 UTC
16:08:00 KST

Zimbabwe’s platinum boom: Where is the wealth?
The metal is generating billions, but mining communities say basic services have failed to keep pace.
Mimosa, Zimbabwe – Zimbabwe’s platinum industry is generating billions of dollars, but residents in mining communities say roads, schools, water and other basic services have failed to keep pace with the wealth extracted from beneath their land.
Platinum prices hit an all-time high of $2,923 an ounce on January 26 during a broader precious metals rally and continued concerns over the platinum supply, according to the World Platinum Investment Council.
For Zimbabwe, home to the world’s second largest known deposits of platinum group metals (PGMs) after South Africa, the price surge offers an opportunity to increase revenue from a sector central to the economy. Mining accounts for about 75 percent of the country’s exports and about 14.5 percent of its gross domestic product, according to the International Trade Administration in the United States.
The mining sector generated a record $8.5bn in export earnings in 2025, up from $5.9bn the previous year, according to John Musekiwa, then-president of the Chamber of Mines of Zimbabwe. He said the increase was driven by strong output and favourable prices, particularly for gold and PGMs.
But in communities surrounding some of the country’s biggest platinum operations, residents said the wealth extracted from beneath their land has not translated into adequate roads, schools, water supplies and other basic services.
In Mhondoro-Ngezi, one of Zimbabwe’s major platinum-producing areas, that tension is visible on the ground.
A rich mineral belt, struggling communities
The Great Dyke, a geological formation stretching across central Zimbabwe, contains extensive deposits of PGMs. Zimplats operates mines, concentrators and processing facilities in the Mhondoro-Ngezi district there.
Inside the mining complex, ore is processed in modern facilities, and heavy trucks move between mines and plants. Outside, residents of Turf, Mamina, Murambwa and nearby villages said infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with the area’s growth.
Ernest Denhere, headman of Denhere village in Ward 3, said mining companies should leave a lasting legacy in the communities where they operate.
“We call upon Zimplats and other mines to build a road from Kadoma/Kwekwe to Turf, Benhura, Mamina, Murambwa and Kadhani, linking to the Harare-Masvingo highways,” Denhere said.
Ward 3 Councillor Emmah Chikwai said some children travel long distances to reach secondary school.
“Children from Jompani, Majoki, Maleti and Makwavarara walk between 15km and 25km [9 to 15.5 miles] to reach Musinambi Secondary School,” she said. “My appeal is for the mines to assist in setting up a satellite secondary school in Makwavarara.”
Schools, water and livelihoods under pressure
During a September 7 visit, Al Jazeera saw pupils at Turf Primary School learning under trees as rising enrolment strained the school’s facilities.
Nearby, women and young men searched through piles of waste for plastic they could sell. Cattle and goats moved among the rubbish.
For Sakina Lice, collecting plastic is how she supports her family.
“I have 11 children and nine grandchildren. Picking up plastics is the only way I survive. When I resell them, I can make maybe $20 a month,” she said.
“I am the breadwinner. My husband is late, so it is just hand to mouth. My wish is for the mine to empower women, so we can start projects and support our families.”
Residents also raised concerns about the Ngwazani River, about 100 metres (330ft) from the dump site, alleging that sewage from the mining area has entered the waterway and affected its use for household needs and small gardens.
Edson Mabure, whose family was relocated as mining activities expanded, said the river has become a problem for residents in his new community.
“Our village was where the mine is today, so we were relocated. From our new village, I cross the Ngwazani River, which is now flooded with sewage coming from the mine,” he said.
“Since the mine started operating, there is nothing tangible that has been done to leave a lasting legacy for the community. I don’t know whether the responsibility lies with the council or Zimplats.”
Agnes Handidikundiona, whom Al Jazeera met crossing the river with her children, said residents once relied on it for household activities and gardens.
“We are facing a serious challenge because the water is no longer clean,” she said. “Before the sewage spill, we used to use this water for domestic purposes, such as washing clothes and watering our nutritional gardens.”
She said flooding also has prevented some children from reaching school.
“Children from many villages cross here to go to school. Sometimes when the river is flooded, they cannot go to school. We need a footbridge here,” she said.
Ward 11 Councillor Nhomboka Kurebwa Javangwe said the area’s population has increased as mine workers and their families have moved in.
He said Zimplats has built classrooms and houses but demand continues to outstrip available facilities. He called for the company to build and operate a primary school.
Javangwe also said local councillors have limited direct access to the company.
“We do not have direct access to the mine to raise the concerns of our people,” he said, adding that only the council chairperson was authorised to meet with Zimplats officials.
Mines point to community investment
The same concerns are being raised in other platinum-producing areas.
In Shurugwi, home to the Unki Platinum Mine, residents have called for more investment in local infrastructure.
“I call upon Unki to consider assisting with classroom blocks for schools, water and sanitation, and roads in Shurugwi town,” said Bulle Madzitire, chairman of the Shurugwi Residents Association.
In nearby Zvishavane, Kamino Simango, chairman of the Zvishavane Residents Association, said the Mimosa Platinum Mine should focus more on infrastructure benefitting the wider community.
Unki told Al Jazeera that it has invested an average of $1.5m a year in community development over the past five years, covering education, healthcare, water and sanitation, agriculture and infrastructure.
Its public relations manager, Evelyn Mawimba, said the mine has built 63 boreholes, supported 32 schools through its STEP-UP programme and contributed $2.75m towards land purchases and development of the Impali housing estate.
Unki also pays about $130,000 a year in municipal levies to the Shurugwi Town Council and contributes about $850,000 annually to the Tongogara Rural District Council, Mawimba said.
Mimosa did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions despite several attempts to contact the company.
Al Jazeera also contacted the chairperson of the Mhondoro-Ngezi Rural District Council, Alderman Ephraim Pepukai Chengeta, about Zimplats’s contributions and development plans. He promised to respond but did not return calls or messages. The council’s chief executive officer, Itai A Mawonde, asked for the questions in writing.
Zimplats’s head of corporate affairs, Hama Saburi, also said he would respond but did not do so by publication.
For residents of Zimbabwe’s platinum belt, the demands are straightforward: better roads, schools, water and other services in communities living alongside some of the country’s most valuable mines.
“What is beneath our land speaks volumes,” Denhere said. “We need to see a lasting legacy for our communities.”

KAPO requests access to bank data register after shutdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:07:00 UTC
16:07:00 KST

KAPO requests access to bank data register after shutdown
Internal Security Service (KAPO) head Margo Palloson has requested restored access to the state Enforcement Register and e-arrest system.
KAPO has been blocked from accessing the register by the Justice Ministry for failing to implement a data tracker tool by the October 1 deadline, and the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) has been hit by the same block.
Palloson says the legislation permits KAPO to continue accessing the register without installing the tracker, at least in the case of national security matters.
"It has now become clear that the Police and Border Guard Board and KAPO have not established the necessary interfaces, which means that these agencies' access to the Enforcement Register and the e-arrest system must be closed. I ask the Center of Registers and Information Systems (RIK) to arrange the immediate technical shutdown of the services," Justice Ministry Deputy Secretary General Mari-Liis Mikli wrote in a letter to the RIK.
However, KAPO Director General Palloson says that, under the Code of Enforcement Procedure, the requirement for a technical solution — in this case a data tracker — does not apply to security authorities when performing tasks stipulated in the Security Authorities Act or conducting security vetting specified in the State Secrets and Classified Information of Foreign States Act.
"Consequently, we request continued access to the Enforcement Register and the e-arrest system for the performance of tasks stipulated in Section 6 of the Security Authorities Act and for conducting security vetting under the State Secrets and Classified Information of Foreign States Act," he wrote.
Palloson also specified which data KAPO wants its right to query restored: the existence of a bank account, account balance, account statement, persons authorized to use the account, who the beneficial owner of the account holder is, and whether a safe deposit box exists.
The KAPO director general confirmed that since October 1 his authority has not made any queries via the Enforcement Register as part of criminal proceedings, and has now also technically disabled the corresponding type of query.
"We also confirm that KAPO has taken measures to ensure the lawfulness of data processing and exercises sufficient oversight over it," Palloson noted.
The Enforcement Register (Estonian: Täitmisregister) is a state channel allowing authorities to query bank account data and place attachments. In 2025 Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise found agencies had been accessing confidential bank data without the correct legal basis. The solution was the data tracker, which lets individuals see who has queried their data. Legislation putting this in place passed at the Riigikogu, with the installation deadline set at October 1. Other authorities initially blocked but now able to access the register, having installed the tracker, are the Tax and Customs Board (MTA) and the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), which combats money laundering.

‘Nobody heard us’ – why Gen Z are leading protests across Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:06:07 UTC
16:06:07 KST

‘Nobody heard us’ – why Gen Zs are leading protests across Europe
BELGRADE/MILAN/BRUSSELS/TIRANA – Maya Gourdel, a 19-year-old student in Brussels, sits at a desk writing slogans against those running her country: “If we burn, you burn with us!”
The slogan, taken from the 2012 film The Hunger Games that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth movements globally, reflects the anger, frustration and desire for change driving Gen Z-led protests around Europe.
From the suburbs of Paris to the squares of Belgrade, thousands have taken to the streets.
The demands are various but often overlapping – frustrations with shabby schooling facilities, perceived lack of economic opportunity, cost of living, corruption, housing and a sense of not being listened to.
At times, those protests triggered violence – with thousands of shops in France alone being damaged or looted in recent weeks – and police firing stun grenades and water cannons.
In October, they also brought real change – student-led protests culminated in the toppling in an election of Serbia’s long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism.
“Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom,” said student protester Stasa Piletic. “Personally, I feel a sense of victory. I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility.”
‘An explosion of rage’
Chiara, a 21-year-old student in protest-hit Milan, believes “it’s vital to take part in people’s spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible”.
“I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream,” she said.
She said Italian students were confronting a reality of schools without enough teachers and crumbling buildings.
“And all of this with the prospect of an underpaid job which we didn’t qualify for and the prospect of living in a tiny, overpriced house, probably away from our city, which we didn’t want to live in.”
Protests led by Gen Zs have caused ructions globally as the generation born roughly between 1997 and 2012 found its voice, from Bangladesh in 2024 and Nepal in 2025, to India in 2026. Now Europe has become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living are a concern for 40% of 16-30-year-olds, according to a European Union survey published in 2025.
Among the 92.7 million people in the EU who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, the highest risk was recorded for young adults aged 18-24 years, at 26.3%, while the lowest was recorded for adults aged 65 years or over, at 18.8%.
Younger people are also wary of shouldering the financial burden of an older generation that tends to vote in greater numbers. People over 60 in France make up a quarter of the population but own 60% of France’s wealth, according to the OFCE think tank.
French pensions are by far the biggest public expense, on track to reach 14% of economic output, as the population ages and voters resist raising the retirement age or reducing benefits.
That is still less than Greece or Italy, which spend the largest proportion of national income on public pensions among OECD countries, at around 16% of GDP, according to OECD figures in 2025.
But it is much more than Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland or South Korea, which spent less than 4% of GDP on public pensions, according to the OECD.
‘Young people in Europe are united’
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris, has been protesting against “deplorable” conditions and staff shortages at his school.
“There used to be rats,” he said. Students were evacuated in 2025 when a roof collapsed on the courtyard, though no one was hurt, he said.
Protests showed “that young people in Europe are united”, he said, adding, “we all agree on one point: That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”
A French government report in October said pension spending had risen by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023 while that for education had declined 0.5.
It also showed 32% of the education ministry’s budget went towards pensions, crowding out money for other areas.
Gourdel, too, has been protesting for better conditions in schools in Belgium.
“We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It’s only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us,” she said.
The protests are still spreading, with a demonstration planned in Germany over cost of living, inequality, war and the state of schools.
Unrest has also hit Albania, where student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government, fuelled by anger over perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, engulfed Tirana and spread to other cities.
“Our Prime Minister spent 130 days not listening to us,” said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.
“If you ask a student in Albania, ‘where do you see your future?’ Everyone says ‘outside this country’,” she said, arguing that at home, even if you have talent, someone with “connections is always going to beat you”.
Serbia’s student movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of.
Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing – something neither the students nor their candidates have any experience of.
Luka Stojakovic, another protester, brushes that aside. “We have seen where people with political experience have brought us.” REUTERS

Israel’s Elections: What Happens Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:03:12 UTC
16:03:12 KST

Israelis voted on Tuesday in their highest turnout for decades, with exit polls showing the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that of his rival are neck and neck.
Exit polls from the three mainstream Israeli television networks gave the two blocs around 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset -- well below the 61 needed to govern -- after initially giving an edge to the opposition led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot’s bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm’s length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
It took Netanyahu 58 days to form his government after the previous election in November 2022.
Israel to Give Verdict on Netanyahu in Pivotal Election
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for anyone that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said that an especially high Arab turnout “indicates a strong desire for partnership”.
Eisenkot has not even entertained the possibility publicly, and Netanyahu relentlessly told Jewish voters in his campaign that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
“Bottom line, at the moment, it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results,” Elovitz said.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel’s extreme polarisation, the prospect of a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on October 16 found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

Elections in Israel give neither Netanyahu nor the opposition a majority - what does this mean
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:06 EET
16:00:06 KST

Elections in Israel give neither Netanyahu nor the opposition a majority - what does this mean
Kyiv • UNN
Netanyahu's bloc is leading after half the votes have been counted, but no political force has 61 seats. Coalition talks await Israel.
Israel may face several weeks of political battles, as exit polls and partial official results showed that neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition bloc led by former General Gadi Eisenkot secured enough seats to form a government. UNN reports this, citing The Guardian.
Details
Polls published by Israel’s main television channels show that Netanyahu’s ruling bloc either matched or nearly matched the opposition group led by Eisenkot, with each receiving approximately 51 seats—fewer than the 61 seats needed to form a majority coalition government.
By Wednesday morning, October 28, election commissions had counted more than half of the votes, and Netanyahu’s bloc was leading with 55 seats, though further changes are expected.
Speaking at 3 a.m. local time, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister promised to form a coalition through agreements between his Likud party, far-right factions, and Jewish religious parties.
"We must create a strong right-wing government," Netanyahu told his supporters, who cheered. "The Jewish and Zionist majority must unite."
Eisenkot, speaking to his supporters in Tel Aviv earlier in the evening, said that "the people have chosen in favor of change" and that Netanyahu should "announce today that he is leaving politics."
The elections, the publication writes, "were marked by record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, a discriminated-against minority that makes up about 20% of the country’s population." Many members of this group sought a stronger political voice after decades of boycotting elections in the Jewish state. Millions of other Palestinians living under Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza cannot vote, leading to accusations of apartheid, the publication notes.
Exit polls predicted that Palestinian parties could win about 18 seats, compared with 10 previously. However, their role in any coalition will be difficult. Netanyahu said it was "impossible" to have a government supported by Palestinian parties, while Eisenkot said that Arab parties did not meet the Zionist criteria for governing.
After more than half of the ballots had been counted, Israel’s Central Election Committee reported that 27 seats had gone to the Likud party and 21 to Eisenkot’s Yashar party, although this figure is expected to change significantly as official results come in. Under Israel’s electoral system, the number of seats can fluctuate sharply over fractions of a percentage point.
The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on the 77-year-old leader, who is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for alleged war crimes,and voter turnout stood at 77.7%, the highest figure since 1999.
Although Israeli television exit polls showed that support for Netanyahu’s broader religious-national coalition had declined, the deadlock could work in his favor, the publication notes.
The deadlock will allow the prime minister, the publication writes, to remain in power as a caretaker, while obstructing the opposition’s attempts to form a coalition and even to hold early elections. Previously, this led to elections being held one after another—between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.
Earlier, exit polls showed that Eisenkot had won a narrow majority of the seats in the Knesset. Israeli exit polls are often revised after publication and are known for their inaccuracy, while the final vote count frequently fluctuates by several seats.
Opposition figures quickly called the exit polls a defeat for Netanyahu, who is embroiled in a lengthy corruption trial over charges he denies and has been accused of being unprepared for the Hamas attacks in 2023.
Another opposition figure and former prime minister, Yair Lapid, said: "Netanyahu’s bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a complete collapse. The public told them to leave."
Netanyahu and several other parties attempted to keep the polling stations open after the set closing time of 10:00 p.m., but the Central Elections Committee refused. The prime minister publicly hinted that the "left and Arabs" were making efforts to steal the election, but the committee rejected this claim.
The campaign, feverish even by Israeli standards, as the publication notes, included Netanyahu posting a photograph of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the opening of the polling stations.
With more than 7 million people eligible to vote, voter turnout stood at 77.7%—approximately 9% higher than in the previous election—with a notable increase in the number of military personnel voting. There were also reports of tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad who had arrived to vote in recent days.

How rebuilding old mosques is bringing Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims together in Punjab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:00:02 UTC
16:00:02 KST

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

A joint petition challenging the SIR was also filed.A day later, Gandhi hosted INDIA bloc leaders for tea at his residence. Following the meeting, the opposition alliance vowed to continue its campaign and take the fight to its logical conclusion.

Japan is eyeing private investment of up to 1 trillion yen (approximately $6 billion) in Bangladesh over the next five years as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi hosted her Bangladeshi counterpart, Tarique Rahman, in Tokyo on Tuesday.
Rahman is on his first visit to Japan since being elected in February.
In a joint statement, Takaichi and Rahman welcomed Bangladesh’s efforts to promote foreign direct investment, citing “a projection of upcoming private investment from Japan to Bangladesh up to one trillion yen with two hundred thousand jobs to be created in Bangladesh by the investment from Japan in the next five years.”
The two leaders also agreed to expand cooperation in energy security and supply chains, according to the statement.
Earlier, the two prime ministers addressed a joint news conference.
“Japan will strongly support Bangladesh’s autonomy and resilience,” Takaichi told Rahman, according to Kyodo News. She added that Japan “looks forward to contributing to regional peace and prosperity.”
“The partnership between Bangladesh and Japan has been built on decades of friendship, trust, and mutual respect. Today, we have an opportunity to take this relationship to new heights. I warmly invite Japanese investors, businesses, and financial institutions to explore the opportunities Bangladesh has to offer and be part of our next phase of growth,” Rahman said.
Bangladesh is seeking investment and low-interest loans from Japan as it faces economic hardship, particularly following conflicts in the Middle East.
The two sides reaffirmed their commitment to “further enhance bilateral security cooperation” amid an “increasingly uncertain geopolitical environment,” the statement said.
They also welcomed the signing and entry into force of an agreement concerning the transfer of defense equipment and technology.
 
Safe repatriation of Rohingya
On the Rohingya issue, the joint statement said Takaichi and Rahman remain “concerned by the worsening crisis in Myanmar and its impact on regional security, displacement of all people, including the Rohingya, and the increase in transnational crimes.”
They shared the view that the “ultimate solution to the Rohingya crisis is to realize a voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return of the displaced persons, including the Rohingya to Myanmar,” it added.
Takaichi and Rahman reiterated their commitment to promoting sustainable peace, security and stability in the Middle East.
They emphasized the need for early de-escalation, as well as the “urgent and full re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz and the safe, secure and unimpeded transit of all vessels… without any additional costs,” the statement said.
They also recognized the strategic importance of maintaining peace and stability in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait for global energy security and the uninterrupted flow of goods.
Japan is Bangladesh’s largest bilateral development partner and a major export destination, with trade between the countries totaling around $4 billion.
The two countries upgraded ties to a strategic partnership in 2023. In their joint statement, the prime ministers highlighted the development of economic cooperation under the partnership in infrastructure, energy, human resource development, trade and investment.
Earlier this month, the two countries signed an agreement to begin recruiting Bangladeshi workers starting next April, offering new opportunities for Bangladeshi workers in Japan with legal protections.

edible sculptures and snap-button metal armatures activate philip johnson’s wolfhouse in NY
the project brings together moving image, edible sculpture, and site-specific interventions, exploring the relationships between memory, landscape, architecture, and the experience of place.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
NO.29 STUDIO STAGES SITE-SPECIFIC EDIBLE SCULPTURES AT Wolfhouse
Presented on October 10th, 2026, at Wolfhouse, a 1949 modernist residence designed by Philip Johnson in Newburgh, New York, Island on Land – A Landscape in Five States is a site-specific exhibition by artists Lang Lang (founder of studio No.29) and Xie Peng. Developed as a spatial translation of Lang’s 2024 experimental short film of the same name, the project merged moving images, ephemeral edible sculptures, and modular metal and acrylic structures across the home’s interior rooms, exterior terrace, and grounds.
ALUMINUM ARMATURES AND ACRYLIC STANDS MAP FIVE FILM CHAPTERS
The installation by No.29 studio mapped five thematic fragments from the film into physical works that juxtaposed durable industrial hardware with biodegradable, consumable media. Indoors, Black Pearls, textured chocolate spheres filled with grape jelly and jasmine cream, sat within spiral spherical recesses on The Panel, a mirrored stainless steel tray reflecting the room as pieces were removed. A Drop Within, a translucent sphere with a deep-red core, was supported by The Stands, an assembly of circular acrylic panels and curved metal joints fastened with fashion-derived snap buttons instead of threaded hardware.
TRANSIENT EDIBLE MEDIA CONTRASTS MODERNIST ARCHITECTURAL SPACE
On the exterior patio framing views of the Hudson River, Red Soil combined buckwheat, fig, and chocolate terrain atop The Table, a two-panel aluminum surface joined with snap fasteners and red steel stabilization rods. White Trace incorporated rice-paper vessels holding watermelon and perilla syrups, set into circular acrylic cutouts on a folding, reconfigurable aluminum screen termed The Partition. Dispersed across the landscape, A Quiet Turn positioned biodegradable door handles directly on the turf. The non-linear sequence allowed attendees to navigate the estate freely, consuming the perishable elements while the fabricated armatures remained.

Trump wants to ban term ‘AI’ in favor of ‘Super Intelligence’
U.S. President Donald Trump has said he wants to officially ban the term “artificial intelligence” and replace it with “Super Intelligence,” arguing that the existing name is inaccurate, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump questioned why The Wall Street Journal still uses the term and said the change would apply to relevant documents and other materials.
“In short order, we will be officially BANNING the term, ‘AI/Artificial Intelligence,’ in all relevant documents, and everything else, due to its inaccuracy,” Trump wrote.
The statement follows an executive order Trump signed on September 29, directing federal agencies to replace “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” with “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in official communications.
The order covers correspondence, websites, reports, policy documents and other materials produced by executive branch departments and agencies, to the extent permitted by law. It does not require changes to previously issued regulations, presidential actions, contracts or other historical documents.
Under the order, “Super Intelligence” currently carries the same legal meaning as artificial intelligence under existing U.S. law. The administration has also instructed its science and technology adviser to propose a new federal definition within 60 days.
Earlier in October, Trump announced the formation of the Super Intelligence Force to coordinate federal efforts in the field and maintain U.S. leadership. The group reports directly to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The White House has argued that “Super Intelligence” better reflects the technology’s advancing capabilities and potential applications in science, medicine, energy and manufacturing.

Ukraine reportedly struck Russia’s largest steel plant and a major chemical factory overnight on Oct. 27-28, with fires reported at both facilities as Russian authorities reported a massive wave of drone attacks across several regions.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The enemy is attempting to attack the industrial infrastructure of Lipetsk. A massive attack is currently being repelled,” the Russian Telegram channel Radar Lipetsk reported.
Later, the channel reported a fire at the Novolipetsk Steel Plant (NLMK). The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ also confirmed a blaze on the facility’s premises, suggesting that a Russian Pantsir air defense system may have failed to intercept an incoming aerial target.
Igor Artamonov, the governor of the Lipetsk Oblast, later said on Telegram that 45 drones had been shot down over the region overnight.
According to him, drone debris shattered windows in an apartment building in Lipetsk. In one of the region’s gardening cooperatives, a drone fell onto a garden plot next to a house. Another drone fell near a residential building in the Dankovsky District.
“Reports are circulating on social media and messaging apps about a major fire at an industrial facility. This is not true. Drone debris fell in a wooded area, sparking a fire that has now been contained,” Artamonov said.
Zelensky: Europe Must Be Included in November Peace Talks
NLMK is Russia’s largest steel plant and ranks among the 20 largest steel producers in the world. The facility has an annual production capacity of 17 million tons of liquid steel. It was previously targeted in an attack on July.
Chemical plant reportedly targeted in Tula Oblast
Early on the morning of Oct. 28, Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyaev also declared a missile alert. He later reported that the region had come under a massive attack by Ukrainian drones.
“As a result of falling drone debris in Novomoskovsk, damage has been recorded to an apartment building, private homes, and infrastructure in the adjacent industrial zone,” Milyaev wrote.
He added that information about possible casualties and the extent of the damage was still being clarified.
Although Milyaev did not identify the specific industrial facility targeted, he said that laboratories from the Tula Oblast state institution Priroda (Nature) and the regional office of Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s federal consumer rights protection agency, had been dispatched to Novomoskovsk.
According to Exilenova+ and the Russian outlet Astra, the target of the latest attack in Novomoskovsk was the Azot chemical plant, which belongs to the EuroChem group and is one of Russia’s largest producers of nitrogen fertilizers.
The facility manufactures ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, and methanol. These substances are used in various industrial applications, including the production of munitions.
Astra previously reported an attack on the Azot chemical plant on June 26. The facility had also caught fire following a Ukrainian attack on the night of June 14.
Moscow claims 531 Ukrainian drones intercepted overnight
The Russian Ministry of Defense reported that air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 531 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27 and 8 a.m. on Oct. 28.
According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tambov, and Tula Oblasts, as well as Moscow Oblast.
The Ukrainian side has not commented on its involvement in the reported strikes as of publication.
Previous Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian industrial facilities
On Oct. 24, Ukrainian drones attacked Tolyattikauchuk, a major petrochemical enterprise in Russia’s Samara region.
A fire broke out at the plant, which is owned by Tatneft, and authorities closed nearby streets. The Tolyatti combined heat and power plant (CHP) was also struck, resulting in disruptions to electricity and water supplies for local residents.
Tolyattikauchuk produces monomers, hydrocarbon fractions, and gasoline additives. Its synthetic rubber products are also used in the production of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.

Russia-Africa Summit: Putin set to address gathering of African leaders in Moscow
Moscow is the stage for two busy days of diplomacy as African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries gather for the third Russia-Africa summit on October 28-29.
Day one opens with discussions on economic partnerships, agriculture, education, healthcare, and artificial intelligence, followed by sessions on energy, mining, and business cooperation through BRICS. Following gatherings in Sochi in 2019 and St. Petersburg in 2023, the summit is expected to produce a cooperation plan for 2027-2029 and agreements spanning trade, investment, and technology.
The summit is being watched closely as African governments seek a greater role in global affairs and broader economic partnerships amid geopolitical tensions. Moscow’s expanding ties with the continent have drawn Western criticism, while Russian officials have accused Western governments of pressuring African states to stay away from the gathering.

Najib has been imprisoned since 2022 following his conviction for corruption and money laundering tied to SRC International, a former subsidiary of 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). The sovereign wealth fund was co-founded by Najib in 2009 during his time as prime minister. He has consistently maintained his innocence.
“Additional recoveries will not eliminate the losses from 1MDB or bring the losses borne by the country below tens of billions of ringgit,” Amir Hamzah Azizan, Malaysia’s second finance minister, told parliament on Wednesday.

15:49:16 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Australia's annual rate of inflation spiked to a six-month high of 4.3 percent in September, according to official data released on Wednesday.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said that the consumer price index rose by 4.3 percent in the 12 months to September, up from 4.0 percent in August and the highest figure since March.
It said that the annual trimmed mean, a measure of underlying inflation preferred by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), rose from 3.5 percent in August to 3.6 percent in September.
Economists from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, the nation's largest bank, had forecast that headline inflation would rise to 4.2 percent in September.
Rachael McCririck, head of prices statistics at the ABS, said that a 5.2 percent rise in housing prices year-on-year was the biggest contributor to annual inflation in September, followed by transport prices, which rose by 8.7 percent due to higher fuel prices.
"On a monthly basis, Automotive fuel prices rose 9.4 percent in September, compared to a rise of 14.8 percent in August. This was driven by higher world oil prices," McCririck said.
The data was released ahead of the RBA Monetary Policy Board's next meeting to consider interest rates at the start of November.
At its previous meeting late in September, the board voted unanimously to raise the cash rate target by 0.25 percentage points for the fourth time in 2026 to a 15-year high of 4.6 percent, citing the inflationary impacts of the conflict in the Middle East.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that the chances of another rate hike in November rose from 60 percent to 79 percent following the release of the latest inflation data. ■

For Kyrgyzstan, a country along the Belt and Road, China's expanding foreign trade presents significant opportunities to increase exports of agricultural products and mineral resources, as well as transit services, Sharsheev said.
It also helps attract Chinese investment in infrastructure, logistics and processing industries, while strengthening Kyrgyzstan's role as a regional transport hub, he added.

Over 100 graves vandalized at Saaremaa cemetery
More than 100 graves were found to have been damaged on Monday in a major act of vandalism at Kihelkonna cemetery on the island of Saaremaa.
Police have opened criminal proceedings into the vandalism and are seeking information about the perpetrators.
Margus Saar, who has worked as a cemetery caretaker for 21 years, was the first person to find the broken graves.
"The police have now established that 105 graves were damaged. Tombstones have been broken – knocked over and then shattered. Expensive granite grave lanterns have had their glass smashed, and flowers have also been damaged. I tend to think it happened on Sunday and that young people were responsible. That's what the footprints suggest," Saar said.
The Saaremaa municipal administration, which manages the municipality's cemeteries, will start to clean up the damage on Wednesday.
"The police have now initiated criminal proceedings under the section of the Penal Code concerning desecration of the memory of the deceased. The punishment for this is a fine or imprisonment. If minors are involved, the type of punishment remains exactly the same. This is the first time vandalism on such a scale has occurred here," said Minna Raun, regional group leader at Kuressaare police station.

EXPLAINER – What to expect from Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:44:41 UTC
15:44:41 KST

Elena Teslova
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
- Twenty-two countries will be represented by heads of state, according to the Kremlin
- Participants are expected to adopt a 2027-2029 action plan and a declaration on cooperation on the use of artificial intelligence
From grain supplies and nuclear energy to education, technology and new trade routes, Russia and African countries are seeking to expand cooperation as leaders gather in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit starting Wednesday.
Delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries have confirmed participation in the two-day summit, with 22 represented by heads of state, according to Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the current African Union chair, will co-chair the gathering.
The program includes summit sessions, bilateral meetings and talks with leaders of African regional organizations, alongside the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
Among the leaders that Putin is scheduled to meet are Egypt’s Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Ethiopia’s Abiy Ahmed.
 
What is on the agenda?
Trade and investment are expected to be among the central issues, alongside energy, agriculture, infrastructure, food security, science, technology, education and humanitarian cooperation.
Trade between Russia and African countries exceeded $27 billion in 2025, according to Ushakov. That compares with around $16.8 billion in 2019, when the first Russia-Africa Summit was held in Sochi.
Transport and logistics are also on the agenda, with both sides discussing ways to expand trade routes, improve connections and increase the range of goods exchanged.
Participants are expected to adopt a final declaration and a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum action plan covering 2027-2029.
A separate declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of artificial intelligence is also planned, along with intergovernmental and interagency agreements in several sectors.
 
Energy and food security
Energy remains one of the most developed areas of Russian-African cooperation.
One of the largest projects is Egypt’s El Dabaa nuclear power plant, being constructed by Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom.
The summit forum also includes discussions on nuclear energy, conventional power generation, renewable energy, mining and development of energy infrastructure.
Several African states are seeking additional electricity-generation capacity as demand grows with population increases and industrial development.
Similarly, agriculture has become another major part of the relationship.
Russia is an important supplier of wheat and fertilizers to several African countries.
After the 2023 summit in St. Petersburg, Moscow delivered 200,000 metric tons of grain free of charge to Burkina Faso, Zimbabwe, Mali, Somalia, the Central African Republic and Eritrea, fulfilling a commitment announced by Putin.
This year’s talks are expected to cover grain and fertilizer supplies as well as agricultural technology, food processing and logistics.
 
What has changed since Sochi?
The first Russia-Africa Summit took place in Sochi in October 2019.
The second was held in St. Petersburg in July 2023, when participating countries adopted a declaration setting priorities for political, economic, security and humanitarian cooperation.
Leaders also agreed to hold the summit every three years. Between summits, Russia and African countries have developed a ministerial-level format.
The first ministerial conference was held in Sochi in 2024, followed by a second meeting in Cairo in December 2025, where preparations for the Moscow summit were discussed.
The Moscow gathering will now review implementation of those earlier agreements while setting priorities through 2029.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:42:46 UTC
15:42:46 KST

Prime Minister Mark Carney (R), and Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, U.A.E. talk during a signing ceremony on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (The Canadian Press via AP)
Canada signed a trade pact with the United Arab Emirates on Oct. 27 to expand access for its exporters as Ottawa seeks to diversify trade beyond the United States.
Once fully implemented, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) will reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99 percent of current Canadian exports to the UAE, the Canadian prime minister’s office said.
It is expected to enter into force in 2027.
The deal will improve access for Canadian pulses and canola, industrial machinery, power generation equipment and aerospace products.
It also aims to reduce non-tariff barriers and expand access for goods and services in sectors including forestry, seafood and engineering.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged to double exports to markets outside the United States over the next decade.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the breakdown of trade talks with Washington have prompted Ottawa to pursue agreements across Asia, Europe and the Middle East.
Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and UAE Foreign Trade Minister Thani Al Zeyoudi signed the pact in Ottawa at a ceremony attended by Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
“We see considerable potential for our private sector,” Al Zeyoudi said, citing export opportunities and investment in logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing.
The UAE is Canada’s largest export market in the Middle East.
Two-way merchandise trade totaled C$3.5 billion ($2.48 billion) in 2025, according to Canadian government figures.
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defense cooperation. 
The UAE last year pledged up to $50 billion in investment in Canada.

Eurozone banks tightened standards for company loans and consumer credit in the third quarter as higher interest rates weakened borrowing demand, a European Central Bank survey showed on Oct. 27.
On a weighted basis, the share of banks tightening criteria for company loans exceeded the share easing them by 9 percentage points, up from 7 points in the previous quarter.
The corresponding figure for consumer credit was 14 points.
Banks cited higher perceived risks and reduced risk tolerance, with some pointing to geopolitical uncertainty and energy market developments.
Mortgage approval criteria were broadly unchanged, but the survey’s housing loan demand indicator fell to its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023. Higher rates, weaker consumer confidence and a poorer housing outlook weighed on demand.
Banks expect further tightening across all loan categories in the final quarter, alongside weaker demand for mortgages and consumer credit. Demand from companies is expected to remain broadly unchanged.
The survey covered 159 banks and was conducted between Sept. 21 and Oct. 6.

Taiwan Central Bank governor rejects claims of funding shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:37:07 UTC
15:37:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Central Bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) said Wednesday that domestic banks have enough money to meet rising loan demand despite growing pressure on their funds.
Speaking at a legislative hearing, Yang dismissed concerns about a nationwide funding shortage. He said strong demand from businesses and investors had made loans harder to obtain for some borrowers, but the banking system remained stable, CNA reported.
Taiwanese banks had an average liquidity coverage ratio of 120.57% at the end of August, above the required 100% but down from 128.79% a year earlier. The ratio measures whether banks hold enough readily available assets to cover expected cash outflows over 30 days, per Economic Daily News.
The artificial intelligence boom has driven factory expansion and increased demand for business loans. Strong stock market activity has also encouraged more borrowing, putting additional pressure on banks, per CTEE.
Yang said changes in banks' deposits had contributed to the decline in liquidity ratios. Large companies can withdraw substantial deposits at short notice, making them less dependable than deposits spread across smaller customers, per Liberty Times.
Banks have responded by seeking more stable deposits, issuing bonds, and adjusting their lending practices. However, they must also keep enough liquid assets to meet regulatory requirements rather than lend out all their available funds.
Taiwan's problem, Yang said, was not a lack of money but how banks distribute their funds. Loans increasingly favor stronger industries, particularly technology companies, while smaller businesses and traditional manufacturers may find borrowing more difficult.
