====================================================================================================

The next phase of military rule in Egypt is here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:36:59 UTC
15:36:59 KST

The next phase of military rule in Egypt is here
El-Sisi’s announcement that he will not run for a fourth term may signal a new leadership arrangement.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi surprised observers when he recently announced his intention to leave office after his third presidential term ends in April 2030.
El-Sisi had been widely suspected of moving to amend the Egyptian constitution to allow him to serve another term, or possibly indefinitely.
But speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy, el-Sisi insisted that his departure was a settled matter and that “no one would tamper with” the constitution.
So what is behind the decision? There has been much speculation that el-Sisi may use this declaration to rally popular support for a fourth term or preempt a move by the military against him. But there is also the possibility that he is setting up the next phase of military rule in Egypt.
It is important to point out first that voluntarily leaving power is a risky proposition for any authoritarian leader.
In el-Sisi’s case, his 2030 departure would leave open the possibility that a future Egyptian government could seek to use him as a scapegoat for the country’s problems, possibly even holding him to account for alleged crimes committed during his presidency.
El-Sisi led a coup in 2013 against Egypt’s first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, which was accompanied by massacres and the jailing of tens of thousands of politicians, activists, and journalists.
El-Sisi’s economic record has also been the subject of criticism, with detractors accusing him and his government of corruption, poor fiscal policy and lavish spending on vanity projects. Egypt’s debt stands at 81 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), with interest payments alone exceeding combined spending on healthcare, education, wages and subsidies. Meanwhile, the Egyptian pound has lost more than 80 percent of its value against the US dollar since 2014, while cumulative inflation exceeds 460 percent.
In this context, el-Sisi’s announcement that he plans to step down in 2030 was rather unexpected. Some have speculated that he has no intention of actually leaving office and could go back on his statement, as he has done before.
In 2013, following Morsi’s overthrow, el-Sisi denied that he would run for president.
After telling the media in 2017 that he was committed to “preserving [the constitution’s] two four-year terms and not changing it”, he helped lead the drive to amend the constitution in 2019.
A judicial source told Mada Masr last week that el-Sisi’s announcement left open the door for a “popular call” for the president to remain in office.
A second possibility is that with this move, el-Sisi may be attempting to preempt a possible military intervention, which could become more likely if the economy continues to falter.
In 2011, the military responded to popular protests against former President Hosni Mubarak by forcing him to step down.
The army could attempt to defuse public anger by presenting el-Sisi as a scapegoat, forcibly removing him from power, and replacing him with someone who can preserve a measure of stability as well as secure its vast economic interests.
In that context, a member of parliament said recently that he has heard el-Sisi say in private meetings that he would rather step down than wait for the military to force him out.
But a third and much more likely possibility deserves particular attention: el-Sisi may be preparing to leave the presidency while ensuring that Egypt’s military-dominated political system survives his departure.
It is perhaps not coincidental that during the announcement, he cited Article 200 of the constitution, which gives the armed forces an extraordinary role in Egyptian politics.
The article, amended in 2019, makes the military responsible for maintaining the country’s “democracy” and the “gains, rights and freedoms” of the Egyptian people.
According to el-Sisi, the aim of the article is “to protect the Egyptian state from any attempt to infiltrate it or allow people to take it over who cannot handle the responsibility of this country or who do not even understand the meaning of ‘state’”.
Article 200, combined with Article 234 — which requires that a president secure approval from the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces before appointing a defence minister — gives the military significant control over Egyptian political life.
El-Sisi’s vision for the selection of Egypt’s next president gives the military an outsized role. His proposal includes setting up a committee of experts to draft legislation for selecting hundreds of highly educated Egyptians to undergo specialised training at the Egyptian Military Academy.
Applicants, el-Sisi proposes, should hold doctoral degrees, be between 40 and 50 years of age, and be prepared to spend 30 months at the academy learning about the Egyptian state.
The programme would also train future ministers, governors and members of parliament.
Combined with Articles 200 and 234, this proposed mechanism seems intended to preserve the military’s dominance long after el-Sisi leaves office. It could be favourable to him as well.
A genuinely independent, civilian president could seek to investigate massacres overseen by el-Sisi, allegations of corruption, or other alleged crimes. A transition process closely managed by the military is highly unlikely to yield such a result.
The open question now is how an increasingly frustrated and critical Egyptian public will respond to a political process managed by the military that effectively wipes out the need for a popular mandate.
For now, el-Sisi and the military appear determined to shape Egypt’s political future. But the people may have the last word.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Experts defer to AI in decision-making, Anthropic study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:33:19 UTC
15:33:19 KST

Experts defer to AI in decision-making, Anthropic study finds
Professional analysts chose options that matched AI assistant’s preference 86 percent of the time, research finds.
Experts using AI overwhelmingly defer to the technology when making decisions, research by Claude creator Anthropic suggests.
In a research paper published on Tuesday, Anthropic said it asked 50 professional analysts to advise a fictional farming cooperative to determine whether experts make decisions themselves when using AI.
Anthropic said the analysts were tasked with assessing whether a fictitious advisory program for the co-op’s members was working effectively and should be expanded.
Participants were asked to make four choices between two defensible options before making a final policy recommendation.
Unbeknownst to the analysts, Anthropic directed each participant’s AI assistant to lean towards to a particular decision to measure whether the analyst’s decision-making was being influenced.
Analysts chose options that matched the AI assistant’s preference 86 percent of the time, compared with a 50/50 outcome that would be expected if they were not influenced, according to the study.
Participants that had a preference before consulting their AI assistant changed their decision 60 percent of the time in cases where the agent disagreed.
While 77 percent of analysts used their AI assistant’s arguments when asked to explain their decision, only 15 percent credited AI as the source of their thinking, according to Anthropic.
Anthropic said the study had some limitations, including that it involved just one task and used AI assistants that had been deliberately set to have a preference.
Anthropic researchers Amaç Herdagdelen, Hailey Joren, and Alex Tamkin said humans’ tendency to defer to AI may be “hard to identify, even for the experts themselves”.
The researchers said their findings raised the possibility that AI’s “priors” could shape consequential policy decisions, including in AI safety.
“If human judgement is to remain a meaningful check as more work is performed with AI, oversight of these decisions has to look at how they get made: Surfacing key decision points as the work proceeds and helping experts articulate the assumptions and values they would otherwise leave unstated,” they wrote in the study.
“A process that lets experts discover their preferences may matter for empowerment as much as the decision itself.”
Anthropic, which is preparing for an IPO valued at up to $2 trillion, and its rivals are at the centre of intense public debate about how to manage the potential dangers of frontier AI.
While AI proponents believe the technology will usher in revolutionary gains in productivity, the rapid pace of its development has prompted widespread concerns about potential negative effects on society, including mass job losses and cyberattacks.

Details
Mbappé quickly apologized on Tuesday, October 27, for comments perceived as insulting Mao Zedong, but criticism continues to spread on Chinese social media. Two major mainland Chinese consumer brands severed ties with him, China’s state television blocked his matches, and some international sponsors removed posts featuring the athlete.
"Once the line is crossed or the public is offended, all the glamour quickly dissipates, and one may even face a backlash," the People’s Daily said in a commentary on Wednesday. "Learning to respect different countries and cultural backgrounds is an important lesson."

Companies such as LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE and Lululemon Athletica Inc. faced damage to their business in China this year after perceived offenses.
China has caused luxury giant LVMH’s sales to plunge13.10.26, 09:09 • 55754 views

For Chinese companies, the immediate damage may prove manageable if they respond quickly. Mengniu’s sales are unlikely to be derailed by public sentiment toward Mbappé, given the company’s swift action to end its sponsorship ties, wrote Elaine Lai, a consumer-business analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence.
However, she added, this misstep "underscores the risks of relying on expensive sponsorship deals to promote a brand."

Ithaca's natural horseshoe harbour is picturesque – but it hides a dirty secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:31:04 UTC
15:31:04 KST

Volunteer divers have removed almost 73 tonnes of solid waste from Greek seabeds across 13 years.
On the Greek island of Ithaca, Vathy is known for its natural horseshoe harbour. But the beautiful port hides a dirty secret.
A volunteer diving team recently removed around 1,300 kilograms of solid waste from the wider harbour area. The two-day operation marked the start of this year's 'We Dive We Clean' campaign.
This was the group's 186th mission, across 13 years of underwater environmental work in different parts of Greece. According to figures released by the team, its total haul now stands at almost 73 tonnes of solid waste recovered from Greek seabeds.
Bottles, nets, tyres and an almost entire plastic boat
The scene that greeted the volunteer divers on the harbour floor highlights the scale of marine pollution and the variety of objects that end up in Greek waters.
Among the waste brought up were plastic and glass bottles, aluminium cans, fishing lines, nets and fish traps, as well as batteries, tyres of various sizes, rugs and assorted plastic items.
Equally striking was the number of objects linked to human activity and navigation in the harbour. Divers recovered parts of boats and dinghies, personal belongings and accessories that appear to have fallen overboard, chairs, traffic cones, bicycles, metal objects and anchors.
One of the most notable finds was an almost complete plastic fishing boat.
Removing such items is an important step towards improving the condition of the seabed, as discarded materials can burden the marine ecosystem, trap sea creatures and undermine the quality of the coastal environment.
13 years of voluntary work in Greek waters
The operation in Vathy forms part of We Dive We Clean's long-term effort to remove solid waste from the Greek seabed and to draw attention to the problem of marine pollution.
Founded in 2013, the group has carried out underwater clean-ups in harbours and coastal areas across the country, building up significant experience in lifting objects of different sizes and weights. Its work combines the practical removal of waste with efforts to raise public awareness about the need to protect the marine environment.
Underwater clean-ups require proper training, specialised equipment and careful planning, particularly when large or heavy items are involved. The process begins with the removal of the largest objects and is followed by the collection of smaller pieces of debris, using the necessary lifting gear.
The volunteers' regular presence in different parts of Greece has helped document a problem that often remains invisible from the surface: the build-up of waste in harbours, fishing shelters and other coastal locations.
Encouraging signs, but no room for complacency
The team says that much of the waste now being recovered from the seabed appears to date back many years.
This creates a sense of cautious optimism among the volunteers, who believe there may be growing public awareness of environmental protection and waste management.
However, this finding does not mean the problem has been solved. Keeping the seas clean calls for continuous effort, responsible behaviour from residents and visitors alike, proper waste management and an end to dumping rubbish in the water or along the shoreline.
The operation in Vathy offers a stark reminder that even today large quantities of objects remain on the seabed of Greek harbours, out of sight in everyday life. At the same time, it highlights the importance of voluntary work and coordinated environmental action.
With almost 73 tonnes of waste already removed from Greek waters, We Dive We Clean is continuing its mission with a clear message: protecting the seas does not stop at cleaning them; it begins with preventing pollution and changing our daily habits.

Freight development, fleet productivity, service quality, top priorities of railways
TEHRAN- The CEO of the Railways listed the development of international rail transport, an increase in the movement of export cargo, faster wagon turnaround, improved safety, and higher quality passenger services as the company’s priorities.
According to an IRNA report from the Railways, Jabbar Ali Zakeri, at a meeting of the High Committee for the Railway Transport Graph, emphasized the need to improve passenger services, especially on routes leading to holy Mashhad, and described providing the required fleet capacity and increasing readiness to offer satisfactory services to pilgrims and passengers as among the Railways’ priorities.
He considered supplying the wagons needed by cargo owners, removing obstacles to international and export freight transport, and reducing wagon dwell times essential for increasing productivity in the freight sector, and stressed the optimal use of locomotive capacity and the formation of heavy freight trains on routes with adequate capacity and suitable technical conditions.
The deputy minister of Roads and Urban Development also described securing infrastructure and ensuring safe train movement as essential, and stressed strengthening cooperation between the railway police and security guard, increasing patrolling along the lines, and countering the theft of railway equipment.
In another part of the meeting, Zakeri presented certificates of appreciation to two Railways athletes who brought honor to the organization on the world stage: Kaveh Riahi, an employee of the General Directorate of Safety and holder of first place in world weightlifting competitions, and Davood Hadavand, employed at the Tehran Railway General Directorate and holder of third place in world wrestling competitions.
He described support for athletes, the development of public and professional sport, and the expansion of sports programs as effective in increasing organizational vitality, and stressed continued support for the participation of Railways athletes in national and international competitions.
Further, Mirhasan Mousavi, Deputy CEO of the Railways, referring to passengers’ welcome for passenger trains, emphasized increasing fleet readiness and carrying out locomotive overhauls precisely in order to improve service quality on high-traffic routes.
He described increasing the share of rail transport in passenger movement as one of the Railways’ priorities, and listed reduced fuel consumption, improved travel safety, fewer road accidents and less air pollution, and better service quality as benefits of developing this sector.
Later in the meeting, the directors general of Railway North 2, West, Yazd, and Hormozgan, and the director of Khavar Sharq, presented reports on plans to increase fleet productivity, identify regional capacities, attract new cargoes, and strengthen the share of rail transport in freight movement.

Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said early Wednesday said Israel had chosen change after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that he would seek to form a new government.

"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.

Eisenkot warns Netanyahu not to 'use Israel's security' for political ends
Israel's elections: What happens next?
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

The bulletin did not specify a payment schedule or compensation amounts.
The brokerage’s liquidation is separate from proceedings involving investment funds established by Tera Portföy. İş Bankası is handling the affected Tera Portföy funds under separate SPK rules setting out procedures for interim and final payments to eligible fund investors.

Türkiye sets Oct 30 start for interim fund payouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:22:45 UTC
15:22:45 KST

Interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to investors in funds undergoing extraordinary liquidation will begin on Oct. 30 through İş Bankası and Ziraat Bankası, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said.
Addressing parliament’s Planning and Budget Commission on Oct. 27, Yılmaz said payments would start with the smallest amounts.
He expected this round of payments to be completed around mid-November.
“I can say that a substantial amount will be paid on Friday,” he said.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK) has given money market funds priority under rules issued after the liquidation law was published in the Official Gazette on Oct. 27.
Interim payments will be calculated separately for each fund and cannot exceed either 1 million liras or the investor’s net investment, calculated without inflation adjustment.
Where cash is insufficient, payments are also limited by the value of investors’ holdings: Sept. 16 values apply to money market funds, while other funds use values from the day before the payment calculation.
The SPK can approve a payment order or a minimum payout to reach more investors.
The SPK assigned the liquidation of Tera Portföy’s affected funds to İş Bankası and those of Pusula Portföy and Atlas Portföy to Ziraat Bankası.
Yılmaz said Atlas’s eligibility for ordinary liquidation was still being assessed.
Payments will draw on remaining fund assets, voluntary returns and recovered gains and proceeds from assets placed under judicial restrictions, Yılmaz said.
The new law gives the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) powers to sell assets more quickly.
Under ordinary liquidation procedures, 68 billion liras had already been paid to 71,899 accounts across 93 funds by Oct. 23, Yılmaz said.
He put the remaining net investment under extraordinary liquidation at 125 billion liras.
Interim payments will be deducted from final entitlements, with fund units surrendered only at the final payment stage.
People and institutions identified by the SPK as having participated in market abuse, insider trading or manipulation involving the affected funds will be excluded from payments.

Iran, Belarus ink energy cooperation MOU
TEHRAN- A cooperation memorandum of understanding was signed between Abbas Aliabadi, Iran’s Minister of Energy, and the Belarusian Minister of Energy, aimed at establishing cooperation between the parties in the energy sector for mutual benefit.
According to an IRNA report from the Ministry of Energy, a cooperation memorandum of understanding was signed between the Minister of Energy of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Minister of Energy of the Republic of Belarus with the aim of promoting cooperation between the parties in the energy sector for mutual benefit.
According to this report, the main axes of this memorandum include promoting cooperation in sustainable energy development, including in the renewable energy sector; promoting cooperation in contracting and energy infrastructure services; and providing the possibility of exchanging experience, training, and technical support.
Also among the provisions of this memorandum are cooperation in the fields of construction and management of energy infrastructure, electricity distribution and transmission systems, joint participation in seminars, conferences, and exhibitions with the aim of attracting investment in the energy field, technical cooperation and exchange of information on engineering and advisory issues, and exchange of visits by senior officials and technical experts responsible for the development and implementation of energy policy.
Back in June, the Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade of Iran, in a meeting with the Deputy Minister of Industry of Belarus, emphasized the development of bilateral cooperation in the fields of industry, trade, transport, logistics, and joint production.
In this meeting, the two sides, referring to the growing economic relations between the two countries, stressed the need to increase the volume of trade exchanges and identify new opportunities for cooperation in various industrial and manufacturing sectors.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, pointing to the industrial capabilities of the two countries, cited cooperation in the supply of mining machinery as one of the important axes of joint cooperation and called for expanding interactions among active companies in this field.
During the meeting, the issue of joint tractor production in Iran was examined, and the two sides emphasized utilizing existing technical and industrial capacities to develop cooperation in this sector. Also, areas of cooperation for the joint production of urban and intercity buses and trucks with the participation of companies from both countries were discussed.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade considered the development of transport infrastructure and facilitation of communication among economic activists as requirements for expanding economic relations and stressed the need to establish direct air lines between Iran and Belarus, as well as facilitating the visa issuance process for traders and citizens of the two countries.
In another part of the meeting, the readiness of Iran to export medical equipment, medicine, and health sector products to Belarus was announced, and the two sides emphasized the development of cooperation in this sector.
Furthermore, the development of logistical cooperation and utilization of the capacities of the North-South International Corridor was emphasized as one of the important axes of joint cooperation. The two sides assessed the use of this strategic route as an effective ground for facilitating trade, reducing transport costs, and increasing economic exchanges between the two countries and the region.
At the end of the meeting, the two sides emphasized the continuation of consultations, follow-up of agreements, and strengthening of joint cooperation in the industrial, commercial, and transport fields in order to enhance the level of economic relations between Iran and Belarus.
Meanwhile, in mid-August, Iran’s Deputy Agriculture Minister for planning and Economy Affairs met with the Minister of Agriculture and Food of Belarus, emphasizing the development of bilateral cooperation in the fields of agricultural fertilizers, machinery, and joint investment.

Another poll shows Center more popular than Isamaa
A third survey monitoring the popularity of Estonia's political parties shows the opposition Center Party has overtaken the opposition Isamaa Party for the first time since 2023.
Earlier this month, the same results were reflected in polls by Emor and Turu-uuringud, and the latest data from Norstat and the Ühiskonnauuringute Instituut confirm the change. Center's four-week average support has risen to 23.1 percent, while Isamaa's has fallen to 22.8 percent.
Center has risen to the top of the party ratings table, with its support increasing by 1.4 percentage points over the week and now standing at its highest level since August 2020.
Support for Isamaa fell by 1.2 percentage points over the week. This is the first time the party has lost the top spot since November 2023.
Support for the Social Democratic Party (SDE) has increased by 1.8 percentage points over the past four weeks to 16.5 percent, reaching its highest level since September 2024.
The top three are followed by EKRE (13.8 percent), Reform (12.3 percent) and Parempoolsed (6.4 percent).
Support for coalition party Reform remains on a slight downward trend, with a fall of 1.7 percentage points over the past five weeks.
Support for the junior coalition partner Eesti 200 stood at 1.4 percent.
The Greens, ERK and Koos all polled below 1 percent.
The coalition parties were supported by a total of 13.7 percent of respondents, while the Riigikogu opposition parties were supported by 76.2 percent.
Based on calculations by political scientist Martin Mölder the Center Party would win 26 seats in the Riigikogu, Isamaa 25, SDE 18, EKRE 14, the Reform Party 12 and Parempoolsed six.
The latest aggregate results cover the polling period from September 28 to October 25, during which a total of 4,000 Estonian citizens of voting age were surveyed.

India evacuates over 180,000 as Cyclone Arnab hits coast
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:15:08 CET
15:15:08 KST

By Jatindra Dash and Rishika Sadam
BHUBANESWAR/HYDERABAD, India, Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least three people were killed, dozens of houses damaged and crops destroyed as a powerful cyclone struck India’s eastern coast from the Bay of Bengal on Wednesday, bringing heavy rain and strong winds, authorities said.
Cyclone Arnab, classified by the India Meteorological Department as a very severe cyclonic storm – the third-highest category on its scale – made landfall in Andhra Pradesh state early on Wednesday, with its centre then moving fully inland, the agency said.
“Andhra Pradesh has been most affected … three people have lost their lives,” Narendra Singh Bundela, a top official at the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), told reporters.
Heavy rain and high winds destroyed at least 180 houses, brought down 220 trees and disrupted power supply in several areas, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu said in a letter to federal Home Minister Amit Shah, updating him on the situation.
Two of the deaths were caused by a tree falling and electrocution, officials in Naidu’s office told Reuters.
Neighbouring Odisha state was not as badly affected, Bundela said, adding that wind-speeds were expected to reduce as the cyclone moved inland.
More than 180,000 people had been evacuated in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of the cyclone’s arrival.
Some schools were closed and some train and flight services cancelled along the eastern coast.
Several NDRF and state teams were working in the affected areas, Bundela said, adding that some neighbouring states were also likely to be affected by heavy rain.
Television images showed trees fallen on highways as workers in rain gear worked to clear the road of branches and leaves.
“No one knew whose house the water would rush into next, or whose home would be submerged,” said Nagi, a resident of Andhra’s Kakinada district.
“Trees have fallen, houses have been damaged, and all our belongings, including our books, have been destroyed,” said Nagi, who did not give a last name.
Fishermen along the coast had been advised against going out to sea, and the weather department said it anticipated losses to crops, as well as damage to thatched houses and communication lines.
Winds of 125 kph to 135 kph (77.7 mph to 83.9 mph) and gusts of up to 150 kph are forecast, with a storm surge of 1 metre to 1.5 metres (3.28 feet to 4.92 feet) above normal tide likely to inundate low-lying areas of Andhra Pradesh, it said.
Operations at three Andhra Pradesh airports were suspended, India’s civil aviation ministry said.
NEPAL SUSPENDS TREKKING PERMITS
In neighbouring Nepal, authorities suspended the issuing of trekking permits to high mountain areas for three days because of the risk of rain and blizzards due to the cyclone, Immigration Department information officer Gita Ghimire told Reuters.
This is peak trekking season in Nepal with around 750 hikers getting permits per day.
On Tuesday, Nepal warned tourists against venturing into high-altitude areas due to fears that Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches in the Himalayan region from Thursday night through Saturday.
Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal, a major region for tropical cyclones that has spawned deadly storms on India’s east coast.
A super cyclone that killed nearly 10,000 people when it hit Odisha in October 1999 remains one of the country’s deadliest natural disasters.
India, however, has over the years developed early-warning systems and preventive measures to minimise loss of life.
(Reporting by Jatindra Dash in Bhubaneswar, Rishika Sadam in Hyderabad, Gopal Sharma in Kathmandu and Sakshi Dayal in New Delhi; Writing by Chris Thomas and Shilpa Jamkhandikar; Editing by Bill Berkrot, Edwina Gibbs, YP Rajesh and Kate Mayberry)

China’s old-age dependency ratio overtakes children for first time
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
07:14:49 CET
15:14:49 KST

HONG KONG, Oct 28 - China is now supporting more people aged 65 and above than children, underscoring the impact of its rapidly ageing population and a declining birth rate.
• Data from China’s National Bureau of Statistics showed the old-age dependency ratio — the non-working-age population compared to the working-age population — was 23.1% in 2025, compared with 22% for children, Chinese state-affiliated media Yicai reported
• The ratio has risen steadily over the years, up from 15% in 2016 to more than 20% in 2021
• There are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above compared with around 213 million children aged 14 and under, the data showed
• China’s population fell for a fourth straight year in 2025, as its birth rate dropped to a record low
• The country’s birth rate has been falling for decades, a result of the one-child policy in place from 1980 to 2015, as well as rapid urbanisation
• Authorities have rolled out a range of measures to encourage marriage and childbearing, including family subsidies, childcare support, and reduced childbirth-related medical costs
• They have also pledged to make urban life more supportive for young people, children and families

By Ricardo Brito, Gram Slattery and Luciana Magalhaes
SAO PAULO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election, three sources said, with the US State Department due to grant him and his family entry visas.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.
The ruling relates to a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.
Argentina’s migration department said on Wednesday that Bolsonaro and his family had briefly entered the country’s Misiones province on Tuesday night through a road crossing, with valid travel documents, before boarding a private plane bound for Guayaquil, Ecuador at 11:30 pm local time (0230 GMT).
Argentina cited the flight plan, for the plane operated by air charter company Baires Fly, as the source for the aircraft’s destination. The Ecuadorian foreign ministry did not respond to an emailed request for comment outside regular hours.
The current location of Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters was not immediately clear.
Speaking to reporters late on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump had said that he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.
“The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States,” a senior State Department official said.
BRAZIL-US RIFT GROWS
Bolsonaro’s departure threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday’s election on a US State Department campaign to restore them to office.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the United States.
“Well, I would approve. I think they’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible. It’s gotten bad reviews. You look at what happened to their market”, Trump said.
“I think it’s so terrible to see it. I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well. The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn’t involved. That’s Brazil. It’s a different country”, he said.
Trump has previously alleged Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. The elder Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
On Monday, Trump had said the Brazilian vote “looked like another rigged election.”
Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just heard that Flavio had left the country, and called it shameful, saying he should have stayed in Brazil and proved his innocence.
Bolsonaro had been favored to win Sunday’s presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result.
ORDERED TO HAND OVER PASSPORTS
On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports, which were canceled after the deadline lapsed, two sources said. In a court ruling seen by Reuters, the Supreme Court cited the risk of Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil and his “significant financial resources” in ordering his passports seized.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, had said on Monday he had no plans to flee.
“I have never thought about leaving the country,” he said. “I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
His departure appeared to have caught his campaign manager off guard.
“We are surprised by the news because, just yesterday, we discussed the need for Flavio — given the 60 million votes he received — to take on this role as leader of the opposition,” Senator Rogerio Marinho told reporters.
FOLLOWING FATHER’S PATH
Although Bolsonaro has yet to officially concede defeat — saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities — his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula’s victory.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro’s younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move.
“If my brother does not win, I’m in favor that he would leave the country,” he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

Political upheaval dominated the Hungarian Press Photo exhibition in 2025. Personal stories on how life is affected by tragedy and new technology such as AI, are at the heart of this year's competition entrants.
If the themes of political change, ballerinas and parental care took pride of place at last year's Hungarian Press Photo exhibition, the show this is dedicated to imminent social revolution sparked by technology.
At the opening of the 44th edition at the Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center in Budapest, managing director Orsolya Kőrösi stressed that the work of photojournalists is becoming increasingly important: "The photojournalist does not just take pictures, but is present, bears witness, selects and interprets, while putting their own name to the claim that what they show is close to reality,"
Kőrösi pointed out that in the age of artificial intelligence, when it is increasingly difficult to distinguish the genuine from content created artificially, the role of a place where authentic photojournalistic work, assumed with a name and responsibility, is presented, protected and celebrated becomes particularly valuable.
More than 6,200 works were submitted by 258 photographers. The exhibition showcases the top three entries and the special prize-winners in each of the sixteen categories.
It also presents works considered by the jury to be exceptionally important or exciting, according to photographer András Bánkuti, who's also chair of the Hungarian Press Association (MÚOSZ) Photojournalists Section.
"With us you cannot retouch a picture even if, say, a politician has a spot. The moment you do that, it counts as interference and the picture is immediately out of the competition," Bánkuti explained. "It can still be printed on any paper; that is not our responsibility. Our responsibility today, when the greatest value and credibility are attached to a picture being real, we have to be very careful about that."
Prize-winning pictures
This year the MÚOSZ Grand Prize went to freelance photographer Diana Nemeh for her series titled "Nimród", while the André Kertész Grand Prize was awarded to Telex photographer Noémi Napsugár Melegh.
Napsugár Melegh has been constant recorder of almost all major protests but her greatest recognition has come from documenting her own personal tragedy. After the death of her 18-year-old younger brother, she spent years photographing her grieving family and his classmates.
"It was very difficult to make these pictures, especially in situations where my brother should have been there. I actually went to the same secondary school as he did, and it was quite surreal that 15 years later I was in the same places, at the same freshers' camp where he should have been," said Napsugár Melegh.
"On the one hand I had to force myself to be there so I could take these pictures; on the other, for a long time I was making them for the drawer, I did not show them to anyone. After a year and a half I began to show them to my closest professional friends, and that broke through something in my own process of mourning as well," she added.
The 44th Hungarian Press Photo Exhibition is at the Robert Capa Center in Budapest until 8 November.

‘Working our fingers to the bone’: Can the UK save its struggling high streets?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:05:27 UTC
15:05:27 KST

‘Working our fingers to the bone’: Can the UK save its struggling high streets?
Small business owners in Britain may get some tax relief in Wednesday’s budget, but they say it will not be enough.
Birmingham, United Kingdom – Taking the reins of a family business can be a source of immense pride, but it also comes with enormous pressures.
When Surpreet Suri’s father started a photography business in Birmingham 40 years ago, his hard work paid off and he expanded to four locations around the city.
Today, the family has just one shop, in a prime location in the city’s Kings Heath High Street. But Suri is now considering relocating.
The reason: It’s too expensive to continue the business there.
When Suri moved the business to its current site, it gave it greater visibility – but also much higher running costs.
“We are at a point now where we are seriously considering how do we get out of this space purely to reduce costs,” he tells Al Jazeera.
Despite having a loyal customer base, Suri says the financial rewards are increasingly difficult to find.
“We’re sort of working our fingers to the bone, and that’s the side that people don’t see.”
Living ‘month to month’
Suri’s experience reflects a broader struggle on Britain’s high streets as the government presents its budget on Wednesday, with attention focused on whether further relief from business rates could help smaller businesses.
Business rates are a property-based tax paid by businesses occupying commercial premises, although some smaller properties already qualify for relief.
For Suri, however, rates are only part of the problem.
There is also the rent, VAT – a type of sales tax – wages, pensions, the rising cost of energy and specialist materials, which are all eating into his earnings. Refilling one of his professional printers with ink, he says, costs about 2,000 pounds ($2,664).
“I pay myself less than the minimum wage [of 12.21 pounds ($16.26) per hour]”, he says when asked how much he earns. “When I say that I live month to month, I literally mean that.”
Another challenge Suri and other independent business owners face is competition from online retailers, which now account for 28 percent of UK retail sales.
King’s Heath high street faces the same challenges as many of Britain’s main commercial thoroughfares: a fight to remain relevant in an age where big businesses, higher taxes and online shopping are squeezing out independent retailers.
While small business owners on the high street face steeper costs, customers increasingly expect prices comparable to those online, even when they are paying for a specialist, personalised service.
“People come to me wanting the quality that we provide, but they want me to match online pricing, which I simply can’t do,” Suri says.
He understands that the cost-of-living crisis he is struggling with also affects his customers.
“You can’t blame the customer or the consumer for not being able to support your business all of the time,” he says, pointing to household living costs.
Decline of the high street
The pressures on retailers come as many customers are feeling increasingly despondent about the state of their high streets.
Boarded-up shopfronts are a more common sight. Pawnbrokers, betting shops, vape outlets, charity stores and big-chain retailers have moved into high street locations that small business owners can no longer afford. Nearly 14 percent of high street retail units are estimated to be vacant.
For many who once regularly used their local high street, this new reality has become a symptom of decline and depression, even putting them off going there in the first place.
“Years ago, you used to come and have a good look, whatever the weather,” one Birmingham shopper tells Al Jazeera. “But it’s just the same up here all the time now.”
Another says shopping online is increasingly preferable. “It’s more convenient as well. Sometimes you come out here and there’s no inspiration.”
Yet the same shopper says they want more distinctive local businesses and adds that the government should make it easier for entrepreneurs to open them.
A struggle to survive
These challenges go well beyond Birmingham.
At a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising Britain’s high streets earlier this month, the chief executive of the British Independent Retailers Association, Andrew Goodacre, argued that recent business rate reforms had failed to deliver the intended benefits for smaller retailers.
He told members of parliament that some independent shops are facing higher bills, even as a large supermarket near his home stood to pay substantially less.
The inquiry heard another troubling argument that legitimate businesses may also face unfair competition from operators which evade taxes. Politicians heard how some central London souvenir shops allegedly use successive limited companies to avoid paying tax, enabling them to pay rents that compliant businesses could not afford.
The evidence highlights the importance of enforcement alongside tax reform, and warnings that a cut in business rates alone will not stem the deterioration of Britain’s high streets.
That warning is echoed by Suri, who says a reduction in rates would be welcome but not enough.
“That’s a small step in the right direction,” he says. “But if the intention really is to help the high streets thrive, there’s a lot of change that needs to be made.”
His challenge to the UK’s Chancellor of the Exchequer is to spend a month or two running a real high street business and experience the pressures first-hand.
For a family business that has survived four decades, the question now is whether it can afford another year in the place it once hoped to grow.
“If [the government] makes it easier to actually run an independent business successfully, that’s the first domino in a positive effect that could really help our country.”

Kumamoto earthquake: Over 1,000 people still living in evacuation shelters
More than 1,000 people are still living in evacuation centers in Japan’s Kumamoto Prefecture, three months after a magnitude-7.1 earthquake damaged tens of thousands of homes, as residents await temporary housing, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Kyodo
The earthquake struck at around 4:27 p.m. on July 28. As of Monday, the death toll had reached 38, including 36 confirmed disaster-related deaths and two suspected cases. The total number of casualties stood at 420.
Evacuation centers remain open at 21 locations across seven cities and towns. Yatsushiro has the largest number of evacuees, with 579 people still living in shelters, accounting for more than half of the total. Another 263 people remain in shelters in Uki, 155 in Hikawa and 65 in Uto.
The earthquake damaged 82,223 homes, including 2,585 that were destroyed.
On Tuesday, Kumamoto Prefecture released a draft restoration and reconstruction plan aimed at helping residents rebuild their lives, including measures to provide temporary housing as quickly as possible.
The prefecture has developed a roadmap extending through fiscal 2028, focusing on restoring livelihoods and rebuilding social infrastructure.
The plan addresses challenges experienced during the disaster, including extreme heat and water outages that took a month to resolve. Proposed measures include revising evacuation shelter operating manuals, strengthening water supply and sewage systems, and expanding physical and mental health support for survivors.
It also incorporates new tsunami countermeasures amid concerns that a fault segment extending offshore near the earthquake’s epicenter did not rupture during the quake.

Traces of Golden Horde-era iron production discovered in Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:03:33 UTC
15:03:33 KST

Traces of Golden Horde-era iron production discovered in Kazakhstan
Archaeologists have discovered evidence of iron production dating back to the Golden Horde era in the Bayanaul district of Kazakhstan's Pavlodar region. The discovery offers new insights into the economic activities and metalworking traditions of medieval nomadic communities, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Researchers have used radiocarbon dating to establish the age of the finds and are now studying the techniques used in ancient iron production.
Ilya Merts, a senior researcher at the Alkey Margulan Joint Archaeological Research Center and a Candidate of Historical Sciences, explained that archaeological studies of medieval sites in northeastern Saryarka have traditionally focused on burial and memorial complexes, while the settlements and everyday production activities of ordinary nomads have received far less attention.
"To fully understand life in steppe society during the Golden Horde era, studying the history of rulers and urban centers is not enough. The daily lives of nomadic communities, the production of tools, the use of raw materials, and the ways people met their everyday needs are equally important aspects of historical research. From this perspective, discovering evidence of ironworking at medieval nomadic settlements is particularly significant," the researcher said.
Researchers analyzed charcoal remains found in iron slag using radiocarbon dating. Laboratory tests conducted in Japan confirmed that the materials date to the medieval period.
According to Merts, radiocarbon dating not only helps determine the age of archaeological finds but also places evidence of ancient production activities within a specific historical period.
Iron slag, a byproduct of metal smelting, can provide valuable insights into ancient production methods. By studying its composition and archaeological context, researchers can identify the raw materials used and better understand the iron-smelting techniques of the time.
The discovery in Bayanaul district offers a new perspective on life in the steppe during the Golden Horde era, shifting attention beyond major historical events and urban centers to the everyday lives, resource use, and production activities of nomadic communities.
Further research could shed more light on medieval iron production in northeastern Saryarka.

Trucker strikes emptied my local supermarket shelves: Shopping locally made all the difference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:02:56 UTC
15:02:56 KST

I didn’t think a trucker strike would really affect me - until supermarkets and petrol pumps were empty.
Last week truck drivers in southern Italy staged a strike - and it had the desired effect. Protesting the rising cost of diesel driven up by the US-Iran war, the truckers’ refusal to work started on a Friday. By Wednesday the supermarket shelves in our area of Sicily, where I live as a foreigner, were empty.
It was much the same across the island and the south of mainland Italy, where drivers set up roadblocks to stop lorries leaving food warehouses. Petrol stations also ran dry and a government minister even said that the Mafia were exploiting the protests by intimidating drivers into taking part and slashing truck tyres.
Strikes are fairly common in Italy - public transport workers often walk out over low pay or working conditions, or rubbish services grind to a halt because of Mafia influence. I’m usually aware these strikes are happening but I’ve never been affected by them. Italian friends had warned me that a truckers’ strike 15 years ago had brought food supplies to a standstill but I foolishly thought that wouldn’t happen again. How wrong I was.
Supermarket stock lasted only a few days
I hadn’t needed to buy food for the first few days of the strike and I hadn’t paid much attention to news about the impact it was having. Then I realised I’d almost run out of a few key essentials - like milk for my toddler and fruit - the go-to when he won’t eat a bite of anything else. That was when I started paying attention to videos on social media of local influencers filming completely empty fridges and aisles in the supermarkets in my local town. I cynically thought they probably went at the end of the day, timing their visit in the hope of catching shocking footage to gain attention.
So I went shopping myself, in the morning, to the local Lidl, Eurospin, a nationwide budget supermarket chain, and a Conad, also nationwide but mid-range. There was no fresh food at all - no meat or fish, no dairy products and no fruit or vegetables. Most of the other aisles looked fairly normal but I could see that in a couple of days, if new deliveries didn’t arrive, staples like pasta, tinned goods and cleaning products would also have disappeared.
It was shocking to realise how quickly the system we all rely on for food can be brought to a grinding halt. This was a well coordinated approach: haulage operators, farmers and shopkeepers, often backed by citizens and students, were all involved in disrupting the transport and delivery of goods, all designed to put pressure on the government to intervene.
Shopping locally became the only option
I left the supermarkets unsure what to do. On my route home I passed a greengrocer’s - charmingly called ‘frutterias’ in Italian. I’d been into this one a couple of times but not regularly, finding it easier to get everything in one go at the supermarket. I pulled up and was delighted to see that it had plenty of fruit and veg. I got a basket full of food and chatted to the owner while I was paying. He said they’d had no problems with stock because local farmers, or their distributors, drive produce directly to his shop. If there’s no logistic chain involved, the logistics can’t be disrupted.
My unexpected visit to the ‘frutteria’ turned out to be one of the best parts of my day: on top of the relief of finding fresh food, my mood was boosted by the friendly chat with the owner - it would never have happened during a rudimentary exchange at a supermarket checkout. On top of that, I got fruit and veg that had only been picked a few days before - it also hadn’t been sprayed with the chemicals needed to make it last long journeys by road.
How did the trucker strike come to an end?
As the strike continued, the fallout got worse and worse. Mozzarella dairies lost €3 million in 24 hours because the buffalo milk needed to produce the cheese couldn’t be delivered. Construction companies were affected when they couldn’t receive deliveries of raw materials.
Eventually the Italian government held an extraordinary cabinet meeting and approved new measures to help truckers, farmers and fishers deal with higher fuel costs, bringing financial aid for the two groups to a combined €540 million in tax credits, up from €434 million.
It’s now been four days since the last roadblocks were opened but I’m still waiting on deliveries I ordered before the strike began, and big companies such as Vinted have notified customers they should expect delays.
Make food transport electric rather than pouring more money into the tank
This protest and its fallout happened for one reason: our addiction to fossil fuels. Almost all of the essential services that keep society moving - like delivery trucks and public transport and production of goods - are powered by oil and gas. The Iran war has caused an unprecedented disruption and shortages of fossil fuels, leading to sky high prices in countries far away from where the war is being raged.
As climate scientists have been saying for decades: we have the solutions to bring down carbon emissions and a big one is electrification - replacing fossil fuels with clean energy sources, like wind and solar, to power transport, heating, factories, everything ideally.
Trucking accounts for roughly 11-17 per cent of total oil demand across the US, EU and China - making it the perfect sector for electrification. The diesel price surge is driving record uptake of electric trucks this year: worldwide, sales of medium- and heavy-duty electric trucks hit a record high in the first half of this year at nearly 160,000 units - up by around 75 per cent versus the first half of 2025.
So as with heat pumps and solar panels, the energy crisis created by the Iran war is actually giving a boost to clean energy. The Italian government would be wise to use tax credits to incentivise hauliers to switch their fleet to electric trucks, rather than pouring more money into fossil fuels.

NEW YORK, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump announced plans on Tuesday to roll back regulations aimed at curbing methane emissions from oil and gas operations, arguing that the move would reduce costs and boost domestic energy production.
"Tonight, I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers 45 billion dollars," Trump said at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas.
The move would "unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas" and allow the production of an additional 210 million barrels of oil, Trump said.
The announcement came amid rising fuel prices driven by the U.S. war with Iran, as Trump seeks to ease energy costs ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the proposed rollback of Biden-era regulations would eliminate a program for identifying and addressing major methane leaks, ease requirements for low-producing oil and gas wells, and relax restrictions on routine flaring of natural gas at oil wells.
The United States is the world's leading emitter of methane from its oil and gas sector, followed by Russia, according to the International Energy Agency. Texas is by far the leading fossil fuel-producing state in the United States.
Methane, the main component of natural gas, is the second-largest cause of global warming after carbon dioxide. It is estimated to be responsible for nearly a third of global warming observed today. ■

The ministers stressed the need for direct security coordination to counter shared threats, protect civilians and combat cross-border weapons and drug smuggling.
The Syrian government said the operation had taken place without prior coordination with Damascus. Its Foreign Ministry later said it had conveyed its objections to Jordan.

Column: Understanding the strengths of China's governance model
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:01:57 CST
15:01:57 KST

by Denis Simon
As China continues on its development path, a range of complex issues will require sustained attention. The good news is that the track record of the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese government demonstrates a number of institutional strengths and development achievements for dealing with these challenges.
To better grasp the capacity of the Chinese government and the CPC to handle the challenges it is confronting, I would like to emphasize three main themes: long-term strategic planning, governance capacity and policy implementation, and the relationship between economic development and improvements in people's livelihoods.
STRENGTH OF CHINA'S GOVERNANCE MODEL
I believe one of the most important strengths of China's governance model is its ability to combine long-term strategic vision with the capacity to mobilize resources and implement policies on a national scale.
One challenge facing many governments today, particularly in developing countries, is the difficulty of maintaining policy continuity. Electoral cycles, political polarization, competing institutional interests, and short-term political calculations can make it difficult to sustain development strategies over a decade or longer. China has developed an institutional approach that places considerable emphasis on long-term planning, policy coordination, and continuity of national development objectives.
The five-year planning system is an important illustration. It allows the government to establish priorities, coordinate national and local development strategies, mobilize public and private resources, and adjust policies as circumstances change. China's experience in infrastructure development, poverty reduction, industrial upgrading, and technological advancement demonstrates the potential benefits of this approach.
I would identify five lessons that may be relevant to political leaders in developing countries: First, the importance of long-term strategic planning. Governments need to look beyond immediate political and economic pressures and develop a coherent national development vision.
Second, the importance of state capacity. Having good policies is not enough. Governments must possess the administrative institutions, professional personnel, financial resources, and organizational capabilities to translate policy objectives into tangible results. China's experience demonstrates the importance of connecting central strategic direction with implementation at provincial, municipal, and grassroots levels.
Third, the ability to mobilize resources around national priorities. Developing countries often face severe resource constraints. China's experience illustrates how governments can coordinate public investment, private-sector participation, financial institutions, and local development initiatives to advance major national objectives.
Fourth, the importance of pragmatism and policy experimentation. One particularly interesting aspect of China's reform experience has been its willingness to experiment with policies at the local level, evaluate results, and expand successful approaches. The establishment of special economic zones is a prominent example. This suggests that effective governance does not require every policy to be perfect from the beginning. It requires institutional learning and the willingness to correct mistakes.
Fifth, the importance of maintaining social stability while pursuing economic transformation. Development requires a reasonably predictable political, social, and economic environment. Governments must address inequality, unemployment, regional disparities, and public concerns if they hope to sustain public confidence.
However, China's governance model should not be regarded as a universal template that other country can simply copy. Every country has its own political institutions, historical circumstances, social structures, and development challenges. Different countries may draw useful insights from one another's development experiences.
Therefore, the most productive international discussion should focus less on competing political labels and more on identifying practical approaches that improve government effectiveness, strengthen accountability, deliver public services, and create opportunities for economic development.
CORE REASON CPC MAINTAINS LONG-TERM GOVERNING VITALITY
In my view, the fundamental reason is the ability of the Communist Party of China (CPC) to maintain a strong organizational structure while continuously adapting its governing priorities to China's changing economic and social circumstances.
The CPC's longevity cannot be explained simply by its size or organizational reach. Its membership of more than 100 million gives it an extraordinary organizational presence, but size alone does not guarantee governing effectiveness. What matters is how that organization functions and whether it can continue to deliver results.
I would highlight three interconnected factors. First, the CPC has developed a distinctive capacity for long-term strategic thinking. It has consistently emphasized national development objectives that extend beyond immediate economic or political considerations. The ability to maintain continuity in major national priorities, while adjusting implementation to changing circumstances, is an important institutional advantage.
Second, the Party has demonstrated a considerable capacity for adaptation. Since the beginning of reform and opening-up, China has undergone enormous transformations in its economic structure, social composition, technological capabilities, and international position.
The CPC has chosen to adjust its governing approaches to accommodate these changes. The transformation from a predominantly agricultural economy into a major industrial and technological power required not only economic reform but also significant changes in governance, administration and policymaking.
Third, the Party has placed considerable emphasis on organizational discipline, cadre development, and the ability to translate central policy decisions into action throughout the country. This capacity for coordination and implementation is an important source of institutional strength.
I would add one further consideration: the ultimate test of a ruling party's vitality is whether it retains the capacity to recognize problems, correct mistakes, respond to changing public expectations, and maintain public confidence. No political organization can remain effective simply by relying on its historical achievements. China's economic and social circumstances today are very different from those of 20 or even 10 years ago. The expectations of younger generations, the challenges of an aging population, the pressures of economic restructuring, and the demands of technological innovation all require new governing capabilities.
CPC'S PEOPLE-CENTERED PHILOSOPHY OF DEVELOPMENT
I consider the people-centered philosophy of development one of the most important aspects of the CPC's governing approach, particularly because it connects national development objectives with the everyday concerns of ordinary citizens. One of the most significant achievements of China's reform and development experience has been the transformation of living conditions for an enormous proportion of its population.
Consider poverty alleviation. China's achievement in lifting hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty is historically significant. It demonstrates what can be accomplished when poverty reduction becomes a sustained national priority, supported by targeted policies, substantial resource mobilization, infrastructure investment, and local implementation.
But the importance of a people-centered philosophy of development should not be measured exclusively by poverty reduction. It also should be reflected in the quality and accessibility of public services, including education, healthcare, employment opportunities, affordable housing, pensions, and social protection.
China has made substantial progress in expanding educational opportunities, improving rural infrastructure, extending healthcare coverage, and developing social security systems. These achievements have helped create a much stronger foundation for social and economic development.
I also would emphasize an important conceptual point: economic growth and improvements in people's livelihoods should not be treated as separate objectives. They are mutually reinforcing. Economic development creates the resources necessary to improve public services, while better education, healthcare, social protection, and employment opportunities strengthen human capital and support further economic growth.
That said, China's people-centered philosophy of development faces an important new test as China has moved into a substantially different stage of development. The challenges today are no longer simply about lifting people out of poverty or expanding basic infrastructure. They increasingly involve improving the quality of development and ensuring that its benefits are shared more equitably.
My overall assessment is that China's experience demonstrates the importance of placing improvements in people's living standards at the center of national development. But the next stage will require moving beyond the achievements of poverty reduction and basic development toward greater equality of opportunity, higher-quality public services, and more balanced and sustainable growth.
EXPECTATIONS FOR FIFTH PLENARY SESSION
I believe the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee comes at an important moment for China. The country is entering a new phase of development, facing a more complicated international environment and a number of significant domestic economic and social challenges.
The principal focus of the Fifth Plenary Session is on advancing the Party's full and rigorous self-governance. Against this background, I expect the Fifth Plenary Session to deliver an important message: institutional self-renewal is essential to long-term governing capacity.
The CPC has repeatedly emphasized the importance of discipline, combating corruption, and strengthening Party self-governance. I believe this is particularly important at a time when China is confronting more complex economic, technological, and international challenges.
But institutional self-renewal must go beyond disciplinary measures. It should also involve improving the quality of governance, strengthening administrative accountability, encouraging innovation, and ensuring that officials at all levels have both the competence and the incentives to address difficult problems.
An effective governing party must be capable of renewing itself before institutional weaknesses become serious obstacles to development.
Looking ahead, I believe the Fifth Plenary Session could strengthen the CPC's institutional capacity and reinforce the importance of administrative discipline and organizational accountability. It could also send an important signal to the international community about China's approach to governance, economic development, and its role in an increasingly uncertain global environment.
Ultimately, my expectation is that the meeting will demonstrate that China's next stage of modernization requires not only strong political leadership and long-term strategic planning, but also continuous institutional reform, greater policy responsiveness, and a stronger commitment to improving people's livelihoods.
The most important outcome should not simply be another set of policy declarations. It should be a clearer demonstration of how the CPC intends to translate its governing principles into practical results for the benefit of the entire population.
Editor's note: Denis Simon is the former Executive Vice Chancellor of Duke Kunshan University in Jiangsu province. He is also a senior faculty member in the Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

SEOUL, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's retail sales grew in single digits last month, boosted by shopping for early Chuseok holidays, the South Korean version of Thanksgiving Day, government data showed Wednesday.
The combined revenue of 26 major retailers, comprising 15 offline and 11 online ones, rose 4.5 percent in September from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.
The earlier-than-usual Chuseok holidays, which fell in late September this year compared to early October last year, led to robust sales of holiday gift sets and traditional holiday food.
Offline retail sales mounted 5.1 percent, and sales by online retailers swelled 4.0 percent.
Hypermarkets posted revenue growth for a second consecutive month, fueled by high demand for holiday groceries, home appliances and toys for gifts and apparel.
Department stores capitalized on Chuseok gift set sales, which pushed up food revenue by 13.0 percent, alongside autumn fashion demand that raised sales of women's casual wear by 15.2 percent and men's clothing by 8.7 percent.
Convenience stores logged a 5.9 percent gain in processed food sales, catering to single-person households looking for ready-to-eat meals during the holidays.
Online retail sales also benefited from the holiday surge, with grocery purchase in cyberspace climbing 6.7 percent.
Online demand for services and others, including food delivery, travel and cultural products and e-coupon purchase, advanced 10.6 percent as more consumers utilized digital grocery services. ■

Rome’s mayor rules out ‘Venice-like’ entrance fee for tourists

Rome’s mayor rules out ‘Venice-like’ entrance fee for tourists
- Rome mayor Roberto Gualtieri rejects a Venice-style entry fee. He says Rome should protect its historic centre by limiting short-term rentals and keeping real local shops.
- Rome has approved stronger housing rules, but new short-term rental laws are still needed. Gualtieri says Venice’s €5 fee suits its smaller size and many day-trippers.
- Rome had record tourism in 2025, with 22.9 million arrivals and 52.92 million overnight stays. Gualtieri also backs a waste-to-energy plant due in 2029 and plans to seek re-election in 2027.
AI generated
ROME – Rome can best preserve the character of its 3,000-year-old city centre with measures like restricting short-term rentals, rather than by increasing taxes imposed on visitors, mayor Roberto Gualtieri said.
“It would make no sense to introduce here an entry ticket to the city, like they did in Venice,” Gualtieri said in an interview with Bloomberg for the video podcast Quello che il potere non dice.
The Eternal City, a destination since ancient times, has no plan to block access, the mayor said.
Visitors want to experience the city as Romans do, and that requires ensuring historic centre isn’t hollowed out, and tourists have access to local shops and restaurants instead of “fake” ones, he added.
“Tourists will always come to Rome,” Gualtieri said. “There have always been tourists and there always will be.”
This past summer, Rome’s city assembly approved an update of rules covering urban development, a process that took nearly 20 years.
Among the changes backed by Gualtieri were stronger protections for residential housing in the historic centre.
Action is still needed to adopt new regulations that apply to short-term rentals.
Venice has tested measures to control the number of tourists and day-trippers visiting the historic centre, including a €5 (S$7.13) access fee which was trialled this summer.
According to Gualtieri, such a system is better suited to the water city because it is smaller, and a large number of visitors do not stay overnight, so they do not pay room taxes.
Florence and Bologna have also passed new regulations on short-term rentals, such as banning a change of use for non-residential properties in their respective historic centres.
Waste to energy
Gualtieri, a former finance minister and a member of the Democratic Party, won election in 2021, pledging to address chronic overtourism and sluggish garbage collection.
To many Romans’ surprise, he jump-started some projects that had eluded predecessors on the left and the right.
A waste-to-energy plant is moving forward after years of resistance, and Catholic Jubilee and European Union recovery funds were used to promote urban regeneration.
Gualtieri confirmed in the interview that the waste plan will become operational at the end of 2029.
Among his remaining priorities is to discourage what he described as hit-and-run tourism, in which visitors “simply consume and give nothing in return”, he said.
According to a survey released in September by real estate company Brixa, Rome’s city centre has more than 122,000 beds available for overnight stays, compared with the 116,000-plus residents of the area.
The research indicated that the trend of short-term lettings, which has traditionally been confined to the historic centre, is spreading to residential neighbourhoods on the outskirts of the city.
“We cannot intervene on existing properties unless we are granted the power to do so,” Gualtieri said. “So we are equipping ourselves with tools to impose restrictions” on various kinds of properties, he added.
His goal is to keep Rome “a great, open city where people want to come back”.
Better-quality tourism, focused on major cultural events that sometimes take place outside the historic centre, will spur a demand for real Roman experiences, Gualtieri maintains.
Rome attracted a record number of tourists in 2025, according to data supplied by the city.
Arrivals totalled 22.9 million, including 12 million from abroad. Overnight stays totalled 52.92 million, another all-time high.
Gualtieri’s term will end in 2027, and he has been tipped as a possible candidate for a centre-left alliance in Italy’s general election in 2027.
The mayor dismissed such an option during the interview, saying he will seek to run for a second mandate.
There are many long-term projects in the city that he wants to oversee, he said.
In 2027’s campaign, Gualtieri said he will be “a mayor, a candidate mayor, and hopefully a mayor again for the next five years”. BLOOMBERG
