As Trump sides with Putin, Europeans are increasingly ready to engage in direct talks with Russia, something they have so far refused to do.
After months of dithering and bickering, Europe is sending its strongest signals yet that it is ready to speak directly with Russia to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and decide the future of the continent's security architecture.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre marched ahead and held a phone call withRussian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the imminent restart of the peace process.
Though Stubb and Støre lacked a mandate to speak on behalf of Europe – they did so as "leaders of their respective countries" – their overture on Tuesday immediately positioned the Nordic duo as preeminent interlocutors.
In its read-out, the Kremlin said that the three leaders had "agreed to maintain direct telephone contact in the future".
Meanwhile, the European Commission and the European Council are preparing a joint team of senior officials to be sent to the next round of talks, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in early November. The exact date is yet to be announced.
Bjoern Seibert, the powerful chief of cabinet of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, is tipped to lead the delegation.
"We are adamantly committed not just to putting an end to the war but to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable. That is our aim and that is the stance we are defending in the ongoing talks," a Commission spokesperson said.
Is it notable that Brussels is now openly statingits intention to hold the upcoming negotiations in a multilateral format, which would mean having Europeans, Ukrainians, Americans and Russians at the same table and at the same time.
This has never happened before in the peace process. Until now, it was primarily the US that spoke with Russia, with episodic trilaterals that also featured Ukraine. (Kyiv and Moscow have a parallel track to release prisoners of war.)
It is even more notable that Russia has not straight-up rejected the European participation, as it has done repeatedly in the past. This time, it seems to seek it.
"It's not enough to talk only to Kyiv. We need to talk to the whole of Europe, which fully supports Kyiv," Yury Ushakov, Putin's close aide, said last week.
Elusive consensus
Whether to break the diplomatic isolation imposed in February 2022 and speak directly with Russia has long been a divisive topic among European leaders.
The debate came to the fore earlier this year, when French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni issued back-to-back calls in favour. The idea of appointing a special European envoy unleashed a flurry of possible names.
Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Luxembourg and Slovakia gradually endorsed the strategy, arguing the stakes were too high for Europe to be absent.
By contrast, Germany, Poland, Sweden, Denmark and the Baltics resisted it, warning that Russia's positions remained as maximalist as the first day of the war.
The lack of consensus was laid bare in June when European Council President António Costa unexpectedly opened a channel of communication with the Kremlin. Costa's decision drew political backlash and was discretely put on hold.
The Stubb-Støre call with Putin also raised eyebrows in some corners.
"I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a rare moment of Nordic divide.
"I honestly don't know what they think can be achieved by this."
Poland's Donald Tusk advised Stubb and Støre to be "vigilant" and proceed with caution in their newfound engagement with Putin.
"Russia's agenda and interests are quite precisely defined, and that one should harbour any illusions about getting an agreement," Tusk said.
There was an obvious point in their warnings. The Kremlin's readout, with evergreen references to the "root causes" of the war and Europe's "confrontational policies", left no doubt that Russia's maximalist demands were still intact.
A turn for the worse
But things are no longer what they were in June, when Costa was rebuked.
Back then, European allies were fresh from a successful G7 summit in France that saw US President Donald Trump promise to reimpose sanctions on Russian oil and discuss licences for Patriot missiles with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Now, they are in shock as Trump cuts a diesel deal with Putin, lifts long-standing sanctions on Russia, lambastes Zelenskyy and demands new elections in Ukraine.
Sudden limits on Kyiv's use the Starlink technology and the early warning system, both crucial to defend itself, set off alarm bells. Overnight, the dreaded scenario that Trump will push Ukraine into a take-or-leave-it capitulation crystallised.
The rapid deterioration prompted Stubb and Støre to hastily organise a new round of talks in Oslo. Following the meeting, Zelenskyy emerged with a tempered attitude. Starlink speeds and the early warning were restored afterwards.
Still, anxiety over Trump's turn to Putin remains palpably high.
European officials have realised the contacts between Washington and Moscow are more extensive than they had previously thought.
The two sides are reportedly discussing more deals involving the Lukoil assets, nuclear technology, Arctic LNG and, most controversially, the restart of the Nord Stream pipeline and the release of immobilised Russian assets.
For Europeans, the US approach is fundamentally flawed because it ignores Putin's fixation with territorial conquest, the core reason why he launched the invasion. No deal, however lucrative, can replace Ukraine's annihilation in Putin's mind, they say.
Adding to the sense of urgency is the blockade in the Black Sea, which has disrupted global supply chains, and the upcoming winter in Ukraine, which Russia plans to make insufferable. The two crises threaten to spur a migratory wave towards Europe.
The need to achieve a ceasefire, even if targeted to the Black Sea and energy facilities, has never been more pressing since February 2022. Putin is certain to demand further sanctions relief in exchange for anything it considers a concession.
This helps explains why Europe, after months of hesitation, is now willing to step up its role and speak directly with Russia: being at the table has become indispensable to defend Ukraine's position, increasingly fragile; counter the US approach, increasingly emboldened; and safeguard the European interest, increasingly side-lined.
Støre said as much as he defended his call.
"If one assumes that the current situation – where communication from the American administration to Moscow serves as the sole channel for discussing Ukraine outside of Ukraine – is the only way, then one is entitled to that view," he said.
"I believe it is important that other voices are heard as well."

Cost of living crisis: How much net income do you need to live comfortably in Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:00:15 UTC
15:00:15 KST

Living comfortably means different things to different people. Euronews Business calculated the monthly net household income needed to reach 150% of the national median which is the starting point of the upper-middle class benchmark.
How much do you need to earn to live comfortably across Europe? This is a very challenging question.
Firstly, "comfortable" is very subjective. Secondly, price levels vary widely both across and within countries. Thirdly, household size also varies. Income also does not take wealth or homeownership into account.
Still, some income indicators can give an idea of how much people may need to live comfortably.
The equivalised disposable income is one of them.
All monetary income received by household members is added together. This includes income from work, investments and social benefits, as well as other household income. Taxes and social contributions are then deducted from the total.
It is then divided by the number of household members converted into equalised adults, meaning this is not directly individual income.
Middle class income bands
The OECD defines the middle class as households with equivalised disposable income between 75% and 200% of the national median.
It divides this into three groups: 75% to 100% of median income is "lower-middle", 100% to 150% is "mid-income" and 150% to 200% is "upper-middle".
There is no established benchmark for how much of the national median income a household should have.
“If information on incomes is all we have, one could probably assume that most households above 150% should have a sufficient income to live relatively comfortably.” Sebastian Königs, senior economist at the OECD, told Euronews Business.
However, other scholars note that an income above 150% of the median does not necessarily guarantee financial security.
Euronews Business calculated 150% of the median income for three household types to show how much net income a household needs to reach the start of the upper-middle-income group.
In 2025, the EU’s median equivalised disposable income is €22,939 a year, or €1,912 a month. A single adult living alone needs €2,867 a month to reach 150% of the median.
Across 34 European countries, this figure ranges from €603 a month in North Macedonia to €6,491 in Switzerland. Within the EU, it ranges from €1,023 in Romania to €6,256 in Luxembourg.
This figure is also above €4,000 a month in Norway (€5,240), Austria (€4,568), Denmark (€4,524), Ireland (€4,392) and the Netherlands (€4,308).
Among the EU’s four largest economies, Germany has the highest benchmark at €3,611. France follows at €3,307, about 15% above the EU figure, while Italy is just below at €2,758. Spain has the lowest of the four at €2,546.
The gap is wide: a single adult in Germany needs €1,065 a month more than one in Spain.
The benchmark is also below €1,000 a month in Albania (€723), Turkey (€755), Montenegro (€825) and Serbia (€975). With North Macedonia, all five are EU candidate countries.
This figure is between €1,000 and €1,900 a month in 11 EU countries, including Portugal (€1,808), Poland (€1,799), Greece (€1,463), Bulgaria (€1,108) and Hungary (€1,099).
Does a couple need twice the income?
A couple without children does not need double the income of a single adult. Because they share costs such as rent and energy, Eurostat assumes they need 1.5 times as much.
So, in the EU, a couple needs €4,301 a month in net income to reach the benchmark. This rises to €6,021 for a couple with two children under 14.
The country ranking does not change for couples or families because every country’s figure is multiplied by the same factor: 1.5 for a couple and 2.1 for a family with two children.
The buttons on the chart show the figures for all three household types in every country.
Purchasing power improve comparison
Euro figures do not reflect price differences between countries. Purchasing power standards (PPS), an artificial currency that removes these differences, offer a better basis for comparison.
The gap narrows, but it remains wide. In PPS terms, the benchmark for a single adult in the EU is 2,830 PPS a month. It ranges from 1,031 PPS in Albania to 4,709 PPS in Luxembourg, a gap of about 4.6 times, compared with 10.8 times in euros.
Within the EU, Hungary has the lowest benchmark at 1,495 PPS. This makes Luxembourg’s benchmark just over three times higher, compared with six times in euros.
Relatively comfortable income can buy different things
These gaps suggest that living comfortably means very different things. PPS figures show what this relatively comfortable income can buy in each country.
“The same relative income position can also buy very different living standards across countries. Being at 150% of the median in one country does not imply the same purchasing power as being at 150% elsewhere,” Prof. Koen Caminada from Leiden University told Euronews Business.
Regional differences within countries
“Purchasing-power-adjusted figures would improve the comparison, but national averages still conceal regional differences, particularly in housing costs,” he added.
Königs also pointed out that many OECD countries have large regional differences in both income levels and the cost of living.
Income is only part of the story, wealth matters too
Königs said income tells only part of the story. Wealth inequality, especially access to homeownership, is a pressing issue in many OECD countries.
“Some people may get by on low incomes just fine because they own their home and maybe live in a place where prices are lower,” he said.
Caminada also pointed to the role of wealth and savings. He said a household with a modest income and savings it can easily use may cope better with an unexpected bill or job loss than a higher-income household with no savings and large debts.
How to define living comfortably
Caminada noted that ‘living comfortably’ should mean more than being able to pay the bills: “A household should be able to afford adequate housing, food, energy and transport, participate in social life, enjoy some leisure, and put money aside. Crucially, it should be able to absorb an unexpected expense or a temporary loss of income without immediately falling into financial difficulty.”
He cautioned that neither 150% nor 200% of the national median income is an established threshold for comfortable living. He underlined that the OECD’s middle-income classification describes a relative position in the income distribution, not the adequacy of a household’s budget.
Dr Markus M. Grabka from the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin) also suggested that an income above 150% of the median does not in itself guarantee financial security.
“An income exceeding 150% of the median provides financial security only when combined with a certain level of private wealth,” he told Euronews Business.

How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:00:04 UTC
15:00:04 KST

Venice is famed for being a floating city, but research shows the land it sits on once lay many miles inland. Dramatic changes in sea level over 10,000 years have reshaped the northern Adriatic coastline, with much of the land that our ancestors roamed now lying beneath the waves.
Samuele Ongaro, at the University of Southampton, and colleagues combined seismic data with sedimentary cores from the coastal basins of northern Italy, Slovenia and northern Croatia to model changes in sea level across the region and reconstruct past landscapes over the past 10,000 years.
Their results, published in Quaternary Science Reviews, show that the present-day Venice lagoon was once dry land extending more than 30 miles from the coast, and that Trieste was previously an area of hills overlooking swamps and lagoons.
Starting just over 10,000 years ago, sea level rose in fits and starts, sometimes by up to 25mm a year, forcing Mesolithic hunter-gatherer populations to shift their hunting and fishing activities as they adapted to a rapidly changing environment. The most dramatic changes occurred in three distinct phases, followed by a period of relative stability over the past 6,000 years, which supported the formation of settlements and the advent of farming in the landscape we are familiar with today.

Vegetarian coconut curry recipes: Maunika Gowardhan’s spicy aubergine baingan and spiced vegetable stew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:00:03 UTC
15:00:03 KST

Both these hearty curries use coconut as part of their base gravy. The region of Kutch in Gujarat is brimming with vegetable curries, and the bhagare baingan features many classic Kutchi ingredients; it has several similarities to the Hyderabadi version, too. I’ve used baby aubergines, but if need be you can use regular diced aubergines instead. Avial, meanwhile, is often served at celebrations in south India, and this version is a Keralan recipe made with a flavourful coconut paste.
Bhagare baingan, or aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves (pictured top)
Prep 15 min
  
Cook 1 hr 30 min
  
Serves 4
For the paste
 
1 tbsp poppy seeds
  
2 tbsp vegetable oil
  
90g finely chopped white onion
  
1 tbsp sesame seeds
  
1 tbsp grated fresh coconut
For the gravy
 
160g fresh tomatoes
  
4 tbsp vegetable oil
  
150g thinly sliced white onions 
  
5 garlic cloves
 , peeled and ground to a paste
 
¼ tsp turmeric powder
  
1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder
  
2 tsp ground cumin 
 
Salt, to taste
 
8-10 baby aubergines, slit open lengthways
 
1½ tsp tamarind paste
  
½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper
  
2 mild dried red chillies
  
12 fresh curry leaves
  
Coriander, to garnish
 
Rice or roti, to serve
For the paste, soak the poppy seeds in 70ml warm water 20 minutes. Meanwhile, put the oil in a small frying pan on a medium heat, then fry the onions for eight or nine minutes, just until they start to change colour. Add the sesame seeds and grated fresh coconut, and fry, stirring, for two minutes. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature. Once cooled, stir in the poppy seeds and their soaking liquid, then blitz the lot to a smooth paste.
Meanwhile, put the tomatoes in a blender and blitz to a smooth puree. In a large, heavy-based frying pan for which you have a lid, heat the oil over a medium heat, then add the onions and fry, stirring regularly, for 17-18 minutes, until softened and lightly browned. Add the garlic paste, fry for 20 seconds, then stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and cumin, and fry, stirring for a few seconds, until fragrant.
Add the pureed tomatoes and fry, stirring, for five minutes, until the mix splits and the oil leaves the side of the pan. Add the ground poppy seed and onion paste and fry, stirring continuously, for four minutes. Pour in 350ml warm water, season with salt to taste, then stir in the aubergines, cover and simmer on a low heat for about 15 minutes, stirring once halfway through. Add the tamarind paste and simmer for a further five minutes.
Take off the heat and stir in the black pepper, whole dried red chillies and curry leaves. Garnish with coriander and serve warm with roti or rice.
Avial, or vegetable stew with coconut, ginger, curry leaves and green chillies
Prep 20 min
  
Cook 40 min
  
Serves 4
For the paste
 
200g grated fresh coconut
  
2½cm x 2½cm piece ginger, peeled and roughly chopped
 
½ tsp cumin seeds
  
1 green bird’s eye chilli
For the curry
 
3 tbsp vegetable oil
  
1 tsp black mustard seeds
  
1 dried mild chilli, roughly broken into pieces
 
7-8 fresh curry leaves
  
70g finely chopped white onion 
  
1 tsp turmeric powder
 
200g medium carrots, peeled and cut into 1cm dice
  
150g potato
  (use a good all-rounder such as red rooster), peeled and cut into 1cm dice
 
200g french beans, all topped and cut into three roughly equal pieces
 
½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper
  
Salt, to taste
 
3 tbsp greek yoghurt
  
Coriander, to garnish
 
Rice or paratha, to serve
For the paste, put the fresh coconut, ginger, cumin seeds and chilli in a blender, add 200ml water and blitz to a smooth paste.
Put the oil in a heavy-based saucepan on a medium heat. Add the mustard seeds, dried chilli and curry leaves. After 15 or so seconds, when they start to splutter and pop, add the chopped onions and fry, stirring, for seven or eight minutes, until they start to soften. Add the turmeric and the chopped carrots and potatoes, fry, stirring, for just a few seconds, then pour in 200ml water, cover and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook gently for 10 minutes, then add the chopped green beans and cook for another eight minutes, until all the vegetables are tender.
Add the coconut paste and the ground black pepper, season with salt to taste, then stir and simmer for another two minutes. Whisk the yoghurt, then stir it into the pan and simmer for a minute more. Garnish with coriander and serve at once with rice or paratha.
- Maunika Gowardhan’s most recent book, Curry: Recipes from Indian Home Kitchens, is published by Quadrille at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, go to guardianbookshop.com

Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon Tisdall

2026-10-28

As another Iran catastrophe looms, one question matters more than any other: how to stop it before it’s too late? Whatever the eventual outcome of Israel’s election and next week’s US midterm polls, Donald Trump, playing the Lone Ranger, and Benjamin Netanyahu, his badass Tonto, appear hell-bent on resuming the illegal war of choice they began in June last year and expanded in February. Like a Shakespearean tragedy moving inexorably to a bloody denouement, the worst is yet to come. And yet three things seem certain: the US and Israel will again fail to totally destroy Iran’s largely hypothetical nuclear capabilities; its regime will survive; and millions of ordinary people, there and around the world, will pay the price for this unjustified, reckless aggression.
Ducking and weaving, Trump is desperate to dodge the blame for the Republicans’ anticipated midterm meltdown, largely triggered by war-related fuel and consumer price inflation. He claimed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were responsible, but that didn’t wash. He cut a treacherous diesel deal with Vladimir Putin but, as usual, Russia’s smirking mafioso conned him. He urged US allies to tap their strategic reserves but, unsurprisingly, vilified and sidelined European leaders, who view his war as an unmitigated disaster and declined to bail him out. Trump also reportedly rebuffed last-gasp, electorally driven pressure from Netanyahu to hit Iran this month, fearful it would unleash a Democratic tsunami.
Yet once the midterm polls close, and whatever the results, all these considerations fall away. What voters think will no longer matter to Trump. At that point, he can do more or less what he wants, in foreign and defence policy, for his final two years. And what he wants has little to do with imaginary Iranian nukes, a democratic uprising in Tehran, or any of his other bogus justifications for waging war. Trump will be free to do what he does best: vendetta politics. Iran’s greatest sin is to have defied the imperial will. He wanted an easy Venezuela-style, regime-altering victory (and sweetheart oil deals). What he got was a middle digit, burnt fingers and a forever war. Just as he vengefully pursues opponents at home, so he now victimises Iranians. It’s not rational or ideological. Like everything with Trump, ultimately it’s personal.
Netanyahu’s reasons for wanting another bash are thoroughly dishonourable too, but in a different way. Given his myriad, chronic failures before and after the 2023 Hamas massacres, his trashing of Israel’s international reputation by his criminal actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and his Trump-ish slide into bigoted, ultra-nationalist authoritarianism, Netanyahu is fighting for his job and, potentially, his freedom. He insists, despite his record, that only he can ensure Israel’s security. He suggests, outrageously, that opposition victory could pave the way for Israel’s destruction in a second, nuclear Holocaust. Israel’s military chiefs suspect he may restart the Iran war in order to dominate and manipulate the inevitable post-election coalition talks – hoping to stay in power and out of jail.
The likely, mortifying consequences of a renewed US-Israel onslaught after 3 November should be fully understood. For starters, the price of oil will spike again, perhaps to unprecedented levels, negatively affecting people all around the world. Pentagon officials, possibly peddling disinformation, suggest Iran is preparing to retaliate with missile and drone attacks against Saudi and other Gulf oil refineries, infrastructure and underwater internet cables, while reinforcing blockades of the strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab strait. The impact on international energy supplies, transportation and international trade generally could be far worse than last spring.
Trump reportedly plans a shock-and-awe, time-limited assault – primarily on the mountain complex where Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium is supposedly stored, plus its missile bases and energy grid. If this sounds familiar, it is. Trump’s chief gunslinger, Pete Hegseth, and his air-force cowboys claim to have destroyed many of these targets already, some more than once. Total success will probably elude them again. What’s more likely is that the war’s duration will lengthen, and more Iranian civilians will suffer the fate of over 100 schoolgirls killed in a Tomahawk missile strike in Minab in February. For that atrocity and others, Trump and Hegseth have never admitted responsibility.
Other foreseeable consequences include: the spread of related conflicts, involving Iranian allies and proxy militias, to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Lebanon; attacks on US embassies and personnel from Jordan to Kuwait; intensified, opportunistic settler violence and land grabs in the West Bank; stepped-up Iranian freelance assassination and sabotage operations in Europe; further undermining of US and Israeli democracy from deliberate obstruction of war-zone accountability, official cover-ups and blatant lying, and restrictions on independent media reporting; another hugely damaging split between Washington and its reluctant European allies; and another geopolitical free lunch for the west’s anti-democratic challengers, Russia and China.
Here are two more questions. By what right does the US, in particular, presume to behave in this way? Forget, if you can, Trump and Netanyahu. What does the American public (or at least, those who vote Republican) say? Have they not learned by now, after so many disastrous interventions that the world does not want, and does not need, to be saved by the US? In the age of Maga, this vulgar exceptionalism has surely had its day. Second, reformulated question: how may this looming catastrophe be prevented? As Albusaidi spoke, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on a last-ditch mission to pre-empt resumed hostilities. All power to them. At least they’re trying.
It would be reassuring to think Trump and Netanyahu are listening. But the bottom line is that, for their different reasons, both men probably want this war. A firm, united course of rapid, preventive action is required to head them off. Britain, its European allies and like-minded governments took a tentative, defiant step in Istanbul last weekend, urging diplomacy over violence. Now they and all the world’s democracies must stand as one and, in a formal demarche, tell the US and Israel they risk a permanent rupture with immediate and long-term negative economic, diplomatic, commercial, military and security consequences if they ignore global opinion and go to war again.
Trump is not king of the world. And Netanyahu cannot do as he likes with impunity. It’s high time they were told.
- Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

A 78-year-old volunteer has claimed a Reform UK councillor accused her of “facilitating the invasion” and being akin to a Nazi collaborator during the second world war because she has helped asylum seekers learn English.
Mair Godley and her husband, Nick, 77, a former chair of Wethersfield parish council, live near the former Wethersfield military base in Essex, where the Home Office accommodates hundreds of asylum seekers.
The couple said the accusations were made against Mair Godley at a parish council meeting on 14 October.
Reform took over control of Essex county council after the elections in May 2026, ending 25 years of Conservative control. The Reform councillor, Carl Johnson, attended the meeting to update members of the parish council about local issues for which it has responsibility, including repairing potholes and “Operation Vanguard”, which involves private security guards patrolling Essex town centres.
Wethersfield is the larger of two former military sites the Home Office uses to provide mass accommodation for asylum seekers. The other is at Crowborough in Sussex.
Nick Godley challenged Johnson at the meeting about the potholes and whether Operation Vanguard was needed to protect local people against asylum seekers. He said crime and antisocial behaviour incidents in nearby Braintree, where asylum seekers sometimes go to, were low.
In response, Johnson asked if anyone in the room had been helping the migrants at Wethersfield and “facilitating the invasion”. Mair Godley said she had previously volunteered to help teach English to the asylum seekers at the facility.
Johnson then reportedly said that by doing so she might as well have been helping Germany during second world war. He said he didn’t want to bring his daughter up to be raped and murdered by asylum seekers.
In a Facebook post the week before the parish council meeting, Johnson had written that people who enter the country “illegally” received things including clothing and accommodation for free while “the rest of us” had to pay for items. “I have never known a country to actively facilitate its own invasion and population replacement,” he wrote. “This is treason.”
According to the draft minutes of the parish council meeting seen by the Guardian the discussion became heated and Johnson was asked to leave the meeting to “restore order”.
Mair Godley said: “I’m nearly 79 years old. I felt violated by his comments. How dare he say that to me? I certainly told him at the meeting, ‘you are not wanted here’. He has left a really bad taste.”
Nick Godley said he had had a “fairly challenging” discussion with Johnson about Operation Vanguard. It was after he had raised concerns that it had been introduced without consultation that Johnson accused Mair Godley of being akin to a Nazi collaborator by helping asylum seekers to learn English.
“It was a member of the public who attended the meeting who suggested forcibly that he should leave. Cllr Johnson’s behaviour was shocking,” said Nick Godley.
He has lodged a formal complaint about Johnson’s comments at the meeting with Essex county council.
A spokesperson for the council said: “We comment on complaints made at a point where they have been investigated and a finding of a breach has been made, but not before that point.”
Reform UK and Johnson have not responded to repeated requests for comment.

Should AI Decide Your Court Case? This Judge Says Yes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

In a few days, judge Geoffrey Vos will retire as Master of the Rolls, the most senior position in England’s civil justice system. As one of his final acts, he’s trying to stoke a debate about whether—and how—judges should be using artificial intelligence.
Under the latest guidance, judges in England are advised to confine their use of AI to administrative tasks, and Vos tells WIRED he uses Microsoft Copilot all the time to locate far-flung documents and summarize large bodies of text. But recently, he visited a court in Shenzhen, China, where civil disputes are already being decided by judges with heavy assistance from AI. Impressed by what he saw, Vos believes that courts across the globe should consider following.
That road is littered with pitfalls. Multiple lawyers have been caught citing case law hallucinated by AI, and in a first for the UK, somebody recently lost their license to practice in part because they misused the technology. Meanwhile, with chatbots as their legal counsel, litigants are flooding the courts with an unprecedented number of claims, some of them bogus.
Yet Vos remains convinced that AI will someday help resolve civil disputes more rapidly and in ways that cost far less. While complicated commercial disputes and sensitive family cases might require a human judge, he believes that personal injury claims, low-value professional negligence cases, and the like could easily be adjudicated by AI.
“What most people desperately want in civil disputes is resolution,” Vos tells WIRED. “The question is, where is the line to be drawn?”
Given his impending retirement, the debate for Vos is largely a philosophical one. But for everyone else in the profession—and for coders, cybersecurity experts, math professors, and a whole host of others—the rules are changing fast.
In October, WIRED met with Vos at his office at the Royal Courts of Justice, London. We discussed the ways that AI is spilling into the courts, the practical and ethical issues it raises, and how the justice system might adapt to serve a new generation raised alongside the technology.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
WIRED: You’re just a few days away from retirement. How do you feel about leaving the post at this particular juncture, as AI begins to reshape how law is practiced and justice administered?
GEOFFREY VOS: When I started as a lawyer, we had foolscap paper, typists, and Tipp-Ex. We moved rapidly into word processors, faxes, and eventually computers.
Lawyers are conservative with a lowercase c. But that doesn’t mean that they should be backward-looking or retrogressive. It means they should be adopting change cautiously, with their eyes open.
The legal system is for the people of this country. You can’t be effective in providing access to justice if you’re not on the same technological wavelength. But it’s time to leave it to a new generation of leadership judges.
How have you built AI into your practice to date?
I don’t use it for writing judgments, but I use it for finding things out, navigating large quantities of material, and checking things. It saves me time. I have 11 meetings a day. I know there’s a document created years ago that’s relevant to my meeting—and Copilot finds it in seconds. I do that every day.
In law, isn’t the devil always in the details? Doesn’t confidence in the legal system depend on the understanding that a judge will review and consider every inch of every court submission?
I’m a little more cautious about using it to read papers for my cases, but that’s because I do the most important cases in the system.
People have confidence in our justice system because they believe that our judges have absolute integrity. In order not to lose that integrity, you have to explain how you’re adopting technology and achieve a broad consensus that it is appropriate.
How is AI spilling into the courts right now? Is it changing how litigants and legal professionals behave? What issues is it throwing up?
It’s changing everything remarkably quickly. We see a 10 percent rise in the number of county court cases started every year—and it looks as if this may increase. That’s because everybody who has a legal problem now puts it into Gemini, ChatGPT, or Claude. Ask it to create a particulars of claim, a case, a claim form—it can.
What proportion of these claims are based on sound legal principles, though? How often are people led by a chatbot to mistakenly believe they have a claim?
We don’t have the data. But I think it’s a mistake to assume that just because a claim is created by AI, it’s totally frivolous.
In a way it’s a good problem, because it shows there’s greater access to justice because of technology. One of the problems with justice in the past is that it’s only been available to rich people.
If people have a problem sufficient to bother ChatGPT, they probably genuinely think they have a claim. When you explore their problem in detail, you might find it is actually a bit different, but it may still be a legal problem and may still be reasonable for them to have wanted to bring it to attention.
People are not generally time wasters. They’re not generally trying to make trouble.
What about the opportunity for AI to fabricate evidence on which judges have previously been able to rely—images, video, voice recordings? Where does that leave the courts?
Often, judges have to decide whether a person is telling the truth. That is the most difficult thing to do, because humans are not bad at lying. But judges make these decisions every day. There’s absolutely no difference—in scale or qualitatively—in somebody producing a false image created by AI.
The only reason we’re all getting so excited about deepfakes is because they are so new. But actually, that is the stuff of judging.
But we’re talking about a whole category of evidence that’s now somewhat compromised. Doesn’t that affect a judge’s ability to decide whether somebody is lying?
It was always thus. We always had to decide whether wills were forged, because people used to do that. It’s exactly the same with voice recordings, and video. It’s just an extension of the type of false information that is produced to the court.
People will find out when they produce fake images to the court that they are committing perjury and they will go to prison, just as if they’d forged a will.
I think we need to be cautious about predicting disaster. I’m very optimistic.
You’ve previously described an “inevitable” future where simpler civil cases are adjudicated entirely by AI. Why are you confident that’s where we’re headed?
You need to find a way to deliver justice that is within the cultural grain. That doesn’t mean you just conduct all your cases on TikTok. But if you don’t understand that people are asking LLMs for the answer to almost every question under the sun, including legal questions, you’re likely to get it wrong when you try to devise a process fit for the 21st century.
It’s all about consensus. It will only be possible to ask people to accept algorithmic decision-making if they consent to the process in a particular case, or if society decides through legislation.
When people go to court and get an adverse outcome, even if they regard the outcome as idiosyncratic or even wrong, when it’s delivered in a human way, it can be accepted over time. With AI, we have to be careful; it may be less easy for people to accept an adverse machine-driven decision.
I very much want to see a very open, international discussion about how we should resolve disputes.
I suspect part of the reason people object to trial by AI is because we can’t know precisely how a model has arrived at a decision. What’s to be done about this problem of explainability?
I don’t think it’s about reasoning; it’s about outcomes. The AI can produce very plausible reasoning. You can’t see how it produced that reasoning, but you can see the reasoning it produced, and you can judge the plausibility.
I don’t think you’ll ever do away with human judges. There’s something almost biblical about the human judge; it’s in the human psyche to want to be judged by their fellow man. But that does not mean that in some situations people wouldn’t rather have a quick outcome—even if it’s not a human outcome.
Where would you draw the line?
I don’t think judges are yet in the position to say. It’s a question for society, politicians, and legislation to resolve. That debate is really important.
I think that custody and family cases are one of the areas where essentially human judgment is expected, even by the younger generation. In complex commercial cases, I think that’s also the case. But I think we will whittle away at how commercial cases are decided by using AI to collate information to make the decision-making process better and easier.
We will allow more people access to justice more cheaply and more quickly using technology. That will be an overall good for the economy and for the people we serve.

New York honours oldest Lithuanian diaspora organisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

A plaque commemorating the oldest Lithuanian diaspora organisation, which has been operating for more than a century, has been unveiled in the heart of New York over the weekend.
The Lithuanian Alliance of America (Susivienijimas Lietuvių Amerikoje) was founded in 1886 by Jonas Šliūpas – a doctor, publisher, and political activist. Initially, the organisation provided assistance to Lithuanians arriving in the United States, later becoming a hub for Lithuanian culture.
The organisation acquired the building in the heart of Manhattan in 1910. Lithuanians who had just stepped off a ship could receive help with paperwork, life insurance, accommodation and a train ticket to their first home in America, where they were ready to work in Pennsylvania’s coal mines or Chicago’s slaughterhouses.
“Often, when we talk about heritage, particularly heritage in America, the news is either bad or worrying. This time, it is certainly a good day,” said Dovydas Špokauskas, Lithuania’s consul general in New York.
Lisa Kersavage, chair of the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission, which granted the building its historic status, highlighted that the Lithuanian-American press was also born within its walls.
“The Lithuanian Alliance has been operating in this building for more than 100 years. There is a great deal of history here. A printing press operated here, helping to preserve Lithuanian-American culture and language. My grandmother was from Lithuania. She came here from Lithuania as a child, on her own. So this means a great deal to me,” Kersavage said.
Historic landmark status is not just an honour but also provides a degree of protection, helping to ensure that the building will not be demolished.
“At a time when relations between our city, our country and immigrants are tense, or even threatening, and many immigrant communities feel unsafe, I think it is very important that New York is taking steps like this. We are honouring what immigration, and Lithuanian immigrants in particular, mean to our city,” said Carl Wilson, a member of the New York City Council.

====================================================================================================

Lithuania pays price for refusing to admit Russian, Belarusian athletes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Lithuania’s refusal to admit Russian and Belarusian athletes is costing the country international sporting events, money and opportunities for its competitors, but officials say they will not compromise on their principles despite growing pressure to reintegrate athletes from the two countries.
The latest setback came when the International Modern Pentathlon Union withdrew Kaunas’ right to host a World Cup stage next year because Lithuania will not allow Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in the country.
The decision has raised concerns about the future of other international competitions planned in Lithuania. Yet the government and national sports federations say they have no intention of changing their position, arguing that Russia and Belarus should remain isolated from international sport because of their countries’ actions in Ukraine.
A sporting setback for Kaunas
Lithuania had been building its reputation as an international centre for modern pentathlon. The country hosted the sport’s world championships for the first time about 18 months ago, followed by world junior and youth championships in Kaunas this summer.
The city had increasingly been regarded as one of the world’s leading modern pentathlon venues. It was due to host a World Cup stage next year, but that event will no longer take place in Lithuania.
Justinas Kinderis, president of the Lithuanian Modern Pentathlon Federation, said the loss was both a financial and a moral blow.
“Organising these events requires a long process. You don’t just show up and get one,” Kinderis said, adding that the federation had already secured a number of agreements.
Hosting the competition would have allowed 16 Lithuanian athletes to compete at home. Instead, the federation expects to send only a few athletes to the event elsewhere.
Kinderis is also concerned about the prospects for other competitions Lithuania hopes to host, including a World Cup stage and junior and youth championships scheduled for 2028.
“After this decision, getting another championship to organise is practically impossible,” he said. “The European Confederation [of Modern Pentathlon] president [Tatiana Ardabieva] will certainly not give us anything, because she’s Russia, and nor will the world federation.”
The financial consequences could be significant, said Kęstutis Bartuškevičius, an adviser to Lithuania’s education, science and sports minister.
International competitions bring prestige to national federations as well as revenue associated with organising major events, he said.
Despite those costs, Kinderis said Lithuania’s position would remain unchanged.
“We will maintain our current position, and I don’t think anything can change it,” he said.
Officials reject pressure to change course
Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys has also defended the policy, arguing that allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to return without restrictions weakens the international isolation imposed on their countries after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“We had agreed that we would isolate those countries,” Budrys said. “When we admit representatives of those countries into sport, we see that this isolation is already crumbling.”
He called the decision to withdraw Lithuania’s hosting rights deeply regrettable and questioned the argument that the sporting community should stop waiting for the war to end.
The modern pentathlon governing body’s decision follows a broader shift in international sport, including the International Olympic Committee’s decision to permit some Russian athletes to participate in competitions under specified conditions.
IOC President Kirsty Coventry has said the organisation would not hold events in Russia or invite Russian government representatives to its programs. She has also argued that athletes should not be held responsible for decisions made by their governments.
The IOC has reiterated its condemnation of the war and pledged support for Ukraine. However, whether Russian athletes will be permitted to compete under their national flag and anthem at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics remains undecided.
Tautvydas Vencevičius, president of the Lithuanian Sports Journalists Federation, said restrictions on Russian athletes were receiving less attention as more international sports organisations allowed them to return.
Lithuania is not the only country opposing that trend. Six countries, including Lithuania, boycotted the opening ceremony of the 2026 Milan-Cortina Winter Paralympics after Russian and Belarusian athletes were permitted to compete with their national flags and anthems following the lifting of earlier suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee.
Budrys said Lithuania wanted the European Union to impose sanctions preventing Russian and Belarusian athletes from competing under their national symbols.
He also said Lithuania was discussing possible visa restrictions with other EU members for Russian athletes linked to the country’s armed forces.
Concerns over political influence and money
Lithuanian sports officials argue that decisions by international governing bodies are not always driven solely by sporting considerations.
Budrys said Russia was devoting political and financial resources to changing the positions of international federations.
“That is blatant corruption in some systems, and we must acknowledge it openly. Political corruption is also a form of corruption,” he said.
Eimantas Skrabulis, president of the Lithuanian Athletics Federation, said the leadership of international sports organisations played a major role in determining whether Russian and Belarusian athletes could return.
“The worldview and understanding of the head of an international federation matter enormously,” Skrabulis said.
He cited Umar Kremlev, the Russian businessman who heads the International Boxing Association and has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s circle. Kremlev has received Russia’s Order of Friendship.
Skrabulis said powerful financial interests were also at play.
“Behind them are enormous amounts of money, billions, Gazprom and all the rest,” he said. “Step by step, through individual federation heads or board members, that avalanche moves forward, and it is doing so very successfully.”
Restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes remain in place in athletics, although policies vary considerably between sports and governing bodies.
The Lithuanian government has so far relied on a recommendation that national federations refuse entry to athletes from certain countries deemed aggressors. Bartuškevičius said the approach was supported by sports federations across Lithuania and that the ministry had received no calls to reverse it.
“We understand that our federations could suffer because international sporting events will not take place in Lithuania,” he said. “But this is a decision based on values. Values cannot be priced or bought.”
The Seimas, Lithuania’s parliament, has also begun considering a proposal from the Foreign Ministry to establish the restrictions in law.
Under the proposal, Russian and Belarusian citizens who directly or indirectly support the Kremlin’s war against Ukraine would be barred from participating in sports in Lithuania. The restrictions could also cover other public activities, including concerts and teaching.
Balancing principles with athletes’ careers
Lithuanian athletes and national teams face a separate dilemma when competing abroad, where Russian and Belarusian athletes may be allowed to participate.
The government is not urging Lithuanian athletes to boycott every competition where competitors from the two countries are present. Vencevičius said a blanket boycott would risk doing more harm to Lithuanian sport than good.
“If Lithuanians don’t participate, everything is lost – all European and world championships and the Olympic Games,” he said. “We would be hurting our own athletes.”
He said Lithuania opposed competing against Russian and Belarusian athletes but had to consider the consequences of withdrawing from international sport altogether.
“If you don’t participate, that’s it – you eliminate yourself from the main international competitions in every sport,” Vencevičius said.
The issue has already arisen in youth football. After FIFA allowed Russian and Belarusian teams to return to football competitions, Lithuania’s under-15 national team is taking part in a tournament in Azerbaijan.
The Lithuanian Football Federation said the tournament’s group allocations and team rankings meant Lithuania was not expected to face either Russia or Belarus. However, the federation said its team would refuse to play if such a match became necessary.

Up to 650,000 special ballots could still turn Israel's election on its head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:57:40 UTC
14:57:40 KST

Hundreds of thousands of ballots cast outside voters' assigned polling stations could still affect the final outcome of Israel's general election, potentially shifting parliamentary seats between parties and altering the political balance. Unlike regular ballots, these votes undergo a separate verification process before being added to the nationwide count, meaning the first results may not fully reflect the final composition of the Knesset.
These votes are known in Israel as double-envelope ballots, a system that allows eligible voters who cannot reach their assigned polling stations to vote elsewhere. They include soldiers, military reservists, diplomats, police officers, prison staff, hospital patients and displaced residents. Each voter places their anonymous ballot inside an envelope, which is then sealed inside a second envelope carrying identifying information. Election officials use the outer envelope to verify that the person has not voted twice before adding the anonymous ballot to the national count.
Because of the war and the large number of mobilized reservists and Israelis displaced from their homes, the Central Elections Committee prepared for an unprecedented number of double-envelope ballots. More than 460,000 were cast in the 2022 election, while advance estimates for this election ranged from 600,000 to 650,000. That volume represents roughly 15 Knesset seats' worth of votes, although those seats are not allocated separately. Instead, the ballots are added to the nationwide totals, potentially changing how seats are distributed among parties.
Historically, these votes have tended to favor Zionist parties across the political spectrum, largely because soldiers make up a significant proportion of voters using the system. Ultra-Orthodox and Arab voters are considerably less represented in this group, meaning their parties' relative share of the overall vote can decline once the ballots are included. The effect is generally limited but can be significant enough to change the allocation of one or two seats.
This means parties such as the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism, as well as the predominantly Arab Joint List and the Islamist Ra'am party, could see their relative electoral strength change when the double-envelope ballots are incorporated. However, the outcome also depends on the remaining regular votes, the performance of other parties and the distribution of surplus votes.
A similar shift occurred in the 2022 election. Before the double-envelope count, United Torah Judaism was projected to win eight seats and Avigdor Liberman's secular nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party five. Once the additional votes were included, United Torah Judaism fell to seven seats while Yisrael Beytenu rose to six. The shift illustrated how a relatively small change in the overall vote distribution can affect individual parties without necessarily changing the balance between political blocs.
In that election, the number of votes required to secure one parliamentary seat under the allocation formula was approximately 36,227. The double-envelope ballots therefore represented the equivalent of roughly 12 to 13 seats. Likud received enough of those votes to represent approximately three seats, Yesh Atid around two, and Religious Zionism and Otzma Yehudit together nearly two. These figures illustrate the voting strength of different parties within the special count, rather than seats awarded directly from those ballots. The final allocation also depends on the electoral threshold and agreements between parties to combine surplus votes.
The pattern was evident in the March 2021 election as well, when approximately 428,000 double-envelope ballots were counted. Their inclusion reduced Ra'am's representation to four seats and increased the left-wing Meretz party's total to six, without changing the balance between the main political blocs.
The counting of double-envelope ballots requires additional checks and can continue after the regular vote count has been completed. Because the votes are incorporated into the national totals rather than counted as a separate electoral category, their impact may not become clear until the final stages of the process. In a closely contested election, even a small shift in parliamentary representation could have important implications for coalition negotiations. Until all ballots are verified and included, initial seat projections remain provisional, and parties could still gain or lose representation before the final results are announced.

Mental Health Investment Bank opens today in Tallinn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:55:45 UTC
14:55:45 KST

Today at 16:00, a Mental Health Investment Bank will open in Ülemiste City, Tallinn, where people can invest time, attention and care instead of money. Created by the Estonian Coalition for Mental Health and Well-being (VATEK), the bank brings together practical tools and recommendations to help people make caring for their mental health an everyday habit.
The bank’s opening marks the culmination of this year’s Mental Health Month, held under the theme “Investing in Mental Health.” Throughout October, the Estonian Coalition for Mental Health and Well-being has encouraged individuals, employers and communities across Estonia to recognise opportunities to invest in their own well-being and that of others.
According to Kadri Haljas, Executive Director of VATEK, the idea behind the investment bank is to change the way we think about mental health.
“We are used to paying special attention to our health when something has already gone wrong. Yet mental health requires the same consistent care as physical health. We should not wait until someone is exhausted or experiencing burnout before thinking about how to support their well-being,” says Haljas.
She emphasises that looking after our mental health does not necessarily require significant spending or major lifestyle changes.
“An investment might be a ten-minute break, a walk, a phone call to someone close to us, or simply deciding to finish work on time. These are small but meaningful steps. We want to help people find activities that work for them and gradually turn them into lasting habits,” Haljas explains.
The Mental Health Investment Bank brings together practical recommendations, worksheets and exercises on a single website, www.vaimsetervisepank.ee, helping people take better care of their mental health.
For example, visitors can receive a randomly selected “quick investment” — a small activity or action they can try to support their well-being.
The bank does not aim to offer a one-size-fits-all solution. People’s needs, circumstances and preferences vary, and there are many different ways to support mental health. What matters is finding activities that fit naturally into each person’s everyday life.
While the investment bank is not a substitute for professional mental health care, it aims to place greater emphasis on prevention and everyday well-being.
“We often talk about how to treat mental health problems once they have developed. That is absolutely essential, but it is equally important to ask what we can do to prevent these problems in the first place. The earlier we can support someone, the greater the chance of preventing both further suffering and rising costs to society,” Haljas stresses.
The opening address will be delivered by Emilia Berg, the noorsootska – the youth representative of King Peko in the traditional Seto Kingdom – and a representative of Tartu, Estonia’s Youth Capital.
Following the ceremony, guests will be invited to make their first investments in mental health by taking part in short practical exercises and activities.
However, the opening of the bank marks not the end of the campaign, but the beginning of its next chapter.
“We want to reach a point where looking after our mental health is not something we think about only in October, or when we are already struggling. Our goal is to make every day a mental health day,” says Haljas.
VATEK plans to keep the investment bank running beyond Mental Health Month and to expand it with new resources and practical tools.

US warns Gulf states of possible escalation against Iran after midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:46:25 UTC
14:46:25 KST

The US has told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a “short, intense military campaign” against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people briefed on the conversations.
The messages, conveyed through diplomatic and military channels, are among growing signs that the US and Israel are preparing a new round of heavy combat operations to weaken Iran and push it towards negotiations, according to the report.
The US military is moving a Patriot missile defence system from Texas to the region and has moved troops from bases where they were vulnerable, while US forces are restocking munitions and preparing bombers and fighter jets for strikes, the newspaper said, citing officials.
An additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit are expected to join roughly 20 US warships in the Middle East next month, it added.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision but is leaning towards a "large post-election attack" that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, the report said, citing people familiar with his thinking.
The White House declined to comment on “sensitive military plans that may or may not exist.”
“President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” it said.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Trump said: “You’ll see Iran in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.”
“We obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury and defeated them militarily, financially and otherwise. And it will all end very soon,” he said.
“It could be over whenever I wanted it to be over,” he added.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the midterms.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to respond with missile and drone attacks in the region and effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
A memorandum of understanding was signed in June to pave the way for a final peace deal, but it collapsed amid disagreements, including over navigation in the strait.

Why India has soured on Trump ahead of US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:43:40 UTC
14:43:40 KST

Why India has soured on Trump ahead of US midterms
Seven years after Modi backed Trump, analysts say New Delhi may now hope US midterm losses leave the president chastened.
New Delhi, India — Standing next to United States President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivered praise after praise.
“Every time [we meet], he has been the same: warm, friendly, accessible, energetic, and full of wit,” he said of Trump, as they addressed a joint rally in a Houston, Texas, stadium packed with more than 50,000 Indian Americans.
That was in 2019, ahead of the 2020 US presidential vote, when Trump was facing a major electoral test – seeking re-election to a second term. Modi was, in effect, galvanising support for him among the Indian-American community, the wealthiest diaspora in the US.
Modi even borrowed a line from his own successful election campaigns, saying: “Abki baar, Trump sarkaar!”, Hindi for “This time, a Trump government.”
But Trump lost.
Seven years later, as Trump prepares for difficult midterm elections that could see him lose significant numbers in the US Congress, potentially crippling his legislative agenda, New Delhi’s equation with Washington could not be more different.
Far from endorsing Trump, Indian officials have in recent weeks been more direct than ever in their criticism of his administration, amid a series of setbacks to bilateral ties. And many analysts believe the Modi government may now actually prefer a Trump chastened by midterm losses.
Striking a nerve
India has long enjoyed bipartisan support in Washington. Yet traditionally, New Delhi’s strategic community has often felt more comfortable with Republican presidents in power.
It was under Ronald Reagan, as the Cold War wound down, that India and the US reset ties after decades of mistrust amid New Delhi’s strong relationship with Moscow. Then, between 2006 and 2008, under George W Bush, India and the US struck a landmark civil nuclear deal. India was allowed access to global nuclear technology and fuel despite not being a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). Under Bush, India and the US also signed major military pacts, including allowing US ships and planes refuelling and logistical access to Indian bases.
By contrast, New Delhi has often seen US Democratic administrations as more critical of India’s human rights record.
The tradition of friendly ties with US Republican presidents appeared set to continue under Trump, amid visible bonhomie between the US leader and Modi. The Indian prime minister even called Trump “India’s best friend in the White House”.
But Trump 2.0 has been very different, from India’s perspective.
So different that New Delhi has chosen to break with a long-held practice. India usually addresses divisive issues with friendly nations quietly, behind the scenes. But months of tensions on a string of issues have pushed India to adopt a more openly critical tone towards the White House.
Last month, speaking at an event in New York, India’s foreign minister, Minister of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, shared a pointed, blunt assessment of the Trump administration: It has been an insensitive partner to India’s concerns over “terrorism”; has warmed to its archrival Pakistan; and has pursued “self-centred” trade policies that have disproportionately hurt the Global South.
“Countries should not be so self-centred that you’re in your own world and take your decision, and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’,” he said.
One of the biggest sticking points between both capitals is an elusive trade deal that could bring relief to India, among the worst-hit countries under Trump’s tariff regime.
Earlier this month, India’s finance minister, Minister of Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman, said that the negotiations had reached a “plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult”.
Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement has also often targeted Indians and Indian Americans, using racist tropes, accusing them of “stealing” jobs in the United States via programmes like the H-1B visa schemes. Anti-Indian rhetoric on US social media is at an all-time high. And early in his second term, Trump sent many undocumented Indian immigrants back home shackled in chains – a visual that stirred outrage in India.
Milan Vaishnav, director of the South Asia programme at the Washington, DC-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank, said the Indian government “can tolerate genuine policy differences with a US administration”. However, “the attacks on India and Indian Americans coming from this administration, and many of their allies in the media and on social media, have struck a nerve,” he said.
Vaishnav, like other analysts, told Al Jazeera that despite recent criticism coming from New Delhi, “the Modi government has shown admirable restraint in its response”.
‘Brought back distrust’
Since Trump returned to office in 2025, the US-India relationship has been beset by a seemingly never-ending series of crises.
Some of the irritants are: punitive US tariffs and stalled trade negotiations; Washington’s pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil; Trump’s repeated claims that he mediated an India-Pakistan ceasefire in 2025, which New Delhi rejects; closer US ties with Pakistan despite India’s concerns over “terrorism”; higher H-1B specialised worker visa fees in the US, and Trump’s wider immigration crackdown affecting Indian workers.
At one point, India was among the countries facing the worst Trump-imposed tariff rates. After the US Supreme Court in February struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs on numerous nations, his administration swiftly turned to other tools, including a new 10 percent global tariff.
Last month, Trump signed a law under which the US can impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries like India that buy Russian oil. However, he paused it to avoid driving up energy prices in the US ahead of November’s midterm elections, while keeping negotiations with Russia over Moscow’s war in Ukraine on track.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited India’s financial hub Mumbai this week, but skipped the capital, said in an interview with The Indian Express that “none of these tariffs are meant to punish or harm India”.
Rubio argued that Washington’s “broader foreign policy, unfortunately, involves a war going on between Russia and Ukraine” — and added that “one of the reasons why [Trump paused the tariff] is because he understands that it would have a very detrimental impact on a very important relationship with India”.
But Rubio did not rule out that similar measures would return in a matter of time. “I think the president is trying very hard to balance that… but it will be a challenge”, he remarked.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera: “Under Trump 2.0, the bipartisan consensus on India seems to have ended in Washington.
“The sentiment [in Washington] seems too strong to be attributed solely to President Trump; it points to the broader American establishment,” Donthi said.
The measures undertaken by the Trump administration “have brought back distrust of the US among the Indian strategic establishment”, he said, referring to Cold War-era tensions.
Can a midterm loss subdue Trump?
The upcoming US midterm elections are crucial for Trump. If he loses control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, it would give Democrats more power to scrutinise his administration’s policies.
Trump is facing the worst approval ratings of his political career amid record-high gas prices in the US due to the global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February this year.
Vaishnav, of Carnegie Endowment, said that “a chastened Trump would be in India’s interests”.
“There are many Democrats on Capitol Hill, not to mention Republicans, who are livid with this administration’s handling of US-India ties,” he said. “While they might have their criticisms of India’s politics, economics, and foreign policy, they genuinely believe in the logic of a strong US-India partnership.”
A Democrat-dominated Congress could have a “moderating impact” on Washington’s foreign policy, he said.
But Michael Kugelman, a Washington-based analyst on South Asia, said he doubts Trump’s foreign policy would be affected by the election results, “at least not when it comes to the question of India”.
Kugelman noted that Trump is entering the last era of his presidency – he cannot legally run for a third term – and “he is going to continue to pursue a policy that he would think could best advance US economic interests” when it comes to dealing with New Delhi.
“If he thinks that could entail threatening additional tariffs on India, then he would do that.”
Crisis Group’s Donthi told Al Jazeera that New Delhi would hope that bilateral relations improve after Trump leaves office, “and that [Washington] can take a more patient, strategic approach”.
But, meanwhile, he said, a weakened Trump might not necessarily bring relief to India, “as there seems to be broader consensus [among Trump-aligned Republicans] on the need to pressure India”.
For New Delhi, that landscape marks a dramatic shift from just a few years ago.
Two years back, days after Trump had won the 2024 election, Foreign Minister Jaishankar said, with a wide smile, that “many countries are nervous about the US today, but let’s be honest — we [India] are not one of them”.
Today, those smiles are gone.

Lapp Reindeer dog Martta lives in Kittilä, Finnish Lapland with her owners Pekka and Anu Nevalainen.
One day she caught their attention with an unusual bark.
For some reason, Martta really wanted to go outside, and took her owners with her.
Pekka and Anu followed Martta onto their neighbour's property and found him stuck in the cold water of a wastewater pit.
By then the man had completely run out of strength, and without help the icy water would likely have claimed his life.
The Nevalainens couldn't manage to lift the man out of the pit, but managed to keep him afloat until rescue services arrived. They struggled to hold onto their neighbour for around half an hour before help came.
Pekka said the worst part of the ordeal was knowing the man's likely fate if they lost their grip.
In recognition of her heroic instincts, Martta will receive the Hero Dog title from the Finnish Kennel Club, alongside seven other brave pups, at the Helsinki Dog Fair in December.
But Martta has already received rewards of ice cream and plenty of praise.
"We're certainly proud of our dog for doing something like this. A great dog, a really great dog," Pekka said.
Kennel Club honouring heroic dogs
Besides Martta, seven other dogs will also receive heroic awards in December. What unites the special canines is that at least one person likely owes their life to each of them.
The awards ceremony will take place on 13 December at the Dog Fair in Helsinki, where 14 other dogs will receive honourable mentions.

South Korea has completed development of a domestically produced marine attack helicopter under a 450 billion-won ($337 million) project, with production expected to begin next year, local media reported Wednesday.
The helicopter, designed for multidimensional amphibious operations, is equipped with air-to-ground missiles and other weapons systems, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing the Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA).

DAPA plans to begin production of approximately 20 helicopters in 2027.

Israel election results: Netanyahu bloc at 56 seats with over 60% of the votes counted
