Israel’s election has left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition challenger Gadi Eisenkot without a clear path to power, as exit polls showed their blocs deadlocked despite record turnout and significant gains by Arab Israeli parties.
Eisenkot, a 66-year-old former military chief, vowed Wednesday to move quickly to form a government, saying voters had rejected Netanyahu’s divisive leadership.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, called for a strong right-wing government and highlighted the prospect of renewed military action against Iran alongside U.S. President Donald Trump.
Neither leader claimed victory. Exit polls from Israel’s three major television networks showed the competing blocs close to evenly matched, with neither securing the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 projected a 51-51 tie, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc a narrow 52-49 advantage. Final results were expected Thursday or Friday, leaving the country facing potentially prolonged coalition negotiations or another election.
Speaking to supporters in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said the public had delivered a vote of no confidence in Netanyahu and urged the longtime prime minister to retire from politics.
“The public has voted for change,” Eisenkot said. “A worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”
He also warned Netanyahu against using national security to advance his political interests, raising concerns about the prospect of renewed military action against Iran while the government’s future remained uncertain.
“Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu did not immediately address supporters after the initial projections. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, an ally of the prime minister, dismissed the opposition’s victory claims as premature.
Arab Israeli parties made some of the strongest gains, with exit polls projecting a combined 17 to 18 seats. Their increased representation could prove decisive in determining whether Netanyahu’s coalition returns to power.
Turnout reached 77.7%, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, the highest in more than two decades and about 7 percentage points above the 2022 election.
The strong participation included a surge among Palestinian citizens of Israel, many of whom voted to prevent Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition from returning to government.
At the headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties, supporters celebrated as exit polls were released. Faten Gattas, a candidate for the alliance, pledged continued opposition to occupation and racism.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” she said in Nazareth.
Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab Israeli political leader, said the right-wing camp had suffered a major defeat and indicated he was open to working with Eisenkot.
However, Eisenkot has largely ruled out forming a government with Arab lawmakers, complicating his route to power. Their parties could still support a minority government in parliamentary votes without formally joining a coalition.
Far-right leader Itamar Ben Gvir warned Netanyahu against forming a unity government with Eisenkot, calling such a move a mistake. Ben Gvir, a prominent supporter of Jewish settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich were projected to win a combined 13 seats, short of the gains some had expected.
Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said Ben Gvir’s polarizing campaign had helped mobilize Arab Israeli voters.
“Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn’t mean Eisenkot won,” Rahat said.
The election was held in the shadow of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, which killed about 1,200 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Israeli figures.
The attack triggered the Gaza genocide and wider regional conflicts involving Hezbollah in Lebanon and Iran.
Netanyahu campaigned on his security record, arguing that Israeli military operations against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iranian targets had made the country safer. He also emphasized his relationship with Trump as an opportunity to confront Iran.
Addressing Likud supporters in Jerusalem early Wednesday, Netanyahu said Israel faced a historic opportunity to eliminate what he described as the Iranian threat.
“Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all,” he said.
Eisenkot, who joined Netanyahu’s wartime government after the Hamas attack before resigning about eight months later, challenged the prime minister’s authority to make major security decisions without a clear public mandate.
He urged the security establishment to resist attempts to put political interests ahead of national security.
Despite presenting himself as a centrist on domestic politics, Eisenkot maintains a hawkish position on Palestinian issues. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
He has described Israel’s campaign in Gaza as a failure because Hamas remains in control. Gaza health authorities have reported more than 74,000 Palestinian deaths during the war.
The exit polls suggested a major setback for Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition, which once held 68 seats but appeared far short of a majority.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 years across several terms and has repeatedly survived political crises. After four inconclusive elections in two years, his opponents briefly removed him from office in 2021. He returned to power in December 2022.
His latest campaign included sharp attacks on Arab Israeli voters. Netanyahu accused them of trying to “steal the election,” while his Likud party unsuccessfully sought to keep polling stations open beyond their scheduled 10:00 p.m. closing time.
The opposition accused him of seeking grounds to challenge the results. Netanyahu also alleged that three senior officials from the United Arab List had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes of cash. Election authorities described the incident as an isolated local case.
Netanyahu entered the election facing criticism over intelligence failures that allowed the Oct. 7 attack and longstanding corruption charges, which he denies. He also faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant related to the Gaza war.
His government’s policies have deepened Israel’s international isolation amid the war in Gaza, expanding settlements and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Eisenkot, meanwhile, has drawn public sympathy after losing his son Gal, who was killed fighting in Gaza, and two nephews during the war. Before voting, he privately visited his son’s grave.
The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would become Israel’s first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent if he forms a government.
The election’s outcome remains uncertain as votes are counted and smaller parties prepare to negotiate their role in the next government.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, described the exit polls as a major blow to Netanyahu’s coalition but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner.
The deadlock could allow Netanyahu to remain caretaker prime minister during lengthy negotiations. If neither camp can assemble a governing majority, another election may be necessary.
Some Israelis returned from abroad to vote. Eilana Zisblit, 55, who has lived in Canada for nearly three decades, traveled to Israel to support a center-right party in Eisenkot’s bloc.
“The country is going in a really, really bad direction,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP), saying the situation affected Jews and Arabs in Israel as well as Jews abroad.
Eisenkot has urged political leaders to avoid another election, arguing that the record turnout demonstrated the public’s desire for change.

Digital currencies could become new payment tool for Russia, Africa — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:05:41 UTC
14:05:41 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Central bank digital currencies could become new instruments for facilitating cross-border settlements between Russia and African countries, according to the authors of a report titled "Russia-Africa: Routes for Capital, Goods, Information, and Specialists," prepared by Vedomosti business newspaper and members of the New Generation International Club of Young Economists with the participation of the Roscongress Foundation.
The report also noted that currency swaps and settlement facilities between the Bank of Russia and African central banks could serve as other effective instruments, with priority given to Egypt, Nigeria, Ethiopia, and South Africa.
The report’s authors point out that the shift away from currencies of unfriendly countries in settlements, along with the risk of secondary sanctions and the lack of direct correspondent banking relationships and ruble-denominated accounts, is keeping trade between Russia and African countries below its potential level.
Other challenges include high costs and delays associated with multiple currency conversions, the near-total absence of accessible direct currency conversion channels for small businesses, and a lack of hedging instruments for currency pairs.
Trade between Russia and African countries totaled approximately $27 bln in 2025. Under the pessimistic scenario outlined by the report’s authors, payments will continue to be routed through third countries at considerable cost through 2030, sanctions could tighten, and bilateral trade could reach $27-30 bln by 2030.

Ex-SC judge Justice Kaul flags ‘punishment’ of prolonged custody before conviction

He said that prolonged legal proceedings can themselves become a form of punishment and that bail should generally be the norm.In an interview with news agency ANI, Kaul said he had generally taken a liberal view on bail, but acknowledged that certain laws explicitly restrict the granting of bail in specific cases."I have taken a generally very liberal view on bail. The process becomes a punishment," former Supreme Court judge said.Kaul said several judges had raised concerns about the issue. He also referred to a judgment written by Justice Sundaresh, with whom he had dealt with the question of bail and the principles governing custody."And many judges have been writing and talking about it. In fact, I, sitting with Justice Sundaresh, had dealt elaborately with the bail itself, trying to say, why are you people under custody? Justice Sundaresh wrote the judgment.
He's, to my mind, a liberal judge on this. And we tried to lay down norms, etc., which were already in existence, but trying to, you know, until this case. So in most cases, our view is, that bail should be the norm. But there are certain acts which prohibit bail," said Kaul.Kaul has co-authored an upcoming memoir, Without Fear or Favour, with Jay Vinayak Ojha. MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia, and several West African countries offer different agricultural investment environments for Russian investors, according to the authors of a report titled "Africa’s Investment Landscape: Conditions, Opportunities, and Models for Russian Business Presence," prepared by the Financial University, the Roscongress Foundation, and Vedomosti business newspaper.

Alishan Forest Railway campaign wins Japan's Good Design Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:01:23 UTC
14:01:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Alishan Forest Railway's campaign celebrating the full reopening of the century-old line has won Japan's 2026 Good Design Award, recognizing its use of contemporary design to promote Taiwan's railway heritage.
The Alishan Forest Railway and Cultural Heritage Office announced the award on Monday, saying the campaign combined visual design, cultural activities, and commemorative merchandise to present the railway's history to a wider audience, per a press release.
Judges praised the campaign for maintaining a consistent visual identity across its events and promotional materials while reinterpreting traditional railway culture through contemporary aesthetics. Elements included original dance performances, Japanese woodblock print-style visuals (ukiyo-e), and specially designed souvenirs.
The railway resumed full-line service on July 6, 2024, after a 15-year interruption caused by typhoon damage. The reopening restored direct train service between Chiayi and Alishan. Celebratory events included a completion ceremony for Tunnel No. 42, a full-line reopening ceremony, and a market combining railway culture, forestry products, and art.
The campaign also extended the railway's identity into everyday life through limited-edition “120,000 Happiness” iPASS cards, commemorative ticket gift boxes, and stamps featuring station landscapes. Searchlight Culture Lab carried out the marketing project, per the press release.
The Good Design Award was established in 1957 and is organized by the Japan Institute of Design Promotion. The 2026 competition received 5,111 entries, according to the railway office.
The Alishan Forest Railway, which has operated for more than a century, is a designated cultural heritage asset in Taiwan. The award highlights efforts to combine heritage preservation, tourism, and contemporary design.

Taiwan economics minister defends energy subsidies to curb inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:01:11 UTC
14:01:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) on Wednesday defended government subsidies for state-owned energy companies, saying that fully passing on higher energy costs to consumers could push Taiwan's annual inflation rate above 3%.
Kung told reporters at the legislature that annual consumer price index growth is about 2%. Citing estimates from the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, he said a 10% increase in international oil prices would raise the CPI by 0.24% if passed on to consumers, while a 10% increase in electricity prices would raise it by 0.27%, per CNA.
He urged lawmakers to support continued budget allocations to Taipower and CPC Corp. to help stabilize energy prices and protect households and small businesses.
He said the two state-owned companies provide essential electricity and fuel while absorbing costs from rising international energy prices, which have contributed to their financial losses. Government funding has helped shore up their finances and maintain stable domestic supplies, he said.
Kung rejected opposition criticism that Taipower's losses stemmed from flawed energy policies, arguing that surging global energy prices had created similar challenges for other countries.
He said governments have responded in different ways, with some allocating public funds to subsidize state-owned energy providers and others freezing domestic energy prices to shield consumers from higher costs.
According to Ministry of Economic Affairs data, Japan and Indonesia have each allocated more than NT$500 billion (US$15.41 billion) to stabilize domestic energy costs, while South Korea has allocated about NT$130 billion for subsidies, per CNA.
Kung said Taiwan's subsidies were intended to balance the financial stability of state-owned enterprises with the need to keep energy affordable. Without government intervention, higher international prices would be passed on to households and businesses, increasing pressure on living costs and inflation.

Gulf states working on multipart peace deal to avert renewal of US-Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:00:55 UTC
14:00:55 KST

A multipronged peace deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted and for the Houthis to withdraw substantial forces inside Yemen are at the heart of Gulf states’ plans to avert what they regard as a disastrous renewal of war between Iran and the US.
The US is aware of the talks’ progress but is holding out for a concession that European powers suggest could involve Iran allowing UN weapons inspectors back into the country.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, urged the Iranians to agree to readmit the UN weapons inspectors when he met the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in New York but so far Iran has refused, saying it will only hold talks in principle on its nuclear programme.
European diplomats believe allowing weapons inspectors to reenter Iran and visit its bombed nuclear sites is a minimum requirement for a breakthrough with the US president, Donald Trump.
But Iran remains focused solely on the guarantees of sanctions relief it would receive in return for reopening the strait of Hormuz. Dr Ali Bagheri, the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, said Iran was willing to reduce its proposal that the strait reopen seven days after economic sanctions are lifted to four days.
In a further sign of flexibility, Iran is starting to acknowledge it has a mediating role in the parallel conflict in Yemen. Iran’s secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, met the Houthi’s ambassador to Iran, Ibrahim al-Dulaimi, on Tuesday.
The meeting took place 24 hours after a high-level delegation from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan travelled to Tehran to discuss Saudi terms for ending the Yemen conflict as well as a longer-term security architecture for the region.
Iran backs the Houthis, and has the power to influence them, including devising proposals that stop short of a Houthi military victory that many say is unobtainable. In return the Houthis are demanding that Saudi Arabia lift what it regards as a naval and air blockade on Houthi-held territory.
Iran successfully prevented discussion of its nuclear programme at the meeting with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and instead ensured the focus was a broader discussion about a long-term regional security vision that would include the Gulf states and Iran and see the US presence in the Middle East reduced or ended.
A new non-aggression pact in which Iran is no longer ostracised by the rest of the Gulf, as it has been since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, would meet Iran’s highest strategic goal.
An agreed commitment to this goal by six Gulf states might also make it easier for Iran to swallow potentially difficult tactical concessions that it would be required to make concerning its nuclear programme.
One of the key advocates of the inclusive security plan, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, said he believed the US administration understood this was the direction the region is heading.
He said: “I think if Iran is fully re-engaged in this idea of having all of us, eight countries at peace with the rest of the world, the economic potential is going to be enormous for all of us in the region and those outside the region who choose to take part in this development. We have really discussed this in at length during the talks between Iran and the United States, and I think there is general acceptance that this will be the direction of travel once we have a deal in place at the end of the day.”
At a televised event in Iran this week Araghchi underlined the importance of a new postwar security pact to Iran, saying: “Recently, there has been talk of a new war but I am already thinking about the postwar period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same.”

====================================================================================================

The pact that aims to return tourism's wealth to residents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:00:12 UTC
14:00:12 KST

A movement born in Malta wants to change tourism rules by involving hotels in local community life, returning visitors' wealth to residents and curbing gentrification.
The boom in international tourism has left many destinations facing a paradox. While large hotels and other businesses increase their revenues, residents are the ones paying the price in the form of rising housing costs, a loss of local identity and neighbourhoods that are being reshaped.
Against this backdrop, Positive Action Community Tourism (PACT) is proposing a different model: Involving the hotel sector in the development of the communities that host it so that part of the wealth generated by visitors also translates into social, cultural and economic benefits for local people.
The initiative, driven by British entrepreneur Mark Weingard, founder of the Iniala Group, was born in Malta with the ambition of bringing together hotels, organisations and local stakeholders so that tourism leaves a positive legacy that goes beyond its economic impact.
Global movement
"We started in Valletta and we want to create a global movement. We are working with the WTTC [World Travel & Tourism Council] to launch it internationally," says Weingard about PACT, which already has 45 members.
"Hotels need to build a relationship with the community in which we operate. It is not enough to arrive in a destination, open a hotel and make a profit. We must also help improve the lives of the people who live there."
His group of luxury hotels, Iniala Group, is actively involved in the local life of the Maltese capital, sponsoring a range of local projects, both cultural and sporting, and working side by side with the community.
"We need the respect of the people who live here, not their hatred, which is why it is so important to work with residents," Weingard explains.
He cites as an example his Iniala Valetta hotel, "a boutique resort on an urban scale", as he describes it. It is the result of several restored historic buildings that blend into the cityscape.
"When I arrived in this city there were buildings with stunning architecture and a history that deserved to be preserved," says Weingard, who believes that the investment has made it possible to restore part of that heritage and bring activity back to certain areas.
"My aim was to restore them and turn them into hotels that could attract travellers from all over the world while at the same time helping the city regain some of its vitality.
"We cannot allow the transformation of a city to end up driving out its residents or destroying traditions, so the commitment has to be to preserve local identity, improving the city without losing its essence."
In his view, the PACT movement is a way of moving in that direction in many other cities, such as Madrid, London, Paris or Lisbon. That is why he is calling for a broad agreement or pact that brings all stakeholders together. "I would like this philosophy to spread to other cities and for more hotels to join the initiative."
Hotels that care about wellbeing
For now, Weingard is going to replicate his hotel model in Lisbon, Athens and Madrid, with "properties that are connected to the culture and identity of each city" and offer unique experiences for travellers.
In his philosophy, architecture, design and gastronomy all play a major role in making guests feel special. To that end, he works with top local designers and architects and runs restaurants with Michelin stars.
In his hotel model, the focus is above all on people and their wellbeing. "We are interested," he says, "in what is happening inside people, how they feel and how they can improve their lives."
That is why his hotels offer a complete wellbeing ecosystem with beauty and personal care services, treatments for skin care and physical recovery after exercise, as well as healthy eating courses and psychological support services, relaxation techniques and meditation.
"Our goal is to bring together in one place accommodation, physical activity, nutrition, personal care, emotional health and all the tools to improve quality of life," he explains. "We do not want guests simply to enjoy a few days of rest, but to leave with knowledge, habits and a plan they can continue to follow afterwards."
In his opinion, this is the trend that will prevail in the coming years, at a time when travellers are looking for more than a destination and somewhere to stay.
They are demanding, discerning travellers who know what they want and are seeking holistic experiences that leave an emotional mark.
If, in addition, they are integrated within the local community, as PACT proposes, it could offer a solution to the problem of gentrification affecting cities everywhere.

Top officials will visit the Chinese capital in the coming months in a bid to persuade Beijing to revalue the yuan, according to sources
5-MIN READ5-MIN

Finbarr Berminghamin Brussels
After convincing China to accept a cap on its hybrid car exports, a stream of top-level European finance and banking officials will descend on the Chinese capital in the coming months on a far trickier mission: persuading Beijing to stop holding down its currency to help save the bloc’s struggling industry.
In the week of November 23, top European Union economy officials led by director general Maarten Verwey will sit down in Beijing for a “macroeconomic dialogue” with their Chinese counterparts.
Plans are in the works, meanwhile, for a heavyweight trio – from the European Central Bank, Eurogroup and European Commission – to follow them there around the turn of the year, though no final date has been set, according to multiple people familiar with the planning.

Obra Blanca 2026 brought together more than 23,000 industry professionals in its seventh edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Direct contact with a material allows one to appreciate textures, compare finishes, and observe how its appearance changes under different lighting conditions. At an exhibition, these possibilities are complemented by exchanges with manufacturers and professionals, helping to understand applications and resolve questions about their use. This relationship between material exploration and architectural practice was one of the central pillars of the seventh edition of Obra Blanca, which drew more than 23,000 professionals to Expo Santa Fe in Mexico City.
Featuring 190 exhibitors across 13 pavilions and 28,620 m² of exhibition space, the event showcased finishes and products for architecture and interior design. The exhibition was accompanied by a program of conferences, forums, and technical talks, alongside a new digital tool designed to consult and organize product information both during and after the visit.
The exhibition spaces offered diverse ways to engage with the products, ranging from material sample exploration to installations showcasing combinations of colors, textures, and finishes. Their layout provided context for understanding how these elements could be integrated into a project and interact with other components of a space.
"The booths are looking increasingly professional, with highly designed, experiential layouts. So, I think it is highly worthwhile to come and experience it firsthand," commented Nadja Borrás of Gensler.
The event also succeeded in bringing suppliers and professionals together in one place to discuss the featured solutions. For architects and interior designers, this exchange complements the technical information found in catalogs and product spec sheets with discussions tailored to the specific needs of their projects.
Spaces for Professional Exchange
The program brought together 70 specialists and featured three international lectures, four national ones, four forums with international guests, and twelve technical talks. Developed in partnership with 32 strategic allies, the agenda expanded the gathering beyond a simple product showcase, creating spaces to share experiences and discuss industry challenges.
For Christele Harrouk, Editor-in-Chief of ArchDaily, the value of the gathering also lies in this professional dialogue: "Beyond presenting products and innovations, I believe one of the event's greatest strengths is the space it creates to discuss architectural practice and the challenges currently facing the profession."
Harrouk spoke with Paula Villar Pastor, co-founder of the Peruvian association Espacio Común, about the Main Floating Stage of Muyunafest 2025, which won first place in ArchDaily's 2026 Building of the Year Award. Their conversation explored how regional conditions, local knowledge, and community collaboration guide design decisions. "Our conversation addressed a broader challenge that architecture faces today: how to respond to increasingly complex social and environmental realities without losing sight of the practical realities of construction," Harrouk noted.
Fernando Lozano Assad, President of Obra Blanca and Director of TCNA Mexico (Tile Council of North America-Mexico), highlighted the collective effort behind the program: "At Obra Blanca, we have always championed knowledge and community spirit. Building an activities agenda like this is the result of the collaborative drive among our 32 partnerships."
The Espacio Obra Blanca, designed by Augusto Quijano Axle, hosted sixteen expert interviews and showcased the Obra Blanca 2027 CMF Dynamic exhibition, titled La tendencia es emocionar (The Trend is to Emotion). Organized in partnership with La Jabonera Centro de Diseño, this initiative brought together twelve architecture and interior design firms from Guanajuato, Querétaro, and San Luis Potosí to explore color, materials, and finishes.
From Exhibition to Specification
One of the key additions to this edition was OB ESPECIFICA, a free digital tool designed for architects, interior designers, and specifiers. Using QR codes, it allows users to access technical specifications for the exhibited products, save selections, and organize them by project.
The platform also offers options to share these selections with design teams and contact sales representatives. Its purpose is to streamline post-event product research, ensuring that information gathered during the visit remains easily accessible when returning to design and specification work.
In this way, the combination of physical samples, professional dialogue, and technical information formed the backbone of the various activities at Obra Blanca 2026. The next edition will take place from October 12 to 14, 2027, at Expo Santa Fe in Mexico City.
For more information, visit the official Obra Blanca website.

Iran ready to expand electricity connection with reg. states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:57:13 UTC
13:57:13 KST

Iran’s Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi said at the 30th Belarusian Energy and Ecology Forum.
The Iranian energy minister emphasized Iran has established electricity connections with its western neighbors and with Pakistan and Afghanistan to the east, adding that links with Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Turkey and Iraq are also in place.
Iran is seeking to connect its electricity network to Russia through a neighboring country, Aliabadi stressed.
He said that regional cooperation is increasingly important as electricity demand rises, particularly with the growth of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies.
He also highlighted the need to expand energy storage and electricity interconnections to balance power generation, distribution and consumption.
The minister said Iran's electricity generation capacity has grown from 7,000 megawatts at the time of the 1979 Islamic Revolution to nearly 97,000 megawatts. He added that Iran manufactures power plant equipment domestically and exports such equipment to regional countries.
Aliabadi said Iran remains committed to developing its electricity industry and is prepared to cooperate with other countries and make use of their capabilities despite sanctions and war.

Cyclone Arnab makes landfall along India's coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:50:42 UTC
13:50:42 KST

Ahmad Adil
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
India’s southern state of Andhra Pradesh evacuated thousands of residents Wednesday ahead of Cyclone Arnab’s landfall along the southeastern coast, where it brought heavy rainfall and powerful winds.
The Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority said the landfall process had remained stationary for two hours.
“The chance of completely crossing the shore by afternoon. Strong gusty winds and rains continue along the shore. People should remain vigilant even today,” the authority said on the US social media platform X.
Authorities in Andhra Pradesh shifted 84,396 people to 290 relief shelters, while a total of 2,199 shelters were designated across the state, All India Radio reported.
The cyclone, which began making landfall early Wednesday, caused widespread disruption, with strong winds uprooting trees and damaging local infrastructure, the broadcaster said.
Authorities in Andhra Pradesh and the eastern state of Odisha also ordered school closures as a precautionary measure. Fishing activities were suspended, while rescue teams were kept on standby to respond to emergencies.
The administration of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands also ordered schools to remain closed for two days beginning Tuesday.
India’s Meteorological Department said a deep depression over the east-central and southeastern Bay of Bengal had moved westward and intensified into Cyclone Arnab.

The billion-dollar cancer bill Australia's sunscreen overhaul may not fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:48:51 UTC
13:48:51 KST

in brief
- The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing.
- But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution.
Australia's sunscreen regulator is planning tougher rules after concerns some products failed to deliver the sun protection promised on their labels.
But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution, with boosting awareness on how Australians need to apply and reapply sunscreen also critical to preventing skin cancer.
In a report published last year, consumer group CHOICE tested 20 popular sunscreens and found that only four met their labelled sun protection factor (SPF), raising questions about the reliability of products Australians rely on to protect themselves from UV radiation.
The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) later recalled several sunscreen products after identifying batches that didn't deliver their advertised SPF protection.
The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing, improve ingredient-quality requirements, and clarify the SPF claims cosmetic products can make.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
What are the proposed reforms?
The TGA is proposing several reforms to address sunscreen quality, with the goal of reducing instances of skin cancer.
Australia has the highest rate of melanoma incidence in the world, with an estimated 17,443 new cases diagnosed in 2025 according to Cancer Australia.
The reforms are:
- Strengthen sunscreen testing requirements
- Develop specific ingredient quality requirements
- Provide a consistent limit for SPF rating that can be claimed for all secondary (cosmetic) sunscreens
- Review sunscreen good manufacturing practice guidance
- Consider labelling for SPF ratings
Professor Terry Slevin, CEO of the Public Health Association of Australia, told SBS News that treating skin cancers costs the country almost $2.5 billion each year.
"We need to invest more in preventing those cancers rather than having to treat them at the tail end," he said.
The TGA told SBS News: "The proposed reforms are intended to provide greater assurance through stronger testing requirements, increased oversight of testing laboratories, testing of finished products and periodic testing over a product’s lifecycle, and improved access by the TGA to SPF testing evidence."
Improving testing
Improving how sunscreen is tested is one way the TGA wants to improve quality and reliability of SPF claims.
Slevin explained that a small number of labs in Australia produce the nation's sunscreen, supplying multiple brands.
Sunscreens can then be tested on volunteers who use the formula and are then exposed to UV radiation; the rate at which skin reddens can then be used to determine the product's quality.
While this method is common, it can also be imprecise.
"People have different skin types, and the amount of product being applied can vary a lot. So having consistent SPF levels relies on a lot of unpredictable variables," Slevin said.
These variations can lead to inconsistent product application and to sunscreens having marginally different SPF than advertised on their packaging.
Should you be worried about SPF levels?
The TGA reforms are looking to ensure that sunscreen manufacturers have clearer guidance and expectations, but SPF levels could still slightly vary from bottle to bottle according to Slevin.
However, variations would be minimal and would have little impact on the sunscreen's efficacy.
"The difference between SPF 50 and SPF 30 may sound significant, but the difference in the amount of UV that’s filtered out is only 3 per cent, a small change," he said.
"The vast majority of sunscreens serve a very useful and effective purpose; these reforms will only strengthen this."
But the main way to achieve the TGA's goal may not be reforming testing, but educating people on how to use sunscreen products best.
Dispelling confusion
Anna Wang, an associate professor in the School of Chemistry at UNSW Sydney, said that improving consumer understanding and behaviour is the best way to improve sun safety.
"What is going to make a bigger impact isn’t whether a sunscreen tests SPF45 using one method and SPF40 using another, but how often we reapply, and whether we put the recommended amount on," she told SBS News.
Experts recommended applying sunscreen generously to all exposed skin every two hours, seeking shade, and wearing a hat and sunglasses.
Towelling off after a swim, or wiping water or sweat off your body, can also remove some sunscreen.
Some cosmetic products, including foundations and moisturisers, also advertise SPF protection.
The TGA is considering a consistent limit on the SPF ratings these secondary sunscreens can claim, aiming to make it easier for consumers to distinguish products designed primarily for sun protection from those intended mainly for cosmetic use.
"In Australia, we have several hundred formulations to choose from so it can be confusing," Wang said.
She supported the TGA's reforms to clarify the distinction between primary and secondary sunscreens.
Investigation ongoing
In the meantime, the TGA confirmed to SBS News its investigation into sunscreens with disputed SPF results is ongoing.
"The TGA is considering the available evidence and providing sponsors with an opportunity to provide additional data or evidence before regulatory decisions are made," it told SBS News.
The regulator said it will issue product recalls or cancellations as needed while it develops the new reforms.
"The TGA intends to publish its findings and learnings and provide further guidance to sponsors and manufacturers to clarify expectations around SPF evidence and testing."
Clarification: This story has been revised to reflect the estimated $2.5 billion cost of skin cancer annually.
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

France minerals envoy says rare earths diversification from China possible within 3-5 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:46:00 UTC
13:46:00 KST

France minerals envoy says rare earths diversification from China possible within 3-5 years
- France’s strategic metals envoy said Western countries could diversify rare earth supplies away from China in “three to five years”.
- China still dominates some rare earth magnets, with up to 90% of production, and its 2025 export curbs hit industries like carmakers.
- Projects in Europe, Australia, the US, Japan, Brazil and India are moving fast, but magnet output may limit progress; the G-7 wants reliance cut below 60% by 2030.
AI generated
SYDNEY – Western countries could achieve an acceptable level of rare earths diversification away from China within three to five years, France’s top envoy for strategic metals said on Oct 27.
Governments and manufacturers are racing to diversify supplies of metals vital to defence, technology and renewable energy, and reduce dependence on China, which accounts for as much as 90% of production of some specialised rare earth magnets.
Beijing rattled global markets in 2025 when export curbs on permanent magnets disrupted industries, including the automotive sector, exposing their reliance on a single source.
Some investors and analysts have questioned whether breaking China’s dominance is achievable, given the scale of investment and technical know-how required to produce the niche metals used in everything from cars and aircraft to electronics and weapons systems.
“You don’t need hundreds of rare earths mines around the world to cover the supply. It’s a limited market, it’s a limited quantity. We have already made some progress,” said Benjamin Gallezot, France’s Interministerial Delegate for Strategic Minerals and Metals Supply.
Expansion projects led by Belgium’s Solvay and France’s Carester, plus others in Australia, the US, Japan, Brazil and India, are developing quickly, he said.
“If you take all together, these projects, and you push to accelerate them, hopefully, you can have a good diversification in the next three to five years,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of a mining conference in Sydney.
While rare earths mines and refining projects were progressing, the amount of magnet manufacturing could still be a limiting factor, he said.
“You don’t need a decade to solve this problem.”
Leaders of the Group of Seven nations agreed in June to step up coordination to cut their countries’ reliance on China for critical minerals.
They aim to reduce dependence on any one supplier outside the G-7 and its partner countries for rare earths and permanent magnets to below 60% by 2030, with an ultimate goal of 50% “as soon as possible”.
“We can do much more,” Gallezot said. REUTERS

Centre deputes a high-level team to investigate death of Cheetah, caused by firearm pellet injuries, in Madhya Pradesh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:41:18 UTC
13:41:18 KST

19-month-old radio-collared male cheetah, an offspring of Namibia-born Cheetah Nirva, was found injured on Oct 25
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Wednesday deputed a high-level team to investigation the death of a 19-month-old male Cheetah of Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh, caused by firearm pellet injuries.The team has been tasked with undertaking a thorough investigation into the circumstances leading to the death of the Cheetah, examining all available evidence and coordinating closely with the Madhya Pradesh forest department to ensure strict and swift action in the matter.The 19-month-old radio-collared male cheetah, an offspring of Namibia-born Cheetah Nirva, was found injured on Oct 25 in the territorial forests of Morena, outside the protected area of Kuno National Park. Preliminary medical examinations corroborated multiple internal injuries associated with the firearm pellets.The incident, the first reported casualty of a shooting since PM Narendra Modi launched Project Cheetah at Kuno in Sept, 2022, is being viewed quite seriously at the Centre, given the critical importance of Project Cheetah and the need to ensure the highest standards of protection for the reintroduced population of the Big Cat.
“As reported by the MP forest department, the injured cheetah was rescued from the Sheopur Territorial Forest Division the same day and provided intensive veterinary care and emergency surgery at the veterinary facility in Jabalpur. During the surgery, five firearm pellets were recovered from its body. Despite the medical intervention, the Cheetah succumbed to its injuries on Oct 27,” said the Union environment ministry in a statement.It said, “The state govt has already constituted a Special Task Force (STF), comprising forest and police officers, to investigate the incident. The central team deputed by the Union environment ministry would work in coordination with the state machinery. It would also examine the implementation of security protocols, as well as monitoring and protection measures being undertaken to avoid any such incident in future.
“The central team would submit its findings and recommendations to the ministry for further directions to the state govt and field authorities.”The central team comprises the Inspector General of Forests, National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), Additional Director, Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB), and Regional Deputy Director, WCCB.

He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

BEIJING, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Taiwan is “provoking confrontation” and stirring anti-China sentiment, a Chinese government spokesperson said on Wednesday, after Taiwanese prosecutors indicted five people for plotting to attack a Taiwanese comedian whose shows mocked Beijing.
Taiwan, the democratically governed island that China claims as its own territory, has accused Beijing of trying to use “transnational repression” against people in Taiwan the Chinese government views as separatists or politically suspect.
Taiwan’s government says China was behind last month’s attack on comedian Huang Yi-hao, who satirised Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Speaking at a regular news conference in Beijing and asked about the incident, Taiwan Affairs Office spokesperson Chen Binhua dismissed Taiwan’s accusations as a fabrication by its ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
“The so-called transnational repression narrative is essentially a way of promoting Taiwan independence and peddling a two-state theory, and it is trotted out every time there is an election on the island,” he said, referring to next month’s local elections in Taiwan.
“The DPP fabricates all kinds of pretexts out of thin air, maliciously smears the mainland, stirs up anti-China sentiment, and provokes cross-strait confrontation, all in an attempt to win political power by misleading the Taiwanese public,” Chen said.
This is a “tired routine” repeated year after year, he added.
Taiwan prosecutors said the defendants, whose full names it has not provided, were paid to fake a car accident and “break the arms and legs” of Huang so he could not perform, though in the end he was only lightly injured.
Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, in a report delivered to lawmakers earlier on Wednesday, said the case of Huang and others showed what he described as China’s expanding efforts to “challenge people’s personal safety, freedom of expression, and the resilience of democratic society.”
Other China critics in Taiwan have also been attacked, including Hong Kong singer and activist Denise Ho in 2019.
Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.

Indonesia beefs up security presence to prepare for student protests
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:32:30 CET
13:32:30 KST

By Stanley Widianto
JAKARTA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Hundreds of Indonesian students and civil society groups staged protests on Wednesday in cities including the capital Jakarta against President Prabowo Subianto’s policies, including the handling of ongoing forest fires.
Worsened by the El Niño weather pattern that leaves peatland vulnerable to fires, Indonesia has been faced with its worst forest fires, and resulting haze, in 11 years, increasing respiratory illnesses and polluting the air of neighbouring countries Malaysia and Singapore.
Protesters crowded a Jakarta landmark roundabout, with some wearing gas masks, holding up signs protesting over forest fires and demanding the government designate the blazes as a national disaster.
Some carried signs that said “If we burn, you burn with us,” and held up the three-finger sign of protest – references to the The Hunger Games movie that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth protest movements globally.
Anggi Aurien, 28, had been wearing a gas mask for three hours at the landmark, protesting about the forest fires that have killed wildlife.
“Animals don’t have a mind of their own. If we kill them, what’s the difference between us and them?” she said.
Other signs included photos of the orangutan, which bears the brunt of the fires, and a cardboard cutout of Prabowo.
Other students, including from the University of Indonesia, were blocked by dozens of police and military personnel, leading to some scuffles.
“Revolution! Revolution!” protesters chanted.
Ezra Al Barra, a student from the University of Padjadjaran, said the fires were “our collective anger,” adding students came from other regions outside Jakarta.
Students also rallied in Makassar, in South Sulawesi, and Bandung, in West Java, with similar demands. Dozens of them on motorbikes filled the main roads.
Protesters called for the the government halt spending on populist programmes such as Prabowo’s free meals scheme, among other demands.
Syahganda Nainggolan, chief of the government’s communications office, urged calm but said the government welcomed the protests and was open to input.
PRABOWO’S POPULARITY
The protests, the second in a week, came as Prabowo’s approval ratings had fallen steadily since late last year, according to surveys by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting, two years into his presidency.
Indonesia has prosecuted companies allegedly linked to the fires and tried methods of modifying the weather to induce rain.
Indonesia’s last major protest took place in August, when hundreds were detained.
In 2025, weeks-long nationwide protests broke out in Indonesia after the police killing of a motorcycle taxi driver, with several more people killed during the unrest.
(Reporting by Stanley Widianto, Johan Purnomo, Heru Asprihanto and Ananda Teresia; Editing by David Stanway and Alex Richardson)

The decision in Erin Patterson’s appeal against her triple murder conviction will be handed down on Friday, with Victoria’s highest court also set to rule on whether she could face more time in prison.
The court of appeal will rule on the two appeals from 10am on Friday, after hearing arguments in August.
Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the poisoned beef wellington lunch after spending weeks in hospital.
Patterson is not expected to attend the appeal decision in person.
There are several possible outcomes to Patterson’s appeal: leave to appeal is not granted; leave to appeal is granted, but her appeal dismissed; leave to appeal is granted, her appeal upheld and a retrial ordered; or her leave to appeal is granted, the appeal upheld, and acquittal entered.
If either of the final two decisions are handed down, there will be no need to rule on the sentence appeal.
If not, either the appeal fails, or it succeeds and Patterson is resentenced.
In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.
Her lawyers argued that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.

Boeing shares tumble after it releases cautious growth forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:30:04 UTC
13:30:04 KST

Investors monitor Boeing shares after a slump on Tuesday weighed on sentiment following an update from the group on its outlook.
Boeing shares slumped around 9% on Tuesday as the company's cautious production growth timeframe surprised Wall Street, deepening questions about how fast recent plane certification and defence procurement wins will translate to the bottom line.
Chief Executive Kelly Ortberg said the company does not expect 737 MAX output to reach 52 per month until the second half of 2027 as it must first "stabilise" output at 47 per month.
Raising 737 MAX output has been viewed by investors as central to revenue and profit growth. But Ortberg, who joined Boeing in the aftermath of safety disasters, defended the approach.
"We're making progress, but we still have more work to do, and I'm expecting it'll take us into next year to get fully stable at this rate," Ortberg said of the 47 plans per month, citing the need for greater predictability in wings production and with the production of fuselages at its Kansas operation.
"It's more important that we do this ramp right than what particular month we achieve a rate break," Ortberg said.
Ortberg also put a timeframe on when the company will achieve $10 billion (€8.98bn) in annual free cashflow, saying it will reach the key target of financial health in 2029.
After Ortberg released this statement, shares fell further, suggesting analysts had expected a quicker timeframe.
"Everybody wants us to go faster. I get that, but we're going to stay disciplined as we ramp up here," Ortberg said.
Ortberg joined Boeing as CEO in August 2024 as the company struggled to move past a pair of deadly 737 MAX crashes and a near-catastrophic 737 MAX flight in January 2024 in which a window blew out mid-flight.
The company at the time faced criticism that the problems stemmed from a culture that chased quick payoffs while short-changing safety.
Boeing is making "slow but steady" progress, aviation expert Richard Aboulafia of AeroDynamic Advisory said in an email to AFP. "But the supply chain remains a major concern and one that's only partly in Boeing’s control."
Smaller loss
Ortberg's comments came as Boeing reported a third-quarter loss of $116 million (€100m), compared with a loss of $5.3bn (€4.6bn) in the year-ago period, mostly from delays to certification of the 777X, the latest generation in Boeing's long-range, wide-body commercial jet family.
The results translated into a larger earnings-per-share loss than analysts expected, but shares did not move significantly after the earnings press release was published.
Ortberg cited the Federal Aviation Administration's certification of the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10, as well as a "transformational" Pentagon award for the US Navy's next-generation fighter jets, as evidence of momentum.
Revenues rose 4% to $24.2bn (€20.9bn), driven by increased deliveries in the defence, space and security business and higher sales in Boeing Global Services.
Revenues for commercial aircraft dipped from the year-ago period, with Boeing delivering 161 aircraft in the quarter, just one more than in the 2025 period.
Boeing executives expressed confidence that the much-delayed 777X would be certified in 2027, projecting deliveries of between 10 and 15 aircraft next year.
"We're providing this with confidence that the team's ready to go execute," Ortberg said of the latest targets.
Ortberg expects free cash flow to gradually grow from about $2bn (€1.7bn) in 2026 to $6bn (€5.2bn) in 2028 and $10bn (€8.6bn) in 2029, with higher levels thereafter.
"As I mentioned, over the last two years, we've made exceptional progress restoring trust, retiring risk, and transforming our culture and rebuilding the foundation of safety and quality that will help ensure durable success," he said.
"We have also been deliberate about not getting ahead of ourselves, given the range of outcomes tied to the production ramp, certification timing, and other critical programme execution," he said.
"But we appreciate that it's been difficult for shareholders to assess how our progress will translate into financial performance. We're now at a point where the range of outcomes is narrowing."

India news: Cyclone Arnab brings heavy rain, disruption

India news: Cyclone Arnab turns weaker but deadly after landfall
Published October 28, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Cyclone Arnab makes prolonged landfall along coast of Andhra Pradesh
- At least three killed in Andhra due to the storm
- New study says India among top countries with highest heatwave exposure for infants and elderly
- Mukesh Ambani's Jio Platforms makes market debut, shares surge over 21%
Here's a roundup of the biggest news from India on Wednesday, October 28:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Cyclone Arnab turns deadly in Andhra Pradesh
At least three people were killed in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, local media cited authorities saying, as Cyclone Arnab made its way further inland after making landfall earlier today.
The storm lost some speed after a prolonged lanfall, downgrading it to a "severe cyclonic storm" from a "very severe cyclonic storm." It is expected to further weaken into a "cyclonic storm" and turn into a "deep depression" by the evening, National Disaster Response Force Inspector General (IG) Narendra Singh Bundela told reporters in New Delhi.
"North of Andhra Pradesh and the southern part of Odisha have been the most affected due to Cyclone Arnab. Strong winds and rainfall are being witnessed in a few districts of the two states," Bundela said.
"Andhra Pradesh has been the most affected... we have been informed that trees have been uprooted, 31 houses of various types have been damaged and three persons have been killed," he said, adding that the impact on Odisha was not serious as per preliminary reports.
The IG said nearly 40 NDRF teams had been deployed to regions along India's east coast to manage the impact of the cyclone.
India faces high economic cost of heatwaves, new Lancet study shows
India ranked among the top countries where the elderly and infants are most exposed to heatwaves, the latest Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change report said, putting the nation in the same basket as China, US and Russia. But that's not all.
As per the report, the economic cost is steep for the nation.
Extreme heat cost Indian workers an estimated $174 billion (€156.5 billion) in potential earnings in 2025. That's 4.2% of the nation's GDP. Moreover, 54% of the losses were from the agriculture sector.
"Increasing heat exposure is affecting health, physical activity, sleep and labor capacity in India, with substantial consequences for livelihoods, particularly in agriculture," the report said.
Published by the presitigious British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.
The report called for climate change to be formally recognized and addressed as a global health emergency.
Jio Platforms becomes second-most valuable firm on stock market debut
Shares of Jio Platforms, a Reliance Industries-backed digital services company owned by India's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, listed on the India stock exchanges with a premium of over 21%.
That instantly made the company the second most valuable on the exchanges.
Jio's telecommunications business serves over 530 million customers and is backed by Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google. Its user numbers are second only to China Mobile on the basis of single-country subscribers.
The listing, the first for the Reliance conglomerate in two decades, furthers Ambani's plan to turn Reliance from an oil-and-chemicals conglomerate into an "everything company" spanning consumer products and technology.
The listing was attended by the Ambani family, that is Mukesh Ambani himself, his wife Nita, eldest son Akash and other children Isha and Anant.
The family patriarch was seen in tears as his youngest son Anant traced Jio's journey in a speech at the ceremony.
Meanwhile, major Indian newspapers on Wednesday carried front-page ads from Reliance Jio, saying "Thank you, India."
India has become the world's busiest IPO market this year in terms of the number of deals, with 246 listings so far, though it ranked fourth by money raised at $13.5 billion, behind the US, mainland China and Hong Kong, LSEG data showed.
High winds, storm surges as Arnab makes landfall
The center of cyclone Arnab had made it to land, authorities told local media on Wednesday morning, as it crawls further inland at 4 kilometers per hour (2.5 miles per hour).
Visuals on social media, from overnight and today morning, show high winds and storm surges. Heavy rainfall flew vertically as old trees struggled to stay upright. Many failed. Local news agencies ANI and PTI showed heavy rainfall and unruly sea water smash the coast of India's southern state, Kerala.
Other footage circulating on social media showed lanes full of fallen trees and broken power lines. Other showed violent winds and heaping waves spill on to a coastal street. These videos were posted by general users and remain unverified.
Old videos of other storms tend to circulate on various channels in such situations. Users are best adviced to remain skeptical and take information provided by verified or government sources.
Cyclone Arnab batters Andhra Pradesh with drawn-out landfall
"Very severe" Cyclone Arnab made a sooner-than-expected landfall along India's east coast and is now "practically stationary" at the edge, authorities said.
The storm, with winds over 125 kilometers per hour (78 miles per hour) and gusts of 150 kilometers per hour (93 miles per hour), is in the third-highest category of storms on a scale of five.
The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) said its landfall would last for over two hours and that the edge of the storm was already on the coast of the south-eastern state of Andhra Pradesh. Its center remains over sea.
Power, transport disrupted
The cyclone brought heavy rains, high winds and disruption to Andhra and its neighboring state of Odisha. Gales rocked trees, winds and heavy rain disrupted power lines and the storm caused the sea to surge like many locals had never seen before. Flight and train services were also impacted.
"There was a cyclone here three years ago, but the water didn't rise this much," a 35-year-old local resident said, adding that the government had warned them to stock up on groceries beforehand.
The weather agency warned of "total destruction" of thatched houses, localized flooding, the uprooting of power and communications poles, and "widespread damage" to standing crops.
No casualties so far
No loss of life has been reported in either states as of Wednesday morning.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu credited advance precautionary measures for preventing casualties so far. He said so during a teleconference meeting to monitor the impact of the storm onground, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
Together, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha evacuated nearly 100,000 people from vulnerable regions in preperation of the storm. They were moved inland fro better shelter.
"Our homes get flooded, and we have to stay in the water," said Rajeshwari, 65, who gave only one name and had been taken to a government-run shelter near Kakinada. "So the government provided us with a bus, and we came here to shelter," she told AFP.
In Nepal, authorities warned tourists against venturing into high-altitude areas due to fears that Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches in the Himalayan region from Thursday night through Saturday.
Arnab formed on Monday morning in the Bay of Bengal, a region known for birthing some of the deadliest storms to batter India. This year's season, however, is turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon which is causing unprecedented warming, experts say.

US midterms: Left-wing influencers like Hasan Piker find a grudging place in Democratic Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:30:00 UTC
13:30:00 KST

US midterms: Left-wing influencers like Hasan Piker find a grudging place in Democratic Party
- Hasan Piker has become a major left-wing influencer for Democrats, helping candidates like Ilhan Omar and Abdul El-Sayed reach young voters through Twitch and live streams.
- His huge reach brings benefits, but his extreme views on Israel, foreign policy and socialism also worry Democrats, who fear he could turn off moderate swing voters.
- Piker says the real problem for the Democratic Party is its lack of clear policies, not his online presence, and he argues that “You can’t podcast your way out of this problem”.
AI generated
PHILADELPHIA – Soon after US President Donald Trump’s victory in the 2024 election, the Democratic Party launched a manhunt of sorts.
Where was the Joe Rogan of the Democrats to be found?
The influential opinion maker, along with many other right-leaning podcasters, was credited by Trump for converting young American men who were once part of the Democratic coalition.
The hunt is ongoing. A US$20 million (S$25.6 million) “Speaking with American Men” project, launched in 2025 by Democratic strategists and donors to bring them back, has one more year to finish the job.
In the meantime, there is Hasan Piker.
The 35-year-old political commentator and live-streamer was something of a kingmaker for insurgent left-wing candidates during the Democratic Party primaries earlier in 2026, helping to test and refine the candidates’ messages, driving grassroots campaign donations and providing political visibility.
As the Democrats look to secure a congressional majority in the Nov 3 midterm elections, a left-leaning influencer like him is a source of traction.
On Oct 26, Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar turned to Piker to rev up her re-election campaign in a state that had hit international headlines for its heavy-handed immigration enforcement operations.
Omar is favoured to win, unscathed by investigations into her immigration history and allegations of abuse of welfare funds, charges she calls politically motivated. The congresswoman was born in Somalia in 1982, and her family was admitted to the US as refugees in the mid-1990s after fleeing civil war.
Still, she sought out Piker, calling his massive reach necessary to tackle a decline in early voting among under-40 progressives.
The late evening event in Minneapolis, where she conversed casually with Piker, reportedly sold out within minutes of being announced. The hour-long session, where they bashed the Trump administration and moderate Democrats, was live-streamed over Twitch, the platform where Piker has more than three million subscribers, mostly young, progressive and male.
Bespectacled and clad almost always in formal shirt, jacket and a tie, Piker goes live for around eight hours nearly every day of the week.
Self-declared socialist-Marxist
Born in New Jersey, Piker grew up in Turkey and describes himself as a cultural but not religious Muslim. His break into broadcasting, during the Covid-19 epidemic, came via his uncle Cenk Uygur, a co-founder of The Young Turks, a left-wing YouTube channel.
In between sharing his gym routine, handing out dating advice and discussing gaming, the highly articulate Piker weighs in with unrestrained emotion and expletives on the controversies of the day. The self-declared socialist-Marxist is usually lambasting Wall Street, big banks, defence and pharma companies for everything from inflation and climate change to workplace safety.
He is at his most volatile when it comes to American foreign policy. He has praised Hamas and warned that American Jewish support for Israel could prompt people to “take action” against them. He has also suggested that the US could learn from the Communist Party of China and described the collapse of the Soviet Union as one of the greatest geopolitical catastrophes of the 20th century. He has also walked back his most controversial comments that “America deserved 9/11”.
As with other streamers, outrage is a critical ingredient in his show, creating virality and deep engagement. It is also a rewarding venture, as remuneration runs into millions of dollars for the top streamers, with money coming from paid memberships, platform advertising, sponsorships, merchandise and other audience-supported products. There is a more sensitive source too: funding from advocacy groups and Democratic-aligned intermediary organisations.
To his viewers, Piker is a habit, a screen presence that validates their grievances and gives them a sense of belonging. From there, the flow into politics is seamless.
Traditional Democratic leaders are wary of Piker, but liberals like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, locked in a tight senatorial race, owe him.
During El-Sayed’s primary battle in August 2026 with sitting congresswoman Haley Stevens, Piker was a bridge to young people distrustful of the Democratic Party but amenable to a personality they watch for hours.
“One of the biggest stories of the 2026 election cycle is Hasan Piker,” said Joel Penney, an associate professor at Montclair State University who studies political communication.
The Democratic Party has had many celebrities and liberal advocates, but this turn of events is new, said Penney, the author of a 2022 book titled Pop Culture, Politics, And The News.
“This is much more interactive and more about the ongoing relationship between the fans and the streamers. Piker is responding to fans in real time, I don’t see a lot of other folks who have become famous for that format, the mix of Democratic politics and lifestyle content,” he said.
Other political commentators in the liberal sphere – such as Pod Save America, led by former Obama speechwriter Jon Favreau; MeidasTouch by a former marine and registered Republican Ron Filipkowski; and The Lincoln Project, which features moderate conservatives and former members of the Republican Party – do not command Piker’s massive numbers nor adopt his unscripted, streaming format.
Piker, inevitably, draws comparisons with Rogan and Rush Limbaugh, the conservative talk radio phenomenon who held sway for three decades starting from the early 1990s and drew a weekly audience of around 15 million.
“At their peaks, Rogan and Limbaugh had much greater audiences, in the tens of millions. I don’t think Piker is at that level. But he’s younger, and there’s always room for growth,” noted Aaron Kall, a political analyst at the University of Michigan.
Piker’s extreme views, however, can be a drag for the Democrats. Being linked with him has constrained El-Sayed’s efforts to broaden his appeal. Trump and the Republicans paint the two as fundamentalist, America-hating liberals.
“Piker’s sort of turned into a main character on Fox News reporting and conservative news outlets, which are putting him in the spotlight with the understanding that he would have a negative impact on the campaign,” Montclair's Penney told The Straits Times.
“He might be inspiring more people to vote who wouldn’t otherwise, but he may also be turning off people or encouraging people to vote for the opponent,” he said.
Will moderate swing voters be alienated?
Indeed, for the Democratic leadership, there is a real fear that the polarising Piker will alienate moderate swing voters.
El-Sayed, who is on course to becoming the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected, has been called to disavow Piker, but he has been reluctant, noted Kall.
“He probably perceives a double standard that right-wing influencers also say controversial things, but the Republicans don’t have to disavow them.”
With Piker by his side, El-Sayed may pick up some voters, but also lose others. In Michigan, with its sizeable Jewish and Arab American communities, that balancing act is especially sensitive.
It is probably the reason the race is very tight and the association with Piker has taken up a disproportionate amount of the campaign, noted Kall.
Penney said it is an open question if Piker can convert his sway with the notoriously unreliable young voters to turnout. “The election day results will be seen as a sort of a verdict on Piker,” he said.
Piker himself sees no risk of attrition of voters because of association with him.
“Getting people to be upset at a Twitch streamer and their affiliation... is going to be very difficult, especially when there are real crises going on in the country,” he said in an Oct 15 interview with National Public Radio, an American public broadcaster.
Democratic Party lacks ‘clear, definable policies’
The Democratic Party stands in its own way, Piker said.
“You can’t podcast your way out of this problem. The problems are with a lack of clear, definable policies that the party represents at the national level.”
The star podcaster claims that this lack of clarity is partly why the Democrats are “still largely very unpopular”.
Even though Trump is the least popular political figure, perhaps in history, Piker said.

NEW YORK, October 28. /TASS/. The Pentagon is deploying an additional Patriot air defense system to Israel, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing sources.
According to the sources, the US military has decided to send the system from Texas to bolster Israel’s missile defenses. The newspaper also reported that an additional aircraft carrier strike group would arrive in the region next month, joining approximately 20 US warships already deployed in the Middle East. According to the WSJ, these moves are intended to give US President Donald Trump a range of options should military operations against Iran resume.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. However, on the night of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing Tehran of violating the terms of the agreements concerning the Strait of Hormuz. Approximately 25% of global oil trade and around 20% of global liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. The US administration subsequently effectively signaled an end to the use of large-scale military force against Iran and a shift toward attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.
