India news: Cyclone Arnab turns deadly after landfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:30:00 UTC
13:30:00 KST

India news: Cyclone Arnab turns weaker but deadly after landfall
Published October 28, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Cyclone Arnab makes prolonged landfall along coast of Andhra Pradesh
- At least three killed in Andhra due to the storm
- New study says India among top countries with highest heatwave exposure for infants and elderly
- Mukesh Ambani's Jio Platforms makes market debut, shares surge over 21%
Here's a roundup of the biggest news from India on Wednesday, October 28:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Cyclone Arnab turns deadly in Andhra Pradesh
At least three people were killed in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, local media cited authorities saying, as Cyclone Arnab made its way further inland after making landfall earlier today.
The storm lost some speed after a prolonged lanfall, downgrading it to a "severe cyclonic storm" from a "very severe cyclonic storm." It is expected to further weaken into a "cyclonic storm" and turn into a "deep depression" by the evening, National Disaster Response Force Inspector General (IG) Narendra Singh Bundela told reporters in New Delhi.
"North of Andhra Pradesh and the southern part of Odisha have been the most affected due to Cyclone Arnab. Strong winds and rainfall are being witnessed in a few districts of the two states," Bundela said.
"Andhra Pradesh has been the most affected... we have been informed that trees have been uprooted, 31 houses of various types have been damaged and three persons have been killed," he said, adding that the impact on Odisha was not serious as per preliminary reports.
The IG said nearly 40 NDRF teams had been deployed to regions along India's east coast to manage the impact of the cyclone.
India faces high economic cost of heatwaves, new Lancet study shows
India ranked among the top countries where the elderly and infants are most exposed to heatwaves, the latest Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change report said, putting the nation in the same basket as China, US and Russia. But that's not all.
As per the report, the economic cost is steep for the nation.
Extreme heat cost Indian workers an estimated $174 billion (€156.5 billion) in potential earnings in 2025. That's 4.2% of the nation's GDP. Moreover, 54% of the losses were from the agriculture sector.
"Increasing heat exposure is affecting health, physical activity, sleep and labor capacity in India, with substantial consequences for livelihoods, particularly in agriculture," the report said.
Published by the presitigious British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.
The report called for climate change to be formally recognized and addressed as a global health emergency.
Jio Platforms becomes second-most valuable firm on stock market debut
Shares of Jio Platforms, a Reliance Industries-backed digital services company owned by India's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, listed on the India stock exchanges with a premium of over 21%.
That instantly made the company the second most valuable on the exchanges.
Jio's telecommunications business serves over 530 million customers and is backed by Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google. Its user numbers are second only to China Mobile on the basis of single-country subscribers.
The listing, the first for the Reliance conglomerate in two decades, furthers Ambani's plan to turn Reliance from an oil-and-chemicals conglomerate into an "everything company" spanning consumer products and technology.
The listing was attended by the Ambani family, that is Mukesh Ambani himself, his wife Nita, eldest son Akash and other children Isha and Anant.
The family patriarch was seen in tears as his youngest son Anant traced Jio's journey in a speech at the ceremony.
Meanwhile, major Indian newspapers on Wednesday carried front-page ads from Reliance Jio, saying "Thank you, India."
India has become the world's busiest IPO market this year in terms of the number of deals, with 246 listings so far, though it ranked fourth by money raised at $13.5 billion, behind the US, mainland China and Hong Kong, LSEG data showed.
High winds, storm surges as Arnab makes landfall
The center of cyclone Arnab had made it to land, authorities told local media on Wednesday morning, as it crawls further inland at 4 kilometers per hour (2.5 miles per hour).
Visuals on social media, from overnight and today morning, show high winds and storm surges. Heavy rainfall flew vertically as old trees struggled to stay upright. Many failed. Local news agencies ANI and PTI showed heavy rainfall and unruly sea water smash the coast of India's southern state, Kerala.
Other footage circulating on social media showed lanes full of fallen trees and broken power lines. Other showed violent winds and heaping waves spill on to a coastal street. These videos were posted by general users and remain unverified.
Old videos of other storms tend to circulate on various channels in such situations. Users are best adviced to remain skeptical and take information provided by verified or government sources.
Cyclone Arnab batters Andhra Pradesh with drawn-out landfall
"Very severe" Cyclone Arnab made a sooner-than-expected landfall along India's east coast and is now "practically stationary" at the edge, authorities said.
The storm, with winds over 125 kilometers per hour (78 miles per hour) and gusts of 150 kilometers per hour (93 miles per hour), is in the third-highest category of storms on a scale of five.
The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) said its landfall would last for over two hours and that the edge of the storm was already on the coast of the south-eastern state of Andhra Pradesh. Its center remains over sea.
Power, transport disrupted
The cyclone brought heavy rains, high winds and disruption to Andhra and its neighboring state of Odisha. Gales rocked trees, winds and heavy rain disrupted power lines and the storm caused the sea to surge like many locals had never seen before. Flight and train services were also impacted.
"There was a cyclone here three years ago, but the water didn't rise this much," a 35-year-old local resident said, adding that the government had warned them to stock up on groceries beforehand.
The weather agency warned of "total destruction" of thatched houses, localized flooding, the uprooting of power and communications poles, and "widespread damage" to standing crops.
No casualties so far
No loss of life has been reported in either states as of Wednesday morning.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu credited advance precautionary measures for preventing casualties so far. He said so during a teleconference meeting to monitor the impact of the storm onground, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
Together, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha evacuated nearly 100,000 people from vulnerable regions in preperation of the storm. They were moved inland fro better shelter.
"Our homes get flooded, and we have to stay in the water," said Rajeshwari, 65, who gave only one name and had been taken to a government-run shelter near Kakinada. "So the government provided us with a bus, and we came here to shelter," she told AFP.
In Nepal, authorities warned tourists against venturing into high-altitude areas due to fears that Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches in the Himalayan region from Thursday night through Saturday.
Arnab formed on Monday morning in the Bay of Bengal, a region known for birthing some of the deadliest storms to batter India. This year's season, however, is turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon which is causing unprecedented warming, experts say.

Putin lectured Nordic leaders on Russian history during latest call, FT reports

Putin lectured Nordic leaders on Russian history during latest call, FT reports
Russian President Vladimir Putin delivered a lengthy lecture on medieval Slavic history to the leaders of Norway and Finland during an Oct. 27 phone call, offering little mention of an immediate ceasefire despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end Moscow's war in Ukraine, the Financial Times (FT) reported.
According to three sources familiar with the call between Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, and the Russian president, Putin spent most of the 90-minute call to deliver a lengthy rant about Russian historical fixations.
The call, which was initially planned to last half an hour, comes ahead of trilateral peace talks expected in the Emirati capital of Abu Dhabi sometime in November between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
Ukraine's calls for an immediate ceasefire were barely discussed during the phone call, the sources added. With one source telling FT that the leaders did not interrupt Putin's rant to gauge his seriousness on future dialogue with Europe.
The Russian leader has often invoked Ukrainian and Russian history to justify aggression against Ukraine, like during his interview with U.S. host Tucker Carlson in 2024.
Amid failed attempts at peace negotiations, Putin has repeatedly espoused his views on Russian history in conversations with world leaders. The Russian president reportedly gave a similar lecture to U.S. President Donald Trump during the August 2025 summit in Alaska, which reportedly included a lengthy lecture on medieval Rus princes, such as Rurik or Yaroslav the Wise, as well as the 17th-century Cossack leader Bohdan Khmelnytskyi.
While the exact details of the discussion remain unclear, Putin's cherry-picked historical narratives and outright distortions have been repeatedly disputed by Western historians as a means to justify Moscow's actions.
The two leaders' call with Putin follows an Oct. 20 meeting in Oslo with Ukrainian, European, and U.S. officials, but they stressed that in the Oct. 27 call, they "did not speak he behalf of Europe as a whole."
The two leaders discussed the call with President Volodymyr Zelensky afterward, who said: "I am grateful for the detailed briefing and for their active support for our diplomacy and the peace efforts we are pursuing together with all our partners."
read also
The phone call between the Nordic leaders and Putin received mix reactions from fellow European leaders with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen telling media that she was "skeptical" of the call and that it had not been coordinated with others.
Meanwhile a European Commission spokesperson reminded that "we have a shared interest in putting an end to this horrific war," in comments sent to the Kyiv Independent.
"On the EU side, we are adamantly committed not just to putting an end to the war but to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable. That is our aim and that is the stance we are defending in the ongoing talks," the spokesperson said.
A senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent to expect a round of talks in Europe before the expected Abu Dhabi meeting, after mixed messages from Kyiv had given the impression that there would be Brussels-based peace talks this week.

Smotrich vows Jewish settlements in Gaza as party defies election polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:27:56 UTC
13:27:56 KST

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich vowed early Wednesday that Jewish settlements would be established in the Gaza Strip, declaring that Israel would not reverse its settlement expansion in the West Bank or withdraw from territory it controls in Lebanon and Syria.
His remarks came after exit polls by Israel's three major broadcasters — Channel 12, Channel 13 and public broadcaster Kan — projected that his far-right Religious Zionist Party had won six seats in the 120-member Knesset, a stronger showing than some preelection surveys had suggested.
During the campaign, the party had repeatedly struggled in polls to clear the electoral threshold of 3.25% of the national vote, the minimum required to enter parliament.
Speaking to supporters at the Religious Zionist Party's election headquarters, Smotrich struck a defiant tone despite initial exit polls showing an advantage for the opposition's pro-change bloc.
"We will not let them celebrate," Smotrich said. "They are celebrating because they think they will be able to reverse our settlement revolution in Judea and Samaria. I am telling them: They will not succeed. Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza."
Judea and Samaria is the biblical name used by Israel for the West Bank, territory captured from Jordan in the 1967 Six-Day War. Most of the international community considers Israeli settlements there illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.
Israel withdrew its settlers and permanent military installations from Gaza in 2005, dismantling 21 Jewish settlements as part of a unilateral disengagement plan. Reestablishing civilian settlements in the Palestinian territory has since become a central demand of some far-right politicians.
Smotrich also rejected the prospect of Israeli territorial withdrawals from Lebanon and Syria.
"They are celebrating because they think, God forbid, that the State of Israel will retreat from Lebanon and the summit of Mount Hermon," he said. "We will not withdraw."
Mount Hermon straddles the border region between Israel, Lebanon and Syria. Israel has maintained control of additional positions in the area following military operations in Syria, while its forces have also operated inside southern Lebanon.
Smotrich blames wasted right-wing votes
Smotrich also criticized rival right-wing political figures whose parties were projected to fall below the electoral threshold, implicitly targeting former IDF general Ofer Winter.
Winter's Amcha Yisrael party failed to secure enough votes to enter the Knesset, according to the exit polls.
Smotrich did not mention Winter by name but blamed the uncertainty surrounding the election results on political rivals who had refused to unite with established parties.
"Tonight, once again, it has become clear how right we were," Smotrich said. "The Arabs united. And, separately, our brothers on the left united. The only reason there is uncertainty is that irresponsible people threw votes into the trash."
Under Israel's proportional representation system, votes cast for parties that fail to cross the electoral threshold do not translate into parliamentary seats, potentially weakening the broader political bloc to which those parties belong.
"Despite those irresponsible people, our voters demonstrated maturity and responsibility," Smotrich said. "We hope to wake up in the morning to results much better than the exit polls."
He urged right-wing voters and politicians to consolidate under the Religious Zionist Party rather than support smaller parties that might fail to enter parliament.
"I call on all our friends and partners among the Israeli public: There is room for all of you in the Religious Zionist Party," he said. "We have had enough of parties that do not cross the electoral threshold. We are coming back together."
A central figure in West Bank settlement expansion
Smotrich has spent the past four years serving as both finance minister and a minister within the Defense Ministry, a dual role that has given him considerable influence over civilian affairs in the West Bank.
During that period, he spearheaded measures to retroactively legalize numerous previously unauthorized settlement outposts and encouraged the establishment of agricultural farms across the territory.
Those efforts form part of a broader strategy he outlined in 2017, known as his "Decisive Plan," which calls for consolidating Israeli control over the West Bank and rejecting the establishment of an independent Palestinian state.
Smotrich became leader of the Religious Zionist Party in 2019, when it was still known as National Union-Tkuma.
In the previous election, his party ran on a joint ticket with Otzma Yehudit, the far-right party led by Itamar Ben-Gvir.
This time, after polls suggested the Religious Zionist Party might fail to enter the Knesset, Smotrich joined forces with former Likud lawmaker Moshe Feiglin and his Zehut party.
Feiglin, a far-right libertarian politician, was placed second on the joint electoral list.
He served as a Likud lawmaker more than a decade ago, previously challenged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the party leadership and later unsuccessfully attempted to bring Zehut into parliament as an independent party.
The alliance with Feiglin was intended to consolidate support among right-wing voters and prevent votes from being lost to parties that failed to meet the electoral threshold.
With six seats projected in the exit polls, the Religious Zionist Party appears to have avoided that outcome, although its final representation will depend on the official vote count.

SEOUL, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's foreign currency deposits broke previous records for a third straight month, propelled by a sharp increase in U.S. dollar holdings from large corporations, securities firms and public enterprises, central bank data showed Wednesday.

S. Korea’s births rise 13% in August to highest level in seven years
Unknown

S. Korea’s births rise 13% in August to highest level in seven years
A total of 23,703 babies were born in August, up from 20,983 during the same period last year, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. The figure was the highest for August since 2019, when 24,371 births were recorded.
South Korea’s total fertility rate, which measures the average number of children a woman is expected to have during her lifetime, increased by 0.09 from a year earlier to 0.87 in August. Despite the improvement, the rate remains significantly below the 2.1 births per woman generally considered necessary to maintain a stable population without immigration.
The country’s birth numbers have continued to rise since July 2024.
From January to August, South Korea recorded 193,783 births, a 14.5% increase from the same period a year earlier. This was also the highest total for the eight-month period since 2019.
The recent rebound has been attributed to several factors, including an increase in marriages in previous periods, a growing population in their 30s and more positive attitudes toward having children.
However, the latest data showed that marriages declined in August. A total of 19,218 marriages were registered, down 1.2% from a year earlier. Meanwhile, divorces increased by 4.4% to 7,510.
The number of deaths also rose, increasing 4.9% year on year to 30,308. As deaths continued to outnumber births, South Korea recorded a natural population decline of 6,605 people in August.
Earlier, Qazinform reported South Korea’s GDP grew 1% in the third quarter on strong exports and investment.

KazAvtoZhol signs $700 million financing agreement with three Kazakhstani banks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

KazAvtoZhol signs $700 million financing agreement with three Kazakhstani banks
Kazakhstan’s national road operator, KazAvtoZhol, has signed a loan agreement worth up to $700 million with a consortium of Kazakhstani banks to support road infrastructure development and expand financing for national infrastructure projects, Qazinform News Agency cites primeminister.kz.
The agreement was signed during a roundtable discussion on financing the road sector and involving second-tier banks in infrastructure development.
The consortium comprises Halyk Bank, Bank CenterCredit and Eurasian Bank. The financing will help expand the pool of investment resources available for KazAvtoZhol’s projects, which previously received support from the Development Bank of Kazakhstan (DBK).
In previous years, the DBK provided financing for road repairs and modernization. Under the new agreement, cooperation will shift to a long-term arrangement extending until 2034. Halyk Bank will serve as the organizer of the syndicated financing and as the agent bank.
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said the agreement would help redistribute the credit burden among financial institutions and free up part of the DBK’s lending capacity to finance new priority infrastructure projects.
Zhumangarin emphasized that the agreement reflects Kazakhstan’s efforts to increase the involvement of commercial banks in financing the real sector of the economy and attract private capital to major infrastructure projects.
He noted that the arrangement does not involve raising new loans for road construction. Instead, it provides for refinancing existing obligations to the DBK using funds from commercial banks.
According to the deputy prime minister, this approach will expand the banking sector’s participation in infrastructure financing while allowing the DBK to redirect its resources toward new development priorities.
Greater involvement of commercial banks in road infrastructure development is expected to mobilize additional domestic investment and reduce the dependence of major national projects on state financing.
The mechanism is also intended to encourage a more active role for commercial banks in economic development without significantly increasing government budget expenditures.
Earlier, Qazinform reported the Development Bank of Kazakhstan (DBK), a subsidiary of Baiterek Holding, had provided financing for the development of a solar power plant park in the Kyzylorda region, supporting Kazakhstan’s transition to renewable energy.

Mahmoud Khalil credits Palestinian activism for reshaping US politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:13:28 UTC
13:13:28 KST

Mahmoud Khalil credits Palestinian activism for reshaping US politics
Khalil returned to Columbia University to discuss memoir detailing his arrest and detention by ICE agents.
Pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil says campus advocacy has shifted public perception and encouraged a generation of leaders to question their views on Israel, speaking as he returned to Columbia University for the first time since his arrest.
The 31-year-old Columbia graduate, who became a figurehead of the campus movement that swept the United States in 2024, returned to campus on Tuesday to discuss his new memoir, No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention, marking his first visit since his arrest on March 8, 2025.
“The American public is finally changing, is finally looking at the Palestinian as an equal human,” he told the AFP news agency in an interview.
While Khalil described the event, attended by about 100 people, as a “victory”, he accused university leadership of seeking “to erase me, to erase any Palestinian voices on campus”.
Some Jewish groups on social media opposed his return to campus. In response, a Columbia spokesperson said the university is “committed to rigorous debate, inquiry, and respectful dialogue across differing perspectives”.
“Columbia supports the right of faculty members to organize academic events,” the statement carried by US media read. “An invitation to speak does not signify university endorsement of a speaker’s views.”
Khalil helped lead student demonstrations at Columbia in 2024, which became the epicentre of nationwide campus protests against Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza. He was later arrested by immigration authorities at the height of a federal crackdown on foreign student activists and held for three months without criminal charge, despite holding permanent US residency.
He has repeatedly slammed the university for its handling of the demonstrations, which included authorising the New York Police Department to clear protesters from the Manhattan campus.
“They chose brutality. They chose repression,” Khalil told AFP.
Columbia maintained at the time that the demonstrations presented a safety threat. Khalil also accused the university of failing to protect him from harassment prior to his detention.
Despite the personal toll, Khalil credited Palestinian student advocacy with driving broader political shifts in the United States, pointing to gains by progressive candidates.
“Also, we can see on the ground that we have more progressive candidates being elected into US Congress and positions of power,” he said, citing candidates like Dr Abdul El-Sayed, running for the US Senate in Michigan, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Khalil was released from immigration custody on June 20, 2025, though the Trump administration continues to seek his deportation.
“A big part of my fight is like fighting for normalcy,” he said. “To go back to being the young father who would go to the park with his son and wife, and no one would bother them.”
Despite the ongoing legal battle, he expressed resolve over his public role.
“My fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country,” Khalil said. “It is about whether, you know, people in this country can speak their minds.”

After years of war, division, Israelis vote in record numbers to shape their future - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:13:25 UTC
13:13:25 KST

Israelis have spent three years at war and in bitter argument at home. On Tuesday, they voted in unusually high numbers.
That participation was strong from the start. By 2 p.m., turnout had reached 44.9%, with more than three million people having cast ballots. It was the highest turnout recorded at that hour since at least 1973. By 4 p.m., the figure had risen to 55.7%, with over four million cast.
The message was already clear: Israelis want a say in what comes next. After everything the country had endured, that willingness to participate deserved celebration.
This was the first national election since the October 7 massacre and the wars that followed. Israelis entered polling stations carrying memories of murdered relatives, fallen soldiers, hostage captivity, months of reserve duty, and displacement from their homes. They brought with them economic worries, bitter arguments over responsibility for the country’s failures and achievements, and disagreements about what those experiences meant and who should lead the country through their consequences.
The campaign had been intensely divisive. Parties had argued over October 7, Gaza, Iran, the courts, haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription, settlements, the economy, and the character of the state itself. Political leaders had accused one another of endangering the country. Voters had heard warnings that virtually every possible result could produce catastrophe.
Millions of voters demonstrate the strength of Israeli democracy
Millions responded by putting a slip of paper into an envelope. They made their own choices, in private, with the same right to participate as the people whose opinions had dominated the campaign. Citizens who rarely attended a demonstration or appeared on television had exactly the same ballot as cabinet ministers.
Participation also mattered because an election gave people a way to turn their grievances into a decision. Public anger over security failures, the burden of military service, or the cost of living could find expression on a ballot. Each voter had an opportunity to reward a record, reject it, or support an alternative.
That opportunity belonged equally to those who had defended the government and those who had demonstrated against it. Their willingness to use the same process was a reason for confidence in the country’s ability to keep making difficult decisions together, even while its citizens remained so deeply divided.
The queues at some polling stations were a visible expression of that determination. They also created practical difficulties, especially for elderly people and voters with disabilities. Election officials had a responsibility to keep the process accessible. The patience of voters, and the work of those administering the ballot, deserved recognition.
The voters in those lines had chosen differing futures. A high turnout could offer encouragement to the public across the political spectrum, regardless of which party ultimately benefited. Broad participation brought more citizens into the decision about the next Knesset and gave more people a direct part in shaping the country’s direction.
Israelis from across society exercise their equal right to vote
That included Arab citizens, whose turnout attracted intense political attention during the day. Their participation was an expression of Israeli democracy. The same was true of haredim, settlers, secular Tel Avivians, residents of development towns, soldiers, and immigrants. Citizenship means having an equal ballot even when other citizens dislike how it is used.
There were complaints on Tuesday about missing or damaged voting slips and other alleged irregularities. Those reports must be investigated seriously. Parties were entitled to identify problems and present evidence. Election authorities must provide the public with clear findings, and sweeping conclusions about the integrity of the vote require substantiation.
The turnout itself gave the country something to appreciate. Even after years in which Israelis had repeatedly been told that the country was coming apart, citizens across its political and social divides participated in the same democratic process. They brought their disagreements into polling stations and entrusted their choices to the ballot.
Democracy depends on citizens believing that their participation matters enough to show up. On Tuesday, millions of Israelis acted on that belief. Their reasons differed, as did their preferred leaders. Yet they participated in a common process for deciding their country’s future. Whatever government eventually emerges from their votes, the scale of that participation deserves recognition. Israelis showed up. That was democracy in action.

Israel election results live: vote count under way as exit polls point to tie between Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Netanyahu's bloc has 54 seats and is predicted to fall short of overall majority
With 70% of the vote (4 million ballots) counted at 11am local time, the base numbers for Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s parties largely haven’t changed but the two Palestinian parties have increased their share.
The Netanyahu bloc now has 54 seats, while the opposition seeking to get him out of office consists of the Eisenkot-led Change bloc with 47 seats and the Palestinian parties with 19 seats.
The Knesset has 120 seats- 61 are needed for a majority.
At the bottom of this post is the current seat breakdown by party – I’ve bolded the Netanyahu bloc.
Netanyahu’s Likud party, while losing support since the last election, has still gained the most number of votes – ahead of Eisenkot’s Yashar. However, critically for Netanyahu, his far-right allies in Ben-Gvir and Smotrich’s parties have seen a decline in their support.
Meanwhile the Palestinian Israeli parties, italicised below, have seen a huge gain, particularly for the Joint List, which is an alliance of smaller Arab-majority parties. They have nearly doubled their representation in parliament.
Leading Palestinian party ready to help 'oust Netanyahu'
The head of the Joint List, the Palestinian Israeli alliance that has performed tremendously this election, has said his party is ready to help remove Netanyahu from office in a partnership with Jewish Israeli opposition parties.
Joint List could be kingmakers, having received the third-largest amount of support so far, behind Netanyahu’s Likud party and Eisenkot’s Yashar. They are an alliance of smaller Arab-majority parties, who have usurped Mansour Abbas’ Ra’am party in galvanising the Palestinian Israeli vote.
Many voters in this camp have said that they needed to turn out for this election for a chance to get away from the racist, discriminatory policies perpetrated against them under the current far-right Netanyahu government.
This morning, Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen called for agenuine Jewish-Arab partnership to replace what he said was Netanyahu’s “government of bloodshed.” He also noted that anyone seeking to form an alternative would need to engage with Joint List.
Eisenkot facing stark choice: Make a deal with Palestinian parties or throw Netanyahu a lifeline
Julian Borger
The leader of the centre-left Democrats, Yair Golan, has made a point about Zionism that has not had much scrutiny until now.
The Palestinian parties are not the only non-Zionist grouping in the new Knesset. Benjamin Netanyahu’s political bloc relies on Jewish ultra-orthodox, haredim, parties that represent non-Zionists who insist on exemption from military service.
By making an early (and seemingly premature) declaration of a victory for a “Zionist mobilisation government”, the leader of the Jewish “Change” bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, was ruling out potential coalition partners, the surging Arab parties, while Netanyahu had no intention of renouncing his potential haredi partners.
Writing in Haaretz, the commentator Noa Landau, argued Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.
While projections of the Knesset results have fluctuated significantly over the past hours, the Palestinian Joint List has held firm at 11 projected seats.[As of the 11am figures, it is up to 13 seats.]
It is the projected strength of the rival Ra’am (United Arab List) which has wavered. It no longer seems feasible for the Eisenkot bloc to make a deal exclusively with the Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, who has shown himself more accomodating towards Zionism, appointing a Zionist Jewish deputy for example.
The choice for Eisenkot will be starker: do a deal with the Joint List, which is far more assertive about Palestinian identity and about the racism that its constituents experience, or throw Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.
Netanyahu's bloc has 54 seats and is predicted to fall short of overall majority
With 70% of the vote (4 million ballots) counted at 11am local time, the base numbers for Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s parties largely haven’t changed but the two Palestinian parties have increased their share.
The Netanyahu bloc now has 54 seats, while the opposition seeking to get him out of office consists of the Eisenkot-led Change bloc with 47 seats and the Palestinian parties with 19 seats.
The Knesset has 120 seats- 61 are needed for a majority.
At the bottom of this post is the current seat breakdown by party – I’ve bolded the Netanyahu bloc.
Netanyahu’s Likud party, while losing support since the last election, has still gained the most number of votes – ahead of Eisenkot’s Yashar. However, critically for Netanyahu, his far-right allies in Ben-Gvir and Smotrich’s parties have seen a decline in their support.
Meanwhile the Palestinian Israeli parties, italicised below, have seen a huge gain, particularly for the Joint List, which is an alliance of smaller Arab-majority parties. They have nearly doubled their representation in parliament.
Golan warns against racist exclusion of Palestinian parties
As the vote count flows in, Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, issued a strong statement rejecting attempts to frame results as a tie, and warning against the racist exclusion of Palestinian representatives from a future government.
Golan leads the only centre-left party in the Jewish-Israeli opposition bloc. Many of the parties in that anti-Netanyahu ‘Change’ grouping have explicitly ruled out governing with Palestinian Israeli parties.
The unofficial leader of the bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, has laid out conditions for joining his coalition that effectively bar the Arab parties.
This morning Golan says:
There is one resounding lesson from the reality we face: we have no future here unless we stop being afraid. And unless we put an end to racism. We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes.
The vote of an Israeli citizen casting a ballot in Tira is worth exactly the same as the vote of an Israeli citizen casting a ballot in Givat Shmuel. Not less. Not approximately the same. Exactly the same.
Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel.
The largest Palestinian-Israeli alliance, the Joint List, is expected to get significantly more seats in the Knesset than the Democrats. With two thirds of votes counted, the Joint List is on track for 12 seats, and the Democrats for 8.
Golan said the clearest message from voters was that Netanyahu’s coalition has lost its majority, and its mandate to rule.
I know how to count to 120 [the number of seats in parliament]. 65 is more than 55. That is how Israeli democracy works. Period.
We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel—a government that serves all Israeli citizens.
It’s worth noting the front page headlines in Israeli media today, printed before dawn so slightly out of date on some of the projections.
But the top headlines for each masthead are notable – with most highlighting the rise in the Palestinian-Israeli parties. The fact that there is no clear government formation had been expected; as we’ve reported, no single political party has ever won an outright majority in Israel’s political history so governments have also been coalitions of multiple parties. The papers did indicate a slight lead among the opposition bloc.
Yedioth Ahronoth:
Eisenkot on His Way to the President
Small Parties Fall Beneath the Electoral Threshold
Surge in Arab Sector Vote
Ma’ariv:
Vote of No-Confidence
Exit Polls on All Channels: Pro-Change Bloc: 52; Netanyahu Bloc: 50; Arab Parties: 18
A Masterpiece of Delicate Embroidery
Ha’aretz:
Exit Polls: 70 Seats for Opposition, 18 of Them from Arab Parties
We’re expecting a sharper picture of results just after 10am local time, where a majority of votes will be tallied and crucially, key counting from areas supporting Palestinian parties will have come in.
As of 9.16am local time, 65% of the vote had been counted showing the Netanyahu bloc on 56 seats, the Eisenkot-anchored ‘Change’ bloc on 48, and Palestinian Israeli parties with 16.
Hours after Israel’s polling stations closed, and with more than half of votes counted, several things are clear.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition has lost its mandate, Palestinian citizens of Israel have secured a key bloc of seats on the back of historic turnout, and the main Jewish-Israeli opposition bloc has no clear path to power without their support.
By 8am Israeli time, partial results put the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot on 49 seats, behind Netanyahu’s coalition at 55 seats. Palestinian-led parties are forecast to secure the remaining 16 seats, but several key towns were yet to report their counts.
A more complete picture is expected by late morning. Exit polls had put Eisenkot in a stronger position, and Israeli political analyst Nadav Eyal said around 6am local time that the pollsters were standing behind their samples.
They haven’t corrected further, and apparently validated their exit polls against the true results at the polling stations. In their view, these will be the final results.”
He noted that samples in Israel have historically been very accurate in forecasting the size of potential coalition blocs, but also that Likud’s strength is often underestimated.
Exit polls also do not capture absentee ballots, although these are fairly restricted under Israel’s voting system. Eligible groups include diplomats, serving soldiers and people medically unable to reach polling stations.
It’s just after 9am in Tel Aviv where Israelis are grappling with the results of yesterday’s elections, with no clear victor and uncertainty guaranteed at this point.
With 50% of the vote counted, Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 55 seats under the current vote share. The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 49 seats and the Palestinian parties on 16 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset, and the final seat projection will probably be updated as more votes are counted.
Exit polls published by Israel’s major TV networks show Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc tied with the opposition grouping led by Gadi Eisenkot on 51 seats each. Earlier exit polls had Eisenkot winning most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin. Israeli exit polls are often revised after publication and are notoriously imprecise, with the final count often swinging by several seats.
Voter turnout surged to the highest level in more than two decades, underscoring the stakes of an election that has been labelled the most important in the country’s history. More than 77% of eligible voters cast a ballot, according to Israel’s central elections committee, about 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
The Palestinian parties are projected to dramatically increase their representation in the Knesset, with exit polls showing they could win as many as 18 seats, up from 10. Experts have said that if Eisenkot falls short of a majority, as the exit polls suggest, he would be obliged to sit down to talk to the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am, to try to form a government – which could take weeks.
Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”. He told his supporters that the country must “establish a strong, right-wing national government” – adding that a government that relies on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.
Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv that the “Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister … a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics.” In his speech, he also warned Netanyahu not to “use Israel’s security” for political ends, playing on fears that the prime minister could use this period of uncertainty to launch a new attack on Iran.
The exit polls were released after a last-ditch effort by Netanyahu and several other parties to keep polling stations open beyond their 10pm deadline was rejected by the Central Elections Committee. The prime minister suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee, which said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.
Turnout among Israeli army personnel was 79.9%, an increase of 6.2% from the 2022 elections, according to the IDF.
In its statement, the IDF said that 809 polling stations were deployed throughout the country’s bases and in combat zones.
Under Israeli electoral law each voter is assigned to a specific polling station and can only vote at that station. However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at; among those afforded this exception are IDF personnel.
Ballot boxes from these special polling stations are transported directly to the Knesset where they undergo a series of checks before they are counted.
One apparent loser from Tuesday’s election was far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was expected to better his party’s result of six seats from the 2022 elections.
But instead there was stunned silence at the watch party for Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) in central Israel as results from the exit polls flashed across the screen, with most channels suggesting the party would remain on just six seats.
Speaking earlier in the evening, Ben-Gvir attempted to revive his supporters spirits by reminding them of all he had achieved in the past four years to further their agenda, including passing a law approving the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of murdering Israelis and worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners.
He also denounced other members of Netanyahu’s coalition who had suggested a unity government with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, which the audience booed loudly.
This is precisely the scenario we warned against – it is a terrible mistake.”
Analysis: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape
The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival.
In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that.
The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, currently projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored.
Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List).
They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben Gvir in this election”.
However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government.
Negotiations with the Joint List, with 10 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinians Israeli citizens, who are currently exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.
With 50% of the vote counted, Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 56 seats under the current vote share.
The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 49 seats and the Palestinian parties on 15 seats.
Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset, and the final seat projection will probably be updated as more votes are counted.
Exits polls earlier in the evening had both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s bloc tied on about 51 seats.
The lead that exit polls gave to the opposition bloc early in the night has disappeared, with Netanyahu’s grouping now neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot.
Israeli television networks gave the two blocs approximately 51 seats each in the 120 member Knesset – well below the 61 needed to govern. Palestinian parties meanwhile saw a surge in support, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
What’s next?
Parties will attempt to reach a majority
No single party has ever reached the requisite 61 seats needed to form a government in the Knesset, so parties must work together to form governing coalitions.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government – not necessarily the party with the most seats – but with the exit polls showing both parties falling short of a majority that process could take weeks.
Coalition building in Israel has always been difficult because mainstream parties usually refuse to collaborate with parties run by Palestinian citizens of Israel. However some have suggested Eisenkot could begin discussions with the Palestinian groupings who have seen a surge in support.
Palestinian grouping Ra’am is seen as a potential kingmaker if Netanyahu fails to secure enough votes to try to form a government. Their leader, Mansour Abbas, participated in a right-leaning government in the past.
However Eisenkot’s camp kept them at arm’s length during the campaign, perceiving their support as a liability. In the past he has said Arab-led parties do not meet Zionist criteria to govern.
For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats, save for defections. Addressing his supporters in the early hours of Wednesday morning, he said that a government that relies on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous and can produce unstable governments. It took Netanyahu 58 days to form his government after the previous election in November 2022.
A minority government could be attempted
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Palestinian parties whose representation in the Knesset is likely to have increase, could play a critical role.
The Joint List – which represents a number of Israeli Arab parties – has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for anyone that ousts Netanyahu from power.
A national unity government?
While appearing fanciful at first glance, Israeli commentators have mused in recent weeks on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.
Amit Segal, the chief political analyst for Channel 12 and journalist seen as close to Netanyahu, suggested that the prime minister’s extortion that the “Zionist majority must come to its senses and unite”, could be interpreted as an olive branch to Eisenkot.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement, but their partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
New elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
However if we a new set of polls is on the horizon, they are not likely to happen for weeks at the minimum, with the candidate designated by the president having 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two week extension.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) has proposed NT$235.7 billion (US$7.4 billion) for NT$10,000 cash payments to eligible recipients under Taiwan’s 2027 central government budget.
Addressing the Legislative Yuan on Tuesday, Cho said central government revenue had exceeded expenditure for nine consecutive years since 2017, per UDN. He said the handout was intended to improve people's livelihoods and ensure that the benefits of AI-driven economic growth were shared more equitably.
Under the Cabinet's proposal, foreign nationals with permanent residency in Taiwan would be eligible for the payment, as would citizens with household registration and nationals without household registration who hold residence permits. Spouses of Taiwanese citizens from China, Hong Kong, Macau, or other countries who hold residence permits would also be eligible.
The eligibility rules generally follow those used for the government’s 2023 and 2025 cash handouts. Taiwanese government employees stationed overseas on official duty, and their dependents who hold Taiwanese nationality, would also qualify.
The 2027 central government budget projects revenue and expenditure of approximately NT$3.927 trillion each, up 13.3% and 31.5%, respectively, from the 2026 statutory budget, UDN reported. The government also plans to repay NT$179 billion in debt through new borrowing, with Cho describing the budget as balanced and requiring no net new borrowing.
Outstanding public debt is projected to reach NT$6.758 trillion by the end of 2027, including supplementary budgets, equivalent to about 23% of average nominal GDP over the previous three years. That ratio would be 2.9 percentage points lower than at the end of 2026 and well below the statutory ceiling of 40.6%, marking the lowest level since Taiwan's provincial government was downsized, Cho said.
Cho urged lawmakers from all parties to support and swiftly pass the 2027 central government budget, per TTV News. He said it would provide the resources needed to care for the public, advance infrastructure projects, maintain Taiwan’s technological lead, and safeguard national security.
In September, KMT Legislative Caucus Convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) called on the government to distribute NT$20,000 to every citizen this year, arguing that excess tax revenue could cover the cost without borrowing. KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said on Oct. 8 that the proposed NT$20,000 payment would be separate from the Cabinet's planned NT$10,000 handout next year.

Ciwas said she had represented Taiwan's Indigenous communities for 24 years and worked to protect their rights. She said she relied on staff to manage her office while she focused on legislation and visiting Indigenous communities across the country, per SETN and UDN.
Her lawyers said Chang oversaw staffing, finances, and other administrative matters. They argued that Ciwas did not know every assistant personally and may have signed documents as a formality without knowing the details.
Defense lawyer Cheng Yu-jen (鄭昱仁) cited amendments passed by the legislature concerning public funding for lawmakers' assistants. He argued that the money was intended to help lawmakers hire staff and that Ciwas had no intention of illegally obtaining public funds, per CNA.
The case also involves allegations that Ciwas illegally imported 74,400 COVID-19 rapid test kits from China in 2022 without the required government approval. Prosecutors allege that she authorized Chang to arrange the imports using other people's names to avoid medical device regulations.

Climate change should be declared health emergency as health risks can no longer be ignored
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:05:57 UTC
13:05:57 KST

Climate change should be declared a global health emergency as its impacts intensify faster than action to address them, authors of a major new report warn.
Climate change has become an escalating chronic global health emergency, with health risks and impacts increasing rapidly since the Paris Agreement entered into force in 2016, according to the latest Lancet Countdown report.
Therefore, the authors of the report are calling on the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations as a whole to formally declare climate change a global health emergency.
They argue that a formal emergency designation would shift global climate action from slow, voluntary commitments to mandatory, coordinated emergency management.
This would lead to strengthened health surveillance and early warning systems, mobilised resources rapidly, established legally binding accountability mechanisms and introduced preventive public health measures.
A measure, they consider, would reflect the scale of the threat.
“As populations grow and age, more people are at risk today than a decade ago, further increasing the scale and urgency of the adaptation task,” the authors wrote.
The report's indicators show that, since the Paris Agreement entered into force, climate-related health risks and impacts have not only increased but have also accelerated across multiple areas compared with the previous decade.
These include some heat-related health risks, drought incidence, extreme precipitation and climatic suitability for dengue transmission. The faster pace of these changes suggests that existing measures are insufficient to protect public health.
Other proposed measures include an immediate global ban on new fossil fuel exploration and exploitation, the complete phase-out of coal-fired power generation by 2035, and a shift towards predominantly plant-based diets.
Climate - related health threats continue to grow
Despite efforts to tackle climate change, greenhouse gas emissions continue to reach record highs. Climate change is increasingly affecting health and threatening lives worldwide, while the window of opportunity to avoid a potentially catastrophic future is rapidly closing.
The past 11 years have been the hottest on record, the report noted, while annual heat-related deaths have risen by nearly 36% over recent decades.
In 2023 alone, heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths, with more than 70% of these deaths attributable to human-caused climate change.
Climate change is also making conditions more suitable for the transmission of vector-borne diseases, including dengue and Zika.
Extreme weather and wildfires are also increasingly threatening human health, particularly among vulnerable populations and in regions with limited capacity to respond to climate-related impacts.
Against this backdrop, the authors say an urgent change of approach is needed “to change course and protect the health and survival of present and future generations.”

Well, what can we say, we do have some of the world's most spectacular toilets. Love, Visit Norway." The post included a link to a feature on its website showcasing what it calls some of the "world's most beautiful toilets," scattered across the Scandinavian country's breathtaking landscapes.
The website features photographs of remarkable public restrooms at Norwegian tourist destinations, explaining that "the toilets along the Norwegian Scenic Routes are architectural masterpieces." It describes Norway's impressive collection of restrooms as examples of how something as ordinary and mundane as a toilet can become a tourist attraction. The Norwegian Public Roads Administration, which is responsible for developing the country's scenic routes and their facilities, still has a few tricks up its sleeve, the website adds.
In a response column published in the Norwegian newspaper Dagbladet under the headline "Straight into the toilet," the writer declared: "Yes, Donald, we are a 'shit house country.' Norway is, after all, the home of the outhouse." The columnist explained that Norwegians are among the last people likely to take offense at being associated with outdoor toilets, which many connect to the country's traditions and its cabin culture, where such facilities were once commonplace.
"Trump has complained about the Nobel Peace Prize so many times that it almost seems like an obsession," the columnist wrote. "No matter how many times both the prime minister and the Norwegian Foreign Ministry explain that the government has absolutely nothing to do with awarding the prize, he continues to blame them."
The writer added: "An overwhelming majority of American voters agree with the Nobel Committee: Trump certainly does not deserve any peace prize. Quite the opposite. The war in Iran is a major source of criticism of Trump, including among his own supporters, second only to the cost of living and the period of inflation and soaring prices. He promised to end the endless wars, particularly in the Middle East. Instead, he joined Benjamin Netanyahu in a war he cannot find a way out of."
Trump's remarks about Norway also drew criticism in the United States. Democratic Sen. Bernie Sanders, a leading figure on the American progressive left, wrote on X: "Norway is one of the most democratic and prosperous countries on Earth. Free health care. Free college Strong democracy. Free press. Trump says 'Norway sucks' and is a 'shit house country' because it won’t give him the Nobel Prize. Insane. We have a mentally unbalanced president."
Sanders' praise for the Nordic country was hardly exaggerated. Norway, with a population of just 5.6 million, is among the wealthiest and most developed countries in the world. Its sovereign wealth fund, known as the Government Pension Fund Global or the Oil Fund, was established in the 1990s using revenues from oil and gas production and is the largest of its kind in the world.
The fund is worth approximately $2.3 trillion and holds an average stake of about 1.5% in all publicly listed companies worldwide. On the United Nations Human Development Index, which measures life expectancy, education and income, Norway ranks second globally alongside Switzerland, behind Iceland. Its gross national income per capita is also among the highest in the world. This year marked the 10th consecutive year that Norway topped Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index.
Trump has argued since his first term in office that he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize, and his demands intensified last year after he claimed to have secured eight peace agreements. In practice, these were not comprehensive peace treaties but primarily ceasefires or conflicts that broke out, some with his backing, and ended relatively quickly when he sought their conclusion.
This year's Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a former judge at the International Criminal Court in The Hague from South Africa and an outspoken critic of Israel who also authored a report accusing the country of genocide.
The Michigan rally where Trump made his remarks about Norway was the same contentious event at which he compared Muslim Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to the terrorists responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks. Trump also made crude remarks about the backsides of other politicians within his MAGA movement and about that of his supporter, rapper Nicki Minaj.

Inhabiting as Inquiry: Threads from the 20th Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Inhabiting a space involves multiple economic, social, cultural, geographic, political, and environmental factors. Beyond these considerations, however, it engages with processes, boundaries, and possibilities that have repeatedly become subjects of architectural inquiry. "We are builders of a society," declared Solano Benitez during his lecture titled The Place of Architecture at the Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial. Through a series of international lectures, exhibitions across different locations in the city, and activities open to all generations, the 20th Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial examined the value of inhabitation, recognizing architecture as the discipline that gives meaning to how and where we live and, consequently, how we exist within society.
Across its six main venues and numerous partner institutions, a common theme emerges: human existence explored through different ways of inhabiting, sharing knowledge, contrasting experiences, and debating the contemporary challenges facing architecture.

EU urges G7 allies to cover Ukraine's budget deficit – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:58:00 EET
12:58:00 KST

EU urges G7 allies to cover Ukraine's budget deficit – FT
Brussels is pressing its Group of Seven (G7) allies to provide funding to Ukraine next year to cover a €70 billion budget deficit amid declining aid from non-EU countries.
Source: The Financial Times, citing European Commission estimates and diplomats
Details: The European Commission has confirmed Ukraine's projection of a €70 billion funding shortfall in 2027. The estimate includes military spending after the remaining weapons supplied under the Biden administration have been delivered. US President Donald Trump has currently halted all direct funding for Ukraine.
Quote from the FT: " According to a forecast by the European Commission, seen by the FT, Kyiv's non-EU allies have so far pledged just €4bn for next year, down from €19bn in 2026. G7 members US, UK, Canada and Japan are collectively set to provide just €1bn, the analysis shows."
Details: The EU has begun contingency planning to secure additional funding to keep Ukraine's finances stable in 2027 if NATO and G7 partners do not step up their aid. European Commission officials are exploring several options, including jointly issuing debt, which is expected to be discussed at the summit in late November.
Brussels is also conducting active bilateral negotiations with London, Ottawa and other capitals. European officials are awaiting the publication of the UK and Canadian budgets for 2027, hoping they will include new financial commitments to support Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Brussels has ruled out covering the shortfall on its own if other allies fail to step up their support. A European Commission spokesperson said that the EU and its member states account for 80% of the promised aid to Ukraine for 2027.
Quote from the European Commission spokesperson: "Europe cannot meet Ukraine's financing needs alone . . . International partners must also step up, including NATO allies."
Details: The position of Kyiv's partners outside the EU currently remains uncertain. A spokesperson for the Canadian finance ministry noted that Ottawa has committed a total of CA$27 billion in aid to Ukraine since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Quote from a spokesperson for the Canadian finance ministry: "I won't speculate on what may or may not be included in next week's budget."
Details: Japan's Foreign Ministry disputed the European Commission's conclusions, emphasising that the government "cannot make any definitive statements regarding the possibility of future financial support to Ukraine".
Quote from a Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesperson: "However, Japan is considering options to address Ukraine's financing needs based on future developments . . . including discussions among G7 members."
More details: Alongside the budget shortfall, allies are also falling short on military aid. The European Commission estimates that NATO's 32 member states are €13 billion short of meeting their pledge to provide Ukraine with €70 billion in defence support this year.

'Not just empty talk': Ra'am's Abbas signals willingness to join next government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:55:05 UTC
12:55:05 KST

Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas said Tuesday that joining a new government could bring meaningful change to the country's Arab minority, after exit polls projected his Islamist party would win seven seats in parliament amid a significant increase in Arab voter turnout.
"If we join a government of change, we will be able to see substantial changes, not just empty talk," Abbas told ynet after the first exit polls were released.
Early projections showing a narrow advantage for the opposition's pro-change bloc initially suggested that Ra'am could emerge as a pivotal player in negotiations to form Israel's next government.
But overnight revisions shifted the advantage toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc, sharply reducing the likelihood of a minority government supported by Ra'am from outside the coalition.
Under Israel's parliamentary system, a governing coalition generally needs the support of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset. Arab parties could play a decisive role if neither major political bloc secures a majority on its own.
Despite the shifting projections, Abbas welcomed the substantial increase in voting among Arab citizens of Israel, including unusually high participation by religious figures.
"We received seven seats according to the polls. We hope to secure an eighth seat so we can bring down the current government and become part of the camp for change, with the aim of fighting crime and violence, home demolitions and racism," Abbas said.
Crime and violence in Arab communities, along with disputes over housing demolitions and allegations of discrimination, have been central issues in Ra'am's political agenda.
Abbas acknowledged that his party still faced significant challenges in translating electoral support into political influence.
"We still have a long way to go before we have an influential voice and a meaningful position on the ground," he said. "We must bring about change across all institutions and invest every effort and resource available to us to achieve that."
He thanked Arab voters for their support, singling out residents of the Negev region in southern Israel, where Ra'am has a significant political base.
"We have invested tremendous efforts to reach where we are today. We have faced challenges and paid a price," Abbas said. "We have endured criticism and attacks, including on a personal level, but despite everything, we will continue on our path with determination."
Abbas reports calls after exit polls
Abbas said he had received numerous telephone calls following the release of the exit polls but declined to identify the callers or disclose the substance of their conversations.
"I received many phone calls after the poll results were published, and I will not reveal their contents," he said. "We want to carefully examine the political landscape, and we will adopt a series of positions and decisions that serve the Arab public."
Ra'am, officially known as the United Arab List, is an Arab Islamist party affiliated with the southern branch of Israel's Islamic Movement. Under Abbas, it has pursued a pragmatic approach to parliamentary politics, emphasizing cooperation with Jewish parties to secure government resources and address problems affecting Arab communities.
The party made history in 2021 when it joined the coalition government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, becoming the first independent Arab party to formally participate in a governing coalition.
Its potential involvement in another government has become a central point of contention in the current coalition negotiations, with Netanyahu rejecting any government dependent on what he describes as anti-Zionist Arab parties.
Ra'am lawmaker Walid Taha described the projected election result as a major achievement.
"We have achieved historic success as an independent party," Taha said. "Now the work begins. If we manage to secure the eighth seat, our strength will be even more significant, and that will have an impact on the government."
Fellow Ra'am lawmaker Iman Khatib-Yasin said the party's campaign reflected years of frustration among Arab citizens over violence, crime and what she described as hostile government policies.
"For four years, we have suffered from many problems that have harmed Arab society," she said. "How deeply we have suffered over the murders and the cries of mothers. We want to act to confront this harsh reality."
Khatib-Yasin also criticized those who had accused Ra'am members of betraying their community.
"What hurt us most was hearing people call us traitors and slander us," she said. "But that did not deter us or divert us from our path. We will continue working with determination and investing tremendous effort."
The final distribution of Knesset seats will depend on the official vote count, leaving Ra'am's ultimate parliamentary strength and its potential role in forming the next government uncertain.

Three Latino Leaders Reflect on Inspiration Across Generations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:47:59 UTC
12:47:59 KST

Three leaders within their respective industries gave toasts at TIME’s Latino Leaders dinner on Tuesday night in Miami, where they each honored their cultures and the people who raised them.
Nelson German, a chef, restaurateur, and author; Julián Castro, the CEO of Latino Community Foundation, the largest Latino-serving organization in the U.S.; and actor, singer, and advocate Sofia Carson, all spoke at the event.
German, who was raised in Manhattan’s Washington Heights, reflected on the experience of growing up in a Dominican immigrant family and shying away from his language and culture as a child.
“We wanted to fit in so badly to reach that American dream,” he said. “But now things have changed … We now are embracing those parts of ourselves more fully. We are embracing our cultures, our heritage, our motherlands.”
The act of honoring one’s culture, he said, is about looking both forward and back.
“It's not just about the future; we have to honor the past. The parents and grandparents who work two, three jobs … They gave us a chance to really stand in these kinds of rooms together, so never forget about that.”
For German, who is the executive chef at acclaimed restaurants in Oakland and San Francisco, passing down Dominican culture is done through his work: food.
“The recipes, the stories, they have to stay alive,” he said. “We have to share them with our kids, with our youth … Let's keep creating opportunities for the next generation while giving them the connection to the generation before them.”
Castro also reflected on his childhood, when he was “always on the lookout for Latinas and Latinos doing great things” while growing up in San Antonio, Texas. He would read through the credits of movies, looking for names like “Garcia,” “Hernandez,” and “Rodriguez,” or scan the library for books by Latino authors.
He paid tribute to his grandmother Victoria, who came to the U.S. in 1922 from northern Mexico after her parents passed away and raised Castro’s mother as a single parent. He also honored his mother, who also raised Castro and his brother alone.
“I am sure that if we went around the room tonight, that that is a very common story here, and that each of you, like me, feels very fortunate and very blessed to have been able to achieve their dreams,” he said. “Our families … have always been strivers and hard workers and people of love, of faith, and of family, and we've always driven progress in the United States of America, and that's true today.”
Castro acknowledged what he described as a "cruelty” being aimed at immigrant and Latino families around the country, but stressed that Latinos remained an integral part of the U.S.
“The destiny of the United States and the destiny of Latinos is more intertwined than it ever has been before,” he said. “Only if Latinos succeed can America succeed in the years to come, and vice versa.”
Throughout Carson’s speech, during which she similarly reflected on those who raised and molded her, she repeated the same line several times: “To be a Latin woman is to be hope.”
She stressed the importance of hope, especially in the face of “oppression, plundering, and abandonment,” quoting the words of the Latin-American author and Nobel Prize-winner in literature Gabriel García Márquez.
Carson said that she has spent her entire life admiring her mother, who taught her poems by Mexican painter Frida Kahlo, and read her novels by Chilean-American author Isabel Allende, and sang her songs by Cuban-American singer Celia Cruz.
“To be a Latin woman is to be hope,” she repeated, honoring the crowd’s mothers, grandmothers, sisters, and daughters. “Hope lives in the DNA of who we are. It flows from our bloodstream into everything we touch. It is the beating of our hearts. It is the language of our soul.”
Latino Leaders was presented by PepsiCo.
