Netanyahu, Eisenkot stake rival claims to lead Israel after deadlocked vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:46:25 CET
12:46:25 KST

By Steven Scheer, Rami Ayyub and Lina Obeid
JERUSALEM, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Benjamin Netanyahu won the support of an unexpectedly clear majority of Israeli Jews in an election billed as a major turning point in his nation’s history, apparently ensuring he will survive as prime minister at least in a caretaker role.
With around 70.7% of votes tallied on Wednesday morning, Israeli media forecast Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties winning 54 seats in parliament, far surpassing 47 for the opposition bloc of rival Gadi Eisenkot. Parties representing Israelis of Arab descent would win 19.
The results could still change as counting continued, but a victory for Eisenkot appeared increasingly out of reach, as his bloc of anti-Netanyahu parties from centre-left to hard-right underperformed pre-election polls that forecast a tight race.
While Netanyahu lost his bloc’s majority in the 120-seat Knesset, as expected, opponents were left with no hope of unseating him without some form of backing of Arab parties, which many have ruled out. Even then, he would remain as caretaker during any coalition negotiations, or until a new election next year.
SECURITY FIGHT SHARPENS
Netanyahu, addressing his Likud party’s faithful after 3 a.m. (0100 GMT) at the party’s election headquarters in Jerusalem, called for the formation of “a strong, right-wing national government”.
He also highlighted Israel’s military successes and raised the prospect of renewed joint military action against Iran alongside his ally, US President Donald Trump.
“Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all. But ulterior motives must not divert us from this sacred mission,” he said.
Trump, who had called on Israeli voters to keep Netanyahu in power so they could “finish the job” in Iran, said Netanyahu had done “very well” thanks to his own endorsement.
“I think when the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot, but I actually heard he did pretty well. It might be winning or tie. The tie is sort of considered a win in that case because it’s a big chess match,” Trump said early on Wednesday at a campaign stop in Texas.
EISENKOT CALLS ON SECURITY CHIEFS TO RESIST PRESSURE
Eisenkot acknowledged that Netanyahu was still in office as a caretaker, but said the prime minister had lost public support and urged him to retire from politics. He also issued a warning that Netanyahu might use security for political ends.
“I call on the heads of the security establishment and the civil service: Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people’s trust,” he said.
“Remember that you serve only the state and the interests of Israel’s citizens. Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you. You have my unequivocal backing. Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel’s security for your political needs.”
The election was the first held in Israel since Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 people and carried off 251 hostages in attacks that shattered the country’s sense of security and plunged it into war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The war in Gaza, which flattened the territory and killed 74,000 Palestinians, has left Israel increasingly isolated on the world stage, with a decisive shift in global public opinion against it, including in its closest ally the United States.
Netanyahu himself is wanted by the International Criminal Court in The Hague on war crimes charges he calls absurd, and faces corruption charges in Israel that he dismisses as an establishment plot.
DECISIVE SHIFT IN ISRAELI POLITICS
His continued support from most Israeli Jews was a clear sign of the decisive shift in Israeli politics that he has presided over as the dominant political figure of the era.
His brand of unapologetic Jewish nationalism, support for settlement on occupied Palestinian land and contempt for all foreign criticism is now firmly entrenched as the Israeli mainstream.
The centre-left that dominated Israel for the first half of its history and had led negotiations to exchange land for peace with Arab neighbours has been reduced to a small fringe.
Nearly all Jewish parties now share Netanyahu’s rejection of any eventual independent state for Palestinians, the basis of internationally endorsed peace talks since the 1990s, when he first came to power as Israel’s youngest-ever leader.
After a spell in the wilderness as a right-wing maverick, he returned to power in 2009 and has remained ever since, apart from a period of 18 months when a rickety coalition of opponents managed to lever him out after four inconclusive elections in two years.
Both sides saw Tuesday’s election as a decisive turning point for the nation, driving turnout to 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
Turnout was particularly high among Israelis of Palestinian descent, who make up more than a fifth of the population but whose representatives have historically been excluded from the cabinet. Many were motivated by what they see as open racism from Netanyahu’s cabinet, which includes a party leader convicted of inciting racial hatred against Arabs.
The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, in a speech at the alliance’s headquarters in Nazareth.

WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A federal grand jury has declined to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson who had provided testimony to a congressional panel that probed the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by President Donald Trump’s supporters, a source familiar with the matter said on Tuesday.
The Justice Department of the Trump administration has been investigating Hutchinson over whether she gave false testimony to the congressional panel. Hutchinson has maintained that her testimony was truthful.

Political experts have raised concerns about efforts by the Trump administration to target his critics and political opponents.

Trump pardoned nearly everyone criminally charged with participating in the 2021 Capitol attack on his first day back in office for a second term in January 2025.
Former Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith and his team secured an indictment in 2023, accusing Trump of plotting to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.
Smith dropped that and another case after Trump won the 2024 election, citing a Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting president.

Sanctions equal economic terrorism, Iran tells UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:45:40 UTC
12:45:40 KST

Iran's chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, said unilateral sanctions amount to economic terrorism and that blockades imposed by armed force are acts of aggression under international law.
Speaking at a UN General Assembly meeting on the need to end US economic, commercial and financial sanctions against Cuba, Darzi said it was the 34th time the assembly has declared its firm opposition to unbridled unilateralism, reckless foreign policies and unilateral coercive measures imposed by a government that considers itself above international law while continuing systematic and severe violations.
Darzi said unilateral sanctions, including those states impose independently, are rooted in unilateralism and coercion and therefore endanger multilateralism, destabilize international relations and undermine the UN Charter and international law.
He said the sanctions, as a tool for collective punishment of targeted nations, violate fundamental human rights, obstruct peace, weaken the right to development and block a just, peaceful and equitable international order.
Darzi said more than six decades of unilateral US sanctions and blockade against Cuba are a clear example of coercive pressure against a sovereign state, imposing widespread suffering on its people, undermining their fundamental human rights and hindering their development.
He said the intensification of these measures under the hypocritical pretext of "promoting democracy" reveals the deep contradiction between claimed goals and devastating humanitarian consequences. This approach, he said, instrumentalizes democracy rather than promoting it.
No government has the right to dictate the political future of an independent nation, Darzi said. From any perspective, such policies and actions, including economic warfare, are illegal, immoral and inhumane. The illegal and inhumane blockade that has lasted decades must end immediately, the imposing government must fully compensate the Cuban people for all damages, and all those involved in perpetuating these policies must be held accountable, he said.
Darzi said the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has itself faced aggression and the consequences of US economic pressure and blockades, once again declares its clear and firm opposition to any sanctions against independent and sovereign states, including Cuba.
He said such sanctions harm ordinary people, especially women, children and the elderly, undermine their health, security and welfare and create serious obstacles to development, which is necessary for the full enjoyment of human rights. These measures, by instrumentalizing the "human rights" of a nation, in fact grossly violate the human rights of that same nation. This is not a defense of human rights but blatant hypocrisy, he said.
Darzi recalled the US president's so-called "help" promise to the Iranian people, saying: "Help is on the way," and days later, on his orders, US forces bombed an elementary school in Minab, ruthlessly killing 168 children aged 7 to 12.
He said the UN General Assembly must compel the United States to implement dozens of resolutions adopted with the overwhelming support of the international community that reject the Cuban blockade and call on the US to end its economic, commercial and financial blockade. The serious legal consequences of unilateral coercive measures for the international legal order must not be ignored or underestimated, especially in the current turbulent international environment, he said.
Darzi said the UN Charter, as stated in Articles 1 and 2, is founded on the principles of sovereign equality, international cooperation and the development of friendly relations among nations. Unilateral coercive measures violate all these principles as well as the principle of non-intervention, especially when their aim is to force states to change their domestic policies, while Article 2(7) prohibits intervention in matters essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of states.
He said invoking human rights can in no way justify measures that impose widespread suffering on innocent people, since sanctions imposed in the name of protecting human rights themselves violate rights such as health, food, development and a dignified life.
These measures target ordinary people and in practice act as a form of collective punishment, hitting the most vulnerable hardest, he said. This is not protection of human rights but denial of human rights through economic pressure, a instrumentalization and weaponization of human rights.
Darzi said that while the Charter considers international cooperation necessary to solve global problems and promote friendly relations among nations, unilateral coercive measures instead strengthen confrontation, deepen divides and weaken the foundations of peaceful coexistence.
He said these measures directly conflict with the text, spirit, subject and purpose of the Charter. Sanctions are a form of economic terrorism, while blockades enforced by armed force constitute acts of aggression under international law, he said. Despite differences in form and severity, these measures share a deeply worrying feature: they undermine the sovereignty of states, cause human suffering and substantively violate international law, and are therefore both illegal and illegitimate.
Darzi said a policy that sacrifices the welfare of millions for political ends is incompatible with the principles of humanity, morality and international solidarity.
He reaffirmed Iran's firm solidarity with the government and resilient people of Cuba in their struggle against the blockade and other unjust coercive measures. Iran will continue to support the elimination of unilateral coercive measures and calls on the assembly to intensify efforts to end these measures immediately, including sanctions against Cuba.
The time has come to end these illegal and inhumane measures, Darzi said. Their continuation is not only a failure of international responsibility but a clear manifestation of humanitarian and moral bankruptcy.

From Iranian drones in Ukraine to Russian military assistance for Tehran
The Russia-Iran relationship has evolved beyond diplomatic coordination and economic cooperation into an increasingly important military partnership.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Iranian-designed Shahed drones have become a major component of Moscow’s long-range strike campaign.
Russia subsequently established domestic production and modified the drones, improving their capabilities for use against Ukrainian targets.
US and European officials have reported that Russia may be transferring upgraded Shahed drones back to Iran, incorporating improvements developed during the war in Ukraine.
Putin and Pezeshkian Pay Tribute to Ayatollah Khamenei, Killed in US-Israeli Strikes
During Tuesday’s talks, Pezeshkian expressed confidence that Moscow and Tehran could deepen cooperation across several sectors, explicitly including security and military affairs.
He thanked Putin for supporting Iran politically and economically, arguing that US pressure had created greater incentives for countries under sanctions to cooperate.
“After the Americans began taking such aggressive steps in the region, it became clear to everyone that we must work toward creating a multipolar world,” Pezeshkian said.

Both leaders paid tribute to Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.

Iran Approves Russian State TV Bureau in Tehran as Ties Deepen

“We are fulfilling all our obligations under all our projects,” Putin said.
The Russian president highlighted continued construction at Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant, where Russia is a major technology and construction partner.

Pezeshkian announced that Iran had cleared the way for Russia’s state television broadcaster VGTRK to establish a bureau in Tehran, following discussions during Lavrov’s recent visit.

At the gas exporters’ summit, both presidents criticized Western sanctions and efforts to restrict their countries’ participation in international energy markets.
Pezeshkian accused the US and Israel of undermining global energy security through military attacks on Iranian infrastructure and restrictions affecting the country’s energy exports.
He urged major gas-producing countries to oppose what he described as destabilizing unilateral measures.
Putin echoed those criticisms, arguing that Europe’s efforts to reduce dependence on Russian gas were harming European industries and households.
“Any attempts to exclude Russia from the global gas market or restrain the development of our industry carry serious consequences,” he said.
The Russian president accused European governments of imposing excessive costs on their own economies by rejecting Russian energy supplies.
The EU has pursued restrictions on Russian energy imports as part of broader efforts to reduce the revenue available to Moscow for financing its war against Ukraine.

He did not identify prospective American companies or specific agreements.

meet otter, the portable newborn warmer designed for hospitals with unreliable power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:34:24 UTC
12:34:24 KST

meet otter, the portable newborn warmer designed for hospitals with unreliable power
design that matters and MTTS rethink newborn warming with an integrated, heat-conducting bassinet designed for the realities of low-resource healthcare settings.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
otter rethinks medical design for real-world conditions
Otter, a portable newborn warmer developed by Design that Matters and MTTS, is designed to prevent and treat neonatal hypothermia in hospitals with unreliable electricity and limited resources. Awarded the 2026 Seoul Design Award Grand Prize (find top 10 finalists here), the device rethinks newborn warming through an integrated, heat-conducting polycarbonate bassinet, a built-in battery, and an intuitive touchscreen interface. Otter addresses the practical challenges of neonatal care in low-resource settings, where power outages, limited maintenance capacity, and the risk of user error can compromise the reliability of conventional devices.
Newborn incubators and radiant warmers often depend on stable electricity, regular maintenance, and specialized equipment, requirements that can become obstacles in rural hospitals, where power outages and limited technical support complicate the delivery of neonatal care. Otter addresses these constraints through a design developed over eight years of field research, expert interviews, and product reviews across Africa and Southeast Asia. The need is particularly acute for premature and low-birthweight newborns, who are more vulnerable to losing body heat. Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC), which relies on skin-to-skin contact between a newborn and their caregiver, is an established approach to maintaining warmth, but interruptions are sometimes unavoidable. A baby may need to be examined, transferred between departments, or temporarily separated from their mother. Otter provides supplemental warming during these moments, including transfers within hospitals.
seamless bassinet replaces the conventional warming mattress
The central design decision by US-based nonprofit Design that Matters and Vietnamese medical device manufacturer MTTS is to replace the removable water or gel mattress found in many conductive warmers with an integrated, heat-conducting polycarbonate bassinet. The smooth, continuous surface has no fabric, seams, or gaps, making it easier to clean and disinfect between patients. It also prevents direct contact between the newborn and the heating element, reducing the risk of burns associated with conventional systems when a mattress is removed or incorrectly positioned. The heating element and temperature sensors sit within a water-resistant housing beneath the bassinet, protected from rough handling. This integrated construction reduces reliance on consumables and replacement parts. Warming mattresses can be vulnerable to punctures, seam failures, and deterioration, while water-filled systems may require additives that are difficult to source in some settings. Otter simplifies the structure of the product, aiming to reduce the maintenance burden throughout its working life.
Otter weighs 3.6 kg and can be carried between clinical departments without interrupting warming. Its integrated battery automatically takes over when mains electricity is disconnected, supporting continued operation during power failures and patient transfers. The battery provides more than two hours of backup at an ambient temperature of 15°C. The touchscreen displays temperature, heating status, and estimated remaining battery life, while alarms alert staff to problems with the sensor, heating element, or power supply. The interface is designed to make the status of the device easy to assess without requiring extensive technical training. Its physical form follows the same principle. Resembling a familiar newborn bassinet, the open structure allows clinical staff to access the baby while making the device less intimidating for parents. This familiar appearance also supports interaction between mothers and newborns during periods when supplemental warming is needed.
testing the device in clinical settings
Five Otter devices have been operating at Kapiri District Hospital in Zambia since May 2025, where an ongoing implementation study evaluates performance, staff acceptance, and integration with existing care protocols. The devices have been used with low-birthweight newborns, including infants weighing as little as 840 grams, and to maintain warmth during transfers between hospital buildings. The study also takes place in conditions that expose the practical challenges the design is intended to address, including documented power interruptions lasting seven to eleven hours and limited access to biomedical support. The project summary reports successful use during transfers, but the implementation study remains ongoing, and its findings should be understood in that context.

UAE honours Indian flydubai pilot for thwarting mid-air attack
NEW DELHI: The UAE has honoured Captain Smit Machchhar and the crew of flydubai Flight FZ1073 for their courage in protecting passengers during a serious in-flight incident. UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan conferred the First-Class Order of Zayed II on the crew on Tuesday.The honour was presented by Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed, in the presence of UAE Vice President, Prime Minister and Dubai Ruler Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, also met the crew members on Tuesday.On September 30, Flight FZ1073, operating from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia following a serious incident in the cockpit. Captain Machchhar was injured, while crew members, off-duty pilots and passengers helped bring the situation under control. The aircraft landed safely, and all 172 passengers and crew were reported safe.During the meeting, the UAE leaders praised the crew for their courage and sense of responsibility in protecting passengers. They stressed that human safety and security remain the UAE's highest priority.While Machchhar was receiving treatment for his injuries, Sheikh Hamdan visited him and praised his courage, sense of responsibility and commitment to protecting human life.
The deputy prime minister expressed pride in Machchhar being part of the "story of our nation"."During a visit to Captain Smit Machchhar… the flydubai pilot who embodied the highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life. From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise. We are proud that he is part of our team… part of the story of our nation… and part of what the UAE stands for… a nation of compassion… a nation of peace… and a nation of life," he wrote in a post on X.In an earlier interview with the UAE's state-owned newspaper The National, Machchhar recalled the attack by the co-pilot and said he suffered several blows before he could open the cockpit door.“The first time when I was hit … my thought was something's gone horribly wrong with the aircraft structure, which has fallen on my head. It almost made me fall on my control column. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, (I realised) it was the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.”“My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head… While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I lost a lot. I was just looking (at) outlines,” he told The National.“Immediately, my hand went to the knob which opens the door. And (I was) screaming for my colleagues. I believe that was the first time when I lost consciousness. I fell face down in the cockpit,” he added.Recalling the moment when the aircraft plunged 17,000 feet, Machchhar said, “The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down.”Despite the attack, Machchhar said his love for flying remained unchanged.
“Did my love die for aviation? Not at all. Not at all. I'm just glad that I was able to do my part.”Machchhar managed to unlatch the cockpit door, allowing passengers and off-duty crew members to enter and restrain the co-pilot. The co-pilot had attacked him with an axe in an attempt to bring down the aircraft. A hijacking distress signal was also sent.The flight was diverted to Tabuk, where it made an emergency landing with the help of passengers who helped land the aircraft. All 180 occupants disembarked without injury, according to the account of the incident.Israeli President Isaac Herzog has also announced that he would confer Israel's Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism on Machchhar.

The United States has urged several Arab Gulf countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign against Iran following next week's U.S. midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing people briefed on discussions between Washington and regional governments.

U.S. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to launch an attack but is leaning toward a broad military operation after the midterms, the newspaper reported. Potential targets include Iranian critical infrastructure and nuclear facilities.
The alternative remains a negotiated agreement with Tehran. Regional mediators continue diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation, but those talks have yet to produce a breakthrough.
The reported preparations include significant changes to the U.S. military posture in the Middle East.
Officials familiar with the matter told the Journal that the U.S. military is moving a Patriot air defense system from Texas to the region to strengthen its defenses against potential Iranian missile attacks.
American forces have also been relocated from bases considered vulnerable to attack as part of preparations for a possible escalation.
According to several officials cited in the report, U.S. troops stationed in the region have replenished their ammunition supplies, while American bombers and fighter jets are being readied for potential strikes.
An additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine Corps expeditionary force are expected to join the U.S. military buildup next month, the newspaper reported.

World Insights: COP17 nears conclusion as negotiators make progress but face hurdles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:30:59 CST
12:30:59 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital of Yerevan has entered its final stretch.
The conference has adopted 14 decisions and secured more than 1.8 billion U.S. dollars in financial commitments. Yet negotiators remain divided over some of the most contentious issues, including who should bear the cost of protecting nature and how global commitments can be translated into measurable results.
With the conference due to conclude on Friday, the focus has shifted from reaffirming global biodiversity goals to reaching agreement on how to achieve them.
TANGIBLE PROGRESS
The COP17 marks the first global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022 with 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
There are encouraging signs of international cooperation, said Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, noting that nearly 90 percent of the convention's parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than 70 percent have submitted national reports.
The negotiations have also yielded concrete results. Parties have adopted 14 decisions under the convention, covering areas such as invasive alien species, biosafety, gender equality and education.
Funding announcements have added to the summit's momentum, with new commitments from governments, philanthropic organizations and other partners.
The Executive Council of the China-initiated Kunming Biodiversity Fund has approved nine biodiversity conservation projects worth roughly 4.5 million dollars for developing nations, Dong Baotong, vice minister of China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment, said Monday.
China has contributed 400 million yuan (60 million dollars) to the fund, which supports biodiversity conservation in developing countries. Schomaker depicted the initiative as an agile instrument for channeling support to where it is needed.
Elsewhere, nine philanthropic organizations pledged 500 million dollars through 2030 for species recovery, while the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund secured over 60 million dollars in new pledges.
These achievements demonstrate that environmental multilateralism is continuing to deliver, even amid profound geopolitical shifts, said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
"Nature is not a luxury we protect when economies can afford it," said Andersen. "Nature is what makes economies possible."
OBSTACLES AHEAD
Securing new financial commitments is one thing; establishing a sustainable, long-term funding model for biodiversity conservation is another.
Despite the pledges announced in Yerevan, countries remain divided over who should contribute to international biodiversity finance, how much they should pay and how the funds should be allocated.
Other sticking points include reforming subsidies and incentives that harm nature, arrangements for indigenous peoples and local communities, and aligning biodiversity action with climate commitments and other international obligations.
Andersen said ministers are attending the conference's final week to help break the deadlock, particularly on resource mobilization and the global review.
"Financing the destruction of nature with 30 dollars against every dollar spent restoring it is like paying 30 people to tear down your house for every one hired to rebuild it," Schomaker said, framing the way forward around three priorities: accountability, alignment and acceleration.
According to Schomaker, "accountability" means identifying where countries are falling short through national reporting and scientific evidence, while "acceleration" means stepping up efforts to meet the framework's 2030 targets. "Alignment" may prove the hardest part, requiring governments to ensure that public budgets, private investment, economic policies and financial incentives reinforce rather than undermine biodiversity objectives.
The private sector is already pressing for change. More than 130 businesses and financial institutions have called for faster reform of incentives harmful to biodiversity.
Yet, for companies and investors, uncertainty remains over how global biodiversity targets will translate into national regulations, investment requirements and standards for measuring conservation results. Without clearer and more consistent rules, even a growing willingness to invest in nature may struggle to produce results at scale.
Meanwhile, the environmental pressures driving the negotiations are intensifying. UNEP's latest Emissions Gap Report warns that global warming could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius this century under current policies, with potentially severe consequences for ecosystems and biodiversity.
The United Nations' State of Biodiversity Action report, released ahead of COP17, found that fewer than half of the national biodiversity targets assessed by countries were on track.
Against this backdrop, much now hinges on the proposed "Yerevan Pathway," a document that identifies measurable priorities to address gaps in implementing global biodiversity targets over the next two years.
The conference has already shown that multilateral cooperation can deliver decisions and mobilize resources. Whether it can also resolve the harder questions of financing and implementation will be the real test of its success.
"COP17 will be judged by the long-term results we achieve together after the conference, rather than the number of statements made in Yerevan," said Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Sixteen years of drills to secure three minutes to safety at rural Chinese school
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:30:25 CST
12:30:25 KST

XINING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Seven-year-old Tenzin Wangso was curled up on his dormitory bed, too frightened to move, when his math teacher Karma Tenzin found him.
The teacher grabbed a quilt, wrapped it around the boy and carried him downstairs to the playground. He then rushed back into the building to make sure no children had been left behind.
A 7.0-magnitude earthquake had struck Baqen County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. on Oct. 22, sending strong tremors through neighboring Jieduo Township of Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in Qinghai Province in northwest China. Most of the 120 boarding students at the township's rural boarding school were already asleep when the quake hit.
Within about three minutes after the quake struck, all 120 had reached the playground, according to the school's surveillance footage. None was injured.
The school, more than 4,200 meters above sea level on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, had been practicing for such an emergency for 16 years.
Chime Tsering, principal of Jieduo Township Central Boarding School, still remembers the morning of April 14, 2010.
He had arrived as vice principal just a month earlier. Back then, the school consisted of two rows of single-story buildings, one for classrooms and the other for dormitories.
When a 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Yushu that morning, teachers and students were attending morning study sessions. Nearly 2,700 people died across the region.
"We had no experience dealing with an earthquake. Everyone was terrified," Chime Tsering recalled.
Teachers and students made it to the playground. Subsequent inspections found cracks in both buildings, which were later demolished and rebuilt.
This experience prompted the school to rethink its emergency procedures. As local education authorities called for more earthquake drills, Chime Tsering and his colleagues began working out how to get students to safety.
At first, they simply designated evacuation routes. Early drills took six or seven minutes. As teachers identified problems and revised the procedures, that duration fell to three or four minutes, and eventually to under three.
They also began holding drills at different times of day, including at night, when children would have to be woken and guided out of their dormitories.
Teachers were given specific responsibilities: waking students, directing them at stairwells and guiding them through exits.
The school now holds emergency drills at least once a month, covering both earthquakes and fires, with two or three nighttime exercises each semester. Its most recent earthquake drill was held roughly two weeks before the Oct. 22 quake.
The dormitory building has two designated evacuation routes and the teaching building has three. Each teacher is also assigned a group of 13 students to look after in daily school life, as well as specific rooms or classes to oversee during emergencies.
Karma Tenzin, who has taught math at the school for three years, was grading homework when the tremors began.
"The ground was shaking violently, and the tables and chairs were moving," he said. It was the strongest earthquake he had felt in recent years.
He and other teachers headed for the student dormitories.
Karma Tenzin was responsible for checking five rooms in the boys' dormitory. Moving from one room to the next, he was most worried about younger pupils, who might be slow to react or fall during the evacuation.
Among them was Tenzin Wangso, the first-grader he carried to safety. The boy had started school only in September.
Another teacher, Pema Wanggyal, also carried a first-grader out of the building.
On the playground, children gathered in coats and quilts while teachers checked attendance and comforted those who were frightened.
The school put up temporary tents that night. Parents began collecting their children the next day.
Most of the school buildings had been rebuilt after the 2010 earthquake. They remained largely intact, although fine cracks appeared in some walls.
"Only through repeated practice can we stay calm when something really happens and protect every child," Chime Tsering said.
The school has more than 170 students, most of them children of local herding families. Many live in remote pastoral areas where mobile phone reception is unreliable.
With in-person classes temporarily suspended, teachers began visiting students' homes on Oct. 25 to inform parents of the arrangements and find out whether the children had the equipment and internet access needed for online lessons.
"We have to visit families one by one," Karma Tenzin noted. "We also need to understand their circumstances before deciding how online teaching can be arranged."
For him, the greatest relief was that the drills had worked when they were needed, and that every child had come through the earthquake unharmed. ■

====================================================================================================

Ozempic was a game changer. Now scientists have another candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:29:28 UTC
12:29:28 KST

Ozempic was a game changer. Now scientists have another candidate
The drug, Orzeyful (oveporexton), developed by Japan-based pharmaceutical company Takeda, received regulatory approval in August for a type of narcolepsy. It belongs to a class of medicines called orexin agonists, which mimic the effects of orexins, brain chemicals that help maintain wakefulness.
Scientists believe these drugs could have a broader impact on medicine, potentially following a path similar to GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic. Initially developed to treat diabetes, GLP-1 medicines later gained wider use for weight management and other conditions.
Orexins influence several brain functions, including sleep, appetite, mood, memory and attention. Researchers are now investigating whether drugs that activate orexin receptors could help treat conditions beyond narcolepsy.
How orexin drugs work
Scientists discovered orexins independently in the 1990s. Early research linked these brain chemicals to appetite, but experiments revealed a more important role in regulating wakefulness.
Researchers found that blocking orexin signals in animals could trigger sudden muscle weakness resembling cataplexy, a hallmark of narcolepsy type 1. Further studies showed that people with this form of narcolepsy often lose most of the brain cells that produce orexins.
These findings helped scientists understand why the condition develops and suggested a way to address its underlying cause.
Unlike existing treatments that mainly manage symptoms, orexin agonists activate the receptors through which orexins work. Researchers hope this approach will help restore more stable wakefulness.
Takeda began investigating the drugs in the late 2000s. An early candidate, TAK-925, showed promising results in animal studies and later human trials. The research eventually contributed to the development of Orzeyful.
People who took the drug during clinical trials reported a striking improvement in alertness, according to Emmanuel Mignot, a Stanford University sleep medicine specialist who led Takeda's late-stage trials.
Beyond narcolepsy
The commercial potential extends beyond the relatively small population of people with narcolepsy. The condition affects an estimated three million people worldwide, although many cases may remain undiagnosed.
Researchers at Alkermes are investigating whether orexin agonists can improve attention and alertness by acting on the brain systems that regulate wakefulness.
In September, the company released preliminary results from an early-stage study involving 50 adults with moderate to severe ADHD symptoms. Participants receiving the highest dose experienced a reduction in symptoms to mild levels after two weeks. The company reported that the drug was generally well tolerated, with no serious treatment-related adverse events.
Takeda has not started a dedicated ADHD trial, but further analysis of its narcolepsy research found improvements in participants' memory and executive function.
Scientists are also exploring whether orexin agonists could reduce fatigue associated with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's disease.

Iran war has cost $47 billion, U.S. military says
The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.
The bulk of the war's price tag is the cost of replacing expended munitions, which CENTCOM pegged at around $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. The military also tallied $6.1 billion to replace lost equipment and around $11.9 billion in incremental costs like support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which were targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.
By comparison, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers three months ago the war had cost around $37.5 billion, not including damaged U.S. bases.
The Congressional Budget Office said last month the war could cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, in part due to the need to replace interceptor missiles to defend against Iranian attacks. That cost could rise during tit-for-tat exchanges between the U.S. and Iran, which were common over the summer but have been quiet in recent weeks.
CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
The Iran war will enter its ninth month this week, and the conflict's future is unclear. President Trump has suggested he might restart hostilities with Iran after next month's midterm elections unless Iran agrees to a deal. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," he told supporters during a rally in Florida last week.
The Pentagon's inspector general said last month the U.S. is facing "strategic inventory shortfalls" due to the number of munitions expended during the war, leading the Defense Department to work to speed up production. The Trump administration has argued the military isn't facing shortages, with Mr. Trump saying in early September, "we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use."
The administration asked Congress to approve tens of billions of dollars in supplemental military funding earlier this year, in part due to the Iran war. That request has not yet passed, and Democrats have pressed Hegseth for a more detailed accounting of the war's cost.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned last week that the US would suffer “an even greater strategic failure” if it opts for renewed military action. State-run broadcaster Press TV, citing a senior Iranian official, reported on Tuesday that Tehran is prepared for an all-out war “without any limitations.”
The prospect of renewed fighting comes amid concerns about dwindling US missile interceptor stockpiles, which Trump has dismissed, insisting that the military has sufficient munitions.
The war remains deeply unpopular among Americans. A Fox News poll published in September found that 71% of registered voters believed the Trump administration lacked a clear strategy for ending the conflict, and 60% said attacking Iran was a mistake. According to a Pew Research Center survey published earlier this month, 65% disapprove of Trump’s handling of operations against Iran, compared with 33% who approve.

Taiwan vaccination uptake rises after health coin program launches

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:13:07 UTC
12:13:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday that the health coin incentive program has coincided with increased vaccination against flu, COVID-19, and pneumococcal disease since launching on Oct. 1.
The program awards adults aged 18 and older 450 health coins for flu vaccination, 900 for COVID-19 vaccination, and 600 for pneumococcal vaccination, whether publicly or privately funded, per a press release. One coin is worth NT$1 (US$0.03) and can be redeemed under the program's rules.
The CDC said that, as of Oct. 26, about 2.725 million publicly funded flu vaccine doses had been administered to adults, up approximately 7% from the same period last year. Another 288,000 doses were privately funded, up about 70%.
For COVID-19, approximately 1.176 million publicly funded doses had been administered to adults, up 35% year over year.
Pneumococcal vaccinations also increased. About 104,000 publicly funded doses and 3,000 privately funded doses were administered to adults, representing 3.5 times and 2.4 times the respective totals during the 26 days before the incentive program began.
The CDC also reported that influenza is circulating widely, with influenza A accounting for most infections and the H1N1 subtype making up 93.4% of detected flu viruses.
During the 2026-27 flu season, Taiwan had recorded 391 severe cases and 57 deaths as of Oct. 26. Of the severe cases, 380 involved H1N1, nine involved untyped influenza A, and two involved influenza B.
Of the deaths, 54 involved H1N1 and three involved untyped influenza A, per the press release.
The second phase of publicly funded flu and COVID-19 vaccinations for adults aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic conditions is scheduled to begin Nov. 2. Eligible people can receive vaccinations at contracted medical facilities or community vaccination stations organized by local health bureaus.
As temperatures cool, the CDC urged the public to get vaccinated and maintain good hygiene, including washing hands frequently, wearing masks when appropriate, and staying home when sick.
People experiencing warning signs such as shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, bloody sputum, chest pain, altered consciousness, or low blood pressure should seek medical attention promptly. Doctors can assess whether antiviral treatment is appropriate.

Jordan’s strikes on Syria killed at least seven people in Deraa and Suwayda, including five members of the same family, three of whom were children. Syria’s Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management said its teams had responded to attacks at four sites.

Australia providing 'extraordinary' support to ICC staff amid Trump sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:10:07 UTC
12:10:07 KST

Australia and other countries supporting ICC amid Trump sanctions
In short:
Australia and other countries are supporting International Criminal Court staff amid ongoing sanctions by the Trump administration, a senior court official says.
ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said the organisation had received help publicly and through "quiet diplomacy behind closed doors".
She said the ICC was determined to protect staff from the financial implications of US sanctions.
A top International Criminal Court (ICC) official says Australia and other countries are providing "extraordinary" support to help protect the court's staff from the Trump administration's latest sanctions assault, while vowing that the court will not be deterred from pressing on with its work.
ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan, a senior court official who has already been personally sanctioned by the US, is visiting Canberra and Brisbane this week for talks with jurists and officials from across Australia and the Pacific.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has labelled the ICC a "rogue court" and has vowed to demolish it "brick by brick".
The Trump administration has rolled out successive waves of sanctions against the court, including new institutional sanctions designed to cripple the ICC by cutting it off from financial and support services.
The latest sanctions will freeze the court's assets in the US, as well as block financial transactions and IT agreements the ICC has with US companies.
Time to step up
Ms Khan told the ABC that while the sanctions had already created some difficulties, the ICC was heartened that many countries had lent support — some in public and others via "quiet diplomacy behind closed doors".
"I think this is the time when states must step up and support this process [of multilateralism] and support the institutions which are under attack," Ms Khan said.
The deputy prosecutor said the court was determined to protect its staff from the financial impacts of the move, and was adopting new systems to circumvent the sanctions and allow it to keep running.
"We have been working very hard to insulate the court as well as ensuring that our work continues," she said.
"Our main priority is that we continue to serve the victims who come to the court, telling us their stories and wanting their voices to be heard."
The ICC drew furious condemnation from the US and Israel when it announced it would pursue Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
More recently it unsealed arrest warrants for several major Taliban leaders in Afghanistan for their policies persecuting women and girls.
Sanctions effect hard to predict
The latest wave of sanctions announced by the Trump administration on October 9 is meant to target the ICC rather than the large cohort of lawyers and staff who work for it.
The measures include a 180-day grace period before they are fully implemented.
But Ms Khan said the impact of sanctions was unpredictable and the court could not know at this stage how many of its staff might struggle with banking or other services as a result.
"We don't know which institutions will over-comply," she said.
The Australian government copped criticism from international lawyers who accused it of moving "sluggishly" after it joined a statement criticising the most recent sanctions about three days after it was first issued.
But Ms Khan praised the response from Canberra, saying its public statement of support behind the court was valuable.
She said Australian officials in the Netherlands had provided "visible" and "really satisfactory" help to Australians working for the court, including on ensuring they could keep accessing banking and financial services.
The deputy prosecutor said the ICC and other multilateral institutions had to hold the line in the face of growing pressure from the Trump administration and other international forces.
"Multilateralism gives everyone a voice," she said.
"Any attempt … to reverse all the work that has gone behind the rules-based order must be a negative step for the world, and the international community."
She said the court had enormous relevance to the Pacific, pointing to a 2024 proposal by Vanuatu, co-sponsored by Fiji and Samoa, calling for ecocide to be recognised as an independent international crime.

The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:02:38 UTC
12:02:38 KST

The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Yale School of Medicine
- Summary:
- A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.
- Share:
A major new study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.
Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces showed lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.
James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.
To gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.
"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.
How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity
McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.
"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland says.
The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.
During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.
They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.
The results showed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.
"The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," says first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.
The researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.
"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.
Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought
Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers new insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.
Recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.
Much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.
By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.
"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland says.
What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support
The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.
Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.
An ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.
"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.
Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.
However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.
"Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland says. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people."
New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis
Another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Currently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.
Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.
The newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.
Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.
"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland says.

Materials provided by Yale School of Medicine. Original written by Isabella Backman. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jason W. Griffin, Alan H. Gerber, Kaylee Litson, Susan Faja, Shafali Jeste, Natalia Kleinhans, Geraldine Dawson, Adam Naples, April R. Levin, Sara Jane Webb, Frederick Shic, Catherine Sugar, James Dziura, James C. McPartland. Decoding the temporal dynamics of face-specific neural representations in autism. Nature Mental Health, 2026; 4 (7): 1109 DOI: 10.1038/s44220-026-00672-y

In brief
- Core inflation rose faster than expected, adding to pressure on the Reserve Bank.
- Fresh inflation data has fuelled expectations of another interest rate hike.
Core inflation climbed 1 per cent in Australia over the quarter, with the Reserve Bank governor warning underlying inflation is still too high.
The September quarter increase in the trimmed mean was in line with economists' expectations but exceeded the central bank's forecast of a 0.8 per cent increase.
On an annualised basis, the trimmed mean — a measure of underlying inflation that removes the biggest price swings — rose 3.6 per cent.
Headline inflation was hotter than expected by the market, at 1.3 per cent over the quarter.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged inflation is persisting "longer than anyone would like" and citing the war in the Middle East as a major factor.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Markets had upped their bets for a November hike after comments in the past week by the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, and chief economist Sarah Hunter, indicating that inflation remained too high.
At the same time as the data was published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, RBA governor Michele Bullock was appearing alongside Hauser, Hunter and other top officials at a Senate estimates hearing.
Elevated underlying inflationary pressures were a sign that the labour market was still tight, Bullock said.
"The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week," she said.
"We'll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time."
Monthly headline inflation rose 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from 4 per cent in the 12 months to August.
"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," said Rachael McCririck, ABS head of price statistics.
Transport was the second largest contributor, rising by 8.7 per cent annually, due to higher fuel costs.
Fuel and the war in the Middle East
Speaking to press in Canberra, Treasurer Jim Chalmers issued a small mea culpa.
"We accept our part in the fight against inflation," Chalmers said.
"We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings and when it comes to managing the budget in a responsible way in the face of this inflation challenge, which is persisting longer than anyone would like."
Chalmers again blamed rising inflation on higher fuel prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East.
"This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living, and for inflation right around the world," he said.
"The point that [Treasury] secretary [Jenny] Wilkinson made today and the point that governor Bullock made today is that global energy prices are much higher than have been assumed. And we know what's driving that."
Speaking to reporters after Chalmers' conference, Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said Australian families need the government to get inflation under control.
"There will be a lot of households, family, sitting around the kitchen tables of the nation figuring out — what is left to cut? Small business owners who will take this inflation data as a kick directly at their future opportunity and their hope."

US national debt hits record high of over $40.5 trillion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:00:01 UTC
12:00:01 KST

WASHINGTON, October 28. /TASS/. The US national debt has surpassed a record $40.5 trillion, according to US Treasury Department data analyzed by TASS.
According to figures published by the department, US sovereign debt stood at $40.52 trillion as of October 26, an all-time high. The debt exceeded $38 trillion in October last year and crossed the $40 trillion mark in August this year, having increased by $20 trillion in less than a decade.
According to estimates by the Peterson Institute for International Economics, the country’s debt could reach $50 trillion in six years unless government spending or taxation is reformed.

EU Public Prosecutor’s Office will be ‘killed softly for doing its job’ says outgoing chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

EU Public Prosecutor’s Office will be ‘killed softly for doing its job’ says outgoing chief
In an exclusive interview with POLITICO to mark the end of her seven year tenure, Laura Codruța Kövesi spoke frankly about the problems facing the EPPO.
A budgetary squeeze and bureaucratic inertia threaten the future of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, its top official told POLITICO.
In a wide-ranging interview, Laura Codruța Kövesi, who wraps up her seven-year tenure on Friday, said: “As I leave my office, I think of this famous Danish TV show Borgen. There is a very famous saying there: ‘In Brussels, no one can hear you scream,’ and unfortunately, this is true,” she said, in a nod to the Ridley Scott blockbuster Alien.
“I am concerned that the EPPO is going to be killed softly because it’s doing its job,” she added in blunt remarks about justice in Europe.
Advertisement
Kövesi also discussed her interactions with the EU institutions, Greece’s farm subsidy scandal and questions of national sovereignty in the interview, which took place via video call from her office in Luxembourg.
This transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Your term concludes this week, so what were the main difficulties during your term and what could should happen in a different way by your successor?
When I was appointed, I promised that I would build an efficient, strong and independent institution, which citizens will trust. I think we managed, together with my colleagues, to do this to a large extent. I’m aware that we didn’t succeed in everything, but no one can dispute that we did a good job.
The most important question now is whether this continues. I listened to all the candidates for the European Chief Prosecutor and I was really worried, because one candidate presented himself saying that his project was to normalize EPPO. For someone like me, growing up during communism, this is very threatening. Another candidate, even worse, spoke about maintaining equal distance between the prosecution office and all the political parties. But how will this be compatible with an independent office?
After the first years of activity, we have results that only few people expected. We have a lot of reactions, and I think we have proved the law is equal for everybody. Now the key challenge for the EPPO and especially for my successor will be to keep the EPPO independent and credible.
Advertisement
What has surprised you most during those this term?
The last seven years was the toughest job that I have ever had. I didn’t have a lot of surprises. But I have to tell you about the attacks or attempts to undermine our independence. The most blatant attempt to intimidate EPPO happened in Greece, where we had this issue with the renewal of the European delegated prosecutors.
The main challenge of the EPPO will be this one: the revision of regulation. It is clear that this will show who is a true friend of an independent judiciary.
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office’s logo is seen at its headquarters in Luxembourg on June 1, 2021. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images
The second example was an attack against our credibility. Everybody knows that we are drowning under work, and I understand that there are many priorities, but we have to see whether this is real or is this just a pretext. Here the surprise comes from Poland. We agreed that we need 24 European delegated prosecutors. The expectations were huge, and our credibility is at stake. In this moment, we have only 15. So how can we be credible in Poland? In Hungary, also, we explained exactly what budget we need to do our job, but the Commission proposed half of what we need.
These are few examples how you can, if you want, destroy the credibility of an institution. As I leave my office, I think of this famous Danish TV show Borgen. There is a very famous saying there: “In Brussels, no one can hear you scream,” and unfortunately, this is true. I am concerned that the EPPO is going to be killed softly because it’s doing its job.
You mentioned pressure from local governments, particularly from Greece and Poland. Was there any support from the EU institutions?
Advertisement
We had support of different stakeholders in some cases, but when I say that I’m concerned that EPPO is going to be killed softly for doing its job, I have three main reasons. It’s easy, it’s a pattern. If you want to destroy an institution, you can do three things, that are happening now. First, you are underfunded. On paper we should have 230 European delegated prosecutors, and we have money only for 180. We have money for only one third of what security service costs, and I would have endless examples.
Second, a lot of delays. Since 2021, we said that the revision of the EPPO regulation has to start earlier. It’s delayed. Thirdly, I have learned that here everything is complicated — and I thought that Romania is complicated. To give you an example, there are these endless discussions about anti-fraud architecture. We discovered a new continent of crime, and we see the criminal organizations are growing, defrauding the EU budget and national budgets. In the middle of this, should be the fight against organized criminality. Instead, we have endless discussion about how to complicate the life of the prosecutors, and we discuss a lot about this joint intake registry. If there is money to have this new registry electronically, how is it possible that money doesn’t exist for what we really need?
Do you feel that you have managed to shake things up? Have people or institutions started behaving differently?
A lot of changes happened due to the EPPO. The level of detection increased in most of the member states, the level of successful cases increased, and obviously the protection of the EU budget is higher with the EPPO. But still, there are things that are not working the way they should be.
If you had the chance to do it all over again, what is the main thing that you would do differently?
Nothing. I would do the same things, but maybe the others should change their behavior. I thought that there is a big difference between Brussels and what I saw in Romania. But in Romania, or other member states, people are used to work with prosecutors, they know what the prosecutors are doing.
Advertisement
In Brussels, sometimes at EU level, they think that they are above the law, and this for me is a problem. In Romania, or other member states, if you are called in for a statement, you show up, because you know that you have to do this. Here, sometimes there is this feeling that you are above the prosecutors, you are above the law, and you don’t come.
Some prosecutors that could be politically motivated, are in a position to delay the outcome of cases, postpone hearings, meetings. Have you experienced that in some countries more than others?
All our European delegated prosecutors are very independent, and our agenda is not based on any electoral campaign or other interests than what is written in our regulation. There are some cases that can be delayed, but this is not because the prosecutors do not want to do their job.
EU flags fly outside the European Commission’s Berlaymont building in Brussels on Feb. 17, 2025. | Thierry Monasse/Getty Images
Some politicians think that they are above the law, and if you are called in for a statement, you have to come, and it’s not all the time the same understanding. So, this is an example in which the prosecutors cannot finalize the cases.
Do you refer to Pfizergate?
I will not comment anything on specific investigations.
Advertisement
You have noted in your reports that the reporting rate from EU institutions has been minimal. Are there instances where they saw corruption cases and they haven’t reported it back?
When I started, I heard that we are a clean country, and we don’t have corruption. And I said many times that there is no clean country. But with the EPPO, this has changed a lot.
But I will not be shy to tell you, that especially when important people are involved in the investigation — be it high-profile politicians or rich people who are connected to the political class — we have difficulties in exercising our competence because we still have this issue of conflict of competences.
Unfortunately, we witness situations in which, when we have opened an investigation and when we were ready to have different measures in our investigation, suddenly on national level, a case with the same object was opened, and the general prosecutor decided that we are not competent to investigate the case. And this is something that affects the capabilities and the capacity of EPPO to make investigations.
In several countries the argument against cooperating with the EPPO is that they would be eliminating their country’s sovereignty. How do you respond to that?
Is it better to have the sovereignty of criminals? Because this is what you have to put in balance. The criminal organizations in Europe are not national anymore, and they take advantage of this fragmentation that exists.
Advertisement
We are still applying the national legislation; we are still going in front of the national court. I don’t think you lose your sovereignty; you win more protection and more security for your citizens. Is it better to let the criminals operate freely, to take advantage of the fragmentation, to take advantage that no one has a helicopter view to see how they operate on the entire territory of the EU?
In Greece some politicians say that they could simply stop working with the EPPO. Can a country that joined the EPPO simply pull out?
Well, I don’t know if they want to go out of the European Union or not, but to go out from EPPO, it’s almost impossible. These kinds of comments don’t do anything else than to prove exactly what I said. There will be attempts to kill the EPPO because we do our job.
Farmers participate in a protest over delays in European compensation payments, in Nikaia, Greece on Dec. 4, 2025. | Thanasis Kaliakoudas/SOOC/AFP via Getty Images
Some politicians speak about an independent and efficient judiciary, until you touch them and until you go close to their inner circle. In that moment, the prosecutors are abusive, they have a political agenda, they are not needed. After that, they start to try to diminish your competence, to let you without money, to dismantle the specialized police.
There are currently cases being investigated in several countries involving political figures or parties, like the OPEKEPE farm scandal in Greece or in France. These countries have elections soon and the EPPO is criticized for being politically motivated. How do you make sure that there is an outcome in all these cases that doesn’t coincide with elections?
You mentioned OPEKEPE, we just finalized some indictments there. The cases are in court. But all the noise was created to blame EPPO that we play politics instead of discussing what happened in reality. You have politicians who want to cover the discussion, try to undermine the credibility of EPPO. You come and you create a smoke. Oh, we will have elections. Look what the EPPO is doing.
Advertisement
If you ask EPPO to abstain and to not do anything because there are elections in Europe, we will not work at all. And our job is not to check when the electoral campaign is, but to check if the honest farmers have access to EU money. Instead, the money was allocated to different people who pretended they are farmers and used the money to go in fancy trips and have luxurious cars, and the honest farmers didn’t get anything. I don’t see any links between what we did, our activity, our cases, and electoral campaigns. The only connection is when you have some unhappy politicians, they want to attack EPPO, and they try to intimidate and stop us from doing our job.
The integrity of the OPEKEPE investigation was questioned here in Greece after a case file was sent to Parliament for lifting the immunity of 11 MPs. Eventually, only four of these were sent to court, and there was criticism it was done hastily. Was something done wrong there?
No, nothing went wrong from our perspective. When we ask for the lifting the immunity, it’s not about the guilt. It’s just a condition to allow the prosecutors to make the investigation and to gather evidences.
What are your personal plans for the future?
Well, let’s not speak about my personal plans. Let’s focus on the EPPO. I will see after I finish my mandate.
