EU prosecutors still have questions for von der Leyen over Pfizergate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

EU prosecutors still have questions for von der Leyen over Pfizergate
Little demonstrable progress has been made on the EPPO’s probe into the Commission chief’s negotiations on Covid-19 vaccines with Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addresses a press conference after a visit to oversee the production of the Pfizer-BioNtech Covid-19 vaccine in Puurs, Belgium on April 23, 2021. | Pool photo by John Thys via AFP/Getty Images
To read the full Q&A with Laura Codruța Kövesi, click here.
ATHENS — Ursula von der Leyen has not yet provided an in-person statement to the European Public Prosecutor's Office for its investigation into the procurement of coronavirus vaccines, according to an individual involved in the effort who was granted anonymity to speak freely.
In 2024, EPPO took over the Belgian-led probe into alleged criminal wrongdoing in connection with vaccine negotiations between the European Commission chief and Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla. Prosecutors have been investigating von der Leyen for "interference in public functions, destruction of SMS, corruption and conflict of interest," according to legal documents seen by POLITICO.
Advertisement
Asked to respond to the assertion that von der Leyen has failed to provide a statement on the so-called Pfizergate affair, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said: "The Commission has demonstrably cooperated extensively with EPPO to clarify facts and assess events."
"This was always done on behalf of and with the full support of the President. The President has always been, and continues to be, very cooperative in answering to any open questions — within the limits of her duties and her availability as President of the Commission.”
In an interview with POLITICO, EPPO chief prosecutor Laura Codruța Kövesi, who wraps up her seven-year tenure on Friday, said she has on multiple occasions dealt with EU officials who refused to answer summons from her office. “Some politicians think that they are above the law,” she said. “If you are called in for a statement, you have to come.”
She added: "I will not be shy to tell you that especially when important people are involved in the investigation — be it high-profile politicians or rich people who are connected to the political class, we have difficulties in exercising our competence."
When asked whether von der Leyen was one of the officials in question, Kövesi said she wouldn't comment on specific investigations.
Killing EPPO softly
EPPO, set up in 2017 and operational since 2021, is tasked with rooting out crimes involving EU funds. As head of the organization, Kövesi said she has faced repeated attacks and attempts to undermine the institution and its work.
Advertisement
“As I leave my office, I think of this famous Danish TV show, Borgen. There is a very famous saying there: 'In Brussels, no one can hear you scream,' and unfortunately, this is true," she said, in a nod to the Ridley Scott blockbuster Alien. "I am concerned that the EPPO is going to be killed softly because it's doing its job."
Kövesi cited three main factors undermining the institution's work: chronic underfunding, delays in the revision of the organization's legal framework and the complexity of its bureaucratic architecture, which she said leads to "endless discussion about how to complicate the life of the prosecutors."
Asked what she would do differently if she could start over again, the chief prosecutor said she “would do the same things, but maybe the others should change their behavior," adding that the biggest challenge her successor, German prosecutor Andrés Ritter, will face is keeping EPPO “independent and credible.”
Greece’s 'blatant' intimidation
Kövesi said that during her tenure, “the most blatant attempt" to intimidate EPPO prosecutors was in Greece, which was hit by a farm funding scandal last year — leading to the resignation of ministers and deputy ministers. The cases of four MPs from the ruling New Democracy party are currently being heard in court. They all plead innocent.
Last May, EPPO sent a formal complaint to the Commission regarding moves by the Greek government to block EU prosecutors from investigating Greek lawmakers. It also complained about the Greek Supreme Judicial Council’s refusal to renew the mandate of European-delegated prosecutors for five years at EPPO's request. Kövesi warned that this could result in EU funding cuts for Greece under Article 16 of the EPPO Regulation.
The cooperation between EPPO and the Greek government has been difficult, with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis hinting at a political agenda by EPPO by complaining of "selective leaks."
Advertisement
“All the noise was created to blame EPPO that we play politics instead of discussing what happened in reality,” said Kövesi. “Some politicians speak about an independent and efficient judiciary, until you touch them and until you go close to their inner circle. In that moment, the prosecutors are abusive, they have a political agenda, they are not needed.”
Some Greek government officials have suggested that Greece could simply opt out of the EU institution, but Kövesi said this is “almost impossible.”
The chief prosecutor also raised concerns about the impact of budgetary restrictions on EPPO's work elsewhere in the bloc. The organization is currently setting up its operations in Hungary, which officially became a participating member of EPPO in August 2026 — but Kövesi is skeptical about how successful it will be.
“We explained exactly what we need to do our job, but the Commission proposed half of [the budget] we need,” she said, adding that EPPO's "credibility is at stake" in countries like Poland, where "expectations were huge" but the organization has not been able to deliver on its promises.
EPPO is also investigating the alleged misuse of more than €4 million by the Identity and Democracy group, a defunct political grouping in the European Parliament whose debts Patriots for Europe could be forced to repay. The latter group includes France’s far-right National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner ahead of France's 2027 presidential elections.
“If you ask EPPO to abstain and to not do anything because there are elections in Europe, we will not work at all,” said Kövesi.

Serbian opposition landslide exposes cost of EU’s bet on ousted Vučić
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian Progressive Party candidate for prime minister, delivers his concession speech in Belgrade on Oct. 25, 2026. | Pedja Milosavljevic/AFP via Getty Images
The opposition Student List’s landslide victory on Sunday ended Aleksandar Vučić’s 12-year run as the EU’s key interlocutor in Serbia. For more than a decade, every step of the candidate country’s accession process and trade negotiations had to pass through him.
“Aleksandar Vučić acted like the go-to person for everything while ignoring all the laws in the country, including the constitution,” Jugoslav Gašić, an assistant professor in medicine at several universities and soon-to-be MP, said in an interview.
Advertisement
When POLITICO reached him, Gašić was in the middle of grading student papers — a fitting snapshot of a new parliamentary majority made up largely of professors, doctors and other political novices.
The Student List won an outright parliamentary majority at the weekend: a stunning result for a leaderless movement born out of protests.
The party’s first order of business will be undoing much the legacy of Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), starting with reversing years of rule-of-law rollbacks. But it will also reset Serbia’s relationship with Brussels, which the Student List argues the former leader managed more as a transactional tool than a genuine path to EU membership.
“Ultimately, [Vučić] always represented his own interests and not the interests of Serbia,” said Gašić.
Representatives for the SNS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Even among Serbia’s most committed pro-Europeans, Brussels’ willingness to route all progress through Vučić personally has left a bitter aftertaste.
Advertisement
“The key lesson that should be drawn from the case of Serbia is that the EU can very easily lose credibility and integrity if it ignores the causes of democratic backsliding in a country,” said Srdjan Majstorović, chairman of the governing board of the European Policy Center (CEP), a think tank.
According to CEP data published earlier this year, as many 41.6% of citizens believe the EU is more interested in pursuing its own political and economic interests in the region than improving the state of democracy and the rule of law in the country.
For years, anytime non-governmental organizations, journalists or activists argued that Brussels should try to include other voices in the EU negotiation process, they were told “that there was no alternative to the regime in Serbia,” Majstorović continued.
Ilija Srdanovic, the first person on the Student’s List, celebrates at the Student’s List headquarters in Belgrade after Aleksandar Vučić conceded the elections. | Andrej Ivanov/Getty Images
The Student List’s election program casts the EU as Serbia’s most important economic partner and pledged to deepen Belgrade’s existing strategic partnerships with EU members such as Greece, Italy, Hungary and France, while seeking closer bilateral ties with other European capitals.
It does not, however, explicitly name EU membership as an immediate goal.
Gašić wouldn’t be drawn on concrete aims for the Serbia-EU relationship, but said: “We don’t want to be cut off by Europe. We don’t want to be an isolated island.”
Advertisement
“I respect how well-ordered they are, the rule of law and democratic principles,” he added. “Yet I think we need to reset our priorities with the EU, where we consider Serbia’s interests first. A one-sided approach doesn’t foster long-term cooperation.”
The Student List grew out of a mass protest movement sparked by a 2024 railway station roof collapse that killed 16 people. Students blamed the deaths on corruption in state construction contracts and began blockading universities, and within months the protests had swelled into the largest Serbia had seen in decades.
Brussels’ response was muted as students marched across the country, with EU officials largely avoided criticizing Vučić directly. EU flags were conspicuously absent from the demonstrations.
The European Commission didn’t respond to a request for comment for this article.
“The Commission must first restore its long-lost credibility after years of propping up Vučić,” said Djordje Bojović, a foreign policy advisor for Greens in the European Parliament.
He said that Serbia has long been demonized and struggled to reinvent its image since the 1990s, an image “only further cemented by Vučić’s repressive authoritarianism.”
Advertisement
Despite those concerns, Serbia’s economic ties with Europe flourished during Vučić’s time in power, with the country becoming one of the region’s leading destinations for foreign investment.
Under Vučić, Serbia went from about €750 million in foreign direct investment in 2012 to more than €30 billion over the following decade, more than the rest of the Western Balkans combined.
In Brussels, figures such as Bojović and representatives of the opposition parties would plead with institutions such as the Parliament and the Commission to meet with them or take their concerns seriously.
“Vučić had convinced all of them that the opposition is not worth talking to and that they’re not credible,” Bojović said.
Now, with SNS firmly relegated to the opposition, Brussels will need to rethink how it works with Serbia. To many Serbians, the EU has 12 years of looking the other way to answer for first.

Tanzania: Authorities weaponize counterterrorism laws to restrict civic space amid pervasive impunity over violent election crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Tanzanian authorities have failed to hold anyone accountable for the violence security forces inflicted on protesters, which left hundreds of people dead and thousands of others injured in the wake of the 2025 general election, Amnesty International said on the first anniversary of the crackdown.
Instead of delivering justice and accountability, authorities have withheld a Commission of Inquiry report from the public and intensified attacks on civic space through the abuse of counterterrorism laws.
Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters. In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponizing counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear,”
Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa
The organization has documented how, over the past year, security agencies have committed human rights violations with impunity against government critics, opposition supporters, media organizations, and dissenting members of the ruling party. These include acts that may amount to torture or other ill-treatment, arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, abductions, and severe restrictions of freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
“Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters. In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponizing counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.
Although the Commission of Inquiry report into the 2025 election-related killings was handed over to President Samia Suluhu in April 2026, it has yet to be made public. She has repeatedly alleged that the post-election protests were funded by foreign actors in a bid to overthrow the government.
In August 2026, President Suluhu inaugurated another Commission of Inquiry to identify those who planned, funded, coordinated, or executed the violence, as well as investigate the excessive use of force and the whereabouts of missing persons.
“President Suluhu’s continued refusal to release the Commission of Inquiry report not only entrenches a culture of secrecy, but it also perpetuates impunity,” said Tigere Chagutah.
“It is imperative that this new commission comprehensively address the role of security forces in the election-related crackdown. Its investigations must be thorough, independent, impartial, and transparent. On concluding its mandate, it must ensure its findings are made public immediately.”
President Suluhu’s continued refusal to release the Commission of Inquiry report not only entrenches a culture of secrecy, but it also perpetuates impunity.
Tigere Chagutah
Between 3 and 17 September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 17 people, including victims of arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances and abductions, as well as journalists, opposition officials, lawyers, and friends and relatives of the victims of the October 2025 election-related crackdown. Amnesty International also verified charge sheets for those arbitrarily arrested and charged with terrorism in different parts of the country.
Tanzanian authorities did not respond to Amnesty’s request for comment.
Abductions, enforced disappearances and torture or other ill-treatment
Amnesty International documented numerous cases of individuals being abducted by suspected state security officers, held incommunicado, and later charged in court. Some of them remain missing.
Among them is Ibrahim Myovella, a youth leader from the opposition party CHADEMA. He went missing alongside two friends on 18 April 2026, after reporting to Central Iringa police station as per their bail conditions following allegations of involvement in the October 2025 protests. The authorities deny ever holding them.
Also missing is Mashaka Nestory Kindikwa, 37, a former official of the ruling Chama cha Mapinduzi (CCM) who was abducted from his home and led away blindfolded by seven men believed to be security officers on 25 June 2026. The police have denied holding him.
On 20 May 2026, David Djumbe, personal assistant to opposition leader Tundu Lissu, was abducted near his Dar es Salaam home by people believed to be state security officers and subjected to severe beatings which may amount to torture or other ill-treatment. He escaped. Police denied involvement and said they had opened an investigation, but there has been no update on progress or findings.
Stefano Patrick*, 26, who expressed support for protests on Saba Saba Day, a national public holiday commemorating the pivotal moment in Tanzania’s struggle for independence, was arbitrarily arrested on 24 July in Dar es Salaam, and detained for 47 days without being charged in court. He told Amnesty International that during his detention, he was tortured and beaten, while also denied food and water.
He said his interrogators demanded to know who was funding the protests: “I was blindfolded… but I could hear some people crying in the next room. Some officers came to me and said, ‘Can you hear how your friends are crying, if you don’t cooperate, we will kill you,’.
“On the first day, they didn’t give me food. When I asked for water, they urinated on my blindfolded face and said ‘that is the price for those of you opening your mouths to make noise’.
I was blindfolded… but I could hear some people crying in the next room. Some officers came to me and said, ‘Can you hear how your friends are crying, if you don’t cooperate, we will kill you.
Stefano Patrick*
“On the second day, I was taken to Gogoni police station where they beat your legs until they get numb but then insist that you must stand. I saw another person’s legs broken at the police station. Even though I was in trouble, I felt pity for what other people were going through”.
Misuse of counterterrorism laws to target critics
Amnesty International documented the frequent abuse of counterterrorism laws to target opposition supporters and government critics. On 9 July 2026, police spokesman David Misime said 130 people had been arrested for allegedly organizing meetings and preparing and circulating messages that encouraged criminal acts aimed at destabilizing the country. Of these, at least 64 were charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, an unbailable offence.
In April 2026, Pendo Jonas Kileo went missing. For two months, the family of the CHADEMA member from Temeke, did not know of her whereabouts. On 27 July, they learned that alongside another CHADEMA member, Kileo had been charged in Temeke District Court with conspiracy to commit terrorist acts as well as participating in terrorist meetings between September 2025 and July 2026.
On 4 July 2026, police arbitrarily arrested university students and CHADEMA student-body members Noah Mwalwange, Gwamaka Mboka, Augustino Wasinyo and Rojas Mpani. They were held at Mbeya Central Police Station until 23 July, when they were charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. A source familiar with their case said they were denied access to lawyers, beaten with batons during interrogation, stripped, and forced to record confessions and name CHADEMA leaders as their financiers.
By resorting to terrorism-related charges against its perceived critics, the Tanzanian government is sending a chilling message that it won’t stop at anything in its effort to repress any and all dissenting opinions.
Tigere Chagutah
On 8 July 2026, Melkisedek Kaijage, a political science lecturer at the University of Dodoma, was arrested on allegations of inciting people to participate in Saba Saba protests. He was detained for 17 days on allegations of engaging in sedition, before the charges were later changed to terrorism. These were eventually dropped and he was released on 10 September but must report to the police in Dodoma every month for a year.
In Iringa, three CHADEMA members were arrested ahead of the July 2026 Saba Saba protests. During their three-week detention, they said police told them to sign a pre-written statement before receiving bail. Instead of being bailed, they were taken to court and charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
“By resorting to terrorism-related charges against its perceived critics, the Tanzanian government is sending a chilling message that it won’t stop at anything in its effort to repress any and all dissenting opinions,” said Tigere Chagutah.
“The authorities must end the abuse of counterterrorism laws to stifle freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. They must immediately and unconditionally drop all terrorism charges against those unjustly detained and end harassment of individuals solely for peacefully exercising their human rights.”
Restriction of civic space and violations of press freedom
Over the last year, authorities have adopted numerous tactics to narrow civic space.
They have restricted access to social media sites, such as Club House and X, and deployed large numbers of security forces to intimidate protesters ahead of planned demonstrations on 9 December 2025 and 7 July 2026. On 26 June 2026, the home affairs minister banned political rallies and mass gatherings, further stifling freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
In February 2026, the Chief Justice issued an order barring lawyers from speaking to the media on cases before the court, violating the rights of lawyers representing their clients, as well as the rights of the media to seek, receive and share information.
Media freedom has also come under increasing and unwarranted pressure.
The authorities must revoke the suspension of Mwanahalisi newspaper, restore access to banned social media platforms, and end censorship of online content. They must also ensure that media outlets are free to operate independently, and that journalists can carry out their legitimate work without fear of reprisals.
Tigere Chagutah
On 2 April 2026, the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA) suspended the online-broadcast licence of Jambo Online TV for 90 days, over content TCRA called unverified and misleading concerning the Commission of Inquiry into the October 2025 general-election unrest. Jambo TV’s licence was reinstated and the station returned to air on 3 July 2026, after the 90-day suspension lapsed.
On 19 August 2026, the Information Services Department suspended Mwanahalisi newspaper’s publishing and distribution licence for six months, over a report that Vice-President Emmanuel Nchimbi had rejected calls to resign.
“The authorities must revoke the suspension of Mwanahalisi newspaper, restore access to banned social media platforms, and end censorship of online content. They must also ensure that media outlets are free to operate independently, and that journalists can carry out their legitimate work without fear of reprisals,” said Tigere Chagutah.

Parents in Japan are taking an increasingly active role in their children’s lives – helping them find marriage partners, navigate job hunting and secure housing – as the line between parental support and personal decision-making continues to blur.

Rights groups oppose UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh for UN chief over Sudan claims
Human rights groups on Tuesday urged countries to reject UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh’s bid to become United Nations secretary general citing allegations that Abu Dhabi funds Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The UAE denies the accusations. Nusseibeh, 48, is seeking to become the first woman to lead the UN.
Several human rights groups on Tuesday urged countries to reject Emirati official Lana Nusseibeh for the United Nation's (UN) top job, over the United Arab Emirates' (UAE) alleged financing of paramilitary forces in Sudan.
The 48-year-old Nusseibeh is vying to become the first woman and only the second Arab to become the United Nations secretary-general.
Read moreEmirati diplomat could become next UN chief despite human rights concerns
Since her official nomination last week, she has garnered the backing of Gulf states but also faced scrutiny over her country's normalisation with Israel and Abu Dhabi's alleged role in Sudan's war.
Sudan has been engulfed in war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since 2023, with the UAE accused of funding the militants, an accusation the country denies.
"I think that Lana Nusseibeh is utterly inappropriate as a candidate for UN Secretary General," Ken Roth, head of Human Rights Watch, told journalists.
"Not just once, but repeatedly she has been asked about the UAE's role in arming and supporting the RSF and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts," he added.
On Tuesday, Nusseibeh said she has taken "a leave of absence from my post as a minister of the UAE" to be "mindful of the obligations of independence" the role would entail, adding that "the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general."
Kate Ferguson, co-director of the British NGO Protection Approaches, also raised concerns. "There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes," she said.
Secretary-general candidates are supposed to be independent from the governments of their home countries given that they are to lead an international body.
Read moreUAE nominates official to lead UN
Nusseibeh is seasoned diplomat who has also served as the UAE's permanent representative to the UN from 2013 to 2024, the first woman to hold the post.
Speaking on Sudan specifically, Nusseibeh said "the loss of human life on the ground is a tragedy."
"The atrocities committed by the RSF are atrocious, and I would support the work of all UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice," she said, adding the first thing the global organisation must do "is stop the conflict."
To win the race for UN chief, a candidate must secure nine out of 15 votes on the Security Council and avoid a veto from one of its five permanent members: the United States, Britain, China, France, Russia.
Nusseibeh comes from a prominent Palestinian family of statesmen, uprooted by the creation of Israel in 1948.
Her family traditionally held the keys to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in the walled Old City of Jerusalem, the holiest site in Christianity that Christians believe marks the spot where Jesus was crucified.

Five key takeaways from Israel’s parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:53:35 UTC
11:53:35 KST

Five key takeaways from Israel’s parliamentary elections
With more than 76 percent of votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc holds slight lead over opposition, but shy of majority.
Israel’s partial election results show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, with neither likely to secure a clear path to a governing majority.
With more than 76 percent of the votes counted by Israel’s Central Elections Committee on Wednesday, Netanyahu’s bloc was on track to win 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, or Israeli parliament, Eisenkot’s alliance was set to win 47, and the Arab parties on track for 19 seats, Israeli media reported.
Tuesday’s vote was largely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and a response to the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, as well as Israel’s subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.
It also came as Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of the country’s neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.
Here are five key takeaways from the Israeli elections so far:
Early results show no clear winner
With 76 percent of votes counted in Israel at 11.45am (09:45 GMT) on Wednesday, Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc was on course to secure 54 seats, seven short of a majority in the parliament, according to election commission tallies published by Israeli media.
Eisenkot’s alliance was on track to win 47 seats, while the Arab parties were set to win 19 seats.
Exit polls published earlier had projected a deadlock, with the two main blocs projected to win 51 seats each.
The exit polls indicated that Netanyahu’s Likud party – which leads his wider bloc – could emerge as the single largest party with an estimated 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar party was projected to win 21 seats, according to projections from Channels 12 and 13 – giving Likud a clear lead over all others in the parliament.
Arab parties were projected to win 19 seats collectively, building on their 2022 performance.
Israelis vote for parties, which then form alliances to create a governing coalition with a prime minister at the helm. No single party has ever won a 61-seat majority.
Released by the major Israeli television networks, exit polls are unofficial indicators of the vote. Preliminary official results are expected on Wednesday, and may vary from the exit polls.
Leaders react, predict end to Netanyahu’s reign
Opposition bloc leader Eisenkot said the Israeli public had voted for change and against the incumbent prime minister.
Addressing supporters at his Yashar party headquarters, Eisenkot said, “This will be a new start. A real new start on a new path. The old era is over, and Israel is starting a new era.”
But the prime minister told supporters that his Likud party is dominant and called for the formation of a “national right-wing government”.
“What we’ve seen is that the Likud party is the largest party – nobody can compete with us,” he said. “The second thing that is clear as well is that the right bloc has a majority. And it is a decisive majority.”
He also accused Israeli television channels of trying to discourage his supporters from voting by projecting stronger results for opposition parties.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told supporters his party was projected to win seven seats, and pledged to continue the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir praised his Otzma Yehudit party’s performance in a speech to supporters at its headquarters.
“We are very proud of our journey”, Ben-Gvir said. “This party was not even existing on the political landscape.”
The Democrats party leader Yair Golan said on X that voters had “fired the Netanyahu government”, and pledged to work with political partners to form a new administration.
The leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas said he hopes the final election results will let the opposition bloc and his party hold the 61 seats needed to form a government. The party was projected to win about seven seats.
Record turnout among voters
The Central Elections Committee reported that 77.7 percent of eligible voters participated in the election, the highest turnout since 1999. Turnout was up 7.1 percentage points from 2022, when Netanyahu, who has served as prime minister off and on since 1996, returned to office.
Israel’s military said turnout among soldiers had climbed beyond 68 percent by 5pm local time (15:00 GMT). More than 60,000 Israelis also returned home from abroad to take part in the vote.
Polling stations closed at 10pm local time (20:00 GMT), but the official elections body said anyone waiting in line at that time would be allowed to vote.
Arab parties as potential tie-breaker
Exit polls and partial results suggested Arab-led parties could win 19 seats, a significant jump from the current 10-seat representation they hold in parliament. That same polling showed Eisenkot and Netanyahu tied at the projected 51 seats each before preliminary official results began trickling in.
Given the 61 seats needed to form a government in Israel, both Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s parties are locked out of the majority without the Arab vote.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu have in the past refused to form a coalition with Arab parties to secure that majority. Netanyahu said the idea of working with Arab leaders would be a “disgrace and a shame“.
Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador, told Al Jazeera that forming a government could be difficult for both parties because of the promise not to form said coalition.
“There’s a price to pay,” Pinkas said, because the “Arabs can’t be kept outside and only being considered and co-opted when you need their votes”.
What could happen next?
After the vote is finalised, the parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach the 61-seat majority.
The bloc with the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister. He will then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
The person nominated will then have up to 42 days to form a government.
As for the two leading parties unifying to create a majority, voters would “never forgive” Eisenkot if he unites with Netanyahu’s bloc, while sharing power through rotating roles would guarantee “dysfunction”, Pinkas said.
If no government emerges, Netanyahu and his current cabinet will remain as a caretaker government.
If negotiations fail and no coalition can form a government, new elections will be called.
The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.

JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot each vowed on Oct 28 to form a government after both came up short in the first election since the Oct 7, 2023 attack traumatised the country.

The strongest gains came from Arab Israeli parties, whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.

Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use a war to push for a unity government. “Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
Addressing Israel’s security establishment, Eisenkot said that they served the state and not Netanyahu, calling him “a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people’s trust”.
‘Public has voted for change’
Eisenkot shares many of Netanyahu’s views on security and has backed the Gaza offensive following Oct 7 that has reduced the territory to rubble.
But Eisenkot has vowed to create a more inclusive atmosphere inside Israel and to rein in extremist settlers in the West Bank who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.
After a turnout of nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, Eisenkot said it would be a mistake to hold a second election and vowed to work “swiftly” to form a government.
“The public has voted for change,” Eisenkot said. “A worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”
The three mainstream Israeli television networks in exit polls gave the two blocs each around 51 seats – well below the 61 needed to govern – after initially giving an edge to the opposition.

Divisive

Netanyahu vows right-wing unity

"We must put in place a strong government of the right," Netanyahu said, noting that Likud was projected to remain the single largest party.
"The Jewish and Zionist majority must unite. It is out of the question to have a government that is backed by Arab parties."
The political confrontation unfolded as broadcaster Channel 12 revised its exit poll projections, showing Netanyahu's right-wing bloc taking the lead with 52 seats against 49 seats for Eisenkot's opposition bloc.
The broadcaster projected Arab-list parties to secure 19 seats.
The latest shift follows earlier projections from Israel’s public broadcaster and Channel 13 that placed both rival blocs level at 51 seats each, with 18 seats for Arab parties.
Channel 13 had projected Likud as the single largest party with 27 seats, followed by Yashar with 23 and Naftali Bennett's Together alliance with 13.
The revisions completely erased an initial lead for Eisenkot's camp, which opening projections had placed at 53 seats against 50 for Netanyahu's bloc.
Crucially, neither camp has reached the 61 seats required for an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Voter turnout reached 77.7 percent—the highest recorded since 1999 and up 7.1 percentage points from 2022, according to the Central Elections Committee.
Vote counting commenced after polling stations closed at 10 pm local time on Tuesday.

Cyclonic storm Arnab has made landfall along the southeastern coast of India, striking the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam (Puducherry) coasts with sustained wind speeds of 125 to 135 kmph and gusts up to 150 kmph.
NEW DELHI: Cyclonic storm Arnab continued making landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday morning, bringing heavy rainfall, strong winds and high tides. Trees were uprooted in Visakhapatnam and Odisha’s Malkangiri, while rough seas and gusty winds battered the Kakinada coastline.
The landfall process was expected to continue for around three more hours from 7am, according to reports. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said the storm was nearly stationary near the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early Wednesday, with sustained wind speeds of 120-130 kmph and gusts reaching 145 kmph.
Visuals from Visakhapatnam showed high tides at RK Beach and a tree uprooted near Andhra University’s College of Engineering for Women. In Odisha’s Malkangiri, strong winds and heavy rainfall were also reported.
Heavy rainfall caused waterlogging in several parts of Kakinada, while nearly 6,000 electricity poles were uprooted in Andhra Pradesh’s Konaseema district, damaging power infrastructure. Officials also shifted residents from badly affected areas, including Pagadala Peta, to rehabilitation centres.
A storm surge of 1 metre to 1.5 metres above the astronomical tide was forecast to inundate low-lying areas of Andhra Pradesh over the following three hours before gradually subsiding.
The Andhra Pradesh School Education Department converted 609 schools into rehabilitation centres, accommodating 854 people across the state as of 5.50am on Wednesday, officials said.
Heavy rainfall, red alert in OdishaThe IMD issued a red alert for extremely heavy rainfall at isolated places in Odisha’s Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada and Nabarangpur districts. Winds of 60-70 kmph, gusting to 80 kmph, were expected in these areas.
Other southern districts of Odisha were under an orange alert for heavy to very heavy rainfall, accompanied by winds of 50-70 kmph. Wind speeds of 40-70 kmph were expected in Bhubaneswar and Cuttack.IMD scientist Sanjeev Dwivedi warned of possible mudslides and landslides in the Koraput region and advised people to avoid unnecessary travel. Strong winds could damage kutcha houses, thatched roofs and other vulnerable structures.Between 8.30am on October 27 and 4am on October 28, Kannuripalem in Anakapalle district recorded the highest rainfall at 261.5 mm. Vizianagaram recorded 259.74 mm, while Visakhapatnam recorded 259.06 mm during the period.Evacuations, emergency teams deployedAhead of the cyclone, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu said the state had identified 2,199 cyclone shelters and prepared evacuation plans, prioritising elderly people, children, persons with disabilities and pregnant women. He said 2,360 pregnant women had been moved to medical facilities.“Twelve NDRF and ten SDRF teams have been assigned to the districts, with deployment underway,” the Chief Minister said, adding that police, fire services and medical teams had been mobilised, while the Navy and Coast Guard were ready to assist.
More than 8,400 power restoration personnel had been mobilised, Naidu said. Arrangements were also being made for food, drinking water, medicines and generators, while control rooms were operating round the clock."I appeal to everyone to remain calm, stay alert and cooperate with the authorities. Move immediately to designated shelters when advised. Fishermen must not venture into the sea until official clearance is given," he said.“Keep essential supplies and charged phones ready. Avoid unnecessary travel, beaches, riverbanks, floodwaters and fallen power lines,” he added.The chief minister urged residents to remain in safe shelters until authorities confirmed that the danger had passed and to follow official advisories.

Is Israel barreling toward another election? 5 scenarios after dramatic night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:39:49 UTC
11:39:49 KST

Israel faces the prospect of another election after updated exit polls early Wednesday showed neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, leaving the country confronting a prolonged political deadlock.
The projections, including overnight revisions, reinforced what had become increasingly apparent during the election campaign: Neither political bloc appears capable of securing the 61 seats needed to control the 120-member Knesset.
Several scenarios remain possible, including another election, a national unity government, a Netanyahu-led coalition supported by defectors from the opposition and a minority government headed by Eisenkot.
But the possibility of an Eisenkot minority government, which appeared viable when the first exit polls were released at 10 p.m. Tuesday, has diminished significantly following overnight updates. One revised projection showed Netanyahu's bloc holding a substantial advantage over the opposition.
The unexpectedly strong showing by Arab parties has complicated coalition calculations for both sides, leaving neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with an apparent path to a majority without their involvement or support.
Scenario 1: Another election
A return to the polls may be the most likely outcome, although it could also be the most damaging for Israel, particularly as the country continues to face security tensions on several fronts.
The large number of seats projected for Arab parties has left both major political blocs struggling to assemble a governing majority without cooperating with them — a prospect that several party leaders have publicly rejected.
President Isaac Herzog could attempt to broker a compromise to prevent another election, potentially with assistance from political figures and international actors.
Under Israel's parliamentary system, the president consults with party representatives after an election and assigns a lawmaker the task of forming a government, generally choosing the candidate considered most capable of securing parliamentary support.
If those efforts fail, Israel could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining in office as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
That would give Netanyahu a significant advantage by allowing him to retain the premiership despite the absence of a new parliamentary majority.
Some figures in the opposition's pro-change bloc also fear that Netanyahu could seek to escalate security tensions to complicate efforts to replace him or pressure rival parties into joining an emergency government.
Those concerns reflect the opposition's suspicions rather than any established plan by Netanyahu.
Scenario 2: A national unity government led by Netanyahu
A unity government headed by Netanyahu remains possible, but only if several political leaders abandon explicit campaign promises.
In his election-night address, Netanyahu gave no indication that he intended to break with his existing right-wing coalition partners. He did not directly appeal to leaders of the opposition bloc or explicitly propose a unity government.
Instead, he declared that "the Zionist majority must come to its senses and unite," without outlining how such an arrangement might work.
Eisenkot, who was introduced as "the next prime minister" during his own election-night speech, appeared equally unwilling to compromise.
"A worthy leader would resign that very day," Eisenkot said, referring to Netanyahu and the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
Eisenkot has repeatedly promised that he would not serve in a government with Netanyahu under any circumstances, even declaring that he would resign the following day if he ever agreed to serve under him.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the Beyachad party, and Avigdor Liberman, chairman of the nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party, have also ruled out joining a Netanyahu-led government.
The updated exit polls, which show Likud and Netanyahu's bloc performing more strongly than initially projected, could further complicate negotiations.
With Likud emerging as the largest party, Netanyahu would be unlikely to relinquish the first term as prime minister under any proposed power-sharing rotation agreement, assuming he agreed to such an arrangement at all.
That leaves a unity government theoretically possible but politically difficult to achieve.
Scenario 3: Netanyahu forms a government with opposition defectors
Netanyahu could also attempt to form a government by persuading lawmakers from the pro-change bloc to defect and join his coalition.
But the updated projections suggest he remains well short of the 61-seat threshold.
Rather than needing one or two opposition lawmakers to cross the aisle, Netanyahu would have to attract a substantial group of defectors to secure a majority.
That would be a considerably more difficult political undertaking, particularly after a campaign in which opposition leaders made replacing Netanyahu a central objective.
The Likud leader could nevertheless seek the presidential mandate to form a government as a tactical move, even if his prospects of assembling a viable coalition remain slim.
Receiving the mandate would give Netanyahu an opportunity to negotiate with potential partners, but it would not guarantee that he could form a government.
Scenario 4: An Eisenkot minority government
An Eisenkot-led minority government initially appeared possible after the first exit polls were released at 10 p.m., when the pro-change bloc seemed poised to emerge as the largest parliamentary grouping.
Under that scenario, Eisenkot could have secured more recommendations from lawmakers than Netanyahu, potentially persuading Herzog to give him the first opportunity to form a government.
Minutes after the initial projections were released, Eisenkot announced that he intended to begin working immediately to establish a government, arguing that his bloc had emerged as the largest.
Such a government would likely have required parliamentary support from Arab parties without necessarily including them as formal coalition partners.
But Liberman, who ruled out a minority government during the campaign, offered no indication in his election-night speech that he was reconsidering his position.
He also declined to answer whether he would cooperate with Ra'am, the Arab Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas.
Liberman instead called for a revolt against Netanyahu, whom he described as "the head of a criminal organization."
The overnight exit poll revisions have made an Eisenkot minority government even less likely, with the pro-change bloc no longer appearing to command enough support to establish a government, even if potential defectors were to join it.
Scenario 5: Replacing Netanyahu's caretaker government
Another possibility would involve replacing Netanyahu's caretaker administration with a temporary government headed by Eisenkot, allowing the opposition to pursue a limited legislative agenda even without a stable long-term coalition.
Such an arrangement could enable the new parliamentary majority to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, and establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attack.
A state commission of inquiry, an independent investigative body with broad powers to summon witnesses and examine government conduct, has been a major demand of Netanyahu's critics.
The arrangement could also allow the opposition to pursue other parliamentary measures while attempting to negotiate a more permanent governing coalition.
But this scenario, too, has become increasingly remote following the overnight revisions to the exit polls.
With Netanyahu's bloc performing more strongly than initially expected and Arab parties holding a substantial share of parliamentary seats, the opposition appears to lack the numbers needed to carry out such a transition.
For now, the projections point to a fragmented Knesset in which neither major bloc can govern alone, leaving Israel's political future dependent on difficult coalition negotiations, possible reversals of campaign pledges or another election.
The final distribution of seats will not be known until the official vote count is completed.

Economic Watch: China, Germany eye broader cooperation in intelligent connected vehicles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:35:48 CST
11:35:48 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- As electrification, digitalization and artificial intelligence (AI) reshape the global auto industry, how China and Germany can build on their complementary strengths to expand cooperation has become a key question facing both countries' industries.
Last week, the 2026 World Intelligent Connected Vehicles Conference (WICV) was held in Beijing, where government and business representatives from both countries held talks on technology coordination, standards alignment and market access. Both sides agreed that there is a strong need for concrete progress.
China and Germany have long cooperated in the intelligent connected vehicle (ICV) sector. Signed in 2018, their memorandum of understanding on ICVs has served as an important platform for bilateral technical cooperation. Last month, the two sides held a plenary meeting in Berlin, where they exchanged views on practical issues such as vehicle type approval, data recording and vehicle-to-everything communications.
"This is exactly the kind of cooperation we need -- concrete, pragmatic, technology-focused and workable," said Hildegard Müller, president of the German Association of the Automotive Industry.
"China has made remarkable progress in electric mobility and digital technology, while German automakers and suppliers have deep expertise in automotive engineering, systems integration and industrial production. The two countries bring important complementary experience to the automotive industry's transformation," Müller said at the WICV.
She acknowledged that harmonizing standards and regulations is no easy task, but "regulatory differences should not become unnecessary barriers to innovation and market access." The goal, she said, is to build enough common ground for innovation to cross borders and ultimately benefit manufacturers, suppliers and consumers in both countries.
China's push for intelligent connectivity is gaining strong momentum. By the end of August, about 61 million passenger cars were equipped with combined driver assistance systems, some 16 million had 5G terminals, and roughly 2 million carried C-V2X (cellular vehicle-to-everything) direct communication terminals.
The country has also rolled out a series of national standards covering combined driver assistance, automated driving, automatic emergency braking and vehicle cybersecurity, and is scaling up connected-vehicle communications through real-world use.
On the German side, companies are deepening their footprint in China. Milan Nedeljković, chairman of the board of management of BMW AG, said the all-new BMW iX3, produced locally in northeast China's Shenyang, will begin customer deliveries in November.
"This model blends BMW's engineering strength with China's vibrant digital ecosystem," he said. "Intelligent, connected new energy vehicles are at the heart of the automotive industry's transformation and a key driver of China's high-quality development. We are confident in the market's long-term potential."
Chinese automakers, for their part, are stepping up their integration into the German and broader European markets. According to Yin Tongyue, chairman of Chery Holding Group Co., Ltd., Chery has set up R&D centers in Germany as it expands into Europe. Chery's cooperation in Europe, he said, has long moved beyond local manufacturing to leverage local talent and embrace local culture, and has achieved localization across the entire value chain, from R&D and manufacturing to procurement and sales.
"In the early days of reform and opening up, Volkswagen, Audi and Mercedes-Benz set up factories in China, helping to develop the country's market, supply chains and talent pool," Yin said. "Today, as China advances in electrification and intelligent technology, China, too, must learn to share with its peers around the world and move toward an electrified, low-carbon and intelligent era alongside established local automakers."
In intelligent driving, Mercedes-Benz is deepening its partnership with Chinese tech company Momenta. Oliver Thöne, member of the board of management of Mercedes-Benz Group AG and head of the board division Greater China, said Mercedes-Benz offers highway driver assistance in China, with the take-up rate for related features doubling year on year, and is now expanding into urban driver assistance.
"We are also working with Tsinghua University to develop a vision-language AI model, which has been applied to our rear-seat systems and will be deployed globally," he said.
Wang Zhiqin, vice president of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, noted that China-Germany automotive cooperation is extending from complete vehicle manufacturing and parts procurement to joint R&D, standards coordination and ecosystem building.
She called on companies from both countries to deepen technological collaboration, conduct joint research and testing in frontier areas, and strengthen cooperation across the ICV supply chain, including in information, communications and software. ■

China, 25 other countries sign UN convention on negotiable cargo documents
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:35:33 CST
11:35:33 KST

ACCRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- China, Ghana and 24 other countries on Monday became the first signatories to the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents at a signing ceremony in Accra, capital of Ghana.
Chinese Vice Commerce Minister Jiang Chenghua signed the convention on behalf of the Chinese government at the ceremony.
Jiang said the institutional innovation fills a gap in international rules and provides an international legal framework for financing transactions involving cross-border transport documents.
It will effectively ease the financial pressure on enterprises engaged in international trade, reduce transaction costs in cross-border overland trade, and inject new momentum into the high-quality development of global trade, he added.
China is ready to work with all signatory states to complete their domestic approval procedures as soon as possible, Jiang said, expressing China's hope that more countries will join the convention so that its benefits can reach more nations and contribute to global trade prosperity and the well-being of people around the world.
Anna Joubin-Bret, secretary of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), said the convention would help reduce uncertainty, enhance resilience, facilitate trade finance, support trade digitalization and improve the efficiency of international supply chains.
She thanked the Chinese government for bringing the convention project to UNCITRAL. "Since the adoption by the United Nations General Assembly, we have greatly benefited from China's steadfast support to the convention and its efforts to promote the broader understanding of this framework," she said.
Around 400 representatives from more than 60 countries and regions attended the signing ceremony.
Initiated and spearheaded by China, the convention was adopted by the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in December 2025. ■

Norway allocates nearly $54M in energy support for Ukraine
This was announced in a press report by the Norwegian government, according to Ukrinform.
“Ukraine is about to enter another wartime winter. To ensure the most stable energy supply possible and avoid severe humanitarian consequences, it is crucial that Ukraine receives funding to purchase equipment to strengthen and restore critical infrastructure damaged by Russian bombing,” Energy Minister Terje Aasland said.
During a visit to Kyiv on Tuesday, October 27, Aasland announced that Norway would provide 500 million Norwegian kroner (NOK) to support Ukraine’s energy sector.
The funding is being provided under the Nansen Support Programme, which runs through 2026. The assistance will be channeled through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund (UESF).
This mechanism allows funds to be quickly directed toward repairs, the purchase of new equipment, and investments where they are most urgently needed.
In particular, the Ukrainian side emphasized the need for new power cables to ensure a stable energy supply.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Norway has allocated more than 16 billion Norwegian kroner ($1.72 billion) for gas procurement, repairs to energy infrastructure, and investment in new solutions.
As previously reported, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Norway would maintain its military, humanitarian, and financial assistance to Ukraine at around $9 billion in 2027.

UN nuclear inspectors see no evidence Iran repaired US-bombed sites

UN nuclear inspectors see no evidence Iran repaired US-bombed sites
NEW YORK – The United Nations nuclear watchdog said it has not detected any efforts by Iran to rebuild nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli strikes over the past two years, even as Tehran continues to block inspectors’ access to most of its atomic sites.
“Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026,” International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi told the UN Security Council on Oct 27.
Grossi’s remarks undercut US President Donald Trump’s narrative that launching a new war against Iran in late February was necessary to halt its nuclear weapons ambitions.
The President has repeatedly said he Is weighing renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.
The assessment echoes a conclusion that former US director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard included in written testimony before a congressional committee earlier in 2026.
She wrote that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been “obliterated” in US and Israeli strikes in June 2025, and that there “has been no efforts since then to try to rebuild their enrichment capability”.
At the same time, the IAEA’s ability to assess Iran’s nuclear activities remains constrained by its lack of access to most of the country’s atomic sites.
Grossi reiterated that inspectors have been unable to verify the status of Iran’s nuclear material – including the previously declared 440kg of uranium enriched up to 60% – and called on Tehran to grant renewed access.
“As at today the IAEA has not been able to verify that there has been no diversion of nuclear material required to be safeguarded,” he said.
The Trump administration has repeatedly claimed it had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities, but offered little evidence to back up its claims.
Trump started the current war against Iran because he said he needed to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, something that most experts said the Islamic Republic was years away from.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has offered other explanations for the war, including that Washington had to act before Israel struck Iran and sparked retaliation against the US.
He’s also said Iran was building up its ballistic missile and drone capability as a conventional “shield” around its nuclear programme. BLOOMBERG

Putin gives 90-minute "history lecture" during call with Norwegian and Finnish leaders
During a phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Russian leader Vladimir Putin spent almost the entire conversation discussing the "initial reasons for the conflict" with Ukraine instead of discussing how to end the war.
Source: Financial Times
Quote: "Vladimir Putin used most of his call with the leaders of Finland and Norway to lecture them about medieval Slavic history, underscoring the difficulties Europe faces in asserting itself in upcoming peace talks with Russia."
Details: Stubb told Finnish media that the call, which was supposed to last less than half an hour, dragged on for 90 minutes.
According to three sources familiar with the conversation, instead of discussing the key issues involved in ending the war, Putin delivered a lengthy monologue to the Nordic leaders about the "initial reasons for the conflict", as the Kremlin calls them.
By contrast, the prospect of an immediate ceasefire – Ukraine's main demand for starting the peace process – was barely discussed, according to the FT's sources.
One source said that the Nordic leaders had decided not to interrupt Putin during his "historical asides" so that they could gauge how seriously he was approaching dialogue with Europe.
It was the first conversation between the Kremlin leader and any of Ukraine's European allies since July 2025, when Putin spoke to French President Emmanuel Macron.
Background:
- On 27 October, Stubb and Støre held a phone call with Putin.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that during the conversation, the leaders of Norway and Finland discussed steps to de-escalate the war, particularly in relation to Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
- The Kremlin's account of the call said that Putin had, among other things, reminded Stubb and Støre of the "root causes" of the war against Ukraine.
- Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen later said she was highly sceptical about the outcome of the call, which had allegedly not been coordinated with other European countries.
- Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed that the call had been coordinated with the Ukrainian side.
- During a meeting with US President Donald Trump in Alaska in 2025, Putin delivered another lengthy "historical" speech about Ukraine. This did not go down well with Trump, who became angry and even threatened to walk out.

'Eretz Nehederet' tackles Israel's election-night drama with Gal Gadot, political satire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:29:46 UTC
11:29:46 KST

As Israelis anxiously awaited the results of one of the most crucial elections in history on Tuesday night, Gal Gadot, the Israeli-born Hollywood superstar, made an appearance on a special two-part broadcast of Eretz Nehederet (Wonderful Country) on Channel 12.
Gadot and the regular cast entertained a politically divided nation as the polls went into their final hour, and Israelis were unified at last in their shared suspense.
Her presence was a high point on an unusual broadcast, half of which was shown before the polls closed and the other half of which was broadcast after the exit polls showed an inconclusive result, which was far from the definitive victory both sides had craved.
In the first half, one sketch featuring Asher (Yuval Semo), the chatty cabbie who always says exactly what is on his mind, focused on a few of the 70,000+ Israelis returning from abroad to vote.
Asher is never speechless, but he was definitely shocked when Gadot stepped out of the airport and into his cab. Their upbeat and, at times, emotional conversation captured the euphoria and emotion of many Israelis who returned to vote after years abroad.
“So, did you come back to vote? Or to be an artichoke on The Masked Singer?” Asher asked Gadot, who had posted a story to her Instagram earlier in the day showing herself voting and saying that she had backed one of the opposition parties, although she did not reveal which one.
“No, I came to vote,” she said.
“Good for you! Good for you,” Asher responded.
“Absolutely,” she said.
“What a Zionist! What a patriot,” he said enthusiastically.
“If not now, when?” she said, echoing the famous quote from the Jewish sage, Hillel the Elder.
“Tell me, how long have you been living abroad?” Asher asked Gadot.
“Almost 12 years,” the actress, who has starred in two Wonder Woman movies and about a dozen others since she made the move, replied.
“So, I can scam you like a tourist!” he said.
Asking her who she was voting for, she agreed to whisper her choice to him. As soon as she did, being Asher, he grabbed his megaphone and started to announce her choice to all the cabbies from his station, but the name of the party was bleeped out and he promised the other cabbies wouldn’t tell anyone, as she laughed.
She also spoke candidly about the difficulty of being an Israeli and a Jew in Hollywood in a period of rising antisemitism. "It's hard these days to be an Israeli abroad," she said and even said that she often wore masks when she went out, as if it were still the pandemic era.
She said she often tried to give "context" that would help Americans understand the issues.
"There's a lot of hate. I try to explain to them, what you see from there isn't what we see from here. And what we see here, you don't see there." She said she planned to return to Israel with her husband and four daughters, three of whom were born in the US, and that they were building a house here.
Finally, frustrated by the Israeli traffic, she told Asher she would drive, since she had starred in Fast & Furious, and after some daredevil moves with his cab, she turned it into a flying car, heading up into the clouds in her quest to make it to a polling place in time to vote.
Eretz Nehederet featured sketches about election candidates
In the first, more optimistic first half of the broadcast, the show outdid itself with an opening sketch in which the political opponents were depicted as professional wrestlers in appropriately absurd costumes.
They fought each other in over-the-top wrestler-style, with weapons like a sawed-off shotgun wielded by Gadi Eisenkot (Yuval Semo), the former chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, and a huge gold suitcase of cash, thrown around by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (Mariano Eidelman), a reference to how his government allowed suitcases containing millions of dollars from the Qatari government to be given to Hamas in Gaza.
In a panel discussion moderated by host Eyal Kitzis, Channel 12 political analyst Amit Segal (Roy Bar Natan) appeared distracted because he was busy writing a victory speech for Netanyahu, a reference to the fact that Segal is alleged to have given the prime minister advice on his campaign speeches.
Another panelist, Dana Weiss (Alma Zack), Channel 12’s political and diplomatic correspondent, ignored calls from an increasingly unhinged Tali Gotliv (Liat Harlev) from the Otzma Yehudit Party.
Netanyahu appeared at a shopping mall and tried to spark fear in voters, saying everyone would die tonight if they did not vote for him. He brandished a toy ceramic mushroom, saying it was a mushroom cloud, a joke about an AI image the prime minister actually released in the final days of the campaign that purported to show Tel Aviv destroyed by an Iranian nuclear bomb.
Eretz Nehederet ribbed Naftali Bennett (Eran Zarahovitsch), the head of the B'Yachad Party, for his campaign visits to “parliamentim,” informal political discussion groups of older citizens around the country. On election day, he had spent so much time with these groups that he realized he had missed his chance to vote and seemed forlorn. Eisenkot, in turn, looked terribly awkward courting the youth vote with a moronic influencer (Liat Harlev).
Expanding on this theme, Eretz Nehederet went back in time and showed AI commercials to a group of former prime ministers from past eras: Golda Meir, Yitzhak Rabin, Menachem Begin, and Ariel Sharon, all of whom totally miss the point. Meir seemed especially mystified when she was given an e-cigarette.
Writers attempt to inject comedy into initial election results
In the second part of the show, after the likely results of the election were revealed, the writers had to try hard to find comedy in the fact that neither side had won enough seats to form a government.
One sketch showed the leaders of the three of the opposition parties, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and Avigdor Liberman (Sharon Taicher) of Israeli Beitenu, playing a game show called “Excuse the Promise,” trying to walk back their campaign promises not to collaborate with Arab or Ultra-Orthodox parties.
Ofer Winter (Yaron Berlad) and Yoseph Haddad (Eli Finish) showed up, upset that their People of Israel Party had not gotten enough votes to enter the Knesset.
Haddad was especially incredulous, saying he couldn't understand how he seemed to be the only Arab who had not gotten elected to the Knesset, a reference to the fact that the Arab parties did much better than expected.
Meanwhile, a grim-faced Netanyahu was shown in the defense headquarters, boasting he was starting up the war with Iran to cement his power as the head of state.
Eretz Nehederet’s staff of quick-thinking writers did what they could to make people smile despite the somewhat grim denouement of a divisive campaign, and the prospect of more uncertainty to come.
One unsettling element was that, instead of Kitzis's usual sign-off line about Israel being a wonderful country, the second broadcast ended with him simply handing the show back to Channel 12 news anchor Yonit Levi.

It’s time to set ego aside: Netanyahu, Eisenkot must form unity government - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:29:12 UTC
11:29:12 KST

Israelis went to the polls in extraordinary numbers on Tuesday, delivering an election result that, according to initial exit polls, left neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot with a clear path to forming a government.
The projections put both blocs around the 50-something mark, with Arab parties slowly approaching a historic 20 seats.
The figures are preliminary, and the final seat distribution could still change. Nevertheless, they raise a question that neither leader can easily avoid: What happens when two rival political camps emerge from an election without the parliamentary majority needed to govern?
One possibility is a national unity government bringing Netanyahu and Eisenkot together.
The truth is, politicians lie, and Israel’s politicians are no exception.
But there are some ideals we cannot stray from in a post-October 7 world, and the next Knesset cannot set itself up to be held hostage by one faction, be they Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) or Arabs.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu must form a true unity government
The solution is simple: Eisenkot and Netanyahu must set their differences aside to form a true unity government.
The mythical broad Zionist government we’ve heard so much about. The chance is here, within our reach.
The only roadblock is the ego of man.
The same ego, by the way, that saw thousands of votes trashed because too-small parties refused to face the music and back out.
Too good to be true
Such an arrangement would require significant compromises from both leaders, who have spent the campaign presenting competing visions for Israel's future.
For Eisenkot, entering a government alongside Netanyahu would raise difficult questions about his campaign commitments, particularly his criticism of the prime minister's leadership and the government's responsibility for the failures surrounding October 7.
For Netanyahu, partnering with Eisenkot would require negotiating with a political rival whose rise has challenged Likud's dominance and whose supporters have demanded major changes to the country's leadership and priorities.
These differences cannot simply be dismissed as personal animosity or political ego. They concern fundamental questions about accountability, democratic institutions, national security, and the direction of the state.
The high turnout, reported at 77.7%, demonstrated the importance voters attached to the contest. But participation alone cannot resolve the disagreements reflected in the resulting parliamentary math.
True unity seems too good to be true. After all our country has been through, can anyone really compromise? Of thinking outside of yourself and doing what's best for the country.
The coming negotiations will test not only the two leaders' willingness to compromise, but also whether their respective parties and potential coalition partners are prepared to accept such an arrangement.
Israel's voters have participated in the democratic process. The responsibility for interpreting the result and translating it into a functioning government now passes to their elected representatives.
Whether a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government can meet that responsibility remains an open question. What Tuesday's election has made clear is that neither leader can resolve the country's political deadlock through declarations of victory alone.
The precedent for cooperation already exists.
Eisenkot served in Netanyahu's emergency wartime government following October 7, before departing alongside Benny Gantz in June 2024.
That experience demonstrated that political rivals can participate in the same government during a national crisis.
They simply need to realize that, even without missiles, we are in a crisis.
Whether the vote was cast for Netanyahu or Eisenkot, we the people voted for stability.
We voted for peace and unity.
It's up to them to deliver it.

OpenAI plans to buy Google’s chips as part of its AI build-out
- OpenAI plans to buy Google’s AI chips to boost its computing power, according to a person familiar with the matter. The deal terms are still unknown.
- The move is part of OpenAI’s wider push to build AI infrastructure fast. It also plans to use its own chips in 2026, including Jalapeno chips made with Broadcom.
- Google’s TPUs, first built for search, are now a rival to Nvidia’s chips. Oracle will also offer TPUs in its cloud, as Google says AI needs “a diverse range of compute”.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – OpenAI intends to buy artificial intelligence computing chips from Alphabet’s Google, according to a person familiar with the matter, part of broader efforts by the ChatGPT maker to build out its AI infrastructure.
The final terms of any deal are not yet known, according to the person, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. OpenAI and Google declined to comment.
The move reflects OpenAI’s multi-pronged bid to quickly add more AI processing power.
The company has already announced plans to start using its own chips to support its artificial intelligence models later in 2026.
It joins a stampede of companies working to develop home-grown AI chips and challenge Nvidia’s dominance in the field.
OpenAI’s in-house Jalapeno chips, developed with Broadcom, were created with help from Google veterans. Richard Ho, who runs the OpenAI internal chip team, was previously involved in the development of Google’s semiconductors – known as tensor processing units, or TPUs.
Google began working on its TPUs more than a decade ago. Initially, the processors were used to speed up the company’s web search engine and improve efficiency.
But the chips soon proved valuable for handling AI work and have emerged in recent years as an alternative to Nvidia’s prized graphics processing units.
Oracle also announced on Oct 27 that TPUs would be available through its cloud-computing infrastructure.
“The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute,” Google executive Amin Vahdat said in a statement announcing that deal.
The Information previously reported that OpenAI was planning to buy Google chips. BLOOMBERG

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The ruling DPP is gaining ground ahead of November's local elections, while the opposition KMT faces growing challenges, Japanese political analyst Ogasawara Yoshiyuki said Tuesday.
Ogasawara, an honorary professor at National Tsing Hua University, said the DPP could win races in Chiayi, Changhua County, and Yilan County, CNA reported. He also saw opportunities in New Taipei and Hsinchu County, although the party could lose Penghu County.
Ogasawara identified New Taipei as the most important race in the Nov. 28 elections. He said DPP candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) had steadily gained on KMT candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), drawing level in the spring before taking a narrow lead after September.
He said winning either Taipei or New Taipei would be a major victory for the DPP. Even if the KMT won 13 or 14 of Taiwan's 22 mayoral and county leader seats, losing New Taipei would still amount to a political defeat, he said.
In Taipei, Ogasawara said DPP candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) had gained ground since September and was now running neck and neck with incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安). He said Shen had stronger momentum but cautioned that the race remained too close to call.
Ogasawara linked the DPP's improving prospects to growing public frustration with the KMT's actions in the legislature. He said opposition efforts to block government spending had delayed approval of this year's central government budget until August, a record 266 days late.
He also cited a dispute over cuts and freezes to the Presidential Office's budget, which forced it to cancel orders for mooncakes from workshops employing people with disabilities. Ogasawara said the controversy had fueled criticism that the opposition had gone too far.
Ogasawara said the KMT may have become overconfident after defeating efforts to remove its lawmakers from office in last year's recall votes. However, he said recall votes and regular elections involve different political dynamics.
Meanwhile, Ogasawara said the DPP had shifted its campaign strategy toward local issues and everyday concerns. Rather than focusing on its message of resisting China and defending Taiwan, the party was paying greater attention to voters' daily needs.
