Ukraine’s Zelenskiy says territory recaptured, forces on the offensive
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:39:53 CET
07:39:53 KST

Oct 27 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces were retaking territory through a series of offensives, including one operation previously unannounced in which Kyiv’s troops used gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions.
Zelenskiy, speaking in his nightly video address, said Kyiv’s battlefield position was the strongest in some time in the 4-1/2-year-long war and could be made stronger with more deliveries of air defence systems from its Western allies.
Zelenskiy, citing a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
He said Operation Veles was conducted near Kupiansk, a city in northeastern Kharkiv region recaptured by Ukrainian forces in late 2022, but since under constant Russian pressure.
“It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions,” Zelenskiy said.
“Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success,” he said.
In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine’s Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres.
That operation was focused to the north of the key strongholds in the region — the so-called “fortress belt” of the cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Their capture would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donbas region.
Zelenskiy in August spoke of success in an offensive further south, with 26 villages being returned to Ukrainian control.
Russia says it favours an overall resolution of the war rather than a short-lived ceasefire and has pledged to pursue its drive to capture all of Donbas.
Russian commanders repeatedly say, often in announcements in President Vladimir Putin’s presence, that their forces are advancing on all sections of the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line.
The chief of Russia’s General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, said this month that Moscow’s forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
Ukraine’s military dismissed the Russian statements.
(Reporting by Ron Popeski and Oleksandr Kozhukhar; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

By Kanishka Singh
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faced widespread rebuke from civil rights groups, healthcare advocates and Democrats on Tuesday over his anti-Arab comments that the Council on American-Islamic Relations cast as “a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry.”
In his remarks on Monday at a campaign event in Michigan where Republican Mike Rogers is running for the US Senate against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the US health secretary falsely claimed that Arabs had not won major international awards and “don’t produce” science and literature.
“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature,” the US health chief said.
Arabs have won all those prizes. Peter Hotez, who is a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and specializes in vaccine development and tropical medicine, said his late colleague, Nobel Prize winner Ahmed Zewail, who was Arab and died in 2016, “would disagree” with the US health chief’s comments.
The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US rights advocates have raised concerns over escalating rhetoric against Muslims, Arabs, immigrants and ethnic minorities by President Donald Trump and his allies during the ongoing midterm election campaign.
“Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vile anti-Arab rant is a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry,” the Council on American-Islamic Relations, which documents hate against Muslims and Arabs in the US, said on Tuesday.
“His sweeping erasure of Arab contributions to humanity is not only maliciously false, but it also fans the flames of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate at a time when communities are already vulnerable to bigoted attacks from other public officials nationwide.”
Kennedy said the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist groups founded almost a century ago, has “created stagnant societies.”
Republicans have claimed, without evidence, El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood even as the Democrat has publicly disavowed the group and denied any connection to it.
El-Sayed, who is Muslim, has faced a host of anti-Muslim attacks during the campaign. Over the weekend, Trump invoked the September 11, 2001, attacks when speaking about El-Sayed, whom he has also repeatedly and falsely called a “jihadist.”
Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy also responded to the US health secretary’s comments.
“I really think everyone needs to pay attention to this coordinated campaign to delegitimize Muslim Americans — not just as citizens but as humans.”
US healthcare advocacy organization and nonprofit Protect Our Care cast Kennedy’s comments as a “wildly racist tirade.”
Kennedy, who has pushed his anti-vaccine views in his role as the top health official, was also in Michigan on Monday to promote funding for Detroit’s health department and touted agreements with hospitals to offer healthier food.
(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; editing by Caroline Humer and Aurora Ellis)

Israel Election: Four Scenarios as Opposition Edges Netanyahu but Falls Short of Majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:37:59 UTC
07:37:59 KST

Israelis went to the polls in the highest turnout for decades on Tuesday, with initial exit polls showing a slight edge but no majority for the opposition, meaning the next government will be formed by whoever can cobble together a coalition.
The country’s main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and Netanyahu’s bloc to win 50.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government – not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu’s Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot’s bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm’s length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
Elections in Israel: Can Netanyahu Hold on to Power?
Following the previous election in November 2022, it took Benjamin Netanyahu 58 days to form his government.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said especially high Arab turnout “indicates a strong desire for partnership”.
Eisenkot has not publicly even entertained the possibility, and Netanyahu in his campaign relentlessly told Jewish voters that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
“Bottom line, at the moment it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results,” Elovitz said.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel’s extreme polarization, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on October 16 found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the center, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., committed Tuesday to a peaceful postelection transfer of power, calling concerns that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans could contest the results if Democrats win control of Congress "absurd."
"We're going to follow the Constitution," Johnson said in Orangeburg, New York during a campaign stop with Republican Rep. Mike Lawler one week before the Nov. 3 midterm election. Trump, who has continued to falsely claim that widespread fraud cost him the 2020 election, has fueled those fears by calling to "nationalize" elections earlier this year and repeatedly questioning the security of mail voting, while also suggesting noncitizens could vote in large enough numbers to skew results. His administration sued California on Oct. 15 in a fight over noncitizens voting.
The Department of Justice also sued Alaska on Oct. 22 to block the certification of its results in the event of voter confusion. GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan will appear on the ballot beside Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whom Republicans have said is on the ballot only as a spoiler candidate.

"Of course we'll have a peaceful transfer of power. But it will not be transferring, because we are going to keep the majority and I'm going to be the speaker of the House and I will keep steady hands at the wheel," Johnson told reporters.

Chancellor targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:34:33 UTC
07:34:33 KST

John Healey has acknowledged the UK faces a “difficult moment” but insisted he would put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget on Wednesday against a turbulent global economic backdrop.
But despite the international uncertainty, the chancellor will signal “fresh hope for the future” as he attempts to sound a more optimistic note, by providing households with breathing space from rising cost of living pressures.
The budget, which will be interpreted as a signal of Andy Burnham’s intent, is nevertheless expected to be a relatively modest affair as Healey grapples with stark fiscal realities, putting off important decisions on tax and spending until next year.
“The world’s a highly uncertain place,” the chancellor said, in a video released before the budget. “Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses and on our public finances.”
Healey insisted the government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, as he attempts to reassure the markets that his plans for longer-term reform will make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.
The chancellor has limited scope for big giveaways because of the stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil caused by the Iran conflict, but changes aimed at easing the cost of living are set to feature heavily.
In his pre-budget address, he added: “This budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”
Healey is expected to offer temporary support for poorer families before a steep rise in typical energy bills in January; while pledging energy market reforms aimed at bringing down bills for all households in the longer term.
Andy Burnham recently told MPs he was keen to see the gas standing charge – a fixed daily levy on all users – abolished. The move would bring down bills for consumers who use less energy, and the cost would be picked up by those who use more.
Industry experts fear further investment in hydrogen and carbon capture is likely to bear the brunt of efforts to rein in extra spending, in a blow to the UK’s net zero targets.
As part of a series of “everyday fixes”, the chancellor is expected to end the carers’ allowance cliff edge, which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit, even by as little as a few pence a week. Healey is also expected to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty.
The government has been under pressure to use the budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030 – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.
But while he is expected to confirm more investment in defence industries – described as a “downpayment” on hitting the target – Healey is expected to wait until next year’s spending review to confirm the timetable.
The budget will also set out a “roadmap” to devolving more tax revenues to local leaders in a significant shift towards moving spending power away from Whitehall to the regions and nations of the UK.
But the detail of Burnham’s devolution agenda in areas such as skills and employment support is not expected until the government publishes a white paper in the weeks ahead.
Cutting energy prices has the added benefit of bringing down inflation, helping to ease pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates. Markets are now expecting the Bank to hike rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.
Healey is also expected to take action to offset part of the hit to the public finances from higher interest rates on government borrowing – the result of rising inflation and turmoil in global bond markets.
The government had to pay the highest yield, or interest rate, on new five-year bonds since 2008 on Tuesday, above 5%.
City analysts say bond market investors will be watching the budget closely – though the upward move in UK yields, or interest rates, have echoed those seen in other major economies.
The UK’s economy has proved more resilient than expected in the face of the Iran conflict but recent data has pointed to a deteriorating outlook.
At a cabinet meeting last week, Healey told ministers that rising inflation caused by the conflict, which hit an in-year high of 3.5% last month, was the political backdrop to the budget.
Consumer confidence has fallen at the fastest rate since Brexit; while the number of businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, according to data published by consultancy BTG on Thursday, with hospitality and construction hardest hit.
Healey struck an optimistic note, however, saying: “Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investment’s up, productivity is growing and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”
Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for younger people under the age of 21 after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs but prompting accusations that Labour had broken a manifesto pledge.
He is also expected to protect pensioners and those saving for their retirement by shielding nearly one million people from paying income tax and is preparing to make the government’s revived Help to Buy scheme more generous, in a boost to middle-earners.
To help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, Healey is poised to raise taxes for Britain’s banks, potentially reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt, which would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Online retailers will be responsible for collecting tax owed by firms selling on their platforms.
The Tories said the chancellor was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the prime minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.
The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Richard Fuller, said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge. A ‘do-nothing’ budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiralling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.”
The Lib Dems warned against a “steady as she goes” budget. Their deputy leader, Daisy Cooper, said: “Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable.”

Israel has voted, but the coalition deadlock is just beginning - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:33:34 UTC
07:33:34 KST

An engaged nation went to the polls in unprecedented numbers on Tuesday and spoke. It will now take weeks, if not months, to figure out exactly what it said.
The exit polls released at 10 p.m. by Channels 11, 12, and 13 all showed the so-called change bloc ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc, but Likud emerging as the largest party.
Neither camp, however, appeared to have the partners needed to form the government it promised.
The distinction matters. Taken together, the parties opposed to the outgoing government won a clear majority of the projected seats. But those parties do not constitute a single bloc willing to govern together.
The Arab parties are central to that gap.
According to the exit polls, they won a combined 17 to 18 seats, making them one of the election’s biggest stories. Their apparent strength helped deny Netanyahu a majority. Yet the change bloc’s commitments against relying on them also complicate its ability to replace him.
The Arab parties’ seats count just as much as anyone else’s. The obstacle is other parties’ willingness to enter a governing arrangement with them.
The result, if it holds, is a clear parliamentary majority against the outgoing government – 1,116 days after October 7 – without a clear agreement on what should replace it.
Expect Netanyahu, Eisenkot both to claim victory
Both camps asked the public for a decisive outcome. Neither got everything it wanted.
Netanyahu apparently emerged at the head of the largest party, but without a clear path to a coalition. Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot emerged at the head of the larger change bloc, but with a gap between the seats opposing Netanyahu and the partners available to form a government.
Expect both to claim victory.
Netanyahu will point to Likud’s lead over Yashar, which trailed it by two or three seats in the exit polls. Eisenkot will point to the balance between the blocs.
Netanyahu knows better than most that the largest party does not necessarily form the government. In 2009, Tzipi Livni’s Kadima won one more seat than Likud. Netanyahu became prime minister because he could assemble a coalition and she could not.
The question now is whether Eisenkot can do what Netanyahu did then.
That will require finding a way around commitments that, during the campaign, sounded unequivocal.
Eisenkot set four conditions for prospective coalition partners that the Arab parties would be unlikely to meet. His camp will now have to confront the consequences of those conditions: a majority for replacing Netanyahu may exist on paper without being available around the cabinet table.
Even a willingness to rely on Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am party would not, on the figures emerging Tuesday night, necessarily close the gap. Support from the Joint List would raise a further set of political obstacles.
The Arab parties, meanwhile, have voters and demands of their own. They cannot simply be penciled into someone else’s coalition arithmetic as though their only function were to provide the missing seats.
Their projected gains came as a result of a strong determination to ensure that another right-wing government does not emerge.
But helping to deny the outgoing coalition a majority and helping to install its replacement are two different achievements. The first appears within reach. The second will depend on negotiations and decisions still to come.
Another route for Eisenkot would be to bring in the two haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, projected together to win 12 seats.
That could provide a majority. It would also give those parties considerable leverage over a government whose prospective partners have promised meaningful changes to haredi conscription.
The difficulty is obvious. Bringing the haredi parties into the government might solve the coalition arithmetic while making one of its central policy commitments considerably harder to fulfill.
There is also an option that jumps off the page: a government comprising Likud, Yashar, Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, and Yisrael Beytenu.
On the projected figures, those parties would together have 67 seats, without the haredi parties, the Arab parties, or the parties on the hard-right (Otzma Yehudit and the Religious Zionist Party) or the hard-left (the Democrats).
Numerically straightforward. Politically, anything but.
If Netanyahu remains at Likud’s helm, such a government would require his opponents to abandon their promises not to serve under him. It would also require agreement on who leads and on what terms.
A coalition that looks doable on paper is anything in real life. That is the central problem emerging from Tuesday’s exit polls.
There are combinations that produce a majority. There are fewer combinations that the parties have said they are prepared to join.
Weeks following election will test final or negotiating positions
The coming weeks will test whether those positions are final or negotiating positions.
First, however, the votes must be counted. Exit polls provide the opening frame for coalition negotiations, not the final count on which they will rest.
But if the broad picture holds, the question will shift quickly from how Israelis voted to what their elected representatives are prepared to do with those votes.
More specifically: which campaign promises will survive contact with the results?
Throughout the campaign, parties told voters whom they would sit with, whom they would never sit with, and what conditions they would insist upon before joining a government.
Those promises matter. A voter is entitled to know whether a ballot cast for one party might help put someone else in the prime minister’s chair.
But when enough parties rule out enough other parties, the result can be a Knesset with no workable majority.
Someone will now have to decide whether the greater obligation is to honor a campaign commitment or to compromise sufficiently to allow a government to be formed.
Those arguing for compromise can be expected to call it national responsibility. Those opposing it will call it a betrayal.
Netanyahu cannot in any way point to these projections and claim that the country gave him a vote of confidence.
His opponents can point to a majority that emerged against his government, but still have to demonstrate that they can turn it into a government of their own.
The politicians now have to decide what they are prepared to change: their conditions, their partners, or their promises.
Failing that, they may eventually ask the voters to try again.

‘Only Bibi’: At Likud headquarters, supporters put their faith in Netanyahu

2026-10-27
22:33:02 UTC
07:33:02 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for a strong right-wing government and warned against forming one dependent on Arab parties early Wednesday, telling activists and journalists at Likud’s election headquarters in Jerusalem to await the final count after exit polls left the outcome unresolved.
“The Likud is the largest party in Israel,” Netanyahu said. He also claimed that the right-wing bloc held a decisive majority among the Jewish and Zionist public and those who supported the Jewish state.
Updated exit polls from Kan and Channel 13 put Netanyahu’s bloc and the four-party opposition grouping at 51 seats each, with the Arab parties on 18. Channel 12 put Netanyahu’s bloc at 52, the opposition grouping at 49 and the Arab parties at 19.
“We must establish a strong, right-wing, national government,” Netanyahu said.
He warned against establishing a government reliant on what he called anti-Zionist Arab parties, accusing them of opposing Israel’s existence and attacking its soldiers. He challenged politicians advocating an alliance of those who serve in the military over the possibility of cooperating with those parties.
His remarks placed the question of reliance on Arab parties at the center of the uncertain coalition arithmetic, even as he urged supporters to wait for the actual results.
Netanyahu recounts government’s military achievements, unfinished work
Speaking to party activists after a night of chants of “Only Bibi!”, Netanyahu recounted what he presented as his government’s military achievements and argued that its work remained unfinished.
“Iran is weaker than ever; Israel is stronger than ever,” he said.
He described an opportunity to work with US President Donald Trump to remove the Iranian threat, while warning that the danger would persist as long as the current regime remained in power.
Netanyahu’s call for patience followed similar messages from Likud MK Amit Halevi and supporters interviewed by The Jerusalem Post throughout the night.
Halevi disputed the initial projection of 50 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc, arguing that it understated its support and would not be the final outcome.
He described the election as Israeli society’s response to the October 7 attacks and three years of war. People had not remained indifferent, he told the Post. They had come out to vote.
Halevi also pointed to the projected strength of the Arab parties. His objection to their political influence, he said, concerned what he characterized as their radical ideology, rather than ethnicity.
He warned that an attempt by Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a government reliant on figures Halevi described as radical advisers to Yasser Arafat would fail.
Inside the hall, classic Israeli songs played in Mizrahi renditions. Journalists, activists, party members and sitting MKs filled the venue, surrounded by Likud’s blue and white and campaign posters.
When Meir Cohen, a longtime Likud member, was asked how Netanyahu would navigate the uncertainty and assemble a government, the answer was simple.
“I trust Bibi,” he told the Post.
Cohen traced his connection to Likud to his birth in 1973, saying Menachem Begin had been his sandak, holding him during his brit milah, the Jewish ritual circumcision.
He expressed distrust of the initial projections from the three main broadcasters and credited Netanyahu with strengthening Israel’s military power and standing abroad.
“He will protect us. He will continue to protect us,” Cohen said.
For supporter Tomer Shlomi Mishkaf Lavan, the evening was about the country’s future and the need to bring Israelis together.
This ship called the State of Israel to safe harbor'
“We are fighting for the future of the State of Israel,” he told the Post, calling for a strong leader who would unite the country.
He returned repeatedly to the divisions between Israelis, describing angry exchanges, burning tires and blocked roads over the past four years. He wanted quiet, an end to the protests and a different atmosphere between people.
“We need mutual responsibility. We need people to love one another,” he said.
Asked what being at Likud headquarters meant to him personally, he again spoke about overcoming divisions.
“I came here to express my opinion. My opinion is unity,” he said.
He wanted Netanyahu to mend the country’s rifts and guide “this ship called the State of Israel to safe harbor.”
Another supporter, who told the Post he had worked for the movement for decades, urged patience with the projections and questioned whether they fairly reflected support for Netanyahu.
Throughout the night, questions about seats and coalition partners repeatedly brought the conversation back to the prime minister himself.
“I trust Bibi,” Cohen said.

Eisenkot and Netanyahu have reason to celebrate, but Israel does not, yet - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:32:13 UTC
07:32:13 KST

If there are two clear winners from Tuesday’s election, at least according to the exit polls, they are Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former IDF chief of staff began this campaign with his party polling in the single digits. If the projections hold, the ended it as the clear head of the bloc seeking to oust Benjamin Netanyahu.
That is no small achievement, and it sends a clear message to Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman: It is time to set aside their plans to force Eisenkot into a rotation agreement that would make one of them prime minister first. The opposition camp has spoken, and the voters have chosen Eisenkot. The others need to respect that decision, and if the opposition is to form a government, Eisenkot should lead it.
Netanyahu also pulled off an impressive win. Based on the projections, he is close to 27 seats, almost nine more than what the final polls said he would get. He couldn't increase his bloc, which is at about 50, but he led the Likud to an impressive accomplishment: ending, despite everything, as the largest party in the Knesset.
But while Eisenkot and Netanyahu scored personal accomplishments, the question is whether the Israeli people have won. That will take time to know.
The exit polls point to a problem that has long been known throughout the campaign: Neither camp has a decisive 61-seat majority, and neither has a clear path to forming a coalition. That leaves us with a simple but unavoidable conclusion. For Israel to form a government in the coming weeks, someone will have to break a campaign promise.
It could be Eisenkot deciding to form a government with the support of Ra’am, the Arab party led by Mansour Abbas. It could be Bennett, Liberman or even Eisenkot deciding to cross the partisan line and join a government with Netanyahu.
That is why the coming days will be so consequential. Because if no one is willing to compromise, Israel could find itself barreling straight toward another election. And after everything this country has endured in recent years, that would be a gamble we simply cannot afford.
Another conclusion from the exit polls is worth noting: a decisive majority of Israelis oppose Netanyahu and want to see him out of office. Based on projections, approximately 70 seats went to parties, Jewish and Arab, committed to ousting Netanyahu.
That does not mean all 70 support Eisenkot or that they can necessarily sit together in one government. But it does mean that Netanyahu and his coalition have lost the support of a majority of the electorate.
And this brings us to another disturbing feature of this election – the Arab turnout and the results that they brought, either 17 or 18 seats. That is unprecedented, despite the campaign that the Likud led in which it warned that Arab citizens were voting in large numbers. The message was unmistakable: high Arab turnout was presented not as a celebration of Israeli democracy but as a threat to Israel’s future.
We have become so accustomed to this rhetoric that we barely notice it anymore. But we should.
Imagine an American politician warning next week that too many Jews were turning out to vote in Michigan. People would be outraged, and rightly so. Why, then, do we accept similar rhetoric about Arab citizens in Israel?
Arab Israelis are citizens of this country. They have the same right to vote as Jewish Israelis. It is one of the founding principles of the state, enshrined in the Declaration of Independence, a document this government has too often tried to cast aside.
Are there legitimate reasons to debate whether Arab political parties should be included in the next government? Yes. But portraying high voter turnout among Arab citizens as a threat to Israel’s future is something entirely different.
The real question now is whether the politicians elected on Tuesday will be able to translate the results into a functioning government.
Even if the exit polls show a decisive majority against Netanyahu, he will not simply step aside. He will hope that Eisenkot, Bennett and Liberman fail to agree on a path forward, fail to agree to sit with the Arabs, and if that happens, he will then have an opening to try to bring one of those parties into his camp.
But that will not be simple. Any party considering joining Netanyahu will come with demands. It will almost certainly refuse to let him take the first turn as prime minister in a rotation agreement; it will demand a state commission of inquiry be established into the failures of October 7, and it will need a real solution to the ultra-Orthodox draft crisis that has torn Israel apart.
Can Netanyahu agree to all of that? Probably not
For Eisenkot and his potential partners, time will be critical, and they will need to move fast if they want to form a government – whether with Arab parties or a minority government. Netanyahu will not sit quietly while they negotiate and he will try to recruit defectors and prevent the establishment of a coalition before it can even take shape.
There is also the looming possibility of another attack against Iran, potentially right after the American midterm elections next week. A new war could give Netanyahu an opening to try to force a national unity government.
In the coming days, we will find out the final results of the vote. Such a high turnout shows us just how concerned Israelis are for the future of their country.
The voters have done their part. Now the politicians need to do theirs.

Caproni told the brothers: “Your conduct was monstrous.”
Tal, 40, and Oren and Alon, both 39, maintained grim expressions during the sentencing but otherwise had little reaction. The prison terms, while lengthy, were less than the life behind bars prosecutors sought. Lawyers for the brothers told the judge they would appeal.
The prosecution was one of the highest-profile sex-trafficking cases to go to trial in recent years.
Oren and Tal were brokers on some of the most expensive residential property sales ever in New York and Miami, claiming US$8 billion (S$10.26 billion) in sales and dubbing themselves the “0.1% of brokers that really sell to the 0.1% of clients”.
At trial, several women testified that they were drugged and raped after being lured to parties, music festivals and other events in glamorous locations such as the Hamptons and Aspen, Colorado.

Before sentencing the brothers, Caproni allowed 12 victims to speak. Many addressed the brothers directly, who showed no visible reaction during the statements. One woman said their “wealth, power and social standing cannot shield them from the consequences of their actions”.
Lawyers for the brothers had asked that they be given no more than 15 years behind bars. They claimed that all the encounters were consensual and accused the government of trying to criminalise the behaviour of successful young men seeking to enjoy their lives as bachelors.
The Alexanders also addressed the court. They maintained their innocence and characterised their actions as youthful partying and womanising that often involved recreational drug use and excessive drinking.
Tal described himself as having a “work hard, play hard mentality”.
“I sometimes behaved in ways I’m not proud of,” he told the judge.
Caproni suggested that the brothers might have been better off remaining silent. “You didn’t have to say anything this afternoon. You did not have to stand up and say you never drugged or raped a woman,” she said.
“In my view, that’s entirely a lie.”
But the judge also said she regarded sentencing them to life in prison as a “draconian penalty” and that she did not believe the brothers were “beyond redemption”.
In a statement, Manhattan US Attorney Jamie McDonald, whose office prosecuted the case, said: “Today’s sentence makes clear that this craven, sinister conduct is extraordinarily serious and will be met with serious punishment.” BLOOMBERG

AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:30:45 UTC
07:30:45 KST

AI bots flooded a government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.
Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.
The attempt to manipulate the outcome of the consultation was disclosed on Tuesday in research published in the journal Tobacco Control by the health policy experts Dr Nason Maani, from the University of Edinburgh, and Prof Anna Gilmore, of the University of Bath.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) used bot-detection methods to identify that 90,835 of the 118,756 responses it received, 76%, were submitted by bots.
All but two of those 90,835 automated responses answered the same question in the “smoke free generation” consultation, in which they opposed Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government’s plan to ban disposable vapes. The submissions were “often duplicated many times and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses”, the DHSC said.
The bombardment “appears to be the first documented instance of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation”, the researchers said.
Maani added that while this attempt was identified, “the threat is that future campaigns become harder to catch, and what we can’t catch, we don’t know about. Such campaigns are a threat because they raise the possibility of a handful of powerful interests looking like a mass movement.”
The DHSC excluded the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. Keir Starmer’s Labour government inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes.
Caroline Cerny, the deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “Evidence that AI bots have been used to swamp a Department of Health consultation is deeply concerning.
“Given the tobacco industry’s history of seeking to undermine public health regulation, we need to be alert to the risk that technological advances can be used to further commercial interests around health policy and put safeguards in place.
“Decisions that affect public health must be based on sound evidence and expertise, not manipulated response numbers.”
Azzurra Moores, the associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, described the attempt to derail the ban as “pretty alarming”.
“Public consultations are one of the main ways government opens up its decision-making, so any interference with them is a serious concern,” she said. “These findings are pretty alarming: if a consultation can be swamped like this, it stops telling policymakers what the public actually thinks and undermines trust in the process.
“This is a problem without easy answers. Every barrier that keeps bots out also makes it harder for real people to take part, and AI makes fake responses far harder to spot. Interference can adapt faster than departments can update their checks. Better screening and more transparency will help, but there’s no single fix.”
The DHSC said its “robust controls” identified the attempt to influence the consultation.
A spokesperson said: “We always have robust controls in place to prevent the manipulation of our public consultations, and those controls worked effectively in this case.
“As a result, the fake responses were removed, and the consultation helped inform the landmark action we are taking to create a smoke-free generation.
“We will remain alert to interference of this kind in future consultation processes, and we will not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.”

Israeli exit polls show deadlock, setback for Netanyahu
Israel’s wartime election appeared deadlocked on Oct 27, exit polls showed, a potential setback for veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if the projections hold, with neither side having a clear path to power but rival Gadi Eisenkot’s larger bloc potentially giving him the first chance to form a government.
The stalemate could yet work in Netanyahu’s favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Turnout was 77.7%, Israel’s Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in the previous election in 2022.
Israel’s three major networks updated their exit polls, giving Eisenkot’s bloc a two-seat edge over Netanyahu’s Likud-led camp, at 52-50 respectively. The remaining 18 seats were allocated to unaligned Arab parties in the exit polls.
Trump will respect US midterm results ‘if they’re honest’
President Donald Trump said on Oct 27 he would respect the results of the US midterm elections “if they’re honest,” in what appeared to be a fresh bid to sow doubt ahead of next week’s crucial vote.
Trump has ramped up his baseless, years-old claims of mass voter fraud as polls show Republicans could lose control of Congress in the Nov 3 elections.
“I will, if they’re honest elections,” Trump told reporters when asked if he would respect the results of the midterms, as he headed on a campaign trip to Texas.
Flavio Bolsonaro, family to receive US visas after leaving Brazil

Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.

Ukraine, Russia say US-brokered Oleshky truce holding
A local truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours.
Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3am local time (9am in Singapore).
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Pope’s cancer a ‘gamechanger’ for papacy

“It’s a bit of a gamechanger,” Archbishop Paul Gallagher told journalists at an event in Rome.
Leo, 71, had part of one lung removed in surgery on Oct 13. His doctors have said the cancer was localised and had not spread, and the pope will not require further treatment.

Russian District in Siberia to Cut 37% of Administrative Staff as Budget Gap Widens
Authorities in Russia’s Irkutsk region have begun cutting public-sector jobs as a widening budget deficit forces local governments to reduce spending, The Moscow Times reported on October 27.
The layoffs have begun in the Nizhneilimsk municipal district, where 37% of administrative staff are expected to lose their jobs by the end of the year, district head Pavel Berezovsky stated.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have major budget problems, and we are cutting our expenses,” Berezovsky noted. He added that the financial strain was affecting not only his district, but the wider region and other parts of Russia.
Among the first positions targeted are night guards at schools, kindergartens, and cultural centers, as well as workers at municipal companies responsible for local infrastructure.
Technical staff at social institutions in the Chunsky district are also expected to be cut. District head Nikolai Khrychov stated that several institutions would each lose four guards and four boiler-room workers.
“We feel very sorry for the people. But otherwise, we will not even have money for electricity at the same facility,” Khrychov was quoted as stating.
An updated 2026 budget proposal submitted to the Irkutsk regional legislature last week showed the deficit had widened to 11.8% of expenditures, up from 8.3% before the latest amendments.
Irkutsk is the second-largest economy in Russia’s Siberian Federal District by gross regional product, behind only Krasnoyarsk region, according to official data cited by The Moscow Times.
The cuts in Irkutsk come as financial pressure spreads across Russian regional budgets. UNITED24 Media reported that around 65 regions were preparing to reduce investment and infrastructure spending between 2027 and 2029, while Russia’s Finance Ministry projects a combined regional budget deficit of about $10.5 billion in 2027.

The US and Canada are talking trade. That doesn’t mean they’re near a deal.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:26:55 UTC
07:26:55 KST

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shows a watch to U.S. President Donald Trump as they attend a work lunch as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, eastern France, on June 16, 2026. | Evelyn Hockstein/Pool/Getty Images
Washington and Ottawa have increased the tempo of their trade talks over the past week, after President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke by phone on Oct. 21.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who helped torpedo a previous round of negotiations over the summer, and Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc have been speaking regularly since then, according to two people with knowledge of the talks, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. They have primarily discussed Trump’s tariffs on sectors like autos and steel that have been a sticking point for Canada all along.
Advertisement
A senior Canadian government official told POLITICO that talks remain informal as of Tuesday.
The uptick in engagement — what Carney called “un petit intensification” speaking in French to reporters in Ottawa Monday — has triggered a flurry of headlines on both sides of the border as well as White House boasts that a deal is near. The North American trade spat will be “settled pretty soon,” Trump predicted at a rally Sunday in Michigan.
But unlike Trump, Carney has little political incentive to make concessions at the moment — or bail out Trump right before congressional elections heavily focused on affordability, including tariffs’ impact on prices. The Canadian prime minister is riding high in domestic polls after standing up to the American president and walking away from trade negotiations in August. And he is days away from welcoming European Union leaders to Montreal for a landmark summit aimed at deepening their alliance — and building an implicit counterweight to the U.S.
Neither side, moreover, has dropped its original demands, according to half a dozen current and former government officials, industry representatives and others with knowledge of the talks. Those outstanding sticking points include Carney’s ask for lower auto tariffs and Trump’s push for increased access to the Canadian alcohol and dairy markets.
The lack of new concessions or tangible breakthroughs is a sign that the recent flurry of outreach may be more of a White House effort to soothe Republicans’ midterm worries — particularly in border states whose economies are tightly connected to Canada’s — than to secure an immediate deal. The people say any denouement between the two countries is likely weeks if not months off, even as they expect the two North American neighbors to ultimately hammer out an agreement to lower tariffs and stabilize one of the world’s largest trading relationships.
“I think that we’re going to make a deal with Canada. I mean, first of all, we made a deal with Canada. They reneged on the deal,” Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said in an interview. Asked if the deal will come before the election, Moreno said, “I don’t know.”
Advertisement
Canada has also been cautious about promising that a deal is near. Carney said last week Ottawa doesn’t care about “the timing” of an agreement to roll back tariffs on each other’s imports. And both Mark Wiseman, the Canadian Ambassador to the U.S., and Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. Ambassador to Canada, suggested at an event in Ottawa Monday that there will be a deal, even if it takes time.
“We have to take a longer timeline into account. And at the end of the day, we have to remember neither of us is moving out of the neighborhood, and we’re going to make it work,” Wiseman said. “The state of the relationship is pretty damn good.”
Trump, however, has been lobbing attacks on Ottawa since he returned to the White House, calling Canada the 51st state and threatening tariffs since shortly after his reelection win. Canada, along with Mexico and China, was one of the first countries he targeted with new duties in 2025 — despite an existing North American free trade deal and deeply entwined economies, particularly in the auto industry.
The tensions hit a crescendo this summer, when Trump announced a preliminary deal with Carney to lower U.S. duties, among other measures, before talks collapsed at the 11th hour. Washington and Ottawa then traded 50% duties on about $20 billion worth of goods, with Trump imposing a ban on certain products, like alcohol, and threatening even more punitive duties come January if their differences have not been resolved.
The forces that caused the deal to unravel in August are still in place. Canada has continued to seek lower tariff rates for key sectors, including autos, trucks, steel and aluminum — policies that are under Lutnick’s purview at the Commerce Department. The previous talks hit a snag over whether the U.S. would lower tariffs on heavy duty trucks, some of which are built in Ontario.
“Any potential Canada deal is going to have the same issue,” said an industry official granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. “And that is Lutnick’s strong reluctance to negotiate on the [sector-specific tariffs], particularly now that he is much heavier involved.”
Advertisement
Lutnick “has signed off on auto [tariff] reductions,” in previous trade agreements the White House reached with partners like the European Union and Japan, “but those often come with promises of large investment.”
A White House official confirmed Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have held discussions with their Canadian counterparts in recent days.
“USTR and the Commerce Department continue to work together on the cross-cutting issues involving trade with Canada,” added the official, who was granted anonymity to share details about the negotiations.
The Commerce Department and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative did not respond to requests for comment.
Industry groups that are in favor of keeping the existing duties on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos insist that Lutnick remains in their corner, even as talks intensify. Representatives for domestic manufacturing met with senior officials at the Commerce Department and USTR over the past week to lobby in favor of sticking with the status quo, according to two people granted anonymity to describe the private discussions.
“”The programs are effective as they are, and they should stay as they are,” said Century Aluminum President and CEO Jesse Gary, adding that Lutnick shows a “clear understanding of what makes these types of industries work.”
Advertisement
The Canada tariffs are unpopular among U.S. voters, however, and have been a headache for Republican candidates running in U.S. border states. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers of Michigan and Republican Senate hopeful John Sununu of New Hampshire have all come out against the deal. The topic has even trickled into competitive races in Texas and Kansas.
Adam Hamilton, the Democrat challenging Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, is making tariffs part of his closing argument in a state where the agriculture industry has been pummeled by the trade war.
Trump and his National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett have sought to play down Republicans’ concerns about the duties by suggesting a deal is close.
Speaking to Fox News on Sunday, Hassett said that the two sides are “very close” to a deal and emphasized Lutnick’s involvement in talks.
“I expect this is supposed to send some sort of signal to … Iowa and Kansas and other states,” said a person close to the administration who was granted anonymity to share details of private conversations with officials. But “no one expects a deal,” the person said.
“Carney would have to have some reason to want to get a deal before the midterms,” the person added. “But I can’t imagine why he would at this point.”
Megan Messerly, Sue Allan, Zi-Ann Lum and Nick Taylor-Vaisey contributed reporting.

Porsche posts earnings rebound but expects lower vehicle sales in 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:25:04 CST
07:25:04 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A senior executive at German sports carmaker Porsche said Tuesday that 2027 was expected to mark a low point for the company, with vehicle sales and operating profit likely to decline, despite a sharp rebound in earnings in the first nine months of 2026.
Porsche chief financial officer Jochen Breckner attributed the expected downturn to gaps in the company's "product portfolio," noting during a quarterly earnings presentation that the combustion-engine Macan was no longer available following the end of its production earlier this year.
According to financial results released Tuesday, Porsche's global vehicle deliveries fell 16 percent year-on-year to 178,532 units in the first nine months, while revenue declined by a smaller 5.9 percent to 25.28 billion euros (28.17 billion U.S. dollars). The company said a higher proportion of high-margin models helped cushion the impact of lower sales volumes.
By contrast, operating profit surged to 1.74 billion euros (1.94 billion dollars) from just 40 million euros (44.6 million dollars) a year earlier, lifting the operating profit margin to 6.9 percent from 0.2 percent.
The Volkswagen-owned carmaker attributed the sharp rebound largely to lower special charges, which fell to around 500 million euros (557 million dollars) in the first nine months from 2.7 billion euros (3 billion dollars) a year earlier.
The charges were mainly related to changes in its electric vehicle strategy and battery operations, alongside workforce restructuring.
In 2022, Porsche announced an ambitious electrification target, aiming for fully electric vehicles to account for more than 80 percent of its sales by 2030.
However, the company revised its strategy late last year amid weaker-than-expected demand for electric vehicles, delaying some electric vehicle projects and extending plans for combustion-engine models. The changes resulted in substantial one-off charges that weighed heavily on last year's earnings.
Alongside the shift in its product strategy, Porsche has also moved to cut costs and reduce its workforce. In July, the company announced plans to cut another 5,000 jobs in Germany by 2035, bringing its planned workforce reductions to around 9,000 positions in the country. ■

Netanyahu's rival Eisenkot says ready to form government as exit polls show Israeli election deadlock

Gadi Eisenkot (C), former Israeli military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar party, delivers a speech at the centrist Yashar party campaign headquarters in Tel Aviv, Israel, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Gil Cohen Magen/Xinhua)
JERUSALEM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot said Tuesday night that exit polls showing his bloc ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's ruling coalition reflected a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu's government, vowing to move swiftly to replace it, as the projections pointed to a parliamentary election deadlock.
Exit polls by public broadcaster Kan and commercial TV Channel 13 projected 53 seats for Eisenkot's bloc against 50 for Netanyahu's, while Channel 12 gave Eisenkot's bloc 52 seats and Netanyahu's 50. Neither bloc reached the 61 seats needed for a majority.
"If these are the final results, this is a victory for Israel's mainstream Zionist majority," Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, said in a statement.
He pledged to act immediately to "implement the people's decision, replace Netanyahu's government and establish a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible."
"The public has fired Netanyahu's government," said Yair Golan, leader of the center-left Democrats party, which supports the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Yair Lapid, the current opposition head, said in a statement that the Netanyahu bloc has suffered "a crushing defeat" and "a total collapse."
Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and the Muslim Ra'am party, were projected to win 17 to 18 seats in the 120-member Knesset or parliament, potentially holding the balance of power. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out forming a coalition with them.
With no outright majority, the results point to potentially prolonged coalition negotiations and political instability.
The exit polls are preliminary, with final official results expected in the coming days or even weeks. ■

Yemen's Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi targets

07:24:56 KST

SANAA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Tuesday it had launched a new wave of drone and missile attacks on several Saudi targets, while claiming to have repelled a fresh ground offensive near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a series of statements posted on social media platform X that a ballistic missile targeted the Saudi Defense Ministry in Riyadh, claiming the missile scored a "direct hit."
Sarea added that two other ballistic missiles targeted Saudi military transport aircraft, one at Najran Airport in Najran province and the other at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, Asir province, asserting both attacks "successfully achieved their objectives."
He also claimed a drone targeted Abha International Airport in the southwestern Asir province and "accurately hit" its target, causing disruption to flight operations.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of the Houthi claim.
Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by Yemen's Houthi group toward Riyadh.
Separately, Sarea said Houthi forces had repelled an advance by government-aligned forces approaching Bab al-Mandab from the south, saying the advancing units were targeted with ballistic missiles and heavy weapons. He claimed the attacks inflicted heavy casualties and destroyed several military vehicles.
The Houthi statements came as government forces renewed their ground offensive near Bab al-Mandab early Tuesday, seeking to dislodge Houthi forces from remaining positions around the strategic waterway linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. The Saudi Arabia-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

New CDC report finds 19 germs cause 50,800 deaths annually in U.S.
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:24:56 CST
07:24:56 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Nineteen pathogens cause an estimated 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the United States each year, according to an updated report released by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Tuesday.
The 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report is the CDC's most comprehensive estimate to date of the impact of drug-resistant bacteria and fungi, as well as Clostridioides difficile, the CDC said.
The report classifies 19 pathogens according to their threat to public health in the United States: four as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats and two as concerning threats.
The four urgent threats are Candida auris (C. auris), carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, and drug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the report said.
Drug-resistant C. auris infections have increased tenfold since 2019, and some strains are resistant to available classes of antifungal drugs, according to the report.
The report also highlighted the rapid spread of resistance genes, which can make infections harder to treat and more deadly.
"Antimicrobial resistance threatens modern medicine and puts millions of Americans at risk every year," CDC Director Erica Schwartz was quoted as saying by U.S. media outlets. "High-quality data help drive action, and CDC is committed to providing easily accessible information to help protect people from drug-resistant infections." ■

MOSCOW, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Russia has barred seven British defense industry executives from entering the country, accusing their companies of supplying Ukraine with weapons and military technologies, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Tuesday.
In a statement published on its website, the ministry said the executives were added to Russia's entry ban list because their companies supply weapons and technologies that are used in Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory.
Three of the executives are from Rotron Aerospace: CEO Alex Head, chief military adviser Kev Oliver and board chairman George Zambellas. The company is involved in the development of the Brakestop long-range missile project, the ministry said.
The other four are Robert Gascoyne, CEO of MGI Engineering, which is also involved in the Brakestop project; Neil Appleton, CEO of drone maker Malloy Aeronautics; Paul Webb, director and co-founder of reconnaissance drone maker Tekever UK; and Julian Cracknell, chief technology and information officer at BAE Systems.
The ministry accused Britain of supplying Ukraine with missile and drone weapons and technologies, with the aim of inflicting maximum damage on Russia. It also criticized the British government's defense spending priorities, arguing that funds allocated to military contractors could instead be used to support Britain's civilian sector amid domestic economic and social challenges. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- With humanitarian needs outpacing relief efforts amid ongoing hostilities in northern Ethiopia, UN humanitarians said Tuesday they were mobilizing additional resources, including by reprioritizing existing funding.

In Tigray, 45 trucks carrying food supplies from partner organization World Vision arrived in Shire Town on Monday, it added. ■

Boeing narrows Q3 net loss as revenue rises 4 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:24:21 CST
07:24:21 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- U.S. aerospace giant Boeing on Tuesday reported a sharp reduction in its third-quarter net loss, while revenue rose 4 percent year on year to 24.19 billion U.S. dollars, driven by stronger defense and services businesses.
For the quarter that ended Sept. 30, Boeing posted a net loss of 116 million dollars, compared with 5.34 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted loss per share narrowed to 26 cents from 7.14 dollars, while core loss per share, a non-GAAP measure, narrowed to 34 cents from 7.47 dollars.
Operating profit reached 354 million dollars, reversing a 4.78-billion-dollar loss, while operating margin improved to 1.5 percent from negative 20.5 percent.
Commercial airplanes revenue fell 3 percent to 10.7 billion dollars, reflecting a less favorable delivery mix. The division's operating loss narrowed to 697 million dollars from 5.35 billion dollars, while deliveries edged up to 161 aircraft from 160.
Boeing said higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and increased supply chain costs weighed on the division's performance. The year-earlier results were affected by a charge related to the 777X program.
Defense, space and security revenue rose 15 percent to 7.94 billion dollars, with operating profit increasing to 492 million dollars from 114 million dollars, partly reflecting a 252-million-dollar gain from the sale of HRL Laboratories.
Global services revenue grew 4 percent to 5.57 billion dollars, while operating profit reached 1.02 billion dollars.
Operating cash flow rose 33 percent year on year to 1.5 billion dollars, while free cash flow, a non-GAAP measure, reached 464 million dollars. Total order backlog rose to a record 745 billion dollars, including more than 6,300 commercial airplanes.
Boeing also reported progress in its aircraft certification programs. The 737-7 received amended type certification from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration during the quarter, while the 737-10 obtained certification in October. The company said the 777X program remains on track for its first delivery in 2027. ■

Britain's shop price inflation keeps surging in October amid cost hikes: BRC
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:24:16 CST
07:24:16 KST

LONDON, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Britain's shop price inflation rose to the highest level in two and a half years amid retailers' limited capability to absorb cost hikes, data from the British Retail Consortium (BRC) showed Tuesday.
Shop prices increased 2.1 percent year on year in October, accelerating from 1.4 percent in September, and well above the 3-month average of 1.6 percent, according to the BRC.
Food inflation accelerated to 2.9 percent from 2.5 percent in September, while non-food inflation rose to 1.7 percent from 0.8 percent.
Mike Watkins, head of retailer and business insight at global marketing research firm NielsenIQ, said global supply chain pressures grew over the last six months, but price cuts by food retailers since the end of summer have delayed some of the impact.
High street retailers will now be more reliant on promotions to drive discretionary non-food spending as consumers are becoming more cautious in the face of higher energy and fuel costs, he added.
Commenting on the record-high shop price inflation, BRC Chief Executive Helen Dickinson said, "The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years."
Although retailers still deliver plenty of promotions on sweet treats ahead of Halloween, price hikes of ambient groceries have driven up food inflation, she noted, emphasizing that non-food inflation climbed to an almost three-year peak as high energy and transport costs pushed up prices.
"The message to the Chancellor ahead of tomorrow's Budget could not be clearer: act now, or prices will keep on rising," Dickinson said, arguing that since retailers cannot endlessly swallow higher business rates, employment costs, energy bills and packaging taxes, October's jump in inflation is only the beginning without a change of course. ■

Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:24:04 UTC
07:24:04 KST

Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
When Donald Trump returned triumphantly to the White House in January 2025, his supporters believed they could finally finish what he started during his first term and reverse the Democrats’ social engineering agenda, commonly known as ‘wokeism’, curb illegal immigration, accelerate technological development, and above all, ‘make America great again’.
Trump moved quickly on the first two priorities, as he revoked 78 of Joe Biden’s executive orders, tightened border controls and gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) greater resources and powers to conduct raids in sanctuary cities, where the local authorities limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
But Trump’s determination to achieve everything at once, from restructuring the federal government and securing favorable trade deals to pursuing ambitions involving Greenland and Venezuela, has kept American politics in a state of turmoil, while his confrontational approach has also unsettled allies and opponents abroad.
The decision to launch joint military operations with Israel against Iran has proven particularly divisive as it fractured Trump’s conservative coalition, with some supporters accusing him of betraying his promise to end America’s ‘endless wars’, while others fear the political consequences for Republicans in the approaching midterm elections.
The Iran war has also hurt American consumers. Over the past year, gasoline prices have risen by 38% and diesel by 71%, while food prices have increased by 2.5%.
The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz isn’t solely responsible, but Democrats and sympathetic media outlets have made it central to their criticism, while they also point to an increase of $3.8 trillion in the national debt since Trump’s return, allegations of corruption within his administration, and questions about the competence of senior officials, particularly Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Republicans, including those who oppose the Iran war, are trying to redirect voters towards the administration’s achievements – despite the turbulence, the US economy has grown by 3.2% since the end of 2024, and investment is booming in certain sectors, particularly technology, while illegal crossings at the southern border have reportedly fallen by 95%.
Vice President J.D. Vance, who is increasingly discussed as Trump’s successor, has urged Americans to give Republicans another chance, or at least another two years, to complete what they have begun – but for now, that opportunity appears uncertain. Yet contrary to expectations, losing control of Congress wouldn’t necessarily be a disaster for Trump.
Even with Republican majorities in both chambers, he has preferred to govern through executive orders, issuing more than 290 since January 2025, and this is hardly unprecedented. Bill Clinton issued 364 over his eight years in office, including during periods when Republicans controlled Congress.
For presidents, demonstrating immediate effectiveness and scoring political points often matters more than ensuring continuity.
Democratic threats to impeach Trump and members of his administration may sound formidable, but removing officials from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate, a much higher hurdle, and even if Democrats capture both chambers, converting their numerical advantage into meaningful political influence will not be straightforward.
They could, however, obstruct legislation, block nominations to senior administration positions and the federal judiciary, and subject the White House to sustained congressional scrutiny.
Their minimum objective would be to turn Trump into a lame-duck president for his remaining two years, but this strategy carries risks of its own – in the 2028 presidential campaign, Republicans can argue that the Democrats prevented them from completing their program.
For Moscow, however, the consequences of the midterms could be considerably more serious.
A Democratic-controlled Congress would almost certainly seek to complicate relations with Russia, and there remains a strong desire in Washington to obstruct Trump’s apparent ambition for a new Yalta involving Russia, China, and the US. Equally persistent is the determination among influential American political circles to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia.
This could explain the Trump administration’s intensified diplomatic activity over Ukraine, given whatever opportunities exist for reaching an agreement today could narrow considerably after the new Congress takes office in January 2027.
The urgency could also reflect an attempt to secure lasting advantages for the administration before the political landscape changes.
The argument that there’s little time left, and that Moscow must therefore accept an agreement now or face worse conditions later, shouldn’t be allowed to overshadow Russia’s own interests.
Russia has an objective interest in normalizing relations with the US, but a settlement of the Ukraine conflict must be based on mutually beneficial terms, rather than unilateral concessions extracted under the pressure of America’s electoral calendar.
Ultimately, as Americans prepare to vote in the midterms, Russia should be concerned less with Trump’s political fortunes than with protecting its own interests.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team

Finland and Norway leaders make rare direct call to Putin, breaking with the West’s diplomatic isolation of the Russian leader to influence Ukraine peace talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:21:42 UTC
07:21:42 KST

Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin on 27 October, urging him to de-escalate Russia’s war against Ukraine and resume negotiations. The roughly 90-minute call was coordinated with Kyiv and came ahead of planned trilateral talks between Ukrainian, US, and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi in November.
The initiative marks a rare direct contact between Western European leaders and Putin since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. The Nordic leaders are reportedly seeking to influence peace efforts increasingly shaped by US President Donald Trump, amid concerns in Europe that Washington is shifting toward Moscow’s position and sidelining Ukraine’s European partners.
Stubb and Støre said they discussed Russia’s war against Ukraine, upcoming negotiations, and security in Europe. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the two leaders had urged Putin to take concrete steps toward de-escalation, particularly regarding attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy says leaders urged energy de-escalation
After the call, Zelenskyy said he had spoken with Stubb and Støre to receive a detailed briefing. He thanked them for supporting Ukraine’s diplomatic efforts and said they had clearly told the Russian leader that real de-escalation steps were needed regarding Ukraine’s energy sector and infrastructure.
Zelenskyy also said the leaders discussed preparations for a trilateral meeting planned for November involving Ukrainian, US, and Russian negotiating teams.
In a joint statement, Stubb and Støre said the call followed their 20 October meeting in Oslo and was held in consultation with Ukraine. They emphasized that Finland and Norway, which both share borders with Russia, would continue their longstanding support for Ukraine.
“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said, adding that the war’s outcome would directly affect Nordic and broader European security. Støre stressed the war’s enormous human and material costs and said the leaders had emphasized the importance of de-escalation.
Moscow gives no sign of changing its position
The Kremlin’s account of the call offered no indication that Putin was prepared to soften his demands, according to Reuters. It said a just and lasting peace was possible only if Russia’s “legitimate interests” were fully taken into account, while blaming EU and NATO policies for prolonging the fighting.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov dismissed the call as offering nothing new on the conflict and accused European countries of seeking a role in negotiations.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin had said the war must end while taking “the realities on the ground” into account. The source interpreted this as meaning Moscow would not compromise on its goal of capturing the entire Donbas region.
Russia has continued its attacks on Ukraine while demanding territorial concessions. Kyiv, meanwhile, has called for meaningful de-escalation and a settlement that preserves Ukraine’s sovereignty and security.
Nordic initiative draws criticism from European partners
The call comes as European governments seek a greater role in peace efforts led by Trump. Western European leaders have largely avoided direct contact with Putin since the invasion, hoping to isolate Moscow, but concerns have grown that Europe is being sidelined in negotiations.
Stubb said Ukraine had sought to open a new channel of communication and that Europe could no longer remain a bystander to peace efforts. He said the initiative had been discussed with Western allies.
However, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the move, saying she saw no signs that Russia wanted peace and arguing that Europe should act together rather than pursue separate initiatives, according to Reuters.
Reuters added that Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said other European leaders had not been informed of the talks and expressed low expectations for the conversation. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also urged caution.
Stubb and Støre stressed that they had acted as leaders of Finland and Norway, not on behalf of Europe as a whole. They said their countries would continue supporting Ukraine while pursuing diplomatic efforts to end the war.
