President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva strongly criticized defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Tuesday, describing the conservative senator’s clandestine departure for the United States as a “shameful” evasion of Brazilian justice.
Speaking two days after winning Brazil's presidential runoff, Lula addressed reports that the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro fled the country to avoid an ongoing money-laundering inquiry.
“He could have stayed and proven that the accusations against him are not true,” Lula remarked. “If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear. A citizen who sneaks out of their own country does so because they have something to hide.”
Confirmation of Bolsonaro’s departure came as a senior US State Department official announced that the US will issue visas to the senator and his family to enter the country.
The flight follows a high-stakes judicial showdown in Brasilia. On Monday, Federal Supreme Court (STF) Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro to hand over all travel documents, including his ordinary, diplomatic, and Italian passports, and imposed a strict departure ban over alleged involvement in a money-laundering scheme linked to illegal digital betting platforms.
After the 24-hour deadline expired on Tuesday morning without compliance, the Federal Police formally revoked his Brazilian passports. Just hours before his departure, Bolsonaro publicly insisted he would not flee.
"I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this farce, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me," he said.
Lula sharply criticized Bolsonaro’s failure to abide by judicial commands, contrasting the senator’s actions with his own historical compliance during previous legal proceedings.
“He has proven himself to be the biggest liar I have ever seen on the face of the Earth,” Lula said. “When I was asked to hand over my passport, I did so. He should have surrendered his to the Federal Police given the suspicion that he might flee. But that is the Bolsonaro family for you, Brazil is only his second homeland. His true allegiance lies with the United States.”
Bolsonaro's sudden flight caps a chaotic three-day period following his unexpected loss in Sunday’s runoff election. After leading the first round on Oct. 4 with 47% of valid votes to Lula’s 45%, Bolsonaro had expressed supreme confidence in victory, dropping hints about his future cabinet appointments.
On Sunday, Lula staged a comeback, capturing 51.76% of valid votes to become the first candidate in Brazilian history to reverse a first-round deficit in a presidential runoff.

Ukraine's Zelenskiy says territory recaptured, forces on the offensive
Oct 27 - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces were retaking territory through a series of offensives, including one operation previously unannounced in which Kyiv's troops used gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions.
Zelenskiy, speaking in his nightly video address, said Kyiv's battlefield position was the strongest in some time in the 4-1/2-year-long war and could be made stronger with more deliveries of air defence systems from its Western allies.
Zelenskiy, citing a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the "Veles" operation using pipelines in Ukraine's northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the "Vivaldi" operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
He said Operation Veles was conducted near Kupiansk, a city in northeastern Kharkiv region recaptured by Ukrainian forces in late 2022, but since under constant Russian pressure.
"It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions," Zelenskiy said.
"Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success," he said.
In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine's Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres.
That operation was focused to the north of the key strongholds in the region — the so-called "fortress belt" of the cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Their capture would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donbas region.
Zelenskiy in August spoke of success in an offensive further south, with 26 villages being returned to Ukrainian control.
Russia says it favours an overall resolution of the war rather than a short-lived ceasefire and has pledged to pursue its drive to capture all of Donbas.
Russian commanders repeatedly say, often in announcements in President Vladimir Putin's presence, that their forces are advancing on all sections of the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line.
The chief of Russia's General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, said this month that Moscow's forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.

Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil amid corruption investigations
October 27, 2026
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left Brazil for the United States after he was defeated in Sunday's presidential election.
The US State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the US, a senior State Department official said.
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured the runoff victory in elections, told supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had left the country.
Brazil is "the second country" of the Bolsonaro family, Lula added.
"The first is licking American boots," the reelected president said. "Those who are not liable do not fear. A fellow who secretly leaves his country, that's because he is liable for something."
Bolsonaro leaves Brazil after losing presidential election: What to know
The Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports to stop him from leaving the country. The senator is facing multiple corruption investigations.
Bolsonaro said that he had received the Supreme Court order outside the home where his father, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest.
He said Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the order, the same judge who sentenced his father to prison.
The senator said in an Instagram post on Monday that he had planned to hand over his passports, but reports on Tuesday said the passports had been canceled after the deadline to turn them in had passed.
Bolsonaro lost the election runoff on Sunday after an incredibly tight voting count through the evening until Lula surged ahead.
The leftist incumbent eventually won by a clear margin of more than 4 million votes.
Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the election results, pointing to the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.
Bolsonaro's Liberal Party on Tuesday acknowledged the results, but the senator has not yet conceded victory.
His refusal to accept the results mirrors how his father Jair disputed his election defeat to Lula four years ago.
Jair is serving a more than 20-year prison sentence for plotting a coup to overthrow Lula after the 2022 election.
How did Bolsonaro exit Brazil?
The Argentinian Migration Department on Wednesday said Flavio Bolsonaro and his family had briefly entered Argentina before taking a private plane to Ecuador.
The department added that Bolsonaro and his family had entered the country through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing in Misiones Province.
It also said that they were holding valid travel documents and that there was "no legal impediment" blocking their entry, despite a court order banning Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil.
Argentine news outlet Infobae reported earlier on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had crossed into Argentina to board a plane to the US.
Bolsonaro's exact whereabouts were unclear, with some reports claiming that he had landed in the US, while others said he was in Ecuador or still en route.
US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he "would approve" of the far-right senator coming to the US.
"I think they're fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews.
Trump also repeated his belief that Flavio's father, Jair, was the victim of persecution by Brazil's judicial authorities.
"The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn't involved," Trump added. "That's Brazil. It's a different country."
Flavio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, said on a podcast last week that his sibling should leave the country if he lost the election.
Eduardo, who lives in the US, was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a warrant was issued for his arrest.
What are the investigations against Flavio Bolsonaro about?
The senator has been accused of laundering money through a sports betting company, money that was taken from government pensions for senior citizens.
A second investigation is looking into Bolsonaro's connections to a disgraced banker from whom he allegedly accepted millions of dollars to finance the biopic about his father, titled "Dark Horse."
Bolsonaro will lose his immunity from prosecution once his senate term ends in February 2027. He has denied wrongdoing in both cases.

Iran calls on gas exporters to strengthen cooperation, safeguard energy security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:16:35 UTC
07:16:35 KST

Iran calls on gas exporters to strengthen cooperation, safeguard energy security
TEHRAN- At the 28th Ministerial Meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, Iran’s Acting Minister of Oil, Hamid Bovard, presented a broad strategic vision linking global energy security to peace, regional stability, the security of critical infrastructure, and respect for national sovereignty.
Speaking as the Forum marked its 25th anniversary, Bovard said the global energy system is passing through one of its most complex periods of geopolitical, economic, and technological change. He thanked Russia for hosting the meeting and honored the memory of those killed in the recent war waged by the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran, including Ayatollah Khamenei, civilians, schoolchildren in Minab, and athletes from Lamerd.
Bovard argued that the recent energy crisis caused by the imposed war demonstrated that energy security is not merely an economic or technical issue. It is inseparably tied to peace, regional stability, infrastructure security, and respect for national sovereignty. The consequences of aggression, he said, can extend beyond the region and affect global energy supply, economic growth, and development. He criticized US military interventions in areas including the Persian Gulf and unilateral economic sanctions, saying they not only target Iran’s legitimate rights and interests but also damage trust, investment security, and the predictability of global energy markets. In Iran’s view, world energy security cannot be achieved without the security of energy producers, respect for their sovereignty, sustainable investment, and effective international cooperation.
He said the GECF must become more than ever a platform for convergence, dialogue, and practical cooperation among producing countries, and described the Eighth GECF Summit as a valuable opportunity to strengthen this approach and set a new horizon for strategic cooperation. While the Forum was founded in Tehran in 2001 and is entering a new institutional phase, Bovard said rapid global changes require members to preserve fundamental principles while reconfiguring priorities, tools, and cooperation mechanisms. Iran’s strategic priorities include flexibility toward global energy crises, strengthening natural gas’s role in the future energy mix, and expanding investment, management, and technological cooperation.
Citing the COVID-19 crisis in 2020 and geopolitical developments in 2026, Bovard said global energy markets are more exposed than ever to unpredictable shocks. The GECF should strengthen its capacity for early risk identification, crisis scenario analysis, and coordinated responses. He called for revising the Forum’s long-term strategy with emphasis on strengthening the natural gas value chain. Natural gas, he said, will remain a key pillar of global energy security and economic development because of its reliability, abundance, operational flexibility, industrial applications, and complementary role in renewable energy development. According to the GECF Global Gas Outlook, global gas demand will rise 31 percent by 2055 to more than 5,400 billion cubic meters, and its share of the world energy mix will increase from about 23 percent to 26 percent.
Bovard proposed that the Secretariat, with member participation, study a roadmap to raise natural gas’s share of the global energy mix to an ambitious 30 percent. Such a roadmap should rest on economic studies, long-term demand assessment, investment requirements, and environmental considerations. He also said members should adopt a coordinated approach, based on technical realities and common interests, toward climate regulations and mechanisms that could impose unbalanced restrictions on energy trade and investment, including the possible effects of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
He stressed that huge underground reserves alone do not guarantee supply security. What converts gas resources into energy security is timely investment, access to technology, infrastructure development, and sustainable demand. The GECF outlook estimates that meeting global needs through 2055 will require about $11.6 trillion in upstream investment and $735 billion in midstream investment—more than $12 trillion in total. This makes a stable, predictable environment with appropriate financing mechanisms essential.
Bovard said member cooperation could focus on three areas: first, joint financing and investment mechanisms for gas projects using national, regional, and international financial institutions; second, technological cooperation, knowledge transfer, training, and joint upstream, midstream, and downstream projects, where Iran has extensive experience; and third, structured dialogue between producers and consumers to increase demand security, reduce investment risks, and balance supplier and consumer interests. The Secretariat could play a more active role in identifying opportunities, facilitating contacts among specialized institutions, and following up on practical results.
As a proposer and main founder of the GECF, Iran has consistently emphasized multilateral cooperation, mutual respect, and common capacities for sustainable gas industry development. Bovard said the 14th government, under the Seventh Development Plan, prioritizes cooperation with international energy organizations, especially the GECF. Iran holds the world’s second-largest proven gas reserves and has strategic geography and extensive technical, industrial, and human capacities.
Despite decades of sanctions and imposed wars, Iran’s gas industry has reached annual production capacity of about 300 billion cubic meters, making it one of the world’s three largest producers. Natural gas accounts for about 70 percent of Iran’s energy mix, and the gas network covers about 95 percent of the population. Bovard said Iran is ready to share these experiences through bilateral and multilateral cooperation and to help develop joint projects and strengthen GECF members’ capabilities.
He concluded that the future of the gas industry depends not only on reserves and production capacity but also on the quality of cooperation, policy stability, and the ability to respond jointly to global challenges. The Forum’s 25th anniversary, he said, is an opportunity to begin a new chapter of results-oriented cooperation, joint investment, and strategic convergence. He expressed confidence that collective will and the Secretariat’s capacities can further strengthen the GECF’s role in global energy dialogue and hoped the ministerial meeting and Eighth Summit would strengthen solidarity and realize the common interests of gas producers and consumers.

What Early Voting Data Is Showing About the Midterm Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:15:02 UTC
07:15:02 KST

Election Day is still a week away. But with early voting for the midterms underway in nearly every state, tens of millions of Americans have already cast their ballots, offering an initial glimpse into how the pivotal elections may play out.
With days of early voting left to go before Election Day on Nov. 3, that figure already represents more than a quarter of the roughly 122 million Americans who voted in the 2022 midterms.
Michael McDonald, a political science professor at the University of Florida who runs the Election Lab, stresses to TIME that early voting data cannot in and of itself be relied on to predict the outcome of the elections. But he says it can reveal other informative aspects of voting behavior.
“Once you start seeing consistency across multiple days of voting and across multiple states, it starts giving us more confidence that whatever we're seeing in terms of relative engagement, that's likely going to carry through to election day,” McDonald says.
Here are some of the notable trends emerging in the early voting data as Election Day nears.
Democrats are outpacing Republicans in early ballots
Registered Democrats so far represent a larger share of early voters in the midterms than Republicans, having cast roughly 45% of early ballots compared to 31% cast by GOP voters, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab data. Another 24% of Americans who have voted early are not registered with either party.
This data is only available for the 27 states that have a formal party registration system, and signifies only the party with which a voter is registered, not the candidates selected on their ballot.
Experts caution that Democrats’ higher turnout in the early vote does not guarantee they’ll maintain that edge, with tens of millions more Americans still expected to show up at the polls.
Republicans are anticipated to make up ground on Election Day, as they have in recent years. A Pew Research survey conducted following the 2024 midterm elections showed that nearly 40% of registered Republican voters cast their ballot in person on Election Day, compared to 28% of registered Democratic voters.
“We expect the Democrats to build up a lead in the early vote, and Election Day tends to be a Republican day, so you can't just look at the early vote as it is now,” McDonald tells TIME.
Polling has shown, however, that Democratic engagement and enthusiasm is higher than it is for Republicans in the lead-up to the elections. According to a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll released on Tuesday, 52% of likely voters said they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district, while 44% would back the Republican candidate. Independent likely voters favored Democratic candidates by 13 points.
More Democrats than Republicans also said in the survey they were very enthusiastic about voting, at 71% and 61% respectively. Another poll from the Pew Research Center earlier this month similarly showed greater engagement and stated motivation from voters backing Democrats: 78% of voters who voiced support for the Democratic candidate in their House district said who controls Congress “really matters,” compared to 69% of voters who backed Republican candidates who said the same. Such polls have suggested a “blue wave” of Democratic support might determine the midterms, but Republicans have pushed back against the numbers.
Bernard Fraga, a political science professor at Emory University, tells TIME that the relative lack of Republican enthusiasm in polls and trailing GOP turnout in early voting shows that support within the party, and for President Donald Trump, has waned.
“This is a story about Democrats who voted in 2024 persisting, and Republicans who voted in 2024 so far at least staying home,” he says.
The midterms come as Trump’s approval rating has hit near record lows amid widespread dissatisfaction with his handling of the war in Iran and the economy. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday put Trump’s approval rating at 32%, up one percentage point from last week, when the same poll recorded the lowest approval rating of his second term.
Fraga says that Republicans are frustrated with what he describes as “failures” of the Trump Administration, which he asserts have decreased GOP voters’ support for their party and led them to stay home rather than casting ballots early.
“Even for steadfast Republican voters, they look at the state of the economy, for example, and say that they're not too enthusiastic about voting,” he says. “Reading the trends, it's clear that Democrats are enthusiastic and mobilized to a much greater degree than even the Republican voters.”
Simon Rosenberg, a long-time Democratic strategist, contends that independents are also more likely to be voting in favor of Democrats, given recent polling, which has shown that more independent likely voters support Democratic candidates. One YouGov poll found that 54% of independents said they’d vote for Democratic candidates, versus 27% who said they’d vote for Republican candidates. Another PBS/NPR/Marist poll showed that independents favored Democrats by a margin of 25 points.
Given such polling, Rosenberg believes that the number of people voting for Democratic candidates is actually higher than the partisan breakdown in early voting data explicitly indicates.
Hispanic voters are turning out early in higher numbers than other recent elections
Rosenberg says that the most significant data coming out of early voting is the number of Hispanic people voting early.
So far, Hispanic early voting participation is outpacing its levels at the same point in the election cycle in 2022 and 2024. Presidential election years such as 2024 typically yield higher voter turnout, which Rosenberg says makes the 2026 figures to date all the more notable and surprising.
“It's almost certain that this heightened performance will carry over through Election Day, and that this will become one of the big storylines of the election,” he says. “It's a universal trend that we're seeing all across the country.”
This trend is most noticeable in states with high Hispanic populations, like Texas.
In one of the most closely watched—and expensive—Senate races this year, James Talarico is vying to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas since 1988 in a tightly contested battle against the state’s Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Over 4 million votes have been cast early, or an estimated 41% of the total votes expected in the race, according to tracking by VoteHub. As of Monday, Talarico held a narrow two-point lead in the early vote.
The state's Hispanic population, one of the highest in the U.S. per capita, represents 24% of the vote as of Monday, according to VoteHub, a percentage point higher than the share it made up in the final vote tally in the 2024 election. Another analysis reported by The Texas Tribune showed that the Hispanic early vote in Texas has already surpassed the early vote numbers from 2024 and 2022.
“What we can see here is just eye-popping numbers for Hispanics,” McDonald said about the group’s early voter turnout not only in Texas, but around the U.S. “If Hispanics are showing up in force now, it's almost with certainty going to change the overall … diversity of the electorate in this election cycle.”
As a result, McDonald contends that “we're going to see larger swings to the Democrats in more diverse states.”
Polling has indicated that Hispanic and Latino voters, a demographic that helped propel Trump back to the White House two years ago, widely disapprove of the President and the Republican Party heading into midterms. Sixty-six percent of Latino voters surveyed in late September by an NBC News/Telemundo poll said that Trump’s deportation policies have gone too far, while 75% disapprove of his handling of the economy and the cost of living. The poll also found that more Latino voters hold a negative view of the GOP than at any point since 2016.
Another Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Oct. 5 showed that just 24% of Hispanic Americans approved of Trump’s performance in the White House, the lowest such rating the President has received across both of his presidential terms. And just 52% of Hispanic voters who responded to the poll planned to vote Democratic, double the level of support for Republicans among the demographic.
How predictive is early voting data?
Rosenberg cautions that early voting “can tell you a lot, but it can't tell you everything,” and that voter turnout can shift from day to day.
He notes that early voting returns showed Kamala Harris leading in the 2024 presidential election, and that she still lost after a strong gain in Republican turnout for Trump.
But he contends that “the lack of intensity that we're seeing in many rural and Republican counties around the country does not bode well for them for Election Day.”
Fraga says that in general, political scientists are skeptical of using early voting data to predict election outcomes. This has been especially true, he notes, in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw Democrats cast early votes by mail at a significantly higher rate than Republicans, who were more likely to vote early at polls, a dynamic that made it harder to draw on the early vote to confidently predict outcomes on Election Day.
Now, though, “the partisan distribution of voters has become somewhat more stable,” he says. “So we can use that information to now have a better comparison, and as a result, early voting data sheds a lot more light on what's likely to happen in November.”
“It's not determinative. It's not going to predict what's going to happen,” Rosenberg says. “But every campaign in the country right now is living and dying on this early vote data.”
Richard Hall contributed reporting.

Israeli political leaders have erupted into fierce public warfare after parliamentary exit polls showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition bleeding its majority and falling short of an outright parliamentary majority.

Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar)
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the opposition Yashar party, framed the numbers as an absolute public repudiation of the ruling administration. "The results indicate a total lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the 'October 7th government'," Eisenkot told Israel's Channel 12.
"If these are the final results, it is a victory for the mainstream Zionist majority in Israel. I will act immediately to carry out the will of the people, to replace the Netanyahu government, and to form a Zionist government of national mobilisation as soon as possible."
Yair Lapid (Yesh Atid)
Former prime minister and Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid delivered a scathing appraisal on X, rejecting any spin from the right wing: "Don’t let them confuse you: The Netanyahu bloc suffered a harsh defeat. This is a total collapse and the public told them to get lost and go home."
Benny Gantz (Blue and White)
Former defence minister Benny Gantz, who withdrew his Blue and White party from the ballot after surveys showed it failing to clear the electoral threshold, insisted the electorate has mandated an overhaul.

Liquidity growth slowed, monthly inflation on a downward trend: economy minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:13:15 UTC
07:13:15 KST

Liquidity growth slowed, monthly inflation on a downward trend: economy minister
TEHRAN- Iran’s Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, Seyed Ali Madanizadeh, told parliament on Tuesday that liquidity growth has entered a declining path and that monthly inflation has been falling over the past four months. Answering a question from MP Mostafa Pourdehqan Ardakani and several other lawmakers, he said the government is fully aware of the pressure that inflation and high prices are putting on ordinary households, retirees, workers, and employees, and that economic indicators are being monitored daily.
He described MPs’ concerns as legitimate and said the fact that the government and parliament can debate such problems openly is itself an achievement of the Islamic Republic’s governance system.
He stressed that his explanations were not intended to deny the hardship people face, and that neither he nor the Ministry of Economy is trying to evade responsibility.
Madanizadeh said that when he received a vote of confidence about a year and a half ago, the country was in an economic-war environment in which multiple economic imbalances and structural crises had converged. He said the Ministry of Economy was handed a difficult situation and responded by setting up an “economic war operations room.” One of its first tasks was to monitor and examine insolvent banks. He said the case of Bank Ayandeh was handled successfully, while other insolvent banks and financial institutions are now on the agenda of the Ministry of Economy and the Central Bank and are going through their legal processes.
He also said bank balance sheets have been placed at the center of efforts to control inflation, and that this work has been pursued seriously since the beginning of the year. According to him, liquidity growth has fortunately taken a declining trend, and its inflationary effects should become visible; he added that the downward trend in monthly inflation over the past four months is already completely clear.
The minister also pointed to the capital market as an alternative source of non-inflationary financing. He said the stock market index rose from around 3 million units to more than 8 million units, a significant increase, and that the market has played an important role in financing the economy.
He said the goal is to direct financing of economic enterprises toward the capital market and the debt market rather than making them dependent on the banking network.
He also referred to the reform of the government bond market after eight years, saying that for the first time in eight years rates were made realistic and corruption and rent-seeking in that market were eliminated. This, he argued, helped financing through the capital market and reduced the government’s dependence on the monetary base, which could otherwise increase liquidity and inflation.
Madanizadeh described the financing of the government budget as another major axis of the ministry’s work, aimed at preventing a budget deficit from spilling over into the Central Bank’s monetary base and creating inflation.
Despite all the difficulties imposed by the war, he said, the government tried to close the budget with the minimum possible deficit and to minimize its effects. He acknowledged the difficulties in collecting taxes from people and businesses, but said the government zeroed out the taxes of 10 million businesses and focused instead on large firms that engage in tax evasion.
He also cited the project to make financial statements transparent and electronic, saying it had been stalled for eight years and was finally implemented with the aim of making economic activity transparent and ending the problem of firms keeping dual ledgers. He said the process began several months ago and is intended to create a basis for economic activity grounded in transparent financial statements and verifiable information.
On facilitating production and reducing cost pressures on firms, he said automatic issuance of permits is among the measures being pursued; only in the past week, about 12,000 permits were issued through the Ministry of Economy’s permit system.
He also mentioned the comprehensive collateral system, designed to make it easier for people and firms to access financing through non-inflationary channels at a time when inflation-control policies impose limits on financial resources.
The minister emphasized the need to increase the share of tax revenues in financing the public budget. He said about 50 percent of public budget resources are now supplied through taxes, and that systematizing tax processes is meant to raise this share. Tax revenues grew by 39 percent last year, and a 70 percent growth is projected for this year.
He expressed hope that with continued progress and a more efficient tax system, a significant part of the country’s budget resources will be supplied through taxes from next year, reducing budget dependence on other sources.
He also said full reports on the causes of imposed inflation have been presented to MPs in private sessions, and that many events cannot be discussed on official platforms. He asked MPs not to use the phrase “the government made the currency expensive,” arguing that the situation was imposed on the country and that access to foreign currency and dollar resources was blocked.
Madanizadeh said the rise in prices had two main causes: the economic-war conditions and imposed pressures on the country. He said 230 million cubic meters of Iran’s export gas and gas allocated to industries were damaged, and that petrochemical and steel facilities were hit. When the sources of foreign-currency supply are damaged, he argued, the government does not have access to foreign currency, and price increases are natural.
He added that when transport costs rise tenfold because of an economic blockade, and when import and export prices rise by 100 percent, all of these affect the exchange rate. He also rejected the idea that the government removed preferential currency, saying preferential currency was not removed but simply ran out.
He said this reality should not be conveyed to the people as a government choice; rather, he said, the US Treasury Secretary framed it as a crime against the Iranian people, and the enemy killed children in the military arena and in the economic arena prevented medicine from reaching people, including through air and sea blockades.
Despite these pressures, he said, monthly inflation has fallen below 4 percent. He described the effort as trying to bring inflation from above 90 percent down to 40 percent, and hopefully to 20 percent next year. He insisted that Iran’s economy has not collapsed and will not collapse. He said the “criminals and killers” who imposed the war first tried to disrupt the economic decision-making system, but the Ministry of Economy responded by launching the economic war room and passing resolutions in the government and the Supreme National Security Council to compensate for the imposed budget deficit.
He referred to a seven-axis plan covering inflation control, trade facilitation, investment facilitation, production facilitation, energy management, and livelihood reconstruction.
He said the ministry has moved toward replacing oil revenues with new sources, managed the treasury’s cash flow, is launching oil certificates, and doubled the stock market index.
He also said a new investment campaign would be launched, and that diplomacy with neighboring countries has been activated. He told the people that the “soldiers” in the Ministry of Economy and Finance have not and will not shrink under pressure and will stand for the elevation of the country until their last breath.
Addressing the enemy, he said: “You have not yet understood the Iranian nation, and you imagine that by closing trade routes and pressuring people’s tables you can break the will of a nation, but that is a vain fantasy. Iran is the land of a people who have stood firm in the hardest storms of history, and the government and parliament, as servants of the people, will defeat the enemy. Iran is a civilization, and a civilization will never be defeated.”

Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

07:11:08 KST

Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
- Published
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.
Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.
That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.
Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".
A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.
Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.
One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.
Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".
The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.
Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".
Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.
Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.
Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.
Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
- Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water 
  - Published24 September
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.
One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.
Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.
"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv.

Vladimir Putin starts work at Russia-Africa Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:06:01 UTC
07:06:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin is beginning an extensive series of events as part of the Russia-Africa Summit.
Wednesday’s agenda includes participation in the third Russia-Africa Economic Summit and Humanitarian Forum, a meeting with the heads of major regional organizations, and a formal reception hosted by the Russian president.
As Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov previously reported, 48 of Africa’s 54 countries will participate in this year’s summit, including 22 represented at the level of heads of state. The current chairperson of the African Union, President of Burundi Evariste Ndayishimiye, will co-chair various events alongside Putin.
The theme of the Economic and Humanitarian Forum is "Developing Mutually Beneficial Cooperation and Unlocking the Potential of Every African Country Together." The Russian president will also participate in its first plenary session.
According to Ushakov, Putin will assess the state of trade and economic relations between Russia and African countries in his address. Particular priority will be given to sovereign development on an equal footing, as well as ensuring African countries’ equitable access to resources, fertilizers, and modern technologies.
Following the plenary session, Putin will tour an exhibition at Gostiny Dvor together with African leaders. The exhibition will have a practical focus. In addition to showcasing ongoing Russian-African projects, it will highlight Russia’s advanced technologies and innovations that Moscow is prepared to share with its partners on the continent.
Program at the Kremlin
However, Wednesday’s events will extend well beyond the forum’s plenary session. The Russian president will receive representatives of Africa’s largest regional organizations who have arrived in Moscow at St. Andrew’s Hall, the most ceremonial and prestigious hall of the Grand Kremlin Palace.
The traditional meeting is expected to bring together representatives of the African Union, the African Continental Free Trade Area, the East African Community, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, the Southern African Development Community, the Economic Community of Central African States, the Economic Community of West African States, the Arab Maghreb Union, and the African Export-Import Bank.
A formal reception hosted by the Russian president is also expected. As is customary, Putin will hold the event in the very heart of the Kremlin, the Faceted Chamber. Dating back to the Soviet era, such formal dinners have traditionally underscored the highest status of these meetings and the particularly warm relations with the countries represented by the distinguished guests.
The series of bilateral meetings that Putin began the previous day will also continue. On Tuesday, Moscow hosted a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum. After holding multilateral discussions with his counterparts, Putin met separately with several of them, namely Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Emir of Qatar Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, President of the Republic of Mozambique Daniel Francisco Chapo, President of Equatorial Guinea Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, and Chairman of Libya’s Presidential Council Mohamed al-Menfi.
The program will continue over the following two days. In particular, plenary sessions of the Russia-Africa Summit and further bilateral meetings are expected.
About the summit
The Russia-Africa Summit is being held for the third time and for the first time in Moscow. St. Petersburg hosted the previous summit in the summer of 2023, while the inaugural summit took place in Sochi in the fall of 2019.

Vance calls Alaskan Senate bid by nearly identically named candidate a ‘big fraud’ amid legal challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:04:59 UTC
07:04:59 KST

Diyar Guldogan
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
US Vice President JD Vance defended the Trump administration’s legal challenge to Alaska’s Senate election, describing the candidacy of a second candidate with a name nearly identical to that of the incumbent as a “big fraud” and arguing that it could confuse voters ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
Speaking to reporters Tuesday as he departed for a campaign rally in Michigan, Vance was asked why Alaskans should not find it "insulting" that the administration appeared to suggest they could not distinguish between the two candidates on the ballot.
“Well, I think the question presumes quite a bit,” Vance responded.
He argued that many voters would recognize the alleged problem but said others might be confused because of competing demands on their time.
"I mean, look, a lot of Alaskans are going to go and look at the ballot and realize exactly what you said, that this is all a big fraud."
“People are busy. People have lives. People have jobs. And when you put a person on the ballot explicitly to try to confuse voters, I think that’s the definition of electoral fraud. And I don’t think that we should endorse it," Vance said.
The comments came after the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit last week seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying its Senate election results under certain circumstances if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses.
The legal dispute centers on Dan J. Sullivan, a second candidate whose name closely resembles that of the incumbent senator. The administration alleges that the challenger's candidacy could mislead voters and affect the outcome of the race.
The filing argues that certifying results affected by the second candidate’s appearance on the ballot would undermine the state’s responsibility to protect election integrity.
Last week, US President Donald Trump accused Democrats of trying to confuse voters in Alaska’s Senate race by fielding a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Sullivan.
“We have a man named Dan Sullivan. So the Democrats, maybe here they're not so dumb. They put another man also with the name of Dan Sullivan. So we have two Dan Sullivans. How about that?” he said.
The president argued that the presence of two candidates with similar names could create confusion among voters ahead of the November midterm elections.

How Hong Kong went from a yuan gateway to a complete currency ecosystem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:00:15 UTC
07:00:15 KST

In FocusHow Hong Kong went from a yuan gateway to a complete currency ecosystem
Yuan can now be used in a wide variety of scenarios in the city, from multi-asset investments to hedging and consumption
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority. In the second part of a four-part series on the globalisation of the yuan, Daisy Wu examines Hong Kong’s evolution from an offshore reservoir into a self-sustaining yuan ecosystem.
Of the hundreds of thousands of people who cross the border between mainland China and Hong Kong every day, many pay with the national currency – the yuan, also known as the renminbi – at turnstiles with the tap of a smartphone.
Yet once that currency passes over the same border and into a Hong Kong bank account, it is treated differently from the renminbi on the mainland. As offshore yuan, or CNH, it falls outside mainland China’s capital controls and trades at a market-driven exchange rate, like the US dollar, the British pound and the Japanese yen.

DNA links serial killer Ted Bundy to 1974 murder of Utah girl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:59:35 UTC
06:59:35 KST

The notorious serial killer Ted Bundy has been found responsible, through DNA evidence, for the murder of a 17-year-old Utah girl who went missing in 1974 before her nude body was found days later, state authorities announced at a Tuesday news conference.
The breakthrough in the investigation of Melissa Ann Smith’s death comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed in April that Bundy had killed another Utah girl, 17-year-old Laura Ann Aime, in 1974.
Bundy had confessed to killing Laura during a string of admissions he made before being executed in 1989 for two of his murders.
Laura was last seen during a Halloween party, before being found dead and severely beaten in late November 1974.
It was not until this year, though, that new DNA testing backed Bundy’s account.
Bodily fluid extracted from Laura’s body was a match to Bundy’s known DNA profile, law enforcement officials said then.
That discovery put into motion the closure of Smith’s homicide investigation.
The Y-STR DNA profile recovered from Laura’s body was a genetic match to one found from Melissa’s body.
“This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence, even when decades have passed,” said the Salt Lake county sheriff, Rosie Rivera, on Tuesday. “We have the ability to take a look at these cases again and again.”
Between 1974 and 1978, Bundy went on a violent rampage, sexually assaulting and killing at least 30 women across the American west and Florida.
“The voices and cherished memories of Melissa Ann Smith and Laura Ann Aime and others involved in these cases ring louder than the hate and sedition of the one that took their lives,” said Mike Reynolds, a sergeant with the Utah county sheriff’s office, on Tuesday. “With every case closure may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out.”

Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman remained silent for 90 minutes after the release of Tuesday night's exit polls before delivering a speech at his party's election headquarters, where he declined to commit to his next political moves.
"I apologize for arriving late. I had to stop by my doctor's office for surgery to lengthen my fuse," Liberman joked, suggesting that patience would be needed before the final results became clear. He said he was not convinced the exit polls accurately reflected the election outcome, pointing out that votes equivalent to roughly 15 Knesset seats were still to be counted from special double-envelope ballots. "I assume we'll only see the actual results early Friday morning or sometime Friday morning," he explained.
According to the exit polls published by Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13, the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu holds a slight advantage over the prime minister's bloc, although Likud remains the largest party. Yisrael Beytenu is projected to win seven to eight seats. Liberman argued that the double-envelope ballots, which include votes cast by soldiers and other voters using special voting arrangements, would reduce the relative strength of the Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties.
"That means it's very important to be patient," Liberman said. "By Friday, we'll know much more, and we'll be able to talk about a much better and more optimistic picture than the one we're seeing today."
Liberman described the election as a difficult campaign. "We competed under unreasonable conditions as a liberal right-wing party, facing an impossible reality," he said. "If we've achieved a reasonably good result, it's thanks to each and every one of you sitting here."
He accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of having "behaved today like the head of a criminal organization, crossing every red line." Liberman also referred to WhatsApp services being disabled and text messages being sent, adding that he would not elaborate.
He stopped short of committing to his party's next steps in the effort to form a government. "We'll wait for the actual results and then consult," he said.
Liberman went on to attack Channel 14 and Netanyahu supporters, whom he accused of inciting against him. "We will establish a Zionist coalition and put an end to the incitement," he declared. "It's important to form a government committed to the values of the Zionist movement. We will build an exemplary movement, a model for others to follow."
He then issued a direct call for rebellion within Likud, urging party members and lawmakers to turn against Netanyahu.
"I received dozens of phone calls from Likud members," Liberman said. "This man must leave the stage, and anyone loyal to the path of Herzl, Trumpeldor and Jabotinsky must get rid of him. Raise the banner of revolt within Likud."
Addressing Likud Central Committee members, local party activists and Knesset lawmakers, Liberman added: "What you say privately, behind closed doors, it's time to say publicly. It's time to tell the truth, not just in closed rooms."
He continued: "This man has destroyed the national camp and is destroying everything good. That's the key to preserving the national camp, rather than leaving it in the hands of a bunch of opportunists protecting their privileges."
The Yisrael Beytenu chairman left the stage to the sounds of the song "You Won't Defeat Me," accompanied by applause.
Liberman founded Yisrael Beytenu in 1999 and has led it ever since, for 27 years. Apart from serving as prime minister, he has held virtually every senior government position, including defense minister, foreign minister and finance minister.
At its peak, Yisrael Beytenu won 15 Knesset seats in 2009. Since then, when running independently, the party has failed to reach double digits. In the previous election, it secured six seats.
For many years, the overwhelming majority of Yisrael Beytenu lawmakers were immigrants from the former Soviet Union. This time, however, only Yulia Malinovsky joins Liberman among the party's senior figures from that background.
Liberman placed Rafi Ben Shitrit, the former mayor of Beit She'an whose son was killed on October 7, 2023, second on the party's electoral list.

Astronomers may have just discovered our solar system’s sixth dwarf planet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:50:43 UTC
06:50:43 KST

Congratulations to Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake—there may be a new sibling to welcome into the dwarf planet family.
On Tuesday astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory announced the discovery of a new dwarf planet candidate in a distant part of the solar system beyond Neptune’s orbit. The new object doesn’t have an official name yet and is instead going by its provisional designation—2026 ED138.
The discovery was made by running billions of pieces of data collected by the Rubin Observatory through a search code developed by Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian astronomers Matthew Holman and Kevin Napier.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said in a statement. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”
When Holman and his colleague Mario Jurić of the University of Washington went to double-check, they found 30 more observations of the object by Rubin that dated to between March and July 2026. Looking at other observation tools, the pair found even more sightings going back to 2016. Together, these data allowed the astronomers to begin mapping out 2026 ED138’s orbit.
The suspected dwarf planet is about 46 times as far from the sun as Earth, making it even more remote than Pluto, which is just 40 times as far. The object is also tilted off the solar system’s plane by around 25 degrees, an arrangement that could be linked to disruptions caused by Neptune’s gravitational pull.
Initial measurements indicate that 2026 ED138 has a diameter between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 and 932 miles), which makes it one of the largest dwarf planet candidates yet detected. But size isn’t all that matters: further observations are required to determine if the object has enough mass to be pulled into a round shape, which is a key requirement for a dwarf planet.
Despite its size, 2026 ED138 was able to avoid detection for all these years because it’s located in a part of the night sky that’s crowded with stars whose light drowned it out. The Vera C. Rubin observatory, which is loaded with state-of-the-art, powerful instruments and only recently came online, made the discovery possible. Now that the object has been identified, astronomers can get to work on learning more about it to see if it can join Pluto and the others in the dwarf planet family.
“If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman said. “Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach.”

Pentagon to Give Startup Stoke Space $150M Loan for New Launch Pad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:49:04 UTC
06:49:04 KST

The Pentagon plans to issue a $150 million loan to Stoke Space Technologies, an emerging space launch provider, to help it expand its footprint at Cape Canaveral Space Force Base, Fla.
The Defense Department announced the plan Oct. 26. The loan, managed by DOD’s Office of Strategic Capital, is contingent on Stoke clearing various financial, legal, and technical requirements.
“The proposed loan from OSC, alongside private capital, would support the buildout of the company’s second launchpad at its existing launch complex at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station,” the Pentagon said in a statement. “The OSC commitment to Stoke Space more broadly supports the expansion of U.S. launch capacity, which is required to meet the rising demand for commercial and national security space launch by the United States Space Force.”
The Pentagon established OSC in 2022 to help connect firms developing critical defense technology with private capital. The loan agreement with Stoke is one of several conditional deals OSC has announced this month alone. On Oct. 8, it revealed a plan to issue a $1.5 billion loan to Wolfspeed, Inc. to build advanced semiconductor components and materials, and on Oct. 17, it signed a conditional commitment with Antheia, Inc., to scale its biomanufacturing efforts.
Stoke’s first launch pad, located at the Cape’s Space Launch Complex-14, is slated to host the debut flight of its Nova rocket in “the first part of 2027,” according to the company’s current schedule. That vehicle is a pathfinder for the firm’s future Nova Block 2 rocket—a fully reusable rocket designed to deliver 15 metric tons to low-Earth orbit.
Stoke plans to fly multiple Nova missions in 2027 and 2028 to fuel its plans for Block 2, which it expects will log its first flight in 2029. The company announced in September that it had raised $1 billion in private capital to accelerate development of its Nova line.
The firm hasn’t disclosed when it expects to break ground on the second facility, and a Stoke spokesperson did not respond to questions about those plans or the OSC deal. In September, it said it has started construction of a new payload processing facility that can service both the first Nova iteration, which it calls Pathfinder, and the Block 2 version. The company has also started work on the offshore platform that will recover both rockets after launch.
While Nova has yet to lift off, the Space Force in 2025 tapped the company to compete for missions under its National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 1 contract, which the service uses to fly smaller payloads with less stringent requirements. To be eligible for Lane 1 flights, firms must have flown their rockets at least once; at the time, Stoke projected Nova would launch by 2026.
Space Force officials are eager for new rockets to enter the market amid broader market concerns about a forthcoming launch bottleneck as SpaceX pursues plans to retire its Falcon 9 workhorse and rely on its Starship super heavy rocket to fly mostly internal Starlink missions. Asked during an Oct. 21 media briefing about the service’s concerns about SpaceX’s new business model, Col. Eric Zarynisky, portfolio acquisition executive for space access, said the Space Force has regular conversations with current and potential NSSL providers about their business plans.
“I’m seeing a lot of growth in those new providers, and being able to use those to support the customers that we see coming on in the national security space launch side,” he said. “We’re talking to all of the providers . . . about their future plans and then talking to them about where we see our manifest going. It is an ongoing conversation.”

By Simon Lewis
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US State Department’s policy chief, Jeremy Lewin, said on Tuesday he was leaving his role after nearly two years in which he helped lead an overhaul of US foreign assistance and implemented President Donald Trump’s policies toward Venezuela and Cuba.
Lewin, a top adviser to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, said on social media he was leaving to return to the private sector.
“President Trump has put decades of post-Cold War malaise behind us — permanently transforming US foreign policy to put Americans first, keep them safe, and drive peace and shared prosperity in key regions,” Lewin said on X.
The 29-year-old joined the government as part of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency and played a leading role in closing the US Agency for International Development. Trump and Musk justified the move by accusing the agency of waste, fraud and abuse.
Some programs were later restored or revamped under the State Department. Lewin oversaw that process as acting under secretary of state for foreign assistance, humanitarian affairs and religious freedom.
In late August, Lewin began his stint as the department’s director of policy planning, in which he focused on US policy toward Venezuela and Cuba, according to his State Department biography.
The biography says Lewin is the only person under 30 to serve in the policy planning role.
The US military captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. Washington has since controlled the sale of Venezuelan oil and holds the proceeds, and Trump has said no Venezuelan oil will go to Cuba.
That move cut off the main source of oil for Communist-run Cuba.

Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after election loss, US says will grant visa

A senior US State Department official said the Trump administration will issue visas to Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the US after news outlets reported that Bolsonaro fled Brazil after losing the country’s presidential election.
The news came on Tuesday, one day after Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to turn over his passports as part of a probe into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro, the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, initially refused to acknowledge the election results and said he would seek their annulment. His party released a statement on Monday saying it accepted the results of the election, which the conservative candidate lost by more than 4.4 million votes.
US President Donald Trump reacted by casting doubt on the election result, telling reporters it “looked like another rigged election”.
No evidence has emerged that the vote was marred by malfeasance. While critics seized on a last-minute decision to extend polling hours, Lula’s eventual victory was commanding, and the extension was unlikely to change the outcome.

Yemen’s armed forces say they carried out ‘precise, direct’ strikes against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:47:19 UTC
06:47:19 KST

Jomaa Younis and Serdar Dincel
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Yemen’s armed forces said late Tuesday that they carried out 1,382 strikes against the Houthi group “in recent hours,” describing the attacks as “precise and direct.”
The operations "neutralized" around 440 Houthi fighters and commanders and secured new field gains in Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, army spokesman Col. Majed al-Nuzaili noted on the US social media platform X.
The operations targeted “field command centers, fortifications, sources of fire, troop concentrations and reserves as well as reinforcements, transport and supply assets belonging to the terrorist Houthi militia," al-Nuzaili said.
In Taiz governorate, al-Nuzaili said army units and Popular Resistance forces backed by warplanes carried out coordinated airstrikes and attacks using various tactical methods.
The operations thwarted Houthi attempts to retake positions they had lost, resulting in new advances on the ground and stronger fire control over several strategic positions and highlands, he added.
Taiz has witnessed intense fighting between the Yemeni army and the Houthi group for weeks, with hundreds killed and wounded on both sides.
On the Bab al-Mandab, Dhubab and Al-Mudhariba fronts in Taiz, al-Nuzaili said army forces thwarted Houthi infiltration attempts and targeted their reinforcements and military vehicles.
He also said army units continued offensive operations along the northern and northwestern approaches to the capital Sanaa and on the eastern front, supported by armored vehicles, artillery and drones.
According to the statement, the operations targeted Houthi movements, command centers, weapons positions, ammunition depots and fortifications, limiting the group’s ability to maneuver and move reinforcements between fronts.
Al-Nuzaili said simultaneous military operations would continue across the front lines to secure further gains, while precautions were being taken to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the Yemeni army’s statement.
The developments come amid a military escalation in Yemen that began in July, described as the most extensive since the relative calm that followed the start of a truce in April 2022.
Operation Dawn of Yemen has been underway since Oct. 5. Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said the operation aims to restore state institutions from Houthi control and take control of Sanaa.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, triggering a civil war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

Australia's appeal to international students plunges over six months as visa rules bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:46:19 UTC
06:46:19 KST

In brief
- Australia's appeal to international students fell sharply in just six months.
- Migration changes and rising costs prompted students to look elsewhere.
Australia's appeal to foreign students has plummeted in just six months, a new report has found.
The crash comes on the heels of the hot debate over migration prompting Labor, the coalition and One Nation to narrow the gangway for foreigners wanting to study in Australia.
Labor will stop higher education entrants from overseas bringing along their families and ensure they can only move between institutions if they're pursuing a higher-level qualification, under measures Immigration Minister Tony Burke announced in August.
New figures from IDP Education, a migration agent, showed less than one in four prospective students put Australia top of their list of potential destinations, down from more than one in three six months ago.
The US, UK and Canada all became more attractive over the same period, hamstringing Australia in a much more fearsome competition for the world's best minds.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Constant chopping and changing of visa rules and fiddling with planning levels had made prospective students take notice.
"The world's best students have got so much choice," IDP's chief partner officer Simon Emmett told AAP.
"Once you've got that uncertainty, the shift to other destinations is something that's difficult to switch back on."
Australia is still considered as a destination by a world-leading 54 per cent of prospective students, IDP found, but that was down five per cent and possibly about to be overtaken by a surging UK.
In July, the cost of a student visa jumped to $2500 for undergraduates and $5750 for postgraduates, making Australia the world's most expensive destination.
Australia's visa refusal rate had the previous month also climbed to a 10-year high of 24.6 per cent, up from just 7.9 per cent a decade prior.
Mr Emmett said Canada, where international enrolments dived 29 per cent after a massive crackdown, should serve as a warning to other countries wanting to lower their migration intake by cutting foreign students.
"We need to be really careful we don't overcorrect on student policies," he said.
"You can make decisions that impact visa decisions now, but it's the prospective students who you'll also impact ... students consider destinations over a long period."
Students already in Australia were also finding life trickier, IDP's report found.
Almost half said finding part-time or post-graduate work was harder or much harder than expected, and more than one in three had trouble with the cost of living.

According to the same report, Witkoff presented Ukrainian negotiators in Florida on Oct. 9 with a postwar “regional prosperity plan,” which envisaged fully restoring Russian oil and gas supplies to Europe through Ukrainian territory.
Weeks of escalation triggered by diesel arrangement
The diesel agreement triggered weeks of severe diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
Around the same time, Trump claimed it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, while, days later, restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite network, disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
Elon Musk claimed such limits were ultimately decided by Trump, not his company; a claim the US president denied.
On Oct. 14, in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan, President Volodymyr Zelensky described Trump’s diesel deal as a victory for Putin, warning that Moscow was exploiting Washington’s decisions to pressure Ukraine into concessions.
Around the time, Zelensky also suggested that Russia was offering Washington potential business ventures and economic projects to influence its decisions.

Israel election turnout hits 77.7%, highest in 25 years, as exit polls show 52-50 split
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:44:12 UTC
06:44:12 KST

Israel recorded its highest election turnout in 25 years on Tuesday, with 77.7% of eligible voters casting ballots by the official 10 p.m. closing time, according to the Central Elections Committee. Meanwhile, updated television exit polls showed a remarkably consistent picture: 52 seats for the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, 50 for his political allies and 18 for the Arab parties.
A total of 5,695,682 Israelis had voted by 10 p.m., an increase of approximately 7.1 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election in 2022. It was the highest turnout recorded at poll-closing time since 2001.
The figure is not yet final. Voters who arrived at their polling stations before 10 p.m. were permitted to cast their ballots even after the official closing time, meaning the total is expected to rise further.
The high turnout was reflected across the country, with particularly strong participation in several Arab and ultra-Orthodox communities. In two small communities in the Arava region, Paran and Shaharut, the reported turnout reached 100%.
Where Israelis voted: The major cities
Among Israel's larger cities, Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut recorded one of the highest turnout rates at 79.2%, followed by Bnei Brak at 77%, Kfar Saba at 74.7%, Petah Tikva at 73% and Rehovot at 72.9%.
Rishon LeZion and Herzliya each recorded 71.3%, followed by Ramat Gan at 71.2%, Ra'anana at 70.8% and Lod at 70.6%.
Turnout in Jerusalem reached 65.9%, compared with 65.4% in Tel Aviv-Jaffa and 61.6% in Haifa, Israel's three largest cities.
In other major population centers, turnout stood at 69% in Holon, 68.7% in Ashkelon, 68.5% in Hadera, 67.8% in Ashdod and Beit Shemesh, and 65.8% in Be'er Sheva.
Netanya recorded 60.2%, while Bat Yam had one of the lowest turnout rates among the major cities listed, at 55.3%.
Arab communities report strong turnout
Turnout was particularly high in several Arab communities, with Sakhnin reaching 86.8% and Kafr Qasim recording 84.9%.
In the southern Bedouin city of Rahat, turnout reached 82%, while Kuseife recorded 81.2% and Hura 79.1%.
Tayibe registered 79%, Shefa-'Amr 75.9%, Umm al-Fahm 75.7% and Nazareth 72.2%.
The figures came as the updated exit polls projected a combined 18 seats for the Joint List and Ra'am, giving the Arab parties a potentially important role in the parliamentary balance.
Ultra-Orthodox communities also see high participation
High turnout was also recorded in several ultra-Orthodox communities. Rekhasim led the group with 86.9%, followed by Elad at 84% and Modi'in Illit at 83.1%.
Beitar Illit recorded 80%, while turnout reached 77% in Bnei Brak and 75.1% in Emmanuel.
These figures come as the main ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, remain part of the projected parliamentary bloc supporting Netanyahu.
Updated exit polls converge on 52-50 split
The latest exit poll updates from Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13 all give the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu 52 seats, compared with 50 for the prime minister's allies. The Arab parties are projected to hold the remaining 18 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The new projections represent a slight setback for former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot's change bloc compared with the initial exit polls, which had given it 53 seats in some surveys.
In Channel 13's updated poll, Naftali Bennett's Beyahad party dropped from 14 to 13 seats, while the Joint List increased from 10 to 11. The change brought the anti-Netanyahu bloc down to 52 seats, with Netanyahu's bloc remaining at 50.
Channel 13 projects Likud as the largest party with 25 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar! with 23. Bennett's Beyahad receives 13, the Joint List 11 and the Democrats nine.
Yisrael Beiteinu, Ra'am and United Torah Judaism each receive seven seats, while Otzma Yehudit, Shas and the Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance each receive six.
Kan 11's updated exit poll also shows Beyahad dropping to 13 seats and the Joint List rising to 11, producing the same overall distribution of 52 seats for the change bloc, 50 for Netanyahu's bloc and 18 for the Arab parties.
Channel 12's update showed a different movement within the change bloc: the Democrats rose to 10 seats, while Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu fell to eight. Its overall bloc projection remained unchanged at 52 seats for Netanyahu's opponents against 50 for his supporters.
The updated Channel 12 poll continues to show Likud leading with 24 seats, followed by Yashar! with 22 and Beyahad with 12. The Joint List receives 11 seats.
High turnout, but no clear parliamentary majority
Despite the unusually high voter participation and the narrow lead for Netanyahu's opponents, the updated exit polls still do not point to a clear parliamentary majority for either main political bloc.
The change bloc's 52 projected seats leave it nine short of the 61 needed for an outright majority. Netanyahu's 50-seat bloc is 11 seats short.
The Arab parties' projected 18 seats could therefore play an important role in determining the next government, although disagreements among the parties seeking to replace Netanyahu remain an obstacle to forming a coalition.
The final outcome will also depend on the official count, including special double-envelope ballots cast by soldiers and other eligible voters whose votes require separate verification.
The unexpectedly high turnout could also affect parties close to the 3.25% electoral threshold, with Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael, the joint party led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, and the Haredi Public Party all projected to fall short in the exit polls.
For now, election night has produced a clear result in one respect: voter participation has reached a level not seen in a quarter-century. Whether that translates into a decisive political outcome remains unresolved.
