Ukraine has launched its own communications satellite – it will become the foundation of an independent network to replace foreign systems
Kyiv • UNN
HIMERA and GomSpace have placed OBRIA NANO into orbit to test a Ukrainian satellite network. Production is planned to be relocated to Ukraine.
The Ukrainian company HIMERA, together with Denmark’s GomSpace, has placed the first OBRIA NANO test satellite into orbit, which will become the foundation of a future independent Ukrainian satellite communications network. The spacecraft has already begun operating in space. HIMERA reported this, UNN writes.
Details
The satellite was launched on October 1, 2026, as part of the SpaceX Transporter-18 space mission. It is currently undergoing scheduled tests that will help verify the technologies needed to create a fully operational satellite system.
The main goal of the OBRIA project is to provide Ukraine with its own satellite communications channels and reduce dependence on foreign operators. Such a system is particularly important during wartime, when stable communications are critically important for the country’s defense.
Ukraine plans to produce its own satellites and terminals
OBRIA NANO is operated by a Ukrainian operator. The results of its tests will be used for the further development of the satellite constellation.
In the future, the developers plan to create a network that will provide communications coverage across the entire territory of Ukraine and complement the capabilities of European satellite systems.
The next stage will be to relocate the production of satellites and ground terminals directly to Ukraine. This will enable the development of domestic space technologies and the gradual expansion of production capacity.
HIMERA is already developing secure communications systems for the Ukrainian military. Its Danish partner GomSpace specializes in developing small satellites and satellite technologies.
At the same time, OBRIA NANO is currently only a test spacecraft, not a ready-made alternative to Starlink. A fully independent network will require the launch of additional satellites and the deployment of ground infrastructure.

European leaders are ‘political masochists’ – Lavrov
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has branded European leaders “political masochists,” accusing them of sacrificing their own citizens’ welfare in pursuit of Russia’s defeat in Ukraine.
Speaking to editors-in-chief of African media outlets in Moscow on Tuesday, Lavrov accused Western governments of pressuring their populations to accept declining living standards to secure Ukraine’s victory in conflict with Russia. 
“They are trying to keep public opinion in a position where people must sacrifice everything: salaries, jobs, healthcare services and social benefits in general, so that Ukraine defeats Russia,” Lavrov said. “People can feel how their situation is deteriorating in European countries,” he added.
He singled out German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as one of the politicians advocating such an approach. “These are masochists, political masochists, if you like,” the foreign minister said.
Merz has defended Germany’s growing military spending and continued support for Kiev while warning that the country can no longer afford its existing welfare system.
The German government has tightened welfare rules, introducing benefit reductions of 30% for repeated violations and, in some cases, complete withdrawal. Berlin’s proposed 2027 budget also envisages billions of euros in savings from pensions, healthcare and other social programs.
Germany has meanwhile earmarked €11.6 billion for Ukraine in 2027, alongside plans to raise defense spending to record levels.
Britain, another major backer of Kiev, has also reduced welfare payments, nearly halving health-related benefits for most new claimants under Universal Credit, a program supporting low-income households and people unable to work.
In September, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called for further welfare cuts to fund increased military spending. “We need to fund our defence, not spend all our money on welfare,” she said. The government, however, rejected her proposal.
France has likewise pursued spending restraint, including a proposed public-sector pay freeze, while increasing military expenditure. The measures have faced opposition from trade unions protesting declining purchasing power and deteriorating public services.
Public discontent has fueled widespread protests across Europe in recent weeks, with hundreds of thousands demonstrating in France over rising living costs, education funding and inequality. Tens of thousands have also taken to the streets in Spain and Portugal over soaring housing costs, while Italy has seen protests over declining living standards.
European NATO members have committed to substantially increasing defense expenditure, citing the perceived threat from Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin last week rejected repeated claims that Moscow was preparing for war with Europe, describing them as part of an ongoing “anti-Russian campaign” on the continent. “They now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. But I hope that it will pass,” Putin stated.
Moscow has repeatedly dismissed claims that it intends to attack NATO countries as “nonsense,” accusing Western leaders of using the alleged Russian threat to justify militarization and continued support for Kiev.

Israel's two main Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, were projected to win six and 12 seats, respectively, according to data published by the Central Elections Committee.
The projections would give the two parties combined 18 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with their five seats each in the outgoing parliament.
The Joint List this year comprises Hadash, a left-wing Arab-Jewish communist party, Ta'al, a secular Arab nationalist party, and Balad, a left-wing Palestinian nationalist party.
Ra’am and the Joint List are unlikely to join a governing coalition, as parties allied with Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud, most notably the parties headed by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, as well as Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman in the opposition, have ruled out including Arab parties in a government. However, Ra’am or the Joint List could still play a role in determining whether either bloc can secure the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority, including by supporting a government from outside the coalition.
The Arab Israeli turnout at this election was significantly higher than in previous years, according to the Central Elections Committee. The unrecognized Bedouin village of Atuana, for example, registered the highest turnout in the country by early noon, at 64%, and two other villages placed second and fourth, at 47.9% and 47.8% respectively.
Arab Israeli vote under scrutiny
The Arab Israeli vote in Israel on Tuesday drew significant attention, with Likud's election integrity headquarters claiming that it had received 620 reports of unusual incidents and suspected irregularities at polling stations in the Arab sector, collected through a network of over 1,500 representatives across the country.
About one-third of the reports concern the recording of voters' personal information and the transmission of information outside polling stations. Some 66 reports concern irregularities involving ballot papers and envelopes, 26 involve difficulties verifying voters' identities and exercising polling station committee members' authority, and 17  concern violence and threats.
The remaining reports involve staffing deficiencies, election campaigning, and documentation issues.
“We categorically reject attempts by elements within the police to link Ra’am to the compromising of electoral integrity,” the Ra’am party said in response to the incident. “The activists were arrested at their homes hours before the polls opened, not in the vicinity of polling stations or voters.

Netanyahu or Eisenkot? Israel's election leaves Herzog with an impossible choice - comment

As the first exit polls emerged on Tuesday night, showing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud as the largest party but Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc holding more seats overall, one wonders what must be going through President Isaac Herzog's mind.
After all, Herzog will soon have to decide which of the two men gets the first chance to form Israel's next government, a decision that could prove particularly complicated given the apparent divisions emerging from the ballot box.
Initial projections from Kan and Channel 13 gave Likud 25 seats, compared with 23 for Eisenkot's Yashar party, while placing the opposition bloc on 53 seats against Netanyahu's 50. Neither side, however, appears to have the 61 seats necessary to command a Knesset majority.
Under Israeli law, the president must consult the Knesset factions before deciding who gets the task of forming a government.
Netanyahu will undoubtedly point to Likud's position as the largest individual party, while Eisenkot has an equally compelling argument in the game of parliamentary arithmetic, pointing to his larger bloc and the bigger chance of forming a government - particularly if the parties opposed to Netanyahu can agree on a common candidate.
The question of how Eisenkot might assemble a coalition remains unanswered. Few of the parties have declared a willingness to sit with the Arab parties, who are projected to receive a record-high 18 mandates, except for Yair Golan’s Democrats.
Herzog knows how this game works well, having led the Labor Party and served as opposition leader before assuming the presidency in 2021. He will also be very aware of the political tensions that have characterized much of his presidency, and the criticism that could follow whichever decision he ultimately makes.
We should remember these are only exit polls, and the final results may still change, particularly with several smaller parties hovering around the electoral threshold.
Nevertheless, the president may soon face the most difficult decision of his tenure, as two political leaders with competing claims to the premiership seek his approval to begin assembling Israel's next government.
Will he go with the long-time leader of Israel, the perceived protector who has led Israel in a multi-front war against its enemies? Or against the potential leader of the largest bloc, at a time when millions of Israelis have taken to the polls and demanded change. Whichever candidate Herzog eventually chooses, millions of Israelis will almost certainly be convinced the other should have had the first opportunity.

What does Yair Golan's Democrats stand for?

On domestic policy, the party advocated for the separation of religion and state, including the introduction of civil marriage and protecting the right of businesses to operate on Shabbat. JERUSALEM – Israel’s wartime election was deadlocked on Oct 27, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.
The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu’s coalition, though the deadlock could allow Israel’s longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations.
“We must establish a strong, right-wing government,” Netanyahu told Likud party supporters after 3am during a speech in Jerusalem, highlighting Israel’s military successes and what he described as a historic opportunity to “remove the Iranian threat.”
Kan 11 and Channel 13 showed the two blocs level, while Channel 12 showed Netanyahu’s Likud-led camp taking a narrow edge over Eisenkot as the night progressed.
None gave either side the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
“The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister... a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics,” Eisenkot earlier told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv.

Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power.
But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power.
Voter turnout was 77.7%, Israel’s Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.
Final results could take days, and Israel’s fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers in coalition negotiations that have run to weeks or months after past elections.
If neither bloc can form a government, another vote may need to be held, something Eisenkot opposed.
“In an election with such a high turnout, it would be a mistake to go to another election,” he said.
The Oct 27 vote was the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu’s coalition, but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted.
Netanyahu setback, no clear winner
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you. The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”
Eisenkot, 66, a hawkish former military chief who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.
He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu’s war Cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the Prime Minister’s leadership.
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu’s leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hawkish security views that have become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack.
He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.

A wartime verdict
Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel’s deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iran that followed.
While Netanyahu was criticised for the country’s biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by assassinating top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
The policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel’s international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel’s foes.

The exit polls were released after a last-ditch effort by Netanyahu and several other parties to keep polling stations open beyond their 10pm deadline was rejected by the Central Elections Committee. The prime minister had suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee that said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.
Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.
Tuesday’s election, which drew the highest turnout in 50 years, had been framed as a referendum on nearly 17 years of unbroken rule by Benjamin Netanyahu, who has most recently overseen three years of unprecedented conflict, instability and growing international isolation.
With more than 7 million people eligible to vote, by 6pm voter turnout was 77.1% – a rise of about 9% on the previous election – with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting. There were also reports of tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad who had arrived to vote in recent days, with many still arriving at Ben Gurion airport to cast their ballots on Tuesday.
Voting was heavy in a number of major cities, including Tel Aviv and Haifa, which some analysts had suggested would benefit the opposition, with long queues to vote in some locations. That pattern was repeated in Israeli-Arab towns, many of which have a long history of boycotting elections.
As polls opened on Tuesday, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition allies launched what critics condemned as a scare campaign to encourage their supporters to turn out, with the familiar racist tactic of warning that large numbers of Israeli Arabs would be voting. Netanyahu made a similar claim to rally support in 2015.
In a recorded message to voters, Netanyahu suggested Arabs and the left were trying to steal the election and Likud claimed suspected irregularities at hundreds of polling stations used by Israeli Arabs.
Israeli citizens of Palestinian origin make up about 20% of the country’s population.
That prompted Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, to say Netanyahu was laying the ground to challenge the result.
“Netanyahu has returned to his familiar tricks, lies and fearmongering to mobilise voters,” he said. “The same lies we saw in previous election campaigns.”
Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023 – an event that many blamed on Netanyahu’s failings – Israel has devastated Gaza with the loss of more than 74,000 Palestinian lives, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war with the US against Iran.
Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners have also attracted international opprobrium for Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank, where violent Jewish settlers have been accused of pogroms against Palestinians and ethnic cleansing.
Despite the many issues confronting the country, much of the focus in the campaign has been on the contrasting characters of the two main party leaders – the machiavellian, grandstanding Netanyahu, who is on trial for corruption, against Eisenkot, the unpolished former IDF chief of staff who rose from humble origins.
The campaign, unusually febrile even by Israeli standards, included a struggling Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.
On Tuesday, encouraging ultra-orthodox voters, Netanyahu – who has long elided his personal and political survival with that of Israel – returned to his apocalyptic language. “The Jewish state is on the brink of ruin,” he said.
In the midst of a major trial for corruption, which has been moving at a glacial pace through the courts, Netanyahu has appeared rattled by the challenge mounted against him by an array of centre-right parties whose unifying pitch has been “anyone but Netanyahu”.
“This is a very moving and fateful moment,” he told journalists after voting, saying he believed the Arab parties that could make or break the election were “receiving massive, truly massive support … heading to the polls in unprecedented numbers”.
Despite tonight’s results, the complexity of Israel’s fragmented political system, with many parties jostling and horse trading, means that it will probably be some time before the shape of any future government – and who will lead it – is clear.
All of which has amplified the importance of Israeli Arab parties, which could emerge as potential kingmakers.
“Our vote will change the government,” the head of the Islamist Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, said while voting, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.
Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for taunting Palestinian detainees and saying some Palestinians in Gaza are “not even people”, said “it will be Mansour Abbas’s government” if Netanyahu and his allies lose.
Underlining the sense of a country at a defining crossroads, an editorial in the left-leaning Haaretz publication had exhorted Israelis to vote, which they did in huge numbers.
“Israel cannot afford another four years under Netanyahu,” it said. “It has exhausted its reserves. The erosion of its diplomatic credit has reached dangerous proportions, and its tired citizens are at the very limits of what they can bear.”

The United Kingdom has simultaneously deployed three of its four nuclear-powered submarines capable of launching nuclear-armed missiles.
According to Sky News, at least one of the submarines is carrying nuclear-tipped ballistic missiles.
This unusual deployment of the majority of the British fleet of strategic nuclear submarines may indicate an increase in their operational readiness.
In recent years, maintaining adequate readiness has been a challenge for the Royal Navy’s submarine force.
The Vanguard-class strategic nuclear submarines include:
All four submarines are equipped with Trident II D5 ballistic missiles with nuclear warheads and provide Britain’s nuclear deterrent.
The constant presence at sea of at least one submarine armed with Trident missiles is considered one of the most important guarantees of the United Kingdom’s security.
“Such action could be used to send a signal to opponents,” the publication notes.
One of the Vanguard-class submarines — HMS Victorious — is currently at the Devonport naval base, where it is undergoing maintenance.
Last year, HMS Vanguard was on combat patrol at sea for over 200 days.
This was likely one of the longest deployments in the submarine’s entire service history. Such a lengthy deployment placed a significant strain on both the crew and the submarine itself.
The longest known deployment of a British nuclear submarine lasted 207 days. It was carried out by HMS Victorious in 2021.
In total, the British Navy has nine nuclear submarines: attack submarines and strategic missile submarines.
Last year, the United Kingdom commissioned its sixth Astute-class submarine—HMS Agamemnon.
Astute-class submarines are designed to conduct covert operations, reconnaissance, protect aircraft carrier strike groups, and deliver precision strikes.

US says it killed five people in strike on alleged drug boat
Unknown

US says it killed five people in strike on alleged drug boat
Latest strike brings death toll of campaign decried as extrajudicial killings to 243 people since September 2025.
The United States military has said that it has killed five people in a strike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the eastern Pacific, continuing a campaign condemned by legal scholars and rights groups as extrajudicial killings.
US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), which oversees military operations in Latin America and the Caribbean, said on Tuesday that five people were killed in the strike.
“On October 27, under the direction of SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific,” it said in a social media post. “Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed five narco-terrorists.”
The administration of President Donald Trump has previously killed at least 238 people in 68 reported strikes in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific since the campaign first began in September 2025, according to a tracker from the Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA), a US-based research group that promotes human rights and democracy.
Tuesday’s strike appears to bring the reported total to 243 people. SOUTHCOM has often accompanied its announcements with videos that purportedly show vessels being struck.
The government has rarely shared details to substantiate its claims that those targeted are involved in drug trafficking, and relatives of some of those killed have said that they were fishermen or workers who were not involved in the drug trade.
The Trump administration has designated numerous criminal groups in Latin America as foreign “terrorist” organisations. Legal experts reject that framing and say that drug trafficking is a criminal activity against which military strikes are not permitted.
“This is the 6th lethal boat strike in the past 4 months,” Adam Isacson, an analyst at WOLA who has tracked the strikes, said in a social media post in response to SOUTHCOM’s announcement on Tuesday.
“The pace is slower than before, but the administration and its commanders persist in grinding out illegal killings every few weeks, with no discernible impact on the drug trade. A bleak pre-midterms message.”

‘I'll act immediately to replace Netanyahu’: Eisenkot responds to Israel exit polls

05:53:50 KST

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar! party, vowed Tuesday night to act immediately to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government after Israel's election exit polls gave the bloc seeking political change a narrow advantage, although neither side secured the parliamentary majority needed to form a government.
"The initial results indicate a complete vote of no confidence in Netanyahu and the government of October 7 by the Zionist majority and the majority of Israeli citizens," Eisenkot said, referring to the government in office during the Hamas-led attack on Israel.
"If these are the final results, this is a victory for the mainstream Zionist majority in Israel," he added. "I will act immediately to implement the people's decision, replace Netanyahu's government and establish a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible."
The average of the exit polls published by Kan 11, Channels 12 and 13 gives the change bloc 53 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu's bloc. The Arab parties are projected to win a combined 17 seats, leaving neither of the two main political blocs with the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Despite the narrow lead for Netanyahu's opponents, Likud is projected to remain Israel's largest individual party, setting the stage for potentially difficult coalition negotiations once the official results are known.
Eisenkot's Yashar! projected to win 19 to 23 seats
Eisenkot's Yashar! party is projected to win 21 seats in Kan 11's exit poll, 22 in Channel 12's and 23 in Channel 13's. The i24NEWS poll gives the party 20 seats, while Channel 14 projects 19.
Across all five exit polls, the former military chief's party averages 21 seats, placing it among the country's largest political factions, behind Likud.
Eisenkot, Israel's 21st IDF chief of staff, entered politics in 2022, three years after leaving military service. He joined Benny Gantz's National Unity alliance and was placed third on its electoral list.
Following the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu's emergency wartime government alongside his party and served as a minister without portfolio.
On December 7, 2023, his son Gal was killed in combat in the Gaza Strip.
In June 2025, Eisenkot announced his departure from National Unity. Two months later, he established Yashar!, which subsequently emerged as a leading party in opinion polls ahead of Tuesday's election.
In recent months, Eisenkot did not rule out forming a minority government with outside parliamentary support from Ra'am and potentially some members of the Joint List. However, Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman rejected that possibility, saying he would not agree to such an arrangement.
With the exit polls showing no outright majority for either main bloc, that disagreement remains a significant obstacle to assembling a governing coalition.
Yair Golan: ‘The public has fired Netanyahu's government’
Democrats leader Yair Golan, a retired IDF major general who has expressed support for a government including Ra'am, also welcomed the exit poll results, describing them as an opportunity to replace Netanyahu.
"The public has spoken. It has fired Netanyahu's government," Golan said. "We have been given a historic opportunity to establish a genuine government of change in Israel, and we have no intention of giving it up."
"We represent an enormous public that has fought in the streets for four years, joined the party and gone out into the field to persuade voters," he continued. "We will do everything we can to ensure that such a government is formed."
Golan said his party was prepared to cooperate with other political factions to overcome disagreements and establish a new coalition.
"We are ready to work with all our partners, bridge the gaps and take responsibility," he said. "The public has spoken. Now it is our turn to do the work."
Sa'ar: ‘The left is celebrating too early’
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, a senior Likud figure, offered a sharply different interpretation of the exit polls, warning Netanyahu's opponents against treating the projections as a victory.
"The celebrations on the left are premature," Sa'ar said.
"According to the exit polls, one thing appears fairly clear: Likud is the largest party in Israel."
His remarks highlighted the central uncertainty emerging from the projections. Although the change bloc holds a narrow lead over Netanyahu's allies in the average of the three main exit polls, Likud remains the largest single party, and neither bloc has enough seats to govern independently.
The final balance could still change as votes are counted, particularly with hundreds of thousands of special double-envelope ballots from soldiers, diplomats and other eligible voters requiring separate verification. Election officials have warned that the count could continue into Friday morning.
Even after the final results are published, President Isaac Herzog will need to consult the elected parties before deciding which lawmaker has the best prospect of forming a government.
For Eisenkot and his allies, the projections represent an opening to replace Netanyahu. For Likud, its position as the largest party provides grounds to challenge claims of an opposition victory. The immediate question is not simply which bloc finishes ahead, but whether any candidate can assemble the parliamentary support needed to govern.

Vatican remains committed to '2-state solution' in Middle East

Baris Seckin and Melike Pala
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Vatican's secretary for relations with states and international organizations, said Tuesday that the Holy See would continue to firmly support a two-state solution in the Middle East, despite some losing faith in the prospect.
Speaking to journalists at the Foreign Press Association in Rome, Gallagher responded to questions on a range of international issues.
Asked about the Vatican’s support for a two-state solution despite opposition to the proposal among some Israeli opposition figures during Israel’s election campaign, Gallagher said the Holy See would continue to firmly advocate for the establishment of two states.
He noted that Israel had been in an extended election campaign atmosphere and said it would be unrealistic to expect opposition politicians to openly support the proposal under the circumstances.
Gallagher stressed that opposition among some Israeli political figures did not mean the international community had withdrawn support for the two-state solution, adding that the proposal continued to enjoy considerable international backing.
He acknowledged, however, that circumstances made its implementation unlikely.
Gallagher underlined that improving conditions in the occupied West Bank was essential for meaningful progress towards a solution, while problems concerning the Gaza Strip also needed to be addressed and resolved.
Russia-Ukraine war
Gallagher also said the Vatican did not consider itself to have a role in negotiating a ceasefire in Oleshky in Russian-occupied southern Ukraine, despite Pope Leo XIV having recently met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Gallagher said the Vatican had the opportunity to convey its views to both during the visit.
He noted that neither side wanted the Vatican to act directly as a mediator or facilitator, but rather preferred it to assume a supportive role.

Three Florida brothers who exploited the wealth and influence of their family’s luxury real estate business to drug and rape dozens of women were each sentenced to 30 years in prison in New York on Tuesday for sex trafficking.
Twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40, were convicted in March on multiple charges after a five-week trial heard details of years of sexual assaults committed in Miami, New York and other high-end locations including the Hamptons; Aspen, Colorado; and on a Caribbean cruise.
A dozen of their victims spoke at the brothers’ sentencing hearing in Manhattan on Tuesday.
Several of the women gave testimony on Tuesday using pseudonyms, and told of how the assaults by the brothers had destroyed their lives and their ability to trust other people.
“I carry a quiet funeral in me for the person I might have become had this not happened to me,” said one woman, who described being raped by Tal Alexander in August 2014, and said the attack changed the way she approached relationships.
“Every second that Tal raped me in that shower felt like an eternity of terror.”
Another told the court that she was raped at a property in the Hamptons after she was drugged and led into a bedroom.
“What looked like a beautiful place became for me a mansion of horror, a mansion of dark secrets,” she said.
The three brothers, dressed in tan prison suits, sat impassively as they listened to the women speak. During their trial, their lawyers conceded that the brothers were “womanizers”, and said they apologized that they were “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times”, but maintained all the sexual encounters were consensual.
The brothers moved from Florida to New York in 2008. Oren and Tal Alexander were star representatives at real estate firm Douglas Elliman, before forming their own brokerage, Official, which made hundreds of millions of dollars selling condos to wealthy and celebrity clientele.
Alon Alexander ran their family’s private security company, and was also deeply involved in their opulent lifestyle of superyachts, private jets, exotic overseas trips, and parties at waterfront mansions in Miami and elsewhere.
Their easy access to money and women, prosecutors said, allowed them to exploit their victims and lure them to parties or on luxury trips, during which the Alexanders would drug and rape them, either together or in the company of others.
“They acted to exert maximum domination over their victims,” the attorneys said in a sentencing submission to the court ahead of Tuesday’s hearing.
“The defendants felt empowered to take whatever they wanted from any woman or girl who agreed to get on a plane, go to a party or sit at their table at a nightclub. The defendants made no effort to have consensual sex with the victims; they did not want that. Instead, they slipped drugs into drinks and forced themselves on to their victims.
“The drugs they used not only rendered a victim immobile, but also impacted her ability to remember every detail of her assault. The defendants’ pattern of mocking and humiliating their victims served the defendants’ goal of maximally dehumanizing these women, and it also shamed the victims into silence.”
Dozens of other women came forward after the allegations against the Alexanders were revealed in a bombshell article published by real estate news outlet the Real Deal in June 2024.
At least 70 women were raped or sexually assaulted by the men, prosecutors said in an earlier court filing that described them as “serial rapists”.
The US district court judge Valerie Caproni said she believed the brothers should not be incarcerated at the same prison because they were a bad influence on each other. The brothers’ lawyers argued on Tuesday that they should be able to serve their sentences together.

Israel exit polls show opposition edge, Arab parties make gains
Unknown

05:44:00 KST

Israeli opposition parties appeared to hold a slim lead over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc in Tuesday's general election, according to initial exit polls, as a surge in Arab voter turnout put Arab-majority parties on course for significant parliamentary gains.
Early projections broadcast by Israeli television networks showed that the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief, had a narrow edge over Netanyahu's bloc, which includes the far-right.
Israeli Arab parties made sweeping gains, likely giving them a critical role in the next parliament, the early exit polls showed.
With no single party winning the majority, Israeli politicians will embark on potentially weeks of high-stakes negotiations on cobbling together a coalition.
The country's main pollsters – Channels 11, 12 and 13 – projected the opposition bloc to win 52 to 53 seats, and Netanyahu's bloc to win around 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in the parliament, with 24 or 25 seats.
In a dash to secure as many votes as possible, Netanyahu had charged that Israeli Arabs were out to "steal the election" and his Likud party unsuccessfully asked election authorities to keep polls open past 10:00 p.m. (2000 GMT).
His efforts led the opposition to charge that he was looking for pretexts to challenge the results.
"We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," a visibly tense Netanyahu told supporters as he tried to bring up turnout in a Likud stronghold.
Nationwide turnout as of 8:00 p.m. stood at nearly 75%, the highest in decades.
Israelis cast their ballots in the shadow of Oct. 7 and the multi-front regional wars that it sparked, with the trauma from the attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.
The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the genocidal military attacks in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza genocide, as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison.
Eisenkot, his main rival, is a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent.
Speaking afterwards at a polling station, Eisenkot called on Israelis to vote to replace "the worst government since the state was established."
Some 7.3 million people were eligible to vote, with tens of thousands of Israelis estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.
Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a center-right party in Eisenkot's bloc.
"The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.
The time to act is "now, or the country really won't survive anymore".
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.
Throughout his career, he has repeatedly raised the spectre of Arab voters as a threat. He warned Tuesday of Arabs voting by the busload, writing on social media that Israel could wake up to a "government of the left wing and Muslim Brotherhood."
The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, said that police had "caught individuals who tried to bribe voters", adding that the unidentified suspects were not at polling stations and were caught near their homes.
He said the matter was a localised case and under investigation.
United Arab List head Mansour Abbas, who could emerge as a kingmaker in a close election, accused Netanyahu of "lying and inciting" to mobilize his voters.
Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists winning 17 or 18 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
In Tel Aviv, left-wing party The Democrats, which is part of Eisenkot's opposition bloc, said police had arrested a man with a knife who had moved threateningly towards its leader Yair Golan.
"Incitement and violence will not intimidate us," Golan said in a statement, blaming the incident on the "poison machine" of Netanyahu.
Netanyahu last returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket and have aggressively championed settlements in the West Bank.
In the last days of the campaign, he posted an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv and talked up his endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who is also fond of alleging election fraud.

German soldier led local branch of Putin-linked Night Wolves biker club for years, The Insider finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:43:49 UTC
05:43:49 KST

A Bundeswehr serviceman spent several years leading the German branch of the Night Wolves motorcycle club, and he continues to hold a leadership position with the group. The Insider found a ruling by a German military disciplinary court dismissing the soldier from service. His name was withheld in the ruling, but The Insider identified him as Alexander Sautner, a dual German-Russian citizen. Sautner initially served as vice president of the club’s “Roads of Victory” division, where he was responsible for organizing international motorcycle rallies. In early 2023, Sautner became vice president of the independent German chapter of the biker club: Night Wolves MC Germania. Despite a disciplinary investigation against him, Sautner continued directing the club’s activities and maintaining contacts with its Russian leadership.
A Bundeswehr soldier
The German military court’s ruling describes in detail how a Bundeswehr serviceman came to hold a leadership position in the Night Wolves.
The soldier is not named in the document, but the charges list the actions that formed the basis of the case against him. They include his participation on April 11, 2022, in a Rossiya Segodnya video conference featuring a Soviet flag in the background, several links to RT and Sputnik material that he posted in 2015, and criticism of Polish authorities for refusing to allow a Night Wolves motorcycle convoy to cross their border. According to publicly available information, the only German participant in the aforementioned April 2022 news conference was Alexander Sautner, and the same posts cited in the ruling can be found on Sautner’s Facebook page (1, 2).
According to the court, Sautner was born in Kazakhstan, moved to Russia with his parents at the age of 2, and relocated with his family to Germany in 1994. He holds both Russian and German citizenship.
Sautner joined the Bundeswehr in July 2007 as a noncommissioned officer candidate and attended the German Air Force’s NCO school. After completing his training, he served in transport units, working in vehicle logistics. In February 2010, he was promoted to Stabsunteroffizier, a junior noncommissioned officer rank, and in January 2013 he was transferred to a logistics battalion.
From July to November 2013, Sautner took part in the International Security Assistance Force mission in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, receiving the Bundeswehr’s bronze deployment medal for his service. He was also awarded the gold-level military service badge.
A September 2013 performance review described Sautner as an experienced, motivated, and results-oriented noncommissioned officer. His commanders praised his openness, honesty, good relations with fellow soldiers, and overall strong performance. In August 2018, at his own request, Sautner transferred to another unit within the logistics battalion.
Sautner’s Bundeswehr contract was not due to expire until June 30, 2032. However, even before the 2018 transfer, Sautner had begun participating in the activities of the Night Wolves motorcycle club — infamous for its longstanding ties to Vladimir Putin, including its role in Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea. According to Germany’s Military Counterintelligence Service, known by its German acronym MAD, Sautner had been a club member since around 2016 and had taken part in its motorcycle rallies even earlier than that.
Sautner later became the first German member of the Night Wolves to achieve “full color” status, meaning full membership in the motorcycle club. In biker culture, “colors” are patches bearing a club’s name and emblem that members wear on their vests. The right to wear the complete set signifies that a person has progressed from supporter and prospective member to a full member of the club.
Sautner later became vice president of the Roads of Victory division, replacing his wife’s uncle in the role. The court ruling does not specify exactly when that happened, but MAD describes him as a longtime vice president and says that until the spring or summer of 2022, he played a key role in organizing and running international motorcycle rallies.
Roads of Victory is a themed Night Wolves division that organizes annual motorcycle rallies around May 9, Russia’s Victory Day commemorating the defeat of Nazi Germany in World War II. Before an independent German chapter was established, Night Wolves activities in Germany were carried out through Roads of Victory, which was headed by Andrei Bobrovsky. Bobrovsky, for his part, is an associate of Night Wolves founder Alexander Zaldostanov, who came under European Union sanctions in 2022. As vice president, Sautner effectively headed Roads of Victory activities in Germany.
The Night Wolves motorcycle club itself was founded by Zaldostanov in 1989. MAD documents say the organization has about 45 chapters in different countries and operates under a strict hierarchy. According to the counterintelligence agency, members are required to follow the club leadership, while Zaldostanov can issue instructions directly to members of foreign chapters.
The Night Wolves and several of the club’s leaders are under EU sanctions for supporting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. The sanctions justification says the organization spreads Russian propaganda, supports pro-Russian armed formations in Ukraine, and maintains close ties to the Kremlin.
German military counterintelligence regards the Night Wolves’ activities as one instrument of Russia’s hybrid warfare efforts against Germany. MAD assesses that the annual motorcycle rallies are used not only as commemorative events, but also to spread pro-Russian political messages.
How the investigation into Sautner began
The first suspicions among Bundeswehr commanders emerged in 2020, when Sautner’s battalion commander and a security officer noticed a Night Wolves emblem sticker on the rear window of Sautner’s car while it was parked on military premises. At the time, Sautner was working primarily as part of the Bundeswehr’s assistance to civilian health authorities. However, after his links to the Russian motorcycle club were discovered, his commanders concluded that he could no longer be assigned to perform work involving classified information.
Sautner’s former direct superior, whose name was withheld in the ruling, testified that the soldier was primarily assisting civilian health authorities at the time, but the restriction on deploying him to posts requiring security clearance created problems for a unit that had commitments to NATO’s rapid-response forces. The situation was compounded by Sautner’s military specialty, which was in short supply, making him difficult to replace.
Sautner also told the court about the circumstances that prevented him from passing the security vetting required for access to classified information, saying that he had retained Russian citizenship because renouncing it would have involved significant expense. He also refused to sign a pledge not to visit certain countries that were considered potential security risks. The ruling does not identify those countries. Holding a second citizenship is not itself prohibited for Bundeswehr service, and the court documents do not indicate that Sautner concealed the existence of his Russian passport from his commanders.
On Feb. 4, 2021, the Bundeswehr’s logistics command formally opened disciplinary proceedings against Sauter, and in December of that year, he was informed of the main findings, which centered on four Facebook posts he had made between 2015 and 2019. Sautner was offered the opportunity to respond, but declined.
On Jan. 27, 2015, Sauter commented on a Sputnik report about Ukrainian military losses in the Donetsk region, writing that Ukrainians could now try out their crematorium. Military disciplinary prosecutors interpreted the remark as incitement to violence and hatred.
On April 27, 2015, Sautner criticized Polish authorities for refusing to allow Night Wolves participants in a motorcycle rally to transit the country on their way to Berlin. He complained that the bikers were being prevented from honoring those killed in World War II and called the Polish authorities “dirty U.S. vassals.”
On Sept. 4, 2015, Sautner shared an article from the German magazine Compact describing the country as an occupied American colony. He posted another article, this time from RT Deutsch, on June 26, 2019. It concerned historical memory and relations between Russia and the West.
The Insider found the first two posts, which were described in detail in the court ruling, on Sautner’s Facebook page. The court ultimately did not consider the four posts in its final judgment, and they were not brought up during Sautner’s disciplinary hearing because they were unlikely to materially affect the type or severity of the punishment.
Notably, despite the investigation, Sautner continued participating in Night Wolves activities. On May 9, 2021, during one of the Roads of Victory rallies, he was seen carrying the flag of the self-proclaimed “Luhansk People’s Republic.” MAD assessed that displaying the symbol of the unrecognized Russian-backed statelet demonstrated how commemorative events were being used to promote Russian political messages.
Instructions from Night Wolves leaders and a pro-Russian demonstration in Berlin
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, German military counterintelligence uncovered evidence of direct interaction between Sautner and the club’s Russian leadership. MAD materials cited in the court ruling say Sautner maintained direct contact with Alexander Zaldostanov and Andrei Bobrovsky and received instructions from them, including while members of the club leadership were in the war zone in Ukraine.
One such episode occurred in early March 2022, mere days after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion on February 24.
In club correspondence from March 4 and 5, counterintelligence officers found discussions of a demonstration in Berlin that was to be held under the stated aim of opposing alleged persecution of Russian-speaking residents of Germany. According to MAD, Sautner received a personal message containing instructions from Roads of Victory president Bobrovsky, who was referred to as Hauptkommandant, or “commander in chief” in the correspondence. Participants were urged to fight on the “information front.”
Sautner then sent a voice message to the German Roads of Victory group chat strongly urging other club members to attend. On March 5, 2022, Sautner appeared with other Night Wolves members at a demonstration at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, where he posed with a Russian flag bearing state symbols and the word “Russia.” Photographs from the event were later reviewed by the court.
Sautner said he attended the demonstration to protest discrimination against Russian-speaking people in Germany, adding that he was particularly concerned about his own children. The court, however, viewed the event as a public display of solidarity with Russia staged against the backdrop of the start of its invasion of Ukraine.
The court ruling also mentions another public appearance by Sautner. On April 11, 2022, he participated by video link in a news conference organized by the Russian state media group Rossiya Segodnya. A Soviet flag with a hammer and sickle was visible behind him. MAD interpreted the episode as a further demonstration of Sautner’s senior position within the Night Wolves leadership.
Raising money for Donbas
During the investigation, German military counterintelligence also examined messages from a WhatsApp group called NW DP GERMANY, which was found on Sautner’s phone.
One message asked club members to contribute 1,000 rubles (around $13 at the time) each by Feb. 1, 2022, and then another 500 rubles per month to support Night Wolves chapters in Donbas. The appeal was posted by Denis N., whom German counterintelligence described as a close confidant of Sautner. The person was Denis Nalyotov, who later became head of the club’s German branch.
MAD assessed that the collected funds could have been used to purchase equipment suitable for armed operations against Ukraine. On Feb. 27, 2022, after the full-scale invasion had begun, Sautner himself called on members of the German Roads of Victory organization to send 13 euros each to a person named Badja. According to the message, the money was intended for humanitarian aid to Donbas.
On March 1, Denis Nalyotov discussed the collection with another club member, Thorsten M. He said the money could be sent by PayPal but that it would be better to wait for an in-person meeting and hand it over in cash so the transfers would leave no record.
On April 26, Sautner said in a WhatsApp voice message that around 1,000 euros had been collected. He said the money had been transferred to a fund called “Humanitarian Aid for Donbas.”
MAD materials also cite correspondence from March 2, 2023, in which Badja again called for donations for humanitarian aid. A Roads of Victory representative in Germany replied that fundraising was already underway.
The court ruling does not establish that Sautner personally purchased military equipment or that the funds collected were in fact used for armed activity against Ukraine. The possible military purpose of the money appears specifically as an assessment by MAD.
How Sautner became vice president of Germany’s Night Wolves
In the spring or summer of 2022, Sautner stepped down as vice president of the German Roads of Victory organization, being replaced by Denis Nalyotov. Сounterintelligence assessed that Sautner may have given up the title because of pressure from German law enforcement. Disciplinary proceedings against him were already underway, and MAD documents also refer to an investigation by Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office. The court ruling does not disclose details of that investigation.
The formal transfer of the post, however, did not mean Sautner stopped playing a leadership role. According to MAD, he continued coordinating all major decisions with Nalyotov, with the two generally making and implementing them together.
In early 2023, the Night Wolves established an independent German chapter, Night Wolves MC Germania. Nalyotov became president of the new organization, while Sautner became vice president.
The two informally divided Germany into two zones. Nalyotov ran the northern chapter from Hanover, while Sautner oversaw the south from Bad Mergentheim in Baden-Württemberg. Flight records reviewed by The Insider also indicate that Sautner and Nalyotov traveled to Moscow together after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. (Nalyotov flew from Kaliningrad to Moscow on Jan. 15, 2023, and returned on Jan. 21.)
Sautner therefore obtained a new formal leadership position in the Night Wolves’ German structure after the Bundeswehr’s disciplinary proceedings had already begun. MAD assessed that Sautner’s appointments as club president and vice president indicated a particularly high level of trust from Alexander Zaldostanov. MAD also found that the Russian leadership continued to control foreign chapters, including the organization of propaganda events in Germany.
At the court hearing, Sautner confirmed that he remained a full member of the Night Wolves and continued to serve as vice president of the German chapter.
Why Sautner was not dismissed from the Bundeswehr until 2026
On March 9, 2022, the proceedings were suspended pending additional disciplinary charges. The Bundeswehr’s Federal Office of Personnel Management later considered dismissing Sautner under a law allowing the expedited removal of soldiers involved in anti-constitutional activities without lengthy court proceedings. Sautner was temporarily suspended from official duties in April 2022, and the hearings continued for several more years. On May 26, 2025, the agency determined that there were insufficient grounds execute Sautner’s expedited removal, and the disciplinary case against him continued.
Then on Oct. 10, 2025, Sautner was served with an amended charge sheet. In addition to the earlier Facebook posts, the case now included three new allegations: participation in the pro-Russian demonstration on March 5, 2022; serving as vice president of the German Night Wolves chapter from at least early 2023 through July 29, 2025; and sending an insulting email to a fellow soldier.
The final incident occurred on April 19, 2025. During the night, Sautner emailed a senior NCO in his unit complaining that he had not been informed about the death of a former fellow serviceman. Sautner said the man had died by suicide and accused the command of inaction. The email contained numerous insults directed at members of the unit.
At the court hearing, Sautner apologized to the recipient. The court nevertheless found that he had deliberately violated his duty to treat fellow soldiers with respect.
The court also heard testimony from Sautner’s former commanders, who described him as an experienced, calm, and reliable soldier widely respected by his colleagues. One commander said he had been surprised by the allegations against him.
At the same time, Sautner’s former superiors said that given his actions, they no longer considered his return to the Bundeswehr possible. According to the court ruling, Sautner had openly discussed his Night Wolves activities on his Facebook page, meaning his links to the club were known within his unit.
When Sautner was asked during the hearing whether he even wanted to remain in the Bundeswehr, he was unable to answer immediately. Ultimately, the judges concluded that Sautner had deliberately violated his soldierly duties to remain loyal to Germany, to uphold its constitutional order, and to refrain from conduct that could undermine trust in the Bundeswehr. The court separately stressed that Sautner’s leadership role in an organization closely linked to the Russian state was incompatible with service in Germany’s armed forces.
The ruling also noted that Sautner did not end his Night Wolves activities after the investigation began. On the contrary, while disciplinary proceedings were already underway, he assumed an even more prominent position in the club. The court considered that to be an aggravating factor.
“He can no longer be the servant of two masters,” the ruling said. The judges were quoting wording used by Sautner’s own defense, although the document does not explain the context in which his lawyer used the phrase.
The judges ruled that the Bundeswehr’s trust in Sautner had been irreparably destroyed. On Jan. 28, 2026, Germany’s military disciplinary court found him guilty of disciplinary violations and ordered his dismissal from service. Sautner was also denied special transitional payments following his dismissal and ordered to pay court costs.
The judgment became final on Feb. 5, 2026. The decision was based on Sautner’s leadership role in an organization that German counterintelligence links to the Russian state, his public participation in a pro-Russian demonstration after the start of the full-scale invasion, and his violations of military duties.

PAC-3 Missiles To Be Maintained in Poland — First Such Center Outside the USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:43:04 UTC
05:43:04 KST

Poland will host the first maintenance center outside the U.S. for PAC-3 anti-aircraft missiles, which are used in Patriot air defense systems.
This was announced by Poland’s Deputy Minister of National Defense, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka.
According to her, four countries — Poland, Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway — competed for the right to host the center. Poland’s proposal received the highest rating as early as the initial selection stage.
The decision was made by the U.S. government in cooperation with the American defense contractor Lockheed Martin, which manufactures the PAC-3 missiles.
According to an official statement from the company, the new facility will carry out the repair, refurbishment, maintenance, and recertification of the interceptor missiles.
The center will service missiles for NATO countries that operate Patriot systems. Its establishment will significantly reduce the time required to return missiles to service, as previously they had to be transported to the U.S. for such work.
Polish Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz previously noted that transporting the missiles to the United States, servicing them, and recertifying them could, in some cases, take up to two years.
According to Reuters, the cost of establishing the center will amount to approximately PLN 1 billion ($253 million). It is expected that it will take about a year or slightly longer to bring the facility into operation.
On July 7, Poland, the United States, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden signed an agreement on the establishment of a European maintenance center for PAC-3 missiles during the defense-industrial forum at the NATO summit in Ankara.
In July, Militarnyi reported that Poland plans to cooperate with Ukraine in the production and maintenance of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems.
That same month, Warsaw also proposed to the U.S. that they launch a trilateral format for the production of these missiles with Ukraine’s participation.

UK Defense Chief Calls on NATO to Brace for Potential Confrontation With Russia
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting warned that Western allies must prepare for a scenario where the United Kingdom and NATO could find themselves in a direct military confrontation with Russia.
Speaking alongside Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz in Warsaw, the official stressed the necessity of strengthening deterrence capabilities across Europe, as reported by The Guardian.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Addressing joint defense efforts, Streeting pointed to historical precedents regarding official assurances from Moscow prior to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“We must be prepared for a scenario in which the United Kingdom and the NATO alliance find themselves at war with Russia. Not because we want war—we have no quarrel with the Russian people and do not seek war with Russia; NATO is a defensive alliance—but when Putin assures that he has no intention of provoking a war with NATO, we remember what he said about Ukraine just a few days before the invasion,” he noted, The Guardian reported.
The defense minister reaffirmed the alliance’s readiness to defend all member territories while maintaining active support for Kyiv.
“The more we are prepared to stand up to Russia, to defend every inch of NATO territory, the less likely we are to find ourselves in such a scenario,” he added.
On May 27, 2026, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed a historic Security and Defense Partnership Treaty in London, officially designating Russia as the primary threat to European stability.
The agreement was designed to elevate bilateral military cooperation to its highest level and enable rapid, direct defense responses in the event of a regional crisis without awaiting unanimous consensus from NATO’s 32 members.
Tusk underscored that while Poland remained fully committed to the transatlantic alliance, building swift, bilateral mechanisms with key allies like the UK and France was essential to counter regional aggression effectively—particularly as Washington prepared to gradually reduce its military footprint on the continent.

The medical negligence case is being dragged out: should victims turn to the European Court of Human Rights?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:40:12 EET
05:40:12 KST

The medical negligence case is being dragged out: should victims turn to the European Court of Human Rights?
Kyiv • UNN
Systematic postponements of court hearings in medical negligence cases may violate victims’ rights. Roman Yedeliev, an associate professor at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, explained when it is possible to apply to the ECtHR, how the expiry of limitation periods affects the case, and whether a closed criminal proceeding can be reopened.
Hundreds of criminal proceedings are registered in Ukraine every year under Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by medical or pharmaceutical workers. According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, 409 such proceedings were registered in 2025, and another 305 in the first eight months of 2026. Some of these cases concern the deaths of patients whose families spend years trying to establish the circumstances of the tragedy and obtain justice. Instead, they face lengthy expert examinations, regular postponements of court hearings, and some cases are closed because the statute of limitations has expired. Can such delays constitute grounds for applying to the European Court of Human Rights? Roman Yedelyev, Associate Professor of the Department of International Law at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, told UNN in an exclusive blitz interview.
Photo caption: Roman Yedelyev, Associate Professor of the Department of International Law at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv.
- Can the systematic postponement of court hearings in medical negligence cases violate victims’ rights and become grounds for applying to the ECHR?
- Yes, it can. However, it is important to understand that not every postponement of a court hearing constitutes a violation of the Convention. If a patient’s death resulted from possible medical negligence, Article 2 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to life, requires the state to ensure an effective and timely examination of the case that will establish the circumstances of the death and clarify the issue of liability. If court hearings are systematically postponed without proper justification, the proceedings make no progress for years, and the delays create a risk that the statute of limitations will expire, this may indicate a violation of the Convention.
Such ECHR case law also exists concerning Ukraine. In particular, in the case of "Sinko and Others v. Ukraine" (2026), the Court found a violation of Article 2 due to shortcomings in and delays to proceedings concerning the deaths of patients. Similarly, in "Lukashenko v. Ukraine" (2025), the Court found that the investigation into the circumstances of a patient’s death, which had lasted for many years, was ineffective.
To apply to the ECHR, it is important to prove not merely that hearings were postponed, but that the delays were unjustified and negatively affected the possibility of an effective examination of the case. In certain circumstances, the prolonged ineffectiveness of the proceedings may justify an application even before their conclusion.
- If criminal proceedings in a medical negligence case are closed because the statute of limitations has expired without a verdict on the merits, will the victims be able to challenge this before the ECHR?
- Yes, victims may apply to the ECHR even after criminal proceedings have been closed because the statute of limitations has expired. However, it is important to understand that the mere fact that proceedings were closed does not necessarily mean that the Convention was violated. The ECHR will primarily assess whether the state ensured an effective investigation and judicial examination. If the limitation periods expired as a result of unjustified delays, inaction by state authorities, or numerous procedural shortcomings, this may constitute a violation of Article 2 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to life.
The case of "Lukashenko v. Ukraine" (2025) is illustrative. In that case, criminal proceedings concerning a patient’s death were closed because the statute of limitations had expired after more than ten years of investigation. The ECHR found a violation of Article 2; moreover, even the compensation received by the victim in civil proceedings did not remedy the shortcomings of the investigation. In "Sinko and Others v. Ukraine" (2026), the Court also confirmed the state’s responsibility for the ineffectiveness of proceedings concerning possible medical negligence.
At the same time, the Convention does not guarantee victims a mandatory conviction. The main requirement is that the state ensure a genuine opportunity to establish the circumstances of the incident and obtain legal protection, including compensation for damage.
- What practical results can victims achieve through the ECHR? Can its judgment contribute to the resumption of the examination of the case and a decision on the merits?
– First and foremost, victims may obtain official recognition that the state violated their rights, as well as financial compensation. For example, in the cases of "Lukashenko v. Ukraine" (2025) and "Sinko and Others v. Ukraine" (2026), the ECtHR found violations of Article 2 of the Convention due to the ineffectiveness of proceedings concerning medical negligence and awarded the applicants compensation for non-pecuniary damage. However, the significance of an ECtHR judgment is not limited to compensation. Under Article 46 of the Convention, the state is obliged to comply with the Court’s judgment, including, where necessary, taking measures to eliminate the consequences of the violation.
Could this lead to the reopening of the criminal proceedings? In theory, yes, but not automatically. Ukrainian legislation provides for the possibility of reviewing judicial decisions after the ECtHR has established a violation of the Convention. However, everything will depend on the nature of the violation established, the circumstances of the specific case, and the existence of appropriate legal grounds.
- What legal steps should victims take now to protect their rights and minimize the risk of the proceedings being closed due to the expiry of the limitation period?
- First and foremost, I would advise victims not to remain passive participants in the proceedings, especially if the expiry of the limitation period is approaching. It is important to use the available legal mechanisms to seek the timely consideration of the case.
First, it is worth submitting written applications to the court requesting compliance with the reasonable time limits for consideration, drawing attention to the risk that the limitation period may expire. Article 28 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine provides for this possibility. If hearings are systematically postponed, it is necessary to demand a proper justification of the reasons and, where possible, propose alternative ways for the accused to participate, including via videoconference.
Second, it is important to document all instances of delays in the proceedings, including the dates of postponed hearings, the reasons for the adjournments, the applications submitted, and the court’s decisions. This may be crucial if it later becomes necessary to apply to the ECtHR.
Third, I would recommend not limiting oneself exclusively to the criminal proceedings, but assessing the possibility of filing a separate civil claim for damages. Even if the criminal case is closed, the possibility of civil-law protection may remain under certain conditions. At the same time, it is important not to miss the time limits for filing such a claim.
Ultimately, the most important thing is not to wait until the limitation period expires. An active procedural position does not guarantee that the proceedings will not be closed, but it may help protect victims’ rights at the national level and create an appropriate evidentiary basis for a possible application to the ECtHR.
In medical negligence cases, time is of particular importance. The longer the proceedings continue, the more difficult it is to establish the circumstances of the incident, gather relevant evidence, and ensure that those responsible are held accountable. Therefore, the ECtHR assesses not only formal compliance with procedural rules, but also the actual effectiveness of justice.

Russia and US exploring Arctic cooperation – Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:37:44 UTC
05:37:44 KST

Russia and US exploring Arctic cooperation – Putin
Russia and the US are exploring opportunities for cooperation in the Arctic, President Vladimir Putin said, stressing that Moscow is ready to work with partners genuinely interested in joint projects.
Speaking at the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow on Tuesday, Putin highlighted growing global demand for natural gas and Russia’s efforts to expand production, particularly in the Arctic.
Natural gas already accounts for a quarter of the global energy mix, and Russia, which holds the world’s largest reserves, is investing in infrastructure and technologies designed to operate in extreme northern conditions, the president stated.
“Russia is systematically strengthening its technological sovereignty,” Putin said. “We have also taken a major step forward by creating our own proprietary LNG technologies, which are already being deployed in the harsh conditions of the Arctic.”
Moscow is “open for cooperation” in technology and other areas, he said, adding that it is “actively working with many nations” in the Arctic. “We are now exploring avenues for joint work with American partners.”
Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Moscow and Washington were discussing a potential venture to use Russian technology to extract natural gas in Alaska, liquefy it and export it.
The proposed company, called Polar LNG, was reportedly discussed last month by Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
According to the NYT, Russian gas producer Novatek has helped finance the venture through a UAE-based firm and is considering taking a minority stake.
Western energy companies have largely scaled back their Russian operations since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. US energy giant ExxonMobil withdrew from the Sakhalin-1 oil and gas project, although the Wall Street Journal reported last year that it is considering a return.
ExxonMobil and Chevron nevertheless retain stakes in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which transports Kazakh oil through Russia to the Black Sea.
Several major European energy companies have also exited Russia, although France’s TotalEnergies retains stakes in Novatek and the Yamal LNG project.
The EU has adopted an increasingly militaristic approach to the Arctic. Its latest Arctic strategy identifies the region as a potential flashpoint for confrontation with Russia, while declaring that the EU “is part of the Arctic” and outlining a range of military objectives.
In August, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned that the EU is seeking to turn the Arctic into a new “hotbed” of tensions. He accused NATO of “driving the region towards militarization” through its military buildup, while stressing Moscow’s commitment to “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation.”
