Egypt orders closure of leading independent news site Mada Masr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:35:18 UTC
05:35:18 KST

Egypt orders closure of leading independent news site Mada Masr
Editor Lina Attalah was freed once a $53,400 fine was paid, only to learn of a one-year sentence passed in her absence
An Egyptian court has ordered the closure of Mada Masr, one of the country’s last prominent independent news outlets, and fined its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, three million Egyptian pounds ($53,400) for running a website without a licence.
The New Cairo Misdemeanour Court also ordered the confiscation of the outlet’s equipment and devices. Attalah was taken into custody after Tuesday’s ruling. She was released several hours later, after Mada Masr paid the fine in full.
During the release procedures, Attalah learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to one year in prison, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. Mada Masr said Attalah’s lawyers have challenged that ruling, and a retrial hearing is scheduled for November 11.
In an editorial published hours after the verdict, Mada Masr said it had entered court “with a measure of faith in the law and the justice system”. It added: “But what we found in court left none of that faith intact.”
The outlet said the court refused its lawyers’ requests to review the case file, submit additional evidence and call witnesses. According to Mada Masr, the judge then appointed “an unknown party” to act as Attalah’s defence lawyer, even though eight of her own lawyers were in court and she herself objected. The editorial said the judge wrote that lawyer’s requests himself “before issuing a verdict carrying the maximum penalty, with no review and no defence”.
Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, attended the hearing. According to Mada Masr, he said the court went ahead with the appointment despite Attalah’s own objection to being represented by a court-appointed lawyer. Mada Masr’s lawyer, Hassan al-Azhari, told the Egyptian outlet Zawia3 that the court rejected the defence’s requests and then appointed a lawyer, a step Attalah and her team objected to.
Egypt’s website laws
Tuesday’s ruling is based on Article 105 of Egypt’s 2018 media law, which sets fines of one to three million Egyptian pounds ($17,800–$53,400), plus closure and confiscation, for operating an unlicensed website.
Mada Masr says it applied for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and again in 2020, without a reply. It says it learned of a rejection only when prosecutors raised it during a previous case in 2022. In 2023, an administrative court upheld the council’s refusal, citing the absence of proof that the outlet’s trademark was registered, although Mada Masr’s lawyer said he had submitted a trademark registration certificate. A new application has been pending since June 2023.
There was no immediate official comment on the verdict.
The head of the Journalists’ Syndicate, Khaled el-Balshy, said the union would take legal action to appeal the ruling.
Mada Masr was founded in 2013 and has been blocked inside Egypt since 2017. It says it has faced six cases in six years, and rights groups say this is the first to reach trial.
“We tried to defend the law,” the outlet wrote, “just as we tried to defend ourselves.”
Amnesty International’s senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said in a statement, “Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.”
“This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country’s last remaining independent media voices,” Ahmed added.
The verdict came on the same day that Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution, which investigates national security cases, renewed the detention of six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash for another 15 days.

A former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, Wayne Couzens, has been found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer.
A court heard that Mark Tyrrell raped the woman – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.
The 57-year-old was then said to have told her “I don’t believe what’s just happened” and “do you realise that what I’ve just done, that was rape?”
Tyrrell had been attached to the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, which is where the convicted rapists Couzens and David Carrick both worked.
He was convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice after a trial at Southwark crown court.
Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC alleged that when the woman resisted Tyrrell’s sexual advances “he simply chose to take what he wanted”.
The court heard that concerns were raised after officers attended her address for a separate matter and found Tyrrell hiding by the side of her bed.
The former PC was found guilty of perverting the course of justice by attempting to delete messages with the woman.

Jurors found him not guilty in relation to 13 other charges, including one count of rape.

Tyrrell previously admitted misconduct in a public office. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to the police about why he was in her bedroom.
The defendant, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced on 16 December.
Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by then Met officer Couzens in 2021. He was later given a whole-life order.
Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.

The $9 billion fuel bill raising questions about Australia's energy security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:32:19 UTC
05:32:19 KST

In brief
- Australia paid a higher price for imported diesel than any other nation during the fuel crisis.
- New analysis linked billions in extra fuel costs to energy security risks.
Australia has paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, with a report putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.
The added cost equates to $324 for every Australian, exceeding the bills incurred by Brazil, South Africa, France and the UK.
The Climate Council released the figures from its energy security scorecard on Wednesday, which also found Australia paid an extra $1.6 billion for petrol imports.
The findings come days after oil prices reached a six-month high amid escalating threats in the Middle East.
The council's report, called Crude Awakening, analysed Australia's energy security, its exposure to rising global fuel prices, and policies and progress towards electric transport and renewable energy.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It found Australia was the world's largest seaborne importer of diesel, with imports responsible for 90 per cent of its supply.
Diesel use in Australia had also more than doubled since 2000 to 33 billion litres in 2025, with about a quarter used in mining.
Australia paid $9 billion in additional costs to import diesel between March and August, compared to an extra $3.5 billion in Brazil and $3 billion in the UK.
The nation also paid an additional $1.6 billion for petrol, or $56 per person.
Climate Council spokeswoman and economist Nicki Hutley said those costs had a widespread impact.
"We're seeing costs (rise) right through the economy, whether it's in inflation at the supermarket or all the way through the supply chain," she told the Australian Associated Press news agency.
"If we keep relying on imported oil, that is leaving our energy security in somebody else's hands, and we're seeing that this year."
Moves to renewable energy had saved Australians from some higher costs, the report found, with electric and hybrid cars cutting $1.7 billion in costs and saving the equivalent of 17.4 million litres of petrol and diesel per week.
Australia was still slow to adopt electric trucks, with the vehicles representing 0.7 per cent of new sales compared to nine per cent worldwide, and had one public charging point for every 41 electric cars, compared to the global average of one for every 11 EVs.
Electrifying more vehicles and removing diesel fuel tax credits could help to protect Australia from future fuel shocks, Hutley said, and state and federal policies should support the transition.
"Every crisis should be seen as an opportunity, and we shouldn't waste that opportunity," she said.
"The best time to do this was yesterday, as they say, and the next best time is today to say what will set us up for a long-term future of energy security at lowest cost to Australian taxpayers."

Ukraine intercepts nearly 60% of Russia’s Geran-4 jet drones, General Staff says, as Kyiv races to counter evolving threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:28:36 UTC
05:28:36 KST

Ukraine’s air defenses have been intercepting nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with the interception rate reaching 80% during some attacks, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine, adding a faster-moving threat to the Shahed-type drones Moscow deploys against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Ukraine is working to improve interception rates while reducing the cost of countering these aerial threats amid shortages of surface-to-air missiles.
The General Staff’s update did not mention interception rates for Russia’s more advanced Geran-5 jet-powered drone.
F-16s, Mirage jets help intercept Russian drones
According to the General Staff, tactical aviation plays a significant role in destroying Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine uses F-16s, French Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29 fighters to intercept them.
The military is also strengthening what it calls “short-range air defense” as Ukraine faces a shortage of guided anti-aircraft missiles. These systems include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft guns, newer Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin systems, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups deployed by different branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped not only with machine guns and supporting equipment but also with man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS). Ukrainian troops have been successfully using these missiles to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones, the General Staff said.
Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones
Ukraine tests cheaper drone interceptors
Ukraine is also seeking to lower the cost of countering Russian aerial attacks by testing new interceptor drones.
According to the General Staff, some models have already downed dozens of Russian Geran jet-powered drones. The military did not provide further details about the interceptor models or the number of drones destroyed.
The rising interception rate reflects Ukraine’s efforts to adapt its air defenses to Russia’s evolving drone campaign while preserving scarce and expensive air-defense missiles for threats that require them.

Verkhovna Rada Simplified Conditions for Legalizing Foreigners Serving in Ukrainian Defense Forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:28:30 UTC
05:28:30 KST

The Verkhovna Rada passed a law extending the deadlines for issuing temporary residence permits to foreigners and stateless persons performing military service in Ukraine.
This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
On October 27, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Bill No. 16094. The resolution was approved by 282 members of parliament.
The bill extends the deadline for applying for a temporary residence permit from six months to one year for foreign military personnel who signed a contract by May 10, 2026.
Thus, they will have until May 10, 2027, to apply for a permit.
The Ministry of Defense explained that due to undergoing basic military training and carrying out combat missions, foreign volunteers are not always able to apply to the migration service in a timely manner.
The law also provides for a number of other changes. In particular, foreigners and stateless persons who sign new contracts will be able to legally remain in Ukraine from the date of signing until they receive their residence permit, but for no longer than three months.
For military personnel who signed contracts after May 10, 2026, but were unable to complete the necessary paperwork in a timely manner, a transition period is provided through May 10, 2027.
At the same time, foreign military personnel who have been discharged from service without having obtained their residence permits will have three months to establish legal grounds for their continued stay in Ukraine.
The law is currently awaiting the President of Ukraine’s signature and will take effect the day after its official publication.
In May, the Cabinet of Ministers simplified the procedure for issuing temporary residence permits for foreign volunteers.
In addition, in September, the Ministry of Defense established an interagency working group to improve the conditions of service for foreign volunteers.

Amid historic voter turnout in Israel's 26th Knesset election, large numbers of Arab citizens turned out to cast their ballots Tuesday. According to television exit polls, the Joint List and Ra'am are projected to win a combined 16 to 18 seats, up from just 10 in the outgoing Knesset.
As of 8 p.m., nationwide voter turnout stood at 74.3%, with particularly high participation recorded in many Arab communities, including Bedouin towns and villages. In the village of al-Aryan in Wadi Ara, turnout reached 90.7%, followed by Sakhnin at 83.5%, Kafr Qasim at 81.3%, Rahat at 79.8%, Kuseife at 78.6%, Bir al-Maksur at 77.6%, Tira at 77.5% and Hura at 76.3%.
However, turnout in several Arab communities remained below the national average. In Shefa-Amr, 72.5% of eligible voters had cast ballots, compared with 70.1% in Umm al-Fahm, 70% in Nazareth and 73% in Tel Sheva. In Tayibe, turnout stood at 74.3%, matching the national average.
Among Bedouin communities, turnout reached 87.3% in Bir Hadaj, 85.2% in the Abu Qrenat tribal community, 84.2% in Kabu'a and 71.3% in Ar'ara in the Negev. In the Galilee, the Bedouin village of Dmeideh recorded 87.9% turnout, while Shibli-Umm al-Ghanam, at the foot of Mount Tabor, recorded 74.3%.
By comparison, turnout in Arab communities was considerably lower during the previous Knesset election in 2022. In Sakhnin, 68.4% of eligible voters participated, compared with 66.88% in Kafr Qasim, 60.6% in Rahat, 57.7% in Tayibe, 51.5% in Shefa-Amr, 49% in Hura and 48.3% in Nazareth.
The most dramatic increase was recorded in Umm al-Fahm, where turnout reached 70.1% by 8 p.m. Tuesday, compared with just 38.3% in 2022, nearly doubling. One possible factor behind the sharp increase is that Joint List chairman Professor Yousef Jabareen is a resident of the city.
Most Arab voters support the Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra'am, which could play a significant role in determining the composition of the next government.
According to the exit polls, the opposition bloc may need the support of these parties to advance measures against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, including legislation that would bar a politician under criminal indictment from serving as prime minister, replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and potentially establishing a government dependent on their support.
However, Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, who appears positioned to receive the first mandate to form the next government, has already declared that he would establish a coalition only on the basis of a Zionist majority.
The Joint List and Ra'am: From 10 seats to a possible 18
The Joint List is an alliance of three Arab parties: Hadash, Ta'al and Balad. Hadash is headed by Yousef Jabareen, who succeeded Ayman Odeh. Ta'al has been led since 1995 by Ahmad Tibi, who has served continuously in the Knesset since 1999. Balad is led by Sami Abu Shehadeh, although he will not enter the Knesset after the Central Elections Committee disqualified his candidacy.
During a hearing on an appeal against the disqualification, the Supreme Court recommended that Abu Shehadeh consider withdrawing his candidacy to avoid the need for a ruling. The Balad chairman subsequently withdrew.
At its peak in 2020, the Joint List won 15 Knesset seats, although all the major Arab parties, including Ra'am, were running together at the time. A year later, when the Joint List ran with the same three-party composition as today, it secured just six seats.
Ra'am has been headed by Mansour Abbas since 2019. The party is considered the political arm of the southern branch of the Islamic Movement in Israel. In the two previous elections, Ra'am ran independently, winning four seats in 2021 and five in 2022.
Following the election to the 24th Knesset, and after also holding coalition negotiations with Likud, Abbas and Ra'am backed the so-called change government, the coalition that replaced Netanyahu. That decision prompted fierce attacks from Netanyahu and Likud, which continued throughout the current election campaign. Netanyahu's central campaign slogan was "Right or Palestine."
This time, for the first time, Abbas placed a Jewish candidate on Ra'am's electoral list: former deputy public security minister and retired police major general Yoav Segalovitz, who was ranked second.

Arab voter turnout would have been lower had there been any other outgoing government - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:25:01 UTC
05:25:01 KST

Throughout this campaign and into its final hours, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sounded the same alarm he has sounded throughout his political career: Arab citizens are flooding the polls and endangering his rule. For once, the outgoing prime minister was telling the truth. Arab Israelis are voting today in numbers not seen in decades, and they may well bring his reign to an end.
The last time this happened was 1999. In one of Israel’s few direct elections for prime minister, Arab voters turned out in large numbers to back Ehud Barak almost unanimously, helping oust Netanyahu for the first time and opening the door of the prime minister’s office to Barak, Israel’s last left-wing prime minister.
Sixteen months later, in October 2000, police under Barak’s government opened fire on Arab demonstrators protesting Ariel Sharon’s visit to the Temple Mount, Al-Aqsa Mosque. Twelve Israeli citizens were shot and killed. The Or Commission of Inquiry later confirmed what every Arab Israeli had already known: There were grave failures in how the police and the state treat Arab citizens. It surprised no one that no police officer was ever charged.
October 2000 became an open wound in Arab Israeli collective memory and a reason to keep a distance from the Israeli mainstream. That memory has kept many Arab citizens home in every election since.
This time is different.
Netanyahu's coalition has abandoned, betrayed Arab citizens
The memory of October 2000 has not faded, but it has been overtaken by the reality of the past four years, under a government that has done far more than neglect Arab citizens.
Israel’s outgoing coalition, the most radical in the country’s history, not only tried to import the reality of the West Bank across the Green Line and into Israel proper. It also taught Israel’s two million Arab citizens that a bad situation can always get worse if they accept their own political marginalization.
This government left Arab communities at the mercy of criminal gangs, living amid anarchy and state absence, with little urgency from those responsible for public safety. Meanwhile, its mouthpieces in the media spewed relentless incitement against Arab citizens: doctors, journalists, elected officials, bus drivers, ordinary people. Without that, Arab turnout today might well have continued its decades-long decline. Instead, the government that did the most to push Arab citizens out of Israeli politics may be the one that brought them back.
The easy reading of this historic turnout is that Arab citizens rallied behind their parties. That reading is wrong. The Arab Israeli political establishment is widely seen as a closed, exclusionary club: outdated, ineffective, and recycling the same faces and the same speeches. Some Arab citizens voted for Jewish-led parties today. Many who voted for Arab lists did so without enthusiasm.
They came out of a sense of citizenship and shared responsibility, just as they did in October 2023, when they stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Jewish Israelis in the country’s lowest, most painful moment. Then and now, they showed that they belong to this state, that they are willing to carry its burdens and share its fate, and that they will not be written out of it. For a community so often accused of standing apart, and even branded an enemy within, today’s turnout declares the opposite. It is a cry from below, from people who have spent four years under the most far-right government in Israel’s history.
Arab citizens, Israel's 'kingmakers'
In 2021, the only government to unseat Netanyahu in over a decade came to power because Ra’am, an Arab party, provided its majority. It was the first Arab party ever to join an Israeli coalition. The opposition took power on that basis and then spent years acting as though it should apologize for it.
In this campaign, its leading figures refused even to say they would govern with an Arab-Israeli partner.
Arab citizens know they are once again the kingmakers. They have put aside their doubts and shown up to defend a democracy that has not always defended them. Voting in such numbers while carrying the memory of October 2000 is an act of extraordinary trust, and trust given twice is not guaranteed a third time.
The opposition need not embrace every Arab politician or every platform. But before coalition talks begin, it must say plainly that at least one Arab party is a legitimate partner in government.
Anything less sends two million citizens a message they have heard before: Your vote counts when it is useful, but your voice has no place in shaping this country.
The hand has been extended. The Jewish-majority opposition can take it, and with it lead Israel toward a different future.
Or it can confirm everything October 2000 taught Israel’s Arab citizens and hand the outgoing coalition the deadlock it desperately needs to stay in power.
The choice is the opposition’s alone. Will Israel be a democracy among the nations, where every vote counts? Or will it keep sliding toward an isolated, undemocratic, and racist ethnocracy?

People of Israel, Reservists-Economic Party, Haredi Public all projected to fall short of threshold

People of Israel, the Reservists-Economic Party, and the Haredi Public, the three new parties that were polling near Israel's electoral threshold, are projected to fall short of entering the Knesset, according to data published by the Central Elections Committee (CEC).
People of Israel, led by former IDF Brig.-Gen. Ofer Winter, the Reservists-Economic Party, led by former communications minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha, and Haredi Public, led by Moti Leitner, were all projected to fall short of the 3.25% electoral threshold required to be allocated any seats in the Knesset.
The Reservists-Economic Party received 2.66% of the vote, with 100,081 valid votes counted thus far. People of Israel received 1.66% with 62,394 votes counted. Haredi Public received 0.21% of the vote with 8,059 eligible votes counted as of 10 a.m. on Wednesday morning
People of Israel campaigned on a right-wing security platform, advocating tougher action against Hamas while also supporting greater ultra-Orthodox participation in military service.
Winter declared his party to be part of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc but challenged the prime minister on several issues during the election campaign and repeatedly called for new faces in Israel's parliament.
Despite challenging the establishment, new parties projected to fall short of Knesset
The Reservists-Economic Party campaigned on expanding military service to include more ultra-Orthodox Israelis and addressing Israel's economic challenges. Hendel did not commit to joining either political bloc, instead calling for a broad Zionist government to be formed following the election.
Haredi Public sought to offer an alternative to the established ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, with a focus on representing the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) public.
The parties' failure to clear the threshold could affect the distribution of Knesset seats among the parties that qualify, as votes cast for parties that fall short are not included in the allocation of seats.
The exit polls are preliminary projections. The final outcome will depend on the official vote count and the allocation of Knesset seats.
People of Israel officials: Winter's campaign did not cost Netanyahu’s bloc seats
Officials from Ofer Winter's People of Israel party said, following an initial analysis of the exit poll results, that the seat distribution would have shifted against the right-wing bloc if Winter had withdrawn from the race.
They claimed that Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha would have passed the electoral threshold, adding four seats to the left-wing bloc.
The officials also argued that the vast majority of votes cast for Winter came from voters outside the governing coalition, dismissing claims that the party had wasted votes as “absurd.”

Israel election exit polls: Netanyahu, Eisenkot deadlocked as both blocs fall short of majority

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is currently expected to enter the Knesset with 54 seats, the Central Elections Committee (CEC) announced on Wednesday morning after over four million votes were counted.
Netanyahu's Likud is projected to enter with 27 seats, while United Torah Judaism is expected to enter with 7, Shas is expected to enter with seven, Otzma Yehudit is expected to enter with seven, and the Religious Zionist Party is expected to enter with six.
The opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and the Democrats, is expected to enter the Knesset with 47 seats, according to data from the CEC.
Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar is projected to enter the Knesset with 21 seats. B'Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, is expected to enter with 11 seats. Yair Golan's Democrats are expected to enter the Knesset with eight seats, and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu is expected to enter with seven.
The latest results by the CEC put 19 seats in the Arab parties, with the Joint List having 13 seats and Ra'am having 6 seats in the next Knesset.
Could Israel be heading toward a unity gov't - or another election?
The prospect of a unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot has appeared unlikely, as Eisenkot has rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in a rotation government. Other opposition leaders have also ruled out joining a coalition led by the prime minister.
Eisenkot has called for the leader of the largest party in the opposition bloc to become its candidate for prime minister, though no agreement on the arrangement has been announced within the bloc.
The exit polls also raised the possibility of a minority government that could win a Knesset confidence vote without holding an absolute majority of 61 seats. However, opposition within the bloc to relying on Arab parties could complicate such an arrangement.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations.
What did Israeli polls indicate on election night?
No clear winner emerged in Israel’s election, according to exit polls published by Channels 11, 12, and 13 on Tuesday night; all showed both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition bloc seeking to replace him falling short of a 61-seat Knesset majority.
However, by Wednesday morning, some polls showed Netanyahu's bloc with a clear lead.
Notably, the exit polls have differed from final results in previous elections, and the official results will be determined after ballots are counted.
On Tuesday, the opposition bloc was projected to win 49-51 seats, compared with 51-52 for Netanyahu’s bloc.
On Wednesday morning, the opposition bloc had fallen to 48-19 across all three channels, and Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 53-57 mandates.
Channels 13 and 11 exit polls on Tuesday projected a tie at 51 seats each for Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition bloc, while Channel 12 projected Netanyahu's bloc to receive 52 seats.
On Wednesday, Channels 11 and 12 projected Netanyahu's bloc to land 56 seats, and Channel 13 projected 55.
Tuesday polling predicted Likud would win 27 seats, with Yashar projected to win 21-22 seats. Neither side appeared to have a clear path to forming a coalition, though the opposition bloc declared victory shortly after the exit polls were released. These numbers were largely unchanged on Wednesday morning, with Likud projected at 27-28 seats, and Yashar winning 21 mandates across all three polls. 
The Joint List and Ra’am were projected to win a record-breaking combined 18-19 seats, potentially making Arab parties pivotal to coalition negotiations. However, opposition leaders have largely ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties, barring the Democrats' Yair Golan. This number was reduced slightly on Wednesday morning, with the upper end of the range, 19, remaining the same, and the lower end dropping to 16.
The final voter turnout number came out as 77.7% when polls closed at 10:00 p.m., according to the Central Elections Committee (CEC), up by 7.1% from the 2022 election.
The small right-wing parties hovering near the electoral threshold, Ofer Winter’s People of Israel and Yoaz Hendel’s The Reservists-Economic party, were both projected to fall short of the required 3.25% threshold, potentially further complicating efforts by Netanyahu’s bloc to secure a majority.
Opposition leaders declare exit poll results a victory for bloc
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders declared the initial Tuesday exit poll results a victory for their bloc, saying Netanyahu’s camp had been defeated.
The Yashar party leader later gave a speech at the party headquarters in Tel Aviv, saying the country had voted against Netanyahu's government and that holding another election would be a mistake.
Eisenkot also addressed the heads of Israel’s security establishment, urging them not to allow Netanyahu to use national security for political gain. He warned against the prime minister issuing a potential attack due to the election results.
“The prime minister is now a caretaker prime minister. Stand firm against any attempt to challenge you. You have my clear backing,” Eisenkot said.
“Netanyahu, do not dare use security for political purposes,” he added.
Earlier, following the release of the initial exit poll results, Eisenkot said they indicated “a complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and his October 7 government among the Zionist majority and the majority of Israeli citizens.”
“If these are the final results, they represent a victory for Israel’s national-minded, Zionist majority,” he added.
“I will act immediately to implement the people’s decision, replace the Netanyahu government, and establish a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible,” Eisenkot said.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid also declared Netanyahu’s bloc defeated.
“Don’t let anyone confuse you: The Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home,” he stated.
Democrats party chairman Yair Golan said the results presented an opportunity to establish a new government.
“The public has spoken. It has fired the Netanyahu government. We have been given a historic opportunity to establish a genuine government of change in Israel, and we have no intention of giving it up,” Golan said.
“We are ready to work with all our partners, bridge the gaps, and take responsibility,” he added.
Politicians in Netanyahu's bloc urged him to wait until later results were given. Ben-Gvir warned against a unity government with Eisenkot, calling it "a terrible mistake."
If Eisenkot were to become prime minister, he would oust Netanyahu, whose right-wing government was in power during the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and went on to serve its full term. Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having held the office for more than 19 years in total.
Following the October 7 massacre and the ensuing war, the opposition bloc has called for Netanyahu to be held accountable for the attacks, arguing that he should no longer serve as prime minister and calling for a state commission of inquiry to be established.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Israel's two main haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), are expected to enter the next Knesset with 14 seats combined, according to data published by the Central Election Committee on Wednesday.
Both parties are expected to get seven seats, after more than 4 million votes were counted by the CEC. UTJ received 6% of the votes, and Shas has 5.5%, according to the latest published data.
Exit polls put each ultra-Orthodox party at 14 seats, seven each
Earlier Wednesday morning, exit polls published by Channels 11, 12, and 13 projected both parties to win six to seven seats each.
The projections would give the two parties a combined 12 to 13 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The results could significantly affect coalition negotiations and the next government's ability to secure a parliamentary majority. However, exit polls are preliminary projections, and the final seat distribution will depend on the official vote count and the allocation of Knesset seats.
Both Shas and UTJ are part of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political bloc, and their combined seat total could prove crucial in determining whether he can secure the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority.
Neither party has committed to joining only a Netanyahu-led coalition, and Shas’s spiritual leader has indicated that he would be open to joining a government led by prime ministerial candidate Gadi Eisenkot. This challenges the assumption that a vote for Shas necessarily translates into support for a Netanyahu-led government.
'Perhaps we will join': Haredi parties won't rule out working with Eisenkot
The ultra-Orthodox parties have not ruled out cooperating with Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot, N12 reported on Wednesday morning.
"If Eisenkot has any sense, he will form a government and not fill the [ministerial positions] that are important to us," source in the Shas party told N12."
"If there is a reasonable conscription law, perhaps we will join later,” the source added.
Eisenkot has previously said that he would not include haredi parties in his coalition, saying they did not meet his criteria for joining the government.
Shas, UTJ back Torah study law amid criticism over haredi draft exemptions
Both haredi parties pushed for legislation that the Knesset recently passed, enshrining Torah study as a fundamental value in Israel’s Basic Laws. Critics argued that the legislation would encourage draft evasion, while the haredi parties defended it as a measure to protect the religious importance of full-time Torah study.
Regarding Gaza, Shas has broadly supported efforts to dismantle Hamas and demilitarize the Strip while opposing indefinite Israeli control of the territory.
Shas and UTJ have maintained close political cooperation, signing a surplus vote-sharing agreement earlier this month ahead of the October 27 election and pledging to continue working together in the next Knesset.
Another central issue for both parties is the relationship between religion and state. Shas and UTJ seek to preserve Israel’s Orthodox Jewish character and maintain the authority of religious institutions, particularly the Chief Rabbinate.
Both parties have strongly opposed expanding alternatives to religious marriage, including civil marriage, and support maintaining the existing system in which Jewish marriages are conducted through the Rabbinate.
Shas, UTJ reaffirm cooperation with vote-sharing agreement ahead of election
Announcing their surplus vote-sharing agreement, Shas chairman Arye Deri and UTJ lawmaker Yaakov Asher said it reflected the “continued cooperation between the factions, in accordance with the instructions of the generation’s leading rabbis and Torah sages.”
Despite their longstanding partnership in Netanyahu’s coalition, Shas and UTJ have faced growing criticism for opposing haredi military conscription amid the IDF’s severe manpower shortage.
Both parties pressed Netanyahu’s coalition to advance conscription legislation that critics argued would fail to significantly increase haredi enlistment during the government’s term.
They also boycotted coalition votes, declaring that they would not resume cooperation until progress was made on the contentious legislation they had been demanding.
Shir Perets contributed to this report.

Olivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:23:46 UTC
05:23:46 KST

The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressive councillors.
The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13-percentage-point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared with his 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city.
Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. On Monday night, she thanked her supporters and Bradford.
“I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.”
Chow, 69, has long been a fixture of the city’s politics. She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what she received in 2023.
Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed.
While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms-related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years.
Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending.
In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate. For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers and other vulnerable institutions.
In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.”
Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost.
Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. While Ford did not endorse her in this election, he told reporters the pair had a “phenomenal relationship” and said people should “read between the lines” when it comes to his preferred candidate. However, the two are likely to spar in a fierce battle over the city’s bike lanes.
Like other major urban centers, Toronto remains locked in a battle over affordability, an issue that is expected to remain a challenge for the incoming council, where a large number of progressive candidates both returned and won for the first time, including Diana McNally Chan, a well-known advocate for unhoused people, who will be the first renter to sit on the city council.

The ultra-orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism won 8 and 7 seats respectively, while new commer Charedi Public Party failed to pass the threshold.
Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit won 7 while their previous electoral ally, Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism Party received 6. This is the first time both parties have entered Knesset without running on a combined list. Religious Zionism Party ran a combined list with Moshe Feiglin's Zehut, marking the first time Zehut has entered the Knesset.
Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beiteinu won 5 seats leaving him the smallest party according to the exit poll.
Preliminary exit polls show neither bloc receiving enough seats to form a government without the support of Arab parties. The coaltion received a total of 55 while the oppositon received 49.
Unless a party switches bloc, it is unlikely either bloc will be able to form a government.
There was high turnout across the country and the electorate with estimates hinting at this being the highest turnout in Israel's history.
The high turnout is likely to have contributed strongly to the Arab parties' results.
Turning to other major polls
Most other major exit polls are in agreement with the exception of Channel 14. Channels 11, 12, and 13 all gave the coalition bloc 50 seats while giving the opposition bloc 52, and the Arab parties 18.
Channel 14 had a much stronger variation, giving the coalition 60 seats and the opposition bloc 43, with Arab parties receiving 17.
Despite the oppostion bloc receiving more seats in most major exit polls, the Likud are still the largets party across all polls. Likud received 24 or 25 from most polls and 30 from Channel 14.
Yashar varied far more with Channel 14 giving them 19 while Channel 13 projected 23. Most other parties received consistent results across all polls, Yisrael Beiteinu varied the most with Channel 14 giving them 4 seats while Channel 12 gave them 9.

UN rapporteur says impunity prevails for killing journalists in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:23:07 UTC
05:23:07 KST

Merve Aydogan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese said Tuesday that the targeting of journalists in the Gaza Strip is part of a deliberate effort to conceal atrocities, describing her latest report as an examination of "truth" that has been "buried under the rubble."
"What is happening is not incidental; it is intentional," Albanese, who briefed reporters virtually, said about the genocide in Gaza.
She said she provocatively called the phenomenon "media side," describing it as "the systematic destruction of the media’s public function."
"In a genocide, the systematic attack on the media is part and parcel of the crime," she added.
Asked for an update on the investigation into Israel’s 2022 killing of Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, she said: "Nothing, nothing happened. So, the update is impunity."
She noted the impunity was not only by Israel but also "impunity by the United States."
Rejecting the terrorist label, Albanese said it "has been the label to kill everyone, to bring famine upon everyone in Gaza, to destroy Gaza."
Even if Israel has a right to self-defense under international law, she said: "Israel doesn’t have and cannot claim the right to wage a war against Gaza."
Responding to a question on whether the International Criminal Court (ICC) had failed Palestinians, she said "the complementarity of international criminal investigation can be triggered," urging prosecutions "starting now with activating domestic courts."
She said citizens of France, Britain, the US and Belgium who served in the Israeli army could face scrutiny, stressing it was "something that cannot be delayed."
Albanese also pointed to "the absence of so many media, especially legacy media" from Western countries, saying she read it as "possibly an act of solidarity" toward outlets named in the report.

Israel election: Anti-Netanyahu bloc ahead, but no majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:21:00 UTC
05:21:00 KST

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- As of 11:00 a.m. local time, just over 76% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."
Netanyahu's bloc trails in Israel election, exit polls say
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest single group in the Knesset, with 25 projected seats.
Challenger Gadi Eisenkot's bloc has emerged as the largest group with a projected 53, just ahead of the ruling coalition on 50, but well short of the 61 needed for a majority.
Neither bloc has a clear majority without the support of Arab parties.
These projected numbers are from public broadcaster Kan 11; other numbers vary by channel, but only slightly.
Polls closing around the country
It's now 10 p.m. across Israel, which means that polling stations around the country either should have closed or should be making preparations to do so as the last people in line cast their ballots.
Exit polls should follow shortly on Israeli television. These have a fairly good reputation overall but of course are only projections.
Results will start to trickle in through the night and are unlikely to be finalized until Wednesday.
And of course, there's every chance that even once the dust has settled and the final results are in, we will have a longer wait until there's clarity about who might be able to form a coalition government.
In any case, stick with us and we'll keep you posted.
Election commission sees 'no need to extend voting hours' after Netanyahu request
The Central Elections Committee has rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and some other groups to extend voting beyond 10 p.m. (2000 UTC/GMT).
"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.
The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.
For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.
The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.
IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign
Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.
DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.
High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc
The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.
According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.
Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.
Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.
Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.
Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.
This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.
The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.
And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.

Polls close in Israeli parliamentary elections as turnout nears 75%

Rania Abushamala
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Polling stations closed in Israel's parliamentary elections Tuesday evening, with voter turnout approaching 75%, according to Israeli election authorities and local media.
Voting in the Knesset elections ended at 10 pm local time (2000GMT), with ballot counting beginning shortly afterward, Israeli media reported.
The Central Elections Committee earlier reported that voter turnout had reached 74.3% as of 8 pm local time (1800GMT).
According to the committee, 5,449,277 people had cast their ballots out of 7,331,981 eligible voters.

Key Event
Rio Tinto boss likely to make $18.5m after 56% pay hike
Speaking of inflation, news just in from London is that Rio Tinto's board has proposed increasing CEO Simon Trott's target remuneration package by 56% to £9.8 million ($18.56 million), according to four people familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by Reuters.
If Mr Trott hits all his KPIs, his remuneration could be closer to $35 million.
Surging pay at defence, aerospace and energy transition firms has left mining companies scrambling to compete for top talent, Reuters said.
According to an investor presentation seen by Reuters, Rio Tinto's board has expanded the list of companies it compares itself to when calculating executive compensation ranges.
Among other companies, it added US energy majors Chevron and ExxonMobil, as well as GE Aerospace, to its peer benchmarking group.
Ben Wyatt, who chairs Rio Tinto's remuneration committee, said the miner was consulting investors ahead of a policy update.
He told Reuters Mr Trott's fixed pay would remain unchanged, but incentives tied to multiyear business outcomes and shareholder returns would be adjusted.
"This is designed to drive business performance in the interests of shareholders, support the delivery of Rio Tinto's long-term strategy, and attract and retain strong leadership in a competitive global market," he said in a statement.
Appointed in July 2025, Mr Trott delivered a 43% jump in first-half underlying earnings this year while pursuing restructuring and asset sales.
Reflecting a compensation overhaul weighted to performance, Trott's maximum remuneration is proposed to grow 63% to £18.3 million ($34.58 million), the briefing documents showed.
Short-term incentives would rise to a maximum of 300% of base salary from 200%, while long-term targets would jump to 900% from 500%.
Mr Trott's new package would apply to the next three years of his compensation.
To come into effect, the expanded framework will require shareholder approval at next year's annual meeting.
Key Event
AUSTRAC says it won't tolerate companies putting profit over compliance
AUSTRAC has responded to the Federal Court's decision to fine casino operator Star $260 million for historical breaches of anti-money laundering laws.
AUSTRAC chief Brendan Thomas said the penalty reflected the seriousness of Star's contraventions and built on previous state and Commonwealth fines to provide ongoing deterrence value.
"The Court found The Star did not simply fail to complete the right checks. It allowed high-risk customers to gamble without properly establishing where their money came from and put profit over compliance on a large scale," Mr Thomas said.
"AUSTRAC will not tolerate companies putting profit over their obligations to the Australian community.
"It permitted a private casino within its casino to operate without appropriate oversight and continued courting customers who had been excluded from gambling in another state.
"The Star allowed junkets to engage in highly suspicious incidents without intervening controls and despite its concerns about these activities, and the known risks associated with junkets, it allowed ongoing access to its private gaming rooms.
"Due to The Star's admitted deficiencies in monitoring we cannot know how much money high-risk customers pumped through its casinos."
"But we do know the risks involving significant amounts of money and instead of closing the door to those risks, The Star's operations exposed the casino and Australia's financial system to them."

Key Event
Have the Kiwis given Aussie borrowers hope?
A lot of Australian borrowers will be looking eastwards across the ditch and thinking wistfully, "maybe there is a chance the RBA won't hike rates next Thursday".
After all, the RBNZ board just thumbed its collective nose at the markets and economist expectations with a surprise interest rate hold today. (Markets had priced in a 100% chance of a NZ rate hike, making the market's punt of a 90% chance for an RBA hike look attractive.)
This is despite NZ inflation heading towards 4% and a very accommodative cash rate of 2.75%.
It was a split decision (4-3) in favour of holding, and that's all Aussie borrowers want.
However, there was an implied threat that the rate-setting committee maintained a hawkish bias and "agreed that tighter monetary policy is likely to be required but remains conditional on the economic outlook".
JP Morgan economist Tom Kennedy said the decision to pause despite markets seemingly green-lighting further tightening is surprising in a global context.
"The RBA has taken a more front-footed approach, hiking on risk-management concerns and pushing the cash rate into restrictive territory despite clear weakening in the local activity data.
"In contrast, the RBNZ is taking a gradualist path while policy remains accommodative and below the central bank's estimate of neutral."
Kennedy said while the RBNZ governor emphasised that inflation remains elevated, he said the broader environment is still favourable for inflation to return to target in the medium term.
"Again, this is quite different to the risk bias shown by some other central banks," Kennedy said.
If the RBA hikes as expected on Tuesday, perhaps Aussie borrowers could offset some of the pain with a cheap holiday in NZ.
In the aftermath of the RBNZ's decision, the Aussie dollar jumped 2% against the Kiwi to hit the highest point since early 2013 at $NZ1.2602
RBNZ narrowly votes to hold rates amid 'abrupt' global downturn fears
If the Anthropic IPO flops and the AI bubble bursts before the end of this year, then a couple of Reserve Bank of New Zealand board members are going to look like geniuses.
This was from the RBNZ's post-meeting statement, after it voted 4-3 today to leave its overnight cash rate (OCR) on hold at 2.75%:
"Members noted that the increase in global long-term yields may partly signal a higher global neutral interest rate, due to higher inflation expectations, war destruction and demand for capital to support AI investment. Higher global interest rates could bring forward a potential global downturn, and the neutral interest rate could decline rapidly in the event of an abrupt global adjustment.
"Prasanna Gai and Anna Breman attached material risk to the possibility that the global environment could shift abruptly. It was therefore appropriate to account for such risks when judging neutral rates and the stance of monetary policy rather than relying on most likely or mid-point measures.
"Members reflected on potential trade-offs associated with increasing the OCR at this meeting or waiting until the December MPS.
"Members discussed that information arriving over the next six weeks could meaningfully change the appropriate policy stance in either direction. There is a risk that inflation becomes entrenched before conventional expectations measures respond, despite the previous two OCR increases. In addition, the world economy could tip abruptly into a downturn causing weaker inflation over the medium term. It is also possible that geopolitical escalation could drive fuel prices higher while weakening global economic activity at the same time."
If the RBA hikes rates next week, for a fifth time this year, and it turns out that the global economy does fall in a heap before the end of the year, the local central bankers are going to have a fair bit of egg on their faces.

- Brent futures: +1.2% to $US115.25/barrel
- WTI futures: +1.1% to $U101.04/barrel.
The claims of an attack on the world's biggest crude exporter by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis renewed concerns around the risks to supply in the Middle East stemming from the conflict with Iran and its proxies.
The Houthis said they had hit Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a missile, intensifying their strikes against the world's second-largest crude producer.
Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike on the 550,000-barrel-per-day facility.
At this stage, oil traders seem to be taking the Houthis' word for it.
Prices were swinging back after dropping nearly $US2 on Tuesday as talks in the Middle East helped ease supply worries.
That was despite data expected to show a rise in crude inventories in the US. Crude oil stockpiles rose by about 15,000 barrels in the week ended October 23, according to a poll of eight analysts by Reuters.
The OPEC+ oil-producing countries are expected to keep their December oil output targets steady on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters, in line with market expectations.
Production in most of the seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — is below their output targets.
Crude oil exports from Russia's Baltic and Black Sea ports could fall next month as domestic refiners increase diesel output following a deal with Washington this month, traders said.
With Reuters
Supply shocks, longer-term inflation expectations, and the RBA's models
In the RBA officials' Senate estimates testimony, Greens senator Nick McKim asked some questions about supply shocks that led to an interesting discussion.
Senator McKim:
"Recently we've seen impacts of COVID on the supply chain, Ukraine, Trump's tariff shocks, Iran, the bond yield leap, we've got our climate system crumbling around us, we've got a record El Niño heading our way.
"These are obviously, or would you agree, that these have a compounding impact on the bank's inflationary outlook in the medium to long term?
"And if you do agree with that, what do you think is going to happen to interest rates as these things continue to compound?
"And how's the bank going to respond to that? And is monetary policy equipped to respond to that?
RBA governor Michele Bullock:
"The first thing is, you've highlighted a number of supply shocks that have occurred, starting with COVID, and [then] continuing.
"Now, what supply shocks do, negative supply shocks, is they basically worsen the trade-off between inflation and unemployment. So for any given unemployment rate or given the state of the economy, inflation is higher.
"A traditional way of thinking about this is that — and all central banks talk about this — is that you would try to 'look through' the supply shock.
"So, if it's a shock, you let it flow through and then once it's flowed through, prices will settle down again, and inflation will settle down again.
"That works, I think, if you've got a one-off shock … [but] if you've got compounding shocks, and they are continuing to raise the level of inflation, then there is a concern that people start to think that inflation is just going to be higher permanently, and if that is the case, then I think it's very difficult for central banks … to completely look through these shocks because it might become embedded in inflation expectations."
Governor Bullock then said fuel price shocks have their own specific problems:
"Something like a fuel price shock is a little bit more difficult because it underlies costs that are embedded in businesses, and if it's a very quick shock, goes up and it comes down again, businesses might think 'Well, I'll just wear it', but the longer it goes on, the more they might think, 'Well, actually, you know what? The fuel price isn't coming down, transport costs aren't coming down, I've just got to start passing this on'.
"So it does make it more challenging for central banks."
And she said the RBA was working hard on updating its models to adapt to a world with more supply shocks:
"We are working very hard on adjusting, adapting our models to try to get better at recognising supply shocks and how to respond to them.
"But I think the bottom line remains that there are going to be a lot of supply shocks, but there are also going to be demand consequences of interest rates, and central banks still need to be involved in setting interest rates to try to make sure that inflation remains low and stable."

ASX limping along, up just 0.1%

Key Event
CBA shifts call to a November hike
One of the more interesting notes out on the inflation figures comes from the CBA's economics team, who have shifted their call from "hold" to "hike" at next week's RBA meeting.
As we posted some hours ago, CBA said an "in line" 1.0% rise in the trimmed mean quarterly figure, delivering a year-on-year 3.7% increase, would likely mean an unchanged rate next week — although there was an important caveat about the composition that kept the decision "live".
CBA's head of Australian economics, Belinda Allen, says there has been a shift in focus by the RBA being driven by a rethink on domestic capacity pressures.
"The labour market has been described as tighter than initially thought. Productivity is an ongoing challenge, and the RBA is clearly worried about anchoring longer run inflation expectations," Allen said
She said offshore factors are also playing a role in the change in RBA thinking.
"The conflict in the Middle East is more prolonged than expected, leading to a sustained shock from energy prices and the global capex boom led by AI is creating inflationary pressures.
"As a result, we see the hike in November as an insurance hike to protect against these forces.
"Acting early and acting decisively should manage the risk of inflation being higher for even longer."
Key Event
Rate hike 'locked in': ANZ
The ANZ's economic team says today's inflation data "cements the case for the RBA to hike rates 25bp in November".
Quarterly trimmed mean inflation printed in line with expectations, rising 1.0% over Q3, while the annual growth in underlying inflation was slightly stronger than expected at 3.7%.
"It appears the upside inflation risks the RBA has been focussing on — around oil prices, the AI tech boom and domestic capacity constraints — are materialising and will see a 25bp rate hike in November," ANZ's head of Australian economics Adam Boyton and economist Madeline Dunk wrote.
"We also expect to see upward revisions to the RBA's inflation forecasts which will be published in the November SMP [Statement on Monetary Policy]," the pair said.
"The monthly underlying inflation 'pulse' is tracking at around 4% and market services inflation recorded its strongest annual growth since 2024."
They also highlighted a key component of the inflation data the RBA will likely focus on.
"Market services ex volatiles and holiday travel was one of the strongest contributors to inflation in Q3.
"This will keep the RBA cautious, given the ties between market services inflation and domestic supply constraints."

Westpac's Luci Ellis says rate hike next week is very likely
Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis says today's inflation data, and the RBA's Senate testimony, have reaffirmed her expectation that the RBA will increase the cash rate again at its November meeting (next week).
"Today’s inflation data and Senate testimony are the final pieces of information before the RBA Monetary Policy Board (MPB) meets next week," she writes.
"Recent data and communication have consistently pointed to the staff recommending an increase in the cash rate. We expect a majority of the external members to agree, though some members might dissent.
"Inflation is above target, and above what the RBA's August forecasts implied. Some upside risks identified in August have partially materialised, particularly energy prices. The RBA is especially worried that above-target inflation will become embedded in people's expectations and pricing decisions. It will therefore deem that further policy tightening is needed.
"The RBA has made it clear that it is down-weighting the recent easing in the labour market, even though this was more than it forecast. It is also relatively sanguine about the current downturn in the housing market.
"The question then turns to the future beyond November.
"While we still expect a hawkish tone in the RBA's communication until inflation has clearly turned down, further hikes beyond next week are not currently our base case.
"Clearly, the risks of another hike — most likely in February — have increased.
"However, a lot can happen in three months, as we have just seen. Risks around energy prices could go either way.
"We note that the RBNZ seems more concerned about the risk of a sudden global downturn than the RBA is," Ms Ellis says.

RBA: Unemployment will rise further, but we don't expect a recession
The RBA officials were asked about the prospect of Australia's economy experiencing a recession.
They said they expect unemployment to keep rising a bit from here, but they're not forecasting a recession.
Greens senator Nick McKim:
"How worried are you about the pace of the increase in the unemployment rate and what pace of increase in unemployment would give you cause for concern that we may be heading towards a recession?"
Governor Michele Bullock:
"We're not worried about the pace of increase in the unemployment rate at this stage. We do forecast that it has to gradually move up, [but] that is very different from saying that people have to lose their jobs. In fact, we are forecasting that employment continues to grow. It just means that the supply of labour is growing a bit more quickly than jobs can keep up with, and I can't be specific about what that number is. What I can say is we think that it's probably above where the unemployment rate is at the moment. So the unemployment rate, in order to ease some of these capacity pressures, probably will be rising a bit further, and that's what will be in our forecast."
The RBA's chief economist Sarah Hunter then jumped in, to add to Bullock's answer.
Sarah Hunter:
"I might just add to the governor's response. In the context of a recession, if you're defining that through the usual sort of technical definition, which is two quarters of negative growth for GDP, we're obviously monitoring a very wide range of indicators across the real economy, including the labour market, but also spending trends across all of the major categories, and there's various sorts of sets of lead indicators and real-time indicators that we can track to look at that.
"And just to reiterate what the governor says, at the moment our assessment is that none of those indicators are suggesting that the economy is in, or heading into, a recession in the near term.
"So that's not what we're seeing or expect to see over the forecast horizon."
