“In connection with preparations for a humanitarian operation in the area of the settlement of Oleshky in the Kherson region, the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation have ceased fire on the Kherson front and introduced a ‘regime of silence’ starting from 4 a.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27, 2026.”
As Lubinets previously said, before the evacuation begins, demining teams will first clear roads of explosives. Humanitarian aid will then be delivered to the city, and registration will begin for residents who want to leave Oleshky. The evacuation is expected to start only after those steps are completed.
The agreement on a ceasefire in Oleshky became public on Oct. 23. The White House announced it first, after which officials in Moscow and Kyiv confirmed the arrangement.
According to the latest estimates from Ukrainian authorities, about 2,000 people remained trapped in Oleshky under a complete blockade — without food, medical care, or a stable electricity supply. In addition to Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV had also joined the efforts to secure a humanitarian corridor for residents of the occupied city, calling Vladimir Putin from a hospital and asking him to halt the fighting in Oleshky as soon as possible.
In late September, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty called for an immediate ceasefire in occupied Oleshky in order to allow unhindered access for humanitarian organizations and the safe evacuation of civilians. He said the humanitarian crisis in the city was rapidly worsening and that civilians, including children, were trapped without adequate food, medical care, running water, or electricity.
In early October, Ukrainian officials reported that the country’s National Guard had carried out a successful operation to deliver humanitarian supplies to Russian-occupied Oleshky. Drones delivered about 400 packages weighing nearly 4 metric tons in total. The shipments contained food, medicine, and supplies for children.

Australia's police chief has a warning about where online hate can lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:44:54 UTC
04:44:54 KST

In brief
- The AFP warned threats against politicians reflected a deeper social problem.
- The recent attack on MP Helen Haines has renewed concerns about safety in public life.
No single measure can undo the shift in social attitudes that is driving political threats, according to the head of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), as it grapples with how to keep parliamentarians safe.
AFP commissioner Krissy Barrett began her late-night appearance at the Senate estimates hearing, noting "a heaviness that hangs across Australia" after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines.
The federal member for Indi lost both her legs and remains in a serious but stable condition in a Melbourne hospital after being struck repeatedly by a four-wheel drive outside her Wangaratta office.
State authorities are leading the ongoing investigation into the motive behind the attack, with the police chief confirming the alleged offender was not known to federal police.
As the nation comes to grips with the attack, Barrett said it has aligned with a global trend of violence emerging with little or no warning from individuals largely unknown to authorities.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Lone actors are being motivated by a convergence of personal grievances, mental health vulnerabilities and ideological concerns," she told the Senate estimates hearing on Tuesday night.
"What helped keep us safe in recent times, such as our geography, analogue systems and far-away criminals, has been impacted by fully integrated technology, social media and artificial intelligence."
Barrett said technology has enabled an "instant pipeline of hate" delivered to people's homes, including teenagers, and workplaces because of the ubiquity of devices.
"Our investigators are charging almost one person a week for targeting Commonwealth parliamentarians or high office holders," she told senators.
The AFP received 785 protective security reports containing "adverse content" about federal parliamentarians in the first half of the year, Barrett said, with 394 directed at male MPs and 371 at female MPs.
She added that while all reports were taken seriously, the "adverse content" sometimes did not meet a criminal threshold.
An AFP psychological analysis of Joint Counter Terrorism Team youth cases from 2020-2025 showed the 55 boys aged between 12 and 17 were entirely or partially radicalised online, Barrett said.
The ideological presentation of those youths had shifted over the past two years away from jihadist extremism or white supremacist ideology, she said, with an increasing number having hybrid or unclear beliefs and displaying "ideological fluidity".
"In three out of five cases, the youths had received support, treatment or intervention for a mental health condition," she added.
Individuals who believe threats and violence are tolerable if their cause is noble are taking to social media, corroding community and normalising violence, creating a fundamental shift, Barrett said.
"It continues to impact on many, most notably the Jewish community. Antisemitism is often the early warning sign of a decay in our society, and the poisoning of our compact with each other," she said.
"Our collective consciousness must be awake to this threat, and acknowledge there will always be another target group of hate if we do not recognise where it can start.
"There is not one single measure alone that will stop the threats, because this goes to a wider societal problem Australia is facing," Barrett said, pledging to work with the home affairs and finance departments to ensure the security of electorate offices and the homes of parliamentarians.
Barrett reiterated she did not seek to judge how parliamentarians "do politics," police free speech or intervene in political discourse.
The federal police commissioner will meet her state and territory counterparts soon to discuss the issue of democratic and parliamentary security.

Three Russian Diesel Tankers Head to US, Including One Sanctioned in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:44:39 UTC
04:44:39 KST

- Category
- World
Three Russian Diesel Tankers Head to US, Including One Sanctioned in Europe
Three tankers carrying around 140,000 tonnes of Russian diesel, including one vessel sanctioned by European authorities, are heading to US ports, the Financial Times reported on October 27.
The shipments are the first licensed by US authorities under President Donald Trump’s recent agreement with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, to exempt Russian diesel from sanctions. The vessels are expected to arrive shortly after the November 3 US midterm elections.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Germany rejected the easing of restrictions, arguing that pressure on Moscow should be increased rather than reduced. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also warned that lifting sanctions without enforceable Russian de-escalation would signal weakness and allow Moscow to prolong the war. Czech President Petr Pavel later argued that the diesel decision weakened Western leverage over Russia and made a ceasefire harder to achieve.
According to the Financial Times, the vessels include the Hong Kong-owned, Sierra Leone-flagged tanker Leruo, which is sanctioned by the UK, EU, and Canada. Ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic showed the vessel signaling an arrival on the US Atlantic coast on November 11.
Leruo departed St. Petersburg on October 17 and was in the North Sea off Norway on October 26. European authorities sanctioned the tanker in 2025 over Russian cargoes and practices including disabling location technology and conducting ship-to-ship transfers.
The vessel was also accused of violating the G7 price cap on Russian oil cargoes, according to OpenSanctions .
Its planned arrival could create legal complications for companies handling the cargo in the US. Jeremy Paner, a partner at Washington-based law firm Hughes Hubbard, told the Financial Times that a tanker sanctioned by the EU, UK, and Canada entering a US port would be “highly problematic” because their financial and maritime systems are closely interconnected.
The US banned imports of Russian oil and refined petroleum products in March 2022. Washington later joined other G7 countries in imposing a price cap on Russian diesel exports.
Trump’s administration has issued a temporary license permitting Russian diesel imports under the new agreement with Moscow. However, members of Congress have challenged whether the administration can authorize the imports without violating restrictions enacted into US law.
On October 26, senior Democrats and Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned US banks, port authorities, and fuel distributors that companies involved in importing Russian diesel could face congressional investigations and legal action.
“Any importation of Russian diesel into the US raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations,” the lawmakers wrote, according to the Financial Times.
They added that companies violating US law could face criminal and civil liability and argued that the transactions raised national security concerns because revenue from the fuel could support Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The first tanker scheduled to reach the US is the Greek-owned Agioi Fanendes, which is carrying around 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel and is expected in New York on November 7, according to ship-tracking data cited by the Financial Times.
If unloaded as indicated, the shipment would be the first Russian gas oil or diesel cargo tracked by commodities platform Kpler to arrive in the US since July 2023.
A second vessel, the 20-year-old Russian tanker Talisman, is scheduled to reach the US East Coast on November 9, followed by Leruo two days later. The Financial Times noted that ship destinations can change and tracking data is not always definitive.
The shipments come as US diesel prices average $6.34 per gallon, compared with $3.66 a year earlier. The Trump administration has presented the Russian diesel agreement as part of its effort to reduce fuel prices.
The Financial Times also reported that legal uncertainty and relatively small shipment volumes could deter major companies from participating. One oil trader told the newspaper that most large firms were likely to avoid handling Russian diesel because of the associated legal risks.
Before the first US-bound cargoes emerged, Russian diesel had already begun returning to its established overseas markets. UNITED24 Media reported that Türkiye accounted for about 34% of Russian diesel shipments in 2026, followed by Brazil at 24% and Morocco at 10%, as exports resumed following the October policy changes.

China's Alibaba wins injunction against Pentagon contract restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:44:32 UTC
04:44:32 KST

(Reuters) -- A U.S. federal judge on Monday granted Alibaba Group Holding's request for a preliminary injunction, ordering the U.S. government not to deny Pentagon contracts to companies because they, their parent companies or subsidiaries do business with firms that engage in lobbying activities for the e-commerce giant.
Alibaba sued the U.S. government in June after the Pentagon added it to a list of companies allegedly aiding China's military, alongside internet search provider Baidu, EV maker BYD and other major Chinese manufacturing and technology firms.
Monday's ruling means Alibaba will be able to retain U.S. lobbyists who also represent Pentagon contractors, removing a potential obstacle to the company's efforts to challenge its designation as a Chinese military company.
Alibaba fired dozens of its Washington lobbyists after the Pentagon action in June, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter who was not authorized to speak to the media.
The designation does not impose formal sanctions, but restricts Pentagon contracts with listed companies and, from 2027, purchases of their products or services through third parties.
Other listed Chinese tech firms were also concerned about the designation's impact on international lobbying activities as well as the indirect procurement ban, which would completely remove Chinese products from US defense contractors' supply chains, the source added.
Alibaba has denied any military ties, saying its products and services are built for retail, logistics and enterprise technology rather than defense or intelligence.
"The determinations have no basis in fact or law," Alibaba said in its lawsuit in June, seeking its removal from the list.
Monday's injunction does not remove Alibaba from the Pentagon list, which the company is continuing to challenge in court.
Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the injunction.
Alibaba is one of several Chinese firms taking legal action to challenge their placement on the Pentagon's list.
Last month, two subsidiaries of the world's largest electric vehicle maker, BYD, sued the U.S. Department of Defense over a federal law banning any Pentagon contractors from hiring lobbyists that also work with blacklisted firms, arguing that it breached BYD's First Amendment rights.
In August, DJI, the world's largest drone maker, appealed its inclusion on the blacklist with the court finding merit in its argument that unclassified records did not support the conclusion that the company contributed to the Chinese defense industrial base.
The appeals court ordered the lower court to reconsider its decision to reject DJI's bid to be removed from the Pentagon list, and the case is ongoing.
The same month, biotech firm WuXi AppTec also won a preliminary injunction from a U.S. federal court, which blocked its inclusion on the list. WuXi said the Pentagon designation was politically motivated.

Protesters storm pro-Vucic TV station in Belgrade (VIDEO)
Supporters of Serbia’s student-led opposition have stormed the Belgrade offices of Informer, a broadcaster supportive of former President Aleksandar Vucic, as celebrations of their election win turned violent. Vucic condemned the attack as an assault on media freedom and accused the EU of turning a blind eye.
The incident came a day after the Student List movement defeated Vucic’s United Serbia coalition in a snap parliamentary election, ending 14 years of rule by his Serbian Progressive Party and its allies.
According to Informer, demonstrators smashed windows and forced their way through the entrance before damaging offices and threatening journalists. Employees reportedly hid in bathrooms and the basement before police arrived and evacuated staff.
Editor-in-chief Dragan J. Vucicevic said attackers destroyed cameras, computers and other equipment worth tens of thousands of euros. Some demanded access to the control room to disconnect cables, he said.

UNITED NATIONS, October 27. /TASS/. United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres has appointed veteran Russian diplomat Gleb Desyatnikov as Assistant Secretary General for Mine Action and Police in the Department of Peace Operations (DPO).
"Mr. Desyatnikov brings to the position more than 35 years of experience in international relations, political affairs and security issues across government, multilateral diplomacy and conflict-affected regions," the Office of the Spokesperson for the United Nations Secretary General said in a press release.
Since 2018, Desyatnikov has served as Russian Ambassador to Jordan. Prior to that, from 2010 to 2018, he was Deputy Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Middle East and North Africa Department.

And between 1994 and 1997, he also undertook several seconded deployments with the United Nations Special Commission on Iraq (UNSCOM).

Melike Pala
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
EU member states remained divided over whether to offer Canada "associate membership" status, with at least four countries opposing the term's inclusion in a joint summit statement, Politico reported on Tuesday.
EU ambassadors failed to reach an agreement on the wording during talks Monday, according to the report.
A subsequent attempt to approve the statement through a so-called silence procedure also failed after Germany and at least three other countries raised objections before Tuesday's midday deadline, two EU diplomats told Politico.
The issue is expected to return to the agenda at another meeting of EU ambassadors Wednesday, a day before the EU-Canada summit begins in Montreal.
Germany is leading efforts to remove the term "associate membership" entirely from the proposed text, the diplomats said.

Four EU diplomats previously told Politico that von der Leyen had not consulted member state capitals before putting forward the proposal.
Von der Leyen, European Council President Antonio Costa, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and several European commissioners are expected to travel to Montreal for the Oct. 29-30 summit.
The talks are expected to focus on strengthening EU-Canada relations and expanding cooperation in trade, energy, education and the Arctic.

GECF member states call for ensuring creation of fair gas price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:42:10 UTC
04:42:10 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Member states of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) have called for ensuring a fair price for natural gas, according to the declaration adopted following the summit in Moscow.
The member countries of the association call for "ensuring the creation of a fair price for natural gas, including through the use of long-term contracts and diversified pricing mechanisms, such as oil-price adjustment, in international gas trade in order to achieve an objective distribution of risks, enhance price predictability, reduce market volatility, and attract necessary investment in gas infrastructure, including underground storage facilities and liquefied natural gas storage," the document reads.
This also refers to ensuring stable gas supplies.
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum includes Russia, Iran, Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates, and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal are observer states. GECF members hold roughly 70% of the world’s proven gas reserves, account for 38% of global gas production and 42% of global gas exports, and represent 47% of global exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

Shackled, shaved and in uniform: first inmates arrive at Costa Rica mega-prison
SAN JOSE, Oct 27 - Costa Rica has locked up the first 123 inmates in a new mega-prison, built with the help of the Salvadoran government in the outskirts of capital San José, the country's justice ministry said on Tuesday.
The ministry shared images showing rows of inmates dressed in orange, seated with shaved heads bowed and their hands behind their necks, in poses resembling photographs from El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), the mega-prison where President Nayib Bukele's government holds tens of thousands of gang members and suspected gang affiliates.
Costa Rica's maximum security prison, which it calls the High Containment Center against Organized Crime (CACCO), has been presented by the government of President Laura Fernandez as a symbol of a new "tough on crime" approach championed by her administration in response to a security crisis facing Costa Rica, once one of the most peaceful countries in the Western Hemisphere.
"Costa Rica is writing a new chapter in its penitentiary history," Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar said in a statement. "CACCO is a monument to national security, a forceful response to organized crime, and a guarantee that the state will exercise its authority without hesitation." Aguilar has said the new facility will also help reduce overcrowding in the prison system.
The prison has a capacity for 5,100 inmates, equivalent to 20% of the country's prison population.
Costa Rica, long regarded as one of the safest countries in Latin America, has in recent years experienced a sharp rise in violence linked to drug trafficking and organized crime. The country recorded a record number of homicides in 2023, although figures have since stabilized. Authorities attribute most killings to disputes between criminal groups over drug trafficking routes and markets. REUTERS

Russian authorities track 6 million  social media profiles critical of the war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:40:36 UTC
04:40:36 KST

Almost half of the 12.5 million social media accounts and profiles monitored daily by Russia’s Federal Agency for Youth Affairs (Rosmolodezh) are critical of Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to the agency’s deputy head Denis Ashirov. Ashirov presented the data on Oct. 26 at a meeting of the expert council of the State Duma committee on family protection, saying that the agency is tracking 6 million profiles criticizing the “special military operation” and the Russian army. Rosmolodezh classifies such publications as “destructive and unlawful information.”
In addition, the agency links another 1.1 million monitored profiles to political violence and criticism of the authorities, 1.5 million to drugs and drug-related content, and 906,000 to the promotion and rehabilitation of Nazism. It is unclear from Ashirov’s remarks what criteria the agency uses to determine the presence of criticism of the war and the authorities, whether the listed categories overlap, and what share of the accounts belongs to minors. It is also not specified how many unique users stand behind these profiles.
The figures were cited in the context of protecting children from dangerous online content. State Duma family protection committee chair Nina Ostanina noted that existing mechanisms for blocking content do not make it possible to fully restrict the spread of banned materials, and teenagers continue to use digital tools to bypass restrictions. At the same time, the lawmaker acknowledged that bans alone cannot solve the problem — as Ostanina herself explained, restrictions can pique heightened interest in banned content among underage users.
At the same meeting, a representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs said that in the first nine months of 2026, Russian law enforcement authorities identified 62,300 people suspected of committing crimes on the internet; 4,220 of them (6.8%) were minors. Another 692 minors were held liable for fraud.
How Rosmolodezh monitors social media users
Rosmolodezh has a Center for the Study and Network Monitoring of the Youth Environment (CISM), created on Vladimir Putin’s instruction. The organization searches the internet for information that the Russian authorities consider dangerous to minors.
As The Insider previously reported, the center takes part in identifying “socially dangerous” schoolchildren and students. According to Rosmolodezh head Grigory Gurov, thanks to the center’s work, Russia opened approximately 500 criminal and several hundred administrative cases in 2024. In addition, thousands of people were subjected to “preventive measures” aimed at countering the spread of banned information.
In August 2026, DOXA reported on the center’s work. Journalists studied the court system and found 48 rulings from 2025 and the first half of 2026 in which information supplied by the center served as the basis for prosecution. Among them is the case of Magnitogorsk resident Sergei Sokolov, who was fined 30,000 rubles ($373) after the center reported him to the prosecutor’s office over his VKontakte comments criticizing the Russian army. In Novosibirsk Region in 2025, the most common category of “destructive” content identified by Rosmolodezh was criticism of the war in Ukraine. Anarchist ideas and drug propaganda came in second and third.
The center has also been mentioned in investigations by international law enforcement agencies. In December 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that, according to the charging documents, several CISM employees were members of the pro-Russian hacker group NoName057(16), which carried out DDoS attacks on government institutions, banks, and infrastructure facilities in various countries. According to the U.S. investigation, center employees also took part in creating the network infrastructure for those attacks. Vot Tak previously linked the center’s leadership to the development of the DDoSia program used by the group to attack the websites of European states.
Earlier, media reports also covered Russia’s development of a system called Generation Index. Its closed part is designed to track the ideological attitudes of young people, including their views on the West, LGBT people, and the war in Ukraine. In particular, the system is designed to assess the share of young people who believe in Russia’s war effort, and low figures are supposed to serve as grounds for the authorities to take “urgent measures.”

AI giant Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei have repeatedly claimed that the company’s models will revolutionize biology and drug discovery. Wherever it’s going, it seems, it will take some time to get there.
Two years ago, Amodei wrote that he was “open” to the idea that AI systems could produce a thousand years of progress in biology in just five to 10 years. In August, he said on X that “Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine.” In the same post, he predicted that AI will make it possible to cure most human diseases in the next five to 10 years and promised a “deluge of AI-accelerated drugs.” The company also promoted the discovery of a “Crispr-like” enzyme by Claude in September.
While the new IPO filing still touts AI’s ability to “profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine” and compress “decades of scientific progress into years,” it’s reserved about how it will turn the potential into the actual.
The company says that its teams “need first-hand experience doing scientific research and drug discovery” and that its life sciences activities will require it “to engage in activities outside our historical experience as a software and research organization.” That includes handling potentially hazardous materials, operating laboratory equipment, and complying with a bevy of regulations.
Anthropic also toned down its language about its enzyme discovery, saying it “might have the potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool, perhaps for gene editing.” (Italics added for emphasis.) Researchers previously told WIRED they were skeptical of the enzyme discovery’s value and utility, and one scientist who had been studying these exact enzymes became suspicious that Claude used his research. (The company said neither its model nor its molecular biology team would have had access to this material.)
The IPO filing indicates that Anthropic no longer sees itself solely as an outside provider of AI tools to the biotech industry; it sees biotech discovery as a core part of its business model. And like all biotech companies, it faces the long timeline of drug development. Any AI-assisted discoveries still have to be researched in a test tube, then in animals, and eventually in people. Even if AI could help sort out which new drugs or targets will work in humans versus those likely to be duds, it will still take years of testing to prove their safety and efficacy.
Anthropic recognizes these challenges in its filing. “Any drug candidates or other discoveries resulting from these efforts would face the lengthy, costly, and uncertain development and regulatory pathways characteristic of the life sciences industry, and may never generate revenue,” the filing says. (For his part, Amodei made the case in his August X post for streamlining regulations for the coming wave of AI-generated drugs.)
US Securities and Exchange Commission filings are generally more cautious than statements made by companies or their executives, given the legal risks of overstating claims to would-be investors. And the IPO makes clear that the company believes its technology will drive revolutionary advancements.
But as Anthropic pushes further into biological discovery, it will face the same conundrum as other biotech companies: proving their worth in trials that can’t be hastened simply by adding computers.

Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro reportedly heads to US despite travel ban after election defeat

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:38:29 UTC
04:38:29 KST

Laura Gamba
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Brazil's defeated presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has reportedly left the country for the United States despite a judicial travel ban, with conflicting accounts of his whereabouts emerging Tuesday as authorities investigate a possible escape through Argentina.
Brazilian news outlet Globo cited sources close to Bolsonaro that it said confirmed he had left Brazil with his family, while official channels have not officially confirmed his departure or established his route.
The reports by came after Brazil's Federal Police canceled Bolsonaro's regular and diplomatic passports Tuesday when he failed to comply with a court order requiring him to surrender the documents within 24 hours.
Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the order Monday, a day after Bolsonaro lost the presidential runoff to incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
The ruling also prohibited the 45-year-old senator from leaving Brazil.
The restrictions stem from an investigation into suspected money laundering and currency evasion involving financial transactions linked to attorney Willer Tomaz, an associate of Bolsonaro.
The senator is also under investigation in a separate case involving the financing of Dark Horse, a biographical film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro. Authorities are examining alleged payments connected to Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of the now-defunct financial institution Banco Master.
Bolsonaro, who denies wrongdoing, said Monday that he had no intention of leaving Brazil.
“I have never thought about leaving the country. I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty,” Bolsonaro said, describing the judicial order as “a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
He made the remarks after visiting his father, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest in Brasilia.
Speculation about his whereabouts intensified Tuesday after Argentine media reported that he had crossed into Argentina by land using his national identity card and planned to board a private flight to Miami with his wife and daughters.
The reports centered on a Gulfstream G400 private jet, registered as LV-JQW and operated by Argentine charter company Baires Fly SA, which arrived at Puerto Iguazu airport near the Brazilian border from Buenos Aires late Monday.
The aircraft had been expected to depart for the US with four passengers and three crew members but remained on the ground Tuesday.
Argentine media reported that aviation authorities had withheld departure clearance over regulatory issues, while other reports indicated that the planned passengers never arrived and the flight was canceled.
However, Argentina's National Directorate of Migration said it had no record of Bolsonaro entering the country and that no flight plan had been submitted listing members of his family.
The agency said authorities had inspected the aircraft and its crew and found the company's documentation in order.
Brazilian federal police also found no record of Bolsonaro leaving the country through an official immigration checkpoint and began examining border crossings and flight records to determine whether he had departed.
Bolsonaro's campaign coordinator, Sen. Rogerio Marinho, initially denied that he had left Brazil, while his brother Eduardo, who lives in the US, dismissed the reports as a "lie."
Bolsonaro's reported departure comes two days after Lula defeated him in Sunday's presidential runoff to secure a fourth term in office.
The senator initially called for the election result to be annulled, although his Liberal Party has acknowledged Lula's victory.

GECF to establish mechanisms to respond to crisis situations on gas market

04:37:38 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Member states of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) intend to establish mechanisms for responding to crisis situations on the gas market, according to the declaration adopted following the summit in Moscow.
"We declare our shared determination to establish mechanisms to respond to crisis situations on the gas market, including the expansion of high-level consultations to assess the impact of external shocks, coordinate actions to ensure reliable gas supplies, and develop effective tools to support energy security," the document reads.
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum includes Russia, Iran, Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates, and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal are observer states. GECF members hold roughly 70% of the world’s proven gas reserves, account for 38% of global gas production and 42% of global gas exports, and represent 47% of global exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

Canada, UAE sign major trade deal amid tensions with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:35:00 UTC
04:35:00 KST

Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a comprehensive trade agreement Tuesday aimed at reducing trade barriers and attracting investment, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to diversify economic partnerships amid strained relations with the United States.
Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Carney has vowed to double Canada's non-U.S. trade over the next decade as President Donald Trump's tariffs have rippled through Canada's economy. Subsequent attempts for a deal with Washington have broken down, and that has pushed Carney to aggressively pursue trade pacts with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and the Middle East.
"Once fully implemented, the CEPA will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99% of current Canadian exports to the UAE. That means new markets for Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola, for manufacturers of industrial machinery and power generation equipment, for our world-class aerospace sector, and other Canadian innovators," The Prime Minister's Office said in a statement.
"The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental, and engineering sectors," it said, adding CEPA is expected to enter into force in 2027.
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defence cooperation.
"We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing - all of which will support our pursuit of a resilient, diversified and globally connected economy,” UAE's Foreign Trade Minister Thani Al Zeyoudi said in a statement.
He signed the CEPA deal with his Canadian counterpart Maninder Sidhu.
UAE is the largest Middle Eastern market for Canadian exports and is a big buyer of Canadian motor vehicles and parts, and machinery. Two-way trade between the countries was worth C$3.5 billion ($2.48 billion) last year. It has been growing at 10% annually for the last few years, according to government data.
The UAE last year also committed up to $50 billion in investment in Canada.
The signing is the last step before Canada’s Parliament can ratify the agreement, a Canadian government source said.

Russia on Tuesday added seven British defense industry executives to its entry ban list over London's military support for Ukraine, the Russian Foreign Ministry said.
The ministry said the move was in response to what it described as Britain's "hostile anti-Russian policy" and its military assistance to Kyiv.
Those targeted are associated with British companies that Moscow alleged were supplying Ukraine with weapons and military technologies, including equipment used in strikes deep inside Russian territory.
The ministry identified Alex Edward, CEO of Rotron Aerospace; Kev Oliver, the company's chief military adviser; and George Zambellas, its chairman.
The list also includes Neil Appleton, executive director of Malloy Aeronautics; Robert Michael Gascoyne, CEO of MGI Engineering; and Paul Webb, director and co-founder of Tekever UK.
Julian Frederick Charles Cracknell, chief technology and information officer at BAE Systems, was also added to the list, according to the ministry.
Moscow alleged that London was supplying Ukraine with missile and drone systems and technologies intended to inflict "maximum damage" on Russia.
The ministry also criticized the British government's defense spending, arguing that the funds could instead support the country's civilian sector amid domestic economic and social challenges.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said it would continue expanding its entry ban list in response to what it considers hostile actions by the British government.

Dutch zookeeper dies after being mauled by leopard
- Published
An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.
The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.
She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.
An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.
Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.
"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.
The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.
Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.
A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.
"They are, and remain, predators."
Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

Analysis: Two ironies emerge out of Israel's deadlocked election
Two ironies have emerged from Israel's election, where more than two-thirds of voters voted against Benjamin Netanyahu.
One is that the lack of a clear outcome means Israel's prime minister will remain in power as caretaker for the immediate future, despite voters clearly rejecting him.
The other is that Arab Israelis, whose voices and concerns were barely mentioned in the campaign, potentially hold the role of kingmakers despite having long been excluded as potential governing partners by the major Jewish Israeli parties.
It will be up to Israeli President Isaac Herzog over the next couple of weeks to decide whether any of the parties can form what he regards as a workable coalition.
For more, read the full analysis below:
Q&A: What effect will the election have on Israel’s diplomatic and security integration in the Middle East?
This will depend on whether Netanyahu forms the next government or not.
If he does, he is likely to continue his current policy of imposing Israel's security presence inside the borders of neighbouring countries.
The IDF now occupies parts of southern Lebanon, southwestern Syria, most of Gaza and has control over the entire West Bank.
That obviously angers Israel's Arab neighbours, and it certainly makes it impossible for Israel to normalise relations with Saudi Arabia.
However, the current Netanyahu government has been able to maintain the Abraham Accords (peace agreements with the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan and Morocco) signed in 2020, which is important in terms of Israel's gradual integration into the Middle East region.
Photos from the scene of Benjamin Netanyahu's speech
Q&A: What would a new leader mean for Israel's relationship with the US?
The US has a broad relationship with Israel, which is not dependent on specific US and Israeli leaders.
President Barack Obama had a poisonous relationship with Benjamin Netanyahu, but the relationship survived his presidency.
Donald Trump has been critical of Netanyahu but has endorsed his candidacy, the first time a US president has expressed a preference in relation to an Israeli election.
However, he is likely to take a pragmatic approach to the relationship whatever the result of the election and would be unlikely to have any difficulty working with Gadi Eisenkot.
Q&A: How might Israel's relationship wtih other countries in the region change after the election?
My answer is that a lot will depend on the actual results of the election and the degree to which, assuming one is formed, it will be able to establish other alternative relations with some of these states.
We do know that, for the first time in many years, there have been US-brokered negotiations between the current Israeli government and the Lebanese government.
The big problem is that the Lebanese government is extremely weak and has very limited authority over the country as a whole and no authority over Hezbollah.
Essentially what has to come out of any negotiation is that Hezbollah is not seen as a threat to Israelis anymore, and there's no sign at this stage that that's going to be the case as a result of the negotiations taking place.
So far it's not clear that a different Israeli government would be able to change the relationship that Israel has with Lebanon while Hezbollah itself is essentially calling the shots.
The other problem is that the new security doctrine that Netanyahu has made in the aftermath of October 7 involves Israel holding territory inside the territory of neighbours it regards as potentially a threat, so it is now holding part of Lebanese territory and Syrian territory.
Keep in mind it could take a very long time for an Israeli government to be formed.
Q&A: How long until there could be a result?
Once we've got an indication of the size of the party in the Knesset as a result of the election result, and at this stage we don't know that, all we know is the exit poll which seems to show Likud may have got a majority.
But the majority itself won't allow Likud to form a government.
The coalition government that Netanyahu was able to put together over the last four years probably won't be able to be reconstituted.
What the process is, is that the Israeli president Isaac Herzog will essentially call on the leader of one of the partyies that he judges to have the best chance at forming a government.
They will probably have up to a month to put together a governing coalition.
That will mean that either Netanyahu or Eisenkot will be given a period to try to put together a government which will be able to form a majority of over 60 seats in the Knesset which is 120 seats.
If that person fails, the Israeli president is at liberty to choose another person who is the leader of a large party and get them to have an attempt.
So we could have up to 6 weeks or two months of an attempt at coaltion forming.
If no coalition is formed because neither party is able to put together a majority coalition, the Israeli electorate will have to vote again.

What would the result mean for the future of Palestinians in Gaza?
Whoever wins the next election will have an influence over the military operations in the Occupied Palestinian Territories. Both Benjamin Netanyahu and his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, vehemently oppose a two-state solution, considering it a security risk and a categorical mistake.
But the surge in support for the Arab parties, with exit polls projecting a combined 17 seats, could mean they'll play a pivotal role as “kingmakers” and may prop up an Eisenkot coalition despite candidates in the change camp, including Eisenkot himself, ruling out such an arrangement.
Gaza is a topic that was barely mentioned by any of the leading candidates. For Israelis on the street, it doesn’t make the top three issues. In terms of policy, there is no clear plan for the future of Gaza from any of the main candidates, beyond Trump’s peace plan.
For Eisenkot, ending Hamas’s rule in the strip within 18 months was a central campaign pledge. Although he shares a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on Gaza, the former military chief views the prime minister’s handling of the conflict as a failure and has said: "As long as Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power, Hamas will remain in power."
Unlike many of the right-wing politcians in Netanyahu’s coalition, Eisenkot has rejected outright the idea of an Israeli military government in Gaza.
The response to Hamas's attacks on 7 October, 2023, which Gazan health authorities say has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and left much of the enclave destroyed, has isolated Israel on the world stage. Eisenkot has said that Netanyahu’s approach to the conflict over the past three years has severely damaged Israel’s international standing.

What would the result mean for the future of Palestinians in the West Bank?
The more than 700,000 Israeli settlers who currently live in the West Bank have the right to vote; the almost three million Palestinians in the same territory do not.
Just days before polls open in Israel, Netanyahu ordered a massive military operation in the area surrounding the southern Palestinian town of Hebron after two Israeli soldiers were killed and others wounded by Palestinians. More than 2,000 families have been displaced, roads blocked and daily life choked in the town.
Some within Netanyahu's cabinet — including the far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben Gvir — himself a longtime settler — have called for the 'voluntary Palestinian emigration' from the West Bank and Gaza — territory Palestinians need and want for a future state.
Since 2022, the current government has legalised more than 100 settlements. Members of Netanyahu's coalition government, such as Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, have advocated continued settlement expansion and what rights group say is tantamount to ethnic cleansing in the area. A UN commission of inquiry report, released yesterday, said Israel had committed war crimes in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, including the West Bank.
Eisenkot mostly supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law. Like a growing number of Israelis, he wants to crack down on what many here call "Jewish terrorism", as violent attacks by extremist Jewish settlers have soared in recent months, according to UN data. Protests on the streets of Jerusalem in recent months against "Jewish terrorism" indicate a growing group within Israeli society who condemn violence being done in their name.
Eisenkot opposes the full annexation of the West Bank, unlike the far-right faction of Netanyahu's coalition, yet he still opposes a fully sovereign Palestinian state. In one interview he raised the possibility of creating the conditions for a "minus state" under ultimate Israel security control.

What will it mean for Netanyahu if his coalition can't form government?
Benjamin Netanyahu has been such a dominant figure in Israeli politics, particularly over the last 20 years, that it is hard for many Israelis to contemplate him losing power. The expectation that this election will not produce a decisive result — and that he may continue in office for some time — has blurred that picture.
But if he does eventually leave the stage, critics say there will be nothing to stop him having to face his ongoing criminal corruption trial. Three cases against him were filed in 2019, and progress has largely been stalled since then.
Both Netanyahu and his far-right allies, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, are also subject to International Criminal Court warrants over alleged war crimes. But no parties in Israel recognise the ICC's authority.
Many of Netanyahu's opponents have also promised to launch an independent state commission of inquiry — akin to an Australian royal commission — into the government and intelligence failures in the lead-up to the Hamas attacks on October 7, 2023. Netanyahu's government has rejected calls for such an inquiry, but he'd be forced to face it if there was one.
There is the broader question, too, of how the powerful business and media networks he has cultivated would reassemble in the future, and what would happen to the far-right parties upon which he has depended particularly and which have pushed such aggressive policies in Gaza and the West Bank.

How closely are other countries watching this election?
Israel said launching the war against Iran in February — alongside the US — was necessary to "remove threats against the state of Israel". But some countries saw it as a clear sign of Israel's ambition to be the dominant force in the region, which was always going to be bitterly opposed.
The sheer aggression of Benjamin Netanyahu — who critics have accused of picking fights to shore up his political position at home — have given countries in the region, but not necessarily on Israel's borders, a particular reason to watch this election closely.
Leaks weeks ahead of the election claiming that the Israeli PM had been directly warned by the UAE and Egypt that Hamas was planning a major attack give some flavour of how the election is being watched in the region. The rest of the world is also watching as Israel has become increasingly isolated from its traditional allies and subject to increasing criticism and sanctions over its actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
While huge changes in security policies are not expected if there is a change of government, it is likely an alternative government will attempt to improve Israel's international standing by taking a tougher line on the further expansion of illegal settlements and settler aggression against Palestinians.
The leading challenger in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, was unequivocal this month, telling an Israeli podcast: "My position on the Palestinian issue has remained consistent: The principle of two states for two peoples is a mistake."

Eisenkot's speech refers to 'all' of Israel
Throughout his speech, Gadi Eisenkot has been speaking in the future tense and frequently referencing "all" of Israel.
“We are one nation, one people, and we want a government that respects all parts," he told supporters.
He has thanked supporters for trusting and believing in him, telling the crowd: "You can tell your children that because of you change is possible."
He signed off his speech by declaring a new chapter in Israel's history.
“We went through difficult years … this is a chance of healing,” he said.
There was a lot of emotion in the room. A lot of party members hugged and Eisenkot looked visibly moved while singing the national anthem.
Key Event
Gadi Eisenkot says Israel is facing a new era
Gadi Eisenkot's supporters have welcomed him to the stage with whooping, cheering, waving flags and the blaring Yashar party anthem.
On stage, he is speaking very much like he is the prime minister, saying the public has voted for change.
“We are one nation, one people and we want a government that respects all parts," he says.
“This will be a real start of a new journey … Israel is facing a new era."
He has said he wants to build a stable Zionist government with all the citizens of Israel.
There is a lot of cheering, clapping and chanting from the crowd as he speaks.
How might Israel’s relationship with other countries in the region, namely Lebanon, change after the election?
This election has been almost entirely focused on domestic issues, particularly Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership. As a result, the plethora of anti-Netanyahu parties have not enunciated detailed policies on foreign and security policy.
If anything, their rhetoric against Iran and its proxies Hezbollah and Hamas has been more hardline — in that they have criticised Netanyahu for failing to wipe out Iran's nuclear program and eliminate Hamas from Gaza.
None of the anti-Netanyahu forces are saying they would immediately withdraw from the large area of Southern Lebanon the IDF now occupies — and where it has been systematically erasing whole villages to stop threats to Israel's northern communities.
Technically, Israel's fight in Lebanon is not with the Lebanese government but with the Iranian-backed Hezbollah. That seems unlikely to change, though a government that is not under as much domestic pressure to demonstrate its security credentials may assess that Israel's interests lie in taking a path which, in future, does not undermine the very fragile governance structures in Lebanon.
One relationship that could possibly change is with Syria. Israel has made increasingly aggressive incursions into Syria in recent months, including an attack on an airbase within Syria, very close to the Turkish border, which it claimed was being used by Turkish troops.
Netanyahu's main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has expressed general support for a security agreement with Syria, which the current prime minister has failed to pursue.

Global affairs editor Laura Tingle is in Israel and is jumping on the blog to answer some key questions about initial exit polling and what that may mean.

Far-right Ben-Gvir denounces suggestion of unity government
A few hundred activists have gathered at a central Israel nightclub that Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) leader and far-right Public Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir party has rented tonight, waving flags and wearing shirts emblazoned with his face.
With his theme song touting his love of guns, Ben-Gvir took to the stage to wild applause despite most exit polls suggesting his party would win six or seven seats.
Ben-Gvir denounced other members of Netanyahu’s coalition for immediately suggesting a unity government with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a name sparking loud audience booing.
"This is precisely the scenario we warned against. It is a terrible mistake," Ben-Gvir said.
Ben-Gvir's agenda has included passing a law approving the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of murdering Israelis and worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners.

Voter turnout was 77.7 per cent, Israel's Central Elections Committee said.
That makes it the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in the previous election in 2022.

Key Event
Result will test unity of anti-Netanyahu camp
Netanyahu’s battle now is the narrative of the outcome of these elections. How will he turn his defeat into a victory? The numbers are clear. At the last election, his party got 32 mandates out of the 120 members in the Israeli parliament. In these elections, the leading exit polls are showing he will receive no more than 25.
Not only that, his coalition, which has a majority in the current parliament, will be getting 50 seats while his opponents will be receiving 70 seats.
Nevertheless, Netanyahu has been working on a new spin. He is predicted to get more seats than Eisenkot’s party. He knows that that fact plays no role, as all governments have to build a governing coalition. That was the case when Tzipi Livni’s party received more seats then Netanyahu back in February 2009, and that did not prevent him from forming the coalition and emerging as the winner as he had more partners to cooperate with.
In order to convince the public that he was not outright defeated, he will undermine the Arab votes. These elections, the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel went out to vote in higher numbers than previous elections, and they are expected to hold some 17 seats. Netanyahu’s claim will be that they should not be part of any governing coalition.
Unfortunately for Netanyahu, the two parties who represent the Arab Palestinians of Israel have made it clear that they will do everything to topple Bibi’s far right coalition, and now they can deliver this promise to the voters.
Netanyahu, by aligning himself with the far right and by placing Itamar Ben-Gvir in charge of the police, has mobilised the Arab voters, who have been suffering from a spike of racism since he established this anti-Arab alliance.
If Netanyahu was a leader in a different country, you might expect him to admit his defeat and resign from leading his party, which has been shattered.
But not Netanyahu, who is facing a trial on three corruption cases and is clinging to power.
Netanyahu will now be calling for unity, he will say that there is a draw and that the Jewish parties have to unite against the Arabs.
The question will be: Are there cracks in the anti-Netanyahu camp. It seems that all the six leaders of the anti-Netanyahu camp — Jews and Arabs alike — are determined to do anything they can to oust Netanyahu and his allies. This of course would mean violating the election promises given by some members of the camp that said they would not lean on the Arab vote. Netanyahu cannot pretend to be too surprised if that happens. After all, throughout his campaign he was saying that this is exactly what Eisenkot would do if he had the upper hand.

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar who merged his party with Likud before the election has warned people against getting ahead of themselves.
"The celebrations on the left are premature," he wrote on X.
"The smugness of the biased commentators — ridiculous. One thing seems quite clear: Likud is the largest party in Israel. It's always good to learn something from the past."

No clear path to power, according to exit polls
Israel's election appears deadlocked, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor rival Gadi Eisenkot showing a clear path to power, exit polls show.
The stalemate could work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
The final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers. No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.
The vote drew a record turnout as Israelis passed wartime judgment on Netanyahu in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Current opposition head Yair Lapid said in a statement: "Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home."
The major networks showed the Eisenkot-led bloc winning between 52 and 53 seats and the Netanyahu-led bloc winning about 50 seats. The remaining 17 to 18 seats were allocated to unaligned Arab parties in the exit polls.
Some Israeli media outlets, including pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, projected a far stronger showing for Netanyahu and his parties, saying they would collectively win 60 seats.
Reuters
How could the election impact Israel's relationship with the United States?
For Israelis, their nation's relationship with the United States is its standout most important relationship. The US's financial support for Israel, along with the close military and intelligence relationship, is seen by Israelis as crucial to their survival.
That relationship is unlikely to change according to whoever is elected in Israel. Both major contenders — Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot — will want it to continue.
The problem for Israel, however, is at the American end. While Donald Trump belatedly endorsed Netanyahu, his relationship with the Israeli PM has been rocky (remember the "f***ing crazy" phone call over Lebanon, as reported by Axios in June?). And from that relationship, it is clear that there are concerns in Washington about Israel's direction.
US Vice-President JD Vance has also revealed a growing crack in the friendship. In June he was asked by media about reports in Israel that Israeli politicians were criticising his attempts to find an end to the Iran war. He said: "If I was in the cabinet of the Israeli government, I might not be attacking the only powerful ally that I have anywhere left in the entire world."
As professional politicians, both Trump and Vance would be conscious of the changing mood in the American public. In April 2026 Pew Research found 60 per cent of American adults had an unfavourable view of Israel. And a Gallup poll in early 2026 found that more Americans sympathised with Palestinians than they did Israelis — 41 per cent to 36 per cent.
Ten years ago the idea that more Americans would sympathise with Palestinians than Israelis would have been unthinkable. The change is largely due to the devastation of Gaza. While most Americans supported Israel's right to respond to Hamas's attacks on October 7, the reduction of Gaza, a home to 2.1 million Palestinians, to "rubble" — a word used by Trump — has changed the reality.
So whatever the outcome of the Israeli election, Israel has a much deeper problem: how it is increasingly being seen by Americans.
What are the key issues driving voters?
Israel is a country which seems to be in a perpetual state of war. Its backers will say it's protecting itself. Its critics will say it brings it on itself by having an aggressive posture in the region.
Regardless of which view people have, national security — or who can keep Israel safe — is a central theme in this election.
Netanyahu’s reputation as "Mr Security" took a battering on October 7, 2023, as Hamas launched its surprise raids and carried out the deadliest attack on Israel since its establishment in 1948.
Since then, wars with Hezbollah in Lebanon and against the Iranian regime in Tehran have put Israel in a precarious position – regardless of its military might.
None of the challengers to Netanyahu are promising wholesale change on management of those multiple wars.
But some of the issues that have erupted because of the conflicts are dominating election debates.
There are calls for a totally independent inquiry into the failures which allowed the October 7 attacks to occur — something Netanyahu has repeatedly rejected. His rivals, including Gadi Eisenkot, are promising such a probe.
The multiple wars have also put the issue of resourcing for the military on the agenda. Every Israeli is meant to complete their compulsory military service when they turn 18, and many continue to perform reserve duty afterwards. The ultra-Orthodox Jewish community was exempt from that until the Supreme Court tore up the policy in 2024.
Critics have accused Netanyahu, whose coalition includes ultra-Orthodox parties that refused to yield on demands to restore the exemptions, of failing to fix the issue.
Issues like the cost of living are also present in the campaign, given Israel is one of the most expensive countries in the OECD. Fuel (95 unleaded) recently had to be capped at 7.77 shekels a litre, which is roughly $3.60.
But it takes a back seat to the greater security and societal problems the country is facing.
The Israelis who flew home to vote
Tens of thousands of Israeli citizens abroad, including estimates of hundreds from Australia, have travelled to Israel to vote in the country's most consequential election in decades.
Political activists mobilised around the world to bring Israeli citizens overseas to the country to vote, given ballots can only be cast in person on election day, with exceptions for serving soldiers and diplomats.
The AID Coalition, a US-based non-profit which describes itself as non-partisan,estimates that as many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its Fly&Vote initiative.
It says about half are flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Among those who have travelled to Israel is Anat Dror, who has been living in Melbourne for almost five years and recently became an Australian citizen.
She said she had flown to Israel to vote against Benjamin Netanyahu:
"The sentiment for us is that right now, voting is absolutely essential. It's something that absolutely comes from the heart and no-one would be able to talk me out of it," she told the ABC.
"I'm coming here at the very expensive cost of missing out on work days and paying for a very expensive ticket and missing my kids at home … All of these are not deterring any of us from coming here to vote.
"This is our motherland and our motherland needs us right now."

Walking into the polling station in Herzliya, you are met with blaring music. Dozens of journalists and voters have gathered to see the man many are hoping will be the next prime minister and unseat Netanyahu.
Gadi Eisenkot is swarmed by crowds as he climbs the stairs of a local school to cast his vote.
After casting his vote, the leader of Yashar — a word meaning straight — addresses the press and the crowd of supporters who have gathered in a school. Chants of "our next prime minister" are heard as the crowd is hushed for the former military chief to speak.

The leader of the centrist Yashar party criticised Netanyahu’s attempt to derail the election and what he said were the prime minister's scare tactics.
For Eisenkot, this was "the most critical day, perhaps since the founding of the state".
Voters at the polling station were casting their ballots for a variety of candidates. We spoke to some who said it was imperative that the country change. For one voter, it was the last chance for democracy.
"It's catastrophe. It’s four years of catastrophe," one voter named Mirijam said.
"The people of Israel are smart people but the people upstairs are terrible," she said.

What do these polls actually mean?
Dear readers, you may well be bamboozled by the various exit polls coming from the Israeli media now that voting in the Israeli election has finished.
What does it all mean?
Well, it's safe to say that Yashar will not be thrilled to be running second to Likud in terms of being the largest party in the Knesset.
All of the public polling to this point had suggested it would be in the box seat.
Likud will be crowing about this, and Benjamin Netanyahu will chalk it up as a win for his campaign and a win for the right wing of Israeli politics.
But even while Yashar has run second, there's still hope for the anti-Netanyahu bloc, with strong figures coming from the Together joint list of former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid and the Democrats.
And the far-right parties that have propped up the Netanyahu coalition in this last term, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich (settlers who have been sanctioned by countries including Australia) will only secure six seats each.
That undermines the Netanyahu bid for forming a coalition.
The other standout here is a strong showing for the Arab parties, often referred to as the Palestinian parties.
High voter turnout among the Arab-Palestinian population, which is 20 per cent of Israel's community, seem to have lifted their standing — the Joint List into double digits, the United Arab List not far behind.
Netanyahu has railed against them in the campaign, trying to de-legitimise them in the eyes of voters.
As much as Israeli politics can throw up some strange bedfellows, it's safe to say the Joint List and United Arab List would be in the sights of the anti-Netanyahu bloc to get them over the line.
How has October 7 shaped the public's perceptions of Netanyahu and his government?
Hamas's deadly attacks on October 7, 2023, continue to cast a long shadow over Israel, Gaza and the broader Middle East region.
What allowed the attacks to happen, as well as how Benjamin Netanyahu handled them, is expected to play a huge role in how Israelis vote this election.
Netanyahu has spent his entire political career carefully cultivating an image of being the security hard man — the man the nation can trust to not only identify and call out threats, but to keep Israelis safe from them.
The October 7 attacks put that image through the shredder. And he's arguably spent the past three years being even more aggressive to try to restore it.
Netanyahu regularly pushes an idea labelled by the Israeli media as "the betrayal theory" or "the treason theory" — a claim he was deliberately kept in the dark by senior defence and intelligence officials about the threat massing at the Gaza border. He has gone as far as to say he wasn't woken up early enough on October 7 to deal with the response.
His political rivals have seized on this defensiveness in their election campaigning, promising that shirking responsibility will become a thing of the past.
Opponents have also pointed to the most extreme voices in the Netanyahu coalition — people like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich (both long-time settlers who have been sanctioned by governments around the world, including Australia, for their policies and rhetoric against Palestinians) — as evidence of how the prime minister has allowed his own desire to hold on to power dictate his government's decision making , arguing extremists are taking Israel down a dangerous path.
An update from Yashar HQ
Yashar anthems are blasting, across all genres from pop to folk, to house to hip hop, as journalists fill the room and anticipation builds for the camp that has vowed to bring change.
It's clear there is a long night ahead.
As polls came in, the music picked up, flags were raised and cheers erupted.
Even though there is no clear winner yet, Eizenkot’s team here told ABC News they are confident this means victory, and that they are on the right track.

Exit polls show Netanyahu's Likud party on track to be largest in Knesset
Polls have closed in the Israeli election, with exit polls from the nation’s media outlets showing Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is likely to be the largest party in the next Knesset.
But it is still unclear whether he will be able to form a coalition government, with the anti-Netanyahu parties recording a significant share of the vote.
Israel’s public broadcaster, KAN, says Likud is on track to secure 25 seats, while challenger Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar will secure 21 seats.
Commercial network Channel 13 is reporting Likud will also receive 25 seats, while Yashar will get 23.
Taking into account the likely coalition partners, the anti-Netanyahu bloc, which includes Yashar, Together, and the Democrats, are still ahead by a handful of seats.
The far-right parties which had propped up the Netanyahu government in the last term of government, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are likely to secure only six seats each.
Could the Arab-Israeli parties end up holding the balance of power?
There were a lot of unknowns in this campaign, and one was them was how many Israelis would cast a vote. Voting is not compulsory in Israel, but records have been broken tonight.
One group which could have a profound impact on the result is the Palestinian citizens of Israel, often referred to as Arab-Israelis.
Traditionally, they have a much lower turnout than the general population. This is a group which feels not only marginalised from the rest of the country but actively discriminated against in terms of policies and resources. Palestinian communities face high crime and poverty rates, among other issues.
But, they make up 20 per cent of the Israeli population.
If these voters showed up and voted, many would likely back the "Arab-Israeli" parties, the United Arab List and the Joint List.
That could put those two blocs in a position of considerable influence in the days and weeks after election day.
On Friday, Channels 11, 12, 13 and newspaper Maariv all put the Joint List at securing nine seats. The same outlets put the United Arab List at securing between five and seven seats.
That puts the two groups in a position where the larger parties, particularly Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, could approach them for support in any coalition agreement.
During the campaign, Netanyahu railed against the idea of cooperation with the Palestinian-dominated parties. Opposition leaders including Eisenkot have also distanced themselves from talk of cooperation with the Joint List or the United Arab List.
But in the mad scramble for power, unlikely bedfellows could quickly emerge, even as Israel remains deeply divided.

Voter turnout breaks records across Israel
Israelis have streamed to the polls in record numbers.
The Central Elections Committee reports voter turnout at 74.3 per cent.
Forecasters were hesitant to guess what impact the strong turnout might have on the result.
A surge in votes from Israelis of Palestinian heritage could limit gains for Mr Netanyahu's right-wing coalition and make it more likely that any government formed to oust him would require Arab parties' support, a contentious prospect among Jewish party leaders.
Ahmed Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said record turnout from Israel's Arab minority would "pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality".

Voters 'know what they want' according to former Knesset member
At the polling station in Rehavia, we picked out of the crowd a familiar face in Israeli politics.
Mossi Raz has been a member of the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, having represented the former left-wing Meretz party from 2000 to 2003, 2017 to 2019, and 2021 to 2022.
This time, he's running for The Democrats, which is the party formed out of the merger of Meretz and the former Labor party.
Anyway, Mossi was fairly clear eyed about how he believed voters would be behave at the ballot box.
"There is a feeling of people, unlike previous elections campaigns, know what they want," he said.
The Democrats are one of the parties which commentators argue will likely join with other anti-Netanyahu parties, such as Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, to form a coalition.
I asked Mossi whether he was worried about polling showing support from the right wing of Israeli voters still propping up the prime minister's Likud party and others in his current government.
"The groups who support Netanyahu in the society grew increased in this last four years," he said.
"There are more religious people, more settlers, more ultra-orthodox, and many liberals who left the country.
"The opposition was very successful in turning people who were supporters of Netanyahu last time to vote for the opposition."
Raz said after polling day, there would be a test for the anti-Netanyahu camp.
"The only question is if it is enough and if the heads of the opposition, I hope the next prime minister, will be honest enough to cooperate with the two Arab Palestinian lists because without them [a change of government] will not happen."
What does the election look like in Israel's suburbs
Having covered Australian politics for a few years before moving to Jerusalem, I can tell you the election looks and feels somewhat familiar when voters are arriving at polling stations.
It was just a bit messier because there are so many more parties running.
Just like in Australia, there are party volunteers lining up outside the entrances armed with flyers trying to win over voters at the last minute. Although in Rehavia, a more affluent Jerusalem suburb, they weren't as aggressive as they may have been in other parts of the country.
There were also no democracy sausages on offer.
A lot of the campaign material focuses on white slips of paper with Hebrew letters on them. This reflects how Israeli voters actually cast their ballot.
Rather than marking a piece of paper, each voter picks a ballot with the lettering representing their desired party and puts it in an envelope.
Parties pick their lettering based on part of their messaging. Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar has a ballot paper saying the Hebrew word for "way" or "street", saying a vote for it is a vote to put Israel on the right path.
Others are more obscure.
I did see some racist campaign material from one of the far-right Haredi parties, called Noam, littered on the ground.
It showed a number of Muslim women and a slogan along the lines of: "Are these the people you want to teach your children?"
Noam is not expected to secure enough votes to secure even a single seat in the Knesset.
And some of the other right-wing party volunteers were having a crack at their team, saying they were pinching votes from the parties which do have a chance of getting in.
