Key Event
Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the main opponent facing Netanyahu?
There are a handful of parties all trying to chip away at Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party. But few seem to have garnered as much support, at least in terms of public polling, as the brand new Yashar party led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants and a former chief of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) — a position he held under Mr Netanyahu from 2015 to 2019.
After retiring from the military he entered politics, joining Benny Gantz's Blue and White party.
It's interesting to note here that Mr Gantz, a one-time high flyer in the Israeli political system, pulled out of this election a week out from polling day because his numbers were so poor.
After the deadly October 7 attacks by Hamas in October 2023, Eisenkot joined the emergency war cabinet — an attempt by Mr Netanyahu to bring together politicians from outside his ruling coalition to show unity of purpose after the terrorist attacks.
But Eisenkot, and Gantz, quit a few months later. And this is where the cracks in the relationship between Eisenkot and Netanyahu really started to emerge.
He accused the government of being beholden to extreme right-wing voices, making decisions about the war which were more about annihilation of an enemy rather than the safety of Israeli hostages.
In mid-2025, he quit the Knesset altogether. A few months later, he established Yashar — which translates to "straight" or "honest".
Netanyahu has spent a lot of time trying to paint Eisenkot as an inept leader and weak on security. He says the former general's grasp on English is weak, calling that a problem for a country like Israel on the world stage. The prime minister also accuses him of being prepared to roll over to Israel's enemies.
But Netanyahu's criticism overlooks one of the key markers in Eisenkot's military career: He was the man who developed the so-called Dahiyeh Doctrine, named after the Hezbollah stronghold suburbs in southern Beirut. It calls for the disproportionate use of force against an enemy, to effectively bomb them into submission.
'No doubt' it's time for Netanyahu to go
Back in Rehavia, a few more voters shared their views on the election with us.
Menachem Lorberbaum said his vote was "private" when asked who he backed at the ballot box.
But he said there was "no doubt" it was time for a change of leadership.
"You don't have to vote for [Gadi] Eisenkot or for anybody, you know, on that side to see that, to speak to people on the street and they'll tell you that people have to know when it's time to go home," he said.
Menachem added that Israel was "undergoing a very deep realignment" of values and attitudes.
"The shifts and the deep divides are elsewhere from where they were 30 years ago, and I think you see this quite dramatically," he said.
"Israel is in a different place today ... no democracy is perfect, no polity is perfect, but I think that this is one of the most dramatic tests of the ability of the self-corrective principles within a republic, a democratic republic, to renew itself."
That division Menachem was speaking about was perhaps evident on some of the Likud party flyers being handed out to voters as they arrived at the primary school.
For weeks, Mr Netanyahu has painted his political opponents as being supporters of the Palestinian cause, as he tried to whip up support and fear about the issue.
His flyers read "Right or Palestine", which in Hebrew rhymes, and featured photos of the anti-Netanyahu party leaders such as Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Golan, Avigdor Liberman and the leaders of the two Arab-Palestinian groups running at the election, Yousef Jabareen and Mansour Abbas.
Netanyahu supporter Etti Brand was clutching one as she arrived to vote.
"He is the only one," she said of the prime minister when asked who she was voting for.
"Yair Golan and Eisenkot are going to bring us to Palestine."
Voters divided on whether it's time for Netanyahu to 'go home'
We spent a bit of time talking to voters at a primary school in the Jerusalem suburb of Rehavia earlier in the day.
It's just around the corner from Benjamin Netanyahu's personal residence in the city, and a short drive from the prime minister's official Jerusalem home.
It was also where Israeli president Isaac Herzog cast his ballot.
Something we've heard a lot in recent weeks from critics of Mr Netanyahu is that it's "time for him to go home".
And some of the residents we spoke to certainly agreed with that sentiment.
Meira Partem didn't say which party she specifically backed, but said she had voted for a "new dawn" — a government without Mr Netanyahu at the helm.
"First of all, it's not democratic, it's the same prime minister for so many years.
"The second thing, after this terrible semi-Holocaust that happened here in my Jewish sovereign state, anyone should have stepped down and apologised.
"And the gall not to do that is very, very disturbing.”
She's talking there about accountability for the defence and security failures which allowed the October 7 attacks to occur in 2023, when about 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
Meira described the prime minister as an "opportunist" who would work with any partner as long as it meant holding on to power.
"If a prime minister tries to have everybody loyal to him, and not to the country, not to the law, that's destructive to the country," she said.
Mr Netanyahu did have support in Rehavia.
"I'm voting Bibi, obviously, because he's our wartime leader and we're still mid-war," voter Yosef Abraham told us.
"I think anybody who wants the government to switch is actually anti-Israel, he wants us to get weaker, because midwar, you don't change leadership.
"I think we need other leadership in different times, but right now we have to continue to support Bibi."
Mr Abraham had very strong views about Palestinian and Arab citizens of Israel, insisting they needed to assimilate or leave.
"Each Arab can place the flag of Israel in their schools, in their houses, and then they remain citizens," he said.
"If they refuse, they are our enemy from within, and we need to cleanse them out."

302,000 Russian soldiers killed or wounded by Ukrainian drones since January, Defense Ministry says
Units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces have killed or severley wounded 302,000 Russian servicemen by using drones since January 2026, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 27.
"Each defeat is recorded on video in the Delta combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster," the Defense Ministry said.
The Ukrainian military uses an incentive system in which the verified destruction of enemy personnel and military materiel awards combat units points that they can exchange for more drones, electronic warfare equipment, and other gear on an internal marketplace.
In September, 46,230 Russian soldiers were killed or irrecoverably wounded, according to figures published by the Ukrainian General Staff.
Of these, 32,739 were killed or wounded by drones, the figures show, amounting to about 70% of the total.
The highest number of casualties Ukrainian drones inflicted on the Russian military was recorded in March, with almost 34,000 soldiers killed or irrecoverably wounded.
Drones of various types now cause the vast majority of casualties on both sides. "The destruction of enemy manpower using UAVs helps preserve the lives of Ukrainian soldiers, making it difficult for the enemy to approach our positions," the ministry said.
The prevalence of drones from both sides has significantly changed assault tactics, making heavy equipment such as tanks a rare sight on the battlefield.
With the "kill zone" reaching 20 kilometers (12.4 miles), Russia has largely stopped using tanks or other heavy equipment for assault operations, Joint Forces Task Force spokesperson Viktor Trehubov said on Sept. 20. Drones have replaced many of the tanks' roles for both sides, since a tank driving close to the front would be easily spotted and hit by much cheaper drones.

====================================================================================================

OpenAI just scooped mathematicians’ work on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:18:23 UTC
04:18:23 KST

If you’ve been keeping up with news in the math world, the story will sound strikingly familiar, right down to its cast of characters.
Using a proprietary internal large language model (LLM), OpenAI just released a result mathematicians have been chasing for decades: a formal proof validating the “quantum chromodynamics” that underpin physicists’ best, most successful description of the universe.
The new proof also scoops the work of two human mathematicians, one of whom just happens to be employed by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic. The duo—Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge and Ethan Sussman, a mathematician at Northwestern University—had publicly disclosed their progress on their own independent proof in the weeks leading up to OpenAI’s historic announcement.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“I’m not going to say that I’m not disappointed,” Sussman says. He and Alpöge first revealed their burgeoning collaboration to the world on October 6. Notably, the pair updated their public GitHub repository with a new set of intermediate results the night before OpenAI’s announcement. “I think we were on the way and maybe even as close as a few weeks away,” Sussman says.
“This is a major advance,” says Michael R. Douglas, a theoretical physicist and artificial intelligence proponent at Harvard University. “Mathematicians have been trying to make quantum field theory rigorous for over 50 years and have made steady progress, but real-world theories like quantum chromodynamics always seemed out of reach—until now. This is just the start..., but we can hope for rapid progress.”
Both camps were pursuing something known as the Yang-Mills problem, which concerns the math that underpins modern physics. The “Standard Model” of particle physics explains all the known forces in the universe with 17 interacting particles. The particles are described by “quantum fields,” mathematical entities that permeate all of space and time, determining how, when and where particles appear in the world, what they are and what they do.
But the math of quantum fields is notoriously gnarly. Physicists use it to reliably predict what happens when they smash particles together at places such as the Large Hadron Collider, but mathematicians worry that the theory has holes.
The Yang-Mills problem is about putting that theory on a solid mathematical footing. The problem has two parts: proving that the theory is mathematically consistent—that it “exists”—and proving that it has a nonzero quantity called a “mass gap,” which has important consequences in the physical world.
In the 1980s mathematician Tadeusz Balaban laid out a coarse path to proving the first part, “existence.” But even just this bare mathematical sketch of a proof was an enormous undertaking, encompassing thousands of pages. And it was far from complete.
“[Balaban’s] papers are not complete and are extraordinarily difficult to read, but experts did not seriously doubt that they could be completed with sufficiently many years devoted to it,” says Roland Bauerschmidt, a mathematician at New York University.
Even so, decades have passed, and no other expert has managed to reach the top of the mountain Balaban built—let alone bridge the gaps he left along the way. Balaban himself eventually tired of the project and moved on.
Hopes for progress ramped up only this summer as the rapidly accelerating capabilities of LLMs catapulted them to the forefront of research-level math. In particular, the superhuman endurance of LLMs has let them blast through numerical tedium to persevere where any human would lose interest and give up. Suddenly, an exhausted mathematician could carefully prompt an LLM, get a good night’s sleep and then wake up in the morning to find a completed proof from the tireless, dutiful model.
Seeing this, Sussman became convinced LLMs were the perfect tool to work on Balaban’s program. “The primary obstacle was the amount of work involved rather than the absence of ideas,” he says. “So from my perspective, this was a rather obvious thing to do.”
At the same time, Alpöge was producing a number of high-profile results with Anthropic’s Claude family of models. In particular, his wrangling of six-dimensional spheres caught Sussman’s attention. “It was the first instance that I had seen of someone being able to get an LLM to produce, reliably, a 100-page proof,” he recalls. That’s the sort of feat that begins to approach the gargantuan tomes typical of Yang-Mills-related work.
So on September 8—which happened to be one of the biggest days in math history—Sussman e-mailed Alpöge. “I essentially told him, ‘Hey, in case no one else has told you, here is something I think would be worth doing,’” he says. Alpöge invited him to collaborate.
The partnership proceeded much like Alpöge’s work with another mathematician, New York University’s Tristan Buckmaster, on the Euler equations (an important precursor to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which OpenAI announced it had solved on September 8). Alpöge would use Anthropic’s internal version of Claude—in fact, many “agent” copies of the LLM working in concert—to churn out thousands of pages of mathematical arcana, essentially unreadable to a human. But he’d then use his agents to validate that the arcana corresponded to some real mathematical truth—and to distill it into something easier to parse. He’d then send it to Sussman—who was flabbergasted by how much was borne out by the LLM’s churn.
“It’s remarkable,” Sussman says. “The vast majority, if not all, of the mistakes in the version we posted on GitHub were produced by me.”
In addition to filling in Balaban’s gaps with a tedious litany of mathematical steps, the agents also made some genuine innovations. “I could tell you exactly how it built on older work,” Sussman says of one example, “but it also was somewhat novel.”
On October 6 Sussman and Alpöge heard the rumors that OpenAI was about to release hundreds of major math results and thought Yang-Mills might be one of them. They decided to proactively start staking their own claim by posting their progress in a public GitHub repository. “I certainly was not the only person to realize this was something worth pursuing,” Sussman says. Their revelation quickly made the rounds on X. Then, when OpenAI’s ensuing “slop drop” didn’t contain a Yang-Mills proof, they continued their work in the open, for all to see.
After making significant progress this past weekend, the pair updated their repository on Sunday evening. They believed they’d solved the three-dimensional version of the “existence problem.” This would have fallen short of the Clay Mathematical Institute’s Millennium Prize Problem criteria, which demand a four-dimensional solution, but “we expect, based on the ‘slop’ that we have, that the key ideas are the same,” Sussman says.
On Monday evening OpenAI claimed a proof of the “existence” part of the Clay problem. The company has yet to release the proof; instead OpenAI opted to hand it off to a group of experts who could “shepherd” it into the mathematical literature. This decision sparked immediate outcry, including from the advisory group of mathematicians the company itself had assembled in response to earlier backlash.
Writing on X, Alpöge expressed a mix of disgust and dismay. “I kept telling [Sussman] to not be too deferential and modest because he would be publicly scooped at any opportunity,” Alpöge wrote. “Instead of contacting him to work with him, as has been suggested publicly many times, the people at OpenAI chose to do this.”
In a blog post, OpenAI stated that its internal model—the same one responsible for the Navier-Stokes proof and the subsequent “slop drop”—arrived at the result on September 9. But according to the post, OpenAI opted to keep it secret until the company could code it into Lean, a programming language that helps ensure mathematical correctness. Notably, the OpenAI said this Lean verification took well more than a month, whereas similar checking only took a reported 17 hours for its Navier-Stokes proof.
“There is no way it took one month to Lean-verify Yang-Mills,” says Buckmaster, whose very public bout with OpenAI over Navier-Stokes remains largely unresolved. “It takes, at most, a couple of days.”
As in the Navier-Stokes controversy, this sequence of events shows how impenetrable the provenance of mathematical ideas is becoming. The ongoing rat race between AI companies jockeying for trillion-dollar initial public offering (IPO) valuations continues to come at the cost of scientific clarity and adherence to academic norms. Everyone involved agrees that new norms need to be discussed and established, but no one seems willing to hold back the deluge while that happens.
Editor’s Note (10/27/26): This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

Trump administration considering lifting sanctions on Russian Direct Investment Fund, NYT says
The administration of US President Donald Trump is considering lifting sanctions on Russia's flagship state investment fund, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, which is regarded as one of the Kremlin's most powerful tools of international influence.
Source: The New York Times, citing sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sources said Russian officials have been pushing for sanctions on the fund to be lifted as part of broader negotiations over its involvement in supplying Russian diesel fuel to the United States.
A US official confirmed that the administration is considering the fund's application for sanctions relief as part of efforts to "improve US-Russia relations and help end the war".
The official praised the fund's head, Kirill Dmitriev, who is involved in negotiations to end Russia's war against Ukraine, describing him as "a helpful envoy".
The lifting of sanctions on the multi-billion-dollar Russian Direct Investment Fund would be a significant reversal of years of US efforts to use economic pressure to force Russia to end its war against Ukraine. The fund has invested billions of dollars in Russian companies, often alongside investors from the Middle East and other regions, helping to expand Russia's global influence.
The Biden administration imposed sanctions on the fund days after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, describing it as a "slush fund" for Russian ruler Vladimir Putin and a symbol of "Russia's broader kleptocracy".
Eric Green, a diplomat who oversaw Russia policy on the US National Security Council at the time, said sanctions against the institution had been an early priority because the fund's access to the Western financial system could have helped Russia finance the war.
The Russian Direct Investment Fund now has a leading role in implementing Trump's diesel deal with Russia.
Dmitriev has been acting as Putin's economic envoy in talks with the Trump administration, spearheading the Kremlin's efforts to convince US officials of the significant potential for business deals with Russia.
Trump's team believes that making business deals with Putin now could help end the war in Ukraine by demonstrating to the Kremlin leader that the US is serious about building new and prosperous relations with Moscow. Many critics of this approach, including some Republican lawmakers, argue that Trump is simply handing economic benefits to Putin without putting pressure on him to end the war.
Meanwhile, the US Treasury Department is following its standard procedure for reviewing applications for sanctions relief. According to sources familiar with the process, this means the fund will have to demonstrate that the reasons for which sanctions were imposed no longer apply.
Background:
- Earlier, Reuters reported that the Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on vessels belonging to Russia's shadow fleet, which transport oil and petroleum products, including from Russia, Iran and Venezuela.
- The New York Times also reported recently that the Trump administration offered Russia several options for economic incentives if it agreed to an energy or maritime ceasefire with Ukraine.

Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:17:55 UTC
04:17:55 KST

The giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, according to government insiders, in a boost to those in the cabinet who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead.
The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, was leaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues, including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval.
Government insiders have told the Guardian the project can be approved on a strict reading of Britain’s climate obligations, in part because once the oil is exported, the emissions from burning it no longer count against domestic targets. “Miatta has more latitude than you might think,” said one.
A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a harmful step away from prioritising net zero – and may see the shift of emissions from one country to another as a trivial distinction.
On Tuesday, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth wrote to the prime minister urging him to consider the cumulative impacts of big decisions on North Sea drilling, Heathrow expansion and grants for heat pumps – rather than viewing each in isolation.
But sources say the Treasury has already accounted for billions of pounds’ worth of tax revenue from Rosebank and so would be faced with a shortfall should it be rejected.
“The climate case against was never the direct emissions,” one source said. “Instead it was the leadership position … the power of a G7 producer seeking to put that into action is the climate point, not the direct emissions.”
Greg Muttitt, a climate researcher at University College, London, said the government was wrong to approve the Jackdaw gasfield last week and would be wrong to approve Rosebank, which would generate around seven times the emissions.
But he added: “It is true that the UK government is not going to find itself in any international court if it approves Rosebank. Approving it is not inconsistent with what the UK has committed to firmly, because most of the oil will be exported and so will count towards other countries’ emissions.”
Fahnbulleh has been forced to make a decision over Rosebank because of a legal judgment that the previous environmental consent was incorrectly given by the Conservative government at the time.
A judge ruled in 2024 that ministers should have accounted for emissions not just from drilling for oil at Rosebank, but also from those which will be generated by burning it.
Given most of that oil will be burned abroad, however, the resulting emissions will not count against the UK’s carbon budgets. Experts estimate that Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, against an overall limit of 90m tonnes.
Fahnbulleh is under an obligation to take into account Britain’s commitment under the Paris agreement to take action to prevent global temperatures rising more than 1.5C.
In her decision to approve the Jackdaw scheme last week, however, she noted Jackdaw would account for about 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions created by the oil and gas industry in 2035.
Some experts believe Rosebank could be approved without meaningfully adding to global temperature changes. But others insist that any new oil and gasfields are harmful to the goal of staying within safe carbon budgets.
Downing Street insiders insist the decision rests with Fahnbulleh, rather than with Andy Burnham. However supportive ministers have interpreted the prime minister’s promise to take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas as a signal he would support giving the green light to Rosebank.
He has also talked of “reindustrialisation” in a speech in Motherwell, North Lanarkshire, this month, language often associated in Scotland with the North Sea. Scottish Labour MPs are believed to be overwhelmingly in favour of approving the oilfield.
Fahnbulleh told the Guardian last week that while she had approved the Jackdaw gasfield on the grounds of national energy security, the same concerns did not necessarily apply to Rosebank.
Her allies say she is leaning away from approving it because the climate damage it would create, while arguably not enough to violate legal limits, would not be overriden by the potential benefits, which those who support its approval argue includes tax take, jobs and investment.
In recent days, however, people close to the chancellor have said he wants Fahnbulleh to approve the project.
The Guardian has learned that part of the reason for this is the Treasury has already accounted for the tax benefits, which Adura, the company operating the field, estimate would be £500m a year by the end of this parliament.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Any decision will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”

By Raul Cortes
MEXICO CITY, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Mexico’s National Electoral Institute (INE) promised on Tuesday to carry out an exhaustive, independent and transparent overhaul to guarantee its continuity, after its chief resigned over allegations of irregularities and corruption.
The leadership upheaval raises fresh questions over the credibility and stability of the autonomous authority as it prepares to oversee Mexico’s 2027 midterm elections.
Lawmakers face the task of choosing a permanent successor to Guadalupe Taddei to steer the INE through an increasingly contentious political environment.
“It is a good time for whoever takes office to exercise transparency and ensure that no department within the National Electoral Institute favors any particular side, and that the Institute fulfills its duties,” Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said at her daily press conference.
INE’s top members announced several measures to overcome the crisis at an unusual press conference led by Blanca Cruz, who earlier was named as interim president. Her designation is due to be formalized later on Tuesday. Cruz, an electoral adviser, joined the INE’s General Council in April.
“The provisional presidency has a clear responsibility: to facilitate dialogue, ensure institutional continuity, and contribute to the decisions that are being shaped through deliberation and consensus,” Cruz said at the press conference.
Taddei resigned on Monday in the most high-profile departure tied to alleged corruption in Sheinbaum’s two-year-old presidency. Sheinbaum said she supported Taddei’s decision.
Mexico’s Superior Audit Office is investigating alleged irregularities involving INE contracts, including possible conflicts of interest and the triangulation of public funds. Taddei, in local news outlets, has been accused of favoring an INE contractor, with whom she has a personal relationship, with contracts worth millions of dollars.
Cruz said the INE council was reviewing officials in decision-making roles, adding that three senior officials had already resigned: the heads of IT Services and the Gender Equality and Non-Discrimination Unit, and the official responsible for material resources. Local media described all three as members of Taddei’s inner circle.
Taddei has not spoken publicly since resigning.
“Over the past few days, rumors, fabricated material, leaks, and versions of events have spread through the media and social networks, and as in all such cases, their authenticity, context, and purpose must be verified and corroborated,” she said in a statement on Sunday announcing her planned resignation.

US’s RFK Jr claims Arabs ‘don’t produce science’: Why he’s very, very wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:12:35 UTC
04:12:35 KST

US’s RFK Jr claims Arabs ‘don’t produce science’: Why he’s very, very wrong
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has claimed that Arabs have not made contributions to math, science or literature.
United States Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has sparked uproar with comments he has made denying Arab contributions to mathematics, science and literature.
In a high-voltage rant on Monday, the US health secretary said, “There’s five hundred million Arabs in the world. And yet they don’t produce science. They don’t win the Nobel Prize. They don’t win the Fields Prize. They don’t win the Wolf Prize. They don’t produce literature.”
RFK Jr, who has been involved in anti-vaccine campaigns and has promoted a debunked theory linking vaccines to autism, made the comments during a US election campaign event in Grand Rapids, Michigan while supporting Republican nominee Mike Rogers, who is up against Arab-American Democrat nominee Abdul El-Sayed, in a tightly contested battle for Michigan’s Senate seat in next week’s midterm elections.
Critics said the comments were racist, Islamophobic and factually inaccurate, pointing to modern and historic Arab innovation in multiple fields.
Here’s how Arabs have made vital contributions to the human understanding of maths, science and literature through the centuries.
Arab contributions to maths, science and humanities
The period known as the Islamic Golden Age, from around 750 AD to 1258 AD, produced many key Arab contributions to medicine at a time when Europe was said to be in its Dark Ages. During this time, Arabic was the language of science and scholarship.
1st-4th centuries: The numerals 0-9, which originated in ancient India, were adopted by Arab mathematicians who spread them across the world. They displaced Roman numerals as a more advanced number system in mathematics.
8th century: Arab and Persian mathematicians were studying the ancient Indian concept of zero in mathematics in Baghdad, long before the Europeans. The number zero was crucial to the development of mathematics – but was absent from widely used Roman numerals in Europe.
813-833: The Arab mathematician Muḥammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi – one of those studying the number 0 – is often referred to as the “father of algebra” as he was the first to treat the method as a separate mathematical discipline in his work, Al-Jabr. This method provided the first linear and quadratic equations, still used as a core part of mathematical study today.
965-1040: Ibn al-Haytham, known as the “father of modern optics”, explained the role that light entering the eye plays in human vision. He was born in Basra in Iraq, but spent most of his working life in Cairo attending to noble families.
936-1013: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, called “the father of modern surgery”, was considered the greatest surgeon in the Middle Ages. He wrote a 30-volume encyclopaedia detailing medical practices and designed and illustrated many surgical instruments. Born in Azahara, in Andalusia, he was known as Abulcasis in Europe.
9th century: Fatima al-Fihri founded the University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco. It is often cited as the oldest continually operating university.
1213-1288: Ibn al-Nafis described pulmonary circulation – the process by which blood passes through the lungs – several centuries before Europeans understood it. He wrote more than 110 volumes of work on surgery, ophthalmology and philosophy while working as a chief physician in Egypt.
915-965: Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi, regarded as the greatest poet in the Arabic language, was Yemeni and grew up immersed in Bedouin Arabic culture. He wrote in classical Arabic and many of his verses became sayings used in everyday Arabic.
1100-1165: Muhammad al-Idrisi was a geographer known for making the Tabula Rogeriana, one of the most accurate and detailed medieval world maps, and a high point of Islamic geography. He was born in Ceuta in Morocco.
Prize-winning Arabs
In more modern times, RFK Jr’s assertion that Arabs do not win Nobel prizes for science and literature is very far from the truth. Here are some of the highlights:
1960: Nobel Prize for Medicine
Peter Medawar won the Nobel Prize for Medicine for work on for work on acquired immune tolerance, which underpins organ transplantation. He was born in Brazil to a Lebanese father.
1966: The Fields Medal
Michael Atiyah won the Fields Medal, the most prestigious award for mathematics, in 1966. He was born in London to a Lebanese father and Scottish mother. Educated in Egypt, he spent much of his childhood in Cairo and Khartoum.
1988: Nobel Prize for Literature
Egyptian Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his body of work, including the Cairo Trilogy, which the Swedish Academy said formed “an Arabic narrative art that applies to all mankind”. He is still the only winner of the prize who wrote in Arabic.
1990: Nobel Prize for Chemistry
Elias James Corey won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for developing retrosynthetic analysis. He is an American of Lebanese descent.
1993: Wolf Prize for Chemistry
Egyptian Ahmed Zewail won the Wolf Prize for Chemistry. The Wolf Prize is an international award which has been presented to living scientists and artists every year in Israel by the Wolf Foundation since 1978.
1999: Nobel Prize for Chemistry
Zewail also won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for pioneering femtochemistry, which is the study of chemical reactions on extremely short timescales. He also won the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 1993.
2005: Nobel Peace Prize
Egyptian scientist Mohamed ElBaradei shared his Nobel Prize with the International Atomic Energy Agency, which he led.
2018: Wolf Prize for Chemistry
Omar M Yaghi, born in Jordan to a Palestinian refugee family, won the Wolf Prize in Chemistry in 2018 for work on metal-organic frameworks. He shared the prize with Japan’s Makoto Fujita. The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) condemned his acceptance of the award because the prize is awarded by an Israeli foundation.
2023: Nobel Prize for Chemistry
Moungi Bawendi won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots. He was born in France to a Tunisian father, but based in the US.
2025: Nobel Prize for Chemistry
Yaghi also won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for developing metal-organic frameworks. These are crystalline materials with large internal cavities that can capture and store gases, harvest water from air, and trap pollutants. He shared the prize with Susumu Kitagawa from Japan and Richard Robson from Australia.
What has the response been to RFK Jr’s comments about Arabs?
In a post on X, vaccine scientist Peter Hotez of the Texas Medical Center weighed in on historical Arab scholarship, saying, “It was the Arab scientists of the Middle Ages who kept Aristotle, Hippocrates, Galen alive to hand it down in the Renaissance.”
Broadcaster Mehdi Hasan described RFK Jr’s comments as “racist” and, in a post on X, wrote: “One of the men who won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry last year was a Palestinian-American, Omar Yaghi.”
The Council on American-Islamic Relations called for the US health secretary to be removed. It said: “To stand on a public stage as a sitting US cabinet official and dehumanise half a billion people – and millions of Muslim and Christian Arab Americans – with fabricated, white supremacist talking points is utterly disqualifying for public office. His sweeping erasure of Arab contributions to humanity is not only maliciously false, but it also fans the flames of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate at a time when communities are already vulnerable to bigoted attacks from other public officials nationwide.”

GECF member states concerned about impact of geopolitics on gas market stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:11:43 UTC
04:11:43 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Member states of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) have expressed concern regarding the impact of geopolitical developments, including those in the Middle East, on the stability of the gas market. They also highlighted increased investment risks and volatility in gas prices, according to the declaration adopted following the summit in Moscow.
"We, the Heads of State and Government of member countries of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, gathered on October 27, 2026, the year marking the 25th anniversary of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, for the eighth Gas Summit in Moscow <…> expressing our deep concern regarding the adverse impact of geopolitical developments, particularly in the Middle East, on the stability, security, and sustainability of the global gas market, including disruptions to gas supplies, heightened uncertainty regarding the security of gas supply and demand, increased investment risks, and significant volatility in gas prices," said the document released on the Kremlin’s website.
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum includes Russia, Iran, Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates, and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal are observer states. GECF members hold roughly 70% of the world’s proven gas reserves, account for 38% of global gas production and 42% of global gas exports, and represent 47% of global exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

Wydrzynska is charged with Isabella’s murder, while both parents have been charged with one count of causing or allowing the death of a child, four counts of causing or allowing serious physical harm to a child, two counts related to the sexual assault of a child and three counts of child cruelty.
The court heard both parents were known to social services and the police.
Isabella died in hospital after sustaining a series of injuries including a fractured skull and ribs, a broken arm and a burn to her entire face, the court was told.
In her opening statement to the court on Tuesday, Annabel Darlow KC said emergency services were called to the Wydrzynska’s home in the early hours of 7 January 2025 where Isabella was found “grey and lifeless”.
Medical experts later concluded Isabella died “because she suffered injuries consistent with a forceful direct impact to her head against a hard surface”, Darlow told the court.
Darlow said Wydrzynska was the only adult present at the home when Isabella was found by police and the injuries were the “devastating culmination of systematic physical abuse”.
“The prosecution say, by the time Isabella died, there was an entrenched pattern of abuse, neglect and mistreatment of the little girl of which both parents were entirely aware,” Darlow told the court.
“Before she died, Isabella was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of both her mother and father,” Darlow added. “Neither defendant has ever provided any explanation for those injuries to their daughter.”
Jurors were told Isabella was born in December 2023 and immediately taken into the care of social services. After being placed in emergency accommodation, Isabella was looked after by foster parents for four months before she was returned to her parents in April 2024 – nine months before her death, the court was told.
Members of the jury were also told Stasiak was arrested by police for common assault after a report was made by Wydrzynska on 14 December 2024, less than a month before Isabella’s death.
Wydrzynska made repeated attempts to withdraw the report, jurors were told. However, Stasiak was placed on police bail and prohibited from living at the family home or contacting Wydrzynska.
In addition, the court was told police officers had attended the family home after a complaint was made by a neighbour in October 2024.
Officers attended the property and were only responded to when the police threatened to force entry, Darlow said. Officers spoke to the parents and saw Isabella and “did not have any immediate safeguarding concerns” after the visit, the court was told.
The trial continues.

====================================================================================================

How a 20-Point Lead Became 2.8: Reading Bulgaria’s Presidential First Round
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:05:25 UTC
04:05:25 KST

A month before Sunday's vote, every major pollster had Iliana Yotova at least 17 points ahead of Andrey Gyurov and some had her within reach of 50 percent. When the Central Election Commission announced the official result, the incumbent president had 528,951 votes, or 34.76 percent, against Gyurov's 486,232, or 31.95 percent. The gap between them is 42,719 votes, a margin of 2.8 points, and both tickets go into the runoff on November 1 with the race effectively open.
Kostadin Kostadinov of "Revival" came third with 190,910 votes, or 12.55 percent, followed by Radostin Vassilev of MECH with 4.61 percent, Ivelin Mihaylov of "Greatness" with 3.79 percent and Ivan Hristanov with 2.39 percent. Another 67,353 people, 4.43 percent, chose the "I do not support anyone" option. Only 1,525,034 of the 6,584,025 registered voters took part, a turnout of 23.16 percent and the lowest of any national election since the fall of communism.
The headline numbers hide a more interesting story. The result was shaped less by voters changing their minds than by which voters bothered to show up and the biggest group that stayed home was the one that had handed Rumen Radev a parliamentary majority six months earlier.
Radev's Voters Did Not Come Back
In April, Progressive Bulgaria won 1,444,920 votes and 131 of 240 seats. On Sunday, the candidate it backed received just over a third of that. According to Alpha Research, only about 29 percent of Progressive Bulgaria's April voters took part in the presidential vote. Alpha's exit poll found that 74 percent of those backed Yotova, 11 percent Kostadinov and 9 percent Gyurov. Trend's exit poll puts her share among them slightly lower, at 71.2 percent, with 12.3 percent going to Gyurov.
Relatively few of Radev's voters defected to her rivals and most of them simply stayed at home. Several explanations are in circulation and they are not mutually exclusive. Six months in government have dented Radev's standing, with Bulgaria among the three EU countries with the highest inflation and the cabinet's cautious line on the Black Sea drone strikes drawing criticism. Polls showing a comfortable lead may have persuaded many supporters that their vote was not needed. And several commentators, from DW's Emiliya Milcheva to Ivan Bedrov in Svobodna Tochka, have questioned how hard Radev himself fought for his former vice president. They point to the case of Sonya Koltuklieva, a reporter for PIK who was knocked to the ground and injured by a National Service for Protection guard escorting Speaker Mihaela Dotsova on October 22. Yotova demanded the resignation of the service's chief, General Emil Tonev, who submitted it, but his dismissal requires the government's agreement and Radev declined to give it until an investigation is complete. Tonev remains in post.
Yotova's own campaign did not help. The "Petrich Escobar" pardon followed her throughout, as she first leaned on the medical commission's findings, then had to explain why a prisoner released on health grounds was again under investigation for drug trafficking and finally sent the file to the prosecutors, after which further questions could be refused on the grounds of investigative secrecy. Her refusal to debate before the first round and her pledge that no Bulgarian soldier would go to Ukraine, a decision that belongs to parliament, which ruled out such participation in February 2025, gave her opponents easy targets. As Novinite's profile put it before the vote, she ran as the status quo, and the status quo turned out to be less popular than the polls suggested.
How Gyurov Closed the Gap
Gyurov did the opposite. We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria won just over 400,000 votes in April, and Gyurov finished on more than 486,000, which means he mobilized his own camp and then reached beyond it. Trend's exit poll shows him taking 86.2 percent of PP-DB voters and, more significantly, 47.6 percent of the GERB voters who turned out, against 22.9 percent for Yotova. Alpha Research puts the GERB split at 39 percent to 22 percent. Whichever figure is closer, a sizable share of Boyko Borissov's electorate voted for Gyurov without any instruction from party headquarters.
His map was the map of urban, younger and educated Bulgaria. He won all three Sofia constituencies, taking 88,681 votes to Yotova's 35,767 in the 23rd alone, and carried Plovdiv city. Trend found him ahead among every age group under 40, with 42.5 percent among 18 to 29-year-olds, and among university graduates by 39 to 31.7 percent. Abroad he won 45.8 percent to Yotova's 22.8 percent, leading in Germany, the United Kingdom, Spain, France, Italy and the United States, while Yotova carried Turkey and Kostadinov topped the small count in Russia.
Yotova's strength lay where Radev's had in April: smaller towns, villages and older voters. She won 56.8 percent of the over-70s and almost every province outside the big cities, and in places like Haskovo, Pleven and Vratsa she polled more than double Gyurov's vote. Varna was closer, at 33,199 to 31,364. DW noted that Gyurov also benefited from being a comparatively new face, unworn by years in politics, which made him an easier choice for voters looking for an alternative to the governing camp without wanting to return to the old parties. Novinite's pre-election profile called his offer the balance, and a third of those who voted took it.
A Record Low Turnout and a Boycott in Plain Sight
Turnout of 23.16 percent is the lowest for any election since 1990, far below the previous low of 34.41 percent at the October 2024 parliamentary vote. Only the 2013 referendum on the Belene nuclear plant, at 20.22 percent, drew a smaller share of voters. In April, by comparison, 51 percent of voters had turned out. Pollsters had expected between 36 and 40 percent, and the gap between that forecast and reality explains much of why they misjudged the margin: their samples of likely voters included a large group of Progressive Bulgaria supporters who never arrived.
The drop was steepest in the strongholds of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS). Delyan Peevski's DPS did not field a candidate and in the week before the vote prosecutors arrested the DPS mayors of Belitsa and Sungurlare on corruption allegations and Kardzhali mayor Erol Mumun was taken in for questioning. Local party structures in Belitsa and Sungurlare called for a boycott. By 4 p.m. turnout stood at 5.65 percent in Belitsa, 5.91 percent in Yakoruda and 6.76 percent across the Kardzhali region. In Turkey, home to many Bulgarian citizens of Turkish origin, it fell to 15.95 percent from 34.63 percent in April. Mumun spent the day posting photos from a farmers' market. Alpha Research estimates that only about 15 percent of April's DPS voters, roughly 40,000 people, took part nationwide.
The boycott can be read as a demonstration of control, with Peevski showing that he can keep his voters at home as reliably as he can bring them out. Radev offered his own explanation for the low turnout, blaming PP-DB, GERB and DPS for convincing people through their constitutional changes and conduct in government that voting changes nothing.
Kostadinov's Partial Revenge
For Kostadinov, the result was a qualified success. Pro-Russian and nationalist Revival won 4.19 percent in April after Radev's new party swept up much of its electorate and on Sunday its leader took three times that share, finishing on 12.55 percent, above every pre-election poll. He fell well short of his prediction of reaching the runoff, finishing more than 295,000 votes behind Gyurov, but the score confirms that part of the nationalist vote Radev borrowed in April is drifting back. Novinite's profile described his campaign as the vengeance, and he has now collected part of the debt.
Together with Vassilev's 4.61 percent and Mihaylov's 3.79 percent, the three candidates can be grouped as the "nationalist vote," sharing a distrust of the EU and a closer view to Moscow's on the war in Ukraine, took almost 21 percent. That bloc is now the largest pool of votes in play and its first move has already complicated both finalists' plans, as the runoff preview explains.
What the First Round Tells Us
The clearest lesson is for Radev. A prime minister who won 1.44 million votes in April could not turn even half of them out for his chosen candidate six months later and whatever the mix of complacency, disappointment and lukewarm campaigning behind that, the government goes into the runoff weaker than it looked a week ago. Lyuben Obretenov wrote in Club Z that "political logic" had returned to Bulgaria after April's surprise, while Bedrov called the result a yellow card for the prime minister.
It is clear that the round exposed two strategic blunders. Yotova's team believed the 20-point leads in the polls and barely campaigned, counting on Radev's April voters and the Bulgarian Socialist Party and falling back on the familiar attacks that tied opponents to the Petrohan case and to warmongering. Moscow might have made the bigger mistake, striking ships off Romania and Bulgaria in the hope of frightening Bulgarians into backing a candidate seen as closer to the Kremlin. If that was the aim, the exit polls suggest it failed: fear appears to have moved mainly Revival's voters, toward Kostadinov, while pro-European voters rallied behind Gyurov. There is no evidence that the attacks were timed to influence the vote and Sofia has not formally attributed them, although EU leaders blamed Russia on October 16. The broader point stands on firmer ground. Neither the comfort of incumbency nor the language of fear produced the result the governing camp expected and a large part of the country showed it is not willing to hand every institution to a single political force without a contest.
For the opposition, Gyurov showed that a pro-Western candidate can expand beyond the PP-DB base when the alternative is a single camp controlling every institution and that GERB voters will act on their own when their party gives them no direction.
The turnout also leaves a problem for whoever wins. Fewer than one in four registered voters took part in choosing the two finalists and unless participation rises sharply on Sunday, the next president will take office with the votes of well under a fifth of the electorate. That is a thin mandate for an office whose main authority rests on being the one official the whole country elects.
This article is part of Novinite's editorial coverage of Bulgaria's 2026 presidential election. It was not commissioned or paid for by any candidate, party or initiative committee, and it does not endorse anyone.

Italy Delaying Transfer of Aster 30 Missiles to Ukraine Due to Political Disputes — Italian Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:01:14 UTC
04:01:14 KST

The Italian government is postponing approval of the 13th package of military aid to Ukraine, which is to include Aster 30 anti-aircraft missiles for the SAMP/T systems.
This was reported by La Repubblica, citing sources in Italian government circles.
According to the newspaper, the aid package has already been prepared, but its final approval is being delayed due to internal political disputes within Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s governing coalition.
La Repubblica’s sources claim that the Italian government may postpone the decision until the U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for November 3, in order to assess the Trump administration’s future policy toward Ukraine.
The document is to be signed by Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.
According to the publication, the delay is also linked to the position of the Lega party, led by Matteo Salvini, which opposes further arms deliveries to Ukraine.
Journalists note that approval of the package had already been postponed from July to September, and later to October. At the same time, according to La Repubblica, the last delivery of Italian military aid to Ukraine took place in December 2025.
Despite the delay, on October 26, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told ANSA that the new military aid package is already ready.
“We stand with Ukraine and will continue to help it for as long as necessary. The next military aid package is already ready, and we will send it to Kyiv as soon as possible,” Tajani said.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto also emphasized that Italy’s position on supporting Ukraine will not change, as Russian aggression poses a threat to the security of all of Europe.
In August, Militarnyi reported on Italy’s preparation of the 13th military aid package, which was to include Aster 30 missiles from the Italian Army’s stockpiles.
These missiles are used in the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense missile systems, which Ukraine employs to defend against Russian air attacks.
In July, France and Italy agreed to expedite the delivery to Ukraine of the previously agreed-upon number of Aster 30 missiles by October of this year.
In addition, Ukraine received licenses from France to manufacture a range of weapons, including Aster 30 anti-aircraft missiles, SCALP cruise missiles, and AASM Hammer air-to-ground bombs.

Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has traveled to the United States following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election, defying a Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports, two sources said.
The U.S. Embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro's lawyer also did not respond.
It was not immediately clear where Bolsonaro was heading, what time he would arrive or whether he would seek asylum. U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has previously alleged Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
Flavio's departure for the United States threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday's election on a U.S. State Department campaign to restore them to office.
Lula's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result to leftist Lula.
On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing, but that deadline has now lapsed, two other sources said, leading to his documents being canceled.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no plans to flee.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
Jair Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former U.S. President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned to Brazil but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
His son has yet to officially concede defeat - saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities - but his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory.
It remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not exited the country via any regular migration point.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move.
"If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

Mexico's electoral body pledges internal overhaul after corruption crisis
MEXICO CITY, Oct 27 - Mexico's National Electoral Institute (INE) promised on Tuesday to carry out an exhaustive, independent and transparent overhaul to guarantee its continuity, after its chief resigned over allegations of irregularities and corruption.
The leadership upheaval raises fresh questions over the credibility and stability of the autonomous authority as it prepares to oversee Mexico's 2027 midterm elections.

"It is a good time for whoever takes office to exercise transparency and ensure that no department within the National Electoral Institute favors any particular side, and that the Institute fulfills its duties," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said at her daily press conference.

"The provisional presidency has a clear responsibility: to facilitate dialogue, ensure institutional continuity, and contribute to the decisions that are being shaped through deliberation and consensus," Cruz said at the press conference.
Taddei resigned on Monday in the most high-profile departure tied to alleged corruption in Sheinbaum's two-year-old presidency. Sheinbaum said she supported Taddei's decision.
Mexico's Superior Audit Office is investigating alleged irregularities involving INE contracts, including possible conflicts of interest and the triangulation of public funds. Taddei, in local news outlets, has been accused of favoring an INE contractor, with whom she has a personal relationship, with contracts worth millions of dollars.
Cruz said the INE council was reviewing officials in decision-making roles, adding that three senior officials had already resigned: the heads of IT Services and the Gender Equality and Non-Discrimination Unit, and the official responsible for material resources. Taddei has not spoken publicly since resigning.
"Over the past few days, rumors, fabricated material, leaks, and versions of events have spread through the media and social networks, and as in all such cases, their authenticity, context, and purpose must be verified and corroborated," she said in a statement on Sunday announcing her planned resignation. The 'very uncomfortable' issue at the heart of Australia's national identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:00:15 UTC
04:00:15 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Ahead of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's appearance at Australia's national multiculturalism conference earlier this month, expectations were high.
It had been decades since a sitting prime minister had addressed the conference, which is run annually by the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia (FECCA) and brings together hundreds of community leaders, researchers and advocates to discuss policy and shape national conversations about migration, social inclusion and cultural diversity.
At a time of heightened community tensions, some hoped the prime minister would use the moment to deliver strong action in support of multiculturalism.
Instead, they were left feeling underwhelmed, describing his keynote address as a missed opportunity.
At the conference, which SBS covered as a media partner, the prime minister spoke positively about cultural diversity in his electorate of Grayndler, which spans parts of Sydney's inner west and has been home to many migrant communities over the years, including Greek, Italian, Portuguese, Lebanese, Islander and Vietnamese.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It means that you can walk around the streets of Marrickville and get groceries from the Filipino shop … [and eat] the best lamb you have ever had in your life [at a restaurant across from my old electorate office]," Albanese said in his speech.
Sociology professor Andrew Jakubowicz from the University of Technology Sydney says it's important that Albanese agreed to speak at the conference, "particularly as situations in Australia seem to be getting more tense and even violent", but he noted the prime minister made no tangible commitments.
"There was nothing said that suggested there was actually a strategy, and we're in an extremely difficult time," Jakubowicz tells SBS News.
[This is a] lost opportunity to make a significant statement about government commitments going forward.
Many of the experts SBS News has spoken with, including Jakubowicz, believe racism is on the rise in Australia, although this is largely based on anecdotal evidence.
There is no single body that consistently collects and reports on race and racism at a national level, so available data tends to be fragmented or infrequent.
A new report released today by the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) is calling for a nationally coordinated approach. It follows a similar recommendation made in 2024 as part of FECCA's Anti-Racism Framework, also commissioned by the AHRC.
Jakubowicz points out that recommendations from the framework, as well as a separate government-funded review on multiculturalism titled Towards Fairness, largely remain unactioned.
The failure to implement most of the significant elements of [the multiculturalism] review means that there is a level of disappointment and cynicism in the multicultural community.
"The government is quite comfortable about making the right noises, and very uncomfortable about doing anything to implement significant change."
Advocates are concerned that, without action, Australia's successful multicultural society may begin to fray.
'Disappointing' response to racism
According to the AHRC's Race Discrimination Commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, Australia has "clearly got a problem" with racism. He points to recent examples of "horrific racist violence", including an antisemitic attack at Bondi Beach that claimed the lives of 15 people, and an alleged act of terrorism at an Invasion Day rally in Perth.
He believes racism has increased online too, particularly following the failure of the Indigenous Voice referendum in 2023.
"When people talk about a lone wolf or a lone actor … that person is never alone," he says.
"They usually have been plugged into an online ecosystem that … taught them how to be violent.
"And it's led to the violence we see on the streets."
Sivaraman says he frequently hears about acts of racism that go unreported, including Muslim women having their hijabs ripped off, Jewish students being screamed at in the street, and young Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders being chased by people in cars.
But he says it's difficult to know the extent of the problem because there's no centralised system to collect data on racism in Australia — something the AHRC is pushing for as one of 16 recommendations in its Data for Change report released today.
The same recommendation was among those included in AHRC's anti-racism framework in November 2024, which Sivaraman says no level of government has endorsed, let alone implemented or funded.
"That is disappointing because it indicates they don't see it as a priority," he says.
He says an AHRC-commissioned audit of government responses to racism found it often involved knee-jerk reactions that pit communities against each other and increase racism or anger.
"There's no monitoring or evaluation of anti-racism work either," he says.
"That is not an effective way to deal with racism."
Jakubowicz says a lack of strategy to encourage intercultural engagement has meant that antagonism between different groups, fuelled in part by social media, has also been allowed to "fester and deepen".
He says much of the significant opposition to multiculturalism often stems from Islamophobia, including from those belonging to migrant communities.
It's one of the reasons some multicultural communities are signalling support for Pauline Hanson's One Nation, which has openly criticised Islam and broadly opposes Muslim immigration.
"One wouldn't necessarily expect to see people who have experienced racism being so strongly supportive of [One Nation], yet we're seeing that occur," he says.
"I think that's partly a consequence of the failure of government to engage meaningfully with the wider Australian population, [to build] cultural links and [address] questions of racism both within and between different migration communities."
Jakubowicz believes there's a need for a national multicultural commission, as well as a research and policy strategy to provide both policymakers and the public with credible, accessible information.
Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly says the government is taking action by strengthening hate crime laws, funding a national anti-racism campaign and establishing the Office for Multicultural Affairs.
"We’re taking a coordinated multi-faceted approach to combating racism, with action underway across a range of portfolios, so we can deliver practical, lasting change," she tells SBS News.
Multiculturalism at risk
Many experts, both at the FECCA conference and beyond, are calling for a similar kind of systemic change to address racism.
Sivaraman says this will ultimately benefit all Australians because it ensures systems and institutions become more transparent, responsive and accountable.
"It means that irrespective of race, gender, sexual identity, class, age [or] disability, a system or institution is inclusive."
He says racism can impede people at every step of their life journey, and dealing with it is critical to Australia being a successful multicultural country.
Racism is affecting kids who go to school, people who want to progress at work, people who are accessing health services, [and] those that encounter the justice system.
Mario Peucker, an expert in place-based anti-racism and associate professor at Victoria University, says data provides a foundation for identifying organisations where racist incidents occur, so pressure can be applied on them to take action.
He believes Australia's failure to address racism adequately is holding it back from achieving genuine multiculturalism — a state in which diverse racial, ethnic and cultural groups co-exist harmoniously.
"There is the need for reckoning with historic injustices, especially because they have ongoing implications for First Nations and multicultural communities."
Whole-of-government approach needed
Bulent (Hass) Dellal is a former director of SBS and chair of the panel that produced the multicultural review. He explains its aim was to identify ways to support a cohesive society in Australia following the COVID-19 pandemic.
The government endorsed the review's recommendations and acted in 2025 to elevate the position of minister for multicultural affairs to cabinet for the first time in Australia's history.
It also announced $85 million in reforms to better recognise the skills of migrants.
Dellal says the review's 29 recommendations are ambitious and acknowledges that full implementation will take time.
"But … one thing that has given communities less confidence is the lack of communication between government and communities about the next steps," he tells SBS News.
In particular, Dellal is concerned about progress on implementing a whole-of-government approach to multiculturalism, which he says has "remained limited".
It shouldn't be just one department being responsible for the reality of who we are — which is a multicultural Australia — it crosses over every department [and] every service provider.
"So, it is important that there is a level of coordination between governments and institutions … [as well as] accountability mechanisms, and these are still often unclear."
Australians need shared civic identity
Dellal says Australia's problem isn't that it doesn't support multiculturalism, but that it hasn't yet built a strong shared civic identity around it.
He points out that 83 per cent of Australian adults agree that "multiculturalism has been good for Australia" according to the Scanlon Foundation's 2025 Mapping Social Cohesion report, but many don't feel like they belong.
Only 46 per cent felt a sense of belonging in Australia "to a great extent", compared to 63 per cent in 2020.
But addressing this rift does not mean Australians of different ethnicities and backgrounds need to become "culturally identical", Dellal says.
He believes a shared Australian identity should be built around fairness, freedom, democracy and equal citizenship. These principles must be applied equally in everyday life for multiculturalism to thrive.
"Fairness must be visible in the workplace," Dellal says.
"Democracy must include the opportunity to be heard, to disagree and to help shape decisions.
"That shared civic identity is credible only when people can see the principles at work."

04:00:04 KST

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s broad and false claims about Arab contributions to humanity's scientific and literary discoveries at a Republican campaign event in Grand Rapids, Michigan, have drawn outrage just days before midterm elections.
"There's 500 million Arabs in the world and yet they don't produce science," Kennedy claimed on the campaign trail, on Monday. "They don't win the Nobel Prize. They don't win the Fields Prize. They don't win the Wolf Prize. They don't produce literature."
The health secretary's comments — widely condemned overnight by critics as untrue and racially biased — were made while campaigning in a state with a large Arab American population.
An HHS representative did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
Arab Nobel Prize winners
Egyptian law scholar Mohamed El Baradei, a diplomat and vice-president of Egypt, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2005 alongside the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Baradei and the IAEA, which he previously chaired, were awarded for their efforts to prevent nuclear energy from being used for military purposes.
Tawakkol Karman, a Yemeni journalist, politician, and human rights activist, was a co-recipient of the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the first Yemeni and the first Arab woman to win the award.
Ahmed Zewail, an Egyptian-American scientist, was awarded the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on femtochemistry.
Egyptian writer Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988.
Jordanian-born Omar M. Yaghi was one of three chemists awarded the Nobel Prize in 2025, and won the 2018 Wolf Prize in Chemistry. Sir Michael Atiyah, of Lebanese descent, was a Fields medalist in 1966.
Yasser Arafat, the former head of the Palestine Liberation Organization, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 for his “efforts to achieve peace in the Middle East."
Arafat died in 2004.
Former Egyptian President Anwar al-Sadat was a co-recipient of the Nobel Prize with then-Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin in 1978 after they signed the Camp David Accords, which ended Israel's occupation of the Sinai Peninsula.
The background of his comments Kennedy made the comments while campaigning for Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who has accused his opponent, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
"Mike Rogers was talking about the Muslim Brotherhood. That’s something I can talk about," Kennedy said.
Kennedy claimed that the world’s 500 million Arabs have not contributed to science or the humanities due to the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood, after he cited Islamic civilisation's contributions to literature in the 13th century.
RFK Jr fact-checked
Protect Our Care president Brad Woodhouse said in a statement that this wasn’t the first time RFK Jr “has trafficked in racism”, but it may be his "ugliest episode yet." Woodhouse was referring to Kennedy's comments on the "High Level Conversations" podcast in 2024, where he implied that Black children with ADHD and on medication should be “re-parented.”
"Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel in Literature in 1988. Ahmed Zewail won the Nobel in Chemistry in 1999, after winning the Wolf Prize. Omar Yaghi won the Nobel in Chemistry in 2025," X user Jordan Guy pointed out. "Algebra is an Arabic word. So is algorithm. The math on this claim doesn’t work."
Dr. Peter Hotez, founding dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor and Texas Children’s Hospital, posted on social media on Monday evening that his former colleague, Nobel Prize winner Zewail, would disagree with Kennedy.
"God rest his soul he didn’t have to endure this, and of course RFK Jr forgets that it was the Arab scientists of the Middle Ages who kept Aristotle, Hippocrates, Galen alive to hand it down in the Renaissance."
The Council on American-Islamic Relations, the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organisation, called for RFK Jr to be fired over the inaccurate comments.
"To stand on a public stage as a sitting US cabinet official and dehumanise half a billion people – and millions of Muslim and Christian Arab Americans – with fabricated, white supremacist talking points is utterly disqualifying for public office," CAIR said in a statement.
"His sweeping erasure of Arab contributions to humanity is not only maliciously false, but it also fans the flames of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate at a time when communities are already vulnerable to bigoted attacks from other public officials nationwide."
Scientists and historians have also emphasised that scholars during the Islamic Golden Age laid the foundations for modern optics, mathematics (including algebra and trigonometry), astronomy, and medicine, preserving vital scientific knowledge while Europe was in the Middle Ages.
Eyad Al-Hamoud, a Saudi Arabian influencer slammed Kennedy, citing four recent Nobel winners.
"The strongest part is that in the responses, they remind the secretary that under Arab rule, the greatest sciences emerged — ones we’re still living off to this day: Algebra and algorithms, development of trigonometry and equations, observatories, surgery and anesthesia, the hospital system, modern optics with Ibn al-Haytham, experimental chemistry and distillation, preparation of acids and water clocks (and much more besides)."
Kennedy is slated to serve as a special guest at the "Make Iowa Healthy Again Rally" in Des Moines on Wednesday.

Dmytro Svyatash holds both Russian and Ukrainian citizenship, but reportedly presented his Ukrainian passport during border control," the report reads.

According to the ruling, Svyatash must submit written comments and conclude the presentation of his position by 10:00 on Wednesday, after which the court will issue its decision.

Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:57:45 UTC
03:57:45 KST

Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools.
The memo, which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.
"We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."
Under CEO Andy Jassy, Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs."
As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment.
Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing, in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks.
In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity.
It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.
"We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.
Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.
The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said.
"Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those."
He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation."
Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task.
"If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo.
The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for."
