American, Israeli Jews report stronger bonds despite challenges of recent years, survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:14:31 UTC
03:14:31 KST

A new survey commissioned by the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA) has revealed that a large majority of American and Israeli Jews feel a deep and growing sense of shared connection, defying prevailing narratives of a widening chasm between the two communities.
Mimi Kravetz, chief impact and growth officer at JFNA, told The Jerusalem Post, “Over the last three years, a surge in Jewish engagement here at home has come alongside a rising sense of connection to Jews in Israel too.”
“Now there’s an opportunity to strengthen those connections using the kind of relationship-building strategies our data show work, including travel, shlichut [emissary work], and community partnerships that our communities have invested in for decades,” Kravetz told the Post.
Writing in a JTA op-ed on Monday, Kravetz and Rebecca Caspi, senior vice president for Israel and overseas and director general of JFNA’s Israel Office, shared the survey's findings, noting that the survey forms the first part of a two-part analysis exploring where the two communities are aligned and where they differ. “Part two will address where American and Israeli Jews see things differently, and why.”
Caspi and Kravetz pointed out that the last three years have been historic for both communities, marked by the trauma of October 7 and ensuing wars in Israel alongside a dramatic rise in security threats, antisemitism, and attacks on Zionism faced by American Jews at home. While it would be understandable if these separate challenges drove the two populations apart, the data reveals that they actually feel closer to one another than they have in years.
JFNA surveys over 4,000 American, Israeli Jews on shared identity and connection
The findings are detailed in the 2026 JFNA Bilateral Relationship Between American and Israeli Jews research initiative published on the Berman Jewish DataBank, which examined attitudes on peoplehood through two separate national surveys conducted earlier this year. The research comprised a national survey of 2,836 adult Jewish Americans conducted by Burson via text-message recruitment between May 4 and May 27, and a parallel survey of 1,323 Israeli Jewish adults conducted by Shmuel Rosner utilizing the Madad Israeli panel and a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) panel between May and June.
The study explored how both populations view their bilateral relationship, tracking a noticeable rise in what the report termed the “rise in peoplehood” since previous major assessments. According to the survey data, 75 percent of Israeli Jews reported feeling “a lot” or “some” commonality with Jews in the United States. On the American side, 72 percent of respondents reported feeling a similar connection with Israeli Jews, rising significantly from 59 percent in a 2020 Pew Research Center survey, with those reporting they have “a lot” in common jumping from 19 percent to 29 percent.
This strengthening bond is also reflected in how members of both communities characterize their relationship through family metaphors. Among American Jews, the share describing Israelis as extended family or part of their community climbed from 46 percent in 2021 to 62 percent, while those feeling no real connection dropped by more than half from 28 percent to 13 percent. Similarly, the proportion of Israeli Jews categorizing American Jews as extended family or part of their community rose from 45 percent to 53 percent, while those reporting nothing in common dropped from 14 percent to 10 percent.
When asked whether Jews around the world, regardless of where they live, share a common fate and must act accordingly, 78 percent of Israeli Jews and 56 percent of Jewish Americans agreed. Furthermore, strong majorities in both countries rejected the notion that diaspora life is a problem to be solved, with 72 percent of American Jews and 72 percent of Israeli Jews affirming that the Jewish Diaspora is a legitimate form of Jewish life.
The research highlighted that this connection translates directly into action, particularly through philanthropic support following the events of October 7, 2025. The Jewish federation system raised $908 million through its Israel Emergency Campaign to fund recovery efforts on the ground. 79 percent of Israeli respondents and 67 percent of American respondents agreed that American Jewish philanthropy remains important to Israeli society, while 68 percent of Israelis stated that post-October 7 giving made them feel Diaspora Jews genuinely care about Israel.
Travel to Israel strengthens American Jews' sense of shared identity
Beyond broad sentiment, the data demonstrates that physical presence and direct engagement dramatically multiply feelings of commonality between the two populations. Among American Jews, travel frequency correlates directly with a stronger sense of shared identity; those who have traveled to Israel once are 1.7 times as likely to feel real commonality with Israeli Jews, those who have traveled more than once are 3.8 times more likely, and those who have lived in Israel are 11.2 times more likely.
A similar dynamic exists on the Israeli side, where casual tourism does not significantly shift connection levels, but deeper immersion does. Israelis who participate in Jewish communal life while visiting the US are 2.8 times as likely to feel a sense of peoplehood, and those who serve as emissaries, work at summer camps, or live inside an active American Jewish community are 2.6 times as likely. Overall, 87 percent of Israeli Jews with real, engaged contact with American Jews feel commonality, compared to just 52 percent among those with no contact.
When American Jews were asked in open-ended discussions why they feel connected to Israel, the responses revealed a consistent set of core motivations. Respondents frequently pointed to seeing Israel as a safe place for Jews, viewing it as the historical homeland where Jewish identity began, and maintaining a belief that Jews are responsible for one another alongside religious or biblical ties. Others highlighted feeling more whole in Israel, recognizing the necessity created by the Holocaust, viewing Israel as part of their own culture, and taking personal pride in Israelis themselves.
Caspi and Kravetz noted that this reawakening of shared peoplehood directly corroborates findings from a separate, comprehensive study conducted by JFNA that tracked trends in Jewish life in the United States. That separate survey revealed that heightened community engagement, known as the “Surge,” had evolved into a sustained behavioral shift rather than a temporary reaction.
Specifically, the research showed that 38 percent of the American Jewish community is part of the Surge and has maintained an active increase in participation across three distinct areas: communal involvement like attending synagogues or joining advocacy groups, educational exploration, and social connection such as hosting private Shabbat dinners or participating in workplace affinity groups.
“We are in another challenging season for the Jewish people,” Caspi and Kravetz said. “It would be easy to conclude that we have more differences than we have commonalities, and to approach discussions from a place of distance and division. But there is an opportunity in this tense moment to recognize our deep sense that we are one community.”
JFNA urges greater investment in travel and community programs to strengthen Jewish ties
Regarding their recommendations for moving forward, Caspi and Kravetz stated, “Our data confirm that today we feel closer than ever, and we recognize that our lives are shaping each other’s. Perhaps even more importantly, our data show what we can do to strengthen and perpetuate this trend. We need to keep investing in things we know build a connection: more travel, more Israeli emissaries in North American communities, and more programs that put people in real contact.”
“And we need to scale innovation that will enable shared volunteer projects, philanthropic partnerships across both communities, stronger business and professional ties, and digital opportunities to learn from one another. These opportunities can ensure impact when travel is impractical, reach those who are less engaged, and ensure that this sense of connection to and understanding of Jews across the world is accessible to everyone in our greater Jewish family and community,” Caspi and Kravetz said.

Iraq deepens ties with Jordan as Baghdad looks to strengthen regional alliances - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:14:02 UTC
03:14:02 KST

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi visited Jordan on Monday for meetings with King Abdullah II and Jordanian Prime Minister Jafar Hassan, highlighting Baghdad’s efforts to strengthen relations with its western neighbor amid regional tensions. The visit resulted in the signing of nine cooperation documents and discussions about expanding trade, energy links, and security coordination.
Zaidi’s visit to Amman was his first official trip to the kingdom since taking office. It followed a visit to Saudi Arabia on October 14 and comes as Iraq is seeking to diversify its economic partnerships and strengthen ties with neighboring Arab countries.
According to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Zaidi returned to Baghdad after meeting Jordanian officials, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, and Iraqi businesspeople and investors. The visit included expanded bilateral talks and the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) covering higher education, environmental protection, consumer protection, diplomatic cooperation, cultural exchanges, and support for small and medium-sized enterprises.
The Iraqi Prime Minister’s Office said the discussions focused on increasing cooperation in economic, commercial, industrial, and security matters. “Jordan is a strategic partner for Iraq, and we look forward to more cooperation and joint coordination to deal with all the challenges and advance the consolidation of bilateral relations,” Zaidi said, according to his office.
The visit illustrates the importance of Jordan for Iraq at a time when Baghdad faces challenges involving Tehran, Damascus, and the security of its country’s borders.
Iraq, Jordan's historic ties rooted in shared Hashemite rule
Iraq and Jordan have longstanding historical, political, and economic ties. Both were ruled by branches of the Hashemite dynasty during the 20th century, until Iraq’s monarchy was overthrown in 1958. Jordan’s Hashemite monarchy continues to rule the kingdom today.
During the 1980s, Jordan became an important economic partner for Iraq. The port of Aqaba provided Iraq with access to international trade routes during the Iran-Iraq War, while the highway connecting Amman and Baghdad became an important commercial corridor.
Amman also maintained relations with Baghdad during Saddam Hussein’s rule, when Iraqi oil supplies and trade were important to the Jordanian economy.
The 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq transformed the relationship. Many Iraqis fled to Jordan as refugees. Extremists also threatened Jordan from Iraq. In subsequent years, the rise of the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria posed another challenge to relations between Baghdad and Amman. ISIS invaded Iraq in 2014. This presented threats to Jordan. The US deployed forces to Jordan and to Al-Tanf military base in Syria near the Jordan-Syria-Iraq border.
Iraq and Jordan have a border that is almost 180 km. long. Trade is important and could grow over the next few years. The security of Anbar Province in Iraq is therefore essential. The province covers a vast area of western Iraq and borders Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia. Its location makes it strategically important for transportation, trade, and regional security.
The importance of this cooperation was underscored by the recent attack on a church in Jordan’s Karak Governorate. Nine people were murdered and 40 wounded in the October 23 attack. Jordanian security forces subsequently arrested three suspects.
Iraq, Jordan discuss proposed duty-free economic zone to boost trade
Economic cooperation was a central focus of Zaidi’s visit. This comes as no surprise since he was a banker before becoming prime minister. According to Rudaw, he emphasized the importance of establishing a duty-free economic zone between Iraq and Jordan. Zaidi said the proposed free zone would increase trade and economic cooperation between the two countries.
Jordanian Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also stressed the importance of implementing existing economic projects.
“We want to move joint economic projects between the two countries to the stage of actual ground implementation, following practical steps and clear timelines,” Hassan said, according to Jordan’s Petra news agency, as quoted by Rudaw.
The nine agreements signed during the visit represent efforts to expand cooperation across several sectors.
However, the announced documents did not include a specific agreement establishing the proposed free trade zone.
Jordan previously imported between 10,000 and 15,000 barrels per day of Iraqi crude oil under a bilateral agreement, reports indicate. According to Rudaw, deliveries have been suspended since late December 2025 following the expiration of the agreement and difficulties obtaining suitable crude.
Jordan’s Energy Ministry said the kingdom imported approximately 2.76 million barrels of Iraqi oil throughout 2025. Another major project under discussion is the proposed Basra-Aqaba oil pipeline, which would connect Iraq’s southern oilfields to Jordan’s Red Sea port. The pipeline could provide Iraq with an alternative export route and reduce its dependence on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq is also increasing exports through Syria.
Jordan offers Iraq both a commercial partner and a potential alternative route for exporting oil.
The two countries also participate in a trilateral cooperation mechanism with Egypt, focused on energy, electricity, infrastructure, and trade. Zaidi is slated to visit Cairo on November 23, according to Egyptian officials cited by Rudaw.
The visit to Jordan also comes as Zaidi is expected to travel to Syria for talks with officials in Damascus. According to previous reporting by Kurdistan24, the Iraqi prime minister had planned to visit Syria before traveling to Jordan, but the trip was postponed.
Iraq seeks stronger ties with Jordan, Syria to secure borders and reduce reliance on Iran
The proposed visit to Damascus is important because Iraq’s western border security is closely tied to developments in Syria.
For Baghdad, improving relations with both Jordan and Syria could help reopen commercial routes and reduce dependence on infrastructure and trade corridors linked to Iran or the Persian Gulf. Security also remains a major issue. Iraq must maintain control of its borders, prevent militant infiltration, and address the influence of armed factions operating within the country.
Jordan has its own concerns about instability in Syria, particularly along its northern border, where smuggling networks and armed groups have posed security challenges. These shared concerns create opportunities for greater coordination among the three countries.
Zaidi’s visit to Jordan reflects a broader effort by Baghdad to strengthen relations with Arab neighbors while managing its complicated relationship with Iran. Iraq has economic and political ties with Tehran, but it is also seeking to expand trade, investment, and energy cooperation with Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other regional partners. This could wean it of Iranian influence. Iraq is doing the heavy lifting now for the future. Jordan and Syria are part of this vision.
This would essentially reunite the three Arab kingdoms that almost came into being in the 1920s. France, at the time, moved into Syria, pushing the Hashemites into Iraq and Jordan. The pan-Arab Ba’ath Party then came to power in Syria and Iraq.
For Jordan, closer ties with Iraq offer economic benefits and opportunities for greater regional integration. The next stage will depend on whether the agreements signed in Amman lead to practical results.
A proposed free-trade zone, electricity interconnection projects, and the Basra-Aqaba pipeline are among the initiatives that could deepen bilateral relations.
The greater question is whether Iraq can translate these diplomatic initiatives into new economic corridors and stronger regional partnerships. Much work remains to be done. Keeping Iran from destabilizing Iraq is vital.

Auterion Developed Talon Interceptor With Rifle-Style Launch System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:13:52 UTC
03:13:52 KST

The German company Auterion has developed the Talon interceptor, which is launched from a handheld, rifle-style launcher.
The company reported that the interceptor has undergone testing by the German Army.
“Whether it’s a single drone or a swarm, Talon can take on both,” Auterion stated.
The handheld launcher enables mobile units to quickly intercept aerial targets in the field.
Talon destroys enemy drones through direct impact rather than detonating its warhead near the target.
The interceptor runs on the AuterionOS operating system.
According to the company, the drone ensures stable navigation and precise target acquisition even in the absence of a GPS signal or when subjected to powerful electronic warfare measures.
The fire-and-forget autonomous mode means that, once launched, the onboard tracking and terminal homing system carries out the interception without further operator intervention.
The exact specifications of the Talon have not been disclosed. However, the company previously unveiled a similar interceptor that is also launched from a handheld launcher.
Its interception speed reaches 60 m/s, its maximum range is 5 km, and its interception altitude is up to 2,000 meters.
The sensor’s operating range is 600 meters, and the claimed probability of hitting the target exceeds 80%. The reload time is less than 60 seconds.
The interceptor combines a high-speed glider, manufactured using 3D printing, with Auterion software. The ability to operate without a GPS signal is ensured by visual guidance during the final phase of flight.
The FLIR Boson 640 LWIR thermal imaging sensor enables the detection of targets day and night, including in low-visibility conditions.
The modular airframe, manufactured using 3D printing, simplifies mass production and allows for rapid replacement of parts in the field.
The system features a multi-tiered architecture and expands the capabilities of short-range air defense for mobile units and fixed installations within distributed command and communication systems.
The SkyBase GCS ground control station, combined with Auterion Mission Control, allows users to plan missions, track their progress, and control the system from a portable station. Mission abort and loitering functions enable the operator to maintain control over mission execution.
The German company is actively collaborating with Ukraine. Previously, Auterion and the Ukrainian company Airlogix began production of more than 5,000 drones for Ukraine.

Swedish border police detain former Ukrainian MP sentenced in absentia to 12 years in prison

Source: Swedish newspaper Expressen, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sviatash is currently being held at the Swedish Migration Agency's temporary detention centre in Märsta.
He arrived in Sweden last week, landing at Arlanda Airport on Thursday.
His lawyer, Mark Safaryan, said Sviatash had travelled to Stockholm to attend a Stevie Wonder concert.
The former MP was detained by border police at passport control and denied entry to Sweden.
Sviatash holds both Russian and Ukrainian citizenship but reportedly presented his Ukrainian passport at border control.

In addition, the former MP has been under suspicion of treason since 2023.
Sviatash fled Ukraine in 2019 and has lived in Russia ever since. He served as a member of Ukraine's parliament from 2002 to 2019 and was a member of the Party of Regions.

Adalah, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, said on Tuesday that it had received numerous reports from Arab voters of attempts to discourage them from casting their ballots. Adalah said it had also been told that queues at polling stations in Arab-majority towns were moving very slowly and, in some instances, had stopped altogether. It also reported a lack of ballot slips printed in Arabic.
The rights group said it had reported the events to Israel’s Central Elections Committee and Regional Elections Committees.
Palestinian politician Sami Abu Shehadeh, who leads the Balad party, praised Palestinian citizens in Israel in a post on X.
“There are racists for whom these pictures are frightening, but for us, they encourage us and we’ll continue with all our might! I call on Arab citizens to continue coming out in droves, it’s in our hands!” Abu Shehadeh said.
Netanyahu has claimed that his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, would be unable to govern without the support of Arab parties. However, Eisenkot has ruled out working with any, citing a lack of shared values.

The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel said Tuesday that Israeli forces had killed 1,080 Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, between Oct. 7, 2023, and Sept. 30, Anadolu reports.
Presenting the findings during a hybrid briefing, with all three members participating virtually, Srinivasan Muralidhar of India said the commission documented the deaths and thousands of injuries during the period.
Muralidhar said the fatalities included at least 784 men, 237 boys, 22 women and seven girls.
He said 10,009 Palestinians had also been injured by Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
The commission called for the international community to take stronger measures regarding Israel’s occupation and settlement activities, urged all states not to recognize the occupation or settlements as lawful and not to provide political, military or economic assistance that helps maintain them.
“Unless there is sufficient pressure brought upon by the international community, and in particular the Security Council upon Israel to honor its commitments and international law … and to take decisive action in stopping Israel from continuing with its acts of genocide in Gaza and crimes against humanity in West Bank, we are not going to see any resolution, immediate resolution, to the very, very grave crisis,” said Muralidhar.
He also urged international actors, particularly the US, to reconsider assistance to Israel, arguing that greater pressure was necessary to halt “this continuing campaign of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.”
Chris Sidoti, an Australian member of the commission, said that its legal analysis had concluded that Israel, “through its political and military authorities, was responsible for the commission of crimes against humanity, of extermination, persecution, torture, rape, and other sexual violence in the West Bank, including through the intentional targeting of Palestinian civilians.”
Florence Mumba of Zambia, another commission member, said Israeli authorities and settlers were seeking to acquire more land and displace Palestinians through violence and mistreatment.
“It’s obvious that the aim by the Israeli authorities and the settlers is to get as much land as possible, get the Palestinians out of the area by ill-treating them, killing them, sexual violence against them, killing the children,” she said.
The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, has seen escalating Israeli military attacks and occupier violence since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

Two days after his crushing presidential election defeat, Brazil was left wondering Tuesday evening where Flavio Bolsonaro had disappeared to. Amid speculation and reports that he might have attempted to flee overland into Argentina, where his political ally, right-wing President Javier Milei, is in power, Argentine authorities said they had no record of Bolsonaro entering the country. Bolsonaro's aides, meanwhile, either declined to say where he was or said they did not know. Brazilians can enter neighboring Argentina using only a national identity card, without a passport.
The Argentine government's statement followed local media reports earlier Tuesday that a private aircraft had landed at Iguazu International Airport, near the Argentina-Brazil border. Authorities inspected the aircraft and its crew but found no flight plan listing members of the Bolsonaro family. A spokesperson for Milei, who has yet to congratulate Lula on his victory, said that "there is no asylum request," declining to provide further details. A senior Brazilian Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not left the country through any official border crossing.
Paulo Figueiredo, a right-wing social media influencer who serves as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family, declined Tuesday afternoon to answer questions about the politician's whereabouts. In a statement, he wrote: "After months of intense work that has been unfairly thwarted, I am not in the mood to speak to the press. If I have any comments to make on any matter, I will get in touch."
Another source close to Bolsonaro said he had been unable to reach him. "I tried to talk to Flavio this morning by phone," the source said. "It rang and it rang, but he didn't pick up."
A film, $12 million and a missed 24-hour deadline
Bolsonaro had been considered the favorite to win Sunday's decisive second round of Brazil's presidential election, leading Lula by 1 to 2 percentage points in opinion polls. But when the votes were counted, he had lost by more than 3.5 percentage points, receiving 48.21% of the vote against Lula's 51.79%. 
The count began late following a decision to extend voting by two hours, prompting Bolsonaro to allege irregularities and announce that he would not recognize the results, just as his father, Jair Bolsonaro, had done after narrowly losing to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. On Monday, however, the younger Bolsonaro's party announced that it recognized Lula's victory.
On Monday, the Supreme Court gave Flavio Bolsonaro 24 hours to surrender his passports amid several ongoing investigations against him, including a complex corruption, money laundering and tax evasion case in which he acknowledged seeking around $12 million from former banker Daniel Vorcaro to finance a film about his father's life. The younger Bolsonaro denies any wrongdoing and promised to hand over his passports, but by Tuesday evening it emerged that he had failed to do so, prompting authorities to cancel them.
The order requiring him to surrender his passports, making it more difficult for him to leave Brazil, came amid fears that he might follow in the footsteps of his father, Jair, who flew to the United States after refusing to concede defeat four years ago and remained there for an extended period. The elder Bolsonaro eventually returned to Brazil, where he was later arrested and sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup.
The demand to confiscate Flavio Bolsonaro's passports also followed a statement by his younger brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in the United States and said that an election defeat would require Flavio to leave Brazil. "If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," Eduardo told podcaster Steven Crowder on October 23.
On Monday, after the election defeat and the order to surrender his passports, Flavio Bolsonaro said in an Instagram video: "I never thought about leaving the country. I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this outrage, which is clearly an attempt to intimidate me, but no one will silence me."
U.S. President Donald Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaro family, also weighed in on Brazil's election Monday, joining efforts to cast doubt on the results and claiming without evidence that the vote had been rigged.
"It looked terrible to me," Trump told reporters before boarding Air Force One. "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election, frankly." He added that elections should be beyond dispute and that the Brazilian vote had looked very bad to him.
Throughout his campaign, Flavio Bolsonaro had promised to strengthen ties with the United States if elected. His defeat this week dealt a blow to Trump's ambitions to further expand his influence in Latin America, where Brazil is the largest country by both area and population, following a series of victories by right-wing politicians in the region, including Chile, Peru and Colombia.
Lula, who has taken strongly critical positions toward Israel, frequently clashes with Trump and has accused him of improperly interfering in Brazil's election. In his victory speech Sunday, Lula delivered a pointed message to the American president, promising that under his leadership, "Brazil is nobody's backyard."

Italy’s Ukraine aid package stalls ahead of U.S. midterms, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:06:08 UTC
03:06:08 KST

- Italy’s 13th military aid package for Ukraine, expected to include Aster 30 missiles, remains frozen ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, La Repubblica reported.
- Rome had promised Macron and Zelenskyy approval by the end of October, but the Copasir committee has not yet been called to review it.
Italy’s 13th military aid package for Ukraine, which is expected to include Aster 30 air defense missiles, is ready but frozen, and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government appears to be waiting for the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 before moving it forward, La Repubblica reported Tuesday.
If the delay continues, Rome would miss a deadline it set with French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to the newspaper, Meloni’s government had promised both leaders the package would be approved by the end of October. With four days left in the month, the parliamentary committee that must be briefed on the package had not been called to meet, and the paper reported no sign that a meeting was imminent.
That committee, known as Copasir, oversees Italy’s intelligence services. Italian aid to Ukraine has been classified since 2022, and the government presents each package to Copasir before it moves forward. The previous 12 packages were authorized through interministerial decrees.
La Repubblica reported that the package has been pushed back several times: first from July, then from September, then until after a congress of the League, a party in Meloni’s governing coalition, and now until after the American vote. The government’s public statements have stayed general, the paper said, and officials in Rome are handling the issue with a mix of caution and embarrassment.
The most pressing item for Kyiv is the Aster 30, an interceptor missile fired by the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense system. Ukraine uses it to protect Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks. Its targets include aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. La Repubblica wrote that only Italy, together with France, can supply the missile.
The October deadline traces back to July. After meeting Macron, Zelenskyy said Italy and France would speed up deliveries of Aster 30 missiles so they would arrive by October 2026.
In August, La Repubblica reported that the 13th package would center on air and missile defense. The paper said it would include four SAMP/T NG batteries, the newest version of the system, along with Aster 30 interceptors and seven long-range radars. It put the package’s value at nearly 3 billion euros ($3.5 billion), funded through European Union loans. The Italian government has not confirmed what the package contains.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto pushed back on those reports at the time. He said they gave the impression the package had already been approved, and that no new aid package for Ukraine had been formally adopted in 2026.
A Copasir briefing planned for Aug. 5 was also postponed, Italian media reported at the time. The reports cited concern in the government about public support and opposition to further arms deliveries from parts of the political right.
La Repubblica reported that Italy’s last shipment to Ukraine was made about 10 months ago. Pagella Politica, an Italian fact-checking outlet, found that deliveries authorized under earlier packages continued during 2026, even though no new package had been approved.

Ukraine Puts First Test Satellite for Its Own Communications Network Into Orbit
Ukrainian radio maker HIMERA and Danish nanosatellite company GomSpace have put into orbit OBRIA NANO, the first test satellite for an independent Ukrainian communications network.
HIMERA told Militarnyi on October 27 that the satellite launched on October 1, as part of SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The company said that the satellite “is successfully undergoing tests of the OBRIA constellation’s capabilities in line with the plan.” The technical trials are intended to provide the company with the practical experience it needs to develop the project and integrate it into Ukraine’s national infrastructure.
A Ukrainian operator will control OBRIA NANO, and the satellite will serve the country’s strategic security. HIMERA co-founder and CEO Misha Rudominskyi described the launch as a first step. “This is an opportunity to lay the foundation of Ukraine’s independent communications network,” he stated.
“We are starting by testing the technology in orbit, and our long-term goal is to develop capabilities that will strengthen the state’s strategic security and reduce dependence on external communications service providers,” Rudominskyi said.
The initiative envisions a constellation of satellites that covers all of Ukraine and complements European satellite networks. HIMERA noted that building such capabilities at home will help Ukraine diversify its communication channels and strengthen its strategic security.
GomSpace CEO Carsten Drachmann welcomed the partnership. “Our shared goal is to strengthen Ukraine’s independent communications potential and to support its long-term security and economic development,” he added.
The next major stage will be localizing the production of satellites and ground terminals in Ukraine.
Denmark’s support for Ukraine’s push to build strategic capabilities beyond the reach of Russian strikes extends well beyond space.
On October 21, Copenhagen agreed to guarantee a $112.6 million loan to the Danish subsidiary of Fire Point, the Ukrainian manufacturer behind the FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missile.
The state backing, provided through Denmark’s Export and Investment Fund (EIFO), was needed because the war prevents the company from borrowing on ordinary commercial terms.
Fire Point is preparing to produce long-range missile fuel in Denmark, with the facility expected to begin operations by the end of 2027.

Household chaos does not directly cause poor grades, twin study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:00:18 UTC
03:00:18 KST

Children who grow up in noisy, disorganized homes often perform worse in school, but a recent study suggests this link is driven by shared genetics and family environments rather than the home’s chaotic nature itself. Researchers found that while household chaos and educational achievement negatively influence each other over time, the relationship is mostly non-causal. The findings were published in the journal Learning and Individual Differences.
Household chaos refers to the level of noise, crowding, and lack of routine that a child experiences in their daily home life. These environments lack predictability, which can cause stress and overstimulation. Prior research consistently shows a correlation between a chaotic home and lower academic performance. It is easy to assume that the noise and disorganization directly distract children from learning.
Yet the relationship between a child’s environment and their development is rarely a one-way street. Children who excel in school might bring their focused habits home, reducing the overall noise and clutter. Those who struggle academically might contribute to a more disorganized home environment. To test these directional influences, researchers need to isolate the effects of the environment from the effects of family background.
Family background includes socioeconomic status, which encompasses parental income, education, and occupation. It also includes genetics, which heavily influence both cognitive abilities and behavioral traits. Because siblings share both their home environment and a portion of their DNA, parsing out what causes differences in school performance requires specialized data. A team of psychologists led by Sophie von Stumm at the University of York sought to untangle whether household chaos actually drives poor educational outcomes, or if both are simply symptoms of shared family traits.
The researchers analyzed data from a large study of 7,591 twin pairs born in the United Kingdom in the mid-1990s. Identical twins share all of their genes, while fraternal twins share about half of their segregating genes. By comparing how similar identical twins are compared to fraternal twins, scientists can estimate how much of a trait is due to genetics versus the environment. Environments are further divided into shared environments, which affect both twins equally, and non-shared environments, which represent unique individual experiences.
The twins in the study reported their perceptions of household chaos at ages nine, twelve, and sixteen using a standard psychological questionnaire. At those same ages, the researchers gathered data on the twins’ educational achievement through teacher ratings and standardized national exam scores. The team then applied a statistical method that analyzes variables across multiple time points while separating genetic and environmental influences. This technique allowed them to track how chaos at age nine predicted achievement at age twelve, and how achievement at age nine predicted chaos at age twelve.
The team observed that higher household chaos at early ages predicted lower educational achievement later on. The reverse was also true, with lower achievement predicting greater subsequent household chaos. The effect sizes for these bidirectional predictions were relatively small. If left at this surface level, the data might suggest a cycle where bad grades cause stress at home, which in turn causes worse grades.
When the researchers decomposed these pathways into genetic and environmental components, the results contradicted the idea of a direct cause and effect. If changes in one trait directly caused changes in the other, those pathways would be driven primarily by non-shared environmental factors. Instead, the team found that the associations were largely due to family-level confounding. The long-term associations between a child’s experience of chaos and their school performance did not reflect causal mechanisms.
To refine their understanding, the researchers ran the model again, this time adjusting the data for family socioeconomic status. After controlling for parents’ education, occupation, and income, the pathway from early educational achievement to later household chaos was entirely explained by shared genetics. Socioeconomic status is known to have a genetic component, and adjusting for it absorbed the remaining shared environmental factors in that direction. This suggests that the same genetic factors influencing a child’s academic success also shape the environment they experience.
In the reverse direction, the pathway from early household chaos to later educational achievement was completely explained by shared environmental factors. Adjusting for socioeconomic status did not change this result. This means that while household chaos predicts later school performance, the prediction is driven by other environmental factors shared by the siblings that are apart from traditional measures of family income or parental education. These might include shared neighborhood conditions, the quality of local schools, or specific parenting styles.
The study relies on a shortened six-item questionnaire to measure household chaos. A brief survey might not capture the full scope of a child’s home environment, which can increase measurement error. The reliance on children’s own reports of their homes introduces a layer of subjectivity. A child’s perception of chaos might reflect their internal psychological state or distress rather than an objective measure of noise and crowding in the physical house.
The statistical model used in the analysis also merges the differences between individuals with the changes occurring within a single person over time. Advanced analytical tools that completely separate these two types of variation in twin studies are not yet available. Without that separation, it is difficult to determine exactly how a specific change in one child’s life alters their personal future trajectory.
Because the study demonstrates that the link between household chaos and academic success is primarily due to shared genetics and broader family environments, simple interventions to organize a home or reduce noise might not improve school grades. Researchers aim to pinpoint the exact shared environmental factors that drive these outcomes. Uncovering these underlying mechanisms will help policymakers design better systems to support children from disadvantaged backgrounds.
The study, “The developmental interplay between household chaos and educational achievement from age 9 through 16 years: A genetically sensitive study,” was authored by Sophie von Stumm, Alexandra Starr, Ivan Voronin, and Margherita Malanchini.

Kyiv without power: how long will the capital be able to remain supplied with water during a prolonged blackout
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:00:15 EET
03:00:15 KST

Kyiv without power: how long will the capital be able to remain supplied with water during a prolonged blackout
Kyiv • UNN
Half of Kyiv’s water supply facilities have backup power, but the duration of autonomous operation has not been specified. The city is preparing water-pumping stations and water deliveries.
The missile-and-drone strikes on Kyiv in October this year demonstrated the vulnerability not only of the capital’s energy system, but also of its water supply and wastewater systems. The vast majority of pumps supplying water to hundreds of thousands of apartment buildings in the city depend on the main power supply system. And just one prolonged emergency or stabilization power outage is enough for water to stop reaching Kyiv residents’ homes.
Whether Kyiv is equipped with backup systems to power the pumps, which areas of the city risk being left completely without water this winter, and whether the capital has an alternative to its centralized water pipeline was investigated by UNN.
Will Kyiv have water during a large-scale blackout?
At the beginning of October, the repeated loss of power at water-supply facilities in Kyiv caused a widespread drop in water pressure in the Shevchenkivskyi, Solomianskyi, and Holosiivskyi districts of Kyiv. Some buildings did not receive water at all. And in many high-rise buildings, residents could not use washing machines, dishwashers, or boilers because of the low pressure.
To determine whether such a scenario could recur in late autumn and winter, UNN contacted PJSC Kyivvodokanal for an explanation. The company explained that in the event of a large-scale power outage in Kyiv, water would not necessarily disappear from all buildings simultaneously. Generators would support some facilities, while artesian wells and water-pumping stations would serve as backup sources.
The company is taking all necessary measures to properly protect and operate critical infrastructure facilities under martial law in Ukraine. As of today, all water-supply facilities in the capital are operating normally
How long can water supply operate without electricity?
The editorial team asked the company how long consumers would continue to receive water in the event of a complete or partial power outage. However, Kyivvodokanal did not provide any specific time frames.
Meanwhile, public-utilities experts explain that a water-supply system is a complex network of stations, pipelines, and pumps. It is not a single "reservoir" with a fixed supply of water, so its resilience depends on the scale of the accident, the possibility of switching to backup power, the availability of fuel for generators, and the preservation of pressure. In the event of a partial power outage, the water situation may differ substantially in various parts of the city.
In particular, in comments to Ukrainian media, Oleksandr Kravchenko, head of the Department of Water Supply and Wastewater Management at the Kyiv National University of Construction and Architecture, explained the operating principle of large pumping stations, saying that they consume as much electricity as an entire urban neighborhood. Therefore, if the network becomes completely empty, restoring water supply to remote consumers may take significantly longer than the power outage itself.
Generators and backup power: how protected is Kyiv’s system?
According to data from the Kyiv City Council, as of October 13, Kyivvodokanal had received 103 generators for use, with capacities ranging from 15 kW to 1 MW.
The company’s General Director Ihor Palamar, in turn, confirmed that approximately half of the water-supply system’s facilities had received backup power.
We are increasing the number of backup power sources; the delivery of additional high-capacity equipment is expected, and the technical possibilities for redistributing water between individual sections of the system are also being used
He also noted that in a difficult situation, artesian wells could provide Kyiv residents and visitors to the capital with drinking water. However, this would cover only minimum needs.
Returning to the issue of purchasing backup power sources, it should be emphasized that (according to information in the Prozorro system), in September 2026, contracts totaling UAH 615.64 million were signed to equip 13 facilities with backup power supplies. The deadline for completing the work is March 27, 2027.
In a letter received by UNN in response to its written inquiry, the enterprise did not specify the status of implementation of these contracts. In other words, signing contracts for the purchase and installation of generators is no guarantee that the equipment will operate throughout the winter and be able to power the pumps during prolonged blackouts.
Are all districts of Kyiv protected from power supply interruptions and guaranteed to retain water
Kyivvodokanal did not provide the editorial office with a list of districts that are guaranteed to retain water during a blackout. It cited the fact that disseminating information about critical infrastructure facilities could lead to disruptions in the provision of essential services and, in turn, result in negative consequences for Ukraine’s national security.
What will happen to the sewage system during a prolonged power outage
Another problem Kyiv residents will face during prolonged power outages is the stoppage of the sewage system. To understand the issue, it is worth recalling how sewage systems operate in high-rise buildings.
Some wastewater moves through pipes by gravity, but it is then pumped onward by sewage pumping stations. If the pumps stop for an extended period, wastewater may accumulate, networks may become overloaded, and localized accidents may occur. The risk depends on the duration of the shutdown and the possibility of activating backup power.
On October 13, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko assured Kyiv residents that the capital’s wastewater disposal system was equipped with backup power sources. Somewhat later, Kyivvodokanal confirmed that the pumps used to remove sewage were operating on generators. In particular, the enterprise’s statement said that four sewage pumping stations that had lost electricity due to Russian shelling of the capital continued operating thanks to generators.
However, experts view the situation skeptically and explain that operating on a generator is no guarantee of unlimited pump autonomy.
What Kyiv utility workers will do in the event of a total power outage
Ihor Palamar, CEO of Kyivvodokanal, assured UNN that he had developed scenarios for the operation of water supply stations during partial and total blackouts. They had even already been rehearsed during practical and command-and-staff exercises.
Thus, for local water supply and wastewater disposal zones, utility workers planned to use diesel generators. In addition, the enterprise’s facilities were equipped with points for filling containers with drinking water. If necessary, district state administrations are to deliver it to predesignated distribution locations.
How Kyiv residents can prepare for possible water supply disruptions
Experts in the utilities sector warn Kyiv residents that even with city generators available, they should not count on an uninterrupted water supply.
People are advised to have at least 3 liters of drinking water and 11–12 liters of non-potable water per person per day. It is advisable to stock up for at least three days, storing drinking water separately from water for household needs.
Boreholes may serve as an alternative. According to data from the city authorities, more than 170 borehole complexes are currently operating in Kyiv, 154 of which, as of January 2026, had the ability to connect to a generator. However, here too, one should not assume that all 154 boreholes will be able to switch to a backup power source in time. Nor is it certain that they will be able to supply water of appropriate quality.
Therefore, the Kyiv City Center for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that Kyiv residents and visitors, in the absence of a centralized water supply, use bottled water, official water distribution points, and verified sources. If the water quality is in doubt, it should not be consumed without proper purification or disinfection.
Reminder
Earlier, UNN reported that water supply disruptions were possible in five districts of Kyiv due to reduced pressure.

Will AI crush the things that make life meaningful?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Economic lifeline or dark force? The questions policymakers aren't grappling with on AI
Do policymakers know what dark forces they're messing with?
In their rush to force AI on us, they're embracing a technology that is exceptionally good at destroying the things that give our lives meaning.
AI has radically devalued the skills of artists, writers, and musicians.
In recent weeks, we've seen footage of mathematicians crying because AI has triggered an existential and spiritual crisis for their profession.
Mathematics professor Francesco Maggi, when discussing the "remarkable ability" that large language models (LLM) have to generate mathematical proofs, says the technology poses a challenge to something deeply human.
So what are we doing?
Do policymakers appreciate that people are extremely concerned about a technology that has a powerful ability to devalue human creative expression?
We're living in a world of major system collapse, and policymakers are forcing technology into our homes (and data centres into our neighbourhoods) that will undermine the very things that bring meaning to our lives, and that would otherwise help us to cope with a collapsing world.
Strangely, we're not talking about it more.
Crushing the arts
It's hard to forget how Apple released a controversial ad in 2024 that featured a giant hydraulic press crushing musical instruments, a record player, piles of paint, books, cameras, sculptures, and other artefacts of human joy.
Apple said it was trying to convey the visual message that its latest iPad Pro could fit a huge amount of technology into a new, thinner model.
But internet users didn't see it that way.
"The destruction of the human experience. Courtesy of Silicon Valley," the actor Hugh Grant wrote on X.
The filmmaker Justine Bateman asked: "Why did Apple do an ad that crushes the arts? Tech and #AI means to destroy the arts and society in general. This is not making things better. This is just making some people insanely wealthy, at the expense of all of us."
The wider public backlash to the ad was so intense that Apple soon apologised and withdrew it from television.
But the PR damage was done. The metaphor was too obvious. And there's been no sign, in the two years since, that Silicon Valley's chief executives really understood why people hated that ad so much.
Enshittification
Now AI technology is coursing through society so quickly that nothing feels immune to its impact, whether good or bad.
For example, this may seem unimportant in the scheme of things, but it's indicative of a larger societal issue. The Reserve Bank recently published a transcript on its website of governor Michele Bullock's "fireside chat" from September 22.
The transcript used the American spelling for labour on seven occasions (i.e. it used "labor" instead of "labour"), so it had Ms Bullock saying this:
"What happens is that we combine labor and capital in a way that allows more output for the same amount of labor and capital, and that's what allows profits to rise, it allows real wages to rise, and improves living standards, and that's what we've observed over the long sweep of time."
And it used the Australian spelling for "labour" on seven other occasions, in the same transcript, with Ms Bullock saying this:
"Productivity, it's a really important concept, which means we use our resources, labour and capital resources, in more efficient ways that allow more output for the same amount of inputs."
That is extremely sloppy.
The RBA has long taken pride in its correct use of grammar and spelling in its written communications. It's always talking about the importance of its "credibility" as an institution. To see it publish such a sloppy transcript on its website was jarring.
If these "AI issues" are affecting the RBA, what's it doing to other institutions?
Now, consider bigger, more important examples.
We're reading stories every week about AI agents "going rogue" and hacking into government systems, bank accounts, and more.
If private citizens were caught doing that, they would end up in prison. But since it's AI agents, it's often framed as though they're "escaping from a lab" and misbehaving like naughty children, with the assumption being that it's just a quirk of the technology that will be fixed over time.
Meanwhile, we're all hoping that we won't wake up one morning to find our personal data stolen and bank accounts drained.
This strange atmosphere of unaccountability for AI agents, mixed with apathy from our leaders, where authorities share little information about what's actually going on and what can be done about it, is creating a lot of anxiety for people.
The 'great white hope' for productivity
Why are policymakers hardly acknowledging the anxiety?
Perhaps it's because governments see the AI investment and data centre boom as an economic lifeline out of our historic productivity slump.
In a speech last week, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said massive investments in the AI boom were ramping up competition for capital globally.
"Capital expenditure by the five largest hyperscalers in 2023 was $230 billion. It's now forecast to quadruple to over $1.1 trillion," he said.
"To finance this, corporate bond issuances by hyperscalers have exploded. Annual issuance averaged around US$40 billion five years ago, but is now projected to average around US$400 billion ($570 billion) in the next few years."
He said Australia was a "digital hub" in the Indo-Pacific with the land, energy, skills and capital to make the most of the AI investment boom.
"As one of the world's top 10 markets for data centre capacity, we have over $150 billion of AI infrastructure scheduled for the next five years, around 5 per cent of current GDP," he said.
Ms Bullock has acknowledged that people see AI as the "great white hope" to improve productivity.
People power
So where does that leave us?
When the ABC spoke to the American journalist Gil Durán recently, he said data centre protests in the US had become a focal point for regular people to come together as a community to fight billionaire power.
"The data centres are viewed, I think, as a physical manifestation of billionaire power on the land that's become this bogeyman, this monster, this alien invasion that arrives in your community to suck up your water and pollute your air and eat up your land, all for the promise that it will fuel a technology that will kill your job and possibly wipe humanity off the face of the planet.
"What's not to love?" he joked grimly.
But another element of the global AI pushback is getting less attention.
Many people also despise how AI is radically cheapening our artistic and cultural output while burning through fossil fuels to do it.
Will our children be able to make a living as artists, musicians, and writers, or are those opportunities disappearing with every new data centre being built?
Where will we find joy in a future where AI has comprehensively debased the arts?
The concerns are genuine. Perhaps our leaders will give them more attention one day.

50,000 people could get compensation for unlawful Centrelink suspensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Centrelink compliance regime resumes after system unlawfully cancelled jobseekers' payments
In short:
The Commonwealth Ombudsman found almost 1,000 jobseekers had their payments cancelled over two years under a Centrelink compliance regime.
Following a review, the department is reinstating the framework, allowing Centrelink payment suspensions and penalties to resume.
What's next?
More than 50,000 people have been invited to apply for compensation over the failure, as advocates question whether enough has been done to address the underlying issues.
More than 50,000 welfare recipients could now get compensation after the government unlawfully stopped their payments, claiming they had failed to meet "mutual obligation" requirements.
That scheme, which was partially paused in July 2024 when concerns it may have been operating unlawfully first arose, has now restarted, with advocates warning the problems have not been fixed.
A Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation last year found 964 payment cancellations were not made in accordance with the law.
Adelaide man Daniel* was one of those affected. His Centrelink payments were suspended in 2022, despite being exempt from mutual obligations with no compulsory activities to complete.
"I kept ringing them and saying, 'I've got zero points, I've got no requirements. Why am I getting these suspensions?' But it just kept happening," he said.
His payments were later cancelled, leaving him without income support for more than three years.
Daniel said without income support, he could not secure rental accommodation, he experienced periods of homelessness and relied on help from family and friends to get by.
"Without my pensioner dad helping me, I honestly don't know what would have happened. There were times I had nowhere to live."
The 51-year-old challenged the Centrelink decision after he was alerted to the ombudsman's findings last year.
A week before his case was due to be heard in October 2025, the department conducted a minister-initiated review, reversed the cancellation decision and paid him about $53,000 in back pay.
The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) said it had fixed the issues identified by the Commonwealth Ombudsman through IT system changes, system testing, improved participant communications and additional training for decision-makers.
But advocacy groups fear not enough has been done to fix the underlying issues, with questions set to be put to the government over the scale of the payment cancellations and what evidence it relied on before resuming the program.
Loading...
The department said one reason identified for the system failure stemmed from an IT system change introduced in December 2020, which caused some welfare recipients to have their payments cancelled up to four days earlier than legislation allowed.
The department's 2025-26 annual report released last week showed $870,000 has been paid in compensation to more than 600 people following the review.
It is now inviting a further 50,652 people to also apply for compensation. However, advocacy groups argue the number of people affected by unlawful cancellations may be substantially higher, with estimates ranging from more than 100,000 people to as many as 300,000.
What went wrong?
Read more
The cancellations occurred automatically under the framework, a system set up to monitor "mutual obligations".
These are conditions people must meet to continue receiving payments, like job hunting and attending interviews.
New laws introduced after the Robodebt scandal required agencies to consider the jobseeker's circumstances before cancelling their payment.
This didn't occur in 964 cancellations between April 2022 and July 2024.
The department then paused the cancellations of payments while it reviewed affected decisions.
Advocates question the fixes
Anti-poverty centre coordinator Jay Coonan said advocacy groups including the Australian Council of Social Service, Economic Justice Australia, National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Legal Services and Inclusion Australia, remain unconvinced the underlying problems of the compliance system have been resolved.
He said the government has yet to demonstrate the system can operate fairly and lawfully at scale.
"We have both publicly raised and privately raised with the department that we do not believe that the targeted compliance framework and the current regime of payment suspensions is used fairly or lawfully," he said.
Despite participating in the department's Targeted Compliance Framework Reference group, Mr Coonan said advocacy organisations had not been provided evidence that the issues identified by the ombudsman had been fixed.
"None. None whatsoever," he said.
Disability groups have also criticised the decision, arguing people with disability are disproportionately affected by payment suspensions and cancellations and calling for the framework to be abolished.
DEWR said it would closely monitor the resumed provisions and noted the most serious cancellation powers remained paused until further safeguards were put in place, with those measures expected to return in 2027.
The department has not publicly disclosed its estimated total compensation liability.
*Daniel is identified by his first name only because of concerns about the impact of identifying him as a recipient of income support payments.

Crossbench push to give Australians a free way to fight back against big tech

Australians could get avenue to challenge big tech under crossbench amendment
In short:
The crossbench is pushing for a free, independent ombudsman to help Australians resolve disputes with tech giants.
Labor argues its proposed digital safety laws already provide stronger complaints protections, but it needs Greens' support to pass them through the Senate.
What's next?
Independent MP Sophie Scamps will move her amendment today, when the bill is expected to pass the lower house.
Australians would have a free and simple way to raise complaints against tech giants under a crossbench amendment to Labor's proposed digital safety laws.
Independents and the Greens are in favour of establishing a new industry-funded online ombudsman to resolve disputes, but the federal government has argued its draft digital duty of care bill already puts the onus on big tech to provide Australians with effective complaint pathways.
Mackellar MP Sophie Scamps will today put forward an amendment that would create an external avenue for appeal in cases such as a small business owner being locked out of their social media account or individuals wanting harmful content addressed.
Labor has the numbers in parliament to pass the bill in the lower house without entertaining any changes, but it needs the support of the Greens, who are also in favour of an online ombudsman, to get the duty of care through the Senate next month.
The Coalition party room yesterday resolved to oppose the legislation after likening the digital duty of care to political censorship.
Labor's proposed duty would require online platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to take reasonable steps to prevent a range of harms for children, including bullying, misogyny and content promoting eating disorders.
Big tech would also have to limit adults' exposure to serious harms such as threats of violence, stalking and the non-consensual sharing of intimate images.
The bill would also let Australians aged 16 and over switch off algorithm-driven feeds and see only content from accounts they choose to follow.
Push for independent big tech watchdog
Ms Scamps said establishing an online services ombudsman within the remit of the existing Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) would help people who currently felt powerless to resolve their problems.
"For many Australians, dealing with big tech platforms can feel like shouting into the void, with complaints met by automated responses, endless online forms or no meaningful response at all," she said.
"When platforms fail to act, there is nowhere independent to turn."
Ms Scamps said Labor's bill provided for stronger internal complaints and dispute resolution processes, but that alone was not enough.
TIO Cynthia Gebert said the crossbench amendment was the missing piece in the government's digital agenda.
"People want someone to turn to when they're locked out of their social media account without warning or a realistic avenue to appeal against big tech companies," she said.
Ms Gebert said thousands of people and small businesses were already reaching out for help she could not provide, despite wanting to.
"The TIO stands ready to expand our role to help people when things go wrong online," she said.
Greens want laws with 'teeth'
Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said her party would fight to ensure the digital duty of care had "real teeth", prioritising tougher fines and the right to sue big tech privately.
"We know that these companies only respond to one thing: penalties that hit them where it hurts," she said.
Senator Hanson-Young said Australians also needed an external complaints pathway that was free from the "whims" of big tech moderators.
"This would put the safety of the user, accountability and basic decency ahead of corporate profits," she said.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government understood how frustrating it was for Australians to report a complaint to a tech company and hear nothing back.
But she said the next step was for Labor's proposed digital duty of care to empower the eSafety commissioner to create enforceable standards to resolve disputes, which currently did not exist.
"The problem right now is that the codes are completely voluntary, completely unenforceable, so let's take the next step to make them enforceable, before jumping several steps ahead and making them externally enforceable," she said.
The Coalition will oppose Labor's bill, with Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson taking issue with what she described as "dangerously vague" definitions and concerns the government would be able to spread propaganda.
"This is information control because of the wide range of discretion, both of the minister and also the eSafety commissioner, to determine what is harm online," she told News24 earlier this week.

Business Council names Victoria worst state for business, again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Victoria the worst state to do business, says Business Council
In short:
The Business Council's annual ranking of states and territories has again put Victoria last for pro-business policies, and South Australia first.
The ranking reflects the peak body's subjective assessment of state and territory policies, rewarding simple regulations and low taxes.
What's next?
Both major parties in Victoria have offered payroll tax relief ahead of the November election.
The peak business body has again branded Victoria the worst Australian jurisdiction to operate in, because of its relatively high taxes and complicated licensing rules.
The Business Council's "regulation rumble", an annual ranking of state and territory policies, has placed the state last every year since the first edition in 2023. South Australia has topped the list every year, and did so again.
Bran Black, the lobby's chief executive, said Victoria "continues to face serious challenges" and that its "high taxes and unnecessary regulation" were factors in the state's sluggish economy and high unemployment.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has attempted to reposition the 12-year-old Labor government as pro-business after taking the leadership in the final months before the November election.
Tax down? Top ranking
The ranking represents the Business Council's subjective assessment of favourable business policies. States are rewarded for lower taxes on payrolls and on land, whether via land taxes or stamp duties.
They are also rewarded for approving planning applications faster, making licensing simpler, and making workers' compensation and insurance cheaper.
While the rankings have not changed much over four years, several jurisdictions have improved their standings by streamlining their planning systems as part of nationwide efforts to boost housing construction.
While Victoria is streamlining planning approvals through its 'Better Decisions Made Faster' laws, this was not factored into the rankings because the legislated reform does not take effect until 2027. The council noted the laws would likely see improvements.
Southern lights
South Australia's strength in the rankings comes chiefly from its payroll tax, which has the lowest average rates. It is also the only jurisdiction to adjust the thresholds for payroll tax for inflation. The Business Council says payroll taxes discourage job growth.
The state is also rewarded for its simplified licensing system, a particular concern for the Business Council. Whereas the most complex state, Tasmania, had 38 separate hoops for a cafe owner to set up shop, South Australia had far fewer.
The Northern Territory bolstered its standing because of its efforts to speed up approvals. New South Wales also sped up its planning system, but its system remains among the most complex and is still wracked with delays. The state ranks fifth overall.
The ACT ranks highly because it does not levy land tax on commercial property and has relatively low stamp duties. The council does not differentiate between the two types of property taxes, although economists say stamp duties are less efficient.
Queensland and Western Australia are ranked sixth and seventh, Queensland penalised chiefly for its heavy restriction on retail trading hours, its disparate planning rules and its high land taxes, and Western Australia for levying payroll tax on smaller businesses.
Mr Black said businesses were "buried under mountains of red tape" across Australia, which was "wasting time and money", but saw some bright spots, especially from the wave of planning reforms.
"Everyone can lift their game by learning from what others are doing well … There's a lot to be optimistic about. Reform is starting to land," he said, adding that the federal government was also working across jurisdictions "to even out the rules".
Business wooed ahead of state election
Both major parties in Victoria have promised to lift the land tax-free threshold, rolling back changes made in 2024 by former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, which captured an extra 250,000 Victorian workers.
Labor's proposed wind-back would be slower than that of the Coalition, which has also pledged to remove payroll tax for private schools and remove stamp duty for first homebuyers.
Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promoted both lower taxes and lower debt as part of her election pitch, though several economists have raised doubts about her "contradictory" policies.
"We have to get business back at the centre of the economy, investing and creating jobs in this state," Ms Wilson told a business lunch on Tuesday for the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
"I want to keep working with you to find competitive advantages and maximise growth and jobs," Mr Carroll told the same forum.
While the Coalition needs to overcome a 16-seat deficit to form a majority government, polling suggests Ms Wilson is most likely to be victorious next month.
The rankings, from best to worst
- South Australia
- Tasmania
- Australian Capital Territory
- Northern Territory
- New South Wales
- Queensland
- Western Australia
- Victoria

Ukrainian Parliament preliminarily approves bill raising bank profit tax to 50% for 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:59:20 EET
02:59:20 KST

The Verkhovna Rada, as expected, passed at first reading a bill on the specifics of bank profit taxation (No. 15262), which provides for another increase in the tax rate for banks in 2027, from 25% to 50%.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, 265 members of parliament voted in favor of the bill, exceeding the required minimum of 226 votes.
"We are making this decision for the fourth time, and the previous three times were quite successful, as we managed to attract additional funds to the budget from the banking system, which generates excess profits even during wartime," said Danylo Hetmantsev, a co-author of the bill, commenting on the vote.
According to him, banks' pretax profit totaled approximately UAH 143.1 billion in the first eight months of 2026, about 5.3% higher than on the corresponding date last year and 2.9 times greater than in the first eight months of 2025.
At the same time, according to the National Bank, net profit for the period fell by 32.7% to UAH 71.66 billion, as the corporate income tax rate was 25% last year.
Hetmantsev noted that the additional revenue from extending the 50% bank profit tax rate has already been incorporated into the revenue side of the 2027 state budget draft and amounts to UAH 38.5 billion.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada first set the bank profit tax rate at 50% for 2023, doing so retroactively. The relevant law did not take effect until December 8. The same law raised the standard tax rate for banks from 18% to 25%.
A year later, parliament again retroactively raised the rate for banks to 50% for 2024 and increased the standard corporate income tax rate for nonbank financial institutions from 18% to 25%, effective in 2025.
The third time the Rada set a 50% tax rate on bank profits was for 2026, passing the relevant law on the morning of the day in question, before the start of the year, in the autumn of 2025.

EU eyes global tax deal revenue to boost next budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:58:36 UTC
02:58:36 KST

European Council President António Costa, center, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, left, give a press conference in Brussels on Oct. 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The European Commission is exploring whether to use revenue from a global tax agreement on multinational companies to finance the EU’s next seven-year budget, four EU diplomats with knowledge of the proceedings told POLITICO.
The idea could facilitate an agreement on new EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, which has emerged as a major stumbling bloc in the ongoing budget negotiations.
The European Council President António Costa has urged countries to approve the new taxes to reduce national contributions to the bloc's budget, which is worth €1.82 trillion according to the latest proposal from earlier this month.
Advertisement
Costa, who is brokering budget talks, is pressuring leaders to reach a budget deal among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in Poland, France and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.
Yet after more than a year of haggling, EU governments are still at odds over five proposed new taxes that the Commission estimates would generate €65 billion per year.
Among the options on the table, a corporate tax known as CORE — which charges a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — has emerged as the most unpopular option and is particularly toxic in Germany.
To break the deadlock, French President Emmanuel Macron supported funneling part of the tax on multinationals to the EU budget during a leaders’ summit in October, said two of the diplomats. They were granted anonymity, like others, to discuss the sensitive plans.
Supporters argue that this idea could garner more political support than CORE as it targets companies’ profits as opposed to their revenue.
“The corporate income tax is about taxing companies based on their profitability. CORE is not about that, CORE is about taking a toll blindly,” said Pascal Saint-Amans, a former OECD official and one of the architects of the global tax arrangement.
Advertisement
The tax deal
Under the OECD tax deal from 2021, EU countries are compelled to levy a 15 percent minimum corporate tax on large multinationals with an annual turnover exceeding €750 million.
Controversially, the U.S. secured an exemption from the rules as it introduced a national tax arrangement that was deemed equivalent to the OECD framework.
The end goal is to prevent countries from competing to offer lower and lower corporate tax rates to attract large multinationals.
Historically, many foreign multinationals operating across the EU such as Apple and Google have set their headquarters in Ireland because of its low taxes and light-touch regulation.
To tackle this phenomenon, the OECD deal compels countries undercutting the 15 percent rate to levy a “top-up tax” on large foreign companies. Currently, the revenue is collected by national governments.
However, European capitals could funnel part of these proceeds to the bloc’s budget, the diplomats said.
Advertisement
This could hit countries such as Ireland and the Netherlands which charge low corporate rates and collect large sums from the top-up tax. The Dutch government alone collected €449 million in 2026 from returns related to the global minimum tax, according to Bloomberg.
Saint-Amans defended the potential new own resource on the grounds that the multinationals’ "activities are taking place in Ireland, but are about managing the EU markets."
“That's how I believe that it could make sense to visualize” the top-up taxes, he added.
Costa’s team and the Commission are looking into this option ahead of bilateral discussions with EU countries starting next week.
Costa will test the waters with governments before proposing new budget figures and EU taxes ahead of a leaders’ summit on Nov. 26 and 27.

Around 1,000 soldiers from El Salvador have deployed to Haiti, source says
