Homes across UK to get low- or no-interest loans to fund solar panels and heat pumps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:28:33 UTC
02:28:33 KST

Households across the UK can now cut their energy bills by hundreds of pounds a year at no upfront cost by applying for interest-free or “low-interest” loans to fund upgrades such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels.
The government-backed Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, could mean thousands more households are able to access low-carbon energy alternative technologies, thanks to loans ranging from £7,500 to up £35,000.
Energy suppliers including British Gas and E.On have partnered with lenders from Tandem Bank and Homeserve respectively to offer the loans directly to customers at a discounted rate compared with those offered by high street lenders.
People interested in swapping their gas boiler for an air-source or ground-source heat pump could secure loans of up to £10,000 or £35,000 respectively, while also drawing on the government’s existing scheme which offers grants of up to £9,000 a year for households installing the replacements for fossil fuel heating.
Installing a heat pump, battery and solar panels could save households up to £550 a year on their energy bills, rising by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.
Soaring energy costs have led to record demand for low-carbon home energy upgrades over the last year, and the government believes the loan scheme means “thousands more households” will be able to cut their energy bills by fitting clean energy technology and spreading repayments over many years.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Energy is an everyday essential that must be affordable for everyone. These government-supported loans will help families across the UK upgrade their homes with no upfront costs to make them warmer and cheaper to run.”
Chris Norbury, the chief executive of E.On UK, said that a recent trial showed that fuel-poor customers in Coventry were able to save more than £250 a year on average by combining a home battery with a time of use tariff that charges lower rates for using energy outside peak demand hours.
He said the Warm Homes Loan scheme was “an opportunity to take that further” by “removing barriers to low-carbon technologies”.
The government set out the terms of the new scheme a day before the chancellor, John Healey, delivers his first budget on Wednesday, which reportedly will include plans to scale back heat pump grants made through its boiler upgrade scheme.
The scheme is not expected to be scrapped altogether, but sources say hundreds of millions of pounds will be cut from its £2.7bn five-year budget because Treasury officials consider it a subsidy used mainly by middle-class households.
It has typically provided grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing a heat pump, meaning households have still required a significant outlay to make up the difference.
The Guardian understands that grants of up to £9,000 a year are likely to remain available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and are forced to rely on high-cost heating oil. These grants could be used alongside the low-interest loans to cover the full cost of a heat pump.
Other lenders taking part in the Warm Home Loans scheme include HTG Finance, Propensio, Secure Trust Bank, Selina Finance, South Manchester Credit Union, Sunsave, The Money Co-op and This Bank.

Finnish and Norwegian leaders discuss Ukraine peace with Putin as a source close to the Kremlin warns of escalating hybrid warfare with Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:27:32 UTC
02:27:32 KST

Finnish and Norwegian leaders discuss Ukraine peace with Putin as a source close to the Kremlin warns of escalating hybrid warfare with Europe
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin. Western leaders initiated the call to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts to end it.
The Finnish president’s office said the call was meant “to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin” ahead of meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi. It was Putin’s first contact with European leaders supporting Ukraine since July 2025, when he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron.
The Kremlin confirmed the call, saying Putin “assessed the current situation” in Ukraine and reminded participants of the “root causes of the conflict.” Putin also pointed to the “confrontational policy of EU and NATO countries, which is prolonging the fighting,” the Kremlin’s press service said.
Volodymyr Zelensky said Stubb and Støre briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure,” Zelensky said. He added that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had discussed preparations for a trilateral meeting between negotiating teams from Ukraine, the United States, and Russia.
Stubb’s office said the call “was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on October 20 and held in consultation with Ukraine.” The Norwegian capital hosted talks that day between Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelensky, with Støre and Stubb also taking part. Witkoff then traveled to St. Petersburg to meet with Putin before returning to Oslo and flying home to the United States.
Those trips produced an agreement on a trilateral meeting between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia, to be held in Abu Dhabi. The meeting will take place after November 4, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said. The day before, on November 3, the United States will hold midterm elections in which Republicans could lose their congressional majority.
Announcing the timing, Ushakov said the peace talks would also have to involve “all of Europe.” Europe has long sought a negotiator to represent the European Union’s interests in talks on ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Stubb has repeatedly been named as a candidate for the role, having built a good relationship with Trump, including on the golf course, and emerged as one of Trump’s main points of contact with European leaders. The Telegraph has also named Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and Czech President Petr Pavel among the candidates.
After Stubb and Støre’s call with Putin, Frederiksen criticized the initiative, saying she was “skeptical” and that the talks had not been coordinated with other European leaders. She added that she sees no sign that Russia wants peace with Europe, either in the hybrid war that continues every day or in Ukraine.
The independent Russian political newsletter Faridaily says contacts between European leaders and the Kremlin amount to “a significant shift in position.” European leaders had “mostly preferred not to talk to Putin at all” since the war began.
However, a source close to the Kremlin said that “events are moving toward escalation, including an intensification of hybrid warfare with Europe.” According to the source, Putin is convinced NATO is waging a hybrid war against Russia and blames Ukraine’s European allies for “comprehensive assistance” in attacks on Russia, including helping identify targets and guide strikes.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin told Stubb and Støre that Russia would not abandon its goal of capturing all of the Donbas. The European leaders responded that a “just” peace was necessary, the source added.

Ukrainian communications company Himera and Danish satellite manufacturer GomSpace have sent Obria nano, a test satellite, into orbit as the first step toward an independent Ukrainian communications network.
Himera told Ukrainska Pravda on Tuesday, Oct. 27, that the satellite reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission on Oct. 1, and is reportedly already operating.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The technical trials should provide the practical experience needed for the project’s further development into Ukrainian national infrastructure,” Himera said.
While the launch relied on a SpaceX rocket, the satellite itself will be controlled by a Ukrainian operator and will serve Ukraine’s strategic security needs. The project comes as Kyiv seeks to reduce its dependence on SpaceX’s Starshield service amid recent disruptions and diplomatic tensions with Washington.
Reducing reliance on foreign technology
Ukraine’s dependence on foreign-made technology creates strategic risks, especially during wartime, Himera argued. Building capabilities domestically, the company said, would widen the country’s communication options and strengthen its security.
In the long term, the company plans to deploy a satellite constellation covering all of Ukraine’s territory.
The network would also complement existing European satellite systems and form the basis of a sovereign Ukrainian communications system.
POW Dispute: South Korea Pulls 8 Diplomats From Ukraine
Moving production of satellites and ground terminals to Ukraine is Himera’s next priority, as this could help Kyiv build its own expertise in satellite communications, while gradually expanding domestic manufacturing.
Ukraine also signed seven agreements with Finland on Oct. 22, including deals to expand Kyiv’s use of Finnish satellite capabilities through Nokia and ICEYE.
“We agreed that we will make greater use of Finland’s satellite capabilities,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier. “This is important for our defense and for Ukraine’s resilience.”
Radios field-tested by military intelligence
A unit of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) had tested Himera’s tactical radios – HIMERA G1 PRO radios and HIMERA B1 repeater – in real combat conditions, the company said in a statement on Oct. 15.
HUR testers reportedly praised the devices’ durable casing, simple setup, compact repeater and a long battery life.
According to Himera, the radios ran for up to four days on a single charge, even in low temperatures and high humidity.
However, the main improvement users requested was much better sound quality for the G1 PRO. At the time, Himera said it had already sent some users a beta version and reported collecting their feedback for the next update.
Russia’s own domestic Starlink: Rassvet
Meanwhile, Russia is working on its own, domestic alternative to Starlink.
Built by the Russian company Bureau 1440, Rassvet is a low-orbit satellite broadband service that users can connect to through dedicated terminals that relay data to satellites overhead.
Major General Ilya Pavlenko, who served as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) from 2015 to 2020 told Interfax-Ukraine that Russia’s growing Rassvet satellite network could eventually allow its forces to control long-range drones over Ukraine in real time.
He cautioned against writing off the project because of problems with its first satellites, arguing that the network could later be used as another tool for hybrid warfare against Europe.
Bureau 1440 says the finished system will operate at an altitude of about 800 kilometers (497 miles), deliver speeds of up to 1 Gbps with delays of up to 70 milliseconds, and use 5G non-terrestrial network standards and laser links between satellites.
According to Pavlenko, Russia is also moving its jet drone factories underground, which could further limit Ukraine’s ability to break manufacturing cycles or destroy the drones.

In Kyiv, the increase in taxi prices during alerts will be limited — Koretskyi
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:24:40 EET
02:24:40 KST

In Kyiv, the increase in taxi prices during alerts will be limited — Koretskyi
Kyiv • UNN
Bolt, Uklon, Uber, and OPTI have limited fare increases in Kyiv to 75% during alerts and transport stoppages. The limit will remain in effect for at least two hours after the all-clear.
Ukraine’s Ministries of Economy and Infrastructure signed a memorandum with the digital platforms Bolt, Uklon, Uber and OPTI to prevent a critical rise in transportation prices in Kyiv during an air raid alert or a suspension of public transportation services. This was reported by Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, according to UNN.
Details
In particular, in the event of the metro or other force majeure circumstances related to logistics in the capital. For example, as happened after today’s attack on the Pivdennyi Bridge.
According to Koretskyi, the memorandum with the operators provides for setting a ceiling on how high prices may rise under such circumstances. This is a maximum of 75% above the base fare.
That is, if the base fare under normal conditions—without air raid alerts, traffic jams, and so on—from point A to point B is, say, 200 hryvnias, the maximum charge will be 350 hryvnias. If it is 300 hryvnias, the maximum will be 525 hryvnias. Passengers will retain the ability to regulate the price themselves, but upper limits will also be established. This price restriction will remain in effect for at least two hours after the all-clear for a red-level alert or until normal public transportation services and bridge traffic are restored. It is often precisely then that demand for rides is highest, while people need to get home
We would like to remind you
At the beginning of the new workweek, diesel and autogas prices surged. The average price of diesel fuel at Ukrainian filling stations currently stands at 103.40 hryvnias per liter, A-95 gasoline at 90.93 hryvnias, and autogas at 54.45 hryvnias.

Jalud families still unable to return to burned homes despite High Court order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:16 UTC
02:22:16 KST

The state acknowledged a sense of “shame and failure” before the High Court of Justice on Monday over an operation to return a Palestinian family to its home in Jalud that ended with its evacuation under attack, as the justices questioned why the residents remained displaced and their homes had burned despite an order intended to protect them.
The Monday hearing returned to the case of three Palestinian petitioners whose homes near the West Bank village, south of Nablus, had been taken over by Israeli extremists. Seven weeks after the court ordered authorities to secure their return, the discussion concerned how to protect workers repairing the damaged houses before the residents could live in them again.
“Sometimes, even when time is needed, there is no time,” Justice Dafna Barak-Erez told the deputy commander of the IDF’s Judea and Samaria Division, pointing to the residents’ inability to live in their homes and the destruction of their property.
Supreme Court President Isaac Amit and Justice Yechiel Kasher also sat on the panel.
Attorney Ghiath Nasser, representing the petitioners, said the case had begun before the houses burned and had now reached a worse position. His clients still wanted to return, he said, and the destruction had not changed that demand.
High Court orders state to secure Palestinian families' return and restore access to homes
On September 6, the court ordered authorities to coordinate the petitioners’ return within 14 days, provide security, and allow in equipment and supplies needed to repair the homes and restore water and electricity. It also required the state to explain why it should not restore access to the homes and remove roadblocks.
The attempted return took place on the night of September 28-29. More than 100 Israeli extremists attacked security forces and prevented the Tubasi family from remaining at home. Three Border Police officers were wounded, and the family’s two houses were burned.
In their account filed with the court, the petitioners described arriving to find broken windows and doors and damaged electrical connections. Within minutes, a crowd began attacking the house with stones. Soldiers gathered the family in a corner to protect them before evacuating them in an armored vehicle under continued stone-throwing.
The state’s October 8 response described Border Police officers shielding the residents with their bodies after exhausting crowd-control ammunition. It said Israelis entered the houses while the family was inside, and the brigade commander ordered the residents evacuated for their protection.
At Monday’s hearing, state attorney Avi Milikovsky acknowledged the operation had ended in failure but rejected the suggestion that this reflected indifference to the court’s order. Officers had risked themselves to protect the residents, he said.
The homes were now burned and unsuitable for an immediate return, Milikovsky told the court.
Dispute over damage assessment delays repairs to Palestinian homes in Jalud
Nasser said his request to bring in engineers to assess the damage had gone unanswered. Milikovsky said coordination was being handled through the military’s local liaison office, which had conducted a damage-assessment visit.
Amit distinguished a brief inspection from the protection needed for sustained repairs. Workers would need to remain at the houses over a period of time, he said. Barak-Erez said that protection was an integral part of allowing the residents to return.
The justices also sought an explanation for Nasser’s allegation that the September fire burned for seven hours without being extinguished.
“If soldiers can be there, fire engines can be there too,” Barak-Erez said after the deputy division commander referred to the difficulty of bringing Israeli fire engines into Area B, where the houses are located.
The officer said he needed to check what happened in this specific incident rather than give an improvised answer. Milikovsky proposed providing a supplementary written response.
Kasher also asked how the third petitioner’s house had subsequently burned. Nasser had informed the court that Tawfiq Shweiki’s home caught fire on October 24, after settlers had been staying there. Responsibility for that fire remained disputed; Nasser told the justices he did not know who had burned the house.
The deputy division commander, identified as Col. A., said the army was bound by the law and responsible for creating conditions for the families’ safe return. The outposts in the relevant Area B sector should not exist, he said.
He cited arrests, search warrants, vehicle seizures and repeated operations against the outposts, while describing competing demands arising from attacks elsewhere, the olive harvest and the election period. A lasting return required preparation, intelligence and forces to protect both the repairs and the families, he said.
Barak-Erez also challenged the failure to meet the original deadline.
“If it is 14 days, it is not 15 or 16,” she said, adding that an extension should have been sought in advance. “That is not the biggest problem in this case; it is only the symptom.”
Petitioners seek NIS 50,000 daily fine as state disputes contempt sanctions
The petitioners have sought enforcement through contempt proceedings, including a daily NIS 50,000 fine. The state opposes that request, arguing that it acted to carry out the order and that the failed operation does not justify contempt sanctions.
Asked to give a timeframe for the preparations, the officer estimated up to 30 days, while stressing that operational circumstances could affect it. His estimate was not a new court deadline.
Amit closed the hearing by saying a decision would follow.
Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

US chooses Poland to host service facility for Patriot missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:13 UTC
02:22:13 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries.
The new centre, the first of its kind ot be located outside the US itself, will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday.
Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”.
Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8
— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026
The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”.
His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate.
Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid.

Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland.
The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre.
“The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.”
Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine.
The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles.
In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”.
Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E

Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted.
After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles.
Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026
The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states.
Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers.
Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles.

Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea.
Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday's presidential election and refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to hand over his passports, two sources said.
The US Embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro's lawyer also did not respond.
It was not immediately clear where Bolsonaro was heading, what time he would arrive or whether he would seek asylum. US President Donald Trump's administration has previously alleged Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
Flavio's departure for the United States threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday's election on a US State Department campaign to restore them to office.
Lula's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result to leftist Lula.
On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing, but that deadline has now lapsed, two other sources said, leading to his documents being canceled.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no plans to flee.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
Bolsonaro follows father's path
Jair Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned to Brazil but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
His son has yet to officially concede defeat - saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities - but his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory.
It remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not exited the country via any regular migration point.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move.
"If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

Feature: Tanzania's Zanzibar seaweed farmers pin hopes on China's import expo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:17:51 CST
02:17:51 KST

Women sort harvested seaweed in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)
DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- After more than two decades of growing seaweed off Tanzania's Zanzibar, Bahati Issa Suleiman is looking to China for better prices and new opportunities for her family.
The 51-year-old mother of eight hopes the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), which opens in Shanghai on Nov. 5, will help Zanzibar's seaweed reach more Chinese buyers and gain wider recognition in the international market.
For Suleiman, seaweed farming has long been a vital source of income, helping her family cover daily expenses and pay school fees. She has also seen fellow farmers use their earnings to buy land and build houses.
"When our seaweed reaches China, we will announce ourselves to the world," Suleiman said, hoping greater market exposure would encourage more people to return to seaweed farming and strengthen household incomes.
Her aspirations reflect Zanzibar's broader efforts to turn its marine resources into a stronger driver of economic growth by moving beyond raw-material exports toward higher-value products.
Zahor Kassim El-Kharousy, deputy principal secretary in Zanzibar's Ministry of Blue Economy and Fisheries, said the CIIE and similar international exhibitions offer an opportunity to connect local producers with buyers and investors, addressing a major challenge facing the seaweed industry.
"Currently, 99 percent of the seaweed that we export outside the country is raw," he said, describing the transition to value-added products as a key government priority.
El-Kharousy said stronger links between producers, processors and markets could encourage investment in processing facilities, expand the range of seaweed-based products and enable Zanzibar to capture a greater share of the value generated along the supply chain.
For farmers, this could translate into more reliable markets and better prices. For local businesses, it could create opportunities in processing, packaging, transportation and export logistics, while generating employment, particularly for women, who dominate seaweed cultivation in Zanzibar.
China is already an important destination for Zanzibar's marine products, including seaweed and sea cucumber, El-Kharousy said.
He added that the ministry was also promoting the production of value-added sea cucumber products to expand the sector's contribution to the blue economy.
The size of the Chinese market offers opportunities for Zanzibar to expand exports, but the ministry official emphasized that businesses must understand consumer preferences and meet prospective buyers' requirements.
Companies participating in the Shanghai expo should therefore use the platform not only to showcase their products but also to establish commercial partnerships and identify opportunities to develop products suited to Chinese market demand, he said.
For Zanzibar, the potential benefits extend beyond immediate export orders. Business contacts made at the expo could attract investment, facilitate technology transfer and help local enterprises improve product quality, processing capacity and access to international supply chains.
China's decision to remove tariffs on eligible imports from Tanzania could provide additional opportunities for exporters, although the benefits will depend on the applicable product coverage and compliance with Chinese import requirements.
Suleiman, meanwhile, said farmers need support to improve production and post-harvest handling. In her village, some seaweed is dried directly on the ground, while cultivation in shallow waters near the shore can damage crops.
She hopes stronger international interest will encourage improvements in farming methods and post-harvest practices, helping farmers supply more consistent, higher-quality products.
Ultimately, she believed, expanding the Chinese market could motivate farmers who have abandoned the activity to resume cultivation, increasing production and strengthening the industry's economic contribution.
"Once our seaweed arrives in China and gets promoted, I believe the price will increase," she said. ■
Zahor Kassim El-Kharousy, deputy principal secretary in Zanzibar's Ministry of Blue Economy and Fisheries, speaks during an interview in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)
Bahati Issa Suleiman, a seaweed farmer, displays harvested seaweed in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)

DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania's northeastern Arusha Region has stepped up measures to prevent the spread of Ebola, training more than 100 health workers, designating an isolation and treatment facility, and intensifying health screening at the Namanga border post following an outbreak in neighboring Kenya, an official said Tuesday.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), there are nine confirmed cases and two deaths in Kenya, with no evidence of wider community transmission.
Arusha Regional Administrative Secretary Toba Nguvila said the measures aim to strengthen early detection and prompt management of suspected infections at the busy crossing linking Tanzania and Kenya.
Nguvila outlined the preparations after inspecting screening procedures and staff readiness at the Namanga One-Stop Border Post in Longido District.
He said more than 100 health workers from all seven district councils in the region had received training on Ebola preparedness and response, adding that a facility had been designated to isolate and treat suspected patients.
Nguvila urged border officials to screen every traveler, including conducting preliminary health assessments and temperature checks, and refer suspected cases for further testing.
He warned that infected travelers entering Tanzania could expose others while traveling to Arusha and other destinations, calling for continued vigilance and strict implementation of preventive measures.
The Ministry of Health has also strengthened screening at the country's points of entry, including health declarations, temperature checks and 21-day monitoring of travelers considered at high risk. ■

Hungary again refused to approve the screening results for negotiating clusters 4 and 5 in Ukraine’s EU accession process, leaving the final two unopened clusters blocked, European Pravda reported on October 27.
The issue was discussed during a meeting of the EU Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession in Brussels. One diplomat told European Pravda that Hungary’s position had not changed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

- Russian ammunition depots near Diakove in the Luhansk region and near Ohorodnie in the Donetsk region;
- a concentration of Russian weapons and military equipment near Krasnohorivka in the Donetsk region;
- materiel and supply depots in the areas of Luhansk, Antratsyt, and Tymonove in the Luhansk region;
- concentrations of Russian personnel near Lahidne and Antratsyt in the Luhansk region, and near Novopetrivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
"The destruction of ammunition reduces the enemy's firepower at the front," the General Staff stated. It added that the loss of stockpiled supplies "hampers the enemy's ability to supply its units."
The General Staff declared that operations against key Russian military targets would continue until Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine ends completely. The post did not provide figures on the damage inflicted or the casualties caused.
The latest strikes follow a similar wave a week earlier, carried out on October 19 and overnight into October 20 across the same three regions. Ukrainian forces then hit a Russian command post near Fedorivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, a military repair unit near Kalmiuske in the Donetsk region, and logistics depots near Kripenskyi, Rivnopil, and Lahidne.
Earlier in October, strikes targeted another repair unit near Chystiakove, a logistics warehouse near Makiivka, and a storage facility near Horodyshche.

VATICAN CITY - Pope Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis and surgery has affected how Catholics view his health and papacy, the Vatican’s foreign minister said on Oct 27, an unusually frank assessment by one of the Church’s most senior officials.
“It’s a bit of a gamechanger,” Archbishop Paul Gallagher told journalists at an event in Rome.
Leo, 71, had part of one lung removed in surgery on Oct 13.
His doctors have said the cancer was localised and had not spread, and the pope will not require further treatment.
Gallagher said that given Leo’s relatively young age for a pope and his physical fitness, some Catholics had thought he was a “Superman” pope.
The illness revealed that Leo “is a poor mortal like the rest of us,” said the archbishop.
“I think that is going to change how we see him and possibly how he sees himself as well,” said Gallagher, a Briton who has served in his Vatican role since 2014.
Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung in an operation on Oct 13.
The pope has been gradually resuming his schedule since returning to the Vatican on Oct 18 and has appeared energetic at public events, speaking in a firm, clear voice.
The Vatican confirmed on Oct 26 he would go forward with a three-country, Nov 6-17 visit across South America, one of the most intense foreign tours arranged for a pope in decades.
“All of the medical advice is very positive... so he feels he can go,” Gallagher said in response to a question about why the pope is travelling only 24 days after his surgery.
“I think he’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go on it,” said the archbishop. “It was obviously quite advanced in the planning.”
Ukraine ceasefire, papal visit to US
Separately, Gallagher also addressed the recent ceasefire agreed by Russia and Ukraine to allow aid into the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
He said that while Leo had recently spoken with both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, he did not believe the Vatican was involved in arranging the ceasefire.
“I don’t think we were,” said Gallagher.
He also spoke about the Vatican’s ongoing agreement with China on the appointment of Catholic bishops in the country, and acknowledged “imperfections” with the accord.
The deal, first signed in 2018, gives Chinese officials some input into whom Leo appoints as bishops in the country.
“It’s not easy, the dialogue is not easy. The imperfections of the agreement are evident, but there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue… and that is what will continue to happen,” said Gallagher.
The archbishop also said he expects Leo, the first US-born pope, to visit the United States “in the not too distant future.”
But he said the visit might not occur in 2027, depending on the pope’s commitments. REUTERS

Russia’s Oil Revenue Hits Highest Weekly Level Since 2022 as Diesel Exports Return
The value of Russia’s seaborne crude exports surged to $2.76 billion in the latest week, marking the highest level recorded since Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine, Bloomberg reported on October 27.
During the week ending October 25, the estimated value of Russian crude shipped by sea jumped by roughly $430 million to $2.76 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The increase came despite falling prices for Russia’s flagship Urals crude. The decline was more than offset by a sharp rise in export volumes and continued gains in the price of ESPO crude, which has now risen for eight consecutive weeks.
Ship-tracking data and industry reports showed that about 37 tankers loaded 26.93 million barrels of Russian crude during the week ending October 25.
That was a substantial increase from the previous week, when 31 tankers loaded approximately 21.87 million barrels.
China and India remain by far the largest buyers of Russian crude, maintaining a wide lead over other importers.
However, the final destination of many Russian oil cargoes is often unclear when tankers first leave port. Some vessels list intermediate destinations such as Suez, Port Sudan, or Singapore and only reveal their ultimate destination after traveling much of the route.
The surge comes as Russian diesel exports are also beginning to return to major international markets following a temporary easing of US sanctions and the lifting of a Russian export restriction.
US President Donald Trump recently said he had spoken with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement covering Russian diesel supplies to the US and global markets.
Under the arrangement described by Trump, Russia is expected to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to American and international markets, followed by another 500,000 tons during November and an additional 1 million tons later.
Shipping data from Kpler and LSEG also indicate that Russian diesel cargoes are already moving back toward traditional destinations. At least two tankers have recently signaled routes toward Türkiye and Brazil.
The renewed diesel flows add another layer to Russia’s energy exports at a time when its seaborne crude business is already generating record wartime revenue.
Previously, US President Donald Trump blocked the implementation of sweeping sanctions and tariffs against Russia and buyers of Russian energy under a law championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, just weeks after signing the legislation himself.

One Russian Warship Down, Another on the Way? Moscow’s New Baltic Dilemma

One Russian Warship Down, Another on the Way? Moscow’s New Baltic Dilemma
Russia may be preparing to send a newly launched missile-armed corvette to the Baltic Sea, potentially replacing a warship previously targeted by Ukrainian drones, despite the vessel originally being intended for the Pacific Fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 26, citing Polish defense outlet Defence24, Russia’s new Project 20380 corvette Grozny has raised questions about its future deployment after appearing with a tactical number associated with vessels operating in the Baltic Sea.
The corvette, launched in October 2026, is officially intended to join Russia’s Pacific Fleet once construction and outfitting are completed. However, Polish analysts identified a detail suggesting that Moscow could have other plans.
Grozny carries the tactical number 551, while vessels assigned to the Pacific Fleet’s 114th Surface Ship Brigade typically have numbers beginning with 3. By contrast, several Russian Baltic Fleet corvettes use numbers beginning with 5, including Steregushchy (550), Soobrazitelny (531), and Boyky (545).
The numbering discrepancy has led Polish analysts to question whether Grozny could eventually be deployed to the Baltic rather than the Pacific. Defense Express further suggested that the vessel could replace Boyky, another Project 20380 corvette that was struck by Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces in June 2026.
However, the outlet emphasized that the potential replacement of Boyky was its own assessment, while the Polish analysis focused on Grozny’s possible reassignment to the Baltic Fleet.
A precedent for changes in Russian naval assignments already exists. The Project 20380 corvette Mercury was initially intended for the Baltic Fleet under tactical number 535 but was later formally assigned to the Black Sea Fleet with number 735.
Despite its official assignment, Mercury has remained in the Baltic Sea because restrictions on passage through the Turkish Straits have prevented its transfer to the Black Sea.
Grozny is equipped with eight Kh-35 anti-ship missiles, a 100-mm naval gun, two AK-630 close-in weapon systems, 324-mm torpedo launchers, and a Redut air defense system with 12 missile launch cells. The 104-meter-long vessel has a full displacement of approximately 2,200 tons and can carry a Ka-27 anti-submarine helicopter.
Despite speculation surrounding its deployment, Defence24 analysts believe Grozny is unlikely to enter operational service for several years. As a result, even if Moscow ultimately redirects the corvette to the Baltic Fleet, it would not provide an immediate replacement for Boyky.
On June 3, 2026, operators from Ukraine’s 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces struck the Russian corvette Boykiy with a long-range drone while it was undergoing repairs at a dry dock in Kronstadt, near St. Petersburg.
The strike was confirmed by Ukraine’s military, while subsequent satellite imagery revealed extensive fire damage and the apparent destruction of the ship’s superstructure.

Immigrant detainee dies at Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:13:54 UTC
02:13:54 KST

Immigrant detainee dies at Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A record number of people have died in ICE custody under the Trump administration, including a person who died Saturday at the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego.
- CoreCivic, the private prison company that operates the facility, said staff attempted lifesaving measures after finding Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, 43, from Guatemala unresponsive.
- Immigration and Customs Enforcement said his death is under investigation.
WASHINGTON — An immigrant detainee died Saturday morning at the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego, marking the 61st such death under the Trump administration.
The death of Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, 43, from Guatemala is under investigation, Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed Tuesday. The cause was not immediately clear.
In a news release, ICE wrote that facility staff found Jimenez Gutierrez unresponsive at around 11:31 a.m. in his assigned safety cell — a segregation cell typically used for people who are suicidal or under psychological observation. The staffers attempted to wake him, contacted medical personnel, declared an emergency and called 911.
Medical personnel began CPR about seven minutes later, the news release states. After paramedics arrived, they continued lifesaving measures but pronounced Jimenez Gutierrez dead at about 12:23 p.m.
ICE wrote that San Diego agents arrested Jimenez Gutierrez on Oct. 9 during an enforcement operation in Escondido, reinstated a prior final removal order and transferred him to the Otay Mesa facility pending his removal to Mexico. The agency did not immediately explain why he would be sent to Mexico despite being a Guatemalan citizen.
Jimenez Gutierrez was convicted in 2024 of selling liquor to a minor, ICE said.
In an emailed statement, an unnamed spokesperson with CoreCivic, the Tennessee-based private prison company that operates the facility, confirmed the death.
“We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care,” the spokesperson wrote, adding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement was immediately notified.
The death was first reported by Daylight San Diego.
ICE said it had notified Jimenez Gutierrez’s family and the Consulate of Guatemala. The agency added that it provides comprehensive medical care and is committed to ensuring safe, secure and human environments for those in its custody.
Terra Lawson-Remer, chair of the San Diego County Board of Supervisors, said the county medical examiner was notified on Saturday, conducted an autopsy Monday and is still working to establish what happened.
“We do not yet know what caused his death, but we know a family has lost someone they love,” she said during a news conference. “They deserve answers.”
Lawson-Remer said she and Supervisor Paloma Aguirre sent a letter Tuesday to the Trump administration and CoreCivic demanding their cooperation with an independent examination and investigation. She said CoreCivic has refused to sign an agreement that would allow public health inspections inside the Otay Mesa facility despite a 2025 state law that allows local public health authorities to inspect ICE facilities.
Aguirre said she asked the county public health officer to determine what kind of follow-up is possible under that state law. She added that county leaders are also asking ICE and CoreCivic to preserve records tied to Jimenez Gutierrez’s detention, care and death, including requests for medical help.
Jimenez Gutierrez is the seventh person to die while in ICE custody in California under this administration, and the first to die at the Otay Mesa facility since 2023.
Deaths have increased as the Trump administration detained record numbers of people, with the population at one point ballooning past 70,000 nationwide.
The most recent death reported by ICE was that of Luis Sandoval, 48, a Salvadoran immigrant who died of apparent suicide Friday. Staff at the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center in Georgia found Sandoval with a ligature around his neck, according to an ICE news release.
ICE policy is to notify the public and Congress within two business days of a detainee’s death. More extensive reports about each death, which were typically three pages, must be released within 90 days, though those have been reduced to several paragraphs.

French slam Macron’s riots response – poll
French voters overwhelmingly disapprove of President Emmanuel Macron’s handling of weeks of violent nationwide protests, with just 12% backing his response, according to a new Ipsos-BVA-CESI poll.
Around 80% of respondents said Macron’s response to the unrest has been inadequate, according to the poll for Le Parisien published on Saturday. The riots also sparked widespread anger, with 58% of respondents expressing outrage.
Macron’s overall approval rating fell to 16%, the lowest since January and down seven percentage points from last month, according to a monthly CSA poll for Le Journal du Dimanche published on Sunday.
The unrest began last month with student demonstrations over teacher shortages, school funding, and deteriorating facilities before spreading nationwide. As trade unions and opposition parties joined the movement, the protests grew into broader demonstrations against soaring living costs, inequality, and cuts to public services.
The unrest escalated sharply on October 17, when around 550,000 people joined the demonstrations nationwide, spilling out into clashes with the police, arson, and widespread looting in several cities.
Immigration also emerged as an issue in public perceptions of the violence. Around 55% believe there is a link between immigration and the October 17 riots, according to a CSA survey published last Thursday.
Last week, Macron responded by announcing a crackdown on public gatherings. Protests deemed unauthorized were banned and limits on marches were imposed – even those organized by recognized groups.
Opposition leaders blamed Macron’s policies for the unrest, accusing him of failing to maintain public order.
Despite the restrictions, the demonstrations continued, drawing around 410,000 people on Saturday, according to Interior Ministry data.
Similar protests took place elsewhere in Europe, with demonstrators in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal voicing concerns about living costs, housing shortages, and public services.
After Western media outlets reported that several EU governments suspected Russia of involvement in the unrest, President Vladimir Putin dismissed the allegations.
“To claim that we are provoking mass protests in major European cities is really going too far,” Putin said, arguing that the accusations reflect European leaders’ inability to address the crisis.

Nearly 5,000 Palestinians displaced in Israel's Hebron siege
Nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been forced from their homes in Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank as Israeli military operations entered their fifth consecutive day, while raids and settler attacks continued across the territory.
The Israeli army has closed all entrances and exits to Hebron while carrying out operations in the neighbourhoods of Deir Baha and al-Jilda, the hometowns of two Palestinians who carried out a shooting attack on Friday that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded others. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to carry out collective punishment against the neighbourhoods following the shooting.
Ola al-Qawasmi, a spokesperson for Hebron Municipality, told The New Arab that municipal records showed 780 families, comprising 4,969 people, had been displaced from their homes.
Those displaced include 336 infants under the age of two, 441 people aged 60 and above, 216 pregnant or breastfeeding women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people with chronic illnesses, al-Qawasmi said.
She added that displaced families had sought shelter with relatives, while the municipality had opened temporary shelters in preparation for further displacement as the Israeli operation and siege continued.
Military raids and settler attacks
The United Nations said on Tuesday that more than 3,000 people had been displaced by Israeli forces in Hebron since Friday, as humanitarian organisations supported local authorities in responding to the needs of affected residents.
Elsewhere in the West Bank, settlers attacked the village of Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, and set fire to three cars, according to village council head Marwan Sabah.
Settlers also stormed the courtyards of Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa Mosque compound on Tuesday morning under Israeli police protection and performed Talmudic rituals. Israeli officials and far-right settlers have increasingly challenged the longstanding status quo at Islam's third-holiest site, under which non-Muslims may visit but are not permitted to pray.
In Nablus governorate, a 44-year-old Palestinian was shot in the foot by Israeli forces at the Huwara checkpoint south of the city. The Palestinian Red Crescent said troops had initially prevented its medical teams from reaching the scene after receiving reports that a vehicle had come under fire. They later allowed medics to enter and evacuate the wounded man to hospital.
A 50-year-old Palestinian was also injured in a settler assault in the town of Burqa, northwest of Nablus, according to the Red Crescent.
Israeli forces also bulldozed memorials erected in honour of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the villages of Beita, Rujeib, Azmut, Madama and Iraq Burin, as well as the town of Beit Furik, east and south of Nablus.
Troops raided several communities across the West Bank, turned homes into military barracks and carried out arrests and house searches in multiple governorates on Tuesday and overnight. Israeli forces also tightened restrictions at checkpoints and roadblocks at the entrances to towns and villages.
In the village of Burin, south of Nablus, Israeli forces had been carrying out a raid since around 2am on Tuesday, according to village council head Ibrahim Omran, who spoke to The New Arab.
Omran said troops had seized a building and converted it into a military barracks while conducting widespread raids on residents' homes. Around 20 Palestinians had been detained, he said, with all but two released by the time he spoke. The raid was still ongoing.
Olive harvest disrupted by settler violence
Settler attacks have also targeted Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest.
In Madama, south of Nablus, a settler uprooted electricity poles, damaging the village's power network and obstructing residents' access to their land. An armed settler also forced four Palestinian families to leave while they were picking olives.
Elsewhere, settlers attacked olive harvesters in several villages around Nablus and Ramallah, smashing a vehicle and stealing harvested olives.
In other incidents, settlers closed off the al-Himma spring in the northern Jordan Valley and fenced off privately owned Palestinian land, cutting off a water source used by residents and livestock, according to Hasan Malihat, director of the al-Baydar Human Rights Organisation.
Israeli forces and settlers also prevented farmers from harvesting olives in Barta'a and Turmus Ayya.
In Masafer Yatta, Israeli forces raided a Palestinian home after settlers attacked the property and assaulted family members, forcing the family to leave. Troops later arrested the homeowner and his son, according to activist Osama Makhamreh.
In Beita, south of Nablus, settlers attacked Palestinian homes and fired live ammunition at residents' vehicles as young men confronted them. No injuries were reported.

I've been singing the praises of merino wool in these pages for over five years. Most people have come around to the fact that merino wool is a super fiber; it's both sustainable and quite remarkable in its capabilities. Merino wool somehow manages to be comfortable in 95-degree heat, and it'll insulate you against below-freezing temperatures. Unlike synthetic fibers derived from petroleum, merino wool resists odors and is naturally breathable. What's not to love? The price.
Merino wool isn't cheap. That's why I love these merino T-shirts from Quince: They're just $42.
The Quince All-Season T-shirt is 100 percent extra-fine merino wool with a 165-gsm weave, which is perfect even on the warmest summer days where I live. (Admittedly, I think the hottest it got this summer was 92 Fahrenheit). I like the relaxed fit here as well. It's neither skintight technical nor overly loose and baggy. It fits like a T-shirt is supposed to. That's what Quince does well in a number of categories: offer a solid, no-nonsense, competitively priced merino wool T-shirt that fits well and feels great. As an added bonus, Quince offers free shipping and free returns for 365 days. I haven't actually tested either—I haven't needed to, my Quince T-shirt is still going strong after two years of use. But there are plenty of customer reviews on Reddit suggesting the company does honor that offer.
Not sold on the idea of a wool T-shirt? I understand. When I started testing merino, I too had visions of lumberjacks in plaid and itchy sweaters someone's grandma had knitted. None of that is merino wool. Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool, which has evolved to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures and is comfortable to wear next to your skin.
One wool myth that's not just a myth is care. Merino isn't cotton. Quince's care instructions for the All Season T-shirt say to wash it in cold water and lay flat to dry. The latter is important, as hanging merino wool to dry will stretch it out (because of the water weight). Can you throw it in the dryer? Yes. I have, for testing purposes only. It will shrink, and it will wear it out much, much faster, but you can do it.

Kernel yields: wheat up 9%, sunflower up 18%, rapeseed up 48%, corn down 13%
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:11:08 EET
02:11:08 KST

Net wheat and sunflower yields at Kernel's agricultural operations increased by 9% and 18%, respectively, year over year, reaching 6.4 tonnes per hectare and 3.1 tonnes per hectare, the company said in a stock exchange filing last week.
"The Group's total acreage under operations increased by 48% y-o-y to 530,000 hectares, following the expansion and optimization of its farming footprint during FY2026," Kernel said.
The company specified that wheat acreage increased by 13%, to 106,000 hectares, while sunflower acreage rose by 90%, to 88,000 hectares. This is expected to translate into increases in their respective harvests of 22.3%, to 678,400 tonnes, and 2.2 times, to 272,800 tonnes.
At the same time, the company noted that sunflower harvesting remains to be completed on 4% of the area allocated to the crop.
As for corn, harvesting has so far been completed on 28% of the planted area. Taking this into account, the net yield is expected to reach 8.1 tonnes per hectare, down 13% from last year, "primarily reflecting the impact of summer heatwaves and insufficient rainfall during key stages of crop development, which severely affected corn yields in one of the Group's clusters," Kernel explained.
However, given that corn acreage increased by 48% this year, to 254,000 hectares, the harvest is expected to rise by 28.6%, to 2 million 57,400 tonnes.
In addition, Kernel increased its rapeseed acreage from 3,000 hectares to 43,000 hectares. Combined with an increase in yield from 2.4 tonnes per hectare to 3.5 tonnes per hectare, this resulted in a 20.9-fold increase in the rapeseed harvest, to 150,500 tonnes.
The company also allocated 39,000 hectares to other crops, compared with 43,000 hectares last year.
Before the war, Kernel ranked first globally in sunflower oil production, accounting for about 7% of worldwide output, and exports, with a share of around 12%. It is one of Ukraine's largest producers and sellers of bottled sunflower oil. The company also grows and sells agricultural products.
In FY2026 (July 2025-June 2026), Kernel increased EBITDA by 20%, to $558 million, and net profit by 35%, to $322 million, while revenue rose 7%, to $4.404 billion.

Spain deports migrants from Ceuta in move criticised by rights group
The deportation was the first of its kind since a mass border crossing into the territory from Morocco in July.
Spain has deported more than a dozen migrants from its North African enclave of Ceuta, prompting criticism from Amnesty International, which said Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s left-wing government was endangering their human rights.
It was the first deportation of its kind since a mass border crossing into the territory from Morocco in July.
The Spanish Interior Ministry said on Tuesday that it had deported the migrants from Ceuta after their asylum applications were rejected, and that Morocco had agreed to receive them.
Nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) told the Reuters news agency that 16 people from African, Middle Eastern and Asian countries had been deported.
About 80,000 people entered from Morocco over a 48-hour period in late July. At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.2sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.
The crisis has evolved into a major political challenge for Sanchez, who is seeking re-election in snap polls scheduled for November 29.
Tens of thousands of protesters have gathered across Spain in recent months to denounce the government’s handling of the situation. Meanwhile, right-wing parties have used the crisis to attack Sanchez.
The leader of the far-right Vox Party, Santiago Abascal, has branded the prime minister a “traitor”.
Human rights guarantees
Amnesty International has warned that the human rights of those deported from Ceuta on Tuesday could be at risk.
“Spain, despite its [progressive] speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” said Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher.
“Morocco does not respect many human rights.”
However, Madrid disputes the rights group’s accusations. In a statement, the interior ministry told Reuters that the European Union considers Morocco to be a safe country, adding that deportations are carried out “with all the necessary safeguards”.
Most of those who entered Ceuta in late July left within days. However, about 8,000 migrants still remain. Some are sleeping on the streets, while others are being housed by Spain, charities and civil society groups.

‘Well-known’ public figure in bid to stop publication of allegations of inappropriate sexual activities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:09:13 UTC
02:09:13 KST

A “well-known individual” attempting to block two media outlets from publishing allegations about him has been accused of inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities with girls and young women, the high court has heard.
The individual, referred to in court as PPT, is seeking a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing the allegations, which he denies. His legal team argued that publishing them would “highly likely lead him to commit suicide”.
In written submissions to the court in London, the news outlets said the allegations involved more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts, as part of a “wide-ranging and rigorous investigation”.
However, at the opening of a two-day trial, PPT’s legal team argued it was a “highly exceptional” case in which publishing was likely to lead to the death of the claimant.
In a written submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team said that he suffered from “very severe mental health problems”.
“It is important to understand that this drastic effect on the claimant is not from guilt of the wrongdoing alleged (which is denied) but because of shame arising from deep-rooted childhood trauma and the fear of ‘trial by media’,” it stated.
Sara Mansoori KC, PPT’s lead barrister, said that he had first attempted to commit suicide in May, when the Guardian and ITN contacted him to give him the chance to respond to the allegations. He was admitted to hospital that afternoon as a voluntary patient.
The court was told PPT made a second attempt to take his life in July, “on that occasion absconding from a secure hospital to do so”.
Submissions to the court by PPT’s legal team stated he is detained in a psychiatric hospital for his own safety and has no intention of returning to public life.
The claimant is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life, article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment” and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.
Setting out the claimant’s case, Mansoori pointed to medical evidence that PPT’s life would be endangered should the allegations be published.
“It would be a travesty if the court didn’t step in to act in these circumstances,” Mansoori said.
According to written submissions from the news outlets, they will argue that the European court of human rights, which enforces the ECHR, has never required a state to prevent publication of journalism in order to protect against the risk of suicide by an individual.
The written submissions argue that any duties the state has towards PPT should come in the form of NHS mental health treatment and its powers under the Mental Health Act.
The news outlets will set out their case to the court on Wednesday.
An independent expert assessment of the claimant’s current wellbeing stated that “community arrangements” would not be sufficient to manage the immediate suicide risk around the prospect of publishing the allegations.
“Publication while the claimant remains in an inpatient psychiatric setting would be significantly safer in terms of reducing the likelihood of a successful suicide,” the expert concluded, according to a summary of his findings.
“The expert does not conclude either that suicide is inevitable if publication occurs, or that psychiatric treatment can eliminate all risk,” the expert’s report states.
Mr Justice Nicklin, the judge overseeing the case, opened the trial with a warning about online speculation over PPT’s identity.
“That speculation has named several different individuals,” he said. “This is a difficult and important case. The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions, while respecting both the principle of open justice and the protective purpose of the orders already made.
“I ask that the court be allowed to perform that task without further attempts to identify PPT or any other person whose identity is protected.”
The trial continues.

In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. Türkiye presents Digital Sovereignty Strategy to Cybersecurity Board
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:08:55 UTC
02:08:55 KST

Seyit Şamil Kurt
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Türkiye's Digital Sovereignty Strategy, aimed at strengthening the country's sovereignty in the digital sphere and reducing dependence on foreign technologies, was presented to the Cybersecurity Board on Tuesday, according to the country's Communications Directorate.
The board met under the chairmanship of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and discussed the implications of global and regional geopolitical developments for the cybersecurity environment, as well as recent cybersecurity incidents worldwide and evolving threat dynamics, the directorate said in a statement.
The board was briefed on how developments in artificial intelligence are affecting the nature, scale, and speed of cyber threats.
It also assessed the effects and risks of algorithmic manipulation and cognitive influence activities carried out through digital platforms on national security and societal resilience.
The meeting stressed the importance of digital sovereignty for national security, identifying the protection of critical infrastructure, strengthening national cyber resilience and deterrence capabilities, and achieving technological independence as strategic priorities in Türkiye's security and development policies.
Against this backdrop, the strategy was presented to the board with the aim of "strengthening Türkiye's sovereignty in the digital sphere, reducing dependence on foreign sources in critical technologies, and developing national technology capacity," the statement said.
The board decided that measures taken in line with the strategy's objectives would be implemented by relevant institutions and organizations within their respective spheres, while implementation processes would be effectively monitored and progress regularly assessed.
The meeting also focused on strengthening interagency coordination, developing joint risk assessment capabilities, and ensuring consistency in implementation, given the ability of cyber threats to spread rapidly and affect multiple sectors simultaneously.
The board reaffirmed its commitment to deepening cooperation among public institutions, the private sector, and academia and developing a comprehensive cybersecurity ecosystem, the statement added.

UN nuclear watchdog demands access to Iran's 440kg stockpile of highly enriched uranium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:08:41 UTC
02:08:41 KST

The head of the UN nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to provide the information and access needed to verify its previously declared nuclear material, including 440 kilogrammes of highly enriched uranium, warning that outstanding safeguards issues remain unresolved.
Addressing the UN Security Council, International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi said on Tuesday that the agency continued to engage with Tehran to resolve questions concerning its nuclear programme and verify material at facilities covered by safeguards agreements.
“One area of particular concern is Iran’s previously declared nuclear material, which includes 440kg of High Enriched Uranium,” Grossi said, adding that the issues had remained outstanding for more than five years.
IAEA seeks access to nuclear facilities
Grossi said the agency had withdrawn all its inspectors from Iran by the end of June 2025 for safety reasons following the start of military attacks.
Although inspectors had been available to return for months, he said Iran had not provided the information and access required to verify previously declared nuclear material at safeguarded facilities, including sites affected by military attacks and those that were not.
The Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant remains an exception, with IAEA inspectors currently conducting verification activities there.
Grossi also said Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization had engaged constructively with the agency to arrange the delivery of safeguards equipment needed to verify spent nuclear fuel before its transfer to a new dry storage facility, expected early next year.
“I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions,” Grossi said, stressing that providing access was Iran’s legal obligation.
Security Council adopts agenda amid divisions
The Security Council opened its session by adopting the agenda with 11 votes in favour, two against from Russia and China, and two abstentions from Pakistan and Somalia.
Grossi highlighted the scale of the IAEA’s global verification work, saying its inspectors spent more than 14,000 calendar days in the field last year, carrying out verification activities at more than 1,400 facilities and locations outside them.
The agency was able to draw safeguards conclusions for 179 states, he said, underscoring the role of inspections in monitoring compliance with nuclear safeguards obligations.
The dispute over access in Iran remains a key challenge for the agency as it seeks to establish the status of previously declared nuclear material and resolve outstanding questions about Tehran’s nuclear activities.

The campaign echoes Netanyahu's previous election tactics, in which he has sought to rally right-wing voters by warning of high Palestinian Arab turnout.
The election is the first since the October 2023 Hamas-led attacks and Israel's subsequent wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Opinion polls ahead of the vote suggested Netanyahu's coalition could lose its parliamentary majority, although opposition parties also faced difficulties securing the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The US selected Poland to host a new European maintenance facility for Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) missile systems, a move aimed at strengthening NATO’s air and missile defense capabilities and improving military readiness on the alliance’s eastern flank, the Pentagon said Tuesday.
The announcement was made on the sidelines of a meeting of NATO’s Conference of National Armaments Directors (CNAD), with the US government coordinating with defense contractor Lockheed Martin and European allies on the initiative.
Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden will lead critical supply-chain integration for the facility, which will establish regional maintenance, repair and overhaul capabilities for PAC-3 missiles within Europe, the Pentagon said in a statement.

The Pentagon said the initiative advances defense-industrial commitments made at the NATO summit in Ankara in July under the framework it described as “NATO 3.0.” The broader objective is to increase European allies’ ability to assume primary responsibility for their conventional defense while maintaining close cooperation with the US.

In Armenia, archaeologists found a coin of Emperor Octavian Augustus

In Armenia, archaeologists found a coin of Emperor Octavian Augustus
Kyiv • UNN
Archaeologists near Metsamor discovered a coin of Octavian Augustus, gold earrings, and a bronze dagger. The tomb dates to different eras.
A coin of the Roman emperor Octavian Augustus, gold earrings, a bronze dagger and other artifacts were discovered by archaeologists during excavations near the Metsamor Historical and Archaeological Museum-Reserve in Armenia. Armenian media report this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Service for the Protection of the Historical Environment and Historical and Cultural Museum-Reserves, the finds date to different historical periods, including the Late Bronze Age, the Iron Age and antiquity.
Excavations at the site under investigation began in 2024 and continued in 2026. The work is being carried out on privately owned land. The structure under investigation is a stone burial chamber surrounded by a circular stone structure.
During excavations in previous years, a burial from the ancient period, dating to the 1st century AD, was discovered in the upper layer of the tomb. Among the objects found were gold ornaments, a coin and other artifacts.
In the lower part of the burial chamber, near its base, archaeologists discovered the main burial, which, according to the preliminary dating of the materials found, dates to the 14th–13th centuries BC.
This layer contained a concentration of horse bones, numerous pottery fragments, a dagger of the Lchashen type, fragments of a belt, pieces of bronze objects and bell-shaped pendants.
