Sardinian restaurants ban families from using phones at the table
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:43:05 UTC
01:43:05 KST

A group of restaurants in Sardinia are banning families from using smartphones and other devices at the table in a quest to encourage conversation.
The initiative, called A tavola senza schermi or At the table without screens, is being spearheaded by Anna Cau, the children’s ombudsman for the Italian island. It is part of a campaign to curtail excessive screen use among children and inspire interaction during meals.
Parents and their children will be required to put their phones away when dining at any of the 15 restaurants that have volunteered to participate in the scheme during a one-month pilot exercise beginning next week.
Cau, a former juvenile magistrate, said: “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others.
“We need real-world settings that strengthen and accommodate the lives of both adults and children. This initiative is a small step within a broader philosophy that guides my approach to this highly complex issue.”
After families hand in their devices, restaurant staff will give them a “reunion kit” containing games and drawings. The kit, which has been designed by the Italian federation of paediatricians, is aimed at helping under-18s start conversations with their parents, such as sharing stories about their day.
The kit includes a brochure outlining the risks of digital overexposure and tips on managing social media use at home.
“The restaurants will offer an alternative activity in the form of a game which is intended to foster interaction,” said Cau. “Obviously, the games are structured with time limits within the context of a restaurant lunch or dinner.”
Cau worked on the scheme with the Sardinian wing of Fipe-Confcommercio, an association uniting the catering, tourism and entertainment sectors.
Emanuele Frongia, president of the federation on the island, said the 15 restaurants had readily agreed to participate. The plan is to expand the initiative on a voluntary basis.
“Restaurants play a vital role in fostering the intimacy that families rediscover when they dine out,” said Frongia. “Yet we increasingly observe that during these moments lively chatter is replaced with stretches of silence as people look at their devices. Often a child is handed one to keep them quiet.”

Kazakhstan, U.S. discuss prospects for small modular reactor technologies use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Kazakhstan, U.S. discuss prospects for small modular reactor technologies use
Kazakhstan and the United States have discussed prospects for the peaceful use of nuclear energy, the development of small modular reactors (SMRs) and scientific and technical cooperation, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Agency for Atomic Energy of Kazakhstan.
The issues were discussed at a meeting between Almasadam Satkaliyev, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy, and Shawna J. Wilson, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Security Assistance Programs.
Particular attention was given to the international FIRST (Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology) program, which conducts technical-economic assessments of SMR technologies to explore their potential use in Kazakhstan.
The sides also discussed expanding scientific and technical cooperation, including joint research in radiation materials science, training scientific personnel and promoting academic mobility.
Other topics included strengthening partnerships between research institutions and universities in the two countries, as well as involving Kazakhstani scientists in international research projects.
Following the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their mutual interest in further developing Kazakhstan-U.S. cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
Earlier, President Tokayev ordered tighter oversight of Kazakhstan's nuclear energy sector.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

Near the Bay of Naples in Italy, the ancient city of Pompeii stands as a remarkable time capsule. In 79 AD, at the height of the Roman Empire’s prosperity, Mount Vesuvius erupted with overwhelming force. Within hours, the city was buried under meters of ash and pumice. This catastrophe turned out to be an unintentional act of preservation, sealing an entire civilization in place for nearly 2,000 years.
Walking through Pompeii, visitors are struck by the sophistication of its urban design and the vivid traces of daily life it preserves. The ash sealed out air and moisture, leaving streets, buildings and everyday objects intact. The city’s well-organized roads, raised sidewalks for pedestrians and public fountains reveal the Romans’ advanced engineering techniques. Written messages can also be seen on walls, including election slogans, restaurant menus and graffiti by ordinary citizens. Together, these features offer a clear picture of a lively and orderly commercial society.
Perhaps the most haunting discoveries are the plaster casts of the victims. As bodies decomposed inside hardened ash, they left behind hollow cavities that retained their final postures. In the 19th century, archaeologists filled these spaces with plaster, capturing the victims’ final moments. Some figures appear to be shielding themselves, while others cling to loved ones or personal belongings. Such details transform historical facts into deeply human stories, connecting us emotionally to people who lived two millennia ago.
Photo: Flickr / 照片： Flickr
Today, Pompeii remains one of the world’s most important archaeological sites. As visitors walk through its quiet streets, they are reminded not only of Roman civilization’s brilliance, but also of this city’s sudden end. No matter how powerful or prosperous a society may be, it cannot escape the forces of nature. The ruins of Pompeii, frozen in time, continue to speak of human vulnerability and the fleeting nature of life.
在義大利的拿坡里灣附近，古城龐貝是一個十分特別的時間膠囊。在西元 79 年，羅馬帝國正值鼎盛之際，維蘇威火山以壓倒性的力量爆發。幾小時內，這座城市便被掩埋在數公尺厚的火山灰和浮石之下。這場災難最終卻成了無意的保存行為，將整個文明原地封存了將近兩千年。
走在龐貝城中，遊客會被它精細的都市設計，以及它所保存的鮮明日常生活痕跡所震撼。火山灰隔絕了空氣和濕氣，使街道、建築物和日常生活用品完好無損。這座城市規劃良好的道路、供行人使用的加高人行道，以及公共噴泉都展現了羅馬人先進的工程技術。牆上也可以看見書寫的訊息，包括選舉口號、餐廳菜單，以及普通市民留下的塗鴉。這些特色共同呈現出一個充滿活力且井然有序的商業社會清晰的面貌。
或許最令人難以忘懷的發現，是遇難者的石膏模型。遺體在硬化的火山灰中分解時，它們留下了保有最後姿勢的中空空洞。在西元 19 世紀，考古學家用石膏填滿這些空間，捕捉了遇難者最後的時刻。有些人形看起來像是在保護自己，有些則緊抱親人或個人財物。這樣的細節將歷史事實轉化成深刻的人性故事，在情感上把我們與兩千年前的人連結起來。
如今，龐貝仍是世界上最重要的考古遺址之一。當遊客走在它寂靜的街道上時，他們不只會想起羅馬文明的輝煌，也會想起這座城市突如其來的終結。無論一個社會可能多麼強大或繁榮，它都無法逃過自然的力量。被時間凍結的龐貝遺跡，持續訴說著人類的脆弱，以及生命短暫易逝的本質。

Former FBI director James Comey has been charged with allegedly disclosing national defense information, the third criminal case brought against the outspoken critic of US President Donald Trump.
In a criminal complaint unsealed on Monday, Comey is accused of communicating the information in October 2016, when he was head of the FBI, to a “person not entitled to receive it.”
Comey was charged in September last year with making false statements to US Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding in what was widely seen as retribution by the Republican president against a political opponent.
Photo: AP
A federal judge threw out the case on the grounds that the US attorney handpicked by Trump who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.
Comey was indicted again in April, this time for allegedly threatening Trump’s life in an Instagram post that showed the numbers “86 47” spelled out in sea shells.
The Trump administration’s Department of Justice has claimed that “86 47” constitutes a threat to the president — “86” meaning to kill and “47” a reference to Trump being the 47th president.
Comey has denied threatening the president’s life.
In the latest case, Comey is accused of directing an unidentified person to “disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.”
“They’re back again,” Comey said in a video posted on his Substack in response to the latest charges.
“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice,” he said. “I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
In a statement to US media, Comey’s attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said the charges in the latest case had been investigated by prosecutors during the first Trump administration and “the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone.”
The unsealing of the court documents came just hours after a US federal judge ruled that firing of Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor in New York, in July last year was unlawful.

====================================================================================================

Super-rich cashing in on climate crisis, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

The world’s wealthiest people are not just profiting from the polluting causes of climate breakdown, they are also increasingly cashing in on the catastrophic consequences, a study by Oxfam showed.
The global equality organization has found that the richest 0.1 percent of the world’s population are heavily invested in disaster preparedness, recovery and reconstruction — a market that is projected to grow from US$70 billion to US$92 billion a year by 2029.
This gives the planet’s wealthiest and most powerful people a “double dividend” from the climate crisis and, more alarmingly, an incentive to delay or disrupt action to solve the problem, the non-governmental organization said.
Photo: Bloomberg
It also worsens global inequality as those least responsible for global heating end up having to pay those most responsible in terms of higher food prices, repairing homes damaged by extreme weather or relocating to other areas.
Oxfam chief influencing officer Jean McLean accused billionaires of turning chaos into profit.
“The super-rich benefit at both ends of the crisis: First, through continued investment in polluting industries, and second, through investment in the booming ‘adaptation economy’ — recovery and rebuilding services are sold back to a warming world,” she said. “The populations who contributed least to the climate crisis are absorbing its worst consequences, while those who caused it are best equipped to protect themselves.”
The richest 0.1 percent on the planet, a group of 8 million people, are responsible for more carbon emissions than the poorest 3.5 billion combined, the report says.
As a result, the richest group have reportedly contributed by 125 times more than the average person to extreme heat events.
That is partly due to lifestyles. For example, private jets release more carbon dioxide in two seconds than most of the world’s people emit in an entire year, but the biggest impact of this group comes from their investments.
Oxfam’s new destroy and rebuild index identifies 217 corporations that either fuel climate breakdown or do business in adapting to it through provision of cooling devices, flood barriers, firefighting equipment, transportation, food, insurance and loans.
Last year, these companies made an average of US$1.8 billion and paid out US$1 billion in dividends to shareholders. Six major asset managing firms, which advise wealthy investors, are on this list in their own right and are heavily invested in other members. Two of the biggest, BlackRock and Vanguard, have shares in 92 percent of the companies in the index, worth a total of more than US$1 trillion, Oxfam said.
Similarly, it said that crises — caused by extreme weather or war — have tended to boost the profits of major food trading companies that are dominated by billionaires, whose wealth has increased by US$120 billion since 2020.
When drought, floods or storms hit crops, any subsequent increase in food prices tends to disproportionately benefit big corporations and their investors at the cost of small producers and regular consumers, Oxfam said.
The group cited the case of a 231 percent surge in cocoa prices after extreme weather in west Africa in 2024, saying that local farmers saw none of the gains.
Such inequality has consequences. The annual emissions for the richest 1 percent would cause 1.9 million excess deaths due to heat, Oxfam said, based on estimated impacts on human health, agricultural productivity and sea level rise.
More than three-quarters of those deaths would occur in low and middle-income countries, which are far less responsible for the crisis, because they produce only 8 percent of emissions.
Wealthy nations and wealthy people are somewhat insulated — at least for now — from the climate crisis, because they are more likely to be able to afford higher food prices, robust houses, emergency evacuation, private healthcare and personal security.
That makes them less likely to use their considerable lobbying power to support climate action, and might even encourage them to slow or block emissions cuts that could affect their personal wealth, Oxfam said, adding that instead, some use disasters to push privatization agendas or encourage poor nations to take out loans.
Alex Maitland, one of the lead authors, said the richest people were not just passive beneficiaries of the climate crisis.
“This is deliberate,” he said. “When you take into account their political influence, this is pretty damning evidence that they’re able to orchestrate that is happening.”
Oxfam is demanding higher taxes on the rich, private jets, oil and gas companies, and polluting companies. The group calls on the British government to improve international climate financing commitments based on grants rather than loans, and to end profiteering from climate disasters.
Nafkote Dabi, the climate change policy lead at Oxfam International, said: “What’s complex about talking about climate change is everyone likes to think it’s a shared problem, but it’s not. Addressing the climate crisis is really easy. Control the richest, curb their power, curb their emissions, and also tax their wealth.”

The National Police Agency (NPA) will step up efforts to prevent election interference by China, gangs and local collaborators, Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) said yesterday.

Comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) has also been subjected to surveillance and attacks allegedly carried out by local collaborators working on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party, while television host and writer Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) might have been pressured into issuing a public apology and saying he did not support Taiwan independence, Lin said.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said that external forces have repeatedly sent military aircraft and warships to harass Taiwan, with these activities growing increasingly brazen and extending into Taiwan’s territory.
The examples cited by Lin clearly show that these operations are directed by foreign forces and carried out with the assistance of local collaborators, he added.
In Shen’s case, the Hong Kongers who allegedly commissioned and funded the operation have fled, Cho said, adding that the sequence of events appears to be a clear example of how transnational repression is carried out in practice.
Noting that effective countermeasures must be developed under the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) and through other relevant mechanisms, Cho said a task force has already been established, and at last week’s Cabinet meeting, he called for measures to protect public safety, including the security of all candidates and related individuals over the next month.
Liu said her ministry, through the NPA, would implement special measures to counter transnational repression, in line with directives from the Presidential Office and the Cabinet.
During the election campaign, enhanced security measures would be introduced for any candidate who experience a surge in online or media attacks, she said.
Since the beginning of this year, the NPA has launched three nationwide crackdowns on organized crime, she said.
Together with its ongoing crime-fighting initiatives, the operations have resulted in 483 cases involving 2,886 suspects, she said.
Some of those involved have ties to specific political parties, and authorities have seized more than NT$700 million (US$21.57 million) in illicit proceeds, she said.
With election campaigning entering its final stretch, Liu said the NPA would direct police agencies nationwide to step up efforts to prevent transnational repression and interference by local gangs and collaborators from affecting Taiwan’s elections.
Such interference would have a negative impact on the development of Taiwan’s democracy, she said.
Liu also called on the Legislative Yuan to expedite amendments to the National Security Act (國家安全法), the Anti-Infiltration Act and relevant laws, saying stronger legal tools would enable the government to take action against those who openly or covertly threaten public safety and national security.

Harry Kane on Monday became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or thanks to his prolific scoring last season.
Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign — he was Europe’s top scorer — and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the FIFA World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.
The 33-year-old Kane said that winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.
Photo: EPA
“Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief,” an emotional Kane said in a message to young players after reflecting on his early-career struggles.
“My journey wasn’t straightforward. I wasn’t the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs,” he said. “I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well.”
Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal — voted best young talent for a third straight year — 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.
Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children and wife.
Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and DFB-Pokal double, scoring a hat-trick against VfB Stuttgart in the Cup final.
At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England’s all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semi-finals, but beat Mbappe’s France for third place, England’s best World Cup placing in 60 years.
An Englishman had not won the Ballon d’Or since Michael Owen in 2001.
“It’s massive for England, for our country. [The ceremony] being here in London was a good omen for me,” Kane said. “It’s been too long. Certainly [there have been] incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I’m extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honor, the thing I love to do the most.”
England coach Thomas Tuchel told Kane that the Three Lions are “lucky to have you as our leader.”
“I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I’m delighted to see that you have now been formally recognized by the football world,” Tuchel said.
Kane planned to celebrate with family and friends, but just a little.
“We have a [DFB-Pokal] Cup game [against second-tier Magdeburg] on Wednesday, so it can’t get too messy,” Kane said, adding that he had an early flight back to Munich in time for team training.
Monday’s ceremony was held in London for the first time in recognition of the inaugural winner 70 years ago, England’s Stanley Matthews in 1956.

Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the off-season, also helped Spain win the Women’s Nations League in December last year.
The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign.
Bonmati, who completed her women’s Ballon d’Or three-peat last year, was not on this year’s shortlist after breaking her leg in December last year.
There was not a women’s Ballon d’Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.
Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with “love and passion.”
“Believe in yourself, that’s the most important thing,” she said. “If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero.”
Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club “something special.”
“I’m really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player” at Barcelona, she said. “What I experienced last year was like a perfect story.”

President William Lai’s (賴清德) trust and approval ratings rebounded to 53 percent and 52.2 percent respectively, both the highest since April last year, surveys released by polling expert Tai Li-an (戴立安) yesterday showed.
Only 35.4 percent of respondents said they did not trust Lai, the lowest rating since December 2024, the poll showed.
Regarding Lai’s overall performance, 52.2 percent of respondents said they were satisfied, while 37.6 percent were dissatisfied.
Photo: CNA
The polls also showed Premier Cho Jung-tai’s (卓榮泰) approval rating rising 5.8 percentage points to 47.7 percent, a record high since he took office.
Asked if they have a favorable impression of the following politicians, with respondents allowed multiple selections, former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) topped the poll at 61.7 percent, followed by three more DPP politicians — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) with 53.5 percent, Lai with 49.7 percent and DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) with 47.8 percent.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) politicians lagged behind, with Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) each getting 36.9 percent, Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) 35.0 percent and KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) 15.5 percent.
Another 8.6 percent of respondents did not provide a clear answer.
The survey was conducted from Tuesday to Thursday last week, collecting 1,075 valid responses with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

NSC says latest Fukushima discharge won’t affect Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:18 UTC
01:42:18 KST

Japan’s latest discharge of treated wastewater containing tritium from the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant is not expected to affect waters around Taiwan, the Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC) said yesterday.
The 25th round of discharges began on Monday and is expected to continue for 19 days, with about 7,800 tonnes of wastewater to be released, the NSC said in a report issued to update the public on each discharge round.
The wastewater is expected to mainly affect waters off eastern Japan, while tritium concentrations in waters around Taiwan are forecast to remain below the minimum detectable level of monitoring instruments, the NSC said, citing forecasts by the Central Weather Administration and information from Japan’s Tokyo Electric Power Co (TEPCO).
Photo: Taipei Times
Japan began releasing treated wastewater from the disabled plant in August 2023. It has since completed 24 rounds of discharges, releasing a total of about 188,000 cubic meters of wastewater, the NSC said.
Taiwan has also been monitoring radiation levels in surrounding waters. Since 2017, authorities have analyzed more than 20,000 samples of seawater, marine life, seafood, beach sand and seabed sediment, with no abnormal radiation detected, the NSC said.

Elderly traffic fatalities rise 3%, ministry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:16 UTC
01:42:16 KST

The number of people aged 65 or older who died within 30 days of a traffic incident rose 3 percent year-on-year to 790 in the first eight months of this year, despite an overall decline in road fatalities, Ministry of Transportation and Communications data released yesterday showed.
The total number of deaths within 30 days of a traffic incident fell 2.8 percent to 1,777 in the January-to-August period from a year earlier, and was down 10.7 percent from the same period in 2023, the ministry said.
In the first seven months of this year, traffic fatalities among people aged 65 or older increased 5 percent, or 33 more than the same period last year, but for the first eight months, it was only a 3 percent rise, or 23 more deaths compared with the same period last year, Department of Railways, Highways and Road Safety Director-General Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Deaths in the age group were highest in motorcycle-related incidents and incidents involving pedestrians, he said.
Among the three administrative regions that recorded the largest increases in elderly traffic deaths, the year-to-date increase in Taoyuan fell from 25 through July to 23 through August, the data showed.
In Hualien County, that figure fell from 13 to 11 for the two periods, while in Taichung, it rose from 14 to 20, the data showed.
Wu urged families to pay close attention to the safety of elderly relatives when they are on the road.
Overall, road safety indicators showed improvement, the ministry said.
In the first eight months of this year, motorcycle-related deaths fell by 217, or 17.1 percent, from the same period in 2023, while fatalities among children and teenagers declined by 29, or 52.7 percent, and deaths in drunk-driving incidents dropped by 99, or 56.6 percent.
Separately, 1,132 people died in “A1” traffic incidents — defined as those resulting in death at the scene or within 24 hours — in the first nine months of this year, down 14.2 percent from 2023 and 6.4 percent from last year.
Meanwhile, 377,039 people were injured in A2 traffic incidents — those resulting in injuries or deaths occurring more than 24 hours later — in the first nine months, down 6.1 percent from 2023 and 4 percent from last year.
Twenty-three fatalities involving drug-driving incidents were recorded in the first six months of this year, while 11 deaths were recorded in July and August, after the National Police Agency broadened the statistical definition, the ministry said.
However, road deaths within 30 days of an incident reached 177 in New Taipei City and 74 on national highways in the first eight months of this year, showing an upward trend compared with the same period in 2023 and last year, the ministry said.
Wu said that secondary collisions on highways were a growing concern, with six such incidents reported in August.
Motorists involved in crashes should move to a safe location away from traffic when possible, he said.
In incidents involving only property damage, drivers should photograph the scene and move their vehicles to a safe location before reporting the incident, rather than waiting for police to arrive, he added.

Taiwan, EU decide their ties, MEP says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

Beijing has no say in Taiwan’s partnerships with European countries, Formosa Club acting chair Rihards Kols, a member of the European Parliament (MEP), told a forum in Taipei yesterday.
The Formosa Club, an interparliamentary group of European lawmakers, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs cohosted the Trusted Technology Forum for Democracies, focusing on artificial intelligence (AI) and drone technologies.
In his opening speech, Kols said it is crucial that people meet and understand each other’s concerns, and work out how they can help.
Photo: CNA
The club has brought European parliamentarians to the second annual forum to understand Taiwan better and seek opportunities for collaboration, he said.
There is a lot of common ground between Taiwan and Europe, he said.
Both want people to live freely and securely, businesses to succeed and to “make our own decisions without someone else threatening to punish us for that,” he said.
There is also a lot the two sides can offer to each other, such as Taiwan’s strengths in semiconductors, electronics and its growing drone industry, and Europe’s experience in manufacturing and industrial technology, he said.
Europe has learned a costly lesson about dependence from treating Russia’s energy as a commercial matter and dismissing warnings about political leverage, and the same mistake cannot be made with the technologies that factories, communications and defense systems rely on, Kols said.
“Before we buy a system, we should know: Who controls it? Where does the data go? Can we repair it?” he said, adding that these questions become more important when hospitals, electricity network and a country’s defense depend on it.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has shown how quickly military designs change and the importance of quickly producing and repairing equipment, he said.
Parliamentarians should work to bring trusted businesses, researchers, investors and policymakers closer together for technology cooperation, he said.
“The European Parliament has called for better market access, greater certainty for investors and closer cooperation with Taiwan on critical technologies. That matters to the company considering an investor, a researcher looking for an industrial partner, or a manufacturer seeking a reliable supplier,” he said.
“Beijing[’s] objections cannot give it a right to decide whom Europeans meet or which partnerships we build,” he said, adding that Taiwan and Europe should be able to pursue opportunities that serve mutual interests.
AI and drones are rapidly becoming fundamental to economies and security, but they carry a heightened vulnerability, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Francois Wu (吳志中) said.
“In an age of geopolitical competition, authoritarian states are treating these technologies as tools of cohesion and related supply chains as instruments of power to challenge the status quo,” Wu said, adding that Taiwan and Europe feel it directly, from Russia and China.
“How do democracies keep the technologies they depend on in trusted hands?” he asked.
Taiwan stands at the heart of many of the world’s high-tech ecosystems, but its greatest contribution to the free world is not just what it makes, but that the nation’s partners can trust how Taiwan makes it and with whom, he said.
“Taiwan is committed to creating non-red supply chains that are secure, transparent and free of coercive control,” he said. “A stronger, more autonomous Europe and a trusted Taiwan are complementary, not competing.”
Europe leads industrial-based world-class research and a drive toward re-industrialization, while Taiwan leads in semiconductors, AI servers, and the coming wave of physical and embodied AI, he said.
“That combination makes us indispensable to each other,” Wu said. “Together Europe and Taiwan can widen the options available to democracies so that no single supplier and no single government can hold our shared future hostage.”

Xi’s lifelong presidency should be opposed: MAC head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:42:15 KST

People of conscience should support calls to end Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) unlimited presidential term, Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said yesterday.
Chiu made the remarks in response to media queries for comment about a petition reportedly circulating on Monday among Chinese university students from 14 institutions, including Peking University, urging the reinstatement of term limits for Chinese presidents.
Monday was also the opening day of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party’s plenary meeting.
Photo: AP
The petition, titled: “A Joint Appeal from a Group of University Students in the Republic,” was first posted on a Chinese-language Web site.
The petition, which was quickly taken down, demanded restoring constitutional term limits on China’s leaders and defining the office’s roles and powers.
It also called for initiating democratic constitutional amendments by convening a national conference of the people and improving the mechanisms for election, supervision and recall processes, and protecting spaces for people to discuss public affairs.
The open letter has also been published on other Web sites.
Chinese university students were “confounded and disturbed” by the authorities’ abolition of the constitutionally mandated term limits for the office of the Chinese president and vice president, the petition said.
“We deeply understand stability and continuity are needed by the nation for its development, but the source of stability should be the predictability of institutions, not dependence on an individual,” it said.
The party should reform itself to ensure that power is subject to term limits and checks, and respect the people’s right to criticize and advocate for public affairs, it said.
Xi in March 2018 oversaw the process for constitutional amendments that made him president for life, an act that allowed him to consolidate power and weaken institutional constraints.
A Radio Free Asia report said it was unable to determine whether the open letter originated in China, as the Siyuan Lake BBS Web site was hosted in South Korea, and no personal name was used.
In Taipei, Chiu told reporters on the sidelines of a legislative meeting that “every intellectual possessing a conscience would support the open letter,” regardless of its origins.
Chinese professors he had met in 2017 before the freeze in cross-strait exchanges had made similar objections to Xi’s move to make himself president for life, Chiu said.
The academics at the time said political tradition demanded that Xi nominate a successor as China’s president, not seek additional terms, he said.
Chinese intellectuals absolutely cannot accept Xi’s presidency for life, Chiu said.
However, after the Chinese Communist Party consolidated power around a single leader, the intellectuals’ ability to correct political errors “disappeared entirely,” Chiu said.
Screen grabs obtained by the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister paper) showed the petition had appeared in at least 17 forums with links to Chinese universities.

EDITORIAL: Choosing a leader with a vision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:13 UTC
01:42:13 KST

Videos of passers-by playing a public piano at the new Tainan Railway Station have gone viral on the Internet. From children to teenagers, from young adults to seniors, people from all walks of life lined up near the piano, waiting to share their music with the crowd who had gathered to enjoy an impromptu performance at a bustling transport hub.
Within just a few days, the station hall has become a concert hall featuring all sorts of music instruments — strings, woodwinds, brass — you name it. Taiwan Railway Corp’s official social media account “clarified” that not every passenger is required to be able to play the piano before they travel to Tainan.
Former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文), in a post on Threads, tagging Tainan Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲) of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and DPP mayoral candidate Chen Ting-fei (陳亭妃), asked whether Tainan Railway Station has become an opera house or a music hall, praising Tainan residents’ musical talent.
Some Threads users attributed Tainan residents’ musical talent to the efforts of former Tainan mayor Hsu Tain-tsair (許添財) of the DPP, who promoted music and art education in elementary and junior-high schools during his tenure from 2001 to 2010. The policy encouraged students to learn at least one musical instrument and every school to have at least one art group.
Hsu in 2009 said more than 90 percent of elementary-school students and 80 percent of junior-high school students could play at least one musical instrument. The number of art groups in schools more than doubled from 102 in 2003 to 237 in 2008, a report by Global Views Monthly in 2009 said.
Hsu said he hoped that while receiving their basic education, every child who grew up in Tainan would also learn to appreciate music. The policy has clearly had a profound impact on the city’s music education.
Universal music education takes time and requires resources. It is not something that would bring instant material benefits or tangible results. However, it breaks the barrier of class, providing equal access to learning music among ordinary households, nurturing cultural literacy in society.
“A musical instrument for every child” is certainly not a policy that aims to benefit the privileged class or a slogan to fight for votes, as it could take years to pay off. It is a policy that requires a long-term vision of a city where future generations would live in the years to come.
This is something worth thinking about ahead of next month’s local elections. In the capital, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), who is seeking re-election, has repeatedly bragged about his “fresh milk for every child” policy, his efforts to turn Taipei into a smoke-free city and the Taipei Dome that opened during his tenure. Recently, out of the blue, he announced his plan to relocate Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) — much to the surprise not only of the central government, but also his fellow KMT candidates, and of course the local residents.
A mayor near the end of his tenure announcing a major urban renewal plan that would involve dismantling an international airport to construct an industrial park — which would likely only benefit developers — without consulting relevant authorities and stakeholders is either reckless, desperate or both.
A Threads user suggested that instead of distributing fresh milk to every child, Chiang might garner more votes by giving out beer to every wage slave in Taipei.
While inspecting the city’s recovery from the aftermath of Typhoon Champi over the weekend, Chiang, surrounded by reporters, picked up twigs on the street and, with the help of district representatives, swept tree leaves with a broom. When critics said he did not know how to properly use a broom, he said he has a different one at home.
When asked whether Chiang was cleaning the street for a photo op, DPP Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) affirmed the city government’s efforts, saying disaster recovery work should not be partisan and that Chiang worked hard at the Central Emergency Operations Center. As for criticism about the way he handled a broom, Shen said he believed Chiang has his own way.
Shen has refrained from attacking Chiang throughout his campaign, despite frequently being maligned himself, showing respect for his political rival.
Taipei residents should take the opportunity to think about what future they want for the city and choose their mayor wisely.

Skeptics counter that much of this manufacturing is mere final assembly — screwdriver work that adds little value. In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Reclaiming Taipei’s public image
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:12 UTC
01:42:12 KST

Upon entering Taipei Railway Station, what greets us at the interchange of Taiwan’s three major rail systems are not testimonies to the city’s technological development or cultural heritage, but an inescapable barrage of cosmetic surgery and aesthetic medicine advertisements.
Advertising itself has always been more than commercial activity; it is a manifestation of the collective unconscious. When the entranceway of the nation is lined with legions of cookie-cutter perfect faces and plastic surgery adverts, it both reveals and provokes society’s collective body-image anxiety.
From a psychological perspective, these advertisements are an exercise in social conditioning of the public. They do more than sell treatments; they pass judgements which say that aging naturally is to let oneself go. Narrow aesthetic standards see age and body fat as flaws, and mainly target women. Diverse forms of beauty are replaced with artificial, mass-produced appearances, pushing ordinary people deeper and deeper into self doubt. It is a perversion of aesthetics, and in the long run amounts to commercial capital holding our collective values hostage.
Among the central transport hubs of neighboring countries’ major cities, Taipei Railway Station’s medical cosmetics advertising problem is singular. Tokyo Station’s historic architecture is subject to strict controls on its visual environment, with billboards largely promoting new technologies and brand identities. Seoul Station was once similarly plastered with plastic surgery posters, but the Seoul Metropolitan Government has since banned such advertising in the subway system. Major MRT stations in Singapore have regulations that completely prohibit advertisements for cosmetic medical procedures involving treatments such as Botox and hyaluronic acid fillers. These stations and metro systems instead showcase technological innovation and urban confidence. Taipei, in contrast, has allowed its most important transport hub to become a marketplace for selling fear over appearances.
There are two parts to addressing this problem.
First, authorities must intervene and impose strict regulations to limit the extent of cosmetic medicine advertising. Inflammatory imagery that discriminates on the basis of gender or imposes coercive and singular beauty standards should be prohibited, restoring commuters’ basic right to a visually clean environment.
Second, we must reclaim control over the city’s public image by reserving prime advertising space for Taiwan’s technological innovation, cultural and artistic achievements, and public service campaigns.
When exactly did Taipei become a city that cannot handle aging? Age should not be reduced to wrinkles with price tags in the halls of its main station.
Cheng Ting-yao is a lecturer at Tamkang University’s Chinese Language Center.

Environmental Impact Assessment: Taiwan’s secret symphony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:11 UTC
01:42:11 KST

The natural world is a noisy place, but our ears miss much of this soundscape. Because the human hearing range is roughly 20Hz to 20,000Hz, we’re effectively deaf to a vast spectrum of acoustic signals generated by living organisms.
Through high-frequency acoustic messages, insects court mates, warn rivals and express distress. Bats’ echolocation clicks are as high as 120,000Hz. Elephant herds coordinate via low-frequency rumbles. Blue whales and fin whales produce pulses and moans as low as 10Hz, which human ears can’t process.
A handful of scientists in Europe were working on aspects of what’s now called bioacoustics — the study of animal sound production, perception and communication — as long ago as the 1920s, but it wasn’t until 1969 that the International Bioacoustics Society was established to formalize it into a recognized academic discipline.
Photo courtesy of Liao Yi-chang
Among Taiwan-based researchers active in the field is Liao Yi-chang (廖一璋). In addition to being an assistant project scientist at the Department of Entomology, University of California Riverside, Liao runs Back to the Wild Insect Ecosurvey Co, a company that’s conducted bioacoustic investigations at several locations around Taiwan.
Back to the Wild focuses on insect surveys and taxonomy, Liao says. Much of its survey work is funded by the Ministry of the Interior’s Marine National Park Headquarters, which oversees both South Penghu Marine National Park and Dongsha Atoll National Park. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) is another source of financial support.
“We also receive smaller grants from local governments to support specific surveys,” Liao adds.
“Mountains and forests are our favorite habitats to survey, but farmland is also an important part of our work,” he says.
Reaching locations deep in Taiwan’s interior often requires hiking, yet Liao says that remote islands are actually more difficult to survey.
“Ferry services are often canceled due to bad weather, which makes it difficult to plan and arrange our field surveys,” he says.
Precipitation can cause other problems, Liao says.
“Rain noise can easily overwhelm insect sounds, and insects also tend to produce less sound during heavy rain,” he says.
UNSEEN YET AUDIBLE
Photo courtesy of Yan Yu-chun
Occasional frustrations notwithstanding, “we love exploring the insect diversity of Taiwan and discovering what species are out there,” Liao says.
Working on a small island in Penghu County, his team identified the “song” (made by rubbing one forewing against the other) of Teleogryllus oceanicus, a cricket species widely distributed across the Pacific islands but never recorded in Taiwan.
“Finding it in Penghu, just west of Taiwan, suggests there may also be undiscovered populations on Taiwan’s main island,” Liao says.
Asked if he has any dream locations where he wants to carry out a bioacoustic survey, but hasn’t yet had the opportunity, Liao responds: “Kenting National Park is one of them. It’s located in a tropical climate zone and has an incredibly high diversity of insects, including many unique acoustic species.”
Pointing to the number of AI-based tools already available for identifying bird and frog species by sound, Liao says Back to the Wild is now working to develop similar technology for Taiwan’s insects.
The miniaturization of equipment has significantly advanced the field of bioacoustics.
“Many insect survey tools have become much lighter in recent years,” Liao says. “The heaviest piece of equipment is probably the generator for our light traps, but nowadays we mostly use lithium batteries instead.”
Asked whether acquiring the necessary hardware or securing sufficient computing capacity to process audio files consume most of the company’s budget, Liao says that human resources are actually its biggest cost.
“We need people with professional knowledge of insects and who are physically fit enough to handle demanding fieldwork. I have to say, people who are willing to spend so much time exploring the wild are becoming harder and harder to find,” he says.
BENEATH THE WAVES
The rapid expansion of wind energy in the Taiwan Strait has raised concerns over the ecological impact of installing hundreds of turbines in waters that teem with life. Among the region’s crustaceans, fish and marine mammals are rare creatures like the critically endangered Taiwan white dolphin (Sousa chinensis taiwanensis) and the vulnerable Indo-Pacific finless porpoise (Neophocaena phocaenoides).
To evaluate these impacts, scientists first need a reliable baseline — and this is why a five-year recording of fish vocalization (2014-2018) reported in the June 2021 edition of Ecological Indicators is of special significance.
Recognizing that “data on species-specific temporal and seasonal changes are still extremely limited,” the paper’s authors speculated that “the daily and seasonal rhythm of fish chorusing might be influenced by ordinary environmental factors, such as temperature, winds and tides” as well as “extraordinary and episodic events, such as intense sediment transport by strong currents, caused due to flooding events or tropical storms.”
More than a decade ago, scientists confirmed that moonlight and water temperature strongly influence when and how intensely various fish species synchronize their acoustic displays.
The authors of the 2021 Taiwan Strait study report increased fish chorusing during the full and new moon, and that the restart of choruses in early spring and their cessation in winter always took place after a full moon.
When the ocean became colder than 21 degrees Celsius “fish choruses tended to reduce in duration and intensity, and a further decrease in temperatures resulted in a total ceasing of fish calls.”
In 2015 and 2016, fish chorusing occurred until early January. In 2017, however, chorusing activity ceased for the winter as early as November. This shortening of the chorusing period, due to cooler waters, “may affect spawning activity and, thus, fish abundance,” the authors speculate.
The study also details how high-energy events such as typhoons and major storms lead to cessations of or reductions in fish chorusing activity. There are two reasons for this. First, churned sediments reduce the amount of lunar illumination underwater, disrupting visual cues. Second, fish temporarily cease vocalizing when they’re unable to compete with the sheer noise of the storm.
The end of the five-year study coincided with the government’s allocation of 5.5 GW of offshore wind capacity across several sites off Miaoli, Changhua, and Yunlin counties. As of this fall, the majority of these wind farms are either fully completed and operational, or in their final construction stages. Now that an acoustic benchmark exists, years from now we’ll have a better idea if they’ve upset the ocean’s ecological balance.
Steven Crook, the author or co-author of four books about Taiwan, has been following environmental issues since he arrived in the country in 1991. He drives a hybrid and carries his own chopsticks. The views expressed here are his own.

Need a smile? This livestream features 6 puppies all day long
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:10 UTC
01:42:10 KST

Every wiggle and wobble, every snuffle and squeak of six newborn puppies snuggling together in Finland is captured by cameras monitoring their development in the first weeks of their lives. For science, of course.
Even though the puppies mostly nap and nurse — no fetching yet — they’ve entranced millions of Finnish viewers and others around the world through Pentulive, a 24/7 slow TV livestream from Finland’s national public broadcaster, Yle. “Pentu” means puppy in Finnish.
The puppies’ mother, a 5-year-old Lagotto Romagnolo dog named Hilkka, gave birth to four males and two females on Oct. 10. The puppies have brown and white fur and weighed roughly 1 kilogram each Thursday.
Photo: AP
“They are just opening their eyes and their ears,” Pirjo Koskinen, a Yle science journalist who came up with the idea for Pentulive, said on Thursday. “They are taking their first clumsy steps.”
The slow TV show is in its sixth season and expected to break viewership records again. In less than two weeks, the livestream had more than 6 million views on social media alone in the country of 5.7 million people. A naming ceremony is set for Saturday.
The programming incorporates science through chat sessions with viewers three times a week, as well as a podcast and online articles detailing the dogs’ development. The audience can watch the puppies grow day by day and track their milestones alongside Yle’s science journalists and the breeder.
The scientific benefits extend to humans, too.
Seeing the puppies attempt to make a mad dash to their mother for milk, for example, can trigger an increase in levels of a hormone called oxytocin in a human brain, Koskinen said. Also known as the love hormone, it can help create social bonding as well as reduce anxiety.
The show is also an escape from the stresses of the rest of the world for viewers and Yle’s journalists alike. One look at those wagging tails and little pink noses and it’s hard not to smile, said Jyri Loikkanen, Yle’s producer of Pentulive.
Loikkanen, who often watches the livestream to decompress from his workday, said a commenter wrote on social media comparing the US considering livestreaming the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan to Finland streaming puppies.
“I think it’s pretty much a sign of the times that people crave for this kind of small escape,” Loikkanen said, from the “doom and gloomy news what we are experiencing at the moment: The politics, the economics, war and strife et cetera.”
The puppies will be adopted mid-December by people chosen by the breeder. Yle keeps the breeder’s name and location anonymous for their privacy and so that they can focus on the dogs’ well-being. The puppies’ new families are selected before the livestream begins each year.
The slow TV style of programming began in 2009 with Norwegian public broadcaster NRK’s minute-by-minute airing of a seven-hour train trip across the southern part of the country. It has since spread with productions in the United Kingdom, China and elsewhere.
In Sweden, for example, remote cameras for “The Great Moose Migration” capture dozens of moose as they swim across the Angerman River, some 300 kilometers northwest of Stockholm, in the annual spring migration toward summer grazing pastures.

The central government’s proposed 2027 general budget, which includes funding for NT$10,000 (US$307.40) cash handouts, was referred to committee review in the Legislative Yuan yesterday.
The bill advanced after Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) answered lawmakers’ questions about the government’s spending plan.
The NT$3.92 trillion general budget proposal includes NT$235.7 billion for the cash handouts, which the government says will be funded entirely by higher tax revenue from growth in technology-related industries amid forecast economic growth of 11.05 percent in 2026.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
The government has said the handouts are intended to let the public share in the benefits of economic growth driven by Taiwan’s booming high-tech sector.
Under the Executive Yuan’s proposal, eligible recipients would include citizens with household registration in Taiwan and nationals without household registration who have obtained residence permits.
Foreign nationals with permanent residence permits would also be eligible, as would spouses of Taiwanese nationals from China, Hong Kong, Macau or other countries who hold residence permits. Government personnel posted overseas and their dependents would qualify if both hold Taiwan nationality.
A competing bill backed by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), which would require the government to issue NT$20,000 handouts instead, was referred to committee review earlier this month. However, the bill refers only to "eligible individuals" and does not specify eligibility criteria.

Apple’s new iPhone Duo receives early complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:04 UTC
01:42:04 KST

The iPhone Duo, one of Apple’s biggest new products in years, is drawing a growing number of complaints from customers who say the foldable display cracked after just hours or days of use.
In these cases, customers reported hearing a crunching sound when unfolding the phone, followed by a large crack forming along the center crease. Some users also experienced a white patch or other display malfunction on the right side of the screen.
Reports of the problem first surfaced on Reddit and other social media platforms. Bloomberg News has since independently verified the issue with more than half a dozen customers, who provided photos showing damage to their devices or evidence of their support conversations with Apple.
Photo: Reuters
Apple acknowledged the issue in a statement, saying it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”
“If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” the Cupertino, California-based company said.
Most Duos are not affected by the problem, and the units that are impacted exhibit the defect quickly, Apple said.
“I went to unfold it, and it felt stuck, harder, slower to open than usual, and when I opened it, it had the lines on the screen,” said Tom Battle, an Apple customer from San Diego, California. “You could feel a bump or loose piece under the display.”
Venture capitalist Jonathan King had a similar experience, saying he heard a crunch-like sound when opening his device on Monday.
“I had all intent to post a positive review of my Duo experience today, until it happened to me,” King said.
“The smaller outer screen works just fine, but the inner screen is now unusable,” he said, adding that the device thinks he is touching the inner screen when he is not.
While the problem appears to affect only a subset of units, it represents an embarrassing setback for Apple, which spent more than a decade developing the device and touted its superior durability, hinge design and display technology.
The Duo, which on Friday went on sale, represents the company’s first foray into foldable phones — and the biggest-ever design change to the iPhone, Apple’s largest source of revenue. Like other foldable phones, the device has a smaller screen on its outer surface and can be opened to reveal a larger display.
Apple chief executive officer John Ternus previously dismissed competing Android foldables as “cheap and crappy.”

Consumer confidence plunges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:04 UTC
01:42:04 KST

Consumer confidence fell this month, with willingness to buy durable goods plunging to its lowest since October 2009, the National Central University said yesterday.
The consumer confidence index fell 2.5 points to 66.27 from last month, a survey conducted by the university’s Research Center for Taiwan Economic Development showed.
The subindex measuring willingness to buy durable goods over the next six months tumbled 10.81 points to 82.97 as rising electronics prices and a sluggish housing market dampened household spending plans, center executive director Dachrahn Wu (吳大任) said.
Photo: CNA
“Rising prices for memory chips and other components are pushing up prices for smartphones and laptops, while weakness in the property market is discouraging home purchases,” Wu said.
The decline highlights a growing disconnect between Taiwan’s export-driven growth and household spending sentiment.
The economy is benefiting from surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware, with GDP projected to grow more than 11 percent this year, but a surge in AI-related demand has pushed up component costs, Wu said.
Apple Inc and Samsung Electronics Co have raised prices for their latest devices, prompting some consumers to delay replacing older models, he said.
The pressure might persist as new production capacity will take two to three years to come online, limiting the scope for near-term relief in electronics prices, he said.
Housing sentiment also weakened, with a separate property-buying index compiled by Taiwan Realty Co (台灣房屋) that measured whether it is a good time to buy real estate falling 8.2 points to 90.64, despite the central bank’s decision last month to ease some restrictions on property lending.
In addition, rising stock prices have drawn funds that might otherwise have gone toward property purchases, while some prospective buyers are struggling to secure mortgage loans, Wu said.
Young people are also increasingly looking to save for home purchases through stock investments before entering the property market, he added.
The survey showed three of the six subindices edged higher this month, reflecting improved sentiment toward job opportunities, consumer prices and stock investment.
However, the gains were outweighed by declines in household finances, the domestic economic outlook and willingness to buy durable goods, Wu said.
Despite double-digit economic growth, the benefits have been concentrated in technology-related sectors rather than spread broadly across the economy, while inflationary pressure continues to weigh on consumer sentiment, he said.

Top bank client numbers increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:04 UTC
01:42:04 KST

The number of clients of Taiwanese banks with assets of more than NT$100 million (US$3.08 million) surpassed 32,000 at the end of last month, Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) data showed.
The local banking sector had 32,326 high-asset clients at the end of last month, up 1,730 from a month earlier, the data showed.
The qualifying threshold is at least NT$100 million in net investable assets plus insurance policy value. Qualifying financial assets need not all be held at the bank providing the service.
Photo: Kelson Wang, Taipei Times
The combined assets of the clients under management by Taiwanese banks totaled NT$3.24 trillion at the end of last month, up NT$129.4 billion from a month earlier, the FSC said.
The growth in financial asset holdings and high-wealth clients reflected in part a sustained increase in the value of stocks and other financial assets, with the TAIEX up 4 percent last month, it said.
Another factor might be that banks are offering wider ranges of financial products, making Taiwan a more attractive wealth management market, it said.
Twenty-six Taiwanese banks had received approval to provide services to high-asset clients as of the end of last month, while 25 had begun providing the service, it said.
With banks expanding their financial product offerings, deposits accounted for 39.3 percent of the total assets of those clients under management at the banks at the end of last month, edging down from 39.4 percent a month earlier, the FSC said.
The ratio was the lowest since March 2022, when deposits accounted for 38.6 percent of the total, it added.
Mutual fund investments accounted for 17.6 percent of those clients’ total assets under management at the end of last month, up from 17.3 percent a month earlier, while insurance products represented 13.6 percent, compared with 13.2 percent in August, it said.
The FSC said that 14.8 percent of the assets was in bonds and about 8 percent was in overseas structured products.
On a year-on-year basis, the proportions of assets invested in all financial products except deposits increased, it said.
In other news, the agency had approved 10 securities firms to conduct high-asset client business through sub-brokerage, wealth management and proprietary trading channels as of the end of last month, allowing clients to place orders for overseas equities through local brokerages without opening accounts abroad.
Cumulative client numbers reached 2,190, up 40 percent from a year earlier, while cumulative transaction value rose 78 percent to NT$685.8 billion, it said.

Dozens killed in attack on Ethiopia Christians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:03 UTC
01:42:03 KST

More than 40 people were killed on Saturday in an attack on Orthodox Christian churches and homes in Ethiopia’s central state of Oromia, residents and a conflict monitor said on Monday.
Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest state with about 40 million people, has faced a long-running insurgency and ethnic tensions between its Muslim, Protestant and Orthodox communities, which have been increasingly exploited by armed groups.
Local residents and the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) conflict monitor said that at least 43 people were killed and 18 wounded when an unidentified armed group attacked villages in the Shirka district of Oromia, about 270km south of the capital, Addis Ababa.
Photo: AFP
“The attack is said to be religiously motivated and to have targeted Orthodox Christians,” ACLED said, adding that the attack led to clashes with local militias and lasted through Saturday afternoon and evening.
Verifying information in Ethiopia is highly challenging due to heavy restrictions on media access.
The state-run Ethiopian Human Rights Commission said only that it was “following the situation.”
“My sister and uncle were killed, and several of my relatives were taken hostage in Chole ward of Shirka district,” one resident said by phone, asking to remain anonymous.
They said 44 people were killed in the region, while another resident put the toll at 51.
ACLED has recorded increasing attacks against Orthodox Christians in the region, starting in February 2023 and escalating since last year.
Ethiopia is a deeply fragmented nation in the Horn of Africa, facing multiple internal conflicts, including heavy fighting that broke out last month in its northern Tigray state. It was not clear if the attacks involved the primary insurgent group operating in the state, the Oromo Liberation Front.
While concerns over political and ethnic representation have been the main drivers of the insurgency, religion has been used to mobilize fighters.
“We are deeply shocked by these tragic killings and are appealing to the government to intervene and restore security,” said a deacon of one of the attacked churches, who put the death toll at 46.

Tony Stark’s Avengers car goes up for auction
The one-of-a-kind Acura NSX Roadster driven by Tony Stark in Marvel’s The Avengers is up for auction, giving fans a chance to own a piece of superhero film history, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
The custom car, created for the 2012 blockbuster, is being offered through Cars & Bids. The online auction will close on October 31 at 2 p.m. Pacific time, according to Acura.
Designed at Acura’s Los Angeles studio, the roadster was built on a first-generation 1991 NSX. Its handcrafted body was inspired by the second-generation NSX Concept, and the vehicle retains the “STARK 33” license plate seen on screen.
The red convertible will be displayed at the Las Vegas Concours on October 31, giving visitors an opportunity to see it before bidding ends.
According to the auction listing, the proceeds from the winning bid will go to a charity agreed upon by the buyer and seller. Acura also said it would guarantee a contribution to the Sundance Institute to support independent artists and emerging voices.
According to the auction listing, the roadster cannot be registered or driven on public roads because it is a movie prop and manufacturer prototype.

AI cycle to last over 20 years: ex-Intel CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:03 UTC
01:42:03 KST

The artificial intelligence (AI) supercycle should last for more than two decades, former Intel Corp chief executive officer Pat Gelsinger told an event in Taipei yesterday, dismissing fears of an AI bubble amid mounting skepticism over massive infrastructure investments.
“We do see that there will be periods of disruption, correction, etc. So, we do not think of it as an AI bubble,” Gelsinger, who is a general partner at Playground Global LLC, said at the US venture capital firm’s second annual Taiwan Deep Tech Summit.
However, “we’ll have some speed bumps as different areas and different technology disruptions occur along it,” Gelsinger said.
Photo: CNA
“Fundamentally, we see AI as a two-decade-plus supercycle of investments and expansion,” he said.
Regarding recent market turbulence, Gelsinger dismissed the panic, saying that “some modest corrections along the way [are] healthy” and serve to keep the industry “in bounds for a long cycle to the future.”
Peter Barrett, another general partner of Playground Global, said there is a massive value migration taking place from the digital realm to the physical world.
Regardless of whether open-source or proprietary models dominate, the one certainty is their reliance on hardware, Barrett said.
This is why Playground Global is heavily invested in its partnership with Taiwan to build the physical foundations of AI, he said.
“Nowhere else in the world do ideas move to reality faster, more significantly than Taiwan,” Gelsinger said. “You and I can have an idea at breakfast, and by lunchtime, Taiwan has produced the prototype. And before dinner, we have early production.”
With Taiwan playing a central role in the global AI infrastructure buildout, accounting for about 90 percent of global AI server production, Playground Global is bringing six start-ups under its portfolio to seek Taiwanese partners, Gelsinger said.
The start-ups aim to tackle critical challenges in AI infrastructure, with focal points ranging from next-generation memory and power management to optical technologies and advanced packaging, he said.
Among them is Atlanta, Georgia-based Nagare Labs, an AI memory start-up that officially emerged from stealth on Monday.
The company is developing Z2RAM — a novel, oxide-semiconductor-based memory architecture designed to shatter the AI memory wall by unifying the speed of SRAM, the density of DRAM and the scalability of flash memory into a single tier.
Gelsinger called Nagare Labs’ work a breakthrough technology that the memory industry has not witnessed in three decades.
“For the AI age, AI is a memory workload,” he said. “I think people have sort of viewed the evolution of AI as being dominated by GPU performance, but it is tipping toward memory at an extraordinary rate.”
AI inference places heavy demands on memory capacity and bandwidth, increasing interest in technologies that combine SRAM-like speed with greater density.
Nagare Labs is in Taiwan to secure foundry partners and build strategic alliances across the ecosystem, cofounder and interim CEO Suman Datta told the summit.
While Datta declined to disclose a specific commercialization timeline, he said a novel memory technology typically requires six to seven years to achieve high-volume production.

Powertech expects net profit to rise from last quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:02 UTC
01:42:02 KST

Chip packaging service provider Powertech Technology Inc (力成科技) expects net profit this quarter to rise from last quarter’s NT$2.61 billion (US$80.43 million), driven by cost-driven price increases and memorychip shortages amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
“As market supply remains tight relative to demand, customers have shown a high degree of acceptance toward price adjustments driven by rising raw material costs,” Powertech chief executive officer Boris Hsieh (謝永達) told an online investors’ conference yesterday.
“For the fourth quarter, profitability is expected to climb further, bolstered by high production utilization and price adjustments,” Hsieh said.
Photo: CNA
The company plans to increase prices by a single-to-double-digit percentage this quarter amid surging costs for substrates and other semiconductor components, coupled with a persistent DRAM and NAND flash memorychip supply crunch, he said.
Last quarter’s net profit rose 17.7 percent from NT$2.22 billion a quarter earlier and surged 70 percent annually from NT$1.54 billion, beating the company’s estimate, Powertech said.
Net profit in the first three quarters totaled NT$6.68 billion, eclipsing the company’s full-year profit of NT$5.54 billion last year, with earnings per share (EPS) climbing to NT$9.05 in the first nine months, exceeding EPS of NT$7.48 for the whole of last year, it said.
Powertech’s overall revenue this year is set to beat its 2022 peak of NT$83.9 billion, the company said.
While the memory shortage is expected to ease next year, supply will still lag behind demand until major chipmakers ramp up new plants, Hsieh said.
The company’s growth engine will start to decouple from the cyclical boom-and-bust cycles of traditional memory chips next year, shifting toward multi-faceted drivers led by advanced packaging technology, he said.
Advanced packaging technologies account for about 30 percent of the company’s revenue and the share is expected to expand, he added.
Powertech chairman Tsai Du-kung (蔡篤恭) said the company has transformed from a traditional memory-focused packaging and testing service provider to an indispensable strategic partner for advanced packaging in the AI era.
The company is on track to ramp up production of its advanced fan-out panel-level packaging (PLP) for chips used in AI and high-performance computing applications, Tsai said.
Mass production of PLP is projected to start late next year or in 2028, with customers including cloud service providers that develop their own AI accelerators, tier-one chip designers and AI chipmakers, he said.
Advanced Micro Devices Inc is one of the company’s first customers to adopt the fan-out PLP technology, which is considered more cost-effective than the mainstream chip-on-wafer-on-substrate technology.
Tsai said the company would prioritize internal demand for fan-out PLP capacity and is capable of providing embedded multi-die interconnect bridge (EMIB)-like packaging technology.
EMIB is an advanced technology developed by Intel Corp.

“Tough win for us, especially early in the season,” said Harden, who added four rebounds and nine assists.
Photo: AP
The Timberwolves, having won their opening three games, led for much of the night, with a 15-point advantage in the first half.
Edwards, only cleared to play late after being listed as questionable with a right knee injury, had made an electric start, with 11 points in the first quarter, but the Cavaliers rallied to pull level in the third quarter and then had to come from behind again after slipping to a seven-point deficit in the fourth.
Harden’s driving floater with 10 seconds remaining tied the game and a blocked Edwards layup with four seconds left sent it to overtime at 113-113.
Photo: David Richard / Imagn Images via Reuters
With just a minute left in overtime, Edwards tied the game again with a three-pointer so close to the arc that a video replay was required.
Mitchell re-established Cleveland’s lead with a go-ahead midrange jumper and when Minnesota’s Jonathan Kuminga missed a free throw with 30 seconds left, the Cavaliers pulled clear.
Harden made two more free throws, leaving the Timberwolves requiring three points, but Edwards’ clutch effort bounced off the rim.
Peyton Watson poured in two more free throws for Cleveland to bury the contest.
“We made a lot of mistakes on both ends of the basketball in that first half ... second half, we did a better job,” Harden said.

Ajay Mitchell led the scoring with a career-high 30, supported by Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who added 26.

Stephen Curry made eight-of-eight field goal attempts for 24 points.

In Boston, the Celtics downed the Chicago Bulls 134-99, while the Milwaukee Bucks beat the Indiana Pacers 110-102.

Anthropic points to AI dangers, soaring sales in IPO filing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:01 UTC
01:42:01 KST

Anthropic PBC, one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies, on Monday made public its plans to sell shares on the stock market, revealing soaring sales but also potentially dire safety risks in a major test of whether the AI boom can deliver profits.
Its filing warns investors of dangers ranging from its conflict with US President Donald Trump’s administration to AI systems acting on their own, alongside huge spending commitments on computing power.
A disappointing reception for Anthropic could dent investor enthusiasm for AI, a sector that has become a key driver of the US economy amid worries of a market bubble.
Photo: Dado Ruvic, Reuters
According to The Wall Street Journal, the company is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, though the timing could change.
The offering could raise as much as US$100 billion in an initial public offering (IPO) that could value Anthropic at between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion, the Wall Street Journal added, citing people familiar with the matter.
The 400-page prospectus devotes over 90 pages to risks specific to an industry that has faced a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways.
It also reflects the dominant belief among researchers inside Anthropic that AI needs to be developed by a safe pair of hands, or otherwise see its extraordinary powers misused with China having the edge.
The filing cited concerns that advanced systems "could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also warned that its "engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action."
The company has been targeted in recent months by Trump’s administration for refusing to lift restrictions on how the Pentagon could use its technology, and the US Department of Defense has since labeled it a national security risk and barred it as a supplier.
Despite these challenges, Anthropic’s business has grown very quickly. Sales reached US$11.6 billion in the April-to-June quarter, up from US$787 million a year earlier. That compares with US$4.6 billion in sales for all of last year.
The company made its first operating profit in that quarter, close to US$1 billion. It still reported an overall loss of US$80 billion for the first half of the year, mostly because of accounting charges linked to its rising value rather than cash spent.
Much of the growth comes from businesses using Claude to write software and handle office work.
Nearly 12,000 organizations now spend at least US$100,000 a year with Anthropic, up from fewer than 1,000 a year ago.
Anthropic warned that its growth is likely to slow, possibly sharply, and investors will be closely looking at the company’s third-quarter figures that will be released before the IPO.
To power its AI, Anthropic has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to computing capacity, including up to US$120.5 billion with SpaceX, about US$110 billion with Amazon.com Inc and an estimated US$125 billion to US$150 billion with Google.
The company warned that if demand falls short of its projections, many of these payments must be made regardless of how much capacity it actually uses.
The company will have a governance structure that gives the power to the founders and not investors.
The company’s seven co-founders, led by chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister, president Daniela Amodei, will keep control of just over half of shareholder votes after the listing, meaning outside investors will not be able to outvote them.
Anthropic is registered as a "public benefit corporation," which requires it to weigh its goal of developing AI safely alongside making money for shareholders.
The co-founders have each pledged to give 80 percent of their shares to charity, though the filing notes these pledges are not legally binding.
