The oldest mistake in statecraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

Diplomats are paid to say unpleasant things pleasantly. Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan (井泉) has managed the opposite.
Asked on Oct. 15 about Philippine Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro Jr’s description of China as the region’s lone troublemaker, he called the remark nonsense, then observed that China “may easily win” against the Philippines, but declines to use force because it loves peace.
A threat dressed as a compliment is still a threat, and Manila heard it correctly. Philippine Secretary of Foreign Affairs Maria Theresa Lazaro on Monday last week summoned Jing to express her concerns about the comments.
What followed was more revealing than the remark. The embassy took to Facebook to belittle Filipino legislators by name and accused them of sacrificing relations to personal ambition. When lawmakers moved to declare the ambassador persona non grata, the embassy replied: “Just do it.”
On Thursday the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs warned of further diplomatic action, and the embassy answered that it “will not remain silent.”
This is not a diplomatic mission. It is a troll farm with diplomatic plates.
Teodoro put the stakes plainly: The embassy has crossed from diplomacy into interference, and the 2028 elections are the target. He has a point. A mission that lists senators as enemies by name is campaigning, not representing. He also rejected the counsel of silence.
“If you give them leeway, they will only push further,” he said.
History supports him.
The claim of easy victory deserves scrutiny, and Jing’s arithmetic omits the Philippines’ position. Manila is bound to Washington by the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty. Its northern islands flank the Luzon Strait, the approach to Taiwan that any serious Chinese planner must worry about.
A war “easily won” would be fought in waters where the Philippine Coast Guard has spent three years publicizing every ramming and water cannon attack, so that the world’s press knows Second Thomas Shoal (Renai Shoal, 仁愛暗沙) by name.
Beijing has won plenty of confrontations against fishers and coast guard cutters. Winning against an alliance is a different proposition. The peace-loving pose is also hard to square with a regime that claims nearly the whole South China Sea and treats the sovereign nation of Taiwan as territory awaiting invasion.
A state that advertises its restraint while rehearsing its power is asking to be flattered, and Manila has declined. Even Beijing’s sympathizers in Manila reach for the excuse that the ambassador was misunderstood, which concedes that he spoke badly.
Pride goes before a fall, and the proverb is old because the pattern is. A nation whose foreign policy rests on bellicosity and the threat of invasion has mistaken noise for strength.

Majority of Taiwanese dislike CCP: poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:58 UTC
01:41:58 KST

Nearly three-quarters of Taiwanese have a negative view of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), including more than half of Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) supporters, polling expert Tai Li-an (戴立安) said yesterday.
Since Tai began his monthly survey of the issue in 2015, the proportion of Taiwanese who view the CCP unfavorably has remained consistently high at 60 to 70 percent.
This month’s survey found that 73.5 percent viewed the CCP unfavorably, unchanged from last month, while 8.9 percent viewed it favorably, up 1.4 percentage points from last month.
Photo: EPA
A cross-analysis found widespread antipathy toward the CCP across all age groups and demographics, with unfavorable views exceeding 75 percent among women, residents of central Taiwan and the Changhua-Nantou-Taichung area, people in the Kaohsiung-Pingtung region, adults aged 20 to 49, those with a university degree or higher, and pan-green supporters.
Among pan-blue camp supporters, 53.7 percent viewed the CCP unfavorably while 30.2 percent viewed it favorably.
Among KMT supporters, 50.3 percent viewed it unfavorably and 34 percent viewed it favorably.
Even among staunch “deep-blue” voters who favor the KMT and hold unfavorable views of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), 46.8 percent viewed the CCP unfavorably while 40.9 percent viewed it favorably.
Among politically neutral respondents, just 3.1 percent viewed the CCP favorably, while 62.5 percent expressed unfavorable views.
A cross-analysis showed that 66.1 percent of respondents who viewed Taiwan’s current economic conditions negatively also held unfavorable views of the CCP. Among those dissatisfied with President William Lai’s (賴清德) performance, 60.4 percent viewed the CCP unfavorably, while 19.4 percent expressed favorable views.
As for preferences ahead of next month’s local elections, 28.5 percent of respondents who wanted their city or county to be governed by the KMT viewed the CCP favorably, while 59.0 percent viewed it unfavorably. Among those who preferred DPP rule, just 1.0 percent had a favorable view of the CCP, while an overwhelming 94.5 percent expressed unfavorable views.
The survey was conducted from Tuesday to Thursday last week, polling 1,075 residents aged 20 or older, with 696 called via landline and 379 via mobile phones.
The survey questionnaire was designed and the data analyzed by Tai, while Beacon Market Research conducted the telephone interviews.

More than 4 million people have received a flu shot since the first phase of the government-funded vaccination program began on Oct. 1, the highest number for the same period in six years, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday, adding that the influenza epidemic period might end next month.
Although medical visits for flu-like illness fell 18.8 percent to 101,746 visits last week from a week earlier, the decline could be due to healthcare facilities suspending operations on Friday because of Typhoon Champi, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Deputy Director Lee Chia-lin (李佳琳) said.
The flu is still in the epidemic period, as 11 percent of the emergency-department visits were for flu-like illness, while 85 severe flu cases and 28 flu-related fatalities were reported last week, she said.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
Of the 391 severe flu cases recorded, including 57 deaths, since the start of the flu season on Oct. 1, 69.1 percent were people aged 65 or older, while 85.2 percent had chronic illnesses and 99.7 percent had not received a flu shot this season, Lee said.
One of the fatalities reported last week was a woman in her 40s, among the youngest flu deaths this season, CDC physician Lin Leng (林稜) said.
She had chronic conditions of the nervous symptoms and was bedridden, and did not get vaccinated, Lin said.
The woman died of respiratory failure about a week after being hospitalized, she said, adding that contact tracing showed that several of her family members who lived with her had also experienced respiratory symptoms.
The woman’s chronic condition is considered a high-risk factor, making her eligible for the vaccine, Lin said, urging people eligible for the vaccine to get one as soon as possible.
As this season’s vaccination program was coupled with the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s “health coin” scheme, people’s willingness to get vaccinated rose significantly, CDC Director-General Philip Lo (羅一鈞) said.
Starting from Oct. 1, people aged 18 or older with National Health Insurance coverage can receive 450, 900 or 600 health coins for receiving the flu, COVID-19 and pneumococcal vaccines respectively, whether the vaccinations are government-funded or paid for out of pocket, he said.
As of Monday, more than 1.83 million people aged 65 or older had received the flu vaccine this season, about 9 percent more than the 1.68 million recorded in the same period last year, bringing their vaccination coverage rate to 38.4 percent, he said.
The number of older adults who received a COVID-19 vaccine also increased by 32 percent to about 940,000 people this season, from about 710,000 people in the same period last year, Lo said.
More than 4 million people received a government-funded flu vaccine between Oct. 1 and Monday, the most for the same period since the program began offering vaccines in two phases in 2021, he said.
About 104,000 people had received a government-funded pneumococcal vaccine and about 3,000 people had paid for one out of pocket, about 3.5 times and 2.4 times the respective totals recorded in the 26 days before Oct. 1, Lo said.
The CDC had originally set a goal of achieving 40 percent pneumococcal vaccine coverage among people aged 65 or older before the end of this year, but Lo said the coverage rate had already risen from 37 percent to 39.9 percent as of Monday.
The second phase of the government-funded flu and COVID-19 vaccination program is to begin on Monday next week, expanding the eligibility to people aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic illnesses, the centers said.

Drug-resistant bacteria alarming researchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:58 UTC
01:41:58 KST

A strain of pneumonia-causing bacteria could be on the verge of gaining resistance against most antibiotics, a Taiwanese medical research team said, citing evolutionary models.
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) and Taipei Veterans’ General Hospital jointly conducted the study on Klebsiella pneumoniae using data gathered by the hospital, the team said in a statement.
The research was published in Emerging Infectious Diseases, a journal of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in collaboration with Chen Liang (陳亮), a professor of pharmacy at the State University of New York at Buffalo.
Photo courtesy of National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
The hospital’s Center for Infection Control director Lin Yi-tsung (林邑璁), who is also a professor of emergency and critical medicine at the NYCU, said multiple drug resistance was observed in bacteria collected from two people’s urine and phlegm samples.
Analysis showed that the K pneumoniae penicillin-binding protein 3 site is blocked by a tetrapetite named tyrosine-arginine-isoleucine-threonine (YRIT), which acts as an armor against antibacterial drugs, he said.
A germ with YRIT is protected against penicillins, cephalosporins and monobactams, the antibiotic triad most commonly used to treat infections, he said.
The study marked the first time a bacterium other than Escherichia coli possessed a genetic mutation that allows the production of the YRIT amino acid sequence in Taiwan, Lin said.
This bacterial strain also contains mutations that make it highly contagious, he said.
Should the bacteria undergo a new genetic mutation that confers resistance to other classes of antibiotics, the pathogen would become untreatable by drugs, making it a threat to global public health, Lin said.
The two people, who were hospitalized during the COVID-19 pandemic, had no relations or contact with one another, he added.
The research proved that the genetic mutation leading to the YRIT sequence can make the species leap from E coli to K pneumoniae, which the WHO deems to pose a high risk of spreading inside hospitals, he said.
The discovery of drug-resistant K pneumoniae showed the urgency for developing a system to monitor germ genetics, new antibiotics and patient containment protocols, he said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:56 UTC
01:41:56 KST

A truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky entered into force early yesterday, after it was announced by US first lady Melania Trump last week.
Both sides said they would observe the truce starting at 3am.
Agence France-Presse was not able to immediately verify whether there had been a decrease in fighting.
Photo: Reuters
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has been caught in middle of the fighting since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Former residents said earlier this year that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.
The Russian Ministry of Defense yesterday said that the truce was in effect.
“In connection with preparations for a humanitarian operation in the area of Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, [Russian forces] have ceased fire in the Kherson sector and introduced a ‘regime of silence,’” the Russian ministry said on its Telegram channel.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said the country was “fulfilling its commitments” to the ceasefire.
“The sides are adhering to the agreements that we reached,” he said on Telegram.
Kyiv continued to be a target for Russian strikes. Yesterday morning, the Ukrainian air force command issued nearly a dozen messages warning of ballistic missiles fired toward the capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said a strike hit the Southern Bridge — one of Kyiv’s main bridges — and damaged its metro infrastructure.
Three-way peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv are set to resume next month after a months-long hiatus.
Neither Russia, Ukraine nor the US have said who would monitor the truce or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it.
Announcing on Friday that she had brokered the ceasefire, Melania Trump said civilian officials from Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and “determine the level of assistance they require.”
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine have said how long the truce would last.
The Russian defence ministry said on Friday that it would halt fire in the “Kherson sector” for the duration of the ceasefire, without giving details.
“To ensure the safety of the population and the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies ... the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy to the settlement of Oleshky, Kherson Region, will be facilitated,” it quoted Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov as saying.
Ukraine has accused Russia of blocking residents from leaving, a charge Moscow has denied.
The city, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, was seized by Russian troops in 2022.
The population has since dropped to about 2,000 today from about 24,000 before Moscow’s invasion, including as many as 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.
Russian Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova on Monday said that most of those who wished to depart had already done so — “entirely of their own volition.”
Former residents said earlier this year that remaining residents were starving, forced to hunt pigeons or subsist on whatever they had in their garden.
“They’ve forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there’s not even flour left,” said Olga, who was in touch with two families still in Oleshky.

Pingtung teacher probed over knife, misconduct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:55 UTC
01:41:55 KST

An elementary-school resource teacher in Pingtung County is under investigation over allegations that they repeatedly brought a fruit knife onto campus, climbed through classroom windows and took special education students out of class without permission, the Pingtung County Department of Education said yesterday.
The school had reported the teacher’s actions through the campus safety system and convened a meeting to determine whether the teacher is fit to continue teaching, the department said.
In a news release earlier yesterday, the National Federation of Education Unions (NEU), citing accounts from classroom teachers and parents, said the resource teacher at elementary school in Changjhih Township (長治) had behaved erratically since the start of the school year.
Photo: Taipei Times
According to the NEU, the teacher refused to teach resource classes — which provide extra help to students with special needs — and failed to draw up legally required individualized education programs, severely impacting students’ education.
The union also alleged that the teacher spent extended periods alone in special education classrooms, praying in the corner of the room.
When locked out, the teacher allegedly climbed through windows.
The teacher also allegedly brought a fruit knife onto campus twice, causing panic and distress among special education students.
In another incident, the teacher allegedly led special education students toward a parking lot without authorization before class had ended, ignoring colleagues’ attempts to intervene.
The union criticized the school’s handling of the incidents, alleging that the principal failed to keep the teacher away from students and instead instructed staff to document the teacher’s behavior.
It also claimed that when teachers sought help during another incident in which the teacher climbed through a window, the principal said police should be called only if a student was actually injured.
The NEU urged the county government to investigate possible administrative negligence, bar the teacher from contact with students pending the investigation and ensure that teachers and staff can report campus safety concerns without administrative interference.
The department said the school had tried to communicate with the teacher, who refused to talk or say what support they needed.
To ensure students could continue attending classes, the school has reassigned the teacher to other duties and arranged a substitute for the resource class.
The department added that it assessed the teacher, but determined that the teacher did not meet the criteria for involuntary hospitalization.

Foreign fund outflows send Taiwan dollar sharply lower: Central bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:55 UTC
01:41:55 KST

Net fund outflows by foreign institutional investors have been a major factor behind the New Taiwan dollar’s sharp depreciation against the US dollar in recent months, the central bank said.
In a written report submitted to the Legislative Yuan ahead of a hearing scheduled for today, the central bank said foreign institutional investors recorded net fund outflows of US$54.3 billion since the beginning of July.
During the same period, the NT dollar depreciated about 2 percent against the US dollar, the central bank said.
Photo: CNA
In the first half of this year, foreign institutional investors recorded net fund outflows of US$23.3 billion, adding downward pressure on the NT dollar amid escalating military tensions in the Middle East and concerns about a hawkish US Federal Reserve, the central bank said.
To ease volatility in the local foreign exchange market, the central bank sold US$17.04 billion more than it bought during the six-month period, it added.
From July through Oct. 21, renewed concerns about military conflict between the US and Iran, along with a global sell-off in technology stocks amid artificial intelligence (AI) spending concerns, weighed on the TAIEX, prompting foreign institutional investors to withdraw more funds from Taiwan’s financial markets, the central bank said.
During the four-month period, foreign institutional investors recorded net stock sales of NT$1.25 trillion, equivalent to about US$38.7 billion. Their total net fund outflows, including capital gains and cash dividends, reached about US$54.3 billion, the central bank said.
Despite the outflows, the NT dollar remained relatively stable compared with several other non-US dollar currencies, the central bank said.
From Jan. 1 through Oct. 21, the NT dollar depreciated 3.23 percent against the US dollar, while the US dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of major trading partners’ currencies, rose 3.49 percent, according to the central bank.
During the same period, the NT dollar’s decline was less pronounced than those of the Swiss franc, which fell 3.89 percent, the euro, which dropped 4.35 percent, and the Thai baht, which tumbled 6.29 percent, the central bank said.
Taiwan is a small, open economy with a relatively shallow foreign exchange market and a heavy reliance on trade, making central bank intervention necessary to stabilize the currency, the report said.
The central bank added that it aims to keep fluctuations of the Taiwan dollar within a relatively narrow range compared with those of the euro, South Korean won and Japanese yen, helping Taiwanese exporters stabilize prices and secure orders, while supporting the broader economy.

Employers, workers groups protest caregiver policies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

Employers and migrant worker advocacy groups yesterday protested outside two government ministries in Taipei, demanding solutions to live-in care issues, but differing over how to protect care recipients and migrant workers.
Outside the Ministry of Labor, an employers’ group challenged Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) to a public debate, accusing the government of neglecting households facing disruptions to care when migrant caregivers go missing or become temporarily unavailable, including during maternity leave.
“We really cannot wait any longer,” International Association of Family and Employers with Disabilities chairwoman Heidi Chang (張姮燕) said.
Photo: Lee Ching-hui, Taipei Times
She called the ministry’s response inadequate to demands the group raised at a May 2 protest on Ketagalan Boulevard.
A woman at yesterday’s protest surnamed Tseng (曾) said that a migrant caregiver hired to care for her mother disclosed she was pregnant, and they agreed to terminate her employment.
Since then, family members have been taking turns traveling to Kaohsiung to care for her partially paralyzed mother, who does not want to move into an assisted living facility, said Tseng, who lives in Taichung.
She said she waited about 20 days for employment termination paperwork and was quoted an NT$18,000 (US$555) fee by a recruitment agency to arrange for a replacement, which she has yet to secure.
“We really feel helpless,” she said, adding that relatives are struggling to balance work, household expenses and caregiving responsibilities.
The association, joined by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Wang Hung-wei (王鴻薇), called for faster replacement procedures and emergency care arrangements to prevent prolonged gaps between caregivers.
“Even one month is too long,” Chang said, adding that she once waited three to four months for a replacement caregiver to arrive from overseas.
Meanwhile, outside the Ministry of Health and Welfare, groups including the Taiwan International Workers’ Association and Independent Living Taiwan said that gaps in care stemmed from inadequate public services rather than migrant caregivers exercising their rights to maternity leave.
The groups urged the government to expand affordable substitute care services, subsidize lower-income households and establish emergency backup arrangements.
They also proposed a system under which institutions, rather than individual households, employ migrant caregivers, allowing workers to take shifts, while ensuring continuous care through replacement staff.
Marni, a caregiver and a representative of Indonesian migrant caregiver union SBIPT, said migrant caregivers sometimes struggle to take time off and in some cases have to pay for substitute workers.
“We are not care machines,” she said.
The health ministry said households employing live-in migrant caregivers have been eligible for community-based care services, including daycare, since September last year, regardless of whether their caregivers are on leave.
The health ministry advised families to request a long-term care needs assessment from a care management center when applying to hire a migrant caregiver, so services can be arranged in advance.
Separately, the labor ministry said that approximately NT$2 billion had been allocated to subsidize respite and short-term substitute care services, which eligible households employing migrant caregivers can use for a combined total of up to 52 days per year.
It said it would work with the health ministry to expand public care resources, improve access to services and enhance caregiver training.
The labor ministry did not say whether Hung would accept the association’s debate invitation.

PRC weaponizing Taiwan handover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:53 UTC
01:41:53 KST

China was waging “cognitive warfare” by marking the anniversary of Japan’s handover of Taiwan with satellite images of Taipei and a military propaganda poster, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said yesterday.
Japan took over Taiwan from China’s Qing Dynasty in 1895 and ruled it until 1945, when it transferred Taiwan to the Republic of China (ROC) government.
On Sunday’s anniversary of the handover, China released high-resolution satellite pictures of Taipei, including the main railway station and the National Palace Museum. The museum holds a vast collection of treasures brought to Taiwan in 1949, when the ROC government fled after losing a civil war to the Chinese communists.
Photo: Taipei Times
The Chinese military’s Eastern Theatre Command also published a poster with a map of Taiwan superimposed on images of fighter jets and warships, with the title “Remember the history of the restoration.”
Speaking to reporters at the Legislative Yuan, Koo said China was using the anniversary to carry out “cognitive warfare.”
“We must stress that the People’s Republic of China was established in 1949. The War of Resistance has absolutely nothing to do with the People’s Republic of China — this is a clear, objective fact,” he said, referring to World War II and the Japanese invasion of China, which began in 1931.
Taiwan’s military marked a different anniversary, the start of an unsuccessful late-October 1949 invasion attempt by the People’s Liberation Army of Kinmen, islands which sit next to the Chinese coast and remain under Taiwan’s control to this day.
Koo said that was a date much more worthy of remembering.
“This reminds us once again that China’s determination to annex the Republic of China and Taiwan by force has never changed. We should be even more vigilant,” he added.

The posts drew tens of thousands

Rays stare at World Series flop

The Milwaukee Brewers on Monday became the first team to score eight runs with two outs in an MLB World Series inning as they routed the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 to take a 3-0 lead in the best-of-seven series.
Tampa Bay’s first World Series game at Tropicana Field in 18 years turned into a record-setter for Brewers batters as they piled on the runs in the fifth inning.
Taylor Walls stabbed at a Brice Turang grounder and felt it glance off his glove.
Photo: Nathan Ray Seebeck / Imagn Images via Reuters
“Knife in the chest,” the Rays shortstop said.
Turang’s two-run single was the second of a post-season-record seven straight two-out hits against starter Freddy Peralta, and relievers Cam Booser and Cole Sulser.
Milwaukee turned a 2-0 lead into a 7-0 advantage with Turang, Garrett Mitchell and Cooper Pratt connecting on three straight pitches. The Brewers went on to score eight runs in a 17-pitch span to open a 10-run advantage.
Photo: AFP
Jackson Chourio had a single and a double in the inning, part of his four-hit night.
“Worst feeling in the world, feeling like you let your team down,” a downcast Booser said in the quiet Tampa Bay clubhouse.
Among 25 previous teams who fell behind 3-0 in a World Series, 21 were swept and four lost in five games. Of 43 teams to trail 3-0 in any best-of-seven post-season matchup, only the Boston Red Sox against the New York Yankees in the 2004 American League Championship Series rebounded to win.
Photo: Kim Klement Neitzel / Imagn Images via Reuters
“It’s kind of that chip and a chair mentality,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “We’ve got a seat at the table. We’ve got to do something with the chip. Obviously the only thing we can do is win tomorrow [this morning, Taiwan time].”
Coming off a pair of one-run wins at American Family Field, the Brewers took a 2-0 lead in the third inning when Christian Yelich and William Contreras hit opposite-field, one-out RBI singles on consecutive pitches.
“They were very disciplined at the plate,” Peralta said. “Just tried to hit the ball the other way.”
Chourio singled with one out in the fifth and Christian Yelich walked with two outs. Contreras grounded to third and Junior Caminero threw to second as umpire Dan Bellino signaled a forceout.
However, the call was reversed in the New York replay operations center by umpire Alfonso Marquez, giving Contreras an infield single that loaded the bases.
Caminero might have had a better chance of throwing out Contreras at first base.
“I knew the speed at first base wasn’t necessarily the best in that situation,” Caminero said through a translator. “So going into the moment, once I got the groundball I was going to second base all the way.”
Booser relieved and Turang’s one-hopper hit the dirt just past the infield grass, bounced off Walls’ glove and into short center field.
“I’d like to have that one back. Those are plays that you’d like to make, that you expect to make even though they may be on the tougher end,” Walls said. “That was pretty much the turning point in the game there.”
Walls dropped to a knee and held out his glove at shoulder level trying to make what would have been an excellent stop, then tumbled as the ball bounced past him.
“You just try to get your eyes as close to where the ball is going to be, the height of the hop,” he said. “Ideally, I guess if you want to talk about fractions, if you can get your glove behind the ball and work more backwards, you have a better chance to make the play than if you’re slightly above it having to kind of work down a little bit, which is where I kind of felt I was.”
Mitchell grounded an opposite-field RBI single through the shortstop hole vacated with Walls shifted toward second for the left-handed batter. Pratt followed with a smash off the glove of a diving Caminero that rolled into the left-field corner for a two-run double.
Sal Frelick sliced an opposite-field double that hit the wall on a hop in the left-field corner, scoring Pratt and chasing Booser.
David Hamilton greeted Sulser by lining a shoulder-high fastball into center for a run-scoring single and a 9-0 lead. Chourio lofted an opposite-field RBI double that hit just in front of the warning track.
Boston set the previous World Series high of seven runs with two outs in the fifth inning of the 2007 opener against the Colorado Rockies, a feat matched three years later by the San Francisco Giants in the eighth inning of Game 2 against the Texas Rangers, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
The Los Angeles Dodgers were the only prior team with eight two-out runs in any post-season inning, scoring 10 with two outs in the first inning of Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the 2020 National League Championship Series.
Griffin Jax said he would put the World Series deficit out of his mind as he prepared to start Game 4.
“We just got our butts kicked tonight. I don’t think there’s really much else to say,” Jax said. “We’ll just kind of forget it and try to sleep it off and come back tomorrow ready to fight.”

Argentina’s economic chainsaw massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:49 UTC
01:41:49 KST

Nearly three years after Javier Milei became Argentina’s president, the chainsaw-wielding free-marketeer has established himself as the darling of the far right. Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro promised in his failed presidential campaign an economic policy that would follow Milei’s lead, and US President Donald Trump calls the Argentine his “favorite president.” Last year, Trump extended Argentina an unprecedented US$20 billion currency swap line to halt its currency’s free fall on the eve of legislative elections, and the gambit worked. Milei’s party won a surprising victory.
More than a mere symbol or role model for the far right, Milei plays a crucial role in Trump’s new “Shield of the Americas,” a security umbrella designed to ward off US rivals and turn Latin America into a resource-rich hinterland of US-compliant partners.
However, since Milei’s contributions to Trump’s hemispheric order depend on Argentina’s economic performance, one must ask how MAGA’s South American poster child has fared.
DEEP CUTS
The “Chainsaw Plan” that Milei unveiled in June 2022 was more than a means to halt hyperinflation. The larger goal was to squeeze the life out of a public sector that had come to be seen as a source of political patronage, and to make Argentina great again as a primary goods exporter.
The vision happily aligns with the Trump administration’s geoeconomic worldview. Investments in lithium fields in the country’s north and hydrocarbons in Patagonia have fueled an economic recovery and bolstered Argentina’s strategic importance to the Shield of the Americas.
Meanwhile, the country has been plastered with billboards declaring that the Malvinas (better known as the Falkland Islands) belong to Argentina, not to the UK.
Milei has no problem pandering to populist nationalism while also nursing claims to newly discovered South Atlantic oil fields.
AUSTERITY
However, the immediate success of the Chainsaw Plan rests on austerity. It was Milei who provided the playbook for Elon Musk’s short-lived (and far from successful) DOGE effort.
Upon taking office, he halved the number of Argentine government ministries to nine, froze public works, fired 51,218 federal employees (plus an additional 23,000 from state companies), and slashed welfare spending. Before long, chronic deficits turned into budget surpluses. After years of volatility and runaway price growth, the inflation rate fell from about 250 percent to 30 percent, and the economy bounced back.
In addition to reining in prices, Milei’s cuts drove capital into the private sector as his government offered tax incentives to foreign investors and promised a vast new private insurance regime to replace state functions.
Austerity compelled workers to follow the money, triggering a flight to for-profit firms in the health, security and education sectors.
Argentina used to have world-class laboratories backed by its national science agency (CONICET); but following salary reductions and budget cuts in research, over 10 percent of CONICET scientists and technicians — primarily biologists, geologists, agronomists and physicists younger than 40 — have left for the private sector.
SCAVENGING
However, the informal sector absorbs most displaced workers. The night before public trash collection, throngs of Argentines walk the streets looking for recyclable metal and paper. At dawn, caravans of shopping carts and horse-drawn carriages haul the scrap to depots where scavengers are rewarded with a few pesos.
Scavenging is but one activity in the informal sector — a traditional cushion in a labor market short on social protections. Without labor contracts, unemployment benefits or pension contributions, informality serves as many Argentines’ only safety net. Once in it, workers tend not to return to formal jobs, with 40 to 50 percent of the labor force now surviving on precarious work.
NO PROMISING PROSPECTS
Young people no longer hope for public-sector jobs or even formal work, and almost 70 percent of Argentines between 18 and 25 toil in informal jobs. When I taught recently at a university in a downwardly mobile district of outer Buenos Aires, all my students had jobs, but not promising prospects. If they were not teachers working for near-minimum wage, they were street vendors, Uber drivers, domestic workers, or food and medicine couriers.
In other words, Argentina’s great recovery is full of misery. By early this year, urban poverty reached 32.3 percent, with extreme deprivation afflicting more than 7 percent of the population. The extent of the destitution is staggering, especially considering how much of it has been masked by the equally staggering growth in personal indebtedness.
DEBT TRAP
Fintech apps, digital wallets, local moneylenders, emergency credit cards and other products designed to help poor families make ends meet have proliferated. Delinquency rates are soaring. With almost 6 million Argentines at least 90 days behind on debt payments, central-bank officials are struggling to forestall a tidal wave of petty bankruptcies.
The chainsaw would continue to grind away. Driving inflation down from 30 percent would require more austerity, but there is less to cut. New commodity frontiers generate growth, but not many jobs, and poor households are running out of options. Yet Milei rushes on. The thought of government intervention to promote economic recovery is, in his characteristically nuanced estimation, “Keynesian garbage.”
Time is running out. With elections coming next year, Milei might not be able to count on a free-spending Trump stopgap. His political base is not to be dismissed, but it is dwarfed by the legions of people slipping into a low-income, low-productivity trap. Milei might be a linchpin in Trump’s geoeconomic vision for now; but he could soon become its weak link.
Jeremy Adelman is director of the University of Cambridge’s Global History Lab and the author, most recently, of The Capitalist Era: The Making and Unmaking of the Global Mind.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Optimists point to Apple Inc’s decision to build an alternative supply chain to hedge against China. A quarter of all iPhones now roll out of factories near Chennai, employing tens of thousands. Skeptics counter that much of this manufacturing is mere final assembly — screwdriver work that adds little value. The fact that a much smaller economy such as Vietnam exports more merchandise shows that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s “Make in India” initiative remains more hype than reality, they said. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

China seeking to undermine US-Taiwan ties: MAC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:49 UTC
01:41:49 KST

Beijing would seek to influence voters ahead of the Nov. 28 local elections and use disinformation campaigns to undermine public confidence in Washington’s commitment to defending Taiwan ahead of a planned meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and US President Donald Trump, the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) said yesterday.
Despite frequent interactions between Trump and Xi this year, significant differences remain between the two countries over trade, technology and geopolitics, MAC Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said at a panel discussion on Taiwan-US-China relations hosted by the Taiwan Inspirations Association.
US-China relations remain defined by strategic competition, he added.
Photo: Chen Yu-fu, Taipei Times
The leaders of the US, China and Russia are reportedly scheduled to attend an APEC summit, but Washington and Beijing hold differing positions on trilateral nuclear disarmament talks, which could affect the course of the summit, he said.
“Whenever Trump and Xi meet, Beijing launches a cognitive warfare campaign to stir up anti-US sentiment in Taiwan and make Taiwanese question Washington’s commitment to defending the nation,” Shen said.
Aside from Taiwan’s local elections next month, the US is preparing for its midterm elections, while China is focused on the ongoing Fifth Plenum of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) Central Committee, he said.
“Our assessment is that China would attempt to influence the local elections in Taiwan. Not only would it use Taiwanese entertainers to manipulate public opinion, but it would also intensify transnational repression to fuel social polarization in Taiwan,” he said.
The Fifth Plenum is expected to pave the way for a personnel reshuffle at the CCP’s 21st National Congress next year, Shen said.
Many CCP Central Committee members were removed from their posts, reported missing or placed under investigation after the Fourth Plenum last year, and the absentee rate at this year’s Fifth Plenum would be higher, he said.
Rather than going to great lengths to interfere in Taiwan’s elections, the CCP should focus on addressing China’s economic, social and political problems, and respond positively to petitions from university students, he said.
“We should not sell ourselves short or give up our democratic way of life. Personally, I think we have reached a point where many democratic countries oppose any unilateral change to the ‘status quo’ across the Taiwan Strait by force,” he said.
Taiwan has a geographical advantage as it lies at the center of the First Island Chain and serves as a key strategic hub in the Indo-Pacific region, Shen said.
Many countries trust Taiwan and seek partnerships with it because of its semiconductor industry, he added.

Securities trading on typhoon days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:45 UTC
01:41:45 KST

Each time a typhoon approaches, Taiwanese inevitably find themselves embroiled in a debate over whether a typhoon day off should be declared. The government must consider the severity of the wind and rain as well as safe commute, while the public is concerned with whether they have to commute during the storm. Financial markets face whether they have to suspend trading.
Yet, despite years of repeated debates over whether to grant a day off, Taiwan has given relatively little thought to a more fundamental question: Should financial markets follow local governments’ decisions to suspend work and classes on typhoon days?
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) has proposed that, as a major financial hub, Taipei should consider whether stock market trading should be decoupled from typhoon days off and whether financial institutions could adopt different contingency measures. The key question is whether ensuring the safety of commuters means that financial markets should also suspend trading.
The purpose of suspending work and classes is to reduce the risks people face when commuting during typhoons, whereas financial markets must consider whether stock trading and subsequent settlement can proceed normally. The considerations behind local governments’ decisions to suspend work and classes are not identical to those behind the decision to close the stock market, so the two do not necessarily need to follow the same approach.
With digital trading and remote work becoming increasingly widespread, the central government should reassess the system and explore whether financial markets could maintain some level of operation when local governments announce work and class suspensions.
Of course, keeping the stock market open does not mean employees should be expected to brave the storm to get to work. If the central government intends to implement such a policy, it should explore arrangements for remote work, staffing requirements for essential personnel and guidelines for handling situations in which employees cannot report to work due to transportation disruptions or safety concerns during their commute.
Otherwise, if the policy is only concerned with the operation of financial markets while shifting risks onto employees, it would defeat the very purpose of institutional reform.
The mayor of Taipei might not have the authority to unilaterally decide whether financial markets should close, but the city can put forward concrete proposals and coordinate with the central government and financial regulators to establish clear guidelines for work suspension standards, financial contingency measures and worker safety.
Shen’s proposal has given society an opportunity to move beyond the binary debate or whether to declare a typhoon day off. As remote work becomes increasingly common and financial trading methods continue to evolve, Taiwan should also rethink how to maintain financial market operations and protect workers’ rights while ensuring people’s safety.
Dino Wei is an engineer.

US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at base in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:44 UTC
01:41:44 KST

One of the US’ biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD Co (比亞迪) over security concerns, the US military in Japan said yesterday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” US Lieutenant Colonel Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US Air Force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
ALL VEHICLES BANNED
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US Air Force base in east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refueling, surveillance and reconnaissance, its Web site says.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported.
US military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other Western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
GROWING LIST
In June, the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Inc (蔚來汽車), e-commerce firm Alibaba (阿里巴巴) and Internet company Baidu Inc (百度).
The US Department of Defense banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei Technologies Co (華為) and ZTE Corp (中興通訊) at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles last year.
It is expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.
Additional reporting by Reuters

Judge rejects prisoner’s challenge to Vegemite ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:41 UTC
01:41:41 KST

A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.”
Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, last year took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of Victoria.
He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to “enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background,” court documents showed.
Photo: AP
Australian Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities’ refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite “limited his cultural rights” under the charter.
However, she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities’ goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.
“The limitation on Mr. McKechnie’s ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner,” Harris wrote in her 47-page verdict.
Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state’s 12 prisons for the past 20 years, because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs’ ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.
McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were “less restrictive means reasonably available” to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes.
Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80 percent of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who were not raised on it.
The last US president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: “It’s horrible.”

Kentec Inc (金運) sees electronics manufacturing services (EMS), thermal management and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure as major growth drivers ahead as it targets opportunities in AI data center construction, company president Asa Kuo (郭丁賀) said yesterday.
Thermal management and AI infrastructure revenue rose 165 percent year-on-year to about NT$168 million (US$5.18 million) in the first half of this year, while EMS revenue increased about 10 percent over the same period, Kuo said.
Kentec posted operating profit of about NT$1.1 million in the first half, reversing operating losses of NT$57.88 million a year earlier, he said.
Photo courtesy of Kentec Inc
The company expects robust demand for AI data center system integration and steady expansion in EMS business to sustain its growth momentum into next year, he said.
Containerized and modular data centers are an important area of development for Kentec, Kuo said.
The company has completed the 3D design of a 5 megawatt (MW) modular data center solution and is awaiting customer approval to move the project forward, he said.
The company has also visited a potential project site with a customer that is considering having Kentec build a 50MW data center, he said.
Kentec also supplies coolant distribution units (CDU), with products ranging from 12 kilowatts to 2.5MW to support high-density graphics processing unit (GPU) computing and large AI data centers, said Daniel Chen (陳敏郎), vice president of the firm’s Research and Development Center.
The company has completed development of its 2.5MW CDU, which is expected to enter mass production this month, while a new 3.5MW model is slated to begin validation next year, Chen said.
Meanwhile, the company plans to provide samples of liquid-cooling couplings and manifolds for customer validation next year, he said.
In Taiwan, Kentec is cooperating with green energy provider Apollo Power Co (阿波羅電力) on AI data center projects in several places, the company said.
Its international footprint includes Japan, North America and Southeast Asia.
Kenmec chairman Kevin Hsieh (謝明凱) said that he expects the company to become more international within three years.

====================================================================================================

Populism’s next chapter is being written in continental Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:38 UTC
01:41:38 KST

Since 2016, the story of populism in the rich world has been dominated by the UK and the US — by the UK’s vote for Brexit and the US’ election of Donald Trump, not once, which might have been put down to naivete, but twice — but things are about to change: Over the next year populism is likely to fade in those countries, but burn ever brighter in continental Europe.
In the US, the Democrats are increasingly optimistic that they will take the Senate as well as the US House of Representatives, forcing Trump to spend the rest of his term dodging subpoenas. Democrats lead Republicans by 9 percentage points in the generic congressional ballot. Only 31 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s job performance. Looking ahead to 2028, no party has ever secured victory in a presidential race when the incumbent president has such a dismal number.
In the UK, Trump’s brother-in-arms, Nigel Farage, is sinking. His party’s approval ratings have been falling for months, thanks to Farage’s taste for pocketing gifts and his foot soldiers’ taste for bad-mouthing minorities. The great theme of British politics today is the recovery of the two-party system.
Illustration: Mountain People
If you like your politics hot, mainland Europe is the place to be. The continent is about to enter a year-long electoral super-cycle, starting with Spain’s general election on Nov. 29 and peaking with the French presidential election in April. Although Germany does not have a federal election, three state elections in April could topple an already doddering German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, if, indeed, he survives that long. Smaller countries that will go to the polls include Finland, Poland and Slovenia.
Even before France erupted in fire and fury on Oct. 17, the populist right was well-positioned to do well out of this super-cycle, thanks to rising living costs, a never-ending refugee crisis and general “grobulation.” Spain might be about to take a sharp turn to the right after eight years of Socialist Workers’ Party rule, with polls suggesting a clear majority for the center-right People’s Party and its putative partner, the radical right Vox.
In France, Marine Le Pen has been ahead in the polls before only to lose decisively in the second round, but this time her poll lead is bigger, and her potential opposition is weaker: So far, the center has been unable to produce a charismatic figure, and the left has united behind someone who is even more divisive than Le Pen, Jean-Luc Melenchon.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has led the country’s longest serving post-World War II government, is favored to continue her winning streak, while in Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is the most popular party in Germany with 28 percent of the vote (and in next-door Austria, the equally right-wing Freedom Party is even more popular, at 39 percent).
The riots in France would surely bolster the right’s position. French President Emmanuel Macron, languishing at 15 percent in the polls, contributed to the sense of centrist fatigue by delivering an address to the nation that one of his former ministers described as “rubbish.” Melenchon appeared to condone the rioting.
Right-wingers across the continent say that civilization is under threat from barbaric hordes. The leaders of Poland and Hungary declared that the riots proved the wisdom of their countries’ hardline policies on immigration. Meloni sent troops to Milan where riots had also broken out.
The populist right is also showing signs that it can harden as well as strengthen. Many centrists have comforted themselves with the idea that the right might be civilized by success: Meloni has governed Italy largely as a traditional conservative and Le Pen has rejected her father’s more revolting policies while adopting social policies that are more gay and female-friendly.
However, Meloni is moving back to the right to fend off criticisms from Roberto Vannacci, a former general who leads the National Future party. Many of Le Pen’s liberal social policies were adopted to strengthen her case against Islam. Meanwhile, the AfD has thrived on extremism.
What will this potential populist turn mean for Europe? The answer clearly depends on how far the populist turn goes — above all, on whether Le Pen wins in France. At the very least, the super-cycle would paralyze the EU machine. Focused on winning votes at home, national leaders would be tempted to play hardball in the EU, particularly on budgets, to curry favor at home. Eurocrats would be absorbed in watching national elections and calculating what to do about them.
A victory for Le Pen would be a bigger blow to Europe than the UK’s vote to leave the EU in 2016, given France’s role in both founding and steering the European project. Le Pen might have abandoned her earlier talk of “Frexit,” but she is nevertheless campaigning on a long-list of anti-Brussels measures, including an initial proposal (since moderated) to cut 11 billion euros (US$12.3 billion) from France’s contribution to the EU budget, pulling France out of the EU’s common asylum policy, giving preference to French companies in public contracts and unilaterally withdrawing from some aspects of the single market; in other words, a partial “Frexit” that would leave Le Pen with a seat on the European Council.
The most obvious winner from any rightward shift in Europe would be Russian President Vladimir Putin, the most obvious loser Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. Le Pen (whose party took a 9.4 million euro loan from a Russian bank in 2014) has promised to stop aid to Kyiv for anything other than military training and to oppose Ukraine’s membership of the EU. Vannacci and Alice Weidel, the leader of the AfD, are loudly pro-Russian.
What about the wider populist project? The most important thing that a European tilt to populism would mean is survival. US commentators, being an introspective breed and fond of writing the end of things, would likely see a defeat for Trump as marking the end of populism. However, Trump is merely the latest manifestation of a much bigger movement.
The current populist wave arguably started in Europe rather than the US (or the UK). Jean-Marie Le Pen began his political career in 1956, when he was elected to the French Assembly, and made his first run for the presidency in 1974. Silvio Berlusconi, Italy’s four-term prime minister in the 1990s and early 2000s, prefigured all too many Trumpian themes, including mastery of the media, dark charisma, womanizing and self-dealing.
The shift to Europe could also mean the intensification of populist themes. The EU is the last great holdout of the neoliberal project of globalization and free markets. A significant populist advance would terminate that already fading project. Europe is closer to the Muslim world than the US and has a substantially larger Muslim population. Hostility to immigration in general and Muslim immigration in particular would be even more central to European populism than to Trumpian populism, spiced with worries about declining birthrates and “civilizational erasure.”
The next phase of populism would be less dominated by grumpy old men than the US phase, featuring women such as Marine Le Pen, Meloni and Weidel and well-coiffed young men such as Jordan Bardella. The populist operation could also become more professional. Trump was so intemperate that he often shot his own side: Ask Pierre Poilievre, who was heading for an easy victory in Canada before Trump announced that he wanted to annex his northern neighbor. Le Pen and Meloni are not only more experienced at navigating domestic politics, but are also more skilled at operating across national borders.
Over the past quarter of a century, we have become accustomed to thinking of the Americans as, on average, hard and the Europeans as soft. Robert Kagan even wrote a book about how Americans are from Mars and Europeans are from Venus. The next turn of the electoral cycle is likely to demonstrate that Europeans can be every bit as hardy as their cousins across the Atlantic.

In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on Monday held talks with Iran to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were “very good.”
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to “de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis,” the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
The talks, which included Saudi Arabian Minister of Defense Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the US, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.
Photo: West Asia News Agency via Reuters
It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they in August formed a defense alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia.
The delegations met with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the parties saying they “agreed to continue discussions,” Iranian state media reported.
However, Iranian Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital, Tehran, were “very good,” state television reported.
POSITIVE ATMOSPHERE
“I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen,” Rezaei said.
He said they agreed that security in the region “should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention,” adding that emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.
Saudi Arabian Prince Khalid, Pakistani Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish National Intelligence Organization Chairman Ibrahim Kalin met Rezaei.
Regional tensions have risen ahead of Israel’s pivotal elections yesterday and next week’s US midterms, where US President Donald Trump’s Republicans are battling to keep control of both chambers of the US Congress.
As the talks in Tehran began, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said it was “essential to stop any escalation” in the Middle East.
“The risk to have the combination of an overwhelming military attack on Iran, and an overwhelming military attack by Iran on the countries of the Gulf, needs to be avoided at all costs,” he told a news conference in Cairo.
‘LAST CHANCE’
Saudi Arabian security analyst and researcher Hesham Alghannam posted on social media that “this historic meeting in Tehran may be the last chance before escalation spirals out of control.”
Fresh explosions rattled Riyadh overnight, which has suffered weeks of attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, after the group claimed a new attack on the Saudi Arabian capital’s international airport on Sunday.
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition in Yemen later reported intercepting three Houthi-launched drones over southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh region.

The Tainan District Court on Monday approved a request by prosecutors to detain a man surnamed Lee (李) who is suspected of involvement in his wife’s death in Japan last week.
Wang Sheng-hao (王聖豪), a senior prosecutor with the Tainan District Prosecutors’ Office, yesterday said in a video briefing that Lee is suspected of being involved in the apparent murder of his wife and attempted fraud.
Prosecutors sought Lee’s detention on Sunday, citing concerns that he could flee or destroy evidence, he said.
Photo courtesy of the office via CNA
Lee’s wife, surnamed Ching (井), was found fatally stabbed at a hotel in Yamanashi Prefecture’s Fujikawaguchiko on Oct. 19, Wang said.
Japanese police arrested a suspect, a woman surnamed Yang (楊) who is also from Taiwan, for her alleged involvement in the case, he said.
On Thursday last week, Tainan prosecutors launched an investigation at the request of the Criminal Investigation Bureau’s International Affairs Division.
Prosecutors found that Lee, who traveled to Japan after his wife’s death to handle the funeral arrangements, had taken out two travel insurance policies on Ching prior to her death — one for NT$10 million (US$308,147) and another NT$20 million, Wang said.
Authorities arrested Lee when he returned to Taiwan on Saturday evening.
They searched seven locations, including his residence, on Saturday and Sunday, Wang said.
Prosecutors said they found records of contact between Lee and Yang, who Japanese authorities suspect of killing Ching, but added that the alleged coordination between the two and their respective roles in the case remain under investigation.
Japanese media last week reported that Ching was found dead on a hotel bed with extensive bleeding.
Yang, 27, was also in the room and later arrested after police found her in possession of a kitchen knife, on suspicion of contravening the country’s Firearm and Sword Possession Control Law.
The women were part of a tour group from Taiwan, the reports said, adding that hotel staff went to check on Ching after she failed to show up before the group’s outing that day.
Japanese police are continuing to investigate the relationship between the two women, with no further details released, reports said.
In Taiwan, the Ministry of Justice said that while the Tainan Prosecutors’ Office had not yet requested judicial assistance from Japan, the ministry would handle any such request in accordance with the law and maintain contact with Japanese law enforcement agencies.

Historical events that are worth celebrating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:30 UTC
01:41:30 KST

Last year, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party reinstated Taiwan Retrocession Day on Oct. 25 as a national holiday. It came under a broader program of “giving holidays back to the people,” adding four new or restored public holidays to the calendar. Naturally, people welcomed the change. But why must this particular holiday be tied to the historically and ideologically contentious “retrocession” day?
In 1945, the Republic of China (ROC) government accepted Japan’s surrender in Taipei, bringing 50 years of Japanese colonial rule to an end. At the time, many Taiwanese had high hopes for the new regime. What came next, however, was a chaotic takeover, the tragic 228 Incident of 1947, and the martial law and White Terror that followed. The end of Japanese colonial rule by no means meant that the people had gained their freedom.
The term “retrocession” means more than just a change of government; it is suggestive of liberation and celebration. The KMT might view Oct. 25 through the lens of victory in the war against Japan, but Taiwanese who experienced political repression also have reason to ask why it should be the day of post-World War II takeover that is designated for celebration. The end of colonial rule can be marked and acknowledged without needing to buy into a single interpretation of history.
Retrocession Day had not been a public holiday for many years. In 2001, civil servants moved to a five-day workweek and Oct. 25 became a day of commemoration without a holiday. In 2017, amendments to the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) to reduce working hours and improve leave entitlements saw private-sector workers also cease to receive the day off. Yet none of this made Taiwan any less able to study and reflect on the history of 1945.
The Legislative Yuan has the power to add public holidays, as well as the power to pick the occasion. If the goal is to protect people’s rights to rest and have time off, why not discuss holidays marking the lifting of martial law, freedom of speech or human rights? Why must it be Retrocession Day that is restored?
Expanding public holidays and choosing which historical events to commemorate are two distinct policy questions; the latter should not be swept away in a policy push for the former.
Last year, China established its own “Commemoration Day of Taiwan’s Restoration,” linking the occasion to its “one China” principle and calls for unification. In 1945, it was the ROC government that accepted Japan’s surrender in Taipei; at that time, the Chinese Communist Party had not yet been founded.
How Beijing uses narratives surrounding “retrocession” cannot determine how Taiwan should judge its own history. However, if Taiwan celebrates the day without critical reflection, it cannot avoid confronting the ongoing significance this term holds in cross-strait politics.
If the concern is truly about workers, then let us discuss working hours and the sufficient right to rest. If the aim is to face up to history, then different perspectives on 1945 must be allowed. Holidays with historical baggage means that people who simply want an extra day off are first asked to concede to particular interpretations of the past.
Oct. 25 can be remembered without being publicly designated for celebrations. Ultimately, what Taiwan should cherish most deeply is the democracy and freedom its people fought so hard to win.
An extra public holiday does not have to mean celebrating so-called “retrocession.”
Steve Ho is a retired engineer.

In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Government studying ways to compensate creators whose work is used to train AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:29 UTC
01:41:29 KST

The government is exploring ways to compensate authors and other content providers for materials used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models, but has yet to determine how content should be valued, licensed or paid for.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Michelle Lin (林楚茵) raised the issue earlier this month during a meeting of the legislature’s Transportation Committee.
She asked whether the Ministry of Digital Affairs would provide content free of charge for AI model training following efforts to obtain voluntarily licensed material from Taiwanese book publishers.
Photo: Reuters
She also asked whether the ministry was developing a mechanism for AI developers to pay news outlets for the use of their content.
Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said the ministry is collecting four types of training content through its voluntary initiative: works whose copyright protection has expired and that are in the public domain, book descriptions provided by publishers, book preview material and works that authors have voluntarily licensed.
The ministry has not sought AI training material from Taiwanese news outlets, he said.
“We are aware that several international news media outlets have signed content authorization agreements with large AI firms, and we would work to facilitate such partnerships in Taiwan,” Lin Yi-ching said.
“Our ultimate goal is for large AI firms, particularly those based in the US, to pay for the content they use to train their models,” he said, adding that the ministry is considering only public-domain and voluntarily licensed material to avoid delaying Taiwan’s AI development through potentially protracted legal disputes over content use.
The ministry began building a corpus of high-quality traditional Chinese content for Taiwan’s sovereign AI models late last year, initially using materials provided by central and local government agencies. On Sept. 15, it announced rules governing the participation of private publishers and e-book platform operators, including provisions for voluntary participation, content authorization and the removal of works by authors who opt out.
As of the middle of this month, the corpus had accumulated 3.3 billion tokens — units of text that AI models use to process and learn language.
The government is also studying ways to encourage AI developers to pay for training materials, but has not specified how payments would be calculated, how any revenue would be shared or when a mechanism might be introduced.
At a separate meeting convened in July by the Taiwan Intellectual Property Office (TIPO), representatives of magazine publishers and broadcast media proposed measures to ensure AI companies pay for the use of their content.
The government should establish a licensing platform to allow media companies to register content for AI companies to use in exchange for payment, CommonWealth Magazine legal affairs director Chiu Ai-lun (邱愛倫) said.
She also urged AI companies to disclose the content they license and the sources of their training data.
Some international AI companies continued to scrape media Web sites even when the owners have explicitly prohibited such activity, Satellite Television Broadcasting Association secretary-general May Chen (陳依玫) said.
She also called for a mechanism to connect content owners with AI companies seeking to license their material.
TIPO’s draft Copyright Guidelines for Generative Artificial Intelligence (生成式人工智慧著作權指引) could give the impression that obtaining authorization was the only way to use copyrighted material, Taiwan Innovative Software and Services Association vice chairman Chang Jung-kuei (張榮貴) said.
Fair-use provisions, which permit the use of copyrighted material without the rights holder’s permission under certain circumstances, should remain available when data sources are lawfully accessed and the AI-generated output does not replace original works in the market, he said.
He also proposed exploring corpus-matching or collective licensing mechanisms.

191 candidates sign on to support gender equality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:41:28 UTC
01:41:28 KST

A total of 191 people running for local government positions have expressed support for gender equality by signing up on the Taiwan Equality Campaign’s “Pride Watch” Web site, the nonprofit group said yesterday.
After registering on the site, candidates completed a questionnaire to indicate their positions on gender equality issues, group representatives said.
Candidates can also use the Web site to list their policy pledges and proposals, they said.
Photo: Screen grab from Taiwan Equality Campaign’s Web site
“Pride Watch” has attracted more than 100,000 views each election cycle since the site was launched in 2018, the Taiwan Equality Campaign said.
In the 2022 local elections, 245 candidates registered, 87 of whom were elected as local councilors, it said.
They put forward at least 233 gender-related proposals and formally questioned local government officials on gender issues on 104 occasions over the following four years, the group said.
In the 2024 presidential and legislative elections, 103 candidates registered on the site, including then-presidential candidate William Lai (賴清德) and his running mate, Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), it said.
The Web site also lets voters submit records of candidates’ past statements on gender equality, the group said.
Gender equality affects people’s daily lives, it said, urging voters to use the site to scrutinize candidates and ensure that their commitments to gender equality are reflected in local policies.
In the Nov. 28 elections, voters would cast ballots for candidates vying for nine different local government posts, including city mayors, county commissioners, and city and county councilors.
Other positions being contested include township mayors and councilors, borough wardens and indigenous peoples’ district representatives.
In total, 11,051 candidates would be chosen for offices at all levels of local governments.
