EU proposes expanded Frontex powers beyond bloc's borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:40:00 UTC
01:40:00 KST

The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled plans to significantly broaden the authority of EU border agency Frontex, including allowing operations outside the bloc, following a surge in migrant arrivals at Spain's Ceuta enclave last summer.
The proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's mandate, allowing it to carry out deportations between non-EU countries, operate outside the bloc and deploy rapid-reaction teams in emergencies.
The proposed legislation is an attempt to make Frontex more reactive to large-scale arrivals at the EU's borders, such as in Ceuta on the North African coast, as European governments push for tougher migration policies despite concerns from rights advocates over accountability.
"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.
But while the proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's role, it would also narrow the scope of its internal rights watchdog, with complaints referred to national authorities to handle.
The proposal comes as member states increasingly focus on returns, arguing that too many migrants ordered to leave the bloc ultimately remain.
Although irregular arrivals have decreased, the arrival of more than 72,000 people in Ceuta from Morocco in late July, most of whom later left, reignited debate over the EU's migration rules and was cited by several member states as evidence for stronger tools.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers by 2041, who would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would create a new EU Return Coordination Centre within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process, from voluntary return counselling to organising returns and reintegration support, the statement said.
The agency would also be empowered to help organise and carry out deportations from one non-EU country to another, subject to agreements with the countries involved and international legal standards, according to the statement.
That would mean Frontex could, for example, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya - one of the main launching points for migrant boats crossing to Europe - back to Bangladesh.
The proposal would also create a new online monitoring centre to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
The Commission proposed allocating €11.8 billion to Frontex for the EU's 2028-2034 budget cycle, nearly double the almost €6 billion earmarked for the agency under the current 2021-2027 framework, as part of a planned expansion of its mandate.
The push comes just a few months after EU lawmakers approved new rules aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc.
Tuesday's proposal was met with criticism from rights groups and some lawmakers.
"Working with third countries, without proper oversight or accountability, is a threat to fundamental rights and respect for international law, while leaving Frontex staff in legal limbo outside of European law," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," she added.

The US and Cuba traded sharp accusations Tuesday at the UN General Assembly, turning a debate about Washington’s decades-old trade embargo into a tense verbal confrontation between the two delegations.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parilla clashed as the General Assembly debated a resolution calling for an end to the US economic, commercial and financial embargo on Cuba.
Waltz launched a forceful attack on Havana, accusing the government of enriching its elite while ordinary people struggle with shortages and economic hardship. He also rejected Cuba’s description of US measures as a blockade.
“There is no blockade,” Waltz told delegates. “A blockade is a ring of military ships around an island. It doesn’t exist.”
The Cuban delegation repeatedly interrupted the speech, prompting the UN president to intervene and remind both sides of the assembly’s rules.
At one point, Waltz turned directly toward the Cuban side and said: “This is America, my friend. This is the United Nations. This isn’t your communist dictatorship. You cannot silence me.”
The Cuban minister fired back, accusing Waltz of making false claims and of disrespecting the forum. “He is offending the dignity of the people and government of Cuba,” said Parilla.
Waltz returned to the embargo, pointing to US trade with Cuba as evidence that Havana’s description of the measures was misleading.
He said American companies had exported more than $876 million in goods to Cuba during the first eight months of 2026, including $230 million in fuel for eligible private businesses.

Unknown Publisher

16:39:15 UTC
01:39:15 KST

In the United Kingdom, sales of emergency preparedness supplies have risen after the government urged citizens to keep a three-day supply of essentials at home.
The BBC reported this, citing data from British retail chains.
Sales of radios, flashlights, portable chargers, and canned goods rose the most.
The Iceland supermarket chain recorded a 40% increase in canned food sales over the weekend. The company also reported high demand for bottled water.
The Robert Dyas chain recorded a 160% increase in radio sales compared to the previous week.
Meanwhile, at Maplin, sales of radios rose by 92%, flashlights by 284%, and portable power banks by 106%. Maplin compared sales after the government campaign’s announcement with figures from the same period the previous month.
Small specialty stores also saw demand surge. The online store Sgt Prepper reported a tenfold increase in sales after the campaign launched. Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, reported a 650% increase in sales.
These changes followed the launch of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign, which urges households to prepare for potential disruptions to essential services. On October 22, UK Defense Minister Wes Streeting urged citizens to keep a supply of water, canned food, baby food, flashlights, and portable phone chargers at home.
The British government recommends keeping at least a three-day supply of essential items for emergencies, including severe storms, floods, power outages, and cyberattacks.
Official recommendations suggest having about three liters of drinking water per person per day, non-perishable food, a battery-powered or hand-crank radio, a flashlight, spare batteries, and a fully charged portable power bank.
The government’s Be Ready campaign is scheduled to run for three years. Officials explain that the campaign is necessary to improve the public’s preparedness for emergencies and reduce the burden on emergency services so they can prioritize helping those who need it most.
Militarnyi previously reported that the defense of Great Britain would require sacrifices from citizens, so the country’s leaders will soon begin a “frank conversation” with them.

AI generated
NEW YORK – Human rights monitors criticised senior United Arab Emirates (UAE) diplomat Lana Nusseibeh’s candidacy to be the next UN chief on Oct 27, citing her role in championing the country’s foreign policy and denying the UAE’s role in fuelling the conflict in Sudan.
Pushback against the prominent Middle Eastern candidate has gathered steam since her late entry last week.
Her bid upended the gridlocked race to replace UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term in 2026.
Despite months of campaigning by several senior UN figures and former country leaders, the competition has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council’s most powerful nations.
Sudan’s war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
“She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts – that is not what we need as UN Secretary-General,” Kenneth Roth, former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told a webinar organised by the campaign.
A UN fact-finding mission said in September that foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks – including individuals and entities in the UAE, among others – are helping sustain Sudan’s conflict.
“This is the opposite of the kind of moral standing of the human rights leadership that we want from a UN Secretary-General,” Roth told the webinar, which was titled “Call to stop UAE minister’s bid for UN top job amid Sudan genocide”.
The webinar also featured Sudanese experts, as well as a survivor of the El Fasher massacre, on their concerns about Nusseibeh’s candidacy and its implications for the UN’s commitment to protect civilians, according to the organisers.
“Electing its senior diplomat as secretary-general would hand leadership of those same institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable,” said Husam Mahjoub a Sudanese advocate and founder of Sudan Bukra TV.
Asked about Sudan during the dialogue with the General Assembly on Oct 27, Nusseibeh said: “If I were to become secretary-general, Sudan would be a number one priority, as one of the most horrific conflicts we have seen in recent history.”
“The loss of human life on the ground is a tragedy, the atrocities committed by the RSF are atrocious and I would support the work of all UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice,” she added.
Nusseibeh told the media at the UN after the dialogue that, as a secretary-general, she would work to be a “risk-taker” and “prime mover in mediation efforts”.
She has also separately said she would “put the UN’s full political and practical support behind ongoing efforts to reach a ceasefire and a credible and inclusive political process that reflects the democratic aspirations of the Sudanese people”.
Nusseibeh, 48, served as UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade. She previously led the UAE’s successful campaign for election to the Security Council.
She is widely known by diplomats working in New York, who say she is a competent manager, skilled negotiator and clear communicator.
An informal council poll in October had placed former Costa Rican Vice-President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow front runner in the race.
But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council – Russia, China, the US, France and Britain.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN and the 193-member body’s declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
The next straw poll could take place as soon as Oct 30, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats. REUTERS

Russian forces struck a warehouse belonging to Ukrainian publishing house KSD in Kharkiv on 27 October, disrupting the publisher’s planned November releases. No employees were injured, but the company is still assessing the damage and losses.
The attack came on the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language, a national holiday celebrating Ukraine’s language and literary heritage. It adds to a series of Russian strikes on Ukrainian publishing houses, printing facilities, and book warehouses that have destroyed millions of books and disrupted the country’s publishing industry.
KSD announced the strike on social media, saying it had planned to greet readers on the holiday and reveal its November releases but instead had to deal with the attack. The publisher said strikes in the area were continuing, preventing it from determining the full extent of the damage.
The company had planned to begin releasing its new books on 5 November. It has now postponed the announcements while it assesses the situation and determines how to proceed.
“We really want to show you the new releases we had prepared for November,” KSD said. “But for now, as we clarify the details, we cannot yet assess the scale of the destruction and understand how we will work going forward.”
The publisher said it would share updates as more information became available.
Russia’s attacks devastate Ukraine’s book industry
KSD’s warehouse is the latest publishing facility affected by Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s book industry. In July and August alone, Russian attacks destroyed around 13 million books, nearly a third of the number Ukrainian publishers printed in all of 2025, according to the Ukrainian publishing industry.
On 1 August, a Russian strike on a warehouse used by the Ranok publishing group in Kharkiv destroyed around 8 million books, including hundreds of thousands of school textbooks. A separate attack on a printing facility in July destroyed print runs and book materials belonging to numerous Ukrainian publishers.
In October, Russian strikes also damaged a Kyiv warehouse belonging to publisher Knyholav, destroying tens of thousands of books, including titles and reprints that had replaced stock lost in an earlier attack.
Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture
These strikes threaten more than publishers’ finances. Destroyed print runs and damaged warehouses delay new releases, deprive readers of Ukrainian-language books, and force publishers to spend scarce resources replacing titles instead of developing new ones.
KSD has not yet disclosed its losses or announced a revised release schedule for its November books.

The fee on the Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard will go up to $150 a year from $99. That is the first hike since 2018, when it raised the fee from $95 to $99, an airline spokeswoman said.
The Citi AAdvantage Business Mastercard will also have a fee increase and will now cost $150 a year.
Airlines and their bank partners have been steadily raising fees on rewards credit cards.
Those cards generate billions of dollars a year for airlines, which make money when miles are sold to banks, which then give them to customers. American's move, announced Tuesday, follows similar increases by rivals such as United Airlines.
Meanwhile, American Express last year raised the fee on its popular Platinum card, which comes with airport lounge access, to $895 a year from $695. JPMorgan Chase increased the annual fee on its competing card, the Sapphire Reserve, to $795 from $550.
The new perks for the American card include three times AAdvantage miles earnings on hotels booked through American's portal, a credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, and a $100 annual statement credit on in-flight purchases like food.
The new fees take effect Jan. 24.

Some 75% of Jewish employees find workplae DEI approaches inconsistent on antisemitism, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:32:33 UTC
01:32:33 KST

A new workplace study published on Tuesday has revealed that 75.5% of Jewish employees feel that Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) approaches within their organizations fail to respond consistently to antisemitism.
The research report titled Yes, But... Antisemitism and the Limits of Workplace Inclusion was published by Pearn Kandola, a business psychology firm co-founded by Professor Binna Kandola. Pearn Kandola is a UK-based occupational psychology consultancy that specializes in diversity, inclusion, and unconscious bias training for corporate and public sector organizations.
The study follows the organization’s 2024 research on workplace antisemitism and Islamophobia, which tracked a nearly 50% increase in antisemitic incidents following the October 7, 2023 massacre.
Following a series of webinars held during Antisemitism at Work Week in June, researchers noted that Jewish attendees repeatedly described a lack of responsiveness from diversity teams regarding antisemitism, prompting a broader investigation into whether these experiences reflected an isolated trend or a systemic pattern.
The research combined a national survey of 1,002 Jewish employees across the UK with qualitative interviews involving participants from various sectors and organizational levels. The interviews included individuals directly involved in diversity and inclusion roles, with some working for large US multinationals and describing interactions with American diversity teams.
Majority of Jewish respondents have misgivings over practical application of corporate commitments to equality
According to the survey findings, while the vast majority of Jewish respondents acknowledged public corporate commitments to equality, major misgivings emerged regarding their practical application. Specifically, 87% of respondents agreed that their organization expressed a clear commitment to tackling racism and discrimination, and 83% agreed that the diversity function was visibly active on these issues. However, 75.5% agreed that their organization’s diversity approach was not consistent in its response to antisemitism, 72.7% noticed a gap between public commitments and actual responses, and 60.5% agreed that antisemitism receives less attention than other forms of racism.
The survey findings also highlighted a severe chilling effect on employee reporting and confidence. Only 15.9% of respondents said they felt able to raise concerns about antisemitism in the workplace. Furthermore, 70.8% of respondents agreed that they had avoided raising concerns because they were unsure how those reports would be received. The report analyzed this low reporting not as an indicator of low prevalence, but as a cycle of futility where employees conclude that speaking up will not yield understanding or action.
The study pointed to organizational listening as a central challenge. The report claimed that providing formal reporting channels or communication pathways is insufficient if institutions lack the capability and motivation to properly receive, interpret, and act upon employee feedback. When concerns are routinely minimized or misread, employees tend to withdraw, creating a dangerous paradox where a low number of complaints mistakenly bolsters corporate confidence that no underlying problem exists.
Problem goes beyond lack of understanding Kandola tells 'Post'
Professor Binna Kandola OBE told The Jerusalem Post: “Our research raises serious questions about the way Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion functions operate. We found that many Jewish employees feel overlooked by the very people whose responsibility it is to promote inclusion.”
Kandola added, “The problem goes beyond a lack of understanding of antisemitism. It concerns the assumptions and frameworks that some DEI practitioners use to understand discrimination. Jews are often stereotyped as wealthy, powerful, influential, and privileged. Because many are white, they do not fit comfortably into models of discrimination that see racism primarily through the lens of power and privilege. As a result, antisemitism can be minimized, explained away, or simply ignored.”
Through in-depth interviews, the research examined how diversity functions can fail to address antisemitism, identifying several recurring rhetorical devices and organizational responses. Among these, denial manifested directly or through silence and omission, such as when Holocaust Memorial Day events omitted references to Jews or when organizations remained silent following October 7. Reversal occurred when individuals raising antisemitism were repositioned as the wrongdoers or accused of self-interest. Liberal arguments regarding merit and fairness were also identified, where perceived Jewish success, wealth, or representation was used to imply that Jewish people do not experience racism or require inclusion support.
Deracialization emerged when antisemitism was reframed as a generic religious matter, an international political issue, or an interpersonal disagreement rather than a form of racial exclusion. Other identified mechanisms included distancing through inaction or framing incidents as isolated anomalies rather than systemic issues, positive self-presentation where inclusion credentials masked operational gaps, trivialization of Jewish safety by making it low priority, and empathizing primarily with perpetrators over targets.
Additional themes from the interviews explored the complexities of Jewish identity, which participants noted encompasses ethnicity, culture, ancestry, and peoplehood rather than religion alone. Interviewees also discussed the distinction between legitimate criticism of Israeli government policy and antisemitism, noting that difficulties arose when diversity teams viewed all Jewish concerns exclusively through the lens of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Employee resource groups, while intended to offer support, were occasionally reported by interviewees as having been utilized by diversity teams to block action or contain antisemitism as a niche issue relevant only to Jewish networks. Furthermore, participants described heightened fear, visibility concerns, and the heavy emotional burden of acting as educators or public advocates for their community.
The report concluded by outlining several core findings regarding the limitations of current diversity practices. The report emphasized that diversity frameworks centered rigidly on power, privilege, and oppression can inadvertently obscure Jewish vulnerability due to persistent stereotypes surrounding influence and success. The report stressed that psychological safety remains ineffective without active organizational listening, and that professional expertise in antisemitism and prejudice cannot be assumed simply through a general commitment to equality or membership in affinity groups.
Professor Kandola told the Post, “Organizations need to take a critical look at their DEI functions. They should examine the assumptions that underpin their work, the evidence supporting their approaches, and whether they are applying the same standards of fairness to everyone. Importantly, these reviews should not be led by the DEI functions themselves.”
Professor Kandola further noted, “We also need to professionalize DEI. A commitment to equality, however sincere, is not a substitute for expertise in the psychology of prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination. Practitioners must be prepared to recognize and challenge their own biases, not just those of others.”
Based on these conclusions, the report provided six key recommendations for organizational leaders: reappraise the purpose and practice of diversity functions through independent review; redefine professional expertise by ensuring practitioners understand the distinct history and contemporary manifestations of antisemitism; separate representation metrics from inclusion experiences; clarify the role of employee resource groups so they do not act as expert advisory bodies or veto mechanisms; build genuine organizational listening capabilities into reporting structures; and introduce reflexive practice so that inclusion teams routinely examine their own underlying assumptions and potential biases.
“Our findings are not an argument for abandoning DEI. They are an argument for fundamentally rethinking how it operates. An approach to inclusion that fails to recognize discrimination because the people experiencing it do not fit a particular model is failing in its most basic purpose,” Professor Kandola told the Post.

Oman: No lasting Persian Gulf security without Iran’s participation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:32:06 UTC
01:32:06 KST

Oman: No lasting Persian Gulf security without Iran’s participation
TEHRAN — Omani Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi has called for an inclusive regional security framework bringing together Iran, Iraq and the six member states of the Persian Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), warning that any arrangement excluding Tehran would be inherently unstable and incapable of delivering lasting security.
Speaking at the University of Cambridge on Monday in a speech titled Inclusive Security in the Persian Gulf, Al Busaidi challenged approaches that portray Iran as a threat around which regional security arrangements should be built, arguing instead that stability depends on cooperation among the countries bordering the Persian Gulf.
He said existing security arrangements had been shaped by the mistaken assumption that Iran and the Arab states of the Persian Gulf were fundamentally hostile to one another, despite centuries of coexistence and shared regional interests.
With a population of approximately 93 million, a history spanning some 3,000 years and a coastline extending along roughly half of the Persian Gulf, Iran is an indispensable part of the region’s security equation, the Omani foreign minister argued.
Foreign military presence has carried political costs
Al Busaidi also questioned the long-term consequences of the Persian Gulf states’ reliance on foreign military powers, pointing to US military agreements, intelligence cooperation, naval deployments and air defense systems.
While stating that such arrangements had delivered certain benefits, he said their political costs over the longer term had been substantial.
His assessment reflects a broader debate over whether an enduring regional security order can be built through external military guarantees or whether it requires direct cooperation among the countries most affected by instability.
From this perspective, excluding Iran from regional security arrangements would leave a major regional power outside the very framework intended to address shared security concerns, undermining the prospects for a sustainable settlement.
Al Busaidi did not suggest that cooperation with international partners should end. Instead, he called for a shift away from military commitments toward investment, economic development and other forms of constructive engagement.
Iran-US negotiations and Strait of Hormuz security
The Omani foreign minister cited the Iranian nuclear issue and negotiations over maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz as examples of regional challenges that have been complicated by external involvement.
Oman has played a mediating role in indirect negotiations between Iran and the United States. According to Al Busaidi, Muscat facilitated five rounds of talks in April and May 2025 and three further rounds in February 2026.
He said substantial progress had been achieved, and an agreement had appeared within reach before the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran disrupted the diplomatic process.
Al Busaidi also reported progress in discussions between Oman and Iran on a preliminary framework for an interim maritime security agreement, while acknowledging that political obstacles remained.
The Strait of Hormuz is a vital international energy transit route, making security arrangements there a matter of importance not only for the Persian Gulf's coastal states but also for global energy markets and maritime trade. The Omani position points to the importance of addressing navigation and maritime security through engagement with the countries directly concerned.
Reviving a regional security initiative
As a way forward, Al Busaidi proposed reviving a 1976 initiative for collective security among the eight states bordering the Persian Gulf: Iran, Iraq and the six GCC members.
He identified a non-aggression pact as a possible foundation for an inclusive regional arrangement, suggesting that a shared commitment to refrain from aggression could help establish the trust needed for broader cooperation.
Such a framework would place regional states at the center of decisions affecting their security and provide a platform for addressing disputes through dialogue rather than military confrontation.
Al Busaidi's proposal also leaves room for continued international engagement but envisages a different role for external partners—one focused more on economic investment and development than on military deployments and security guarantees.
The central message of his speech was that lasting stability cannot be imposed on the Persian Gulf through arrangements that exclude one of its principal coastal states. Instead, he argued, security must be built through the participation of all regional countries and grounded in their shared responsibility for peace and stability.
The proposal reinforces the importance of regional diplomacy at a time when tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel have heightened concerns over military escalation, maritime security and the wider consequences for energy supplies and regional stability.

Polish-Vietnamese bilateral relations elevate to strategic partnership
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:31:37 CET
01:31:37 KST

Polish-Vietnamese bilateral relations elevate to strategic partnership
26.10.2026
On 24-26 October 2026, Prime Minister Donald Tusk paid an official visit to Vietnam invited by Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng. The most important outcome of the talks in Hanoi was the elevation of Polish-Vietnamese relations to the status of a strategic partnership. This decision marks a new chapter in the relations between the two countries, which have spanned more than 75 years, and set out the direction for cooperation in the fields of politics, the economy, security, and defence. The Polish government delegation included MFA Undersecretary of State Robert Kupiecki, who also serves as Prime Minister's security advisor.
The establishment of this strategic partnership confirms Vietnam’s growing importance as Poland’s partner in South-East Asia and the Indo-Pacific region within Polish foreign policy. The new formula of bilateral relations is intended to give new momentum to political and economic cooperation, as well as to strengthen dialogue on security and key international challenges.
Security and defence
An important item on the agenda was fostering Polish–Vietnamese cooperation in the fields of security and defence. Deputy Minister Robert Kupiecki took part in talks on the development of a military partnership, including between the defence industries of the two countries. Both sides also declared their willingness to strengthen cooperation within UN peacekeeping operations.
One key area of discussion was countering contemporary security threats. Poland and Vietnam announced the enhancement of cooperation on combating cybercrime, cross-border crime, human trafficking, and illegal migration, as well as on the protection of critical infrastructure and exchange of information and experiences.
Economy, trade, and transport
One of the priorities of the strategic partnership is to increase trade and mutual investment and to create more favourable conditions for entrepreneurs. Poland and Vietnam reaffirmed the importance of making full use of the EU–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), reducing non-tariff barriers, and facilitating access to the markets in both countries. The development of Polish agri-food export, industrial cooperation, and modern technologies is of particular importance.
Regular meetings of the Polish–Vietnamese Working Group on Cooperation in the Field of Agriculture, the next session of which should take place by April 2027, will serve to further develop economic cooperation. The launch of a direct LOT Polish Airlines air link between Warsaw and Hanoi, scheduled for the first quarter of 2027, will also create new opportunities for businesspeople and tourists alike.
Regional cooperation and international affairs
During the talks, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of the UN Charter, international law, and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.
Poland and Vietnam emphasised the need to achieve a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine, in accordance with international law and the principles of the UN Charter, including the prohibition on the use or threat of use of force.
The two sides also acknowledged the importance of peace, stability, and freedom of navigation and overflight in the South China Sea. They also spoke for peaceful resolution of disputes in line with the international law, particularly with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS),
and agreed to strengthen cooperation in multilateral forums, including within the framework of Poland’s and the EU’s relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Vietnam expressed its support for Poland’s efforts to strengthen cooperation with countries in the region.
Science, modern technologies, and people-to-people contacts
The strategic partnership will also include the development of cooperation in the fields of digitalisation, innovation, scientific research, and the medical and pharmaceutical industries. Both sides announced plans to expand cooperation between universities and research institutes, to organise exchanges of students and experts, and to support the teaching of Polish and Vietnamese.
Interpersonal contacts remain an important element of relations, including the role of the Vietnamese community in Poland, which is instrumental in bridging the two countries.
The Joint Action Plan for 2026–2030 will serve to implement the agreed priorities. It is intended to translate the strategic partnership into specific political, economic, and social ventures.
Lastly, Prime Minister Donald Tusk invited Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng to pay an official visit to Poland.

German court sinks bid to cancel Nord Stream trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:29:36 UTC
01:29:36 KST

German court sinks bid to cancel Nord Stream trial
A German court has rejected an attempt to end the trial of Nord Stream bombing suspect Sergey Kuznetsov, after the defendant’s lawyers claimed that he cannot be convicted without a confession.
Kuznetsov, a Ukrainian military officer whom German prosecutors claim carried out the sabotage of the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in 2022, stayed silent in the opening hearing of his trial earlier this month. As Kuznetsov was an active duty soldier at the time of the bombings, his legal team claimed that he cannot be forced to defend himself without divulging state secrets, and filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him.
The Higher Regional Court of Hamburg rejected the motion on Tuesday. “According to German law, the defendant is not restricted in his defense,” presiding Judge Anne Meier-Goring told the court, explaining that the terms of Kuznetsov’s service in Ukraine do not apply in Germany.
Kuznetsov is accused of causing an explosion, disrupting public utilities, property damage, and being an “accomplice to war crimes.” He has neither admitted nor denied carrying out the attack.
Prosecutors claim that he led a seven-person team into the Baltic Sea on a rented pleasure yacht and planted timed explosives on all four individual lines comprising the Nord Stream 1 and 2 projects, three of which completely destroyed the pipes. They did this, prosecutors allege, despite the well-documented limitations of the yacht and the logistical and technical difficulties in carrying out multiple deep-sea dives in a single night.
The case rests on a relatively flimsy body of evidence. Although Kuznetsov was allegedly seen in Germany prior to renting the yacht in Rostock, his fingerprints were not among those lifted from the vessel, and a phone call to his wife in which he defended the bombing as “an official military operation” is the closest thing to a confession that prosecutors can work with.
Russia maintains that the version of events presented in Hamburg is implausible from the outset. “Five people were sitting around drinking, having a laugh, and decided ‘Why don’t we blow up the Nord Stream pipelines?’ They had diving skills, allegedly hired a little boat, sailed to the place where the Nord Streams were passing, went down, planted explosives and detonated them,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov commented in 2024. “If someone can actually believe this version, then it’s only people who are afraid of the truth and are trying to protect the criminal Kiev regime in any way possible.”
American journalist Seymour Hersh has put forward an alternate theory. Citing sources in the intelligence community, Hersh claimed that CIA divers, working with the Norwegian Navy, used NATO’s June 2022 BALTOPS exercises in the Baltic Sea as cover to plant remotely-detonated explosives on the Nord Stream lines, which were triggered three months later with a sonar buoy.
Another lead came from a Danish harbormaster, who claimed in September 2024 that he had approached a US amphibious assault ship – with its transponder switched off – at the location of the pipelines five days before the explosions. The harbormaster claimed that he was ordered to turn away by the Danish Naval Operational Command and forbidden from discussing the incident.
His claims were never investigated. Denmark closed its investigation into the bombings seven months before the harbormaster came forward with his claims.
Back in Hamburg, Kuznetsov’s trial is expected to run into the new year.

Bagheri: Tehran quadrilateral meeting reflects Iran’s defense capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:29:12 UTC
01:29:12 KST

Bagheri: Tehran quadrilateral meeting reflects Iran’s defense capabilities
TEHRAN — Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy for international affairs at the Secretariat of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has described the quadrilateral meeting between Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in Tehran as a product of the Iranian nation’s resistance and the courage of its Armed Forces, saying the gathering reflected a growing recognition among regional countries that 'lasting security must be built through cooperation and reliance on domestic capabilities.'
Speaking after Monday’s meeting, Bagheri Kani said the talks took place against the backdrop of major strategic developments in the region over recent months, the “brutal aggression” of the Israeli regime and the “terrorist US government.”
He said Iran’s resistance had thwarted Washington’s objectives and left the United States facing a difficult situation. He also maintained that developments following the Israeli regime’s aggression against Iran had not unfolded according to its plans.
Bagheri Kani identified two major outcomes of the confrontation: Iran’s ability to withstand military aggression through its domestic capabilities and the demonstrated effectiveness of its indigenous defense industry.
Indigenous capabilities and resistance to sanctions
The official said the Islamic Republic had relied on its national resources and domestic capabilities to withstand two separate acts of aggression, adding that Iran had succeeded in confronting both.
He noted that the United States and Western countries had imposed sanctions on Iran for decades, particularly targeting strategic sectors and restricting the country’s access to advanced military equipment and technology.
Despite those restrictions, he said, Iranian military personnel and specialists had made significant advances in defense capabilities, demonstrating their effectiveness under operational conditions.
He maintained that Iran’s experience demonstrated the strategic importance of developing indigenous capabilities rather than depending on external powers for national security.
The official also pointed to a broader lesson for countries across West Asia, saying some regional states had believed that aligning themselves with a major power such as the United States would shield them from security threats. In practice, however, he said, events had shown that such expectations did not necessarily correspond with reality.
He argued that regional countries therefore had growing reasons to pursue security through regional engagement, cooperation and the pooling of their respective capabilities.
Israeli policies and the case for regional security cooperation
Bagheri Kani said developments involving the Israeli regime had created an important basis for greater understanding among regional countries about the sources of insecurity and instability.
He argued that the regime’s actions, particularly following developments in recent years, had demonstrated its 'aggressive conduct and lack of restraint in pursuing its ambitions.'
Referring to the concept of “Greater Israel,” he said the idea encompassed a number of countries in the region and had reinforced concerns among regional states about the implications of Israeli policies.
According to Bagheri Kani, the growing recognition of the Israeli regime as a source of instability had helped create common ground for regional countries to work toward establishing security within the region.
He identified this assessment as 'one of the key points reflected in the Tehran meeting,' alongside the emphasis all four participating countries placed on self-reliance and the development of domestic capabilities.
The official said Iran regarded reliance on internal resources as a fundamental strategic principle and that the other participants had also acknowledged the importance of self-sufficiency.
“This is a very important point and a fundamental cornerstone on which we can move toward the future,” he said.
Bagheri Kani added that regional security could not be sustainably achieved by relying exclusively on external powers. Instead, he argued, countries in the region needed to strengthen their own capacities and establish cooperative arrangements capable of addressing shared security challenges.
How the quadrilateral meeting came to Tehran
Bagheri Kani also outlined the process that led to the meeting between Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, explaining that the initiative emerged from earlier consultations among the three other countries and their subsequent efforts to bring Iran into a regional dialogue on security.
He said Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan had previously held a meeting in Pakistan and had expressed a strong interest in Iran's participation. However, circumstances at the time had prevented the Iranian side from attending.
The three countries subsequently held another meeting in Turkey, where they again expressed their desire for Iran to take part in the discussions.
This time, however, they proposed travelling to Iran themselves to hold a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran, Bagheri Kani said.
He cited a previous visit to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, during which the Pakistani commander met Major General Rezaei and conveyed the three countries’ interest in convening a meeting in the Iranian capital.
Four countries seek a framework for broader regional engagement
The Iranian official emphasized that the meeting was not an attempt by any one participant to impose its particular outlook on the others. Rather, he said, the four countries sought to develop a common framework capable of accommodating their respective perspectives and encouraging practical cooperation.
He described this approach as a significant feature of the gathering, arguing that a cooperative framework among the four countries could also encourage other regional states to participate in efforts to strengthen security.
Bagheri Kani said Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan had the potential to play an influential role both across the wider region and in the Muslim world if they worked together.
He stressed that their cooperation could serve as a foundation for broader regional participation, enabling countries to address shared security concerns through dialogue, coordination and the development of mutual capabilities.
Its emphasis on self-reliance, regional cooperation and the need for a common approach to security, Bagheri Kani said, reflected a shared interest in developing practical mechanisms for addressing the region’s challenges.

Forced retreat of neighbors

Forced retreat of neighbors
Khorasan examined the reopening of borders by Iran’s eastern and western neighbors, Pakistan and Iraq, after a forced retreat from restrictive policies. The paper argued that recent statements by Scott Bessent regarding cooperation between Washington and Iran’s neighbors to limit land routes represented a new stage in economic pressure on Tehran. However, developments on both borders showed that isolating Iran through regional blockades is neither easy nor cost-free.
According to the report, Iran remains an important partner for neighboring countries in sectors such as energy and essential goods. Any political decision designed to pressure Tehran for a limited period could result in the long-term loss of valuable markets. The newspaper noted that Iran provides substantial opportunities for foreign exporters, manufacturers, and service companies. Restricting access to this market would reduce sales and may even negatively affect employment in neighboring states. For this reason, attempts to economically isolate Iran could ultimately damage the interests of regional countries as much as, or even more than, Iran itself.
Ettelaat: Shadow of war and a window for diplomacy
Ettelaat focused on the complicated relationship between military developments and diplomacy. It wrote that disagreements over negotiation terms have intensified the challenges facing both Tehran and Washington. Iran seeks relief from economic and maritime pressures as well as guarantees against future confrontations. The United States, in contrast, continues to emphasize nuclear restrictions and security arrangements. The analysis stated that neither side wants to enter negotiations from a position of weakness, making a comprehensive agreement difficult to reach. Declining trust is another major obstacle. When confidence erodes, even establishing common ground on basic issues requires more time and stronger assurances. The newspaper added that economic pressure may be increased in an effort to force concessions, but such measures can also reduce the likelihood of compromise. Successful diplomacy requires a willingness to understand the concerns of the opposing side and to search for realistic solutions rather than simply repeating demands.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Mediators on the move
Arman-e-Emrooz highlighted regional and international mediation efforts aimed at preventing further escalation. The paper noted that several actors are simultaneously attempting to create opportunities for dialogue. Qatar has sent a delegation to Tehran, Pakistan has expressed readiness to mediate, and Russia may assume a more active diplomatic role. According to the report, Iran has made clear that it is prepared for negotiations but only under conditions it considers acceptable. Issues related to the Strait of Hormuz and restrictions on ports are viewed by Tehran as interconnected and cannot be discussed separately. The newspaper argued that meaningful progress depends on confidence-building measures and practical actions by all parties. Maintaining stability is especially important because any serious escalation could affect neighboring countries, international trade, global energy markets, and broader security concerns.
Arman-e-Melli: Why Europeans have become active
Arman-e-Melli examined increasing European diplomatic activity toward Iran. The newspaper argued that since the outbreak of recent tensions and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, many analysts have viewed European countries as among the most vulnerable to the resulting economic and political consequences. As a result, Europe appears to be searching for a new path out of the current situation. The European troika is reportedly interested in playing a more influential role in future discussions between Iran and the United States through a revised framework for negotiations. Political and security indicators suggest that European governments are working to avoid becoming directly involved in policies that could deepen confrontation in the region. However, Europe faces several challenges. Among them are unexpected developments involving energy cooperation between the United States and Russia, as well as growing speculation about a possible accommodation between Russia and Ukraine. These factors have complicated European strategic calculations and encouraged greater diplomatic engagement.
Farhikhtegan: How Iran should deal with US
Farhikhtegan discussed strategic principles that should guide Iran’s approach toward the United States. The article outlined four main recommendations. First, Iranian proposals should be framed in terms of mutual interests rather than demands. This approach can present negotiations as constructive opportunities rather than confrontational exchanges. Second, if circumstances lead Washington to support ending tensions and pursuing an agreement, Iran should seek structural guarantees instead of relying solely on written or verbal commitments. Third, Tehran should expand the number and diversity of mediators, partners, and supporters involved in diplomatic efforts. Fourth, despite their limitations, international organizations should remain important instruments for advancing national objectives and protecting interests. The article concluded by arguing that the United States should be judged by its actions rather than its statements. Real policies, treatment of allies, and tangible outcomes are ultimately more important than public rhetoric in determining intentions and future relations.

The “Tiepolo 2026” Award to Giovanni Ferrero and Benito Tesier of Brembo
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:27:21 CET
01:27:21 KST

Giovanni Ferrero, executive chairman of the Ferrero confectionery group, and Benito Tesier Sierra, general manager of Brembo Iberia, are the winners of the 2026 Tiepolo Award, an honor bestowed upon business leaders who contribute to strengthening economic and commercial ties between Italy and Spain.
                                    
The award, now in its 29th edition and established in 1996, is presented jointly by the Italian Chamber of Commerce and Industry for Spain (CCIS) and the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE), under the auspices of the Italian Embassy in Madrid. The award ceremony will take place on November 17 at the Italian Embassy, in the presence of Ambassador Giuseppe Buccino Grimaldi and representatives from institutions and businesses in both countries.
                                    
The jury sought to recognize, in particular, the Ferrero Group’s strategic decision to focus on Spain as an industrial and technological platform for growth in Europe, as well as Tesier’s contribution to the development and consolidation of Brembo in the Iberian market.
                                    
The group, founded in Alba, Piedmont, in 1946, is celebrating 80 years of operation this year as a family-owned business, now in its third generation. As one of the world’s leading manufacturers of packaged confectionery products, it employs over 50,000 people, operates in more than 170 countries, and generates revenue of nearly 20 billion euros.
                                    
Its relationship with Spain dates back to 1985. In 1988, Ferrero Ibérica was established, with headquarters in Barcelona. Today, the company employs approximately 200 people on the Iberian Peninsula, across its offices in Cornellà de Llobregat (Barcelona) and Lisbon. On the Spanish market, the group is represented by the Ferrero Rocher, Kinder, Nutella, and Raffaello brands.
                                    
Under the executive presidency of Giovanni Ferrero, the group has also expanded its operations into the ice cream segment, identifying Spain as a strategic market for the development of this category. In 2021, it acquired Ice Cream Factory Comaker (ICFC), which has its headquarters and production facility in Alzira, in the province of Valencia.
                                    
The facility is set to become Ferrero’s European technology hub for ice cream production. To carry out the project, an initial investment of 140 million euros was approved, earmarked for technological and industrial modernization, the expansion of production capacity, and the introduction of new processes. The jury emphasized that this decision strengthens Spain’s role in the group’s European industrial strategy and serves as an example of how Italian investments contribute to the growth of Spain’s manufacturing sector.
                                    
The second award recipient, Benito Tesier Sierra, is the general manager of Brembo Iberia and a key figure in the development of the Italian group’s operations in the Spanish market. The jury recognized his contribution to integrating local entrepreneurial expertise into an international industrial and commercial strategy.
                                    
Brembo’s presence in Spain has evolved from its initial establishment in the Molins de Rei area, near Barcelona, to the consolidation of its operations in Aragon, in part through the collaboration between the Bombassei and Tesier families. The group has expanded its presence in the automotive sector and in the aftermarket—the market for replacement parts and post-sale services—including through the acquisition of J. Juan, a Spanish company specializing in motorcycle braking systems.
                                    
In his leadership role, Tesier helped integrate the expertise and business relationships developed in the Spanish market with Brembo’s technological, industrial, and international capabilities, fostering business continuity and the company’s growth. With over 30 years of experience in the automotive sector, Tesier has also served as president of Ceoe Aragón since January 2026. 
 According to the award citation, his career path demonstrates the value of collaboration between international capital and local entrepreneurial expertise in strengthening companies’ industrial capacity and international reach.

Explainer: Why the CPC puts people's well-being at the heart of self-governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:26:42 CST
01:26:42 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- In northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, eligible residents can receive certain forms of medical assistance and other support without submitting an application. Government departments share the information needed to provide the benefits.
The provincial bodies responsible for disciplinary inspection helped drive the change. They prompted civil affairs departments to build a data-sharing network connecting 33 departments and institutions, enabling 12 frequently used assistance services to be provided without applications.
The initiative offers a concrete example of how the self-supervision of the Communist Party of China (CPC) improve public services and help ensure that benefits reach those who most need them.
Earning public trust through tangible improvements in people's lives is a defining feature of the CPC's full and rigorous self-governance, which is high on the agenda of the fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee. The key meeting, which opened Monday in Beijing, is considering a draft decision of the CPC Central Committee on major issues concerning strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance.
COMMITMENT TO THE PEOPLE
The CPC constitution commits the Party to serving the people, and states that it has no special interests of its own apart from those of the working class and the broadest possible majority of the people.
Without seeking self-interest, the CPC can keep its spirit of thorough self-reform, and by swiftly detecting and resolving its own problems, the Party can prevent any interest group, power group or privileged stratum from preying on or corrupting its members.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has led an unprecedented anti-corruption campaign since 2012, driven by a determination to "offend a few thousand rather than fail 1.4 billion." The campaign has targeted corrupt officials at both high and low levels.
Gyula Thurmer, president of the Hungarian Workers' Party, said serving the interests of the people is a central principle of the CPC.
He added that the Party's anti-corruption efforts have achieved significant results, strengthening internal discipline and helping implement major economic and social development programs.
SAFEGUARDING PEOPLE'S INTERESTS
Xi has called on Party members to bear in mind that "benefiting the people is their greatest political achievement."
An official review of work in 2025 reported that disciplinary and supervisory bodies nationwide investigated 967,000 cases of misconduct and corruption affecting people's daily lives, returning or helping recover about 77.6 billion yuan (11.5 billion U.S. dollars) in money and property to the public.
Faruk Boric, president of the Association of Friendship between China and Bosnia and Herzegovina, said China's efforts to pursue corrupt officials at both senior and lower levels send "a clear message that no official is above the rules, regardless of their position."
He said China's experience offers important lessons in linking clean governance with people's well-being. Protecting public funds, he added, helps direct more resources toward health care, education and other public services.
BUILDING BETTER GOVERNANCE
On several occasions, Xi has called for taking simultaneous, coordinated, and comprehensive steps to ensure that officials do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to become corrupt.
In his article on the Party's self-reform, Xi urged efforts to improve Party conduct, enforce discipline, and fight corruption, while integrating Party self-supervision with public oversight to deeply advance the Party's self-reform.
Lyazid Benhami, a member of the Paris Association of French-Chinese Friendship, said rigorous Party self-governance can clarify officials' responsibilities, improve coordination and help sustain development programs.
He highlighted China's emphasis on long-term planning, infrastructure, education and research, adding that the country has achieved a profound transformation regarding such priority areas and improved the well-being of its people.
Those administrative strengths matter as China implements its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). In January, Xi urged efforts to confine power to an institutional cage in a more well-conceived and effective manner, and press ahead with the anti-corruption fight with a clearer understanding and stronger resolve, thus providing a strong guarantee for achieving the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan period.
Volker Tschapke, honorary president of Germany's Prussian Society, said the CPC's courage to "turn the blade inward" demonstrated a "moral strength that I truly admire." He stressed that rigorous Party self-governance ultimately serves the fundamental interests of the people.
"I have seen with my own eyes what that has achieved: how villages have blossomed through targeted poverty alleviation, how rural areas have found new hope, how high-speed rail connects people and hearts," he said. ■

Iran opposes nuclear technology monopoly, calls for equal access to advanced technologies

Iran opposes nuclear technology monopoly, calls for equal access to advanced technologies
TEHRAN — Iran has called for equitable global access to advanced nuclear technologies, urging the international community to eliminate discriminatory barriers, expand technical cooperation and strengthen protections for peaceful nuclear facilities.
Hossein Derakhshandeh, deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) and chief executive of the Nuclear Power Production and Development Company of Iran, outlined four priorities for the equitable development of nuclear power at the International Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power in South Korea on Tuesday.
He stressed the need to remove discriminatory restrictions, facilitate access to advanced technologies, broaden technical cooperation and reinforce international measures to protect peaceful nuclear facilities, warning against the use of nuclear technology to establish monopolies.
Derakhshandeh also called for equal access to advanced nuclear technologies in accordance with international law and without double standards. He reaffirmed the inalienable right of states party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) to conduct nuclear research and development and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.
Emphasizing the importance of upholding the rights of NPT signatories, he called on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to function as an independent, technically focused and development-oriented organization, in line with its Statute. The Agency’s mandate includes promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and facilitating technical cooperation among member states without discrimination, he said.
However, Derakhshandeh argued that developments in recent years had shown the Agency to be increasingly influenced by political considerations, undermining its impartial implementation of its statutory responsibilities. He cited the US-Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities as an example of the challenges facing the international nuclear framework.
He described the attacks as a flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter, international law, and IAEA General Conference resolutions prohibiting attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities. He also criticized the Agency for an 'inadequate response,' saying it had failed to uphold the fundamental principles of impartiality and professionalism effectively.
Derakhshandeh stressed that protecting peaceful nuclear infrastructure was a shared international responsibility. He also condemned 'international silence over violations of the Iranian people’s rights' in areas including energy, healthcare, food security, the environment and industry.
He further criticized the Israeli regime, the United States and certain European countries for 'politically motivated campaigns' against Iran, involving unfounded accusations and negative media coverage.
His remarks underscored Iran’s call for a nuclear order grounded in equal access to technology, respect for the peaceful-use rights of NPT signatories. and the consistent application of international law, free from political pressure and discriminatory treatment.

MOSCOW, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday called on natural gas-exporting countries to strengthen cooperation to maintain stability in the global market.
Addressing the plenary session of the eighth Summit of Heads of State and Government of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) at the World Trade Center in Moscow, Putin said natural gas accounts for about a quarter of global energy consumption, and worldwide demand is expected to reach 5.5 trillion cubic meters annually by the middle of this century.
The escalation of tensions in the Middle East, disruptions to gas supply routes, and restrictions imposed by some countries on the procurement of gas equipment and technologies have increased the risk of prolonged imbalances in the global gas market, he said.
Putin noted that GECF member countries collectively hold about 70 percent of the world's natural gas reserves and account for around 40 percent of global gas exports.
To address challenges facing the global gas industry, exporting countries should deepen cooperation and develop open and trust-based partnerships on the basis of mutual benefit and respect for each other's interests, he said.
Putin also highlighted Russia's role in the global gas market, saying the country has the world's largest natural gas reserves and ranks second in production.
Any attempts to exclude Russia from the global gas market or hinder the development of its gas industry would have serious consequences and drive up costs for gas consumers in other countries, he warned.
Founded in 2001 and formally established as an organization in December 2008, the GECF aims to strengthen cooperation and dialogue among natural gas-producing and exporting countries, and promote stability and security in the global gas market. ■

News Analysis: Burnham pushes for devolution, closer EU ties in first 100 days as PM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:26:13 CST
01:26:13 KST

by Zhao Jiasong
LONDON, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first 100 days in office, which fell on Tuesday, have seen him put forward plans to devolve more power to the regions, reconsider Brexit, and pursue a more independent foreign policy.
Since taking office on July 20, the former mayor of Greater Manchester has helped the Labour Party recover from the stark drop in popularity it experienced under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
An analysis of polling data by the Press Association shows that Labour's average support has risen by around 10 percentage points compared with the period immediately before Starmer announced his resignation in June.
Nevertheless, Burnham faces growing pressure to turn his proposals into results, with constitutional tensions, the legacy of Brexit and disagreements with Washington testing his government.
DEVOLUTION UNDER PRESSURE FROM NATIONALISTS
Devolution has been central to Burnham's political agenda. After nearly a decade as mayor of Greater Manchester, he has brought his approach to regional governance into Downing Street.
Just three days after becoming prime minister, Burnham opened "Number 10 North" in Manchester, a government office intended to give regional development a greater role in national decision-making.
He also revived the National Economic Council, bringing together ministers and regional leaders to discuss investment and economic growth. His government has proposed giving local authorities greater powers over skills training, employment support and taxation.
Ian Scott, an academic at the University of Manchester, told Xinhua that the establishment of Number 10 North carries "considerable symbolic importance." However, questions remain over "how much decision-making power would actually move away from London."
He added that Manchester's experience, built over years of cooperation between local authorities and central government, could not easily be reproduced elsewhere.
Burnham's plans are also under pressure from nationalist parties in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
On Sept. 14, leaders of the Scottish National Party, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Fein met in Cardiff and signed an agreement calling on the British government to prepare for constitutional change. The parties support Scottish independence, Welsh independence and Irish reunification, respectively.
Jennifer Todd, a political scientist at University College Dublin, said the meeting was "largely symbolic," given the different political circumstances and objectives of the three parties. She noted that Brexit had increased discussion of Irish reunification, though public attitudes remain complex.
Nevertheless, the meeting showed that nationalist parties are seeking closer cooperation as Burnham prepares to transfer more powers from Westminster. His government now faces demands for greater autonomy from parties that ultimately want to leave the United Kingdom (UK).
REOPENING DEBATE OVER EU RELATIONS
Burnham has also taken a different approach from his predecessor on Britain's future relationship with the European Union (EU), suggesting that the country should consider closer integration with the bloc.
In an interview with The Sunday Times published over the weekend, Burnham said Britain needed an "honest discussion" about restoring free movement with the EU.
He argued that immigration patterns have changed since Brexit, with more migrants settling permanently in Britain rather than moving between countries for temporary employment.
In the near-term, Burnham raised the possibility of Britain rejoining the EU single market or customs union, while in the longer-term, returning to the EU itself could be considered. The leader acknowledged that rejoining the bloc would require another referendum, while other arrangements might not.
The BBC reported on Tuesday that Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said British officials would discuss possible future arrangements with their EU counterparts, including free movement, ahead of a summit on Nov. 20.
For now, the government is concentrating on agreements covering food trade, emissions trading and youth mobility. Burnham has pledged to respect Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return to the single market, customs union or free movement during the current parliamentary term.
His comments have drawn criticism from Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who accused him of betraying the Brexit vote. Some Labour lawmakers also fear that reopening the debate could alienate voters in constituencies that supported leaving the EU.
Britain continues to face trade barriers following Brexit, while businesses have called for closer economic cooperation with Europe. Burnham's challenge is to persuade voters that a new relationship would bring economic benefits without reviving the divisions that have shaped British politics for a decade.
UKRAINE, PALESTINE AND RELATIONS WITH WASHINGTON
In foreign policy, Burnham has continued Britain's support for Ukraine, while taking positions that at times differ from those of the United States.
On Aug. 24, he chose Kyiv for his first overseas visit as prime minister, where he reaffirmed Britain's commitment to military and political support for the country.
Differences with Washington became more apparent this month after restrictions on Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite communications system raised concerns over Kyiv's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
During a telephone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 23, Burnham stressed the importance of Ukraine having full access to Starlink.
He also acknowledged Trump's efforts to bring Russia to the negotiating table. The two leaders agreed to work with international partners towards ending the conflict.
Regarding Palestine, Burnham has supported stronger measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In September, Britain, France and Canada announced plans to ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements and impose targeted measures against those involved in settlement expansion. The three governments said such actions were necessary to protect the prospects of a two-state solution.
These measures drew criticism from Israel and the United States, pointing to differences between Britain and its allies over the Israel-Palestine conflict. ■

The Achilles’ heel of the Iskanders: why the Defense Forces are attacking rubber plants
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:26:13 EET
01:26:13 KST

The Achilles’ heel of the Iskanders: why the Defense Forces are attacking rubber plants
Kyiv • UNN
FP-1 attacks damaged six Russian enterprises producing solid rocket fuel components. An immediate reduction in shelling should not be expected.
The Defense Forces attacked a number of enterprises in Russia’s rubber industry with long-range FP-1 drones. Their products are used in the production of solid rocket propellant, including for Iskander-M ballistic missiles. Will the attacks affect the intensity of shelling of Ukraine? UNN investigated together with military expert Oleksandr Kovalenko.
Why Ukraine is attacking Russia’s rubber plants
There are around ten large enterprises in this industry in Russia overall. According to Fire Point, as of October 25, six of them had sustained 11 successful attacks. Tolyattikauchuk came under attack most often, having been targeted at least four times. The Sterlitamak Petrochemical Plant was targeted three more times.
In just the past few days, FP-1 attack drones struck three major enterprises in Russia’s rubber industry at once: Voronezhsintezkauchuk, Omsk Rubber, and Tolyattikauchuk.
At first glance, the rubber industry does not appear to be directly related to weapons production. However, these enterprises manufacture not only materials for automobile tires but also polymers used in the production of solid rocket propellant.
One of them is polybutadiene-acrylonitrile. It binds the components of rocket propellant into a single solid grain while also serving as an additional fuel. Replacing such a component is not easy—it requires new formulations and testing. Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles operate on solid propellant. Strikes on the rubber industry are strikes against the chemical foundation of Russia’s missile production
Will strikes on the rubber industry lead to a reduction in Iskander production?
According to military expert Oleksandr Kovalenko, polymer components play an important role in the production of solid rocket propellant. Therefore, damage to enterprises that supply the relevant raw materials could potentially affect the operations of Russian missile manufacturers.
Rubbers and related polymers are used to create solid rocket propellant. In particular, the 9M723 ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system are equipped with solid-fuel engines. In general, missiles of this class, including ballistic and aeroballistic missiles, primarily use solid-propellant propulsion systems. Accordingly, polymer components play an important role in the formation and stabilization of rocket propellant
According to him, damage to several plants does not mean that Russian ballistic missile production will stop. moscow may seek alternative sources for the necessary components, including in China, India, and other countries with developed chemical industries.
However, replacing domestic production with imports could result in additional costs for the kremlin, more complicated logistics, and increased dependence on foreign partners.
If Russia is forced to purchase the necessary components abroad, this could increase the cost of production, including rocket propellant and finished missiles. In addition, the dependence of Russia’s military-industrial complex on external suppliers will increase, while the capabilities of domestic production will come under additional pressure
Systematic attacks will lead to more serious consequences
In Kovalenko’s view, one of the decisive factors in the effectiveness of strikes is the nature of the damage to industrial enterprises. If only auxiliary facilities are hit, production will be restored relatively quickly. By contrast, damage to technological equipment, power-supply systems, purification systems, or other critical production units could cause plants to remain idle for considerably longer.
In one case, an enterprise may resume operations after relatively uncomplicated repairs in two or three weeks. In another, restoration may take months. And if complex equipment is involved—equipment that Russia cannot obtain promptly because of sanctions—repairs may turn into a much more serious problem
Repeated attacks are particularly painful, according to the military expert. Even if a single strike does not shut down a plant for long, regular damage forces the enterprise to spend resources on repairs instead of maintaining stable production.
In such a case, it is precisely the systematic nature of the strikes that may have significantly more serious consequences than a single attack
In this context, the repeated attacks on TolyattiKauchuk and the Sterlitamak Petrochemical Plant will have a cumulative effect.
Will Russia reduce the intensity of its shelling of Ukraine
Despite the potential problems for Russia's missile industry, according to the military expert, an immediate reduction in the number of ballistic missile strikes against Ukraine should not be expected.
Kovalenko explains that the intensity of the shelling depends not only on current missile production, but also on stockpiles already accumulated, the rate at which they are used, and Russia's ability to quickly compensate for production losses.
Even if damage to chemical plants leads to a reduction in the production of new missiles, the Russians will use accumulated missiles for some time.
Kovalenko explained that assessing the effectiveness of Ukrainian strikes requires monitoring the production dynamics of Iskanders, changes in production costs, the duration of the production cycle, and the dependence of Russian plants on imported components.
If, as a result of systematic strikes, Russia really begins producing fewer missiles than it uses during attacks on Ukraine, this will gradually affect its ability to maintain the previous intensity of shelling. However, this effect will not necessarily be immediate: it will depend on existing stockpiles, the ability to compensate for losses, and the speed at which damaged production facilities are restored
Thus, strikes against Russia's rubber industry, and especially systematic and repeated attacks, increase the economic and production pressure on the chemical base of Russia's missile industry. However, the extent to which this will affect the production of Iskander missiles and their use during attacks on Ukraine will depend on the ability of Russian plants to quickly resume operations and on existing missile stockpiles.
