By Anton Zverev
LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A Russian IT specialist has been sentenced to 13 years in jail on charges of financing terrorism after the cryptocurrency exchange Binance passed details to Moscow of his donations to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns.
The 2nd Western District Military Court on Monday convicted 49-year-old Yuri Belenkiy and sentenced him to three years in prison plus 10 years in a strict-regime penal colony, according to a court statement.
Belenkiy, who has a Bulgarian residence permit, was detained in September last year when he flew to Moscow for a visit, and has been in custody since. He denied the charges, according to the court.
Belenkiy had responded to online appeals to help buy medical equipment for Ukrainian soldiers by transferring money from his Binance accounts to the Ukrainian military, according to Russian law enforcement documents seen by Reuters. Some payments went to the Azov Brigade or Azov Regiment, a particular bete noire for Moscow.
BINANCE ACCEPTED RUSSIAN INVESTIGATORS’ REQUEST
The same documents showed that Binance provided Russian investigators with Belenkiy’s transaction history last year, including records of transfers to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns, in response to a Russian request, and that the records were instrumental in prosecuting him, Reuters reported in August.
According to the records, Belenkiy sent more than $700 to the Ukrainian military in response to an online appeal by Arkady Babchenko, an exiled Russian critic of the Kremlin who supports Ukraine.
“The response from Binance serves as key evidence in the criminal case against Belenkiy,” said Yevgeny Smirnov, a lawyer with the rights group First Department, which assists people facing politically motivated prosecutions in Russia.
Rights advocates who monitor such prosecutions say dozens of Russians have been convicted in recent years for donations made through cryptocurrency platforms to causes that authorities later classified as extremist or terrorist. Many used cryptocurrency because they believed it would keep their identities secret.
Asked on Tuesday about the sentence, Binance referred Reuters to a previous statement in which it said the exchange “does not make or enforce the laws of any jurisdiction, determine charges, or decide how any government uses information in legal proceedings”. It said it does not comment on confidential law-enforcement requests or individual cases.
A lawyer who specialises in crypto regulation, Mike Bystrov, told Reuters in August that Binance, which left Russia in 2023 following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent imposition of Western sanctions, had been under no obligation to provide Belenkiy’s data.
He said it might, in fact, have had obligations under European Union data-protection law not to do so because of Belenkiy’s Bulgarian residency status.

Dueling proofs from OpenAI and Anthropic astound scientists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:50:47 UTC
00:50:47 KST

Just a few weeks after dropping hundreds of artificial-intelligence-generated math breakthroughs on a field that’s already in crisis, OpenAI is piling on more.
Yesterday the company dropped three massive proofs that touched on math, physics and computer science, sending shockwaves rippling through those fields. Experts are still staggering.
These latest releases from OpenAI continue to contradict the recommendations of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), the expert panel the company organized in response to widespread criticism from mathematicians. The large language model (LLM) that produced the new proofs remains proprietary, and the exact prompts used, time spent computing and “chain of thought outputs” involved have not been made public. Two of the results coincide with closely related work involving OpenAI’s competitor Anthropic.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
OpenAI’s approach to two of the three results also directly violates a clarifying statement AGMAI issued just a day before they were released by designating specific experts to shepherd the results into the public sphere. Among the work of such experts, a paper relating to the “million-dollar” Yang-Mills problem (one of seven Millennium Prize Problems set by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000) has still not been made public. Writing that “there is no scientific reason for delaying ... any further,” AGMAI has already called on OpenAI to release the paper.
Here’s a quick breakdown of what the three new results are and why they matter.
Kakeya
The Kakeya conjecture is about swirling a needle or stylus around in the air cleverly—so that it points in every direction once but sweeps out as little volume as possible. Specifically, the conjecture says that the volume cannot be less than a certain number. Surprisingly, this simple geometry problem is one of the most important conjectures in harmonic analysis, the study of how all kinds of mathematical objects can be built from waves.
Last year mathematicians Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved the conjecture in three dimensions in one of the biggest math breakthroughs of this century. The feat won Wang a Fields Medal—math’s highest honor—at this summer’s International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia. But the problem remained open in higher-dimensional spaces.
In last month’s “slop drop,” OpenAI’s internal model solved the four-dimensional Kakeya problem. Now it’s solved the problem in every dimension, proving that there’s a limit to how small a space a high-dimensional stylus can take up.
Yang-Mills
The Yang-Mills problem, one of Clay’s five million-dollar Millennium Prize Problems that remain open, is about particle physics. Specifically, it asks whether the mathematics that underpins the “Standard Model” of particle physics is actually sound.
This question comes down to two parts, referred to as “existence” and “mass gap.” The Clay Mathematics Institute’s definition of the problem asks for answers to both. Today OpenAI claimed to prove the first of the two—that the “Yang-Mills theory” is mathematically consistent in all relevant cases: in other words, it “exists.” The part of the Clay problem that remains open is more quantitative, asking whether a certain number in the theory, called the “mass gap,” is always bigger than zero.
In the late 1980s, a little more than a decade before the Clay Mathematics Institute existed, mathematician Tadeusz Balaban published a series of massive, dense papers that sketched out a path to prove the “existence” part of the problem. As voluminous as “Balaban’s program” is, it only codifies the problem’s broad contours—filling in the gaps to construct a mathematically rigorous proof would demand far more laborious and exhaustive calculations. The project is so immense—and Balaban’s papers are so difficult to parse—that no one has carried it out more than three decades later. “He basically did it,” says Roland Bauerschmidt, a mathematician at New York University. “But I think there’s no one who understands these papers and can tell whether they’re correct or not.”
Recently, sensing that a race was on to finish Balaban’s program, some experts began using LLMs to churn out the necessary tomes of tedious mathematical steps. Working with Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge, Ethan Sussman, a mathematician at Northwestern University, created and publicized a public GitHub repository to do just that. They were making considerable progress and believed they were near to finishing the program. OpenAI’s claim—with no publicly available proof—appears to have beaten them to the finish line.
Exponential Time Hypothesis
The exponential time hypothesis (ETH) is about computational complexity—the science of ranking computer science problems by how hard they are.
Specifically, ETH suggests that a famous task called the 3-satisfiability, or 3-SAT, problem cannot be solved in less than exponential time. This means that as the number of variables in the problem increases, any algorithm that solves it will run exponentially slower. OpenAI’s proof provides an algorithm to solve 3-SAT that is just a tiny bit faster than exponential time, refuting ETH.
ETH is important because of its relationship to “P versus NP,” which is another of the Clay institute’s Millennium Prize Problems and widely considered to be one of the most difficult, with major implications for modern encryption.
First suggested in 1999, ETH can be thought of as an even stronger version of P ≠ NP (the conjecture that P does not equal NP, which the majority of people in the field believe) and has been treated as a bedrock tenet of computer science by most experts. Because 3-SAT is a problem computer scientists know to be central to the debate, ETH would show that there were problems that were not only fundamentally hard to solve but that would also scale up so brutally that they would be effectively unassailable.
Although the new result doesn’t necessarily translate to a transformative breakthrough about P versus NP, the potential effects are so sweeping that OpenAI has tapped outside experts to vet its claim. Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, two computer scientists at the University of California, San Diego, who first suggested ETH, as well as Ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, are now working with OpenAI to perform an independent investigation of the result. The company will also sponsor a computer science conference about the proof as part of this investigation, according to Williams.
The result hasn’t been without controversy, either. Mere hours after OpenAI’s announcement, Anthropic posted its own independent result disproving ETH, based on work by an internal Anthropic model.

UK sets pace on new undersea sensors to detect threats, as AUKUS partners test advanced kit in San Diego
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:49:26 GMT
00:49:26 KST

UK sets pace on new undersea sensors to detect threats, as AUKUS partners test advanced kit in San Diego
The UK will lead development of three advanced undersea sensor payloads for uncrewed vehicles under AUKUS, following a week of testing at the Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego.
- UK to lead development of three pioneering payloads for uncrewed underwater vehicles, as part of AUKUS security partnership
- Announcement wraps up Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego, enhancing integration of uncrewed systems across AUKUS fleets in another step towards a UK Hybrid Navy
- Work builds on AUKUS Pillar II framework, strengthening security and deterrence across Euro-Atlantic and Indo-Pacific
The UK will lead the next stage of delivery of cutting-edge undersea sensing technologies which will be deployed from uncrewed underwater vessels as part of the AUKUS security partnership.
The announcement rounds off a week of testing and demonstrations at the Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego.
This advances the first signature project under AUKUS Pillar 2 - announced in May as part of the trilateral security partnership between Australia, the UK and the United States - seeks to pool the innovation of each nations’ defence sector to develop advanced military capabilities to strengthen deterrence and security around the world.
The UK will lead development and delivery of three pioneering sensor payloads for uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs): a Synthetic Aperture Sonar, a Deployable Anti-Submarine Warfare Sensor, and a Deployable Non-Kinetic Effector.
These capabilities will collect detailed underwater information, deploy sensors to detect and classify underwater threats, and generate underwater effects. The payloads will help UUVs provide surveillance of large ocean areas and protect underwater infrastructure.
The payloads will be available across the three nations’ UUV fleets from 2027, enhancing the reach and effectiveness of those fleets and reinforcing strategic deterrence across the Euro-Atlantic, High North and Indo-Pacific.
The project positions AUKUS at the forefront of autonomy and uncrewed systems in the maritime domain and wraps up the latest series of exercises conducted last week at the Maritime Big Play (MBP) exercise in San Diego, a proving ground where autonomous marine capabilities are integrated and tested before wider adoption across the AUKUS partnership.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard said:
  The UK is all in on AUKUS, and this cutting-edge technology shows why. By leading development of these sensor payloads, we’re putting British innovation at the heart of AUKUS and strengthening our collective undersea capability.
In places like Frome, Basingstoke and Dorchester, British companies large and small are driving this work forward, creating skilled jobs and backing our plan to deliver a modern, Hybrid Navy fit for the threats we face.
Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the Prime Minister’s Special Representative on AUKUS, said:
  AUKUS is a uniquely powerful partnership, and the depth and breadth of our cutting-edge capability and strength in the maritime domain has been demonstrated this week in San Diego.
The UK is now stepping forward to lead development of three of the most advanced undersea sensor payloads any of our three nations have fielded, sharpening our collective edge and reinforcing security across the Euro-Atlantic and the Indo-Pacific.
The AUKUS partnership is backed by the Defence Investment Plan, which set out £298 billion of UK defence spending over the next four years, marking the largest sustained increase since the end of the Cold War.
The Maritime Big Play exercise aims to shorten the path from innovation to capability by testing new maritime technologies in realistic operational environments. Exercises at MBP-Pacific tested how Australian, UK and US crewed and uncrewed systems operate together across four strands: anti-submarine warfare, lethality, contested resupply, and subsea and seabed warfare.
The UK led the anti-submarine warfare (ASW) strand, contributing thirteen uncrewed surface vehicles, two ASW targets and four underwater gliders from six industry partners. The testing supports the transition to a Hybrid Navy: a more flexible, modern force blending crewed and uncrewed platforms, able to detect underwater threats to the UK and allies’ critical undersea infrastructure.
Royal Navy Captain Keith Taylor said
  Maritime Big Play-Pacific gives AUKUS a unique opportunity to turn autonomy into operational advantage. By bringing scientists, industry and warfighters together, and developing the common control solutions that allow diverse autonomous systems to operate and fight as one, we can rapidly build an integrated allied force with greater scale, combat effectiveness and deterrent effect.
The event also showcased two of the four UK winners from the AUKUS Maritime Innovation Challenge – SEA Ltd, based in Frome, and Decision Analysis Services Ltd, based in Basingstoke – demonstrating their cutting-edge technology to trilateral partners and media at MBP-P.
The two companies, along with A2i (based in Dorchester) and US company MSI Transducers, make up the four suppliers that won the Maritime Innovation Challenge, and a share in £3 million of funding to develop innovative capabilities enabling the command, control and cooperation of undersea systems.
The winners show the breadth and diversity across AUKUS innovation, with one SME, two large suppliers, and one micro-consultancy. MBP featured 12 UK industry partners showcasing their role at the forefront of development in the maritime domain, demonstrating how the AUKUS partnership is driving economic growth across the UK, creating skilled jobs and opportunities for companies of all sizes.
Maritime Big Play and the announcement on delivery progress for the first signature project follows a strong month for UK delivery against AUKUS Pillar 2. This includes the successful test firing of a US-Australian heavyweight torpedo from a UK extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle, XV Excalibur, a historic first for an uncrewed submarine and an important milestone in enhancing interoperability and delivering the signature project.

fiat’s tiny multiplina brings 1950s italian microcar design into the electric age

fiat’s tiny multiplina brings 1950s italian microcar design into the electric age
inspired by the 1956 fiat 600 multipla, the electric concept fits four passengers into a retro-inspired body at just under ten feet long.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
fiat brings the spirit of the 1956 multipla to paris
Fiat has presented its Multiplina concept at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, introducing a tiny electric four-seater inspired by the original 1956 Fiat 600 Multipla. Measuring just over three meters (9.8 feet) long, the new concept revisits an idea that shaped some of the Italian automaker’s most inventive early vehicles: how much space can a car offer while taking up as little room as possible? With its rounded body, cheerful orange paintwork and contrasting cream roof, the Multiplina brings the familiar character of Fiat’s small city cars into a new generation of electric mobility.
The reference is the original Fiat 600 Multipla, which managed to accommodate six passengers within a body measuring only 3.5 meters long. Introduced seventy years ago, the unusual little people carrier challenged conventional automotive proportions by pushing the passenger compartment forward and making efficient use of its compact footprint. The Multiplina follows a similar approach, with an upright windshield and a short front end that give most of the vehicle’s length over to its occupants. Alongside the Multiplina, Fiat also unveiled its Multiplay concept in Paris — check it out here.
a microcar with rounded bodywork and retro details
The Fiat Multiplina takes the shape of a small, almost continuous volume, with its cream-colored upper section wrapping around the windows and extending toward the front. Below, the orange bodywork has gently inflated surfaces and short overhangs. The wheels sit close to the corners, emphasizing the generous cabin relative to the vehicle’s size. Round, color-coordinated wheel covers reference Fiat’s earlier small cars, while the tiny rectangular headlights introduce a contemporary detail to the otherwise retro appearance.
A few recognizable elements connect the concept more directly to the 1956 Multipla. The horizontal lines across the front recall the original car’s distinctive moustache-like treatment, while similar ribbed detailing appears across the rear hatch. Vertical oval taillights sit at either edge of the body, leaving the rear surface largely uninterrupted. Along the sides, expansive windows reveal striped seating inside, and a rolled fabric roof adds another familiar touch from Fiat’s open-air city cars.
four seats fit within a three-meter electric vehicle
Despite its small proportions, the Multiplina accommodates four passengers across two rows of seats. It measures 1.4 meters (4.6 feet) wide and 1.53 meters (5 feet) high, dimensions that place it close to Fiat’s two-seat Topolino, although the additional length makes room for the rear passengers. The long side windows and forward-positioned windshield reinforce this emphasis on interior space. Even the car’s simple, upright silhouette contributes to the packaging, allowing the cabin to occupy a substantial portion of its overall volume.
The concept uses a fully electric L7 heavy quadricycle architecture, a European vehicle classification that places it between lightweight urban runabouts and conventional passenger cars. Fiat describes the proposed category as a Multi-Purpose Quadricycle, combining the compactness of a microcar with the practicality of four seats. The company has yet to announce the Multiplina’s battery capacity or driving range, although the concept is intended to offer greater versatility than the smaller Topolino.
fiat explores how much car a city really needs
The Multiplina forms part of Fiat’s broader approach to micromobility, which already includes the Topolino and the three-wheeled Tris. Within that family, the new concept occupies an interesting position. Its four-seat configuration makes room for passengers beyond the driver and a companion, while its dimensions remain suited to narrow city streets and limited parking space. Fiat sees potential for the vehicle in short journeys and urban commuting, where the size of a conventional car can feel excessive.
The Multiplina draws attention to how much can fit inside a small footprint, and how an approachable, slightly eccentric little car can still offer a practical response to urban mobility. For now, it remains a concept, with production details yet to be confirmed. Its proportions, however, make a convincing case for the continued relevance of the microcar.

Postal service Nova Post says it has already shot down Russian Shahed drones, as Ukrainian businesses take air defense into their own hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:48:58 UTC
00:48:58 KST

Ukrainian postal company Nova Post has established its own private air defense capability and has already shot down Russian Shahed attack drones, company co-owner Viacheslav Klymov said on 27 October, according to Interfax-Ukraine.
As Russia increasingly targets Ukrainian factories, warehouses, transport hubs, and other civilian infrastructure, localized air defense is becoming more important. Ukraine’s expanding private air defense program allows businesses to help protect their facilities while operating within the country’s military air defense command system.
“We are one of the few companies that has implemented this project. I don’t want to disclose figures, but we have Shahed shootdowns,” Klymov said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum, according to Interfax-Ukraine.
Klymov also argued that businesses can take on responsibilities that were previously considered exclusively the state’s domain. He pointed to firefighting as another area where companies can strengthen their own response capabilities.
Nova Post employees already extinguish many fires caused by Russian attacks on the company’s facilities without waiting for the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) to arrive, he said. Large businesses are also looking for fire engines in Europe to establish their own firefighting units.
Private air defense expands across Ukraine
Ukraine began allowing private companies to establish air defense units under a government-approved framework in November 2025. These units operate under Air Force command, with the military coordinating their missions and integrating them into the national air defense network.
Nearly 100 companies have reportedly joined the experimental program. About 50 air defense groups had been formed, and crews from six companies were already carrying out combat missions. By 14 October, the groups had downed more than 60 aerial targets, mostly Russian drones, according to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry.
The program allows participating businesses to help defend industrial sites and critical infrastructure using capabilities that include interceptor drones and remotely operated heavy machine guns. The approach adds another layer of protection without requiring the military to cover every facility with its own units.
The need for such protection has grown as Russia continues launching long-range attack drones against civilian and industrial targets across Ukraine. Localized air defense can help protect specific sites and reduce the burden on military units, although it remains part of a coordinated national system rather than an independent replacement for military air defense.
Ukraine’s air defense goes private: businesses can now buy point coverage for their own sites
Not every company sees private air defense as the answer
The approach has its limits. On 26 October, Kateryna Zahorii, chair of the board of directors of major pharmaceutical company Darnytsia, said her company had studied private air defense but decided against deploying it, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
Zahorii said the changing nature of the threat could make the investment difficult to sustain, as companies might need to keep upgrading their defenses. Darnytsia is instead prioritizing attack monitoring, employee shelters, and safety procedures. The company has been hit by Russian forces three times in September, according to NV.

Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for auto industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:48:32 UTC
00:48:32 KST

DETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday.
President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.
"That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.
Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.
Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend the USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.
Trump negotiated the USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."
Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.
She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum.
"Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."
Honda is the second-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor, but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.
While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants.
"I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.
The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

Poland to host European Patriot maintenance centre, government says
WARSAW, Oct 27 - A maintenance centre for Lockheed Martin's Patriot interceptor missiles will be established in Poland, Deputy Defence Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on Tuesday.
Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have strained stocks of air-defence interceptor missiles and caused delivery delays, prompting countries to seek maintenance and production capabilities closer to home.
"Four countries competed for the European location of this investment: alongside Poland — Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway," Sobkowiak-Czarnecka wrote on social media platform X. "This success was not a given," she said.
The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the United States, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said.
The Pentagon said, in a statement on its website, that the European Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Maintenance Facility (MMF) "will be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden."
"By establishing regional maintenance, repair, and overhaul capabilities directly within the European theater, the MMF will dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines," the statement said.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told reporters during a briefing in Brussels that the value of the investment would be around 1 billion zlotys ($253 million) and that it would take a dozen or so months to make the centre operational. REUTERS

Boeing stock sinks 9% as company says it won't significantly ramp up 737 Max production until late 2027

Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected because of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock fell 10% in trading Tuesday.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster, but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
Third-quarter earnings
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
- Loss per share: 34 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 21 cents expected
- Revenue: $24.19 billion vs $23.84 billion expected.
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
Certification wins
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10, the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

Breadcrumb
Kuwait sentences 3 to death over assassination plot, 'working for Iran, Hezbollah'
A court in Kuwait has sentenced three men to death over an alleged plot to assassinate the country’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad al-Yusuf al-Sabbah, in a case involving charges of spying for Iran, joining Hezbollah and planning hostile acts against the state.
The Criminal Court’s State Security and Terrorism Division issued the sentences on Monday, while eight other defendants received prison terms.
Kuwaiti media reported that the eight were sentenced to five years in prison each. The verdicts are not final and can be appealed, according to Kuwait Times newspaper.
The three men sentenced to death were identified as Shia cleric Hussein Abdullah al-Maatouq, secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Hassan Abdulhadi Hajieh and Iranian national Abdulreza Haidar Dehqani, according to local media reports.
The defendants were convicted of charges including alleged harming of Kuwait’s national interests, collaborating with Iran, plotting to assassinate senior officials and joining the Lebanese Shia militant group Hezbollah, which Kuwait classifies as a terrorist organisation.
According to two judicial sources cited by AFP, one of the men sentenced to death had previously been convicted of terrorism in 2016 and later received an amnesty from the emir before being arrested again in April.
The prosecution said the case involved 11 defendants, including nine Kuwaitis, an Iranian national and another non-Kuwaiti. Three of the defendants were outside the country. It also said that three defendants had previously received final criminal sentences in state security cases in 2015 and 2017.
According to Kuwait’s Al-Qabas newspaper, prosecutors accused the defendants of attempting to use explosives to carry out the assassination plot. One defendant was separately accused of attempting to bring explosives into the country to enable the others to carry out the alleged operation.
In its reasoning, the court said the defendants had sought to undermine Kuwait’s security, spread social unrest and erode public confidence in the authorities’ ability to protect lives and property.
Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai reported that the indictment accused the defendants of seeking assistance from and communicating with Iran and groups acting in its interests, including Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on 28 February, at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
The indictment also accused the defendants of joining and participating in a banned organisation, knowingly supporting its objectives and spreading ideas intended to undermine the country’s fundamental political and social systems through unlawful means.
Prosecutors further alleged that the defendants had engaged in activities harmful to Kuwait’s national interests, including attempting to use explosives to carry out the assassination and cause public panic. One defendant was accused of attempting to procure explosives to enable the others to commit the alleged crimes.
The court’s ruling is subject to appeal.
In March, Kuwait announced the arrest of dozens of people it said were linked to Hezbollah and plotting attacks in the Gulf state, which was repeatedly targeted by Iranian missiles and drones after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered a regional war.
Hezbollah, engaged in conflict with Israel for more than three years, has denied it has a presence in Kuwait.

Africa's Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases, mainly in DR Congo

Africa's Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases, mainly in DR Congo
Africa's outbreak of the Ebola virus has passed more than 10,000 cases, health authorities said Tuesday, with the vast majority located in Democratic Republic of Congo. There are currently no approved vaccines for the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola driving the current infections.
Africa's latest outbreak of Ebola has passed 10,000 confirmed cases, the vast majority of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Congolese health authorities said on Tuesday.
According to the DRC's figures, 10,060 people have been infected and 4,887 have died since the virus was first detected in May in the vast central African country's deadliest outbreak in its history.
Cases have likewise been detected in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda, with the World Health Organization warning that Africa faces a "complex" task to contain an outbreak spanning the east, west and centre of the continent.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
Read moreNigeria records first Ebola case as outbreak spreads across Africa
After recording a total of 20 cases and two deaths, neighbouring Uganda was declared Ebola-free by the WHO in late August.
Kenya, which had not reported a single case of the contagious virus until October 6, has likewise suffered two deaths from the virus.
The only case so far confirmed in Nigeria, a Swiss woman who contracted the virus following a trip to Uganda with her husband, was evacuated back to the Alpine nation on Monday.
Fifty-three of the patient's contacts have been identified by the Nigerian health authorities, in a bid to stop the virus spreading across Africa's most populous nation.
Some experts are worried that the virus – caught through contact with bodily fluids – could have spread after the Swiss couple landed back in Nigeria on October 3.
The WHO said the patient developed symptoms on October 7, sought care in Abuja on October 11, then tested positive for Bundibugyo on October 20.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Von der Leyen’s Canada ‘associate membership’ spurs battle of words with EU capitals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:44:50 UTC
00:44:50 KST

Germany, Italy, France and Greece objected to a draft EU-Canada declaration that cites von der Leyen’s ‘associate membership’ offer, as the member states fear legal uncertainty and a precedent for other third countries ahead of the Montreal summit on Thursday and Friday.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made a bombshell offer to Canada: to become the first EU “associate member”. Now the term is proving hard to swallow for several member states, including her own Germany.
Ahead of the EU-Canada summit, meant to chart what many see as the closest partnership between the bloc and a non-member country, European capitals led by Berlin have pushed back against a term that has yet to be clearly defined, five EU diplomats told Euronews.
“The main concern is that this is unknown terminology, it might bring up legal uncertainty and expectations from other third countries,” one of the diplomats said. “This was not communicated previously from the Commission. We don’t know what we are talking about.”
Last week, a revised draft of the joint declaration explicitly mentioned the notion, vowing regular exchanges with Canadian authorities on major policy and regulatory initiatives and to define the full scope of the partnership at the 2027 summit.
Naming the term outright in what would be the first EU official document of major political significance to include it has drawn strong pushback from Germany, Italy and Greece, and scepticism from other countries, including France.
A new draft circulated on Monday evening added wording that distanced member states from the concept, specifying that it was “put forward by the European Commission," wording suggested by the Italian government.
The text was due to be adopted on Tuesday through the so-called silent procedure, under which a document passes unless a member state objects. Germany, Italy, France and Greece all raised objections before the deadline.
Italy's objection does not relate to associate membership, since its proposed wording was accepted, but it asked to change a paragraph related to competitiveness and technological sovereignty for a balanced decarbonisation transition.
The office of European Council President António Costa is now expected to circulate a new version, with another round of talks at ambassador level on Wednesday, before the summit opens in Montreal on Thursday.
Von der Leyen floated the idea of offering associate membership to Canada in her annual State of the Union speech to the European Parliament in September, with Prime Minister Mark Carney as guest of honour.
The idea had been put to the Canadians before, but it was never discussed with member states or within the Commission, catching capitals including Paris and Berlin off guard.
Even Carney did not seem fully sold on the nomenclature, preferring to call it an “alliance of the future”. “What matters is the substance,” he said when asked whether he was comfortable with the term.
With governments now finalising the joint declaration, to be adopted at the summit on Thursday and Friday, that initial lack of consultation is coming back to haunt the bid.
For Berlin, the main issue is that member states should first define what the cooperation package contains, and only then agree the terms for the declaration, not the other way around.
There is broad consensus on seeking closer cooperation with Canada in areas such as defence, critical raw materials, energy, trade and border security. It is the associate membership label that has drawn scrutiny.
Others took aim at its legal implications, arguing these must be carefully studied before the term enters a political declaration.
“It does not mean anything, it is not in the treaties,” a second EU diplomat said, adding that “we want to find a way to make the concept work.”
Von der Leyen is not new to launching new ideas and forging ahead with initiatives without consulting with the member states. In 2023, she announced a migration deal with Tunisia and was criticised for lacking a formal mandate to do so.
“In the case of Tunisia, member states fully agreed with the objective of reducing arrivals, but they had to say that they did not 100% agree with the way it was done. It is a bit the same case here,” a third diplomat told Euronews.
For this diplomat, the EU should not view the label as merely institutional, but as a way of packaging what would otherwise inevitably look like a sector-by-sector technical exercise in bringing Canada closer to the bloc.
For von der Leyen’s critics, she has a habit of making grand announcements before figuring out the implications. For her supporters, her strength is staying ahead of the curve, setting out a political vision and letting the bureaucratic machinery do the rest.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was the first to propose associate membership, but pitched it as a way to anchor Ukraine to the EU, with security guarantees, as Kyiv progressed through the accession process.
Applying it to Canada carries a very different connotation: it would offer a blueprint for the closest possible partnership with a non-European country that could never join the bloc.
“A lot of other countries want to come closer to the EU, but we don’t know what to offer them. Whatever deal we reach with Canada might be an important motivator for others,” an EU official told Euronews.
This story was updated with additional information.

German Court Rejects Motion to Halt Nord Stream Trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:44:39 UTC
00:44:39 KST

The trial in Hamburg over the Nord Stream pipeline bombing will continue despite a motion filed by the lawyers of the Ukrainian defendant.
The German outlet WELT reported this.
The Higher Regional Court of Hamburg rejected the defence’s motion on the second day of the trial.
The lawyers asked to halt the trial, arguing that the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov, a former officer, was bound by state secrecy obligations.
As a result, he was allegedly unable to consult fully with his lawyers or testify in court.
The court rejected this argument. Presiding judge Anne Meier-Göring said the defendant’s right to a fair trial had not been violated.
“Under German law, the defendant is not restricted in his ability to present his defense,” the judge noted.
According to her, Germany’s freedom of expression is not restricted by a foreign state’s civil service rules.
In late November 2025, the Italian Supreme Court approved the extradition to Germany of a Ukrainian suspected of involvement in the Nord Stream pipeline bombing in the Baltic Sea.
The trial of former Ukrainian serviceman Serhii Kuznietsov, whom Germany accuses of involvement in the Nord Stream pipeline bombing, began in Hamburg in mid-October.
The Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipelines were designed to transport Russian natural gas to Germany and other EU countries.
The pipelines, which run along the seabed of the Baltic Sea, were severely damaged by explosions in September 2022, several months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At the time, the pipelines were not in operation.
According to the prosecution, Kuznietsov allegedly planned the sabotage with other servicemen and later led a team that planted explosive devices on the pipelines.
According to Germany’s Federal Public Prosecutor General, Ukrainian state authorities allegedly ordered the sabotage.
Ukrainian authorities deny involvement in the pipeline attacks.

Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on how to end the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022, and long-range airstrikes by both sides have increased this year while battle lines have remained largely static.
"The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.

Breadcrumb
Syria closes Jordan border after strikes kill seven civilians
A major diplomatic dispute has erupted between Syria and Jordan after Jordanian airstrikes, launched in retaliation for a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church, killed seven Syrian civilians, including three children, and prompted Damascus to close its main border crossing with the kingdom.
The Syrian government condemned Monday's bombardment of southern Syria as a violation of its sovereignty, accusing Jordan of carrying out the operation without prior coordination and demanding an explanation for the strikes.
Jordan launched the attacks in response to Friday's killing of nine people at a church funeral in the village of Hamoud, in the southern Jordanian governorate of Karak, claiming that the perpetrators were linked to militant organisations operating across the border in Syria.
However, Syrian authorities said the airstrikes hit civilian areas in Daraa and Suweida provinces, killing five members of one family and two elderly men.
Syrian Civil Defence said rescue teams responded to four locations targeted by Jordanian warplanes, recovering the bodies of seven people, including three children, three men and a woman.
Five members of one family were killed and three others injured when a strike hit a tent in the village of al-Taff, in the Lajat area of rural Daraa.
An 80-year-old man was also killed when Jordanian aircraft struck a farm near the Nasib border crossing, while a 60-year-old man died after a house was bombed in the countryside of Suweida.
Jordan acknowledged the civilian deaths on Tuesday and expressed regret, but insisted its operation had targeted Islamic State militants connected to the church attack.
Jordanian government spokesman Mohammed al-Momani said Amman respected Syria's sovereignty and remained committed to cooperation with Damascus against terrorism and cross-border arms and drug smuggling.
Jordan claimed that its aircraft had killed more than 20 Islamic State militants and destroyed a large weapons depot during the operation, which its military named "Jordanian Deterrence – Hamoud".
The Syrian Foreign Ministry said it had formally conveyed its objections to Amman, stressing that military operations inside Syrian territory without prior coordination were unacceptable.
It added that communication between the two countries was continuing to establish the circumstances of the operation and address its consequences.
The dispute deepened on Tuesday when Syria's General Authority for Ports and Customs announced the closure of the Nasib border crossing, suspending passenger movements and commercial trade in both directions.
The crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, is a vital commercial artery linking the two countries and facilitating trade between Syria, Jordan and the wider Gulf region.
Syrian authorities said the closure was necessary to protect travellers and border personnel amid the security situation in Daraa, without specifying when operations would resume.
The Jordanian strikes followed Friday's attack on mourners attending a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud, which left nine people dead and 34 wounded.
Jordanian security forces subsequently arrested three suspects, identified as two brothers and their brother-in-law, following an extensive manhunt.
Public Security Director Obeidallah al-Maaytah described the men as extremists who had adopted takfiri ideology, but said they had decided to carry out the attack spontaneously, without advance planning.
Jordanian authorities also indicated that the suspects did not belong to an organised militant group.
However, the Jordanian military subsequently asserted that the attackers were connected to the organisations targeted in southern Syria, without publicly identifying those groups or presenting evidence establishing their involvement.
The apparently conflicting accounts have raised questions about the justification for the cross-border military operation, particularly given the civilian casualties reported by Syrian authorities.
The bombardment and subsequent border closure mark a significant setback in relations between Damascus and Amman, which had sought closer security and economic cooperation following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Despite their disagreement over the operation, both governments have indicated that diplomatic and security contacts will continue in an effort to prevent further deterioration in relations.

The ‘Queen of the Chinese’ and a forgotten history on the US-Mexico border
As descendants rediscover their Texas roots, past discrimination against Chinese immigrants echoes in new restrictions on foreign nationals
At Texas’ dusty Concordia Cemetery, grass grows over graves in a 140-year-old Chinese burial ground. Some headstones have been stolen or vandalised; others have been marked by flat concrete slabs etched with names in Chinese and English. The slabs were harder to steal than traditional headstones. Still other graves have no visible markers.
“I don’t think many people go out there,” says Linda Chew, a retired judge in El Paso, the state’s sixth-largest city.
Yet interest in the history of the Chinese community in the Lone Star State is growing. “There’s a real resurrection in understanding the influence of the Chinese in Texas,” Chew adds.

Turkey pushes to reunify Libya as rival factions hold talks

Breadcrumb
Turkey pushes to reunify Libya as rival factions hold talks
Turkey has intensified diplomatic efforts to reunify Libya's rival eastern and western administrations, hosting negotiations aimed at establishing a unified military command and government capable of managing the country's vast natural resources.
The latest talks, held in Ankara on Friday and Saturday, ended without a final agreement, as disagreements persisted over the structure of the military leadership and its relationship with civilian political authorities, Libyan sources familiar with the discussions told The New Arab.
Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of the eastern-based military leadership, and Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, undersecretary at the defence ministry of the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, arrived in Ankara on Friday evening for Turkish-sponsored negotiations.
The discussions centred on a draft agreement to unify Libya's institutions, although the two sides remained divided over whether the deal should focus exclusively on military and technical arrangements or extend to senior political positions, including the Presidential Council.
Sources said the negotiations produced broad understandings on the structure of a unified military institution, but no decisive breakthrough.
Both delegations agreed to consult their respective leaderships in Tripoli and Benghazi before resuming negotiations, although no date has been set for further talks.
The initiative comes as Ankara seeks to consolidate its influence across Libya, strengthen its position in the eastern Mediterranean and secure the future of a controversial maritime boundary agreement signed with Tripoli in 2019.
The agreement has faced opposition from Greece, Egypt and other regional actors over competing maritime claims.
The Benghazi-based House of Representatives' approval of the maritime agreement has been viewed as an important step in Turkey's efforts to build closer relations with eastern Libya, after years of maintaining stronger ties with the Tripoli authorities.
Erdogan calls for Libyan unity
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan reiterated Ankara's opposition to Libya's continued division on Monday, saying his government wanted to see unity and solidarity across the country.
Speaking after a cabinet meeting, Erdogan said Turkey was working to reduce regional disputes and expand cooperation.
He also defended the 2019 maritime agreement, rejecting suggestions that Ankara was seeking to undermine other countries' interests in the eastern Mediterranean.
"Our policy towards the eastern Mediterranean is completely clear. We are not seeking to score goals against any party in the eastern Mediterranean," Erdogan said.
He maintained that Turkey was seeking to protect its maritime jurisdiction, rights and interests while advocating dialogue to resolve disputes.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also acknowledged Egyptian reservations about the maritime agreement last Friday, calling for dialogue to address Cairo's concerns.
Turkey's renewed engagement with both Libyan camps comes as the country's oil resources attract growing international attention, particularly as the war involving Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupt energy supplies and push up global prices.
A unified Libyan government could help stabilise oil production and exports to European markets, although significant political and security obstacles remain.
Ankara also hopes to expand commercial and investment opportunities, particularly in construction and infrastructure, sectors in which Turkish companies have historically maintained a substantial presence in Libya.
Military leadership remains major obstacle
Turkish researcher and writer Cahit Tuz told The New Arab that Ankara viewed Libya as a single state and opposed its permanent division.
He said Turkey's priorities included preserving Libya's territorial integrity, establishing a single administration and ensuring that the country's natural resources benefited its population.
Tuz argued that Turkey's diplomatic efforts had already produced tangible results, pointing to the eastern parliament's approval of the maritime agreement as evidence of improving relations.
He also claimed that some regional and international actors, including Israel, were uncomfortable with Turkey's expanding influence in Libya.
Journalist and political commentator Hamza Tekin told The New Arab that Ankara's approach had evolved from working primarily with one Libyan faction to establishing direct relationships with influential political and military figures on both sides.
He said this shift had helped Turkey reopen channels of dialogue between Tripoli and Benghazi.
"Turkey's efforts in Libya stem from a fundamental conviction that the continuation of political and institutional division does not serve Libyans," Tekin said.
He argued that Ankara was seeking to create the conditions for a unified Libyan state rather than merely bringing rival factions together for negotiations.
However, he warned that the central challenge was translating broad agreement on reunification into workable arrangements.
"The real test begins when determining who will assume military command, how responsibilities will be distributed, which political authority the institutions will answer to, and how to ensure that no single party monopolises power," he said.
Tekin stressed that any lasting agreement would depend on the willingness of Libyan factions to compromise and avoid turning institutional reunification into another arrangement for dividing political influence.
He said Turkey's expanding contacts with both camps offered an opportunity for progress, but cautioned that a sustainable settlement must reflect the will of Libyans rather than an externally imposed agreement.
Libya has remained politically divided for years, with rival authorities and competing military structures obstructing efforts to establish a unified government.

New Israeli TV exit polls show opposition, Netanyahu blocs even
New Israeli exit polls early Wednesday showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc even with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the premier's rivals.
Among the three mainstream networks, Channels 11 and 13 both put the blocs even at 51 seats -- neither enough for a majority -- while Channel 12 still gave an edge to the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot after Tuesday's vote.
Eisenkot says Israel has chosen change, hopes to form government
Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot said early Wednesday said Israel had chosen change after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that he would seek to form a new government.
In remarks to supporters, Eisenkot also issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu who has stepped up warnings in the final days of the campaign that he will attack Iran -- an emergency that could potentially delay efforts to form a coalition.
"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Exit polls showed the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot with a tiny edge over Netanyahu's right-wing bloc in Tuesday's election but with neither side securing a majority.
"The people have spoken against the continuation of Netanyahu's rule," Eisenkot said. "In an election with such a high turnout, it would be a mistake to go to another round of elections."
Eisenkot warns Netanyahu not to 'use Israel's security' for political ends
Israel's elections: What happens next?
Here are four possible scenarios:
1. Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
2. Minority government
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
3. National unity government
Considering Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
4. Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

UN nuclear watchdog chief urges Iran to grant IAEA access to verify nuclear material
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:39:06 UTC
00:39:06 KST

The head of the UN nuclear watchdog on Tuesday urged Iran to provide the agency with the information and access needed to verify its previously declared nuclear material, including 440 kilograms (970 pounds) of highly enriched uranium, Anadolu reports.
The UN Security Council began the session by voting to adopt the agenda, with 11 votes in favor, two against from Russia and China, and two abstentions from Pakistan and Somalia.
Addressing the Council, Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), said the agency continues to engage with Tehran, “seeking avenues to encourage it to clarify all remaining safeguards issues.”
“One area of particular concern is Iran’s previously declared nuclear material, which includes 440kg of High Enriched Uranium,” he said.
Grossi said the issues “have now been outstanding for more than five years.”
He recalled that the agency had to withdraw all its inspectors from Iran by the end of June 2025 for safety reasons after military attacks began.
READ: Iran insists enriched nuclear material must remain in country, sets conditions for US talks
“Inspectors have been available to return for many months now,” he said.
He stressed that Iran has not provided “the requested information and access so that the IAEA can verify previously declared nuclear material at Iran’s facilities under safeguards, both those that have been affected by military attacks and those that have not.”
Grossi said the only exception was the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, where inspectors were conducting verification activities.
“The one exception is the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP), where our inspectors are currently undertaking verification activities,” he said.
He added that the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran had engaged constructively with the agency to arrange the delivery of safeguards equipment needed to verify spent fuel before its transfer to a new dry storage facility, expected early next year.
Grossi also said the agency’s inspectors spent more than 14,000 calendar days in the field last year, conducting verification activities at more than 1,400 facilities and locations outside them, and were able to draw safeguards conclusions for 179 states.
“I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions,” he said, adding that Tehran must provide access “as is Iran’s legal obligation.”

HONG KONG, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Hong Kong's food safety authority decided on Tuesday to suspend the import of poultry meat and products from Lolland Municipality in Denmark and Jackson County in the State of Minnesota in the United States due to avian influenza outbreaks in these regions.
The Center for Food Safety (CFS) of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government's Food and Environmental Hygiene Department has instructed the trade to suspend the import of poultry meat and products, including poultry eggs, from these areas with immediate effect to protect public health in Hong Kong.

Thailand's auto output falls in September as floods disrupt parts supply

00:38:48 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's auto production dropped in September as flooding disrupted parts suppliers and forced several assembly plants to halt temporarily, data from the Federation of Thai Industries (FTI) showed on Tuesday.
Automakers produced 120,319 vehicles in Thailand last month, down 6.08 percent from a year earlier, reversing from a 10.93-percent gain in August, according to the FTI.
The federation attributed the decline to supply chain disruptions, particularly for internal-combustion-engine (ICE) vehicles, which require more parts during manufacturing.
Output of fuel-powered passenger cars fell 27.78 percent in September, despite 55.20 percent growth in pure electric vehicle (EV) production.
For the first nine months of 2026, auto production inched up 0.39 percent over the same period last year to 1,080,030 units, said FTI Automotive Industry Club spokesperson Surapong Paisitpattanapong.
Domestic auto sales rose 14.28 percent year-on-year to 55,255 units in September, driven by deliveries of passenger battery EVs, which rose 80.13 percent and accounted for 29.69 percent of all vehicle sales, Surapong told a news conference.
Meanwhile, sales of passenger ICE cars dropped 14.50 percent, making up 14.07 percent of total sales, Surapong said.
The Southeast Asian nation's finished car exports increased 4.55 percent from a year earlier to 89,972 units in September, even with shipments to the Middle East falling 30.60 percent due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, the spokesperson said.
The group kept its 2026 production target at 1.45 million vehicles, including 900,000 for export and 550,000 for the domestic market, noting that manufacturers planned to speed up production to make up lost output. ■

Can AI replace government jobs? World is watching the Dutch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:37:00 UTC
00:37:00 KST

Can AI replace government jobs? World is watching the Dutch
- The Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 civil servant jobs, about 15%, to save €3.5 billion a year from 2035. Police and defence are exempt.
- The plan is part of a wider push to use AI to make government smaller, but experts say public services are behind private firms and many tasks still resist automation.
- AI may also create new problems, such as floods of complaints and data security worries. Union resistance and public concern could make the cuts hard to deliver.
AI generated
The Dutch government’s AI-led efficiency drive to cut 25,000 civil servant jobs is perhaps the most ambitious government plan yet to use technology to reduce the state’s payroll. Making it work – and rolling out similar programmes in other countries – could prove tricky.
The Netherlands intends to lose roughly 15% of its civil servants to save €3.5 billion (S$5 billion) a year from 2035, the government said on Oct 26. Police and defence are among the exempted areas, while ministries, inspectorates and implementing agencies could see headcount reductions of as much as 60%.
Translated to the US, that would mean about 150,000 job cuts, according to calculations by Bloomberg. That is around half the number of federal employees who left their jobs in 2025 after efforts by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency in the early days of the second Trump administration to reshape the government workforce.
The equivalent in the UK would be sbout 75,000 jobs, while in France it would be slightly above 50,000, although it is hard to directly compare civil servant numbers and roles across countries.
The size of government bureaucracies is a political issue in many advanced economies. Dutch government headcount surged 41% between 2018 and 2025. Britain’s civil service has grown by more than a third in the last decade to more than 500,000. There, the opposition Conservatives promise to reverse that increase, while Reform UK has pledged to go even further.
Some argue such ambitious and controversial targets can be achieved. The Tony Blair Institute, set up by the former British prime minister, argued in a report published in July 2024 that artificial intelligence could partly automate over 40% of public sector tasks, saving a fifth of workers’ time. (The report itself was criticised for using AI in its analysis). “The speed with which these gains are realised is within the government’s gift to determine,” it said.
Blair this summer called for “not civil-service retraining, but a new cadre of workforce”. He has argued that AI can help to square the circle of being able to afford ageing populations and the increasing cost of health and pensions, and that a politics focused on issues such as tax, spending and nationalisation rather than AI is decades out of date.
While private companies have already announced waves of AI-driven job cuts since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, governments are some way behind. Their AI use “trails the private sector” and initiatives “often remain in pilot phases”, according to a report by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development in September 2025. They are behind on adopting the technology, getting more work from AI rather than less, and there are plenty of tasks they do not want automated.
Until AI Minister Kanishka Narayan intervened in October 2026, Britain’s official AI guidance recommended keeping prompts short, using smaller models, not saying thank you, and only using AI when needed, to lessen its environmental impact. Guidance given to Bloomberg by the country’s Environment Department still refers to Google Bard, a brand that was retired in favour of Gemini almost three years ago.
In a Treasury announcement last week detailing £16 billion (S$27.3 billion) of efficiencies and savings, AI gets relatively scattershot mentions and no price tag. And in places, talking about AI is a bit like putting the cart before the horse. As recently as February 2025, almost 10% of English health trusts still lacked an electronic patient record.
The French government said in June it is rolling out a conversational AI assistant to all public sector workers after a 10-month trial. During the test phase, the assistant cut the time spent on writing tasks by about 12% and by 16% for summarising documents. However, France’s government has said it will not accept an AI that replaces civil servants or dehumanises relations between citizens and the administration.
Meanwhile, governments are finding that AI is creating more work, not less, as voters and businesses embrace the technology.
A study by a team including Chris Schmitz of Berlin’s Hertie School and co-authors published in August documented 84 cases across 11 countries of what they call “agentic flooding”: an AI-facilitated surge in complaints, court claims and other requests to government. Most involve chatbots drafting polished, legal-sounding text. The quickest fixes, such as fees, risk shutting out people with genuine claims, the authors warn.
Even where AI could technically do the job and respond to that deluge, there are tasks governments may decide it should not. Britain faced a massive backlash to proposals to curb trial by jury, let alone trial by AI judge.
“The big question is whether this government will be able to meet its targets,” ING chief economist Marieke Blom said of the Dutch plan, adding that previous cuts to civil servant headcount have been followed by increased hiring. “AI can lower the number of people working in the government, but it can also lead to ‘needs’, such as when government institutions are bombarded by complaints as people use AI agents to file them.”
Then there is sovereignty. With few cutting-edge AI models built in Europe, policymakers might be reluctant to outsource swathes of the civil service to US or Chinese products. (The Dutch say they will favour domestic and European suppliers.) Britain’s reliance on US cloud giants is already alarming its politicians, while a flagship £330 million data contract with Palantir for the health service has grown increasingly contentious over questions of value for money and data security.
“The thing the British public really doesn’t like is their private sensitive data, particularly their healthcare data, going to foreign billionaires,” Narayan said in September.
Governments are also seeking to reassure their citizens that AI will not lead to widespread job cuts, and to encourage them to adopt rather than fear the technology. Narayan regularly talks about developing and adopting technology “in line with Labour values”.
Even if a government tries to cut swathes of jobs, civil servants are often highly unionised and likely to resist. Across high-income countries analysed by Bloomberg, union membership among civil servants was on average more than double that of the workforce as a whole. More than a quarter of US federal employees belong to a union, versus a tenth of all workers. In South Korea, it’s two-thirds versus 13%.
Perhaps AI is simply a convenient cover. Labour MP Anneliese Dodds told Bloomberg last week of a growing number of “performative mentions of AI as a reason for redundancy” among companies. “It seems like perhaps the redundancies were already in train, but there’s a belief that using the term AI will somehow make the company look more cutting edge,” she said. BLOOMBERG

Nordic call to Putin opens rift in Europe on Ukraine

Nordic call to Putin opens rift in Europe on Ukraine
A phone call with the leaders of Finland and Norway’s with Russian President Vladimir Putin has exposed divisions among Ukraine’s European backers. Denmark criticized the initiative and Sweden complained that it had received no advance notice.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store contacted Putin on Tuesday ahead of renewed Russia-US-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi next month. The leaders discussed efforts to resolve the conflict, as well as security and stability in Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea.
Most Western European leaders have shunned direct contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, but now appear to be desperately seeking a seat at the negotiations table. Both Stubb and Store have been named as potential candidates to represent Brussels at the talks, but neither spoke on Europe’s behalf during Tuesday’s call.
Following the conversation, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen accused her Nordic colleagues of breaking ranks, saying she was “very skeptical about this Norwegian-Finnish initiative” because it had “not been coordinated with the rest of us.”
Frederiksen said Europe should stick together rather than go solo, doubting anything can be achieved through unilateral contacts with Moscow.
Her opposition to the diplomatic initiative comes as Copenhagen is backing Kiev’s efforts to expand its weapons production to Danish soil. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point plans to build a missile-fuel factory in Denmark.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also lamented that he had not been informed of the call to Putin beforehand and said he had “pretty low expectations for this kind of conversation.”
Western leaders have repeatedly faced backlash for contacting Putin or advocating direct talks with Moscow. Earlier this year, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever sparked a wave of backlash from his colleagues after arguing that Europe’s strategy of arming Kiev and sanctioning Russia had failed, leaving negotiations as the only viable option.
His comments elicited an immediate retort by EU Foreign Policy chief Kaja Kallas, who has consistently dragged the bloc down the warpath with Russia. She argued that normalizing ties with Moscow would lead to “more wars.” De Wever’s own foreign minister also described the move as “a signal of weakness.”
In 2024, then-German Chancellor Olaf Scholz was also accused of opening a “Pandora’s box” by calling Putin, with Estonia and other Baltic states decrying contacts with Moscow a “strategic mistake.”
Russian officials have repeatedly accused European governments of prolonging the conflict and obstructing a settlement while demanding a place at the negotiating table. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in March that the EU had “completely discredited itself” as a mediator, citing its failure to uphold previous agreements and its support for deploying Western troops in Ukraine.
Moscow has nevertheless expressed willingness to engage with a European representative committed to negotiations. On Sunday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a negotiator from Brussels would be welcome, but stressed that such a person would need to be “someone genuinely committed to facilitating a peaceful settlement.”

Canada introduces bill to allow people to be euthanized after they lose capacity to decide
OTTAWA, Oct 27 - The Canadian government will introduce a new bill on Tuesday to allow people to request being euthanized at a later date when they have lost the mental capacity to make that decision, in a potential further expansion of one of the world's most liberal assisted dying programs.
• Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the new legislation will allow adults to consent to being euthanized in advance "so their wishes could be respected if they are diagnosed with an incurable illness that could take away the ability to make this decision."
• Fraser said the government would work with provinces and territories on implementation, with "rigorous safeguards to protect people and ensure the decision remains voluntary and free from external pressure."
• Making an advance request will not mean euthanasia is automatically provided later, the government said. New safeguards will be introduced and people will have to be experiencing "intolerable suffering" at the time when they are killed.
• Canada first legalized euthanasia in 2016 for people who were terminally ill and broadened its law in 2021 to allow people with incurable but not terminal conditions to seek death.
• If the bill passes, provinces and territories will still have to decide whether to make advance requests available in their jurisdictions; it is already allowed in Quebec.
• Advance requests for euthanasia are also legal in countries including the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain.
• Krista Carr, CEO of Inclusion Canada, a disability rights charity, has raised concerns about advance requests for euthanasia, saying that a person consenting to their death "is the most basic protection a person has" and that "Parliament should not take it away." REUTERS
