A red carpet against the odds at Gaza Women's Cinema Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:36:00 UTC
00:36:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Even in Gaza's darkest days, the International Festival for Women's Cinema rolls out the red carpet for its second edition
Amid the devastation of Israel's genocidal war, mass displacement and starvation, Gaza is hosting the second edition of the International Festival for Women's Cinema.
Running from 26 to 31 October 2026, the festival brings film screenings to the tents of displaced Palestinians, affirming the importance of Palestinian women's stories, culture, and creativity even as Israel's war continues to shape their everyday lives.
The festival was first held in Deir al-Balah, in the central Gaza Strip, from 26 to 31 October 2025, coinciding with Palestinian Women's National Day.
Through the event, organisers hope to show that Palestinians can continue to create art and tell their stories despite the devastation of Israel's genocidal war.
"We want to prove that the people of Palestine are still able to create beauty and life, even while they are living in tents under immense pressure and pain," Ezzeddin Shalh, the festival's founder and president, told The New Arab.
The decision to hold the festival comes amid widespread displacement, documented malnutrition and the loss of loved ones as Israel's brutal war on the besieged enclave continues.
The Final Gaza Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment reported that more than 1.9 million people had experienced internal displacement, while more than 1.2 million Palestinians had been left without homes.
The destruction has also affected Gaza's economy. The Report on UNCTAD assistance to the Palestinian people: Developments in the economy of the Occupied Palestinian Territory states that 92% of Gaza's economic establishments had been damaged or destroyed by Israeli forces.
A red carpet amid the ruins
Despite these conditions, Ezzeddin said the scale of the destruction had strengthened the organisers' determination to hold the festival.
Asked what motivated them to go ahead with the event, he said Gaza should not be defined solely by the devastation.
"Gaza should not be limited to wars, death and destruction. This was the main motivation," Ezzeddin said.
"We are people with lives, culture, art and stories to tell. The scale of the destruction and genocide we have experienced in Gaza has made us feel more responsible for taking meaningful action, not less," he added.
For Ezzeddin, that meant going ahead with the Gaza International Festival for Women's Cinema rather than waiting for conditions to improve.
He explained, "We could say that conditions are difficult and that holding a festival is out of reach. But that raises the question: if we keep waiting for normal conditions, will they ever come? And if they do, when?"
But Ezzeddin does not ignore the reality on the ground, stating that the event was not an attempt to ignore the suffering in Gaza, but a way to preserve Palestinian voices and memories.
"We are not hosting a festival because we are disconnected from reality, but because it is part of life. Culture for us is a form of survival and a way of preserving Palestinians' voices and memories," he told The New Arab.
That belief also shows in the decision to keep the red carpet, a familiar feature of international film festivals, despite the conditions under which this edition will take place.
"We want to have a red carpet so that people, despite their suffering, can experience what it feels like to attend an international film festival. The red carpet is an essential part of the festival's atmosphere and identity," Ezzeddin said.
But unlike a conventional international film event, with its celebrities, press coverage, cameras and sense of celebration, the festival's screenings and activities will take place among the tents of displaced Palestinians and damaged buildings, rather than in a cinema or prestigious theatre.
The organisers also recognise that attending a festival may not be a priority for people dealing with displacement, loss and psychological distress.
Ezzeddin said they were not asking people to put their suffering aside to take part.
"We are fully aware of the psychological difficulties people are facing. We are not asking them to forget the pain, loss and suffering they have endured to attend the festival," he said.
"That is why we will screen the films among the tents, bringing cinema closer to people and their everyday lives."
A platform for Gaza's women
By bringing screenings closer to displaced communities, the festival aims to make cinema accessible to people living through Israel's war.
For Gaza's residents, cinema also preserves memories and identity, lets them express themselves, and helps them share their stories.
As Ezzeddin explained, organising an international film festival in Gaza was far less difficult before Israel's war. The current circumstances have changed what is possible.
"Everything has changed. Three years ago, we could have imagined hosting an international film festival where the main challenge would have been organising an event to welcome and celebrate filmmakers and their films," he said.
Today, the organisers face practical difficulties, including power cuts, poor internet connections, mental health struggles among the population and a scarcity of resources.
"The festival relies mainly on voluntary efforts and contributions from individuals and the community. We are doing our best to make use of the limited resources available to organise the festival," Ezzeddin added.
Despite these challenges, the festival has attracted submissions from dozens of filmmakers worldwide. The women-centred event selected 73 films from 24 countries, including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Finland, the Netherlands, India, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others.
Ezzeddin said the organisers had selected films that reflected the festival's purpose and message.
"We tried to select the 73 films that reflect the festival's identity and message," he shared.
The selected films focus on women's experiences in Gaza, with this year's edition taking the slogan Women Creating Life From Death to highlight their efforts to sustain life despite Israel's war.
"It was chosen to highlight the reality facing women in Gaza and their determination to keep going and sustain life despite the war," Ezzeddin said.
"We see women who have lost their homes and loved ones and are living in tents, yet they still wake up every day to provide for their children and families, even in the face of death."
Alongside screening films about women's experiences, the festival aims to give women in Gaza the opportunity to tell their own stories through filmmaking.
Ezzeddin said 25 women from Gaza had already been selected and trained to produce films about their lives and communities.
The films premiered on the festival's opening day, and organisers also plan to continue supporting local filmmakers through the Gaza Cinema Academy after the festival ends.
Ultimately, the festival aims to show that Palestinians are not merely subjects of the world's gaze, but storytellers who can tell their own stories through their own lens.
Rabie Jan is a Syrian student, writer and actor. He is also an ambassador for the Sharjah International Film Festival for Children and Youth and served as a junior juror in its 2023 edition

====================================================================================================

Israel's record turnout could change everything: Who survives and who governs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:34:25 UTC
00:34:25 KST

Israel's record-breaking voter turnout could do far more than signal heightened public interest in Tuesday's election. It could fundamentally change the political landscape, raise the number of votes smaller parties need to enter the Knesset, reshape the balance between rival blocs and leave the identity of the next government uncertain until the final ballots are counted.
By 4 p.m., turnout had reached 55.7%, compared with 47.5% at the same hour in the previous election, marking the highest participation recorded at that point in the day since 1973. The surge caught even senior political figures by surprise. While many had anticipated stronger voter participation, the numbers have far exceeded expectations.
But the significance of the surge extends well beyond the headline figures. Higher turnout changes the electoral mathematics, potentially determining which parties survive, which disappear from parliament and whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or his opponents can assemble a governing majority.
More voters, a higher bar for smaller parties
The most immediate consequence concerns parties hovering around Israel's electoral threshold, the minimum share of votes required to enter the 120-seat Knesset.
Under Israeli election law, a party must win at least 3.25% of all valid votes to secure parliamentary representation. While that percentage remains fixed, the actual number of votes required rises as more people participate.
In the November 2022 election, parties needed more than 154,000 votes to cross the threshold. If Tuesday's unusually high turnout continues through the evening, the number could rise by tens of thousands, creating a significantly tougher challenge for smaller parties.
Among those facing particular uncertainty are Amcha Yisrael, led by former IDF general Ofer Winter, and the Reservists-Economic Party, headed by former minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha. Both have been fighting to secure enough support to enter parliament, and the growing number of ballots could make that task considerably harder.
The effects could extend to established parties whose support is concentrated within particular communities. Even if their own voters turn out in substantial numbers, a larger overall electorate could reduce their relative share of the vote, potentially costing them parliamentary seats.
However, the national turnout figure alone cannot reveal which parties or blocs stand to benefit. The geographic distribution of voters, and which communities are participating in greater numbers, will ultimately determine how the surge translates into seats.
Netanyahu's dilemma: A small party could help or hurt his bloc
The electoral threshold could have particularly significant consequences for Netanyahu's efforts to secure a parliamentary majority.
Despite Netanyahu's aggressive campaign against Winter, the former general's party could ultimately strengthen the Netanyahu bloc if it crosses the threshold and wins seats in the Knesset.
But if Amcha Yisrael fails to reach 3.25%, its votes will be excluded from the allocation of parliamentary seats. That could leave a substantial number of right-wing votes without representation, potentially pushing Netanyahu further away from the 61 seats needed to form a majority government.
The situation surrounding Hendel and Zelekha is more complicated. Their party appeals to voters from both major political blocs, particularly those concerned about equal responsibility for military service and greater economic fairness.
It remains unclear which side would lose more votes to the alliance, or how its entry into parliament might affect the balance of power.
In an election where even a handful of seats could determine who forms the next government, the fate of parties hovering around the threshold could prove decisive.
Why the final results could take until Thursday
The record turnout also adds another layer of uncertainty to an election whose outcome may not become clear on Tuesday night.
More than 650,000 special double-envelope ballots are expected to be cast by soldiers, diplomats, displaced residents and voters with disabilities, among others. These ballots are counted separately from ordinary polling station votes and could significantly alter the final distribution of seats.
With several parties potentially finishing close to the electoral threshold, those votes could determine whether a party enters the Knesset or falls short, potentially changing the balance between the competing blocs.
That means the exit polls released when polling stations close at 10 p.m. may provide only a preliminary picture of the election outcome. Even by Wednesday evening, the political balance could remain unclear, with a more definitive result potentially not emerging until Thursday.
For Israel's political leaders, the unusually high turnout presents both an opportunity and a risk. More voters may strengthen some parties, weaken others and dramatically alter the prospects of forming a government.
The central question is no longer simply how many Israelis are voting, but who they are voting for, which parties cross the threshold and how hundreds of thousands of ballots still to be counted could transform the final result.

A Russian court sentenced Yuri Belenky, director of the IT company DiHouse, to 13 years in prison on terrorism financing charges, Radio Liberty reported on 26 October. The case concerns cryptocurrency donations that investigators believe were meant for Ukraine’s Armed Forces, the outlet said. The court also fined Belenky 500,000 rubles ($6,200), according to the report.
Since 2022, Russian courts have imprisoned Russians and Ukrainians under treason, terrorism, and other national-security laws over donations to Ukrainian causes. Binance, one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, left Russia in 2023 but says it cooperates with lawful law-enforcement requests in different countries.
Belenky had lived in Bulgaria with his wife and child since 2015. In September 2025, he traveled to Moscow on business, and police detained him at the airport for allegedly using obscene language, Radio Liberty reported. In court, Belenky denied swearing, but the judge gave him 13 days of administrative detention. On the 10th day of his detention, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a criminal case against him under an article on terrorism financing, based on a report from the Federal Security Service, according to the report.
Binance shared account records with Russian investigators, rights group says
In October 2025, Russia’s Investigative Committee contacted Binance to request information on six users who had transferred funds to a cryptocurrency wallet published by journalist Arkady Babchenko, the Russian human rights project First Department said on 17 August 2026. The exchange provided investigators with Belenky’s detailed account history, including his personal information, copies of identification documents, and cryptocurrency transaction records, according to the organization. The human rights project said the materials helped investigators identify nine more transfers, which went into the final charge against Belenky. Binance told his lawyer it does not give law enforcement user account data without a court order or an equivalent ruling, the group said.
Belenky’s alleged offense was transferring donations totaling 126,000 rubles ($1,560) between 2022 and 2024 to an account published by Babchenko, Radio Liberty reported. The court ordered that sum confiscated.
Russia sentences Ukrainian women from Zaporizhzhia Oblast to 14 years for donating $120 to Ukrainian forces
The court said the money in Babchenko’s account went to Ukraine’s Armed Forces and the Azov battalion, which Russia designates as a terrorist organization, Radio Liberty reported.
In a statement dated 14 October 2025, Babchenko said he had not received transfers from Belenky to the cryptocurrency wallets he had published. He emphasized that he had raised money for civilian humanitarian needs, not to support the military.
Binance’s exit from Russia and previous data-sharing concerns
In September 2023, Binance announced that it would sell its entire Russian business to cryptocurrency exchange CommEX, according to the company’s website. Operating in Russia was incompatible with Binance’s compliance strategy, the exchange’s chief compliance officer, Noah Perlman, said in the announcement. Binance said it would fully exit the Russian market, receive no share of future revenue from the sale, and retain no option to buy back the business.
CommEX said on 29 September 2023 that it was not owned by Binance but confirmed that it had hired some former Binance employees during the platform’s six-month development, Cointelegraph reported.
UK sanctions crypto exchanges and “A7 network” in crackdown on Russian evasion systems
The exit came after earlier questions about Binance’s dealings with the Russian state. In April 2021, Russian financial intelligence officials met with Binance’s head of Eastern Europe and Russia in Moscow and asked the exchange to provide customer data, including names and addresses, Reuters reported in April 2022. The Binance executive agreed to the request in a message to a business associate, saying he didn’t have “much of a choice,” the outlet said. Binance told Reuters it had never been contacted by Russian authorities about Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny.
In February 2026, 11 US senators asked the Treasury Department and the Justice Department to investigate Binance’s compliance with sanctions and anti-money laundering rules, Cointelegraph reported. They cited reports that about $1.7 billion had moved through Binance to Iran-linked entities, as well as possible activity related to evading Russian sanctions. The senators also warned that Binance payment cards launched in parts of the former Soviet Union could facilitate sanctions evasion. Binance rejected the allegations.

Without auctions and starting from UAH 1 per sq. m: the Cabinet simplified the lease of state property for businesses and data centers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:31:09 EET
00:31:09 KST

Without auctions and starting from UAH 1 per sq. m: the Cabinet simplified the lease of state property for businesses and data centers
Kyiv • UNN
The government allowed affected businesses and data centers to lease state property without auctions. The rate for warehouses is UAH 50, and for data centers, UAH 1 per sq. m.
The Cabinet of Ministers simplified the leasing of state property for businesses and data centers affected by Russian shelling. Enterprises will be able to lease state and municipal premises without auctions. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, according to UNN.
Details
The government simplified the leasing of state and municipal property for affected businesses and digital infrastructure. Enterprises that suffered due to Russian aggression will be able to lease state and municipal premises without an auction. This will enable businesses to find new premises and resume operations more quickly
Cloud service providers and data center service providers, state authorities and local self-government bodies, as well as state and municipal enterprises and institutions, will also be able to lease premises without an auction in order to promptly locate or relocate equipment.
We are also simplifying leasing for providers of electronic communications networks and services that deploy network infrastructure
Supplement
According to Cabinet Resolution No. 1329 of October 23, 2026, during the period of martial law and for six months after its termination, state and municipal property that may be used as warehouse space may be leased to businesses without auctions if their property was destroyed by Russian shelling.
The fact that the property was destroyed or damaged is confirmed by an inspection report for the facility, a technical inspection report, or a fire report and a conclusion on the causes of the fire.
Prospective tenants intending to lease property that may be used as warehouse space shall submit an application indicating the need to conclude a lease agreement, together with the documents specified above.
Within five days, warehouse owners shall send businesses a list of available properties that may be leased.
The monthly rent for state property that may be used as warehouse space is also set at 50 hryvnias per 1 sq. meter.
Also, during the period of martial law and for six months after its termination, business entities that provide cloud services and/or data center services are entitled to lease state and municipal property without an auction, but exclusively for the purpose of locating, setting up, and ensuring the operation of data centers; deploying information systems, information and communication systems, Category I technological systems for the impact of disruption of the functioning of an information technology facility; or recovery systems and backups of information, information and communication systems and Category I technological systems for the impact of disruption of the functioning of an information technology facility.
The monthly rent for state property used to locate data centers is set at 1 hryvnia per 1 sq. meter.
Reminder
In Ukraine, the leasing of premises belonging to state-owned companies for telecom businesses and data centers has been simplified to enable a swift recovery after attacks.

Germany’s economy minister hails Poland as “example of great success”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:30:25 UTC
00:30:25 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries.
Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries.
She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle.
Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year.
Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs.
Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe.
Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany, while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters.
Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026
Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań.
Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average.
Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20.
Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.
He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.”
Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia.
“I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports.
“We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”.

Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry.
The meeting was attended by representatives of 21 EU member states and European Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné. Discussions focused on protecting and strengthening European industry’s competitiveness and economic security amid geopolitical challenges.
“Today, we are facing the consequences of the fact that, in the past, competitiveness was often relegated to second, third or fourth place. Competitiveness took a back seat to other priorities, with the result that European industry now faces serious challenges,” said Domański.
He proposed making competitiveness a core EU policy priority, cutting red tape, strengthening the single market, lowering energy costs, investing in strategic technologies such as AI, and tightening trade protections against unfair foreign competition.

A woman’s world was “tilted on its axis” when she discovered that for years her former husband had been drugging her and inviting men into their family home to sexually assault her while she was restrained and blindfolded, a court has been told.
Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard.
In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into “an inanimate state” where anything could be done to her by whoever answered the adverts, jurors were told.
The businessman has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.
The jury of eight men and four women is hearing the trial of four men jointly charged with sexually assaulting Joanne Young, 49.
Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, Wiltshire, denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016. Richard Wilkins, 62, of Toothill, Swindon, has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration in July 2016.
Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. Mohammed Hassan, 38, of Swindon, has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching in February 2023. Philip Young is named in each of the counts as having committed the alleged offence with the other men.
Sarah Jones KC, prosecuting, said Joanne Young had no idea what had been happening to her when police arrived at the family home in Swindon, Wiltshire.
She said: “The world she thought she knew had entirely tilted on its axis. The relationship she thought she had appears now to be wholly unreal – she does not even know what she doesn’t know.”
Jones told jurors they were going to have to contend with “some depressingly awful and sordid material”. She told them: “You are going to see videos of things you cannot then un-see and may find you can’t forget.”
Jones said the videos that formed the bulk of the evidence showed Joanne Young was the victim of her husband’s fantasy to watch her being “crawled over” by men “plucked from the internet”.
The barrister said the case was about whether it was ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first. “Whether it is ever reasonable to think someone truly can give consent on another’s behalf,” she added.
The barrister said the pair married in 2004 and had three children, now young adults. She said: “From the outside they seemed a normal couple with a normal family life.”
Joanne Young characterised her sex life as “fairly normal” and was emphatic that she and her husband were “monogamous … physically and emotionally … the traditional sense of marriage … it was us two kind of till the end.” She didn’t like being out of control, not even liking to take a sleeping tablet, the prosecutor said.
The court was told her husband had some “preferences” in their sex life, such as blindfolding and using restraints on his wife, which she did not object to.
In 2015 a packet of a sedative drug that had been posted to Philip Young from India was intercepted at customs. Police visited him and he denied any knowledge of it, telling them someone must have obtained his name through his business.
Jones said this helped build a picture of Young searching from 2015, at least, for drugs that could be used on their own or with alcohol to send Joanne Young into “a deep sleep where she would be disoriented, unaware of her surroundings and unlikely to be able to recall what happened”.

While she and her husband were having sex, she “felt someone else’s hand on my wrist and it wasn’t his [her husband’s] hand”.
She said: “I was obviously really shocked because, obviously you don’t expect someone else to be in your bedroom. Phil said to the person: ‘Get down’, and the person ducked at the end of the bed.”

Sky Sentinel Goes Mobile—Ukraine Mounts AI Anti-Drone Turret on Military Vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:29:02 UTC
00:29:02 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Sky Sentinel Goes Mobile—Ukraine Mounts AI Anti-Drone Turret on Military Vehicle
Ukrainian forces have revealed a mobile version of the Sky Sentinel robotic anti-aircraft turret, mounting the AI-assisted system on a military vehicle to create a rapidly deployable defense against Shahed-type drones and other low-flying aerial threats.
The 1021st Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade released footage of the system on October 26.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The video shows Sky Sentinel installed on a HAMMER military vehicle, with the robotic gun mount positioned at the rear. Inside the vehicle is an operator station equipped with a monitor and control panel.
Sky Sentinel is a Ukrainian-developed air-defense system built around automated targeting, machine vision, and artificial intelligence.
Using targeting data from radar systems, the turret can automatically acquire and track an aerial target, calculate its speed and flight path, and determine the necessary lead for firing.
Its software can even account for wind conditions, reducing the need for the operator to continuously aim the weapon by hand.
Known configurations of Sky Sentinel use the 12.7mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun. The turret can rotate through 360 degrees and adjust the weapon’s elevation, allowing it to engage aerial targets approaching from different directions.
The system is primarily intended to intercept Shahed-type attack drones and other UAVs. Developers have also said it can engage faster targets traveling at speeds of up to 800 km/h, or roughly 500 mph.
Its engagement range is still limited by the machine gun itself, meaning Sky Sentinel is designed mainly for close-range protection of critical facilities rather than replacing longer-range air-defense systems.
Mounting the turret on a vehicle adds another advantage: mobility. Instead of transporting the system separately and setting it up at a fixed position, crews can move between firing locations quickly as the threat changes.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine’s Defense Forces destroyed more than 4,700 aerial targets and neutralized over 48,000 additional tactical-level drones throughout September.
The reported results included the destruction of 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, and eight Zircon missiles. Ukrainian forces also intercepted six Iskander-K cruise missiles and six Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles.
Russian-made Shahed drones accounted for a significant portion of the reported interceptions. Ukrainian forces destroyed 2,722 Shahed-131/136 drones and 1,935 Shahed-238 drones, bringing the combined total to 4,657.
In addition, the military reported destroying 86 S8000 Banderol weapons, 1,009 reconnaissance drones, and 719 Lancet loitering munitions.

Russia’s Newest “Jamming-Resistant” Cruise Missile Crashes in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:28:45 UTC
00:28:45 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Newest “Jamming-Resistant” Cruise Missile Crashes in Ukraine
Russia’s latest upgraded Geran-5 K5-K cruise missile, designed to navigate without satellite signals and resist electronic warfare, has crashed in Ukraine’s Odesa region, with newly released photographs showing the advanced weapon lying largely intact in an open field.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 27, the missile, bearing serial number ANS-3031, was discovered following a Russian attack. The circumstances surrounding its fall remain unclear, with no confirmation of whether it was intercepted by Ukrainian air defenses, disrupted by electronic warfare, or brought down by a technical malfunction.
The photographs reveal the redesigned fuselage of the Geran-5 K5-K, one of Russia’s newest jet-powered strike weapons, which reportedly entered combat use in late September 2026.
Unlike earlier versions, the upgraded missile features smaller swept-back wings, a modified tail section, and a turbojet engine integrated directly into its fuselage rather than mounted externally. One of its most significant upgrades is an autonomous optical navigation system designed to operate without satellite signals.
According to Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, the system compares images of the terrain below with stored reference data, allowing the missile to adjust its flight path even when satellite navigation is unavailable or disrupted by electronic warfare.
This technology is intended to make the weapon more resistant to Ukrainian electronic warfare systems, which are widely used to interfere with Russian drones and missiles.
Russian developers are reportedly seeking to increase the upgraded missile’s speed to as much as 900 km/h (559 mph), although it remains unclear whether the latest version has achieved that capability.
Russia first deployed the original Geran-5 against Ukraine in January 2026. Ukrainian military intelligence identified the weapon as a turbojet-powered cruise missile with a conventional aerodynamic configuration resembling Iran’s Karrar drone.
The original Geran-5 measures approximately 6.5 meters in length, has a wingspan of 3.2 meters, and carries a warhead weighing around 90 kilograms. Its reported operational range reaches approximately 1,000 kilometers, with cruising speeds between 450 and 600 km/h.
Earlier, Russia’s Alabuga plant in Tatarstan reportedly reached a production capacity of over 3,500 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones per month, alongside more than 3,000 Shahed-type drones, with support from Chinese technology and components.

Donald Trump Jr. Hunted With Kremlin-Linked Russian Oligarch in Mongolia, FT Reports
Donald Trump Jr., the eldest son of US President Donald Trump, spent several days hunting in Mongolia in late August with Kremlin-linked Russian businessman Umar Kremlev, the Financial Times (FT) reported on October 27.
The FT reconstructed the trip using testimony from local guides and officials, flight data, social media posts, and public records.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the newspaper, Kremlev flew by charter aircraft from Kazakhstan to Ulaanbaatar before traveling to Trump Jr.’s hunting camp in western Mongolia.
Russian businessman Arthur Martirosov, a partner in the US-sanctioned venture fund Voskhod, traveled with Kremlev. The FT reported that Trump Jr. and Kremlev spent two days together before Kremlev returned to Ulaanbaatar.
One local participant in the trip told the FT that Trump Jr. and Kremlev were careful not to be photographed together while staying at the camp.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. described the relationship as personal rather than commercial, explaining that the two men were introduced through a mutual acquaintance in the hunting community.
“Don has made clear that he has a personal friendship, not a business relationship, with Umar,” the spokesperson stated. “Their friendship is largely based on their shared love for hunting, fishing and the outdoors.”
“It shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone that they went hunting together earlier this year,” the spokesperson added.
The FT also cited counterintelligence concerns surrounding contacts between members of the US president’s family and people with links to Russian authorities.
“It really doesn’t matter if people have the most above board intentions,” Holden Triplette, a former director of counterintelligence on the US National Security Council during Trump’s first term, told the newspaper.
“The moment the Russian security and intelligence services figure out someone has a relationship with anyone of high value, they will try to weaponise that,” he added.
During the Mongolia trip, Trump Jr. also hunted a rare Altai argali, an endangered wild sheep, and met Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh, according to the FT.
Kremlev, 43, is president of the International Boxing Association and previously headed the Russian Boxing Federation from 2017.
The Mongolia trip was not the first reported instance of Kremlev providing significant personal support to Trump Jr. In September, UNITED24 Media reported that Kremlev had allegedly helped finance Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas, including the rental of a private island and a fireworks display.

Fly in, vote, fly out: Israelis return home for election, some for just hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:27:26 UTC
00:27:26 KST

Even on Tuesday morning and afternoon, hours after polling stations opened, planes continued landing at Ben Gurion Airport carrying Israelis who had returned to vote in the 2026 election. "I spent 18 hours in the air on three flights from Goa, India, just to vote," Ariel Bar Yosef, 22, told ynet after cutting short her post-military trip through Asia. "I debated whether to come back or keep traveling, and in the end decided I wouldn't be able to sleep at night if I didn't vote."
Ariel's father, who was waiting excitedly for her in the arrivals hall at Ben Gurion Airport, added with a smile: "At least something has come out of the election: my daughter is back."
According to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, around 810,000 Israelis eligible to vote live abroad, while many others are overseas on vacation, traveling or spending limited periods abroad for work and business. Tens of thousands have returned to Israel in recent days. According to an estimate by Fly&Vote, an initiative aimed at encouraging Israelis abroad to exercise their voting rights, some 67,000 people have returned, potentially equivalent to about one and a half seats in the Knesset, Israel's parliament.
Among those arriving on a flight around midday was the Zak family, a couple and their baby who came from the Greek island of Paros, where they live. "It's nice to come here, both to visit family and to exercise our democratic right to vote," said the father, Moshe. "I know who I'm voting for. I don't want to say who, but I hope it will be the right side."
Mirav Ben Simhon Rothstein also arrived from Greece with her husband and baby daughter, although they were on an extended trip rather than living abroad. "We came back to vote especially for her," Mirav explained, pointing to her daughter Luli, who was in a baby carrier. "We had planned to keep traveling, but in the end we decided to return. I came to change the way things are."
A flight arriving from Bucharest, the Romanian capital, also carried Israelis returning to vote. "I came for a few hours to vote, and I'm going back to Bucharest this afternoon," said Karnit Weinberger. "The most important thing is to vote for Gadi Eisenkot and make a difference. We deserve better. I'm not thinking about the money I've spent. Buying the ticket isn't what's important. The most important thing is to make an impact so Eisenkot gets elected."
Asked how the flight went, she replied: "We talked politics. I tried to persuade the person sitting next to me on the plane. Let's hope I succeeded."
Asaf Yosef, who arrived from Thessaloniki, had attended a concert there the previous night but hurried home, missing the chance to enjoy more of what the Greek city has to offer tourists. "We did everything we could to get back to Israel specifically to vote," he said. "It was a short night after the concert, and then we went straight to the airport. We came home to bring about change, but it's important that Israeli society becomes united again after the election. Things haven't been good in recent years, and a change of direction is needed."
Yaffa Yaakobi from Yavne had booked a trip abroad to celebrate her husband's birthday long in advance. But about three months ago, when the election date was set, they discovered it coincided with their vacation. "We moved our return flight forward so we could vote, and paid another 800 shekels per ticket," she said.
Was it worth paying that much just to vote?
"Absolutely, absolutely. Especially if we win. The plane was full of people flying to Israel to vote."

Iran’s calculations as US escalation looms: Trust, midterms, Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:26:59 UTC
00:26:59 KST

Iran’s calculations as US escalation looms: Trust, midterms, Hormuz
Tehran remains firm on demands despite diplomatic urgency to prevent escalation in the ongoing US-Israeli conflict.
As regional powers step up diplomatic efforts to prevent another escalation in the eight-month United States-Israel war on Iran, Tehran is showing little sign of backing down from its red lines.
The announcement by China on Tuesday that Beijing will be sending an envoy to relevant countries in the region soon to help avoid another round of escalation highlights the growing urgency of finding a peaceful solution to a conflict that has disrupted global energy markets and spilled over across the region.
On Monday, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye – the three nations which signed the Mecca defence pact in August – met with high-ranking Iranian officials, promising to continue discussions related to “peace and security” in the region.
However, Tehran appears determined not to budge on its demands, particularly as it holds considerable leverage over the future of maritime trade in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) were shipped before the war.
“Iran’s priority is not simply to secure another ceasefire, but to end the war permanently and establish deterrence so that the cycle of military attacks by the US and Israel does not keep repeating itself,” Negar Mortazavi, editor and host of The Iran Podcast, told Al Jazeera.
Tehran continues to insist on sanctions relief, an end to the US naval blockade on its ports in the Gulf and guarantees that the US will not renew attacks, in exchange for helping to resume normal traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. The US wants Iran to give up more before a final peace settlement is negotiated – including making concessions about its nuclear programme.
Experts say Iran’s current calculations are being driven by several factors, including its deep distrust of Washington – which has launched strikes on Iran three times since June 2025 while conducting talks – the belief that continued economic pressure could force more attractive US concessions, and much-anticipated elections in Israel and the US this week and next.
Lack of trust
At the heart of Iran’s position is a belief that previous diplomatic efforts have failed to provide sufficient protection against renewed US and Israeli attacks. The US and Israel launched the first strikes of the war on February 28, just as peace talks were ongoing in Oman. Last year, Israel launched its 12-day war on Iran in June, which the US joined.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker a memorandum of understanding in June this year aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, ending the US blockade of Iranian ports and laying down the conditions for the start of negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme.
But the arrangement quickly unravelled as both sides resumed attacks, leading to sustained US attacks on Iran for several weeks in July, followed by retaliatory strikes from Iran on US military assets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf countries, as well as in Jordan.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy (CIP), said the failure of that arrangement had hardened Tehran’s position.
“Iran believes previous negotiations and ceasefire arrangements failed to protect it from renewed military attacks, and it is therefore seeking more tangible and durable guarantees,” he told Al Jazeera.
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has remained ambiguous over what course of action he will take in the near future. “My question is, do I make a deal with them or do I finish them off?” Trump told reporters on Sunday. He had previously said attacks on Iran would not take place until after the US midterms on November 3.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said last week that the country’s armed forces were prepared to respond to any new attacks, including by invading Tehran’s neighbours and hitting bases used in US military operations as part of its new “offensive” strategy in its war with the US.
He also said Iran would only reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin peace talks once Washington took concrete steps to rebuild trust, including meeting Iran’s latest set of conditions – suspending sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and giving concrete assurances that it will not begin strikes again.
US midterms, Israel elections loom
The US midterms next week, when all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats will be up for grabs, will determine which party has control of the US Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. The war, already deeply unpopular with Americans, is becoming an increasingly contentious domestic issue.
A Reuters/Ipsos survey earlier this month found just 34 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s handling of the conflict – his lowest rating during either of his presidential terms. Republican majorities in both houses of Congress are already wafer-thin – at 53-47 (including two independents who vote with Democrats) in the Senate and 218-214 in the House.
The war has also driven up energy prices – particularly diesel, which has nearly doubled in price, causing a major burden for farmers and small businesses – adding to concerns about inflation and affordability that are dominating the election campaign.
Some reports citing Iranian officials say Tehran may be deliberately prolonging negotiations to deny Trump any sort of political victory before the elections.
A Republican setback could further constrain Trump’s room for manoeuvre, particularly if Democrats gain congressional control and increase scrutiny of the administration’s conduct of the war.
“Tehran wants to teach a lesson to Washington, including future American presidents, that attacking Iran comes with a high price,” analyst Mortazavi said.
“Its deterrence strategy is multilayered, aimed at imposing military, economic and political costs that extend well beyond the battlefield.”
Before the US midterms is Israel’s election on Tuesday, which introduces another dimension to Iran’s calculations. A defeat for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could complicate renewing joint attacks with the US on Iran, as experts say he was the main force behind Trump greenlighting the war.
While some believe an opposition victory led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot could potentially ease regional tensions, Netanyahu’s removal would not necessarily translate into a softer Israeli position towards Iran.
Eisenkot is himself a former military chief, and has repeatedly expressed concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme and regional influence.
Nevertheless, Mortazavi said, while Iranian officials are closely watching the political consequences of the war for both Washington and Israel, they recognise the danger of renewed escalation after the elections, “making a durable diplomatic settlement even more urgent”.
Iran’s Hormuz leverage
Iran’s control over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains one of its strongest bargaining chips.
The waterway carried about one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies before the war began on February 28, giving Tehran considerable leverage over global oil markets.
October has recorded the highest number of attacks on commercial shipping around Hormuz, according to data collected by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Brent crude surged above $117 a barrel last week – compared with about $72 pre-war – following Iranian attacks on tankers, while shipping through the strait remains nowhere near pre-war levels.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, said he believes Iran is deliberately exploiting this economic pressure as part of a wider contest of endurance with Washington.
“They know they are in an attritional race with the US to see who breaks first,” Beauchamp told Al Jazeera. “For now, however, they are happy to keep attacking shipping to push prices higher.”
Uncertainty over diplomatic efforts
The latest diplomatic initiative reflects a growing concern among regional powers about the consequences of another round of fighting.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye agreed with Iranian officials on Monday to continue discussions about regional peace and security, amid fears that the conflict could escalate again.
The talks in Tehran come amid heightened regional tensions following weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, who are also engaged in a conflict with forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government.
Pakistan and Turkiye maintain close strategic ties with Saudi Arabia and have committed to supporting Riyadh militarily under the recently established Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between the three Muslim-majority nations.
Political analyst Rami Khouri, a nonresident fellow at the Arab Center in Washington DC, said the meeting had several objectives, some more immediate than others.
“The most immediate goal: to de-escalate and to try to return to the diplomatic process, to have a permanent ceasefire, and then define the issues and address them with much stronger mediation, supported by these three countries [Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye] and maybe others,” Khouri told Al Jazeera.
He added that talks could mark the beginning of a shift away from a regional security order dominated by Washington, towards one in which Middle East countries and other regional nations can exercise greater influence.
Meanwhile, CIP’s Toossi said regional powers are increasingly recognising that their own security cannot be separated from that of Iran, despite their differences with Tehran.
“It will be difficult to stabilise Yemen while the wider US-Iran confrontation continues, just as it will be difficult to reach a durable settlement with Iran while regional military escalation remains a constant threat,” he said.
Ultimately, however, the biggest obstacle remains Iran’s lack of trust in Washington, Iran Podcast host Mortazavi said.
“After two wars, Tehran is deeply sceptical of American commitments and wants concrete guarantees that any agreement will not simply become another temporary pause before the next attack,” she said.
“Iran is willing to negotiate and has already demonstrated flexibility by presenting a proposal to end the war. But Tehran believes it retains significant leverage, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, and will not surrender that leverage under military or economic pressure. The goal is a permanent end to the war, not another temporary ceasefire that leaves the underlying conflict unresolved.”

One of those charged, Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, has been accused of assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police believe to be Iran's.
Two men have been charged under the UK's National Security Act following an incident near a military air base last month, police announced on Tuesday.
The pair have been named as Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, also 24.
It comes after five men were arrested near the RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire, South West England, in late September after police received reports of several suspicious vehicles in the area.
“Earlier this morning, Nouman Essghir, 24, a British national from the Borough of Westminster, London, was charged under Section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, for suspected activity on Saturday 22 August. He was first arrested at the scene in Gloucestershire on Sunday 27 September, and re-arrested on 20 October," assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of UK National Counter Terrorism Policing, said in a statement shared on Tuesday.
He added that Abdulkarim "has been charged under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, which makes it an offence to assist a foreign intelligence service."
"In this case, we believe that country to be Iran," Taylor said.
Both were due to appear in court on Tuesday.
Five other men arrested in connection with the case remain on police bail.
RAF Fairford is home to the US Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing headquarters and the 420th Air Base squadron. It has also served as the USAF Global Strike Command's preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe.
In July, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it was aware that the base was being used by US bombers as part of Washington's military operations against Iran and warned the UK that "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces."
The US has now withdrawn its bombers from Fairford, with President Donald Trump saying the decision had been made in response to "threats."
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier this month that the September incident was "almost certainly directed" by the IRGC.

How is the Western world reporting on Israel's 26th Knesset elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:26:15 UTC
00:26:15 KST

Israel’s elections are taking center stage in international media coverage on Tuesday, with headlines framing the vote as a test of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political future and a decision on the country’s direction after three years of war.
Alongside discussion of a possible change of government, the outlets surveyed also emphasize the uncertainty surrounding the outcome: the election could end without a clear result that would allow either camp to form a government.
“Netanyahu’s political survival on the line as Israel votes,” reads the Reuters headline.
The Associated Press opted for more direct wording: “Israeli voters decide whether to oust Netanyahu after three years of war.” Both headlines place the prime minister at the center of the first election since the October 7 attack and the wars that followed.
Britain’s Financial Times chose the headline “Israelis head to polls in historic election.”
Germany’s Tagesschau described the vote as a “fateful election,” while Spain’s El País framed its significance in terms that extended beyond Israel’s borders: “Netanyahu puts his future on the line in an election decisive for the entire Middle East.”
'Yes or no to Bibi'
Alongside straight news reporting, some outlets published sharply worded opinion headlines.
In the American magazine The Atlantic, the headline “Netanyahu Enters Full Panic Mode” appeared above an article by commentator Graeme Wood. Germany’s Der Spiegel used similar language: “Netanyahu shifts into panic mode.” In both cases, the headlines reflect analysis of Netanyahu’s conduct and campaign messaging, rather than reporting on the election results.
The Italian edition of Euronews summed up the election’s personalized framing with the headline “‘Yes or no to Bibi’: Israel’s election has become a referendum on Netanyahu.”
By contrast, Brazil’s Folha de S.Paulo focused on the figures surrounding the two main contenders: “Israel’s election pits Netanyahu against a former general, but other leaders may determine who governs the country.”
British coverage also highlights the gap between winning at the ballot box and actually forming a government.
The Times published a guide to the electoral system, the candidates, and possible scenarios. The Wall Street Journal emphasized in its subheadline that Israel’s parliamentary system could leave the outcome unclear for weeks.
In France, Le Monde took a more personal approach to the election, publishing a field report on Israelis living abroad who are returning to the country to vote. The headline opens with the words “‘What is at stake is existential!’,” quoting one of the people interviewed. The report describes voters traveling from various countries to take part in the election.
Elections on 'a knife's edge'
On election day, Der Spiegel also published a news report with a different focus: “Families remember Hamas victims, and demand answers.” Thus, alongside its sharp commentary on Netanyahu, the magazine also gave space to families demanding an investigation into the failures surrounding the attack.
The drama surrounding the election is also reflected in Australian headlines. SBS described the vote as being “on a knife’s edge,” while ABC focused on Netanyahu’s increasingly hard-line security rhetoric in the run-up to the election.
Across the coverage examined, one distinction repeatedly emerges: the question of which party or candidate will receive the most votes is not the same as the question of who will ultimately be able to govern. That second question may remain unresolved even after the polls close.

Ukrainians fled west for safety. Now Russian drones are following them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:23:40 UTC
00:23:40 KST

Ukrainians fled west for safety. Now Russian drones are following them
Children play on the playground at Lutsk Lyceum No. 4 during the early autumn school break in Lutsk, Volyn Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 22, 2026. (Alona Malashyna/The Kyiv Independent)
Andrii Mazur has spent 24 years with Ukraine's State Emergency Service in Volyn Oblast, but during all that time, nothing has compared to the situation that has unfolded in recent weeks.
He and his team have been dispatched to disaster areas eight times in seven days, operating round the clock as swarms of Russian jet-powered drones bombard Western Ukraine.
"Above all, we fear for our colleagues on site, as nothing outweighs the worth of a human life," he told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia has intensified its attacks on western Ukraine in recent weeks, increasingly targeting regions far from the front line, including Volyn and Rivne oblasts in the country's northwest.
The escalation comes as Russia expands its production and use of Geran jet-powered attack drones, which are faster than conventional versions and far harder to intercept.
Local residents in the regional capital of Lutsk say drones are "terrorizing" them day and night, as air alerts last hours and drones constantly target critical infrastructure.
The attacks have caused civilian casualties in Lutsk and Rivne. On Oct. 14, a drone strike in Lutsk killed six people and injured 12, damaging a food warehouse and a residential building. That same day, drone strikes in Rivne injured eight people, following an attack a day earlier on a university building that injured 25.
Kateryna Kovalchuk, founder of the Katelab clothing brand, designed minimalist T-shirts featuring a subtle Ukrainian emblem early in Russia's full-scale invasion. She sent them to President Volodymyr Zelensky, who wore them often in the war's early months.
Kovalchuk experienced the impact of the recent attacks firsthand when an explosion shook her apartment building this week. The blast wave shattered the window of a neighboring apartment where her friend lives. Her friend moved from Kyiv to Lutsk with her two children, hoping to find a safer place to spend the winter, as many Kyivans are doing by relocating to western cities.
"It's hard for me to call Lutsk safe now," Kovalchuk said. "Drones cross our skies constantly. That illusion of peace is completely gone."
On the morning of Oct. 23, much of Lutsk was without electricity following a Russian attack targeting energy infrastructure. In the city center, generators hummed loudly in the streets. The noise gave way to silence as a convoy carrying a fallen Ukrainian soldier passed down the main street.
People stepped out of cafes and lined the road to pay their last respects as the convoy passed. Hours later, air defenses brought down a drone. A deafening blast ripped through the city center, sending pedestrians on the bustling street running for a shelter nearby.
Mazur's family remain in Lutsk, clinging to the hope that the city would remain a relatively safe haven away from the front lines. But the fear of the situation taking a turn for the worse is never far away. When emergency calls come in, there is little time for reassurance, let alone a proper goodbye.
"Fighting a fire, deployed right now," he messages her, or simply: "I'm safe. Still here."
Among the most agonizing duties is retrieving victims killed by Russian strikes and observing the anguish of surviving relatives. Reflecting on the recent strike targeting a commercial storage facility where six individuals perished, Mazur remembered family members gathering to confirm the deceased.
"Nothing compares to the sorrow when families show up to identify loved ones," he said. "Watching a son learn that his mother, father, and their friend lie dead inside is agonizing. Every loss of life hurts, but facing those grieving relatives remains the most painful for me."
read also
Kovalchuk said she has no plans to leave Lutsk for now, but is preparing for possible power and heating outages by storing water and charging her power station.
If heating is significantly disrupted this winter, she may move to her mother's village around 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the Belarusian border, despite the risks. During a recent visit, she saw an attack drone flying low over houses, seemingly directly above her mother's home.
Some of Kateryna's friends with children, however, are considering leaving Ukraine. For families with school-age children, the decision also raises questions about whether they can continue their education safely.
According to Oksana Shchyboruk, a biology teacher and deputy director at Lutsk's Lyceum No. 4, schools have adjusted their routines around ongoing air alarms, yet continuous disruptions severely hinder regular classes.
Educational institutions across Lutsk have implemented a blended instructional model, granting families the choice between physical attendance and remote learning. Educators try to teach during brief lulls between alarms, while students on campus must constantly retreat to shelters.
"Sometimes we have normal classes, but on certain days, our time was mostly spent repeatedly moving back and forth between the classrooms and the shelter," Shchyboruk said.
Heightened security risks prompted municipal authorities in Lutsk to move the scheduled autumn school break forward, acting mayor Andrii Razymovskyi announced on Oct. 21.
Olha Paliona, a senior researcher at the Kramatorsk History Museum in Donetsk Oblast who specializes in local embroidery from her home region, relocated to Lutsk in the summer of 2026 after enduring years of Russian bombardment.
The persistent danger posed by Russian first-person-view (FPV) drones in Kramatorsk made daily routines agonizingly hard. Local residents were often forced to stay hidden inside almost all day to avoid FPV drones hunting them.
Paliona opted for Volyn Oblast largely due to bonds forged amid the full-scale war, including connections with servicemen from the Lutsk-based 100th Brigade and a local ceramic artist. Upon arriving in Lutsk, Volyn Regional Historical Museum staff "embraced her warmly." Together, they curated an exhibition that bridged Kramatorsk's heritage with Lutsk's.
Having survived Russian strikes herself, Paliona is not yet alarmed by the attacks. She said they are an inevitable consequence of the war. But she urged Lutsk residents to take air alerts seriously and move to shelters rather than staying out in the open during alarms as they usually do now.
Lviv, where the threat becomes psychological
Further west, in Lviv, residents have yet to face the same pressure as those in Lutsk, but many are bracing for the possibility that deadly Russian attacks may soon reach them, too.
"I've come to realize that sooner or later, this could happen in any city, including Lviv," says Anastasiia Polianska-Maherovska, an IT specialist living in Lviv, when talking about the recent strikes in the Volyn and Rivne oblasts.
"You can never fully prepare for something like this, or simply stop caring about it. But at the same time, this has become our everyday reality. It's a terrible psychological burden to live with this contradiction."
"We try to focus on daily life and not think about the future hardships of winter in Ukraine."
Vira Kostenko-Kuznietsova, a strategist and media expert who lives in the western city with her husband and 10-year-old son, speaks bluntly: "I think (the increasingly heavy attacks will come), but that’s the reality of war."
Although only an hour's drive from the Polish border, Lviv has never been truly safe from Russian drones and missiles. Like other cities in Ukraine, it has periodically sunk into darkness during Moscow's winter onslaughts against the Ukrainian power grid.
Yet compared to Kyiv and eastern regions, Lviv has been a relative refuge for much of the year. Air raid alerts have been sparse throughout the summer and early autumn, while the capital faced near-endless attacks.
read also
That is beginning to change as Russian jet-powered drones probe the city, sometimes circling at high altitudes, keeping the entire population on edge about where — or when — they will hit.
So far, the drones have come in small numbers and caused little damage, but air raid alerts are becoming near-daily.
"It's frustrating," says Dmytro Maherovskyi, Polianska-Maherovska's husband, who also works in the IT sector. "Power cuts are back, and businesses have to suspend their work more often. So even if a drone doesn't hit its target, there is still clear economic and psychological pressure."
Polianska-Maherovska says she has to center her daily routine around air-raid alerts — from doctor visits to buying groceries to walking her dog.
But Maherovskyi says he can't say for sure whether he feels more in danger than before. The city has faced worse attacks, and the situation is a far cry from the threat facing cities like Kyiv, Dnipro, or Zaporizhzhia, he says.
"Maybe we've become somehow desensitized to the threat over time. And we've been lucky, too, as our street hasn't suffered any damage."
As the temperature drops, locals are preparing for another brutal winter of Russian attacks, stocking up on power banks, blankets, food, and warm clothes. Having endured four wartime winters, Lviv denizens know what to expect and what precautions to take.
But preparing oneself mentally is a different challenge, one that grows harder as the full-scale war approaches its fifth anniversary in just a few months.
"We try to focus on daily life and not think about the future hardships of winter in Ukraine," Kostenko-Kuznietsova says. "But we do plan a trip to visit relatives abroad in the middle of this winter to make it end more quickly."
"I try to believe that we'll get through the winter more or less okay and make it to the spring and warmer weather," Polianska-Maherovska says, adding she tries to enjoy little things in everyday life rather than focus on the coming difficulties.
"I try not to dwell on the worst-case scenarios, although that gets harder every year."
read also
Chernivtsi, where safety is relative
For Ukrainians who have fled Russian occupation and bombardment, Chernivtsi has offered something increasingly difficult to find: a place where daily life can begin to feel normal again.
In the southwestern city, located near the Romanian border, the war has so far been less immediate than in much of Ukraine. Aside from a Russian drone and missile attack in July 2025 that killed five people, Chernivtsi has avoided major mass-casualty strikes. Residents are more likely to experience the war through blackouts caused by Russian attacks on the energy grid and funeral processions for fallen soldiers than through the sounds of air defense.
But as air raid alerts become more frequent across the region, the question of how long that relative safety will last is becoming harder to ignore.
For Oksana Kudria, a psychotherapist who fled Russian-occupied Kherson and settled in Chernivtsi in spring 2022, the answer is shaped by what she has already lived through.
"It won't be more dangerous than it was during the Russian occupation or than it is now in Kherson," Kudria told the Kyiv Independent. "I trust in our air defense."
After four years, Chernivtsi has become "her" city, and she has no plans to leave. She is drawn to its cultural heritage, including that of Olha Kobylianska, the pioneering feminist writer who made her mark in the city in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Yet leaving Kherson and following the daily attacks on those still living there has taken an emotional toll. Kudria attends therapy herself to work through the experience, even as she helps her own clients do the same.
"How we process and work through these experiences really affects how well our minds can adapt," she said.
Kudria is not alone in finding a second home in Chernivtsi. Iryna Kolomiets arrived with her family from Vyshneve, a town less than an hour from Kyiv, three months ago. They left after a Russian attack on July 5-6 struck an ammunition warehouse belonging to a state defense-industry enterprise, killing nine people and damaging hundreds of homes in secondary explosions.
"We just didn't have the emotional strength to put up with it anymore. We have three children," Kolomiets told the Kyiv Independent.
The frequent air raid alerts in Chernivtsi worry her, but she says they are different from those she experienced at home and in other regions under constant attack.
Like Kudria, Kolomiets has been struck by the city's "magical" quality. In three months, she says, she has not met "a single unpleasant person." She hopes her family will eventually return to Vyshneve.
She's just not sure they will be able to do so by spring.

USA Reinforced the Island of Guam with a New Air and Missile Defense Battalion Equipped with THAAD, Patriot, and UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:23:23 UTC
00:23:23 KST

The U.S. Army has formed and activated a new air and missile defense battalion on the island of Guam in the Pacific Ocean.
The press office of U.S. Army Pacific reported on this.
The ceremony marking the formation of the 3rd Battalion, 43rd Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment, 38th Air and Missile Defense Brigade, part of the 94th Air and Missile Defense Command, took place on October 16.
The newly formed unit replaced Task Force Talon, which was deactivated this summer. That task force had been operating on a rotational basis since 2013.
The new battalion will operate THAAD and Patriot anti-aircraft missile systems as well as unmanned aerial vehicles.
THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) is a U.S. ground-based missile defense system designed to intercept short-, medium-, and intermediate-range ballistic missiles in the exoatmospheric phase.
The system’s key feature is its ability to destroy aerial targets both in the upper atmosphere and beyond it—at altitudes ranging from 40 to 150 km and at ranges of up to 200 km.
To detect and track ballistic threats out to 1,000 km, the system uses a powerful AN/TPY-2 active phased array radar (APAR).
Guam hosts key U.S. military facilities, including Andersen Air Force Base, which can accommodate strategic bombers, and a naval base that serves as a homeport for nuclear submarines and support ships.
Beyond hosting combat units, the island serves as the main logistics and supply hub for U.S. military operations in the region, with massive fuel storage tanks and ammunition depots.
The U.S. Marine Corps previously formed the first battalion designed to launch medium-range missile strikes.
The upgraded unit’s main weapon is the NMESIS (Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System) missile system.

Israel election turnout highest in 50 years as voting continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:20:48 UTC
00:20:48 KST

Israel election turnout hits 77.7%, highest since 1999
More than 5.69 million voters cast their ballots amid reports of record turnout by Palestinian citizens of Israel.
More than two-thirds of Israeli voters have cast their ballots in Israel’s consequential legislative election, according to the country’s Central Elections Committee, exceeding the total number of votes cast in the last election.
The commission said at least 77.7 percent of eligible voters – or more than 5.69 million of about 7.33 million voters – turned out to cast their ballots in Tuesday’s election.
The figure is about 7.1 percentage points higher than the 70.63 percent recorded in the previous election in 2022, and the highest turnout in a Knesset election since 1999, when 78.7 percent of eligible voters participated.
Israel’s Channel 12 also reported that voter turnout among the Arab community inside Israel reached about 80 percent, five percentage points higher than the 1999 record.
Earlier, Israel’s military said turnout among soldiers had climbed beyond 68 percent by 5pm (15:00 GMT) – higher than the 65 percent tracked at the same stage of the 2022 election.
Polling stations closed at 10pm local time (20:00 GMT), but the Central Elections Committee said anyone still waiting in line at that time could vote. This came as local media reports say the committee rejected a request by Likud to extend voting hours beyond 10pm.
Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has issued an 11th-hour appeal for right-wing voters to cast their ballots, saying that turnout “in the Arab sector is unprecedented” and that a “dangerous left-wing government” could take power.
“Do not despair! It is still possible to win,” Smotrich said in a post on X.
Prominent politicians from Arab-led lists have accused right-wing figures of incitement against Palestinian citizens, who make up 20 percent of Israel’s population, and of questioning their legitimacy to vote.
Near-record turnout
Mitchell Barak, a pollster and former aide to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, earlier told Al Jazeera that voter turnout “is really high and that’s good”.
“I think … it will probably pass its historic peak in ’73 – when Israel was also involved in a huge war – so draw what conclusion from that you will,” he added.
The election is largely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s handling of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the wars that followed, the most intense period of combat for Israel since the 1973 surprise military campaign by Egypt and Syria.
“Those numbers are going to help the incumbent parties,” Barak said, “as the 3.25 percent threshold a party needs to get into the Knesset remains, the number of votes you need to meet that threshold increases dramatically.”
Israeli officials noted that several polling stations faced exceptionally long lines, attributed to high voter turnout despite rainy and blustery weather in parts of the country, and a flood warning in some areas.
‘Fateful moment’
In a message more than five hours after polls opened, Netanyahu urged supporters to vote, saying turnout was high among his opponents on the left and among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
“We need it to be high too. You all need to stream to the polls,” he said. “This is a fateful moment.”
Netanyahu had repeatedly warned supporters of the prospect of high turnout among Palestinian citizens in Israel ahead of the vote, seeking to mobilise his base under the slogan “the right or Palestine”.
Those voters were casting ballots in “unprecedented” numbers, Palestinian candidate Ahmad Tibi said.
Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, have ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, although some possible scenarios envision them propping up a minority government to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
Meanwhile, an Israeli rights group has filed a complaint with the country’s election committee warning that widespread delays could be suppressing the vote among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Although delays could reflect high voter turnout, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) said in its complaint to the Central Elections Committee that delays had been reported in at least 18 communities. It asked the committee to investigate “whether these delays are deliberate”.
The ACRI also reported “a large presence” of police and National Guard officers at a polling station in the Negev desert, raising concerns that officers were using crowd control as a pretext to prevent people from entering to vote.

UN inquiry confirms Israel continued Gaza genocide, committed torture and rape in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
