UN inquiry confirms Israel continued Gaza genocide, committed torture and rape in West Bank
TEHRAN — Israel has kept committing genocide in Gaza since the U.S.-backed “ceasefire” took hold last October, and across the occupied West Bank it has committed crimes against humanity that include extermination, torture, rape and the systematic persecution of Palestinians.
That is the finding of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, in a report published on Monday, October 27.
The report covers October 7, 2023, through September 30, 2026. It appeared one day before Israel’s general election, and three days after Netanyahu ordered al-Khalil (Hebron) sealed. Reacting to the report, Israel’s mission in Geneva demanded the commission’s dissolution.
A ‘truce’ that has changed little on the ground
The commission says Israel is “continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
The report says that the “ceasefire” lowered the volume of the war without ending it, and the Israeli military used the lull to advance. When the deal was signed, Israeli forces controlled 53 percent of the Strip. They now hold at least 60 percent.
Those seven points came with a grim body count. Fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, among them 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls.
Commission chair Srinivasan Muralidhar said the expansion continues to kill and injure civilians who approach or cross the so-called Yellow Line.
In May, Israeli vehicles shoved its concrete markers dozens of meters west. On Monday, medical officials reported at least five more killed in air strikes, including a seven-year-old girl.
Gaza Health Ministry’s overall toll now exceeds 74,500, and nearly everyone in the territory has been displaced.
In September 2025, the commission found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and in June it concluded that Israeli forces were deliberately targeting Palestinian children.
The West Bank under a widening assault
In the West Bank, the commission describes military operations, reinforced by sustained settler violence, as a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians, meant to collectively punish residents for October 7.
Its legal conclusion names extermination, torture, rape and other sexual violence, plus persecution based on nationality, race and ethnicity “at its core.”
The air war is the clearest measure. From 2008 to October 6, 2023, six Palestinians died in air attacks in the West Bank. Between October 7, 2023, and September 30 this year, 254 died.
That works out to about 85 a year against fewer than one. Muralidhar tied the killings and the demolition of homes, together with Israel’s refusal to accept responsibility, to a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and “impose conditions of life that are unlivable.”
Rape and torture in custody
The report also documents sexual violence in detention. The commission says it recently recorded six cases in which guards at the Sde Teiman military prison abused male detainees from Gaza.
In one, a detainee was raped with a stick. In another, guards tied a plastic cord around a man’s genitals and ordered him to urinate.
Women describe invasive strip searches, including of a pregnant detainee, and denial of sanitary pads.
Al-Khalil and the ministers
Al-Khalil (Hebron) is where it is playing out now. Netanyahu ordered the city sealed on Friday after a shooting nearby and told security forces to prepare a lockdown of the whole West Bank.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said Monday that more than 2,000 Palestinians have already been forced from their homes, houses have been demolished, and residents are confined to their neighborhoods.
Threats to empty and erase neighborhoods, he said, raise “serious concerns of ethnic cleansing.” He called the measures punitive and said that “collective punishment is a grave violation of international law.”
Israeli ministers speak openly about where this leads. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told Ynet last month that Israel should “go to war” in the West Bank and repeat what it did in Gaza.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, backing the closure, said soldiers’ and settlers’ lives were “a million times more important than freedom of movement.”

Ex-FBI official's lawyers slam unusual new criminal charge: 'Outrageous government conduct'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:19:50 UTC
00:19:50 KST

A judge on Tuesday sharply criticized federal prosecutors for failing to get judicial approval before filing a new criminal complaint overnight against two ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about investigations of Hunter Biden.
Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said he would not sign off on the new complaint, which added a charge of obstruction against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides in U.S. District Court in Washington.
"I am not going to bless it as a superseding complaint," Faruqui said at a court hearing, after Floris' lawyers filed a motion arguing the new complaint was legally deficient and filed in bad faith.
He told prosecutors that if they wanted to file a superseding complaint, a judge first would have to find probable cause that a crime had been committed, instead of sending him the complaint in the middle of the night and expecting him to sign it.
Faruqui said he did not believe that federal prosecutors had previously sought to file a criminal complaint without a judge's signature.
"It is not our court's practice … that unsigned complaints are filed in the docket," Faruqui said.
"I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"
The superseding complaint that prosecutors in the office of D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro filed in court early Tuesday contained a signature block with Faruqui's name typed out. But the judge had not personally signed the complaint.
It was filed hours before prosecutors and defense lawyers were due to appear before Faruqui for a preliminary hearing on the original complaint.
That first complaint, made public last Friday, accuses Floris and Benavides of making false statements to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 about their involvement in investigations of Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden.
Floris and Benavides were arrested Friday and have been released.
The new complaint sought to charge them with obstruction and attempted obstruction of a congressional proceeding.
Typically, criminal cases for conduct that occurred well in the past — as this one alleges — are lodged through an indictment, not a criminal complaint. To obtain an indictment, prosecutors must present evidence to a grand jury, which then determines whether the evidence is sufficient to charge a defendant.
A criminal complaint only requires a judge's signature. It is often used to obtain an arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly.
At Tuesday's hearing, Faruqui homed in on the way prosecutors filed charges.
"This case was charged by criminal complaint on Oct. 20, for testimony that occurred over a period of time in 2023," he said. "As I noted, and I think it continues to be the case, that it's unusual in a case that has conduct like this to be charged by criminal complaint."
"This has to get to a grand jury," Faruqui said.
Under federal rules, prosecutors generally must obtain an indictment within 30 days of a person's arrest, or risk the case being dismissed.
Floris' lawyers, in an emailed statement to CNBC on Tuesday morning, criticized the prosecutors' conduct.
"In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," the attorneys wrote.
"In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed. That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself," they wrote.
"Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom," they said.
"We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing," Floris' legal team wrote.
In their motion to strike the superseding criminal complaint, the lawyers argued the document "represents a serious abuse of the criminal charging process, a troubling disregard for the judicial safeguards governing the initiation of criminal proceedings, and a calculated effort to evade judicial scrutiny and shield the government's allegations from adversarial testing at the scheduled preliminary hearing."

Israel destroys West Bank memorials in war on Palestinian memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:17:35 UTC
00:17:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel destroys West Bank memorials in war on Palestinian memory
Israeli forces demolished around nine memorials commemorating Palestinians killed by Israel across six towns and villages near Nablus in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, as part of a widening campaign targeting Palestinian national symbols and public spaces.
The demolitions took place in Madama, Burin, Iraq Burin, Beit Furik, Rujeib and Azmut, where Israeli forces destroyed stone monuments, memorial plaques and structures bearing the names and photographs of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces.
The latest raids follow days of similar operations across the occupied territory, during which dozens of memorials have been destroyed in Palestinian cities, villages and refugee camps.
Palestinian academics and analysts told The New Arab that the campaign represented an attempt to reshape public spaces in the West Bank by removing symbols of Palestinian identity, resistance and collective memory.
The operations come as Israeli forces and settlers continue attacks on Palestinian communities, including the destruction of agricultural land, attacks on olive harvesters, livestock theft and restrictions on movement through military checkpoints and gates.
Beyond these attacks, Palestinians say Israel is increasingly targeting the physical symbols through which communities commemorate those killed during decades of occupation.
Across the West Bank, memorials bearing the names and photographs of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces have long been a feature of streets, public squares, refugee camps and university campuses.
Many have stood for decades, serving as reminders of individuals whose deaths remain part of local and national history.
Their destruction has coincided with the growing visibility of Israeli flags and Hebrew-language signs along roads connecting Palestinian towns and cities, particularly near Israeli settlements.
Settlers have also written threatening messages on concrete barriers at military checkpoints, including the Arabic phrase "No future in Palestine".
Israeli forces target memorials in Palestinian cities
On 5 October, Israeli forces raided Birzeit University near Ramallah and destroyed a memorial commemorating Palestinians killed by Israel, leaving no trace of the structure.
Similar operations have taken place in central Nablus, its historic neighbourhoods and Jenin, where Israeli troops deployed military vehicles and bulldozers to demolish stone monuments bearing the names and photographs of Palestinians.
Memorials have also been targeted in Ramallah and Tulkarm, including areas classified as Area A under the Oslo Accords, where the Palestinian Authority was granted responsibility for internal security and civil administration.
Israeli forces have distributed leaflets warning Palestinians against erecting or maintaining monuments commemorating people Israel accuses of carrying out attacks.
Israeli authorities have justified the removal of memorials on the grounds that they allegedly glorify "terrorism".
However, Palestinian academics argue that the campaign goes beyond individual monuments and forms part of a broader effort to suppress expressions of Palestinian national identity.
'A war on memory'
Abduljawad Omar, a writer and assistant professor at Birzeit University, told The New Arab that the demolitions served two purposes.
The first, he said, was to reinforce the visible presence of Israeli military forces in Palestinian communities and deter political and social mobilisation.
The second was a direct attack on Palestinian collective memory.
Omar drew parallels with Israel's destruction of Palestinian homes and neighbourhoods in Gaza, arguing that the loss of buildings and personal possessions also erased physical records of Palestinian lives and history.
He said the campaign in the West Bank had taken two forms: the proliferation of Israeli flags and symbols asserting control over the territory, and the removal of Palestinian flags, monuments and other expressions of remembrance.
According to Omar, Israel was using legal and political language centred on incitement to justify targeting memorials and other social practices associated with Palestinian identity.
He argued that the occupation itself, rather than the commemoration of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces, remained the principal source of resistance.
'A war on Palestinian consciousness'
Adel Shadid, an analyst specialising in Israeli affairs, told The New Arab that Israel viewed the commemoration of Palestinians killed during the occupation as a means through which resistance remained embedded in collective memory.
He argued that memorials gave those commemorated a lasting social, religious and moral significance, allowing their stories to influence subsequent generations.
Shadid said Israeli authorities were attempting to undermine the cultural and political significance of Palestinian resistance by removing the symbols associated with it.
The campaign, he argued, reflected a wider effort to reshape Palestinian political consciousness through military pressure, educational changes and restrictions on public commemoration.
He also questioned the continued relevance of the territorial divisions established under the Oslo Accords, pointing to Israeli military operations in areas nominally under Palestinian Authority control.
According to Shadid, Israeli forces now operate across virtually the entire West Bank, with Palestinian Authority security headquarters among the few places generally treated differently.
He argued that the demolitions demonstrated the extent to which Israel was prepared to deploy military resources against even small monuments made of stone or marble.
"Israel is forced to bring out its tanks, not to confront another tank, but to confront a memorial made of a piece of marble or stone bearing their name and photograph," Shadid told The New Arab.

Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere have reached an all-time high: the UN warns of consequences lasting for centuries
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:17:34 EET
00:17:34 KST

Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere have reached an all-time high: the UN warns of consequences lasting for centuries
Kyiv • UNN
In 2025, levels of CO₂, methane, and nitrous oxide reached an all-time high. The UN warned that warming would intensify for centuries.
The concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere has reached an all-time high. The UN warns that the further accumulation of these substances will intensify global warming, and its consequences may be felt for centuries, UNN reports, citing a new bulletin from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published on October 27.
According to the organization, in 2025, the concentration of carbon dioxide (CO₂) reached 426.8 parts per million, which is 153% of the pre-industrial level in 1750. Meanwhile, the concentration of methane rose to 1,948 parts per billion, or 267% of the pre-industrial level, while nitrous oxide rose to 339.1 parts per billion, equivalent to 126% of the 1750 level.
Details
"Another year, another record. Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, creating conditions for more extreme weather events and the associated risks for the economy and society," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
According to her, the past 11 years have been the warmest on record, and this trend is likely to continue. Because carbon dioxide remains in the atmosphere for a long time, its impact on the climate will be felt not only for decades but also for centuries.
The organization also drew attention to the accelerating rate of CO₂ accumulation. Since the 1960s, the average annual rate of increase in its concentration has tripled. While the figure was about 0.8 parts per million per year at that time, it rose to 2.4 in 2011–2020. From 2024 to 2025 alone, the concentration of carbon dioxide increased by another 2.8 parts per million.
WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova explained that the somewhat slower growth rate compared with the previous year was linked to the recovery of the ability of terrestrial ecosystems to absorb carbon and a reduction in emissions from wildfires following the powerful El Niño climate phenomenon in 2023–2024. She also warned that CO₂ concentrations will continue to rise in 2026 due to the use of fossil fuels and the development of a new powerful El Niño, which could affect natural carbon-absorption mechanisms.
In addition, scientists are concerned about the accumulation of other gases, including sulfur hexafluoride, which is used in the power sector and can remain in the atmosphere for more than a thousand years.
Context
The new WMO report was published ahead of the UN climate conference COP31, which will take place on November 9–20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. One of the main issues is expected to be the implementation of international commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and curb global warming.
For reference
Earlier, we wrote that over the next five years, the average temperature on Earth could, for the first time, exceed the 2°C threshold. The reason is the record concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

Sanctions to be lifted for gas market stabilization — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:16:43 UTC
00:16:43 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Europe hits its own industry and social sphere by rejecting Russian energy resources, President Vladimir Putin said at a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF).
It is necessary to think of termination of conflicts and sanctions lifting for stabilization of the international gas market, the head of state said.
TASS collected the key statements of the Russian leader.
GECF
The dialogue among GECF participant is evolving "without any behind-the-scenes maneuvering and market manipulation attempts."
Member-countries of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) account for approximately 40% of global gas exports.
Participants and observers of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum have resources to tackle the most difficult tasks in the gas industry.
Gas-exporting countries do not create any "cartel" and do not breach international law by their cooperation.
Gas demand
Natural gas accounts for a quarter of the planet’s energy balance.
The role of natural gas as a pillar of the global energy sector, industry, and the agricultural sector will only continue to strengthen.
LNG, which currently accounts for half of global trade, could help resolve the issue of disruptions in worldwide gas supplies. "Large volumes of supply have been removed from the market in a short period, with demand remaining," said the Russian leader.
Natural gas demand will continue growing over time. Accordingly, there is a need "to develop new fields, upgrade processing facilities and invest in transport projects, including marine fleet and infrastructure for liquefied natural gas shipments and intake. Obviously, this means large-scale, long-term investments."
Global gas demand will grow to 5.5 bln cubic meters per year by 2050 and international deliveries will grow by about 1.5 times.
International gas prices increased dramatically and the sector found itself in the state of uncertainty. Nevertheless, "they can also roll back sharply, return to the previous level,"
There is a direct connection between the gas industry and global food security. "Another important thing that we noted and that I would like to note too is how the gas production and development is connected to food security. We know that fertilizers that multiple countries rely on directly for food security are produced from natural gas."
Development of cooperation
Efficient interaction mechanisms should be built up in the gas sphere.
Russia and the United States are exploring an option of the joint work in the Arctic.
Moscow "is open for cooperation, for exchanges of technological developments in the gas sphere."
Proposals for gas-exporting countries
A professional and responsible approach is required in the green agenda sphere. "The only issue is not to abuse this green agenda for domestic political reasons. We must act responsibly and professionally, and take into account the gas industry’s capabilities during the transition period and in the future." Gas-exporting nations need to work on optimizing fuel supply routes to markets.
Gas-exporting nations need to expand consultations concerning crisis situations in the market and threats to infrastructure, "to assess risks - including physical threats to gas infrastructure - in a timely manner, and to coordinate approaches to carrying out supplies."
Russia’s role as gas supplier
Russia ranks first globally in terms of natural gas reserves and is second in production.
Russia is a responsible gas supplier abroad, reliable and predictable partner.
The country is systemically strengthening its process sovereignty, including in the gas sphere.
Any attempts to exclude Russia from global gas market players have serious consequences. "Any attempts to exclude Russia from participants of the global gas market and restrict development of this sector in our country have serious consequences. Above all, these are growing exorbitant costs for foreign end consumers of gas, companies, businesses and households," Putin said.
Importance of stability
Rising spot gas prices are not welcome news for producers, as stability in the global market is more important,
Sanctions are used as a tool for unfair competition, which leads to severe consequences for everyone, most notably for those who initiate such measures.
Termination of conflicts and lifting of sanctions should be considered in order to stabilize the global gas market.
The sovereignty of one nation cannot be ensured at the expense of other countries, including in the energy sphere. "All energy sovereignty, and sovereignty in general in the broad sense of the word, in the literal sense of the word, cannot and should not be provided by one country at the expense of other countries," the Russian leader said.
European problems
Europe itself is undermining its industries and social sphere by rejecting Russian energy. "This is what we are currently witnessing in Europe, which is harming its industries and social sphere by its own actions, by refusing Russian energy and terminating long-term contracts," Putin said, citing the proverb "don't dig a pit for others and fall into it oneself."
Created as an association of coal and steel, the European Union is now preventing developing economies from using hydrocarbons.
European countries have reopened coal mines amid energy challenges, despite their commitment to the "green agenda."
Situation around Nord Stream gas pipelines
The bombing of Russia’s Nord Stream gas pipelines is a direct terrorist act. "Direct terrorist acts were committed against Russian gas pipelines running to Europe. They were blown up."
Climate change
Russia has first-hand experience of climate changes as they largely occur in the North, which accounts for 70% of the country’s territory.
Permafrost processes are being observed in Russia and they have serious consequences for a number of regions.

Myanmar: Is US undermining EU's diplomatic blockade?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:16:00 UTC
00:16:00 KST

Myanmar: Is the US undermining the EU's diplomatic blockade?
October 27, 2026
The US government has begun a quiet reproachment with Myanmar's military-backed government, holding two rounds of talks since September with State Department representative Michael Vance. American diplomats reportedly meet Myanmar officials in Naypyitaw and then in Tokyo earlier this month.
Washington wants to tackle online scam centers, secure the release of imprisoned American businessman Adam Castillo, and potentially gain access to Myanmar's rare-earth resources. The market for the valuable minerals is currently controlled by the US rival China.
Meanwhile, Southeast Asian governments are also increasingly questioning their policy of isolating Myanmar's military leadership. Multiple countries have already renewed direct diplomatic contacts.
The EU, however, continues to reject the legitimacy of the military junta in the war-torn country. The European bloc has also remained unmoved by the 2025/2026 election, which ended with military chief Min Aung Hlaing becoming the president. The military retains control over the political system.
EU's sanctions still in force
The EU responded to Myanmar's February 2021 military coup by suspending direct financial assistance to the government, imposing targeted sanctions and sharply reducing diplomatic engagement with the military authorities.
Its sanctions currently cover 105 individuals and 22 entities connected to the military. In April, the EU extended these measures for another 12 months.
At the same time, Brussels is providing humanitarian assistance to displaced communities and Rohingya refugees and is supporting civil society organizations.
The EU also stopped short of withdrawing Myanmar's preferential trade access because of concerns about the consequences for workers, particularly the mostly young women employed in the country's garment industry. Last year, bilateral goods trade was worth about €4 billion ($4.46 billion), up from €3.4 billion in 2019.
Brussels supports ASEAN's peace deal
The civil war triggered by the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people. Rebel groups still control or contest large swathes of Myanmar, and over 4 million people have been internally displaced, according to UN data.
The EU "continues to uphold its policy of non-recognition of the current military regime," in view of "the ongoing violence and the attack against its own population," an EU spokesman told DW.
At the same time, the bloc "is closely monitoring developments in the discussions and positions of the United States, Japan, ASEAN countries and other major actors with representatives of Myanmar's military regime."
"It also supports ASEAN efforts, in particular the Five-Point Consensus, which has yet to be fully implemented," the spokesperson added, referring to the peace deal proposed by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2021.
Myanmar diplomats reach out to European partners
In the aftermath of the coup, ASEAN took the unprecedented decision to exclude Myanmar's military leaders from its highest-level meetings after the junta failed to implement the regional peace plan.
However, ASEAN's position is showing signs of change. Some member states, most notably Myanmar's neighbor Thailand, signal growing frustration with the lack of progress towards ending Myanmar's civil war.
Last week, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow welcomed Washington's renewed engagement and suggested that ASEAN members would hold substantive discussions about Myanmar's future at their summit in Manila next month.
Myanmar's authorities are also seeking to break their diplomatic isolation. In September, Myanmar's leader Hlaing gave an interview to Time magazine, his first with a major Western publication since the coup, as part of an apparent effort to rebuild relations with Western governments.
On October 22, Burma Campaign UK, a London-based human rights organization, accused the British government of making a "significant shift in approach" after the British Foreign Office hosted Win Zeyar Tun, the charge d'affaires of Myanmar's military-controlled embassy in London, at an ASEAN diplomatic gathering days earlier.
According to an article published by Intelligence Online this month, the regime's charge d'affaires in Brussels, Khin Thidar Ay, has also sought contacts with European politicians, including Czech MEP Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament's delegation for Southeast Asia.
EU's isolation 'has achieved relatively little'
Kristina Kironska, of Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic and an expert on the EU's policy on Myanmar, told DW that the EU has little reason to follow Washington's apparent shift towards engagement with the Myanmar junta.
The US strategy "appears to be pursuing specific interests" such as rare earth mining and cybercrime, she said.
However, the most important rare earth mining operations are no longer controlled by the military, but by rebels such as the Kachin Independence Organization in Kachin State. "It remains to be seen what the US can achieve through negotiations with the junta," she said.
The EU has long positioned itself as a defender of democracy and human rights in Myanmar, "so abandoning this now because the US is exploring a new, perhaps more transactional approach would undermine the EU's credibility," Kironska added.
"At the same time, isolation has achieved relatively little. The question is therefore not whether the EU should engage, but rather with whom and under what conditions."
Balancing act between Myanmar's rebels and junta
The EU is forced to consider risks to its own influence. If Washington, ASEAN governments and other regional powers increase their engagement with Myanmar's authorities, the EU risks becoming increasingly marginal in discussions about the country's political future.
Yet greater engagement with the military could undermine Brussels' relations with Myanmar's democratic opposition and ethnic resistance organizations, many of which control substantial territory.
"The key question for Brussels is whether it can remain a credible defender of democratic change while ensuring that it still has a meaningful voice in the negotiations that will determine Myanmar's future," Sabe Soe, director of the NGO Burma Centre Prague, told DW.
One possibility is for Brussels to maintain its sanctions against military leaders and their businesses while expanding diplomacy through ASEAN, the UN and other regional partners. The EU could also tie any easing of restrictions to humanitarian access, improvements in political freedoms and progress towards peace.
Soe also suggested that the EU could pursue economic engagement in areas administered by revolutionary and ethnic resistance forces, offering an alternative to engagement centered on the military authorities in Naypyidaw.
This approach would allow the EU to remain involved in Myanmar's future without necessarily recognizing its military-backed government, she said.
For now, Brussels seems to have little appetite for a fundamental policy rethink. But this could change as more governments reopen their doors to Myanmar's generals.
Edited by: Darko Janjevic

Norwegian media sue Meta over plans to use their journalism for AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:13:35 UTC
00:13:35 KST

Publishers say new terms for Facebook and Instagram business accounts could allow Meta to collect articles, images and videos from their websites without permission.
A coalition of Norwegian media organisations has launched legal action against Meta, arguing that the company’s new terms for business accounts could undermine publishers’ control over their own journalism and allow it to be used in AI products without their agreement.
According to the 10 media groups, the new terms would give Meta — which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads — the right to collect their articles, photos and videos, including those behind a paywall, and use them to develop artificial intelligence products, among other things.
Meta quietly announced it was changing its Commercial Terms on 8 October, with plans to roll out on 30 October. However, the company postponed the roll-out after receiving widespread pushback from European publishers and antitrust authorities.
The launch is now set for 20 November, "to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what's changing and what's not", said Meta.
Critics say news publishers are being forced into an "all-or-nothing" choice by the US tech giant: allow Meta to scrape their journalism, potentially for AI training, or lose their Facebook and Instagram presence entirely.
The Norwegian media groups’ legal challenge will test whether publishers can block the changes before they take effect.
"The fear is that the companies will use this power to secure rights over journalistic content," the head of the Norwegian Media Businesses' Association (MBL), Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, said in a statement.
"Meta uses media groups' investments to develop artificial intelligence services that compete with them directly. This is both unacceptable and distorts competition," she added.
According to the plaintiffs, Meta’s new terms of use would apply to all professional account holders — media outlets as well as companies and retailers — and would leave them no way to opt out other than deleting their accounts.
They said they had filed a request with the Oslo District Court for a provisional injunction against the entry into force of the terms of use, pending a ruling on the substance of the case.
The plaintiffs include public broadcaster NRK, media groups Schibsted, Amedia, Polaris and Aller, as well as Norwegian news agency NTB.
On 14 October, MBL and NRK had also threatened to sue Meta, accusing the American tech giant of profiting from fraudulent advertisements impersonating them in order to defraud internet users.
A global shift
The Norwegian case reflects a broader dispute over the rights of publishers whose journalism appears on major tech and AI platforms.
Since May this year, more than 340 local and national news sites including the Guardian, the New York Times and USA Today have blocked internet archive crawler bots to prevent them from collecting data for training AI models.
And in June, France’s competition authority warned Meta that its approach to copyright talks with news outlets could "seriously harm" the press.

Russia's weekly seaborne oil exports generate record revenue since start of full-scale war – Bloomberg
The value of Russia's seaborne oil exports reached US$2.76 billion last week, the highest figure since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: The value of Russian seaborne oil exports rose by around US$430 million to US$2.76 billion, setting a record for the period since the start of the full-scale war, Bloomberg said.
The decline in prices for Russia's Urals crude was offset by a sharp increase in supply volumes and a rise in the price of Russia's ESPO grade.
According to vessel-tracking data and industry reports, about 37 tankers loaded 26.93 million barrels of Russian crude in the week ending 25 October.
A week earlier, 21.87 million barrels were loaded onto 31 tankers.
China and India remain the largest buyers of Russian crude. However, the final destination of individual cargoes cannot always be determined until vessels have travelled a substantial part of their route. As a result, many recent tanker shipments list only intermediate destinations, Bloomberg noted.
Meanwhile, Russia shipped its lowest volume of oil in more than a month, despite the rapid resumption of operations at its main Baltic port following an earlier shutdown.
In the four weeks to 25 October, Russian oil exports fell to 3.55 million barrels per day. This was 30,000 barrels per day below the figure for the period ending 18 October and the lowest level in five weeks.
Background:
- Russia's energy revenues fell by 17% this year, despite oil prices reaching their highest level in more than a decade.
- Russia increased diesel production in October after the government granted producers export quotas under a supply agreement between the Kremlin and the United States.
- Russia subsequently began resuming diesel supplies to Türkiye and Brazil.

Italy

From digital monitoring to
nature-based solutions, the project aims to protect
Mediterranean communities and critical infrastructure from
extreme weather events.
                                    
The fifth meeting of the partners involved in the European
cooperation project Med-IREN took place in Larnaca, Cyprus, on
21-22 October. The project brings together nature-based
expertise and engineering developments to protect critical
infrastructure from the impacts of climate change.
                                    
The meeting in Cyprus provided an opportunity to review the
project's progress and discuss the next stages of work, with a
particular focus on moving from the development of methodologies
to their practical application in the participating territories.
                                    
Med-IREN is a joint initiative involving several European
countries, including Italy. It provides local authorities,
academics and civil society with an opportunity to share
experiences and best practices to address the specific
challenges facing their territories.
                                    
During the two-day meeting, partners presented the latest
developments in the Digital Toolset, a suite of tools combining
monitoring systems, satellite data, digital models and
indicators to assess climate risks and support decision-making
processes.
                                    
Discussions also focused on integrating nature-based solutions
with traditional infrastructure, taking into account the
specific characteristics and vulnerabilities of different
territories.
                                    
Larnaca serves as a case study for monitoring water flows in the
Kamares area and investigating urban heat islands in Ayioi
Anargiroi. The activities include tools to assess thermal
comfort and environmental monitoring initiatives.
                                    
The Med-IREN project involves nine European regions in total.
                                    
Five Mediterranean areas are testing solutions to strengthen
climate resilience, while four other EU regions are replicating
the activities to assess their applicability in different
contexts. The case studies address a range of climate-related
risks, from heatwaves and wildfires to floods and coastal
erosion.
                                    
The next project partners' meeting is scheduled to take place in
Ischia during the week of 5-11 April 2027.

15:11:39 UTC
00:11:39 KST

Israel's parliamentary election recorded its highest voter turnout at 8 p.m. since 1988, with 74.3% of eligible voters having cast their ballots Tuesday, according to the Central Elections Committee.
The figure represents a surge of eight percentage points compared with the same hour in the November 2022 election, when turnout stood at 66.3%. More than 5.4 million Israelis had voted, with two hours remaining before most polling stations were scheduled to close.
Acting Central Elections Committee Director-General Dean Livne announced the latest figures, continuing a day of unusually high participation that had already broken records at several earlier reporting intervals.
By 6 p.m., turnout had reached 66.7%, compared with 57.7% at the same hour in 2022. The nine-percentage-point difference represented a relative increase of 15.6% over the previous election's pace. At that point, 4,892,186 Israelis had already cast their ballots.
"By 6 p.m., we have surpassed the number of people who voted by 10 p.m. in the previous election," Livne said, referring to the number of ordinary ballots cast, excluding special double-envelope votes.
Earlier, turnout reached 55.7% by 4 p.m., compared with 47.5% in 2022, and 44.9% by 2 p.m., compared with 38.9% four years ago. Each milestone reflected the unusually strong participation throughout Election Day.
The latest turnout also exceeded the previous election's final participation rate of 70.63%, with two hours still remaining before the scheduled closing time.
Long lines and heavy demand at polling stations
The surge in participation brought long lines to polling stations in several cities, including Ra'anana and Ramat Gan, with some voters reporting unusually lengthy waits. Election officials urged the public to remain patient as the number of voters continued to climb.
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg said waits at some polling stations had reached 15 to 20 minutes. Officials stressed that anyone arriving before the scheduled closing time would be allowed to cast a ballot, even if the line continued moving afterward.
Participation was also high among military personnel. According to the IDF, 68% of eligible service members had voted by 5 p.m., compared with 65% at the same hour during the previous election.
At the Jalame military base south of Afula, unusually heavy demand forced the IDF to deploy an additional polling station after soldiers reportedly waited more than two hours to vote. Other soldiers reported waits of approximately 90 minutes at a base in central Israel.
The military said it had prepared for high turnout by operating more than 850 fixed polling stations, alongside mobile voting stations serving troops in the field, and was deploying additional facilities where necessary.
Where is turnout highest? Some communities surpass 90%
Figures published by the Central Elections Committee earlier in the evening revealed striking differences between communities and major cities across the country.
The highest turnout among regular polling stations was recorded in Timorim, a community near Kiryat Malakhi in southern Israel, where 91.6% of eligible voters had already cast their ballots. Close behind was Yuval, near the Lebanese border, with 91.5%, followed by Shorashim in northern Israel at 90.1%.
Other communities reporting exceptionally high participation included Bat Hen at 87.7%, Hazon and Shavei Darom at 87% each, Nataf at 86.4%, Netiv HaLamed-Heh at 86.2%, Yesodot at 85.3% and HaBonim at 85.2%.
Among larger cities, Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut stood out with a turnout rate of 70.1%, one of the highest among the major urban centers included in the committee's earlier update.
Tel Aviv recorded 58.6%, Jerusalem 55.3% and Haifa 54.5%. Rishon LeZion reached 61.3%, Petah Tikva 63.1%, Ashdod 59.4% and Netanya 50.6%.
In the south, Be'er Sheva recorded 55.8% and Ashkelon 58.8%. Holon reached 58%, while Ramat Gan recorded 61.9%, Bnei Brak 64.3% and Rehovot 63.8%.
Herzliya recorded 63.1%, while Bat Yam stood at 47.6%, one of the lowest turnout rates among the major cities included in the update.
The local figures reflect voting at regular polling stations as of the earlier reporting period and should not be confused with the updated nationwide turnout figure for 8 p.m.
Election committee rejects bid to extend voting hours
Israel's Central Elections Committee rejected a request Tuesday to extend voting beyond the scheduled 10 p.m. closing time, following a political dispute between coalition and opposition parties amid record voter turnout and long lines at polling stations.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party had submitted a formal request to extend voting hours, citing heavy turnout and lengthy waits. The proposal gained support from the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the ultra-Orthodox Shas party, headed by Aryeh Deri.
Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party also supported the proposal, calling for an additional hour of voting.
Opposition parties rejected the request. Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party, Naftali Bennett's Beyahad party and the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, all opposed extending voting beyond the scheduled closing time.
Yashar! said it "strongly opposes" Likud's request, arguing that no exceptional circumstances justified changing the voting hours.
"No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify approving the request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for claims against the integrity of the election, following the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning," the party said in a statement.
Following a meeting of the committee's presidium, chaired by Justice Sohlberg, officials concluded that there was no justification for a nationwide extension.
"The high national voter turnout across all sectors reflects the public's strong engagement in the democratic process, and under these circumstances, no need was found to extend voting hours," the committee said.
Under the decision, most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. as originally scheduled. However, anyone who arrives before closing time will still be allowed to vote, even if they remain in line after 10 p.m.
The committee separately approved extending voting in Hebron until 10 p.m. because of a power outage that had disrupted the voting process.
Why the final results could take until Friday
A total of 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in the election for the 26th Knesset, with 12,018 polling stations operating nationwide. Most are scheduled to close at 10 p.m., when television networks traditionally release their exit polls.
However, the final results could remain uncertain for several days. More than 650,000 special double-envelope ballots are expected from soldiers, diplomats, displaced residents, voters with disabilities and others voting away from their registered polling stations. These ballots require separate verification and counting.
Livne warned that the number of special ballots could be higher than originally anticipated and that counting might not be completed by Thursday evening, potentially continuing into Friday morning.
"It is possible that the number of double envelopes will be higher, and it is possible that we will not finish counting them by Thursday evening," he said, adding that the count would be broadcast live.
The unusually high turnout could also have significant political consequences, particularly for smaller parties attempting to cross Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold. The threshold itself remains fixed, but as the total number of valid votes increases, so does the absolute number of votes a party needs to enter the Knesset.
With several parties potentially finishing close to that threshold, special ballots could alter the final distribution of seats and change the balance between rival political blocs.
The record turnout has already transformed the scale of Israel's election. Whether it will also transform the political balance will become clear only when the final ballots are counted.

Russians transfer Ukrainian prisoners from occupied Makiivka to Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:11:00 EET
00:11:00 KST

Russians transfer Ukrainian prisoners from occupied Makiivka to Russia
Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian political prisoners, as well as individuals convicted of criminal offences, have been transferred to Russia from penal colony No. 32 in occupied Makiivka, Donetsk Oblast.
Source: Novyny Donbasu (News of Donbas) news outlet
Details: According to the news outlet, some of the Ukrainian political prisoners and criminal convicts were transferred to strict-regime penal colony No. 1 in the city of Tambov. They were placed alongside Russian convicts serving their sentences there.
Another group of political prisoners and criminal convicts was moved to strict-regime colony No. 5 in the town of Morshansk, Tambov Oblast.
Several Ukrainian political prisoners remain in Makiivka penal colony No. 32 awaiting transfer to Russia. Their exact destination is currently unknown.
Meanwhile, about 100-120 convicts held in the settlement colony attached to penal colony No. 32 will remain in Makiivka for the winter period.
The transfer of prisoners from the Makiivka colony began in August 2026. The first to be taken to Russia were five Ukrainian servicemen and one civilian political prisoner.
The whereabouts of Ukrainian prisoner of war Vitalii Chmil, who was transferred from Makiivka in mid-August, have also become known. He was initially held in a pre-trial detention centre in Krasnoyarsk before being moved to strict-regime colony No. 1 in the city of Kyzyl in the Tyva Republic, near Russia's border with Mongolia.
The soldier was able to inform his relatives of his whereabouts with the help of Russian volunteers.
It is known that about 35 Ukrainian political prisoners and servicemen were held in colony No. 32, including five soldiers on the exchange lists.
Most of them have been in captivity for 7-9 years. The Russians sentenced them to 10 to 17 years in prison on charges of "espionage", "terrorism" and "extremism".
The administration of the Makiivka colony cited the inability to ensure proper living conditions in winter as one of the reasons for moving the prisoners to Russia. Specifically, this refers to a lack of funds to purchase coal for heating, as well as water supply interruptions and power outages in occupied Donetsk Oblast.
In addition, the relocation is linked to changes in Russian legislation, which stipulate that those convicted of terrorism and extremism must serve their sentences as far away from home as possible, as well as the fact that the premises of colony No. 32 do not meet Russian standards.
The vacated premises are already being refitted, including the installation of CCTV cameras.
Background:
- On 23 October 2026, two Ukrainian servicemen held in colony No. 32 returned from captivity during a prisoner swap: Anatolii Kapitskyi, captured in 2020, and Serhii Heremes, who had been in captivity since 2018.
- Meanwhile, over 30 Ukrainian prisoners from colony No. 32 who are on the exchange lists remain in captivity.

Israeli military detains Egyptian national who crossed border
Egyptian man held after crossing into Israel near Nitzana, his motive for the crossing still unknown.
Israel’s military has said that it detained an Egyptian civilian overnight after he crossed a border fence from Egyptian territory into Israel near Nitzana and that he was transferred to security forces for further questioning.
The military, which made the announcement on Tuesday, provided no additional details on the man’s identity, his motive or whether he was carrying anything at the time of his detention. Israeli state broadcaster Kan 11 reported that surveillance identified the suspect crossing the border and that troops were dispatched to the scene to arrest him.
Nitzana is a small community in southern Israel’s western Negev (Naqab) Desert, sitting directly adjacent to the Egyptian border opposite the Egyptian side’s Al-Awja area. The Nitzana border crossing, also known as the Eliav crossing, primarily handles cargo transport between the two countries rather than serving as a major passenger channel. It lies roughly 75km (47 miles) south of Beersheba.
The incident occurred as Israel maintains heightened alert levels along the Egyptian border. Israeli outlet Ynet reported that the military was treating the incident seriously and that it was under investigation.
Egyptian officials have not publicly commented on the detention.
Drug and arms smuggling takes place across the border between Egypt and Israel, neighbouring countries that signed a peace treaty in 1979 but whose relationship remains largely chilly.
Ynet reported the crossing came less than a year after Israel’s defence minister ordered the area adjacent to the Egyptian border declared a closed military zone and announced changes to open-fire regulations following earlier smuggling activity.

UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:10:26 UTC
00:10:26 KST

A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.
The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.
The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”
“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”
The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.
Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.
Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.
“We’re dealing with people’s lives. We’re talking about people that have faced some of the worst circumstances, and we’re meant to be making decisions based on facts and on understanding harm,” Labour backbench MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy tells WIRED. “I just don’t think it’s appropriate that machines are doing that.”
A Home Office spokesperson says, “Use of Artificial Intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders, and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.”
Ribeiro-Addy, Alsherif, and the Public Law Project, which has separately been investigating the tools, also worry that well-documented “cultural bias” in GPT models could lead to language barriers and the loss of cultural nuances in the summaries, which could in turn result in discriminatory decisions. An OpenAI spokesperson highlighted to WIRED the company’s ongoing work to improve its models’ accuracy and pointed out that the company will be retiring GPT-4 in January.
In the absence of regulation, the UK’s “AI Playbook” mandates that departments must be transparent about the algorithmic tools they use in decision-making processes and make information on them available to the public, including listing those tools on a public repository. The Home Office’s case summarization and policy search tools are not on that list.
Asylum seekers are also not told when these AI tools are used in their case. “Migrant organizations, legal practitioners, not many of them know about the actual use of this tool,” says Alsherif, who leads ORG’s migrant digital justice program. “So we need to let them know about this, let them know how it works, so they can challenge it.” Not being able to contest an incorrect AI summary of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws, Cloisters lawyers wrote in an independent legal opinion commissioned by ORG. The Home Office states that parts of the decision-making process may involve automation in its privacy notice.
Both groups have sent their findings to UK data regulator, the Information Commission, which is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to tell ORG how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.
Public Law Project senior research fellow Caroline Selman also notes that the ACS and APS tools are just two of the 11 high-risk AI systems that her team has found being used across government but absent from the public repository. She’s concerned there may be more deployed across government that even researchers, let alone the individuals they are being used on, are unaware of.
“Other tools are being used but not being publicized at all,” says Selman, “and you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.”

Hegseth heads to Manila to shore up US ties with Asia-Pacific partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:08:59 UTC
00:08:59 KST

Hegseth heads to Manila to shore up US ties with Asia-Pacific partners
The Iran war and Donald Trump’s criticisms of allies have led countries in the Asia-Pacific region to recalibrate their calculations.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will attend a Southeast Asian defence meeting this week alongside his counterparts from India, South Korea and Japan as Washington looks to solidify ties with the region after a year overshadowed by the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.
The meeting will bring together defence officials from the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) plus eight of the bloc’s dialogue partners.
Australia, New Zealand, Russia and China are also expected to send representatives to the talks, which run from Wednesday to Thursday in the Philippines.
Known as the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), the meeting will be held alongside a parallel ASEAN members-only event for Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam.
India is among the dialogue partners that will host bilateral meetings on the sidelines of ADMM-Plus to “review the ongoing defence ties and explore ways to further strengthen strategic partnerships”, according to state media.
William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that the focus will be on regional security concerns like Myanmar’s ongoing civil war and maritime disputes between ASEAN states and neighbouring China.
“The South China Sea dispute is going to be front and centre because the Philippines is the chair of this year’s summit,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that he expects Manila to push for ASEAN to finalise a code of conduct with China to outline how to approach maritime disputes and handle conflicts in the globally important waterway.
The Philippines, China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan all have overlapping territorial claims to the South China Sea, although Beijing claims most of it as domestic waters.
These disputes often leave Beijing at odds with its neighbours, and particularly Manila, as both sides claim the uninhabited Scarborough Shoal and parts of the Spratly Islands.
Tensions escalated sharply this month with at least “eight close encounters” in the South China Sea and nearby Luzon Strait, according to the US Naval Institute.
The spat turned into a war of words when Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan said Beijing could “easily win” a war with the Philippines, prompting a Philippine senator to call for his expulsion.
Beijing has yet to confirm whether Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun will attend ADMM-Plus in person, but he could still make a last-minute appearance. The Chinese defence chief attended ADMM-Plus 2024 and 2025, according to Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund’s Indo-Pacific Program, and Hegseth’s presence could factor into Beijing’s calculations.
China and the US have spent the past year thawing their relationship. A face-to-face meeting between Hegseth and Dong could also lay the groundwork for two meetings between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping scheduled for later this year, following two previous meetings between Trump and Xi this year.
“It is certainly possible that he will attend again this year,” Glaser told Al Jazeera by email. “I would not be surprised if Dong meets with Secretary Hegseth, especially since China has repeatedly said that it attaches importance to strengthening crisis communications and preventing crises between the US and Chinese militaries.”
Analysts, however, say that the bulk of Hegseth’s work at ASEAN will be reassuring the bloc and its dialogue partners that the US remains committed to the region amid its months-long conflict with Iran.
The US has raised eyebrows in Asia over the past year by moving some of its military assets from South Korea and Japan to the Middle East, while Trump has also sent mixed signals on his views on Taiwan, another potential flashpoint for the region.
Trump has reportedly delayed a major arms package to Taiwan, an unofficial US ally, ahead of an upcoming meeting with Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in November, before the Group of 20 (G20) Leaders’ Summit in December.
“What Hegseth says and does will be interesting,” said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore, because of recent comments by US defence official Elbridge Colby suggesting that Washington would focus less on empty gestures and more on substance in the Asia-Pacific region.
“How Hegseth keeps to these lines while trying to keep a US advantage will be interesting, since these are not easy calibrations to make,” Chong said.

Palestinians protest against military demolitions in West Bank as Israelis vote
Unknown

15:07:42 UTC
00:07:42 KST

Israeli troops fired a stun grenade on Tuesday to disperse Palestinians who gathered to protest against an Israeli military operation that has displaced thousands of residents from a neighborhood in Hebron in the West Bank.
The unrest, which follows the deaths of two Israeli soldiers shot by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint last week, unfolded as Israelis were voting in an election in which the country's posture in the West Bank has been a major political issue.
Some Palestinian officials have accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of launching a crackdown in the West Bank to coincide with the vote, as a way to energize his right-wing supporters. The government says its operation is a response to the attack on its soldiers.
A group of Palestinian men, women, and children gathered at Tuesday's protest. One elderly man held a placard that said: "No to collective punishment, no to closures, and no to displacement."
The military said it had fired a stun grenade to disperse them so that its operation could continue.
UN says over 3,000 Palestinians displaced by Israeli military operation in Hebron
On Monday, the United Nations said that over 3,000 Palestinians had been forced from their homes by the Israeli military operation, which targeted neighborhoods near the checkpoint where Palestinian gunmen killed the two Israeli soldiers on Friday.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," said UN human rights chief Volker Türk in a statement. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
The Israeli military said in a statement on Sunday that troops would carry out demolitions in the area. It said soldiers had not located any weapons in searches of the houses.
Since Friday's attack on the checkpoint, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns across the West Bank, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement.
Noura Nassar, a displaced resident who attended the protests, said she had struggled to get medical treatment because of the blockages.
"Where is the democracy in all of this? Their elections are today, sure, but what about us? Aren't we human beings? We want to go out, we want to visit the doctor," said Nassar.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot oppose Palestinian statehood as Hebron residents question election's impact
Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot both oppose the creation of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. Residents expelled from the Hebron neighborhood said Tuesday's election in Israel would do little to change the reality on the ground in territories Israel has occupied since 1967.
"Among themselves they will elect who is the oppressor and who will destroy the Palestinian people. That is their election," said Sana' Salman Abu Sneineh, another expelled resident.
Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements, which are deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Under Netanyahu's right-wing coalition, there has also been a surge of militant settler violence against Palestinians.

27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Trade unions at Belgian public broadcaster VRT urged its management on Tuesday to reconsider its decision to participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, calling on it to follow the example of the Netherlands.
The unions urged VRT management not to wait for additional staff action before reversing its decision, after Dutch public broadcasters announced that the Netherlands would not participate in next year's contest.
"Perhaps our management also needs 500 signatures from employees first to reverse its decision. In that case, we will gladly collect them," Carlos Van Hoeymissen of the ACV-VRT trade union told the broadcaster.
He added that conversations showed support for VRT's participation in the contest was limited.
Another trade union, ACOD-VRT, said the Dutch broadcaster NPO had made "the only morally acceptable decision" by withdrawing from an event in which Israel continues to participate.
The two unions have already filed a strike notice covering the Eurovision broadcast dates of May 11, 13 and 15, 2027, in protest against VRT's decision to send a candidate.
Israel's participation in Eurovision has prompted growing calls for boycotts and renewed pressure on broadcasters to withdraw from the contest in protest against Israel's genocidal war in Gaza.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Apple introduced the M6 iMac with a significant leap in AI performance

Apple introduced the M6 iMac with a significant leap in AI performance
Kyiv • UNN
The new iMac features the M6 chip, Wi‑Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and a Center Stage camera. Orders open on October 28, starting at $1,499.
Following the presentation of the new iPad mini, Apple is continuing the phased release of its "Pro and Tell" products with the launch of its latest iMac model. Equipped with the new Apple M6 processors, it promises a "significant boost" in performance and AI capabilities thanks to additional cores and new neural accelerators in each core. UNN reports this, citing Engadget.
Details
The M6 processor first appeared in the Mac mini and Mac Studio, but it is now also available in entry-level iMac desktop computers.
As noted, the M6 chip offers not only greater performance per core but also more cores overall: up to a 12-core CPU, a 12-core GPU, and two 16-core neural processors. This processor, together with higher memory bandwidth of 170 GB/s, will make the iMac twice as fast graphically compared with the previous iMac M4 model, accelerating resource-intensive tasks such as photo editing and gaming, Apple said. Models start with 16 GB of unified memory, with options for 24 GB and 32 GB.
Since it is primarily intended for work, Apple claims that the iMac is 50 percent faster in tasks such as Microsoft Excel compared with the iMac M4, or 2.5 times faster than the M1 model. However, these machines are more than capable of handling resource-intensive tasks such as photo editing and even video editing. According to Apple, it also delivers up to twice the gaming performance with ray tracing.
However, as with the Mini and Studio models, Apple is focusing on promoting the iMac’s artificial intelligence capabilities. The additional speed is much more noticeable there: on-device AI performance in LM Studio is up to five times higher compared with the M4 model, or 12 times higher than with the M1 model.
This AI performance, the publication writes, is important given that the iMac running macOS 27 operates on the next generation of Apple Intelligence with Siri AI, which Apple calls significantly more functional than the old Siri. iMac users will be able to use this AI for tasks such as setting tasks and searching for information in emails and photos. Siri AI is also integrated into Spotlight, so, as noted, users can find answers to any questions and ask questions. At the same time, it is noted that Apple Intelligence is not yet available in Europe.
The 4.5K 24-inch Retina display with 500-nit brightness and wide P3 color gamut remains unchanged. However, the iMac with the M6 processor has new Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 capabilities, as well as 2.5-gigabit Ethernet, providing 250 percent more speed than before. Unlike the latest version of the Mac Studio, it supports only Thunderbolt 4, rather than the twice-as-fast Thunderbolt 5. Nevertheless, up to two external 6K displays can be connected if additional workspace is needed.
Other features include a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera, a choice of seven colors, as well as color-matched accessories and Touch ID. Orders for the new iMac with the M6 processor will open on October 28 at a starting price of $1,499 with a 10-core processor, a 10-core processor, and 16 GB of RAM, or $1,699 with a 12-core processor and a 12-core graphics processor.

The pair will appear at London's Westminster Magistrates' Court later on Tuesday.
Police said that six other people, four of whom are British nationals who were arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27, remain on police bail.
The decision to bail suspects after an apparent major incident had drawn scrutiny, but on Tuesday police said that decision had helped secure charges against the two men.
UK counterterrorism chief defends police decisions in RAF Fairford investigation
"We know the decisions made during our investigations can sometimes appear illogical to those on the outside, but I want to make it very clear that there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them," said Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK.
"In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I have announced today."

Israeli and US elections could hasten the end of Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:07:05 UTC
00:07:05 KST

Israeli and US elections could hasten the end of Iran war
LONDON - Alongside military and economic calculations, the Knesset elections in Israel and midterm congressional elections in the U.S. are emerging as factors influencing the duration of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and the terms under which it might end. These electoral considerations also shape the relationship between Benjamin Netanyahu’s political future and Donald Trump’s decisions.
Netanyahu’s political future may be linked to the future of the confrontation with Iran. If Netanyahu loses the Israeli elections, Trump may have a greater opportunity to withdraw from the war while declaring that the United States has achieved its objectives.
Under this scenario, the withdrawal could be presented to the American public as a victory, even if the actual outcome more closely resembles Iran’s success in enduring the confrontation and maintaining its ability to shape the future of the region and beyond. In this way, Trump could end America’s direct military commitments while attempting to avoid admitting that the war failed to achieve its stated objectives.
However, if Netanyahu wins the elections, the confrontation could be prolonged, increasing the likelihood that it would continue for the remainder of Trump’s term. This would result from Israeli calculations favoring the continuation of the war and an attempt to avoid ending it before achieving results that could be presented domestically as an accomplishment.
Nevertheless, if Netanyahu remains in power, it does not necessarily mean that Washington will be able to continue the war indefinitely. American decision-making will remain subject to the costs of mobilization, attrition, the global economy and relations with allies. Elections, therefore, are not the sole factor determining the end of the war, but they could accelerate or delay the decision to withdraw.
What if Netanyahu and the Republicans in the U.S. lose the elections? In that case, political pressure to end the war could intensify, whether through an agreement or through an American withdrawal without an agreement. The ultimate outcome would depend on the nature of the settlement, the conditions of withdrawal and the ability to translate military results into political gains.
In either case, the central argument remains that electoral changes could politically provide the American administration with an exit from the confrontation. However, they would not guarantee that the strategic consequences of withdrawal would match the narrative presented to the public.
The United States, particularly the Trump administration, faces a dilemma that extends beyond achieving an immediate military gain. The American objective is not simply to leave the war, but to do so in a way that allows the outcome to be presented to the American public and allies as a victory.
The problem, however, is that Washington’s available options are now constrained by substantial strategic costs, meaning that none appears to be free of losses. These options can be summarized in three main scenarios: maintaining a state of neither war nor peace, withdrawing without an agreement, or withdrawing under an agreement.
Maintaining a state of neither war nor peace
This scenario involves maintaining the current situation without reaching a final settlement and without returning to open warfare at the same intensity. At first glance, this option may appear to offer a way to postpone a decisive outcome while keeping pressure on Iran. However, it raises a fundamental question: how long can the United States maintain this situation?
Keeping forces mobilized and on continuous standby, rotating units, securing supplies and covering military and logistical expenses all impose accumulating burdens. These burdens increase when troops are deployed far from American territory, particularly in a region of critical importance to energy security and global trade.
Withdrawal without an agreement
The United States may withdraw without reaching a comprehensive agreement, while maintaining its policy of sanctions on Iran.
Under this scenario, the Trump administration might attempt to construct a narrative of victory by launching a rapid military strike against Iranian targets, such as nuclear facilities and then claiming that the mission had been accomplished and Iran’s capabilities had suffered decisive damage.
However, such a declaration could be an attempt to disguise the withdrawal rather than a genuine indication that the confrontation had been decisively resolved.
Withdrawal under an agreement
The third option involves reaching an agreement that would allow the United States to end the confrontation on the basis of a memorandum of understanding containing 14 clauses. The memorandum itself calls the objectives of the war into question and grants Iran some of its rights. However, such an agreement would present Washington with a different strategic problem.
If the agreement leads to the lifting or easing of sanctions, the opening of economic and financial ties with Iran, and its reintegration into the regional and international systems, Tehran could transform its resources and capabilities into those of a major regional economic power.
Here lies one of the greatest concerns reflected in the agreement: the United States would appear to have been defeated and to have achieved nothing, while Iran, benefiting from economic openness, could become a regional economic giant—or what might be described as the “economic China of West Asia.”
Iran has demonstrated, through its development of national strength under sanctions, that it can mobilize its natural and human resources, geographical position and trade relationships. Without the restrictions imposed on it, Iran could become a major regional power and contribute to the establishment of a new world order.
An agreement that opens these doors could therefore alter the regional balance of power in ways that extend beyond the military results of the war itself.
