Strong winds and high water to ease as calmer weather reaches Denmark
Denmark’s week will begin with strong winds and elevated coastal water levels before calmer and sunnier conditions arrive around Thursday.
The strongest winds Monday morning were along Jutland’s west coast between Blåvandshuk and Skagen, Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Mette Zhang said.
Some areas continued to experience storm-force gusts, although the wind was expected to weaken during the day.
DMI maintained warnings for elevated water levels around the Wadden Sea, the central western coast of Jutland and parts of the Limfjord.
Water levels in the Wadden Sea reached more than three meters above normal overnight but were beginning to fall.
Western Denmark will experience the most clouds Monday, while eastern areas will have clearer conditions. Showers are expected in several places before conditions improve later in the day.
Temperatures will range from 9 to 13 degrees Celsius.
A new front will bring clouds, rain and stronger southerly winds overnight into Tuesday. Winds could reach gale force along the west coast, although less rain is expected than during the weekend.
Wednesday will bring a mixture of rain, showers and sunshine.
A high-pressure system is expected to stabilize the weather from Thursday, bringing less wind, drier conditions and more sunshine.
Fog may form overnight into Thursday and Friday. Clearer skies will also increase the risk of overnight frost, particularly heading into Saturday.
Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.
Danish Crown confirms slaughter without stunning at Polish subsidiary
Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.
Several animal welfare organizations criticized the company’s involvement.
Søren Kent Pedersen, a veterinarian with animal welfare organization Dyrenes Beskyttelse, described the practice as animal cruelty and accused Danish Crown of hypocrisy because the company publicly emphasizes animal welfare.
Danish Crown’s website states that “good animal welfare is the core of our business” and that the company protects animals’ well-being from farms through slaughter.
Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.
Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Danish road safety authorities are urging parents to check electric scooters used by their children after police stopped underage riders and scooters capable of greatly exceeding the legal speed limit.
Riders must be at least 15 years old to use an electric scooter alone in traffic. Scooters may travel no faster than 20 kilometers per hour, and helmets are mandatory.
Children under 15 may ride in traffic only when accompanied by an adult.
The Danish Road Safety Council identified 21 reported cases between September 13 and October 13 involving children who were too young or scooters that could travel too fast.
The figure came from media coverage and police reports rather than a complete national count.
Children as young as nine were stopped, while some scooters could reach speeds of up to 90 kilometers per hour.
“Parents should take it seriously and check the rules before saying yes to an electric scooter,” council chief executive Jakob Bøving Arendt said.
Emergency departments in Odense and Svendborg have treated 811 people injured in electric scooter accidents since 2021. Twenty-five percent suffered serious injuries.
Odense University Hospital physician Jens Lauritsen said crashes can cause severe injuries even at legal speeds.
Modified scooters capable of traveling 60, 80 or 100 kilometers per hour could endanger both riders and others, he said.
Denmark to cull 27,000 turkeys after bird flu outbreak on Lolland
Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.
It is Denmark’s second confirmed outbreak of the highly contagious disease within one week, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said.
Another outbreak was identified Friday in a flock in Bøgelunde in Slagelse Municipality.
“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.
Owners should prevent wild birds from reaching their animals, drinking water and feed. The agency also recommends changing footwear before entering areas where birds are kept.
Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the infected flock on Lolland. Poultry owners within those areas must follow stricter disease control requirements.
The restrictions will remain until authorities complete their investigations and determine that the risk of further transmission has declined.
The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Queen Margrethe has received a 25th anniversary medal recognizing her work as a costume and set designer for Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens.
Tivoli chief executive Susanne Mørch Koch presented the medal during a private ceremony at Fredensborg Palace.
“Queen Margrethe has had a truly exceptional significance for Tivoli’s performing arts,” Koch said.
The former Danish monarch has contributed to nine productions at Tivoli during the past 25 years.
Seven were staged at the Pantomime Theatre, while two appeared in Tivoli’s Concert Hall.
Her first production was Hans Christian Andersen’s “Love in the Dustbin” in 2001, for which she created costumes, scenery and an interpretation of the story.
“Queen Margrethe’s contribution has become part of Tivoli’s cultural heritage,” Koch said.
Margrethe has also contributed costumes and set designs to a new production of “The Nutcracker,” opening at Tivoli’s Concert Hall on November 26.
Three ballet dancers were honored during the ceremony. Tori Cooper and Allan Clausen marked 25 years at Tivoli, while Tommy Edvardsen celebrated 50 years at the Pantomime Theatre.
All three have performed in productions involving Margrethe, including “The Tinderbox,” “The Swineherd” and “Cinderella.”
Margrethe, 86, became Denmark’s monarch in 1972 and abdicated in favor of her son, King Frederik, on January 14, 2024.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Denmark delays new citizenship screening model – what it means for applicants
The expert group tasked with examining the possibilities for a screening model for citizenship applicants is facing further delays in its work.
The Ministry of Immigration and Integration writes this in a press release.
– Due to the scope and complexity of the work, we cannot manage to deliver our recommendations around the turn of the year. Instead, I expect that we will conclude our work in mid-March next year, says Henrik Thomassen, chairman of the expert group, in the press release.
The granting of citizenship in particular has taken up a significant amount of the political debate recently.
Most recently, the Danish People’s Party entered the debate because the party wants a Pakistani man removed from an upcoming bill that next year will make 2,055 foreigners Danish citizens.
DF’s citizenship spokesperson, Mikkel Bjørn, has found a Facebook post from 2016 in which the man, according to DF, supported an Islamic execution.
– The government should strip him of the opportunity to obtain citizenship. If they are not willing to do that, they must at the very least be willing to let us meet this man eye-to-eye so we can see the matter for ourselves, Mikkel Bjørn told DR on Thursday.
Last week, Liberal Alliance found a woman who, according to the party, has repeatedly praised Hamas and the former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Therefore, the party wants the person summoned for an interview with the Folketing’s Naturalisation Committee.
The central element in the debate regarding a bill granting citizenship to 2,055 new individuals has been whether they have been sufficiently investigated for anti-democratic views.
Every six months, a bill is introduced in the Folketing granting new individuals Danish citizenship after an often lengthy and comprehensive application process.
This also applied to the then SVM government.
But the latest granting of citizenship coincided with the calling of the general election held in March of this year, and the bill regarding the citizenship of the 2,055 individuals was therefore postponed.
A screening model must be created for people who apply for Danish citizenship to investigate whether they have anti-democratic views. The government announced this earlier in October.
However, the government has ultimately decided that it will introduce the bill before a screening model is ready.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, just as “other relevant authorities are being kept closely informed”.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness and the Agency for Public Security write in a press release Friday evening that the authorities are monitoring the cyber incidents at the University of Copenhagen and Aarhus University.

– The Agency for Public Security generally assesses that universities in Denmark are exposed to the threat of cyberattacks. Among other things because they are leaders within a range of research areas. I know that the universities are working actively to counter that threat.
The minister states that “relevant higher education institutions have been informed about the incidents and have received advice from the Agency for Public Security.”
The attack against the University of Copenhagen was discovered on Tuesday and “was subsequently brought under control”.
The university is in the process of analyzing the exact scope and preventing similar or further attacks from taking place, it is stated.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.

Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.
During Sunday, winds will shift toward the southwest and intensify, bringing strong gusts and severe gales to coastal areas.
DMI warns that the conditions could affect traffic on several Danish bridges.
Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.
Wanner said the forecast reflects Denmark’s transition into its windier autumn and winter months.
“We are genuinely entering the windy season in Denmark. It is not at all unthinkable that there will be more episodes with storm-like conditions leading up to and throughout the winter,” he said.
DMI will continue monitoring the weather and publishing updated forecasts as the storm approaches.
Denmark to end mink farming by August 2029 under EU ban
Denmark’s remaining seven mink farms will have to close by August 7, 2029, after the government decided not to seek an exemption from an upcoming European Union ban.
The Ministry for Nature and Animal Welfare announced the decision, citing animal welfare concerns and the industry’s limited economic contribution.
“An industry should not continue solely because it has existed for a long time. It must also make sense for society, for the economy, and for the animals,” said Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats).
The EU added mink to its list of invasive species last summer, introducing a ban on breeding and production that takes effect August 7, 2027. Existing farms will have a two-year transition period.
Denmark previously opposed the EU measure and had planned to seek an exemption allowing existing farms to continue operating.
Carl Valentin, animal welfare spokesperson for Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, welcomed the government’s decision.
“As we see it, it is not good animal welfare to have mink in tiny cages,” he told Ritzau.
Denmark’s mink industry was severely affected in 2020 when authorities ordered approximately 15 million animals culled over concerns about coronavirus mutations.
A temporary farming ban followed, lasting until January 2023, when some producers resumed operations.
The total estimated cost of pandemic-related compensation, farm demolition and administrative work reached 29.1 billion DKK in early 2026.
The government has yet to determine compensation costs for closing the remaining farms.
Valentin said an earlier estimate was around 14 million DKK, although the final amount could be higher.
Politicians push to change rules for dogs suspected of being banned breeds
Several Danish opposition politicians are calling for changes to the country’s dog laws after reports of legally owned dogs being kept in kennels for months while authorities investigate their breeds.
Under Denmark’s Dog Act, 13 breeds are banned from ownership, breeding and importation, including pit bull terriers and American bulldogs. Crossbreeds containing any of the prohibited breeds are also illegal.
When police suspect a dog belongs to a banned breed, its owner must provide documentation proving otherwise. During the investigation, the animal may be placed in a boarding kennel.
Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten has reported cases involving dogs that were eventually found to be legal but had spent months in kennels.
Danmarksdemokraterne (the Denmark Democrats), an opposition party, has proposed allowing dogs to remain with their owners while investigations take place, potentially using electronic tracking devices instead.
Borgernes Parti (the Citizens’ Party) and independent lawmakers Nadja Natalie Isaksen, Cecilie Liv Hansen and Emilie Schytte have also criticized police powers to order euthanasia based on visual assessments of a dog’s breed.
The law requires police to euthanize dogs found to belong to prohibited breeds.
The restrictions were introduced in 2010 following incidents involving dog attacks on people and other animals.
Christian Rabjerg Madsen, Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare from Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats), told Jyllands-Posten he was open to discussing changes to the law and its enforcement.
He said the challenge was balancing public safety with fair treatment of owners who struggle to document their dogs’ breeds.

Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.
Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.
Meanwhile, competing retailer Coop, which operates Brugsen, SuperBrugsen, 365discount and Kvickly, has not decided whether to establish similar stores.
Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.

“It is completely, completely the wrong way to go, and it actually makes me furious. While Russian missiles rain down on Ukrainian cities, while innocent civilians are being killed, and while Russia is waging hybrid warfare against Denmark and our allies, a Danish member of parliament apparently believes that the time has come to sit down at the table with Putin’s representative,” Lund Poulsen wrote.
Mohammad Rona, political spokesperson for the Moderates, and Mette Abildgaard, parliamentary group leader for the Conservatives, also criticized Harris.
“Why is Harris turning his back on Denmark? Harris’ loyalty apparently lies somewhere else. Sad that a Danish parliamentarian can sink so low,” Rona wrote on X.
Abildgaard wrote: “He becomes a useful idiot in the Russians’ propaganda machine. If he wants to be a great diplomat so badly, then apply for a job in the Foreign Service instead.”
Sigurd Agersnap, political spokesperson for the Socialist People’s Party (SF), described the planned meeting as “deeply naive”.
Harris risks giving the Russian ambassador exactly what he needs: “An image that Danish politicians are softening toward Russia while the attacks on Ukraine continue,” Agersnap said in a written comment to Ritzau.
“Of course we must have diplomacy. But a lasting peace requires that we stand firm on the Ukrainians’ right to freedom and self-determination. Harris does not help that by showing up for this meeting,” he added.
Trine Pertou Mach, the Red-Green Alliance’s foreign affairs spokesperson, told DR that the meeting was “decidedly stupid”.
Harris announced the planned meeting with Barbin in a Facebook post on Thursday. He also said he expected criticism from fellow politicians.
He has defended the decision, arguing that meeting a foreign ambassador is not an act of disloyalty.
“Speaking with a foreign ambassador is not treason. Seeking diplomatic solutions is not treason. And working to ensure that Denmark is not dragged into a war is certainly not treason either,” Harris wrote on Facebook.
Harris is an independent member of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. He was elected in March as a member of Borgernes Parti, or the Citizens’ Party, but was expelled a few days later.
He has since established a “working partnership” in parliament with fellow independent Cecilie Liv Hansen, who supports his decision to meet the Russian ambassador.
“I think it is reasonable to meet with ambassadors, regardless of where they come from. Jacob Harris has also tried to reach out to several, including the Ukrainian one,” Hansen told DR.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four and a half years ago. Denmark and several other countries have supported Ukraine since then, including through financial assistance and weapons deliveries.

21-22 October. The project brings together nature-based
expertise and engineering developments to protect critical
infrastructure from the impacts of climate change.
                                    
The meeting in Cyprus provided an opportunity to review the
project's progress and discuss the next stages of work, with a
particular focus on moving from the development of methodologies
to their practical application in the participating territories.

countries, including Italy. It provides local authorities,
academics and civil society with an opportunity to share
experiences and best practices to address the specific
challenges facing their territories.

developments in the Digital Toolset, a suite of tools combining
monitoring systems, satellite data, digital models and
indicators to assess climate risks and support decision-making
processes.

with traditional infrastructure, taking into account the
specific characteristics and vulnerabilities of different
territories.
                                    
Larnaca serves as a case study for monitoring water flows in the
Kamares area and investigating urban heat islands in Ayioi
Anargiroi. The activities include tools to assess thermal
comfort and environmental monitoring initiatives.
                                    
The Med-IREN project involves nine European regions in total.
                                    
Five Mediterranean areas are testing solutions to strengthen
climate resilience, while four other EU regions are replicating
the activities to assess their applicability in different
contexts. The case studies address a range of climate-related
risks, from heatwaves and wildfires to floods and coastal
erosion.

Ukrainian intelligence says Russia’s missile makers use gear from seven countries—and the Chinese machines run on European, Japanese, and Taiwanese parts

2026-10-27
14:52:36 UTC
23:52:36 KST

Machine tools and other equipment from seven countries, led by China, work at Russian plants that make ballistic missiles and their components, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said on 26 October. The 30 items are a small slice of HUR’s War&Sanctions portal, which lists 1,698 machine tools at 223 Russian plants.
Seventeen of the 30 were made outside China, in Germany, Taiwan, the US, Türkiye, Switzerland, and Italy. One of HUR’s proposals reaches past Russia and China, to the firms that supply parts for Chinese machine tools. The list comes two weeks after the EU blacklisted 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and executives. More than half of those listings hit the ballistic missile supply chain, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said. Sanctioning a company, though, does not stop the machines in its workshops.
A Chinese machine at the Iskander plant
HUR’s statement leads with a GX-650 five-axis machining center made by China’s Hyper Machine Tool. Such computer-controlled machines cut complex metal parts from several angles. HUR said it works at the Votkinsk Plant, which the agency described as the maker of 9M723 missiles for the Iskander-M system and the missile section of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal, an air-launched ballistic missile.
Kinzhal is 90% identical to Iskander-M: Ukraine’s intelligence identifies 58 companies in production chain
HUR has flagged Votkinsk before. In November 2025, it published hackathon findings showing that Russian companies supplied Chinese and Taiwanese machine tools to the plant after the full-scale invasion began.
Chinese Shtral turning and milling centers work at PEMZ Molot, which builds electronics units for Iskander-M missiles, according to HUR’s statement. At UPKB Detal, which makes altimeters for hypersonic Zircon cruise missiles, HUR found measuring equipment from Germany’s Rohde & Schwarz.
The portal entries paint a broader picture. Only four of the 30 entries list a ballistic missile among the plant’s weapons. Most of the rest list cruise missiles, glide-bomb kits, guided artillery shells, or Geran-2 attack drones. HUR did not publish its evidence, though the portal says partner agencies can request it.
Foreign parts inside Chinese machines
Russian plants use the equipment to make missiles and parts such as altimeters, control surfaces, and gyroscopes, HUR said. The agency noted a growing number of Chinese machine tools, including five-axis models. According to HUR, those Chinese machines contain European, Japanese, and Taiwanese components, from numerical control systems to precision spindles and bearings. In HUR’s assessment, Russia still cannot replace equipment from leading foreign makers with its own.

US Justice Dept asks Washington state not to count ballots from possible noncitizens
Oct 27 - The US Justice Department has asked Washington state not to count any mail ballots received from more than 400 residents who it says may not be US citizens, opening a new front in the Trump administration's push to expand control of election administration ahead of the November 3 midterms.
The letter, which resembled a request earlier this month that California not count any ballots received from around 20,000 alleged noncitizens, marked an escalation in the Trump administration's pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting. Multiple state audits and independent studies have found that voter fraud, including voting by noncitizens, is very rare and has not affected election outcomes.
The pressure campaign is a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process in the weeks before an election. President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain slim majorities in both chambers of the US Congress, and centrist Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez's campaign to hold onto her southwest Washington seat is one of 10 key races that could decide control of the US House of Representatives.
In the letter dated October 26, the top federal prosecutors in Seattle and Spokane asked Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the state's top elections official, to determine whether the more than 400 people were in fact US citizens and to not count their ballots until their citizenship was determined. The letter said the Justice Department would seek "emergency relief" if the state could not take those actions by noon local time (1900 GMT) on Wednesday.
There were 5 million registered voters in Washington state as of 2024, according to the secretary of state's office.
In a statement, Hobbs said his office would only respond to requests that follow due process.
“The timing of this request — one week before the General Election — is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results," Hobbs said.
A Justice Department spokesperson said, "With his (Hobbs') help, we can ensure that only American citizens vote in Washington's elections."
In California, after state election officials said complying with the Justice Department's demand would be impractical and questioned the accuracy of its information on alleged noncitizens, federal prosecutors filed a lawsuit seeking to block the state from counting any ballots received from the alleged noncitizens.
A hearing is scheduled in that case for 1 p.m. PDT (2000 GMT) on Tuesday before US District Judge David Carter in Los Angeles. A federal appeals court on Monday night denied the Justice Department's request to block California from counting any ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.
Democrats and voting rights advocates say federal data on citizenship is often outdated, meaning naturalized citizens registered to vote are often mistakenly flagged as noncitizens.
In its letter to Washington state officials, the Justice Department acknowledged that some of the individuals flagged as possible noncitizens may have since naturalized, but it did not say how many. REUTERS

‘Mosquito toilets’: How scientists are using mosquito poop to detect viruses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:49:38 UTC
23:49:38 KST

Researchers have developed a “mosquito toilet” — a tool to analyse mosquito waste for pathogens — that could be an early warning system for emerging health threats.
Mosquitoes are considered the world’s deadliest animals because of the diseases they transmit. Monitoring them could help scientists detect viruses circulating in the environment before they pose a threat to humans.
To gain a better understanding of the viruses and bacteria circulating in the environment, Dana Price, an entomologist at Rutgers University in the United States, developed a tool to analyse mosquito waste.
The device, which Price calls a “mosquito toilet”, collects small amounts of liquid excreted by mosquitoes, which can then be analysed for genetic traces of pathogens.
“Our question is, is this virus in the environment?” Price told Euronews. “You just have to look for it. If you don't look for it, you won't find it,” he said, adding that the findings suggest the range of viruses that mosquitoes may be naturally infected with is much broader than previously thought.
Having such a tool could give scientists an advantage in responding to new viruses, Price explained. Detecting traces of COVID-19 before it jumped to humans, he said, could have given researchers “a large head start” in understanding the virus and developing vaccines.
The mosquito toilet is a 3D-printed funnel coated with a water-repelling material that causes liquid to bead up and slide into a collection tube. Researchers placed 50 Culex mosquitoes collected from a garden in New Jersey into the container, where they drank from a cotton pad soaked with sugar water and red food colouring.
Their excrement, containing genetic traces of viruses and other organisms, collected over 18 hours, was later analysed in a lab.
Unlike traditional methods, which involve trapping and grinding up mosquitoes, analysing their waste reduces the amount of mosquito DNA in samples, making viral genetic material easier to detect.
Using this seemingly simple device, the team identified the first known evidence of a Hedwig-like virus in the Americas and detected several viruses that may be new to science.
They also recovered a complete West Nile virus genome, which shows that mosquito waste contains enough high-quality genetic material to rebuild an entire virus's genetic code and allows researchers to identify specific variants or mutations of the virus.
Yet, Price said there is no reason to be alarmed by anything the study found.
Identifying previously unknown viruses, or detecting them in places where they have not been found before, does not necessarily mean they pose a threat, he added. Instead, it may just indicate that they have been circulating undetected.
What’s next?
While Price’s tool has shown promise in detecting viruses carried by mosquitoes in a limited area, the team’s next step is to expand the geographical scope of its research and improve the device to keep samples stable for longer, enabling extended collection periods.
“The idea is that you could go, place these traps kind of in the middle of nowhere or some place that's really hard to reach and then go back in a few days or maybe even a week,” Price said.
Being able to leave traps in remote locations for longer could make it easier to monitor pathogens in areas that are difficult to access regularly. However, further research is needed to establish how effectively the approach could be used for ongoing disease surveillance.
The researchers are also working to develop devices that can be deployed in the field and combine mosquito trapping with excreta collection in a single step.

Lithuania tightening rules on buying smartphones: renting instead of instalment plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:49:00 UTC
23:49:00 KST

Buying smartphones and other smart devices in instalments through mobile operators will become more complicated in Lithuania from November 20, when new European Union rules introduce stricter creditworthiness checks. Customers unable to pay the full price upfront may increasingly turn to device rental or other financing options.
Under the changes, people seeking to buy phones or other telecommunications equipment in instalments through mobile operators will undergo financial assessments similar to those required when applying for other types of credit.
Currently, about seven in 10 customers buy phones and other smart devices from operators using instalment plans. The new requirements are expected to affect how these purchases are financed, with licensed credit providers becoming involved in the process.
“When buying a phone or other telecommunications equipment in instalments through an operator, customers will have to sign a credit agreement, which was not previously required,” said Asta Buitkutė, head of public relations at Tele2 Lithuania. “For this, we will need to work with a licensed partner that already has creditor status.”
The new system will require providers to check customers’ existing financial commitments and determine whether they can afford additional payments.
Jaunius Špakauskas, head of corporate communications at Bitė Lietuva, said customers could expect the purchasing process to take longer.
“In practical terms, it means I will spend a little more time in the store because they will have to check my creditworthiness,” he said. “And when we feel the impact on our wallets, smartphones will become almost a luxury item for some people.”
Rental and alternative payment options
The changes have prompted concerns among consumers who rely on instalment plans to spread the cost of new devices over time.
Some residents of Vilnius said they might have to save up and pay the full price upfront rather than go through the more complicated financing process.
One woman said instalment plans had been particularly convenient for families buying phones for their children. Parents could purchase newer models for their children and then use the older devices themselves, sometimes financing the purchases through successive instalment agreements.
Others questioned whether the changes would make smartphones less affordable, noting that the devices were essential for everyday communication and work.
Customers who cannot afford their preferred model upfront may have to choose a cheaper phone or consider renting a device instead.
Audrius Stasiulaitis, a spokesman for Telia Lietuva, said rental arrangements could allow customers to pay for a device for a year before switching to a new one.
Another option would be a residual-value arrangement, similar to financing used for cars.
“This means that you pay a certain amount in instalments for a couple of years and then decide whether to buy the device or leave it,” Stasiulaitis said.
Operators promise prices will not rise
Mobile operators acknowledge that the new rules could frustrate some customers but say they will continue offering ways to access smartphones at different price points.
Tele2's Buitkutė said phones would remain available at a wide range of prices, from about 200 euros to more than 1,000 euros.
“There will always be good offers, and we will continue arranging those offers so that customers are not left without phones,” she said, describing smartphones as an essential means of communication.
Špakauskas said smartphones had become indispensable for education, work and staying in touch with family and friends, making the changes particularly significant.
Stasiulaitis said customers would still have several ways to obtain devices, even if the arrangements and terminology changed.
Operators do not expect the new requirements to increase device prices.
The timing is a concern for some consumers who have already planned to buy smartphones for relatives as Christmas gifts. Some residents of Vilnius said they would now try to complete their instalment purchases before the new rules take effect on November 20.

Is there a limit to delaying the proceedings: the case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors may be closed due to the expiration of the statute of limitations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:47:20 EET
23:47:20 KST

Is there a limit to delaying the proceedings: the case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors may be closed due to the expiration of the statute of limitations
Kyiv • UNN
On October 27, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa was unable to continue hearing the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors due to a motion filed by the defense. The next hearing is scheduled for October 29.
On October 27, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa once again failed to continue hearing the case concerning the medical negligence of doctors at the private Odrex clinic. According to the publication’s sources, this time the reason was a motion filed by Yuliia Duz, the lawyer for defendant Maryna Bielotserkovska, who is occupied with other court proceedings. As a result, the hearing scheduled for October 28 was also postponed, UNN reports.
The next hearings in the case are scheduled for October 29 and 30. However, whether they will take place remains an open question. The court proceedings in the case concerning the medical negligence of Odrex doctors are overwhelmed by postponements, which may raise suspicions that the process is being deliberately protracted in order to allow the statute of limitations to expire.
In September, the court managed to hold fewer than half of the scheduled hearings in full—6 out of 13. October risks becoming an even greater mockery of the Ukrainian judicial system. Of the 16 hearings scheduled for the month, as of October 27 only three had taken place in full, while another 11 had been postponed. Even if the final two October hearings do take place, the court will end the month with a record of "5 out of 16".
Two years after Adnan Kivan’s death: will the court manage to deliver a verdict?
It is symbolic that the latest postponement of the hearing took place precisely on October 27 and 28 — the second anniversary of the death of Odesa businessman Adnan Kivan. He died on October 27, 2024, while being treated for cancer at the private Odrex clinic.
According to the investigation, after the surgical intervention, doctors Rusakov and Bielotserkovska may have failed to provide appropriate treatment for postoperative complications. This could have contributed to the development of sepsis, which, against the backdrop of the cancer, may have led to Adnan Kivan’s death.
Surgeon Vitalii Rusakov and oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska are charged under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—improper performance by a medical professional of their professional duties, resulting in serious consequences for a patient.
Neither doctor admits guilt. The court must provide a final assessment of their actions or inaction. However, it is unknown whether this process will be completed before the statute of limitations expires.
Under Article 49 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, the limitation period for the offense charged against the doctors is three years. If the actions or inaction attributed to them took place in October 2024, the issue of the statute of limitations expiring could arise as early as autumn 2027—unless there are grounds established by law for suspending or interrupting it.
At the same time, the law establishes an important condition: the limitation period is calculated up to the moment the verdict enters into legal force. Thus, even if the court of first instance manages to issue a decision, subsequent appellate proceedings may be relevant to the application of this provision.
What does this mean for the defendants? If the conditions established by law are met, the court may release them from criminal liability because the statute of limitations has expired, without finally resolving the issue of guilt. At the same time, closing the proceedings in this manner is not an acquittal and does not establish a person’s innocence.
If the doctors are confident of their innocence and seek specifically an acquittal in order to defend their professional reputation, they may insist that the court proceedings continue.
Who will be held responsible for delaying the court proceedings?
The constant postponement of hearings raises another fundamental question: who must ensure that a high-profile criminal case is heard within a reasonable time if the defendants’ lawyers regularly file motions to adjourn the hearings?
Earlier, retired judge of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine Oleksandr Sytnykov emphasized in a comment to UNN that responsibility for observing reasonable time limits for court proceedings also rests, in particular, with the presiding judge. Even if delays are caused by the actions of the participants in the proceedings, the court must use the mechanisms provided by law to ensure the timely consideration of the case.
"A judge has procedural time limits, compliance with which may also make the judge subject to disciplinary liability," Sytnykov emphasized.
According to him, обращения to disciplinary bodies because of the conduct of participants in the proceedings does not release the presiding judge from the duty to respond to further delays.
Let us remind you
The presiding judge in the Odrex doctors' case, Viktor Chaplytskyi, responded to the systematic absences of defense attorneys more than a month and a half ago. Chaplytskyi deemed the reasons for the defense lawyers' absence from September 1 to 10 unjustified and sent the corresponding ruling to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar (QDСB).

Old aviation — new possibilities: “MS AVIA-GRADE” explained the role of helicopter modernization
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:46:59 EET
23:46:59 KST

Old aviation — new possibilities: “MS AVIA-GRADE” explained the role of helicopter modernization
Kyiv • UNN
“MS AVIA-GRADE” noted that modernizing aviation equipment makes it possible to continue operating time-tested helicopters and avoid significant costs associated with purchasing new aircraft.
The high cost of developing and procuring new aircraft worldwide is prompting the aviation industry to seek ways to use existing equipment more efficiently. One such way is modernization, which makes it possible to combine time-tested designs with modern equipment and technologies. UNN asked Oleksandr Nahapetyan, Deputy Director for Airworthiness at MS AVIA-GRADE, what determines the possibilities for such an upgrade.
Details
Aviation is an industry that requires significant financial and time resources to renew its technical fleet. Creating a new aircraft or helicopter model is a highly complex process that can take years. Therefore, alongside the development of new aircraft, the modernization of those already in service plays an important role.
The age of an aircraft or helicopter alone does not always determine how effectively it can be used. The condition of the structure, remaining service life, availability of spare parts, maintainability, and compliance with current requirements are all important.
The modernization of existing aviation equipment is now one of the key trends in the global aviation industry and military affairs. Against the backdrop of the rapidly increasing cost of developing and procuring new aircraft, upgrading time-tested platforms is becoming the most economically beneficial solution. An aircraft or helicopter may have been built decades ago, yet its airframe often has an enormous strength reserve. That is why completely scrapping equipment because of moral obsolescence is an unjustified waste
From repairs to comprehensive upgrades
Modernization is often perceived as replacing outdated parts or installing new equipment. In reality, it is a comprehensive process that usually begins with a major overhaul and restoration of the service life of the fuselage and main load-bearing elements.
The greatest changes affect the machine's "internal content"—outdated analog instruments are replaced with modern digital avionics. The installation of a "glass cockpit" concept with multifunctional displays radically improves ergonomics and reduces the workload on the crew
Depending on the aircraft's purpose, navigation systems, satellite communications, and night-vision equipment may also be upgraded, making it possible to carry out missions around the clock in all weather conditions.
Mi-8 as an example of the long-term operation of an aviation platform
One example of a platform that remains widespread in various countries around the world is the Mi-8 family of helicopters.
Developed back in the last century, this mass-produced helicopter remains an indispensable workhorse in dozens of countries thanks to continuous improvements
The long-term operation of the Mi-8 family has been accompanied by the emergence of various modifications that differ in equipment and technical solutions.
For example, modern Mi-8MSB modifications receive more powerful engines with an electronic control system, which significantly improves flight performance in high-altitude and hot conditions. Thanks to the installation of modern Western or advanced domestic protection systems, the old transport helicopter becomes resistant to the latest man-portable surface-to-air missile systems.
Such changes make it possible to adapt the helicopter for both civil transport and complex search-and-rescue or airborne missions.
The modernization of other types of aviation equipment, including Mi-24 helicopters, may also involve upgrading onboard equipment and individual systems. The scope of the changes is determined by the technical condition of the specific aircraft, its design features, and the requirements for its further operation.
No less illustrative is the story of modernizing the Mi-24 attack helicopter, known for its unique concept. Despite the platform's considerable age, its thorough modernization allows it to compete confidently with newer examples of attack aircraft. Modern avionics, guidance systems, and onboard defense systems enable the "old platform" to perform missions under modern combat conditions
The balance between technology and economic feasibility
Of course, modernization cannot always replace the procurement of new equipment. However, in cases where the aircraft's technical condition and the scope of work required make it possible, it can become a way to extend its service life and use available resources more efficiently.
Updating equipment makes it possible to maintain high defense capability and logistical potential without astronomical costs. Extending the relevance of old aircraft and helicopters is not merely a compromise, but a sober and pragmatic calculation. By investing in new technologies, aviation gains a second life and remains in service for many more decades

UN political mission in Somalia to cease operations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:45:57 CST
23:45:57 KST

MOGADISHU, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will complete its two-year transition and cease operations on Oct. 31, the United Nations (UN) said on Monday.
The closure follows UN Security Council resolutions 2753 (2024) and 2809 (2025) and comes in response to a request from the Somali government.
On the same day, UNTMIS Officer-in-Charge Raisedon Zenenga and Somali Deputy Prime Minister Salah Jama co-led a ceremony marking the conclusion of the mission's mandate.
The ceremony was attended by senior government officials, international partners, civil society representatives and senior UN personnel.
"As UNTMIS concludes its mandate, we do so with gratitude for the trust and partnership extended to us, with pride in the dedication and achievements of UN personnel in Somalia, and deep respect for the resilience and determination of the Somali people," Zenenga said in a statement.
"Above all, we leave with the conviction that the partnership between Somalia and the UN will endure, together with our shared hope for a peaceful, stable, and prosperous Somalia," he added.
Unlike military missions, UNTMIS was a political mission that provided support to Somali authorities in areas including elections, justice, security sector reform and human rights.
The closure will not affect the separate African Union mission deployed to support security and stabilization efforts in Somalia, including operations against al-Shabab.
Zenenga emphasized that the closure did not signal the end of UN support for Somalia or diminish the commitment of its international partners. Instead, he said, the transition marked a new chapter in the partnership between the UN and Somalia.
The closure marks the end of a UN political mission presence in Somalia that dated back to 2013, when the United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM) was established.
UNSOM was replaced by UNTMIS in November 2024 as part of a two-year transition aimed at transferring the mission's functions to Somali institutions and the UN country team. ■

Sudan’s war steals children’s future with school closures and displacement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:45:41 UTC
23:45:41 KST

Sudan’s war steals children’s future with school closures and displacement
The conflict in Sudan has left millions of children without education, as they work to help their families.
Nine-year-old Abkar Mohammed works cleaning and polishing shoes on the streets of Port Sudan every day. He arrived in the eastern Sudanese city with his mother and three siblings from Khartoum days after the country’s armed conflict erupted on April 15, 2023.
Abkar lost his father before the war began and the family live in a rented a home in al-Kasara, a low-income neighbourhood in Port Sudan.
Due to the family’s financial situation, he doesn’t go to school but does attend classes at a traditional “khalwa” where he learns the Quran.
“When my lesson finishes, I pick up my shoe-cleaning equipment and head to busy areas to work,” he told Al Jazeera. “In the evening, I take public transport home, making sure I get back before sunset.”
He gets around 1,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.11) to clean or stitch a pair of shoes, and by the end of the day, he earns around 10,000 pounds ($1.08). He gives the money to his mother to cover the family’s daily needs.
“My 23-year-old brother works on casual jobs in the markets to cover most of the household expenses,” he said.
Abkar’s story echoes the lives of eight million of the country’s 17 million school-age children who are out of school, according to UNICEF.
In Darfur, one of the areas of Sudan hardest hit by the war, about 80 percent of schools remained closed with 70 percent of children in the area not attending classes.
Save the Children estimates that children in Sudan have missed on average about 484 days of classroom learning since the war began in April 2023, due to prolonged school closures, fighting, displacement and damage to education facilities.
The Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in conflict with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since 2023, has been accused of targeting schools and universities in drone strikes, along with other civilian infrastructure.
In September 2026, a drone attack on two warehouses in North Kordofan destroyed more than 330,000 school textbooks and other learning materials.
Sulaima Ishag, head of the Government Advisory Council for Women and Children, told Al Jazeera that children who live in conflict zones, such as Darfur and parts of Kordofan, are at greatest risk of permanently losing access to education. This can have a dire impact on their future, particularly for girls.
“[There are] cases of school dropouts and child marriage reported, alongside sexual violence. [Girls] face additional risks, including adolescent pregnancy and increased domestic responsibilities, which can further limit their chances of returning to education,” Sulaima told Al Jazeera.
“The absence of schools as safe and protective environments leaves children increasingly vulnerable to a range of threats, including child labour, early marriage, recruitment and use by armed groups, exploitation, sexual violence, trafficking and family separation. It also takes a significant psychological and social toll on children … [particularly those] from the poorest families … even in areas considered relatively safe.”
Eva Hinds, UNICEF’s head of advocacy and communication in Sudan, said that nearly half of all school buildings in the country no longer function as classrooms, due to war damage.
“Displaced children, many of whom have been forced to flee several times, face additional barriers, as repeated displacement disrupts their learning and separates them from teachers and classmates, often leaving them without learning materials or a safe place to study,” Hinds told Al Jazeera.
Children who no longer attend school lose access to a safe space and are exposed to the risks associated with child labour, recruitment by armed groups, and other abuses.
Hinds warned that the longer children remain out of school, the harder it will become for them to make up for lost learning. This disruption can deepen existing inequalities and mean that a generation of Sudanese children and young people will be unable to contribute to the country’s future peace, recovery and development.
“The conflict in Sudan continues to have a devastating impact on children’s education. The consequences extend far beyond the classroom,” said Hinds.
Psychologist Hanaa Mohamed told Al Jazeera that prolonged displacement and interruptions to schooling have taken a significant psychological toll on children. Many are in a constant state of fear, experience sleep disturbances and have difficulty focusing.
“These pressures have also led to changes in behaviour, including increased aggression or social withdrawal,” she told Al Jazeera. “Being out of school deprives children of an important protective environment. The absence of that protection has also helped bring cases of violence and sexual exploitation against children to light.”
Sudan’s economy has been set back 30 years by the war, with 60 percent of Sudanese now living in poverty.
Families fleeing the conflict often enter new towns or camps where they have few social connections and sometimes are just carrying the clothes on their backs. Sudan’s dire financial situation means that there are few jobs available for adults, forcing parents to turn to their children for essential income.
Saliha Omer, who sells tea on a street in Port Sudan, said her meagre finances prevented her from enrolling her 11-year-old son in school.
He currently works at a grocery shop in Port Sudan, but Saliha plans to return to Khartoum in the coming days so he can attend school.
“I couldn’t enrol him because of our financial circumstances after we were displaced,” Saliha told Al Jazeera.
Mahmoud al-Ghali, 16, has not been to school since the war broke out when he was aged 13, and has been displaced several times during the war.
For the past three years he has sold sweets and crisps on the streets of Port Sudan to provide his family with extra income.
Mahmoud remembers his final days at school, when he and his classmates sat their end-of-year exams. They were preparing for intermediate school and a new chapter in their lives, but the war changed their plans.
“After reaching Al-Fao in December 2023, I worked as a street vendor until I managed to save some money. Then I came to Port Sudan with my uncle in July 2025, hoping to earn more so I could help my family with household expenses,” he told Al Jazeera.
Mahmoud buys packets of crisps or sweets from local shopkeepers and sells them on the streets. At the end of the day, he pays the trader back for the goods he bought and keeps the small profit of around 20,000 Sudanese pounds, less than $3 a day.
This hand-to-mouth existence and the constant financial pressure on his family, worsened by rising cost of living, means he also has little hope of returning to school.
But his two younger brothers have now returned to classes in their village in Gaziera State after the SAF regained control of the area. Mahmoud hopes to save enough money to expand his small trading business.
“I’ve got used to working because circumstances have left me with little choice,” he said. “I no longer feel as strongly about going back to school as I once did, but I’ll keep trying so my younger brothers can finish their education.”

A UN report published on Oct. 19 says Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid may amount to crimes against humanity.
The report, penned by the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine and submitted by the UN secretary general, says the attacks show the Russian military’s intent to deprive the Ukrainian civilian population of the necessary means of survival.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The Commission assesses that the Russian commanders ordering the attacks had the knowledge that the heating facilities they targeted in large civilian agglomerations were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter,” the report says.
Russian authorities have made declarations to attack Ukraine’s energy grid, the report says, adding that the attacks were “carried out with intent and pursuant to a state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering.”
The UN report also notes that Russia has been launching similar attacks since 2022 – including the winter of 2025-26, when attacks on heating facilities turned off heating in subzero temperatures – before noting that the attacks have “intensified.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed to strike Ukraine’s energy grid in December 2022, with recent Kremlin statements suggesting that it aims to pressure Kyiv towards capitulation this winter.
Russia Pounds Kyiv’s Energy Infrastructure: How Are Residents Preparing for Winter?
After the previous winter, Russia has begun to target Ukraine’s energy grid in earnest in October 2026, with regular blackouts already introduced nationwide ahead of the coldest months.
Water disruptions were also reported in Kyiv and other cities after Russia targeted facilities needed to power the pumps, with Ukrainians interviewed by Kyiv Post calling it a major concern ahead of the winter.
Ukraine’s energy minister said Kyiv has obtained detailed Russian plans on the energy attacks, including but not limited to the use of roughly 1,000 weapons to disable power facilities nationwide.
On Oct. 19, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia damaged 28 Ukrainian substations overnight.
“The Commission has concluded that the Russian authorities have committed war
crimes of intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects and the crimes against
humanity of other inhumane acts,” the UN report adds.
With Russia’s suffering frontline setbacks in Ukraine’s Donbas region, where Ukraine has liberated much of the territory Russia occupied in 2026, speculators suggest both sides expect each other to break this winter.
No energy truce in sight
Ukraine has sought to intensify attacks on Russian refineries – a major revenue source for the Kremlin – after a summer campaign that reportedly disabled 43% of Russia’s refining capacity, while Russia has sought to decimate Ukraine’s already-battered energy grid.
US President Donald Trump touted an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow in October, though the terms appeared to cover only refineries, not other energy facilities, favoring Moscow.
After Trump demanded Kyiv stop hitting Russian refineries, Kyiv paused briefly before resuming about a week later after Russia continued hitting Ukraine’s energy grid.
On Monday, the Kremlin said the ongoing peace talks, with trilateral talks involving the US, Russia, and Ukraine under discussion, would not slow down Russian attacks on Ukraine.
