Asia-Pacific Community: China-Indonesia healthcare cooperation brings hope to rare-disease patients
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:45:00 CST
23:45:00 KST

JAKARTA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A four-year-old Indonesian boy suffering from severe drug-resistant epilepsy experienced three to five seizures a day. Despite repeated attempts with various anti-seizure medications, doctors struggled to bring his condition under control.
A breakthrough came through genetic testing. Using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) technology provided by China's BGI Genomics and its Indonesian partner PT Naleya Genomik Indonesia (NGI), doctors identified genetic variants associated with neuronal excitability and ion channel function, allowing them to adjust the boy's treatment.
Two months later, his major seizures were completely controlled, and his quality of life had improved significantly.
The case highlights how growing healthcare cooperation between China and Indonesia is making a tangible difference in the lives of local patients.
For many Indonesian families with children suffering from rare diseases, obtaining an accurate diagnosis can be a long and difficult journey. Complex symptoms and limited access to specialized medical services often force patients to visit multiple hospitals and undergo repeated examinations, sometimes taking months or even years to identify the underlying cause.
Lydia Pratanu, a senior clinical geneticist at Indonesia's Harapan Kita Women and Children's Hospital, said specialized diagnostic services remain limited even in Jakarta.
Some children from distant regions, including Papua and Medan, have to fly to Jakarta for medical examinations, placing an additional financial burden on their families and potentially delaying treatment, she said.
In recent years, the introduction of Chinese genetic testing technologies has offered new possibilities for addressing these challenges.
Achmad Rafli, a pediatric neurologist at Indonesia's Cipto Mangunkusumo National Central General Hospital who was involved in treating the boy with epilepsy, said conventional diagnostic methods previously yielded detection rates of only around 5 to 15 percent in certain complex cases.
With the introduction of advanced technologies, the diagnostic yield for complex epilepsy cases at his medical center has risen to approximately 45 to 48 percent.
For some patients, the time required to reach a definitive diagnosis has been shortened from years to just a few weeks.
"These technologies have not only improved diagnostic accuracy and efficiency but also enabled doctors to identify the genetic causes of diseases more precisely, providing a basis for subsequent personalized treatment," Rafli said.
Behind these technological advances lies the steadily deepening healthcare cooperation between China and Indonesia.
In 2024, the two countries agreed on further cooperation in healthcare, infectious disease prevention and control, medical personnel training, and the establishment of more sister-hospital partnerships.
From intergovernmental agreements to clinical practice, the cooperation has produced concrete results.
In 2024, the Cardiovascular Hospital of Xiamen University in China established cooperation with Indonesia's Dr. Soetomo General Academic Hospital. Chinese medical experts traveled to Indonesia to provide guidance on cardiovascular interventional procedures and help train young Indonesian doctors.
In January this year, Xuzhou Medical University and Indonesia's National Standardization Agency signed a cooperation agreement to jointly establish the China-Indonesia Joint Laboratory for Digital Medicine and Proactive Health.
In July, Indonesia's Ministry of Health announced the unveiling of a prototype quadrivalent dengue mRNA vaccine jointly developed by the University of Indonesia, China's Tsinghua University and an Indonesian biotechnology company, underscoring the potential for bilateral cooperation in medical innovation.
Meanwhile, medical training, technical seminars and joint research projects have helped strengthen Indonesia's local diagnostic capabilities.
Pratanu expressed hope that advanced genetic testing technologies could eventually be made available in more Indonesian cities, reducing the need for patients to travel long distances to Jakarta for medical care.
Heru Dharmadi, president director of NGI, said combining China's expertise in technology development and large-scale genetic testing with Indonesia's local clinical needs could help build a more comprehensive healthcare system.
"I hope that in the future, more Indonesian professionals will lead innovation in medical technology, and more families will have access to the healthcare services they need," he said. ■

Rare “angel of death” mushroom found growing in Soest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:44:34 UTC
23:44:34 KST

Rare “angel of death” mushroom found growing in Soest
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
An extremely rare poisonous mushroom known as the “angel of death”, or formally Amanita virosa, has been discovered growing in Soest, a town in the Utrecht countryside.
It is considered a “notorious” species of fungus among mycologists, according to RTV Utrecht, for its toxicity and rarity. It was presumed extinct in the region and is designated as endangered.
Mycologist Rob Chrispijn told RTV he “jumped for joy” when he found one growing while leading a tour of the De Paltz estate in Soest. The species’ decline has come amid increased acidity in the soil, something related to the nitrogen crisis.
The fungus can be easily mistaken for an edible button mushroom, but failing to distinguish it before picking and eating could be life-threatening.
Chrispijn said that symptoms wouldn’t be immediate, but later you could suffer severe gastrointestinal problems and nausea after digesting, and “after two days, the liver and kidneys are affected, and the consequences can be permanent.”
Only two of the mushrooms were found on the estate, one of which is being examined for research. The other is remaining in the ground where it was, but Chrispijn said he isn’t worried anyone will be careless enough to eat it.

Bulgaria has the highest number of road fatalities in the EU in 2025
Unknown

News
Bulgaria has the highest number of road fatalities in the EU in 2025
Tuesday 27 October 2026 15:34
Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 15:34
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
Bulgaria has the highest road traffic fatality rate in the European Union, according to data for 2025 published by the European Commission, BNR correspondent in Brussels Angelina Piskova reports. Last year, 71 people per million inhabitants lost their lives in road accidents in Bulgaria. At the other end of the scale, Sweden recorded 19 fatalities per million inhabitants, compared with an EU average of 43.
Despite these alarming figures, Bulgaria is among five countries on track to meet the EU target of halving road deaths by 2030. The other countries are Belgium, Denmark, Poland and Romania.
Older people are the most frequent victims of road traffic accidents. Those at greatest risk include car occupants and vulnerable road users such as pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists. Most road fatalities occur on roads outside built-up areas. For every person killed in a road accident, five others sustain serious injuries.

Neil Young sues Donald Trump's political committee for copyright infringement - again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:42:59 UTC
23:42:59 KST

Neil Young has filed a $10 million suit against Donald Trump's political action committee, Trump 47 Committee Inc., for using his hit song ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ - six years after a prior settlement over the same song.
Legendary Canadian rocker Neil Young has filed a lawsuit against Donald Trump’s political committee, alleging copyright infringement over the organisation’s ongoing use of his song ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ during midterm election rallies. The 1989 hit is frequently used as Trump's walk-on music.
Young’s camp is requesting $10 million (approx. €8.9m) in damages and that Trump’s team be barred from playing the song in public.
The lawsuit, filed on Monday and seen by Variety, highlights how Trump 47 Committee Inc.’s unsanctioned use of Young’s song violates the terms of a past settlement, as the musician and his publishing company, Silver Fiddle Music, filed a copyright infringement suit against Trump’s presidential campaign in 2020.
Young later dismissed the lawsuit, but only after reaching a settlement with the Trump campaign – which included the promise that they would not use ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ without permission.
“The Committee does not now have, and did not at the time of the Youngstown Rally or any other rally financed and conducted by the Committee, have a license or Young’s permission to play the Song at any public political event,” states the new lawsuit.
The lawsuit also highlights that Trump has clearly not listened to (or bothered to read) the song’s lyrics, as it is a famously anti-Republican.
Young wrote the track as a critical commentary on politics and American society during the George H.W. Bush years. The song clearly paints the contradictions and pitfalls of the so-called "American Dream".
“‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ is a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” the document states. “The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits - a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity -while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all.”
“In short, the song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for."
The opening lyrics to the song are: "There's colours on the street / Red, white and blue / People shufflin' their feet / People sleepin' in their shoes / But there's a warnin' sign on the road ahead / There's a lot of people sayin' we'd be better off dead / Don't feel like Satan, but I am to them / So I try to forget it any way I can...”
For most, it's hardly a difficult metaphor to grasp...
The suit also alleges that Young “has suffered and continues to suffer from great injury” over the alleged infringement, adding that he also “suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. Trump in any way.”
Young has been a longstanding and vocal critic of Trump. Last year, he came to the defence of Bruce Springsteen and Taylor Swift, both of whom Trump had criticised and even threatened.
At the time, Young shared a new blog post on the Neil Young Archives website, where he defended his fellow musicians.
“Bruce and thousands of musicians think you are ruining America. You worry about that instead of the dyin’ kids in Gaza. That’s your problem. I am not scared of you. Neither are the rest of us.”
He continued: “You shut down FEMA when we needed it most. That’s your problem Trump. STOP THINKING ABOUT WHAT ROCKERS ARE SAYING. Think about saving America from the mess you made.”
“Taylor Swift is right. So is Bruce. You know how I feel. You are more worried about yourself than AMERICA. Wake up Trump!! Remember what the White House is?”
He finished his blog entry by writing: “You are forgetting your real job. You work for us. Wake up Republicans! This guy is out of control. We need a real president!”
Earlier this year, Young even offered Greenlanders free access to his music in the wake of Trump's threats of annexation.
He wrote on his website: “I’m honoured to give a free year’s access to neilyoungarchives.com to all of our friends in Greenland. I hope my music and music films will ease some of the unwarranted stress and threats you are experiencing from our unpopular and hopefully temporary government.”
Young is far from the only high-profile musician to take legal action against the Trump administration for playing their songs without authorisation.
Everyone from Creedence Clearwater Revival to Tom Petty, via The Rolling Stones, Adele, Foo Fighters, Céline Dion, The White Stripes, ABBA and many more have called out Trump for using their songs without permission.
Other cases include Bruce Springsteen objecting in 2016 to Trump blasting 'Born in the U.S.A.' as a patriotic anthem, when it’s actually a scathing indictment of the treatment of Vietnam vets; Rihanna demanding that Trump stop playing 'Don’t Stop the Music' after the song played at a 2018 rally; and R.E.M. being outraged that their tracks 'Losing My Religion', 'Everybody Hurts' and 'It’s the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine)' were used at rallies.
In 2020, Leonard Cohen’s estate issued a statement criticizing Trump's unauthorized use of Cohen’s ‘Hallelujah’ at the Republican National Convention – having specifically rejected permission for its use. The estate, rather brilliantly, added that they would have only realistically considered approving Cohen's song ‘You Want It Darker’.
In June, Ariana Grande became one of the latest artists to protest Trump's antics, calling out the White House for using one of her songs in a social media post promoting ICE arrests.
She wrote: “Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense. F*** ICE."
The 2026 United States midterm elections are scheduled to be held on Tuesday 3 November.

Long-term defense agreements with European partner countries can undermine the Russian leadership's strategy of waging a war of attrition and are part of a plan to achieve peace in Ukraine through strength, Ukrainian MP and European Solidarity party leader Petro Poroshenko believes.
"Putin hopes that he will exhaust Ukraine, exhaust Europe and wait until our societies grow tired, fall out with each other and turn away from one another. We must ensure that each successive year undermines Putin's calculation. This requires long-term defense agreements with European partners, joint ventures, joint development projects, production lines with funding already allocated and orders placed years in advance, rather than blocking joint production with partners in Ukraine and Europe for corrupt purposes," Poroshenko said in a video address published on YouTube on Tuesday.

Poroshenko outlined six points in a plan that, he believes, would "stop this war so that our children inherit a secure country and the freedom to choose their future."
The other five points include strengthening Ukraine to improve its negotiating position, with this reflected in the military budget, and weakening Russia's ability to wage war through strikes on key military targets on the territory of the aggressor state. He also called for tighter sanctions until continuing the war becomes unprofitable for Russia.
The plan also calls for ensuring that any ceasefire is monitored and that violations have inevitable consequences. The final point is reparations and the country's reconstruction.
"First and foremost, we must do everything possible to ensure that Ukrainians return home. This plan must look forward. We must not restore the old economy but build a new, post-industrial, modern, European and technologically advanced Ukraine, with modern energy infrastructure that is harder to destroy, protected infrastructure, education that opens up opportunities, and cities where a person recovering from injury can move around freely, work and finally live," Poroshenko said.

The French government explored ways to block access to social media and mobile internet in specific areas during last Saturday’s protests to prevent protesters from coordinating, according to a media report Tuesday.
In the week leading up to Oct. 24, the Interior Ministry contacted telecom operators to explore ways of cutting access to social networks or even mobile internet in specific areas to prevent “rioters” from coordinating, Politico reported, citing a government official and an employee of a telecom company.
The discussions culminated in Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu directly asking French telecom operators to be prepared to block access to some social media platforms, including US social media company X, in a letter revealed by French digital outlet Blast, which first reported on the government’s request.
The report noted that officials from Lecornu’s office, the Technology Ministry and the Interior Ministry neither denied the move nor the existence of the letter.
“What they wanted, above all, was to block the communication channels that allow gangs to meet up and organize,” said an employee of a telecommunications provider who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The government also considered another option that would disable location-sharing features “to prevent gatherings of people who don’t know each other, for example,” according to the official from the prime minister’s office.
The Interior Ministry said Sunday that authorities arrested more than 1,300 people during nationwide demonstrations Saturday, while 53 security personnel were injured.
According to the ministry, 410,000 people took part in Saturday’s demonstrations across France, including 110,000 in Paris.
Trade unions, however, estimated nationwide turnout at nearly 800,000, with 250,000 protesters in the capital.
The ministry also said 24 businesses were looted during the demonstrations, compared with 1,522 a week earlier, representing a decline of more than 98%.

Russia’s agricultural exports to India soared in the first nine months of the year, powered by sunflower oil shipments, the Russian agency Agroexport has said, citing estimates.
The federal agency told Interfax that shipments had reached 1.3 million tons between January and September, an 11% surge in volumes

Karmen Turk: Why Estonia's gambling license is not attracting foreign operators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:42:00 UTC
23:42:00 KST

Karmen Turk: Why Estonia's gambling license is not attracting foreign operators
Estonia has strengthened its regulations through economic and money laundering crises, but along with the rules, the procedural environment has also changed, no longer conforming to good practice but instead deterring international companies, attorney-at-law Karmen Turk writes.
No one is disputing that a gambling operator is required to combat money laundering. The law requires it. The question lies elsewhere: do Estonia's rules prevent money laundering, or do they primarily act as a barrier to new companies coming to Estonia? Unfortunately, experience over the past year points more towards the latter.
The recently amended Remote Gambling Tax Act has brought into focus international opportunities for financing Estonia's state budget and, in particular, sport and culture. The environment here could be attractive given the purpose of an Estonian license is simple: to bring tax revenue earned elsewhere into digitally advanced Estonia. International remote gambling operators will not be targeting Estonian players. Their customers are in other countries, around the world. An Estonian license, however, means that taxes on their activities are paid into Estonia and go towards financing our sports and culture. Every license brought into Estonia is thus a victory for Estonian culture and sports, yet without increasing gambling in Estonia. To achieve this goal, however, companies need to actually come to Estonia. But what is deterring companies today? The simple answer is: fear-driven regulation that diminishes the legal opportunities created in Estonia, because every applicant is treated primarily as a potential risk.
To explain in more detail, a gambling operating license is issued by the Tax and Customs Board (MTA), but it must first be approved by the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU). The applicant must submit their internal anti-money laundering regulations, appoint a person who will communicate with the FIU (the so-called contact person), and submit documents concerning its owners and managers. Companies already operating must meet these requirements by January 1, 2027, at the latest. Gambling operators are now essentially treated in the same way as financial companies and cryptocurrency firms are. The purpose of stricter rules is understandable. The problem lies in how they get applied in practice.
The contact person must work in Estonia
Under current law, the contact person must be working on a permanent basis in Estonia. The FIU's training materials even state that "the entire department should be located in Estonia." In addition, the contact person must have suitable education, experience and an impeccable reputation, while the FIU must approve their appointment.
What does our regulation mean for an international company? Usually, the people responsible for its anti-money laundering controls work in the same location as its IT and payments teams would do, for example in Latvia, Italy or Malta. In order to obtain an Estonian license, however, it must find someone who works in Estonia, understands the risks of the gambling sector and passes the FIU's checks. The FIU has also indicated that one person may serve as a contact person for no more than two companies, and must have a replacement during vacation periods. In reality, consequently, one contact person is not sufficient; two experts meeting the same criteria are needed – but this is an over-regulation of the requirements. Estonia is small and there are few such specialists. This is as a result not merely a formality, but a real barrier to market entry.
Where the contact person sits says nothing about the quality of their work. The FIU's own updated guidelines do not mention location either. They require the contact person to report directly to the management board, to be competent and to have access to all the necessary information at all times. Even an entire department can serve as the contact person. None of these conditions depends on the country. On the contrary, actual knowledge and control are more effective when they are "close" to the operations themselves. According to the FIU's own data, the sector's real weakness is also the detection of suspicious transactions. In 2025, only about 14 percent of reports were related to genuine suspicions, while nearly 94 percent of all reports came from only about a tenth of all companies. This problem is solved by a good monitoring system and a skilled team, not by whether the contact person sits in Tallinn or in Rome. If a company's international team is stronger than an individual specialist who can be found in Estonia, the Estonian requirement may n fact weaken controls. This also raises a question of EU law. Companies with Estonian licenses often belong to groups managed in other EU countries and mainly serve foreign customers. The EU guarantees companies the right to operate and provide services in other member states. The European Court of Justice has allowed countries to restrict gambling, but only if the restriction has good grounds, genuinely helps achieve its objective, is applied consistently and does not go further than necessary. Estonia's location requirement is questionable in light of the last two conditions. First, it is not consistent: according to the FIU's guidelines, customers from other EU countries are considered lower risk, but a specialist working in another EU country is considered a risk. Second, less restrictive solutions exist. It would be sufficient for the contact person to be available at all times, communicate with the FIU in Estonian and ensure that the FIU has access to the data. In addition, a uniform EU anti-money laundering regulation will take effect on July 10, 2027. It is therefore appropriate to ask whether Estonia's additional requirements, which the EU does not demand, are even still necessary.
Documents must be in Estonian
The second obstacle is the language requirement. According to the experiences of companies, the FIU requires internal rules and other documents be in Estonian. It is natural that communication with the authority would take place in Estonian. However, an international company's internal rules are an everyday working tool. They are used by employees in various countries and so get written in a language that everyone understands. If a separate Estonian-language version has to be prepared for Estonia, two documents are created: one that is actually used at work and another that is shown to the authority. This contradicts the FIU's own objective, however. The FIU will check exactly whether the rules are actually being used or exist only on paper. The updated guidelines state that the rules must be understandable to employees and describe what the company actually does. In the case of customer documents, the guidelines themselves recommend avoiding translation if the original is in a comprehensible language, such as English. There is no requirement in the guidelines for internal rules to be in Estonian. The obligation to translate does nothing to help combat money laundering.
A procedure whose duration and outcome are unknown
In 2024, the Chancellor of Justice examined the FIU's licensing procedures and identified several problems. First, the FIU does not tell applicants when all their documents are in order. As a result, applicants do not know when the statutory 60-day deadline for making a decision starts. Second, in the course of an interview, an applicant may be advised to replace the contact person, an owner or a management board member, or to withdraw the application, but these interviews are not logged in the minutes. Based on the experiences of several companies from 2026, these interviews have gone on for hours, with three to four officials questioning one person all at the same time. For a company planning investments in Estonia, uncertainty of this kind is the worst possible signal. An official refusal can be challenged in court. However, if the outcome of the procedure depends on interviews that are not recorded in minutes, the company will simply choose another country where the procedure is clear and predictable.
Rules must be based on actual risks
The state fully knows what the sector's risks are. According to the national risk assessment, the money laundering risk posed by gambling operators is high because Estonian licenses are used mainly to serve foreign customers and business partners are often located abroad. The FIU focuses on the origin of funds, the use of front persons, the splitting of transactions and cryptocurrency. These are the right issues. But having the contact person live in Estonia or the rules written in Estonian does nothing to counter these risks. What is needed is good transaction monitoring, rapid information exchange and access to data for the FIU. The latter is already guaranteed by law, even when the server is located abroad.
The law itself requires proportionality: the extent of controls must correspond to the risk and be reasonable. The same should apply to the state when it decides what to require of a new market entrant. Penalties are already severe: a fine of up to €1 million can be imposed for violating the requirements for internal rules.
Estonia does not have to choose between strict anti-money laundering controls and an attractive license in order to regulate the market and generate tax revenue. But the success of controls must be measured by whether they stop suspicious money flows. Neither an office address in Tallinn nor the language of the documentation demonstrates this.
The author of this piece advises international gambling operators.

Critics attack 'anti-democratic' French bill making rioters pay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:41:04 UTC
23:41:04 KST

Critics attack 'anti-democratic' French bill making rioters pay
PARIS, Oct 27 - A proposed French law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 ($11,150) for damage they cause faces a backlash from rights groups and some lawyers who say it attacks the basic democratic right to take to the streets to protest.
President Emmanuel Macron's government, under pressure to quell social protests accompanied by some of France's worst unrest in years, says the law is needed to compensate victims of the vandalism that often follows protests, such as the looting and rioting seen across the country on October 17.
But critics say the draft bill, being debated in parliament this week, is worded in such a way that legitimate protesters who happened to be close to the scene of any violence could also be deemed legally responsible for it and face prosecution.
"Around the edges of a protest there can be those who engage in violence or damage with no involvement from the vast majority of peaceful, legitimate demonstrators," said Hanna Bouchareb, a Paris-based lawyer who represented some of those accused in fast-track trials of taking part in rioting on October 17.
"It's very problematic because it undermines the right to protest," she told Reuters.
The text states that anyone who knowingly formed part of a group of people would be held jointly responsible for any damage caused by any member of that group.
It further allows the state to seize welfare entitlements of those convicted, or those of their parents if they are minors, to help pay the costs.
French businesses and retailers say they have lost millions of euros either through looting or vandalism or by being forced to shut their shops and board their windows during protests.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who offered his resignation to Macron last week after security forces were overwhelmed by the unrest, rejected arguments the law undermined the principle that individuals were only accountable for their own actions.
"What this draft law changes is that we are creating a joint responsibility - not a collective one," Nunez, whom Macron asked to remain at his post, told broadcaster TF1.
That is a distinction rejected by France's Human Rights League (LDH) and a group of trade unionists who signed a column in Le Monde newspaper this weekend demanding it be scrapped.
Police were accused in 2020 of using excessive force against "yellow vest" anti-government protesters and there was criticism then of a subsequently watered-down law banning circulation of images of police officers in some circumstances.
In recent weeks, protesters have again accused police of heavy-handed tactics against the student protesters while lawyers including Bouchareb have raised legal concerns over the fast-tracked convictions of some of those accused of rioting.
Backers of the proposed new law point to surveys showing broad public support for it. The National Rally (RN) party of Marine Le Pen - the far-right frontrunner for next year's presidential election - said it would go even further.
"The vandal's law is good in that it recognises the principle of joint responsibility," RN senator Edwige Diaz told French television. "But not with a cap at 10,000 euros." REUTERS

Germany’s next fighter jet puts its defense partnerships to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:40:37 UTC
23:40:37 KST

A mock-up of the New Generation Fighter for the Future Combat Air System is displayed during the Paris Air Show in France on June 18, 2023. | Julien de Rosa/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Germany faces a consequential choice over building its next fighter jet: join an existing project with the U.K., Italy and Japan, or develop a new aircraft with Sweden and Spain. The decision will shape its military capabilities and diplomatic alliances for decades.
Defense ministry assessments favor partnering with Stockholm and Madrid, citing military requirements and opportunities for German industry, while chancellery officials, according to industry and diplomatic officials who spoke with POLITICO on the basis of anonymity to discuss sensitive issues, see diplomatic advantages in aligning with London.
Advertisement
“On the one hand, all countries want to support their national industries,” Defense Minister Boris Pistorius told lawmakers in September, asked about European defense cooperation following FCAS's collapse. “At the same time, everyone ... also wants joint European armaments projects,” he said. “Resolving this dilemma is no simple matter.”
Berlin's overarching goal is to become less dependent on American military technology. And while that ambition predates Washington's increasingly unpredictable approach to European security, President Donald Trump’s threats to leave NATO and criticism of allies have raised the stakes.
At a campaign rally last week, the U.S. president warned that America would have “no choice but to leave” Europe — implying American troops on bases — if its leaders failed to change course on immigration. He also criticized NATO allies for refusing to support Washington’s war against Iran.
Ukraine’s recent difficulties with American-controlled SpaceX satellite communications, delays in deliveries of American-made air defense missiles and problems with intelligence sharing have also highlighted how countries relying on U.S. technology can remain vulnerable to decisions made in Washington.
The fighter jet decision is the most immediate test of a broader effort: Germany is also planning its own military satellite communications network that could cost €10 billion, and is working with Britain to develop European long-range missiles capable of striking targets more than 2,000 kilometers away. It also aims to meet NATO’s core defense spending target of 3.5 percent of GDP by 2029 — six years ahead of the alliance’s deadline.
But spending more will not automatically make it militarily independent. Germany cannot develop every advanced weapon by itself, so it needs partners that can deliver military capabilities while giving Germany a lasting role in developing and controlling them.
The collapse showed how partner disputes can tie up billions in taxpayer money in delays and abandoned ambitions. Now Germany’s immediate challenge is finding a replacement.
Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz give a press conference in Brühl, Germany on July 17, 2026. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images
One possibility comes from Britain, which is already developing a next-generation aircraft with Italy and Japan under the Global Combat Air Programme, or GCAP. During a visit to Berlin earlier this month, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham offered Germany the opportunity to join.
For London, German participation could help share the enormous costs of developing one of the world’s most advanced military aircraft. For Berlin, joining an existing program could offer a path forward without having to establish an entirely new project.
But the proposal has met with reservations within Germany’s defense ministry. As POLITICO previously reported, internal ministry assessments recommend pursuing a new fighter program with Sweden and Spain instead.
Advertisement
German officials fear joining GCAP would leave domestic industry with little say over key technologies and production, since responsibilities are already divided among the existing partners. Defense ministry officials see advantages in the Swedish option, including more compatible military requirements and greater opportunities for German industry.
But that may not necessarily align with Berlin's broader diplomatic ambitions.
Two political approaches
Germany and Britain have been strengthening their relationship after Brexit, including with a new friendship treaty focused in part on security and defense, and cooperation on long-range missiles. A jet partnership would deepen those ties further, tying the two countries together in one of Europe’s most strategically significant defense projects.
According to an official familiar with Airbus’ thinking, granted anonymity to speak freely on sensitive issues, officials in the chancellery appear drawn to GCAP partly because of those geopolitical advantages.
For Berlin’s political leadership, closer defense ties with Britain could help keep a major European military power and key NATO ally closely involved in the continent’s security as Europe is pushed to assume greater responsibility for its own defense.
That leaves Germany weighing the potential diplomatic gains of partnering with Britain against the military and industrial priorities officials see in a project with Sweden.
Advertisement
Diplomacy ahead
The political calculations could become more pressing in the coming weeks.
Merz is scheduled to visit Japan on Wednesday, offering an opportunity to discuss Germany's possible involvement in GCAP with one of the program's founding members. Japan's agreement would be essential to any German entry, while Tokyo is particularly concerned about preserving the 2035 deadline, as its aging F-2 fighter jets are due to begin retiring around then.
During Burnham’s visit, he and Merz agreed to task their defense teams with examining the prospect of German participation. Industry and diplomatic officials expect Merz to raise the issue during his visit to Japan.
For Merz and Pistorius, the challenge is to choose partners who can help Germany build up its defense capabilities while advancing its political, military and industrial interests.

Kyiv plans to allocate UAH 1 billion for a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said following a meeting of the Kyiv Defence Council on Tuesday.
"Today, a meeting of the capital's Defence Council took place. Among the issues considered was the implementation of a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them," Klitschko wrote on his Telegram channel.
He said the initiative had been put forward by the state and the government had adopted a resolution on the project.
The locations of the crossings will be determined by the military command and approved, among others, by the Kyiv City Military Administration. "The city, on the government's recommendation, will find the funds – UAH 1 billion for this project," Klitschko said.
As reported, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine approved an experimental project to build combined water crossings and access roads in several regions. The government adopted Resolution No. 1295 on Oct. 15.

Sudan seeks justice in face of humanitarian crisis in El Fasher, says envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:40:04 UTC
23:40:04 KST

Gulsum Incekaya, Gokhan Kavak, and Seyit Kurt
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Sudan is seeking justice amid the humanitarian crisis caused by the conflict in the country, Sudan's Ambassador to Türkiye Nadir Yousif Eltayeb said Tuesday, highlighting severe food shortages faced by civilians in El Fasher.
Speaking at a Tuesday meeting on Sudan held at the headquarters in the Turkish capital Ankara of the Foundation for Political, Economic and Social Research (SETA), Eltayeb criticized the international community's approach to the conflict in Sudan and said government forces had made intensive efforts to break the siege of El Fasher.
Eltayeb said the city has been under a complete siege for around 30 months.
"About 1 million people were surviving on aid delivered by the armed forces by air. People could not access enough food, to the point that they had to eat tree bark," he said.
He said Sudanese government forces had made more than 200 attempts to break the siege of El Fasher.
"The international community has taken a biased approach to this issue, preventing it from being resolved," he said.
'What happened in El Fasher is genocide'
Eltayeb alleged that rebel forces in Sudan are being supported by foreign countries, arguing that they would not have been able to advance without external support.
He also claimed that armed groups in El Fasher have specifically targeted certain tribes.
"What happened in El Fasher is genocide," he said.
Eltayeb said the number of people killed in El Fasher and the wider Darfur region remains unknown.
"Due to pressure from the UAE (United Arab Emirates), Sudan cannot submit reports on the massacre to the UN Security Council. The UAE supports the armed groups, but because this has not been proven, the international community cannot do anything," he claimed.
Abu Dhabi has repeatedly denied the allegations.
Eltayeb also thanked Türkiye for supporting Sudan.
"We are seeking justice for Sudan," he said.
Dire humanitarian situation following siege of El Fasher
The city of El Fasher, under siege since May 2024, fell under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on Oct. 26, 2025, following around 18 months of fighting.
The city, capital of the North Darfur state in western Sudan, had been the last major city in the Darfur region held by the Sudanese army before the RSF seized control.
Throughout the siege, access to food and medical supplies became increasingly difficult, leaving civilians facing severe humanitarian conditions as basic necessities ran out.
According to the UN Human Rights Office, more than 6,000 people were killed in the first three days of attacks after the RSF seized the city.
Following the RSF takeover, allegations emerged of killings, forced displacement, torture, and sexual violence against civilians in the city.
The UN warned that violence against civilians, including women and children, was continuing and that it had received reports of executions and sexual violence.
Around 138,200 people were displaced from El Fasher and surrounding settlements between Oct. 26, 2025 and March 1, 2026.
The city, which had a population of more than 1 million before the war, is now estimated to have fewer than 70,000 residents.
Alongside continuing security problems, access to food and health services remains severely limited.
The flight of large numbers of civilians from the city following the RSF takeover has further deepened the already severe humanitarian crisis in Darfur.

Ukraine’s Drones Have Eliminated or Wounded an Army of 300,000 Russians in Less Than a Year

Ukraine’s Drones Have Eliminated or Wounded an Army of 300,000 Russians in Less Than a Year
Ukraine’s expanding use of battlefield drones is reshaping the war against Russia, with unmanned systems now responsible for an average of more than 1,000 Russian soldiers killed or wounded every day in 2026.
Ukrainian drones have killed or wounded more than 302,000 Russian soldiers since the beginning of 2026—a number equivalent to the personnel strength of a large military force—in less than ten months of fighting, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The figures highlight the scale of Ukraine’s drone operations, which have inflicted an average of more than 1,000 Russian personnel casualties per day throughout the year.
According to the ministry, every recorded strike was documented on video through Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
March was the deadliest month for Russian troops targeted by Ukrainian drones, with 33,989 soldiers killed or wounded. April followed closely with 33,961 casualties, while February recorded the lowest figure at 26,204.
The monthly figures show that Ukrainian drone units have consistently inflicted tens of thousands of Russian casualties, with more than 30,000 recorded in January, March, April, May, July, and September combined with other monthly totals.
In September alone, Ukrainian drones killed or wounded 32,739 Russian troops. During the first 25 days of October, another 27,829 Russian personnel were recorded as killed or wounded in drone strikes.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said that drone operations play a central role in reducing Russia’s manpower, weakening the combat effectiveness of its military units, and slowing offensive operations.
Earlier, on October 16, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported that Russia had gained a net 144.5 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory between January and September 2026, roughly 45 times less than the 6,500 square kilometers claimed by Vladimir Putin.

Ukraine-Moldova Defense Deal Covers Air Defense, Cybersecurity and Joint R&D

Ukraine-Moldova Defense Deal Covers Air Defense, Cybersecurity and Joint R&D
Ukraine and Moldova signed a five-year military-technical cooperation agreement covering defense technology, air defense, cyber defense, equipment maintenance, and joint research projects, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence reported on October 26.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Moldovan Defence Minister Anatolie Nosatîi signed the agreement in the presence of Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi and Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The agreement creates a framework for exchanging technologies, practical knowledge, and battlefield experience while developing joint defense projects.
“Ukraine has experience that cannot be gained through exercises,” Khmara stated. “We are ready to share this knowledge with our partners and help them better understand the equipment’s capabilities and use it more effectively.”
Khmara added that Ukraine is already advising Moldova on the development of its air defense capabilities.
“Our task is to strengthen our own defense and help our partners become more resilient to modern threats,” he stated.
The agreement covers the modernization, repair, and maintenance of military equipment, as well as cooperation on logistics, engineering, and protection of personnel and critical infrastructure.
The two countries will also work together on specialist training, testing and evaluation of military products, technology transfers, and the development and procurement of military equipment.
Other areas include joint research and development related to military production and capability development in cyber defense, surveillance, and airspace protection.
Cooperation will primarily take the form of consultations, exchanges of technical and scientific information, professional experience, and joint work on selected projects.
The agreement will remain in force for five years and can be extended automatically. Ukraine’s Defence Ministry stressed that its implementation will not affect Moldova’s constitutionally enshrined neutral status.
The agreement comes as Russia has repeatedly violated Moldova’s airspace during its war against Ukraine. UNITED24 Media reported that Moldovan airspace has been violated more than 100 times since the full-scale invasion began, prompting Chișinău to adopt Ukrainian anti-drone tactics.

Trump Struck a Russian Diesel Deal—But US Buyers Could Still Face 20 Years in Prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:39:39 UTC
23:39:39 KST

- Category
- World
Trump Struck a Russian Diesel Deal—But US Buyers Could Still Face 20 Years in Prison
American businesses that import Russian diesel could still face severe criminal penalties—including fines of up to $1 million and up to 20 years in prison—despite President Donald Trump’s recent fuel agreement with Moscow, Rep. Jamie Raskin warned on October 26.
Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, issued the warning in a letter to the American Petroleum Institute, the US Chamber of Commerce, and American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He argued that the Trump administration cannot simply override a federal prohibition on Russian energy imports that Congress enacted after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Your members are now on notice that taking part in any effort to help President Putin hawk Russian diesel in the US is a clear and dangerous violation of federal law,” Raskin wrote.
The warning centers on the bipartisan Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act and restrictions first imposed under Executive Order 14066 in 2022. Congress later codified the prohibition, meaning lifting it requires more than a unilateral change in White House policy, Raskin argued.
“Those who choose to act in this way proceed at their own risk and will undoubtedly be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law, whether in this Administration—or the next,” he added.
According to the House Judiciary Committee Democrats, violations can carry civil penalties of up to twice the value of a prohibited transaction, while criminal violations can result in fines of up to $1 million and prison sentences of as long as 20 years. The applicable statute of limitations is 10 years.
The dispute follows Trump’s agreement to purchase nearly 2 million tons of Russian diesel. His administration subsequently issued an Office of Foreign Assets Control license intended to provide sanctions relief, but Raskin maintains that such a license cannot override the statutory import ban enacted by Congress.
Raskin said the President does have a legal path to ending the prohibition—but only after consulting Congress and certifying that Russia has met conditions established in law.
Those conditions include Russia agreeing to withdraw its forces and cease hostilities in Ukraine under terms accepted by Ukraine’s freely elected government, no longer posing an immediate military threat to NATO members, and recognizing Ukrainians’ right to choose their own leadership.
Raskin accused the administration of trying to bend existing US law to provide economic relief to Moscow.
“Even as Russia actively supplies weapons to Iran that are being used to kill American service members, President Trump has been stretching American law beyond the breaking point to throw a lifeline to Russian President Vladimir Putin and his imperialist war machine attacking the people of Ukraine,” he wrote.
Previously, US President Donald Trump blocked the implementation of sweeping sanctions and tariffs against Russia and buyers of Russian energy under a law championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, just weeks after signing the legislation himself.

The Ukrainian city of Konotop, in Sumy Oblast, is suffering its fourth consecutive day without power, following a massive Russian attack on Oct. 24, Konotop Mayor Artem Semenikhin said in a statement on Oct. 27.
There are currently "no forecasts" for the return of the city's electricity supply, Semenikhin said.
The sustained blackout follows a series of Russian drone strikes on 24. Oct, which heavily damaged the city's electrical grid.
“Schools have been damaged, and even our hospital is currently running on generators. It was a treacherous strike on civilian infrastructure in the middle of the night," Semenikhin said in an interview on Oct. 26.
Water is currently being heavily rationed in the city, with supplies only available for six hours per day, Semenikhin said. "Water is being supplied according to a schedule: from 6:00 am to 9:00 a.m. and from 6:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m.,” he said.
While Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy system have been ongoing throughout the year at a low level, Moscow has recently ramped up mass attacks to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure for its fifth winter offensive during the full-scale invasion.
Ukraine is in a vulnerable position. In just the week of Oct. 5-11, there were around 200 hits on power sector facilities and 17 on the oil and gas sector, the Energy Ministry’s press department told the Kyiv Independent. And Ukraine lacks critical air defense against Moscow’s expanding arsenal, energy specialists told the Kyiv Independent.
The recent attacks have already left hundreds of thousands of citizens in Kyiv and front-line regions suffering power and water outages.
"The overall pattern is systematic: the strikes damage the network, force emergency restrictions, and slow down repairs, especially when crews cannot work safely during air-raid alerts," Viktoria Gryb, a lawmaker and head of the parliament’s subcommittee on energy security, told the Kyiv Independent.

A stronger Frontex for better protection of the EU’s external borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:39:06 UTC
23:39:06 KST

Summary
- The European Commission proposed to further strengthen Frontex, turning it into the EU’s central actor for protecting external borders and organising returns across the Union.
- To operationalise the new EU rules on returns, the Commission has also proposed a Regulation to digitalise return, readmission and reintegration.
- It is now for the European Parliament and the Council to agree on the proposals.
On 27 October, the European Commission proposed to further strengthen Frontex, turning it into the EU’s central actor for protecting external borders and organising returns across the Union.
Frontex already plays a critically important role in supporting Member States to manage Europe’s external borders. Under the new rules, its mandate will be further reinforced, enabling it to act faster and more effectively. Key novelties include: more resources and operational capacity, a Quick Reaction Force to intervene in crisis situations, and a new Online Monitoring Centre for the early detection of potential threats at the borders. Frontex will have a dedicated Return Coordination Centre and it will now be able to help carry out returns from third countries.
To operationalise the new EU rules on returns, the Commission has also proposed a Regulation to digitalise return, readmission and reintegration. This will simplify and accelerate the management of returns across the EU, reducing administrative burden.
These proposals are delivering on the commitments announced in the 2024-2029 political guidelines and reiterated by President von der Leyen in her State of the Union address this year, to reinforce Frontex, and especially to speed up returns. It is now for the European Parliament and the Council to agree on the proposals. The Commission will support co-legislators to advance on negotiations for both Regulations.
A new Frontex Regulation
The proposed rules will ensure that Frontex has the mandate and the right tools to support Member States at the external borders and help them to carry out returns effectively. The Regulation sets out three priorities:
- More resources and operational capacity: Frontex pools resources, expertise and operational capacity that no single Member State alone could provide. To ensure a consistent high standard of border control across the EU, the Commission proposes to:
- Gradually increase Frontex’s standing corps to 30 000 officers by doubling the amount of Frontex's own standing corps officers and creating a new ‘European border and return reserve’ of 17 000 officers ready to be deployed when needed. This comes in addition to the already existing 7 000 officers seconded from Member States.
- Easier access to state-of-the-art equipment and technology. Frontex will be able to acquire, lease and co-own equipment and to carry out, coordinate or participate in joint procurement with Member States. Frontex will be able to act as a central purchasing body, also for digital and AI-enabled tools.
- Stronger on returns: Frontex will have a more proactive and strategic role to steer EU-wide return operations, maximising the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of its support, with:
- A dedicated Return Coordination Centre to collect and analyse operational information and support planning and coordination. Frontex’s support will cover the full spectrum of the return process, from early identification and voluntary return counselling to carrying out return operations and providing reintegration assistance.
- Capacity to support third countries on returns, both for technical and operational support. Frontex will be able to help organise and carry out return operations from one non-EU country to another, subject to the conclusion of an agreement with the country concerned, in compliance with fundamental rights and international standards.
- Effective crisis response: Frontex will be able to help detect dangerous trends early and to intervene quickly when there is an emergency or a crisis. This is a response to the lessons learned from this years’ crisis in Ceuta.
- A dedicated Online Monitoring and Response Centre, with the explicit mandate for Frontex to monitor publicly accessible social media content, detect developments relevant for external border management, and support action against illegal online content linked to border-security risks.
- A Quick Reaction Force to be deployed at very short notice to assist Member States to swiftly address any crisis and emergency at the external borders. The decision to deploy can be taken by the Frontex’s Executive Director following a request by a Member State facing an emergency situation.
- Improved information exchange in crisis situations, including with an obligation for Member States to report events with potential significant impact on EU borders within 24 hours in the dedicated EUROSUR network.
Digitalisation of returns
Alongside the Frontex Regulation proposal, and following the entry into force of the new Return Regulation on 16 October, the Commission is proposing a new Regulation to digitalise return, readmission and reintegration procedures across the EU. The aim is to modernise the handling of return cases, simplify and speed up administrative procedures through digitalisation, reduce administrative burden, and improve data collection and sharing.
The new rules will also strengthen Frontex’s role in developing a new EU digital architecture for the Member States, and support the new Return Regulation, complying with data protection standards and fundamental rights.
Background
The current Frontex Regulation entered into force in 2019. Since then, the role of Frontex has continuously grown, in view of the unprecedented challenges from the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the migration weaponisation attempts at the EU’s external borders.
Effective European integrated border management and an efficient return policy are mutually reinforcing and central for the Schengen area. Frontex continuously engages in capacity-building, sharing intelligence and expertise with all Member States and with neighbouring non-EU countries affected by migratory trends and cross-border crime. Always in full respect of fundamental rights and human dignity, which are built into the Frontex mandate and operations.
For more information
Regulation amending the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation - Migration and Home Affairs

Umar Kremlev, a businessman with criminal convictions and close ties to the Kremlin, joined Donald Trump Jr. on a hunting trip to Mongolia after paying hundreds of thousands of dollars for festivities at the US president’s son’s wedding.
Kremlev, president of the International Boxing Association (IBA), hunted with Trump Jr. for two days during an August trip, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Tuesday, Oct. 27.

The US president’s son spent about a week in Mongolia and shot an Altai argali, a wild sheep species subject to conservation protections.
The FT reconstructed Kremlev’s movements using accounts from hunting guides and Mongolian officials, flight data, social media posts, and public records.
                                                                                                                                                                         (Screenshot from the Financial Times report)                             
On Aug. 27, Kremlev flew by charter jet from Kazakhstan, where the IBA had held a press conference, to Ulaanbaatar. He then traveled by helicopter to a hunting camp in western Mongolia where Trump Jr. was staying.
Kremlev was accompanied by Artur Martirosov, a businessman and partner at the US-sanctioned venture capital fund Voskhod.
Kremlev later flew via Ulaanbaatar to Yakutsk to attend an IBA fight event.
The trip followed revelations in September that Kremlev had attended Trump Jr. and Bettina Anderson’s wedding in the Bahamas in May.
Russia Says Three Tankers With Diesel En Route to US
An investigation by ProPublica found that Kremlev had paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward the celebrations, including the rental of a private island and fireworks. His team also helped organize the event.
Anderson described Kremlev as a “dear friend” who had given the couple an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift,” arranging two celebratory evenings after the ceremony.
Trump Jr. subsequently repaid Kremlev, according to the Washington Times. President Donald Trump said there was nothing illegal about paying for a friend’s party, adding that he had done the same himself.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told the FT that the two men had a personal friendship rather than a business relationship and had been introduced by a mutual friend from hunting circles.
“Their friendship is based on a shared love of hunting, fishing and outdoor activities,” the spokesperson said.
Security experts warned that such personal ties could be exploited by Russian intelligence services.
Holden Triplett, who served as director of counterintelligence at the US National Security Council during Trump’s first presidency, told the FT that Russian security and intelligence services could seek to exploit anyone with connections to an influential figure, regardless of that person’s intentions.
Kremlev, whose real name is Umarali Lutfulloev, has longstanding ties to Putin’s circle. He was a member of the Night Wolves motorcycle club, which actively supports the Russian president and his policies.
According to Russian investigative outlet Proekt, Kremlev used his connections through the club to build ties with Alexei Rubezhnoy, who later headed Russia’s Presidential Security Service.
Rubezhnoy helped Kremlev become head of the Russian Boxing Federation in 2017. Kremlev has criminal convictions for extortion and assault, according to reporting cited by the FT.
After taking over the IBA in 2020, Kremlev made Russian state-owned energy giant Gazprom the association’s sole sponsor.
In 2023, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) withdrew recognition of the IBA, citing unresolved governance, financial and corruption concerns. The IOC also took control of boxing competitions at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
Kremlev is also linked to major Russian betting companies Liga Stavok, Pari, and Fonbet. He controls Russia’s Unified Gambling Regulator, which records bookmaker bets across the country.
In 2024, Russian authorities transferred control of Rolf, one of Russia’s largest car dealership groups, to Kremlev. The state had seized the company a year earlier from its founder, Sergei Petrov, who had moved to Austria and criticized Putin’s policies.

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The sovereignty of one nation cannot be ensured at the expense of other countries, including in the energy industry, Russian President Vladimir Putin said, commenting on speeches made at the summit of the Forum of Gas Exporting Countries.

This is a key point, he said.

Norway and Finland take Ukraine peace push to Putin, drawing Danish rebuke
- Finland and Norway held a 90-minute “frank and substantive” call with Vladimir Putin to explore ways to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
- The call, made “in consultation with Ukraine”, followed talks in Oslo with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
- Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen criticised the “solo” move, while the Kremlin blamed the EU and NATO for prolonging the war.
AI generated
HELSINKI – Finland’s President and Norway’s Prime Minister held a “frank and substantive” discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct 27 about efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Nordic leaders said.
It was the latest effort by Kyiv’s allies to de-escalate the most deadly conflict in Europe since World War II, which erupted when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
“The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a joint statement with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The statement noted that the call was “held in consultation with Ukraine” and followed a meeting in Oslo on Oct 20 between Store, Stubb and Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as US envoy Steve Witkoff.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, also took part in the meeting remotely.
After the Oslo talks, Witkoff travelled to St Petersburg to meet Putin.
Speaking to reporters in Helsinki, where Nordic leaders are meeting, Store said the 90-minute call highlighted “big differences in views” on Ukraine.
According to a statement from the Kremlin, Putin stressed during the call that it was the European Union’s and NATO’s “confrontational policy” that was “leading to a protraction of hostilities”.
The Kremlin said the three leaders “agreed to continue maintaining direct contact by telephone”.
Stubb and Store initiated the call to discuss “efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe”, their statement said.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call, we stressed the importance of de-escalation,” Store said.
Stubb described the discussion between the three as “frank and substantive”.
Shortly after the announcement of the call, Kyiv said Zelensky spoke to the Nordic leaders about the conversation with Putin.
Denmark ‘sceptical’
Stubb confirmed the talks with Zelensky in a social media post and commented: “Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace”.
The leaders stressed they were representing their own countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe, but Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen bemoaned that they had gone “solo”.
“I’m very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn’t been coordinated with any of the rest of us,” she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordic leaders, including Store and Stubb, in Finland.
“I honestly don’t know what those two countries think they can achieve with this,” she said.
Store rejected the criticism.
“In the times we live in, it cannot be that only the US administration has a channel to talk to the Russian leadership. European countries must be able to do that as well,” he told reporters.
Relations between Ukraine and the United States have become strained again after Trump suddenly announced in October a deal with Russia to obtain diesel, as part of his efforts to lower oil prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Ukraine reacted with dismay after Trump also waived sanctions against Russia and appeared to again pivot to Putin.
The Oslo meeting followed furious diplomatic efforts in Washington, Kyiv and Western capitals to calm the situation.
Norway and Finland, both NATO members, share borders with Russia and the statement emphasised that the countries are “firm supporters of Ukraine”. AFP

Protecting Europe with stronger climate-resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:37:40 UTC
23:37:40 KST

From wildfires to droughts, the summer of 2026 showed us the devastating impact climate change is having on our homes, communities, and nature. It also showed us why Europe must move beyond reacting to disasters, to get ahead of the climate impacts and avoid damages. The new EU framework for climate resilience will do just this, taking a more proactive and systemic risk management approach to protect Europeans and the EU economy.
The Commission has put forward today a European climate resilience law to equip and empower public authorities, businesses and communities. A common approach to assessing and responding to climate risks, and to supporting broader systemic change will help better protect people, essential services and infrastructure when climate-related disasters occur.
The tools to support this common approach are
- the European Climate Viewer, to understand what the shared warming trajectory means for different parts of Europe .
- the Navigator of Climate Resilience Tools that helps users find relevant climate resilience tools based on their location, sector, and the specific risks they face.
- the Mission Solutions Explorer showcases adaptation solutions developed through the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change. These examples will help others adapt, replicate, and scale up proven approaches.
The EU continues to be committed to becoming climate neutral by 2050. This new framework prepares us for the climate impacts that are already unavoidable. It will help protect jobs and livelihoods, and create new opportunities for European innovation and investment.
Looking ahead, the Commission will further strengthen Europe's capacity to prepare for and respond to climate extremes with a European heatwave plan, a climate insurance alliance, and a European water initiative. It will also launch a PreparEU Advisory Group on disaster preparedness and an initiative to identify Europe’s 100 most climate-vulnerable territories.

Seven stitches: shrapnel wounded a man in the neck during the shelling of a university in Kyiv — photo report
Kyiv • UNN
In Kyiv, shrapnel from a Russian strike wounded a driver who was passing by a university. The man received seven stitches, and his car was damaged.
As a result of the overnight Russian shelling of Kyiv, the educational buildings and dormitories of the State University of Trade and Economics were damaged. Near the institution, a fragment wounded a local resident, Serhii. Medics from an ambulance that was nearby provided the man with first aid. This was reported by an UNN journalist from the scene.
Details
According to preliminary information, Serhii works in delivery, and at the time of the strike he was driving past the university while carrying out an order. According to him, the explosions occurred directly in front of the car.
I was just driving to deliver an order. There was an explosion right in front of my car. I was injured, and the car was damaged too. I was driving past the university; there was a flash, then a second explosion and immediately a third. I felt that something on my neck was wet. I touched it with my hand—it was blood
The fragment struck the man's neck but did not hit an artery. In addition, he was lucky that an ambulance was nearby.
The "ambulance" was still there; the ambulance was damaged too. I ran up to that ambulance. The ambulance crew were also injured; everything inside had been overturned, and the vehicle was damaged, but they provided me with first aid, wrapped my neck and checked whether there were any fragments there. Then they sent me to the hospital. At the hospital, they took an X-ray, and after the X-ray, the doctors decided to stitch up the wound. Seven stitches. So I was born under a lucky star—I survived
Serhii also reported a concussion, a mild contusion and dizziness. According to him, there were many people in the street after the explosions.
There were a great many people, but I was in a state of shock. I saw that some people were, well, lying on the pavement, calling for help. Many people ran out of their homes. Everyone helped as best they could
We remind you
As a result of the overnight Russian shelling of Kyiv, the educational buildings and dormitories of the State University of Trade and Economics were damaged. Several people are known to have been injured, while there were no fatalities among students and staff.

Nigeria panel says 37 detained miners died from overcrowding and neglect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:36:11 UTC
23:36:11 KST

Nigeria panel says 37 detained miners died from overcrowding and neglect
ABUJA, Oct 27 - A group of 37 suspected illegal miners died in detention in Nigeria as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and neglect, according to a government investigation into their deaths.
The investigating committee, set up after the deaths last month sparked outrage in Nigeria, rejected earlier claims by officials that an outbreak of disease was to blame and called for compensation for victims and survivors as well as an overhaul of the agency involved.
The deaths, which included many teenagers working in artisanal gold mines, triggered protests in Nigeria, raising fresh concerns about conditions in detention facilities and the treatment of suspects awaiting trial.
Jonathan Kure, chairman of the committee, said the deaths were "entirely preventable" and a result of severe overcrowding, deprivation of basic necessities and ignored warnings.
"The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities, and the welfare of persons in custody," Kure said after his committee reviewed evidence, including detention records, autopsies, hospital reports and communication logs.
NSCDC officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The evidence showed the victims died from asphyxia, an acute respiratory failure caused by prolonged confinement in a severely overcrowded, poorly ventilated cell, worsened by heat stress and dehydration, Kure said.
"The evidence did not support claims that the deaths resulted from a disease outbreak," Kure said.
The Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), the paramilitary agency that locked up the miners as part of efforts to regulate mining, initially suggested the detainees may have died from an unspecified disease before later saying the cause had not been established.
The panel recommended 30 million naira (about $22,500) in compensation for each victim's family and 10 million naira for each of the 41 survivors.
The findings are in line with testimonies from survivors who told Reuters that dozens of artisanal miners were crammed into a small holding cell and repeatedly ignored after complaining of overcrowding.
The government has suspended senior NSCDC officials pending the investigation, but the panel called for a sweeping overhaul of the agency's leadership. REUTERS
