What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:36:00 EET
23:36:00 KST

What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
This op-ed was co-authored with Kateryna Kyrychenko, a Ukrainian international lawyer and Head of Ukraine Legal Affairs and Programme Management at the Public International Law & Policy Group (PILPG). Her work covers international criminal law, accountability for Russian war crimes, peace negotiations and transitional justice. She is pursuing a PhD in international criminal law at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.
On a sunny September afternoon, Kyiv almost seemed at peace. People sat outside the Food Market, talking and eating. Between meetings, we discussed Bosnia's and Ukraine's shared experience. For one of us, war is a memory shaping life three decades later; for the other, an immediate reality of air-raid alerts, sleepless nights and uncertainty about the next Russian attack. We returned to one question: what does it mean for war to end?
A month earlier in Sarajevo, a meeting with Ukrainian officials and civil-society representatives had focused on how Bosnia and Herzegovina handled post-war return and reconstruction. Families crossed former front lines to reclaim homes; property disputes took years, and people returned to areas governed by forces that had driven them out. These challenges are familiar to Bosnians. For Ukrainians still at war, the question was not simply how people had managed to return, but what it had taken to rebuild their lives in places from which they had once been driven.
Pressure to negotiate is mounting in Kyiv, yet little attention goes to a peace framework with credible guarantees. After more than 12 years of Russian aggression, including nearly five of full-scale invasion, Ukraine's weariness is understandable. Millions have lost homes, loved ones or livelihoods; families have been separated for years, and communities live between air-raid alerts and the next attack. They want the war to end, but exhaustion is not willingness to accept peace at any price. Distant negotiators may see this desire for relief as a chance for a quick deal. What seems a breakthrough in Washington or a European capital can have different consequences for those living with its terms. Bosnia shows the gap between signing an agreement and the reality that follows.
Ending the war is only the beginning
Dayton, Ohio, is remembered for producing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war. Its annexes covered the constitution, military arrangements, elections, human rights and refugee return. Unlike an archived document, it had force behind it: some 60,000 NATO-led Implementation Force (IFOR) troops separated armies, oversaw territorial transfers and enforced military provisions. Peace required troops on the ground, and the money and governments willing to keep them involved after Bosnia left the front pages.
Ukraine knows the limits of a mission without enforcement powers. From March 2014, the OSCE Special Monitoring Mission monitored the security situation, established facts and reported violations, while also facilitating dialogue and supporting local ceasefire arrangements; it had no power to enforce compliance. Its mandate expired on 31 March 2022 because OSCE consensus on an extension could not be reached owing to Russia's position. The Minsk agreements, meant to end hostilities in eastern Ukraine, proved vulnerable to manipulation: repeated ceasefire violations, unresolved security questions and incompatible readings of political provisions. They neither secured peace nor prevented Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. For Ukraine, the question is not whether another agreement can be signed but what would make it different from arrangements Russia has already violated: who would verify compliance, respond to renewed attacks and impose consequences?
Dayton was possible under different conditions: the parties accepted IFOR's deployment and undertook to facilitate its operations, while the UN Security Council authorised the force. Russia, by contrast, is Ukraine's aggressor and holds a UN Security Council veto. A guarantee it can veto offers little protection. Ukraine's security cannot rest on monitoring or diplomatic assurances: its ability to defend itself, maintain military capabilities and choose security partnerships must be central to any settlement. Restricting its self-defence while Russia can rearm risks another war.
Civilian implementation was equally demanding. Dayton created the Office of the High Representative, but implementation soon exposed serious obstacles. In December 1997, the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn supported the exercise of what became known as the Bonn Powers: the High Representative could impose binding decisions on specified implementation issues and remove officials who obstructed Dayton commitments.
Ukraine faces a less favourable international environment. Beyond Russia's veto, other major powers' interests may not align with its security needs. Those conditions cannot simply be recreated. Proposals for Ukraine must start from this reality, not assume guarantees will enforce themselves.
The unfinished business of peace
Property return showed that work went beyond the text. Annex 7 gave refugees and displaced people the right to return home and have their property restored, or to receive compensation where restoration was impossible. Laws and administrative procedures were developed and enforced, with municipalities monitored and pressed to comply. People could receive house keys yet find the hardest part of return ahead. For some returnees, especially those returning as an ethnic minority, the label "returnee" can be a reminder that the return of property does not necessarily restore their place in society.
Much will be familiar in Ukraine: destroyed or occupied homes, separated families and repeated displacement. The scale of destruction, mines and unexploded ordnance, displacement of millions and Russia's systematic efforts to alter the demographic, legal and cultural realities of occupied territories will compound Ukraine's challenges. Restoring Ukrainian governance requires more than replacing flags or reopening offices. It must address documented pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, property expropriation, the replacement of Ukrainian education and the suppression of Ukrainian identity, forcible transfers or deportations of civilians, including children, to the Russian Federation, arbitrary detention by Russian forces or occupation authorities, and the consequences of occupation.
War's end brings difficulties beyond rebuilding homes and institutions: disputes over education, integration, national symbols, history, heroes and victims. Who decides what schools teach, whose suffering is recognised and whose history becomes official? Bosnia has grappled with these issues since 1995; many remain unresolved. Survivors and victims' families still face denial of the Srebrenica genocide, historical revisionism and glorification of convicted war criminals, according to the Srebrenica Memorial. Reconciliation efforts have sometimes emphasised moving forward rather than confronting the past. Ukraine should heed the warning: ending a war and reconciling societies are different things.
Despite its achievements, Dayton left unresolved questions, notably the struggle over the Bosnian state. Its two entities and political system enabled obstruction and challenged state authority. Bosnia's experience is not a warning against decentralisation or minority rights. Nevertheless, trouble begins when arrangements protecting communities let a neighbouring government prevent a country from deciding for itself. For Ukraine, a Russian veto over defence or European integration would be especially dangerous. Russia has sought to use the status of occupied territories to influence Ukraine's internal affairs. A settlement must not institutionalise that interference as political compromise or minority protection.
What happens after the diplomats leave?
We sought no Ukrainian version of Dayton. and Dayton's unfinished business in Bosnia makes it no blueprint. But it stopped the war, and some people returned and homes were rebuilt because outsiders stayed to enforce commitments local politicians resisted.
Ukraine's partners should ask what they will do on the first day after the war, not just what they will sign, propose or pressure others to accept. Bosnians understand Ukraine's reluctance to accept promises without guarantees: they have been down that road and, in many ways, still are.
These answers will matter years later, when another crisis dominates headlines and Ukraine leaves the global spotlight. Who will remain engaged, provide assistance or step in when agreements are violated or institutions fail?
"At least nobody's shooting" was common in post-war Bosnia. It is a painfully modest definition of peace, hardly a foundation for the future, especially for those living with unresolved consequences.
Nedim Jahić and Kateryna Kyrychenko

Rada Extends Residency Deadline for Foreign Soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:35:09 UTC
23:35:09 KST

Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada approved legislation Tuesday, Oct. 27, giving foreign and stateless military personnel more time to arrange temporary residence permits and clarify their legal status after leaving service.
Lawmakers adopted bill No. 16094 both at first reading and as a whole, Suspilne reported, citing its correspondent in the Ukrainian legislature.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The measure extends an existing transitional application period from six months to one year for personnel serving under contract in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the National Guard and the State Special Transport Service.
It also provides a separate three-month period after signing a contract and establishes arrangements for regularizing immigration status after discharge.
The Verkhovna Rada’s bill tracker listed the legislation as adopted and being prepared for signing. The legislature’s press service said it would enter into force the day after publication.
Extension addresses approaching November deadline
The legislation responds to a deadline that could leave some foreign service members without a clear legal basis to remain in Ukraine.
Under the existing transitional rules, personnel covered by the requirement must apply for temporary residence permits by Nov. 10, 2026.
The Verkhovna Rada’s human rights committee said that military duties and tasks connected with defending Ukraine had prevented some eligible personnel from submitting their applications on time.
Finland, Norway Push Putin for Peace
The committee warned that failing to extend the deadline could create legal uncertainty and expose service members to negative consequences associated with losing lawful residence status.
The additional time concerns applications for residence documentation. It does not mean that temporary residence permits themselves will be valid for only one year.
The existing six-month transition originated in legislation that entered into force May 10, 2026. It applied to foreigners and stateless people who had signed military contracts before that date. During the application window, their military registration document or service identification confirms their lawful temporary residence.
Separate 3-month window follows contract signing
The bill also addresses the period between signing a military contract and obtaining a residence permit.
Its provisions recognize lawful stay while the permit is being obtained, for up to three months from the contract’s signing. This is separate from the extended transitional period for personnel already covered by the earlier legislation.
The measure also establishes a period for former service members to regularize their status following discharge, rather than leaving their immigration position unresolved when military service ends.
The legislation concerns residence documentation and lawful stay. It does not itself grant Ukrainian citizenship.
Military units told to help with applications
The Defense Ministry had already issued guidance in September to help military units organize residence applications for foreign personnel.
The recommendations assign units responsibility for checking contract dates and existing documents, preparing paperwork and coordinating submissions with the State Migration Service.
Service members still attend procedures requiring their personal presence, including photography, biometric collection and signing documents.
“This will reduce the administrative burden on individuals and the time they have to spend away from service,” Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan said.
The guidance also allows units to arrange visits by mobile migration-service teams when personnel are receiving inpatient treatment and cannot travel. Where combat duties or security conditions prevent attendance, units are instructed to contact the migration authorities about extending lawful stay and arranging a safer opportunity to submit documents.
Foreign volunteers have served in Ukrainian units throughout Russia’s full-scale invasion. The International Legion, established in 2022, provides one route into the Armed Forces.
The new legislation covers contract personnel across all three named service branches, extending beyond volunteers serving through the Legion. Its immediate purpose is to give those already defending Ukraine sufficient time and clearer procedures to document their right to remain.

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- As of 11:00 a.m. local time, just over 76% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
- Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Little shift in numbers as three-quarters of votes tallied
Partial results issued by the Central Elections Committee and cited by the Times of Israel showed little movement in results with 76.8% of votes counted, with the pro-Netanyahu bloc on 54 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc on 47.
However, the United Arab List, commonly known by its Hebrew abbreviation Ra'am, saw a gain of two seats, bringing the Arab parties to 19.
The results will change as counting progresses.
Both main blocs remain short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.
Left-wing leader calls for 'courage' to unite with Arab parties
Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, the Democrats, has called on partners in the opposition alliance to be ready to work with Arab parties to gain a majority and take government.
"We must no longer accept [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X.
"We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens," he wrote.
Arab parties have around 16 seats amid the ongoing count, while the anti-Netanyahu bloc under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is on around 48, meaning that a coalition between them would produce the necessary majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu's bloc had some 56 seats after around two-thirds of votes had been counted.
Several opposition parties have so far rejected working together with the Arab parties.
Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee
Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party currently leads with a projected 27 seats, with challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party coming in at 21 seats projected.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
The Likud and Yashar parties are leading their respective blocs.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.
"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.
"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.
Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.
Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck
Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.
Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.
However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.
"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."
He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.
Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.
"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.
The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.
"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.
"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.
A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.
Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show
Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.
While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.
The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.
Ra'am party becomes political power broker
The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.
The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.
Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.
As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."
Netanyahu's bloc trails in Israel election, exit polls say
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest single group in the Knesset, with 25 projected seats.
Challenger Gadi Eisenkot's bloc has emerged as the largest group with a projected 53, just ahead of the ruling coalition on 50, but well short of the 61 needed for a majority.
Neither bloc has a clear majority without the support of Arab parties.
These projected numbers are from public broadcaster Kan 11; other numbers vary by channel, but only slightly.
Polls closing around the country
It's now 10 p.m. across Israel, which means that polling stations around the country either should have closed or should be making preparations to do so as the last people in line cast their ballots.
Exit polls should follow shortly on Israeli television. These have a fairly good reputation overall but of course are only projections.
Results will start to trickle in through the night and are unlikely to be finalized until Wednesday.
And of course, there's every chance that even once the dust has settled and the final results are in, we will have a longer wait until there's clarity about who might be able to form a coalition government.
In any case, stick with us and we'll keep you posted.
Election commission sees 'no need to extend voting hours' after Netanyahu request
The Central Elections Committee has rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and some other groups to extend voting beyond 10 p.m. (2000 UTC/GMT).
"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.
The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.
For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.
The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.
IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign
Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.
DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.
High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc
The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.
According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.
Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.
Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.
Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.
Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.
This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.
The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.
And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.

Intact Russian Missile of Unknown Type Found in Odesa Region—Photos Were Previously Published by Flash

An unknown Russian cruise missile was found in the Odesa region; it had crashed in an open area and was relatively intact.
Photos of the missile were published by the local Telegram channel ODESSA INFO LIVE.
Based on the published images, the missile sustained minimal damage during the crash, allowing Ukrainian experts to study its design in detail.
In terms of its design, this missile is a small-sized cruise missile with a rectangular fuselage cross-section and rounded edges, as well as a swept-back wing.
The boxy fuselage contours and flat faces likely simplify production and the layout of internal compartments.
This design choice may also be part of measures to reduce the vehicle’s radar signature.
The missile is equipped with a small turbojet engine, with its nozzle located in the V-shaped tail section, while the power plant’s air intakes are positioned on the fuselage sides.
The image also shows tail fins with an offset geometry. The fuselage itself is made of dark-colored composite materials to reduce the cross-sectional area (RCS).
As a reminder, the first photos of the new rocket were released by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov on October 22.
Although he also calls the new missile the Geran-5 K5-K, its external appearance differs significantly from the known Geran-5 K5-K version.
“The missile’s distinctive features include an optical navigation system, increased range, speed, and flight altitude,” he said.
You can read more about these upgrades and the missiles’ operational capabilities in the article published by Militarnyi on October 23.

Ukraine’s last two EU negotiation blocks stay shut as Hungary’s new government keeps Orbán’s veto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:34:14 UTC
23:34:14 KST

Hungary on 27 October again refused to approve the screening results for clusters 4 and 5, the last two blocks of Ukraine’s EU accession talks that remain unopened, at a meeting of the EU Council’s enlargement working party in Brussels, European Pravda reported, citing several EU diplomats. It was Budapest’s second refusal in a week.
Ukraine is pursuing EU membership while fighting Russia’s full-scale invasion, and for years its path ran into vetoes from Viktor Orbán’s Hungary. Orbán lost power in April to Péter Magyar, who promised to bring Hungary back to Europe. His government is now the one blocking the last two clusters.
Brussels knew Budapest would say no
One of the diplomats said that “Hungary’s position has not changed.” Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the EU Council, knew in advance that Budapest would not move but put the item on the agenda anyway. Another diplomat described the repeat vote as a political move to raise pressure on Hungary rather than a real attempt to get a yes.
Hungary’s arguments were not disclosed on 20 October, when it first blocked the step. Cluster 4 covers transport, energy, trans-European networks, the environment, and climate. Cluster 5 covers agriculture, fisheries, regional policy, and budget rules.
Kyiv paid for two clusters, and the last two stay shut
Earlier this month, Ukraine’s parliament passed the minority-language schooling law Budapest had demanded, and the EU opened clusters 2 and 3 on 13 October. Magyar’s government has tied its support to Kyiv meeting 11 demands on the rights of the Hungarian minority.
On 16 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held his first one-on-one meeting with Magyar in Brussels and thanked him for opening the two clusters, adding that work was underway to open the remaining two by the end of the year, his office said. Ten days later, Zelenskyy set out why the timing matters.
“It is very important that the remaining two negotiating clusters for Ukraine are opened by the end of this year, and that during the Lithuanian presidency we could already close negotiating chapters,” he wrote.
Lithuania takes over the EU Council presidency in January.
Budapest’s next moves may also decide whether Ukraine and Moldova still advance together.
Moldova’s President Maia Sandu discussed the opening of her country’s last two clusters with Magyar during a visit to Budapest last week, and in July Hungary already offered to move Moldova ahead on its own.

A Russian IT worker joined the army to ‘benefit society’ and was promised a job operating drones. Now he’s missing in Ukraine, and his wife believes his commanders stole his money.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:32:28 UTC
23:32:28 KST

A Russian IT worker joined the army to ‘benefit society’ and was promised a job operating drones. Now he’s missing in Ukraine, and his wife believes his commanders stole his money.
An IT specialist from Chelyabinsk signed a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry that promised him service in the drone forces. Instead, he ended up in what’s known as a “meat grinder regiment.” He was sent on an assault and went missing, his wife told the independent Russian investigative outlet iStories.
Nikolai and Irina (names changed) had been together for 20 years and raised two children. The family didn’t need money: Nikolai developed software for government agencies at a large IT company.
In the summer of 2026, Nikolai decided to go to war to “benefit society.” “When the special military operation started in the country, a lot of our friends left for abroad. We kind of looked down on that. I can’t explain it now. But still, we had a question: who’s going to defend the country then? Defend its interests?” Irina told journalists.
An appendix to the contract specified that Nikolai would serve as a drone operator and undergo training for that role. Instead, he was sent to military unit No. 95378 in the Samara region, home to the 1437th Motorized Rifle Regiment, where he spent several months. He received no training or weapons instruction at all, doing “housekeeping work” and serving as a “company clerk” instead.
Russia’s Defense Ministry has been actively recruiting Russians, including students, into the drone forces since late 2025. Recruiters promise high salaries, one-year contracts, and service far from the front line, but in reality, the contracts are open-ended, and recruiters cannot guarantee any special conditions of service.
In conversations with his wife, Nikolai said that his unit practiced extortion and harshly punished discipline violations: putting offenders in a pit or sending them on assaults.
In September, Nikolai called his wife and said he was being sent on a combat mission:
One day he called from someone else’s phone number and said he was being sent on a combat mission and wanted to say goodbye. At first I didn’t understand anything. I said, how is that possible? Were you even trained for anything? What mission are you being sent on? He said he didn’t know, and to be honest, he started crying. Then the call cut off.
Soon after, his wife received a notice from command that Nikolai had gone missing on September 28 “while performing tasks during the special military operation.” What exactly happened to him on the combat mission remains unknown.
Irina found a notification from the online marketplace Ozon in her husband’s email showing that Nikolai, while at the front, had bought five laptops for 120,000 rubles. She believes someone among his commanders stole about one and a half million rubles from his bank card. On social media, she found complaints about commanders from relatives of other servicemen who served in the same unit.
The 1437th Regiment, where Nikolai served, is part of the 15th Separate Guards Motorized Rifle Brigade. Its unofficial name is the “Black Hussars.” Before Russia’s full-scale war with Ukraine, it was the only “peacekeeping” brigade in the Russian army. Its soldiers carried out missions in Georgia and Nagorno-Karabakh and likely took part in the annexation of Crimea.
In the war against Ukraine, the brigade took part in the occupation of the Kyiv region. Brigade servicemen are suspected of torturing and killing civilians. The unit itself also practices torture and extrajudicial killings, the independent Russian news outlet Verstka reported.
The 1437th Regiment is commanded by Colonel Vladimir Teslo, 31, iStories found. In 2024, Vladimir Putin awarded him the title Hero of Russia “for the totality of heroic acts and personal courage.”
“On the one hand, the regiment commander is a Hero of Russia. On the other, that same commander sees his soldiers as walking wallets. First he empties their bank accounts, then he gets rid of the soldiers themselves. I want people to know about this Teslo. He may be a hero for one thing, but he’s a murderer for another. I don’t know what will come of speaking out. It’s too early to tell. These are deranged men with guns,” Irina told journalists.

Greenhouse gases hit record highs, further rise expected with El Nino, UN weather agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:32:00 UTC
23:32:00 KST

Greenhouse gases hit record highs, further rise expected with El Nino, UN weather agency says
- Greenhouse gas levels hit record highs in 2025, with carbon dioxide at 426.8 ppm, or 153% of pre-industrial levels, the WMO said.
- Methane, nitrous oxide and SF6 also reached record highs, and the WMO warned these gases will keep trapping more heat and worsening extreme weather.
- The WMO expects CO2 to rise again in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and a powerful El Nino.
AI generated
GENEVA – Greenhouse gas levels in the atmosphere reached unprecedented highs in 2025, potentially further warming the planet and leading to more extreme climate events, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in a report on Oct 27.
The global average concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide reached 426.8 parts per million (ppm) in 2025, about 153% of the 1750 pre-industrial level, the report said. The level rose by 2.8 ppm from the previous year, a bigger annual increase than the average over the past decade.
Concentrations of other important greenhouse gases – methane and nitrous oxide – reached record highs in 2025, standing at 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The report measures the amount of gas that accumulates in the atmosphere, not new annual emissions.
The WMO will share the findings with negotiators at the COP31 UN climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, in November, and warned that a powerful El Nino could push concentrations higher in 2026.
“Every additional part per million matters because it traps additional heat. In effect, we are supercharging the ocean and the atmosphere,” WMO deputy secretary-general Ko Barrett said.
“That means that heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for.”
In 2026, parts of the world including Europe saw scorching summer temperatures, as well as devastating floods in Asia and elsewhere.
El Nino likely to add to the problem
The WMO said it expected carbon dioxide concentrations to rise further in 2026 due to fossil fuel burning and the onset of a powerful El Nino, which will cause drier weather and make it harder for carbon sinks to absorb emissions.
The WMO also raised concern about sulfur hexafluoride, or SF6, a greenhouse gas widely used in electrical equipment, saying its increase in 2025 was a record high. The global warming potential of SF6 is more than 24,000 times that of carbon dioxide and it can remain in the atmosphere for more than 1,000 years.
The agency also pointed to rising hydrogen concentrations, which increased 5.3% between 2010 and 2024. Although hydrogen is not a greenhouse gas, leaks from infrastructure used to produce, transport and store it can affect atmospheric chemistry and indirectly contribute to warming. Hydrogen produced using renewable electricity can be used as a low-carbon fuel for transport.
The WMO said both hydrogen leakage and the long persistence of SF6 could undermine some of the climate benefits of the global energy transition.
“The energy transition is essential and welcome, but as with every transition, it has to be done in a smart way and informed by environmental observations,” Barrett said. REUTERS

EU prepares for a grim future with new climate-proofing law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:30:45 UTC
23:30:45 KST

BRUSSELS — Hope for the best, prepare for the worst.
The European Commission updated its approach to dealing with climate change along those lines on Tuesday with a package aimed at improving the bloc’s response to mounting disasters such as extreme heat, supercharged storms and worsening wildfires.
Unveiling its first-ever law to boost the bloc’s resilience to global warming, the EU executive conceded that merely slashing planet-warming emissions is insufficient as climate extremes wreak havoc across the continent.
Advertisement
“There is no alternative to continue to cut emissions more forcefully and to move full-frontal into clean energy,” Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told reporters. “But at the same time, we do have to acknowledge that the problems we're facing have morphed into something that is so large that just doing that alone unfortunately no longer is good enough.”
The Commission’s proposed Climate Resilience Law asks governments to draft plans to prepare for a world that’s 2 degrees Celsius hotter in 2050 and 3C hotter by the end of the century, aligning with the United Nations’ latest projections that current global climate policies can only limit warming to 2.8C.
The same U.N. report also warned that the world can no longer limit warming to 1.5C, the lower bound of the Paris Agreement’s dual goals, and that steep emissions cuts are needed to achieve the best-case scenario of halting the rise in global temperatures at 1.8C.
The Commission insisted that Tuesday’s package did not amount to Brussels resigning itself to catastrophic levels of warming.
“Let me just be crystal-clear on the 1.5C, that remains our goal,” said Hoekstra. “At the same time, it would be unwise not to prepare for… the current trajectory the world is on.”
Regulation for the deregulation era
Under the proposed law, governments are “encouraged” to take the 3C scenario into account when designing policies, budgets and investments.
Advertisement
Countries will have to carry out national climate risk assessments every five years starting in 2029, and subsequently draw up climate-proofing plans by the end of 2030. These strategies should also indicate which public authorities are in charge of managing certain climate risks to avoid inaction and finger-pointing among ministries and agencies.
The fairly light-touch legislation reflects the prevailing mood in the EU. Brussels itself has committed to a deregulation agenda, and national governments have called for fewer rules, not more, particularly where climate and the environment are concerned.
Efforts to improve resilience to weather extremes, such as flood prevention or urban greening, are also largely a national and even local responsibility, with the EU holding limited powers.
Wopke Hoekstra looks on during the European Industry Summit in Antwerp, Belgium on Feb. 11, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
Even the limited rules proposed on Tuesday are already raising eyebrows.
“I strongly support a clearer allocation of responsibilities,” said Peter Liese, the lead climate lawmaker of the center-right European People’s Party. But, he added, “we need to examine whether the plans, in the form proposed by the Commission, are necessary. Plans alone do not protect people and could tie up resources unnecessarily if we do not design them pragmatically.”
Others argued the law was too limited. "The danger is a framework that tells us exactly how exposed we are and then commits us to nothing," said Greens-affiliated lawmaker Kai Tegethoff. "Europe needs binding resilience targets and clear, measurable goals for the sectors most at risk."
Advertisement
The Commission, for its part, has sought to appeal to governments' concerns over the EU’s economic competitiveness by emphasizing the wealth-destroying threat of climate disasters and the business potential of climate-proofing technologies.
“Some may say resilience is expensive. But the right question is, what is the real cost of being unprepared,” said Teresa Ribera, the Commission’s executive vice president in charge of the green transition. Both she and Hoekstra cited data showing the impact of heat on GDP as an example. “Europe cannot be competitive without being resilient,” she added.
In the wider package presented Tuesday, the Commission also highlighted the emerging market for climate technologies such as drought-resilient crops and cooling solutions, casting European industry as a front-runner in that sector.
As the EU is currently negotiating its next long-term budget, the package does not come with any funding attached, despite financing often acting as the biggest barrier to climate-proofing efforts. The bloc needs to invest around €70 billion a year by 2050 to adapt to a warmer world but currently only spends €29 billion.
More where that came from
While presenting new obligations for governments, the Commission also promised to push ahead with work in Brussels.
The European Environment Agency will draw up bloc-wide climate risk assessments, with the next one due in June 2028, and the Commission will present an EU “strategic plan on climate resilience” by the end of September 2028.
Advertisement
Progress will be assessed regularly based on four criteria — climate-related deaths, economic losses attributable to global warming, the share of uninsured losses, and related fiscal costs. The Commission’s Eurostat agency will start compiling EU-wide statistics on climate-related deaths and economic losses by the end of 2030, according to the regulation.
Beyond the legislative efforts, the EU executive also presented a wider package that includes several digital tools, including a “climate viewer” that converts the new warming scenario into local projections policymakers can use.
The Commission also vowed to take into account the new 3C warming scenario in all its future policy proposals. Further steps, including a heat wave action plan and a climate insurance alliance, are planned for next year, it said.
"I wouldn't say that we're nearly done," said Hoekstra. "Much of this is going to be work in progress." And if climate change continues getting worse, he added, “this package might well need to be beefed up.”

A Spanish judge on Tuesday gave the government 15 days to declassify intelligence reports on mass migrant arrivals in Ceuta in July, including assessments of Moroccan authorities' actions, local media reported.
National Court Judge Maria Tardon formally requested that the Council of Ministers release the documents within the specified period, according to Spanish news agency EFE.
The judicial order seeks "all notes and reports made by the (National Intelligence Center) CNI and disseminated to authorities from July 30, 2026 onwards relating to the investigations into the events that occurred on July 30 and 31, 2026."
The request specifically includes intelligence relating "to the actions of the Moroccan authorities to date."
Around 72,000 people crossed irregularly from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on July 30-31, according to estimates from Spain's central government.

Expert Insights: Two life science career fairs coming to Lund and Copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

About the author: David Zepernick is the Director of Member Engagement and Communication at Medicon Valley Alliance. He is also a columnist for The Copenhagen Post, where he writes about careers.
The general hunting season in Denmark opens for most species starts on September 1, though individual game types have distinct individual schedules.
Looking at the daily timeframe, hunting is generally only permitted from 1.5 hours before sunrise until 1.5 hours after sunset (with extended windows for certain waterfowl and deer)
Furthermore, hunters must hold a valid hunting license, submit annual game bag returns, and follow specific public/private forest access guidelines outlined via the Danish Agricultural Agency.
If you are hunting for your new life science job, or if you represent a life science related company hunting for the best talent, these restrictions fortunately do not apply. It is basically hunting season all year round. There are, however, distinctive time and place bound hunting grounds where the likelihood of success is significantly better.
In the Greater Copenhagen area, often referred to as Medicon Valley when focusing on life science only, November present two opportunities in the form of Career Fairs you should certainly consider. 
Unfortunately, they take place on the very same day, 25th of November, which means you either need to choose or do a 50-50 split and start in the Swedish city of Lund and the arrive in Copenhagen early afternoon.
In Lund I can recommend the  Life Science Career Day 2026 at the science park Medicon Village, which runs from 08:30 to 15:00co-organized by Medicon Village and Lund University.
The days includes both a Track 1: Opportunities in Pharma-related Life Science applications and a Track 2: Opportunities in MedTech and Business-related Life Science applications and then of course the opportunity to mingle with the exhibiting companies.
In Copenhagen I suggest you explore the Life Science Career Fair Copenhagen 2026, which takes place at the Mærsk Tower starting early afternoon and is organized by the non-profit student-driven organization Synapse Life Science Connect. 
Here you will be able to meet top employers from the life science sector and get a head start to your job search, get inspired about the vast number of possibilities within the life science field, learn more about the requirements for your dream job, network with like-minded students and get feedback on your CV from experienced career counselors. They also offer a free professional picture for your applications!
Enjoy hunting and best of luck! Remember that you miss 100% of the shots you don’t take”

‘No Kings’ sees public mobilization as essential to defending US democracy, says American activist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:29:58 UTC
23:29:58 KST

‘No Kings’ sees public mobilization as essential to defending US democracy, says American activist
Rebecca Winter discusses the role of mass protests, electoral participation and community organizing in challenging authoritarianism
TEHRAN- Rebecca Winter, executive director of Massachusetts 50501, is involved in organizing grassroots efforts to defend democracy and oppose authoritarianism in the United States. The movement, which emerged from a nationwide call for protests in February 2025, seeks to mobilize Americans through demonstrations, boycotts, voter participation and community action.
As the No Kings movement seeks to sustain public engagement beyond the US midterm elections, Winter spoke to the Tehran Times about the Trump administration, threats to democratic institutions, immigrant rights, and the role of grassroots activism in holding elected officials accountable.
Below is the full text of the interview:
 
Could you tell us a little about how Massachusetts 50501 began and what its main goals are?
We started with the national 50501 call to action on February 5, 2025. The original call to action was for a protest in every state capital: 50 states, 50 protests, all on one day. That eventually grew into a single movement.
Our organization’s goal is to protect democracy in the United States and fight authoritarianism. Once we hopefully overthrow the current authoritarian regime through nonviolent methods, we want to repair our democracy so that it actually works for everyone.
How would you describe the movement’s main concerns about the Trump administration?
We are incredibly concerned about how authoritarian Trump and his regime’s goals are. We see him acting against our Constitution and undermining the rule of law. He is also clearly more interested in supporting corporations and billionaires than working-class Americans.
Could you tell me about your role in leading the movement and what motivated you to become a political activist?
I am the executive director of our organization, and I wear several hats because we are an entirely volunteer-run organization without funding.
Honestly, many things motivated me to get involved. I am a mother, and I work at a school, so I am always thinking about the world I want these children, especially my own children, to grow up in.
I am also queer and disabled, and those are two populations that Trump and his regime are attacking. Basically, anyone from a marginalized group is very vulnerable right now.
In addition, many of my friends, family members and co-workers are immigrants or come from immigrant families. That is something we have always celebrated in the United States.
As a white woman, I recognize that I have a little more privilege under this regime. I believe it is my duty to stand up for my country and my community right now.
What do you consider the movement’s most important achievement since it began in February 2025?
It is the momentum we have built. We have held rallies that were among the largest protests in the United States, and we have done that four times now. This shows that people do not support this government and gives people a great deal of courage and hope to stand up in their own communities.
We have also organized several successful boycotts. Using our money to fight back is one of the most powerful things we can do.
Just this past weekend (October 17–18) , we also saw the largest day of early voting in the United States. That was the result of the nationwide No Kings: Vote Early call to action.
Why did the latest No Kings action focus on early voting rather than another mass rally? What results do you hope to achieve by changing your strategy?
It was incredibly important for us to focus on voting right now. Free and fair elections are a fundamental pillar of democracy and are what ground us in our Constitution.
Another reason we have ended up with the president and officials we have today is that not enough people have turned out to vote. People have lost faith in voting, and we are here to help restore that faith.
We want people to turn out in large numbers and demonstrate the values of the people through their votes.
Another reason we did not organize a protest this time is that, if there is election interference, we may have to take to the streets nonviolently and stand up very soon. People need to prepare for that possibility.
In this case, we needed to shift our energy and focus. We need to vote now, and we may need to take to the streets later.
Some critics might argue that these demonstrations have little real political impact. How will you turn the energy of the protests into lasting change, beyond the midterm elections?
Everything we do is action-oriented. The protests are highly visible, and that is intentional. They give people hope and show the media and people watching at home that Americans really care about what is happening in our country. They also show people that they should not be afraid, but should feel empowered to stand up and become part of this movement.
At our events, as is the case with most similar events across the country, a protest is never the only component. There is always another element focused on action.
For example, we often have different organizations come to our events to educate people and share information about their work. They recruit volunteers and collect donations. We also support mutual aid and find ways to give back to our communities.
We often turn people who attend our events into activists right there on the spot. Once we have their attention, we continue supporting them after the rallies through education and additional opportunities to help and volunteer.
We are constantly trying to bring people into the movement and give them tangible things they can do so that they feel they are making a difference.
Do you expect the movement to grow after the midterm elections, regardless of the outcome?
I do expect the movement to grow, and I think much of that depends on how the midterms go.
We know that we are not going to remove the regime through these midterm elections. The threat to our people is not going to disappear at the ballot box.
We hope things will turn around so that our legislative branch can be more effective than it is now. However, we will still need a strong people’s movement to hold our elected officials accountable and continue pushing them to oppose authoritarianism.
Apart from the movement’s position, I would also like to know your personal view. Which actions by the Trump administration do you consider most dangerous to American democracy, particularly over the past year?
It is very difficult for me to quantify that because this administration is doing so many harmful things.
As someone who volunteers in the immigrant justice movement, what concerns me most is what is happening to immigrants in our country. People are being taken away from their families and picked up off the streets by masked men without identification or warrants.
Many of those who have been detained have legal documentation. They are not violent. They are either working to obtain legal citizenship or hold visas or green cards. At least 500 U.S. citizens have already been detained.
The level of fear this creates, and the damage it does to our image around the world, are enormous.
We have always been a country that welcomes immigrants and celebrates diversity. I grew up in New York State, near the Statue of Liberty, and I always thought of the United States as a safe place for people from all over the world to come.
Now, it is very clear that this administration is trying to change our history and our image, and that will affect us negatively for generations.
Is there any message or plan you would like to add that we have not covered in our questions?
I think those are really the main points. We exist because we see that marginalized communities, in particular, will be hurt the most as our democracy continues to be undermined. It will take everyone in America standing up and engaging in our democracy.
Our country was founded by the people, and I think many people have become passive. We need to return to that original spirit: this is our government, and we need to take an active role in it.

Ballon d'Or ceremony raises case of French sports journalist jailed in Algeria
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:29:39 GMT

Ballon d'Or ceremony raises case of French sports journalist jailed in Algeria
- Published
The plight of French sports journalist Christophe Gleizes, who is serving a seven-year prison sentence in Algeria, was highlighted at the Ballon d'Or ceremony.
Run by France Football magazine, the prestigious football awards were held in London where presenters Kate Scott and Thierry Henry dedicated the occasion to the 37-year-old reporter.
On a large screen behind them, it stated that he had been in jail for one year, three months and 27 days and alongside his photo was the hashtag "#FreeGleize".
He was arrested on a trip to Algeria where he had gone to report on a football club in Kabylie, a region where some people want self-determination. The authorities accused him of supporting terrorism.
"The Ballon d'Or France Football family would like to take this opportunity to dedicate this ceremony to Christophe Gleizes," said British broadcaster Scott and former Arsenal player and French striker Henry as the ceremony kicked off on Monday evening.
The event, held in London for the first time in its 70-year history, saw England and Bayern Munich strike Harry Kane crowned the world's top footballer of the year and London's City's Spanish midfielder Alexia Putellas taking the female prize.
- Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or wait - how he bucked the trend 
  - Published1 day ago
- Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or 
  - Published1 day ago
Gleizes, who contributes to French magazines So Foot and Society, travelled to Algeria in May 2024 to report on Jeunesse Sportive de Kabylie (JSK), one of the country's best-known football clubs.
It is based in Tizi Ouzou, about 100km (62 miles) east of the capital Algiers, in the mountainous Kabylie region, which is mainly home to the ethnic Amazigh people (historically known as Berbers).
It is also the base of the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylie (MAK), which Algeria designated a terrorist organisation in 2021.
Gleizes was accused of possessing publications deemed harmful to national security.
The case centred on his contacts with a JSK official who was also associated with the MAK.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF), which has campaigned for his release, says the exchanges took place in a journalistic context and that some contacts predated the outlawing of the group.
During his appeal hearing last December, Gleizes acknowledged mistakes in his reporting and said he should have applied for a journalist visa rather than entering Algeria on a tourist visa.
"I beg your mercy so that I can be reunited with my family," he told the court.
Prosecutors argued that he had not travelled to Algeria to carry out journalistic work, but to commit a hostile act.
The Algerian authorities have yet to commented on the decision by the Ballon d'Or, which is organised by France Football magazine in partnership with European football governing body Uefa, to dedicate the ceremony to Gleizes.
RSF has announced a solidarity football match for 11 November, marking Gleizes's 500th day in detention, as part of its campaign calling for his release.
Former France internationals Robert Pirès and Vikash Dhorasoo, along with Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire, are among the first participants announced.
Gleizes's case comes amid wider concerns over the prosecution and imprisonment of writers and other public figures in Algeria.
Franco-Algerian writer Boualem Sansal was sentenced to five years in prison for undermining national security before receiving a pardon from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune following mediation by Germany's president in 2025.
Gleizes's arrest also came during a period of heightened diplomatic tensions between France and Algeria, marked by the withdrawal of ambassadors and reciprocal expulsions of diplomats.
Relations deteriorated further after France recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in July 2024. Algeria supports the pro-independence Polisario Front, which seeks independence for the disputed territory.
As relations began to improve in May, France's Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin visited Algiers and urged the Algerian authorities to allow Gleizes to reunite "not with France, but with his mother".
He said that he believed President Tebboune would be receptive to the request.

President Vladimir Putin warned Tuesday that efforts in the West to isolate Russia from the global natural gas market will hurt European consumers, as he confirmed potential joint energy projects with the United States in the Arctic.
“Any attempts to exclude Russia from the global gas market or restrain the development of our industry carry serious consequences,” Putin said at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow.
“First and foremost, these are skyrocketing costs for foreign end consumers of gas: businesses, companies and households,” he said.
Putin noted that Europeans are already struggling with high energy costs as the EU moves toward a phase-out of Russian natural gas imports by fall of next year in a bid to deprive the Kremlin of funding for its war against Ukraine.
“We have a saying in Russia: ‘Don’t dig a hole for someone else or you’ll fall into it yourself.’ This is precisely what happened in EU countries,” the president added.
Russia’s share of EU gas imports plummeted from 45% in 2021 to 19% by 2025, though seaborne LNG shipments partially offset pipeline losses.
On Tuesday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow has supplied $320.7 billion in energy resources to the EU since 2022, including $21.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026.
At the forum in Moscow, Putin also revealed that Russia was exploring potential energy cooperation with U.S. companies in the Arctic, confirming recent media reporting on his latest talks with White House special envoy Steve Witkoff.
“Until recently, European partners worked alongside us in our fields, and Chinese partners are still working there. Now, we’re exploring the possibility of joint work with American partners,” he said.

He drove a taxi in Jakarta and once worked in the US. Russia trained him as a machine gunner for a week and a half, then sent him into his first and last battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:27:15 UTC
23:27:15 KST

An Indonesian taxi driver who went looking for work abroad ended up in Russia's army and died in his first battle in Ukraine, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said. Russian recruiters found him through a job application, and he reached the front in Donetsk Oblast within weeks of signing. HUR calls him one more foreigner drawn into Russia's war through deception.
Russia's war against Ukraine consumes men faster than the Kremlin is ready to replace them through another mobilization at home, so it keeps hiring abroad. Ukraine has identified nearly 46,000 foreigners who signed with Russia's army since 2022. On 26 October, a UN commission found “compelling evidence” that Russia trafficked men from 29 countries into its forces.
A résumé that reached Russian recruiters
Taufiq Muhammad, born in 1978 in Sorong, Indonesia, drove a taxi in Jakarta and had once worked in the US. Russian recruiters found him through a résumé he had sent out while looking for work, the agency said. He probably believed promises of “easy money” and traveled to Moscow. HUR sees his case as part of a pattern.
“In fact, he became yet another victim of Russia's scheme of recruiting foreigners for the criminal war through deception,” HUR said.
A week and a half of training, then the front
Muhammad signed a one-year contract with Russia's army in Korolyov, near Moscow, on 19 April 2026. HUR called that term typical for foreigners Russia uses as “disposable” infantry. Russia made him a machine gunner and gave him only a week and a half at a training center near Voronezh, Army Inform reported, citing HUR.
Russia moved him to occupied Ukraine in early May. He died almost at once, in his first battle. Russian troops were trying to advance from the village of Zelena Dolyna toward Novoselivka and Drobysheve in Donetsk Oblast, Militarnyi reported.
Indonesia is the newest recruiting ground
Russia's recruiters have been working in Indonesia for months. In August, Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service said it held documents on at least eight Indonesians recruited into Russia's army.
Another Indonesian, Rendi Apriyanto, 30, was reportedly killed in September, his family learned from an Indonesian fighting for Russia. Rendi had told his family he was recruited for logistics work, The Jakarta Post reported.
HUR has traced the same fast track before. In January, it identified a Filipino recruit killed in a Donetsk Oblast assault after one week of training. A Nigerian, 34, died in Kharkiv Oblast after a similar week of training, HUR said in May.
Russia courts Africa ahead of a summit
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry has counted at least 2,982 Africans recruited into Russia's army, and 486 of them have died. Ahead of a Russia–Africa summit on 28–29 October, Moscow plans military and port-access deals with a string of African states, HUR said. The deals would help expand the campaign of Russia's Africa Corps, the Defense Ministry-controlled force on the continent, Army Inform reported, citing HUR.
Each recruit Ukraine identifies gives his home government a documented case to act on. Jakarta has said citizens shown to have been deceived will get its protection, while those who enlisted by choice could lose their citizenship.

Fatal Rotterdam explosion suspect acquitted for lack of evidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:26:38 UTC
23:26:38 KST

Fatal Rotterdam explosion suspect acquitted for lack of evidence
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A man suspected of causing an explosion in Rotterdam two years ago, in which three people died, has been acquitted.
Jalal O., a 37-year-old man who rented a garage in the Schammenkamp area of the city, was accused of using the premises as a drugs lab for processing cocaine.
In the aftermath of the explosion he climbed through the rubble looking for victims, and was initially perceived by local residents as a “hero”, according to media reports.
The explosion tore through the apartment complex above it, spreading a fire and partially collapsing the building. Besides the three who died, several were seriously injured and some lost their homes permanently.
After investigators analysed the scene, they found evidence including more than 40 acetone containers, traces of cocaine and procaine, and other paraphernalia. Prosecutors also found app messages between O. and his nephew they said were related to drug dealing.
In a procedural hearing after O.’s arrest in 2024, it was also disclosed that he had a previous conviction for drugs offences in Spain. He has always maintained his innocence and said at the time he had never been involved in the drug trade.
Prosecutors sought a seven-year sentence. If he had been convicted, the surviving victims would also have been eligible for compensation. They could instead take out a civil case against O. now that he has been acquitted.
The court found there was not enough evidence to convict him, and found no proof that the premises had been used as a drugs lab. It noted that the exact reason for the explosion remains unknown.
O. was a tenant of the garage but had sublet the space, and the court said the prosecution could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that he was responsible.

Who could Brazil's Lula pick for finance minister?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:25:54 UTC
23:25:54 KST

Who could Brazil's Lula pick for finance minister?
BRASILIA, Oct 26 - A sharp selloff in Brazilian markets on Monday after leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise reelection is pressuring the veteran leader to pick a finance minister who can send a signal of fiscal discipline and reassure markets.
Sources say Lula is likely to take his time to make a decision. But three sources who spoke on condition of anonymity said two key names have emerged: Vice President Geraldo Alckmin and Rafael Fonteles, the re-elected governor of Piauí state who revitalized Lula's flagging campaign after trailing in the first round to right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Here is a rundown of Lula’s choices:
WHO IS FONTELES?
Mathematician Fonteles, 41, is seen as a fiscally disciplined technocrat who could bridge the gap between Lula's administration and wary investors.
He holds a master's degree in mathematical economics and served as Piaui's finance secretary from 2015 to 2022. He also completed two terms as head of Comsefaz, which represents state finance secretaries.
WHO IS ALCKMIN?
Alckmin, 73, comes from the Brazilian Socialist Party and was once the president's center-right rival who lost to Lula in the 2006 presidential election. He is also a former two-term governor of São Paulo and ex-trade and development minister.
Reuters reported earlier this month that Lula was weighing Alckmin as finance minister to bolster his fiscal credibility and win over centrist voters.
WHAT IS WORKING FOR OR AGAINST FONTELES?
Fonteles gained prominence in Lula’s campaign after a shakeup that followed Lula’s first-round finish behind Bolsonaro.
A member of Lula's Workers' Party (PT), he is a close ally of Lula’s former education minister and senator-elect Camilo Santana. The two worked together on Lula’s campaign in Brazil’s Northeast, where the president secured a commanding lead.
In his victory speech, Lula thanked Fonteles for his role in the campaign, but noted that the governor still had a “mission to fulfill in Piauí,” which some allies read as a sign he may be reluctant to bring him into the cabinet so soon.
WHAT IS WORKING FOR OR AGAINST ALCKMIN?
In his victory speech, Lula lavished praise on Alckmin’s loyalty and even handed him the microphone before speaking himself. Lula wants a finance minister he trusts completely, one of the sources said. Alckmin is someone Lula trusts “100%,” another source noted.
"There are very few people outside the PT who have that kind of relationship with Lula today," one of the sources said.
Lula, however, may ultimately decide to retain current Finance Minister Dario Durigan, said the sources.
While Durigan lacks the political weight of some rivals, Lula is said to value him highly and view him as an "effective operator," according to a fourth source.
IT COULD COME DOWN TO THE CHIEF OF STAFF
The three sources said Lula’s choice of finance minister has become increasingly intertwined with whether Lula makes former Finance Minister Fernando Haddad his chief of staff.
Haddad, a member of the PT, left the Finance Ministry earlier this year to run for governor of Sao Paulo at Lula’s request - despite polls pointing to a likely defeat - to bolster the president’s base in Brazil’s most populous state. He lost.
Both Durigan and Alckmin, who are from outside the PT, are seen as having close ties to Haddad, which would also help ensure alignment between the Finance Ministry and the presidential palace.
Two sources also said that Lula understands that, given current market conditions, a PT figure alone would struggle to curb the slide in the Brazilian real or the surge in long-dated interest rate futures. This could boost Durigan and Alckmin's chances of being finance minister if Haddad is chief of staff. REUTERS

Qatar emir meets Iran president in Moscow amid mediation efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:24:14 UTC
23:24:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatar emir meets Iran president in Moscow as mediation efforts continue
Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow on Tuesday to discuss regional tensions, ongoing negotiations and the Strait of Hormuz, as Doha reaffirmed its commitment to preventing renewed conflict in the region.
The meeting took place at the emir's residence in the Russian capital ahead of the eighth summit of heads of state and government of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), according to Qatar's Amiri Diwan.
The two leaders discussed regional developments, the latest progress in negotiations, maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and energy supplies, alongside issues on the summit's agenda.
The talks came as Qatar's foreign ministry said mediation efforts aimed at halting regional tensions and securing a lasting agreement were continuing in coordination with Pakistan and other regional and international partners.
Ibrahim al-Hashimi, director of the ministry's Media and Communication Department, told a weekly press briefing in Doha on Tuesday that diplomatic efforts were moving in a positive direction.
He said the mediation was being conducted in coordination with Pakistan and other partners, with the aim of reaching a sustainable agreement that would bring the regional crisis to a definitive end.
Al-Hashimi also confirmed that a recent Qatari delegation's visit to Tehran formed part of ongoing consultations and mediation efforts.
The visit involved exchanges of messages, proposals and views aimed at resolving the crisis, he said, stressing that contacts through mediators and with the parties to the conflict had continued without interruption.
Qatar calls for reopening of Strait of Hormuz
Al-Hashimi said efforts by the countries involved in the Mecca Pact complemented the mediation led by Qatar and Pakistan, with diplomatic contacts focused on encouraging dialogue and preventing a resumption of hostilities.
He reiterated Doha's position that the region needed a collective security framework based on respect for state sovereignty and non-aggression.
Qatar and other Gulf Cooperation Council states were prepared to begin work towards establishing such a framework, he added.
The spokesman said Doha had heard positive statements from Iran regarding regional security but stressed that these needed to be translated into practical measures demonstrating goodwill and a commitment to stability.
He called on Tehran to stop threatening countries in the region and reopen the Strait of Hormuz to maritime traffic, describing the restoration of navigation as an important part of efforts to resolve the crisis.
His remarks followed a meeting in Tehran on Monday between senior Iranian officials and representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey under the framework of the Mecca Pact.
A joint statement issued after the meeting said the four countries had agreed to continue dialogue and consultations to strengthen cooperation, particularly in regional peace and security.
The meeting was hosted by Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
The participants agreed to maintain consultations aimed at promoting stability and cooperation across the region.
Energy cooperation on Moscow agenda
Meanwhile, Iranian news agencies Tasnim and IRNA reported that Pezeshkian and Sheikh Tamim had discussed ways to strengthen bilateral relations and expand political and economic cooperation.
The leaders reviewed developments in relations between Tehran and Doha and emphasised the importance of making greater use of both countries' economic capabilities to deepen their partnership.
Energy cooperation featured prominently in the discussions, alongside trade and investment and coordination between gas-exporting countries.
The Iranian agencies did not provide further details about any agreements reached during the meeting.
Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani attended the talks, alongside Amiri Diwan chief Abdullah bin Mohammed Al Khulaifi and other members of the Qatari delegation.
Iran was represented by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei and other senior officials.
Sheikh Tamim arrived in Moscow on Monday for the gas exporters' summit, where he was received at Vnukovo International Airport by Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov and Qatar's ambassador to Russia, Sheikh Ahmed bin Nasser bin Jassim Al Thani.
The summit brings together leaders of major gas-exporting countries at a time when regional tensions and disruptions to maritime trade have placed energy supplies and transport routes at the centre of diplomatic discussions.
Separately, al-Hashimi reiterated Qatar's support for dialogue between rival parties in Libya, calling for a political settlement based on relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions and other UN decisions.
