News coverage of psilocybin often outpaces the science, systematic review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:02 UTC
23:00:02 KST

News outlets and clinical studies report positive effects of psilocybin therapy at nearly the same rate, according to a new systematic review published in JAMA Network Open. However, while scientific papers tend to emphasize small sample sizes and study design flaws, news articles frequently present the compound’s medical benefits as established fact and extend them to conditions with little or no clinical trial backing. The findings suggest a gap between preliminary scientific evidence and public media narratives surrounding psychedelic medicine.
Psilocybin is a naturally occurring psychoactive compound found in hallucinogenic mushrooms. When a person ingests psilocybin, the body converts it into psilocin, a chemical that binds primarily to serotonin receptors in the brain and alters mood, emotion, and sensory perception. Medical researchers first began studying psychedelics in the 1940s, though legal restrictions in the 1970s slowed clinical studies to a near standstill for decades. Since the 1990s, scientific interest has rebounded, with modern researchers testing whether psilocybin can help treat mental health and substance use disorders.
Despite the surge in scientific interest, the clinical evidence supporting psilocybin remains in its early stages. For instance, a 2024 scoping review by several of the same researchers, which cataloged 193 published and 80 ongoing psilocybin studies, found that only 12 percent were randomized clinical trials, the standard medical test in which participants are randomly assigned to receive either an active treatment or a comparison substance. Most of the existing studies were small preliminary tests with a median of 22 participants.
Additionally, a 2023 systematic review of 10 psychedelic trials found that blinding, which keeps participants and staff unaware of who received the active drug versus a placebo, was either unsuccessful or never checked, likely because the drugs’ effects are so noticeable.
The authors argue that public interest has outpaced this preliminary evidence base. Between 2018 and 2021, the use of hallucinogens other than LSD, such as psilocybin, nearly doubled from 3.4 percent to 6.6 percent among young adults in the United States, and some people now use the substance off-label for mental health conditions without regulatory approval. Because many people rely on news coverage to inform health decisions, lead author Kim Madden of McMaster University’s Department of Anesthesia, senior author Anthony Adili, and their colleagues set out to compare the tone, safety details, and effectiveness claims in news articles against clinical trial publications.
“Psychedelics are having a renaissance, receiving increasing media coverage in recent years,” said Adili, a professor and vice chair of the Department of Surgery and an associate member of the School of Biomedical Engineering at McMaster University, as well as the chief innovation officer, head of orthopedics, an orthopedic surgeon, and director of the Centre for Health Innovation and Research in Psychedelics at St. Joseph’s Healthcare Hamilton. “While the socialization of these substances is helping facilitate research initiatives, we wanted to investigate how aligned media reporting is with the current published trials.”
To conduct their two-part systematic review, the researchers updated their earlier scoping review, searching four medical databases for English-language clinical trials of psilocybin targeting any medical condition between January 1, 2014, and October 10, 2024. They included randomized clinical trials and phase 1 or phase 2 nonrandomized trials, excluding review papers and studies on recreational use.
Next, the team searched the Factiva database for English-language news articles discussing clinical uses of psilocybin published between January 1, 2014, and April 22, 2025. They extended the media search six months past the trial cutoff to account for the delay between a study’s publication and subsequent news coverage, while excluding press releases, stock reports, and brief summaries.
Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data from every eligible trial publication and news story, with a third researcher resolving disagreements. For the trials, the team recorded the medical condition treated, sample size, dosing details, whether psychotherapy was included, safety outcomes, and the authors’ conclusions on whether the treatment worked. They also assessed randomized trials for bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. For the media articles, reviewers logged the target audience, specific health claims, discussions of side effects or drug policy, and overall tone, which they classified as favorable (combining optimistic and cautiously optimistic pieces), neutral, or skeptical.
The final dataset included 70 trial publications and 172 online news articles. Annual counts for both trial publications and media stories climbed starting in 2018, when trial publications rose from zero in 2017 to eight, and peaked in 2023. Most of the trials were conducted in the United States and the United Kingdom, while most news articles came from outlets in the United States and Canada. Nearly all media articles (163, or 95 percent) targeted the general public rather than medical professionals (9, or 5 percent), and 115 articles (67 percent) referenced at least one published clinical trial.
Of the 70 trial publications, 36 (51 percent) were randomized clinical trials, 30 (43 percent) were nonrandomized experimental studies, and 4 (6 percent) consisted of two nonrandomized crossover studies, one pooled analysis, and one secondary analysis. Nearly all of the trial publications described small sample sizes of fewer than 100 participants, accounting for 65 of the 70 papers (93 percent), and follow-up durations were often short or incompletely reported. Quality assessments indicated that 19 of the 36 randomized trials had a high or uncertain risk of bias regarding the blinding of participants and personnel, alongside concerns related to for-profit funding.
When comparing overall conclusions, trial publications and news stories reported positive outcomes at similar frequencies, though the two figures measure different things: a trial’s own conclusion about its main outcome versus any favorable claim in a news story. Forty-nine of the 70 trial publications (70 percent) concluded that psilocybin benefited patients on the primary clinical outcome, 5 (7 percent) reported mixed effectiveness, 1 (1 percent) found no benefit, 4 (6 percent) had inconclusive findings, and 11 (16 percent) provided no efficacy conclusion.
In the press, 125 of the 172 media articles (73 percent) made at least one positive claim about psilocybin’s effectiveness for a health condition, while 47 (27 percent) made none. In total, 122 media articles (71 percent) adopted a favorable tone, comprising 98 (57 percent) optimistic and 24 (14 percent) cautiously optimistic pieces, while 45 (26 percent) were neutral and 5 (3 percent) were skeptical.
Beneath those parallel numbers, scientific papers and news outlets framed the evidence quite differently. “The most practical significance of this systematic review is that there is a disconnect between media publications and the hard science,” Adili told PsyPost.
While trial authors routinely emphasized methodological limitations and the preliminary nature of their work, news articles tended to present benefits as established fact. Both groups focused primarily on depression, which was examined in 47 trial publications (67 percent) and mentioned in 138 media articles (80 percent). Other conditions examined in the trial publications included substance use disorders in 11 papers (16 percent), cancer-related distress in 5 (7 percent), headaches or migraines in 4 (6 percent), anxiety in 4 (6 percent), bipolar II disorder in 3 (4 percent), and body dysmorphic disorder in 2 (3 percent), plus single publications (1 percent each) on obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), autism, anorexia nervosa, and demoralization.
In contrast, news coverage frequently promoted psilocybin for conditions with little or no clinical trial backing. Most notably, 74 media articles (43 percent) referenced PTSD and 5 (3 percent) mentioned Alzheimer disease or other neurodegenerative conditions as clinical uses, even though zero eligible trials tested psilocybin for those conditions. Similarly, 72 news stories (42 percent) highlighted anxiety and 18 (10 percent) discussed anorexia nervosa or other eating disorders, despite the trial literature containing only four studies on anxiety and one on anorexia nervosa. Media reports also occasionally cited OCD (12 articles, or 7 percent), chronic pain (5, or 3 percent), and long COVID (4, or 2 percent).
The researchers also found differences in how treatment context and safety were reported. In 51 trial publications (73 percent), psilocybin was administered alongside psychotherapy, typically at doses of 25 milligrams or higher. While 107 news articles (62 percent) mentioned psychotherapy, 143 (83 percent) omitted dosing information entirely.
For safety, 31 trial publications (44 percent) reported safety outcomes, with 24 (34 percent) documenting short-term adverse events like temporary anxiety, nausea, or headaches, and only 4 (6 percent) assessing long-term safety. Media coverage addressed safety even less often, with only 51 articles (30 percent) mentioning adverse effects. When news stories did discuss harms, they focused on psychosis or challenging psychological experiences, with 12 articles (7 percent) noting potential long-term psychological risks that were not consistently tied to specific trial findings.
“Something surprising to me was how minimally media articles reported on safety,” Adili noted. “Based on the lack of safety reporting, we want audiences to be more aware that media articles may bias positive results without discussing safety concerns. As a result, patients may enter into trials with preconceived notions of the outcomes leading to potential disappointment if their expectations aren’t met.”
Policy themes were also widespread in the press. Across the 172 media articles, 48 (28 percent) discussed legalizing or decriminalizing psilocybin for clinical use, and 45 (26 percent) advocated for expanding patient access. Another 28 articles (16 percent) discussed reducing stigma around psychedelics, whereas only 8 (5 percent) mentioned the potential for misuse or abuse. The authors noted that pairing calls for expanded legal access with optimistic efficacy claims could foster public expectations that exceed the current medical evidence.
“We hope that the average person is more critical of overly positive media portrayal of psychedelics and is empowered to do their own research,” Adili explained. “When possible, reference the study that the media article references, delve deeper into potential safety concerns, and conduct further research.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The findings concern how psilocybin research is communicated, not whether the compound works; the trials remain early-phase, while public enthusiasm and policy changes in places like Oregon and Colorado have moved ahead. Additionally, the media review was limited to English-language, text-based online news articles in the Factiva database, primarily from the United States and Canada. The analysis did not capture television, radio, podcasts, or social media, which may convey different narratives to the public.
On the clinical side, the 70 trial publications included several papers reporting different analyses of the same underlying trials, along with conference abstracts and a dissertation, so they do not represent 70 independent experiments. The review also relied on each paper’s own conclusions about whether psilocybin worked, rather than a formal grading of the strength of the evidence.
Evaluating the tone and messaging of news articles also involves some subjectivity. Even though two reviewers coded each article independently using predefined criteria, their initial agreement was moderate, meaning another research team might classify certain content differently. Moving forward, the authors suggest that scientists prioritize larger, high-quality randomized trials with longer follow-up periods and thorough safety reporting. The authors also suggest that media outlets can support informed health decisions by avoiding sensationalism and explaining study limitations, sample sizes, and remaining scientific uncertainties.
“At the Centre for Health Innovation and Research in Psychedelics (CHIRP), our next steps are to design and conduct rigorous randomized controlled trials to produce evidence and actionable outcomes that can improve patient care,” Adili added. “Long-term, we hope to provide novel solutions for patients with few alternate options across a wide range of subspecialties from gut-brain health to neurodegenerative disease, chronic pain, and women’s health.”
The study, “Clinical Evidence on Psilocybin and Its Representation in Media Reporting: A Systematic Review,” was authored by Kim Madden, Breanne Flood, Imad Kashir, Rayan Ahmad, Hiba Ali, Rotem Petranker, James MacKillop, and Anthony Adili.

New poll upends narrative that Democratic voters are split on El-Sayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

In the final televised debate for Michigan’s Senate race, GOP candidate Mike Rogers used his closing remarks to claim that Jewish Democrats were supporting him because they view his Democratic opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, as “too extreme” on the subject of Israel.
“Jewish Democrats who are afraid for their children when their daughters can’t wear their Star of David walking across Michigan’s campus, these are real,” Rogers told the audience. “My opponent’s rhetoric, his vitriol, is having consequences.”
The idea that El-Sayed’s criticisms of Israel have alienated Jewish Democrats is certainly not limited to propaganda from the Rogers campaign. In recent weeks, multiple articles have used this very narrative as their thesis.
“Michigan Democrats at odds over Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed as November nears,” a Quartz headline declares.
“Questions about El-Sayed’s stance on Israel, accusations of antisemitism, and his campaign’s relationship with [left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan] Piker have kept the party’s attention away from its general-election opponent, Republican Mike Rogers,” insists the piece. “The divisions come as Michigan’s statehouse and governor’s races are also closely contested.”
Division was also the theme of an NPR piece claiming that Democrats were trying to “unify” before the midterms. The article asserts that “healing the fractures is proving complicated” and quotes multiple Democratic voters who express reservations about the candidate over Israel.
“Democrats are still struggling to unite behind El-Sayed after the primary exposed deep disagreements over Israel,” says PBS News.
CNN said a “ruptured” Democratic Party is “trying” to unite around the candidate.
The Detroit-based Super PAC TFM is attempting to ride this purported wave, spending nearly $6 million on ad campaigns connected to a “Democrats for Mike Rogers” effort.
“We believe in the true spirit of the Democratic Party, always standing against hate and bigotry, no matter where it comes from, who it targets, or whether it is politically inconvenient or not,” reads the campaign’s website. “We believe every American deserves dignity, respect, and equal protection under the law.”
This past weekend, a planned “Democrats for Mike Rogers” rally in Pontiac, Michigan, drew almost no one.
The Bulwark’s Joe Perticone shared images of the event on Twitter, showing three people in an empty parking lot and one person operating a camera.
“When your astroturf campaign meets actual turf,” joked the liberal social media account MeidasTouch.
The low turnout probably wasn’t a surprise to anyone who read a recent Marist survey of Michigan voters. Despite the media narrative detailing a massive split among Democratic voters, 95% of Democrats say they’re voting for El-Sayed, and just 4% say they’re voting for Rogers. 3% of Michigan Republicans actually say they’re voting for El-Sayed, but this minuscule number certainly hasn’t led to a host of stories about divisions within the GOP.
“The Democrats have a six-point advantage against the Republicans on the generic congressional ballot question among Michigan likely voters,” reads a write-up summarizing the poll’s findings. “That leads opens up to 10 points among registered voters, little changed from the nine-point lead the Democrats had in September. President Donald Trump’s approval rating is upside down in Michigan, and a plurality of likely voters express worry about their personal finances.”
If this is reality, why do many articles on the race tell the story of a divided party, and why do they rely primarily on testimony from rare voters to convey a wider trend?
Furthermore, why do so few of these pieces point out that Israel has grown deeply unpopular among Democratic voters and that El-Sayed’s positions are consistent with the vast majority of the base? An April 2026 Pew poll found that 80% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents held an unfavorable view of Israel, compared with 53% in 2022.
This framing goes well beyond El-Sayed. The idea that the Democratic Party is divided on Israel is a consistent theme in the mainstream press, despite the fact that voters are effectively aligned on the issue.
“There’s only one problem with the tensions,’ ‘divided,’ and ‘wedge issue’ framing: It is not supported by any polls,” wrote media critic Adam Johnson in The Intercept earlier this year. “The ‘divide,’ such as it is, is increasingly not among Democrats or even liberals; it is between the supermajority of Democratic Party voters and party leadership. While party leaders such as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and big Democratic donors, are pro-Israel, actual Democratic voters have moved on from Israel with remarkable speed and consistency.”
The pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC recently announced that it would stop issuing endorsements or directly earmarking contributions to political candidates. The move comes less than five years after the organization began making such endorsements. The shift exposes a clear truth: voters view AIPAC as a toxic entity, and their public support is doing more to hurt candidates than help them.
This was clear during Michigan’s Democratic primary, when El-Sayed highlighted opponent Haley Stevens’s connections to the group. An August Axios report showed that Mike Rogers even expressed concerns about an AIPAC endorsement, although he has since publicly welcomed their help.
This all seems relevant to next week’s election or, at least, more relevant than a split that doesn’t exist.

EU eyes better preparadness for climate risks with new strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The European Commission presented on Tuesday a new climate strategy aiming to better identify droughts, floods, wildfires and other effects of climate change and to manage the risks more effectively.
Climate resilience should be taken into account in all major EU policy areas in the future, the commission said.
"Europe is warming at double the global rate. To become truly climate resilient, we need to adjust and learn along the way," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Today, we are presenting a European approach to climate risks, to anticipate, to prepare for and to manage. We are ensuring that climate resilience will be included in policies across the continent, supporting investment, innovation and long-term growth," she added.
A new Climate Resilience Act is intended to ensure that EU countries assess their climate risks and plan their preventive measures using the same basic assumptions.
The specific ways in which the member states protect themselves against heat, drought and flooding will largely remain up to the individual countries, depending on their risks and priorities.
A website entitled the European Climate Viewer will show potential hazards for specific locations and periods. For example, users should be able to identify railway routes that may be particularly exposed to high temperatures or heavy rainfall, allowing targeted protective measures to be planned.
Other platforms will help public authorities identify suitable, proven measures for addressing specific climate risks.
The aim of the initiative is to anticipate the effects of climate change and prevent damage through action at EU, national and local levels, the commission said.
According to the commission's estimates, economic losses caused by climate-related damage amounted to around 200 billion euros ($223 billion) between 2022 and 2025, or 50 billion euros per year.
In September, von der Leyen announced that the initiative would pursue a whole-of-society approach, down to the local level.
According to data from the EU Earth observation programme Copernicus, the past summer was the hottest on record for Western Europe.
Up to Sept. 2, the area of land that burned in wildfires in the EU was almost twice as large as the average for 2006 to 2025.
According to estimates by British scientists, heat killed around 50,000 people in European cities over the summer, more than ever before.
In Germany, some 16,000 people died as a result of heat, according to estimates by the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), a government health agency.

Russia targets Kyiv as Finnish, Norwegian leaders hold rare call with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:59:37 UTC
22:59:37 KST

Kremlin downplays rare Putin call from leaders of Finland and Norway
Strikes hit a major bridge in the Ukrainian capital as leaders push for ‘direct discussions’ to end the war.
The leaders of Finland and Norway held a rare direct phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, describing the conversation as “frank and substantive”.
The call was initiated by President Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store from Helsinki “to discuss Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe”, Stubb’s office said in a statement.
“We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” said Stubb.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation”, said Store.
The pair spoke with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy afterwards, and the country’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been coordinated with Kyiv, calling it “the right approach”.
“We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process,” he said.
Russia sought to dampen the importance of the call, with the Kremlin’s readout of the exchange stating that long-term peace was possible “only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account”.
The readout also said that “attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU [European Union] and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities”.
Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov also downplayed the Finnish and Norwegian initiative, saying that European countries were merely seeking a role in future negotiations.
Nordic criticism of Putin call
Most Western European leaders have avoided direct contact with Putin since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, and there was a rare Nordic rebuke to Finland and Norway from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said she was “very sceptical” of reaching out to Putin.
“I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo,” said Frederiksen.
Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was also cautious about the outcome of the 90-minute conversation. Swedish public broadcaster SVT quoted him as saying, “If talks lead to peace, talks are good. My experience is that the results so far after the German and French talks have been very modest. And if you look at what Russia is doing on the ground every day, I don’t think there is anything to suggest that it is peace they are after – it is submission.”
A member of the European Parliament from Stubb’s own National Coalition Party cautioned against Finland playing such a visible role in ending the war. Mika Aaltola said there could be “propaganda value” for Moscow in such a move.
“Putin and the Russian media have already used Stubb’s earlier comments [about the conflict] as proof of the West’s wavering,” Aaltola said, while citing a “lack of coordination” and warning that “a single call weakens the common line”.
The Kremlin gave no hint that Moscow is ready to back down from its key demands, insisting that any lasting peace settlement must fully accommodate Russia’s interests.
Zelenskyy said Russian attacks, including relentless strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, must stop in order to open a path to peace.
“There must be peace, de-escalation is needed, and Russia must stop dragging out the war,” Zelenskyy said on X.
Russian attacks continue
Meanwhile, Russian attacks on Ukraine continued Tuesday, with a strike on transport infrastructure in Kyiv targeting a major bridge.
Officials in Kyiv said the South Bridge was hit in overnight attacks on the city that included 16 ballistic missiles and more than 280 drones. Zelenskyy said Russian forces struck again while emergency crews were still dealing with the aftermath of the initial strikes.
“This is a serious escalation in Russia’s campaign targeting our logistics,” he said.
Russian attacks also caused deaths and injuries in the cities of Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Telegram that its forces had targeted transport infrastructure in Kyiv and a logistics hub in the Kharkiv region, along with industrial sites and cargo vessels it said were serving military purposes.
Officials in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhia region said a drone strike on a bus killed one person and injured 30 others.
One person was also killed and six others were wounded in a drone attack on the Russian city of Bryansk, near the Ukrainian border.
The attacks come as the warring sides prepare for talks. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow said they had agreed to hold United States-mediated technical meetings in Abu Dhabi in early November.
In a separate development, US President Donald Trump has credited his wife, First Lady Melania Trump, with securing a localised ceasefire in the southern Kherson region, which took effect on Tuesday to allow aid into the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky.

In His Reporting, Japanese Journalist Yuki Imai Revealed a Fascination With Russia. Then He Was Arrested.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

In his last dispatch from Russia, the recently arrested Japanese journalist Yuki Imai reflects on the rising number of North Korean laborers in the country’s Far East. On the street, one asks him for a cigarette, while he sees others singing Soviet-era songs at a restaurant and buying jewelry in a shopping mall.
“Japan has no diplomatic relations with North Korea, but here on Sakhalin, I find myself catching glimpses of a people who otherwise remain entirely out of reach,” he writes, referring to the large, far-flung Russian island where he did the bulk of his reporting.
North Korean workers are some of the biggest victims of labor abuses in Russia, to say nothing of the isolated country’s shadowy involvement in the Ukraine war.
While the report makes no mention of those issues, the recollected encounters show how Imai, 34, didn’t shy away from the kinds of politically sensitive topics that have landed other foreign correspondents in trouble with the Russian authorities.
At some point, that reporting may have angered the wrong people.
Two weeks ago, a group of masked men broke into Imai’s hotel room in Sakhalin’s largest city, Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, and wrestled him to the floor. They were Federal Security Service (FSB) agents, arresting Imai on espionage charges likely related to his journalistic work. He is now awaiting trial in Moscow’s notorious Lefortovo Prison, where he faces up to 20 years in prison.
In Japan, his case is enveloped in secrecy. Few who knew Imai — including his employer, the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper — are willing to talk publicly about his background, the kind of journalist he is and what motivated him to report on the ground in a contentious region, despite the mounting risks for foreign correspondents.
But a review of his limited online presence and published articles reveals a picture of someone who was deeply fascinated by Russian culture, had family connections to the Far East and was committed to explaining the complexities of his home country’s relations with Russia.
The Hokkaido Shimbun declined to comment for this story, saying that it was still “gathering information” about the criminal charges against its journalist. In an open letter signed by Editor-in-Chief Takeshi Yamamoto, the newspaper said it was “responding with our highest priority on ensuring our reporter’s safety.”
Foreign correspondents are often criticized for parachuting into unfamiliar territory, firing off a quick report and leaving without ever developing a deeper understanding of their subject. Imai wasn’t that kind of journalist.
An acquaintance of his told the exiled news outlet IStories that Imai first came to Russia in 2014 for Russian language studies at St. Petersburg State University. According to the report, he also took an interest in Russian politics and literature.
It doesn’t appear that interest waned, even after Imai reportedly returned to Japan to continue his studies.
In recent years, Imai channeled his curiosities through journalism. He started reporting for the Hokkaido Shimbun, a daily newspaper located in the capital of Japan’s immense northern island of the same name. Owing to its proximity to both the Russian mainland and the disputed Kuril Islands, the newspaper publishes a robust section focused on Russian affairs, with a particular emphasis on bilateral relations.
The Far East is a geopolitically complicated region. Both Russia and Japan claimed and contested large areas of territory there during the 19th and 20th centuries before World War II largely sealed the matter, handing the Soviets control over most of it.
The enduring disagreement over ownership of the four southernmost Kuril Islands, which are controlled by Russia, has prevented the two countries from formally signing a peace treaty to end World War II.
Imai’s articles interrogated the conflict’s legacy and Japan’s absence from the islands that were once its territory, reporting on everything from the construction of a controversial war monument to the recent demolition of a disused Japanese government-funded medical clinic.
He also covered developments in politics and defense, from Russia’s recent parliamentary elections and relations with North Korea to the rise in military drone production on Sakhalin.
It’s unclear if any of these stories were the reason for Imai’s arrest, but it’s easy to see how officials might have felt his coverage was prodding at delicate topics, even if it wasn’t particularly intrusive.
For Imai, Russia and Japan’s fractured relationship was not merely a subject of professional fascination. He had roots in Russia’s Far East, noting in an article published this summer that his grandfather had lived in the Sakhalin town of Kholmsk — then called Maoka — before World War II, something that drew Imai to the same place a decade ago.
“My grandfather had lived in Maoka before the war,” he wrote, “and I wanted to see the remnants of Japan that remained in the town.”
The “remnants” he referred to are the long-abandoned buildings of a former Japanese paper factory. In the same article, Imai writes about the melancholic experience of walking past this area in August of this year after the factory was demolished. Gazing at the lot where the factory used to stand, he felt “as if a part of the town’s history had been lost.”
‘Most of the population doesn’t know his name’
Outside of his social media account and articles for the Hokkaido Shimbun, details about Imai’s background are scarce. That may come as a surprise to outsiders who remember the blitz of news coverage surrounding the arrest of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in Russia on spying accusations in spring 2023.
In Imai’s case, there has so far been no public outcry and no media campaign spearheaded by colleagues or family, as happened with Gershkovich and other foreigners arrested in Russia on dubious charges in recent years.
Aleksandra Bielakowska, the advocacy manager of Reporters Without Borders’ Asia-Pacific Bureau, said this is a common tack the government and families take when a Japanese reporter is arrested overseas.
“Usually how it works in Japan is that the Japanese government takes the lead, and they very rarely allow anyone else to intervene with any type of engagement,” Bielakowska said. “They will be very strict about not sharing any information or insight into what’s going on.”
In the past, that’s extended to even naming the individual, she added. The only reason the Japanese public knows Imai’s name in this case is because it was released by the Russian side. Publicly, Japanese officials have still not acknowledged that he was the person arrested.
In a statement to The Moscow Times last week that did not name Imai as the detained individual, Japan’s Foreign Affairs Ministry called on the Russian government to release the journalist and treat him in a “humane, fair and impartial manner.” On Tuesday, the Hokkaido Shimbun announced that officials from the Japanese embassy had finally met with Imai after nearly two weeks of no contact.
Part of the reason for this secrecy comes down to deeply rooted cultural norms.
“It’s just sort of the Japanese way of doing everything. They always prefer to avoid any sort of loud confrontation. They always prefer to deal with things behind the scenes,” said James D.J. Brown, a professor of international relations at Temple University, Japan Campus.
But that quiet approach could backfire by encouraging Russia to target others, Brown argued.
“This poor guy is being locked up, and most of the population doesn’t know his name. I also feel that if you don’t publicize it, there’s more risk of other people falling into the same danger,” he told The Moscow Times.
The biggest unanswered question is what Russia wants from Japan. Japan doesn’t hold any Russian prisoners that the Kremlin would like to see returned home. Still, Brown speculated that Imai could end up as part of a multinational prisoner swap, similar to the 26-person exchange in 2024 that freed Gershkovich.
However, Brown thinks Russia may care less about a prisoner swap and more about punishing Japan over larger policy issues.
Authorities in Tokyo have made a series of recent decisions that have unsettled the Kremlin about security in the Far East, including hosting American Typhon intermediate-range missiles.
Japan has also helped pay for weapons for Ukraine through a NATO initiative, while Japanese companies, like the drone manufacturer Terra Drone, have started doing business with the Ukrainian military.
“I think that, for all of that, Russia has decided that they want to apply pressure on Japan,” Brown said. “And frankly they regard Japan as likely to concede, so they feel they probably have a good chance of forcing some concessions.”
“It’s almost certain they will,” he said, referring to Japan giving in to at least some of Russia’s demands, whatever those may end up being. “That also explains the low-key approach. They want to perhaps have the freedom away from the public eye to cut a deal.”

Employing veterans could help address the labor shortage in Ukraine — MP Anatolii Ostapenko
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:58:56 EET
22:58:56 KST

Employing veterans could help address the labor shortage in Ukraine — MP Anatolii Ostapenko
Kyiv • UNN
MP Anatolii Ostapenko noted that, to help veterans return to work, it is necessary to help them adapt their skills to civilian professions and create appropriate working conditions.
Ukrainian veterans can help overcome the labor shortage, but their return to civilian working life requires the development of professional retraining, the adaptation of workplaces, and the practical implementation of state support programs. MP Anatoliy Ostapenko, head of the Subcommittee on Social Protection of Veterans’ Rights of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Social Policy, said this in an exclusive comment to UNN.
Details
Earlier, Tetiana Karelska, head of the HR and CSR direction at the European Business Association, said in a comment to UNN that Ukrainian companies are gradually developing practices for employing and reintegrating veterans. Businesses are training teams to interact with colleagues who have combat experience, creating adaptation and retraining programs, and some companies are introducing dedicated positions to support veterans. At the same time, it is still too early to talk about mass employment because of the dynamics of the military operations.
Preparing employers is only one component of veterans’ return to working life. State support mechanisms and professional retraining for defenders are also necessary. MP Anatoliy Ostapenko also emphasizes this.
Veterans can help solve the labor shortage problem, because many of them were already working before mobilization and had professions, experience, and qualifications. Our task is to help them return to civilian life and, where necessary, adapt their existing skills to new conditions
According to him, many veterans already had professions, experience, and qualifications before mobilization that may be in demand on the labor market. At the same time, some defenders return from the war with disabilities, which requires working conditions to be adapted to their abilities.
That is why professional retraining for veterans is extremely important. We must help people master civilian professions, acquire new competencies, and find work in accordance with their abilities and the needs of the market. This will not only support veterans but also partially meet the staffing needs of Ukrainian businesses
In his opinion, amid a significant labor shortage, employers effectively have no choice but to more actively involve people returning from military service in the workforce.
At the same time, this process requires a systematic approach: it is not enough simply to offer a veteran a vacancy - it is necessary to create conditions in which they can work effectively
Among such mechanisms, the MP mentioned compensation for the costs of equipping workplaces for people with disabilities, as well as opportunities for professional retraining and obtaining additional education. According to him, the key task remains the practical application of these tools and informing employers about the opportunities available.
It is necessary to ensure their practical application, inform employers about available programs, and help veterans take advantage of these opportunities. Only in this way will we be able to build a system in which a veteran has the opportunity to realize themselves in civilian life, while businesses can attract qualified workers
We remind you
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine is also working to support veterans. According to Serhii Byzov, chairman of the FPU, the Federation’s sanatoriums provide medical rehabilitation services to military personnel, while the organization itself, together with relevant ministries and the National Health Service of Ukraine, is developing programs to support, socially adapt, and employ veterans. According to the FPU, more than 32,800 military personnel have undergone medical rehabilitation at its sanatoriums.

Japan Confirms Dispatch to India to Explore Anti-Ship Missile Drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:58:00 UTC
22:58:00 KST

Japan has dispatched personnel to India to explore possible live-fire training involving Ground Self-Defense Force (GSDF) surface-to-ship missiles and small attack drones, GSDF Chief of Staff General Arai Masayoshi confirmed at a press conference on October 27.
“It is true that we dispatched personnel to coordinate various matters with India,” the head of the GSDF said.
The confirmation followed an October 21 report by public broadcaster NHK that Defense Ministry officials had traveled to India in mid-October and spent about one week inspecting test facilities and firing ranges.
The missile system for any prospective exercise has not been selected, and no decision has been made to conduct the training. But the exploratory talks attempt to solve a new problem for Japan.
“When operating relatively long-range missiles, such as surface-to-ship missiles, how to conduct training that makes use of their range is a major challenge,” Arai said.
The service is examining how to secure suitable training environments in Japan while also considering overseas facilities, he added.
The issue is becoming increasingly important as Japan expands its stand-off defense capabilities. Acquiring missiles capable of reaching targets hundreds of kilometers away is only part of the challenge. Personnel must also be trained to deploy and operate these weapons effectively.
Japan’s newly deployed Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missile illustrates the growing training requirements.
The GSDF deployed the missile to Camp Kengun in Kumamoto Prefecture in March 2026. Its range is believed to be around 1,000 kilometers, compared with around 200 kilometers for the earlier Type 12 surface-to-ship missile.
On October 25, during Keen Sword 27, a large-scale Japan-U.S. joint exercise running from October 19 to 29, the GSDF demonstrated the Type 25 to reporters at a training area spanning Nagasaki and Saga prefectures. Personnel demonstrated procedures for deploying a mobile launcher and preparing it for firing, but no missile was launched.
Such exercises help troops practice operating the system, but live-fire training that makes full use of its range presents additional challenges involving safety, airspace, maritime areas, and coordination with relevant authorities.
There is no confirmation that the Type 25 specifically would be used in India.
Japan has previously conducted surface-to-ship missile firing exercises in the United States and Australia. During the Philippine-U.S. Balikatan exercise in April and May 2026, the GSDF conducted such training in the Philippines for the first time, firing its Type 88 surface-to-ship missile.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro later told the Asahi Shimbun that the Type 88 was one of the leading candidates for acquisition by Manila.
Access to training facilities in India could further expand Japan’s overseas options while creating opportunities for closer cooperation with New Delhi.
“India is an important partner in the Indo-Pacific region, and we recognize the importance of promoting various forms of defense cooperation and exchanges amid an increasingly severe and complex security environment,” Arai, the GSDF chief, said.
Japan and India already conduct bilateral military exercises and cooperate with the United States and Australia through the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, or Quad, against the backdrop of growing concerns over China’s maritime activities.
However, the latest discussions concern possible bilateral arrangements, not an announced Quad military exercise. Potential Japanese missile training in India would add a practical dimension to bilateral defense cooperation.
Asked specifically about small attack drones, Arai confirmed that training involving such systems was also among the possibilities being explored.
He identified several challenges associated with training involving these systems, including radio frequencies, training content, suitable locations, operational conditions, and safety management.
Training arrangements must also reflect when, where, and how the GSDF expects to employ the drones, Arai explained. The service is considering both domestic training environments and possible overseas alternatives.
The general said no decision had been made on whether overseas training would precede domestic exercises or proceed alongside them. Conducting live-fire training in Japan would require coordination with relevant local governments and other authorities, taking account of the training activities and safety requirements.
For now, the India discussions remain exploratory. Neither the location nor the timing of any prospective exercise has been announced.
As Japan’s weapons gain greater reach, deciding where and how to train with them is becoming a matter of diplomacy as well as military planning.

Eisenkot is hoping to beat Netanyahu, but what does the Yashar leader stand for? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:57:45 UTC
22:57:45 KST

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot hopes to beat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and his bloc of political allies to get the first chance to form the next government.
However, due to the size of the Israeli-Arab parties, which are not specifically affiliated with a bloc, Eisenkot is not expected to be able to easily form the next government even if he wins more votes than the Netanyahu right-wing bloc.
Instead, he is expected to need to undertake complex negotiations with his coalition partners, especially Yisrael Beytenu's Avigdor Liberman, to convince them to form some kind of government or minority-voting bloc arrangement with the Israeli-Arab parties.
Eisenkot's campaign on Tuesday started early in the morning at Ofakim and Nir Oz in the Gaza Strip corridor, calling attention to the failures of the past government in preventing Hamas's October 7 invasion.
He then traveled further north to Ashdod, with other stops along the way, before voting in Herzliya at 1:45 p.m. and eventually reaching his election-night headquarters at the National Sports Complex in Tel Aviv.
The former IDF chief also went with his wife, Hana, to visit the grave of his son, Gal Eisenkot, who died in Gaza in late 2023.
Already by late morning, Yashar had filed complaints with the Israeli Election Commission complaining of alleged systematic vandalism and destruction of ballots carrying the party's name at various voting sites.
Eisenkot's largest support comes from voters who blame Netanyahu for October 7 or who blame him and his bloc for failing to draft the haredi sector into the IDF even after over 1,000 Israeli soldiers died in recent years.
What are his views on other issues?
Iran: Eisenkot less willing to take risk in attacking
There are few major differences between Netanyahu and Eisenkot here, though some nuances remain. Both would oppose a "bad deal" if US President Donald Trump's administration opts for one.
In that sense, the main difference is how they would address such a bad deal.
Unlike Netanyahu, Eisenkot would likely keep his opposition private in order to try to improve the deal quietly, while viewing American public opinion as something he has less control over.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot would be ready to attack Iran in some circumstances, but most would agree that, at this stage, Netanyahu would be willing to take on more risk and might interpret the point of no return as earlier than Eisenkot.
Gaza: Eisenkot has no real plan except Trump's
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a real plan for Gaza. Both have promised to eliminate Hamas's control of the Strip, Eisenkot within 18 months, and Netanyahu by the end of Trump's term, but neither has a clear path for doing so.
Eisenkot has no clear plan of his own, but unlike Netanyahu, is willing to push forward with Trump's ceasefire plan without significant resistance, including empowering Palestinian Authority-linked technocratic leaders and police, and international peacekeepers in Gaza.
He would likely be ready to allow partial rebuilding for partial Hamas disarming, if for no other reason than to pause and maybe even push back the diplomatic tsunami which is already threatening Israeli national security and economic stability.
These differences could have implications over the next year and years, but Eisenkot has made it clear he will not move toward a Palestinian state, certainly not in any first term.
West Bank: Eisenkot harsher on Jewish extremism, settlement expansion
If there are strong commonalities between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on Iran and Gaza and the differences are more in the nuances, they are night and day on the West Bank.
The only thing they both have in common is a strong commitment to fight Palestinian terror as the number one issue.
But on fighting Jewish extremism and on expansion of the Israeli settlements, the number two and three issues, they are far apart.
Eisenkot would immediately reinstitute administrative detention of Jewish extremists, which Defense Minister Israel Katz suspended in January 2025, and which Netanyahu has allowed to remain suspended for nearly two years despite losing control of Jewish extremists.
In addition, Eisenkot will clean house at the police, injecting officers who will come down hard on the Jewish extremists.
He will likely also fire Shin Bet Director David Zini and replace him with a new chief who will crack down more on Jewish extremists.
Regarding the over 100 new "farms" which Netanyahu's government expanded under Bezalel Smotrich's authority within the defense ministry, Eisenkot will likely clear most or all of them.
He will certainly freeze new settlement building or limit it to the "natural" expansion of existing settlements.
Collectively, these actions would help pause or even roll back the diplomatic tsunami which has started to engulf Israel's national security and economic stability.
However, Eisenkot has no vision for how to resolve the standoff with the West Bank Palestinians, which has lasted since 1967. Once again, he opposes a two-state solution in the near and medium term.
Lebanon: Netanyahu, Eisenkot aligned
There seem to be no major differences between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on Lebanon.
Both would maintain a security zone. Both are open to partial withdrawals in exchange for the Lebanese army partially clearing Hezbollah from the security zone, and neither trusts that the Lebanese army will do its job sufficiently.
Under light pressure from Trump (heavier pressure will be on Gaza and likely the West Bank), might Eisenkot agree to partial withdrawals faster than Netanyahu? Maybe.
But Eisenkot has said he would draw a line at eight kilometers so that Hezbollah cannot fire anti-tank missiles into Israel.
The only major nuanced difference might be that Eisenkot will try to return France to a productive role, hoping to score some diplomatic points with them on other fronts, whereas Netanyahu now relishes public conflicts with Paris.
Syria: Eisenkot to keep security zone, has trouble trusting al-Sharaa
Netanyahu and Eisenkot also likely differ little on Syria.
Once again, both want to keep a security zone, and both have dropped hints at times that they might agree to partial withdrawals, but both have strong doubts about trusting Syrian leader Ahmad al-Sharaa because of his al-Qaeda past.
Diplomatic relations: Eisenkot to improve European ties
Eisenkot would heavily improve relations with Europe.
He might reach some new understandings with Middle Eastern countries who once liked, but now loathe, Netanyahu.
All of those diplomatic wins could help on various national security and economic stability issues.
But the most crucial prize is the US.
Despite Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu, if Eisenkot wins and is more compliant with some of Washington's demands in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria, they will likely figure out how to get along.
More importantly, Eisenkot will not give up on the Democratic party, which has turned more against Israel than in any time in decades.
He will try to hit "restart" post-Netanyahu.
The bad news is that he has no clear plan for doing this, and the gulf between Israeli and American expectations about the Middle East really is large, even if Netanyahu exists stage left.
Whether Eisenkot could bridge that gulf would be one of the key challenges and uncertainties of his premiership.

Palestinians protest against military demolitions in West Bank as Israelis vote
HEBRON, West Bank, Oct 27 - Israeli troops fired a stun grenade on Tuesday to disperse Palestinians who gathered to protest against an Israeli military operation that has displaced thousands of residents from a neighbourhood in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
The unrest, which follows the deaths of two Israeli soldiers shot by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint last week, unfolded as Israelis were voting in an election in which the country's posture in the West Bank has been a major political issue.
Some Palestinian officials have accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of launching a crackdown in the West Bank to coincide with the vote, as a way to energise his right-wing supporters. The government says its operation is a response to the attack on its soldiers.
A group of Palestinian men, women, and children gathered at Tuesday's protest. One elderly man held a placard that said: "No to collective punishment, no to closures, and no to displacement."
The military said it had fired a stun grenade to disperse them so that its operation could continue.
On Monday, the United Nations said that over 3,000 Palestinians had been forced from their homes by the Israeli military operation, which targeted neighborhoods near the checkpoint where Palestinian gunmen killed the two Israeli soldiers on Friday.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," said UN human rights chief Volker Türk in a statement. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
The Israeli military said in a statement on Sunday that troops would carry out demolitions in the area. It said soldiers had not located any weapons in searches of the houses.
Since Friday's attack on the checkpoint, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns across the West Bank, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement.
Noura Nassar, a displaced resident who attended the protests, said she had struggled to get medical treatment because of the blockages.
"Where is the democracy in all of this? Their elections are today, sure, but what about us? Aren't we human beings? We want to go out, we want to visit the doctor," said Nassar.
Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot both oppose the creation of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. Residents expelled from the Hebron neighbourhood said Tuesday's election in Israel would do little to change the reality on the ground in territories Israel has occupied since 1967.
"Among themselves they will elect who is the oppressor and who will destroy the Palestinian people. That is their election," said Sana' Salman Abu Sneineh, another expelled resident.
Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements, which are deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Under Netanyahu's right-wing coalition there has also been a surge of militant settler violence against Palestinians. REUTERS

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

22:55:38 KST

The Sofia City Prosecutor’s Office has asked a court to keep Turkish businessman Eyup Temiz in permanent detention after charging him with the intentional killing of former Member of the European Parliament Slavi Binev, while media reports have raised questions about a business dispute and footage has emerged showing a second SUV following the vehicle used by the suspects.
The killing took place at Binev’s home in Sofia’s Pavlovo district on Saturday morning, following a heated confrontation. Details of the incident are expected to emerge during court proceedings, while accounts of the circumstances and possible motive have so far appeared in media reports.
The Varna-based website Afera first reported that a personal dispute was behind the shooting. According to the outlet, Niya Temiz, the accused man’s wife, was a business partner of Binev in the company Evinko. Binev and the Temiz family had spent Friday evening in the same social circle.
Afera reported that after returning home, Niya told her husband that Binev had threatened her. The following morning, Temiz went to Binev’s home and shot him in the head after a brief conversation. People close to Binev have rejected claims that he made threats, describing the incident instead as a domestic tragedy.
The newspaper 24 Chasa has reported further details about the financial dealings between the two men. According to the publication, Binev received 500,000 euros from Eyüp Temiz for helping mediate a major business dispute between Niya Temiz and architect Kalin Tiholov.
Binev and Temiz had known each other for years, partly through taekwondo. Tiholov confirmed to 24 Chasa that the former MEP had participated in negotiations over the division of corporate assets.
The newspaper reported that Binev had a heated telephone conversation with Temiz’s wife on Saturday morning, blaming her for the collapse of the deal and warning that the assets could be lost altogether. Niya reportedly began crying during the conversation.
Enraged, Eyüp Temiz allegedly went to the Pavlovo property with his personal driver and another associate. He confronted Binev over the offensive remarks, suspecting him of secretly working in the architect’s interests to secure valuable properties. After Binev failed to dispel his suspicions, Temiz struck him in the face and shot him in the head with a legally owned Sig Sauer pistol, according to the report.
Security camera footage from a nearby property shows three men leaving the scene after the shooting and walking toward a silver Range Rover parked on the street. Two initially approach the vehicle, look around and then return to the fence.
According to 24 Chasa, the men struggled to leave the property and had to climb over the fence. Temiz’s interpreter, who has a larger build, reportedly had particular difficulty. The other two returned to help him before all three entered the vehicle and drove away.
The website Mediamall has also published footage showing the suspects’ vehicle pulling away while following closely behind another SUV of the same model. Although the two vehicles could have been traveling together by coincidence, the second SUV’s identity remains unknown, raising questions about whether it was part of a planned escape and whether other suspects were involved.

KABUL, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Afghanistan's Foreign Minister Mawlawi Amir Khan Muttaqi on Tuesday described illicit drugs as an international problem, calling on the international community to help Afghanistan overcome the challenge.
Illicit crop cultivation and drug production are not confined to a specific geographical area, and the fight against this menace is a shared responsibility of Afghanistan and the international community, Muttaqi said at a gathering attended by Kabul-based diplomats and government officials.
As part of efforts to combat the drug menace in Afghanistan, Muttaqi urged the international community to help farmers switch to alternative crops, cooperate in providing treatment for drug addicts, and assist in combating drug trafficking networks.
Although Afghanistan has made significant progress in combating illicit drugs in the post-war period, sharply reducing poppy cultivation, drug production and processing, and trafficking, the country still needs more time to become drug-free. ■

Lebanon’s lost olive season: harvesting olives under drones and warplanes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:54:43 UTC
22:54:43 KST

Lebanon’s lost olive season: harvesting olives under drones and warplanes
Lebanon’s olive harvesters are facing dangerous conditions, with the potential for attacks and fear of cluster munitions.
Beirut, Lebanon – Every year, Khaled Farhat tends to his olive trees in the southern village of Majdel Selm, a task carried out year after year amid the din of war.
“I own an olive grove with about 200 trees. I tend to them in my spare time whenever I’m not on duty at the school,” he told Al Jazeera by phone.
This year, reaching his olive grove, which is just a 20-minute drive from the border with Israel, is more complicated due to the ongoing Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon. His town of Majdel Selm lies just north of Israel’s “Yellow Line”, below which the Israeli military is demolishing homes and local infrastructure.
To reach his land, Farhat said, he had to request access from his local municipality, which forwarded the request to the Lebanese Army. The army then coordinates with a mechanism established after June’s Tripartite Framework Agreement between the United States, Israel and Lebanon to get permits for locals to tend to their olive groves.
American University of Beirut’s Ramy Zurayk, a professor specialising in landscape design and ecosystem management, said the widespread damage to farms and buildings in southern Lebanon, along with restrictions on movement, is an attempt by Israel to make the area “sterile”.
“The Israeli project is to eliminate humans and living organisms from the land,” Zurayk told Al Jazeera. “They are doing this via a variety of methods, including destroying the habitat and the components of the landscape that provide life, which destroy the relationship between the people and this land.”
Many of the border areas’ olive trees have been burned to the ground or uprooted by Israeli bulldozers. Lebanon’s Environment Minister Tamara Elzein said more than 16,000 hectares (about 40,000 acres) of land have been torched since Israel began bombing, and later invading, Lebanon in October 2023, including through the use of white phosphorus, a highly flammable substance.
Israel continues to occupy nearly 630sq km (243sq miles) of southern Lebanon, which includes swaths of farmland and dozens of villages.
In areas where the olive groves are still intact, Israel’s occupation has complicated this season’s harvest. Farmers and landowners say they work with Israeli drones flying overhead and live with the fear of unexploded ordnance on the ground. An hour earlier, an Israeli shell had landed near Farhat.
“Drones are constantly in the sky. You look up and see one, two, three of them sometimes just moving back and forth,” Farhat said. “Warplanes sometimes pass by and carry out strikes nearby, taking a toll on us psychologically and emotionally.”
Permission to access own land
Israel has placed tight restrictions on Lebanese farmers’ access to their land, which has cost them their crops. Farhat said he was given just a two-week window to work his land, and the neglect of his farmland is already evident.
“Usually, there shouldn’t be any weeds. But since the time for tilling and clearing the land happened during our displacement, we weren’t able to clear it. The land remained as it was because we couldn’t reach it,” he said.
“We’re in the middle of the harvest now. If we manage to finish harvesting everything directly from the trees within this timeframe, then great. Otherwise, whatever remains will go unharvested.”
The time spent clearing these weeds eats into the limited time he has to pick his olives. But they could also conceal a deadly surprise. Farmers and landowners said working their lands in the south is rife with unexploded ordnance, including from cluster bombs.
In early October, at least two people were killed in olive groves in south Lebanon. A retired soldier was killed in Yater village in the Bint Jbeil district by Israeli artillery fire. Another young man, who worked as an engineer, was killed when Israeli ordnance exploded while he was harvesting olives in the village of Froun, also in Bint Jbeil. A day later, a member of Lebanon’s police force tending to farmland in the southern village of Ain Ebel, a predominantly Christian village, was also killed in an explosion.
“There is a constant fear of being targeted [by Israeli attacks], especially in areas near the sites of attacks, as well as the risk of encountering cluster bombs or other remnants of war, which pose a grave danger to human life,” Hicham Hoteit, a journalist and olive farmer from Babliyeh town in south Lebanon, told Al Jazeera.
Explosives have been a recurring problem for farmers in southern Lebanon since the final days of the 2006 war, when Israeli forces dumped cluster bombs containing between 2.6 and four million submunitions in the area, according to a Human Rights Watch report.
“One of the biggest challenges we’ve seen in southern Lebanon since the 2006 war is how long cluster munitions continue to affect people’s lives long after conflict has taken place,” Hiba Ghandour, Lebanon’s programme manager for the Mines Advisory Group (MAG), a nongovernmental organisation that aids communities affected by landmines, unexploded ordnance, small arms and light weapons, told Al Jazeera.
“Millions of submunitions were scattered across the region, including farmland, and many failed to explode on impact. They were left hidden in fields, olive groves and orchards – many of which we are still clearing today.”
According to a 2022 Lebanese Mine Action Center (LMAC) report, the government announced that much of the contaminated land had been cleared. “The Lebanese government announced that only 5 million square metres of land remained contaminated with cluster munitions [18 percent of the baseline to be cleared],” Ghandour said, citing the report.
“Since October 2023, the situation has become more complex. The latest hostilities have added a new layer of explosive hazards.”
Ghandour said MAG had identified 444,000sq metres of confirmed hazardous areas for farmers, but with research still ongoing, this figure is likely to rise significantly.
Despite these dangers, Lebanon’s dire economic situation has pushed many Lebanese to work their lands out of necessity.
“In our experience, clearing agricultural land is especially challenging, as the contamination can be concealed within vegetation or beneath soil, which takes us longer to clear,” Ghandour said.
“When people are under pressure to earn a living, they often feel they have no choice but to return to their land before it has been made safe, making clearance all the more challenging. Repeated bombardment has also damaged agricultural land and made it harder for our clearance teams to reach some of the communities most in need.”
Political analyst Bassel Doueik told Al Jazeera that many Lebanese citizens have been harassed by Israeli forces and barred from harvesting their olive trees.
Doueik used Kfarshouba, a predominantly Sunni border village, as an example. On Monday, he said, about 200 Israeli soldiers entered Kfarshouba and searched houses in several neighbourhoods, while at least three Merkava tanks and other military vehicles infiltrated the area around the village.
Hope for a better future
The widespread use of white phosphorus has led some Lebanese to hesitate buying produce from the south over concerns that it could be exposed to hazardous chemicals.
Zurayk, the AUB academic, said in a panel hosted at his university on October 21 that the panic was unfounded and there was no evidence that any of the olives or other produce from south Lebanon was dangerous to consume.
For many in Lebanon, including in areas beyond the south, harvesting olives is serious work but is also an opportunity for their families or communities to come together.
Many people with farmland across south Lebanon have said this year, due to the threat of Israeli attacks, they will leave their children and other relatives behind when they head to their crops. Back in Majdel Selm, Farhat said the dangers are evident in the south this harvest season.
“People hear that the situation is dangerous, they hear that there is shelling, but for someone who is actually in the midst of the shelling, or living under it, it is certainly a different experience,” he said.
“The reality on the ground is something else entirely. Still, thank God, hopefully, this is just a phase that will pass. Hopefully, the situation will not escalate further and will begin to de-escalate and move towards something better.”

Photos show Ukraine's Starlink was down during fatal strike

Photos show Ukraine's Starlink was throttled during Russian strike that killed 5 in park
Kharkiv, Ukraine – Yulia Spichak, a 34 year-old makeup artist in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, dropped her son off at an English-language lesson on Oct. 19 and sat down in a nearby park to send a selfie to her sister, Alina. Seconds later, a Russian drone slammed into the park, killing Spichak and four others, including a 1-year-old girl.
The attack came six days after Elon Musk's SpaceX throttled Ukraine's access to Starlink, which Ukraine has been using to coordinate its defenses against Russian attacks and for some of its offensive operations. In a post on X, Musk accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by also using it for attacks on Russia.
Ukrainian officials told CBS News that the restrictions imposed without advance notice affected ground-based air defense radars and drone interceptors, hindering the military's ability to stop incoming Russian strikes.
"It's an essential part of the air defense infrastructure," Vadym Ivchenko, a Ukrainian member of parliament on the National Security, Defense and Intelligence Committee, told CBS News Monday. "I couldn't say that all other air defenses stopped working, no. But this part is quite essential for the defense of civilians in Ukraine."
CBS News obtained photographs that show Ukraine's ground-based air defense radars' Starlink connectivity dropping to .1 megabytes per second on Oct. 19, the day of the Kharkiv drone attack. That would not be enough to load a webpage, let alone power air defense radars, according to a source familiar with the technology who requested anonymity because he was not permitted to comment on the matter.
On Saturday, Ukrainian officials confirmed that Starlink's access had been restored across the country, with Musk admitting that SpaceX had throttled connectivity.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."
Ukrainian officials have also complained of connectivity problems with Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade network, which runs on the same constellation of satellites as Starlink and serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations. But Musk said the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment, and the White House referred CBS News to President Trump's comments last week, during which he told reporters that he did not order the Starlink restrictions in Ukraine.
Alina Spichak, the sister of Yulia, the make-up artist who died in the strike in Kharkiv, revisited the park where she died with CBS News on Sunday. She said the Geran-4 Russian jet-powered drone that killed her sister arrived so quickly the victims didn't hear it coming.
"I understand that everyone has their own lives and nobody wants to look at these horrors. But I believe that the whole world has to know what is happening in Ukraine, that there is a war here and we are being attacked," Alina Spichak said. "I really hope that it will end soon."

====================================================================================================

Sri Lanka: Outrageous organized crime bill granting authorities unchecked powers must be withdrawn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:53:52 UTC
22:53:52 KST

A new bill before Sri Lanka’s parliament that grants the authorities sweeping arbitrary powers to tackle ‘organized crime’ and deny suspects’ human rights should be immediately withdrawn, Amnesty International said today.
The Prevention of Organised Crimes bill, tabled in Sri Lanka’s parliament on 6 October, contains provisions that would make confessions extracted under duress admissible in court, enable the detention of suspects for up to two years without trial, and ban the media from reporting on court proceedings. The bill also confers the police with wide powers to conduct searches without a warrant, and imprison people for not providing information to authorities.
The bill mirrors many elements of Sri Lanka’s repressive Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), which has been misused since the 1970s to target minorities and repress dissent.
“This extraordinary bill is the most alarming in a string of repressive laws proposed by the National People’s Power (NPP) government. It reintroduces most of the very worst elements of the PTA and applies them to a wide range of offences,” said Smriti Singh, Amnesty International’s South Asia Director.
We urge the Sri Lankan government to withdraw the bill in its entirety
Smriti Singh, Amnesty International’s South Asia Director
“The bill entrenches impunity and risks reviving the conditions that enabled arbitrary detention, torture and other ill-treatment under the PTA, including the use of coerced statements to secure convictions. It allows what effectively amounts to secret trials and it removes virtually all the safeguards designed to prevent the abuse of police power. The international community, which saw and decried the abuses under the PTA, should shudder.
“We urge the Sri Lankan government to withdraw the bill in its entirety and engage in meaningful public consultations around how to tackle organized crime while protecting human rights.”
The bill also empowers police to obtain personal information from telecommunications, satellite, digital and data service providers – including subscriber identities, call records and device location data – without a court order. This would infringe on the right to privacy and create significant risks of abuse, including the surveillance of journalists’ contacts, lawyers’ communications, and organizers of lawful assemblies.
The bill covers offences already criminalized under Sri Lankan law, including intellectual property violations, Penal Code offences such as obstructing public servants and secret wrongful confinement, but subjects them to fewer due process safeguards when committed by an organized criminal group, to support prosecutions.
An organized criminal group is defined in the bill as “a structured group of three or more persons, existing for a period of time and acting in concert… in order to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit”.
To determine whether an individual is a member of such a group, courts are allowed to consider a range of circumstantial evidence including their “style of dress, hand signs, language or tattoos used by known members of the organised criminal group” or whether they visit places known to be used by organized criminal groups. Courts are also allowed to consider past conduct and association as admissible evidence to prove membership of an organized criminal group.
Statements made before a magistrate by persons who can’t be cross-examined – on account of their being dead or because they cannot be found – are also permitted as evidence of criminal conduct, while a provision in the bill making it an offence to knowingly do “any other act… in furtherance of a common criminal object borne by the members of an organised criminal group” is extremely vague, and subject to possible abuse.
“Criminal guilt must be based on actual evidence of individual wrongdoing from objective factual circumstances defined by law with sufficient precision, not appearance, association or suspicion. Provisions that allow people to be branded members of criminal groups based on how they dress, whom they know or where they go risk discriminatory profiling and undermine the prohibition of arbitrary detention and the right to a fair trial,” said Smriti Singh.
Criminal guilt must be based on actual evidence of individual wrongdoing
Smriti Singh
The proposed bill risks facilitating torture and other ill-treatment by weakening key safeguards against coercion and undermining fair trial guarantees. By making confessions to police officers above the rank of Assistant Superintendent admissible evidence and removing protections against torture and other ill-treatment, it increases the risk that coerced confessions could be used to secure convictions.
The bill also reverses the burden of proof in relation to torture and other ill-treatment, with the onus placed on accused persons to prove that abuse occurred.
Judges are permitted to alter indictments mid-trial from organized crime offences to ordinary offences when there is no evidence of the former, instead of discharging the suspect and the prosecution filing a new indictment for the correct offence.
These provisions further undermine fair trial rights, due process and safeguards against arbitrary detention and risk reproducing features of the PTA, creating conditions conducive to torture or other ill-treatment and impunity for perpetrators.
Under its provisions, an individual accused of being a member of an organized criminal group can be detained for up to a year before being charged and for a further year in pretrial detention. It also creates a legal obligation to give information to police, including information that would otherwise be protected by privilege, with punishments of up to seven years in prison and/or a fine of up to 200,000 rupees (approximately 600 USD) for failing to do so.
“Sri Lanka is following a dangerous path by introducing legislation that weakens safeguards against torture and other ill-treatment and that puts fair trial guarantees at risk, repeating the mistakes of the PTA. This must stop. Allowing statements that could have been obtained by torture or other ill-treatment to be admissible in court while shifting the burden onto victims to prove their abuse risks entrenching impunity and undermining the fundamental rights of anyone accused of a crime,” said Smriti Singh.
Background
The National People’s Power government recently passed into law amendments to the Financial Transactions Reporting Act, the Convention on the Suppression of Terrorist Financing Act, and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, which civil society organizations have criticized for undermining the rights to freedom of association and expression.
The government is currently in the process of repealing the draconian Prevention of Terrorism Act by attempting to replace it with the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Act, which Amnesty International has also raised alarm over.
