Fighters of the Freedom of Russia Legion Started Shooting Down Shaheds with Interceptor Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:53:04 UTC
22:53:04 KST

Fighters of the Freedom of Russia Legion have mastered a new area of combat operations and have begun using interceptor drones against Russian attack drones.
The unit reported this on its official channels and released a video of combat training and target engagements.
“Defending Ukrainian airspace is one of our top priorities, and it is important for us not to stand still, but to develop and be useful where it is truly needed,” Legion Commander Maksimilian Andronnikov reported.
To ensure air defense capabilities, the fighters undergo specialized training and practice rapid deployment procedures.
The crew training process covers the full cycle of operations—from installing antennas and configuring communications to testing the control systems for interceptor drones.
The unit is equipped with high-speed, vertical-takeoff quadcopter interceptors with antennas, and mobile command posts.
The video also shows the interception of a Russian Geran-2-type strike UAV.
Using drones to destroy enemy strike UAVs conserves anti-aircraft missiles for traditional air defense systems.
Legion operators carry out missions as part of mobile fire teams and specialized unmanned aerial vehicle crews.
Freedom of Russia is a volunteer unit composed of Russians within the Defense Intelligence of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, deployed to carry out missions in various sectors of the front.
Previously, the insurgent movement in Russia carried out strikes on railway tank cars, destroying over 10,000 metric tons of fuel.
As a result, operations at several key rail junctions halted, blocking supplies and disrupting key logistics corridors.

Flemish Ardennes booming as staycation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:52:37 UTC
22:52:37 KST

The Flemish Ardennes, an area of outstanding natural beauty in East Flanders province, are becoming increasingly popular with tourists. In 2025, 487,070 overnight stays were recorded. That is 5.5 per cent more than in 2023. The towns of Oosterzele and Brakel stand out in particular: the number of overnight stays in Oosterzele rose by 72.6 per cent, and in Brakel by 56.2 per cent. In Brakel, the mayor has clearly noticed this growth. “We get enquiries about opening new holiday accommodation almost every week,” says Marleen Gyselinck.
The figures from Statistics Flanders and Tourism Flanders show the East Flemish town of Geraardsbergen recorded the highest number of overnight stays in the Flemish Ardennes, with 96,734, followed by Oudenaarde with 83,123. Brakel ranks third with 50,654 overnight stays.
Not all municipalities have seen this growth. In Ronse, the number of overnight stays fell by almost 12 per cent, to 40,762. Oudenaarde also saw a slight decline of just over 3 per cent.
Oosterzele and Brakel stand out
Oosterzele has seen the largest percentage increase of all municipalities. The number of overnight stays rose from 6,664 in 2023 to 11,499 in 2025. Brakel is also performing remarkably well: from 32,438 to 50,654. “A lot of B&Bs and holiday homes are springing up here,” says Brakel’s mayor, Marleen Gyselinck.
“We’re receiving more and more applications, practically every week. People are inheriting houses from their parents and converting them into holiday lets. Most holiday lets are fully booked every week. I see this happening in my own neighbourhood too. It really is a beautiful region, and one we can be quite proud of it.”
Cycling tourism also plays a part, but Brakel’s appeal is not limited to the racing season. “Tourists flock to Brakel even outside the cycling season. In fact, we welcome visitors all year round,” says Gyselinck.
In Oosterzele, the number of holiday lets has risen further. Six new ones have been added since 2024. Sixteen of the 21 accommodation options in Oosterzele are lets. The council is pleased with the figures, but notes that the number of overnight stays in holiday lets is an estimate by Statbel, and therefore not an exact figure.
Tourism generates nearly 6,000 jobs
The tourism sector of East Flanders is estimated to account for 5,945 jobs and an annual turnover of 85.4 million euros. “Compare it to two or three large factories,” says Boris Dewolf, team lead for researchers at Tourism East Flanders. “These jobs are locally based and often have low entry barriers.”
Cycling contributes to the appeal of the Flemish Ardennes, but it is not the only reason why people stay overnight there. “We record the highest number of overnight stays in the summer. Often, these are people taking a short holiday at home,” says Dewolf.

Australia warns of ‘unprecedented’ AI-powered cyberattacks. Here’s what’s driving them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:52:08 UTC
22:52:08 KST

The country’s cyber security agency says AI is helping criminals and state-backed hackers exploit vulnerabilities faster, as recent incidents expose risks to government systems and critical infrastructure.
Artificial intelligence poses an "unprecedented" threat as foreign governments turn it loose to hack computer networks and critical infrastructure, Australia's cyber security agency warned on Tuesday 27 October.
It comes at a time when governments around the world are struggling to deal with the scale of the threat posed by AI as it is used in new ways to discover and exploit digital vulnerabilities, such as last week’s PHP security flaw which saw governments shut down their websites to protect themselves from cyberattacks.
The Australian Signals Directorate, which used some AI tools to compile its own Annual Cyber Threat Report, said rapidly advancing AI models could be of huge benefit if harnessed for good.
But recent months had also shown how AI was helping criminals and state-sponsored hackers launch attacks at "greater scale than ever before", the directorate said in the report.
"AI has been the defining force in the cyber threat landscape over the past year, allowing malicious actors to find vulnerabilities faster and exploit them at unprecedented scale, speed and sophistication," the report read.
"In recent weeks, new threats have emerged from the unintended actions of AI agents and model testing."
Global worries about the power of advanced AI tools are mounting after a string of hacking incidents and rogue AI actions involving models from leading developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
In June, an OpenAI model bypassed safeguards during training and hacked an Australian government website. The company only discovered the incident in August and later revealed it to Australian authorities in September, a breach Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described as ''obviously unacceptable''.
What the report found
The report documented a stark increase in cyber security incidents.
The Australian Signals Directorate issued more than 4,400 warnings about potentially malicious activity over the past year — an 80 percent increase compared to the prior 12 months.
"State-sponsored cyber actors continued to target Australian organisations primarily to gain access to sensitive or non-public information.
"This activity extends beyond government networks, and includes critical infrastructure entities, private businesses and individuals."
The report said hackers linked to China, Russia and North Korea had targeted Australia or its allies in recent times.
It’s not the first time Australia has sounded the alarm on cyberattacks. In June 2020, then prime minister Scott Morrison announced that Australian governments, industry, political bodies, health networks and critical infrastructure had come under sustained cyberattacks from a sophisticated state-based actor.
Defence Minister Richard Marles said the nation could not ignore the AI revolution.
"AI is here and it's real. People need to engage," he told reporters.
"There's no turning the clock back in relation to that. Malicious actors are using AI to find vulnerabilities in systems."
Marles urged Australians to update their computers and "harden their systems".
Governments and firms have in recent days been rushing to fix critical flaws in a programming language that runs a large share of the world's websites.
The vulnerability was found using a powerful model from OpenAI.

Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil refinery, blasts shake Riyadh
Yemen's Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a ballistic missile on Tuesday, as blasts shook the capital of the world's top crude exporter.
Saudi Arabia, the Middle East's largest economy, has suffered weeks of strikes from the Iran-backed Houthis against oil and civilian sites including Riyadh's international airport.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces were able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, saying the strike caused "massive fires".
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis earlier said it had shot down three missiles fired by the group towards the Eastern Province.
A resident in the city of Al Khobar, south of the Ras Tanura complex, told AFP he heard explosions around dawn and received a text message alert.
"We got the alert on the mobile and then heard a very loud bang," the resident said.
Maritime security agency Vanguard said a fire was reported in the Ras Tanura area in the early hours of Tuesday after an attack.
"The fire has reportedly been contained, while the extent of damage and any impact on oil-loading operations remain unclear at current," Vanguard said.
The Ras Tanura facility along Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast is home to one of the largest refineries in the Middle East and a cornerstone of the kingdom's energy sector.
The complex has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. It has been repeatedly targeted by strikes blamed on Iran, including a drone attack in early March that forced a partial shutdown of the refinery.
Meanwhile a series of explosions echoed across the capital, Riyadh, shaking office windows in the city centre. A text message alert warned residents to seek shelter.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted two ballistic missiles that were fired at Riyadh.
Egypt 'declared war'
Earlier, a Houthi official said the Egyptian parliament's decision to authorise defensive military support for Saudi Arabia amounted to a declaration of war.
Egypt's parliament authorised the measure on Monday, following a request from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
"It is truly remarkable that while these people go to discuss what they call 'peace in the region', Egypt and its parliament declare support for the so-called defence of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, declare war against the Republic of Yemen," said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, in a Telegram post.
It was not clear exactly what support was on offer from Egypt, which has the Arab world's largest military.
Al-Houthi's statement also pointed to Monday's visit to Tehran by the Saudi defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief, in a bid to de-escalate tensions in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad recently signed a NATO-style defence pact in Mecca, pledging to consider an attack on one country as an attack on all three.
Turkey and Pakistan have not announced any strikes on the Houthis during the group's weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia.
'Not afraid of any alliance'
The Houthis said the group was "not afraid of any alliance that may be formed".
Yemen's largely dormant conflict reignited in July, further destabilising the region months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.
The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing swathes of Red Sea coastline in a major offensive in September.
The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi strikes targeting areas under their control.
This month the Houthis ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, forcing the cancellation of flagship events and shutting down Riyadh's airport for two weeks.
The Houthis' war with the Saudi-led coalition began in 2015, months after they ousted the internationally recognised government from the capital Sanaa in September 2014.

170-million-year-old fossil in northern Iran presented for scientific study

Unknown Publisher

170-million-year-old fossil in northern Iran presented for scientific study
TEHRAN - A fossilized tree trunk estimated to be 170 million years old and discovered in Iran’s northeastern Golestan province has been presented as a valuable resource for scientific research, natural heritage conservation and the development of science tourism.
The fossil was identified in 2021 during road-widening work along the Azadshahr-Shahroud route and was subsequently transferred to the Golestan Department of Environment after officials confirmed the discovery, IRNA reported on Tuesday.
Preliminary assessments suggest that the specimen belongs to a group of coniferous trees, although further specialist studies are needed to determine its precise classification and geological age.
Mahmoud Shakiba, head of the wildlife protection and management, natural history museum and genetic resources department at the Golestan Department of Environment, said the fossilized trunk was among the province’s valuable natural heritage assets.
He said the specimen could help researchers investigate the region’s geological history and ancient vegetation while raising public awareness of paleontology and natural heritage.
Although the fossil has been estimated to be around 170 million years old, its precise geological period remains uncertain. Further expert examination is required to establish whether it dates to the Late Triassic or Middle Jurassic, Shakiba said.
A fragment of the fossilized trunk has been donated to the Department of Environment’s Biodiversity Museum in Tehran, a move intended to make the specimen more accessible for scientific and educational purposes.
Shakiba said the provincial environmental department had collected about 100 fossil specimens of different plant and animal types, which are being kept at its museum. Recently, 50 specimens were sent to the biodiversity museum in Tehran for further identification and taxonomic assessment.
Fossils provide important evidence of the history of life, past environmental conditions and changes in the Earth’s ecosystems over geological time. Proper preservation and documentation in specialized museums can support scientific research and help transmit knowledge of the natural world to future generations.
Shakiba said identifying, protecting and presenting fossil discoveries was part of the broader responsibility to safeguard Iran’s natural heritage. He added that greater public awareness of such resources could strengthen conservation efforts and improve understanding of the country’s natural history.
The fossil discovery also highlights Golestan’s wider potential for nature-based and educational tourism. The province is home to part of the Hyrcanian forests, an ancient forest ecosystem whose history extends back tens of millions of years.
Unlike fossilized remains, these forests are living ecosystems that preserve elements of ancient vegetation and provide important evidence for understanding long-term ecological change.

Riga considers postponing Vanšu Bridge repairs as plans for temporary bridge remain uncertain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:48:51 UTC
22:48:51 KST

The reconstruction of Riga's Vanšu Bridge could be postponed by three to six months, from the fourth quarter of 2027 to mid-2028, unless effective traffic management solutions are developed and implemented, Riga Mayor Viesturs Kleinbergs of the Progressives said on Tuesday during a discussion organised by the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI).
The mayor explained that several solutions are currently being assessed simultaneously, including redesigning intersections to increase traffic capacity and constructing a temporary bridge to partially alleviate congestion during the reconstruction.
"If we see that certain preparations cannot be completed by the deadline, we will postpone the start of the repair works," Kleinbergs said.
Kristaps Kauliņš, Director of Riga City Council's Department of Outdoor Space and Mobility, said the current plan envisages reconstruction beginning in late 2027 and continuing until 2030.
The first two stages are not expected to involve significant traffic restrictions, as they will focus on reconstructing the Daugava river embankment and Krišjāņa Valdemāra Street.
During the third stage, when the bridge itself undergoes major repairs, traffic will be reduced to one lane in each direction. Exceptions will apply during the replacement of the bridge's suspension cables, which is planned for nights and weekends.
Kauliņš explained that there are 20 signal-controlled intersections around Vanšu Bridge. The municipality is examining ways to increase their capacity and redirect traffic away from the bridge.
Possible measures include additional traffic lanes, redesigned turning arrangements and adjustments to traffic light timings.
Kauliņš also said that the start of the bridge's main reconstruction works could be postponed until the second quarter of 2028 without significant difficulties.
The overall project has been divided into three separate construction projects, each with its own building permit, allowing the stages to begin independently.
Mārtiņš Lazdovskis, Chairman of the Board of Latvian State Roads (LVC), explained that the government has begun replenishing its strategic material reserves and has signed a contract to purchase temporary bridge structures, as the existing bridges in state reserves have reached the end of their service life.
Two years ago, LVC launched the procurement of modern bridge spans and signed an agreement with an Austrian company to purchase single-lane bridge sections measuring 45 metres in length and capable of supporting loads of 100 tonnes.
Initially, deliveries were scheduled to take place gradually until 2029.
However, Lazdovskis explained that if the government decides to bring forward the funding allocated for 2028 and 2029 to 2027, the Austrian manufacturer could produce and deliver the required bridge components within eight months.
"At the same time, we must remember that these are only Lego blocks from which the bridge is assembled. Temporary supports or pontoons are also needed, along with access roads," Lazdovskis said.
Guntars Vītols of the United List, an adviser to Finance Minister Māris Kučinskis, stressed that funding for the temporary bridge could be found because the economic losses caused by severe congestion should be avoided.
However, the Ministry of Finance is concerned that planning for the temporary bridge may have started too late.
Vītols added that a political decision is needed to simplify procurement and design procedures.
Guntis Āboltiņš-Āboliņš, Chairman of the LCCI Construction and Real Estate Development Committee, recalled that a temporary bridge design originally developed for Rail Baltica is already available.
He suggested that a temporary bridge could therefore become operational within a year.
"It is urgently necessary to examine the riverbed, determine what should be installed where, and establish which supports are required," Āboltiņš-Āboliņš said.
Riga Deputy Mayor Māris Sprindžuks of the United List argued that approximately 80% of the solution would depend on reorganising traffic.
In his view, the priority is to avoid delays in launching accelerated design-and-build procurements for intersections that would allow traffic flows to be redirected.
Sprindžuks believes a temporary bridge could realistically be installed in 2028, but traffic arrangements must be redesigned before then.
Kauliņš explained that Riga City Council favours placing the temporary bridge alongside Vanšu Bridge on the Old Riga side.
Under this option, vehicles on the left bank would access the temporary bridge via the existing Ķīpsala exit near the Saules akmens office building.
On the right bank, a temporary intersection would need to be constructed connecting the bridge to 13. novembra krastmala.
However, LCCI representatives, including road engineer and entrepreneur Jānis Vasaraudzis, argued that the temporary bridge should connect to Muitas Street, on the side of Riga Passenger Port.
Kauliņš said the final decision would be made by engineers and designers.
He pointed out that the Daugava riverbank near the port is privately owned and that the river is considerably deeper there than on the Old Riga side.
Kleinbergs added that both fixed-support and pontoon-based bridge solutions remain under consideration.
Dace Zīle, a researcher at the University of Latvia's LV PEAK research institute, said Vanšu Bridge is crossed daily by between 55,000 and 60,000 vehicles.
In addition, 759 Riga public transport services cross the bridge each day, carrying approximately 20,000 passengers.
According to LV PEAK research, if daily travel times increased by 30 minutes, the resulting losses would amount to 1.2 million person-hours per month, equivalent to 12.5 million euros.
The additional congestion would also generate 222.6 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.
Zīle explained that the economic impact of an additional 30 minutes of congestion on Vanšu Bridge would correspond to 23.3% of Latvia's gross domestic product generated during a 30-minute period.
LETA previously reported that the most significant reconstruction works on Vanšu Bridge were scheduled to begin in 2027.
To manage traffic during the reconstruction, Riga City Council has proposed installing a temporary bridge.
Earlier plans envisaged one traffic lane in each direction, with construction costs estimated at approximately 20 million euros.
Officials have previously suggested that such a bridge could also serve national civil and military purposes, rather than being used exclusively by the municipality.
However, there has been no definitive agreement on how the temporary bridge would be provided.
The mayor previously promised to discuss potential cost-sharing arrangements with the finance minister and prime minister.
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs of the United List described the proposal for a temporary bridge during the reconstruction as an "outside-the-box" idea.
However, he stressed that state participation in financing the project would depend on several factors.
"It is good that solutions are being considered from a national perspective," Kulbergs said.
He acknowledged that, at first glance, the possibility of reusing the temporary bridge elsewhere in the future appeared reasonable, provided it was technically feasible.
The tender for the reconstruction of Vanšu Bridge was won by the Vanšu tilts consortium, which offered to complete the works for 69.8 million euros excluding value-added tax.
The consortium comprises Hanza Construction Group, Tilts and Baltijas mākslīgo būvju projektēšanas birojs Vektors T.
The reconstruction is expected to require up to 6.7 million euros in 2026, up to 42 million euros in 2027 and up to 35.76 million euros in 2028.
Vanšu Bridge has a total length of 593.6 metres, while its main pylon reaches a height of 108.7 metres.
The project includes resurfacing the roadway and creating separate pedestrian and cycling infrastructure.
The pedestrian pavements will measure 1.7 metres wide on one side of the bridge and 1.9 metres on the other.
The bridge railings will be restored to their original height of 1.3 metres.
The reconstruction will also include replacing the suspension cables, which will have a combined weight of 385.5 tonnes.
New protective coverings will be installed along 3,084 metres of existing and replacement cables to ensure long-term durability and protection against environmental conditions.
The reconstruction will be carried out using the design-and-build approach, under which a single contractor is responsible for both preparing the construction design and completing the works.
This approach is intended to ensure consistent planning, coordination and accountability throughout the contract.

U.S. Army launches Project Griffin to automate cyber defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:48:38 UTC
22:48:38 KST

- The U.S. Army selected Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology on Oct. 23, 2026, for a $2.6 million Project Griffin cyber defense pilot.
- Project Griffin aims to build an autonomous, superintelligence-driven platform that helps U.S. Army cyber defenders detect, divert and deceive threat actors faster.
The U.S. Army has picked Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology to help build an autonomous cyber defense system that can find and stop network threats with little human involvement, choosing the two companies on Oct. 23, 2026, for a Project Griffin pilot worth a combined $2.6 million.
The U.S. Army said it wants an autonomous, agentic platform driven by what it calls superintelligence, or SI, that can spot and neutralize cyber threats faster than human analysts, removing the weak points that come from manual data analysis and human action, though it did not say how the $2.6 million is split between the two companies or how long the pilot will run.
“Project Griffin is one of the first efforts under Project ARDS, which is advancing the Army’s adoption of SI-enabled cyber defense capabilities through rapid sprints in conjunction with industry partners. We will swiftly implement SI-enabled cyber tools to detect, divert and deceive threat actors, and rapidly adopt agentic SI to securely scale network defense and disruption,” said Brandon Pugh, principal cyber advisor to the secretary of the U.S. Army.
Project Griffin is one of three fast-tracked efforts under Project ARDS, short for Army Rapid Defensive of Cyber Systems, which Pugh’s office leads together with the assistant secretary of the U.S. Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, Army Cyber Command and the U.S. Army’s chief information officer to find, buy and hand over promising tools to the soldiers who defend its networks.
The pilot will be managed by Project Manager, Cyber Warfare, part of the Portfolio Management Executive for Intelligence and Spectrum Warfare, with Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, handling the contract.
“Through our flexible procurement methods, we were able to quickly seek out SI solutions that will advance the cyber warfighter,” said Col. David Bergmann, project manager for cyber warfare.

Saffron festival added to Iran’s intl. tourism events calendar
TEHRAN - The National Saffron Day festival in Iran’s northeastern Khorasan Razavi province has been registered as an international event on the country’s tourism calendar, with a permanent secretariat established at the province’s Chamber of Commerce to promote Iranian saffron and strengthen its value chain from production to export.
Samira Sabzevari, secretary of the National Saffron Day conference, said the registration marks a significant step in efforts to safeguard the position of Iranian saffron and expand activities related to the prized agricultural product.
Speaking to ISNA, Sabzevari said the Khorasan Razavi Chamber of Commerce had placed a range of initiatives on its agenda following the festival’s registration and the establishment of its permanent secretariat.
The initiatives aim to preserve saffron’s standing in domestic and international markets while strengthening links among producers, processors, traders and exporters, she said.
Over the past two years, the National Saffron Day festival has featured exhibitions, conferences, urban advertising campaigns and plans for promotional caravans and tourism tours in different counties across the province.
This year’s program takes an integrated approach to the saffron value chain, covering all its stages and related industries, she added.
Also, an international saffron exhibition was inaugurated in the presence of officials and featured traditional and cultural programs intended to celebrate the local heritage associated with saffron cultivation.
Sabzevari said the festival’s registration as an international event on Iran’s tourism calendar had been secured through follow-up with the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
Known as “red gold,” saffron is a valuable agricultural product widely used in Persian cuisine, where it lends distinctive aroma and color to dishes and desserts. It also has a long-standing place in traditional Iranian medicine and cultural practices.
Iran is one of the world’s major saffron-producing countries, with much of its cultivation concentrated in the country’s eastern and northeastern regions. The annual harvest generally begins in early November, when saffron’s vivid purple flowers emerge across fields in otherwise dry landscapes.
Beyond its economic value, the harvest season offers opportunities for rural tourism, allowing visitors to experience saffron picking and learn about the cultivation and processing of the spice. Organizers’ plans for promotional caravans and tourism tours reflect efforts to connect the product more closely with the region’s cultural heritage and travel industry.

Concluding his address, Pezeshkian expressed confidence that constructive cooperation among GECF members can ensure the security of supply and demand, the fair pricing of natural gas, and its elevated role in the global energy basket while respecting vital environmental considerations.

Melania or the pope: Who brokered Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:45:01 UTC
22:45:01 KST

Melania or the pope: Who brokered Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky?
Competing claims over the ceasefire mark the latest tensions between the White House and the Vatican.
A critical localised ceasefire in Ukraine that promises to help more than 1,000 civilians has set off an unlikely contest over who brokered the truce.
The White House insists that United States’ First Lady Melania Trump mediated the ceasefire in Oleshky between Russia and Ukraine, after weeks of increasingly alarming reports from the town warning of a growing humanitarian crisis.
But the Vatican has offered its own narrative, suggesting that the pope was responsible for helping the pause in fighting through phone calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Here’s what we know about the Oleshky ceasefire, and why the diverging versions of what led to the truce matter:
What’s the ceasefire about?
Russia took the southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky in the Kherson region in the early days of the invasion in February 2022 and has retained control over it since.
But the town has suffered from extensive war damage and was later hit by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in 2023.
According to residents and officials, those who remain in the town, which the US estimates at 1,700-2,000 residents, have reported severe shortages of food, medicine, and other supplies.
Then, on October 23, a brief ceasefire was announced. Ukrainian and Russian officials have said the pause in fighting over Oleshky will allow the delivery of humanitarian assistance and the evacuation of those who want to leave the Russian-occupied town.
They’ve added that humanitarian corridors would be established to allow for aid deliveries.
Both sides have said this ceasefire, which is scheduled to end on Sunday, is not a comprehensive end to hostilities. Multiple diplomatic efforts to end the war have so far failed.
Still, the Kremlin said on Monday that the truce might set a precedent for similar localised ceasefires in the future.
On Telegram, Russia’s Ministry of Defence announced that it had stopped shelling in the direction of Ukraine’s city of Kherson from 4am Moscow time (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday, to prepare for the effort in Oleshky.
“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments,” Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said in a Facebook post confirming Russia’s timing of its halt.
What have Melania and the White House said?
Announcing the ceasefire on Friday, US First Lady Melania Trump said the situation in the town was “dire”, and it was on the “brink of disaster”.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said in a statement issued by the White House.
It added that Melania and her representatives had worked closely with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire.
“Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require. Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” said Melania.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets also publicly thanked the first lady and her team for helping coordinate the talks. Russian officials confirmed the agreement.
What is the Vatican saying?
The morning after the White House announcement, the Vatican published a front-page article in its official newspaper, L’Osservatore Romano. The headline: Humanitarian truce for Oleshky.
The article underscored that the ceasefire was secured after Pope Leo spoke to Russian and Ukrainian leaders, urging them to agree to the pause in fighting to help save trapped civilians.
Pope Leo spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin via phone call on October 16 and expressed his “deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky”, adding that he had called for a ceasefire to allow for food and medical assistance.
The pontiff made the phone call while he was in hospital recovering from surgery to remove a cancerous tumour in his lung.
Three days later, on October 19, Pope Leo also spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the situation in Oleshky.
The pope’s special envoy, Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, had pressed Russian authorities on conditions in Oleshky during a visit to Moscow in late September.
Hasn’t Trump tussled with the pope before?
US President Donald Trump and Pope Leo have had a strained relationship.
Pope Leo, the first US pope in history, has criticised Trump’s decision to launch the Iran war, saying it violated Catholic moral principles of a “just war”.
In April, responding to Leo’s critiques, Trump said the pope was “weak on crime, weak on nuclear weapons”, and that he would not have been elected pope if Trump wasn’t president – claiming, without evidence, that his presidency had helped Leo into the position.
“Leo should get his act together as Pope, use Common Sense, stop catering to the Radical Left, and focus on being a Great Pope, not a Politician. It’s hurting him very badly and, more importantly, it’s hurting the Catholic Church!” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.
Does this matter for the US midterm election?
Among Catholics, Trump’s popularity is low. Refusing to even mention the pope’s role in the Oleshky ceasefire is unlikely to help him.
The midterms, scheduled for next week, often reflect a sitting president’s performance as voters decide whether Trump’s Republicans can retain control of Congress.
A Pew Research Centre study conducted between September 28 and October 4 suggested that Trump’s approval rating among Catholics has fallen from 47 percent at the start of his second term in January 2025 to just 30 percent in October 2026. As many as 20 percent of US adults identify themselves as Catholic.
Among white Catholics, Trump’s popularity has fallen from 59 to 39 percent, while among Hispanic Catholics it has crashed from 31 to 18 percent.

Details: Despite being injured, the paramedic continued to provide assistance to other injured people.
That day, the ambulance crew had just finished a call, but as soon as the medical workers returned to their vehicle, an explosion rang out nearby. The blast wave shattered the vehicle's windows, injuring both team members.

"Emergency medical workers operate in difficult and dangerous conditions every day, saving people's lives. Their safety and them getting to come home after every call remain extremely important," the department said.

Widening gap between aid, development needs threatens global security: Stockholm Peace Institute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:42:46 UTC
22:42:46 KST

Efe Ozkan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A widening gap between official development assistance and global development and humanitarian needs could have serious consequences for human security and political stability, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) said in a report released Tuesday.
The report said the gap could be closed with only a small fraction of the resources being directed toward increased military spending.
Global military expenditures reached a record $2.9 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 2.5% of global gross domestic product, according to SIPRI data.
At the same time, official development assistance (ODA) has declined since 2024, based on figures from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
SIPRI said core official development assistance spending began to stagnate in 2021, a trend temporarily obscured by increased aid to Ukraine following the start of the war in 2022 and higher spending by donor countries on hosting refugees.
The largest declines in core official development assistance spending have been seen in economic infrastructure and health, according to the report.
“Wealthy states in Europe and beyond have sharply increased their military spending in response to rising military threats,” said Xiao Liang, a researcher with SIPRI's Military Expenditure and Arms Production Program.
“But this has coincided with deep cuts in other budget lines, including development and humanitarian aid. This can create widespread insecurity for people and states that rely on aid.”
'Sustained withdrawal of vital humanitarian and development assistance' even as needs 'are growing'
SIPRI researchers estimate that official development assistance funding needs could reach as much as $326 billion in 2028, depending on developments related to armed conflicts, natural disasters, and other factors.
That would leave a potential funding gap of $179 billion, exceeding the total amount of official development assistance expected to be committed in 2028.
“We are in the middle of a sustained withdrawal of vital humanitarian and development assistance at a time when needs for it are growing,” said Nan Tian, the director of SIPRI's Military Expenditure and Arms Production Program.
He added that the projected funding gap represents only a fraction of the additional resources being allocated to military spending and that meeting future official development assistance needs remains affordable.
The report examined recent development aid and military spending policies in Germany and the UK, finding that governments had cited the need to finance higher military spending when justifying cuts to official development assistance.
However, SIPRI said the reductions in aid made only a marginal contribution to planned increases in military expenditure.
“With the weakening of international cooperation and rising geopolitical tensions and militarization, it is understandable that states are seeking to invest in their security,” Liang said.
“But military capabilities alone do not guarantee security. Development aid can address long-term drivers of insecurity and should therefore be seen as complementing military spending, not competing with it.”

Permanent handicrafts exhibition planned at Shams Tabrizi shrine in northwest Iran
TEHRAN - A permanent handicrafts exhibition themed around the spiritual and literary traditions of Shams Tabrizi and Jalal al-Din Rumi is planned at the shrine of Shams Tabrizi in Khoy, West Azarbaijan province, as part of efforts to promote local artisans and strengthen cultural tourism.
Rita Khazrzadeh, deputy director of handicrafts at the West Azarbaijan Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department, announced the plan during a meeting with handicrafts producers and artists in Khoy on Tuesday.
Khazrzadeh outlined the department’s plans for the county and discussed artisans’ concerns, calling on them to produce competitively priced handicrafts inspired by the shrine and the life and legacy of Shams Tabrizi.
The products would be marketed to tourists and visitors interested in Shams and Rumi, the renowned Persian mystic and poet whose spiritual outlook was profoundly influenced by his encounter with Shams.
Khazrzadeh said the permanent exhibition would provide an opportunity to showcase the skills and creative potential of Khoy’s artisans to pilgrims and tourists visiting the cultural and religious complex.
The initiative also aims to create a dedicated space for presenting locally made products and connecting the region’s handicrafts with its rich spiritual and cultural heritage.
Ali-Akbar Chitsaz, cultural and artistic affairs director at Khoy Municipality, welcomed the proposals and pledged municipal support for developing the handicrafts sector.
He said the municipality was prepared to cooperate in organizing specialized handicrafts exhibitions and setting up regular open-air markets at suitable locations, with careful planning.
Chitsaz stressed the need to implement the initiatives promptly to provide artisans with better opportunities to sell their work and contribute to the local economy.
During the meeting, participating artists and craftspeople also raised concerns and shared their views on the challenges facing the development of handicrafts in Khoy.
The proposed exhibition comes amid broader efforts to develop the Shams Tabrizi shrine as a destination for cultural and spiritual tourism.
Earlier this month, a vast extension to the original mausoleum was officially inaugurated after two decades of anticipation, marking another step in efforts to promote the legacy of the Persian mystic.
The shrine complex covers 7,000 square meters and includes a domed chamber, a library housing 8,000 volumes and research facilities. The site was inscribed on Iran’s National Heritage List on October 3, 2026.
Shams Tabrizi, a Persian mystic who lived in the 13th century, is widely known for his transformative spiritual relationship with Rumi, whose mystical poetry became a major contribution to Persian literature and Sufi tradition. Rumi’s Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi bears the mystic’s name and reflects the significance of their relationship.

Bird flu detected at Dutch farm, 45,000 laying hens to be culled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:41:35 UTC
22:41:35 KST

Aysu Bicer
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Bird flu has been detected at a poultry farm in Lutjegast, a village in the northern Dutch province of Groningen, prompting authorities to cull 45,000 laying hens, the Dutch Agriculture Ministry said.
The outbreak is the first reported in the Netherlands since July, according to the ministry.
The affected farm keeps laying hens, regional broadcaster RTV NOF reported.
Authorities immediately imposed a transport ban within a 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) radius of the farm to prevent the virus from spreading.
The ban prohibits the transport of birds, eggs, manure and used bedding within the designated zone, which extends across parts of the provinces of Groningen and Friesland.
The restricted area includes 21 other agricultural businesses, according to the report.
The ministry said the outbreak does not currently warrant a nationwide or regional confinement requirement for poultry.

Kryvyi Rih HOAs can receive backup power equipment grants from URCS
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:40:06 EET
22:40:06 KST

Homeowners associations (HOAs) in Kryvyi Rih will be able to receive grant support to purchase backup power equipment from the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS).
"The Ukrainian Red Cross, with the support of the Norwegian Red Cross, is launching a grant support program for HOAs in Kryvyi Rih. The funding will help acquire backup power equipment to ensure the operation of basic in-house systems during prolonged power outages," the URCS reported on Facebook.
The application period began on October 26 and will last through November 15, 2026.
HOAs registered as legal entities that manage apartment buildings in one of the three districts of Kryvyi Rih - Pokrovskyi, Metalurgijnyi, and Saksahanskyi - are eligible to participate in the program.
A single HOA may submit several applications if it manages multiple buildings. A separate application and a corresponding packet of documents must be prepared for each building.
Participation in the program is competitive: applications will be checked for compliance with the terms, and winners will be determined based on the selection results. Submitting an application does not guarantee funding.
The grant amount depends on the height of the building: UAH 100,000 for up to 6 floors inclusive; UAH 200,000 for 7 to 16 floors; UAH 300,000 for 17 floors and above, or for buildings from 4 to 16 floors inclusive with three or more entrances.
Grant funds can be used to purchase gasoline, diesel, or gas generators, inverters, batteries, solar panels, and high-voltage battery control units.
Equipment installation costs, related materials, and other additional expenses are not covered by grant funds. If necessary, HOAs and/or building residents may cover them through their own co-financing.

Decoupling ‘would be a big mistake’, says Germany’s Merz as he seeks balanced ties with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Decoupling ‘would be a big mistake’, says Germany’s Merz as he seeks balanced ties with China
- Germany’s Merz said a balanced China policy needs a united, strong and competitive Europe. He warned that decoupling would be “a big mistake” and backed “de-risking and diversification” instead.
- He spoke in Singapore during a five-day Asia tour, amid rising EU-China trade strains. He cited China’s “€360 billion” trade surplus and called for more dialogue on trade, security and world order.
- Merz linked China to wider security issues, urging Beijing to help end Russia’s war in Ukraine. He also backed stronger EU-ASEAN trade ties and said any peace deal must include Ukraine.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Building a balanced relationship with China requires Germany and Europe to be united, innovative and competitive, said German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“Wise China policy begins at home,” he said on Oct 27 in a lecture in Singapore where he is on a two-day official visit, amid trade tensions between Europe and China that have threatened to escalate into an all-out trade war.
“We will be better equipped to build balanced relations with China if we ourselves are united, strong, resilient, innovative and competitive.
“We are working systematically towards that goal, both in Germany and at the European level,” he said, as he delivered the 49th Singapore Lecture organised by the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.
Europe-China talks earlier in October resulted in China agreeing to cap hybrid electric vehicle exports to the European Union over a four-year period. Brussels is alarmed at a ballooning trade deficit that reached €360 billion (S$515 billion) in 2025 – or about €1 billion a day.
China’s manufacturing might is causing frictions with European industries, in sectors from electric vehicles to chemicals, pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery.
Germany has advocated stronger defensive trade tools against what it views as unfair trade practices by other countries. Merz visited Beijing in February to address issues such as Germany’s growing trade deficit and Chinese industrial overcapacity.
Speaking at the Singapore Marriott Tang Plaza Hotel in Orchard Road, Merz said that it is imperative to continue dialogue with great powers, “even where our interests and values only align in part”.
“This also applies to China. Our view of Beijing has become more nuanced. China’s pivotal role in world politics raises deep questions regarding trade, security and international order,” he said, adding that dealing with these challenges is a major long-term strategic task for Europe.
But decoupling “would be a big mistake”, he said, as doing so would make Germany neither safe nor more prosperous. “Instead, we are pursuing de-risking and diversification.”
How Germany intends to manage its growing strains with China was a key theme of Merz’s lecture, alongside the existential nature of the Russia-Ukraine war for Europe, and advancing cooperation in research, technology and people-to-people exchanges.
His 20-minute speech was titled Germany and the Indo-Pacific: Partnership, Competitiveness and Resilience in a Changing World.
‘New geopolitical era’
He described a “new geopolitical era” shaped by new dynamics among great powers, technological revolutions and by the erosion of an international order. This erosion is “at odds with our fundamental values and interests”, he added.
Nowhere was this more evident than in Ukraine, he said, as Russia – “a great power pursuing a militant, revisionist agenda” – invaded Ukraine, its neighbour, unprovoked.
He reiterated European calls for China to play a greater role in restraining Moscow.
“As a permanent member of the Security Council, China bears a particular responsibility for upholding international law. China’s voice carries weight in Moscow. We encourage China to use her power to help bring about a just peace in Ukraine, rather than enabling Moscow’s war of aggression.”
Merz said that Germany intends to play its part for order, peace and security in the Indo-Pacific, with the German government’s “continued adherence to its One-China policy” with regard to Taiwan.
“We know as well as our partners in the region: Any escalation or violent change to the status quo in the Indo-Pacific would have grave consequences for global security and prosperity.”
Merz is on a five-day tour of Singapore, Japan and South Korea, which he described as “three of our most important partners in the region”. Germany is also forging closer ties with India, Indonesia and Vietnam, he added.
His lecture was chaired by Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo, who said that Germany is one of the most important trading partners with ASEAN within the EU, as well as the largest exporter of goods to the region.
With the international rules-based order and globalisation coming under great strain, Germany is a trusted and reliable partner for the region in cooperation to support international law, free trade and economic resilience, said Teo.
In a question-and-answer session following Merz’s speech, Jens Ruebbert, chairman of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, asked the German leader if the German government could do more to advance a bloc-to-bloc free trade agreement (FTA).
He cited the initial FTA deal between the Philippines and the EU reached in September, which could pave the way for an eventual ASEAN-EU FTA.
Merz said he was in favour of such an FTA, “provided we have enough in common to do it fast”.
“If not, I would like to see as a step in between to have preliminary FTAs with those who are in this area and willing to move forward. But the best way to move forward would be a bloc-to-bloc agreement.”
Ian Storey, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, asked about speculation that US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin may meet at the APEC summit in November to discuss the Russia-Ukraine war.
What steps are Germany and its European partners taking to ensure that Europe plays a central role in this peace process, Storey asked.
Merz said Europe was trying to find ways in which it can engage Russia, not just involving the so-called E3 grouping of the United Kingdom, France and Germany, but also others such as Poland, Italy and Norway.
While the US and Russia might negotiate, “they can never find solutions without Ukraine”, he added. “This is absolutely not acceptable – that one day Russia, perhaps China and the United States of America, find a way to bring this war to an end without having Ukraine at the table.
“I want to make no doubt that this is in our European interest to defend this country, because we’re not just defending the territorial integrity of this country, we’re defending the entire political order of the European continent, and that’s the reason why we’re still engaged.”

Brussels wants to turn Frontex into deportation agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:38:33 UTC
22:38:33 KST

Brussels wants to turn Frontex into deportation agency
The European Commission wants to make Frontex the key player in deportations. On Tuesday it proposed a new mandate for the agency. The proposal also affects Switzerland, which is involved in Frontex through the Schengen Agreement.
The European Border and Coast Guard Agency is to provide additional support in the return of deported people, according to a statement from the European Commission. A return coordination centre is to be set up for this purpose.
The agency’s staff is also to be tripled from 10,000 to 30,000. According to Brussels, this increase is to take place gradually by 2041. Among other things, a rapid reaction force for crisis situations is to be set up.
More
EU border agency remains under scrutiny
The proposal will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the Council of Member States for consideration.
Frontex was founded in 2005. The agency supports EU Member States and Schengen countries in securing the external borders of the Schengen Area. Switzerland contributes to the funding of Frontex.

China to Tighten Export Controls on Drone Engines, Autopilots and Communication Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:38:27 UTC
22:38:27 KST

China will introduce updated export controls on drones and their components from November 18, 2026.
The Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China (MOFCOM) published the new rules.
They will tighten controls on the export of engines, autopilots, communication equipment, and other components and technologies.
The updated rules introduce export controls on drones with specific flight characteristics. These include aircraft capable of controlled beyond-visual-line-of-sight (BVLOS) flight for between 30 minutes and three hours, provided they can take off and maintain stable flight in wind gusts of 46.3 km/h or higher.
The restrictions will also cover drones capable of flying for at least three hours, as well as certain models with a flight range of 300 km or more.
China will also tighten controls on certain drone components, including specially designed autopilots, certain aircraft engines, onboard radio communication equipment and high-performance brushless electric motors.
For the latter, the rules set technical thresholds including a voltage of 48 V or higher, power output of 3 kW or more, a power-to-weight ratio of at least 3 kW/kg, and a rotational speed of up to 3,000 rpm. The controls will also apply to the corresponding electronic speed controllers and certain carbon-composite propeller blades.
In addition, exporters must provide customs authorities with the technical specifications of the goods, their intended use, and information about the end user. If customs officials doubt the accuracy of a declaration, they can detain the shipment for inspection.
Penalties will apply for the illegal export or resale of products, as well as their use for purposes other than those declared.
MOFCOM said the changes were necessary to protect national security, meet international non-proliferation obligations, and maintain stable global production and supply chains.
China’s new rules could complicate the supply of certain components for Ukrainian and Russian drones, although the actual impact may vary.
For example, Russia could obtain components with the Chinese government’s approval, helping supply amid Russian drone production’s significant dependence on Chinese components.
Meanwhile, for Ukraine, which does not have such close ties with the Chinese government, the new rules could delay the supply of certain components, add inspections, and raise costs.
This mainly affects components that meet the new export controls’ specific criteria, including specialized autopilots, high-power electric motors, electronic speed controllers, communication equipment, and certain types of long-range UAVs.
However, some Chinese products reach Ukraine through intermediaries in Poland, the Czech Republic and other countries.

Eurovision in crisis: Netherlands make U-turn and pull out of Eurovision 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:38:08 UTC
22:38:08 KST

The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to participate.
The Netherlands will not participate in 2027's Eurovision Song Contest after all.
NPO, the umbrella organization for public broadcasters in the country, has reversed its earlier decision to return to the contest, after Dutch public broadcaster AVROTROS had announced in August that it would not take part because of Israel's presence in the line-up.
The decision to return to the competition was met with widespread criticism and around 400 NPO employees signed a letter urging the organisation to reconsider its participation.
In a statement, NPO's director Jet de Ranitz said that NPO was unable to secure a broadcaster who would send a Dutch artist.
“In our coordinating role, we held discussions with the broadcasters to investigate whether there are any broadcasters willing to facilitate the participation of a Dutch artist. In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return,” De Ranitz said.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027." He added: "Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO will still broadcast the event.
Eurovision director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
He said in a statement: "We recognise that opinions about the Contest are deeply and sincerely held at the moment, and that they differ widely, both within countries and between them. We do not dismiss any of those views. Public service media exist to serve their audiences, and it is right that our Members weigh these questions carefully, in dialogue with their own communities."
He added: "At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience. That spirit of unity is what the Contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
"We are very happy that the 2027 Contest will still be broadcast in the Netherlands and look forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again whenever NPO, its members and audiences feel the time is right."
Ireland has already announced it will not take part in Eurovision 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.
The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.
Last year, five countries - Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia - boycotted Eurovision after organizers declined to exclude Israel over its military actions in Gaza and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
The Spanish broadcaster RTVE said at the time that it would not broadcast the contest or the semi-finals and criticised the decision-making process as “insufficient”. They said that the EBU’s decision to keep Israel as a competitor “increases RTVE’s distrust of the festival’s organisation and confirms the political pressure surrounding it.”
Irish broadcaster RTÉ stated: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation remains unconscionable given the appalling loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.” As for Slovenian broadcaster RTVSLO, they said last year that taking part “would conflict with its values of peace, equality and respect” and that it was pulling out of the competition "on behalf of the 20,000 children who died in Gaza".
The 2026 competition drew 131 million viewers, down 35 million from the year before.
Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year.

A large-scale hacker attack on the information systems of Italy’s Chamber of Deputies was recorded, affecting the email inboxes of a number of parliamentarians, including Giorgia Meloni. ANSA reports, writes UNN.
Details
The large-scale attack affected the entire system; however, specialists from the Chamber of Deputies continue to monitor the situation.
In particular, regarding the prime minister’s mailbox, sources at Palazzo Chigi clarify that it is not used by the President of the Council of Ministers for government correspondence.

The same sources clarify that "all protective measures have been taken, including in cooperation with the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN), with which a special protocol is in place. These measures may also include the temporary disabling of certain information-system functions in accordance with established practice.
Furthermore, it is known that over the past few days, similar attempts to attack and exert pressure on the information systems of other national, European and international institutions have become more frequent."

Israel detains Egyptian man who crossed the border fence
Israeli forces have arrested an Egyptian man who crossed the border fence into Israel overnight on Tuesday, in an event the army described as "serious".
The Israeli military said it identified a man crossing the border from North Sinai into Israeli territory near the Nitzana settlement.
Soldiers detained the man and transferred him to security forces for interrogation, it said in a statement on social media.
It said it "views the incident with severity and continues to maintain a high level of defensive readiness in the area".
Egyptian authorities are yet to comment on the incident.
There have been a number of security incidents on the Egypt-Israel border since the Israeli military began its genocidal offensive in Gaza.
In June 2023, an Egyptian policeman shot and killed three Israeli soldiers after crossing the border near Nitzana.
There have been several exchanges of fire between Egyptian and Israeli troops since Israel began its genocidal offensive in Gaza.
In October 2023, an Israeli tank struck an Egyptian military position at the Kerem Shalom border crossing into Gaza. The following May, Egyptian and Israeli troops fired on each other after Israeli forces invaded Rafah.
There have been dozens of incidents involving drones, which are used to smuggle drugs and weapons over the border.
Tensions have risen between the two countries over Israel's assault on Gaza, which sparked concerns in Cairo that Israeli forces could attempt to forcibly displace hundreds of thousands of Palestinians into Egypt.
Egypt has responded by increasing military deployments in the Sinai, triggering accusations from Israel that it is in breach of the 1979 peace treaty.

EU Commission proposes expanding powers of border police force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:36:04 UTC
22:36:04 KST

EU proposes major Frontex expansion, curbs internal rights oversight
BRUSSELS, Oct 27 - The European Commission proposed a major expansion of the powers of the EU border agency Frontex on Tuesday, including giving it the capacity to act beyond EU territory, in the aftermath of the massive rush to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta last summer.
The proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's mandate, allowing it to carry out deportations between non-EU countries, operate outside the bloc and deploy rapid-reaction teams in emergencies.
The proposed legislation is an attempt to make Frontex more reactive to large-scale arrivals at the EU's borders, such as in Ceuta on the North African coast, as European governments push for tougher migration policies despite concerns from rights advocates over accountability.
"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.
OVERSIGHT CONCERNS
But while the proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's role, it would also narrow the scope of its internal rights watchdog, with complaints referred to national authorities to handle.
The proposal comes as member states increasingly focus on returns, arguing that too many migrants ordered to leave the bloc ultimately remain.
Although irregular arrivals have decreased, the arrival of more than 72,000 people in Ceuta from Morocco in late July, most of whom later left, reignited debate over the EU's migration rules and was cited by several member states as evidence for stronger tools.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers by 2041, who would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would create a new EU Return Coordination Centre within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process, from voluntary return counselling to organising returns and reintegration support, the statement said.
The agency would also be empowered to help organise and carry out deportations from one non-EU country to another, subject to agreements with the countries involved and international legal standards, according to the statement.
That would mean Frontex could, for example, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya – one of the main launching points for migrant boats crossing to Europe – back to Bangladesh.
The proposal would also create a new online monitoring centre to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
The Commission proposed allocating €11.8 billion to Frontex for the EU's 2028-2034 budget cycle, nearly double the almost €6 billion earmarked for the agency under the current 2021-2027 framework, as part of a planned expansion of its mandate.
The push comes just a few months after EU lawmakers approved new rules aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc.
Tuesday's proposal was met with criticism from rights groups and some lawmakers.
"Working with third countries, without proper oversight or accountability, is a threat to fundamental rights and respect for international law, while leaving Frontex staff in legal limbo outside of European law," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," she added. REUTERS

Netanyahu warns of high Arab voter turnout, urges Likud supporters to vote in Israeli elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:35:21 UTC
22:35:21 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday issued an urgent appeal to supporters of his Likud party to vote in the country’s general elections, warning of high turnout in Arab communities and the possibility of a left-wing government supported by Arab parties, Anadolu reports.
“Buses are heading to the polling stations, and huge lines are being reported in Arab communities,” Netanyahu wrote on US social media company X.
“Meanwhile, the right-wing strongholds are not waking up!” he added.
Netanyahu warned that unless his supporters mobilized, Israel could end up with what he described as “a government of the Arab parties.”
“We must not stay home. Every vote counts!” he said, urging voters to cast their ballots for Likud.
In a separate post, Netanyahu issued an “emergency appeal” to Likud voters, calling on them to ensure their relatives, friends and neighbors also reached polling stations.
“Today, no one stays home. No beach, no barbecue,” he wrote.
“At stake is the future of our Jewish state: a strong right-wing government or a left-wing government supported by the Arab parties,” Netanyahu added.
His appeal comes as Israelis voted Tuesday to elect the 120-member Knesset, with Netanyahu seeking to retain power against an opposition camp led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Opinion polls ahead of the vote indicated that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition was assured of securing the 61 seats required to form a government, raising the possibility of complicated coalition negotiations.
Arab parties, which represent citizens making up around 20% of Israel’s population, have expressed willingness to provide parliamentary support for an Eisenkot-led government without formally joining the coalition.
Such support would be conditional on measures addressing concerns of Arab citizens of Israel, including halting home demolitions, combating crime and opening a political horizon with Palestinians.
Eisenkot has not publicly committed to accepting the proposal and has previously ruled out including Arab parties in his governing coalition.

2026-10-27
13:34:58 UTC
22:34:58 KST

A Ukrainian company is beginning to assemble interceptor drones designed to launch from unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), with specialized launch boxes being developed for their deployment.
Taras Ostapchuk, founder of Ratel Robotics, announced the plans in an interview with Forbes, as cited by RBC-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The company has previously demonstrated the launch of strike FPV drones from its ground robots. It now plans to adapt the concept to counter aerial threats.
Ratel will initially focus on multi-rotor interceptor drones before moving on to fixed-wing, airplane-type models.
The company is also developing launch boxes for deployment from UGVs and integrated software to enable data exchange between ground and aerial platforms.
Under the concept, a UGV would carry interceptor drones to a designated position and launch them to engage enemy aerial targets.
Ostapchuk told Forbes that integrating different types of unmanned platforms was a key direction in robotics development. By combining their capabilities, the systems could enable operators to perform a wider range of tasks remotely.
Vsviti, which also cited the interview, reported that Ratel is currently focusing on multi-rotor interceptors that do not use jet engines. Fixed-wing drones are planned for a later stage.
The company is also working on unified software for ground, aerial and, eventually, maritime unmanned systems. The software is intended to improve data exchange and interoperability between different platforms.
Germany’s Helsing Unveils Low-Cost Highspeed Drone Interceptors
As part of this effort, the company is testing an autopilot system for ground robots that it plans to adapt for aerial drones.
According to Ostapchuk, Ratel has already invested approximately $200,000 in developing its aerial division. Developing fixed-wing drones could require several million dollars.
Ukrainian troops have completed their first logistics mission using a domestically developed amphibious UGV, traveling more than 40 kilometers (nearly 25 miles) across land and water to deliver supplies to frontline positions, Ukraine’s defense ministry said.
The vehicle can cross rivers, canals, and marshes without switching platforms, allowing it to continue operating where conventional ground robots might be unable to pass.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps has begun using unmanned ground vehicles for assaults on Russian positions. Its NC13 unit equipped kamikaze robots with Bullspike grenade launchers and deployed them against Russian troops, including positions inside shelters.
The corps has also tested dropping UGVs from Gryphon heavy bombers and used robotic platforms to strike Russian positions and logistics targets up to 15 kilometers (about 9 miles) from the front line.

NAIROBI, October 27. /TASS/. At least 60 people were killed in two attacks by armed groups in the Arsi area of the Oromia region of Ethiopia, Africanews TV channel quoted a statement from the Ethiopian Orthodox Church as saying.
According to the statement from the Holy Synod, 14 people were killed on October 20 in the Merti district, and 46 more on October 24 in the Shirka district. All the dead were Christians. More than 20 houses were burned down in the attacks, and over 20 people were hospitalized with serious injuries.
Earlier, local online publication The Abay Times said armed men killed at least 48 people, including women, children and the elderly, in the settlements of Chole and Birbo in the Shirka district. According to eyewitnesses, the attackers used automatic weapons, looted houses and killed civilians.
The attackers are yet to be established. The Oromian authorities and representatives of the armed opposition accuse each other of carrying out violent acts. The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission said it was investigating the claims.

Hong Kong lawmakers raise concerns about fresh HK$27 billion funding for tech hub
Government outlines second-round proposal for San Tin Technopole as panel members question timeline, budgeting and pond-filling works
Hong Kong lawmakers have raised concerns about the hefty cost of developing a flagship tech hub and a neighbouring wetland park near the city’s border with mainland China, as the government seeks to secure a fresh HK$27 billion for the second round of works.
During a Legislative Council development panel meeting on Tuesday, government officials explained the HK$27.2 billion proposal. It covers forming 175 hectares (432 acres) of land at the San Tin Technopole, establishing more than one-third of the 348-hectare Sam Po Shue Wetland Conservation Park and building an effluent polishing plant.
The funding request comes less than two years after the legislature’s finance committee approved HK$27.3 billion in December 2024 to commence the first stage of works at the 540-hectare technopole and design the first phase of the wetland park.

Russia's return to global sports gathers momentum as EU mulls response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:34:30 UTC
22:34:30 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — The EU is working on how to stop Russia from laundering its reputation through international sporting events, but as it talks, Moscow creates new facts on the ground.
"Sports and culture must not become vehicles for whitewashing Russian aggression," the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas told journalists on Oct. 13.
But since then, there have been at least two instances in which Russia has been able to advance its sports agenda.
Lithuania was stripped of its right to host an April 2027 international pentathlon tournament on Oct. 19 after it refused to grant visas to Russian and Belarusian athletes for the event.
And on Oct. 25, the International Weightlifting Federation announced that its 2030 championship would take place in Moscow, the first time such a high-level contest has been awarded to Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In both cases, the condemnations and expressions of disappointment have come thick and fast.
Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys called the pentathlon decision "shameful" and said the EU "must tighten restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes competing under national colors, expand visa bans and sanctions, and cut support for those enabling state-sponsored propaganda."
And Ukraine's Sports Minister Matvii Bidnyi told public broadcaster Suspilne that Kyiv would boycott the weightlifting tournament in Moscow.
The minister added that he considers the choice of host "an alarming and unacceptable signal," which "suggests that the influence of Russians in some international federations is extremely strong."
Likewise, European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova told the Kyiv Independent that the EU's executive arm "regrets" both of those decisions.
"In line with the autonomy of sport, international federations are responsible for decision-making on where to host international competitions. However, both federations and member states should act in line with EU sanctions and values," Hrncirova said.
Beyond criticism, the EU is also preparing measures in a bid to tackle the issue.
Kallas said on Oct. 13 that the EU's diplomatic arm, the European External Action Service, "together with the Commission, will put forward proposals on how to sustain Russia's isolation in global sports."
And Hrncirova said that "the Commission is facilitating and supporting coordinated action among member states and with like-minded international partners to resist the instrumentalization of sport by Russia and Belarus."
However, it remains unknown when the new measures will be announced. In the meantime, Russia's lobbying to return to sports continues unabated.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

LNG accounts for half of global gas trade now — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:32:38 UTC
22:32:38 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. LNG, which currently accounts for half of global trade, could help resolve the issue of disruptions in worldwide gas supplies, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit.
The key problem now is the disruption of gas supplies to global markets, he said. "Large volumes of supply have been removed from the market in a short period, with demand remaining unchanged. This means we need to work on optimizing transport routes, taking into account the geographical locations of the Forum’s member countries, through mutual operations among them, that is among us," Putin explained.
The growing flexibility of the gas market driven by the widespread use of liquefied natural gas makes this possible, he noted. "After all, LNG supplies do not depend on international pipelines, and LNG already accounts for about half of global gas trade. I would like to emphasize that replacing lost volumes and revising logistics is no simple task: it is essential to strike a balance between the interests of gas suppliers and consumers, while also fulfilling existing contractual obligations," the Russian leader said.

NSDC enlists Weatherman Foundation to help identify fallen Ukrainian defenders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
