====================================================================================================

German Ambassador: Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:26:00 EET
22:26:00 KST

German Ambassador: Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way
Boris Ruge has been Germany’s new ambassador to Ukraine since August.
Ukraine is not new to him, though. Until recently Ruge was a senior NATO official, serving as Assistant Secretary General for Political Affairs and Security Policy – essentially the third-highest position in the Alliance’s civilian hierarchy. And, of course, he was closely involved with Ukraine and supported closer ties for Ukraine with the Alliance.
Now Ruge speaks on behalf of Berlin.
And when he tells European Pravda in this interview that Germany supports NATO membership for Ukraine, that represents a clear German position. But his statements on EU membership for Ukraine are even clearer and more detailed.
This and much more in the ambassador’s first interview in office.
"We are absolutely determined to stay here"
In your view, what does Ukraine mean to Germany?
Ukraine is a very important partner for Germany – in technical terms we could say a strategic partner, as we agreed in the spring of this year. We understand how important Ukraine is for European security, and we also understand its weight as a major economic player.
You’ve worked at NATO, so you’ll know that pretty much every member is described as "a highly valued ally". It’s the same for Ukraine, isn’t it?
No, it’s not the same for Ukraine. Ukraine is a big country, and it is, unfortunately, at the heart of the largest war in Europe since 1945, which has been going on for more than four years now – tragically so. The outcome of this war will determine Europe’s future security order.
As far as we are concerned, Europe’s future security order should include a Ukraine that is sovereign, independent and democratic – and able to move towards and join the European Union, certainly. And NATO as well: we said a few years ago that the future of Ukraine is in NATO.
All of these things matter. At the core is a fundamental point: Ukraine must be able to exercise its own choices and be part of what, in the old days, we would have called the free world. And I think that is very relevant today – if we look at what Russia represents today, it is definitely not the free world.
So, NATO membership, EU membership, and a democratic Ukraine. Those are encouraging messages at the start of our interview, and we’ll come back to each of them later. But first let me say that I’m particularly happy to see you here in Kyiv after last night’s missile attack [the interview took place on 22 October]. Do you know why I say that?
No.
Because we Ukrainians remember 2022, when one embassy after another was leaving Kyiv. Can we be certain that this won’t happen again?
Yes. I think you can be absolutely sure. You remember that Chancellor [Friedrich Merz] came to Kyiv on 4 October. And on 3 October, we were told [by Moscow] that all foreigners should leave Kyiv because it was dangerous and we risked losing our lives by staying here.
But the Chancellor was not deterred from coming here.
We are here. We know that the coming months will be difficult – over the past two months, we have already seen the security situation become more difficult. We need to handle that, and we need to look after the security of our people, but we are absolutely determined to stay here. It’s the same for all our European and NATO partners.
"EU membership won’t happen in 2027 or 2028. That's impossible. It's not doable"
You’ve already said that you see Ukraine as a member of the EU. But is that goal achievable within a reasonable timeframe? And what exactly is a "reasonable timeframe"?
That’s a good question. As we all know, to become a member of the European Union, a country has to adapt its legislation, regulations, institutions and so on. That’s not arbitrary, and it’s not something we’ve made up to make things complicated. It’s simply that the European Union is so highly integrated and demands so much of its members. Ukraine needs to go through those steps – and doing so will also make Ukraine a more European country in a broader sense.
I don’t think you will find a government in the European Union that is more forward-leaning on EU membership than Germany. I remember that you interviewed my predecessor, Heiko Thoms, about the letter that Chancellor Merz wrote back in May [on a special format for Ukraine’s integration into the EU].
Among other things, the letter called for full membership for Ukraine – I think it says so three times in a single letter – and, basically, for opening all negotiation clusters now.
And it says that, as Ukraine moves towards the European Union, Ukrainians – representatives of Ukraine – should be brought into the institutions: the Commission, the Parliament, the Council, the European Court of Justice. It’s a very forward-leaning, very positive vision of how we see Ukraine and of our wish for Ukraine to advance rapidly.
How long it will take is a very difficult question.
I think it's a good thing that
people here in Kyiv have moved away from the notion that it will happen in 2027 or 2028.
It will not happen then. It’s impossible. It’s not doable.
We’re now hearing hopes that Ukraine could join by 2030, and this is being discussed in Brussels as well, not just in Kyiv. Is that an achievable goal, even if it is an ambitious one?
2030 is ambitious. First of all, it depends on how Ukraine performs. And then, of course, the reality is that it’s also a very political process, because there are 27 members of the European Union and they all have a say. So it’s difficult to predict, but I think the geopolitical case for Ukraine joining the European Union is very strong.
What matters is that, together, we keep Ukraine on track, moving forward as fast as possible towards full membership – so that people in this country can feel that this is something they can work towards, and that they have a real opportunity to become a member of the European Union within a reasonable time.
Is it theoretically possible for Ukraine to join the EU while the war is still ongoing?
I don't know whether the European Union has taken a position on whether a continuation of the war would stand in the way of Ukraine becoming a full member. I don’t know that. I don’t believe that’s the case.
We should work with Ukraine, even under these very difficult circumstances, to move forward on the path to the European Union. And then we’ll take it from there.
"There's an understanding, but I remind people that this is the case"
The path to EU membership is first and foremost about reforms.
Last week, several laws were passed that are relevant to the European Union and to Ukraine’s membership – including the law on minorities, but many others as well. There’s a whole list of things – I think they’re very well known to the Office of the President, to the government, to the Rada [Ukrainian parliament] – that need to be done. And in some cases, draft laws or executive decisions are relevant to unlocking funding from the European Union for Ukraine, which is hugely important.
And we keep reminding people that, given the overall situation, we can only encourage Ukraine’s institutions to adopt this legislation as soon as possible, so that the funding the European Union has available for Ukraine can be released.
Do you think the Ukrainian government and our MPs understand that all the reforms must be implemented? That cherry-picking reforms is not an option?
I think there’s an understanding, but I can tell you that I do remind people that this is the case. To raise the very significant resources – the massive resources – needed to support Ukraine and help it defend itself, we also need to be able to tell people in the German parliament, the Bundestag, in the European Parliament and in the European Council that Ukraine is doing its part and delivering on the reform agenda.
Is Ukraine making tangible progress on the rule of law and the fight against corruption?
I mean, there are issues with corruption. There were very prominent cases. But at the same time, we can see that Ukraine has institutions, created after the Revolution of Dignity, that are able to investigate and prosecute people even in very high positions. That’s pretty significant. Maybe it’s not perfect, but nothing ever is.
There is real action on anti-corruption, and that’s extremely important because – again, in Germany – to make the case for supporting Ukraine, there has to be a credible anti-corruption architecture in place and credible action against people who misuse funds for their own purposes.
I remember interviewing German and other European ambassadors five or ten years ago, and even earlier. Time and again they would describe how corruption was hurting their investors. Is that still the case today?
I don’t think that is the main problem for German companies today. And that’s good.
"Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way"
I’d like to ask you about the war, but first, let’s talk about what’s happening around these so-called peace negotiations. I think the best word to describe it is a mess. Would you describe it differently?
No, I don’t have another word for it. I think everyone, first and foremost the people in Ukraine, would like to see the war come to an end – after four and a half years of full-scale war and, before that, eight years of a bloody war at a lower level.
I can see that there is an American-led effort to bring the war to an end. But I would also say, as a German diplomat, that it is clear that Europe has to be part of the picture. The first point is that Ukraine and the people of Ukraine have to decide on what basis they are willing to end the war.
We are grateful to America for trying to bring the war to an end. But Europe – and Germany too – certainly has a big stake in how this war ends, and so we will be there and find a way of articulating our European interests and working with Ukraine to make sure that we end up with a result that is acceptable.
Is Europe playing a sufficiently meaningful role in the process right now?
What we can see is that, as you remember, the national security advisors of France, Britain and Germany have been to Kyiv twice most recently in September. We also had some national security advisors in Oslo just now. So there is a presence, recently in Miami as well.
At the same time, we’re hearing criticism from Poland, our closest EU neighbour. Polish officials don’t hide their frustration that they’re never invited to these discussions. What’s the reason for that?
I don’t know whether it’s true that they’re never invited. But Poland is clearly very important. It’s an important member state of the European Union and an important ally in NATO. It is a neighbour, and it is very much impacted by this war. So I think Poland’s desire to be closely involved is important, clearly. I think there are questions about what the formula will ultimately be.
In a sense, we could say that we have not yet entered into a proper negotiation process. And if we’re serious, we can also say that the Russian Federation has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way. They have always stuck to their basic demands, which essentially amount to Ukraine capitulating – so that is not a negotiation. So I would say we’re not yet in a real negotiation process, and we will see what format it takes.
So for now, as far as I understand, you don't see Russia being ready for serious steps.
Exactly. I mean, last night [21 October] is a demonstration that Russia talks in very vague terms about its willingness to engage, to meet and so on – and in the meantime it attacks Ukraine with its jet drones and ballistic missiles, killing civilians, attacking civilian targets and committing war crimes. So that’s not exactly the mindset of peace. I think we have to be very clear about that.
There was a change in the Ukrainian position beginning in 2025, when the president signalled that he would be willing to accept a ceasefire – a full ceasefire. Since then, we have been talking about the Black Sea deals, grain deals and energy ceasefires – all sorts of things. Russia has rejected every single one of them, and I think the record is perfectly clear.
"I wouldn't say NATO is stepping back. Part of the response is not visible"
Is there a risk that Russian attacks could extend beyond Ukraine?
Russia’s strategy consists of fighting on land. But the front line is relatively stable. Ukraine has done quite a good job of slowing Russia down and, obviously, of retaking territory recently as well.
There’s a war happening in the air, with cruise missiles and drones, where Russia is unfortunately having an impact on the energy infrastructure and attacking the economy – the steel industry, for example. And then there’s a third element: Russia’s hybrid campaign against NATO and EU states, which has been going on for years. Russia is not engaging in a military conflict with NATO, but it is pushing the limits of its hybrid campaign.
In my view, when an explosive-laden drone attacks Leipzig Airport, that’s no longer a hybrid attack. It’s more like a conventional attack, isn’t it?
In the case of Leipzig, Germany made an attribution. We did our homework: we didn’t go out the next morning and say it was Russia – our intelligence services did their homework, and then we attributed it to Russia. And then we took a number of measures: we closed the consulate in Bonn, we closed the Russian House in Berlin, and we did a number of other things to push back.
But you still consider it a hybrid attack?
You know, people argue about hybrid, and I accept that hybrid is perhaps a problematic term. You could say it’s grey-zone – a kind of grey-zone campaign that they’re waging.
But Russia is not engaged in a large-scale military campaign against NATO. And why is that? Because NATO’s deterrence against Russia has worked. So they have been trying to operate below the threshold of an actual military attack.
They've been testing us. And we have to find ways of pushing back.
I was in Berlin at the beginning of September for our ambassadors’ conference. Mark Rutte was there to speak, and he said – and I agree entirely – that if Russia engages in these hybrid operations, the response should be more support for Ukraine, not less, because Russia’s objective is to undermine our support for Ukraine.
And you could see it when Chancellor Merz came here on 4 October with a package of one billion [euros] in military support for Ukraine. So maybe people in Moscow should register that, despite Leipzig and everything else that has been going on against EU states, NATO states and Germany, our support for Ukraine has not gone down. It has gone up.
And yet I’m seeing attacks that ten years ago would have been considered conventional acts of military aggression – Russia is striking NATO member states with drones, targeting Turkish ships, and sinking ships in the territorial waters of Bulgaria or Romania. And nothing happens! There’s no response from the Alliance. So Russia keeps raising the stakes, and NATO is stepping back.
I wouldn’t say NATO is stepping back, but I can tell you that I’ve talked to many Ukrainian colleagues and I know that this is the perception here: that Russia is pushing and NATO has not come up with a strong response. I think part of the response is not visible. But I’ve been telling colleagues from NATO, my former colleagues, that this is the perception here and that they should think about it: The impression that NATO is not responding strongly enough to Russia’s campaign. I think that’s a point people should reflect on in Brussels.
"Germany wants Ukraine to be as close to NATO as possible"
I’m glad to hear that you see Ukraine as a future NATO member. But there’s one opponent to us joining, and that’s the United States. Do you think Ukraine will join the Alliance despite that opposition?
For Ukraine to join NATO, you need all 32 NATO allies to agree. And if you look at the procedure, there are actually several steps where 32 ambassadors need to raise their hand and say "Yes, we agree."
What we said in Washington – and that is the NATO position, as Mark Rutte has reminded people – was that the future of Ukraine is in NATO and that Ukraine is on a… I can’t come up with the adjective right now. Незворотній is the Ukrainian term.
Yeah, absolutely! Незворотній.
Irreversible! Sorry.
So you know the Ukrainian word better!:)
Exactly – so I do remember only the Ukrainian word.
It’s on an irreversible path to full Euro-Atlantic integration. When exactly that will happen is, again, a political issue. The difference today, at least from a German point of view, is that it’s very clear that Ukraine is not just the recipient of our assistance, but also a major element of Europe’s defence today.
We need Ukraine, with its armed forces and its expertise in modern warfare, to be part of our defence against a very aggressive and imperialist Russia whose ambitions go beyond Ukraine. That is our analysis.
What is your vision for Europe’s future security architecture, and what role would Ukraine play in it?
In my view, it revolves around NATO. I’m a former NATO person, so maybe that’s logical. But NATO is the organisation in charge of collective defence. I think the role that the United States plays in NATO is changing – we can see that – because of the change in US force posture globally. As you know, that has been going on for 20 years: Barack Obama talked about the pivot to Asia, and that was in the years after 2008. And now China has become even stronger, and the US is required to play its balancing role in the Indo-Pacific.
So Europeans will have to step up and play more of a role. But to my mind, Ukraine is already very, very close to NATO. We have the NATO-Ukraine Council, and we do a lot of things together. We have the Joint Analysis Training and Education Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland, and we are learning from Ukraine today when it comes to unmanned systems.
We don’t know when Ukraine will be able to join NATO as a full member, but, from a German point of view, we want Ukraine to be as close to NATO as possible, because in reality you are already part of our collective defence.
What are the key elements of a peace settlement that is acceptable to Europe? And please don’t just say that it’s for Ukraine to decide. You have your own position too, don’t you?
Sure. Our position is that Ukraine should survive as a sovereign, independent, democratic nation that can make its own choices.
What about other conditions, particularly concerning Russia? Some people say that to secure a lasting peace, Europe would need to restore ties with Russia and resume supplies of Russian oil and gas through Ukraine. What’s your view on that?
I don’t believe that’s the case. If you look at the German-Russian relationship after 1991, you could say two things.
One is that Germany got it terribly wrong. We were wrong to assume that we could develop a partnership with Russia. Russia walked away from the partnership we tried to establish and turned into an aggressive, imperialist actor that is trying to overturn the entire political order of Europe. That’s one way of looking at it, and I think in many ways it’s accurate.
Another way of looking at it is that Germany and the rest of Europe tried very hard to build a constructive and positive relationship with Russia. You can see it in the NATO-Russia Council, and you can see it in the way we developed the energy partnership with Russia, and so on. So we tried, and it failed.
We made an honest effort to have a positive, forward-looking relationship with Russia, and Russia threw that out of the window and turned to the use of military force, aggression and this hybrid campaign, this manipulation of information and politics.
This attempt of ours was a failure. But what is important is that we sincerely made efforts to build forward-looking relations with Russia. So the people in Europe today, including in my country, Germany, who say we should go back to that and build a positive relationship with Russia have obviously forgotten that we spent 20 years doing exactly that, and it turned out to be a massive failure.
And it turned out to be the biggest failure on energy in particular. The idea at the time was that if Russia had a major market in Western Europe, it would have a stake in maintaining peace and building a positive relationship. But that is not what Mr Putin ultimately decided.
We are not going back to that. I don’t believe you will find a majority in Germany for that. Maybe people in Washington DC think we should re-establish that energy partnership between Western Europe and Russia, but I think in Western Europe you will find precious few people willing to make themselves dependent on Russia in any way today.
Interview by Sergiy Sydorenko
Video by Mykhailo Alekseev

In the trenches, on duty and in shelters: how Ukraine held the National Unity Radio Dictation

In the trenches, on duty and in shelters: how Ukraine held the National Unity Radio Dictation
Kyiv • UNN
On October 27, Ukrainians took part in the National Unity Radio Dictation based on a text by Artur Dron. It was written by military personnel, officials, schoolchildren and celebrities.
Today, October 27, on Ukrainian Writing and Language Day, the National Unity Radio Dictation was traditionally held in Ukraine, written by politicians, famous stars and military personnel, reports UNN.
Details
Despite another difficult night, when the enemy attacked our cities with ballistic missiles and hundreds of drones, despite the fatigue, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians sat down together to write a dictation in their native language. The enemy may destroy buildings, but it is unable to destroy what makes us Ukrainians: our language, culture, history and unity. They cannot be broken by missiles, drones or any other weapon. Our resilience and our unity rest on this foundation. And this is our response to every attempt to intimidate or break us. Thank you to everyone who joined the National Unity Radio Dictation today
Olena Ivanovska, the Commissioner for the Protection of the State Language, representatives of the Commissioner in the regions and the Secretariat team also joined the radio dictation.
"A Letter That Does Not End" by Artur Dron brought together millions of Ukrainians in different parts of Ukraine and far beyond its borders. Military personnel and veterans, teachers and schoolchildren, volunteers, civil servants, and Ukrainians scattered around the world by the war all wrote it. It was precisely for the sake of this unity that the tradition of the Radio Dictation was born 27 years ago
Minister of Culture Tetiana Berezhna also showed a photo of herself writing the dictation at the Scientific and Technical Library of the National Technical University "Kyiv Polytechnic Institute."
"Language truly knows no boundaries." Artur Dron's very poignant text for this year's National Unity Radio Dictation is called "A Letter That Does Not End." And I really wanted this letter not to end. I joined the dictation. I have been writing it for many years, and I get nervous every time. This time, I allowed myself the right to make a mistake and enjoyed the text and its reading. I love this tradition very much: in different cities and countries, Ukrainians pick up their pens and listen to the same text. Everyone has their own handwriting, their own doubts about commas, and their own history of relations with the Ukrainian language. And at the same time, there is a shared feeling of closeness. In Artur's text, language protects us when the present is frightening and helps us create the future. It preserves memory, passes on experience, and provides words for what matters most. For a conversation with an entire country and for a personal "I love you"
The mayor of Ivano-Frankivsk, Ruslan Martsinkiv, also showed how he wrote the dictation together with students.
I joined the National Unity Radio Dictation. The most important things we have are Ukrainian statehood and the Ukrainian language! Thank you to our Defenders
As usual, Ukrainian military personnel also joined the radio dictation; in particular, some of them wrote it from the front line, right in the trenches.
And how did your radio dictation go this year?
The soldiers of the 50th Separate Artillery Brigade, the 92nd Assault Brigade named after Koshovyi Otaman Ivan Sirko, the 10th Separate Mountain Assault Brigade "Edelweiss," the 1st Separate Heavy Mechanized Siverska Brigade, the 22nd Separate Unmanned Systems Battalion and the 39th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment also joined in writing the dictation at their combat positions.
On Ukrainian Writing and Language Day, service members of Operational Command "West," organized by specialists from the personnel psychological support structure in cooperation with representatives of the communications structure, joined the traditional Nationwide Radio Dictation. It is the same weapon that the enemy tried to destroy for centuries but never managed to break. Today, we are defending not merely our borders, dignity and sovereignty; we are defending the right to speak, think, read and write, and simply to live in Ukrainian on our own land. Our native word is our "friend-or-foe" password, and as long as our commands are heard in Ukrainian over the radios, we will stand, endure and win
Ukrainian border guards also wrote the dictation.
Border guards from various units and agencies of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, together with thousands of Ukrainians, joined the 2026 National Unity Radio Dictation. This year's text, titled "The Letter That Never Ends," was written by Ukrainian writer and veteran of the Russian-Ukrainian war Artur Dron. For border guards, participating in the radio dictation is not only an opportunity to test their knowledge of their native language, but also a chance to join a shared tradition that unites Ukrainians regardless of their profession, location, or circumstances
In addition, the Strategic Communications Center of the Armed Forces of Ukraine showed how service members from various brigades wrote the dictation at their positions, including soldiers from the Presidential Brigade, the 128th, 82nd, and 29th brigades, the 20th Corps, and cadets of the Military Institute of Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv.
Celebrities also joined in writing the dictation. In particular, war veteran and public figure Oleksandr Teren showed a photo of himself writing the dictation together with singer "Leleka," actress Maryna Koshkina, bloggers Dasha Kubik and Vlad Shevchenko, as well as chef Yevhen Klopotenko.
By the way, Yevhen Klopotenko shared his alphabet of Ukrainian cuisine on Instagram.
I love how simply and logically we name dishes. You study food—you discover new words
We would like to remind you
Ukrainian singer and model Dasha Astafieva shared an intimate photo on social media of herself on horseback. "I'm flying to you," she captioned the photos ahead of the National Unity Radio Dictation.

Giant metal 3D printer to build hypersonic systems in Indiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:24:52 UTC
22:24:52 KST

- Kratos has bought an AMCM M 8K large-format metal 3D printer with eight 1.2-kilowatt lasers for its hypersonic payload facility in Odon, Indiana.
- The system will support MACH-TB, the U.S. Department of War hypersonic test program for which Kratos is the prime contractor.
Kratos Defense & Security Solutions has bought one of the largest metal 3D printers on the market, an AMCM M 8K additive manufacturing system, for its new hypersonic payload facility in Odon, Indiana, where the company prepares the experimental test vehicles it flies for the Pentagon’s MACH-TB hypersonic test program.
Germany’s EOS, whose AMCM unit builds the machine, announced the sale on Oct. 27, 2026, saying the printer will be installed at the Kratos Indiana Payload Integration Facility near Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane Division, though neither company disclosed the price or when the system will begin producing parts.
The M 8K was developed for space and defense work and can print metal parts inside a build volume of 800 by 800 by 1,200 millimeters (31.5 by 31.5 by 47.2 inches) using eight high-power 1.2-kilowatt lasers, with built-in thermal management, gas flow control, filtration and in-process monitoring meant to keep large, complex components accurate and consistent from one build to the next.
“As we change the paradigm on low-cost, high-cadence hypersonic testing for programs like MACH-TB, this type of capability is critical to achieve the goal,” said Mike Johns, senior vice president of Kratos SRE.
Kratos is the prime contractor for MACH-TB 2.0, the U.S. Department of War’s effort to run frequent, affordable flight tests of hypersonic technologies, under a contract worth up to $1.45 billion awarded in January 2025, and printing large metal parts in-house is meant to help the company build test hardware faster and in greater numbers than traditional machining allows.
The printer will join a site that is still ramping up, after Kratos finished the $50 million, 68,000-square-foot (6,317-square-meter) Indiana Payload Integration Facility ahead of schedule in July 2026, with room to prepare up to six hypersonic payloads at once and plans for more than 100 high-tech jobs in its first phase.
“The M 8K was built for exactly these kinds of applications, large, complex parts where scale, precision, and process reliability all matter,” said Martin Bullemer, managing director of AMCM.

Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:23:32 UTC
22:23:32 KST

Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US elections
The US and Israel have teased strikes around their elections, particularly against Iran’s civilian infrastructure.
Israelis have gone to the polls to decide whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in power. On November 3, midterm elections in the United States will take place and likely impact President Donald Trump’s final years in office.
Many Iranians are watching both elections closely, knowing that the way Israelis and Americans vote could have serious consequences for their future. Since Israel and the US launched an unprovoked war on Iran on February 28, Iranians have experienced bombings, a blockade and sanctions.
But despite a sharp decrease in US and Israeli attacks since a memorandum of understanding was reached between Washington and Tehran in June, the threat of war has re-emerged. Many political commentators believe that the US and Israel could restart the war after the elections, and Iranians are anticipating further strikes.
“I haven’t followed the Israeli election very closely. But I think there will be more fighting whether Netanyahu wins or Eisenkot or someone else,” 37-year-old Tehran resident Sajad told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous due to security reasons.
He believes that the rhetoric of Israeli officials signals that their ambition in the war is still for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic, which has controlled Iran since a 1979 revolution.
This has gained some support from Iranians inside and outside the country, who are opposed to the government. But cyber intelligence operations by both Israel and Iran make it difficult to accurately gauge online reactions to the prospect of Netanyahu winning another election.
Iranian authorities have described pro-Israeli Iranians as “homeland sellers” and continue to severely punish any perceived cooperation with Israel based on national security charges.
They also fully blame the US and Israel for Iran’s nationwide protests in January, during which thousands of civilians are believed to have been killed. The United Nations says Iranian security forces committed crimes against humanity while cracking down on the protests.
Shayan, a 32-year-old Tehran resident, said he believes that any Iranians who might have hoped for the overthrow of the government at the start of the war are disillusioned after witnessing US and Israeli conduct since then, with thousands of civilians killed and the US blockade and sanctions hitting most people’s incomes.
“I think some people’s viewpoints adjusted after some of the comments from the US and Israel, and after they bombed infrastructure that we need to live, like oil and gas, power and steel,” he told Al Jazeera.
“I think most Iranians don’t have a choice in the matter, but want some stability and peace.”
President Trump has threatened to bring about the “death of a civilisation” in Iran and suggested the country’s map may look different after the war.
He has also repeatedly threatened to launch more major strikes against Iran’s power plants, bridges and other civilian infrastructure if hostilities resume. US media report that the country’s military is prepared to attack over the coming days if an order is given.
The other option Trump has threatened is prolonging a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place since July, which has stopped the country’s oil exports and significantly disrupted trade. Together with some of the most stringent sanctions imposed against any country, the US measures have made Iranians poorer and more isolated from the international community.
The Netanyahu government has also threatened to strike Iranian infrastructure again, including energy facilities. Defence Minister Israel Katz has repeatedly said in recent months that he wants to send Iran “back into the Stone Age”.
His election opponents and other prominent opposition figures, including Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Yair Golan, have all cheered the US-Israeli attacks on Iran both during the current war and during last year’s 12-day war.
They have also been united in wanting to remove Iran’s enriched uranium stockpiles from Iran and dismantle the country’s nuclear programme. Another goal is eliminating the Tehran-backed “axis of resistance” of armed forces who oppose Israel and the US across the region.
Israeli politicians, both the government and opposition, are generally united on the war aims of overthrowing the Iranian establishment, but differ on the method.
Eisenkot, for instance, has supported Netanyahu’s military strikes against Iran and praised Trump’s decision to launch attacks as courageous. But he also says that military operations cannot realistically overthrow the Islamic Republic, and that change must come from Iranians themselves.
Some Iranians have been mentally preparing themselves for conflict when the elections end.
Some Iranians said they have established groups with friends living in different parts of the country to warn each other of imminent strikes if they hear fighter jets flying overhead.
Some of the groups are in domestic messaging apps or over text message since Iranian authorities have said they will impose more internet and communication shutdowns if deemed necessary.
“In all seriousness, 90 million people have our eyes to the sky to see when there will be war. Damn this life we’ve lived,” a user named Ali wrote on X.

Top Indian media dispute Modi's new data privacy rules in top court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:23:00 UTC
22:23:00 KST

India's Supreme Court Tuesday ordered the government to respond to a challenge by news publishers who argue that new data privacy rules threaten press freedom.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government introduced rules last year to implement a personal data protection law, but critics say their sweeping scope risks undermining public interest reporting.
The new rules "fail to provide any exemption for journalistic activity" and "threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity," a petition from the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said. The DNPA represents some of India's biggest news organizations.
Members include Network18, part of the Reliance conglomerate led by billionaire Mukesh Ambani and NDTV, owned by the Adani Group, founded by Gautam Adani. Both tycoons are close to Modi.
"We think it could impact investigative journalism and compromise sources," Sujata Gupta, with the DNPA, said.
Data privacy laws in many parts of the world, including the European Union, include specific exemptions for journalism.
The law's requirement to disclose all personal data processed, without a public interest exemption, would "seriously hinder investigative reporting and could discourage whistleblowers from coming forward," Reporters Without Borders, an international media watchdog, said.
Independent activists and smaller news organizations also challenged provisions removing exemptions for personal information sought under India's Right to Information (RTI) transparency law.
"The removal of the public interest override ... of the RTI Act now allows information offices of the government to withhold information that is deemed 'personal' even if it has significant connection to a public activity or public interest," a legal challenge filed by investigative news website The Reporters' Collective argued.
Critics have long accused Modi's Hindu nationalist government of undermining press freedom, a charge the government denies. The court will hear the matter next on Nov. 17.

Russia tries to drag a village north of Kupiansk into no-man’s-land after its losses in Ukraine’s underground operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:22:33 UTC
22:22:33 KST

Russian troops are trying to drag Radkivka, a village on the northern edge of Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast, into the gray zone so their infiltration groups can keep reaching the city, Viktor Trehubov, spokesperson for Ukraine’s Joint Forces Grouping, said on national television on 27 October, Ukrinform reported. Russian forces made three attempts to advance toward Radkivka on 26 October, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
Russia has tried for more than a year to retake Kupiansk, a city on the Oskil River, largely by slipping small groups through a disused gas pipeline under the river. They kept using it even after Ukraine said in September 2025 that it had flooded three of the four pipe strings, until Ukrainian troops went into the pipes themselves in Operation Veles, announced on 22 October.
Russian groups now have to move above ground
The pipe Russian groups used to seep toward Kupiansk has been put out of action, so they now have to go through Radkivka or neighboring Holubivka, Trehubov said. They move along the bank of the Oskil and a nearby tree line, but the foliage will soon be gone, which will make that much harder.
On the western bank of the Oskil, Russian forces took losses from Ukraine’s Khartiia Corps and in Operation Veles, and their logistics have “suffered noticeably,” Trehubov said. Advancing there is now harder for them than it was a month ago, he added.
Everything now depends on how the fights for Holubivka and Radkivka end, Trehubov said.
“If Ukrainian control can finally be established there, the Russians will have nowhere much to crawl through,” he said.
Several dozen Russian soldiers remain in low-rise buildings in northern Kupiansk, and Ukrainian forces are working to cut off their rotations, Trehubov said on 23 October.
Each side wants the other off its bank of the Oskil
On the eastern bank, Russian forces keep pushing toward the village of Podoly and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi, a railway junction town southeast of Kupiansk, aiming to wipe out Ukraine’s foothold there, Trehubov said. Ukraine wants to destroy the Russian foothold on the western bank.
“For that, we will need to at least somehow throw them out of Dvorichna,” Trehubov said, referring to a town north of Kupiansk.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that Russian forces conducted no offensive operations on the Kupiansk axis on 26 October, likely because Ukraine now controls the pipeline, a view at odds with the General Staff’s report for that day.
Ukraine reported confident control of Kupiansk as early as February, yet Russian groups kept slipping into the city for months afterward. Trehubov’s latest assessment stops short of declaring that threat over: Russia will still try to advance, he said.

How to balance a career and a master’s in the Netherlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:22:11 UTC
22:22:11 KST

Partner content
How to balance a career and a master’s in the Netherlands
Working full time while studying for a master’s can be a tough balancing act. Melina Gkiolma, a sustainability consultant and currently a student on the Online Master Sustainability Management at Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University (RSM) in Amsterdam, talks about how she handles the burden.
For many internationals in the Netherlands, going back to university means fitting lectures and assignments around a full-time job, family commitments and trips back home. Finding the time and the energy is often the biggest hurdle.
Melina, who is originally from Athens, has worked in the sustainability sector for five years, having spent the past 2.5 years as a sustainability consultant at Kōan, a boutique consultancy in Amsterdam. She started her career at Deloitte Luxembourg. She helps organisations deal with sustainability reporting requirements and changing regulations across Europe and beyond.
She wanted a part-time course she could follow online, so she could keep working while building her academic background in a field where she sees her long-term career. “This programme seemed like the perfect fit because it met all the criteria I was looking for,” she said.
Finding a routine
Returning to study took some adjustment. “I admit that returning to academic study after several years in the workplace was a little challenging at first,” she said, “but I’ve found a balance that works for me.”
She tries to join the live class every week and usually studies in the evening after work, when she is “already in a productive mindset”. She also puts in some time at weekends, but makes a point of keeping time free to relax.
Weekly updates from the programme managers on upcoming activities and assignment deadlines help her stay on top of the workload, she said.
Studying on the move
Because the course is entirely online, Melina can keep studying wherever she is – at home, on work trips or visiting her family in Greece.
She also found it more sociable than she expected. “People often assume online learning can feel impersonal, but my experience has been the opposite,” she said. Live classes, discussion forums and informal virtual coffee chats have helped her build strong ties with classmates around the world.
The international mix is one of her favourite parts of the course, with students from almost every continent. “It’s eye-opening to hear about people’s different experiences depending on where they live and their different professional backgrounds,” she said.
Theory into practice
Melina has been able to use what she learns at work straight away. Earlier in the programme, students were asked to develop key performance indicators (KPIs) for a logistics company. When a new client later asked her for help setting KPIs for its carbon emissions, she drew on the research she had done for that assignment.
“The master’s has also helped me broaden my horizons in sustainability. Because I work in sustainability reporting, there are many topics I hadn’t explored in depth before. One module I found particularly interesting focused on ethics and leadership. It made me reflect on what I want to stand for in my work, my moral compass, and the purpose behind the things I do. It really got me thinking.”
“Be kind to yourself”
Her advice to anyone thinking of combining a job with a part-time master’s is to go easy on themselves. “Working full time while studying for a part-time master is a significant challenge, but you can find the balance that works for you,” she said.
“And remember, pursuing further education while advancing your career is a major achievement in itself.”
Applications for the Online Master in Sustainability Management at RSM are now open for cohorts starting in 2027. Find out more about the programme and apply here.

Air defense chief vists units stationed in south Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:22:10 UTC
22:22:10 KST

During the inspection visit to the Southeast Air Defense District and the defense units stationed on the three islands of the Persian Gulf recently, Brigadier General Alireza Elhami reviewed the operational capacity and combat readiness of the personnel, met with the troops stationed there, and commended their efforts and role in downing the American A-10 aircraft during the Third Imposed War in summer.
Appreciating the day-to-day efforts and struggles of the army’s air defense forces, he emphasized the importance of maintaining service morale, intensified efforts, ismart monitoring of threats, and improving defense capabilities, and stated: Producing sustainable security and defending calmness for the people are among the main priorities of the army’s air defense.
The commander of the country's Khatam al-Anbiya (PBUH) Joint Air Defense Headquarters also met with the troops deployed in the three islands of the Persian Gulf, and while wishing them strength, emphasized the necessity of maintaining comprehensive combat readiness and improving the operational capacity of the units.

====================================================================================================

China Is Learning to Sell Japanese Culture Better Than Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:22:00 UTC
22:22:00 KST

What would Japanese youngsters respond when asked about Chinese culture? Chances are that they will point to the neon-lit streets of Yokohama Chinatown, the culinary tradition that invented gyoza and mapo tofu, and perhaps something they overheard from friends, classmates, and coworkers who are part of the 900,000-strong Chinese diaspora in Japan.
But what about Genshin Impact, the role-playing video game created by Shanghai-based miHoYo?
It certainly is wildly popular. After launching in 2020, it earned $10 billion in revenue by the end of 2025, becoming the fastest mobile game ever to reach that milestone. In Japan, it was ranked first in popularity as late as 2024, and remains within the top 20 for new downloads, more than six years after launch.
While created by a Chinese firm, Genshin Impact draws heavily from Japanese pop culture. Its graphics use the typical nijigen visuals perfected through the country’s anime and manga industries, while the gameplay features gacha mechanics of obtaining mystery items, so culturally rooted in Japan’s gachapon capsule toy vending machines.
MiHoYo, branded internationally as Cognosphere, had been publishing games for China’s otaku community since its founding in 2011. The co-founders stated that their inspiration for creating games came from personal love for Japanese anime and technology. However, their business has expanded far beyond those roots. Only 5 percent of Genshin’s total downloads come from Japan despite the game’s popularity in the country. And as miHoYo increasingly expands globally, its games now mix Japanese, Chinese, and Western elements to attract a more diverse audience, as the transnational visuals of its successful Honkai series attest.
Translating Japanese cultural vocabulary for the global audience has become a source of success for other Chinese firms too. Toymaker PopMart manufactured a global fad for its Labubu dolls by applying that same gacha mechanics to its blind boxes, compelling fans to buy more to chase those rare varieties. Consumer goods retailer Miniso – much derided in Japan as “(Daiso + Muji) / 2” – has become an international promoter of Japanese characters such as Chiikawa and Hello Kitty through licensing agreements.
Notably, Miniso has more than 8,000 stores in 110 countries. With Japanese firms largely absent from large swathes of Africa and South America, Chinese firms have become the first point of contact local consumers have with Japanese aesthetics.
Now, these Chinese firms are ready to sell Japanese culture back to Japan. If miHoYo’s success in Japan through Genshin was accidental, the next wave of Japanified Chinese products will be anything but.
Following PopMart’s entry into the Japanese market in 2022, Miniso-owned toymaker TopToy entered Japan in 2025 using the same formula. Mellojoy, leveraging Japan’s love for punipuni, engineered a craze among young Japanese women for its own handmade squishies. Even Miniso itself is making a return to Japan through a pop-up shop in collaboration with renowned idol Lisa.
Japanese firms will now be in an unusual situation of competing for Japanese consumers in products they have long believed to be idiosyncratically Japanese. The case of the BYD Racco is illustrative. The Chinese electric vehicle giant became the first foreign company to ever launch a dedicated Japanese kei car, a class of ultra-compact cars found only in Japan. Japanese carmakers long considered the kei class to have a technological, cultural, and regulatory moat deep enough to deter foreigners. After the Racco sold more than 1,000 two weeks after its launch, domestic rivals were driven out of their complacency and compelled to respond. Suzuki’s recent launch of the e SKY, an electric kei car using BYD-made batteries, will surely ignite more competition in the previously insular market.
As that competition heats up, Japanese firms may come to discover that consumers no longer really care what it means for a product to be culturally Japanese. A coordinated effort to promote the country abroad through the Cool Japan Fund’s investments in media and retail proved a costly failure, while Miniso plans 900-1,000 new stores every year and BYD is readying the Racco for the international market.
As Genshin Impact showed us, people are interested in a Japanese aesthetic that anyone can access affordably. That means commercialized and scalable products, rather than ones completely made by Japan.

Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:21:36 CET
22:21:36 KST

CAIRO, Oct 27 (Reuters) - An Egyptian court convicted the editor-in-chief of leading independent news website Mada Masr of running it without a licence on Tuesday, ordered the site closed and held her in custody for five hours, her lawyers and the outlet said.
Lina Attalah of the online newspaper Mada Masr, which has won numerous international awards for its reporting, was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds ($53,400), her lawyers told Reuters. She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, the newspaper said.
The ruling targets the most internationally prominent independent outlet in a media landscape mostly dominated by the state, and it comes a month after authorities arrested the entire newsroom of the fact-checking outlet Matsaddash. Rights groups have criticized the case against Attalah. Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, regularly publishes stories on politically sensitive topics.
Her lawyers said the court rejected their requests during Tuesday’s session to review the case file and submit additional evidence and instead issued her a court-appointed lawyer despite her objection. State authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The court gave her the maximum penalty, ordering the website to be shut down and its equipment confiscated, Mada Masr said in a statement.
The independent outlet said in a separate statement that during release procedures, Attalah was informed of a one-year prison term handed to her in absentia in 2024 on charges of disseminating false news and managing an unlicensed website. It said a retrial of the separate case was set for November 11 after her lawyers took steps to challenge the 2024 ruling.
Prosecutors referred Attalah to trial last Thursday.
A group of 119 rights groups and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, called the case an “unprecedented attack on press freedom.”
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, said in a statement on the social media platform X on Friday that the charges were baseless and that “journalism is not a crime.”
Egyptian authorities say the state is committed to upholding freedom of expression but that the media must operate within the law, respect national security and counter misinformation.
YEARS OF LEGAL BATTLES
Egyptian authorities have blocked Mada Masr inside the country since 2017. Mada Masr says six cases have been brought against it and its journalists over the last six years, though rights groups say this is the first of its kind to be referred to trial.
Attalah was named one of the world’s 100 most influential people by Time magazine in 2020.
Mada Masr says it has asked for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation repeatedly since 2018 but heard nothing back and learned of a rejection only when prosecutors raised the issue during an earlier case in 2022.
The outlet contested that decision in court and said its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
The council has not commented on the case but has said that it facilitates procedures for outlets that meet official requirements and is keen to promote freedom of expression.
In September, the US waived rights conditions, which include protecting media freedoms, on a portion of the roughly $1.3 billion of military aid it sends Egypt each year.
(Editing by Alexander Dziadosz, Aidan Lewis and Matthew Lewis)

BELGRADE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Protesters entered a Serbian television station supportive of former President Aleksandar Vucic late on Monday, interrupting broadcasting to call for the arrest of its editor, as tens of thousands took to the streets for a second night of post-election celebrations.
Serbia’s Student List, born out of a student-led anti-corruption protest movement, unseated Vucic in a historic election on Sunday, bringing to an end 14 years in power for a man who served as information minister under Slobodan Milosevic and who maintained tight control over the media.
Live footage broadcast by Informer TV showed around 30 people walk into its newsroom on Monday evening and surround editor-in-chief and owner Dragan Vucicevic. Some protesters shouted: “This is how it is in free Serbia” and “Where is Vucic now?” Some also called for Vucicevic’s arrest.
On his personal Instagram account, Vucic, dressed in a jumper displaying the crossed-out word “sorry”, called the event an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.
CALL FOR CALM
The student movement has no clear leader and Serbians are waiting to see whom it will appoint as prime minister and to other key positions. The leading candidate on its election list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, called for calm.
“We ask of you to stay calm and dignified until the end of the electoral process, just like you have been until now,” he said in a video posted on his Instagram account. “Don’t resort to any form of violence. Your Student List and your student movement urge you on this.”
The Independent Association of Journalists of Serbia said in a statement that it would submit an application on Tuesday to have Informer TV’s broadcasting licence revoked, citing systematic violations of law and programme obligations.
“On the very first day of (Student List) power, they want to ban the media. They have said everything about themselves, and nothing about us,” Informer’s Vucicevic told Reuters.
A group of people also gathered outside the private pro-Vucic Pink TV station in Belgrade on Monday evening, which was cordoned off by police.
Earlier, public broadcaster RTV in the Vojvodina region began its evening news bulletin by apologising to viewers for failing to fulfil its role, citing uncritical one-sided reporting.
The announcement was reminiscent of a move by the main Hungarian state TV channel, which in July, following the election defeat of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s Fidesz party three months earlier, displayed a black screen with the message: “Public media cannot lie. We apologise for doing so for many years.”
Serbia was ranked 104th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders, its lowest position ever, and worst in the EU-Balkan region.
The Crta election monitor said last week that television stations with national reach gave three-quarters of the time allotted to politicians to government representatives. The Student List was portrayed negatively more than 80% of the time it was discussed, Crta added.

Spain deports African, Asian asylum seekers to Morocco amid rights group outcry
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:20:57 CET
22:20:57 KST

By Corina Pons
MADRID, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Spain has returned to Morocco more than a dozen sub-Saharan African and Asian migrants who reached the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and were turned down for asylum, the first deportation of its kind from the enclave since a mass border crossing in July.
The Interior Ministry said the group had been sent back to Morocco after it agreed to receive them and they remained on Moroccan territory at present. It declined to give numbers or nationalities but migrant and rights charities operating in Ceuta said 16 people from Senegal, Nigeria, Yemen, Cameroon and Bangladesh were deported.
The NGOs claim such returns fail to take into account the risks associated with Morocco’s treatment of migrants from other countries and fly in the face of the values espoused by Spain’s leftist government.
Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher, said Spain’s posture was hypocritical.
“Spain, despite its (progressive) speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” she said. “Morocco does not respect many human rights.”
Neither Morocco’s Interior Ministry nor the International Organization for Migration, which cooperates with Moroccan authorities on voluntary return programmes for third country nationals or migrants, responded to Reuters requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Spain’s Interior Ministry told Reuters that Morocco is considered by the EU to be a safe country, and deportations are carried out “with all the necessary safeguards”, without providing further details.
Over 48 hours in July, some 80,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a tiny enclave that along with Melilla represents Europe’s only land borders with Africa.
While most returned within days, thousands remain and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government is under pressure from the EU and a frustrated populace to fix the Ceuta crisis before elections on November 29.
Spanish authorities are housing 8,000 migrants in reception centres and processing asylum applications lodged by the majority of people remaining in Ceuta.
Several NGOs including Amnesty International have complained to the Spanish ombudsman that some of the more than 13,000 people the government says have returned to Morocco voluntarily since the middle of August were forced to leave, including non-Moroccans.
(Reporting by Corina Pons, editing by Aislinn Laing and Keith Weir)

At a market in Türkiye's central Kayseri province, a humanoid robot moves between inspecting products and chatting with shopkeepers, checking price labels one moment and joking about bananas the next.
Named MEGA, the AI-powered robot accompanies municipal police officers on inspections in the Melikgazi district, where its unusual interactions with shopkeepers and customers have brought new energy to the market.
At Carsi Melikgazi, the robot scans shelf labels, compares displayed prices with those charged at checkout and provides information about product shelf lives and hygiene standards. It also relays its findings to relevant municipal departments in real time.
But MEGA's duties go beyond inspections. It reminds shopkeepers to label their products, informs shopkeepers with deficiencies about the applicable rules and thanks businesses that comply with regulations.
Acquired by Melikgazi Municipality, MEGA is part of the local government's efforts to adapt to emerging technologies.
Melikgazi Mayor Mustafa Palancioglu told Anadolu that the country, its cities and districts were seeking to adapt to technological advances, adding that robots could eventually be used in fields ranging from security and disaster response to cleaning and public information services.
Noting that robots were increasingly becoming part of everyday life, Palancioglu said those used in police, security and military services in various countries could also take on roles in the work of local governments.
"As Melikgazi Municipality, we use our robot in different areas to serve our citizens. Today, it is conducting inspections at Carsi Melikgazi as a municipal police officer and informing citizens. At the same time, it makes people smile and boosts morale," he said.
“Shopkeepers have welcomed encountering a robotic municipal police officer that makes suggestions and issues warnings to help maintain order," he added.
Palancioglu said AI-powered robots needed to be trained in advance to perform specific tasks, noting that staff from the municipality's research and development and information technology departments were working on MEGA.
"The robot we acquired is becoming increasingly involved in public services, taking on new tasks and interacting with our citizens. If you use technology for good, it can bring about many different benefits,” he said.
He also highlighted the municipality's efforts to train young people in technology through high schools and workshops, saying projects such as Gokturk Melikgazi aimed to equip them with skills to develop unmanned aerial vehicles and robotic systems.
Greengrocer Ahmet Murt said MEGA had brought new activity to the market and established a friendly rapport with local businesses.
“There has been quite a change since MEGA came to the market. It inspects us and even comments on our hair and beards. It tells us to put labels on products that don’t have them,” he said.
“Customers really like it and chat with it,” he added. “For example, when they offer it something to eat, MEGA says it only uses oil and cannot eat or drink. That makes us laugh.”
Another greengrocer, Mahmut Ozgoncu, said MEGA's arrival had brought more activity to the market.
He said children were interested in the robot, their families could shop comfortably and customers were happy to see MEGA.
Ozgoncu added that the robot also checked the produce on his stall.
“It paid attention to me and looked at the pomegranates and mandarins on my stall. It said, ‘You have very nice products.’ It was pleased that our products were of good quality. I offered it a banana, and it said, ‘I have diabetes, I can’t eat it,’” he said.

Egypt: Court order to shut down and fine Mada Masr a devastating blow to media freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:18:54 UTC
22:18:54 KST

Responding to the news that the New Cairo Misdemeanours court today convicted editor in chief Lina Attalah on charges of operating an unlicenced website, ordering the shutdown of prominent independent outlet Mada Masr and taking her into police custody pending payment of the maximum penalty of three million EGP fine (54,467 USD) Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Regional Impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said:
Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.
Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International
“Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country. By imposing a 3 million EGP fine, ordering the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its property, and detaining Lina Atallah until payment is made, the Egyptian authorities are sending a clear and ruthless message: critical, independent reporting will not be tolerated.
“This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country’s last remaining independent media voices. Lina Atallah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job. The Egyptian authorities must immediately overturn this outrageous verdict, halt the forced closure of Mada Masr, and end the systematic persecution of journalists.
“Mada is one of the most fearless and staunchly independent media outlets in the country, and they have continued to report professionally and operate in full transparency. The media outlet has repeatedly attempted to apply for a licence since the new media law was passed in 2018, but the authorities have continuously denied or failed to respond to their application.
“The speed with which the investigation and trial were scheduled and the judge’s refusal to adjourn today’s session to give defence lawyers adequate time to prepare and his refusal of all other requests by the defence, including to submit additional documentation or to summon witnesses, raises serious due process concerns.
“Under no circumstances is shutting down a media outlet a proportionate response to operating without government authorization. International human rights standards are clear on the fact that registration systems should not be used as a mechanism of prior restraint or to pick and choose which media outlets governments like and which they wish to silence.
“Today’s verdict comes at a time when independent journalism in Egypt is under assault and just weeks after the arbitrary detention of six journalists from the Matsadaash fact-checking platform amidst the continued blocking of hundreds of news websites and civil society organizations across the country.”
Background
Mada has for years operated in full transparency as a non-profit company, while actively attempting since 2018 to register under the 2018 Law Regulating the Press, Media, and the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. Mada applied for a licence twice in 2018 and 2020 but received no response from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation (SCMR), the government body overseeing the media.
In 2022, Mada learned that the SCMR rejected their application without providing reasons. In the same year, Mada appealed the rejection in court but later lost the case. At a hearing in 2023, the SCMR stated its grounds for the first time. Mada reapplied this year and submitted all the documents the SCMR said were missing but never received a response.
The ruling follows years of harassment and intimidation against Lina Atallah as editor in chief of Mada Masr who has faced six criminal investigations over the past six years over their reporting. Most recently, on 4 August 2025, the authorities summoned Atallah for questioning on unfounded charges, including “spreading false news” and “operating a website without a license,” over an article published on 31 July 2025 about deteriorating detention conditions in Badr 3 prison. She was released on bail pending investigation.
At least 18 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Hundreds of websites remain blocked in the country, including Mada Masr, other media outlets and independent NGOs.

Germany’s Helsing Unveils Low-Cost Highspeed Drone Interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:17:49 UTC
22:17:49 KST

Helsing, a German military AI company, unveiled its Contra AI-controlled autonomous air defense system via a video posted on X on Monday. Helsing described it as a cost-effective system optimized to tackle jet-powered drone and missile attacks.
Helsing’s Contra system is intended to solve the existing air defense conundrum where the only current way of effectively intercepting jet-powered drones such as Russia’s Geran 4s and 5s is the use of multimillion-dollar interceptors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Contra is intended to control two relatively inexpensive interceptor missiles: the AD-1 Inferno and AD-2 Ambush said to cost less than $100,000 each compared with Patriot PAC-3 missiles at $4-5 million a unit and the NASAMS (AMRAAM / AIM-9X) at around $1million a throw.
The military issues website Defense News cites recent intelligence reports, that Russia is increasing jet-powered drone and cruise missile production, to as much as 4,000 units a month, which, along with launch sites, could bring parts of the EU within range.
Artificial intelligence and interceptor speed, the key
While still at the developmental stage, Helsing bills Contra, based on its well-proven Altra C2 platform, as an autonomous AI-based operation that will allow the real-time detection and engagement of hundreds or more drone and missile threats into a single air defense picture.
It is anticipated to be “field-ready” by late 2027, with Helsing saying its seekers rely on European supply chains and is free from Chinese components.
Russia Says Three Tankers With Diesel En Route to US
Intercepts would be achieved through a combination of two, advanced radar guided, container-launched missile interceptors whose performance is designed to overlap and supplement each other’s capability.
The AD-1 “Inferno,” which Helsing Chief Executive Gundbert Scherf says is intended as the “workhorse” of the counter-drone system, is powered by a jet engine, and flies at around 700 kph (435 mph) at a range of around 20 kilometers (12 miles). It can loiter over a defended area, swarm with other interceptors, and make repeated passes.
The AD-2 “Ambush,” intended as a rapid interceptor against drones and missiles that break through the AD-1 “net,” has a solid rocket motor and is said to have a flight speed of Mach 2.5 (1,900 mph, 3,000 kph) at a range of in excess of 20 kilometers (12 miles).
Both systems are able to be redirected mid-course by the Contra ground stations with an onboard radar-seeker for all-weather terminal guidance. While designed for, and capable of, stand-alone operation, Helsing said the system is set up to rapidly integrate with third-party counter-drone systems including missile interceptors, lasers, and guns. The company said Contra has already demonstrated such hardware integrations to multiple military customers.
Niklas Köhler, Co-Founder and President of Helsing, says: “Contra ends the air defense dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometers (6+ miles) high – affordable and at industrial scale.”

Estonian foreign minister briefed on Norway-Finland call with Putin

A statement from the Finnish president's office described the call as "a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on October 20 and held in consultation with Ukraine."
The call was initiated by Finland and Norway, which border Russia, and its aim "was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin." The statement said it was related to the upcoming meetings in Abu Dhabi between Russia and Ukraine.
While Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was critical of Tuesday's call, Tsahkna said that only increased pressure on Russia will make it take peace negotiations seriously.
He added that there is currently no indication whatsoever that Russia has changed its strategic objectives or is genuinely interested in negotiations.
Only increased pressure on Russia will make it take peace negotiations seriously. Every contact with Russia must convey Europe's unity and determination to support Ukraine and maintain pressure on Russia, while making clear that Europe will not negotiate away the fundamental principles underpinning its security. Ukraine wants peace, and Estonia supports all efforts to achieve it. But there is no indication that Russia has changed its strategic objectives or is genuinely interested in negotiations. Russia's goal is not merely to seize parts of Ukraine, but to subjugate the entire country and undermine Europe's security order, founded on NATO and the EU. Putin believes that Western support for Ukraine may weaken, which is why he remains motivated to continue the war, Tsahkna said.

"It is also important to make clear that Europe will not negotiate over the fundamental principles underpinning its security arrangements. These include the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity, the understanding that borders cannot be changed by force, and every country's right to decide its own security arrangements," he added.
