Rare North American bird spotted in southern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:31:00 UTC
21:31:00 KST

A buff-breasted sandpiper spreads its wings in Manavgat’s Ulualan area.
For the very first time in the country’s history, birdwatchers have recorded a buff-breasted sandpiper in the southern province of Antalya, officially bringing Türkiye’s total recorded bird species to 506.
A Dutch birdwatcher first spotted the bird in Ulualan, where the Manavgat River meets the Mediterranean Sea. Members of the Antalya Bird Watching Community then documented it with photographs and video, making it the 361st bird species recorded in Antalya.
Türkiye Bird Committee Chairman Mustafa Erturhan said the species normally lives in North America, including Alaska. Some individuals stray from their usual routes and turn up in Europe, but this was the first record in Türkiye, he said.
Around 20 members of the Antalya Bird Watching Community, which has about 200 members, were among the first to see the bird, Erturhan said. Birdwatchers from other parts of Türkiye have since traveled to the area, while others have set off for Manavgat.
The Manavgat wetland is an important area for birdwatching and wildlife in the western Mediterranean, offering birds places to rest and feed during migration, he said. Rare species can be seen in important bird areas, and Manavgat attracts both Turkish and foreign birdwatchers and nature enthusiasts, he said.
The wetland’s natural structure must be preserved to protect the area’s natural wealth, Erturhan said.
Gökçe Irmak, one of the community’s youngest members, said seeing the rare bird in Manavgat had excited her.
“I was excited to see a rare species like the buff-breasted sandpiper here. I came to photograph it, and I did. I am truly happy right now,” she said.
The buff-breasted sandpiper breeds in Arctic Alaska and Canada and winters in the grasslands of Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina. Unlike many other shorebirds, it uses dry, grassy habitats during migration, including pastures and farm fields. It feeds on insects and other invertebrates, picking prey from the ground.

Protesters enter Serbian pro-Vucic TV station, call for arrest of editor
BELGRADE, Oct 27 - Protesters entered a Serbian television station supportive of former President Aleksandar Vucic late on Monday, interrupting broadcasting to call for the arrest of its editor, as tens of thousands took to the streets for a second night of post-election celebrations.
Serbia's Student List, born out of a student-led anti-corruption protest movement, unseated Vucic in a historic election on Sunday, bringing to an end 14 years in power for a man who served as information minister under Slobodan Milosevic and who maintained tight control over the media.
Live footage broadcast by Informer TV showed around 30 people walk into its newsroom on Monday evening and surround editor-in-chief and owner Dragan Vucicevic. Some protesters shouted: "This is how it is in free Serbia" and "Where is Vucic now?" Some also called for Vucicevic's arrest.
On his personal Instagram account, Vucic, dressed in a jumper displaying the crossed-out word "sorry", called the event an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.
CALL FOR CALM
The student movement has no clear leader and Serbians are waiting to see whom it will appoint as prime minister and to other key positions. The leading candidate on its election list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, called for calm.
"We ask of you to stay calm and dignified until the end of the electoral process, just like you have been until now," he said in a video posted on his Instagram account. "Don’t resort to any form of violence. Your Student List and your student movement urge you on this."
The Independent Association of Journalists of Serbia said in a statement that it would submit an application on Tuesday to have Informer TV's broadcasting licence revoked, citing systematic violations of law and programme obligations.
"On the very first day of (Student List) power, they want to ban the media. They have said everything about themselves, and nothing about us," Informer's Vucicevic told Reuters.
A group of people also gathered outside the private pro-Vucic Pink TV station in Belgrade on Monday evening, which was cordoned off by police.
Earlier, public broadcaster RTV in the Vojvodina region began its evening news bulletin by apologising to viewers for failing to fulfil its role, citing uncritical one-sided reporting.
The announcement was reminiscent of a move by the main Hungarian state TV channel, which in July, following the election defeat of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party three months earlier, displayed a black screen with the message: "Public media cannot lie. We apologise for doing so for many years."
Serbia was ranked 104th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders, its lowest position ever, and worst in the EU-Balkan region.
The Crta election monitor said last week that television stations with national reach gave three-quarters of the time allotted to politicians to government representatives. The Student List was portrayed negatively more than 80% of the time it was discussed, Crta added. REUTERS

With diesel deal, Trump is teaching Reagan’s lesson to a larger class

With diesel deal, Trump is teaching Reagan’s lesson to a larger class
Like Ronald Reagan, who lifted sanctions on a Russian pipeline in time for the midterm elections, Trump is showing his allies that American restrictions are for sale
In June 1982, Ronald Reagan imposed sanctions to prevent European firms from using American technology to help build a pipeline that would carry Soviet gas to western Europe. He warned that Europe was making itself a hostage to the Kremlin and contributing to the Moscow’s war chest. Then, 18 days before that November’s congressional elections, he offered to sell the Soviet Union up to 23 million tonnes of grain.
Europeans, told to tear up their own contracts while American farmers were invited to feed Moscow, cried hypocrisy. Even the Kremlin’s own news agency called the offer an electoral ploy. Reagan’s Republicans lost 26 House seats anyway, and about 10 days after the vote he lifted the pipeline sanctions.
Forty-four years later, the commodity is diesel. Last week, a tanker left Russia for New York carrying 40,000 tonnes of the fuel, an import Congress banned in 2022. It sails under a temporary Treasury licence meant to bring down pump prices before the November 3 midterm elections, though its cargo arrives four days after polls close.

Swiss tourism expected to recover slightly this winter
Swiss tourism is expected to grow again this winter, following a decline in overnight stays over the summer – the first such decline since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Economists at BAK Economics are forecasting growth in overnight stays, although the consequences of the war in Iran are likely to continue to hamper business with tourists from the Far East.
During the summer season, the number of overnight stays fell for the first time since the Covid-19 pandemic, following several previous record highs, BAK Economics noted in its forecasts for Swiss tourism published on Tuesday. It fell by 0.8% to just under 25 million.
However, moderate growth is now expected for the winter, the report added. According to the tourism forecasts commissioned by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), overnight stays in the winter of 2026/27 are expected to rise by 0.9% to 18.9 million.
More
Switzerland ranks among top ten in WEF Tourism Index
War in Iran continues to weigh on the sector
The war in Iran remains a drag on tourism. This has significantly disrupted international air traffic, and the rise in kerosene prices has made air travel considerably more expensive, BAK Economics added. The Middle East conflict is therefore continuing to dampen tourism demand in long-haul markets, particularly in Asia.
Nevertheless, BAK Economics expects overall growth in overnight stays of 1.3% for the summer of 2027. Demand from long-haul markets is set to recover, with an increase of 3.3%. However, visitor numbers from Asia will remain below pre-war levels.
For 2027 as a whole, BAK Economics anticipates a 1.1% increase in overnight stays to 44.2 million. And in 2028, tourism demand is likely to gain momentum as air travel continues to normalise. Consequently, an increase in overnight stays of 1.3% to 44.8 million is expected in the 2028 tourism year.

'Get the Flock out': Americans respond to AI cameras in bipartisan backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:26:54 UTC
21:26:54 KST

'Get the Flock out': Americans respond to AI cameras in bipartisan backlash
ATLANTA, Georgia – AI-driven Flock cameras made by an Atlanta-based company are sprouting up across the US, sparking alarm and bipartisan, citizen-driven campaigns as the new technology emerges as a 2026 midterm campaign issue. While politicians hedge and local officials rush to sign contracts, community volunteers attempt to address an issue with major implications for future generations. But it might be too late.
Standing near a nondescript black pole topped with a solar panel on a leafy side street lined by family homes in an Atlanta exurb, Noah* confesses that he feels an immense sense of disquiet as the US heads into the midterm elections.
“I truly think that this is the most observed that Americans have ever been in political history. And I think that Flock is a massive step into these surveillance states that we have the ability to decide whether or not we are okay with,” said the 27-year-old software engineer.
“Flock” refers to a brand of AI-driven surveillance cameras produced by Atlanta-based company Flock Safety, which was started in 2017 by three alumni of the Georgia Institute of Technology, commonly called Georgia Tech. The cameras scan licence plates and capture, analyse and store details of passing vehicles, including location, time, car models and bumper stickers.
The surveillance cameras emerged as a lightning-rod campaign issue across the US amid a backlash against AI, alarm over the sweeping power of the technology and questions about the unchecked growth of the industry as President Donald Trump pushes a pro-tech agenda.
Watch moreAI on the ballot? Voters in US midterms revolt
In Atlanta, capital of the southern state of Georgia and a city that has gained a reputation as one of the country’s fastest-growing technology hubs, candidates were repeatedly grilled about their positions on AI and the little cameras, topped with solar umbrellas, that have sprouted up across the state, earning the wrath of many Georgians.
When the two candidates were asked about the cameras during the only televised debate in the gubernatorial race to replace Georgia’s outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp, Democratic hopeful Keisha Lance Bottoms noted that, “the challenge that we have with Flock cameras and other licence-plate reader technologies is that the technology has gotten ahead of the policy”. When pressed on her platform on the issue, Bottoms said she was “not opposed to a moratorium on Flock cameras”.
Her Republican rival, Rick Johnson, said he “would not put a moratorium” on Flock cameras “because I don’t want crime to go up”. The billionaire, whose business connections with a Texas data centre have been under scrutiny in the Atlanta press, said he would instead “fix” the AI camera problem. “I’m telling you, there’s 15 people at Georgia Tech that can solve this in one week,” he said.
The televised exchange nailed the arguments for and against the hi-tech cameras. Flock Safety says the cameras help law enforcement officials fight crime by connecting “vehicle sightings across jurisdictions to uncover patterns, strengthen investigations, and securely collaborate with trusted partners”, according to the company website.
But critics concerned about security breaches and privacy issues are not persuaded. Their numbers are growing across the US, with their opposition getting increasingly vocal, visual and visceral.
Police use Flock to stalk ex-girlfriends, spouses
Strolling down the streets of Woodstock, an affluent, predominantly White area of Cherokee County in northern Atlanta, Noah says he watched the gubernatorial candidates debate the Flock camera issue and was not impressed.
“I was honestly kind of disappointed by how both candidates discussed it. They would either say that they were OK with it, or they would look into it, or they just wanted some sort of guardrail on it, whereas Flock cameras already have guardrails and they’ve been broken over and over and over again,” he noted.
Noah knows a thing or two about Flock guardrail failures. In his free time, the young software engineer volunteers as one of the coordinators of DeFlock Cherokee, a local chapter of a larger, decentralised DeFlock movement that tracks Flock and other AI-driven surveillance cameras across the US.
In Cherokee – a county with a population of around 260,000 – alone, there have been a number of high-profile cases of breaches that have made headlines in recent months. The suspects in most cases are, or have been, law enforcement officials with a duty to protect the people.
In August, the Cherokee County Sheriff’s Office arrested and fired a fourth deputy, Jerry Shellhouse, for allegedly misusing Flock licence plate readers. The office had previously arrested and fired three other deputies for abusing Flock, but missed Shellhouse until they were contacted by a USA TODAY investigative team that found the 57-year-old Cherokee law enforcement official had searched one tag at least 840 times.
County authorities said he had misused the Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) system between October 2023 and December 2025, before the office updated its Flock policy to include multiple audits a year and limit access to authorised users.
While the details of the Shellhouse case have not been released, news reports reveal a pattern of Flock misuse across the US. Most cases involve a current or former law enforcement official surveilling the movements of an ex-spouse or partner.
In Dallas, another northern Atlanta exurb near Cherokee, a 911 emergency response director was arrested and fired after the USA TODAY team found she had searched more than 2,500 times for cars belonging to her estranged husband and his new girlfriend. The searches were accompanied by persistent stalking of the couple, the report revealed.
At least 100 police department employees across the US were charged with or accused of misusing licence-plate readers for unauthorised purposes, according to a September report by The Washington Post. And cases covered by the media could simply be the tip of the iceberg, analysts warn.
Beneath each case lies a human story of harassment and, at times, tragedy. In Jefferson, a northern Atlanta suburb, a police chief committed suicide in April, according to local officials, before he could face trial for stalking his former girlfriend. Text messages between the police chief and his ex, who confronted him about his repeated harassment, revealed the law enforcement official confessing to being “on a spiral” and promising never to “look again” at the Flock database.
Flock insists that it takes allegations of misuse seriously and regularly updates its guardrails. Last year, the company changed its systems to make officers' misuse more difficult for the public to unearth, according to InvestigateTV.
But the reports of misuse keep coming, and with them, company rebuttals. In a response to the USA TODAY report, Flock’s public relations manager Paris Lewbel said the company was “committed to setting a baseline for where safeguards and transparency for our industry should be, and welcome further conversations and regulations from local communities about the rules of the road that they want to set for public safety technology”.
Blocking, destroying, locating cameras on apps
Local communities in counties such as Cherokee are having plenty of conversations about public safety in the face of sweeping AI surveillance technology. The problem is, most lack the time or wherewithal to frame policy. And for those who try, such as Noah, it’s an uphill slog against the odds.
Emerging from a coffee shop at a strip mall in Woodstock, a town in Cherokee, Chanel Dennis, 46, said she was against the use of Flock cameras. “It’s an invasion of privacy that shouldn’t be allowed and people are using it for not the purposes it's intended,” she said. “I think it's also a problem that we are being taxed to provide these services from private companies.”
At the Woodstock city centre park, Zeke Sims, a 27-year-old resident, said he does not “support the surveillance and the misuse” of Flock cameras.
“There's been several stories on how the police force and law enforcement have used them to track certain people, specifically exes and stuff like that. I just don't think it's something that should be there in the first place,” he said.
Both Dennis and Sims said the use of Flock cameras was an election issue for them in the midterms, although they declined to divulge which party they would be voting for.
On social media, videos show opponents how to place signs, attached to household items such as mops and rakes, to block Flock camera lenses. Photographs of “Get the Flock out” signs on the cameras flood the internet.
Another genre of anti-Flock posts features video clips of people destroying the cameras, but some are AI-generated spoofs.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Meanwhile, community-run campaigns abound. Noah pulls out his phone to display a user-generated DeFlock Cherokee app, which he helped create with a few friends, to pinpoint the location of the cameras. “The website started a couple of months ago, and everyone started flooding in to try and help with research, outreach and everything. It's been quite a movement,” he said.
DeFlock apps also offer drivers alternate routes to avoid the AI cameras. But in the Atlanta area, finding a Flock-free route is a challenge. A local journalist tried the app to buy an “afternoon sweet treat” but found the route took too long on a working day and he could not avoid a key intersection that had a Flock camera.
‘Flock’s evil twin’
Most Americans are alarmed by the explosive growth of the AI industry and the infrastructure, such as mega data centres, required to power it. Around 70% of US citizens and residents oppose the construction of data centres due to high energy consumption, water use, contamination, sound pollution and other environmental problems, according to polls.
Watch moreThirsty giants: Big tech's data centres multiply
These concerns cut across ideological divides.
Flock cameras purport to reduce crime, often a key concern for Republican voters. But the statistics on the technology’s crime reduction results so far have been mixed. A recent working paper by researchers at the University of South Carolina found ALPR networks reduced motor theft. But the Arlington, Virginia-based Institute for Justice disputed the study and questioned the interpretation of the findings, adding to the disquiet about a technology that appears to be more than the public is ready for.
In the trade-off between surveillance and security, the alleged abuse of ALPR technology by law enforcement officials has raised alarm bells, even among voters who traditionally rate being tough on crime as a key election issue.
“One of the craziest things about this movement is just how bipartisan it is. One of the most American things is not to trust the government. And this is government master surveillance. I'm seeing very similar rhetoric on both sides and people are uniting across the aisle,” explained Noah.
Across the United States, city, county and town council meetings have seen residents show up to protest and voice their opposition to Flock cameras in desperate bids to slow down contract approvals and draw attention to the issue. At a San Francisco meeting this summer, a resident dressed as Darth Vader sarcastically expressed his support for the cameras. “They are following children in parks and gymnasiums, and we need this. I need this so I can stalk my ex-girlfriend,” he said.
Noah believes raising public awareness about the issue is a civic duty. “The greatest thing somebody can do is just to be loud about it, to tell your neighbours about it, to educate them, and inform them, because most people don't know,” he said.
But it takes tenacity to keep up the fight, Noah acknowledges. Earlier this week, for instance, DeFlock Cherokee alerted residents about a Tuesday, October 20, meeting, where commissioners were set to vote on a $37 million police security contract including AI surveillance technology for the county. But on the designated day, the vote was postponed to November 3 – the date of midterm elections, increasing the frustration among activists, who viewed it as an attempt to keep the public out.
The targets are also getting more diverse with the AI surveillance options multiplying, pitting activists against a growing army. As a growing number of councils scrap contracts with Flock due to the backlash, other surveillance companies are stepping in to fill the gap.
The latest $37 million police contract bid for Cherokee does not concern Flock, but another company, Axon, also promising AI-driven monitoring. DeFlock Cherokee campaigns now describe Axon as “Flock’s evil twin” and warn that, “Axon clearly sees itself as the alternative to Flock for agencies that want out, yet it's the same kind of mass surveillance company, with all the same problems.”
As the surveillance systems expand with new players entering the scene, Noah admits that the challenges can at times be daunting. But he’s determined to keep at it.
“I'm very motivated to keep pursuing anti-surveillance action. It's partially just because I see how much support I get for it and how widespread the backlash against mass surveillance is. It can definitely be exhausting at times, because the surveillance state has a way of sort of firing on all cylinders,” he said. “It's an enormous ecosystem that I’ve spent months, if not years, researching, and I feel overwhelmed by it. So I can't imagine how overwhelmed and in the dark the average person feels about it. And I feel like I have an obligation to try to educate and fight on their behalf.”
*Full name withheld upon request due to security concerns.

EU Commission proposes expanding powers of border police force
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:26:20 CET
21:26:20 KST

By Amina Ismail and Inti Landauro
BRUSSELS, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The European Commission proposed a major expansion of the powers of the EU border agency Frontex on Tuesday, including giving it the capacity to act beyond EU territory, in the aftermath of the massive rush to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta last summer.
The proposal would significantly broaden Frontex’s mandate, allowing it to carry out deportations between non-EU countries, operate outside the bloc and deploy rapid-reaction teams in emergencies.
The proposed legislation is an attempt to make Frontex more reactive to large-scale arrivals at the EU’s borders, such as in Ceuta on the North African coast, as European governments push for tougher migration policies despite concerns from rights advocates over accountability.
“Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns,” Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
“It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis,” Brunner added.
OVERSIGHT CONCERNS
But while the proposal would significantly broaden Frontex’s role, it would also narrow the scope of its internal rights watchdog, with complaints referred to national authorities to handle.
The proposal comes as member states increasingly focus on returns, arguing that too many migrants ordered to leave the bloc ultimately remain.
Although irregular arrivals have decreased, the arrival of more than 72,000 people in Ceuta from Morocco in late July, most of whom later left, reignited debate over the EU’s migration rules and was cited by several member states as evidence for stronger tools.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex’s standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new “European border and return reserve” of 17,000 officers by 2041, who would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would create a new EU Return Coordination Centre within Frontex and expand the agency’s role across the entire deportation process, from voluntary return counselling to organising returns and reintegration support, the statement said.
The agency would also be empowered to help organise and carry out deportations from one non-EU country to another, subject to agreements with the countries involved and international legal standards, according to the statement.
That would mean Frontex could, for example, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya – one of the main launching points for migrant boats crossing to Europe – back to Bangladesh.
The proposal would also create a new online monitoring centre to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
The Commission proposed allocating €11.8 billion to Frontex for the EU’s 2028-2034 budget cycle, nearly double the almost €6 billion earmarked for the agency under the current 2021-2027 framework, as part of a planned expansion of its mandate.
The push comes just a few months after EU lawmakers approved new rules aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc.
Tuesday’s proposal was met with criticism from rights groups and some lawmakers.
“Working with third countries, without proper oversight or accountability, is a threat to fundamental rights and respect for international law, while leaving Frontex staff in legal limbo outside of European law,” said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
“The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration,” she added.
(Reporting by Amina Ismail and Inti Landauro; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Alex Richardson)

Hungary refused to approve the screening results for negotiating clusters 4 and 5 within the framework of Ukraine's EU accession negotiations during a meeting of the Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession to the EU (COELA) in Brussels on Tuesday 27 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing EU diplomats familiar with the course of the meeting
Details: European Pravda noted that Hungary has not yet supported the further advancement of the process to open the final two clusters 4 and 5 in accession negotiations with Ukraine. One of the diplomats said that Hungary's position has not changed.
According to sources, the Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU was aware in advance that Hungary had no intention of altering its stance regarding Ukraine's further progress towards opening these two clusters.
Despite this, the issue was again included on the working group's agenda for 27 October.
Another diplomat expressed the view that bringing the matter up for re-discussion was more political in nature and served as a means to increase pressure on Budapest, rather than representing a real attempt to secure a positive decision at this specific meeting.
Cluster 4, Green Agenda and Sustainable Connectivity, covers transport, energy, trans-European networks, the environment and climate change. Cluster 5, Resources, Agriculture and Cohesion Policy, includes agriculture, fisheries, regional policy and budgetary provisions.
These are the final two negotiating clusters that have not yet been opened for Ukraine. The Ukrainian authorities are counting on their opening by the end of 2026.

DUBAI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a body set up by Tehran to manage passage requests in the Strait of Hormuz, said on Tuesday all vessels belonging to South Korean shipping company Sinokor would face “legal action” starting on November 1.
Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the strategic waterway by attacking shipping there since US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28. It has restricted transit to try to gain leverage over Washington, while disrupting oil flows from Arab Gulf oil producers, especially to their customers in Asia.
The authority said on X that Sinokor vessels had committed the highest number of crossing violations in the strait over the past three months, and “appropriate actions” had been taken against at least seven of them.
The Korea Shipowners’ Association said on Wednesday the vessels in question were not owned by Sinokor but had been sub-chartered to an overseas oil company, and had no South Korean crew, with only foreign seafarers on board.
The association said it had confirmed this through a Sinokor official.
Sinokor was unaware of the authority’s separate warning of legal action and was checking the details, the association said.
Ships owned by Sinokor were previously included on a list issued by Iran in August of 45 tankers that it said had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
In response to Iranian attacks, the United States also imposed a naval blockade against ships linked to the Islamic Republic in the strait.
While the blockade has all but choked off Iranian exports, Gulf producers have adapted to attacks on shipping by relying on so-called dark transits — switching off tankers’ tracking systems to evade detection — to protect the oil flows that underpin their economies.

Trump Jr. went hunting in Mongolia with a Putin-linked oligarch — FT
Kyiv • UNN

Donald Trump Jr., the son of the U.S. president, spent two days hunting in Mongolia together with Umar Kremlev, a Russian businessman with ties to the inner circle of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin. Financial Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, at the end of August Donald Trump Jr. flew to Mongolia’s capital, Ulaanbaatar, and from there traveled to a hunting camp in Uvs Province. On August 27, Umar Kremlev, a convicted oligarch with close ties to Vladimir Putin’s personal security service, flew to Ulaanbaatar on a charter plane and joined the group.
"One of the guides said that during the trip Trump Jr. killed an Altai argali — an endangered species of sheep valued for its enormous horns. Since 2019, the president’s son has hunted argali in Mongolia at least twice more. A still from the 2022 short film "Lost in Mongolia," in which Donald Trump Jr., on the right, shoots an Altai argali during a previous trip," the publication writes.
"Don made it clear that he has a personal friendship with Umar, not a business relationship," a representative for Trump Jr. said.
He also added that they were introduced by a mutual friend from the hunting community.
"Their friendship is largely based on a shared love of hunting, fishing, and outdoor recreation. It should not be surprising that earlier this year they went hunting together," the representative noted.
Who is Kremlev and why the trip attracted attention
Umar Lutfulloyev, better known as Umar Kremlev, has headed IBA since 2020. Before that, he ran Russia’s boxing federation, and during his presidency the international organization received significant sponsorship funding from the Russian state-owned company "Gazprom." In May this year, Kremlev was also part of Putin’s delegation during his visit to China. According to the Financial Times, Kremlev was also convicted of extortion and assault at a young age.
"In 2010, he changed his Tajik surname to the more Russian-sounding Kremlev, which means "one who belongs to the Kremlin." After that, he began a new phase of his life as a successful boxing promoter, building connections among biker gangs, the police, and later the highest circles of the security services," the publication writes.
Journalists also established that he was accompanied during the trip by Artur Martirosov, a Russian businessman and partner at the venture capital fund Voskhod, which is under U.S. sanctions.
"The meeting in Mongolia took place after Kremlev attended Trump Jr.’s wedding celebrations in May on a private Caribbean island and paid some of the expenses. ProPublica was the first to report on the Russian’s role in Trump Jr.’s wedding. The president later said that his son had repaid Kremlev," the publication writes.
At the same time, according to the publication, intelligence experts believe that such ties could become an object of Russian propaganda.
"In reality, it does not matter whether people have the best intentions. As soon as Russian security and intelligence services learn that someone has a relationship with a person who is of significant interest to them, they will try to use it for their own purposes," said Golden Triplett, who served as director of counterintelligence at the U.S. National Security Council during Donald Trump’s first presidential term.
After the hunt, Trump Jr. also met with Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh.
"A government representative posted photographs on Facebook and wrote that they discussed relations between the United States and Mongolia, as well as potential business opportunities. "The president held an informal meeting and had lunch with Trump’s son. Relations are in fairly good shape. They did not discuss politics or official visits," a representative for Khurelsukh said.

Russia’s ‘sci-fi fortress’ in Antarctica goes viral (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:23:33 UTC
21:23:33 KST

Russia’s ‘sci-fi fortress’ in Antarctica goes viral (VIDEO)
A video of Russia’s revamped, futuristic-looking Vostok Station in Antarctica has gone viral, with its elevated complex drawing comparisons to a sci-fi spaceship and a video game fortress.
Russia’s only operational inland Antarctic research station, Vostok, is around 3,500 meters above sea level and 1,400-1,500 km from the coast, in the planet’s notorious ‘Pole of Cold’. It holds the world record for the lowest directly measured air temperature – a bone-chilling -89.2 C (-128.6 F), recorded on July 21, 1983.
Footage posted on X on Saturday – which shows the station’s exterior painted in blue and the colors of the Russian flag, almost entirely cloaked in snow and frost – received over a million views in just two days before spreading to Instagram and Facebook.
“This place looks like it’s straight out of a sci-fi game! Just imagine: working there at a temperature of -89 C. Simply unbelievable,” one user wrote.
“It looks like Star Wars,” another person said. Others described the station as “otherworldly,” with a “Dune vibe” and an appearance “straight out of the Star Wars movies.” Some likened it to a fortress from the ‘Metal Gear Solid’ video game series.
Founded in 1957, the station received its futuristic makeover in 2024, replacing an aging complex largely buried under snow. Stretching 140 meters and rising up to 17.5 meters, the five-module complex stands on 36 three-meter-high supports to keep it above accumulating snow. Outside, crews face oxygen-poor air, extreme dryness, intense UV radiation, and around five months of polar darkness. Inside, however, it’s a different world.
Spanning over 3,000 square meters, the station houses up to 35 people in summer and 15 in winter, offering private rooms, laboratories, a gym, sauna, recreation areas, a medical center with an operating room, and other amenities. Insulation up to 95 cm thick, Russian-made heating and power systems, heat recovery, water recycling, and multiple backups help sustain operations, with food and fuel reserves sufficient for two years.
Vostok is a major scientific outpost operated by Russia’s Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute. Researchers analyze ancient ice cores to trace Earth’s climate history, monitor extreme weather, cosmic rays, and the planet’s magnetic field, and study Lake Vostok – a vast freshwater lake sealed beneath nearly 4 km of ice for millions of years. The station’s isolation also makes it a testing ground for future space missions, while its historic drilling facility is protected under the 1959 Antarctic Treaty system, which reserves the continent for peace and science.

The Ministry of Finance&apos;s general tax consultation will help resolve the issue of criminal prosecution of airlines over leasing
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:21:55 EET
21:21:55 KST

The Ministry of Finance's general tax consultation will help resolve the issue of criminal prosecution of airlines over leasing
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Finance is preparing a consultation on the taxation of aircraft leasing, which the Economic Security Bureau is reclassifying as royalties. It may help in disputes that have already been opened.
The issue of taxing Ukrainian airlines’ leasing payments to non-residents requires a solution not only going forward, but also with regard to tax and criminal proceedings that have already been initiated. A general tax consultation (GTC) from the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine could resolve the contradictions. Since a GTC is not a regulatory legal act and does not create new tax rules, but explains how to apply the current legislation, its conclusions will also be taken into account when considering disputes that arose earlier. The Ministry of Finance has already used this approach to eliminate ambiguities in tax legislation, UNN writes.
Airlines faced problems because of a new interpretation of aircraft and helicopter leasing
Since 2024, the State Tax Service and the Economic Security Bureau have begun reclassifying Ukrainian airlines’ leasing payments to non-residents as royalties. This led to tax claims and criminal proceedings involving at least five Ukrainian air carriers.
The key contradiction lies in the legal classification of such transactions. Airlines pay foreign aircraft owners rent or lease payments for the use of aircraft. The Economic Security Bureau, however, treats these transactions as the lease of equipment rather than air transport and regards such payments as royalties, which entails a different tax treatment.
At the same time, the relevant provisions of the Tax Code and Ukraine’s international treaties on the avoidance of double taxation were in force before 2024 as well. There were no legislative changes that directly established a new taxation procedure for such transactions. At the same time, airlines have successfully undergone tax audits and, according to the State Tax Service, only one carrier had faced a claim concerning aircraft leasing.
Representatives of the aviation industry point out that aircraft leasing is a global practice and that no country treats it as royalties. For the industry, this contradiction is systemic, since more than 80% of the aircraft operated by Ukrainian commercial air carriers are leased. Accordingly, the ambiguous interpretation of such payments creates risks for the vast majority of airlines.
The situation is complicated by the fact that, due to russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukrainian airspace remains closed to civil flights, while Ukrainian airlines are forced to operate abroad in order to preserve their fleets and personnel. Despite this, from 2022 to 2025, aviation industry enterprises paid almost UAH 27 billion in taxes and fees to the Ukrainian budget.
Under such circumstances, additional pressure creates risks of lost liquidity, reduced operations, and even the cessation of activities by individual air carriers.
To resolve the situation, they approached the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine, which, as the regulator, can put an end to differing interpretations of the legislation. The Ministry of Finance agreed to develop a general tax consultation (GTC) to resolve the issue. The Ukrainian Air Transport Association has now established a working group to prepare specific examples of the incorrect interpretation of leasing transactions and develop a draft general tax consultation, which it plans to submit to the ministry for consideration.
Eliminating the ambiguous interpretation of the legislation going forward will not fully resolve the problem. After all, the claims of the supervisory authorities cover previous tax periods. That is why representatives of the aviation industry insist on the need for a comprehensive settlement of the situation, which would not only prevent new disputes but also create legal grounds for resolving those that already exist.
The Ministry of Finance’s GTC may put an end to disputes over aircraft leasing
It is important to understand that a GTC does not establish new taxation rules, but explains how to correctly apply the provisions of the legislation that are already in force.
Pursuant to paragraph 52.6 of Article 52 of the Tax Code of Ukraine, the Ministry of Finance analyzes the circumstances indicating ambiguity in the application of certain provisions of legislation and approves generalized tax consultations. At the same time, the Procedure for Providing GTCs, approved by Order No. 811 of the Ministry of Finance dated September 27, 2017, expressly stipulates that such consultations "are not regulatory legal acts".
This is a fundamental legal distinction. A regulatory legal act may establish new rules of conduct and change the rights and obligations of participants in legal relations. A GTC, by contrast, merely explains the procedure for applying legislative provisions that already exist; it does not create new tax rules.
It is precisely this feature that creates the legal grounds for taking the conclusions of a GTC into account when considering disputes that arose before its approval.
Why a GTC may be applied to existing tax disputes
The issue of applying a GTC to previous tax periods is directly related to its legal nature.
Since a GTC is not a regulatory legal act, rules concerning the entry into force of new legislative provisions cannot be applied to it mechanically. It does not change the legal framework but clarifies the meaning of provisions that were previously in effect.
Therefore, if the Ministry of Finance determines the correct procedure for applying a provision of the Tax Code that has remained unchanged for many years, the relevant clarification may be used to assess transactions carried out during that period.
At the same time, it should be taken into account that a GTC does not have automatic retroactive effect. However, its conclusions may be used as an argument in existing disputes if they concern the same legislative provisions that were in effect at the time the relevant transactions were carried out.
Otherwise, a legal contradiction arises, because identical transactions carried out under unchanged legislation receive different tax classifications solely depending on when the Ministry of Finance published its clarification.
This is particularly significant in the case of aviation leasing, since tax claims against airlines concern past periods.
If a future GTC confirms a particular procedure for taxing lease payments on the basis of provisions that were in effect for decades, its conclusions should be taken into account when considering the relevant disputes.
The Ministry of Finance has already used GTCs to eliminate contradictions concerning provisions in force
The practice of the Ministry of Finance shows that generalized tax consultations have repeatedly been used to resolve ambiguities that had already arisen in the application of legislation.
In particular, by Order No. 22 dated January 19, 2021, the Ministry of Finance approved a GTC on the application of certain provisions of the Tax Code to financial institutions and companies engaged exclusively in leasing activities.
The purpose of the consultation was to eliminate differing interpretations of the relevant provisions of tax legislation. In other words, the Ministry of Finance clarified provisions that were already in effect and being applied in practice, rather than establishing new taxation rules.
Another example is Order No. 673 of the Ministry of Finance dated August 3, 2018, by which four generalized tax consultations on VAT matters were approved. They concerned, in particular, the taxation of transactions of permanent establishments of non-residents, documentary confirmation of the destruction of fixed assets, and the transfer of property under a financial lease. The Ministry of Finance established a unified approach to applying the provisions in force instead of the contradictory clarifications previously issued.
A similar mechanism was used in Order No. 7 of the Ministry of Finance dated January 12, 2022, concerning certain issues related to the registration of taxpayers. The basis for preparing the consultation was ambiguity in the application of legislation, amendments to which had been adopted as early as 2014 and which created preconditions for tax disputes.
The examples cited confirm that the Ministry of Finance has a practice of resolving contradictions in the application of current legislation without amending the Tax Code itself. These decisions demonstrate the possibility of reviewing the approaches of the controlling authorities to legal relations that already existed at the time these consultations were approved.
For Ukrainian airlines, it is fundamentally important that the future general tax consultation not be limited to determining the procedure for taxing lease payments going forward. In that case, it would prevent new disputes from arising, but would not resolve the problem of tax assessments already made or criminal proceedings already opened.
Undoubtedly, the GTC itself does not cancel tax notices-decisions or terminate investigations into criminal proceedings. However, it will be a significant legal argument during the administrative or judicial appeal of additional tax assessments, as well as when assessing the validity of claims by law enforcement authorities. This is particularly so if the Ministry of Finance expressly determines that the approach set out in the consultation follows from the provisions of the Tax Code and international treaties that were in force during previous tax periods as well.
It is also important that the consultation contain a clear position on the application of Ukraine’s international treaties on the avoidance of double taxation. Representatives of the aviation industry emphasize that only a comprehensive solution to the problem will restore legal certainty for Ukrainian airlines, reduce the risks of further tax claims, and create conditions for preserving an industry that continues to operate and contribute to the state budget despite the war and the closure of Ukraine’s airspace.

UN commission finds Russia’s grid strikes are crimes against humanity, citing last winter at minus 21°C. Now they’re intensifying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:21:20 UTC
21:21:20 KST

Russian authorities committed war crimes and crimes against humanity through attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine said in a report to the UN General Assembly on 26 October.
International Criminal Court (ICC) warrants for former Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu and Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov, issued in June 2024, already covered alleged crimes linked to Russia’s 2022–2023 strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The UN commission’s new report reaches into last winter, 2025–2026, and the cumulative toll since 2022, documenting what the attacks did to civilians living through outages in freezing temperatures.
“As the cold season approaches, the attacks have intensified once again, raising serious concerns about the threats to civilians’ lives and health,” commission chair Erik Møse said.
Russian commanders knew heating facilities were vital
The commission said Russian commanders knew that heating facilities in large cities were indispensable to civilians, particularly during winter. Russian authorities also made official declarations about further attacks and referred to a plan to carry them out, it said. It found that Russian authorities intentionally directed attacks against civilian objects, constituting war crimes.
The commission also concluded that the attacks were carried out under a state policy aimed at depriving civilians of electricity and other essential energy-dependent services and causing suffering. It classified these acts as crimes against humanity in the form of “other inhumane acts.”
Minus 21°C, weeks without heat, and shelters out of reach for older people
Last winter, temperatures fell to minus 21°C as millions of Ukrainians endured prolonged disruptions to heating, electricity, water, and gas, the commission said.
The commission relied on the accounts of 255 people from Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr Oblasts, alongside officials, doctors, and nongovernmental organizations.
Older people and those with limited mobility were particularly affected. Fear of becoming trapped in elevators during blackouts prevented some residents from reaching shelters during air raid alerts. They remained in unheated homes, sometimes without access to life-support equipment.
A 53-year-old Kyiv resident told investigators he tried to stay awake at night because he feared he might not wake up if he fell asleep in the cold.
Meanwhile, school closures disrupted children’s education, and children fell ill in unheated homes, the report said.
Russia rejects the findings
Russia’s UN mission said Moscow did not recognize the commission’s mandate and dismissed its findings as “falsified data,” the Associated Press reported.
The commission also examined Ukrainian attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and Russian-occupied Ukraine. It said it could not investigate their impact fully because Russia denied access and did not respond to its requests.
Foreign recruits trafficked to the front
The same report found “compelling evidence” that Russian authorities trafficked men from 29 countries into the Russian armed forces through deception and coercion.
Recruitment agents arranged visas and travel, presenting themselves as legitimate businesses. After arriving in Russia, the men were forced to sign military contracts in Russian and were sent to the front, where many were killed or went missing, the commission said.

Frozen housing market sends remodelers mixed messages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:20:59 UTC
21:20:59 KST

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
Home remodelers have always served two different markets, but the current state of housing is now pulling them opposite directions. First, people tend to remodel when they move, but high interest rates, high home prices and weak consumer sentiment have put the housing market in a deep freeze. Homeowners also tend to renovate when they are unable or don't want to sell. So which way will the remodeling market shift?
Annual spending on home improvements and repairs is expected to remain relatively flat through late 2027, according to the latest Leading Indicator of Remodeling Activity (LIRA) from the Remodeling Futures Program at the Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University. It puts spending growth on renovation and repairs at just 1.5% year-over-year by the third quarter.
"Retail spending on building products has been flat to negative, and remodeling permits have stagnated, which points to continued sluggish renovation activity," said Rachel Bogardus Drew, director of the remodeling futures program at the Center, in a release. "We expect annual spending to hover around $525 billion through the third quarter of next year."
The U.S. Census Bureau's monthly read on single-family housing starts for September came in well below expectations, as did building permits, an indicator of future construction. Pending home sales, measured by signed contracts, also plunged beyond expectations, according to the National Association of Realtors.
"These ongoing headwinds could slow growth in remodeling spending even further in the quarters ahead," said Chris Herbert, managing director of the center in the release.
A separate October report from the National Association of Home Builders on sentiment among home remodelers was slightly more positive, but also did not forecast big growth in 2027.
"Remodeler sentiment remained stable in the third quarter, although remodelers in certain parts of the country continue to report issues with high material costs and finding enough labor to finish projects on time," said Elliott Pike, national chair of the NAHB remodelers council and a remodeler from Homewood, Alabama. "Remodelers also report that economic uncertainty is making some potential customers hesitant to move forward with projects."
Finally, another October report from Houzz, an AI platform for construction and design professionals and homeowners, showed an improved outlook, with some caveats.
"Construction pros are closing out 2026 with optimism, as expectations reach their highest level since early 2022 following a rebound from a long stretch of slow activity. Design firms are more measured, though cautiously optimistic," said Marine Sargsyan, head of economic research at Houzz. "Fuel costs remain a pressure point for most businesses, with some pros passing them on to clients through higher prices and surcharges and others absorbing them in their margins."

Iranian strait authority says Sinokor vessels will face legal action
DUBAI, Oct 27 - Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a body set up by Tehran to manage passage requests in the Strait of Hormuz, said on Tuesday all vessels belonging to South Korean shipping company Sinokor would face "legal action" starting on November 1.
Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the strategic waterway by attacking shipping there since US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28. It has restricted transit to try to gain leverage over Washington, while disrupting oil flows from Arab Gulf oil producers, especially to their customers in Asia.

Sinokor did not immediately comment on the authority's statement.
Ships owned by Sinokor were previously included on a list issued by Iran in August of 45 tankers that it said had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
In response to Iranian attacks, the United States also imposed a naval blockade against ships linked to the Islamic Republic in the strait.
While the blockade has all but choked off Iranian exports, Gulf producers have adapted to attacks on shipping by relying on so-called dark transits — switching off tankers' tracking systems to evade detection — to protect the oil flows that underpin their economies. REUTERS

Christopher Moseley, champion of Estonian literature in English, dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:19:00 UTC
21:19:00 KST

Christopher Moseley, champion of Estonian literature in English, dies
Christopher Moseley, the Australian-born translator and language teacher who devoted his career to bringing Estonian, Latvian and Nordic literature to English-language readers, has died. He was 76.
Moseley was born in Australia and came to Britain in 1974 to study Scandinavian languages, but his interests soon moved somewhat eastwards to Finland and the Baltic states, even while the latter countries were still shackled under the Soviet occuption.
He studied Finno-Ugric languages in Finland and the UK, and his fieldwork on Livonian between 1987 and 1993 was his first direct work with a minority language. It led to his Master's thesis at the School of Slavonic and East European Studies (SSEES), part of the University College London (UCL), and later to his book Livonian (2002).
He also authored the Estonian language installment of British publisher Routledge's "Colloquial" range, and co-authored its Latvian course too.
For many years he taught Estonian language and Baltic literature at SSEES and UCL, along with evening courses in Estonian and Latvian. He also worked as a translator and journalist specializing in Baltic affairs at BBC Monitoring for nearly two decades, before becoming a freelance translator and editor.
Moseley's own translations from Estonian into English included A.H. Tammsaare's classic "Põrgupõhja uus Vanapagan", Andrus Kivirähk's "The Man Who Spoke Snakish", Indrek Hargla's "Apothecary Melchior" series, and Ilmar Taska's "Pobeda 1946". His final translation, Rein Raud's "The Sun Script", was published by Norvik Press just this year.
From 2008 Moseley was General Editor of UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger, which became a key reference for the world's threatened languages. He was also a dedicated member of the Foundation for Endangered Languages.
In 2018, he was one of the speakers at the opening of the University of Latvia's Livonian Institute.
The Estonian Literature Center remembered Chris as a warm and friendly person with unceasing passion for languages and literature.

Safran to Produce 2,000 AASM Hammer Bombs Annually
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:18:31 UTC
21:18:31 KST

French company Safran plans to double its defense production between 2025 and 2030, focusing on increasing production of AASM Hammer guided bombs and engines for SCALP/Storm Shadow cruise missiles.
According to La Tribune, Safran plans seven projects by 2028 to expand production capacity. These include building new factories and expanding existing facilities across Europe and the United States.
Production of AASM Hammer guided bombs is set to increase significantly. In 2022, Safran produced 200 units per year. Output is expected to reach 1,400 units in 2026, with the company planning to produce up to 2,000 bombs annually from 2027.
Safran is also expanding its rocket engine production. The company has tripled output between 2022 and 2026 and aims to increase it tenfold by 2030.
Safran engines power SCALP/Storm Shadow cruise missiles, Exocet MM40 and NSM anti-ship missiles, as well as RBS-15 missiles and BQM jet-powered drones.
Over the past four years, production of optoelectronic missile seekers has increased sixfold, while output of Geonix inertial navigation systems has risen sevenfold.
Production of M88 turbofan engines for Rafale fighter jets is set to double between 2025 and 2029. Safran is also increasing production of engines for NH90, Tiger, H225M and H145M helicopters.
Safran is also expanding into the land-based weapons sector. A consortium formed by Safran and MBDA has been selected to develop the Thundart multiple-launch rocket system, designed to strike targets at ranges of up to 150 km.
The Thundart project provides for the delivery of 26 launchers and 300 munitions. In addition to meeting France’s domestic needs, the developers expect export demand from allied countries.
Safran is building a new factory in Germany that will specialize in the production of optoelectronic equipment and navigation systems.
In the United States, Safran plans to double its production capacity for small turbojet engines. A new assembly line forTR40 engines is scheduled to open in Texas by 2028. These engines power Norway’s Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship missiles.

Togo’s China Pivot: Building a Strategic Gateway to the Sahel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

As Togo’s President of the Council of Ministers Faure Gnassingbé concluded his eight-day visit to China on October 16, much of the geopolitical attention surrounding the deepening relationship between Lomé and Beijing naturally centered on China’s expanding commercial and strategic influence in West Africa. Yet an equally important question deserves attention: What does Togo stand to gain from its growing partnership with China?
For Togo – a relatively small coastal country with significant maritime assets and ambitions to become a regional economic hub – China offers opportunities that extend beyond conventional bilateral cooperation. Togo is seeking to leverage its geographic position, particularly the strategic Port of Lomé, to strengthen domestic development while expanding its commercial influence across West Africa, including the landlocked countries of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).
During the visit, both countries elevated their bilateral relations to a “China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era,” alongside agreements spanning agriculture, industry, infrastructure, finance, and security.
From Togo’s perspective, three strategic opportunities stand out: building domestic productive capacity, consolidating its position as a maritime gateway to the Sahel, and expanding financial and strategic optionality.
Moving Beyond Raw Commodity Exports
One of the most important opportunities for Togo lies in leveraging Chinese investments, technology, and market access to accelerate domestic industrialization. The composition of Togo’s exports to China illustrates the challenge. According to U.N. Comtrade data reported by Togo, the country exported approximately $18.1 million in merchandise to China in 2025, compared with $14.8 million in 2024. Leading products included sesame seeds, unwrought aluminum alloys, cocoa beans, copper scraps, and manganese ores.
These figures reveal an export relationship still heavily concentrated in primary commodities, metals, and limited processing activities. They also illustrate the considerable scope for Togo to capture economic value domestically. During this visit, Gnassingbé toured a smart farming park in Shaanxi, and the Third Institute of Oceanography in the coastal city of Xiamen. He further expressed that Togo will learn from China’s comprehensive production ecosystems as it pursues a sustainable blue economy.
The significance of these engagements becomes clearer when considered alongside Togo’s existing industrial ambitions. At the Adétikopé Industrial Platform, a major industrial and logistics zone near Lomé, Chinese manufacturer Vivace Group inaugurated a building-materials factory in April 2025 following an investment of about $13.6 million. The facility has a reported annual production capacity of 10,000 tonnes and is intended to supply Togo and neighboring markets.
These developments suggest that Chinese engagement could complement Togo’s efforts to establish a broader industrial production ecosystem rather than remain predominantly a channel for merchandise imports. China’s zero-tariff access arrangements for eligible African exports and the newly signed phytosanitary protocol for Togolese soybeans could further expand export opportunities.
Position Lomé as the Gateway to the AES
The second opportunity concerns Togo’s maritime geography and its potential to becomes an increasingly important commercial intermediary between China and the landlocked economies of the Sahel. The Port of Lomé is central to Togo’s development strategy. Its maritime facilities and the connections to inland transport corridors give the country a structural advantage in serving neighboring economies without direct access to the Atlantic Ocean. For the AES countries of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, reliable access to coastal infrastructure remains essential for international commerce, industrial supplies, and economic development.
Togo’s ambition is to convert this geographic advantage into a durable regional logistic position. During his China visit, Gnassingbé emphasized maritime security, technological capacity, and the need to capture greater economic value from port activities. He spoke highly of China’s record in terms of global maritime governance. The China–Togo joint declaration similarly identified port cooperation, logistics infrastructure, and the development of Lomé as a West African commercial gateway as areas for further engagement.
The timing is particularly significant because Togo and the AES have been pursuing closer customs and trade coordination to harmonize their customs and trade frameworks. Experts from the four nations met in Ouagadougou between October 12 and 14, while Gnassingbé was in China. Their objectives revolved around defining the interconnection of custom IT systems, the adoption of community regulations, and boosting capacity for customs administrations. The strategic benefits of these developments cause a multiplier effect especially in coordination with China.
For Togo, the benefits could extend beyond port traffic to include warehousing, freight services, customs administration, logistics employment, industrial distribution, and greater regional diplomatic influence.
However, Togo must compete with alternative coastal corridors through Benin, Ghana, and Côte d’Ivoire. Its advantage will ultimately depend on transport costs, customs efficiency, infrastructure reliability, and the security of inland routes. This is where Togo’s relationship with China could become strategically consequential. Chinese capabilities in logistics infrastructure, industrial system, and transport technology could complement domestic and regional investments, helping Togo strengthen its competitiveness as a gateway economy.
Diversifying Togo’s Strategic and Economic Partnerships
The third opportunity concerns Togo’s ability to use its relations with China to diversify development financing, strengthen financial connectivity, and expand its room for strategic maneuver. Chinese financing has already played a role in Togo’s infrastructure development.
Research on China’s overseas lending estimated that Togo’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors reached approximately $740 million in 2021. This figure demonstrates the scale of earlier financing relationships, although it does not represent Togo’s current outstanding obligations. During Gnassingbé’s visit, the Togolese government also announced an agreement providing partial cancellation of debt owed to China.
Beyond conventional lending, the most significant new development concerns financial infrastructure. On October 10, the pan-African banking group Ecobank, headquartered in Lomé, signed a memorandum of understanding with China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to strengthen renminbi-denominated payment connectivity between China and African markets. With operations across 34 African countries, Ecobank provides a potentially important institutional bridge between Chinese financial infrastructure and African commercial networks.
Gnassingbé reaffirmed Togo’s support for the One China principle, and both leaders spoke on the importance of connecting immediate security conditions to long-term development planning. The wider implications of these connections were expressed in the joint declaration on October 15 where Gnassingbé and Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivered five main points as the foundation of the China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era. First was to undertake joint contribution towards the promotion of an orderly and equal multipolar world. Second was to work together to implement the Global Development Initiative. Third was to implement the Global Security Initiative. Fourth was to collaborate toward implementing the World Civilization Initiative and finally, to establish the Global Governance Initiative.
By maintaining economic connectivity with the landlocked Sahel while deepening its engagement with China, Togo is positioning itself as an increasingly important intermediary in the region’s evolving economic architecture. However, the success of this strategy will ultimately depend on Togo’s ability to convert diplomatic agreements into financed projects, domestic technical capabilities, efficient institutions and productive economic activity.

Jordan acknowledges civilian casualties in Syria airstrike
October 27, 2026
The Jordanian government admitted on Tuesday that a number of civilians had been killed in airstrikes conducted against so-called "Islamic State" militants in southern Syria on Monday night.
The Jordanian air force carried out the strikes on "terrorist groups" in the region in retaliation for last week's attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan in that killed nine people, adding the strikes killed more than 20 IS fighters.
However, Syrian authorities contradicted the claim, saying the strikes in the Daraa and Sweida provinces had killed seven people including three children and a woman. Two men who were killed were reportedly elderly.
One resident, Masoud al-Salim, said he lost his wife, son and three grandchildren in one of the strikes that hit his home in the Syrian border village of Al-Tuff.
"I came running and found there was no house anymore, no tent, nothing. I couldn't find anyone," he told the Associated Press, which said he was rummaging through children's schoolbooks and toys in the rubble.
"I started looking under the rubble. I thought they might be buried there."
Jordan admits civilians killed
On Tuesday, Jordanian Communications Minister Mohammed al-Momani acknowledged the civilian casualties, which he said the Hashemite Kingdom regretted.
"Jordan always takes all precautions to avoid harming civilians," he said in a post on social media, insisting: "The operations were carried out based on field intelligence to neutralize confirmed threats and terrorist operations against Jordan."
He said the Jordanian air force had inflicted "heavy losses in IS ranks, estimated at more than 20 elements" and destroyed a "massive weapons depot belonging to the organization."
"Jordan refrained from targeting sites where intelligence indicated the presence of civilians and regrets the occurrence of civilian casualties," he added.
Syria condemns 'violation'
Monday's operation sparked anger in Syria, where the Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as an "unacceptable violation [of] and encroachment [into]" Syrian airspace.
While the Jordanian military claimed the strikes were conducted in coordination with Damascus, the Syrian government said they were carried out without prior coordination and announced an investigation.
Jordan and Syria maintained strong bilateral ties following the downfall of the Assad dynasty in December 2024 and the emergence of interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa's Islamist-led government.
Despite Monday's airstrike, Syria asserted that that both countries' leaderships will strengthen security coordination to "obstruct any efforts to destabilize the two countries' security and spill the blood of its people."
No group has claimed responsibility for the initial attack on the Greek Orthodox funeral in Jordan, but Jordanian security forces arrested three men – two brothers and their in-law – following a shootout earlier on Monday.

Syria defends textbook changes erasing women and democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:14:41 UTC
21:14:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria defends textbook changes erasing women and democracy
Syria's education ministry has defended controversial revisions to school textbooks that include covering up female figures, removing historical artworks and deleting lessons on democracy and political participation.
The changes, independently verified by Syrian fact-checkers, have provoked criticism from educators and women's rights advocates, who fear the country's new authorities are imposing an increasingly conservative ideological vision on its education system.
In a statement on Monday, the Ministry of Education insisted that revisions made since the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 were limited to a single round of changes announced in January 2025, intended primarily to remove symbols and ideological material associated with the former regime.
The ministry said its reforms were designed to protect Syria's social and religious diversity, promote citizenship and encourage respect for others, dismissing some of the information circulating online as inaccurate.
However, the independent Syrian fact-checking organisation Ta'akkad said the statement did not address the specific alterations it had verified, including the removal of lessons concerning democratic participation and changes to depictions of women.
Ta'akkad also found that one of the illustrations published by the ministry to demonstrate diversity was itself a revised image previously identified by investigators.
Women covered up, historical artworks removed
The controversy erupted after Syrian journalist Mohammed al-Salloum published comparisons between older editions of school textbooks and versions distributed to pupils for the 2026–2027 academic year.
Ta'akkad examined digital and printed copies of the books and confirmed that female characters had been removed from some illustrations, while others had been altered to include hijabs or more conservative clothing.
In one first-grade textbook, an illustration of a female doctor was modified to include a hijab, although the same character appeared without one elsewhere in the book.
Other changes included replacing illustrations of women and girls, modifying depictions of historical figures and removing artwork.
An image of an ancient Egyptian statue was altered to cover its exposed torso with a striped shirt, while illustrations of ancient sculptures associated with the civilisations of Mari and Ugarit were removed.
A depiction of Elissa, the legendary Phoenician founder of Carthage, was also altered to cover her neck and chin.
The changes extended beyond illustrations.
A sixth-grade social studies textbook originally published during the Assad era was reissued without several lessons addressing local government, political life, citizenship, the media and democratic participation. Content glorifying the former regime was also removed.
Ministry insists changes reflect Syrian values
Ismat Ramadan, director of Syria's National Centre for Curriculum Development, told The New Arab that the previous textbooks had been shaped by Baathist ideology and that the new authorities were seeking to rebuild the country's educational identity.
He acknowledged that images had been altered, but argued that the changes were intended to reflect Syria's cultural and religious diversity.
Ramadan said the curriculum should also respect the values of the majority of Syrian society, including parents' wishes that younger children not be exposed to material they considered inappropriate, such as nude statues.
He argued that removing a particular illustration did not necessarily mean removing knowledge of the historical period it represented.
However, critics say the changes risk replacing the ideological restrictions of the Assad era with new forms of exclusion.
Aswan Nahar, director of the Syrian educational organisation Roya for Change, told TNA that the problem was not the inclusion of women wearing hijabs, but the exclusion of other representations of women.
She argued that textbooks should reflect the full diversity of Syrian society and allow girls to see women occupying different roles.
Nahar also warned that deleting lessons on citizenship, local administration and democratic participation could deprive children of important opportunities to understand their rights and responsibilities.
Educationalist Abdullah al-Shahrour similarly criticised the alterations to historical artwork, warning that concealing sculptures and depictions of the human body risked presenting art and history as something shameful.
The Syrian Feminist Lobby has called for the revisions to be reviewed with the participation of educators, specialists and civil society representatives, to ensure that school curricula respect equality, social diversity, human rights and democratic values.
Syria's Education Ministry announced in August that a unified curriculum would be adopted across the country's provinces for the 2026–2027 academic year, with further work underway on new national educational standards.
The controversy has revived questions about the direction of education under Syria's post-Assad leadership, particularly whether reforms intended to remove decades of authoritarian propaganda will also preserve the country's cultural and political diversity.
