====================================================================================================

CEC Justice Sohlberg bars UTJ from reporting voter numbers in real time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:10:52 UTC
21:10:52 KST

Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg issued a temporary order on Tuesday barring United Torah Judaism and its representatives at polling stations from reporting voter turnout figures, prompting the Movement for Quality Government to demand immediate police enforcement nationwide.
The order prohibits reporting the number of people who have voted at a polling station either in real time or through periodic updates. Issued following a petition by the movement, it required UTJ to respond by 2:15 p.m.
In its response, UTJ said it was complying with the High Court’s rulings and was not transmitting information from polling stations. It said it had instructed all its polling-station representatives at 9:27 a.m. not to report voter numbers by any means, before Sohlberg issued Tuesday’s order.
The party said it had initially understood the October 22 ruling to prohibit only digital reporting and had prepared to transmit figures by other means. It claimed it learned on Tuesday morning of a subsequent decision prohibiting transmission by any means, and issued the instructions after obtaining that decision from the elections committee.
UTJ asked Sohlberg to dismiss the petition and award costs, arguing that MQG could have established its compliance by contacting it before filing.
The intervention brings to Election Day a dispute that has moved through the elections committee and the High Court of Justice since August: whether representatives stationed inside polling stations to administer and supervise voting may pass information obtained there to their parties for campaigning.
The petition followed a report by Channel 13 journalist Yoeli Brim and forms obtained by MQG. The outlet reported that the forms instructed UTJ polling-station representatives to record voter numbers and report them by telephone to a Degel Hatorah system from outside the polling room.
In its subsequent letter to Police Commissioner Daniel Levy, senior police officials and Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara, MQG said the order had been issued at 1:08 p.m. and requested enforcement “immediately and without delay” at polling stations throughout the country.
It also asked police to investigate suspected violations where necessary, collect testimony, identify those involved, and gather and preserve evidence.
Movement for Quality Government urges immediate enforcement of court rulings on Election Day
“The High Court’s decisions and the election committee chairman’s order are binding, and on Election Day there is no time to wait,” said Jacqueline Bracha, an attorney in MQG’s economic department.
“We expect the police to enforce the order issued today at all polling stations immediately, so that voters can vote without fear and without party representatives tracking voter numbers in real time.”
The dispute initially concerned reports identifying individual voters who had cast ballots. Systems such as Elector allowed campaigns to compare that information with their databases and contact likely supporters who had not yet voted. The information revealed whether someone voted, not how they voted.
Sohlberg prohibited the practice in August, finding that information available to polling-station officials for election administration could not be transferred for party campaigning without legal authorization. He also provided for the committee to release aggregate turnout figures, giving parties information about participation without identifying individual voters.
Likud challenge leads elections committee to permit identified reporting under restrictions
Likud challenged the prohibition, including Sohlberg’s authority to impose it alone. Under an arrangement approved by the High Court, the issue went before the full elections committee, which voted on September 6 to permit identified reporting subject to restrictions.
On September 17, the High Court unanimously overturned that permission. Justices Yael Willner, Alex Stein and Khaled Kabub held that polling-station representatives perform public functions and lack legal authority to transfer identifiable voter information to their parties for campaign purposes. The court also found that the practice violated voters’ privacy. Parties remained free to contact voters and encourage participation using information they could lawfully use.
The next dispute concerned whether representatives could report numerical totals without identifying anyone.
In an October 14 clarification following a request from Likud attorney Ilan Bombach, acting committee director-general Dean Livne permitted polling committee members and party observers to digitally count voters and transmit those numbers to their parties, provided they did not identify the voters.
Israel Democracy Guard challenges legality of collecting and transmitting voter information
The Israel Democracy Guard organization challenged that permission. Its argument was that removing names did not resolve the separate question of whether officials inside polling stations were authorized to collect and transmit information for party headquarters.
The state and Likud defended the distinction between numerical reporting and identifying individual voters, arguing that turnout figures could help parties encourage participation.
On October 22, the High Court rejected the permission in a two-to-one decision, with Kabub and Justice Ruth Ronnen in the majority and Justice David Mintz dissenting. That ruling barred digital counting and real-time transmission of voter totals by party representatives serving on polling committees or as observers.
Tuesday’s order specifically addresses UTJ and its representatives, expressly prohibiting periodic reports and real-time updates.

Singapore, a major refining hub in the Southeast Asian region, accounted for half of Indonesia’s gasoline needs and supplied 28.36% of its oil and gas imports in the first half of 2026. However, Indonesia slashed its piped gas exports to the city state last week, days after Jakarta slammed neighboring countries that had complained about haze from intense forest fires on its territory.
The cuts have led to tensions between the two countries. Singapore depends on imported natural gas for about 95% of its electricity generation. The city state has not resorted to any retaliatory action, but its foreign minister is visiting Indonesia on Tuesday.
Jakarta is also facing severe fuel supply disruptions across its provinces, due to surging demand and distribution bottlenecks, apart from geopolitical uncertainties, Reuters reported.
Indonesia is not the first country to look toward India for its fuel needs amid the global oil crunch. Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio termed India a “refining superpower” as Washington sought to tap New Delhi’s oil refining capabilities to cool global fuel prices.
Indian refineries, especially the Jamnagar refinery complex owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, are configured to process both Russian and Venezuelan heavy crude. The latter, especially, is considered key to lowering global fuel diesel prices, as it yields a higher volume of the fuel.

China Focus: Chinese research institutes, enterprises co-innovate from lab to factory
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:08:43 CST
21:08:43 KST

Huang Xiaohua, who is in charge of the Industrial Development Center at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, introduces the technology achievement supermarket in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Yu Fei)
SHENZHEN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- At a special supermarket in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province in south China, shelves are stocked not with fruits or vegetables, but cards featuring cutting-edge scientific achievements and top research talent.
The cards at the supermarket in the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology (SIAT) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences represent more than 1,000 frontier achievements arranged by track, covering medical equipment and scientific instruments, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, advanced electronics and energy materials, and synthetic biology.
Every card carries a unique QR code, which helps entrepreneurs gain access to the technology's highlights, application scenarios, potential collaboration directions, together with the developer's contact information. If something catches their eye, they can connect directly, with no more wading through thick archives of research files.
In the past, researchers' achievements often lay dormant in academic papers and patent offices, while companies desperate for new technologies had nowhere to turn. Today, with the results stocked on supermarket shelves, complex academic papers are transformed into "visual products" that companies can grasp at a glance. Supply and demand finally meet face to face, and the commercialization of research achievements is put on the fast track.
The supermarket's entire inventory comes from the SIAT's 10 research divisions. Over the past five years, SIAT has produced an average of 6.6 patents per day, with new achievements hitting the shelves every month.
FROM LAB TO PRODUCTION
The supermarket is re-imagining the way scientific and technological achievements are commercialized: connecting frontier laboratory technologies precisely with industrial needs, so that more research results can travel from the lab bench to the production line more efficiently.
Huang Xiaohua, who is in charge of the Industrial Development Center at SIAT, said: "Through this matching platform, companies find technologies of interest, and technologies are directly exposed to real corporate needs."
Jiangsu Apon Medical Technology Co., Ltd., which has been deeply engaged in the brain-computer interface field for many years, is a "treasure seeker." The company urgently needed new technological breakthroughs in the neural regulation domain, particularly in non-invasive deep brain stimulation. The platform helped connect the company's technological request with relevant research from SIAT.
In 2025, the company precisely matched with SIAT's non-invasive brain regulation technology, and the two sides quickly reached a consensus, establishing a "brain-computer interface" innovation consortium in early 2026 to jointly tackle temporal interference stimulation technology, exploring diagnostics and treatments for epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and emotional brain disorders.
Since opening in February 2025, the supermarket has facilitated the commercialization of research achievements worth more than 200 million yuan (about 30 million U.S. dollars). In 2025, the SIAT's average achievement conversion rate exceeded 29 percent, and the success rate of technology matchmaking through the supermarket has risen by more than 10 percent, according to Huang.
The achievement supermarket has expanded beyond Shenzhen, taking root across China in cities including Zhuhai, Jiangmen, Ningde, Wenzhou and Wuhan.
INTEGRATED INNOVATION
The supermarket model is a vivid snapshot of the growing integrated innovation between Chinese research institutions and enterprises in recent years. Companies have moved beyond simply buying technologies to co-developing them with scientists, unleashing a stronger combined force for innovation.
Carbon dioxide emitted from industrial processes used to be taken as waste gas in many people's eyes. But as a result of the cooperation between SIAT and China Merchants Group, it has become a treasure.
The two sides have jointly developed a remarkable technological pathway: electrocatalytic processes powered by renewable electricity convert carbon dioxide into organic carbon feedstocks, which are then used in fermentation to sustainably produce flavors and fragrances, protein feed, bulk chemicals and other products, supporting food security and China's dual carbon goals of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060.
A joint laboratory for green conversion of carbon dioxide and biorefining has been established by the two sides, with cooperation funding approaching 100 million yuan. A 100-tonne-scale demonstration facility has already been commissioned, and a 1,000-tonne-scale platform has completed design verification.
The SIAT has also teamed up with China Nuclear Power Engineering Co., Ltd. to conduct research on and apply multimodal human-machine interaction systems for nuclear power plants, developing solutions oriented toward human-machine interaction needs in plant operations to reduce operator workload.
Cooperation with the Shenzhen Research Institute of the China National Coal Group Corporation focuses on another key technical frontier. The two parties are jointly developing high-performance proton exchange membranes based on ordered subnanochannels. The technology holds huge potential for long-duration energy storage, with promising prospects for further expansion into semiconductor, biomedical and environmental applications.
SIAT's research team has also partnered with China Resources Mixc Lifestyle to bring AI into property inspections, service dispatching, on-site handling, and operational evaluation. The system has been deployed in more than 1,000 property projects, improving overall operational efficiency by 35 percent.
China has recently released a set of guidelines on promoting the deep integration of scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation.
Issued by the General Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council, the guidelines require efforts to deepen the implementation of the innovation-driven development strategy, with the goals of developing new quality productive forces and building a modern industrial system, and with a focus on establishing an enterprise-led, multi-stakeholder collaborative system for integrated industry-academia-research innovation, so as to form a new pattern in which sci-tech innovation and industrial innovation promote each other. ■

Sri Lanka to establish national committee to tackle wildlife threats to aviation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:08:36 CST
21:08:36 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- The Sri Lankan government approved on Tuesday the establishment of a national committee to address wildlife-related risks to aircraft operations, in line with international aviation safety requirements.
The National Wildlife Hazard Management Committee for Aviation Safety will coordinate efforts among relevant agencies to monitor and manage wildlife hazards at and around airports across the country.
The proposal, submitted by the minister of Ports and Civil Aviation, follows guidelines issued by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which recommend national-level coordination to reduce the risk of collisions between aircraft and wildlife.
As a signatory to the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation, Sri Lanka is required to maintain systems for recording and reporting wildlife strikes, identifying potential hazards and regularly assessing risks near airports.
These requirements also include submitting wildlife collision data to the ICAO's Bird Collision Information System and ensuring that risk assessments are conducted by qualified personnel.
The committee is expected to strengthen cooperation among government agencies and improve the monitoring, reporting and management of wildlife hazards affecting civil aviation. ■

EU cybersecurity revision could cost the Netherlands up to 2.2 bln euros in first year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:08:34 CST
21:08:34 KST

THE HAGUE, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A proposed revision of the European Union's Cybersecurity Act, known as CSA2, could lead to losses ranging from 290 million euros (324.02 million U.S. dollars) to 2.2 billion euros (2.46 billion dollars) for Dutch businesses in the first year of implementation, according to a report by SEO Amsterdam Economics.
The report, titled The Price of Security and commissioned by the Netherlands China Business Council (NCBC), cautions that the impact could extend beyond businesses directly affected by the restrictions, spreading through supply chains and hitting firms in other sectors of the Dutch economy.
The legislation was proposed by the European Commission at the beginning of this year. The draft introduced "non-technical risks" in the name of cybersecurity and supply chain security. In particular, the draft would identify "countries posing cybersecurity concerns" and "high-risk suppliers," and exclude listed countries and suppliers from relevant EU supply chains across 18 sectors, including energy, transport, and information and communications technology.
However, the economic implications of restricting suppliers could be substantial, particularly for businesses that rely on existing information and communications technology infrastructure and have limited short-term alternatives, according to the report.
Companies may also need to modify existing systems, adjust production processes and reorganize supply chains to accommodate replacement products. These changes could generate additional costs beyond the losses estimated in the report.
"Security measures do not exist in an economic vacuum," NCBC Chairman Jochum Haakma said at a seminar on the report on Monday, adding that restrictions on suppliers, changes in procurement policies and the replacement of existing ICT infrastructure can affect entire supply chains, investment decisions and ultimately the competitiveness of the European economy.
In a letter to parliament on June 19, Dutch Minister of Justice and Security David van Weel said the government was concerned about the European Commission's proposed power to designate entire countries and suppliers as high-risk, citing potentially far-reaching economic, legal and geopolitical consequences, as well as insufficiently clear and detailed criteria and procedures.
The report notes that restrictions on supplier choice could also yield other adverse consequences, as diminished competitive pressure may result in higher prices, lower quality and reduced innovation.
"Strategic autonomy is an important European ambition, but autonomy should not lead to isolation," Haakma noted. ■

Serbia releases preliminary results of parliamentary election
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:08:24 CST
21:08:24 KST

BELGRADE, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A list backed by student groups led Serbia's parliamentary election, projecting to win 140 seats, an outright majority in the 250-member parliament that would enable it to form a government independently, preliminary results showed Monday.
According to the interim tally released by the Republic Electoral Commission, the "Student List - Students Win" list came first with 52.71 percent of the vote, and the "Aleksandar Vucic - United Serbia" list, led by the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), came second with 39.17 percent and was projected to secure 104 seats.
The results showed that the two lists were the only ones not representing national minorities to cross the 3-percent threshold for parliamentary representation.
Meanwhile, four electoral lists representing national minority communities secured a total of six seats, the results showed.
Serbia held early parliamentary elections on Oct. 25, with 18 electoral lists featuring 2,418 candidates competing for the 250 seats in the National Assembly. About 6.45 million voters were registered for the election, with 8,392 polling stations set up across the country. The preliminary results covered 8,187 polling stations.
Under the Serbian constitution, the election of a new National Assembly will initiate the process of forming a new government. After lawmakers elect a new parliamentary speaker, the speaker, who is currently serving as acting president, will nominate a candidate for prime minister. The nominee must present a government program and a proposed list of cabinet members and secure the support of a majority of National Assembly deputies to form a new government.
On Sept. 5, Vucic, then president, accepted the nomination by the SNS to lead its parliamentary election list and run as its candidate for prime minister. He signed a decree dissolving parliament on Sept. 9 and called early parliamentary elections for Oct. 25.
Vucic resigned as president on Sept. 27, after which National Assembly Speaker Ana Brnabic assumed the duties of acting president.
Under Serbian law, a presidential election must be held by the end of December. ■

Interview: China plays crucial role in advancing Asia-Pacific free trade, says Malaysian scholar
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:08:23 CST
21:08:23 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- China is playing a crucial role in advancing the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) through sustaining regional growth and strengthening economic integration, according to a Malaysian scholar.
With its vast domestic market, extensive industrial networks and commitment to opening up, China is well positioned to play a constructive role in turning the long-standing vision of the FTAAP into practical cooperation, Ong Chong Yi, executive director of BRI Caucus for Asia Pacific (BRICAP), told Xinhua in a recent interview.
"The FTAAP has been discussed within the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) framework for two decades. Although progress toward a comprehensive agreement has remained limited, the institutional foundations for regional integration are now stronger than ever, " he said.
Ong noted that the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) have established two major, partly overlapping frameworks for trade liberalization in the region and that the FTAAP's central challenge is to reconcile high standards with broad participation.
"A successful framework must offer meaningful market access while ensuring that economies with different regulatory capacities can implement their commitments effectively. It must also generate tangible benefits for businesses, particularly micro, small and medium-sized enterprises," he said.
"This is where China can make an important contribution. China can help promote greater coordination between existing regional trade agreements. China can strengthen confidence in regional cooperation through continued unilateral opening up and domestic reform," he said.
Ong added that China, especially through its ASEAN partners, can help identify regulatory differences, develop workable solutions and facilitate cooperation among a wider group of APEC members and provide support by contributing market opportunities, technical expertise and capacity-building resources, while encouraging inclusive participation and the development needs of different economies.
"China's leadership can be most effective when it works alongside ASEAN members, other major regional economies and the business community to develop practical and inclusive solutions," he added.
"Priority areas should include customs procedures, electronic trade documentation, rules of origin, digital trade and mutual recognition of technical standards ... Genuine trade facilitation therefore requires not only technological connectivity but also legal recognition of electronic signatures, documents and authentication mechanisms," he explained.
"Similarly, differences in product testing, certification and carbon-accounting standards can impose substantial costs on businesses, even when tariffs have been reduced. Addressing these practical barriers would help transform regional integration from a policy aspiration into measurable economic benefits," he added.
Ong cited the Hainan Free Trade Port as an important example of how domestic institutional innovation can contribute to wider regional cooperation, adding that it could serve as a testing ground for regulatory cooperation involving China and regional partners such as Malaysia and Singapore.
"By comparing clearance times, compliance costs and business participation before and after implementation, policymakers could identify effective solutions and consider extending them to other sectors and economies...It can help translate that vision into practical results by supporting regulatory coordination, expanding market opportunities and working with regional partners on measurable reforms," he said. ■

The court further ordered that Wang be deprived of his political rights for life and that all his personal property be confiscated.
From 1998 to 2025, Wang took advantage of his official positions in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and at the CSRC to provide assistance to relevant units and individuals in matters such as business operations and fund-raising. In return, he illegally accepted money and property totaling more than 436 million yuan (about 64.88 million U.S. dollars), the verdict noted.
Wang's bribery amount was particularly huge, while his conduct caused especially significant losses to the interests of the state and the people, for which his crimes warranted the death penalty in principle, the court said.
However, Wang truthfully confessed his crimes after being taken into custody, voluntarily disclosed criminal facts not yet known to the investigators, admitted his guilt and showed remorse, while some of the bribery offenses were attempted rather than completed. Part of the bribes he received had been recovered. The court thus imposed a lenient sentence on him, the verdict explained.
The case was heard publicly by the court on July 17. During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence, while Wang and his defense counsel cross-examined the evidence and made their arguments. Wang made a final statement in court, pleading guilty and expressing remorse. ■

Asua worked with young players, helping them maintain family ties, continue their education and develop values such as respect and humility.

Simon also paid tribute to Athletic legend Jose Angel Iribar, widely regarded as the club's greatest goalkeeper, who remains an ambassador at the age of 83.

"I have learned to love the club's colors, its history and, above all, its fans, to whom I am eternally grateful. It is because of all of them that I am here today to receive this award, so thank you all very much," Simon concluded.
His remarks offered a reminder that, even at football's highest level, success can be measured by more than trophies and individual honors. ■

Ukraine says it hit drone hangars at Crimea’s Hvardiiske. Now an OSINT channel spots 20+ bermed shelters there
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:07:15 UTC
21:07:15 KST

Russia is expanding drone storage at the Hvardiiske military airfield in occupied Crimea, Ukrainian OSINT channel Dnipro Osint reported on 26 October, citing new satellite images. The channel did not say who took the images or when. Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said it struck drone hangars at the same airfield in July, and the military said strikes on 13 October damaged four drone storage sites nearby.
Hvardiiske has stayed in use since then. Ukraine’s General Staff has listed it among the sites Russia launched attack drones from in every daily report since 7 October. The airfield was on the list again on 24, 25, and 27 October, the night Russia aimed its main strike at Kyiv. The new construction, as the channel describes it, adds protected storage at a base Ukraine has already shown it can reach.
Shelters and “garages”
The images show more than 20 small shelters under construction, each protected by earth berms, the channel said. It also counted about 40 smaller structures it calls “garages.” It said they are meant for storing, servicing, and preparing Geran drones for launch.
Geran is the name Russia gives the Iranian-designed Shahed drones: the Shahed-136 became the Geran-2, which Russia now builds itself. The images show at least one hangar damaged by a Ukrainian drone hit, Dnipro Osint noted.
Launched from vehicles
Hvardiiske, north of Simferopol, uses mobile launch platforms instead of fixed installations, according to Dnipro Osint. Crews load drones onto specially equipped vehicles, which then launch them from the runway.
Struck repeatedly since June
On 24 June, the SBU said it hit infrastructure at Hvardiiske and at the Saky airbase. On 3 July, the SBU reported that its drones struck two hangars at Hvardiiske that stored Shaheds and aviation equipment. Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces struck the airfield again overnight on 5 July, and the SBU said a day later that it hit three hangars with aviation equipment there. A strike on 3 August destroyed nine aviation-fuel tanks and damaged two aircraft hangars, the General Staff said. Strikes on 13 October damaged four drone storage sites near Hvardiiske, with signs of secondary detonation, it reported two days later.
Not the only base Russia is building up
Hvardiiske is not the only Russian drone base Ukrainian OSINT channels have flagged this month. On 13 October, the anonymous channel Absolutely Reliable Source said Russia had nearly finished the first section of a launch site for jet-powered Geran-5 drones near Millerovo in Rostov Oblast, with eight launcher positions and 32 drone-preparation spots. Hvardiiske and Millerovo were both among the launch areas the General Staff listed for the night of 27 October, when Russia launched 280 Shahed-type drones, 69 of them jet-powered, with Kyiv as the main target.

China to license export of engines for Russian Geran drones
China has introduced export licensing for certain categories of drones, along with their components and technologies.
Source: Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, citing a clarification from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce
Details: Vlasiuk said the new rules will take effect on 18 November and will cover, among other things, the engines used in Russian Geran attack drones.
Quote: "Formally, the core of Russian long-range attack drones has fallen under control. This includes engines for Gerans, turbojet engines for jet-powered modifications, autopilots and jam-resistant navigation. However, whether anything will change in practice depends on how these rules are applied."
Details: Vlasiuk stressed that licensing does not equate to an export ban, adding that "general permits for up to three years are envisaged for 'reliable' exporters, alongside broad grounds for refusal".
At the same time, Vlasiuk noted that the new requirements largely do not apply to components for mass-produced frontline FPV drones.
"The new thresholds do not cover motors and speed controllers for FPVs, batteries, cameras or fibre optics. Production equipment is not covered either," he explained.
Vlasiuk described China's decision as an opportunity for Ukraine, since Beijing is officially taking responsibility for controlling specific categories of goods.
"We will demand that the new rules be applied to known suppliers of the Russian defence industry. Together with our partners, we will track licences, transit channels and re-exports," he stated.
Vlasiuk said the introduction of the new rules is big news and grounds for cautious optimism.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Russia had begun learning to produce Chinese Telefly TF-TJ2000A jet engines for the Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. They are assembled from Chinese kits at the Alabuga industrial facility.
- It was also reported that Russia is experiencing problems in procuring Chinese jet engines for drones. According to Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), this is the result of sanctions imposed by Ukraine and its partners.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said Tuesday that polling stations may remain open beyond the scheduled closing time of 10 p.m. (2000GMT) amid high voter turnout in the country’s general elections.
Dean Livne, acting director general of the committee, said polling stations would continue operating after the deadline if voters were still waiting in line, The Times of Israel news outlet reported.

Voting began at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) across Israel, with more than 7.3 million eligible voters choosing representatives for the 120-seat Knesset.
The Election Committee earlier reported that voter turnout had reached 31.5% by noon (1000 GMT), more than three percentage points higher than in the previous elections and the highest figure recorded at that hour since 1973.
Approximately 2.39 million voters had cast their ballots by noon, according to the committee.
The elections are Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

New homes but for whom? Syria's housing faces affordability test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:06:27 UTC
21:06:27 KST

Breadcrumb
New homes, but for whom? Syria's housing recovery faces an affordability test
Driving through Damascus, billboards for new residential developments offer a vision of the future: modern apartments, landscaped surroundings, and the promise of a fresh start.
But for Syrians navigating damaged homes, rising rents, and the cost of returning after years of displacement, the question is how much of that future they can actually afford.
In Qudsaya, west of the capital, Abyat Hills illustrates both the ambitions and the limits of Syria’s investment-led housing drive.
The development brings together Saudi company Abyat Investment and Real Estate Development and Syria’s General Housing Establishment, which operates under the Ministry of Public Works and Housing. Under the partnership, the state provides the land while Abyat develops the buildings and facilities.
Its published subscription contract sets first-phase prices at $950–$1,150 per square metre. On a simple 100-square-metre illustration, that amounts to somewhere between $95,000–$115,000.
These prices are not unprecedented within Damascus’s property market. Listings published by local agency Elmas include a 150-square-metre apartment in Mashrou Dummar, just south of Qudsaya, advertised at $300,000 and a 180-square-metre property in the southwestern neighbourhood of Kafr Souseh at $450,000.
But the relevant comparison for many Syrians is not with another expensive neighbourhood. It is with what they earn.
The European Union Agency for Asylum’s July country report cited February figures putting average monthly wages at roughly $102 for entry-level public-sector employees and $120 in the private sector, indicating the scale of the gulf between locally earned income and the capital required to enter such developments.
"A housing development may attract substantial investment while its residential units remain beyond the financial reach of families who lost their homes, jobs, and savings during the conflict," Fadel Abdulghany, founder and director of the Syrian Network for Human Rights, told The New Arab.
"If public reconstruction policies fail to take these families’ needs into account, urban development may expand without contributing sufficiently to the conditions necessary for displaced people to return sustainably."
Investment promises, everyday pressures
The affordability question has become more politically visible as households confront rising living costs.
In September, a government decision to raise diesel prices by 40 percent and petrol prices by approximately 26–28 percent triggered protests and roadblocks across Syria. Demonstrators burned tyres, blocked major routes, and demanded the increases be reversed.
The government subsequently announced cheaper diesel categories for heating, agriculture, and some productive sectors, while leaving the standard diesel price and the higher petrol and gas prices in place.
The fuel protests essentially exposed the economic pressures against which promises of recovery and foreign investment are being judged: whether households can afford transport, heating, and daily necessities, rather than simply whether new projects attract buyers.
For many displaced Syrians, the immediate challenge is even more dire - not about purchasing a new apartment but making their existing home habitable.
Liban Abdullahi Jimale, housing, land and property advisor for the Norwegian Refugee Council in Syria, said families frequently tell the organisation that they want to return but cannot afford repairs.
"The choice is often stark," he told The New Arab.
Some live in damaged properties, pitch tents nearby or repair a single room. Others go back to displacement camps or sites because they offer better shelter than what remains at home.
Renting can also be precarious. According to a sector assessment cited by NRC, rents rose in 84 percent of assessed communities in rural Damascus, with the increases attributed mainly to returns.
NRC’s legal-needs assessment found that only 48 percent of surveyed returnee households reported owning or renting a dwelling, compared with 70 percent across the surveyed population. Around one in five renting returnee households faced eviction risk, mostly because of unpaid rent.
These figures therefore illustrate why increasing the number of apartments does not automatically give displaced families somewhere secure to live.
Whose land, whose recovery?
At Abyat Hills, questions about access to housing have been accompanied by another dispute: the rights of people claiming an interest in the land beneath it.
On 26 September, residents from Qudsaya and other rural Damascus communities protested over expropriation, compensation, and ownership claims concerning land allocated to developments. Some told state news agency SANA that they had received no compensation; others said historical payments were inadequate.
The governorate subsequently opened an office to receive claims concerning land within Abyat Hills and Sham View. The ministry said most contested expropriation decisions dated back decades and that each property’s status had to be established through land records and compensation documents.
It also argued that public housing projects could include commercial components and private partners. Abyat maintained that its work was lawful and that government bodies and courts should settle ownership disputes.
Similar tensions surfaced in Homs, where residents protested over expropriated land they associated with the Boulevard project. The city council said the properties had entered public ownership through legal procedures and were designated as a park under an older approved plan; residents sought a review of the records and compensation arrangements.
For Abdulghany, the danger is that redevelopment can make unresolved claims harder to remedy.
"The greatest risk is that reconstruction projects may consolidate the consequences of past property seizures, making them increasingly difficult to remedy or reverse," he told The New Arab.
Once disputed land is transferred, built on, used as collateral or sold to new purchasers, additional interests and financial obligations can emerge. Recovering an original property may become more complicated even where an earlier claim has a sound legal basis.
More than a new apartment
Abyat Hills’ contract includes measures presented as supporting residential use rather than speculation: one subscription per family, restrictions on transferring subscriptions and controls on resale. It states that the homes are intended for Syrian families. But these provisions do not themselves bridge the gap between a household’s income and the money required to buy.
Nor does building an apartment resolve the documentation problems that can prevent a family from reclaiming a different home.
Abdulghany said lost records, incomplete registration, inheritance disputes, and properties registered in the names of detained or disappeared people continue to obstruct recovery.
"The fundamental distinction is between the legal recognition of rights and enabling rights holders to recover and exercise them in practice," he said.
Families of missing people face a particularly difficult bind when a property remains registered in their relative’s name. Abdulghany said Syrian law allows them to seek a judicial representative without first obtaining a declaration of death, but the representative’s limited powers mean significant property transactions or some legal proceedings may require further court approval.
Women face additional barriers. Abdulghany said SNHR’s July report documented how property confiscations intersected with discriminatory registration practices, inheritance obstacles and economic dependency. For these families, rebuilding a house does not necessarily mean being able to reclaim, manage or securely inhabit it.
Jimale described civil documentation as a foundational need. Missing identity and family-status records can obstruct inheritance claims, access to services and legal proceedings, leaving families navigating expensive and complicated procedures after they return.
The contrast with a fully serviced new development is therefore about more than finishes or sale prices. It is about the conditions that allow people to live somewhere securely.
What should count as recovery?
Private investment can expand housing supply and help finance reconstruction. Abdulghany’s argument is not that commercial development should stop, but that it cannot replace a public response to housing need.
He called for priority to be given to repairing existing neighbourhoods, restoring essential services, strengthening tenure security and developing affordable housing and rental programmes.
Jimale also stressed the need for international financial and technical support, alongside continuing assistance for people who cannot yet return.
"When people return to their areas but lack housing, basic services, livelihood opportunities, or legal documentation, pressure to leave temporary shelters may simply transfer displacement from camps into informal settlements and urban areas rather than resolve it," he said.
Abyat Hills may demonstrate that there are buyers for new housing around Damascus. What it cannot establish on its own is whether families living in damaged homes, struggling with rent or contesting old expropriations are gaining a viable route to recovery.

Donald Trump Jr. went hunting in Mongolia with a Kremlin-linked Russian businessman who helped bankroll his wedding
Donald Trump Jr., 48, the son of U.S. President Donald Trump, traveled to Mongolia in August 2026 to hunt, spending two days there with Umar Kremlev, head of the International Boxing Association and a businessman close to the Kremlin, the Financial Times found.
Umar Kremlev, whose real surname is Lutfulloyev, has led the International Boxing Association (IBA) as its president since 2020. Under him, the organization has received tens of millions of dollars from Gazprom. In 2023, the International Olympic Committee stripped the IBA of the right to hold Olympic boxing tournaments, citing, among other reasons, a lack of transparency in its finances.
In 2024, Kremlev became the new owner of the car dealership Rolf, which had previously belonged to businessman Sergei Petrov and had been placed under temporary management by a decree from Putin. The Russian investigative outlet Proekt reported that Kremlev acquired Rolf because of his friendship with Alexey Rubezhny, head of the Russian president’s security service. Kremlev also obtained a number of assets in the lottery and bookmaking businesses through that same friendship, Proekt wrote.
Kremlev is also tied to the Trump family. In September 2026, it emerged that he had paid part of the costs of Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas, and Democrats in the U.S. Congress launched an investigation. Trump Sr. later said that his son had repaid the money to Umar Kremlev.
A charity auction raffled off the trip to Mongolia in the company of the U.S. president’s son. One of the winners did join Trump Jr. to hunt mountain sheep. Kremlev, who did not take part in the auction, also joined the trip, along with longtime Republican Party donor Kevin Small.
Trump Jr. flew into the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar, in late August, after his wedding on a private island in the Caribbean Sea — a wedding Kremlev partly funded. He then traveled several hundred kilometers to a camp in western Mongolia, where he stayed with a small group of hunting guides, drivers, and cooks. Kremlev joined him there, accompanied by Arthur Martirosov, a businessman and partner at the venture fund Voskhod, which is under U.S. sanctions.
On August 30, Kremlev posted two videos to his Telegram channel. In one, he says he is flying to Mongolia with Martirosov, while in another he shows footage from the trip. In the caption, Kremlev asks, “How do you feel about hunting?”
One participant in the trip said Trump Jr. and Kremlev tried not to be photographed together while at the camp. Trump Jr. does not appear in Kremlev’s video either, though two organizers of his hunting trips do.
According to one guide, Trump Jr. killed an Altai argali — an endangered mountain sheep prized by hunters for its large horns — during the trip. After the hunt, he returned to the Mongolian capital. However, his trip did not end there — he held a series of other unofficial meetings, including a dinner with Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh.
As a member of the president’s family, Trump Jr. traveled with a U.S. Secret Service detail. The U.S. Embassy in Ulaanbaatar paid $18,715 for hotel rooms linked to an unspecified “visit” by Secret Service agents from August 23–September 6.
A representative for Trump Jr. said a mutual friend from hunting circles introduced him to Umar Kremlev. “Don has made clear that he has a personal friendship, not a business relationship, with Umar. Their friendship is largely based on their shared love for hunting, fishing and the outdoors. It shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone that they went hunting together earlier this year,” the representative added.
However, intelligence experts polled by the FT believe these relationships create favorable conditions for manipulation.
“It really doesn’t matter if people have the most above board intentions,” said Holden Triplett, former director of counterintelligence at the U.S. National Security Council. “The moment the Russian security and intelligence services figure out someone has a relationship with anyone of high value, they will try to weaponize that.”

The decision came after the clip spread on social media across China, where jokes about Mao, who died in 1976, are seen as disrespectful.
Kylian Mbappé has lost several of his biggest sponsorship deals in China after a video circulated online in which he appears to joke about Mao Zedong, the founder of the People’s Republic of China, that led to a backlash that he has now apologised for.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement he published in French, Chinese and English on Tuesday.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."
Energy-drink maker Dongpeng and dairy group Mengniu both ended their partnerships with the Real Madrid forward with immediate effect.
“Our company is firmly opposed and applies a policy of zero tolerance towards any behaviour that offends national feelings,” Dongpeng said, announcing the end of “all forms of cooperation” with the player.
Mengniu said in its own announcement that it was ending all cooperation with the captain of the French national team in a move that shows how political and national sensitivities can weigh on international brands.
What sparked the backlash?
Mbappé reportedly made the 'insensitive' comment on the French talk show The Bridge, where he was asked about the online memes about him being a 'dictator' and the ones which amuse him the most.
He then said the one that makes him laugh most is a video of a man he thinks is "a Chinese dictator".
Mbappe laughs as the programme cuts to a meme showing his own face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.
The meme is part of a running joke on social media in which Mbappe is called a "dictator" over his huge influence on and off the pitch.
Why did the video cause such a reaction?
The decision by several brands to drop Mbappe came after the clip spread across China, where jokes about Mao, who died in 1976, are seen as disrespectful.
Both companies’ statements stressed the need to protect national feelings and clearly distanced themselves from Mbappé.
The split is a sharp reversal for the 27-year-old, who until now has been hugely popular with Chinese fans and has millions of followers on the country’s social platforms.
During this year’s World Cup, Chinese viewers regularly saw Dongpeng adverts featuring AI-generated images of him drinking the brand’s energy drink.
He is also affectionately known in China as "Guigui", which translates as "turtle", a nickname linked to a meme inspired by the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

The Association of European Journalists in Bulgaria (AEJ-Bulgaria) has accused the government press office of creating conditions for censorship after it instructed media outlets to report Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s statements accurately and in full, amid a controversy over his support for presidential candidate Iliana Yotova.
In a position paper released on Tuesday, the association called the press office’s attempt to define professional journalistic standards dangerous, arguing that the executive branch has no authority to dictate how journalists should cover political statements.
“The media are not merely platforms for publishing government press releases, and journalists are not simply ‘microphone stands’ expected to unquestioningly relay whatever the Prime Minister, or any other government official, chooses to say,” AEJ-Bulgaria said.
The association stressed that the Bulgarian Media Ethics Code requires accuracy but does not oblige journalists to reproduce the positions of government officials in their entirety. Media outlets may focus on particular parts of a statement and examine them critically, it said, adding that such scrutiny should not be confused with manipulation or the imposition of political narratives.
AEJ-Bulgaria also said the Commission on Journalistic Ethics is responsible for overseeing compliance with journalistic standards, while the Council for Electronic Media (CEM) acts as an independent regulator. It argued that the government was attempting to assume powers belonging to neither a self-regulatory body nor an independent regulator.
The association said the government press office’s position conflicts with the European Media Freedom Act, which requires EU member states to safeguard the editorial independence of media service providers. It also cited Article 40, paragraph 1 of Bulgaria’s Constitution, which states that “the press and other mass media shall be free and not subject to censorship.”
The controversy began after the government press office issued guidance on how media outlets should cover Radev’s statements. The office said journalists were responsible for providing timely and accurate information about the prime minister’s public positions and activities.
“Even if certain journalists or media outlets do not share the Prime Minister's positions, professional journalistic standards require that these positions be reported accurately and in full,” the government press office said.
It also warned that it would not follow what it described as negative examples of media outlets omitting, distorting, manipulating or abridging the prime minister’s words, placing them within political narratives, or engaging in censorship or self-censorship.
The statement provoked criticism and ridicule from journalists and members of the public. A post on the Council of Ministers’ Facebook page drew more than 3,700 laugh reactions and over 2,000 comments.
Journalists and citizens argued that the government had no right to dictate professional practices, with some comparing its stance to approaches used by repressive regimes in other countries.
Journalist Alexander Detev questioned the press office’s authority in a Facebook post, asking, “By what right does the Council of Ministers' press office presume to lecture the media on how they should do their job?”
Journalist Polina Paunova also rejected the idea that government officials could determine journalistic standards. She recalled a 2020 statement by the Sofia City Prosecutor’s Office (SCPO) concerning an article by journalist Boris Mitov about prosecutor Boryana Betsova, who was involved in an investigation into leaked audio recordings featuring then-Prime Minister Boyko Borissov.
At the time, the SCPO said Mitov’s article contained a “violation of the Code of Ethics for the Bulgarian Media.” The Commission on Journalistic Ethics subsequently clarified that it alone was authorized to rule on violations of the code.
The dispute over the government press office’s statement followed a complaint submitted to the Central Election Commission (CEC) by presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov. He alleged that official government communication channels had been used to campaign for his runoff opponent, Yotova, who is backed by Radev.
On Monday, Radev urged voters to support Yotova in the presidential runoff scheduled for November 1. His appeal was published on the Council of Ministers’ website and its official Facebook page.
“This is an official state channel, funded by all taxpayers. The Council of Ministers is not an election campaign headquarters; the state is not the property of a political party,” Gyurov said.
Representatives of Democratic Bulgaria (DB) and We Continue the Change (PP), both of which support Gyurov, also accused the government of violating the Electoral Code by using official state channels for campaigning.
The initiative committee that nominated Gyurov filed a complaint with the CEC, arguing that campaigning had taken place through a state institution and that public administrative resources had been used free of charge.
Bozhidar Bozhanov and Ivaylo Mirchev, co-chairs of Yes, Bulgaria, likewise accused the government of using official channels for election campaigning. Radan Kanev, leader of the Democrats for a Strong Bulgaria (DSB), identified the use of the Council of Ministers’ official page for political messaging as a problem.
Asen Vassilev, chairman of PP, also accused Radev of using the Council of Ministers for partisan purposes, saying the government should not be turned into an election campaign headquarters.
The first round of the presidential election took place on Sunday, with Yotova receiving 34.7% of the vote and Gyurov 31.9%, sending both candidates into the November 1 runoff. During a briefing on Monday, Radev framed the contest as a choice “between peace and war” and “between democracy and the corrupt model of the 'assembly' [GERB and PP-DB joint rule].”
The presidential and vice-presidential candidate pair of Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev will deliver their campaign addresses first on Bulgarian National Television (BNT) and Bulgarian National Radio (BNR)

Glutamate receptors may help explain the brain structure behind children’s math and reading abilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:00:57 UTC
21:00:57 KST

A brain signaling system important for learning and memory appears to be linked to the brain structure that supports children’s math and reading abilities, according to a study published in Nature Communications. Across two groups of children, brain regions where gray matter volume was most closely tied to academic skills tended to be regions rich in NMDA receptors, which respond to the chemical messenger glutamate.
Scientists have long known that mathematics and reading rely on networks of brain regions rather than a single “math area” or “reading area.” Less understood is how the brain’s chemical signaling systems relate to the development of these networks.
The researchers expected two systems to be especially relevant: glutamate, the brain’s main excitatory chemical messenger, and GABA, its main inhibitory messenger, since the balance between the two is thought to be important for learning. NMDA receptors, which are proteins on brain cells that respond to glutamate, play an important role in plasticity, the ability of connections between neurons to change and strengthen with experience.
Previous studies have linked levels of glutamate and other neurotransmitters to academic abilities, but they have generally concentrated on selected areas of the brain. The new study instead asked whether the brain-wide distribution of different chemical receptors corresponded with structural patterns associated with children’s math and reading skills.
Led by Yuan Zhang of Stanford University, the researchers analyzed structural brain scans and academic test scores from 991 typically developing children between the ages of 7 and 14. The initial sample included 760 children (average age 9.7 years; 275 girls) from the Child Mind Institute’s Healthy Brain Network, a large research dataset. The findings were then tested in an independent sample of 231 children (average age 9.2 years; 98 girls) drawn from studies conducted at Stanford.
Children completed standardized tests of numerical calculations, mathematical problem-solving, word reading and reading comprehension. The researchers examined gray matter volume across 218 brain regions to identify patterns associated with stronger academic performance, accounting for age. They then compared these patterns with an existing atlas, based on PET scans, showing the typical brain-wide distribution of 19 different neurotransmitter receptors and transporters.
Of those 19 systems, NMDA receptors produced the most consistent finding. In both groups of children, regions where gray matter volume was more strongly tied to math and reading performance tended to have higher densities of NMDA receptors. These associations were modest, with NMDA receptor distribution accounting for between 8% and 20% of the variation across brain regions.
Other chemical systems, including those involving dopamine, acetylcholine, serotonin and GABA, produced weaker or inconsistent findings. Some, such as acetylcholine and histamine for math, showed associations in one sample but not the other, making NMDA receptors the only system that replicated across both groups for both skills.
There were also differences between academic skills. For mathematics, NMDA receptor distribution corresponded with structural patterns across several brain networks, including the default mode, salience and higher-order visual networks. For reading, the relationship that held up in both samples was concentrated within a network involved in higher-level visual processing, which includes regions important for recognizing written words.
Math and reading scores were strongly correlated, and additional analyses suggested that the NMDA associations mainly reflected brain structure shared by both skills. The researchers suggest glutamate-related signaling may be a common biological feature of academic learning that is expressed through somewhat different brain systems depending on the skill.
Zhang and colleagues summarized, “NMDA receptor distribution showed robust and spatially selective associations with brain structural organization for both mathematical and reading abilities across two independent cohorts.”
Some limitations should be noted. The researchers did not measure NMDA receptors or glutamate in these children. Instead, the receptor maps came from previous imaging of more than 1,200 healthy adults and were used as a reference against which the children’s brain structures were compared, and because neurotransmitter systems change during development, adult maps may not accurately represent children’s brains.
Because the analysis compared patterns across brain regions rather than measuring receptors in individual children, it does not show that children with more NMDA receptors are better at math or reading. The study was also cross-sectional and included only typically developing children aged 7 to 14, so it cannot establish whether glutamate signaling shapes the development of these skills.
The study, “Glutamatergic signaling underlies brain structural organization for mathematical and reading abilities in children,” was authored by Yuan Zhang, Hyesang Chang, Dawlat El-Said and Vinod Menon.

“The operation was based on field intelligence aimed at neutralizing confirmed threats and planned terrorist attacks against Jordan,” he said.
“Initial results of this operation indicate significant losses among ISIS, estimated at more than 20 members, as well as the destruction of a major weapons depot belonging to the group,” Momani said.

Momani said Jordanian authorities were following up on the matter with their Syrian counterparts.

The ministry said coordination was underway with Jordan to establish an urgent joint civilian and security committee to investigate the incidents, prevent their recurrence and strengthen security cooperation along their shared border.

The Israeli army entered a fifth day of a large-scale offensive in Hebron Tuesday, displacing nearly 5,000 Palestinians from their homes.
The Hebron municipality said in a statement that 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families have been forcibly displaced from the Deir Bahha and al-Jilda areas since the Israeli military campaign began Friday.
Among those displaced are 336 infants, 441 elderly, 216 pregnant and nursing women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people suffering from chronic illnesses, the statement said.
The municipality said the figures document families forced out from their homes since the start of the Israeli campaign amid growing humanitarian consequences, particularly for people requiring special care.
The army has shut all entrances to Hebron and surrounding villages since Friday following a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.
Türkiye's Anadolu Agency reported Palestinians being stopped, searched and mistreated by Israeli forces at military checkpoints near al-Jilda Roundabout.
Witnesses said new military reinforcements also arrived in Ein Deir Baha, where Israeli forces have taken over several Palestinian buildings and turned them into military posts.
According to the Palestinian Prisoner Society, the Israeli army has arrested 85 Palestinians across Hebron governorate since Friday.
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces arrested at least nine Palestinians in military raids and closed all main entrances to Ramallah.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli forces raided the eastern neighborhood of Jenin as well as the towns of Meithalun, Jaba and Qabatiya, arresting at least six Palestinians, according to local sources.
A Palestinian man was detained during a raid on Aqraba, southeast of Nablus, while Israeli forces stormed the southern al-Hawouz area of Qaffin in Tulkarm governorate and raided a home in the town’s western neighborhood.
In the central West Bank, Israeli forces closed all main entrances to Ramallah, including the Ein Sinya and Atara checkpoints, the Rawabi gate and the Nabi Saleh and Aboud gates, and set up additional checkpoints on alternative roads.
In Al-Bireh, the army turned a Palestinian home into a military post, held four residents inside and confiscated their phones, according to local sources.
Palestinian farmers were also expelled from their land in Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, while Israeli forces raided Tuqu southeast of Bethlehem with tracked military vehicles.
In Hebron governorate, Israeli forces also repeatedly raided the town of Taffuh and searched the homes of former prisoners.
Israeli troops assaulted a Palestinian man in the Hawara area south of Hebron before arresting him and his son, according to local sources.
Separately, Israeli occupiers set fire to three Palestinian vehicles early Tuesday in the village of Umm Safa, west of Ramallah in the central West Bank.
Municipal chief Marwan Sabah told AA that a group of occupiers stormed the village around midnight and set three vehicles ablaze.
"Confrontations broke out between residents and the attackers, forcing the occupiers to withdraw," he said.
"Umm Safa has repeatedly come under attack by Israeli occupiers involving assaults on residents, vehicle arson, intimidation and harassment," Sabah said.
He added that occupiers have seized large areas of the village’s land.
Israeli occupiers also established a settlement outpost at the northern entrance to al-Bireh overlooking the al-Balou neighborhood, the Bedouin rights group al-Baidar said.
According to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli occupiers attempted to establish 21 new settlement outposts across the West Bank in September, including 10 in Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate.
The incidents come amid intensified Israeli army raids and attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.

Record carbon dioxide levels will impact us for centuries, says UN weather agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Record carbon dioxide levels will impact us for centuries, says UN weather agency
Levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere caused by burning fossil fuels reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term global warming, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said on Tuesday.
The agency’s latest Greenhouse Gas Bulletin indicates an average global concentration of CO2 at 426.8 parts per million (ppm) last year, or 153 per cent of the 1750 pre-industrial baseline.
“Every additional part per million matters because it traps additional heat. In effect, we are supercharging the ocean and the atmosphere. That means that heat waves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for,” WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett told journalists in Geneva.
Equally worrying, levels of methane and nitrous oxide – the second and third most important long-lived greenhouse gases caused by human activities – also hit a new peak in 2025.
“Another year, another new record. Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies,” Ms. Barrett stressed. 
“The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. CO2 has a very long lifetime and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries.”
When the Bulletin was first published in 2004, the annual average level of CO2 measured by WMO’s Global Atmosphere Watch network of monitoring stations was 377.5 ppm, compared with nearly 427 ppm today.
El Niño accelerator
Growth rates of CO2 have tripled since the 1960s, accelerating from an annual average increase of 0.8 ppm per year to 2.4 ppm per year in the decade from 2011 to 2020.
The “exceptional [3.5 ppm] surge” of 2023-2024 coincided with a strong El Niño “which reduced the efficiency of the biosphere through more drought, drier vegetation and more wildfires”, said WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova. 
She noted that although the 2.8 ppm annual increase from 2024-2025 represented a more modest increase, it was nonetheless “a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning. We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Niño which will impact land carbon sinks as it did in 2023-2024.”
CO2 growth rates triple
The agency’s Bulletin reports on the amount of gas that accumulates in the atmosphere and not new annual emissions. About half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere and the rest is absorbed by Earth’s land ecosystems and oceans.
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Annual Greenhouse Gas Index shows that from 1990 to 2025, the warming effect on our climate caused by greenhouse gases increased by 56 per cent, with CO2 accounting for about 81 per cent of this increase, known as “radiative forcing”.
Energy transformation concerns
WMO noted that as countries transform their energy systems towards decarbonization, careful attention should be given to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulphur hexafluoride (SF6).
Widely used as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution, SF6 use has risen steadily in the past three decades in line with increased global electrification. “It has an atmospheric lifetime of over 1,000 years and has the highest 100-year global warming potential of approximately 24,300 times that of CO2. The increase of SF6 in 2025 was a record high,” the agency’s report notes.
Hydrogen concentration has increased by 5.3 per cent between 2010 and 2024. Hydrogen is being used as an energy storage medium for hard-to-decarbonize sectors such as steelmaking, shipping, and long-duration energy storage, as well as for renewable sources and as an energy source for transport. 
“Its leakage into the atmosphere from production facilities, pipelines, storage tanks, and fuel cells poses a growing concern,” WMO said, highlighting that although hydrogen is not a greenhouse gas, “it influences atmospheric chemistry” and has a strong indirect effect on warming, the agency explained.
“Both H2 leakage and SF6 persistence represent potential threats that could undermine the climate benefits of the energy transition,” WMO said. “Careful monitoring of the composition of Earth’s atmosphere is essential to detect, understand and prevent unintended consequences of these changes.”.
WMO releases the Bulletin to provide authoritative scientific data for negotiators attending the annual UN Climate conference. The aim of the Conference of the Parties meeting (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November is to turn climate commitments into concrete action.

General Assembly weighs US embargo against Cuba ahead of 34th vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

General Assembly weighs US embargo against Cuba ahead of 34th vote
The General Assembly opened its annual debate on the US economic embargo against Cuba on Tuesday. On Wednesday, 28 October, Member States will vote for the 34th time on a resolution calling for it to end.
Every year at around this time, the assembly – where each of the UN’s 193 Member States has one vote – takes up the “necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba”.
And every year, whatever the political climate, the issue generates plenty of diplomatic heat. The debate usually spills over two days as countries and regional groups take the floor to explain their positions.
A 33-vote record
The assembly has called for an end to the embargo, first imposed in 1960, on 33 previous occasions.
Support has grown markedly since the first vote in 1992, when 59 countries backed the resolution, three opposed it, 71 abstained and 46 did not vote.
It peaked at 191 votes in favour in 2015, 2016 and 2017, during the thaw in relations under US President Barack Obama. The United States and Israel voted against in 2015 and 2017; in 2016, both abstained.
Some countries have shifted position as governments have changed, but many have held the same line for decades. Canada, China and Russia have long voted in favour, while the United States, backed by Israel, has voted against every year bar one.
A tightening squeeze
This year’s debate comes as the Trump administration has tightened the embargo – a move that has led to an energy crisis and possible humanitarian collapse, according to the UN Resident Coordinator in Cuba, Francisco Pichon.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has also warned that energy shortages are taking a toll on health.
In May, senior UN officials reported that more than 100,000 surgical procedures had been postponed. Cuban authorities have repeatedly pointed to further damage to the health system, including delays to vaccination programmes and patients with chronic illnesses unable to get a stable supply of medicines.
This year, President Donald Trump has also raised the possibility of military intervention in Cuba.
Successive UN High Commissioners for Human Rights and independent UN experts have condemned the embargo and other unilateral US sanctions, warning that they threaten Cubans’ rights to health, life, food and development.
Tensions spill over
Those tensions were on display in the chamber on Tuesday when Cuba’s Foreign Minister, Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, interrupted the US Ambassador, Mike Waltz, on a point of order midway through his statement.
The exchange escalated into a heated row between the two, prompting the President of the General Assembly to briefly suspend the session. The debate later resumed without further incident.
Mr. Waltz rejected the premise of the debate, arguing that Cuba’s crisis was the fault of its own government, not the embargo.
“There is no blockade,” he said. If there were, he argued, there would be no explaining US exports to Cuba – which he put at more than $876 million in the first eight months of 2026 – or shipments from Canada, Spain, Mexico, China, Russia, the European Union and UN agencies.
The country’s wealth had not vanished, he said, but had “simply” passed from ordinary Cubans into the hands of the ruling elite.
Mr. Rodríguez is due to deliver his statement on Wednesday.
What the resolution says
As in previous years, the Cuban-drafted text reaffirms the sovereign equality of States and the principles of non-intervention and non-interference in their internal affairs, as well as freedom of international trade and navigation – all enshrined in numerous international legal instruments.
It also voices concern over laws such as the Helms-Burton Act, enacted by the United States on 12 March 1996, whose extraterritorial effects, it says, undermine the sovereignty of other States, the legitimate interests of people and entities under their jurisdiction and freedom of trade and navigation.
It calls on all States to refrain from adopting such measures and urges those that still apply them to repeal them.

The safety of UNOPS staff has been compromised too many times, he said, stressing that all parties to the fighting in Gaza must uphold their obligations to protect civilians and humanitarian personnel.
Guterres condemns West Bank attacks
Meanwhile, Secretary-General António Guterres continues to express his deep alarm over the intensifying violence in the West Bank as an Israeli offensive in Hebron continues.
Associate Spokesperson Daniela Gross told journalists at the daily briefing in New York that the UN chief is following the situation there closely.
“He is deeply alarmed for this offensive…the intensifying violence in the West Bank. He condemns the violence. And he also firmly opposed the settler attacks in the region.”
Between January 2025 and the end of September 2026, 331 Palestinians, including 77 children, were killed in the West Bank, and more than 42,000 have been displaced, according to the UN aid coordination office. OCHA. Over the same period, 21 Israelis were killed in the West Bank.
OCHA also recorded 3,684 attacks by Israeli settlers during the period that resulted in casualties or property damage.
Flood risk
Despite restrictions and funding shortfalls, the UN and its partners continue to bring limited supplies into Gaza. On Monday, UN teams brought in food, blankets, winter clothes, school items and fuel, according to OCHA.
Over the past week, partners distributed school bags to more than 8,000 children. The week before, they provided stationery to about 22,000 boys and girls and furnished some 300 classrooms supporting around 60,000 children.
Many families are living in deteriorating tents and shelters with little protection from the cold, wind and rain. Around 950,000 people are living in displacement sites at medium to high risk of flooding, and stocks of supplies to support them are insufficient, a shelter assessment found.
Media under attack
Also on Tuesday, Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied, briefed journalists virtually on her latest report, which focuses on the media.
She reminded reporters that she was unable to attend in person because of sanctions imposed on her by the United States.
According to Ms. Albanese, nearly 300 journalists and media workers have been killed in Gaza, citing UN sources, and more than 100 have been detained, many of them tortured.
Some 150 media centres and offices – 80 per cent of Gaza’s media infrastructure – have been destroyed, she said, while in the West Bank more than 139 attacks on journalists have recently been recorded.
She also criticized Israel’s ban on foreign journalists entering Gaza and said there had been no accountability for the killing of Palestinian journalist Shireen Abu Akleh.
“The update is impunity,” she said.
Her report also documents intimidation and repression of Palestinian journalists by Hamas in Gaza and the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, she said.
