Estonian media association: Meta is planning the largest theft of content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:46:00 UTC
20:46:00 KST

Estonian media association: Meta is planning the largest theft of content
Estonian media companies have warned US tech giant Meta's new business terms would let it use news content without consent or payment.
The companies are urging the European Commission to intervene over the terms, due originally to take effect October 30.
The Commission says Meta has postponed them to 20 November, following discussions, but the Estonian Association of Media Companies (Eesti meediaettevõtete liit) says the delay changes little.
The Estonian Association of Media Companies has appealed to policymakers and regulators over Meta's new business terms, which would require business users — including news publishers — to grant Meta permission to access their web content by automated software. Meta could then index, store, search and update that content for its business purposes, without separate permission or payment.
Meta initially sought the right to use content for AI training. After publisher protests, it removed the word "training," but the association says the remaining terms are broad enough to permit AI-related use anyway.
In the association's view the terms threaten media business models, as Meta could build competing products from journalistic content without paying for it. Publishers now face a choice: allow the use of their content, or lose a key channel for reaching readers.
Media association board member Väino Koorberg called the development potentially the largest theft of content, while in the U.S., the News/Media Alliance, representing nearly 2,000 American publishers, has written Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, demanding the terms be withdrawn. A further four European publishers' organizations have approached the Commission with similar concerns.
"In European Union terms, Meta is a so-called major gatekeeper, on whose activities the visibility of others hinges, hence why stricter rules have been established for them," Koorberg said.
He added that Meta is also testing restrictions on link sharing on Facebook. "Only two links can be shared free of charge during a month," he said, which serves to limit the platform as a marketing channel.
The association says the situation threatens access to reliable information: more than half of people get daily news from social media, and reduced visibility for journalism could increase vulnerability to disinformation.
Koorberg said Estonia should send a clear message. "For example, state institutions can end cooperation with Meta and leave those platforms, because the change in terms also affects them," he said.
Elis Paemurd, deputy head of the European Commission Representation in Estonia, said Meta had postponed the terms to November 20 following discussions, adding that the Commission is ensuring Meta complies with EU law, including the prohibition on abuse of a dominant position.
Koorberg said the delay does not mean media have escaped. "Meta itself explains that it wants to specify and clarify how the terms should be interpreted," he said, adding that it may be a step toward neutralizing possible legal action. The association has told members to follow developments closely, and that the most extreme step would be to end all cooperation with Meta's products.
Estonian media companies have warned US tech giant Meta's new business terms would let it use news content without consent or payment.

What’s next for Brazil after Lula’s victory and Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:44:37 UTC
20:44:37 KST

- 'Bolsonaro rejecting the result (when he lost) is not surprising – some would say ‘like father like son’,' says Mahrukh Doctor, a political economy expert
- Lula's victory is particularly 'significant' for a region that has recently seen a marked turn towards far-right leaders, says Consuelo Thiers of University of Edinburg
Brazil’s election dispute has entered a new phase, with presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro yet to formally concede defeat, despite his Liberal Party (PL) recognizing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory.
Bolsonaro initially threatened to seek annulment of Sunday’s election, which Lula won by more than 4.4 million votes.
He later said he would seek to have Lula’s electoral ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of political and economic power.
Bolsonaro also said he had been ordered to surrender his passports and barred from leaving Brazil under a separate investigation.
The dispute comes as Lula prepares for a fourth, non-consecutive presidential term, which is due to begin in January. He faces a strengthened conservative opposition in Congress, economic concerns and strained relations with US President Donald Trump.
Trump also questioned the election on Monday, saying it “looked like another rigged election” without presenting evidence of fraud.
Meanwhile, Brazil’s real recorded its steepest daily fall against the US dollar since 2002, according to media reports, following Lula’s victory.
 
Legal challenge unlikely to overturn result
Bolsonaro initially threatened to seek annulment of the election over a two-hour extension of voting hours but later shifted to seeking the disqualification of Lula’s electoral ticket.
The extension followed requests from both campaigns. About 34,330 votes were cast after the original closing time, far below Lula’s winning margin of approximately 4.4 million votes.
Mahrukh Doctor, a professor of comparative political economy at the University of Hull, said the circumstances gave Bolsonaro grounds to challenge the result but that annulment was highly unlikely.
“Bolsonaro rejecting the result (when he lost) is not surprising – some would say ‘like father like son’,” she said.
Consuelo Thiers, a lecturer in international relations at the University of Edinburgh, warned that rejecting election results could erode public trust, undermine democratic institutions and deepen political divisions.
She noted that former President Jair Bolsonaro also did not publicly concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022. His party’s subsequent challenge over electronic voting machines was rejected by the electoral court.
“The margin between Bolsonaro and Lula is quite large to be attributed to the extension of voting time (about 4 million votes), which makes Bolsonaro's attempts to contest the results less credible,” Thiers said.
 
Divided government awaits Lula
Analysts say that Lula’s victory does not necessarily signal a broader revival of left-wing politics across Latin America, where right-wing forces have gained ground in several countries.
Thiers said Lula benefited from the mobilization of voters who had not participated in the first round, an effective media campaign and his political experience.
But she cautioned against interpreting the result as a renewed left-wing surge.
“I think we should be cautious about presenting Lula’s victory as a signal of a renewed rise of the left, since other factors are at play,” she said.
Many voters, she added, may have supported Lula primarily to prevent another Bolsonaro presidency rather than out of strong personal loyalty to the incumbent.
Thiers, however, said Lula's victory is particularly "significant" for a region that has recently seen a marked turn toward far-right leaders, such as Keiko Fujimori in Peru, Jose Antonio Kast in Chile, and Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia.
"Brazil now remains one of the few countries in the region led by a left-wing president.
"Lula’s victory in the last elections in Brazil came as a surprise in several ways. It was the first time since Brazil’s return to democracy that a candidate who lost the first round went on to win the run-off. It also ran counter to the broader anti-incumbency trend in which governing parties tend to lose elections."
Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at International Crisis Group, said the election had produced a divided government, with the presidency remaining in left-wing hands while right-wing parties gained ground in the legislature.
“What we see is that really Brazil will have an essentially divided government because the parties on the right, did advance and did gain representation in the legislature and Lulas holds on to the presidency,” she said.
Dickinson warned that the arrangement would complicate efforts to build consensus.
“What that likely means is that it will be a few difficult years, in terms of governing, in terms of passing legislation, finding consensus, and that is really the political challenge that stands ahead for Lula as he enters his next term,” she said.
Lula’s priorities include managing public finances, addressing social and economic concerns and reducing political polarization. Negotiations with a more conservative Congress will determine how much of his program he can implement.
Meanwhile, Doctor called the result a rejection of ‘Bolsonarism’ and what the populist far-right stood for in terms of inclusion, human rights and progressive societal values.
 
Relations with Trump under scrutiny
The election also has implications for Brazil’s relations with Washington, where Trump has questioned Lula’s victory despite the absence of evidence of electoral fraud.
Doctor said the US could initially increase trade pressure on Brazil but would eventually have incentives to adopt a more pragmatic approach.
“It is likely to switch to resolving trade issues on more technical rather than ideological grounds,” she said.
She pointed to US interest in Brazil’s critical minerals and rare earth resources as a reason for continued engagement between the two countries.
Lula is expected to pursue a foreign policy centred on multilateralism and balanced relations with partners including the European Union, China, India and others.
Dickinson said Brazil’s position in global supply chains and the future of the Amazon would remain important issues for the incoming administration.
“The Amazon, we know, is home to many of the minerals that are needed and in high tech and defense industries and the sort of rapid interest in these minerals, I think has placed Brazil really at the center of the geopolitical debate,” she said.
Thiers said that the Trump administration was probably expecting to gain another ally in the region, as they would have benefited from having the largest country and economy in Latin America within the US sphere of influence.
"In this sense, Lula’s victory is a setback for US plans in the region and the expansion of the Donroe doctrine."
“This victory comes at a time when the US is attempting to increase its influence through initiatives such as the Shield of the Americas, a US-led security coalition that has already attracted support from several conservative and far-right governments," she said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) on Tuesday defended the government’s decision to deny entry to Chinese actor Zhang Linghe, citing the sensitive timing ahead of the November elections.
Zhang, who stars in the Chinese television series “Pursuit of Jade,” was reportedly scheduled to visit Taiwan later this month, but MAC formally rejected his application Wednesday.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office criticized the move as “undermining cross-strait cultural exchanges,” saying it was “against the wishes of Taiwanese youth.”
On Wednesday, MAC Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) pointed to the unclear purpose of Zhang’s application and his participation in the Straits Forum as reasons for the rejection.

At the Legislative Yuan, Chiu told reporters Tuesday that Taiwan welcomes cultural exchanges based on “mutual respect, parity and dignity,” but the agency had doubts about the true purpose of Zhang’s visit.
With the elections approaching, his visit could cause social unrest, and it would be better for him to consider arranging a cultural exchange event at another time, Chiu added.
Zhang’s planned visit has been in the public eye since late April, when KMT Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) asked at a Legislative Yuan session how the Ministry of Culture would respond if the Chinese actor came to Taiwan for a fan meeting. Culture Minister Li Yuan (李遠) did not answer directly, saying Zhang had not applied for a visit.

Hozier, Kneecap join Macklemore at sold-out launch of Free Palestine tour

27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Irish artists Hozier, Kneecap and Beoga joined US rapper Macklemore as surprise guests Monday at the sold-out opening of his Free Palestine tour in Dublin.
The concert at the 13,000-capacity 3Arena marked the first European date of the benefit tour Macklemore organized after being removed from Ed Sheeran’s US tour over his public support for Palestine.
“I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people,” Macklemore told the audience. “We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath.”
Palestinian flags and keffiyehs were visible throughout the arena as the audience repeatedly chanted “Free Palestine.”
“Six weeks ago, two words is all that it took,” Macklemore said, referring to the declaration that led to his removal from Sheeran’s remaining concerts.
“Those two words are so threatening to some people that we’d rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean,” he said. “Somehow those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary.”
Macklemore was joined by Palestinian singer Lina Makoul, Palestinian American DJ Habibeats and the US political hip-hop group Dead Prez, alongside Irish performers Hozier, Kneecap and Beoga.
Actors Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon and the Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas also appeared in recorded video messages.
Hozier performed some of his best-known songs, including Take Me to Church and Too Sweet. Screens behind him displayed a QR code linking to a petition for 55 Palestinian students from Gaza who reportedly have been unable to obtain visas to study in Ireland.
Irish-language rap group Kneecap drew one of the strongest reactions of the night. Opening their appearance with a pointed reference to Macklemore’s removal, a member of the group jokingly thanked Sheeran for “organising this concert.”
Beoga, who performed on Sheeran’s hit Galway Girl, also appeared after withdrawing from his tour in solidarity with Macklemore.
The rapper performed tracks including Thrift Shop, Same Love and Chant, as well as Hind’s Hall, his 2024 protest song supporting Palestinians and the student-led Gaza solidarity movement.
The Dublin concert was the first of three announced European performances, followed by shows in Paris on Thursday and London on Friday. All three dates sold out.
Proceeds will support organizations providing Palestinians with medical care, humanitarian assistance, education and community services.
Macklemore was removed from Sheeran’s tour after declaring “Free Palestine” and criticizing Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank during performances at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium in September.
Several other performers subsequently withdrew from Sheeran’s tour in solidarity. Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was made after promoters were told venues would not permit further concerts with the rapper on the bill.

The AI social paradox: Better at communicating, worse at connecting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:40:59 UTC
20:40:59 KST

A text from a family member. An email from the boss. A friend seeking advice after an argument. These are ordinary moments that are part of everyday interactions. Yet, increasingly, there is another participant in these conversations, one that neither feels emotions nor has any personal stake in the relationship - artificial intelligence.For generations, people learnt social etiquette, understood different perspectives and navigated relationships through actual interactions. They often said the wrong things, misunderstood intentions and learnt from those experiences.Now, with AI offering an instant answer to every social dilemma, some of that effort can be outsourced.So, why has replying to an ordinary message become something we might need assistance with? Also while AI may make us more articulate, polite and confident, does that necessarily make us better at connecting?
A 'social animal' with AI?
Humans have long been described as social animals. Relationships are shaped not merely by what one says, but by how they listen, react, disagree and adapt to one another.AI, however, offers something human relationships rarely can: immediate attention, endless patience and responses tailored to specific concerns. There is no awkward silence, no raised eyebrow and seemingly no fear of embarrassment.This was highlighted by Shailesh K Nevatia, founder director of Grandeavour Communication, having spent nearly 25 years in the communication industry but described himself as shy when it comes to open communication concerning himself.
He said AI helps him navigate differences of opinion, offering perspectives he might otherwise overlook. "With humans we may have certain opinions, views, or thoughts, while with AI, the most valuable thing it offers is not the right answer but a different perspective than us," he said.
"AI can be a guide"
Nevertheless, he maintained that the emotional depth, vulnerability and shared experiences of human relationships cannot be replicated by a chatbot.
When the robot does the talking
The concern with AI-assisted communication is not just that people are using it to find the right words, but that repeated reliance on it could weaken their confidence in finding those words themselves.For instance, Riddhi turns to ChatGPT almost instinctively when responding at times. Whether she needs to sound polite yet firm in a professional email or find a way to decline plans with friends, AI helps her navigate the interaction. "It's not like I can't reply without AI, but having someone to proofread the convos is better than just listening to how they sound in my head," she said.Yet, the reassurance comes with a trade-off for her. "AI has such a grasp on my writing that I am not very confident even while writing this, and that is, without being said, one of the biggest disadvantages." She also called to embrace AI but be careful.
Now that AI has become a new normal, its not possible to go back to the non-AI era, but its also important to not let it become the master of ourselves.
Riddhi
Her experience pointed to a potential paradox: a tool intended to make communication easier can also leave users less confident about communicating independently.The stakes may be higher when AI is used not just to frame a response, but to interpret another person's intentions. Consider someone who turns to a chatbot after an argument and asks who was at fault. The response can sound considered and convincing, but it is based on the account presented to the system, which may omit details or reflect the user's own biases.In that context, Reshmithaa Nair, counselling psychologist at SPARSH Hospital, Hennur Road, warned that such interactions can reinforce confirmation bias, making people more convinced of their existing interpretation rather than open to another perspective.That matters because disagreements are also opportunities to develop social skills. Understanding another person's point of view, managing uncomfortable emotions and responding to unexpected reactions require practice, not simply a well-worded reply."Social skills are learned in actual situations that involve emotions, misunderstanding, conflict, and sometimes rejection," Nair further explained.
"Connections develop through shared connections'
Repeatedly delegating these situations to AI could reduce opportunities to develop empathy, emotional intelligence and the ability to navigate uncertainty. A person may learn to phrase a difficult message more effectively without necessarily becoming better at handling the conversation that follows.
The missing human touch
A message is not simply a collection of sentences. Its meaning can change with the relationship between the people involved, their shared experiences and even the pauses between words.Ritu Mehrotra, Founder and CEO of Shunya Labs, a voice AI company, pointed out that natural communication involves much more than language."Communication is not only about words, it’s also about tone, pauses, context, emotion and all the things we communicate without explicitly saying them."Advances in voice AI are making it possible for technology to interpret language, intent and context with greater sophistication, including across different accents and communication styles. Yet, recognising emotional signals is not the same as experiencing emotions."And as AI is becoming a part of more and more personal conversations, we have to realise that understanding emotion is not feeling it. Trust, privacy, and transparency must be fundamental," she said.
AI should help people connect with one another, not replicate human empathy or replace human relationships.
Ritu Mehrotra, Founder & CEO, Shunya Labs
A chatbot may recognise expressions of sadness or affection and produce an empathetic-sounding response. But recognising emotional patterns is different from sharing the emotional responsibility of a human relationship. For ex, an AI chatbot was asked to give advice to reply on a (hypothetical) "text to a friend who was laid off"
Response of AI
While the response was considerate, it was also generic. It offered comfort without knowing the friend's emotional state, personality or the nature of the relationship. Even a seemingly caring question like “Are you OK?” may fall flat when the person is looking for encouragement rather than a question whose answer seems obvious. A more personal response might acknowledge the setback while affirming the friend's abilities: “OMG, that's awful. I know the job market is tough, but you're talented. You'll land on your feet.”The difference is not simply about choosing warmer words. It is about understanding what a particular person might need in that moment, something a chatbot may struggle to judge without sufficient context.There is also the question of authenticity. When a message is carefully constructed by AI, it may communicate the intended information effectively. But does it still sound like the person sending it?
The robot speaking
In this example, of AI removing the human touch, another chatbot was asked "Someone close to me is grieving. I don't know what to say, and I'm afraid of making things worse. What should I tell them?". It gave a response, which is not wrong but is too robotic. "I am here with you. I care about your pain. Speak if you wish; silence is acceptable." Perfect words but not someone who is comforting says in such "rigid tone"The little hesitations, imperfect expressions and familiar phrases that characterise someone's communication can disappear beneath polished language. A message can become more grammatically correct while feeling less personal.
What aI can't do when comes to social interactions
Not all bad
Dismissing AI as a threat to social skills, however, would overlook how it can help people who struggle to express themselves.For Pooja, a college student who hesitates to speak up in front of the entire class or repeatedly ask friends to explain something, AI offers a space where she can ask questions without worrying about others' reactions.She uses it to understand complicated topics and brainstorm ideas, sometimes asking ChatGPT to explain something as though she were a 10-year-old.
What I love most is that I can ask the dumbest questions without feeling embarrassed. But I also feel it's very easy to become too dependent on it.
Pooja
Yet, she recognises the possibility of becoming overly reliant on it. "AI can give you answers in seconds, but actually understanding and learning something is still on us."For others, AI serves as a sounding board before difficult conversations. It can also help people become more mindful of how their words might affect others. It can suggest more inclusive language, flag potentially insensitive phrasing and help users consider perspectives they might otherwise overlook. For someone unsure how to communicate across differences, this can offer a starting point for more thoughtful interactions.But knowing which words are considered appropriate is not necessarily the same as understanding why they matter. Genuine inclusivity requires empathy and a willingness to understand experiences different from one's own, qualities that must extend beyond the words suggested by a chatbot.Also, in such cases, might not give you the perfect answer, but may help you think in the right direction and give you options that you may not have thought about. In another hypothetical test, a chatbot was asked how to support a family member struggling with their mental health without pushing them away. While its response was not fully correct, it offered different approaches to consider, giving the person a starting point for thinking about how to respond.
AI bot's advice giving suggestions on comforting a family member
Thus, the value, then, may not lie in AI providing the perfect answer, but in helping someone see possibilities they had not considered. The important distinction is whether people use these suggestions to develop their own judgement or simply follow them without question.As Shruti Rajan Kappil, clinical lead, excellence and quality at a mental health care platform Amaha, explained, that while the need to feel heard and supported is fundamental to human relationships, not every concern feels safe to share. Shame, embarrassment and fear of judgement often prevent people from opening up, particularly where stigma remains prevalent.
"AI offers space"
AI offers an alternative, but Kappil pointed to an important distinction. "Good support often needs honest disagreement or gentle challenge with a different point of view. AI tends to be agreeable more often than not, and being agreed with is easily mistaken for being helped."She also noted that repeatedly seeking AI's approval before sending a message can become a form of reassurance seeking. While it offers immediate relief, constantly checking whether one's words are "correct" may gradually undermine confidence in one's own judgement.Shristi Chaudhari, senior executive, regulatory intelligence and market research at Bureau Veritas, uses AI almost daily to condense regulatory updates. Increasingly, she also turns to it for interpersonal communication.From identifying emotional undertones to making messages warmer and more polite for colleagues and professional contacts, AI has become a useful sounding board.
While AI can refine written communication, help us anticipate reactions and interpret conversational nuances, it cannot replace the soft skills, verbal cues and lived experiences that shape genuine human connections.
Shristi Chaudhari
These experiences suggest AI can help people prepare for conversations, overcome language barriers and articulate thoughts they might otherwise struggle to express.
Perfect talks, weaker bonds?
Communication is one of the ways human beings establish connection. But effective communication and meaningful connection are not necessarily the same thing.
What AI can and can't do
One involves expressing something clearly. The other requires understanding, trust, emotional involvement and vulnerability.Tanvi Mankodi, assistant professor at SPJIMR, believes the deeper concern is not whether AI will replace human relationships, but what excessive dependence might do to our ability to participate in them."For me, the essence of human relationships is about our vulnerabilities, about our imperfections, and about how we try to relate with each other with our discomforts and uncertainties," she said.Misunderstandings, difficult conversations and moments when people struggle to find the right words are also experiences through which patience, compassion and empathy develop."Rather than worrying about AI replacing human relations, I am more worried about how if we use AI in a way that we are dependent on it, it might reduce our ability to be vulnerable and to be human," she added.
Impact of AI-dictated communications
Her concern captures the paradox: in trying to eliminate the discomfort of human interaction, we may also remove experiences that make relationships meaningful.
Of course, not every AI-generated message weakens a relationship, and the long-term effects of outsourcing everyday communication are still being understood. AI may help some people overcome barriers to social participation while encouraging others to avoid interactions through which confidence develops. But, the concern is can it address the individuality and complexity of human behaviour?However, using AI to prepare for a difficult discussion is one thing. Allowing it to decide how we interpret another person's intentions and what we say in every interaction is another.The point is not whether AI can offer thoughtful, nuanced or well-structured answers to human dilemmas. It is whether those answers can replicate the emotional understanding, vulnerability and lived experiences through which we learn to navigate relationships and grow socially. After all, relationships are not assignments to be completed with perfectly structured answers. They evolve through disagreement, compromise and sometimes saying something imperfectly but sincerely.Perhaps the real challenge is not learning how to communicate better with AI, but ensuring that, in the process, we do not forget how to connect without it.
Trisha Mahajan is a journalist with The Times of India digital, with keen interest in covering business and corporate affairs. She also reports on key national and world developments and global news trends. A keen reader with a strong interest in storytelling that adds context, clarity, and depth to complex issues.

Rule of law improves in Latvia, but corruption remains a key weakness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:40:53 UTC
20:40:53 KST

Latvia has climbed two places in the latest World Justice Project Rule of Law Index, although further improvements are needed, particularly in combating corruption and strengthening the criminal justice system, according to the Ministry of Justice.
Latvia ranks 19th among 143 countries and jurisdictions assessed in the index.
The country ranks ahead of France, Spain, the United States and Italy, reinforcing its position among the world's most developed democracies, according to the ministry.
Latvia's overall score reached 0.75 on a scale from 0 to 1 this year, representing an increase of 1.6% compared with the previous year.
Justice Minister Edvards Smiltēns of the United List (AS) noted that global trends indicate a continued weakening of the rule of law, with growing pressure on democratic institutions and judicial independence.
Against this background, Latvia's ability to strengthen the rule of law is particularly important, he said.
At the same time, Smiltēns stressed that a high position in the index does not eliminate the need to address existing shortcomings and ensure that individuals and businesses can defend their rights more easily and quickly.
The report indicates that more than 86% of the countries assessed have experienced a sustained deterioration in at least one key indicator of democratic protection over the past five years.
These indicators include constraints on government powers, open government and fundamental rights.
According to the Ministry of Justice, Latvia is not among the countries experiencing such deterioration.
The ministry also highlighted that Latvia's performance in freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association, and public participation has not declined, despite widespread deterioration in these areas globally.
In the latest index, Latvia received its highest rankings in the protection of fundamental rights and government transparency, placing 17th worldwide in both categories.
These areas assess respect for individual rights and freedoms, access to government information and opportunities for public participation in decision-making.
Progress has also been recorded in the civil justice system, where Latvia's score has improved by 9.4% since 2021, placing the country 18th globally this year.
This category evaluates the ability of individuals and businesses to protect their rights, access to courts, judicial impartiality and the effectiveness of dispute resolution.
However, the Ministry of Justice acknowledges that several areas still require improvement.
Latvia ranks 26th worldwide in the absence of corruption category and 21st in the criminal justice system assessment.
Denmark, Norway, Finland and Sweden occupy the leading positions in the World Justice Project Rule of Law Index.
The index is an annual international study that assesses the state of the rule of law across 143 countries and jurisdictions.
It is based on public surveys and evaluations by legal experts, examining eight key dimensions of the rule of law.

At least 20 killed in airstrikes on Sudan’s South Darfur: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:40:43 UTC
20:40:43 KST

Sahin Demir
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
At least 20 people, including members of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), were killed and dozens injured in airstrikes on the city of Nyala in Sudan’s South Darfur state, local media reported Tuesday.
The strikes hit several locations across the city late Monday, including a crowded night market and positions belonging to the RSF, Sudan Tribune reported, citing local sources and eyewitnesses.
A local source said at least 20 people were killed and dozens injured when airstrikes targeted two locations in Nyala.
One of the strikes hit the Tanguj Station night market in the Domaya area, where civilians and RSF recruits were reportedly present, resulting in heavy casualties.
Videos circulated by pro-RSF activists on social media purportedly showed bodies of RSF fighters killed in a drone strike on a gathering in Domaya.
Eyewitnesses said other strikes targeted the headquarters of the 16th Infantry Division, nearby positions and houses believed to belong to RSF commanders in the Al-Nahda, Al-Riyadh and Airport neighborhoods.
The attacks also reportedly hit a student housing complex belonging to Nyala University.
According to the report, the Sudanese army has intensified its air operations in Nyala over the past week, targeting RSF military positions, command facilities and air defense systems near Nyala International Airport.
Military sources said the operations were aimed at weakening the RSF’s defensive and offensive capabilities ahead of a possible ground offensive in Darfur and Kordofan.
There was no immediate comment from the Sudanese army or the RSF on the latest strikes.
Sudan has been engulfed in a conflict between the army and the RSF since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and millions displaced.
The fighting has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with widespread food insecurity and famine reported in several parts of the country.

Netherlands to stay away from Eurovision Song Contest after all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:38:51 UTC
20:38:51 KST

Netherlands to stay away from Eurovision Song Contest after all
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands will not take part in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest after public broadcaster NPO said there was “not enough support” for sending an act.
The decision reverses a previous U-turn after AVROTROS, the broadcasting company that is usually responsible for the Dutch entry, said it would boycott the contest for a second year in 2027 because of Israel’s continued participation.
NPO said last month it would make alternative arrangements to participate in the contest in the Bulgarian coastal city of Burgas next May.
But on Tuesday Jet de Ranitz, chair of NPO’s board of directors, said after holding talks with networks and staff that there was “not enough support” for a Dutch entry.
AVROTROS said in September it would be staying away until “transparent rules” were drawn up on countries involved in military conflicts to restore the “neutrality” of the event.
The Netherlands was one of five countries not to send an entry last year, but news broadcaster NOS still sent a team to cover the event and will do so again next year. Ireland has also said it will continue its boycott in 2027 and is not broadcasting the contest.
Staff critical
Around 500 NPO employees signed a letter a week ago criticising the broadcaster’s decision to look for a replacement for AVROTROS, saying that “the desire to take part in an entertainment programme is considered more important than the countless lives of people who are being murdered.”
De Ranitz did not directly mention Israel’s participation, but said NPO had concluded after consulting broadcasting licence holders that “it is too early at the moment to take part in the Eurovision Song Contest”.
“Because of the sensitivities around the issues that are taking place now, we have decided to step aside for now,” she said.
NPO is in charge of the Dutch broadcasting infrastructure, but programmes are made by autonomous licensed companies.
The European Broadcasting Union, which organises the song contest, said it regretted NPO’s decision. It said it recognised the “deep-rooted and genuine opinions about the song contest and that they vary strongly”, but argued the event was an opportunity to bring unity to a “divided world”.
Culture minister Rianne Letschert said NPO had made an “editorial decision” and it was not her place to intervene.
“The song contest is an event that touches many people and understandably gives rise to widely differing opinions,” she said. “I understand that none of the broadcasters are prepared to take over the entry for the song festival for 2027.”

For Pope Leo, there was little choice but to go to Latin America
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:37:50 CET
20:37:50 KST

By Joshua McElwee
VATICAN CITY, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Since undergoing surgery on October 13 to treat lung cancer, Pope Leo has weighed a major decision: whether to press ahead with an intense, three-country tour of South America just 24 days after having part of one lung removed.
But in the end, according to a biographer and other experts, Leo had little choice but to continue with a visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru as the Vatican announced on Monday, to show he remains up to the job of leading the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics.
Leo, 71, was born in the US but spent decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. He is also devoted to that country, where he became a citizen and which he considers an adopted home.
“Cancelling would have meant … sending a certain message that this (surgery) has been a real rupture in this pontificate,” Massimo Faggioli, a papal historian, told Reuters.
“The message is now, ‘No, that health crisis is over. And I can do it,’” said Faggioli, a professor at Villanova University, near Philadelphia, where Leo earned one of his diplomas.
Elise Allen, author of a biography of the pope for Penguin Peru, said his decision “shows an incredible determination to continue with the mission that he believes has been entrusted to him by God.”
FOREIGN TRIPS NOW INTEGRAL PART OF PAPACY
Travelling abroad has become a major part of the modern papacy, with popes seeking to meet local Catholics, spread the faith, and conduct international diplomacy.
They often draw large crowds, and officials in Argentina have estimated that some seven million people will attend events with Leo over his three days in that country.
Making foreign trips has become an integral part of being pope, said Faggioli. “That has become the real test of the papacy, if you can do exhausting trips or not,” he said. “The papacy is … a global job and you have to be there in person.”
Leo’s November 6-17 South America tour is set to be one of the most intense taken by a pope in decades. He is scheduled to travel some 31,000 km (19,300 miles) over the 10-city tour and give 36 speeches.
The Vatican said on Monday that the pope was fit for the trip, citing Leo’s personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone.
Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, said the risks of complications for the pope related to the surgery now appear “quite low.”
He said that Leo being cleared to fly by his doctors should indicate that his operated lung has fully expanded and any surgical wounds are healing without signs of infection.
“My primary advice for patients in this situation is not to push themselves too far and to listen to their body when it asks for rest,” Liu told Reuters.
“I would expect his team would primarily be watching for any signs of exhaustion” during the trip, said the doctor.
CATHOLICS WILL WATCH TRIP CLOSELY
Leo is recovering from surgery two weeks ago in which doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung to treat lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The pope’s doctors said last week that further examinations of the tissue removed in the operation had confirmed the cancer was localized and he would not require any further ongoing cancer treatments.
The Vatican said on Monday the trip would go forward with no changes to the previously planned itinerary, which includes 12 flights and two helicopter trips.
The Vatican press office did not immediately respond to questions about whether there would be any additional emergency planning for the trip or additional medical personnel added to the tour.
“It is very intense and I think the risks are very real,” said Allen, the only journalist to interview Leo since his May 2025 election. “But obviously, Leo is confident in how he’s feeling and his medical team is confident in what they’re seeing.”
Faggioli said he expects Catholics across the world will be watching the trip closely, to see how Leo is faring.
“Everyone will look at every speech he gives, every hand he shakes,” said the academic. “This decision will keep some people, as we say in Italian, ‘sulle spine’ (on tenterhooks).”
(Reporting by Joshua McElwee, editing by Keith Weir)

GUWAHATI, India, Oct 27 (Reuters) - India has deployed hundreds of additional security personnel in its remote northeast, authorities said on Tuesday, after youth protesters clashed with police last week over a plan to build a mega-dam to counter a Chinese hydropower project upstream.
Protests in Arunachal Pradesh’s Siang Valley, which borders Tibet, turned violent last week, triggering clashes with police, who made at least 21 arrests.
Police fired tear gas shells, while youth protesters pelted stones and set fire to a police station and an office of the state-owned National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, authorities said.

Villagers who oppose the project fear that the dam would submerge ancestral villages belonging to the Adi tribe.
“We will keep opposing this dam till they cancel it. If it is constructed, 27 of our ancestral villages will be completely submerged. At least 40 or 50 more will be affected,” Gegong Jijong of the Siang Indigenous Farmers’ Forum told Reuters.
The Siang river flows into Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet, where it is known as the Yarlung Zangbo. China announced plans in December 2024 to build the world’s largest hydropower dam upstream, triggering fears in New Delhi that its longtime strategic rival could weaponise its control of the river.
China claims Arunachal Pradesh, which it calls Zangnan, as part of southern Tibet. India says the state is an integral and inalienable part of its territory.
Arunachal Pradesh’s chief minister, a member of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, has called the Chinese project an existential threat and said the government would protect national interests while respecting the rights and aspirations of the people of Siang Valley.

ATHENS, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Egypt, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates aligned with Greece to denounce a Turkey-Libya maritime accord as a threat to regional security and international legal order in a long-standing dispute over sea borders in the eastern Mediterranean Sea.
Libya’s eastern parliament last week approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey, originally agreed in 2019, drawing swift condemnation from Greece and Cyprus, which say it infringes on their own maritime claims.
In a joint statement delivered by Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis at the United Nations in New York on Monday, Greece and the three Arab countries said the maritime accord raised “serious concerns for regional security and stability” and could set a bad precedent by allowing “arbitrary bilateral arrangements” to undermine established rules of international law.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday that reactions from the European Union and others to the approval of the agreement had no legitimate basis, defending Ankara’s policy in the eastern Mediterranean.
The Arab support to Greece signals efforts to turn a bilateral dispute into a broader regional push for respect of maritime rules, increasing diplomatic pressure on Turkey and Libya over maritime zones and future energy projects in the Mediterranean Sea.
Since the 2019 Libya-Turkey deal, Greece has awarded a Chevron -led consortium a licence to look for gas off the island of Crete and has sought a separate agreement with Libya on demarcating their maritime zones.
Gerapetritis said on Monday that Athens stood ready to continue the effort and called on Libya to foster good relations with neighbours in line with maritime rules as part of a political transition.
Libya broke apart into rival eastern and western administrations more than a decade ago during a civil war after a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.
The Libya-Turkey accord was agreed by Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in the west, but the rival eastern administration under military commander Khalifa Haftar had withheld its approval for years.
Turkish support was crucial to repelling an assault by Haftar’s forces on Tripoli in 2019-2020.
But relations have steadily improved in recent years, with Turkish officials paying regular visits to Haftar’s de facto capital, Benghazi, and investing heavily in construction and other sectors.

Iraq revives shipping line after 50 years as Hormuz crisis bites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:37:29 UTC
20:37:29 KST

Breadcrumb
After 50 years, Iraq revives national shipping line as Hormuz crisis drives up costs
Iraq has resumed operations on its national commercial shipping line after more than five decades, as rising freight and insurance costs linked to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz place growing pressure on the country's import-dependent economy.
The relaunch marks an attempt by Baghdad to restore its presence in regional maritime trade, reduce reliance on foreign shipping companies and expand transport options for Iraqi businesses.
The General Company for Maritime Transport, which operates under Iraq's Ministry of Transport, announced on Monday that the vessel Basra had arrived at Umm Qasr port carrying containers from Jebel Ali port in the United Arab Emirates.
The voyage marked the first step towards reviving the Iraqi Line, the country's national commercial shipping service, which had been inactive for more than 50 years.
Ahmed Jassim, director-general of the company, said the resumption would provide traders and importers with additional shipping options while strengthening commercial links between Iraqi and Emirati ports.
He added that the initiative formed part of wider efforts to develop Iraq's national maritime carrier and expand its role in regional and international trade.
The transport ministry announced on 5 October that the shipping line was preparing to resume commercial operations, noting that its last voyages dated back to the mid-1960s.
The ministry also said Iraq's ports had a combined annual handling capacity exceeding 79 million tonnes and a container capacity of more than 3.6 million containers, with measures underway to ease congestion and improve roads and storage facilities.
However, Iraq's national fleet currently consists of just six vessels, raising questions about whether the revived service can compete with established international shipping operators.
Hormuz disruptions drive up shipping costs
The relaunch comes as instability in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime route connecting the Gulf to international markets, has increased freight and insurance costs and disrupted delivery schedules.
Jassim al-Moussawi, a member of Iraq's parliamentary Oil and Gas Committee, said developing the national fleet had become increasingly important as regional tensions drove up transport costs.
Speaking to The New Arab, Moussawi said Iraq needed a larger fleet of nationally owned vessels to reduce its dependence on foreign companies.
He estimated that transport costs had risen sharply because of regional disruptions, reaching almost half the value of exported oil, according to his calculations.
Expanding Iraq's maritime transport capacity could save the state treasury millions of dollars, he argued, by reducing freight and insurance expenses and improving the country's ability to respond to disruptions in international shipping.
Iraqi trader Halim Hamid also welcomed the reopening of the route between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr, describing it as an opportunity to provide importers with more shipping options.
"The resumption of the line between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr represents a positive step towards expanding shipping options for importers, particularly following the rise in freight and insurance costs and delays in the arrival of goods caused by the Hormuz disruptions," he told TNA.
Hamid said fluctuations in shipping costs and unreliable delivery schedules were affecting the price of imported goods in Iraqi markets.
He added that an effective national carrier could increase competition with foreign companies, provided it offered competitive rates, reliable sailing schedules and efficient customs clearance.
"The success of the line depends on providing integrated services covering booking, transport, unloading and delivery according to clear schedules," he said.
Traders, he stressed, make shipping decisions based on overall costs and reliability rather than the nationality of the carrier.
While expanding the service could gradually reduce import costs, Hamid cautioned that it would not necessarily lead to an immediate fall in consumer prices without sufficient shipping capacity and competitive logistics services.
Can Iraq's shipping revival deliver economic gains?
Economists say the return of the national shipping line could help Iraq develop an additional source of non-oil revenue by capturing a greater share of the country's substantial import and freight market.
Economic expert Karim al-Hilu said Iraq's heavy reliance on foreign shipping operators presented an opportunity for domestic companies to expand their role in maritime transport and logistics.
Citing Ministry of Planning figures, Hilu said Iraq imported approximately 23.46 million tonnes of goods through its ports in 2025, an increase of 10.5% from the previous year.
Despite the growth in cargo volumes, revenues at the General Company for Maritime Transport fell by 10.9% to 213 billion Iraqi dinars ($163 million), highlighting a gap between expanding trade activity and the earnings of the national carrier.
Iraq's merchandise imports totalled approximately $72.3 billion in 2025, including $49.3 billion transported through seaports, according to Hilu.
He said the figures demonstrated the potential for greater investment in shipping, warehousing, maintenance and other port-related services, which could create jobs and generate more economic value domestically.
However, Hilu warned that reviving the national line would require a carefully planned commercial strategy, particularly given the small size of Iraq's fleet and competition from international operators.
"Unplanned expansion could turn the project into a financial burden rather than a sustainable source of revenue," he said, calling for a clear operational and investment plan to ensure economic viability and strengthen the national carrier's regional competitiveness.

====================================================================================================

Israeli ad tech company targeted Starlink internet users in suspected attempt at espionage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:35:43 UTC
20:35:43 KST

Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company heavily targeted users of Starlink's satellite internet service, likely to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro, concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX's Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.
The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI's telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted. Bidding refers to the complex auction system advertisers use to secure space inside people's browsers and apps.
SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two weeks.
TrendAI released a report on October 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79.” The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.
TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding "hype-driven labels" or "unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions."
Finding ways to track Starlink users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals. Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas, or coordinate action across battlefields. Starlink has become a particularly important resource in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service for frontline communications and directing drone strikes.
In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process.
Canadian watchdog, New York ad tech firm, name Discover-Tech
The same day TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology firm Confiant named Discover-Tech.
Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad-bidding process, which can leak internet-user data back to the bidder.
Over time, bidders can collect that leaked data, collate it, and merge it with other information to de-anonymize users, follow them around the web and, in some cases, set them up for targeting with surveillance software.
Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads had been shown inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organizations, governments and tech firms.
In response to the investigations, Google, Comcast, and other companies said they had removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms.
At least one big US tech company and one international organization recently launched internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech's ads targeted their employees, according to one of the people and a seventh person familiar with the matter.
TrendAI's report cited suspicious bidding patterns that suggested Shadow-Earth-79 was running "targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation."
In addition to noting the "obvious skew" towards buying ads aimed at Starlink users, the report said that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top buyer of ads in Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan and was the No. 2 ad buyer in Afghanistan even though "the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero." It said the entity won "an implausibly dominant share" of bids in several countries including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan, and Venezuela.
Researchers drop plan to name Discover-Tech in suspicions due to legal concerns
TrendAI researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind the suspicious bidding activity and discussed naming the company in TrendAI's report, according to the six people familiar with the matter. But they eventually dropped the idea of publicly attributing the activity to a named company after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of the sources said.
Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say.
Earlier this year, US cybersecurity company Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign even though its researchers were confident the hacking could be pinned on Beijing, Reuters reported at the time. Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that calling out China would harm Palo Alto's operations there, which were already under scrutiny after a Beijing directive ordered domestic companies not to use its products. Palo Alto said the lack of attribution in its report was not correlated with "procurement regulations in China" and that any suggestion otherwise was "speculative and false."

Right-leaning voters in Jerusalem share core values for future gov't but split over who should lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:35:10 UTC
20:35:10 KST

Security, religion, and loyalty remain the core values Jerusalem residents shared as they prepared to vote in the 26th Knesset elections, with opinions sharply split over whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should remain prime minister.
The Jerusalem Post recently conducted street interviews at Shuk Mahane Yehuda and on Ben Yehuda Street in the city, where residents were asked who they plan to vote for in the elections and their reasons behind the choice.
These individuals dictate the fate of the political dynamic of the country for the next four years. All voters interviewed leaned right, but were split over which party should lead. The interviewees were randomized and remained completely anonymous, with their gender being the only characteristic recorded.
In a tight race, with the opposition widening its lead, Yashar party head Gadi Eisenkot remains ahead of Netanyahu. About 60% of Israelis favor a unity government, though votes shifting between right-wing parties could decide whether the bloc reaches 61 seats.
Many people in Jerusalem said they feel strongly loyal to Netanyahu. Two voters said they would vote to re-elect him, saying, “He is a great ally to America, America is a great ally to him,” and that “his policies are the right ones to follow.”
Many citizens, however, remained unsure about who to vote for and said they are relying on their families to influence their decisions.
A woman in Nachlaot, who said she wants a government that “supports Torah learning” and "lower prices," admitted that “we love Netanyahu, but I don't understand too much politics, so I'm not sure, I have to ask my husband what exactly we are doing”
With 120 seats in the Knesset, and 61 needed to govern, the gap between Israel's coalition and opposition blocs has widened to six seats ahead of Tuesday's Knesset election, despite the two largest parties being separated by just two seats, according to a Maariv poll by Lazar Research published Friday.
Several people said they resent Netanyahu and the current government and are voting for his rivals, with one man saying, “probably something not in the current government. I'm not sure I can explain, to be honest. I don't like part of their attitude.”
Another female supporter of former prime minister Naftali Bennett said that “the list of people that are with him are going to do good for the country and want to make good rules in Israel.”
“He really cares about the country and not about populism or making money for himself,” she added.
Current voter turnout expected to surpass that of 2022 election
The Maariv poll also found that the proportion of Israelis who are certain they will vote in Tuesday's Knesset election continued to rise, reaching 81%. The figure suggests a potential increase in voter turnout compared with the 2022 election, when turnout stood at 71%.
In 2022, Likud won about 23% of the vote, Yesh Atid about 17.79%, and the Religious Zionist Party 10.84%, according to the official Knesset website.
Voters backing a different right-wing party believe that their religious values feel aligned with those of certain parties such as Shas and RZP, both of which are “good for the religious people, the Haredi people,” according to the people of Jerusalem.
Two individuals said they will vote for Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich for a multitude of reasons:
“I think I want to vote Smotrich because I'm part of the party... and I believe in the same values, and I think it's the best way for Israel, for the next [few] years,” said one interviewee.
“One of them [the reasons] is bitachon (security). It's a bit funny, but he has that I believe in it. Also, I come from the Religious Zionist community, so he gives me things that I believe in and helps me with what I need,” said another.
Many people prioritize safety and security, and the street interview data reports one man in Mahane Yehuda voting for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for these exact reasons. Additionally, many people say their rabbis advise them not to share who they plan to vote for.
'Just not Bibi'
This week’s Maariv poll shows that, nationally, support for the coalition appears to be slipping, and the coalition bloc has weakened by three seats compared with the previous week's poll. In the last days before the vote, akin to the previous poll, 60% of Israelis would prefer the formation of a unity government if the Knesset election produces no clear result.
Some voters interviewed in Jerusalem reflected that shift. “I just know I don’t want Bibi,” said a woman in Mahane Yehuda who is leaning toward Bennett, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.
Most, however, said they would back parties in the current coalition, and their answers focused on a right-wing government rather than a unity one. “For sure we want right wing,” said a woman in Nachlaot.

Lithuanian conservative leader proposes universal conscription from 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:35:00 UTC
20:35:00 KST

Lithuania should introduce universal military conscription from 2030, opposition Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas said Tuesday as he registered legislative amendments proposing an overhaul of the country’s draft system.
Kasčiūnas and a majority of the party’s parliamentary group proposed replacing the annual conscription quota and lottery system with mandatory initial military service for nearly everyone on the annual draft list from January 1, 2030.
Under the proposal, young men would be subject to mandatory conscription, while women could serve voluntarily. Exemptions would apply to people excused from service, those granted individual deferments, and certain final-year students and vocational trainees studying for professions in short supply in the armed forces. The option of alternative service would remain.
The Defence Ministry’s draft list for this year included 42,556 young people, of whom 5,000 were scheduled to be called up.
Kasčiūnas said the proposed changes would require a fundamental review of the conscription system to reflect the changing nature of warfare and the military’s staffing needs.
“We propose to conduct a very serious review of the conscription concept, related to the fact that new warfare requires new approaches to drafting,” he said. “Take drone operators, for instance. Perhaps sometimes strong physical training is not required if a clear drone operator training program can be opened.”
He added that the armed forces could adopt more flexible approaches to training personnel for different roles and assess whether everyone needed to serve in barracks under the traditional model.
Kasčiūnas said the priority should be to establish a new system before determining the additional funding it would require.
“We need to start primarily with the system, with the concept of how it should work, and then see how much it might cost,” he said. “I believe we can really move from talk to decisions now.”
If the amendments are adopted but preparations fall behind schedule, the transition period could be extended, he said. However, he argued that lawmakers should approve the legislation and set a hard implementation deadline rather than continue debating the issue indefinitely.
Kasčiūnas acknowledged that the conservatives failed to introduce universal conscription when they headed the government between 2020–2024. However, they adopted amendments allowing more conscripts to be called up and established a military commandant system, which he described as a transitional model that revealed both strengths and weaknesses in the existing system.
“The times and the political situation also require it,” he said, arguing that Lithuania needed to move to a new stage of military preparedness.
Defence officials support expansion
Lithuania’s military leadership has also outlined plans to expand conscription in the coming years.
Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras said the armed forces aimed to draft “nearly everyone who is willing and able” by 2030 and increase the number of conscripts to 7,000-8,000 through different forms of military service.
Conscripts currently serve for nine months, although an option introduced this year allows mandatory service to be completed in three, six or nine months.
School graduates aged 18–22 are also being called up, with their numbers expected to increase annually. Some politicians have described the measure as a step toward universal conscription.
In mid-September, the National Universal Defence Coordination Council, chaired by President Gitanas Nausėda, announced that it would propose accelerating the introduction of universal conscription.
Nausėda has said the transition to universal conscription is only a matter of time as Lithuania establishes a national division. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has also said the country is moving toward universal conscription but must first make the necessary preparations.
Public support for the proposal appears substantial. A survey commissioned by the Universal Defence association in August found that nearly 80% of the population supported introducing universal conscription, with priority given to drafting men.

Just under 270,000 people on welfare in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:35:00 UTC
20:35:00 KST

Just under 270,000 people on welfare in Switzerland
Just under 270,000 people received social assistance in Switzerland in 2025. The social assistance rate stood at 2.9%, which is in line with the previous year’s figure.
The number of people receiving social assistance thus rose by 4.5% compared with the previous year, as the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) announced on Tuesday. As in previous years, children and young people had the highest rate of social assistance among all age groups, at 4.8%. The FSO noted that the rate decreases steadily with age.
The highest social assistance rates by region were recorded in several cantons in French-speaking Switzerland and in Basel City. Rural cantons in Central and Eastern Switzerland, as well as the cantons of Fribourg, Graubünden and Valais, recorded lower rates. These differences are linked, among other things, to regional economic and demographic structures, as well as to the particular pressures faced by urban centres, the report added.
More
How Swiss welfare works
Single parents
In a separate study published on Tuesday, single parents in Swiss towns and cities are more likely than average to rely on social assistance. This is shown by the key figures report by the Urban Initiative on Social Policy.
In many towns, around a quarter of single-parent households with children under the age of 18 receive social assistance. The risk of poverty for single-parent households is almost five times higher than that for all households.
Many single parents receive social assistance on top of their wages because their earnings are not sufficient to support their families. The report identifies education and training, suitable childcare and supplementary family benefits as effective forms of support.
Every year, the City Initiative compares social assistance figures across 14 cities. Last year, the social assistance rate stood at 3.9%, slightly below the previous year’s figure. Overall, social assistance figures remained stable.

France Unveils RAVEN Mine-Hunting Underwater Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:32:41 UTC
20:32:41 KST

French company SEABER has unveiled the RAVEN autonomous underwater drone, designed to detect naval mines.
Bretagne Économique reported the system’s capabilities, citing the manufacturer.
During mine countermeasure operations, RAVEN can survey potentially mined areas and record the coordinates of suspicious objects. Divers or specialized underwater vehicles can then use this information to inspect and neutralize the mines.
RAVEN can be equipped with a side-scan sonar, which generates acoustic images of the seabed.
SEABER offers two variants of the underwater drone. The SCAN-MAG version includes a magnetometer to detect and locate metallic objects underwater.
The other version, SCAN-LUMEN, is equipped with a high-resolution camera and a lighting system that outputs 24,000 lumens. This equipment enables visual inspection of previously detected objects and helps determine their nature.
The RAVEN weighs 13 kilograms, measures 131–137 centimeters in length, and has a 12-centimeter hull diameter. It can dive to depths of up to 300 meters, reach speeds of 3–6 knots, and operate autonomously for up to eight hours. Only one operator is required to deploy it into the water.
One of the drone’s key features is SEABER’s proprietary LYNX inertial navigation system, which operates in conjunction with a Doppler velocity log (DVL) that measures speed relative to the seabed. The manufacturer claims a cumulative positioning error of less than 0.2% of the distance traveled during straight-line navigation.
Before diving, the drone determines its position using a dual-antenna satellite navigation receiver, which the manufacturer claims offers enhanced resistance to radio-frequency interference.
An acoustic modem provides underwater communication, enabling command transmission and vehicle tracking at distances of up to 2–3 kilometers. When operating on the surface, the drone uses a UHF radio link and Iridium satellite communications. Infrared lights, visible through night-vision devices, provide visibility in darkness.
According to company president Vidal Teixeira, SEABER aims to offer capabilities comparable to expensive autonomous underwater vehicles at about one-third the cost. However, the manufacturer has not disclosed the RAVEN’s specific price, its first customers, or the expected start of deliveries. Overall, the company reports having sold more than 200 unmanned vehicles of various models on the international market.
Militarnyi previously reported that Ukrainian naval personnel had practiced detecting and neutralizing naval mines using SeaFox underwater vehicles during exercises in the United Kingdom.

The Israeli army continued a large-scale offensive in the West Bank city of Hebron for a fifth consecutive day on Tuesday, forcing nearly 5,000 Palestinians from their homes, Anadolu reports.

Among those displaced are 336 infants, 441 elderly people, 216 pregnant and nursing women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people suffering from chronic illnesses, the statement said.
The municipality said the figures document families forced out from their homes since the start of the Israeli campaign amid growing humanitarian consequences, particularly for people requiring special care.
The army has shut all entrances to Hebron and surrounding villages since Friday following a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.
Anadolu footage showed Palestinians being stopped, searched and mistreated by Israeli forces at military checkpoints near Al-Jilda Roundabout.
Witnesses said new military reinforcements also arrived in Ein Deir Baha, where Israeli forces have taken over several Palestinian buildings and turned them into military posts.
According to the Palestinian Prisoner Society, the Israeli army has arrested 85 Palestinians across Hebron governorate since Friday.
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces arrested at least nine Palestinians in military raids and closed all main entrances to Ramallah.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli forces raided the eastern neighborhood of Jenin as well as the towns of Meithalun, Jaba and Qabatiya, arresting at least six Palestinians, according to local sources.
A Palestinian man was detained during a raid on Aqraba, southeast of Nablus, while Israeli forces stormed the southern Al-Hawouz area of Qaffin in Tulkarm governorate and raided a home in the town’s western neighborhood.
In the central West Bank, Israeli forces closed all main entrances to Ramallah, including the Ein Sinya and Atara checkpoints, the Rawabi gate and the Nabi Saleh and Aboud gates, and set up additional checkpoints on alternative roads.

In Hebron governorate, Israeli forces also repeatedly raided the town of Taffuh and searched the homes of former prisoners.
Israeli troops assaulted a Palestinian man in the Hawara area south of Hebron before arresting him and his son, according to local sources.

“Confrontations broke out between residents and the attackers, forcing the occupiers to withdraw,” he said.
“Umm Safa has repeatedly come under attack by Israeli occupiers involving assaults on residents, vehicle arson, intimidation and harassment,” Sabah said.
He added that occupiers have seized large areas of the village’s land.
Israeli occupiers also established a settlement outpost at the northern entrance to Al-Bireh overlooking the Al-Balou neighborhood, the Bedouin rights group Al-Baidar said.
According to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli occupiers attempted to establish 21 new settlement outposts across the West Bank in September, including 10 in Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorate.
The incidents come amid intensified Israeli army raids and attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.
