Trump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:00:38 UTC
20:00:38 KST

Sweeping cuts to the premier US climate agency under Donald Trump have severely hampered the country’s capacity to forecast, research and respond to extreme weather events, former government officials and scientists have warned, as the US faces a cascade of hazards fueled by a potentially historic El Niño this winter.
From the start of his second term, the president has taken aim at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), slashing staff levels, canceling contracts and grants, and shutting down databases and research laboratories. The agency that has long been considered a global crown jewel in climate science and forecasting has lost roughly 20% of its staff since January 2025.
The National Weather Service, which is housed within Noaa, has also taken a hit. Weather stations have had to delay data collection and cut operating hours, with hundreds of meteorological and other technical positions still vacant across its 122 forecast offices.
The effects have already been felt at Noaa, where a chaotic and volatile environment has sent morale plummeting, increased burnout and hampered vital work. While capacity has quietly unravelled, a large-scale disaster will quickly expose the most dangerous gaps.
“The system has not really been tested since all the cuts happened,” said Tom Di Liberto, a former Noaa climate scientist who now works as the media director of Climate Central.
That test could soon be coming.
This year’s super El Niño, a climate phenomenon characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the ability to fuel extreme weather events around the world. It’s already climbing off the charts and is expected to strengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter.
Along with dangerous spikes in temperature, El Niño will supercharge storms in parts of the American west, raise sea levels in California by up to a foot, and set the stage for debris flows, landslides and flash floods.
“Whether we as a country can handle the kind of coast-to-coast extremes that could potentially happen this winter is a big question,” Di Liberto said.
Noaa plays a pivotal role in public safety and provides key insights and forecasts relied upon by a vast array of communities and industries, from weather shifts that could affect crop schedules, to emergency response preparations when hurricanes are brewing or fire conditions are aligning. The agency operates early warning systems for tsunamis, monitors seafood supply chains and provides ocean data needed for safe shipping and port operators.
While the losses are expected to have a profound effect on the American public, they will be felt globally, too. Scientists and forecasters around the world depend on Noaa satellites, studies and intelligence, including data-sharing arrangements that track severe weather across Europe, coordination for disaster response in the Caribbean, and deforestation monitoring and the effects of the climate crisis in the Amazon rainforest.
“I worry about loss of life and about our inability to be protected at a time when we need our government the most,” said Monica Medina, who served as the principal deputy administrator of Noaa during the Obama administration.
The risks are but a taste of what’s to come as the world warms. “If this is a real test” of a hotter, more precarious future, she added, “we’re going to flunk”.
Budget and research cuts
Gaps in staffing, operations and engagement with the public are the top three concerns for Rick Spinrad, who spent three decades at the agency and served as Noaa administrator for the Biden administration.
The agency was already shorthanded in those areas when Trump took office, according to Spinrad. But since January 2025, Noaa has lost more than 3,000 staffers, according to workforce data from the US office of personnel management that was last updated in August this year.
It’s the biggest staffing drop in the last decade, and includes hundreds of people who lost their jobs during massive layoffs or who took incentives to retire or resign as the administration worked to systemically shrink the size of the federal government last year, along with those who left voluntarily.
Some departments have been hit harder than others.
The public affairs team that helps disseminate important information was roughly halved. Information technology management workers, who provide vital support for forecasting and data infrastructure among other things, were reduced by roughly 27%. The data showed a loss of more than 500 staffers across a range of science positions with only 46 new hires.
There were also about 10% fewer meteorologists and meteorology technicians as the US went into autumn this year, even after the National Weather Service rushed to staff up in the aftermath of the Trump administration’s massive 2025 layoffs.
The NWS analyzes and collects roughly 6.3bn observations each day. They release 1.5m forecasts and up to 50,000 warnings each year. Cracks have begun to show as the agency has tried to takes on its enormous and essential workload with fewer people.
Staffers had to work double shifts to keep some forecasting offices open, the Washington Post reported last September. Staffers who spoke to the Post at the time described an agency pushed to its limits.
Only 40 meteorologists were added to the ranks across Noaa between January and August this year, with hundreds of vacancies across the country still open as a tumultuous winter approaches.
Overall, the agency was able to bring on just 525 new hires since January 2025, leaving a gaping 2,500-person deficit.
Already, staffing limitations have shown up in delayed or limited weather balloon launches that left parts of the Great Plains unprepared for tornadoes and limited warnings to rural communities in Alaska, where more than 1,500 people were displaced by floods earlier this year. The NWS also failed to adequately provide multilingual weather alerts due to staffing and funding cuts, the government accountability office (GAO) found, leaving 26 million people in the US at higher risk.
“There has been this hollowing out – there’s no time to do anything other than the very basics,” said Dr Anna Zivian, a climate researcher and policy expert. “I suspect we haven’t seen the worst outcomes from the loss of capacity yet. You can’t pick up that kind of slack.”
Meanwhile, the Trump administration terminated dozens of grants representing a loss in more than $28m in funding for states, cities, non-profits and universities, according to calculations from Grant Witness, an organization that tracks science-related grant making by the federal government. Climate research has been the most affected, according to their analysis, which found that the number of grant awards in fiscal year 2026 was 37% lower than the 2021-2024 average.
Despite these concerns, the administration has outlined more plans to slash budgets and research capacity.
Trump has proposed cutting $1.6bn in Noaa funding – a 26% drop – for next year’s budget. While many of the cuts won’t make it through the budget process, they showcase how the president views the essential services the agency provides the American public and puts more pressure on the staff still working at Noaa.
“People at Noaa are nervous,” Di Liberto said, adding that employees across the organization were afraid they would get in trouble if they said something that conflicted with the administration’s anti-climate narrative.
“You want people doing their best work when we face these extremes,” he said. Denials of human-caused climate crisis coming from the top have only made their jobs harder, as scientists and forecasters work to put urgent information into context for the American public and others around the world.
“It’s incredibly difficult,” Di Liberto said. “Imagine being told the number six doesn’t exist and then being asked to do math.”
A missed learning opportunity
An El Niño year can be high risk, but it’s also an incredible chance to learn and prepare, offering a glimpse of what the world might expect as temperatures rise. In that regard, experts worry a shrunken Noaa is missing a vital research opportunity.
“This El Niño is so useful in a sense of getting an understanding about where we stand for dealing with extreme weather around the world,” Di Liberto said. “Unfortunately we’re going to learn a lot this winter about our ability to deal with multiple extremes happening at the same time.”
He and other experts have also expressed concerns that not enough has been done to ready communities for the coming hazards or capture important data that will inform the future. “When it comes to preparing for El Niño events – or any weather extreme – the preparation happens during the off season,” he said.
During the last strong El Niño a decade ago, the agency deployed planes, weather balloons, unmanned aircraft and a research ship to collect data. This year, only “a handful of unmanned watercraft” will be deployed into the Pacific, NPR reported in September.
The Trump administration had also begun removing ocean monitoring systems that provide important data during El Niño, but restored them after widespread outcry from scientists, fishers and public officials.
Roughly $6bn has been shaved off an investment secured for weather satellites that would have propelled major advancements in future weather predictions. The sharp reduction could create a gap in satellite coverage, according to an analysis from the government accountability office, severely disrupting data.
Funding for a decade-long project to monitor the oceans using autonomous robotic devices called biogeochemical-argo floats – part of a global effort – will also expire at the end of October.
A Noaa spokesperson responded that efforts to monitor and collect data this year have built on past efforts by using “new, cutting-edge technologies” that were previously unavailable.
“NOAA has never been more equipped to study, prepare for and respond to an ENSO event [El Niño southern oscillation event],” a Noaa spokesperson said in an emailed statement that highlighted updated modeling tools and the use of uncrewed systems. “These advanced capabilities have allowed NOAA to streamline resources and study this year’s El Niño more effectively than ever before.”
Spinrad and other experts agreed that new technologies had helped advance data collection and improve forecasting ability.
“We are more capable than we have been in the past because of the developments in the technology, the satellites that we’re flying, the observing systems that we’ve put in place,” Spinrad said. “But everything that this administration is doing suggests that we cannot and will not sustain those capabilities. So the real question is – are we at a turning point now?”

Italy delays Ukraine military aid package ahead of US midterms: Report

2026-10-28

Necva Tastan Sevinc
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Italy’s latest military aid package for Ukraine remains on hold as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government awaits the outcome of next week’s US midterm elections, Italian daily La Repubblica reported Tuesday.
The 13th package is ready but has yet to receive final approval, the newspaper said, citing government sources. Italy’s previous aid shipment to Ukraine was last December, according to the report.
Rome had assured French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that it would approve the package by October, with missile deliveries expected by the end of the month.
However, the parliamentary committee overseeing intelligence services, known as Copasir, had not convened to examine the decree as of Monday evening.
The package includes Aster 30 air defense missiles sought by Ukraine to protect Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks.
The decree requires signatures from Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.
Crosetto and Tajani support approval, while some government sources suggested Giorgetti was hesitating over potential opposition from League leader Matteo Salvini, the report said.
The final decision rests with Meloni, and Crosetto had privately warned of a political obstacle that needed resolving.
Approval has already been delayed several times, with expectations shifting from July to September and then until after the League’s party congress.
Government sources now favor waiting for the US midterm elections next Tuesday to assess Washington’s future approach and adjust Italy’s position accordingly.
Domestic political considerations are also contributing to the delay, including opposition to arms supplies from former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte and concerns about giving political momentum to Roberto Vannacci.
Italian officials have informally asked their Ukrainian counterparts to remain patient, according to the report.

Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic or existential' AI risks in IPO filing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:00:16 UTC
20:00:16 KST

Efe Ozkan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
US artificial intelligence company Anthropic warned Monday that its technology could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," citing concerns about increasingly autonomous AI systems that may act unpredictably or resist human oversight.
The company behind the Claude AI model issued the warning in a registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission ahead of its planned initial public offering (IPO).
The filing contains more than 90 pages of risk factors, accounting for roughly one-third of the document.
Anthropic said its AI models could behave unexpectedly, act autonomously in ways that conflict with human values and carry out harmful actions without being explicitly instructed to do so.
The company also warned that AI models, including its own, have demonstrated unexpected self-preserving behavior, such as resisting attempts to shut them down.
In some cases, models have generated responses resembling manipulation or blackmail of human users in attempts to remain operational, according to the filing.
Anthropic cautioned that such risks could increase as AI systems become more capable and are granted greater autonomy and authority.
It highlighted potential dangers in high-risk sectors, including health care, scientific research, law and government, where unintended model behavior could cause serious harm.
The company said it and other researchers had raised concerns that advanced AI systems could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" if deployed without adequate safeguards.
Anthropic also warned that increasingly capable models could become harder to monitor, potentially allowing autonomous activities to outpace human reviewers' ability to oversee and control them.

Mecca Agreement aims to strengthen regional security, Turkish official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:00:12 UTC
20:00:12 KST

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan aims to strengthen regional security through cooperation and collective defence, the Turkish deputy foreign minister said on Tuesday.
“The Mecca agreement is not only an extension of the special friendly relations between the three countries, but also a concrete product of the regional ownership increasingly needed in our region,” Ambassador Levent Gumrukcu told the Turkish Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee.
Gumrukcu submitted the agreement for approval by the committee and the Turkish parliament, as lawmakers continued their deliberations on the proposed legislation.
He recalled that the agreement was signed in Mecca on August 7 by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
He said Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had completed their domestic ratification procedures and submitted the required official notifications.
Gumrukcu said the agreement marked an initial step toward establishing a regional security framework based on cooperation and collective defence, adding that the three countries aimed to take responsibility for addressing regional challenges rather than waiting for solutions from outside the region.
He said the framework was intended to contribute not only to the security of the three signatories but also to that of the wider region by strengthening dialogue and cooperation based on mutual trust and promoting lasting stability.
Deal 'envisions integration rather than bloc-building in region'
Gumrukcu stressed that the agreement was entirely defensive in nature and did not target any country.
He said it was open to all regional countries that respect international law, including the principles of state sovereignty and territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force except in self-defence, the peaceful settlement of disputes and non-interference in internal affairs.
"The agreement envisions integration rather than bloc-building in the region, embracing an inclusive rather than divisive vision," he added.
Defence cooperation and NATO commitments
Gumrukcu said the agreement envisaged strengthening collective deterrence, holding regular consultations on international security issues, and improving interoperability between the countries' armed forces through personnel exchanges, joint training programs, and military exercises.
It also provides for closer defence industry cooperation, including joint production and technology sharing, stronger joint counterterrorism efforts, and logistical support between the parties in implementing the agreement, he said.
The deputy foreign minister emphasised that the agreement would neither replace nor undermine Türkiye's obligations under its existing alliances and agreements.
He said the initiative was expected to complement Türkiye's participation in multilateral platforms, particularly NATO, by contributing to security and stability across the broader Middle East and supporting European security in light of the interconnected nature of the two regions.

====================================================================================================

AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.
Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.
“I’m kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.
Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.
“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. “We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.
Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.
Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.
What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.
“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”
At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.
“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.
The two initial Direct feeds are aimed at corporate clients. The first, which launched this fall, gives the AI agents of Axios Pro Deals subscribers access to merger and acquisition content. The second feed will act as a source to train in-house large language models, and will launch next year.
Starting with feeds aimed at businesses makes sense. Corporate budgets tend to have more tolerance than individual subscribers for experiments, especially if these unproven concepts could offer even a slight business advantage. But the third Axios Direct feed, which the company plans to develop next year, will be consumer-facing—a way for individual subscribers to have Axios’ reporting sent directly to their agent. All three feeds will look similar to RSS feeds—not aesthetically pleasing, as they aren’t intended for the human eye, but instead taking the form of standardized lines of text.
While Axios is trimming its (already brief) content to satisfy AI, Every is taking a different approach. The six-year-old tech media and software company, which announced a $2 million funding round from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman last year, expects its subscribers to treat AI as almost an extension of themselves.
Every’s founder Dan Shipper says the most common way Every’s content differs from a typical article is that its writers include prompts in pieces whenever possible, allowing readers to test concepts themselves. An article about a new model, for example, includes a series of prompts the reader can copy-paste into AI, demonstrating how the model answers questions and evaluates input.
Certain types of articles—such as guides—also include buttons that readers can press to “Read With Claude” or “Read With ChatGPT.” Clicking pulls up a prompt, instructing AI to “Start with a tight summary: one paragraph, bulleted. Then offer to go deeper.” Writers pack stories with details without worrying about losing readers’ attention, knowing agents will pick out the most relevant bits.
Two years ago, the outlet launched its first “extendable” article: a long-form feature accompanied by a database of reporting, from interview recordings to news articles to YouTube videos. Readers could query a chatbot, which would fetch additional details from the database.
Recently, Every published a 8,000-word article about Codex that subscribers can consume in even more forms. Drawing from the database, subscribers’ agents can tailor a new piece—be it an article, podcast, or video—to suit their interests. One reader might want a bulleted summary, while another could request a short film of interview bits.
“As a writer, you have to make choices about what goes into the story you’re telling,” Shipper says. “And there’s always a question about, are those the right choices? Or, are those the right choices for a particular reader?” With AI, journalists no longer choose.
“People are gonna do crazy, crazy stuff with this,” Shipper adds.
As outlets eye AI agents as a new audience, another question looms: Can publishers actually make money off of this?
Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, a professor of communication at the University of Copenhagen, says that while the market of publishing for agents is “emerging,” it remains immature and “extremely uneven.” Major questions remain, he says, about price points and how AI agents will interact with content in the future.
Cameron and Allison Murphy, Axios’ chief operating officer, are optimistic about AI as an audience proxy. According to the executives, Axios’s short-form, highly structured style has already made the publisher a favorite for AI to pull from, when responding to prompts. “Time is money for crawlers,” Murphy says. “They don’t want to have to go three quarters down the page to find the main point. So, that’s something that’s already benefiting us.”
But does AI crawling its content actually benefit Axios’ bottom line? Even if readers don’t actually visit the Axios homepage, the brand visibility in and of itself can be positive, Nielsen says. It’s not unlike publishers making content for social platforms like TikTok and Instagram that rarely bring viewers back to their websites.
Publications in general are grappling with how difficult it has become to monetize certain types of content when a chatbot can offer up answers on a silver platter. People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have. At Every, that means in-the-weeds guidance on AI and how to use it; at Axios Pro Deals, it’s speedy access to information that could move the market. An all-access Axios Pro Deals subscription costs $2,499 a year, while an annual Every subscription costs $288.
Shipper sees that $288 as a subscription for a human reader, along with their agents. “I may not want to read all of your stuff every month,” Shipper says. But if his subscription can include his agent, “I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’”
Murphy says that Axios’ starting point is one of acceptance: People are already using AI to absorb information, and that more people will be doing so in the near future.
“I also try to make it a little less existentially terrifying by thinking, this isn’t the first time this has happened in media,” Murphy says. People get their news via social media, via short-form video, via podcasts. “It isn’t really AI as the audience,” Murphy adds. “It’s AI as a tool that helps us reach our audience.”

Following seven years of closure, Chatillon Architectes implements contemporary solutions and state-of-the-art facilities, bringing this distinctive building back to life, first as an Olympic training site and then for its subsequent return to the local community. The first images of the restored Grande Nef de l'Île-des-Vannes sports complex in Paris have been revealed ahead of its role as an Olympic training facility. UK and Poland strengthen defences on Europe's Eastern flank
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:59:30 GMT
19:59:30 KST

UK and Poland strengthen defences on Europe's Eastern flank
Britain will be more secure as a result of a new defence agreement with Poland designed to deter Russian threats.
The Warsaw Defence Plan comes as Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and his counterpart Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz today meet in Warsaw. Under the agreement, the two nations will work together across sea, land, air, cyber and industry to strengthen security and deterrence across Europe’s Eastern Flank.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:
  Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies - from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century.
The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.
From collaborating on NATO exercises that deter our adversaries to working together to support Ukraine in its fight for freedom, we are committed to standing together for European security whilst boosting our economies with stronger defence industries.
The agreement sets out the first phase of defence cooperation under the new UK-Poland Security and Defence Partnership Treaty and demonstrates the UK stepping up on European security to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.
It will strengthen joint work on defence between the UK and Poland across a number of key areas, including:
- Collaboration on the manufacture and development of the next generation of air defence missiles.
- Co-development of drone and counter-drone technologies to deter threats to civilians and critical national infrastructure, as Russia steps up its campaign of drone incursions across the UK and Europe.
- Boosting cooperation on cyber security and resilience to help both countries defend defence and civilian sites from hostile threats.
- Sharing lessons and experience from developing frigate capabilities, the British Type 31 and Polish Miecznik, which are built from a common design.
- Increasing defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea.
The UK and Poland will also work together to further strengthen cooperation between their defence industries through closer defence procurement coordination, building on major deals such as Poland’s procurement of its Narew air defence system from MBDA UK.
UK and Polish defence industrial partners BAE Systems and Poland’s PGZ will expand large-calibre ammunition production capacity and capability. More widely, both nations’ defence industries will collaborate to promote defence education, training and workforce mobility to build shared expertise.
Continued UK and Polish participation in large-scale exercises such as Steadfast Defender, Polish Dragon and Joint Warrior will also ensure both nations remain ready to respond to the conflicts of the future, including counter-drone warfare, electronic warfare, and missile defence.
It comes as the UK and Poland plan for a major Coalition of the Wiling exercise in Poland next month, which will see thousands of personnel take part to ensure the Multinational Force Ukraine is ready to support the military training and post-war rebuilding that Ukraine will need.

Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation issues recommendations for development of social services in Kyiv region based on new study
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:59:21 EET
19:59:21 KST

Currently, the most in-demand services include social support, home-based care, transportation, and social adaptation. This is according to the findings of a study conducted by the Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation in cooperation with Kyiv Regional State Administration as part of the Seeing the Invisible project. The results were presented at a press conference held at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Tuesday.
"There is plenty of work for everyone: state, municipal, and non-governmental organizations alike. As part of the Seeing the Invisible project, we carried out a comprehensive study. It involved approximately 100 social sector professionals and over 600 residents of Kyiv region," said Vladyslav Zhyliaiev, an advocacy specialist at the Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation.
According to him, the study’s results show that "the needs, as assessed by both residents and professionals, align very closely."
"I always say that if a person’s basic needs aren’t met, if they have nothing to eat, nothing to wear, or no way to pay for housing (which is especially true for internally displaced persons, or IDPs), then, unfortunately, we cannot even begin to discuss anything beyond that. That is why we keep urging the international community to focus on the needs of Kyiv region in particular, as it is in dire need of assistance," emphasized a representative from Caritas Kyiv.
"As the figures show, the region is constantly taking in internally displaced persons. It was one of the first to welcome them, and to this day, it continues to host the largest number. Consequently, while the needs are only set to grow, the available aid is shrinking; yet, we must continue to devote ever-greater attention to these internally displaced persons," he said.
Zhyliaev also noted that special attention should be paid to veterans and their families, families with children facing difficult life circumstances, children with disabilities, people with disabilities, and the elderly.
"What kind of services are needed most? These include social support, in-home care, material assistance, transportation services, social adaptation, supported living, and respite care. We can provide assistance to these families—who are in need—on several occasions, helping them overcome their difficult life circumstances and reach the level of stability they require," he emphasized.
According to the study, Zhyliaev pointed out, "the services that residents feel are most lacking include transportation, respite care, material assistance, social adaptation, and collaborative social work involving the non-governmental sector, municipal institutions, and the public sector."

Slovakia plans to develop cooperation with Russia in areas not covered by sanctions
Kyiv • UNN
Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár said after his visit to Moscow that cooperation with Russia would be developed outside the scope of international sanctions. The opposition called the trip a disgrace.
Slovakia plans to develop cooperation with the russian federation in areas not covered by international sanctions. The country’s Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár said this after his visit to moscow on October 26. Slovak opposition politicians criticized the trip. DW reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Juraj Blanár headed the Slovak delegation at the 22nd meeting of the bilateral intergovernmental commission on economic and scientific-technical cooperation. The previous meeting took place in 2021. The russian delegation was headed by the Minister of Science and Higher Education of the russian federation, valery falkov. During his visit, Blanár also met with russia’s Foreign Minister sergey lavrov.
"The parties discussed Slovakia’s energy security, bilateral relations with an emphasis on economic cooperation, as well as the war in Ukraine. In particular, Juraj Blanár stated that it was necessary to maintain dialogue with russia in order to resolve 'situations arising in connection with the European Commission’s decisions to abandon russian energy resources' by the end of 2027. The Slovak Foreign Ministry’s website emphasizes that lavrov assured Blanár that russia 'is still ready to fulfill its contractual obligations.' Commenting on the war in Ukraine, the Slovak minister said that representatives of the two countries understood how 'important it is to take into account the root causes of this conflict and actively support dialogue with all parties' in order to end it," the publication writes.
According to Blanár, lavrov called his proposal to hold 'preliminary talks at a lower level' in Bratislava 'acceptable.'
At the same time, according to available information, Blanár’s visit drew criticism from opposition politicians. In particular, Gábor Grendel, a representative of the conservative Nova party, called the trip an 'international disgrace' and demanded that the minister explain 'what exactly his trip to moscow gave the citizens of Slovakia.'
Meanwhile, former Slovak Foreign Minister Ivan Korčok, who represents the liberal Freedom and Solidarity party, called Blanár the 'gravedigger of Slovakia’s foreign policy.' According to him, Blanár intended to ask Lavrov for permission to increase the number of employees at the country’s embassy in moscow. Other representatives of the Slovak opposition had previously made similar assumptions.
"However, Blanár’s visit at the head of a delegation was not the first trip by high-ranking Slovak officials to Russia in recent times. On May 8, the country’s Prime Minister Robert Fico flew to moscow. On the eve of Victory Day, he laid flowers at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, and the following day met with Russian President vladimir putin. At the same time, Fico did not attend the parade on Red Square," the publication notes.
Background
The Slovak delegation arrived in moscow for talks on energy and Russian gas. Bratislava fears arbitration claims of up to €16 billion.

Polish far-right leader charged over confrontation with abortion doctor and inciting hatred against Jews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:59:04 UTC
19:59:04 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion.
The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections.
Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej
Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.…
— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026
As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges.
Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read.
In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges.
Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hannukah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”.
Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups.
Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison.
In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month.
The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher.
Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”.
For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term.
Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it.
Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition.
The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025
Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions.
In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”.
Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%.
If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition.

Tit-for-tat Sudan drone strikes kill 21, cause mass power outages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Retaliatory drone strikes between Sudan's warring factions killed at least 21 people in Darfur and caused widespread power outages in the east, witnesses and medics said Tuesday.
A drone strike on a market in Nyala, the de facto capital of Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Darfur, killed 21 people and wounded at least 40 others, a medical source and witnesses said.
One Nyala resident said a market in the city's north was struck by a drone on Monday around 8:00 p.m. (6 p.m. GMT).
Another said the market was frequented by young men, particularly Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters.
"Twenty-one people were killed in last night's bombing, and more than 40 others injured," a medic at Nyala Hospital said, though he was unable to identify how many were RSF fighters.
Sudan's military, at war with the RSF since April 2023, regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has declared an administration rivaling the army-backed internationally recognized government in Khartoum.
The RSF has in turn launched repeated strikes targeting Khartoum's airport, as well as dams and power stations across the country's east.
On Tuesday, "RSF militia drones targeted the Al-Markhiyat transformer station, disrupting the power supply across large parts of Khartoum and Al-Jazira states," a source in the national electricity company said on condition of anonymity.
The strike comes a day after a coordinated RSF drone attack on six power stations left millions without power in Al-Jazira, White Nile, Sennar and Gedaref states.
The war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks from across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October alone, drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a U.N. tally.
Since it began, the war has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate and has triggered the world's largest humanitarian crises.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people.
Close to 3 million people have returned to Khartoum state since it was recaptured by the army last year, but many have struggled to rebuild their lives in a scarred city.
Power and water supplies remain unreliable, much of the capital remains unsafe from unexploded bombs and many struggle to put food on the table in a collapsed economy.
On Monday, 30 countries including the United States, France and the United Kingdom warned that urgent action was needed to prevent famine expanding across the country.
Sudan is facing "an alarming deterioration" of food security, they said, citing the war, a currency in freefall, higher fuel prices due to the Middle East war and a drought induced by the El Nino climate phenomenon.
Sudan's Foreign Ministry Monday insisted the country's food security was "reassuring," in an attempt to "refute claims of famine."
It accused "some countries and organizations" of "politically exploiting the humanitarian situation."
The army has for years denied claims of documented famine and has been accused of blocking access to humanitarian aid.

Saab announces new Sea Giraffe AMB D radar
Saab introduces Sea Giraffe Agile Multi Beam D (AMB D), the latest evolution of its Giraffe AMB radar family, providing naval forces with enhanced 3D surveillance and tracking of air and surface targets in increasingly complex maritime environments.
Sea Giraffe AMB D can detect, track and classify aircraft, drones, missiles and crewed or uncrewed surface vessels, with a range of up to 250 km for air targets and 50 km for surface targets. It provides early warning and accurate target information to support decision-making in distributed, multi-domain operations, where reliable sensors are the foundation of operational advantage.
Designed for demanding maritime environments, the radar combines advanced Electronic Counter-Countermeasures (ECCM) capabilities against jamming attempts, with a modular architecture that enables integration with other naval systems. Its software-defined architecture also enables continuous upgrades as operational requirements evolve.
“Sea Giraffe AMB D takes a proven naval radar capability to the next level, combining increased performance with a low footprint and an architecture built for continuous development. It is designed to meet the demands of today’s naval forces while giving customers the flexibility to evolve with future threats,” says Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s business area Surveillance.
Building on more than 70 years of radar innovation and over two decades of ongoing operational success with Sea Giraffe AMB radars, the new Sea Giraffe AMB D leverages Active Electronically Scanned Array radar hardware with a new software architecture and modern processing capabilities to provide enhanced air surveillance performance.

AI generated
Audi chief executive officer Gernot Dollner said he acted in the interest of the carmaker when he took part in US President Donald Trump’s campaign rally that announced the company would build a US$4 billion (S$5.1 billion) plant in the country.

Audi is particularly exposed to the US trade shift because it still imports most of the vehicles it sells there, leaving the brand vulnerable to tariffs that have already raised costs across VW’s North American business. Media groups challenge India’s privacy law at top court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:56:22 UTC
19:56:22 KST

Media groups challenge India’s privacy law at top court
News organisations are challenging the law, arguing it could hamper investigative journalism and endanger sources.
The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounts to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups have told the Supreme Court.
A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s law on Tuesday, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow the government to identify journalists’ sources, according to The Indian Express newspaper.
“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), told judges.
“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission … it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”
The Supreme Court said it would hear the case next month.
Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written exemption for journalists as in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.
The DNPA’s members include Ambani’s Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani’s NDTV and other high-profile media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.
Fear of putting sources at risk
A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, says the group’s filing, cited by the Reuters news agency.
A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent “would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses”.
The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which the DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report.
News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for noncompliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the “interests of the general public”, which would curtail press freedom, the DNPA said.
From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organisation handling personal data “to furnish such information as it may call for”, putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said.
It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued.
The “nakedly unguided” provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power “can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant.”

Is Jagan Reddy's 'regret' message a calculated alliance pitch for Congress?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:55:55 UTC
19:55:55 KST

A successful alliance with the INDIA bloc hinges on the YSRCP and Congress aligning, which could be Jagan Mohan Reddy’s biggest challenge
NEW DELHI: Is YSRCP supremo YS Jagan Mohan Reddy signalling a drift towards the Congress-led INDIA bloc? Or is he trying to break free from the image of being soft on the BJP?The former Andhra Pradesh chief minister has provided issue-based support to the BJP-led NDA government on several key legislations in Parliament while he was in power in the state. However, he has stayed away from joining any alliance till now. So, when Jagan Reddy recently regretted his “mistake” of supporting the 2023 NDA legislation for selecting the Chief Election Commissioner, it fuelled speculation about his future political moves."We regret supporting the process under which the ruling party nominates the Chief Election Commissioner at the Centre. Neither the CEC nor the SEC should be appointed by the ruling party. The selection committee should comprise the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition and the Chief Justice of India (CJI), with all three exercising their voting rights," the YSRCP chief said recently, calling the current selection system "flawed."The timing and context of Jagan’s remarks are significant. So, is he rethinking his “solo” politics? And if yes, will the Congress be ready to tango with him in Andhra Pradesh? After all, alliances with regional parties have been the Congress’s biggest Achilles heel across states.
Jagan’s support for NDA’s key Bills
Jagan Mohan Reddy’s MPs backed the Modi government several times between 2019 and 2024, both in Lok Sabha and in Rajya Sabha, on many important legislations. However, when it came to stitching an alliance for the 2024 elections, the BJP ignored Jagan’s help and joined hands with his arch-rival Chandrababu Naidu. Together, TDP and BJP swept the polls in Andhra Pradesh, winning 164 out of 175 seats in the assembly and 21 out of 25 seats in Lok Sabha. The YSRCP was reduced to 11 seats in the assembly and 4 in Lok Sabha.Despite being spurned by the BJP and his party’s shock defeat, Jagan Mohan Reddy remained confident about his BJP ties. After all, he still had 15 MPs (4 in Lok Sabha and 11 in Rajya Sabha) to provide the much-needed support to the BJP’s minority government at the Centre. Jagan even announced that his MPs would extend issue-based support to the NDA government in matters concerning national and state interest.But with the BJP heavily dependent on Chandrababu Naidu’s support for survival of its government at the Centre, there was little room for the saffron party to accommodate Jagan Reddy. Nearly two and a half years down the line, Reddy seems to have accepted this harsh reality and is perhaps gearing up to chart a new path for the next political challenge in 2029.
Jagan vs Congress
However, for any successful alliance with the INDIA bloc - the YSRCP and the Congress will have to be on the same page. And that perhaps would be the biggest challenge for Jagan Mohan Reddy.Jagan Mohan Reddy had a bitter parting from the Congress in 2010, a year after the death of his father YS Rajasekhara Reddy. YSR Reddy was in his second term as the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh when he died in a helicopter crash on September 2, 2009. Jagan’s supporters, who were many in number, lobbied hard with the Congress high command for the top post, but Sonia Gandhi did not budge and made K Rosaiah the chief minister. The Congress leadership did not approve of Jagan’s Odarpu Yatra, which was part of his announced plan to meet the families of many people who had sacrificed their lives after his father’s death.That set the stage for his eventual exit from the Congress, which he announced on November 29, 2010 in an open letter to Sonia Gandhi carefully written to ensure there was enough public sympathy for his second phase of political career.In the 2014 assembly elections, the YSRCP made an impressive debut and won 67 out of the 175 seats with a vote share of 44.46%, while the Congress could manage only a vote share of 2.8%. The Congress decision to bifurcate the state and create Telangana played a huge role in the party’s declining political fortunes in the state.On November 6, 2017, Jagan embarked on the Praja Sankalpa Yatra and covered 3,648 km in 341 days, crossing 134 assembly constituencies. The Yatra, from YSR Ghat at Idupulapaya to the northeastern tip of Ichchapuram, powered Jagan Mohan Reddy to a historic mandate of 151 seats in the 175-member assembly in the 2019 elections. The Congress’s vote share was reduced to less than 1%.The Congress, since then, has been making efforts to reclaim its lost political space in the state. It roped in Jagan Reddy’s sister Y S Sharmila as part of the party’s revival plan. Sharmila, who started her political career with her brother Jagan Mohan Reddy eventually drifted towards the Congress and was appointed president of Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee in January 2024.However, both Jagan Mohan Reddy and his sister Y S Sharmila failed to make an impact in the 2024 elections. The 2024 elections saw a dramatic collapse of Jagan’s electoral fortunes, and his party was reduced to only 11 seats. The Congress once again failed to make its presence felt.
The 2029 challenge
And that brings us to the 2029 elections - a do-or-die challenge for both Jagan Mohan Reddy and the Congress. Jagan’s remark on backing the CEC appointment Bill is his first open “regret” for backing the BJP.But does this “open regret” mean an olive branch for the Congress?Former Congress leader and senior political commentator Sanjay Jha strongly feels that Jagan and Congress should come together, though he admits that this may not be easy.“Politics is the art of the possible and I'm sure Jaganmohan Reddy is aware that Chandrababu Naidu has been an extremely close alliance partner of the Modi government. While the Congress doesn't have a base in Andhra like it used to have once upon a time. The support base of Jaganmohan Reddy is basically the Congress vote which moved away from the traditional Congress to the Congress that Jaganmohan Reddy, branded as the Congress of his father. So, if the merger were to happen, it would, frankly speaking, give them a huge advantage because then both the Central Congress and the Jaganmohan Congress could be on the same page,” Sanjay Jha says.However, he accepts that merger of the two parties could be a difficult process while stitching an alliance may be easier. “Once a political party becomes independent and has power, they don't like to give it up in a hurry. The TMC or the NCP are good examples. In which case it could be an alliance,” Sanjay Jha adds.The third option, according to Sanjay Jha, is for the Congress to resurrect itself on its own strongly in Andhra by capturing both the anti-incumbent votes against Chandrababu Naidu and winning back the loyalist voters of the Congress who had moved over to Jaganmohan Reddy.
This is easier said than done. The Congress has a poor track record when it comes to winning back states it has lost. We have seen several states across the country where the Congress has lost its government and eventually its support base but does little to reclaim it.In Andhra Pradesh, Chandrababu Naidu and the BJP are going all out to consolidate their position. Naidu’s call for greater cooperation and coordination among southern states at a recent conference is perhaps an effort to keep his importance and relevance intact. We saw DMK’s MK Stalin make similar moves before he lost power to Vijay’s TVK in the last assembly elections.Jagan Mohan Reddy and the Congress face an uphill electoral battle in 2029. It will be interesting to see if they can agree to an alliance to take on Chandrababu Naidu and the BJP.

It’s hard breaking up with Washington: Why Canada’s European defense turn has limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:54:46 UTC
19:54:46 KST

Canada and Europe both want an insurance policy against Donald Trump — and they are turning to defense partnerships to do so.
The military and industrial relationship between Ottawa and Europeans is accelerating, driven by the U.S. president's repeated threats to annex Canada and his undermining of the traditional American commitment to European security.
But European officials, diplomats and analysts who spoke to POLITICO describe a welcome with conditions. Neither side, for one thing, wants a total rupture with Washington, highlighting how delicate reshuffling alliances can be.
Advertisement
Ottawa is “in a phase of constrained rapprochement [with Europe], but they don’t want to completely break away from the U.S.,” said Camille Grand, a former NATO assistant secretary-general who now leads the Aerospace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe.
Later this week, the leaders of the European Union and Canada will meet in Montreal for a summit to deepen their cooperation, including on critical raw materials and defense.
Over the past year, Ottawa has been admitted to the EU’s €150 billion Security Action for Europe loans-for-weapons scheme. It has applied to join a U.K.-led northern European military coalition, although not all existing members are on board. Canada has also selected a German submarine-maker and a Swedish early-warning plane for two of its largest military hardware purchases.
Tore O. Sandvik takes part in a panel discussion during the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland on Oct. 12, 2026. | Omar Marques/Getty Images
Canada is a natural partner for northern European countries on Arctic security. Asked how closely Canada should be integrated into Europe’s defense policy, Norway’s Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik replied: “Very. It’s an Arctic nation, a G7 country and a formidable economy.”
Canada is not starting from scratch. It is a founding member of NATO, leads the alliance's Multinational Brigade in Latvia and Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier works closely with European aerospace firms like Saab.
For Europe, Canada is “an easy partner in a way that some of the other countries are not” because Australia, Japan and South Korea are further away and Turkey poses political problems, said Anand Sundar, special adviser to the director of the European Council on Foreign Relations. “A lot is happening outside of the EU. As NATO tries to become more Europeanized, the question is how to do that without leaving Canada out.”
Advertisement
Amid warnings that Russia could attack NATO by 2030, Canada has critical raw materials crucial to Europe’s arms-makers, know-how in Arctic warfare and decades-long continental air defense expertise.
Canada’s International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu reinforced the need for deeper cooperation at a meeting with EU counterparts last week in Dublin.
Maninder Sidhu speaks during the G20 Trade Ministerial in Wisconsin, U.S. on Oct. 1, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images
“Some of those shared opportunities we're seeking here in Europe is on supply chains, critical mineral supply chains,” he said. “Canada is also working our way up in terms of defense spending, but we can't do it alone. And this is why we want to build up more capacity with our European partners.”
European access — with limits
Canada’s access to the SAFE scheme doesn’t mean all new EU defense instruments are now automatically open to Ottawa.
Attention has now shifted to negotiations on the EU’s seven-year budget, and whether third countries will be eligible for some of the €131 billion defense and space program proposed by the European Commission.
Countries such as Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland are open to broader participation, while France, Greece and others want to favor European companies. In late October, the European Parliament also signaled that it was open to letting third nations in, under some conditions, according to internal documents obtained by POLITICO.
Advertisement
EU budget negotiations “are where the depth of Canada’s integration in defense schemes will be decided. It’s an ongoing debate and … it’s up in the air until the very last minute,” said Sundar.
The idea of opening access to the European Competitiveness Fund’s defense money “is more aimed at Canada and the U.K.” than the U.S., added one diplomat. They argued that the requirement that third countries contribute financially to take part makes Washington less likely to participate.
Although Canada struck a deal to take part in SAFE-financed procurements almost a year ago, only one small deal has been announced — a C$10 million contract to supply tactical radios to Poland. Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty is, however, optimistic that there will be “more to come.”
David McGuinty speaks to the journalist during the International Defence Industry Exhibition in Kielce, Poland on Sept. 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images
For now, the deepening Canada-Europe defense cooperation is mostly illustrated by bilateral agreements between Ottawa and European capitals. This summer, the Canadian government chose German shipbuilder TKMS over South Korea’s Hanwha Ocean to build a new fleet of 12 non-nuclear submarines.
The submarine deal, which has yet to be officially signed, is "bringing us very much closer together,” said Norway’s Sandvik.
Cautious hedging against the U.S.
A major test of Canada’s willingness to pivot away from the U.S. toward Europe will be Canada’s choice between U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets and Sweden’s Gripen E.
Advertisement
Canada is replacing its aging fleet of CF-18 fighters. It planned to buy 88 F-35s and has committed to 16; the remaining 72 are under review by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government, potentially snubbing Lockheed Martin in favor of Saab.
Asked repeatedly about its status, McGuinty always gives the same answer: “under review.” In July, Ottawa also became an observer to the Global Combat Air Programme, the British-Italian-Japanese effort to build a sixth-generation fighter jet.
Buying Swedish warplanes would anger the Trump administration when trade relations are already under strain; Canada’s economic ties to the U.S. are much larger than its ties with the EU.
Earlier this year, U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra specifically warned that procuring Swedish aircraft instead of the remaining F-35s would have consequences for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, the military organization through which the U.S. and Canada jointly defend North American airspace.
“NORAD, the most important element of Canada’s defense, isn’t part of NATO but bilateral with the U.S., which explains part of the constraint,” Grand said.
McGuinty did not agree to an interview for this article.
Advertisement
No consensus on JEF membership
Another test for European governments is whether Canada’s application to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force will be accepted — and so far, not everyone is on board.
The U.K.-led force includes the three Baltic states, five Nordic countries and the Netherlands.
Last month, Carney formally applied to join. But while some members, such as Norway, are very open to adding Canada, others are more reluctant.
“Canada is a fellow NATO member; defense relations should remain in NATO. Russia is a threat in the north so it makes sense that they collaborate more with Europe — but within NATO,” said a diplomat from a Baltic country.
Given the Trump administration’s unpredictability, JEF is seen as an additional layer of defense insurance. It’s described by the U.K. as a “first responder” ahead of NATO.
The group’s structures are less clear-cut than NATO’s, but another official from a JEF nation noted that, despite Britain’s role as the grouping's leader, the application would require agreement among all members.
Advertisement
At a meeting in Iceland earlier this month, JEF defense ministers only “noted” Canada’s application, according to a joint statement. A spokesperson for the U.K. Ministry of Defence said London was “consulting” JEF countries on the way forward. A decision could come at a leaders’ summit hosted by Iceland next spring.
Ottawa joining, two diplomats from JEF nations said, could shift the organization’s primary geographical focus from the Baltic Sea to the Arctic. One of them added that it may send a bad signal if Canada were accepted over European nations.
“It would make sense geographically to include Canada in JEF, but then why not Poland and Germany? They are Baltic Sea countries,” the Baltic diplomat echoed.
In Canada, however, the case for a European role goes beyond any one forum. “In both world wars, Canada was involved in Europe years before the U.S. got involved,” said Wendy Gilmour, a former NATO assistant secretary-general who’s now vice chair of the CDA Institute, a Canadian think tank.
She added: “I can envisage situations where Canada engages where the U.S. may not.”
Laura Kayali reported from Paris and Warsaw, Mike Blanchfield from Ottawa, Jacopo Barigazzi from Brussels and Mason Boycott-Owen from London.

In Lubbock, Texas, Trump attacks Talarico for showing compassion for transgender children
In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.
The president began by repeating a string of false claims about Talarico and then insisted, falsely, that the Democrat, who is Presbyterian seminarian, said that “God is transgender”.
In fact, as a selection of statements from Talarico that Trump played for his rally crowd showed, what the state lawmaker actually said, during an October 2021 debate on a Texas bill barring trans children from competing on school sports teams, was that “God is nonbinary”.
“The first two lines of the Bible, the first two lines in Genesis use two different Hebrew words to describe God – one is the masculine Hebrew noun for divinity, the second is the feminine Hebrew noun for spirit. God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary,” Talarico said.
In Genesis 1:26 and 1:27, Talarico added, “God speaks of God’s self in the plural, saying ‘Let us make human beings in our image, to be like us’. That’s the infinite multitude of God, the masculine, the feminine and everything in between. Asked then to name one thing that he loves, Talarico paused a moment and said: “Um, I love… and I just say this because it’s on my mind, the trans children who showed up yesterday at the state capitol to advocate for their humanity; they shouldn’t have to but it was an inspiration to watch.”

Apparently unaware of its origin, Trump once again uses the phrase ‘to the victor belong the spoils’ to claim Venezuela's oil
Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.
The president told reporters before the event that he intends to re-gift the oil, giving it to the people of the United States of America.
During his remarks, Trump pointed to the tanker, which can hold an estimated 800,000 barrels of oil, and said: “See that little ship out there? It’s got one million barrels of oil on it from Venezuela.”
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump continued. “‘To the victor belong to spoils’, right?” he added, referring to a phrase he has used in the past to suggest the US has a rightful claim to Venezuela’s oil since US forces kidnapped its leader.
Trump first used the phrase in public during an April 2011 appearance on Fox News, when he told the host Bill O’Reilly that, if elected president, he would not withdraw US troops from Iraq but redeploy them to secure its oil fields.
“In the old days, when you had wars, you win, right? You win. ‘To the victor belong the spoils’. So when we go to Iraq, we spend $1.4 trillion so far and thousands of lives are lost … and we’re going to leave,” Trump said. “I like the old system better: You won a war, you stay there, and you keep the oil. And you know, then those people will not have died in vain.”
“You stay and protect the oil, and you take the oil and you take whatever is necessary for them and you take what’s necessary for us and we pay our self back $1.5 trillion or more,” Trump added.
Since the US military operation seized Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, Trump has repeatedly used the same phrase to lay claim to the country’s oil, but the president appears to be unaware of its original meaning.
The phrase was first used in 1832 by New York senator William L. Marcy during a speech in defense of president Andrew Jackson’s right to reward his supporters with appointments to public office, arguing that “to the victor belong the spoils of the enemy.”
The phrase gave rise to describing the system of political patronage as “the spoils system”.

US Federal Election Commission’s website targeted by hackers - report
Reuters reports that the US Federal Election Commission’s website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, disrupting the agency’s electronic filings system to disclose campaign spending a week before the midterm elections.
In a statement to the news agency, the FEC said, “at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service.” The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage.
The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters’ ability to cast ballots, although it will keep information on how much political groups are spending on specific races from the public as they cast ballots.
“We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer said in an email seen by Reuters.
In Texas, Trump repeats a stream of false claims and screens misleading edit of CNN polling data segment
Near the end of his speech to a Republican campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, Donald Trump just screened two short clips, edited from longer CNN segments first broadcast in August and September, highlighting polling data that flatters him.
As we have reported previously, screening these brief clips has become a routine part of Trump’s argument as he tries to convince supporters, and perhaps himself, that he is far more popular than other polling suggests.
The clips, however, were created by editing out negative information the president does not want his supporters to hear.
The first clip is 43 seconds of CNN’s chief data analyst, Harry Enten, showing viewers in September that Trump remains very popular with self-described “Maga Republicans,” which is to say people who describe themselves as loyal to his Make America Great Again movement.
“Maga GOP on Trump. In the 2024 election versus Kamala Harris, he got 99% of the Maga GOP vote—perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it’d be 100%, but it was 99% percent,” Enten said in the first part of the clip. “Compare that to his approval rating now with the Maga GOP. It’s 98%; that is, there’s been no real decline in Maga support.”
“Look, now in terms of the congressional vote, 98% of them say they’re going to be voting for House Republican candidates,” Enten added. “So, that support is actually really holding up strong. It’s really, really strong when it comes to Maga GOP and Republicans holding on to that vote.”
However, a look at the full 14-minute segment broadcast in late September shows that what the White House edited out was Enten carefully explaining that Trump’s approval rating among Republicans who do not describe themselves as Maga loyalists had suffered a sharp drop, plunging from +56 points in the 2024 election to just +7 points in September 2026.
“You know, when it comes to non-Maga, this is where we’ve absolutely seen Donald Trump’s numbers plummet into the ocean,” Enten said, in a part of the report Trump did not screen at the rally.
The president also screened for his supporters a portion of a prior CNN segment, from August of this year, in which Enten showed viewers that according to polling conducted in May, Trump was, at that time, called the president Republicans most admire by 53% of Republicans, ahead of Ronald Reagan at 18% and Abraham Lincoln at 8%.
Trump is so fond of these two cherry-picked pieces of data, from months ago, that he included both in his 1,300-word social-media tirade against the comedian Bill Maher on Sunday.
Trump cited the data as supposed proof that Maher was wrong to say that the president is unpopular. “I have High Ratings and, more importantly, he said that I’m losing the support and approval of the Republican Party when, in fact, CNN just came out with a Poll showing that I’m at 98 and 99% support within the Republican Party, an All Time Record High,” Trump wrote.
Given that the president has repeatedly screened the clip of Enten clearly saying these were his ratings with Maga Republicans, not the party as a whole, this is not the evidence that he seems to think it is.
