Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.

Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.

Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.
Jacob Harris has been banned from managing or sitting on the board of a company for three years following a ruling by the probate court in Roskilde on Friday.
TV 2 reported the decision, citing trustee and bankruptcy lawyer Morten Bjerregaard.
The ban also means Harris, an independent member of the Danish parliament, cannot own a company unless he accepts personal liability.
The ruling concerns Harris’ activities in Krokodille ApS, a company for which his wife, Tetiana Harris Nielsen, served as director. The court declared the company bankrupt in the autumn of 2025.
According to TV 2, Harris’ wife has also received a three-year bankruptcy ban. The ruling was reportedly based on the couple’s conduct in the company, whose bookkeeping was deficient and entirely absent for 2025.
Krokodille ApS was founded in Hedehusene, west of Copenhagen, in December 2021 under the name Vostok Sokol ApS. A holding company owned by Tetiana Harris Nielsen is registered as its founder. The company changed its name in March 2022 and moved its registered address from the couple’s home to an address in Ringsted in October 2025, shortly before its bankruptcy.
Harris was elected to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, for Borgernes Parti in the March election but was expelled from the party days later. The party said he had “not provided truthful information to the party and, moreover, repeatedly acted contrary to the party’s values.”
Harris has also faced criticism over plans to meet Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, on 10 November.
Responding to the controversy, Harris wrote on Facebook: “Talking to a foreign ambassador is not treason.”

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.
Netanyahu orders West Bank lockdown after shooting near Hebron
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered an immediate closure of the city of Hebron and instructed the military to prepare to shut down the entire West Bank following a shooting that left at least five people injured.
Netanyahu announced the measures in a post on X, according to the French news agency AFP.
“I have ordered the IDF and the security forces to impose an immediate closure of the city of Hebron and to prepare a full shutdown of all of Judea and Samaria effective from today,” he wrote.
Judea and Samaria are the names Israel uses for the territory known internationally as the West Bank. It remains unclear what the planned shutdown will mean in practice.
Netanyahu said the military had begun “counter-terrorism operations” in the area, including searches of homes belonging to people suspected of involvement in terrorism.
“Soldiers are currently operating inside the homes of terrorists and other suspects,” AFP reported.
The announcement follows a shooting early Friday near Hebron, during which two Palestinian men were shot by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). They are suspected of carrying out an attack that left at least five people injured.
The incident involved an exchange of fire between the two men and Israeli forces at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint near Hebron. According to AFP, the Palestinians were armed with a pistol and an automatic rifle.
Netanyahu praised the military for preventing what he described as “a major terrorist attack” and vowed to pursue Hamas members.
“You have nowhere to hide,” he wrote.
Israel is due to hold parliamentary elections next week. Following the shooting, Netanyahu cancelled all political meetings.
Israel’s National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, also responded to the shooting by calling for the dissolution and demilitarization of the Palestinian Authority.
“We have to act before it is too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dissolved and demilitarized, and its terrorist infrastructure must be completely eradicated,” he said.
The Palestinian Authority administers parts of the West Bank and was established under the Oslo peace agreements. It is led by President Mahmoud Abbas, whose Fatah party is a rival of Hamas.
There is currently no indication that Palestinian Authority officials were involved in the shooting.
Hamas praised the attack but did not claim responsibility, according to AFP.
“The attack is a natural and legitimate response to the ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people,” the group said, describing it as “an exceptional heroic operation”.
Retail sales in Denmark rose by 0.4 percent in September compared with August, despite growing pessimism among consumers, according to figures from Statistics Denmark.
The increase is adjusted for seasonal fluctuations, price changes and the number of trading days.
For the third quarter, covering July through September, retail sales rose by 1.6 percent compared with the previous quarter.
Sales trends varied across industries in September. The largest increases were recorded among retailers selling second-hand goods, household equipment, furniture and building materials.
By contrast, sales fell the most at gas stations and pharmacies. Danish supermarkets also recorded a slight decline.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said the increase in retail sales was encouraging given the growing pessimism among Danish consumers.
On Thursday, Statistics Denmark’s consumer confidence indicator stood at minus 17.2, down from minus 13.7 in September.
A negative reading indicates that consumers have a pessimistic view of the country’s current and future economic situation.
Despite the decline in confidence, Morten Granzau, deputy director at the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri), believes retail sales could continue to grow in the coming months.
“Consumers’ purchasing power is fundamentally good. High employment, growth in real wages, and the lower electricity tax provide breathing room in many households’ budgets. This creates good opportunities for retail sales to maintain progress through the autumn,” he wrote in a comment.
Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.
During Sunday, winds will shift toward the southwest and intensify, bringing strong gusts and severe gales to coastal areas.
DMI warns that the conditions could affect traffic on several Danish bridges.
Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.
Wanner said the forecast reflects Denmark’s transition into its windier autumn and winter months.
“We are genuinely entering the windy season in Denmark. It is not at all unthinkable that there will be more episodes with storm-like conditions leading up to and throughout the winter,” he said.
DMI will continue monitoring the weather and publishing updated forecasts as the storm approaches.
Denmark to end mink farming by August 2029 under EU ban
Denmark’s remaining seven mink farms will have to close by August 7, 2029, after the government decided not to seek an exemption from an upcoming European Union ban.
The Ministry for Nature and Animal Welfare announced the decision, citing animal welfare concerns and the industry’s limited economic contribution.
“An industry should not continue solely because it has existed for a long time. It must also make sense for society, for the economy, and for the animals,” said Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats).
The EU added mink to its list of invasive species last summer, introducing a ban on breeding and production that takes effect August 7, 2027. Existing farms will have a two-year transition period.
Denmark previously opposed the EU measure and had planned to seek an exemption allowing existing farms to continue operating.
Carl Valentin, animal welfare spokesperson for Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, welcomed the government’s decision.
“As we see it, it is not good animal welfare to have mink in tiny cages,” he told Ritzau.
Denmark’s mink industry was severely affected in 2020 when authorities ordered approximately 15 million animals culled over concerns about coronavirus mutations.
A temporary farming ban followed, lasting until January 2023, when some producers resumed operations.
The total estimated cost of pandemic-related compensation, farm demolition and administrative work reached 29.1 billion DKK in early 2026.
The government has yet to determine compensation costs for closing the remaining farms.
Valentin said an earlier estimate was around 14 million DKK, although the final amount could be higher.
Politicians push to change rules for dogs suspected of being banned breeds
Several Danish opposition politicians are calling for changes to the country’s dog laws after reports of legally owned dogs being kept in kennels for months while authorities investigate their breeds.
Under Denmark’s Dog Act, 13 breeds are banned from ownership, breeding and importation, including pit bull terriers and American bulldogs. Crossbreeds containing any of the prohibited breeds are also illegal.
When police suspect a dog belongs to a banned breed, its owner must provide documentation proving otherwise. During the investigation, the animal may be placed in a boarding kennel.
Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten has reported cases involving dogs that were eventually found to be legal but had spent months in kennels.
Danmarksdemokraterne (the Denmark Democrats), an opposition party, has proposed allowing dogs to remain with their owners while investigations take place, potentially using electronic tracking devices instead.
Borgernes Parti (the Citizens’ Party) and independent lawmakers Nadja Natalie Isaksen, Cecilie Liv Hansen and Emilie Schytte have also criticized police powers to order euthanasia based on visual assessments of a dog’s breed.
The law requires police to euthanize dogs found to belong to prohibited breeds.
The restrictions were introduced in 2010 following incidents involving dog attacks on people and other animals.
Christian Rabjerg Madsen, Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare from Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats), told Jyllands-Posten he was open to discussing changes to the law and its enforcement.
He said the challenge was balancing public safety with fair treatment of owners who struggle to document their dogs’ breeds.
Danske Bank announces third round of layoffs this year
Danske Bank is cutting 106 jobs, around half of them in Denmark, in its third round of layoffs this year.
The bank announced the cuts in a press release on Thursday, saying they are intended to help create a “more efficient and competitive bank”.
The remaining positions are in the bank’s operations in Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Poland and Sweden.
“We continue to develop Danske Bank to meet our customers’ expectations, strengthen our competitiveness, and realize the ambitions in our Forward ’28 strategy,” Karsten Breum, the bank’s head of human resources, said in the release.
“This means that we continuously simplify the organization, invest in new competencies, and move resources to the areas where we create the greatest value for our customers.
“It is a natural part of running and developing a large company.”
The latest cuts follow two previous rounds of job reductions in 2026.
In February, Danske Bank announced that it would cut 420 positions across the organization. At the time, the bank said it wanted to adapt to customer needs, invest in technology and advisory services, and become more digital.
Three months later, a further 262 positions were affected. The bank gave broadly similar reasons for those cuts.
Both earlier rounds primarily affected employees in Denmark.
Breum acknowledged the impact of the latest decision on employees.
“Decisions like these affect people,” he said in Thursday’s press release.
“For the colleagues who are affected, it is a difficult situation. Therefore, it is important that we implement the changes responsibly and give our affected colleagues the support and respect they deserve throughout the entire process.”
All employees affected by the latest cuts have been notified.
Danske Bank says on its website that it has more than 20,000 employees across its international operations.
Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.

Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, will join the returning television program Junior MasterChef Australia as a special guest in 2027, Australian broadcaster Network 10 announced Tuesday.
While some reports described Meghan as a co-host, the official announcement said she would work alongside host and MasterChef Australia judge Poh Ling Yeow to guide the young contestants.
“I had an incredible time with the whole team at MasterChef this past April, so when they approached me to come back and work with this young group of talent, it was an easy yes,” Meghan said.
“I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun. I can’t wait to see what they cook up!”

Yeow said she was pleased that the children’s version of the cooking competition was returning after six years.
“I had a lovely time filming with Meghan earlier this year, and being reunited will be a real treat,” she said. “I can’t wait to meet our pint-sized culinary adventurers – I’m expecting plenty of delicious surprises and a little mischief, too.”
Meghan has previously presented food and lifestyle content in the Netflix series With Love, Meghan, which ran for two seasons and a Christmas special. She also appeared as a guest judge on the US program Chopped Junior in 2016.
Before marrying Britain’s Prince Harry in 2018, Meghan was best known for playing Rachel Zane in the legal drama Suits.
She and Harry stepped back from their roles as senior members of the British royal family in 2020 and subsequently pursued independent media and commercial projects.
Junior MasterChef Australia, produced by Endemol Shine Australia, will return to Network 10 in 2027. Further details about Meghan’s role, the contestants and the broadcast schedule have not yet been announced.

U.K. charges 2 men arrested over alleged Iran-linked terror plot against RAF Fairford air base used by U.S.
London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.
Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."
The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.
Abdulkarim was arrested by Counter Terror Police under the National Security Act last week, along with another 25-year-old man — a British-Iranian dual national who was released on bail pending further investigation.
Police are still investigating a suspected terror plot against Fairford after five men were initially detained on Sept. 27 near the base in western England. All five of those men were also released on bail, but police said they remained under investigation and would be monitored.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the base, which prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford. The base had been home to U.S. long-range bombers for many years, and it was used during the war with Iran to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic.
Residents of a nearby town were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police and bomb-disposal experts searched the area on Sept. 27. They found gasoline in three vans that had been driven by the five initial suspects, parked close to an entrance to the base, but no explosives.
Iranian officials have said repeatedly that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. The Iranian Embassy in London, however, said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Police said Tuesday that six men remain free on bail in relation to the incident, four of whom were arrested on Sept. 27 — all U.K. nationals and London residents in their 20s — and two others who were detained subsequently, including the 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national who was detained on Oct. 1.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT mayoral candidates have reportedly sidelined party Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) at campaign rallies, with Cheng either given an opening speaking slot or not invited at all.
Liberty Times reported that when Cheng attended the Oct. 4 opening of Taichung mayoral candidate Johnny Chiang’s (江啟臣) campaign headquarters, organizers did not arrange for her to share the stage with Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) and Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕). Cheng reportedly drew the ire of Chiang’s campaign team by greeting and shaking hands with KMT supporters along the central walkway leading to the stage without being prompted to do so.
The same pattern reportedly continued at a rally for New Taipei mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) that afternoon. Cheng left the stage before Lee joined Han, Hou, and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安).
The newspaper reported that Cheng reprimanded KMT Vice Chair Li Chien-lung (李乾龍), who was responsible for communicating with Lee’s campaign team, over the arrangements.
At Chiang Wan-an’s campaign headquarters opening on Monday, his team reportedly planned to follow the example of Taoyuan Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政) and exclude Cheng from the event. However, Chiang’s team ultimately agreed to let Cheng speak about an hour before Hou, Han, and Lu arrived to show their support for Chiang.
Chiang Wan-an responded to the report by saying there was no such problem and that the speculation was unwarranted, per Mirror Media.
Asked to comment, DPP lawmaker Chung Chia-pin (鍾佳濱) suggested that the reported arrangements reflected an internal power struggle within the KMT, per Liberty Times. He characterized the divide as a choice between seeking power through the electoral process and pursuing it through the destruction of the democratic system.
Chung suggested that Cheng’s speeches, which often focus on her time as a DPP member or developments in China, do not appeal to voters.
DPP Legislator Kuo Yu-ching (郭昱晴) agreed, arguing that Cheng’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping had prompted KMT candidates to distance themselves from the party chair, per Liberty Times. She also predicted another round of internal infighting within the KMT after the election, suggesting that the party’s public displays of unity on stage were merely for show.

The Prospekt shopping and entertainment center in Kyiv, owned by Arricano, suffered minor damage in a Russian strike overnight on Tuesday, the company's press service told Interfax-Ukraine.
"As a result of the enemy attack on Kyiv on October 27, the Prospekt shopping center was damaged. The shopping gallery suffered minor damage and is operating as usual. The Auchan Ukraine hypermarket is temporarily closed today," the company said.
Arricano suspended operation of its City Mall in Zaporizhia in early September, citing the current security situation, after it was significantly damaged in a Russian strike, and said it plans to restore it.
Russian drones struck the Sonyachna Galereya mall in Kryvyi Rih twice on August 21, killing 16 people and injuring 130.
Overnight on July 19, another massive Russian missile strike on Kyiv damaged the construction site of a shopping and entertainment center in Lukianivka that is being built by Arricano. There were no casualties.
Arricano Real Estate PLC (Cyprus) owns four shopping centers in Ukraine through its Ukrainian subsidiaries: Prospekt and RaiON in Kyiv, City Mall in Zaporizhia and Sonyachna Galereya in Kryvyi Rih. It also owns 49.9% of Sky Mall in Kyiv and land plots for the further construction of three facilities that are at the design stage. Taiwan receiving 6 MS-110 reconnaissance pods for F-16Vs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:36 UTC
19:50:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is scheduled to receive six US-made MS-110 Multispectral Airborne Reconnaissance System pods by the end of December, enhancing its F-16V fighter fleet's surveillance capabilities and speeding access to battlefield intelligence.
The defense ministry confirmed the updated delivery schedule in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan, per Liberty Times. The procurement program has a budget of NT$9.63 billion (US$302 million), with two pods already delivered and the remaining four expected by the end of the year.
The Air Force began installation testing and personnel conversion training in June. In August, F-16Vs operating from Hualien's Chiashan Air Force Base carried the first two pods on flights that completed the initial phase of flight-performance evaluations.
The MS-110 is expected to double the imaging capabilities of the Air Force's existing tactical reconnaissance pods, commonly known as the Phoenix Eye system, Liberty Times reported. Its seven spectral bands — blue, green, red, near-infrared, shortwave infrared, and two midwave infrared bands — enable multispectral imaging for target identification and surveillance.
Military sources said the system has an effective imaging range exceeding 148 kilometers and can capture high-resolution imagery at a rate of up to 26,000 square kilometers per hour. This would allow F-16Vs operating east of the Taiwan Strait median line to monitor Chinese coastal military deployments and troop movements without flying deep into contested airspace.
The system also lets the Air Force receive reconnaissance imagery in real time, rather than waiting for aircraft to land and retrieve recorded images, according to Liberty Times. Its digital data link transmits high-resolution imagery to ground stations while airborne.
If terrain or low-altitude flight disrupts the signal, the pod stores imagery internally and automatically transmits it when connectivity is restored. The Air Force has established four ground receiving stations that relay imagery through military data networks and fiber-optic connections to the Heng Shan Military Command Center and operational theater commands.

Underwater data centers may be coming to the U.S.—smack in the middle of endangered whale habitat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:19 UTC
19:50:19 KST

The battle over where to put data centers is heading below the waves: the Trump administration is considering proposals to build two massive underwater data centers off the country’s coast. The sites selected for the projects—one in Cook Inlet, Alaska, and one in the Gulf of Maine—are smack in the middle of two endangered whale populations’ habitats.
Whales are “skittish animals,” says Arial Brewer, a beluga researcher at the University of Washington and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “A massive-scale project like this could really stress them out in a lot of different ways.”
Data centers, with their thousands of servers, generate considerable heat that can damage equipment if not offset in some way. Land-based facilities use massive amounts of fresh water to cool down. By putting a data center underwater, the ocean can easily dispel that heat. “Cooling is a large part of what a data center costs to run, and seawater is a free sink,” says Vishal Misra, a computer scientist and professor at Columbia University.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Microsoft showed that the concept could work with a pilot project off California in 2015 and another off Scotland a few years later. Currently, there are only two operational underwater data centers in the world, one off the Chinese island of Hainan and another off the coast of Shanghai, and they’re a fraction of the size of the proposed centers at the two U.S. sites.
In the Maine project, a cluster of what official documents call “subsea-compute hives” or “data center pods” would rest on the seabed, powered by up to 50 tidal turbines across 27 acres. In Cook Inlet, the data center would be made up of 66 pods and more than 300 tidal turbines. Its footprint would span 1,650 acres—more than 1,000 football fields.
The locations were chosen by DeepGreen Holdings LLC—a U.S.-based developer—because of their potential for tidal power, which works by harnessing the movement of water.
But each spot is also home to beleaguered groups of whales. A distinct population of around 300 critically endangered beluga whales lives in Cook Inlet. And the Gulf of Maine hosts feeding grounds for the North Atlantic right whale, a species whose numbers have dropped below 400 individuals.
The primary concern over data centers underwater is the same as for those on land: they are exceedingly noisy. “Pumps, fans and especially turbine arrays make continuous low-frequency sound, and pile-driving during construction is louder still,” Misra says.
Shipping noise has doubled every decade since the 1960s, and there’s evidence to suggest that when the volume goes down, marine mammals are less stressed. One study found that when ship noise decreased immediately after 9/11, right whales in the Gulf of Maine had lower levels of stress hormones. As for the belugas in Cook Inlet, they are particularly sensitive to noise, Brewer says. Because of glacial runoff, the bay is very turbid. “It literally looks like chocolate milk,” she says, so the belugas there rely almost entirely on echolocation to feed, mate and move around.
The purpose for putting the data centers underwater—heat shedding—also threatens the whales. When a pattern of warming waters hit the Gulf of Maine in the early 2010s, right whales started to abandon their feeding grounds. “Ocean warming is a big, big deal to them,” says Philip Hamilton, a senior scientist at the New England Aquarium.
In Alaska, salmon are one of the main prey sources for belugas—and the fish need cold water to develop their eggs, keep their metabolism stable and prevent energy depletion during long migratory journeys. “All that hot energy, what’s that going to do to very delicate salmon populations that rely on cold water?” Brewer says.
Community backlash has been fervent: The city of Eastport, Maine, issued a moratorium halting all permits and applications for all industrial data centers. The local Passamaquoddy tribe has also publicly expressed that it has no interest in any sort of collaboration with DeepGreen. Several groups have filed motions to intervene with the proposal for Cook Inlet.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which oversees such energy projects, notes that these proposals are just that: proposals. “A preliminary permit does not authorize construction of any kind,” says Celeste Miller, a FERC representative.
Indeed, FERC found the original proposals for both projects “deficient,” citing a lack of details and insufficient identification of Indigenous tribes who have historic ties to the local areas. But the agency has accepted amended versions; the Maine project, which originally called for 170 turbines on 400 acres of seafloor, now has a smaller proposed footprint. The public comment period for Maine closed on October 19, but the one for Cook Inlet is open until November 2. After that, FERC will review the applications and comments and issue preliminary permit decisions.
“We have no intent to build at this stage,” Louis Wolfson, the luxury real estate developer behind DeepGreen, says. “If equipment cannot operate safely well within federal marine mammal thresholds, it will never be licensed or deployed.”
But over the past two years, the federal government has sought to strip back those very thresholds. For example, the Senate is considering a bill that would delay new protections for right whales against entanglements in fishing gear. And though belugas and right whales have historically been protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, proposed amendments to it would drastically draw back protections.
“It feels like every day they’re chopping at another protection,” Hamilton says.

Why we’ll never have another Black Death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:10 UTC
19:50:10 KST

Scientists disagree over how scared we should be by the mysterious death of a worker at a Russian plague lab. A young laboratory technician died earlier this month of an undisclosed illness after working on research at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East. Although officials have not released details about the cause of death, scientists agree that if it was caused by ordinary plague, the wider world has little to worry about. This bacterial illness is infamous for the explosive killing spree known as the Black Death, which wiped out between a third and half of the population of Europe between 1347 and 1353. Today, however, plague is curable and extremely unlikely to blow up into a new pandemic, experts say. That’s thanks to a combination of antibiotic development, scientific understanding and luck.
Experts who study plague are reluctant to say it’s been completely conquered. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently reported approximately 3,800 infections and 423 deaths from plague between 2019 and 2025. And scientists haven’t cracked all the mysteries behind the plague bacterium, known as Yersinia pestis—one of the biggest being how it hides for years in cryptic reservoirs only to spring out in unpredictable new waves of infection in humans or other animals.
The disease is endemic in rodents living in the Americas, Central Asia and Africa, says David Wagner, a plague expert who directs the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “It’s constantly cycling between rodents via fleas, and it just does that in perpetuity in a manner we poorly understand, despite 100 years of research.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Studies of ancient DNA show plague-infected prehistoric hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago. Plague is known for causing three major pandemics: in addition to the one that started with the Black Death, which peaked between 1347 and 1351 and was followed by outbreaks into the 18th century, there was the plague of Justinian from C.E. 541 to 549 and a third pandemic that started in the 1800s and spread to every inhabited continent by 1900. That last pandemic was accelerated by a boom in rail and steamship travel but was eventually quashed by advances in science.
In 1894 French-Swiss bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin isolated the plague bacterium and connected rat infestations to the disease. Rat eradication campaigns followed around the world, drastically slowing the spread of plague, Wagner says. Though it was really the fleas that spread the disease to people, rat control worked because fleas are very specific about hosts. Different animal species have their own flea species, so rats and plague-carrying fleas traveled together.
Quarantines also helped, Wagner adds, because doctors started to recognize that the bacteria could sometimes spread from person to person through respiratory droplets. In the 1940s, when antibiotics had become widely available, doctors started curing plague cases with the drugs. Several vaccines have been developed over the years and deployed in severe outbreaks, in which they offered partial protection. No vaccine has been deemed effective enough to gain approval from the WHO or the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but labs in Russia and the U.S. continue to work on them.
Today most plague cases occur in Madagascar. Because food can be scarce there and people fear theft, individuals will store rice in their dirt-floor homes, Wagner says, allowing close contact with the rats that infest the island.
Though fleas are picky about their hosts, plague-carrying fleas in the U.S. are commonly found on prairie dogs, thanks to the animals having some functional similarities to rats. The plague bacterium now infects all five known species of prairie dogs and is one of the factors that contributed to a population decline in these social, burrowing rodents of about 98 percent from their historical levels. Because prairie dogs are a food source for other animals, including the critically endangered black-footed ferret, plague has been wreaking ecological havoc.
Even now it’s not clear where Y. pestis hides out between detectable outbreaks, Wagner says, and it’s surprising that it can be transmitted both by respiratory droplets and through fleas. But important clues about how the sickness operates are emerging from the latest studies of bacterial DNA in ancient bones and teeth.
The plague bacterium appears to have emerged as a human pathogen more than 5,700 years ago, evolving from a soil bacterium called Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, says Hendrick Poinar, a biologist at McMaster University, who works with ancient DNA. For the next 3,000 years, it infected Late Stone Age hunter-gathers and Bronze Age herders. Scientists suspect it was transmitted from human to human via respiratory droplets or via contaminated food because it hadn’t yet acquired the genes needed to travel through fleas.
Despite the versatility of Y. pestis, we’re lucky it can’t spread between humans unless an infected person is very sick and the contact is very close. Because of this limitation, even the emergence of an antibiotic-resistant strain won’t necessarily spark a new pandemic, Wagner says, noting that such strains have already shown up in Madagascar.
Though most scientists aren’t too alarmed about the situation in Russia, some are speculating that the death was caused by some highly genetically modified version of the plague bacterium or a different germ entirely. There’s no evidence for this, though the lack of transparency from Russia is unnerving. Regardless of the cause, the death of the worker is tragic. But if it was caused by the plague we know, the rest of us need not worry.

GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:49:45 UTC
19:49:45 KST

DETROIT — General Motors plans to transfer shares of its common stock from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq as the automaker attempts to position itself more as a technology-focused company.
The Detroit automaker said Tuesday that it expects to begin trading as a Nasdaq-listed company on Nov. 17. Its ticker symbol is expected to remain "GM," the company said.
"GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," GM CFO Paul Jacobson said in a release. "We're grateful for our long-standing partnership with the New York Stock Exchange and its remarkable legacy."
GM noted the move will provide eligibility for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 Index.
Current shareholders do not need to take any action with respect to the transfer, the company said.
The switch marks a notable loss for the NYSE, as GM first listed on the exchange in 1911. The Detroit automaker also relisted on the stock exchange in 2010 following a government-backed bankruptcy.
GM follows other companies such as Walmart, DoorDash and Palantir Technologies that have transferred from the more traditional NYSE to the historically technology focused Nasdaq in recent years. Hilton Worldwide Holdings last week also announced plans to move trading from the NYSE to Nasdaq.
The key drivers for a listing transfer differ from company to company, but the Nasdaq in 2024 said common reasons include "index inclusion opportunities, cost effective fee structure, brand visibility partnership, access to Nasdaq's event space, and Nasdaq's suite of investor relations and ESG products."
GM's decision comes a week after the automaker held a technology-focused event where executives laid out the company's roadmap for artificial intelligence and self-driving vehicle technologies.
Shares of GM, which has been aggressively buying back stock, have more than doubled since 2024. GM stock closed Tuesday at $80.54 a share, up 5%. The company's market cap is roughly $64.4 billion.

Oct 27 (Reuters) - Jordan said on Tuesday its forces had killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on southern Syria the previous evening, following a deadly church attack in Jordan that authorities linked to militants operating across the border.
The strikes, which followed a rare attack in Jordan, have inflamed tensions between the two US allies.
Jordan has been a longtime partner to the US in its fight against extremism, while the Islamist-led government of Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who wants to restore the country’s relations with the West after overthrowing longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, said it was seeking to curb extremism.
Syria said the strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman. Jordan regrets the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed al-Momani said in a post on X.
Jordan said on Monday its air force had struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week’s church attack were linked to “terrorist groups” based there. Jordanian security officials said separately that security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law following a shootout linked to the church attack, which killed nine people.
Local resident Salah Mahwash, speaking to Reuters during the funeral of four people including three children in Al-Mismiyah in southern Syria, said:
“At around 10 p.m., there was an explosion and the sound of aircraft overhead. We went to the site, and it was a poor family whose father had gone missing during the events and was in Sednaya prison.
“Today, as you can see, these are people just trying to make a living, tending to their sheep and goats and doing manual labour. We condemn what happened in the Jordanian state, of course.”
Attacks such as the church shooting are rare in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. No group has claimed responsibility for the shooting, although Jordan said the militants it targeted in Syria were members of Islamic State.
Monday’s strikes have nevertheless sparked anger in Syria. While the Jordanian military said they were conducted in coordination with Damascus, Syria’s government said they were carried out without prior coordination. It also said it would hold an investigation.
Statements in recent days by Jordanian authorities that there appeared to have been no prior planning of the church attack have added to the confusion, seemingly at odds with Jordan’s justification for Monday’s cross-border strikes.
Syria’s Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as a violation of the country’s sovereignty.
It said, however, that Damascus was coordinating with Amman and would establish a joint security committee to strengthen border security and prevent similar incidents.
Last year, Jordan and Syria agreed to form such a committee to secure their border, combat arms and drug smuggling and work to prevent any resurgence of Islamic State militancy.

Fukuda, who died on Thursday from heart failure at the age of 90, used his brief period in office to seek closer ties with Asian neighbours, particularly China, with which relations have periodically been tense.
Fukuda was a Japanese politician of integrity and responsibility, as well as an old friend of the Chinese people, Xi said in his message, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Fukuda “upheld a correct view of history,” Xi said.

In his message on Tuesday, Xi said he “hopes Japan’s current leaders to cherish the hard work and efforts made by the older generation of politicians, abide by the four political documents between China and Japan, and earnestly safeguard the political foundation of bilateral relations.”
China would remember Fukuda’s contributions to China-Japan relations and to Asia’s development, Xi added.

Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:49:20 UTC
19:49:20 KST

Ukraine made significant progress in countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some air defence units reporting interception rates around 80%. But recent restrictions on US satellite services exposed Kyiv's reliance on US technology as it races to develop cheaper, more effective interceptors.
Ukraine's improved interceptor drone technology has helped it counter Russia's jet-powered drones, but disruptions to US Starshield satellite services threaten those gains.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Ukraine's interception rate fell slightly from 77% to around 74% during disruptions to the military-grade satellite service between 14 and 24 October.
The figures nevertheless represent a marked improvement on early September, when Ukrainian officials reported intercepting around 60% of Russia's jet-powered drones.
Some Ukrainian air defence units have reported interception rates exceeding 80%, although these figures reflect individual units' performance rather than nationwide results.
The Starshield restrictions, which affected high-speed drone operations, were lifted on 24 October, according to Ukrainian officials. However, the disruption highlighted the country's dependence on US satellite communications to sustain its air defences.
ISW warned that maintaining and improving interception rates would require Ukraine to develop and deploy affordable, high-speed interceptor drones on a much larger scale.
Russia has increasingly turned to jet-powered versions of its Shahed-type attack drones, which travel considerably faster than conventional propeller-driven models, leaving Ukrainian air defence crews with significantly less time to detect and intercept them.
Ukraine relies on a combination of interceptor drones, fighter aircraft and ground-based systems to counter the threat.
Interceptor drones have proved particularly effective, according to ISW, but many depend on Starshield connectivity to operate at the speeds required to engage faster Russian targets.
Ukrainian forces also use F-16 fighter jets, either firing air-to-air missiles or engaging targets with onboard guns. Both approaches have drawbacks: missiles are expensive and scarce, while gun engagements demand considerable pilot skill and expose aircraft and crews to additional risks.
Using fighter jets against drones also increases maintenance requirements and diverts aircraft from other missions.
Ukraine has installed ground-based gun turrets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, although expanding these systems nationwide would require considerable time and resources.
The race for cheaper interceptors
The growing threat has accelerated efforts by Ukrainian manufacturers to develop faster, more affordable interception systems.
One such project is the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor being developed by Ukrainian company F-Drones, which plans to incorporate artificial intelligence into its guidance system.
The company aims to keep the unit cost at approximately $7,000, compared with an estimated $20,000 to $70,000 for other high-speed interceptor drones and around $1 million for an air-to-air missile launched from an F-16.
Although the F-Jet 80 remains under development, its manufacturer says it has already successfully intercepted several Russian drones.
For Ukraine, the challenge extends beyond developing effective technology to producing it in sufficient numbers to counter Russia's expanding use of jet-powered drones.
ISW argues that integrating affordable interceptor drones into Ukraine's existing air defence network offers the strongest prospect of sustaining high interception rates as the country approaches another winter of Russian aerial attacks.

Pope Leo to return to his adopted home on South America tour
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:48:56 CET
19:48:56 KST

By Marco Aquino
ZAÑA, Peru Oct 27 (Reuters) - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America next week, many Peruvians remember him as the priest who helped feed hungry families, delivered aid after floods and walked alongside migrants in the country he would eventually call his own.
When the pandemic emptied the streets of northern Peru and one of the world’s longest quarantines left many struggling to eat, Bishop Robert Prevost, as Leo was known, helped launch a soup kitchen in 2020 in the small town of Zaña.
“He gave us an example of human charity, and we prepared the ‘aguadito con fe’,” recalled former cook Betty Burga Campos, referring to the traditional soup of rice, meat and vegetables that volunteers served.
Prevost left Peru for Rome three years later after Pope Francis tapped him to lead the Vatican office that recommends candidates for bishop appointments worldwide.
After rising from missionary and bishop in Peru’s far north to cardinal and ultimately pope, Leo, 71, is set to revisit the country where he became a citizen and built some of the relationships that defined his ministry, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer. The Vatican confirmed on Monday that his November 6 to 17 South America tour remained on schedule.
Across northern Peru, regional governments are refurbishing churches and residents are preparing celebrations for his visit, which also includes earlier stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
For many Peruvians, memories of the Chicago-born head of the Catholic Church are less about Vatican titles than muddy boots, long drives across the country’s rugged north and a hands-on approach to helping people.
“He had become Peruvian, even in the way he spoke. He no longer had much of that American accent,” said José Manuel Zamora Romero, a priest in Lambayeque who knew him for years.
The share of adults in Peru who identify as Catholic has fallen from 76% to 67% over the decade to 2024, according to Pew Research Center. The decline is often linked to social changes and distrust of institutions, following years of political instability that have caused Peru to cycle through nine presidents in a decade.
A BISHOP ON THE MOVE
Prevost arrived in Peru in 1985 at age 30. After years based in the United States and Rome with his Augustinian order, he returned in 2014 and became bishop of the Peruvian city of Chiclayo in 2015. In 2023, Pope Francis brought Prevost to the Vatican. Francis named him a cardinal later that year and he was elected pope in 2025.
Across northern Peru’s sun-baked farm belt, residents and priests recall a churchman constantly on the move.
For the future pontiff, “the distances were not limits, the distances were opportunities,” said David Farfán, a priest in Zaña, one of the towns on the pope’s upcoming itinerary.
Many remember Prevost riding horseback to isolated Andean communities. Others recall him driving hundreds of kilometers himself across Peru’s rugged north.
“His hobby was driving,” Zamora Romero said. “And I know he taught some priests to drive so they could get their licenses … and they all passed the test.”
That practical approach became evident during emergencies.
When severe flooding linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon inundated northern Peru in 2023, photos circulated on social media of Prevost wading through knee-deep water in rubber boots as he helped deliver aid.
When natural disasters occurred, “he was on the front lines to bring the help that the population needed,” said Rev. Jorge Villegas of Chiclayo, where the pope will spend two full days.
Residents pointed to moments like those as evidence of a bishop who preferred action over visibility.
“He wasn’t very focused on being with the press; he was more with the poor and in social conflicts,” said Verónica Castillo, a journalist in Chiclayo who witnessed his intervention during a 2015 labor conflict.
“He was a bishop who intervened, who took action, and people remember that,” she added, recalling how Prevost helped mediate the prolonged protest by workers against a sugar company, which turned violent.
‘PUT HIMSELF IN SHOES OF A MIGRANT’
Migration has reshaped much of Latin America over the past decade, as millions of Venezuelans fled economic collapse and political turmoil. Peru hosts the world’s second-largest Venezuelan diaspora community, with more than 1.5 million migrants. Many arrived without proper documentation and live with inadequate access to healthcare and basic services.
Prevost founded a Catholic organization in Chiclayo in 2018 to assist newcomers.
“He put himself in the shoes of a migrant first and foremost and knew what the situation was like,” said Augusto Martínez, who leads the organization.
The group has assisted thousands of Venezuelans.
As pope, Leo has called for migrants to be treated with dignity, condemned human trafficking and warned traffickers to repent or face divine judgment. He has criticized anti-immigration policies, including measures pursued by US President Donald Trump.
“He supported migrants on how to have a dignified life here in Peru,” said Lisbeth Coromoto Díaz, who received help through the Chiclayo organization and said he held Masses in honor of migrants.
Leo’s planned return to Peru has revived hopes among Catholics in Eten, near Chiclayo, that he could advance a long-running campaign to secure Vatican recognition of the town’s reported Eucharistic miracle. As bishop, he supported the cause, presenting historical records and thousands of testimonies of faith in Rome, linked to a 1649 apparition in which devotees say the image of the Christ Child appeared in a consecrated host.
Tourism officials are promoting routes tied to the places Leo lived and worked. Souvenir shops are stocking shelves with pope-inspired hats, key chains and pins.
In a shop window in the capital Lima’s Gamarra textile district, an image of Leo on a T-shirt depicts him smiling while enjoying a plate of Peruvian food.
“We’ve got the pope looking spirited; we’ve got the pope as a foodie, enjoying delicious ceviche and rotisserie chicken. We even have the play on words: ‘The Pope and the papa (potato) are Peruvian’,” said clothing maker Victoria Quiñones.
Quiñones predicted a 200% increase in her workload and was running low on fabric for the T-shirts.
Nearby, Maria Rodriguez, 70, was shopping for pope T-shirts.
“I’m buying several,” Rodriguez said.
“I’ll be wearing them all through November because I am Catholic: Roman and Peruvian,” she added.

Exclusive-Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:48:45 CET
19:48:45 KST

By Raphael Satter
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink’s satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro, concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.
The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI’s telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted. Bidding refers to the complex auction system by which advertisers secure space inside people’s browsers and apps.
SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two weeks.
TrendAI released a report on October 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79.” The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.
TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding “hype-driven labels” or “unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions.”
Finding ways to track Starlink users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals. Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields. Starlink has become a particularly important resource in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service for frontline communications and directing drone strikes.
In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process.
DISCOVER-TECH ACCUSED OF WIDER SPY EFFORT
The same day that TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology firm Confiant outed Discover-Tech by name.
Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder.
Over time, bidders can collect that leaked data, collate it and merge it with other information to de-anonymize users, follow them around the web and, in some cases, set them up for targeting with surveillance software.
Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads had been shown inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organizations, governments and tech firms.
In response to the investigations, Google, Comcast and other companies said they had removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms.
At least one big US tech company and one international organization recently launched internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech’s ads targeted their employees, according to one of the people and a seventh person familiar with the matter.
TOP ADVERTISER IN YEMEN, SOUTH SUDAN
TrendAI’s report cited suspicious bidding patterns that suggested Shadow-Earth-79 was running “targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation.”
In addition to noting the “obvious skew” towards buying ads aimed at Starlink users, the report said that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top buyer of ads in Syria, Libya, Yemen and South Sudan and was the No. 2 ad buyer in Afghanistan even though “the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero.” It said the entity won “an implausibly dominant share” of bids in several countries including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan and Venezuela.
TrendAI researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind the suspicious bidding activity and discussed naming the company in TrendAI’s report, according to the six people familiar with the matter. But they eventually dropped the idea of publicly attributing the activity to a named company after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of the sources said.
Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say.
Earlier this year, US cybersecurity company Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign even though its researchers were confident the hacking could be pinned on Beijing, Reuters reported at the time. Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that calling out China would cause problems for Palo Alto’s operations there, which were already under scrutiny following a Beijing directive ordering domestic companies not to use its products. Palo Alto said the lack of attribution in its report was not correlated with “procurement regulations in China” and that any suggestion otherwise was “speculative and false.”
(Reporting by Raphael Satter; editing by Chris Sanders and Rod Nickel)

Swiss house prices continued to rise over summer
House prices in Switzerland have continued to rise unabated. The upward trend continued in the third quarter of 2026 for both detached houses and flats.
From July to September, the Swiss Residential Property Price Index (IMPI) rose by 1.7% compared with the previous quarter to 129.8 points, as announced by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) on Tuesday. Year-on-year, prices have climbed by as much as 4.4%.
At national level, prices for detached houses have risen by 2.1%. Prices for flats have also increased by 1.3% compared with the previous quarter.
The sharpest rises in property prices were seen in urban municipalities within a small conurbation or outside a conurbation (+3.4%). The smallest price increase, at 0.6%, was recorded in so-called intermediate municipalities, which exhibit both urban and rural characteristics.
More
Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
Significant year-on-year increase
In the longer term, the upward trend in the property market is continuing despite prices already being high. Compared with the previous year, both detached houses (+3.3%) and flats (+5.4%) have risen significantly in price.
The IMPI is a relatively new indicator: it has only been published quarterly since the third quarter of 2020. According to the FSO, it is calculated based on an average of around 7,000 transactions from all regions of Switzerland. The FSO obtains data from the 28 largest mortgage lenders in Switzerland. These cover a very large market share, as the vast majority of property purchases are financed by a mortgage.
