Bulgaria’s Mobile Entertainment Economy: Choice, Consumer Safeguards and the Search for Recognised Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:23:00 UTC
19:23:00 KST

We have switched to winter astronomical time
Bulgaria switched to astronomical time last night, after clocks were set back one hour to 3:00 a.
Bulgaria’s digital entertainment habits are becoming ever more mobile-first. Whether people are reading the news, listening to music, watching live sport or browsing online services, the smartphone has become the handy starting point.
That shift brings plenty of choice, but it also raises sensible questions. Who is behind a service? How are payments handled? What happens to personal data? And, where an online activity is regulated, how can users check that the operator is permitted to offer it in Bulgaria?
These aren’t fussy details. They’re part of making informed decisions online, particularly when a familiar brand or game appears in search results and may be presented differently from one country to another.
The appeal of mobile entertainment is obvious. A single device can hold messaging, streaming, shopping, banking and a huge range of entertainment services. Faster mobile connections and broad access to smartphones have made discovering new platforms feel almost effortless.
That convenience has changed expectations. People increasingly expect:
Clear sign-up journeys
Reliable payment options
Pages that work properly on a smaller screen
Information in a language they understand
Customer support that is easy to find
Straightforward controls over accounts and notifications
Yet the same ease of access can make it tempting to skip the small print. A polished website or a recognisable logo is not, by itself, evidence that a service is authorised locally or that its terms suit your circumstances.
For regulated online services, including gambling, the sensible approach is to pause before registering or adding payment details. Look at who operates the site, where it is licensed, how it verifies users and which rules apply in your location.
Bulgaria’s public institutions have an important part to play here. The country’s National Revenue Agency has responsibilities connected with gambling oversight, while the Ministry of Finance sets out wider financial-policy information. For consumer matters more broadly, the Consumer Protection Commission provides a public route for information and complaints.
Mobile use isn’t just about portability. It changes how people find things.
Search engines, app stores, social platforms and recommendation systems can put a service in front of someone in seconds. That can be useful when you’re looking for a particular publisher, entertainment brand or recognised title. It can also mean that results from other markets sit alongside locally available services without much explanation.
The difference matters.
A page aimed at the UK, for example, may have different eligibility rules, payment arrangements, licensing information and customer-protection processes from a service available to Bulgarian residents. The language may be familiar and the site may look established, but availability is never something to assume.
Digital wallets and other online payment methods have also made account funding more immediate. That makes clarity particularly important. Before using any regulated service, it is worth checking:
Which company receives the payment?
What is the payment method’s own protection process?
Can you see the full terms before committing?
Is the service intended for your country?
A quick check may feel a little old-fashioned in a world built around tapping and scrolling. Still, it can save confusion later.
For any regulated online service, consumer protection should be visible rather than buried. You shouldn’t need detective skills to work out who is responsible for an account or how to raise a concern.
Start with the basics. A legitimate operator should clearly state its company name, registered address and relevant licensing details. If you cannot find those details, or if they appear inconsistent across pages, treat that as a reason to stop and investigate further.
In Bulgaria, gambling activity is subject to national rules and oversight. The precise legal position can change, and individual services may have different permissions, so it is sensible to rely on current official information rather than old forum posts or social-media claims.
Terms and conditions are rarely anyone’s favourite read, but a few sections deserve attention:
Account eligibility
Geographic restrictions
Identity checks
Payment and withdrawal rules
Privacy notices
Account closure and complaint procedures
Limit-setting and self-exclusion options, where relevant
The wording should be understandable. If a provider makes key conditions hard to locate, or writes them in a confusing way, that tells you something about the service.
Age verification is an essential safeguard, not an inconvenience. Gambling services are for adults only, and operators should take steps to confirm that a user meets the legal age requirement in the relevant jurisdiction.
Identity checks can also help prevent fraud and support safer payments. You may be asked for evidence of identity, address or ownership of a payment method. Only provide such documents through a secure, verified operator channel, never through an unexpected message or a link sent by an unverified contact.
Personal information is valuable. A provider should explain what it collects, why it collects it and how long it keeps it. You can also check whether the site uses secure connections, usually indicated by https and a padlock symbol in the browser.
For users in Bulgaria and elsewhere in the EU, the European Commission’s guidance on data protection is a useful starting point for understanding your rights under data-protection rules.
Be cautious with any service that asks for more information than seems necessary, particularly if it has not explained the reason. And never reuse a password from your email or banking account. A password manager can make this much less of a faff.
Problems happen. A payment may be delayed, an account may be restricted, or a user may believe a term was applied unfairly. What matters is whether the operator has a clear process for resolving it.
Keep copies of correspondence, screenshots of relevant pages and transaction references. If you cannot resolve an issue directly, Bulgaria’s Consumer Protection Commission may be a useful point of reference for consumer rights and complaint options.
Responsible use is not just a message at the bottom of a webpage. It is about setting your own boundaries before an activity becomes part of your routine.
Gambling is strictly for people aged 18 and over. Adults who choose to use gambling services should approach them as paid entertainment, not as a way to produce a particular financial outcome.
A few practical controls can help keep decisions deliberate:
Set a personal spending limit before depositing anything.
Decide how much time you are willing to spend and stick to it.
Avoid using a service when you are tired, upset or distracted.
Take breaks rather than making rushed decisions.
Review account settings for deposit, session or cooling-off controls.
Keep gambling separate from essential household spending.
There is no reliable way to predict or control the result of a gambling product. Recognising that upfront helps put the experience in its proper place.
If gambling no longer feels manageable, confidential support is available through organisations such as GamCare, which provides information and support for people affected by gambling-related harm.
It’s understandable to search for a title you recognise. Still, a game brand can appear on multiple sites, under different arrangements, and may not be available in every country.
Before accessing a familiar title, check:
Whether the operator accepts users in Bulgaria
Whether the service has the necessary local permissions
Whether the site’s terms name Bulgaria among eligible territories
Whether its age-verification requirements apply to you
Whether its customer support and complaint processes cover your location
A recognisable name is only one part of the picture. The operator, territory, rules and protections matter just as much.
## Entertainment resources

France Brings 10 European Allies Into Its Nuclear Deterrence Plan Against Russia

France Brings 10 European Allies Into Its Nuclear Deterrence Plan Against Russia
France is expanding its nuclear deterrence posture across Europe in response to nuclear threats from Russia, increasing its warhead stockpile for the first time in decades and placing its arsenal size under total secrecy, as reported by The Wall Street Journal.
As the only European Union member state possessing nuclear weapons, France holds approximately 290 nuclear warheads and is scaling up production while ending public reporting on its stockpile.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The move extends nuclear deterrence in Europe beyond the US nuclear weapons stored in five European countries under NATO’s nuclear sharing program. France has reached agreements with 10 European countries to join the strategic initiative: the United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark.
The framework centers on temporarily deploying nuclear-capable French Rafale fighter jets across Europe alongside the construction of specialized infrastructure, new communication systems, early warning capabilities, and intelligence-sharing mechanisms.
French President Emmanuel Macron has described the expanding nuclear umbrella as “advanced deterrence,” intended to complicate strategic calculations for Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Xavier Chatel, strategic advisor to the French president, stated that the initiative provides France with “new options for positioning nuclear forces in the event of nuclear escalation.”
Military experts note that this setup poses a more immediate tactical challenge for Russia than NATO’s traditional nuclear sharing program. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide noted that France holds a strategic capability that complements existing US security guarantees.
Analysts highlight that French ASMP-A cruise missiles carried by Rafale jets are designed to target major Russian cities with a high probability of reaching their targets, establishing a distinct level of deterrence.
Nicole Grajewski, a Russian and nuclear policy expert at Sciences Po in Paris, observed that while it remains unclear whether the posture will convince Russian strategists that France would risk a retaliatory strike on Paris for allies like Warsaw, Russian military officials are actively monitoring the expansion, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Earlier, Germany and France put their nuclear-deterrence cooperation into practice for the first time, staging a joint air force drill with nuclear-capable French Rafale jets and German Eurofighters.

Norway, Finland call Putin ahead of potential Abu Dhabi peace talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:22:35 UTC
19:22:35 KST

Editor's note: The article was updated following Russia's read-out of the call, and to include reactions from Ukraine, Denmark, and the EU.
The leaders of Norway and Finland held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 27, as part of a renewed push to bring Moscow's war in Ukraine to an end.
"Finland and Norway border Russia. They are firm supporters of Ukraine. The aim of the call was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin," reads a press statement published by the Norwegian and Finnish governments.
The two leaders' call with Putin follows an Oct. 20 meeting in Oslo with Ukrainian, European, and U.S. officials, but they stressed that in the Oct. 27 call, they "did not speak he behalf of Europe as a whole."
"The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation," said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The two leaders discussed the call with President Volodymyr Zelensky afterward, who said: "I am grateful for the detailed briefing and for their active support for our diplomacy and the peace efforts we are pursuing together with all our partners."
However, not all European leaders welcomed the news.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told the Danish news channel TV2 that she was "skeptical" of the call and that it had not been coordinated with others.
"I actually don't know what the two countries think can be achieved with this. I think we should stand together and speak with one voice," Frederiksen said.
Meanwhile a European Commission spokesperson reminded that "we have a shared interest in putting an end to this horrific war," in comments sent to the Kyiv Independent.
"On the EU side, we are adamantly committed not just to putting an end to the war but to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable. That is our aim and that is the stance we are defending in the ongoing talks," the spokesperson said.
The call also comes ahead of trilateral peace talks expected in the Emirati capital of Abu Dhabi sometime in November between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
Though Europe is not expected to be at the table for the talks, it is engaging in multiple ways to support Ukraine ahead of any trilateral gathering, with specific countries and the EU itself participating in various talks.
A senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent to expect a round of talks in Europe before the expected Abu Dhabi meeting, after mixed messages from Kyiv had given the impression that there would be Brussels-based peace talks this week.
Finland and Norway rank among Ukraine's strongest supporters. Norway is the only non-EU country to have made a pledge to support Kyiv's 2027 financial needs.
And Finland has provided 35 different packages of financial support, and its tech companies ICEYE and Nokia recently announced a partnership with Ukraine to build out its own satellite communications system.
Russian state news agency TASS confirmed that the call had taken place and provided the Kremlin's main talking points.
Among those points, "The president of the Russian Federation and the leaders of Norway and Finland reaffirmed the importance of complying with international maritime law and the principle of freedom of navigation."
At the time of publication, at least five ships are believed to be carrying Russian diesel to the U.S.: the Maltese-flagged Agioi Fanendes, two further ships reported by the Financial Times, and two additional ships pointed out by Ukraine's sanctions chief, Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
Two of those five ships have been identified as sanctioned vessels belonging to Russia's shadow fleet — the Sierra Leone-flagged tanker Leruo and the Russian-flagged Primorye — which means European authorities are required to stop them if they enter their territorial waters.

Richest 0.1 percent emit more carbon than poorest half of humanity combined: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:21:54 UTC
19:21:54 KST

A new Oxfam analysis released on Tuesday revealed that the world’s richest 0.1 percent, comprising around 8 million people, produce more carbon pollution than the world’s poorest 3.5 billion people combined.
The report found that a person in the richest 0.1 percent contributed nearly 400 times more to today’s extreme heat waves than someone in the poorest 50 percent of the global population, while the richest 0.1 percent collectively produce more than three times as much carbon pollution as the entire population of sub-Saharan Africa.
The report also found that the world’s richest one percent have been responsible for 20 percent of global warming since 1990, with per capita emissions 100 times higher than those of the poorest half of humanity.
The study estimated that a single year of emissions from the richest one percent could cause 1.9 million excess heat-related deaths, with 78 percent of these deaths projected to occur in low- and lower-middle-income countries, which account for just eight percent of global emissions.
The report further projected that emissions from the richest one percent would cause nearly $53 trillion in economic damage by 2050.
The report also highlighted private aviation as a stark example of carbon inequality, finding that private jets collectively emit more carbon pollution in two seconds than a person in the poorest half of the global population produces in a year.
“While the super-rich are responsible for a disproportionate share of carbon pollution, it is ordinary people who bear the brunt of the resulting floods, fires and famine,” the report noted.
The report also warned that climate crisis could displace up to a billion people, around 10 percent of the global population, by 2050, with most expected to be in the Global South.
“The climate crisis is often described as a shared human challenge. It is not. Those who have done the least to cause it are losing their homes, their harvests and, increasingly, their lives. Meanwhile, the super-rich can buy their way out of danger,” said Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar.
Behar noted that the super-rich also actively profit from the consequences of their pollution.
“This is not a tragedy of shared fate; it is a crime of extreme inequality,” Behar added.
The report also cautioned that climate disasters are increasingly being used to advance policies that deepen inequality, including privatisation, land grabs, deregulation and tax breaks for the super-rich.
“The ultra-rich are setting the planet on fire and then charging the rest of us for the extinguishers,” Behar said, adding: “They profit from the pollution. They profit from the disaster. And they profit again from the clean-up.”
Oxfam called on governments attending COP31 to make wealthy polluters pay through higher taxes, significantly increase public climate finance for the Global South and triple adaptation funding by 2035.
It also urged governments to reduce inequality through climate-resilient public infrastructure and services, and curb corporate profiteering from climate disasters.

designboom listens: paola pivi remembers what music leaves behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

designboom listens: paola pivi remembers what music leaves behind
for the Italian artist, music is less a tool for inspiration than a vessel for memory, carrying her back to moments, places, and feelings that remain long after a song ends.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
what does creativity sound like to paola pivi?
Paola Pivi rarely turns to music for inspiration or concentration, and when she gets stuck, her response is simple: ‘I act. I move. I search. I despair.’ Music enters her life in other ways, through memories of late-night Italian television, songs that transport her back to the 1990s, and the live performances of her husband, composer Karma Culture Brothers. This week on designboom listens, the Italian artist reflects on the songs that have stayed with her, the ones she can barely listen to anymore, and why she believes music and visual art operate on different terms.
In our weekly series, we explore the music behind creative practice, asking people from different fields what they listen to when they need inspiration, get stuck on a project, or find themselves drawn back to a particular memory. Pivi approaches these questions on her own terms. She describes conventional song structures as restrictive, prefers the unpredictability of experimental music, and finds that a song can sound entirely different depending on how and where she hears it. A recent performance of Franco Battiato’s Summer on a Solitary Beach through a 24-channel speaker system at Triennale Milano brought back memories of a car ride decades earlier. Yet, when she played the same track online afterward, she found it ‘annoying and disturbing.’ This sensitivity to the conditions of an experience also informs how she thinks about her art. Discussing Leoni, 68,000 Watts of Light, an installation that uses twelve large lights to alter viewers’ perception, Pivi questions the idea of pairing visual art with a soundtrack. As she puts it, ‘Because music needs time and visual art is instant.’ Read on for Pivi’s answers, and discover the songs and memories behind her listening habits.
the italian artist on music, memory, and the experience of art
 What song best captures your creative practice?
Paola Pivi (PP): Sex Pistols, God Save the Queen.
 What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project?
PP: No, no, no, no, no, inspiration and a new project need all the space in the world, there is no space for music in those moments. It would be disturbing.
 Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past?
PP: Well of course, tons of them. The last one was a song I saw 2 days ago on IG by Gianluca Grignani, La mia storia tra le dita. Very sentimental. Quite uncool to mention here. I saw a clip of him extremely young singing that song on the TV program Non è la Rai, a program that aired in Italy in the 90s with a large group of teenage girls hanging out together every afternoon. The girls appeared and sounded uncannily easygoing and interesting, in a twisted way, which was very captivating. In fact, their skills were manipulated because they were improvising with their authentic innocence but at the same time they were secretly prompted in an earpiece by adult authors.
It was fun to re-see what I probably, likely, had seen back then and sense the younger me watching that video, thanks to the emotions of the song, which drew me back in time to that precise moment, and feel the years in between in a sort of time lapse.
Another song that truly gave me a real time-machine trip back into a specific car ride in the 90s was Summer on a Solitary Beach by Franco Battiato, which I re-heard a couple of weeks ago in a magnificent way through the 24-channel speaker system of Voce, the new space at Triennale Milano dedicated to sound and music, curated by Carlo Antonelli. It is a place where music truly becomes a physical, dense mass in the space.
What song is stuck in your head right now?
PP: To tell you the truth, today really none, no song. I am not very inclined to music myself at all, I do not look for it, I do not play it. The melody of Battiato’s Summer on a Solitary Beach stayed with me for a few days after the performative experience of listening to it through the 24 speakers. Peculiar, though, that just now I re-searched for it online, to make sure I was quoting it right, and the music this time sounded annoying and disturbing to me. Often I find ‘regular’ music extremely boring with its 8 times 8 times 8 times… bridge, up and low. In this regard, I much prefer crazy music like Popol Vuh’s or the music of my husband, Karma Culture Brothers, which is not structured like that but free. He plays every day, so every day I have the extreme luxury of having a live chamber concert at home. Living with a composer is pretty cool, I suggest it. Also, having songs written about oneself is pretty nice. There are also certain Arabic music and songs that have stayed in a part of my memory and will never leave. They are two or three songs that Palestinian Instagram creators used a lot in 2024 and 2025.
What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track, the one you secretly know every word to?
PP: I have never memorized an entire song as far as I remember, but parts of some, yes, absolutely. My 2 AM song is Patti Smith’s Because the Night. It played every day at about 2 am in the early 90s on Italian TV. I used to stay up late every night to look for interesting programs on TV (Italian TV offered a lot back then), and that song marked the end of the night programming, or the beginning of the deep-night programming, Fuori orario. Cose (mai) viste (Outside of time. Things (never) seen) by Enrico Ghezzi, with niche movies often unwatchable.
The song played identically every night over images from the 1934 silent movie L’Atalante by Jean Vigo. It marked the end of the day for me; it had become a ritual. I totally adored the sounds and the images, but now, when I encounter the same song somewhere, I play it and… can hardly listen for more than a few seconds, because I find structured music too constrictive. A good song to end the day is also Into My Arms by Nick Cave.
What song do you put on when you’re stuck and need a breakthrough?
PP: When I am stuck I would never listen to music. I act. I move. I search. I despair. I stay stuck, but no music. When I felt very strong anxiety, at times, I sought the effect of Karma Culture Brothers’ solo flute, which is deeply touching and healed me.
What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you’re making right now?
PP: I do not use speakers, as the music flows up from the stairwell from Karma’s studio. Live, true. Live music does not make me feel the chains of time, like recorded music often does for me.
What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details?
PP: Honestly, details of art need silence. When I am doing repetitive activities, then I listen to what is happening in the world through news or IG. My life is already loaded with music because I live with a person who creates it live every day. It is part of the air in the house. I do not search for it on the web or through speakers.
If people were wearing headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing?
PP: My latest work in a show was Leoni, 68,000 Watts of Light, a performative piece that is a wall of light in a group show, made of 12 large Arri lights, fed by a generating truck, and inundating a room with bright light that is so intense it plays with the perceptive system of the viewers in different ways. Even the same person can have extremely different reactions to the amount of light on different visits, according to their status.
Which song is this piece? None, really. Because music needs time and visual art is instant.
What is your favorite album cover art?
PP: By far, Robert Crumb’s cover for Janis Joplin’s Cheap Thrills with Big Brother and the Holding Company. But then, on a second thought, I also truly like the cover of the album Circle by Karma Culture Brothers, conceived by him and photographed by Hugo Glendinning, where Karma is kissing the hand of our son as if with the respect due to a mafia boss.
What track best describes your favorite project you’ve worked on so far?
PP: Today Is the Day by Karma Culture Brothers. Karma composed this song when he and I were in India fighting a very long and dangerous legal battle against the Tibetan Children’s Village to save the rights of our son and our family from some very aggressive, evil people. The court case, which also changed Indian law, was definitely my favorite project. It changed Indian law, making sure that Tibetan children in India can be adopted and can adopt parents. The song, with its fast pace and ‘make me dizzy and crazy,’ is totally adherent to how we lived. Karma made an album and book about this arduous time of our life in India titled Circle. I am the editor of the book. The music is online, and the book can be read here,

Google Cloud unveiled a national cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) upskilling academy in partnership with the Informatics Industry Association of Türkiye on Tuesday to certify more than 1,000 professionals within a year.
Announced at Google Cloud Day Türkiye 2026 in Istanbul, which gathered more than 800 business leaders, developers and officials, the initiative supports the company's planned $2 billion local cloud region investment.
The program aligns with the Industry and Technology Ministry's 2026-2030 AI action plan, which aims to mobilize $10 billion and deploy one gigawatt of computing capacity.
"Advanced technology only creates sustainable economic value when local talent has the capability to drive it," said Onder Guler, country manager for Google Cloud Türkiye.
"Alongside our planned $2 billion local cloud region investment, we are equipping Turkish developers, engineers, and enterprise leaders with the certified skills required to deploy and govern production-grade AI systems," he added.
Funded by Google Cloud's Economic and Community Development division, the Türkiye Cloud and AI Upskilling Academy will offer subsidized certifications for developers, strategic training for executives and modernization roadmaps for local companies.
The event also marked the first anniversary of Google Cloud's 10-year, $2 billion local cloud region project in partnership with Turkish telecom operator Turkcell.
Speaking at the event, Guler said physical data center construction in the capital, Ankara, is progressing ahead of schedule and that local partner firms now employ more than 750 Google-certified engineers holding over 1,000 advanced certifications.
He said the upcoming Ankara facility will bring the same technological capabilities, security, speed and flexibility that power global services such as Google Maps, YouTube and Gemini for billions of users.
He added that this momentum will accelerate further in 2027 as partners increasingly help enterprises optimize business processes through artificial intelligence.
Google Cloud is also working closely with the Industry and Technology Ministry, the Cybersecurity Directorate and the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency to support regulatory compliance across key sectors.
To support startups, the company highlighted its collaboration with Türkiye's Small and Medium Enterprises Development Organization, providing entrepreneurs with financial and technical access to cloud computing and Gemini.
During the summit, Turkcell showcased its new hybrid-cloud data platform built on Google Cloud technologies for nonregulated digital services. 
90% of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini  
Also speaking at the event, Andrew Love, Google Cloud's AI go-to-market executive operations lead for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, highlighted the shift toward autonomous AI agents in business.
Love praised Turkish glassmaker Sisecam, noting that the 90-year-old global manufacturing powerhouse, with over 25,000 employees, including 11,000 in Türkiye, is undergoing an agentic transformation.
"AI is just a tool; it's the people who are the actual multiplier when it comes to your business," Love said, adding: "The model is just raw power; it's what you do with that model and who you give the model to that actually transforms a business."
Citing research showing that employees spend 40% of their time on "work about work" across multiple software windows, Love said 90% of Fortune 100 companies are already using Gemini Enterprise to streamline operations.
He said Gemini Agent functions as a universal agent with shared enterprise memory and unified security controls across platforms such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, ServiceNow, Jira and Salesforce.
"We're the only cloud provider in the world where you can get these models today, along with open weight and open source models that we will continue to add," Love said, referring to unified platform access to Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI models.

HSBC says ‘no pressure’ to move HQ out of UK despite prospect of higher bank taxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:21:03 UTC
19:21:03 KST

A top executive at HSBC has tried to quash speculation that the bank could move its headquarters out of the UK over tax increases expected to be announced in Wednesday’s budget.
HSBC’s chief financial officer, Pam Kaur, said there was “no pressure”, particularly from shareholders in its cornerstone Hong Kong market, to shift out of London despite lobbyists warning higher tax bills could drive big banks’ business abroad.
HSBC on Tuesday revealed a 32% rise in third-quarter profits to $9.6bn (£7.2bn), alongside plans to give $2.7bn to shareholders through dividends and buybacks.
Lobby groups have for months warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills, with the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, saying he could even scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if Britain became “hostile” to banks.
A handful of wealthy businesspeople have already said they are leaving the UK, with some criticising Labour’s tax policies.
The Guardian revealed earlier this month that the chancellor, John Healey, was planning to tax Britain’s banks in Wednesday’s budget. He is likely to reverse the previous Conservative government’s cuts to the bank surcharge.
“Irrespective of what happens on taxes, we are there to support our customers, and that is what we will do,” she told journalists during a media call on Tuesday. “We are very comfortable, we are domiciled in the UK and we remain in the UK. So that question is just not on the table,” Kaur said.
HSBC has a strong shareholder base in east Asia, where it makes the bulk of its profits, and has twice been pushed to shift or split its operations in reaction to UK policies.
That includes in 2015, when growing regulatory burdens and a new bank levy led HSBC to consider shifting its headquarters out of London to Hong Kong. The Conservative government later scaled back the levy to cover only UK-based assets, in a boon to HSBC.
HSBC later faced pressure to separate the bank’s profitable Asian business from the rest of its operations in 2022, amid anger that the UK had forced the bank to cancel its dividend during the first Covid lockdown.
Kaur gave broad backing to Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, saying the bank was “very encouraged by the government’s growth agenda”, adding that the bank would “just have to see how businesses and customers react”.
The lender’s profit in the July to September quarter was boosted by higher interest rates, lower loan losses and smaller legal provisions compared with last year. However, its UK-listed shares fell 5.4% on Tuesday, causing it to lose its status as the biggest company on the FTSE 100.
Kaur speculated that investors may have expected stronger forecasts for net interest income – which is the difference between what banks charge for loans versus what they pay out in deposits.
HSBC’s net interest income rose to $9.3bn in the third quarter, up from $8.8bn a year earlier. That metric has been a flashpoint for groups campaigning for a UK bank tax, including the Trades Union Congress, which said bank profits have been driven by higher interest rates rather than their own improving performance.
However, HSBC said its net interest income grew in the third quarter as a result of hedging strategies and a growth in deposits in Hong Kong, while UK deposits stayed flat.
The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said HSBC’s results still showed banks could comfortably shoulder higher taxes. “Some in the finance lobby have tried every which way to stop tax rises in the budget. But these results make it blatantly obvious banks can afford to contribute more.”
Abhijay Sood, an economist at the New Economics Foundation thinktank, said HSBC’s strong profits would be “difficult news to swallow for households struggling with rising mortgage costs”.
He added: “Like other big banks, its profitability has depended on keeping interest rates on savings accounts low, and a stealth subsidy from taxpayers via the Bank of England due to quantitative easing.
“While the rumours of a bank tax change in the budget are welcome, it is unlikely to go far enough …
“The chancellor should go further by clawing back the stealth subsidy, and use this to fund inflation-busting investment and keep the essentials of life affordable for ordinary people.”

James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:20:52 UTC
19:20:52 KST

James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- University of Birmingham
- Summary:
- A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.
- Share:
Astronomers have discovered surprising evidence that a scorching planet covered in molten rock may be protected by a reflective layer of clouds that acts like a giant sunscreen. Scientists previously believed that the planet's extreme conditions would make it nearly impossible for an atmosphere to survive, but new observations suggest otherwise.
An international team of researchers, including Dr. Anjali Piette, an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham, reported the findings in The Astronomical Journal. Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the scientists monitored a rocky exoplanet called TOI-561 b, located approximately 280 light-years from Earth. Over 37 hours, they observed nearly four complete orbits around its host star.
The observations indicate that TOI-561 b may be surrounded by a substantial atmosphere, although its conditions would be far too hostile for life as we know it. This atmosphere appears to help the planet reflect much of the radiation coming from its star. One possible explanation is a layer of highly reflective silicate clouds that prevents the surface from reaching the extreme temperatures expected on an exposed rocky planet. The atmosphere also appears to move heat from the permanently illuminated dayside toward the nightside, further reducing temperatures on the star-facing side.
A Lava Planet With an Atmosphere That Should Have Disappeared
Scientists still do not know exactly which gases make up the atmosphere of TOI-561 b. One possibility is a thick layer of carbon dioxide, resembling the atmosphere of Venus but under much hotter conditions. Another is an atmosphere dominated by sulfur dioxide, a gas released by volcanic activity on Jupiter's moon Io.
Dr. Anjali Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said: "Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.
"Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface, acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere."
James Webb Reveals Why the Planet Is So Reflective
Earlier measurements revealed something puzzling about TOI-561 b. Its dayside was significantly cooler than researchers predicted for a dark, rocky planet orbiting so close to its star. That unexpected temperature suggested that much of the incoming energy was either being transferred to the nightside or reflected back into space before it could heat the surface.
To investigate, the team observed the planet throughout its orbit, allowing them to examine its nightside for the first time. Because the same side of TOI-561 b always faces its star, the nightside receives no direct starlight. However, the measurements showed that this darker hemisphere was not warm enough to explain all the missing heat.
The findings instead indicate that TOI-561 b reflects approximately 75% of the starlight reaching it, a remarkably high proportion comparable to Venus.
To determine what could produce such strong reflectivity, the researchers compared the telescope measurements with computer models of the planet's climate. Their simulations suggest that clouds containing silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium silicate (MgSiO3), may form over the dayside. If present, these clouds could reflect incoming radiation before it reaches the surface, functioning as a natural sunscreen.
Professor Lisa Dang, who led the project at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, said: "We measured how the planet's brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere."
Could a Global Ocean of Lava Keep the Atmosphere Alive?
The new findings strengthen earlier evidence gathered by Professor Lisa Dang, Dr. Anjali Piette, and their collaborators that TOI-561 b has a thick atmosphere that may be continually replenished by gases escaping from its molten interior.
That possibility could help explain how the planet has maintained an atmosphere despite enduring intense radiation from its star for billions of years. Rather than simply losing its gases to space, the planet's vast reservoir of molten rock may be constantly releasing new material into the atmosphere.
Researchers now hope to determine whether TOI-561 b is more like an extremely hot Venus or a much more intense version of the volcanic moon Io. Additional observations with JWST at longer wavelengths could reveal important details about the atmosphere's chemical composition and help resolve the mystery of its long-term survival.
Professor Dang added: "The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b's atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of lo. Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years."

China Focus: Shenzhen pushes embodied intelligent robots into real-world use
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:20:02 CST
19:20:02 KST

SHENZHEN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- South China's tech hub of Shenzhen in Guangdong Province is advancing its embodied intelligent robot industry with moves such as opening a robot school to empower machines with practical capabilities for real-world production and everyday chores.
The Jubaopen Embodied AI Innovation Community was launched last month, offering a variety of scenarios for companies to collect data, train and test robots. In Chinese, Jubaopen literally means that embodied intelligence treasures gather together.
True to its name, Jubaopen now serves as a public treasure house for robot companies, acting as a functional community in the Embodied Intelligence Hub in Bao'an District of Shenzhen.
Shenzhen is one of China's most dynamic cities for the embodied intelligence industry, home to more than 1,100 companies spanning the full industrial chain, from core components to complete-robot manufacturing. Bao'an District alone boasts more than 600 AI and robot firms through major initiatives including the Embodied Intelligence Hub.
The robot school buzzes with learning and training activities. Many robots are stationed across a rich variety of scenes: beside beds, next to shelves, and inside bathrooms. Some are repeatedly picking up and putting down water bottles, while others are gathering scattered clothes into a laundry basket.
In a simulated living room and kitchen, technicians from Shenzhen Physen AI Technology Co., Ltd. (Physen AI) are collecting data while performing household chores. Right next door, a fleet of robots mirrors the technicians' movements, with all motion data recorded precisely.
The data generated at the school is fed back, cleaned, labeled, and turned into "textbooks" for robot learning, supporting subsequent rounds of training.
Once the training is complete, robots are tested in real-world scenarios on skills that include picking up a water bottle, folding clothes neatly and moving smoothly. Technicians then assess their behavior to decide what data needs improvement, and the training cycle repeats to make the robots smarter and more capable.
"In the real-world application scenarios built by this robot school, we collect data on-site immediately and test whether it works, greatly cutting our data-collection costs," said Huang Zhishen, founder of Physen AI.
Shenzhen's robotics sector reached historic highs in 2025. Humanoid robot production surged 83.1 percent year on year to 343,400 units, while the total robotics industrial output value exceeded 240 billion yuan (about 35.7 billion U.S. dollars), up over 20 percent year on year.
This rapid ascent is a reflection of Shenzhen's strategic focus on high-end innovation, such as embodied intelligence, while leveraging the broader manufacturing capabilities of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.
The Jubaopen Embodied AI Innovation Community integrates embodied intelligence data services with frontier technology business incubation, aiming to form a closed loop from data collection and training verification to business incubation and industrial deployment, according to Wang Maolin, co-founder of Jubaopen.
The robot school now covers more than 6,000 square meters. Its standardized robot training scenarios span six core fields: smart home, motion capture, elderly care services, new retail, 3C manufacturing, and AI for Science.
Beyond these training scenarios, it also connects to real-world venues such as sports stadiums, elderly care institutions, semiconductor factories, and commercial complexes, creating a closed loop of data collection, scenario iteration, and model optimization.
The school also provides public services to sci-tech companies across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, including standardized data collection, algorithm training, model iteration and product testing. These services help companies effectively reduce R&D spending and shorten commercialization cycles.
"Challenges of the robotics industry often lie not in concepts or breakthroughs in individual technologies, but in the continuous journey from prototype to engineering and then to scaled production," said Tan Weijia, secretary-general of the Shenzhen Robotics Association.
Targeting the huge market gap for tens of millions of hours of data required for the commercial deployment of robots, Bao'an District enables robot companies to go through the entire process -- from data collection and model training to real-world scenario testing -- through the robot school and other initiatives.
Zhang Xutao, deputy director-general of the Science, Technology and Innovation Bureau of Bao'an District, said the launch of Jubaopen precisely fills the embodied intelligence industry's gaps in data supply and early-stage incubation.
"It effectively tackles pain points such as high R&D costs, fragmented scenarios, and difficult data reuse. Empowered by capital, technology, and real-world scenarios, it helps frontier sci-tech projects take root and grow," Zhang added.
Jubaopen will move from the training ground to real-world sites such as factories, homes and stores, allowing robots to collect data and further verify their capabilities, according to Wang.
"It will also upgrade to take on the comprehensive roles of data production, model training and application verification, serving not only as a training hub for embodied intelligent robots, but also a solid public service base for the industry," Wang said. ■

Feature: Afghan entrepreneurs look to China's annual import expo to unlock global markets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
18:20:00 CST
19:20:00 KST

A worker of Jahan Saffron selects saffron for display at the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Herat Province, Afghanistan, Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Mashal/Xinhua)
KABUL, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- For a growing number of Afghan entrepreneurs, the China International Import Expo (CIIE) has evolved from a promotional platform into a strategic gateway, one that offers access to international buyers, investment prospects and commercial partnerships capable of lifting local enterprises beyond the constraints of the domestic market.
As the annual gathering in Shanghai draws near, Afghan companies specializing in handwoven carpets, premium saffron and rose-based products are preparing to showcase their goods with a clear objective: to deepen ties with Chinese partners and open pathways to wider global markets.
Hamed Rauf, vice president of Qader Rauf Company, is among the Afghan entrepreneurs seeking to strengthen the country's presence in China's lucrative carpet market through sustained participation in the expo.
"We hope that this year's exhibition will be as successful as in previous years and that we will be able to attract more customers. I hope we can display 80 to 90 percent of our products at this exhibition," Rauf told Xinhua.
The company, which currently employs between 350 and 400 women, has built much of its success around its participation in the CIIE since the event's inaugural edition in 2018. Rauf has attended the expo every year since then, using the platform to cultivate business relationships and introduce Afghan carpets to prospective international customers.
"By participating in the China International Import Expo, good doors were opened for us. We were able to meet and establish connections with Chinese traders," Rauf said.
The firm exported approximately 6,500 square meters of handwoven carpets to China so far in 2026, illustrating both the strength of existing trade links and the scope for further expansion.
Similar ambitions are driving Jahan Saffron, an Afghan enterprise preparing to showcase one of the country's prized agricultural products at the international trade event in Shanghai.
"We hope to return from this year's exhibition with better results and make progress towards securing a market for Afghan saffron in China," said Farhad Omid, who is in charge of Jahan Saffron.
Omid said closer links with Chinese buyers could help Afghan producers reach new customers, explore export opportunities and expand their presence in international supply chains.
"China purchases tonnes of saffron annually from various countries. This presents an excellent opportunity for Afghanistan to supply the Chinese market with saffron and other products, including dried fruit," he said.
The drive to expand internationally is also reaching Afghanistan's traditional rose-based fragrance industry, where producers are seeking to connect local resources and craftsmanship with international demand.
Dara-e-Noor Rose Herbal Pharma, based in eastern Nangarhar province, is preparing to participate in the China International Import Expo in Shanghai for the first time. The company hopes to use the event to introduce its products to a wider audience, establish relationships with international traders and explore opportunities to expand its overseas markets.
"We want to establish links in China with international traders involved in the production and processing, as well as the buying and selling, of rose products, so that we can develop markets for our products globally," Shirin Aqa Raouf, the company's sales manager, told Xinhua inside his company in Behsud district of Nangarhar.
The company sees international market access as an opportunity not only to increase sales, but also to expand its production base and strengthen links with local growers.
"We hope to return from the exhibition with sufficient marketing opportunities to expand our operations throughout Dara-e-Noor district, as well as into other cooler districts of Nangarhar and Kunar provinces, and ultimately across Afghanistan," Raouf said.
For these Afghan enterprises, the China International Import Expo is far more than a temporary showcase. It offers a rare platform to build lasting commercial partnerships, diversify export markets and integrate into global value chains, objectives many local business leaders see as vital to the country's longer-term economic recovery. ■

ABC to take legal action against One Nation over 'shocking' use of Bluey in party's videos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:19:52 UTC
19:19:52 KST

IN BRIEF
- One Nation is under fire for its use of Bluey in a 2024 episode of the party's Please Explain series.
- In the episode, it's implied that Bluey mows down Daniel Andrews and Anthony Albanese with a car.
Communications Minister Anika Wells says the ABC is "well within its rights" to be concerned about a One Nation video in which its beloved character Bluey is run over by a car.
The Australian cartoon dog appeared in a 2024 episode of One Nation's Please Explain series, now the subject of legal action by the ABC.
In the episode, a car driven by former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews hits Bluey, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the passenger seat.
The episode implies the battered Bluey mows down the premier and prime minister later in the episode, titled The State of Melbourne.
"Bluey is one of Australia's biggest, most large, most well-known exports. I think the ABC's well within its rights to be concerned here," Wells told ABC RN on Wednesday morning.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Wells acknowledged the video series is satirical, but said there is a line between satirising politics and making a politician's life "unbearable".
"It's certainly not something that I would produce or that I would ever ask my team to produce," she said.
'We will be taking further action'
ABC managing director Hugh Marks said it was a "shocking use of Australia's most loved character" in a Senate estimates hearing on Tuesday.
"Probably the globally most loved character in a video that is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia," he said.
"I can't substantiate it either legally, or on the basis of its usage."
Labor senator Varun Ghosh described Bluey's use as "heinous", particularly in light of the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines on 19 October, where she was hit by a car and lost both legs.
To Marks' knowledge, One Nation had not licensed Bluey's likeness from BBC Studios, which distributes the TV show, but could still be entitled to show the character under fair use provisions if Please Explain is considered satire or parody.
But the ABC boss said he did not think that defence would suffice.
"It's not a parody of any Bluey work, it's not a minor use of the (intellectual property). In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property," he said.
"I think it's a blatant use.
"We will be taking further action. I can assure you."
The broadcaster will write One Nation a cease and desist letter demanding the video be taken down, with Marks flagging it may seek damages.
The party used Bluey in another Please Explain episode about Queensland, where the dog did not drive into any politicians.
Wells declined to comment on any legal proceedings when asked, but she added: "Bluey has a lot more production value than One Nation's cartoons. We can all learn a lot from Bluey."
Joyce accuses critics of 'sanitising beyond satire'
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has said the Please Explain cartoons were satire and were not meant to be taken seriously.
"You get to a point where you are sanitising beyond satire and you are starting to put restrictions on us," he told ABC TV on Tuesday.
"You've got to have some form of tolerance."
Joyce has previously apologised for another One Nation cartoon calling Liberal frontbencher and former Special Air Services soldier Andrew Hastie a "traitor".
The episode remains on YouTube.
The party's leader Pauline Hanson has also said sorry for a Please Explain episode making fun of Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie's vaginal prolapse, which has been taken down.

Ukraine receives 12 Patriot missiles per month from US, Zelensky says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:04:13 UTC
19:04:13 KST

Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month from the U.S. throughout 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalist on Oct. 27 at a closed-door press briefing.
Ukraine needs to intercept around 150 Russian ballistic missiles per month but receives about 150 Patriot missiles from the U.S. annually, according to Zelensky.
The president said some European countries have agreed to provide additional missiles from their stockpiles, but the transfers require approval from Washington. Zelensky pointed to documents awaiting action by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
"We want the Americans to start signing off on the supply of antiballistic missiles – interceptor missiles – to Ukraine from the countries we've reached agreements with. Because without Hegseth's signature, it's simply impossible," Zelensky said.
Zelsnky said on Oct. 26 that Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Hegseth to approve missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems. Ukrainian officials have described the delays and disruptions as an example of political pressure from Washington that could put civilian lives at risk.
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, including NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the United States.
The shortage also affects missiles for NASAMS air defense systems, which Ukraine receives through the PURL initiative.
Zelensky also said he had asked U.S. President Donald Trump for a special package of interceptor missiles ahead of winter during a meeting in New York on Sept. 22. Trump promised to make efforts to secure the missiles, Zelensky said, but noted that the U.S. also needed them for their own defense.
"These are the circumstances I live in today: every week, we have to put together new packages, find new missiles, and secure new air defenses. We need them every day to save the lives of our people from Russian ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, Russia has launched over 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since Oct. 14.
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to "bad weather conditions."
Zelensky added that the war in the Middle East has reduced military and financial support for Ukraine, making it more difficult for Kyiv to secure the air defense supplies needed to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
"The war in the Middle East is having a negative impact on the whole world. The energy challenges around the world are caused exclusively by the Strait of Hormuz. All the other challenges are also affecting Ukraine. The military and financial support Ukraine receives has definitely declined because of the war in the Middle East," he said.

The Dutch government on Oct. 28 outlined a package of non-military aid worth 1.2 billion euros (about $1.3 billion) for Ukraine, to be disbursed over the next three years and directed toward the country's economic recovery.
"Support for recovery and reconstruction can't wait for a ceasefire. Ukraine needs our help right now: military support, but also social and economic assistance," Dutch Foreign Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma said during his visit to Kyiv.
"However successful you are on the battlefield, it's also essential that energy systems, hospitals and food production keep ticking over."
The package includes 878 million euros (close to $977 million) previously outlined in the Dutch government coalition agreement, plus an additional 327 million euros ($364 million) announced on Sept. 15.
The funds will be disbursed between 2027 and 2029 and are separate from Dutch military aid to the war-torn country.
The Netherlands unveiled further details about the package on the occasion of Sjoerdsma's visit to Ukraine's capital, which comes as the country braces for another brutal winter of Russian attacks against energy infrastructure.
The bulk of the package will be directed to support Ukraine's energy and water sectors.
Under this assistance, the Netherlands will provide 40 million euros ($45 million) to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund by the end of the year, as well as 55 million euros ($62 million) to fund energy equipment from Dutch companies via the Netherlands Enterprise Agency.
The package also includes support for Ukraine's private sector, and Sjoerdsma will sign a memorandum with Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko on 10 million euros ($11 million) for Ukraine's Ramstein initiative — a project aimed at restoring and modernizing the country's industrial base.
A significant part of the aid will be channeled to Ukraine via the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the World Bank, and the European Investment Bank (EIB).
"We will be with Ukraine however long and whatever it takes," Sjoerdsma told the Kyiv Independent in an interview, noting he will hold talks with Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi and other Ukrainian officials during his visit, and possibly hold a call with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The Dutch minister added that "if demands change, if the situation changes, whether it's in Kyiv or in Ukraine, we will adapt our support accordingly... because it's not about what we want to offer you, it's about what Ukraine needs."

Ambassador Schiavo presents the Stella d’Italia to writer Amara Lakhous
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:17:21 CET
19:17:21 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Algeria, Alessandra Schiavo, presented the Italian-Algerian writer Amara Lakhous with the title of Knight of the Order of the Star of Italy, an honor conferred upon him by President of the Republic Sergio Mattarella back in 2021 but which could not be presented at the time due to the pandemic.
                                    
The ceremony, held at the Italian Residence, brought together members of the diplomatic corps, representatives of the Italian community and the “Scuola Roma” in Algiers, senior officials from the University of Algiers 2, the Faculty of Languages, and the Department of Italian Studies, the director of the Italian Cultural Institute in Algeria, Paola Cordone, and numerous Algerian publishers, journalists, and artists.
                                    
Ambassador Schiavo recalled the reasons for awarding the honor to this writer, who was born in Algiers and later moved to Rome during the “Black Decade.” Having acquired dual citizenship, Lakhous mastered Italian to such an extent that he has become one of the world’s rare examples of perfectly bilingual writers.
                                    
He is the author of a prolific body of work in Arabic and Italian—with some of his novels translated directly from the Italian text into numerous European and non-European languages —Lakhous has distinguished himself for his tireless commitment to promoting the Italian language and culture, which he now teaches in the United States at Yale, one of the most prestigious universities on the international stage.
                                    
“By making the encounter between languages one of the defining elements of his work,” said Ambassador Schiavo, “Lakhous has shed light on the themes of exile and identity, contributing to reflection on many contemporary urban contexts.”
Amara Lakhous’s visit to Algeria is part of the program promoted by the Italian Embassy and the Italian Cultural Institute in Algiers on the occasion of the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, dedicated this year to the theme “Brilliant Language: Conceive, Design, Create with Italian.” The program includes meetings with students and faculty from the Italian Studies departments of four Algerian universities (Annaba, Algiers, Blida, and Oran), as well as the author’s participation in the 29th edition of the Salon International du Livre d’Alger (SILA), scheduled for October 28 through November 7.
                                    
The book fair will mark the 20th anniversary of the Italian publication of “Clash of Civilizations Over an Elevator in Piazza Vittorio,” one of the author’s best-known novels and a significant work of contemporary literature on the transformations of multicultural societies.

Can Oleshky truce pave way for wider Russia-Ukraine peace?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Kanyshai Butun
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
- Truce in Russia-controlled Ukrainain city of Oleshky aims to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations amid worsening humanitarian crisis
- Analysts say sustained ceasefire could build momentum for broader negotiations, but doubt it will hold amid failed truce attempts
A temporary ceasefire has taken effect in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, but analysts remain skeptical about whether it will hold.
The ceasefire, announced by US first lady Melania Trump, took effect Tuesday and could serve as a test of broader US-mediated efforts to end the war.
Eugene Chausovsky, senior director at the New Lines Institute, told Anadolu that a ceasefire sustained beyond a “few days” could signal that both sides were willing to consider similar arrangements across a wider geography of the conflict.
Failure to sustain it, however, would reinforce the "status quo" amid already high levels of mistrust, he said. 
Truce could test prospects for peace talks
The truce comes ahead of trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US scheduled for the first half of November, raising the prospect that a successful local arrangement could inject momentum into broader negotiations.
Chausovsky said a successful truce in Oleshky “could breathe new life” into the upcoming talks and have important implications for the overall conflict.
“It is possible that this localized ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a significant test for broader US-mediated ceasefire arrangements to be put into place between Ukraine and Russia,” he said.
Timothy Ash, an associate fellow in the Russia and Eurasia program at Chatham House, was more skeptical that a localized ceasefire would change the course of the war, saying Russian President Vladimir Putin still believed he held the upper hand.
"It’s possible that if the ceasefire holds it could generate some positive vibes around broader peace talks - but I doubt it," he told Anadolu.
Ash questioned whether the truce would alter Putin's approach to the war, arguing that Moscow's ambitions remained “maximalist," with Russia rejecting several ceasefire efforts and believing that US Donald Trump could reduce US support for Ukraine, weaken the Western alliance and ultimately make concessions to its demands. 
Humanitarian crisis
The truce comes as Moscow and Kyiv trade blame for the worsening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, a city in Ukraine's southern Kherson region that Russian forces captured in 2022.
Oleshky had a prewar population of around 24,000, but estimates suggest only 1,700-2,000 people remain, many of them older residents unable to leave.
Thousands of people lost their homes to massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023, with both sides accusing each other of blowing it up.
Ukraine has accused Russia of trying to turn the city “into a death trap,” saying the only exit route and a nearby river are mined and monitored by attack drones.
“Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in homes, as Russians forbid residents from burying them. Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
He added that the local hospital had run out of medicine and residents feared they would not survive the winter.
Moscow has rejected Kyiv's accusations.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov described the situation in Oleshky as critical, saying Kyiv “is doing literally everything it can” to prevent food and medicine deliveries.
Trump described the situation as “dire,” saying that without intervention, bringing humanitarian aid into the city and evacuating the elderly would be “impossible.” 
Will truce hold?
Although Russia and Ukraine agreed to halt fighting in the area from Tuesday morning to facilitate the humanitarian operation, analysts remain sceptical that the ceasefire will hold, given the broader military and political objectives of both sides.  
“Failure of the Oleshky ceasefire would signify that diplomatic mediation efforts are still unable to overcome the competing objectives of Russia and Ukraine in their protracted conflict,” Chausovsky said.
“I think the war goes on and we see a winter of escalation by both sides,” Ash said.

Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:15:50 UTC
19:15:50 KST

Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
- TrendAI said an Israeli ad tech firm, likely Discover-Tech, heavily targeted Starlink users. Researchers said the ads may have been used to geolocate or spy on them.
- Citizen Lab and Confiant later named Discover-Tech, saying it abused ad bidding to leak user data. Google, Comcast and others removed it from their ad platforms.
- The firm was a top bidder in more than 100 countries, including Syria, Yemen and South Sudan. TrendAI held back the name over legal fears, showing how cyber firms self-censor.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Experts at a digital defence firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink’s satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro, concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.
The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI’s telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted.
Bidding refers to the complex auction system by which advertisers secure space inside people’s browsers and apps.
SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two weeks.
TrendAI released a report on Oct 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79”. The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.
TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding “hype-driven labels” or “unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritisation, and trigger inappropriate response actions”.
Finding ways to track Starlink users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals.
Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields.
Starlink has become a particularly important resource in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service for frontline communications and directing drone strikes.
In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process.
Discover-tech accused of wider spy effort
The same day that TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology firm Confiant outed Discover-Tech by name.
Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder.
Over time, bidders can collect that leaked data, collate it and merge it with other information to de-anonymise users, follow them around the web and, in some cases, set them up for targeting with surveillance software.
Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads had been shown inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organisations, governments and tech firms.
In response to the investigations, Google, Comcast and other companies said they had removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms.
At least one big US tech company and one international organisation recently launched internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech’s ads targeted their employees, according to one of the people and a seventh person familiar with the matter.
Top advertiser in Yemen, South Sudan
TrendAI’s report cited suspicious bidding patterns that suggested Shadow-Earth-79 was running “targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation”.
In addition to noting the “obvious skew” towards buying ads aimed at Starlink users, the report said that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top buyer of ads in Syria, Libya, Yemen and South Sudan and was the No. 2 ad buyer in Afghanistan even though “the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero”.
It said the entity won “an implausibly dominant share” of bids in several countries including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan and Venezuela.
TrendAI researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind the suspicious bidding activity and discussed naming the company in TrendAI’s report, according to the six people familiar with the matter. But they eventually dropped the idea of publicly attributing the activity to a named company after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of the sources said.
Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say.
Earlier in 2026, US cybersecurity company Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign even though its researchers were confident the hacking could be pinned on Beijing, Reuters reported at the time.
Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that calling out China would cause problems for Palo Alto’s operations there, which were already under scrutiny following a Beijing directive ordering domestic companies not to use its products.
Palo Alto said the lack of attribution in its report was not correlated with “procurement regulations in China” and that any suggestion otherwise was “speculative and false”. REUTERS
