Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

The Franklin County board of elections building at 1700 Morse Street in central Columbus, Ohio, is an early voting site for next week’s midterms. It is also located in the middle of the large Somali American community that was targeted by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s Operation Buckeye last December. The campaign was designed, the agency said, to find “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens.”
The result was a paltry number of arrests, months of sustained harassment, and a lingering feeling that ICE agents could return at any minute, especially around election time.
“Here in central Ohio, our early voting location is located in a neighborhood that's been the hardest hit by ICE, and it's an immigrant community neighborhood,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with the 614 ICE Watch group and the Ohio Good Neighbor Network, tells WIRED. “So we knew that that neighborhood was at risk and that people were going to be going to vote there, and a lot of the community there, like our Somali community that can vote, our Latino community, they walk to the location.”
Baiman’s group is responding to the threats from the Trump administration to target immigrant communities during the midterms. Dozens of volunteers are already patrolling near early voting sites in Columbus every day, Baiman says, and the figure will rise to around 250 on Election Day. They have been trained to document, record, and report any sightings of federal immigration agents, sharing the information in dozens of Signal and WhatsApp groups.
“We teach people that they have to observe the behavior. We show them what to look out for, what does ICE look like, this is the type of uniform that agents wear, these are the types of vehicles that they drive,” Baiman says. “We show them examples so that they can get familiar with what they might see.”
These efforts are being repeated in towns and cities across the country. WIRED spoke to a dozen people taking part in this effort, whose groups are working together to combat what they see as an existential threat to American democracy. Central to this response are training sessions run by massive national groups like Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Indivisible, as well as local groups like Living United for Change in Arizona and NorCal Resist, that have created massive groups of people who can document and record what ICE is doing, understand voters rights, and in many cases, prepare for worst-case scenarios.
Officially, the Department of Homeland Security has said that it has no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on Election Day. “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED, but added: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”
For the past six months, President Trump and his allies have declined to rule out possible deployments to voting locations during the midterms, even though they would be illegal under federal law. When asked in May if he would deploy the National Guard or ICE during the midterms, Trump said: “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections.”
“Why are there objections to sending ICE officers to polling places?” Todd Blanche, then acting attorney general, said in July. “Illegals can’t vote.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.
Some election experts simply don’t believe it will happen: “ICE and troops will not be at the polls,” David Becker, a former Justice Department trial attorney who is now head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said at a recent media briefing. “It won't happen. If it happens at all, it will be isolated. It will be accidental. It just won't happen.”
But for organizations on the ground interacting with voters in communities that have been targeted by ICE during Trump’s second term in office, the reality feels very different. Hundreds of different groups are part of the fight against possible ICE intimidation at the polls, and they are all working in coordination with each other.
“I've been up and down this state, in and out of Reno, in and out of Las Vegas, into our rural counties, and the number one question I get is about federal agents at polling locations,” Cisco Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, tells WIRED.
Beatriz Lopez, the executive director of Voto Latino, a group encouraging Hispanic and Latino citizens to register to vote, agrees, particularly when it comes to the communities her organization is focused on.
“We know that Latino voters are in the crosshairs of this administration because we know our electorate, our voting bloc, is what's going to shape and determine the elections of so many competitive races,” Lopez tells WIRED. “There is legitimate fear among our community.”
Lopez’s group, like many others WIRED spoke to, will be operating a war room on Election Day, with the specific goal of identifying and debunking viral disinformation that could dissuade citizens from voting. But they are also preparing for more troubling, real-world concerns.
“One of the scenarios that we're anticipating is that at the same time that we're trying to get people out to vote, there might be home raids by ICE in some of these neighborhoods, which has a real chilling effect on people,” Lopez said.
To combat this scenario, groups like 614 ICE Watch in Columbus are organizing patrols in neighborhoods near polling locations. “We send our folks in pairs or in groups. We never want to send anyone alone; we always want to have multiple people there so they can help take control of the situation,” Baiman says, adding that they have trained volunteers in a unique method of de-escalation: “If it starts to get very tense, we teach our folks to hum, to sing, to calm themselves down.”
The goal is not to interact with ICE agents but to document what they are doing so that events can be properly recorded and shared publicly. In January, just days after Alex Pretti was shot and killed in Minneapolis, more than 200,000 people logged into an “Eyes on Ice” Zoom training session, designed to teach people how to properly document ICE activities. Those skills are now being deployed during the midterm elections, Ezra Levin, cofounder of Indivisible, a group founded to stop the rise of authoritarianism in the US, tells WIRED.
On a much smaller scale, Living United for Change in Arizona has been training volunteers to become “constitutional defenders” in person, as the group prepares for next week’s vote. To track ICE activity, the group created a heat map that volunteers use to log and track ICE activity. The map is not available publicly, but WIRED was given access to the website and reviewed hundreds of recorded incidents of ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties.
Groups are also using social media to draw attention to what is happening. Last week in Sutter County, California, six ICE vehicles showed up in the parking lot of the Yuba City board of elections building, where a ballot drop box is located. Following a call from a local resident, NorCal Resist, a mutual aid organization, was able to send one of its trained volunteers and post an alert on Instagram.
“They don't like the attention, [and] when there's more community attention, they do often leave,” Giselle Garcia, programs director with NorCal Resist, tells WIRED.
DHS denied it was conducting immigration enforcement at a polling location, and said its agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation against an illegal immigrant from Mexico. “ICE parked in front of a polling center—with permission from a representative of the center—while waiting for the target to exit the courthouse,” Chandler Rebel, a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.
Much of this work, however, is being done in private, a move Lopez says is necessary to protect the online infrastructure they have put in place over the course of the past two years. Levin said that Indivisible’s leadership team would be hunkered down in an Airbnb in an undisclosed location on Election Day, on alert to deploy their sizable resources wherever they are needed.
Despite the fear that pervades minority communities about what Trump and his federal agents will do next week, every group leader, activist and volunteer WIRED spoke to in recent weeks has repeated one central belief: They are prepared.
“You have all this traditional election protection infrastructure that's really, really robust, but then there is this grassroots infrastructure,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, which combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They've done all this tactical documentation training. They know how to be constitutional observers, and I'm pretty confident that when and if we have an uptick in federal enforcement at the polls, it's going to get documented really, really quickly, and it's going to be beamed out to the world that it's happening.”

AFP boss warns boys as young as 12 being radicalised at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:13:56 UTC
19:13:56 KST

AFP boss reveals new youth radicalisation data, with warning signs for teen boys
In short:
AFP boss Krissy Barrett says new youth teen radicalisation data shows the evolution of youth extremism, revealing warning signs and shattering previous assumptions.
Commissioner Barrett has also revealed that female parliamentarians are three times more likely to receive abuse or threats, showing a clear gender divide.
What's next?
Commissioner Barrett will raise security for politicians at an upcoming meeting with state and territory police commissioners.
Australia's top cop Krissy Barrett has warned teenage boys as young as 12 are being radicalised in their bedrooms, lured by a chaotic blend of violent jihadism, white supremacy and anti-government rage.
A statement from Commissioner Barrett tabled at Senate Estimates details an internal AFP analysis of 55 radicalised children aged 12 to 17, revealing a chilling evolution in modern extremism.
All of the subjects were male, and every single one was radicalised all or in part online.
While violent jihadism remained the most prevalent belief system, it was closely followed by anti-authority and white supremacist ideologies, with an increasing number of boys displaying no clear ideology at all.
"The ideological presentation in youths has shifted over the past two years, with fewer presenting with clearly defined ideologies, and an increasing number having mixed/hybrid ideologies, unclear/ incoherent ideologies, a superficial understanding of ideologies and ideological fluidity," she said.
The data shatters long-held intelligence assumptions that youth extremism is confined to broken homes, revealing that boys from stable families with secure parental bonds are increasingly being weaponised by digital algorithms.
While more than one-quarter did not have a stable male role model and about one-third had witnessed or experienced violence from their caregivers, Commissioner Barrett said there "were also youth cases where there was a secure bond to one or both caregivers."
"This shows kids who come from stable family environments and have few vulnerabilities are also becoming radicalised and manipulated,"
she said.
Commissioner Barrett did point to some clear warning signs among the cohort, including 13 per cent being suspended or expelled in primary school, with more than a third kicked-out from high school.
"In three out of five cases, the youths had received support, treatment or intervention for a mental health condition," she said.
She also warned presentations were not clear-cut and increasingly complex, with "no single profile of a radicalised young person and no one pathway to violent extremism."
She said she hoped the study would help the federal police and policy makers intervene earlier to prevent youth offending.
Parliamentarian security
In the wake of last week's attack on independent MP Helen Haines, Commissioner Barrett told Senate Estimates the AFP handled nearly 800 protective security reports targeting parliamentarians in the first six months of the year.
She warned basic policy debate is increasingly triggering direct threats against politicians.
"At times there is an almost immediate link from a policy announcement or comment, to a threat being sent," Commissioner Barrett said.
"It would be wrong to think only inflammatory comments are creating the flood of threats. In some cases, just the debate causes the hate."
Detailing the drivers behind the harassment, the commissioner said AFP caseloads showed hostility is typically triggered by four factors: policy, perceived performance, profile, and personality.
"In some cases, parliamentarians are being targeted because of their accent, what they look like, or their political party," she said.
The evidence presented to the committee exposed a stark gender divide in the abuse directed at elected officials with female parliamentarians three times more likely than their male colleagues to receive sexualised or gender-based threats.
That toll is highest for female MPs from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, who report the most frequent and varied attacks.
Male parliamentarians are also subject to gender-based abuse, with Commissioner Barrett noting that threats directed at men frequently rely on "accusations of weakness, femininity or subordinate masculine traits."
Facing pressure from MPs and senators over the adequacy of current protection measures, Commissioner Barrett acknowledged the AFP needed to "do better" in demonstrating how seriously threats are managed.
She committed to implementing more consistent officer training and confirmed she would raise parliamentarian security at an upcoming meeting with state and territory police commissioners.
Social media and technology
The surge in threats against politicians is unfolding against a broader, more alarming shift across Australian society, one Commissioner Barrett warned is driven by an "instant pipeline" of digital hostility home-delivered into everyday lives.
"The threats are instant and voluminous. And they instantly shock and cause legitimate fear," she said.
"Perceived or real anonymity have given cowards courage."
Pointing to a dangerous convergence between digital platforms, social hostility, and ideological obsession, the commissioner warned that online abuse is spilling into physical violence.
"The contagion of online hate has breached the digital compound and is spilling into the physical world. This is corroding our communities and has normalised violence — and it continues to impact on many, most notably, the Jewish community," she said.
Crucially, Commissioner Barrett warned that hyper-connectivity and artificial intelligence have erased the geographic isolation that historically shielded Australia from global threats.
"Across the world, we are witnessing a trend where violence emerges with little or no warning, particularly where individuals do not have a protection intelligence footprint," she said.
"Lone actors are being motivated by a convergence of personal grievance, mental health vulnerabilities and ideological concerns. What helped keep us safe in recent times, such as our geography, analogue systems and far away criminals, has been impacted by fully-integrated technology, social media and artificial intelligence."

OPINION - Brazil has chosen, and Lula must deliver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:13:02 UTC
19:13:02 KST

Marcus Vinicius De Freitas
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Marcus Vinicius De Freitas is a visiting professor at the China Foreign Affairs University and a senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, based in Morocco.
Brazil’s voters have given President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva another chance to govern. His victory also preserves the country’s freedom to negotiate its international partnerships. The election results leave Lula responsible for demonstrating what he can deliver in a fourth term. Whether an octogenarian president in a Latin America that is turning conservative can do so is a defining question for the next four years.
Lula won 51.79 percent of valid votes, compared with Flavio Bolsonaro’s 48.21 percent, reversing a 1.87-point deficit from the first round. Almost half of voters cast valid ballots for his opponent. A fourth presidential victory demonstrates extraordinary personal resilience, but it cannot be read as an endorsement of his entire record.  
Anatomy of a comeback
The comeback required mobilization beyond Lula’s loyal base. National abstention fell from 21.08 percent in the first round to roughly 19.2 percent. Lula’s campaign stepped up its outreach to those who had stayed home or remained unconvinced.
The electoral geography is clearer. Gains in Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Bahia together brought Lula millions of additional votes compared with the first round, widening his overall margin over Bolsonaro. Lula recovered Minas Gerais and reinforced his advantage in the Northeast. He also won the city of Sao Paulo, although Bolsonaro carried the state. The decisive expansion therefore went beyond familiar Workers’ Party strongholds.
Pre-election polling had shown Lula stronger among poorer voters and women. These constituencies help explain his coalition, but claims about specific vote transfers require further evidence. Politically, the result suggests that dissatisfaction with Lula did not automatically translate into confidence in a Bolsonaro successor. Voters could demand change while remaining uneasy about the alternative.  
Foreign interference and national autonomy
Foreign involvement complicated that choice. Donald Trump’s pressure, Javier Milei’s campaigning and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s endorsement gave Bolsonaro international visibility. What Flavio Bolsonaro expected to be a decisive asset for his campaign proved instead to be a poisoned chalice. It enabled Lula to link his defense of sovereignty to a tangible concern: whether Brazil’s next government would negotiate independently or import foreign patrons’ priorities.
Foreign involvement helped Lula politically by giving his sovereignty argument a concrete target. Establishing the precise electoral effect of this foreign pressure, however, is harder. The result alone cannot tell us how many voters rejected Bolsonaro because of outside backing. Nevertheless, economic pressure gave the president grounds to frame autonomy as a protection for Brazilian livelihoods, including those affected by tariffs, rather than as an abstract diplomatic ambition.
The election offers a difficult lesson. Jair Bolsonaro's decision to promote his son reinforced the movement’s dependence on one family. A modern conservative alternative needs credible programs for security and public spending, as well as leaders with executive experience. Social media reach helped conservative candidates compete, but winning national office requires proving that their organisations have the competence to govern.
Lula faces a related succession problem. His fourth victory confirms how heavily the Brazilian left depends on him. He should use this term to strengthen party institutions and groom leaders capable of carrying his platform beyond his presidency. Repeating past achievements will not satisfy younger voters seeking better education, productive employment and protection from violence.  
Pragmatism abroad
Abroad, the outcome favours continuity of strategic autonomy. Brazil should negotiate constructively with Washington on trade and security while maintaining its partnerships with China and the wider Global South. Chinese demand sustains key Brazilian export sectors, where the United States is actually a direct competitor, particularly in soybeans. Sacrificing commercial opportunities to demonstrate political loyalty would cost Brazilian producers.
BRICS gives Brazil a forum to help shape institutions alongside other major developing economies. Lula should use that position to secure finance and technological cooperation that support development at home. International prominence needs practical results to retain domestic support.
The immediate political task is reconciliation. The late extension of voting hours, amid transport and weather difficulties, requires a transparent explanation. Institutions should answer questions with evidence and follow lawful procedures to protect confidence in the result and prevent grievances from hardening into a permanent refusal to accept electoral defeat.
Lula’s legacy will ultimately depend on confronting corruption, improving learning outcomes and making communities safer. That requires investigations that reach politically connected offenders, schools that teach pupils to understand what they read and security policies that protect residents from organized crime. Success must be visible in public services and opportunities, including for those who voted against him. Political parties must also recruit and prepare capable public servants rather than treating online popularity as a sufficient qualification. The next four years offer Brazil an opportunity to begin renewing both political camps. Voters have entrusted Lula with another mandate; the country now needs a government that can turn that mandate into improvements people can recognize.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Two ballistic waves hit a Kyiv campus, the center, and the Southern Bridge
Shortly after 22:00 on 26 October, Russian missiles hit near a metro station in Kyiv's left-bank Desnianskyi district, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. An ambulance crew that had arrived at a call came under fire, and two medics were injured.
The missiles struck the grounds of one of Kyiv's universities, its campus, Kyoto Park, nearby homes, and the area beside a metro station, Zelenskyy wrote. “There is no military facility nearby,” he said.
In Dniprovskyi district, the blast wave blew out windows in a medical facility's intensive care unit, Klitschko said. A three-story non-residential building in the district partly collapsed.
The evening strike also damaged the metro between two left-bank stations and the exits of Lisova station, Klitschko said.
Kyiv gets no warning of the first of two Russian ballistic waves, hours after Zelenskyy said US alerts were back
A second wave followed before dawn on 27 October. Missiles hit an administrative building in Podilskyi district, Klitschko reported, and at 05:04 he said Russia had hit the Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it.
Police closed the bridge to traffic, and green-line trains stopped crossing it. Russian strikes had already damaged metro infrastructure on the same bridge on 22 October.
The overnight attack set two non-residential buildings on fire in Obolonskyi district, and two more people were injured.
By morning, a 46-year-old woman was dead and 15 people were injured, among them dormitory residents and two medics, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said. Prosecutors counted at least 12 damaged apartment blocks, as well as a burns center, a shopping mall, and a tram.
Kyiv was the main target of the night, the Air Force said, as Russia launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 280 drones. Air defenses downed two of the missiles and 255 drones.
Zelenskyy put the night's total at 16 ballistic missiles and called the attack “a serious escalation in the Russian operation against our logistics.” He blamed delays in deliveries of interceptors for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.
“Artificial and lengthy delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriots and NASAMS, which unfortunately have been happening lately, directly help Russia achieve the goals of its terrorist campaign. Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
Russian strikes kill two in Kharkiv and wound civilians across Ukraine
Russian strikes on Kharkiv's Novobavarskyi district on the evening of 26 October killed two men and injured four people, including a 17-year-old girl, oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. On the morning of 27 October, a Russian missile hit Izium, damaging eight houses.
In Zaporizhzhia, a Russian strike on a gas station wounded two people, and a later strike on a car wounded a 17-year-old boy, the oblast administration said. In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian drones and aerial bombs injured three women in Synelnykove district overnight.
In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian attacks set homes on fire and injured six people, including a child, the oblast administration said. In Chernivtsi Oblast, a drone attack damaged an energy facility, cutting power until 02:15 and injuring two security guards, oblast head Ruslan Osypenko said. Russian attacks have also critically damaged electrical equipment in northern Khmelnytskyi Oblast, the regional power company said.
Over the past day, Russian attacks killed civilians in Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv oblasts
On 26 October, Russian attacks killed three people in Donetsk Oblast and wounded 22, oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. His breakdown puts 16 of the wounded in Yasnohirka, where Russian aircraft dropped guided bombs. A Russian drone strike on Pavlohrad killed one person and wounded seven, and a drone killed a woman in Shevchenkove, Kharkiv Oblast. In Kherson, a Russian drone hit a health facility and wounded a nurse. Most of Konotop in Sumy Oblast has been without power since Russian strikes on 24 October, with no forecast for its return, the mayor said.
Patriot systems are the only ones in Ukraine that reliably stop Russia's Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and their missiles have waited almost a month for a US signature. Every week of that wait leaves cities like Kyiv facing waves like this one with fewer interceptors, which is why Kyiv is also asking Lockheed Martin directly for more.

2026-10-27
10:12:07 UTC
19:12:07 KST

Israel will build a new patrol vessel for the Cyprus Naval Command to strengthen the protection of the country’s maritime borders.
The Israeli Ministry of Defense reported this.
The vessel is a Sa’ar 62-class ship that Israel Shipyards will build.
Defense contractor Rafael Advanced Defense Systems will equip the vessel with combat systems tailored to the customer’s requirements.
Under the same agreement, the parties will also upgrade Cyprus’s patrol vessel Ioannides, which Israel Shipyards also built. The work will include upgrades to its onboard systems.
The Ioannides was launched in Haifa in September 2017.
The new vessel will belong to the Sa’ar 62 class, developed by Israel Shipyards based on the Sa’ar 4.5-class missile patrol boats. It is designed for extended high-seas patrols, maritime surveillance, and the protection of maritime borders.
Depending on the configuration, the vessel can carry radar systems, electronic intelligence equipment, stabilized weapon stations, and medium-range missiles.
Israel Shipyards launched Cyprus’s first vessel of this class, Commodore Andreas Ioannides, in Haifa in September 2017. It entered service with the Cypriot Navy in January 2018.

Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in Saudi Arabia postponed
TEHRAN - The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) has officially announced the postponement of the 6th Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games, originally scheduled to take place in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in December 2026.
According to the new schedule, the Games will be held from March 28 to April 8, 2027. The decision was made following consultations between the OCA, the Local Organizing Committee, national Olympic committees, and other relevant stakeholders.
Organizers explained that the postponement was necessary to address logistical and operational requirements, improve coordination, and ensure the widest possible participation of Asian countries.
Despite the change, Saudi Arabian officials emphasized that preparations remain on track and that the country is fully committed to delivering a successful international sporting event.
More than 4,500 athletes representing over 45 National Olympic Committees are expected to participate in the competition.
The Games represent an important milestone for Saudi Arabia, marking the country’s first opportunity to host a multi-sport event under the Olympic Council of Asia.
The postponement also provides additional time for participating nations to finalize their preparations and logistical arrangements.
Organizers remain confident that the rescheduled event will strengthen sporting cooperation across Asia and contribute to Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 objectives.

Billions allocated to Rail Baltica, but politicians delay decisions – RB Rail chief sharply criticises Latvia's approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:55:23 UTC
18:55:23 KST

The Rail Baltica railway project has reached a point where one of the greatest risks to its further progress is no longer technical readiness or construction capacity, but delayed and inconsistent political decisions, according to Marko Kivila, Chairman of the Management Board of the Baltic joint venture RB Rail.
While the leaders of the Baltic states and Poland have repeatedly reaffirmed their commitment to completing the project at the European level, public debate in Latvia has once again turned to whether the country can afford it, Kivila noted.
He stressed that European Union (EU) support for Rail Baltica is not merely a political declaration. This is demonstrated by the 4.5 billion euros in funding already allocated, reflecting the project's strategic importance at the European level.
"Therefore, at this stage of the project, the most important question is not whether Latvia can afford Rail Baltica, but how Latvia will continue construction, fulfil its commitments and make full use of this substantial EU support," Kivila said.
He recalled that on 16 October, the leaders of four countries reaffirmed their commitment to completing Rail Baltica during the next EU multiannual budget period in a joint letter to EU leaders, calling for predictable European funding for the project.
Project implementers take such commitments seriously because construction planning and contractual obligations are based on them.
They also take seriously public statements that raise doubts about the project's financing prospects.
Kivila pointed out that such signals reach other EU member states and Brussels, making it difficult to demand predictable European funding when Latvia's own decision-making remains unpredictable.
"The financing challenges facing Rail Baltica are well known. Simply repeating them will not build a single kilometre of railway. Latvia did not arrive at its current situation overnight. It has also been shaped by postponed decisions, including those concerning the project implementation schedule, financing plan and infrastructure manager, as well as inadequate financial planning and the inability to agree on priorities in time," Kivila said.
In his view, it would be paradoxical to use these same problems as arguments for further delaying the project.
Kivila explained that several financing scenarios are available, combining EU co-financing, national contributions and other financial instruments while spreading investments over a longer period.
He believes Latvia needs a concrete decision that reflects the country's fiscal capacity.
According to Kivila, Estonia has recently demonstrated how such challenges can be addressed in practice.
Its revised schedule envisages completing the Tallinn–Pärnu connection by 2032 and the cross-border section by 2034.
At the same time, planned investments for 2027 have been reduced from 919 million euros to 541 million euros, while investments for 2028 have been cut from approximately 1.06 billion euros to 453 million euros.
Kivila emphasised that Estonia's plan also depends on future EU funding and that the country has not resolved all its financing challenges.
However, Estonia has made decisions on how to address them. He believes Latvia needs an equally concrete approach.
Rail Baltica construction is already underway in all three Baltic states, Kivila noted.
More than 40% of the first phase of the main railway line is either under construction or ready for construction to begin.
In Latvia, construction contracts cover more than 200 kilometres, but the actual pace of work is significantly slower than in neighbouring countries, Kivila acknowledged.
Meanwhile, the implementation deadlines for several Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) funding agreements expire in 2028, with some extending into 2029.
Kivila stressed that EU funding deadlines will not wait for Latvia to finish discussing why making decisions is difficult.
"Moreover, Latvia is not alone in this project. Estonia and Lithuania are investing millions to establish a connection with the rest of Europe, and its full operation also depends on the Latvian section. Our neighbours can make their own decisions and build their own railways, but they cannot build Latvia's section for it. Latvia's delays also postpone the return on their investments. This is a responsibility that extends beyond Latvia's national budget," Kivila said.
He explained that slowing construction is not a cost-free solution.
It creates risks associated with renegotiating contracts, price indexation and additional expenses.
Kivila stressed that unused EU funding means the same construction work will cost more in the future.
At the same time, delays postpone the benefits of the new railway connection with Europe, including opportunities for freight and passenger transport, business development and military mobility.
Kivila also highlighted that construction investments generate fiscal returns.
According to project estimates, approximately 19–21% of invested funds return to the national budget through tax revenues.
As previously reported, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis of New Unity (JV) said on Monday, 26 October, during TV3's programme 900 Seconds that the new government would have to assess whether and how Latvia could afford to continue implementing Rail Baltica while preparing the next national budget.
Kozlovskis explained that Russia's war in Ukraine and other geopolitical developments require serious consideration and decisions, as it is clear that Latvia can no longer continue with the approach used so far.
Furthermore, there is currently no clarity regarding funding from the EU in future planning periods or financing from the European Commission.
LETA previously reported that the first phase of Rail Baltica's main railway line in Latvia is planned within the existing scope.
This includes establishing a cross-border Rail Baltica connection from the Lithuanian border to the Estonian border, as well as completing construction at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station to enable connections between Rail Baltica and the existing railway network.
Consequently, the first phase does not include the so-called Riga loop.
It has also been reported that the first phase of Rail Baltica could cost 14.3 billion euros across the Baltic states, including 5.5 billion euros in Latvia.
However, after accounting for price indexation, Latvia's costs could reach six billion euros.
According to the project's cost-benefit analysis, the total cost of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 23.8 billion euros.
The previous cost-benefit analysis, conducted in 2017, estimated the project's total cost at 5.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica aims to establish a European standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian–Polish border, connecting the Baltic states with the wider European railway network.
The project envisages constructing 870 kilometres of new European standard-gauge railway tracks, with a gauge of 1,435 millimetres, across the Baltic states.
Trains on the new railway are expected to reach maximum speeds of 240 kilometres per hour.

At least 10 killed as 2 high-speed trains collide in central Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

At least 10 people were killed Wednesday when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, derailing carriages and prompting the suspension of rail services connecting Madrid with southern Spain, authorities said.
Officials warned that the death toll could rise as emergency crews worked to rescue passengers and assess the damage.
The collision occurred shortly after 9 a.m. near the towns of Mora and Orgaz, in Toledo province, on the high-speed line linking Madrid and Seville, according to Spain's rail infrastructure operator ADIF.
The crash involved trains operated by state-owned Renfe and private rail company Iryo. A Renfe train struck the rear of an Iryo train that had stopped, knocking two Iryo carriages off the tracks, regional authorities said. The cause of the collision was not immediately known.
Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, confirmed 10 deaths and warned that the number would likely increase as rescue operations continued.
The two trains were carrying hundreds of passengers. The Renfe train had 397 people aboard, while the Iryo service was carrying 147, according to regional authorities.
ADIF announced on X that rail traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed line had been suspended following the collision. The disruption affected services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Emergency services mobilized rescue teams to the scene to assist injured passengers. Manuel Galán, the mayor of nearby Urda, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that emergency officials had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to accommodate passengers affected by the crash.
Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, said on X that he was traveling to the crash site.
The collision came months after another deadly rail disaster in southern Spain. In January, 46 people were killed when a train derailed near Adamuz in Cordoba province and collided with an oncoming train.
That crash was Spain's deadliest rail accident since 2013, when a train derailed near Santiago de Compostela, killing 80 people. The January disaster raised concerns about railway safety and public confidence in the country's extensive high-speed rail network.
Investigators will seek to establish what caused Wednesday's collision. Meanwhile, emergency crews continued responding to the crash, and rail services remained suspended along the affected route.

At least 36 people have been killed in a drone strike on a crowded market in Sudan’s Darfur region, a medical aid organization said Tuesday, as attacks on civilian areas intensify and the country’s humanitarian crisis deepens.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said Sudanese armed forces struck a market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, on Monday evening, causing what it described as “complete devastation.” A second drone strike hit a residential area.
The MSF-supported Nyala Teaching Hospital had received 36 bodies by Tuesday, including 21 people dressed in civilian clothing, the organization said. More than 150 injured people had also been treated in the hospital’s emergency department, many suffering from shrapnel wounds and severe burns. Children were among the wounded.
The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudan’s military since April 2023, gave a substantially higher toll, saying 188 civilians had been killed and another 356 injured. The figures could not immediately be independently verified.
The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) had not commented on the attack as of Tuesday.
MSF called on both sides to protect civilians and refrain from attacking markets, residential buildings and essential civilian infrastructure.
The strike is the latest in a series of deadly attacks on civilian gathering places. At least four people were killed and many others injured in a similar drone strike on another market in Nyala on Oct. 16. A separate attack on a market in the Abyei region, near the border with South Sudan, killed at least 80 people.
The United Nations has also reported drone strikes at several locations in the capital, Khartoum, in recent days, including an area near the airport. Other attacks have been reported in West Darfur, South Darfur and North Kordofan.
Drones have become an increasingly prominent feature of Sudan’s civil war. According to the U.N. Human Rights Office, drone strikes killed at least 1,120 civilians during the first half of 2026. Both sides have been accused of carrying out attacks that have endangered civilian lives.
The conflict, which erupted in April 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The latest violence comes as Sudan’s government seeks international accountability for atrocities in Darfur, where the RSF’s takeover of El Fasher has left civilians facing severe food shortages, displacement and widespread reports of abuses.
Sudan’s Ambassador to Türkiye, Nadir Yousif Eltayeb, said Tuesday that the international community had failed to take an impartial approach to the conflict and had not done enough to address the suffering of civilians.
Speaking at a meeting on Sudan at the Foundation for Political, Economic and Social Research (SETA) in Ankara, Eltayeb said El Fasher had endured a complete siege for about 30 months, leaving residents dependent on limited aid deliveries.
“About 1 million people were surviving on aid delivered by the armed forces by air. People could not access enough food, to the point that they had to eat tree bark,” he said.
Eltayeb said Sudanese government forces had made more than 200 attempts to break the siege but had failed to restore access to the city.
“The international community has taken a biased approach to this issue, preventing it from being resolved,” he said.
The RSF captured El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, on Oct. 26, 2025, after about 18 months of fighting and a siege that began in May 2024. The city had been the last major urban center in Darfur under the Sudanese army’s control.
Eltayeb accused foreign countries of supporting the RSF, arguing that the paramilitary group would not have been able to advance without outside assistance. He also alleged that armed groups had deliberately targeted particular tribes in El Fasher.
“What happened in El Fasher is genocide,” he said.
He added that the full death toll in El Fasher and the wider Darfur region remained unknown.
Eltayeb further alleged that pressure from the United Arab Emirates had prevented Sudan from submitting reports on the killings to the U.N. Security Council. He accused Abu Dhabi of supporting armed groups involved in the conflict but acknowledged that the allegations had not been proven.
The UAE has repeatedly denied accusations that it supports the RSF.
“We are seeking justice for Sudan,” Eltayeb said, thanking Türkiye for its support.
The fall of El Fasher marked a major shift in the conflict, but the fighting and its aftermath have left the city’s remaining population facing dire conditions.
The U.N. Human Rights Office said more than 6,000 people were killed during the first three days of attacks after the RSF seized the city. Subsequent reports described killings, forced displacement, torture and sexual violence against civilians.
The U.N. has warned that abuses against civilians, including women and children, have continued, citing reports of executions and sexual violence.
The takeover also triggered a mass exodus. About 138,200 people were displaced from El Fasher and surrounding settlements between Oct. 26, 2025, and March 1, 2026, according to figures provided in the humanitarian assessment.
Before the war, El Fasher had a population of more than 1 million. Its population is now estimated to have fallen below 70,000.
Those who remain face continuing insecurity and severely restricted access to food, medical care and other essential services. The departure of tens of thousands of residents has further strained already limited humanitarian operations across Darfur.

Kazakhstan sees 5.6-fold increase in cargo transit over decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:16:44 UTC
19:16:44 KST

Kazakhstan sees 5.6-fold increase in cargo transit over decade
Cargo transit through Kazakhstan increased 5.6-fold over the past decade, rising from 6.5 million tons in 2015 to 36.3 million tons in 2025. The strongest annual growth came in 2025, when transit volumes jumped 70.8%, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Energyprom.kz.
According to Kazakhstan's Bureau of National Statistics, which cited data from the Ministry of Finance's State Revenue Committee, cargo transit volumes grew steadily over the decade, reaching 11.6 million tons in 2020, 15.6 million tons in 2022, and 21.3 million tons in 2024.
The upward trend continued in 2026, with government figures showing that 32.6 million tons of cargo transited through Kazakhstan between January and September, a 13.1% increase from the same period last year.
Kazakhstan aims to raise annual cargo transit volumes to 100 million tons by 2035 through the construction of new railway lines and the modernization of existing infrastructure.
Rail transport accounted for the largest share of transit cargo in 2025, with volumes rising from 13.3 million tons in 2024 to 18.7 million tons. Meanwhile, cargo transported by road vehicles, including trucks and trailers, nearly tripled to 16.8 million tons, up from 5.7 million tons a year earlier.
China remained a major source of transit cargo, with shipments to Uzbekistan reaching 6.5 million tons in 2025. Another 4 million tons consisted of consolidated cargo from China destined for Kazakhstan and other countries.
The China–Russia route handled 3 million tons of cargo, while other major routes included Uzbekistan–Russia (2.2 million tons), China–Iran (2.1 million tons), and China–Poland (1.6 million tons).
Cold-rolled iron and steel products accounted for the largest share of transit cargo by commodity, totaling 5.6 million tons. They were followed by motorcycles, mopeds, and similar vehicles at 2.2 million tons, passenger cars at 619,200 tons, certain polymers at 482,400 tons, and automotive parts at 478,200 tons.
Meanwhile, Kazakhstan transported 712.1 million tons of cargo across all modes of transport in the first nine months of 2026.
However, year-on-year comparisons were affected by a change in statistical methodology, which excluded empty railcars from railway freight calculations. When both periods are measured using the same methodology, total freight volumes show a 0.9% increase.
Between January and September, road and urban electric transport carried 270.4 million tons of cargo, followed by railways at 248.5 million tons and pipelines at 189.8 million tons.
Transport companies generated 4.5 trillion tenge in revenue from freight, baggage, and cargo-baggage services during the nine-month period, up 5.3% from a year earlier.
Rail transport accounted for the largest share of revenue at 1.8 trillion tenge, followed by pipeline transportation at 1.4 trillion tenge and road and urban electric transport at 1.2 trillion tenge.
The expansion of transit routes is opening up new opportunities for Kazakhstan's transport sector, with logistics services, warehousing, and vehicle maintenance and repair playing an increasingly important role alongside growing cargo volumes.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan had announced plans to expand its international route network to 160, with Europe, China, India, the U.S., Türkiye, and Russia identified as priority destinations.

Rostec’s new Obereg GR body armor incorporates bleeding control system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:12:27 UTC
19:12:27 KST

MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. The modernized Obereg GR body armor, manufactured by the Oktava plant (managed by RT-Capital, a subsidiary of the Rostec State Corporation), has been equipped with a bleeding control system, the corporation’s press service reported.
"The Oktava plant has modernized the Obereg GR body armor for humanitarian demining specialists. The gear includes an integrated automatic tourniquet system that allows users to quickly stop blood loss in critical situations, thereby increasing the chances of saving a life. A prototype of the equipment is currently undergoing testing," the press service said.
It noted that one of the key advantages of the Obereg GR is its low weight and comfort, combined with a large area of body protection. The body armor weighs about 5 kg and does not restrict movement, allowing it to be worn for extended periods of work.
Rostec specified that the mechanism built into the Obereg GR operates on the same principle as a household blood pressure monitor. Along with the body armor, the deminer wears cuffs with airbags on the arms and legs, and a battery-powered pump is located on the back of the gear. A system of tubes runs through the inside of the gear. These tubes inflate the cuffs with air to constrict an injured arm or leg, functioning like a tourniquet. The system’s control panel is located in a protective pocket on the chest. To use it, the wearer must pull a special cord. Then, using the four buttons, the operator can select which limb needs to be constricted. Both arms and both legs can be constricted, if necessary. When help arrives, the cuffs can be unfastened, or the valve can be opened to release the air. In an emergency, the user can cut the pneumatic tourniquet.
"The modernization of the Obereg GR is a direct response to the real needs of specialists working in high-risk environments. The combination of reliable ballistic protection and new features makes the gear as effective as possible in the field. Stopping bleeding is a key step in first aid for limb injuries, and with the new version of the body armor, this can be done independently using a remote control in a matter of seconds. This saves precious time before evacuation to a hospital and increases the chances of a favorable outcome. A prototype of the new equipment has been created, and testing is currently underway," Rostec reported.
According to the state corporation, the Obereg GR is being supplied to humanitarian demining teams in new regions. The gear features ballistic inserts with special protection classes C2 and Br1+. They can withstand pistol bullets and shrapnel, as well as protect against the main types of modern anti-personnel mines. The body armor is equipped with a large collar, eliminating gaps when worn with a helmet with a visor, and it provides extensive protection for the groin and inner thighs. At the same time, the gear is highly ergonomic - a deminer wearing this equipment can work kneeling on one knee.

Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases, mainly in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:03:30 UTC
19:03:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases, mostly in DR Congo
The latest outbreak of Ebola in the African continent has passed 10,000 confirmed cases, the vast majority of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Congolese health authorities said on Tuesday, with almost 5,000 fatalities.
According to the DRC's figures, 10,060 people have been infected and 4,887 have died since the virus was first detected in May in the vast central African country's deadliest outbreak in its history.
Cases have likewise been detected in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda, with the World Health Organisation warning that Africa faces a "complex" task to contain an outbreak spanning the east, west and centre of the continent.
While some 2,684 have recovered from the virus in the DRC, the epidemic's fatality rate appears to be close to 50 percent, according to the Congolese National Institute of Public Health.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
After spreading under the radar for weeks, the virus was first detected in the northeastern Congolese province of Ituri, kicking off the DRC's 17th outbreak of the disease.
It has since spread across swathes of the country's north and east, which is plagued by a litany of violence by various armed groups and where trust in a faraway and long-absent state is low.
Ituri and the eastern North Kivu province, the latter of which is partially controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 militia, account for the majority of reported cases.
Swiss woman evacuated
After registering a total of 20 cases and two deaths, neighbouring Uganda was declared Ebola-free by the WHO in late August.
Kenya, which had not reported a single case of the contagious virus until October 6, has now seen two virus deaths from nine cases, most of them from recent travellers to the DRC.
The only case so far confirmed in Nigeria, a 42-year-old Swiss woman who contracted the virus following a trip to Uganda with her husband, was evacuated to a hospital in Geneva on Monday.
Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), Congolese Jean Kaseya, told AFP his organisation was still trying to track how the patient came into to contact with the virus.
"We saw that the genomic sequencing of the Kenyan case is similar to the Nigerian case. And we discovered that yesterday with some cases in Beni," he explained. "Today it's an outbreak in three regions. We didn't see that since we started to have experience of Ebola outbreaks. We were not thinking that Nigeria could be an at risk country."
When the outbreak was declared, just three zones of one province were affected, he said. "Today we are talking about eight provinces, more than 66 health zones. To give you an idea, it's like twice the size of the UK."
Fifty-three of the patient's contacts have been identified by the Nigerian health authorities, in a bid to stop the virus spreading across Africa's most populous nation.
Some experts are worried that the virus—caught through contact with bodily fluids—could have spread after the Swiss couple landed back in Nigeria on 3 October.
The WHO said the patient, the wife of an employee of the Swiss embassy in the capital Abuja, developed symptoms on 7 October.
She then sought care in Abuja on 11 October, before testing positive for Bundibugyo on 20 October.
A Ugandan government spokesperson dismissed the idea that the Swiss woman could have contracted the disease while in the African Great Lakes nation.
Nurse killed
The response to the DRC's outbreak has been hampered by the distrust of parts of the population.
A nurse was killed and a health worker seriously wounded in the northeastern Tshopo province on Saturday, according to the WHO.
Doctor Marcel Likolo, chief medical officer of the Bafwasende health district, told AFP that young people from the area had accused the victims of trying to infect locals with tablets before attacking them.
The Ebola treatment centre where the incident took place has since shut down, he said.
Since it first emerged half a century ago, Ebola has killed more than 15,000 people across Africa.
Testing of the Ervebo vaccine, which has already proven to be effective against the more common Zaire strain of the virus, has begun in recent weeks to determine whether it could also provide protection against the Bundibugyo variant.

Small and very scary: Rare miniature T.rex dinosaur skeleton fetches €42 million at auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:15:33 UTC
19:15:33 KST

A dinosaur that looks like a tiny Tyrannosaurus rex is now one of the world's most expensive fossils having been sold at a Sotheby's auction for €42.6 million in New York.
A rare skeleton of a smaller cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex has sold for a record €42.6 million at an auction in New York.
The Nanotyrannus, nicknamed "Jodi" after the person who discovered the remains in 2019, was bought by a mystery buyer after a 12-minute bidding battle online and over phones. Sotheby's had expected it to fetch anywhere from €4 to €7 million.
In a statement, the auction house said the deal now ranks the junior T.rex as the world's second most valuable dinosaur ever sold. This summer, a T. rex fossil known as “Gus” sold for a record €44 million at Sotheby's
Close family claws and controversy
A Nanotyrannus was about half the length of an adult T. rex, and the two creatures coexisted during the Cretaceous period some 67 million years ago. Nanotyrannus had relatively longer forelimbs and larger hand claws, as well as more slender, blade-like teeth than its famous cousin.
“Jodi” is one of only three such skeletons known to exist. Standing 2.9 metres and stretching nearly 6 metres, it has been on display at the auction house’s upper Manhattan headquarters since earlier this month, and is considered almost 70% complete.
However, some scientists have opposed such private sales, saying “Jodi” and other significant fossils should be displayed in museums or other institutions so they can be studied by researchers and viewed by the public.
Sotheby’s, in a statement, thanked the team of professional fossil hunters whose efforts to discover and excavate the specimen were the focus of the Discovery Channel documentary series “Dino Hunters” in 2020.

The joint Baltic company RB Rail has submitted a new application to the European Commission seeking an additional 357.5 million euros in funding for the Rail Baltica railway project, including 37.3 million euros for work in Lithuania, Lithuanian rail group LTG said.
The funding would be provided through the European Union’s Connecting Europe Facility (CEF).
Of the amount requested for Lithuania, 8.96 million euros would go toward designing train control, command and signalling systems and procuring the necessary software and hardware.
Another 28.37 million euros would cover connecting high-voltage power networks at traction substations in Panevėžys, Išorai and Liudvinavas, producing and testing railway switch and rail expansion joint prototypes, acquiring land for the Panevėžys railway junction and carrying out other work.
“These technical systems are an integral part of the future high-speed railway, ensuring safe traffic management, efficient infrastructure maintenance and smooth railway operations,” Mindaugas Ivanavičius, head of Rail Baltica in Lithuania, said in a statement.
“We plan such work well in advance so that, once one stage of the project is completed, we can move immediately to the next and maintain a steady pace of implementation,” he added.
Rail Baltica has received about 4.5 billion euros in EU investment under 12 CEF grant agreements to date.
The European Commission and the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency, CINEA, will assess the new applications. The results are expected to be announced in spring 2027.
The first phase of Rail Baltica, intended to connect the Baltic states with the rest of Europe via a single railway line, is expected to cost 15.3 billion euros across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. The estimated cost of building a second track is about 23.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica is designed to connect Tallinn, Pärnu, Riga, Panevėžys, Kaunas, Vilnius and Warsaw. The railway line will run for 392 kilometres through Lithuania.

Netanyahu or Eisenkot? Can you form Israel’s next coalition government?

The next government, like every government in Israel’s history, will have to be a coalition.
The question now is who can secure at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats to form a government and become Israel’s next prime minister.
Al Jazeera has built an interactive tool that lets you test different combinations of parties. Start with any of the four exit polls or enter your own seat numbers. Then add parties until your coalition reaches 61 seats. You can add an entire bloc at once or select parties individually.
Who is ahead?
Initial counting by the Central Elections Committee put Likud ahead as the largest single party, with 27 seats.
Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 54 seats, against 50 for Eisenkot’s.
Four exit polls published on election night showed how close the race is.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 put Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc level at 51 seats each. Channel 12 gave Netanyahu 52 seats to Eisenkot’s 49, while Channel 15 was most favourable to the incumbent, projecting 55 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc against 49 for the opposition.
How many seats are needed?
Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. Parties win seats in proportion to their share of the national vote, provided they clear the 3.25 percent threshold to enter parliament.
A government needs the support of at least 61 politicians to secure a majority.
Neither of the main blocs has reached that number in the exit polls or the initial count. The next step is to find enough parties willing to join forces to make up the difference.
Why is forming a government so difficult?
The Arab-led parties Ra’am and the Joint List could hold the balance of power, with exit polls putting their combined support at between 16 and 19 seats.
But the political obstacles are considerable. Netanyahu has described a coalition with Arab parties as “shameful”, while leading figures in the Jewish-led opposition have also ruled out governing with them.
That leaves potential coalitions that may work on paper but face serious political barriers.
Which parties belong to each bloc?
Netanyahu’s bloc spans Likud, the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism, and the far-right parties Religious Zionism, led by Bezalel Smotrich, and Otzma Yehudit, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc includes his Yashar party, the Together list associated with former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu and Yair Golan’s Democrats.
What happens next?
Once the results are certified, the president gives the mandate to the member of the Knesset considered most likely to assemble a majority.
That politician has 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. If they fail, another lawmaker can be given a chance. If no one can form a government, Israel may have to hold another election, as it did repeatedly between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, with 19 years in office across three stints, remains caretaker prime minister while coalition negotiations unfold. He is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.
Official results are due on November 4. Negotiations to form a government could take considerably longer.

Israel’s stock market drops as exit polls show no clear election winner
Benchmark Tel Aviv 125 index drops more than 3 percent amid uncertainty over who will lead the next government.
Israel’s stock market has fallen sharply amid exit polls showing no clear winner in the country’s parliamentary elections.
The benchmark Tel Aviv 125 index dropped as much as 3.5 percent in early trading on Wednesday as investors weighed the unclear results of Israel’s first election since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza.
Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor the opposition bloc headed by Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot appeared on track to gain a parliamentary majority in the 26th Knesset.
With more than 76 percent of votes counted as of 09:30 GMT, Netanyahu’s coalition was on course to win 54 seats, while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc was headed for 47 seats, according to tallies published by Israeli media.
Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority in the unicameral parliament.
Israel’s economy has been running hot despite being on a war footing for the past three years amid an influx of investment in the local tech sector.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025 and 3.2 percent in the first half of 2026, according to government figures.
The Bank of Israel last week raised its GDP growth forecast for all of 2026 to 5.6 percent, up from 4 percent, citing ramped-up production by Israeli firms overseas.
The central bank has forecast that GDP growth for 2027 would reach 7.5 percent, far surpassing estimates for advanced economies such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan.

Ukraine lacks unified vision for postwar reconstruction – IMF Alternate Executive Director Rashkovan
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:18:59 EET
19:18:59 KST

Funding for Ukraine's recovery following Russian aggression, which the World Bank currently estimates at $588 billion, should be viewed as part of a broader model and institutional architecture for reconstruction, with a vision for the postwar country being a key element, Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternate Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), believes.
"This vision must be shared and supported by the majority of Ukrainians. Frankly speaking, we do not yet have such a vision," he said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12–18.
Rashkovan said that the IMF does not develop such a vision because the Fund's task is to ensure current macrofinancial stability: preventing high inflation, sharp currency depreciation, and crises in the banking sector, the budget and the balance of payments.
"Structural reforms are being implemented for this purpose, but overall, this is merely a foundation for further development. Some criticize Ukraine's IMF program for lacking ambition. But its purpose is to sustain our resilience," Ukraine's representative at the Fund explained.
According to him, the Future Economy initiative, launched by the Ukrainian government and the Ministry of Economy, is intended to help shape a broader vision. The IMF participates in the initiative as an analyst rather than a strategist. "The World Bank provides more active assistance, but the key role belongs to the Ukrainian authorities and society," said Rashkovan, who has been working on issues related to Ukraine's reconstruction for many years.
He added that an interesting discussion is also underway around the Prosperity Plan: what Ukraine should become after the war and how much funding and investment will be needed for it to become a new European tiger.
"However, neither this plan nor the Future Economy initiative is a Marshall Plan at this stage. They are more like ideas that need to be developed. Money does not solve everything: an institutional architecture is needed that can sustain reconstruction over several political cycles in Ukraine and partner countries," the IMF's alternate executive director said.
He added that Ukrainian ownership of the process is one of the key principles on which reconstruction should be built. "No one will take better care of us than we do ourselves, and no one will shape a vision for Ukraine's future on our behalf," Rashkovan explained.
The expert said that this vision must be translated into strategies. "We already have many regional and sectoral strategies, perhaps even too many. They need to be aligned. And again, it is important not merely to have strategies but to live by them. All of them must contribute to realizing a shared vision," the IMF's alternate executive director said.
In his view, reconstruction is not a task that can be completed in a day or a few months; it will take decades, if not generations. Therefore, it must be planned, and the necessary institutions must be established in advance.
In addition to the IMF program focused on macrofinancial stability, without which long-term investment planning is impossible, he also cited security guarantees as a prerequisite for reconstruction.
At the same time, Ukraine's representative at the IMF believes that the end of the war is not a mandatory condition for beginning reconstruction.
"We are already rebuilding a great deal despite the war. Not on the scale we would like, but billions of dollars have already been spent on recovery," he said.
Among the other elements of the reconstruction model, he also cited European integration, noting that if Ukraine is moving toward the European Union, reconstruction should be planned in accordance with EU standards.
As for financing, Rashkovan noted that a considerable number of instruments are already available. These include the Pillar 2 investment component under the Ukraine Facility; the EUR 1 billion European Flagship Fund for the Reconstruction of Ukraine, managed by Dragon Capital and Amber Infrastructure; projects supported by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), resources from the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD); and the Co-Investment Platform, which brings together 19 development finance institutions from different countries.
"All of these are working for Ukraine's benefit, but we are still far from the scale required. We need to understand that the probability of all $588 billion coming from public funds provided by international partners is zero. Historical experience shows that 75–85% will come from private sources," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said.
He clarified that private investment typically arrives significantly later than donor funding, which is why Ukraine is currently relying more heavily on donor resources.
Finally, Rashkovan said the importance of structural reforms to attract private capital, including protection of property rights and the continuation of land and anti-corruption reforms. He recalled that the Czech Republic and Poland attracted most of their private investment before joining NATO and the European Union, driven by strong investor expectations.
"If the world expects Ukraine to join the EU and we maintain the pace of reforms, the same could happen here, especially amid friendshoring – the relocation of production and procurement to geopolitically friendly countries," the expert believes.
